nuance: It is the child, not the householder, who sees the stranger at the door and calls him in.
event: The boy sees the hungry ascetic at the door and invites him to the meal.

tamil: கை கவி நறு நெய் பெய்து கன்னல் அம் குடங்கள் கூட்டிப்
பெய் பெய் என்று உரைப்ப யானும் பெருங் கடல் வெள்ளிக் குன்றம்
பெய்து தூர்க்கின்ற வண்ணம் விலாப் புடை பெரிதும் வீங்க
ஐயன் அது அருளினால் யான் அந்தணர் தொழிலன் ஆனேன்.
reading: Pouring handfuls of fragrant ghee and bringing pots of jaggery, the boy kept saying 'serve, serve', till the teacher's sides swelled as if the silver mountain were being poured into the great sea to fill it; by the master's grace, he says, he became one who does the work of the learned.
nuance: The hunger is the measure of the cure: what is poured in is a mountain into the sea. அந்தணர் தொழிலன் ஆனேன் turns the cured ascetic into a teacher, so the meal is the cause of Civakan's education. The verse credits the cure to the boy's grace (ஐயன் அது அருளினால்), a child's gift doing what a vow could not.
event: Fed without stint at the boy's bidding, the ascetic is cured of his hunger and becomes a teacher.

tamil: சுரும்பு உடை அலங்கல் மாலைச் சுநந்தையும் துணைவன் தானும்
விரும்பினர் எதிர் கொண்டு ஓம்ப வேழ வெந்தீயின் நீங்கி
இருந்தனன் ஏம முந் நீர் எறி சுறவு உயர்த்த தோன்றல்
கரும்பு உடைக் காளை அன்ன காளை நின் வலைப் பட்டு என்றான்.
reading: Sunandai of the bee-thronged garland and her husband welcomed and cared for him, and freed from the elephant-fire he stayed on, caught, he tells Civakan, in the net of a youth like the god of love with the sugarcane bow.
event: Kantukkatan and Sunandai keep the cured ascetic in their house, and he stays for love of the boy.

tamil: நிலம் பொறுக்கலாத செம் பொன் நீள் நிதி நுந்தை இல்லம்
நலம் பொறுக்கலாத பிண்டி நான் முகன் தமர்கட்கு எல்லாம்
உலம் பொறுக்கலாத தோளாய் ஆதலால் ஊடு புக்கேன்
கலம் பொறுக்கலாத சாயல் அவர் உழை நின்னைக் கண்டேன்.
reading: Your father's house, he says, holds red-gold wealth the earth could not bear and is open to all the people of the four-faced Lord under the Pindi tree; therefore he entered it, and there saw the boy among the women.
nuance: பிண்டி நான் முகன் is the Jina seated under the asoka (பிண்டி), and தமர் his followers: the foster home is a Jain household, and its hospitality to ascetics is why the meeting happened. நுந்தை here is Kantukkatan, the foster father.
event: The teacher explains that he came to the merchant's house because it received the Jina's devotees.

tamil: ஐயனைக் கண்ணில் காண யானைத்தீ அதகம் கண்ட
பை அணல் நாகம் போல வட்க யான் பெரிதும் உட்கித்
தெய்வம் கொல் என்று தேர்வேற்கு அமிர்து உலாய் நிமிர்ந்ததே போல்
மொய் குரல் முரசம் நாணும் தழங்கு குரல் முழங்கக் கேட்டேன்.
reading: When he saw the boy, the elephant-fire within him shrank like a hooded snake that has seen the antidote; awed, wondering whether this was a god, he heard a resounding sound, as of nectar rising, that would put a war drum to shame.
nuance: The sound of line 4 is not identified: it may be the boy's voice, or a sign that marks him; read as the teacher's sign that the child was more than human. அதகம் is the antidote that subdues a snake.
event: At the sight of the boy the ascetic's disease abates and he hears a sound like a drum.

tamil: கோட்டு இளந் திங்கள் சூழ்ந்து குலவிய திருவில் போல
மோட்டு ஒளி முத்தம் சூழ்ந்து முருகு கொப்பளிக்கும் தாரோய்
கேட்டு அளப் பரிய சொல்லும் கிளர் ஒளி வனப்பும் நின்னைச்
சேட்டு இளஞ் சிங்கம் அன்னாய் சாதகம் செய்த என்றான்.
reading: He tells the young lion, whose garland of pearls rings him like a rainbow about the young crescent, that his words beyond measure and his bright beauty were made by his horoscope.

tamil: கோள் இயங்கு உழுவை அன்ன கொடும் சிலை உழவன் கேட்டே
தாள் இயல் தவங்கள் தாயாத் தந்தை நீ ஆகி என்னை
வாள் இயங்கு உருவப் பூணோய் படைத்தனை வாழி என்ன
மீளி அம் களிறு அனாய் யான் மெய்ந்நெறி நிற்பல் என்றான்.
reading: The tiger-like bowman, hearing this, says that with penance as mother and the teacher as father he has been created anew, and blesses him; the teacher replies that he will now stand in the true path.
nuance: The prince who has just learned that his mother left him in the forest and that he was raised by a foster house now names a third parentage, the teacher's.
event: Civakan calls the teacher his father, and the teacher announces that he will return to the ascetic path.

tamil: மறு அற மனையின் நீங்கி மா தவம் செய்வல் என்றால்
பிற அறம் அல்ல பேசார் பேர் அறிவு உடைய நீரார்
துறவறம் புணர்க என்றே தோன்றல் தாள் தொழுது நின்றான்
நறவு அற மலர்ந்த கண்ணி நல் மணி வண்ணன் அன்னான்.
reading: If one says 'I will leave home without stain and do great penance', the teacher says, the greatly wise speak of no other dharma but bid him take up renunciation; and he stood worshipping the prince's feet.
nuance: Who speaks lines 1 to 3, and who is நல் மணி வண்ணன் அன்னான் in line 4, is not fixed by the verse; it is read as the teacher asking leave and bowing to the prince he has called master (ஐயன், 400), but it could be Civakan giving leave. துறவறம் is set against பிற அறம், which includes the household life the teacher has lived in the merchant's house.
event: The teacher asks Civakan's leave to renounce and bows to him.

tamil: கை வரை அன்றி நில்லாக் கடுஞ் சின மடங்கல் அன்னான்
தெவ்வரைச் செகுக்கும் நீதி மனத்து அகத்து எழுதிச் செம்பொன்
பை விரி அல்குலாட்கும் படுகடல் நிதியின் வைகும்
மை வரை மார்பினாற்கும் மனம் உறத் தேற்றி இட்டான்.
reading: Having written into the mind of the lion-like prince, whose fierce anger will not stay in bounds, the policy by which enemies are destroyed, the teacher consoled the merchant's wife and the merchant who dwells among sea-borne wealth.
nuance: The construal that the teacher wrote the policy into Civakan's mind, rather than into his own, is the more natural reading of lines 1 and 2 but not certain.
event: Before leaving, the teacher instructs Civakan in the policy of defeating enemies and comforts his foster parents.

tamil: அழல் உறு வெண்ணெய் போல அகம் குழைந்து உருகி ஆற்றாள்
குழல் உறு கிளவி சோர்ந்து குமரனைத் தமியன் ஆக
நிழல் உறு மதியம் அன்னாய் நீத்தியோ எனவும் நில்லான்
பழவினை பரிய நோற்பான் விஞ்சையர் வேந்தன் சென்றான்.
reading: Sunandai, melting inwardly like butter by the fire, her flute-like voice failing, asks whether he will leave the boy alone; he would not stay, and the Vidyadhara king went away to do the penance that wears down old deeds.
nuance: பழவினை பரிய நோற்பான் names the aim of the renewed penance as wearing away (பரிய) old deeds, the Jain account of release; it closes the account begun in 396, where those deeds broke his first penance.
event: Ignoring Sunandai's plea, the teacher leaves to resume his penance.

title: கோவிந்தையார் இலம்பகம் 409-429 (1/4)
theme: The Kovindaiyar ilampakam opens with the release of Civakan's teacher Accanandi and a portrait of Civakan as the young man every maiden takes for Kama, then turns to the cattle raid: hunters seize the king's herd despite their own omen-reader's prophecy that one man in a chariot will break them, the herders ignore an ill omen of their own and are routed, and their outcry is carried to the usurper seated at ease on his throne.
source_issues: Verse 416 line 4: உடைதுஞ் சுடுவிற்றே னுடைந்த வண்ணமே is hard to divide and may be corrupt; the smoked-honey simile is a conjecture.
Verse 419 line 2: ஆய்த்தியர் நலக் காசெ றூணனான் cannot be divided with confidence and may be corrupt.
Verse 420 line 2: the text flag reports a repaired ௌ read as ெள (எள்ளன்மின்).
Verse 427 line 4 lacks the closing full stop the other verses carry; no text seems lost.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by a merchant, who wins eight brides, regains his father's kingdom and renounces
Civakan's teacher, who renounces and attains release
the deceitful hunters whose seized herd Civakan frees
the hunter who reads bird-omens and foretells the raid's outcome
the hunter who scorns the omen and urges the raid
the herders' announcer, who warns of an ill omen
the herdsmen of the king's cattle
the herdswomen of the cattle hamlets
Saccandan's minister, given the rule, who usurps it

reading: The narrator tells how Accanandi, having cut out the root of desire, went away and performed austerities in the shade of the Hero's feet, and then, while the gods worshipped, left his embodied form, vanishing like a bubble in the rain.
nuance: The ilampakam opens by closing the teacher's story before the hero's adventures begin. The order is threefold: the root of desire is cut, austerity follows, and only then does the body go. வீரன் is the Jina's epithet, so the verse places the release under a Jain master without stating a doctrine in so many words. The bubble is not an image of life's frailty here but of how cleanly the embodied form ends.
event: Accanandi, Civakan's teacher, renounces, performs austerities at the Hero's feet and attains release.

reading: In this fine city like the city of the Nagas, Civakan rides about on gold-caparisoned elephants, chariots with long red-gold banners and horses, like the god of spring whose passing makes hearts burn.
nuance: வேம்ப (so that they burn) makes the hero's display a torment to those who watch him, preparing the next two verses.
event: Civakan rides through Rajamapuram on elephant, chariot and horse.

reading: In breadth of learning, delight to the eye, mastery of the bow and the wealth of the vina, the broad-chested Civakan became one without a second in the world.
The poet announces that he will tell what befell the prince whom the young maidens, taking him for Kama, drank in with their lotus eyes as he went about.
nuance: கூறுவாம் is the poet's own voice turning to a new episode; the maidens' gaze sets up the marriage that ends this ilampakam.

reading: The herds of the land are pictured: jasmine blooms as if the rains had come, the cattle crowd round their calves and pour out milk, and the noise of the herds is greater than the sea's.
On a hill where elephants' musth mixes with honey and fills the springs to overflowing, men strong as lions gathered.
event: The hunters gather on the hill.

reading: As the hunters said the king's herd was near and that on an auspicious day they would take it, one among them who knew all, reading the cry of a bird, spoke first.
nuance: புட்குரன் is read here as புள் குரல் (the bird's cry) run into முன்னம்; the reader is a hunter who interprets bird-signs, not a royal soothsayer.
event: The hunters plan to seize the king's herd, and an omen-reader among them speaks.

reading: The omen-reader foretells that they will get the herd, and that when they do the king's army will break, leaving its umbrellas and peacock-feather standards, but that afterwards they themselves will be broken by one man in a chariot, as bees scatter from smoked honey.
nuance: The prophecy gives the whole battle in advance, both the raiders' first victory and their defeat by Civakan, who is not named. Line 4 is hard to divide and may be corrupt; the smoked-honey simile is read from தேன் உடைந்த.

reading: When he had said this, a hunter answered his fellows that even if the one man in the chariot were Death himself, what could one man do, and urged them to rise and take the herd that day; and they went.
nuance: ஏழை வேட்டுவீர் (foolish hunters) may be the answering hunter scorning his fellows' fear, or the poet's own judgment folded into the speech; either way the boast is set up to be broken.
event: The hunters dismiss the warning and set out for the herd.

reading: Having drunk honey-toddy swarming with bees, with tondakam drums and thudi sounding, they bowed to their deity, saying 'may we win', and fell on the herd at daybreak.
event: The hunters drink, worship their deity and attack the herd at dawn.

reading: A man with a pearl garland on his chest, among herdswomen bearing gold like the flowering kongu, spoke about that herd: he was the herders' valluvan, the announcer.
nuance: Line 2 (ஆய்த்தியர் நலக் காசெறூணனான்) cannot be divided with confidence, so who the valluvan is and what he wears is unclear beyond the pearl garland.
event: The herders' announcer speaks of the herd.

reading: He warned that an ill-omened bird had entered and spoiled the day, so they should not scorn it and should keep the herd in today; yet the herdsmen, shoulders shining like silver bracelets, went out with the cattle in their strength.
nuance: பிள்ளை is taken as the name of an omen bird. The herders, like the hunters in 417, hear an omen and go ahead.
event: The herdsmen take the herd out despite the announcer's warning of an ill omen.

reading: While the herd grazed scattered in the forest like the stars, the hunters of cruel trade shouted together and loosed arrows like rain, and the herdsmen were churned like curd under the churning stick.
event: The hunters attack the grazing herd with arrows and throw the herdsmen into confusion.

reading: Dropping flute and axe, the cowherds fled through the forest; the calves broke their tethers and ran round the yards, and in the hamlets the sweet-voiced women were thrown into confusion and cried out.
event: The cowherds flee and the hamlet is thrown into uproar.

reading: Saying that the hunters had driven the herd off, as a churning rope let go at one end is not let go at the other, the women smelling of broken sour curd all crowded together.
nuance: The churning-rope simile is hard to fix: it may picture the cattle pulled one way while the women hold the other, or the unbroken report passed from mouth to mouth.
event: The herdswomen gather in alarm at the news that the cattle are driven off.

reading: Like deer caught in a net, like peacocks, the herdswomen, the pearls on their breasts and the cool garlands in their hair tangled together, beat their bellies and wept.
event: The herdswomen weep and beat themselves.

reading: The herdswomen lamented with the calves of their houses, asking them how they would live now that the hunters of the cruel border had driven off their mothers in pain.
nuance: The women address the calves as orphans: the loss is framed as a family's, mothers taken from children, not as property.
event: The herdswomen grieve over the calves whose mothers were taken.

reading: With curd, milk and ghee spilled on the rocks like a river and the hamlet in tumult, the herdsmen's force fought back and broke, scattering flowers in the mud as it hurried away.
event: The herdsmen's attempt to fight back fails.

reading: Passing through the flowered pasture and crossing the lotus-filled farmland, they carried their outcry to the king of the old city girt with a shark-filled moat and a strong wall.
event: The herdsmen go to the city to bring their complaint to the king.

tamil: கொடுமர வெயின ரீண்டிக் கோட்டிமி லேறு சூழ்ந்த
படுமணி நிரையை வாரிப் பைந்துகி லருவி நெற்றி
நெடுமலை யத்தஞ் சென்றா ரென்றுநெய் பொதிந்த பித்தை
வடிமல ராயர் பூசல் வளநகர் பரப்பி னாரே.
reading: The herdsmen with oiled hair and flower garlands spread the cry through the rich city that the bow-bearing hunters had gathered, swept off the belled herd with its humped bulls and gone up the long hill path where waterfalls hang like silk.
event: The herdsmen spread the news of the raid through the city.

reading: The strong-shouldered king sat on the lion throne, maidens fanning him with jewelled chamaras, his great makara earrings flashing, holding a fragrant blue water lily.
nuance: The king is not named, but 438 shows the complaint reaching Kattiyankaran, the usurper; the picture of him fanned and holding a flower while his herds are being driven away is set against the herders' outcry.
event: The king sits at ease on his throne as the outcry reaches the city.

title: கோவிந்தையார் இலம்பகம் 430-450 (2/4)
theme: Hunters seize Kattiyangaran's herds; the king's great army is routed by them, the herd chief Nandagon offers his daughter to whoever recovers the herd, the city's men refuse, and Civakan vows to protect the herd and drives out alone against the hunters, who taunt him, lose heart before his chariot and, blaming their omen-reader, make a last charge.
source_issues: Verse 433 line 4 prints நீர்டிவிளை; read as நீர்விளை, with a stray டி.
Verse 431 line 2 divides குப் பாய மிலேச்சனை; read as குப்பாய மிலேச்சனை (a jacketed Mleccha).
Verse 449 line 3 prints புளி ஞருள், a word (புளிஞர்) split by a space.
Verse 445 line 4 புண்மொழிந்தான் may be புன்மொழிந்தான்; the doubled மொழிந்தான் is hard to construe.
Verse 450 was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the join reads correctly.
The cast id for the usurper is kattiyangaran here, as in ch001 and ch011; ch010 and ch012 spell it kattiyankaran.

cast.role: the hero, raised as a merchant's son in Rajamapuram
the usurping minister, now ruling as king
the army Kattiyangaran sends to recover the herd
the forest hunters (வேடர், எயினர், கானவர்) who seize the king's herd
the herdsmen of the royal herds
the herd chief, father of Govindai, who names himself Govindan in 477
a Mleccha in Kattiyangaran's court whom the king rebukes
the men of the city who refuse Nandagon's challenge
the man who tells Civakan of the raid
the hunters' omen-reader, blamed for a false omen

reading: A herdsman, sword and herding staff in hand, joins his palms and bows at the fierce king's feet; told to say what the uproar is, he reports that the herd has been seized and begs the king to protect it.
nuance: The appeal கொண்டனர் நிரை போற்று puts the protection of the herd on the king, which is the duty the rest of the chapter shows him failing and Civakan taking up.
event: A herdsman reports to Kattiyangaran that hunters have seized the herd and asks him to protect it.

reading: The king, eyes reddening and blazing, shouts at a jacketed Mleccha with red eyes, coarse hair and a fierce face, crushing the flower in his hand like killing Death.
nuance: Who the Mleccha is, an attendant or officer of the court, is not said; குப் பாய is read as குப்பாயம், a jacket, across the printed word break.
event: Kattiyangaran, enraged, shouts at a Mleccha in his court.

reading: Understanding the herdsmen's words, the guardian king with the killing spear looks at his sea-like army and roars like a lion's thunder that they must go swift as wind and recover the herd.
event: Kattiyangaran orders his army to go quickly and recover the herd.

tamil: கார்விளை மேக மன்ன கவுளழி கடாத்த வேழம்
போர்விளை யிவுளித் திண்டேர் புனைமயிர்ப் புரவி காலாள்
வார்விளை முரசம் விம்ம வானுலாப் போந்த தேபோ
னீர்டிவிளை சுரிசங் கார்ப்ப நிலநெளி பரந்த வன்றே.
reading: The army sets out: musth elephants like rain clouds, war chariots, plumed horses and foot soldiers, with drums booming and conches roaring, as if the sky were marching, and the earth bends under it.
event: Kattiyangaran's army marches out with all four arms.

tamil: காலகம் புடைப்ப முந்நீர்க் கடல்கிளர்ந் தெழுந்த தேபோல்
வேலக மிடைந்த தானை வெஞ்சின வெயினர் தாக்க
வால்வளை யலற வாய்விட் டிரலையுந் துடியு மார்ப்பப்
பால்வளைந் திரவு செற்றுப் பகலொடு மலைவ தொத்தார்.
reading: Like the sea rising when the wind beats on it, the spear-thick army meets the fierce hunters' attack amid wailing conches, horns and tudi drums, so that the dark hunters and the army seem like night closing round to fight the day.
event: The hunters attack the king's army.

tamil: விற்பழுத் துமிழ்ந்த வெய்ய வெந்நுனைப் பகழி மைந்தர்
மற்பழுத் தகன்ற மார்பத் திடங்கொண்டு வைகச் செந்நாச்
சொற்பழுத் தவர்க்கு மாண்மை சொல்லலாந் தன்மைத் தன்றிக்
கொற்பழுத் தெரியும் வேலார் கொடுஞ்சிலை குழைவித் தாரே.
reading: The hunters' fierce arrows lodge in the broad chests of the king's warriors, whose manhood proves to be a thing only the red-tongued talkers speak of, and the spearmen's bows go slack.
nuance: Line 3 is read as the narrator's sarcasm that the army's valour was only boast; whose bows are made to sag in line 4 (the army's own, or the hunters' bent to shoot) is not certain.
event: The hunters' arrows strike down the king's warriors, who falter.

tamil: வாட்படை யனுங்க வேடர் மாற்றவண்சிலை வளைய வாங்கிக்
கோட்புலி யினத்தின் மொய்த்தார் கொதிநுனைப் பகழி தம்மால்
வீட்டினார் மைந்தர் தம்மை விளிந்தமா கவிழ்ந்த திண்டேர்
பாட்டரும் பகடு வீழ்ந்த பனிவரை குனிவ தொத்தே.
reading: As the swordsmen weaken, the hunters swarm like a pack of tigers bending strong bows and destroy the warriors with burning-tipped arrows, leaving dead horses, overturned chariots and fallen elephants like bowed snowy hills.
event: The hunters slaughter the king's warriors, horses and elephants.

tamil: வென்றிநாங் கோடு மின்னே வெள்ளிடைப் படுத்தென் றெண்ணி
யொன்றியுள் வாங்கு கென்ன வொலிகட லுடைந்த தேபோற்
பொன்றவழ் களிறு பாய்மா புனைமயிற் குஞ்சி பிச்சம்
மின்றவழ் கொடியொ டிட்டு வேற்படை யுடைந்த வன்றே.
reading: Thinking that they will win by drawing the enemy into open ground, the army's men call to fall back together, and the spear-army breaks like a roaring sea, leaving behind gold-hung elephants, horses, peacock plumes, parasols and banners.
nuance: The speaker of the call in lines 1 and 2 is not named; read so, the tactical withdrawal is the cause of the rout.
event: The king's army pulls back to draw the hunters into open ground, and the retreat becomes a rout.

tamil: பல்லினாற் சுகிர்ந்த நாரிற் பனிமலர் பயிலப் பெய்த
முல்லையங் கண்ணி சிந்தக் கால்விசை முறுக்கி யாய
ரொல்லென வொலிப்ப வோடிப் படையுடைந் திட்ட தென்ன
வல்லலுற் றழுங்கி நெஞ்சிற் கட்டியங் கார னாழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The herdsmen run with all their speed, the mullai garlands they had strung on fibre stripped with their teeth scattering, crying out that the army is routed, and Kattiyangaran sinks into grief.
event: The herdsmen bring news of the rout and Kattiyangaran is plunged in grief.

tamil: வம்புகொண் டிருந்த மாதர் வனமுலை மாலைத் தேன்சோர்
கொம்புகொண் டன்ன நல்லார் கொழுங்கயற் றடங்கண் போலு
மம்புகொண் டரசர் மீண்டா ராக்கொண்டு மறவர் போனார்
செம்புகொண் டன்ன விஞ்சித் திருநகர்ச் செல்வ வென்றார்.
reading: They tell the lord of the rich city with copper-like walls that his chiefs have come back carrying arrows like the carp eyes of the women they love, and the warriors have gone off with the cows.
nuance: The simile turns the wounds into the love-wounds of women's eyes, a mocking report of an army that fled; the speakers are taken to be the herdsmen of 438.
event: The king is told that his chiefs returned wounded and the hunters kept the cows.

tamil: மன்னிரை பெயர்த்து மைந்தர் வந்தனர் கொள்க வாட்கட்
பொன்னிழை சுடரு மேனிப் பூங்கொடி யனைய பொற்பிற்
கன்னியைத் தருது மென்று கடிமுர சியம்பக் கொட்டி
நன்னகர் வீதி தோறு நந்தகோ னறைவித் தானே.
reading: Nandagon has the marriage drum beaten in every street of the city, proclaiming that to the warriors who bring back the king's herd he will give the maiden with sword-like eyes, like a golden creeper.
nuance: Where the king's army has failed, the herd chief turns the recovery into a bride contest, the pattern of Civakan's other marriages, which each come as a prize won.
event: Nandagon proclaims his daughter as the prize for whoever recovers the herd.

tamil: வெதிர்ங்குதைச் சாபங் கான்ற வெந்நுனைப் பகழி மூழ்க
வுதிர்ந்தது சேனை யீட்டங் கூற்றொடு பொருது கொள்ளுங்
கருந்தடங் கண்ணி யன்றிக் காயமா றாக வேகு
மரும்பெற லவளு மாகென் றாடவர் தொழுது விட்டார்.
reading: Remembering how the army's host scattered under the hunters' arrows, the men of the city bow and decline, saying that not only the dark-eyed maiden to be won by fighting Death, but even a celestial woman hard to win would not tempt them.
nuance: காயம் ஆறாக ஏகும் is read as one who travels by the sky, a heavenly woman; the line is compressed and the refusal is inferred from தொழுது விட்டார்.
event: The city's men refuse the challenge despite the bride offered.

tamil: கார்விரி மின்ன னார்மேற் காமுகர் நெஞ்சி னோடுந்
தேர்பரி கடாவித் தேந்தார்ச் சீவக னருளிற் போகித்
தார்பொலி புரவி வட்டந் தான்புகக் காட்டு கின்றாற்
கூர்பரி வுற்ற தெல்லா மொருமகன் உணர்த் தினானே.
reading: As the lustful men's hearts follow the lightning-like girl, Civakan is out driving his chariot horses and showing the circling paces of his garlanded horse when a man tells him all that has caused the great distress.
nuance: அருளிற் போகி may mean Civakan goes out of compassion or that another goes by his favour; the subject of காட்டுகின்றான் is taken to be Civakan.
event: A man tells Civakan, at his horse exercise, of the raid and the rout.

reading: Civakan swears that if he does not protect those the world names, the good cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins, let him become like the eunuch who, having seen his wife in another man's arms, still hurries to his sweet rice.
nuance: The vow has the shape of the Sangam vanjinam, a self-curse on failure, but its curse is the shame of a பேடி who swallows dishonour for food; the list of the protected is the classical one, given here by a merchant's son and not the king.
event: Civakan vows to recover the herd.

tamil: கார்க் கொண்மு மின்னி னிமிர்ந்தான்கலி மான்கு ளம்பிற்
பார்க்கண் ணெழுந்த துகளாற் பகன் மாய்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: He makes ready the war gear, yokes and harnesses the horses, fits out the chariot, strings the bow and chooses arrows, and rises like lightning from a cloud, and the dust from his horses' hooves blots out the sun.
event: Civakan arms himself and drives out against the hunters.

reading: As the youth whose arrows sink as flawlessly as young women's glances turns his strong chariot to face them, one hunter speaks a mean word, that this is no time to engage him and they should go.
nuance: முழுது என்று and the doubled மொழிந்தான் are hard to construe; புண்மொழி may stand for புன்மொழி, a mean word.
event: Civakan turns his chariot on the hunters, and one of them urges retreat.

reading: Saying that if the crocodile is strong in deep old water, in the forest they will see off even the strong, the hunting band, like a hungry snake that has seized its prey, hurries on without letting the herd go.
nuance: The hunters take the crocodile maxim for themselves: the forest is their deep water. The story keeps them in their forest and still defeats them (453).
event: The hunters refuse to give up the herd and press on.

tamil: கடற்படை யனுங்க வென்ற கானவ ரென்னுங் கூற்றத்
திடைப்படா தோடிப் போமி னுய்யவென் றிரலை வாய்வைத்
தெடுத்தனர் விளியுஞ் சங்கும் வீளையும் பறையுங் கோடுங்
கடத்திடை முழங்கக் காருங் கடலுமொத் தெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: Putting horns to their mouths, the hunters cry that the enemy should run and save themselves rather than fall into the Death that is the foresters who routed the sea-like army, and their calls, conches, whistles, drums and horns roar through the wasteland like cloud and sea rising together.
event: The hunters raise a war cry and taunt Civakan's party to flee.

tamil: கைவிசை முறுக்கி வீசுங் கொள்ளியுங் கறங்கு மேய்ப்பச்
செய்கழற் குருசில் திண்டேர் விசையொடு திசைக ளெல்லா
மையென வளைப்ப வீர ரார்த்தன ரவரு மார்த்தார்
மொய்யமர் நாட்செய் தையன் முதல்விளை யாடி னானே.
reading: Like whirled firebrands, the anklet-wearing lord's chariot circles so fast it seems to ring every direction in darkness; his heroes shout and the hunters shout back, and the lord plays the opening game of the crowded battle.
nuance: முதல் விளையாடினான் makes the battle Civakan's play, against the army's terror before the same men.
event: Civakan opens the fight, wheeling his chariot round the hunters.

tamil: ஆழியா னூர்திப் புள்ளி னஞ்சிற கொலியி னாகம்
மாழ்கிப்பை யவிந்த வண்ணம் வள்ளறேர் முழக்கி னானுஞ்
சூழ்துகண் மயக்கத் தானும் புளி ஞருள் சுருங்கிச் சேக்கைக்
கோழிபோற் குறைந்து நெஞ்சி னறமென மறமும் விட்டார்.
reading: As snakes faint and fold their hoods at the sound of the wings of Garuda, mount of the discus-bearer, so the hunters, under the roar of the generous one's chariot and the whirl of dust, shrink like coop hens and give up valour from their hearts, as they had given up dharma.
nuance: அறமென மறமும் விட்டார் pairs the two losses: men who had no dharma now lose their courage too, so the raiders' fall is given a moral as well as a martial cause.
event: The hunters lose heart before Civakan's chariot.

tamil: புள்ளொன்றே சொல்லு மென்றிப் புன்றலை வேடன் பொய்த்தான்
வெள்ளந்தேர் வளைந்த நம்மை வென்றியீங் கரிது வெய்தா
வுள்ளம்போற் போது நாமோ ரெடுப்பெடுத் துய்ய வென்னா
வள்ளன்மே லப்பு மாரி யார்ப்பொடு சிதறி னாரே.
reading: The hunters say that the scrawny hunter who told them the bird-omen alone decides has lied, that victory is hard now that the flood of chariots surrounds them, and that they must make one charge fast as thought and escape; and with a shout they shower arrows on the generous one.
nuance: புள் ஒன்றே சொல்லும் is read as the omen-reader's assurance; the omen that drove the raid fails them, and the blame falls on the augur, not on the raid.
event: The hunters blame their omen-reader and charge Civakan with a rain of arrows.

title: கோவிந்தையார் இலம்பகம் 451-471 (3/4)
theme: Civakan routs the hunters who seized the cowherds' herd, turning it back by the sound of his bow with no man lost; the city hails him as an Arjuna, and its women throng the street in a long scene of longing, praising his mother's penance, praying for him in dreams and paling as his chariot passes, until he enters his home and the chariot is housed with offerings.
source_issues: 456, 461, 469 (lines 2 and 4) and 471: the tool repaired a TSCII slip (ோ் read as ேர்); the repaired readings (தேர், ஏர்) fit the sense.
451 and 452 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.
453 line 1: ஐந்நூறு நூறு தலையிட்ட ஆறாயிரவர் can be counted two ways (six thousand under five hundred, or six thousand five hundred).

cast.role: the hero, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan, who recovers the seized herd
the hunters who seized the cowherds' herd, also called கானவர்
the cowherds whose herd is recovered
Civakan's companions
the usurping ruler, taken here as the one angered by the news
the women of the city who throng the street to see Civakan

tamil: மால்வரைத் தொடுத்து வீழ்ந்த மணிநிற மாரி தன்னைக்
காலிரைத் தெழுந்து பாறக் கல்லெனப் புடைத்த தேபோன்
மேனிரைத் தெழுந்த வேடர் வெந்நுனை யப்பு மாரி
கோனிரைத் துமிழும் வில்லாற் கோமகன் விலக்கி னானே.
reading: As wind rising in a line blows apart the dark rain that falls clinging to a great hill, the prince with his bow, which spits arrows in a row, wards off the rain of hot-tipped arrows the hunters loose in ranks.
event: The hunters shower arrows on Civakan, and he parries them with his own arrows.

tamil: கானவ ரிரிய வில்வாய்க் கடுங்கணை தொடுத்த லோடு
மானிரை பெயர்ந்த வாய ரார்த்தன ரணிசெய் திண்டோ
டானொன்று முடங்கிற் றொன்று நிமிர்ந்தது சரம்பெய் மாரி
போனின்ற வென்ப மற்றப் பொருவரு சிலையி னார்க்கே.
reading: As the foresters flee before the fierce arrows set to his bow, the herd turns back and the cowherds shout, while of the matchless archer's strong shoulders one bends and one straightens, so that he is said to stand like a cloud raining arrows.
nuance: The rhythm of the drawing arm, one shoulder bowed and one straight, is the poet's picture of continuous shooting; the herd is not driven back by him but turns of itself once the raiders run.
event: The hunters flee, the herd turns back and the cowherds cheer Civakan.

reading: When the six thousand hunters, with five hundred at their head, rain arrows by hundreds on his body, he cuts away the bows and arrows in their hands, and in a moment they vanish as the minds of kohl-eyed women do.
nuance: The count in line 1 can be read as six thousand under five hundred leaders or as six thousand five hundred. மாய்ந்தார் may mean they perished or that they vanished from the field; the simile of women's changing minds, the epic's own view of women here, favours vanishing, and the next verse speaks of no blade drawing blood.
event: Civakan cuts down the hunters' bows and arrows and the hunters vanish.

reading: With neither the edge of a sword nor the point of an arrow, the young man turns back the herd by the mere twang of the bow on his shoulder and returns, like the full white moon that the tall god freed from the planet's mouth.
nuance: Line 1 does not say whose body went unwounded: it can mean the recovery cost the hunters no blood or that Civakan came back untouched; the moon released whole from Rahu fits either. The god is named only as நெடியான், the tall one.
event: Civakan recovers the herd by the sound of his bow and comes back.

reading: When word comes that, with no man of his lost, he of the blooming garland with his companions has recovered the seized herd of the cowherd, one who heard it raged like a man whose last day had come, as if a spear had been thrown into a sword wound, and the city roared.
nuance: The one who rages (வெகுண்டான்) is not named; that he is Kattiyankaran, whose rule Civakan's success shames, is a reading from the story so far, not from the verse. கோவன் here is the herd's owner, not Civakan.
event: News of the recovery reaches the city, which cheers, while one who hears it rages.

tamil: இரவிதோய் கொடிகொண் மாடத் திடுபுகை தவழச் சுண்ணம்
விரவிப்பூந் தாம நாற்றி விரைதெளித் தாரந் தாங்கி
யரவுயர் கொடியி னான்ற னகன்படை யனுங்க வென்ற
புரவித்தேர்க் காளை யன்ன காளையைப் பொலிக என்றார்.
reading: The townspeople spread incense smoke over the sun-touching bannered mansions, scatter powder, hang flower garlands, sprinkle scent and, holding garlands, hail the young man as like the young hero of the horse chariot who wasted the wide army of the snake-bannered king, saying 'may he flourish'.
nuance: The comparison is to the Mahabharata: the snake banner is Duryodhana's, and the hero who routed his host is Arjuna, who in that story too recovered seized cattle; the poet sets the merchant's foster son beside an epic prince.
event: The city decorates its streets and blesses Civakan on his return.

tamil: இன்னமு தனைய செவ்வா யிளங்கிளி மழலை யஞ்சொற்
பொன்னவிர் சுணங்கு பூத்த பொங்கிள முலையி னார்தம்
மின்னிவர் நுசுப்பு நோவ விடலையைக் காண வோடி
யன்னமு மயிலும் போல வணிநகர் வீதி கொண்டார்.
reading: Women with red mouths like sweet nectar, the lisping speech of young parrots and rising breasts spotted with gold-bright freckles run to see the young man until their lightning waists ache, and fill the street like swans and peacocks.
event: The young women of the city run into the street to see Civakan.

tamil: சில்லரிச் சிலம்பின் வள்வார்ச் சிறுபறை கறங்கச் செம்பொ
னல்குற்றே ரணிந்து கொம்மை முலையெனும் புரவி பூட்டி
நல்லெழி னெடுங்கண் ணம்பாப் புருவலில் லுருவக் கோலிச்
செல்வப்போர்க் காமன் சேனை செம்மன்மே லெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: With the small drums of their anklets sounding, their hips decked as golden chariots yoked to the horses of their breasts, their long eyes as arrows and their brows as bows bent, Kama's army rises against the young lord.
nuance: The whole verse is a war in reverse: the hero just home from routing an army now meets one made of the women's bodies, and it is he who is the target.

tamil: நூல்பொர வரிய நுண்மை நுசுப்பினை யொசிய வீங்கிக்
கால்பரந் திருந்த வெங்கட் கதிர்முலை கச்சின் வீக்கிக்
கோல்பொரச் சிவந்த கோல மணிவிரற் கோதை தாங்கி
மேல்வரல் கருதி நின்றார் விண்ணவர் மகளி ரொத்தார்.
reading: Binding in their bodices the fiery breasts that swell till their waists, finer than thread, bend, and holding garlands in fingers reddened by the plectrum, they stand waiting for him to come, like the women of the gods.

tamil: ஆகமு மிடையு மஃக வடிபரந் தெழுந்து வீங்கிப்
போகமும் பொருளு மீன்ற புணர்முலைத் தடங்க டோன்றப்
பாகமே மறைய நின்ற படைமலர்த் தடங்க ணல்லார்
நாகம்விட் டெழுந்து போந்த நாகர்தம் மகளி ரொத்தார்.
reading: Women with wide flower-like eyes, standing half hidden with only their breasts that bring forth pleasure and wealth showing, look like the daughters of the Nagas risen from their underworld.

tamil: வாளரந் துடைத்த வைவே லிரண்டுடன் மலைந்த வேபோ
லாள்வழக் கொழிய நீண்ட வணிமலர்த் தடங்க ணெல்லா
நீள்சுடர் நெறியை நோக்கு நிரையிதழ் நெருஞ்சிப் பூப்போற்
காளைதன் றேர்செல் வீதி கலந்துடன் றொக்க வன்றே.
reading: All the wide flower eyes, long beyond men's measure, like two whetted spears met in fight, crowd together along the street where his chariot goes, as nerunji flowers with their rows of petals turn to watch the course of the sun.

tamil: வடகமுந் துகிலுந் தோடு மாலையு மணியு முத்துங்
கடகமுங் குழையும் பூணுங் கதிரொளி கலந்து மூதூ
ரிடவகை யெல்லை யெல்லா மின்னிரைத் திட்ட தேபோற்
படவர வல்கு லாரைப் பயந்தன மாட மெல்லாம்
reading: Shawls, silks, ear-rolls, garlands, gems, pearls, bracelets, earrings and jewels mingle their light, and as if lightning were ranged along the old city's every boundary, every mansion brings forth women with hips like a snake's hood.

tamil: மாதுகு மயிலி னல்லார் மங்கல மரபு கூறிப்
போதக நம்பி யென்பார் பூமியும் புணர்க வென்பார்
தோதக மாக வெங்குஞ் சுண்ணமேற் சொரிந்து தண்ணென்
றாதுகு பிணையல் வீசிச் சாந்துகொண் டெறிந்து நிற்பார்.
reading: Peacock-like women speak the customary words of blessing, some calling him a young elephant of a man and some wishing that he wed the earth too, and they shower powder everywhere, toss cool pollen-dropping garlands and stand flinging sandal paste.
nuance: பூமியும் புணர்க, 'may he join the earth too', is a wedding blessing that makes rule a second bride; the women do not know he is the dead king's son. போதகம் in line 2 is taken as the elephant calf; the sense of the epithet is not certain.
event: The women bless Civakan with auspicious words and shower him with powder, garlands and sandal.

tamil: கொடையுளு மொருவன் கொல்லுங் கூற்றினுங் கொடிய வாட்போர்ப்
படையுளு மொருவ னென்று பயங்கெழு பனுவ ணுண்ணூ
னடையுளார் சொல்லிற் றெல்லா நம்பிசீ வகன்கட் கண்டாந்
தொடையலங் கோதை யென்று சொல்லுபு தொழுது நிற்பார்.
reading: Others stand worshipping, saying that all the learned who walk in the fruitful subtle books have told of one unequalled in giving and one in sword-fighting crueller than killing Death, and all that we have seen in Nambi Civakan of the garland.
nuance: The pairing of கொடை and படை repeats the Sangam measure of a man, the patron and the fighter, and the women make Civakan the proof of the books rather than the books the measure of him.
event: Women worship Civakan as the one in whom the books' ideal of giver and warrior is seen.

tamil: செம்மலைப் பயந்த நற்றாய் செய்தவ முடைய ளென்பா
ரெம்மலைத் தவஞ்செய் தாள்கொ லெய்துவம் யாமு மென்பா
ரம்முலை யமுத மன்னா ரகம்புலர்ந் தமர்ந்து நோக்கித்
தம்முறு விழும வெந்நோய் தந்துணைக் குரைத்து நிற்பார்.
reading: Some say the good mother who bore this lord must have done penance; some ask on which mountain she did it, so that they too may attain the like; and women with nectar breasts, dried up within, stare at him and tell their friends of the burning sickness they suffer.
nuance: எய்துவம் யாமும் leaves open what they hope to attain, a son like him or the man himself; the next lines on their longing lean to the second.
event: Women praise Civakan's mother's penance and tell their friends of their longing.

tamil: சினவுநர்க் கடந்த செல்வன் செம்மல ரகல நாளைக்
கனவினி லருளி வந்து காட்டியாங் காண வென்பார்
மனவிரி யல்கு லார்தம் மனத்தொடு மயங்கி யொன்றும்
வினவுந ரின்றி நின்று வேண்டுவ கூறு வாரும்.
reading: Some ask that the lord who overcame the angry hunters grace them by coming in a dream tomorrow and showing his red flower-like chest so they may see it, while others, bewildered in their minds, stand saying what they want with no one asking them.
event: Women pray that Civakan visit them in a dream, and others voice their desires unasked.

tamil: விண்ணகத் துளர்கொன் மற்றிவ் வென்றிவேற் குருசி லொப்பார்
மண்ணகத் திவர்க ளொவ்வார் மழகளி றனைய தோன்றல்
பண்ணகத் துறையுஞ் சொல்லார் நன்னலம் பருக வேண்டி
யண்ணலைத் தவத்திற் றந்தார் யார்கொலோ வளிய ரென்பார்.
reading: They say none on earth matches this lord of the victorious spear, perhaps only those in heaven, and wonder who they might be, the poor fortunate ones, whose penance has given them the elephant-like hero so that women whose words dwell in music may drink his beauty.
nuance: அளியர் can be pity or envy ('poor things' or 'blessed ones'), and whether the penance is the women's or their families' is not stated. யார்கொலோ அளியர் is the Sangam turn of wonder at a hero (Purananuru 257 has யார்கொலோ அளியன்), here moved from the hero to the women who would have him.

tamil: வட்டுடைப் பொலிந்த தானை வள்ளலைக் கண்ட போழ்தே
பட்டுடை சூழ்ந்த காசு பஞ்சிமெல் லடியைச் சூழ
அட்டரக் கனைய செவ்வா யணிநலங் கருகிக் காமக்
கட்டழ லெறிப்ப நின்றார் கைவளை கழல நின்றார்.
reading: The moment they see the generous one in his bordered garment, the coins of their silk girdles slip round their soft feet, their lac-red mouths scorch, and they stand burning in the fierce fire of desire with the bangles sliding off their hands.

tamil: வார்செலச் செல்ல விம்மு வனமுலை மகளிர் நோக்கி
யேர்செலச் செல்ல வேத்தித் தொழுதுதோ டூக்க விப்பாற்
பார்செலச் செல்லச் சிந்திப் பைந்தொடி சொரிந்த நம்பன்
றேர்செலச் செல்லும் வீதி பீர்செலச் செல்லு மன்றே.
reading: As the women with swelling breasts watch him go, praising his bearing and worshipping him, their shoulders droop, and on this side bangles shower to the ground, so that the street where the lord's chariot runs turns pale as the beerkan flower.
nuance: The pallor of longing, which akam poetry lays on one woman's skin, is spread here over a whole street; the chariot leaves a pale track behind it.

tamil: வாண்முகத் தலர்ந்த போலு மழைமலர்த் தடங்கண் கோட்டித்
தோண்முதற் பசலை தீரத் தோன்றலைப் பருகு வார்போ
னாண்முதற் பாசந் தட்ப நடுங்கினார் நிற்ப நில்லான்
கோண்முகப் புலியோ டொப்பான் கொழுநிதிப் புரிசை புக்கான்.
reading: Tilting their rain-flower eyes as if to drink the young man and cure the pallor on their shoulders, the women stand trembling, held back by the noose of shame; he, like a fierce-faced tiger, does not stop, and enters his rich walled home.
nuance: Shame (நாண்) holds the women where they stand, and the hero's not stopping (நிற்ப நில்லான்) is set against their standing; the sequence of the crowd scene ends in one line of his action.
event: Civakan passes the women without stopping and enters his walled home.

tamil: பொன்னுகம் புரவி பூட்டு விட்டுடன் பந்தி புக்க
மன்னுக வென்றி யென்று மணிவள்ள நிறைய வாக்கி
யின்மதுப் பலியும் பூவுஞ் சாந்தமும் விளக்கு மேந்தி
மின்னுகு செம்பொற் கொட்டில் விளங்குதேர் புக்க தன்றே.
reading: The horses unyoked from the golden yoke go into their stalls, people fill gem bowls wishing that his victory last, and bearing sweet offerings of liquor, flowers, sandal and lamps, the shining chariot is brought into its gold-bright shed.
nuance: மதுப் பலி, an offering of liquor or honey, is made to the victorious chariot; the verse gives no sign of any Jain reserve about it.
event: The horses are stabled and the chariot is housed with offerings for lasting victory.

title: கோவிந்தையார் இலம்பகம் 472-492 (4/4)
theme: The Govindaiyar ilampakam closes: Civakan is welcomed home after the herd's recovery, and the herd chief Nandagon, telling in confidence how the old king fell and how he himself turned back from suicide in hope that the line survived, offers his daughter Govindai with gold and the herd's wealth and argues from the gods that lineage is no bar; Civakan, holding that a man must first marry a woman of his own rank, accepts her for his friend Padumukan, and the herders' wedding is told in dairy rites and a bridegroom's unbounded pleasure.
source_issues: Verses 473 and 474 end with the same speech formula (தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும்), but only 474 is followed by a speech; 473's formula may be doubled from 474, or a speech of Civakan's foster father may be lost.
Verse 488 line 2 is a repaired line (TSCII slip, ோ் read as ேர்); the repair gives சேர்த்தி, which fits the sense.
Verses 480-482 are in a different, shorter metre from the surrounding viruttams; the text gives no rubric for the change.
Verse 489 line 1 ஏறங்கோண் is obscure as divided and may be corrupt or misdivided.

Cast id for the usurping minister differs across this book's chapter files (kattiyankaran in ch010 and ch019, kattiyangaran in ch011, ch012 and ch020); this chapter names him only in Nandagon's speech and does not cast him.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father
the women of the city who welcome Civakan with the auspicious objects
the herd chief, father of Govindai, who names himself Govindan in 477
Nandagon's daughter, given to Padumukan
Civakan's friend, for whom he accepts Govindai
the herdsmen of the royal herds
the herdswomen of the cattle hamlets

tamil: இட்டவுத் தரிய மெல்லென் றிடைசுவல் வருத்த வொல்கி
யட்டமங் கலமு மேந்தி யாயிரத் தெண்ம ரீண்டிப்
பட்டமுங் குழையு மின்னப் பல்கல னொலிப்பச் சூழ்ந்து
மட்டவிழ் கோதை மாதர் மைந்தனைக் கொண்டு புக்கார்.
reading: A thousand and eight women with flower garlands, their upper cloths slipping and ornaments ringing, carry the eight auspicious things and lead the young hero into his house.
nuance: The welcome continues the procession of 470-471; the number ஆயிரத்தெண்மர் repeats the thousand and eight of the auspicious marks, a ritual figure rather than a count.
event: Women bearing the eight auspicious objects escort Civakan home after the herd's recovery.

tamil: தாயுயர் மிக்க தந்தை வந்தெதிர் கொண்டு புக்குக்
காய்கதிர் மணிசெய் வெள்வேற் காளையைக் காவ லோம்பி
யாய்கதி ருமிழும் பைம்பூ ணாயிரச் செங்க ணான்றன்
சேயுய ருலக மெய்தி தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும்.
reading: His foster father, more to him than a mother, comes out to receive the youth of the shining spear and takes him in with care, as if Indra's son had come to the high world, and then, the verse says, the noble one speaks these words.
nuance: The closing formula தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும் is repeated word for word at the end of 474, which introduces Nandagon's speech; no speech of the father follows here, so either the formula belongs to 474 alone or a speech has been lost. Whether தோன்றல் here is the father or Civakan is not clear.
event: Kantukkatan receives Civakan at the house and guards him.

tamil: தகைமதி யெழிலை வாட்டுந் தாமரைப் பூவி னங்கட்
புகைநுதி யழல வாட்கட் பென்னனாள் புல்ல நீண்ட
வகைமலி வரைசெய் மார்பின் வள்ளலைக் கண்டு வண்டார்த்
தொகைமலி தொறுவை யாளுந் தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும்.
reading: The noble lord who rules the great herds, seeing the bountiful hero whose broad chest Fortune of the lotus embraces, speaks these words.
nuance: The herd chief is named by his office (தொறுவை யாளும்), not by name; the name comes from his own mouth in 477.
event: Nandagon, the herd chief, comes before Civakan and begins to speak.

tamil: கேட்டிது மறக்க நம்பி கேண்முதற் கேடு சூழ்ந்த
நாட்டிறை விசயை யென்னு நாறுபூங் கொம்ப னாளை
வேட்டிறைப் பார மெல்லாங் கட்டியங் காரன் றன்னைப்
பூட்டிமற் றவன்ற னாலே பொறிமுதல் அடர்க்கப் பட்டான்.
reading: Nandagon asks Civakan to hear and then forget what he tells: the king of this land, who first brought ruin on himself, desired Vijayai, laid the whole burden of rule on Kattiyankaran, and by that man was crushed at the root of his fortune.
nuance: Nandagon blames the king's own choice (முதற் கேடு சூழ்ந்த, 'who first plotted the ruin') and says nothing of a former deed, whereas the narrator at 215 says a destiny formed before sprouted in the king; the epic keeps both causes, in two voices. The irony, which the hero cannot yet share, is that the listener is the dead king's son. பொறிமுதல் may be 'fortune at its root' or point to the machine (பொறி) of the peacock flight; the sense of line 4 is not certain.
event: Nandagon recounts in confidence how Saccandan handed his rule to Kattiyankaran for love of Vijayai and was destroyed by him.

tamil: கோலிழுக் குற்ற ஞான்றே கொடுமுடி வரையொன் றேறிக்
காலிழுக் குற்று வீழ்ந்தே கருந்தலை களைய லுற்றேன்
மால்வழி உளதன் றாயின் வாழ்வினை முடிப்பல் என்றே
ஆலம்வித் தனைய தெண்ணி அழிவினுள் அகன்று நின்றேன்.
reading: Nandagon says that when the sceptre fell he climbed a high peak meaning to throw himself down and end his life, resolving to die if no heir of the great line survived, but thinking of the banyan seed he drew back from destruction.
nuance: The banyan seed (ஆலம்வித்து) is the tiny seed of a vast tree: his hope is that one surviving child of the line could regrow the house. மால்வழி is read here as 'the great line'; it could be taken otherwise, and the sense of line 3 turns on it. The servant's loyal suicide is withheld, not condemned.
event: Nandagon tells how, at the king's fall, he went to kill himself and turned back in hope that the royal line survived.

tamil: குலத்தொடு முடிந்த கோன்றன் குடிவழி வாரா நின்றே
னலத்தகு தொறுவி னுள்ளே னாமங்கோ விந்த னென்பே.
னிலக்கண மமைந்த கோதா வரியென விசையிற் போந்த
நலத்தகு மனைவி பெற்ற நங்கைகோ விந்தை யென்பாள்.
reading: Nandagon names himself: he comes of a family in the service of the king whose line ended with him, he lives among the herds and is called Govindan, and his wife, who came swift as the Godavari, bore the girl called Govindai.
nuance: The daughter's name is formed from the father's. 'The king who ended with his clan' is what Nandagon believes of Saccandan; 476 has just shown him hoping it is not so.
event: Nandagon names himself and his daughter Govindai.

tamil: வம்புடை முலையி னாளென் மடமகள் மதர்வை நோக்க
மம்படி யிருத்தி நெஞ்சத் தழுத்தியிட் டனைய தொப்பக்
கொம்படு நுசுப்பி னாளைக் குறையிரந் துழந்து நின்ற
நம்படை தம்மு ளெல்லா நகைமுக மழிந்து நின்றேன்.
reading: Nandagon says that his young daughter's bold glance went into men's hearts like a pressed-in arrow, and that among all his people who begged for the slender girl and suffered he stood with his smile gone.
nuance: Line 4 can also be read of the herd's loss before the raid was undone (நம்படை, 'our men', who had stood beaten); the reading here takes it of the suitors among his own people whom he could not satisfy.

tamil: பாடகஞ் சுமந்த செம்பொற் சீறடிப் பரவை யல்குற்
சூடக மணிந்த முன்கைச் சுடர்மணிப் பூணி னாளை
யாடகச் செம்பொற் பாவை யேழுடன் தருவ லைய
வாடலில் வதுவை கூடி மணமக னாக என்றான்.
reading: Nandagon offers Civakan the girl of the golden anklets and bangled wrists together with seven statues of fine gold, and asks him to join her in an unfailing wedding as her bridegroom.
nuance: This keeps the proclamation of 440, that the maiden would go to whoever brought back the herd; the seven golden statues are added here.
event: Nandagon offers Govindai to Civakan in marriage with seven golden statues.

reading: Nandagon praises his daughter in the goods of the herd: her sweetness wells like butter, her speech is sweet as the cream of milk, her body is like melted ghee, and her two eyes are karuvilam flowers.
nuance: The metre changes here for three verses (480-482). The herdsman's similes are all dairy: the poet gives him the idiom of his trade, as the Sangam mullai poems give it to herders.

reading: Nandagon promises to fill the underworld with the ghee of red cows, sweet milk and thick curd, and asks Civakan to garland his handmaid with flowers, knowing all that must follow.
nuance: He calls his daughter உன் அடிச்சி, 'your servant woman', offering her below the hero's station before the hero raises the question of rank in 483.
event: Nandagon presses his offer with a promise of boundless dairy wealth.

reading: Nandagon tells Civakan not to think of lineage: fragrant-garlanded Murukan enjoyed the beauty of Valli, and the husband of the Earth took the sweet nectar of the lips of Nappinnai of the long herds.
nuance: Both precedents are gods who married beneath them by birth: Valli is a hunter's daughter and Nappinnai a herdsman's. The father argues from myth, not from doctrine, and the argument is his own interest.

tamil: கன்னியர் குலத்தின் மிக்கார் கதிர்முலைக் கன்னி மார்ப
முன்னினர் முயங்கி னல்லான் முறிமிடை படலை மாலைப்
பொன்னிழை மகளி ரொவ்வா தவரைமுன் புணர்தல் செல்ல
ரின்னதான் முறைமை மாந்தர்க் கெனமனத் தெண்ணி னானே.
reading: Civakan reflects that men do not first unite with women unequal to them in birth before they have married a maiden of their own high lineage, and that this is the rule for men.
nuance: This is the hero's thought, not his speech. It does not deny 482 that unequal marriage is possible; it orders it, so that rank governs which wife comes first. Lines 1-2 are hard to construe and the reading follows their sense with lines 3-4.
event: Civakan considers the offer and decides it would breach the order of marriage for him to take Govindai first.

tamil: கோட்டிளங் களிறு போல்வா னந்தகோன் முகத்தை நோக்கி
மோட்டிள முலையி னாணின் மடமக ளெனக்கு மாமான்
சூட்டொடு கண்ணி யன்றே யென்செய்வா னிவைகள் சொல்லி
நீட்டித்தல் குணமோ வென்று நெஞ்சகங் குளிர்ப்பச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Civakan, like a young tusker, looks at Nandagon and says, so as to cool his heart, that the girl is to be the crest and garland of one dear to him, and asks whether it is fitting to delay with such speeches.
nuance: The sense turns on மாமான் in line 2, a kinship word whose referent is not clear; 489 shows that he accepts Govindai on behalf of Padumukan, and the reading takes the line in that light.
event: Civakan accepts the offer and urges that the marriage be made without delay.

tamil: தேன்சொரி முல்லைக் கண்ணிச் செந்துவ ராடை யாயர்
கோன்பெரி துவந்து போகிக் குடைதயிர் குழுமப் புக்கு
மான்கறி கற்ற கூழை மௌவல்சூழ் மயிலைப் பந்தர்க்
கான்சொரி முல்லைத் தாரான் கடிவினை முடிக வென்றான்.
reading: The herd chief, in his wreath of honeyed mullai and red cloth, goes off in great joy into the crowd where curd is churned and orders that the wedding be performed in the pavilion of mayilai ringed with jasmine.
event: Nandagon orders the wedding to be held in the herders' pavilion.

tamil: கனிவளர் கிளவி காமர் சிறுநுதல் புருவங் காமன்
குனிவளர் சிலையைக் கொன்ற குவளைக்கண் கயலைக் கொன்ற
வினியுள ரல்ல ராய ரெனச்சிலம் பரற்றத் தந்து
பனிவளர் கோதை மாதர் பாவையைப் பரவி வைத்தார்.
reading: The women bring the girl, whose brow outdid Kama's bow and whose kuvalai eyes outdid the kayal fish, her anklets crying out, and set her down with praise.
nuance: Line 3 (இனியுளர் அல்லர் ஆயர்) seems to give the anklets' cry that the herders are 'no longer' something to her, perhaps that she now passes out of her people; the sense is not clear.
event: The herdswomen bring Govindai to the pavilion.

tamil: நாழியு ளிழுது நாகான் கன்றுதின் றொழித்த புல்தோய்த்
தூழிதோ றாவுந் தோழும் போன்றுடன் மூக்க வென்று
தாழிருங் குழலி னாளை நெய்தலைப் பெய்து வாழ்த்தி
மூழைநீர் சொரிந்து மொய்கொ ளாய்த்திய ராட்டி னாரே.
reading: The herdswomen dip in ghee, in a measure, grass the young cow's calf has eaten from, bless her to grow old with her husband age after age like cow and stall, pour ghee on her head and bathe her with water from a ladle.
nuance: The rite is wholly of the herd: calf-grazed grass, ghee, a blessing in the image of cattle. Line 2's comparison (ஆவும் தோழும்) is read as cow and stall; it may be cow and bull.
event: The herdswomen perform the herders' bridal anointing and bathing of Govindai.

tamil: நெய்விலைப் பசும்பொற் றோடு நிழன்மணிக் குழையு நீவி
மைவிரி குழலி னாளை மங்கலக் கடிப்புச் சேர்த்திப்
பெய்தனர் பிணையன் மாலை யோரிலைச் சாந்து பூசிச்
செய்தனர் சிறுபுன் கோலம் தொறுத்தியர் திகைத்து நின்றார்.
reading: They take off the gold ear studs bought with ghee and the gem pendants, fasten the auspicious bridal thread, put on a garland and sandal paste, and make her a small simple adornment, and the herdswomen stand amazed.
nuance: நெய்விலைப் பசும்பொன், 'gold bought at the price of ghee', marks the herders' wealth as dairy wealth. The small adornment (சிறுபுன் கோலம்) is plain, yet it amazes the herdswomen themselves.
event: The herdswomen adorn Govindai for the wedding.

tamil: சாறெங்கு மயரப் புக்கு நந்தகோன் றன்கை யேந்தி
வீறுயர் கலச நன்னீர் சொரிந்தனன் வீர னேற்றான்
பாறுகொள் பருதி வைவேற் பதுமுக குமரற் கென்றே.
reading: As the drums sound the herders take her and go through the festive old town, and Nandagon, holding the pitcher, pours its water, which the hero receives, saying it is for prince Padumukan of the spear.
nuance: The pouring of water seals the gift of the bride; the giver's promise in 440 is kept, but the winner passes the prize to his friend. ஏறங்கோண் in line 1 is unclear; it may name horns or the bull-catch drums of the herders.
event: Nandagon gives Govindai by pouring water, and Civakan receives the gift on behalf of his friend Padumukan.

tamil: நலத்தகை யவட்கு நாகா னாயிரத் திரட்டி நன்பொ
னிலக்கணப் பாவை யேழுங் கொடுத்தனன் போக விப்பா
லலைத்தது காமன் சேனை யருநுனை யம்பு மூழ்க
முலைக்குவட் டிடைப்பட் டாற்றான் முத்துக முயங்கி னானே.
reading: Nandagon gives her two thousand young cows and the seven fine golden statues, and then Padumukan, struck by the sharp arrows of Kama's army, embraces her pearl-adorned breasts.
event: Nandagon gives the dowry and Padumukan is united with Govindai.

reading: Drinking without tiring the nectar of her sharp teeth, whose eyes are like paired kazhuneer flowers and whose garland is fragrant, the garlanded spearman falls into a sea of pleasure that cannot be contained.
event: Padumukan delights in Govindai.

reading: Wondering whether she is the nectar the gods churned from the sweet ocean of milk or a daughter of the herders, while the girl melts, Padumukan becomes one with no awareness left but of his unguarded pleasure.
nuance: ஓம்பா ஒழுக்கத்து உணர்வொன்றிலன் can mean he kept no guard on himself or that he lost every awareness but this one; the narrator does not blame him. The nectar churned from the milk ocean answers the dairy similes of 480: the herd girl is made the gods' amrita.
event: Padumukan is lost in love for Govindai.

title: காந்தருவதத்தையார் இலம்பகம் 493-516 (1/15)
theme: The Gandharvadattai ilampakam opens with the merchant Sitattan, who, scorning those who blame former deeds and praising wealth as the only true thing, sails to a golden island, trades and enjoys himself for six months, and on the voyage home meets a storm in which he exhorts his crew with maxims on courage, the measured life-span and refuge in the Jina's feet; the ship sinks, all others drown, and he is cast alone on a strange shore.
source_issues: Verse 494 line 2 (கொன்னொழுகு வேலியவ தத்தன்) and line 3 (காளைசீ தத்தனவன்) are divided oddly; the father's name and whether Padumai's husband is the father or the son cannot be fixed from the verse.
Verse 496 line 4 and 514 line 4 carry repaired glyphs (FLAG repaired); the repairs read correctly.
Verse 515 line 3 carries a repaired glyph (FLAG repaired); செவ்வனஞ் சேர்ந்தாங் reads correctly after it.
Verse 507 ends on நாய்கன் without a verb, which comes only at the end of 508 (கூறும்); the two verses form one sentence.

cast.role: merchant's son who sails for wealth and is shipwrecked
those aboard Sitattan's ship
king of the gold-yielding island

reading: While Civakan and his companions live happily, a merchant rich in treasure gathered from the sea sets out to sail with ships, like great elephants on the waves, to bring back wealth.
nuance: Line 1 (இங்கு இவர்கள் இவ்வாறு இருந்து இனிது வாழ) closes the previous ilampakam's household and opens a new thread; the merchant is named only in the next verse.
event: A wealthy merchant resolves to sail abroad for wealth.

reading: The merchant is introduced: the husband of the bright-jewelled Padumai, a man of the lance-fenced line of Dattan, and his son Sitattan, a bull of that line, like a fighting tiger dwelling on a golden hill.
nuance: The word division of line 2 (வேலியவ தத்தன்) leaves the father's name unsure, and whether Padumai's husband in line 1 is the father or Sitattan himself depends on reading அவன் தன் போல் in line 3 as 'like his father'.

reading: Sitattan reflects that even artisans, by heaping up wealth from things as small as grains, come to ride elephants with frontlets, and that when fortune turns upside down, like a grindstone floating and a gourd sinking, to sulk and blame one's former deeds is not understanding.
nuance: The reflection runs from here to 498, closed by என்று எழுந்து போந்தான்; it is the merchant's view, and within a few verses he himself will put his survival down to old deeds (510, 511).

reading: If a man of resolve strives, a flood of wealth may fall to him in a single day, since nothing fails to yield to effort; but to sink into sloth at the words of hollow-minded men is as bitter as the mockers' jeers.
nuance: Line 4's comparison (எள்ளுநர்கட்கு ஏக்கழுத்தம் போல) is compressed; the sense that sloth gives one's mockers their triumph is a reading.

reading: Make wealth: there is no other steel that can subdue those who would subdue you, it works even while one sits still, and without doubt it brings pleasure, virtue and everything else; true wealth alone is wealth, and nothing else counts.
nuance: The verse gathers the Kural's chapter on making wealth (751, 759, 760) almost clause by clause, but in its own words: செய்க பொருள் and எஃகு are the only shared words, short of an echo. The shipwreck of 512 to 514 puts the creed to the test.

reading: As old trees fill with hanging bats when they decay, so when a lofty lineage weakens the heroes born in it must hold it up, while shunning the evil talk that bows the head is the women's part; with that he rose and went.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 divide duty by sex: upholding the line falls to the men, guarding against shaming talk to the women. Whether line 1 means the lineage is already declining or only that it may decline is open.
event: Sitattan resolves to restore his family's fortune and leaves to make ready.

reading: Loading great quantities of goods without stint, the hill-chested man whose pollen-thick garland bore the marks of women's sword-like eyes set out with a flawless aim.
event: Sitattan loads his cargo and sets out.

reading: The patron whose fame reached the sky gave suppliants whatever they asked, like rain, then boarded with his fragrant hair and bade the ship run sweetly without harm.
event: Sitattan gives gifts to suppliants, boards and orders the ship to sail.

reading: With flags flying from the mast-tops and three sails set high, the young men cheering and conch and drum sounding over the sea, the ship ran sweetly like an elephant that does not trample the coral.
event: The ship sails out under full sail.

reading: Striking the conches the waves bring, spilling clustered pearls, leaving the wind's arrows behind, the ship cleft the sea as if splitting a mountain lying in it and sped on, scattering the herds of the islands.
nuance: Line 4 (இரை இடறிப் பாய்ந்து இரிய) is open: the ship may scatter flocks or fish feeding at the islands.
event: The ship crosses the sea at speed.

reading: It reached an island of fine gold, rich in cleanliness and goodness, where women like lightning, flower-creepers and soft blossoms, with the gait of swans and peacocks and a nectar-like grace, live close and happy.
event: The ship reaches a gold-yielding island.

tamil: கோவினைக் குறிப்பிற் கண்டு கொடுத்தருள் சுமந்து செம்பொற்
நாவினு ளமிர்தங் கேட்டு நாடக நயந்து சின்னாள்
reading: Landing on the island, the honey-garlanded lord saw its king and, reading his wish, gave him a fine pearl necklace and carried away his favour; then for some days he listened to the nectar of the speech of women like Lakshmi of the lotus and delighted in their dramas.
event: Sitattan presents a pearl necklace to the island's king, wins his favour and enjoys the island's women and dramas.

tamil: புணர்ந்தவர் பிரித லாற்றாப் போகமீன் றளிக்குஞ் சாய
லணங்கினுக் கணங்க னாரோ டறுமதி கழிந்த பின்றைக்
கொணர்ந்தன பண்டம் விற்ற கொழுநிதிக் குப்பை யெல்லா
முணர்ந்துதன் மதலை யேற்றி யொருப்படுத் தூர்க்கு மீள்வான்
reading: After six months with women whose grace yields a pleasure lovers cannot bear to leave, he reckoned up the heaps of rich wealth from the goods he had sold, loaded his ship and made ready to return home.
event: Sitattan sells his goods, loads the proceeds and prepares to sail home.

tamil: அரசனைக் கண்டு கண்ணுற் றவர்களை விடுத்து நன்னா
ளிரைவதி வியாழ வோரை யிருஞ்சிலை முளைப்ப வேறிக்
கரைகட லழுவ நீந்திக் காற்றினுங் கடுகி யைஞ்ஞூ
றுரையுடைக் காத மோடி யோசனை யெல்லை சார்ந்தே,
reading: Taking leave of the king and of those he had met, on a good day when Revati, Jupiter's hour and the rising of Sagittarius met, he embarked, crossed the deep sea faster than the wind and ran five hundred kathams to the edge of the voyage's yojanas.
nuance: The care over the auspicious moment (line 2) sets up the storm that follows: a well-chosen day does not keep off what comes.
event: Sitattan departs on an auspicious day and sails most of the way home.

tamil: களித்தலை மயங்கி யிப்பா லிருத்தலுங் கலந்தோர் காற்றிற்
றுளித்தலை முகில்க ளீண்டித் தூங்கிருண் மயங்கி மான்று
விளிப்பது போல மின்னி வெடிபட முழங்கிக் கூற்று
மொளித்துலைந் தொழிய வெம்பி யுரறிநின் றிடிப்ப நாய்கன்.
reading: As they lingered in joy on this side, clouds heavy with drops gathered on a wind, the darkness thickened, lightning flashed as if calling, and the thunder roared and struck so fiercely that Death itself might hide, while the merchant...
nuance: The verse ends on நாய்கன், whose verb is கூறும் at the end of 508: the merchant's words are held back through a whole verse of storm.
event: A storm breaks over the homeward ship.

tamil: எண்டிசை வளியு மீண்டி யெதிரெதிர் கலாவிப் பவ்வங்
கொண்டுமே லெழுவ தொப்பக் குளிறிநின் றதிர்ந்து மேகந்
தண்டுளி பளிக்குக் கோல்போற் றாரையாய்ச் சொரிந்து தெய்வங்
கொண்டதோர் செற்றம் போலுங் குலுங்கன்மி னென்று கூறும்.
reading: The winds of the eight quarters met and clashed head-on, the sea seemed to rise up, the clouds roared and poured cold rain in streams like crystal rods, like the wrath of some god, and he says 'do not shake'.
event: In the storm Sitattan tells his crew not to tremble.

tamil: இடுக்கண்வந் துற்ற காலை யெரிகின்ற விளக்குப் போல
நடுக்கமொன் றானு மின்றி நகுகதா நக்க போழ்தவ்
விடுக்கணை யரியு மெஃகா மிருந்தழு தியாவ ருய்ந்தார்
வடுப்படுத் தென்னை யாண்மை வருபவந் துறங்க ளன்றே.
reading: When trouble comes, laugh without tremor, steady as a burning lamp, for that laughter is a steel that cuts the trouble; who has ever survived by sitting and weeping? Do not shame manliness: what must come will come, he says.
nuance: Line 1 opens as Kural 621 opens (இடுக்கண் ... நகுக) and line 3 turns its claim into an image (நக்க போழ்து அவ் இடுக்கணை அரியும் எஃகு), but the run of shared words is under four, so it is not marked as an echo. எஃகு recalls 497, where wealth was the steel; here composure is.
event: Sitattan exhorts his crew to face the storm without fear.

tamil: ஆடகச் செம்பொற் கிண்ணத் தேந்திய வலங்கற் றெண்ணீர்
கூடகங் கொண்ட வாழ்நா ளுலந்ததேற் கொல்லும் பவ்வத்
தூடகம் புக்கு முந்நீ ரழுந்தினு முய்வர் நல்லார்
பாடகம் போலச் சூழ்ந்த பழவினைப் பயத்தி னென்றான்.
reading: If the span of life held in the body like clear water in a golden cup is spent, the sea will kill; but even plunged into the deep, the good survive by the fruit of their old deeds that surrounds them like an anklet, he says.
nuance: The man who in 495 called blaming former deeds a failure of understanding now makes former deeds the ground of hope; the story does not mark the turn, but the two views sit four verses apart. The outcome bears him out: all the rest die (512) and he alone is cast ashore (513).

tamil: வினையது விளைவின் வந்த வீவருந் துன்ப முன்னீர்க்
கனைகட லழுவ நீந்திக் கண்கனிந் திரங்கல் வேண்டா
நனைமலர்ப் பிண்டி நாத னாண்மலர்ப் பாத மூலம்
நினையுமி னீவி ரெல்லா நீங்குமி னச்ச மென்றான்.
reading: Do not swim this sea weeping with melting eyes over the unbearable suffering that ripened deeds have brought; all of you, think on the flower-feet of the lord of the budding pindi tree and cast off fear, he says.
nuance: பிண்டி நாதன், the lord of the asoka (pindi), names the Jina. The refuge offered is not rescue: the feet are to be remembered so that fear goes, while what the deeds bring is still to be borne.

tamil: பருமித்த களிற னானும் பையெனக் கவிழ்ந்து நிற்பக்
குருமித்து மதலை பொங்கிக் கூம்பிறப் பாய்ந்து வல்லே
நிருமித்த வகையி னோடி நீர்நிறைந் தாழ்ந்த போதி
லுருமிடித் திட்ட தொப்ப வுள்ளவ ரொருங்கு மாய்ந்தார்.
reading: As the merchant, like a caparisoned war elephant, stood quietly bowed, the ship heaved, the mast broke, it ran as it had been built to run, filled with water and sank, and all aboard perished together as if thunder had struck them.
nuance: Line 1 (பருமித்த களிறனானும் பையெனக் கவிழ்ந்து நிற்ப) may describe the merchant standing bowed or the ship itself heeling over; the reading taken here makes it the merchant.
event: The ship founders and everyone aboard except Sitattan drowns.

reading: While the sea, bitter as neem, swallowed the wealth he had guarded and gathered and the people he loved, he stood without haste, clung to a broken piece of the mast, and the waves washed the fresh-garlanded man ashore.
nuance: ஓம்பிப் படைத்த பொருள் (line 1) is the wealth 497 called the only wealth; it goes down while the man who made it is kept, as 510 said the good would be.
event: Sitattan clings to a piece of the mast and is washed ashore.

tamil: போவாய் தமியே பொருளைப் பொரு ளென்று கொண்டாய்
reading: 'Having lost your ship, you swim alone through the midnight with no one beside you; you took wealth to be the thing of worth; you did not first make what would keep you from death, you made only deeds; my poor self,' he says, and goes on to a dune of white sand.
nuance: பொருளைப் பொருள் என்று கொண்டாய் answers 497's பொய்யில் பொருளே பொருள் in the speaker's own mouth. Line 3 (வீவாய் என முன் படையாய் படைத்தாய் வினை) is compressed and the sense of what he failed to make is a reading; என் பாவாய் may be addressed to himself or to some other.
event: Sitattan reproaches himself and reaches a sandbank.

reading: Reaching a lovely red grove where ஞாழல் and புன்னை trees with rough bark were in flower and striped bees and honey-bees hummed, the hill-chested man sat there grieving.
event: Sitattan reaches a flowering shore grove and sits in grief.

reading: In the long neytal grove, where crabs rolled over and over as the running waves kicked them, making the swans wonder, the noble one sat withering, watching for a ship to come.
nuance: The crab tumbled by the waves (lines 1 and 2) mirrors the castaway tossed ashore in 513.
event: Sitattan waits on the shore watching for a ship.

title: காந்தருவதத்தையார் இலம்பகம் 517-540 (2/15)
theme: The shipwrecked merchant Sridattan tells his loss to a stranger, Dharan, who promises by magic to restore his drowned companions and goods and flies him on a ram to the Vidyadhara city on the silver mountain, which the poet describes at length; there Dharan begins the story of King Kaluzhavegan's daughter, whose horoscope places her destined husband in Rajamapuram on earth.
source_issues: Verse 528 line 2 and verse 530 line 1 carry repairs of TSCII conversion slips (FLAG repaired); the repaired readings make sense.
Verse 537 line 2 prints the king's name split across words (கலுழனாய கலுழவே கற்கு); 546 confirms கலுழவேகன்.
Verse 537 line 1 (மாடியந் தானை) and verse 532 line 1 (உருளி மாமதி ஓட்டொழித்து) are obscure as printed.
Verse 522 line 2 reads பகும்புயல், possibly for பசும்புயல்.
Verse 540 lines 3 and 4 name no speaker.

cast.role: merchant of Rajamapuram, friend of Civakan
Vidyadhara in the service of Kaluzhavegan, who stages the wreck and brings Sridattan to the Vidyadhara city
Vidyadhara king, father of Gandharvadattai
Kaluzhavegan's astrologer
kings who came seeking the princess

reading: Cast up on the shore grove, the strong-shouldered merchant meets a man of strong stride and, calling him kin, begins to tell him what has befallen him.
nuance: The stranger is not yet named; 519 calls him Dharan, and 574 reveals he is the Vidyadhara who staged the storm, so the merchant here confides his loss to its author.
event: Sridattan meets a stranger in the seashore grove and begins to tell him his misfortune.

reading: He tells the man how his ship went down in the black sea under the wind, how his goods were ruined, and how he survived by clinging to a hard-won float.
event: Sridattan recounts the shipwreck and his escape on a piece of wreckage.

reading: When the mighty merchant has told his grief so that even deer and trees pity him, the stranger's flawless words, sweet as honey and nectar, cool his heart.
nuance: The listener is first named here, in the dative தரனுக்கு; the comfort is described before its content is given in 520.
event: Sridattan finishes his tale to Dharan and is comforted by his reply.

reading: Dharan says he is master of magic arts and will, without any deceit and in the blink of an eye, give back the dead companions together with all the wealth that remains, so the merchant should not grieve.
nuance: 'Without any deceit' (வஞ்சம் ஒன்று இன்றி) is spoken by the man who, as 574 says, raised the storm by deceit; the promise to return 'dead' companions is kept because they were never dead (580, 582).
event: Dharan promises to restore Sridattan's companions and goods by his magic arts.

reading: Having made his word believed, Dharan says 'let us climb the mountain', mounts the merchant on a swift ram and flies off carrying him.
event: Dharan sets Sridattan on a flying ram and carries him up through the air.

reading: They split the sky-climbing clouds at speed, the cold rain wetting their sides, and come gladly to a hard mountain with fragrant groves on its dripping slopes.
event: Dharan and Sridattan fly through rain clouds and land on a mountain.

reading: The merchant takes ripe fruits hanging from the branches, sweet to see and rare, fit for the lotus goddess, eats them like nectar, and his body is cooled.
nuance: Third use in a few verses of the image of cooling (519 heart, 523 body): the poet stages relief in steps after the wreck.
event: Sridattan eats the mountain's fruits and is refreshed.

reading: Looking on the groves of saffron, naga trees and sandal on the cloud-wrapped mountain, the jewel-chested merchant rejoices.
event: Sridattan views the mountain groves with delight.

reading: Dharan tells him that a kaatham beyond this cool mountain of garland-like falls lies a fine city where the lord of flag-hung walls dwells, and bids him come; they go and reach it.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 carry Dharan's words (…உண்டு அங்குப் போதும் எழுக) inside the narration without a speech tag.
event: Dharan leads Sridattan onward to the Vidyadhara king's city.

tamil: மேகமே மிடைந்து தாழ விருள்கொண்ட வெள்ளிக் குன்ற
மாகத்து விளங்கித் தோன்றும் வனப்புநாம் வகுக்க லுற்றா
னாகந்தான் கரிய தொன்று கீழ்நின்று நடுங்கக் கவ்விப்
பாகமே விழுங்கப் பட்ட பான்மதி போன்ற தன்றே.
reading: The poet begins the description: the silver mountain, cloaked below by dark clouds and shining above, looks like the white moon half swallowed by a black serpent gripping it from beneath.
nuance: An eclipse image: the dark serpent of the eclipse holds the moon from below, so the white peak shows only in part. The silver mountain is the Vidyadhara range named in 546 (வெள்ளிவேதண்டம்).

tamil: துளங்குபொன் னகரின் றன்மை சொல்லலாஞ் சிறிதோர் தேவன்
விளங்குபொன் னுலகத் துள்ள துப்புர விடங்க ளெல்லா
மளந்துகொண் டின்பம் பூரித் தணிநக ராக்கி மேலா
லிளங்கதிர்ப் பருதி சூட்டி யியற்றிய தென்ன லாமே.
reading: The golden city, the poet says, can be described a little as if a god had measured out every fine place of the shining heaven, filled it with delight, built it into a city and crowned it with the young sun.
The golden city looks as though the thousand-eyed god's golden city, red eyes blooming like a thousand lotuses, had come to rest on the mountain with its fragrant-haired women.
nuance: The thousand eyes like a thousand lotuses are Indra's; the comparison sets the Vidyadhara city beside heaven's capital, as 535 does again.

reading: The bright flags on the moated walls seem to pat the moon with hollowed palms, as though calling it like the faces of the doe-eyed women, so that the moon is cooled within.
nuance: The sense of line 3 (உடங்கு வெண்மதி உள்குளிர) and of கொம்மை கொட்டுதல் is uncertain; the conceit pairs the moon with the women's faces, as 532 does.

reading: The sounds of girdles, anklets, harps, flutes and tuned drums make the bright city seem to open a noisy mouth and cry out, 'whose is beauty like this?'
The gem finials on the gold mansions, scorched by the long rays of the burning sun, seem to break out in blisters of gold.
Because the moon, its chariot halted, rests on the lofty mansions, the faces of the deer-eyed women seem in kindness to soothe its heat.
nuance: Line 1 (உருளி மாமதி ஓட்டொழித்து) and the moon's 'heat' (அழல்) are hard; the reading that the moon pauses on the towers and is cooled by the women's faces is tentative.

reading: Jewels and garlands of fresh gold lie where they fell, with no one wanting to pick them up, so that the streets look as if the sky had come into flower.
nuance: The city's wealth is measured by indifference to it: dropped jewels lie unclaimed, a sharp contrast to the merchant who in 514 is reproached for taking wealth to be the only thing of worth.

reading: The rich smoke of teak-dark agil mixed with honey, pent in the mansions, escapes slowly as they open, as though the mansions were breathing out sighs.
If one asks what the splendour of this matchless city of truthful Vidyadharas is like, it is like the gem casket Indra longs for, opened.
nuance: The city's people are called தப்பில் வாய்மொழி, of faultless speech, in the same chapter whose host has just lied to bring the merchant there (520, 574).

tamil: நன்னகர் நோக்கி நாய்கன் நாகங்கொல் புகுந்த தென்னப்
பின்னவன் விருந்து பேணிப் பேசினன் பிறங்கு தாரான்.
reading: Seeing the fine city, the merchant wonders whether they have entered the serpents' world; they go in, descend into a gold mansion among the clouds, and Dharan entertains him as a guest and speaks.
event: Dharan brings Sridattan into his mansion in the city, entertains him, and begins to speak.

tamil: மாடியந் தானை மன்னர் மாமணி நாக மாகக்
தோடலர் கோதைத் தொல்சீர்த் தாரணி சுரும்புண் கண்ணி
யாடவ ரறிவு போழு மணிமுலை யணங்கி னன்னாள்.
reading: Dharan begins: the king Kaluzhavegan, a Garuda to rival kings who are like great gem-bearing serpents, has as queen Dharani of ancient fame, bee-haunted eyes and breasts that pierce men's judgment, a goddess among women.
nuance: The king's name is split across words as printed (கலுழனாய கலுழவே கற்கு) and is confirmed in 546; the opening phrase மாடியந் தானை is obscure.

tamil: விண்ணகம் வணங்க வெண்கோட் டிளம்பிறை முளைத்த தேபோற்
பண்ணகத் தினிய சொல்லாள் பாவையைப் பயந்த ஞான்றே
யெண்ணிட மின்றி மன்ன ரிம்மலை யிறைகொண் டீண்டி
யண்ணலங் களிற்றி னுச்சி யருங்கல வெறுக்கை யீந்தார்.
reading: When the sweet-voiced queen bore a daughter, like the young white crescent rising for the heavens to worship, kings without number crowded onto this mountain and offered rare jewels and wealth from the heads of their elephants.
nuance: The princess is not named here; 550 names her Gandharvadattai.
event: At the princess's birth, kings gather on the Vidyadhara mountain bringing gifts to win her.

tamil: மந்திரத் தரசன் வல்லே நிமித்திகன் வருக என்றாற்
கந்தரத் தோடு கோளின் சாதக மவனுஞ் செய்தா
னிந்திர திருவி லேய்ப்பக் குலவிய புருவத் தாட்கு
வந்தடை பான்மை மண்மேல் இராசமா புரத்த தென்றான்.
reading: The king called for his astrologer, who cast the princess's horoscope from the planets and declared that the one she is destined to join lives on earth, in Rajamapuram.
nuance: பான்மை, one's allotted portion, is the word the king will take up in 554 (பான்மையார் விலக்குகிற்பார்). The prophecy points down from the sky-dwellers' city to the human town where Civakan lives.
event: The astrologer reads the princess's horoscope and names Rajamapuram on earth as the place of her destined husband.

tamil: அவனுரை தெளிந்து வேந்த னாசையு ளரசர் நிற்பக்
கவனங்கொள் புரவிக் கொட்பிற் காதலுங் கரந்து வைத்தா
னவனதே கருதிற் றாங்கொ லன்றுகொ லறிய லாகா
திவணது மறிது மென்று கோயிலுக் கேகி னானே.
reading: Trusting the astrologer's word, the king kept the suitor kings standing in hope and hid his intent like the wheeling of a swift horse; unable to tell whether he meant it or not, they resolved to learn the matter there, and he went to the palace.
nuance: Who speaks lines 3 and 4 (அவனதே கருதிற்றாங்கொல் … அறிதும் என்று) is unclear: the waiting kings guessing the king's mind, or the king weighing the astrologer's word; the subject of ஏகினான் is the king.
event: Kaluzhavegan keeps the suitor kings waiting while concealing his plan, and withdraws to his palace.

title: காந்தருவதத்தையார் இலம்பகம் 541-564 (3/15)
theme: At the court of the Vidyadhara king Kaluzhavegan the merchant Sridattan is welcomed as kin of seven generations, shown the princess Gandharvadattai, and entrusted with her: she is to go to his city and belong to whoever defeats her at the vina.
