theme: The battle over Gandharvadattai ends: Padumukan's elephant and arrows and Civakan's conch rout the envious kings, who take him for Murugan and scatter, and the narrator declares that victory goes to the virtuous mind. Civakan brings the bride home, the wounded are treated and rewarded, he expiates the sin of the battlefield by a golden image of the Jina, a festival and gifts and worship at the Tirthan's feet, and the stores for the great wedding pile up, led by Nandagon's pots of milk, curd and ghee.
source_issues: 807 line 3: கண்ணுட் டீயாற சுட்டு looks corrupt for கண்ணுள் தீயால் சுட்டு.
808 line 1: the word division is broken (சிலை கால்கு னிந்த for சிலை கால் குனிந்த).
811 line 1: தெழிக்ப் is a misprint for தெழிக்கப்.
812: printed with the number 811; read as 812 (the tool's numbering flag).
817 line 2: உழதசெஞ் reads as a misprint for உழுத செஞ்.
819 line 3: பதுமுகன் பாவை மார்பி னெய்க்கிழி is hard to construe; the line may be corrupt.
821 line 2: சேடங் கூலித் is doubtful; கூலித் gives no clear sense.
824 line 4: தாங்கொர்பால lacks the final pulli of the refrain ஒர்பால் found in 825 to 827.
Verses 805, 807, 808, 809, 812, 819: TSCII repairs of ோ் to ேர் (flagged by the tool); 814 to 817: stanzas printed in eight half-lines and joined.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, who has won Gandharvadattai at the vina
Civakan's friend, who fights from an elephant and tends the wounded
Civakan's companions, who fight beside him
the kings who came seeking the princess and make war over her
the Vidyadhara kings who watch and cheer Civakan's fight
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, won by Civakan at the vina, now his bride
the women who give the wounded ghee food as medicine
the herd chief, keeper of the king's herds, who brings milk, curd and ghee for the wedding

tamil: கடல்விளை யமுதங் கண்ட பொழுதினெய் கனிந்த தீஞ்சொற்
றடிசிலஞ் சுவைமிக் காங்கு மண்ணலங் குமர னொன்னா
ருடலின்மேற் றிரியுந் திண்டேர் காண்டலு மைந்தர் நெஞ்சத்
திடல்பிளந் திட்ட வெஃகஞ் சுமந்தமர்த் திறத்தின் மிக்கார்.
reading: As rice cooked with ghee grows sweeter when nectar from the sea is added, the warriors, seeing the young lord's strong chariot rolling over the bodies of his foes, carry the spears that have split their chests and fight the harder.
nuance: The simile makes the sight of the leader's chariot a seasoning: it does not change the fight but sharpens what the warriors already have. Whether மைந்தர் are Civakan's men or the enemy's is not stated; the sense of growing valour points to his own side.
event: Civakan's chariot drives over the enemy dead and his men, though wounded by spears, fight on more fiercely.

tamil: கடாந்திறந் திட்டு வானிற் களகள முழங்கும் வேழம்
படாந்திறந் தூழித் தீயிற் பதுமுகன் காட்டி யிட்டான்
தடாம்பிறை மருப்புத் திண்கை யபரகாத் திரங்க டம்மாற்
கொடாம்பிற குமரிப் போருட் பிறர்க்கெனக் கொன்ற தன்றே.
reading: Padumukan drives forward a roaring elephant in musth, like the fire at the end of an age, which with its crescent tusks, strong trunk and hind legs kills in the battle for the maiden as if refusing to give her to others.
nuance: குமரிப் போர் names the war for what it is, a fight over a girl; the elephant is made to fight as if it too were a suitor who will not yield her (கொடாம் பிறர்க்கு).
event: Padumukan sends his war elephant into the battle fought over the princess, and it kills the enemy.

tamil: மருப்பினால் வேழம் வீழா மன்னரை வாலிற் சீறா
முருக்கித்தேர் தடக்கை தன்னான் முழங்கிப்பாய் மாக்கள் காலி
னெரித்திடாக் கண்ணுட் டீயாற சுட்டுநீ றாக்கி நெய்த்தோ
ரொருக்கிப்பேய் பாடி யாட வுறுசிலை யுடன்று கொண்டான்.
reading: Felling kings with its tusks, lashing with its tail, crushing chariots with its trunk, trampling leaping horses under its feet and burning foes to ash with the fire of its eyes, the elephant makes blood flow while demons sing and dance, and the rider angrily takes up his strong bow.
nuance: The rider who takes the bow is not named; continuing from 806 he is read here as Padumukan, though the bow-work that follows could belong to Civakan. Line 3 (கண்ணுட் டீயாற சுட்டு) looks corrupt for கண்ணுள் தீயால் சுட்டு.
event: The war elephant destroys kings, chariots and horses, and its rider takes up his bow.

tamil: கொண்டான் பகழி தொடுத்தான் சிலை கால்கு னிந்த
reading: He took his bow, fitted the arrows, the bow bent in a circle, and seeing chariots, elephants' heads, the flanks of bee-swarmed horses and the fierce kings, he poured a rain of arrows that fell among them all.
nuance: The verse runs on the verbs கொண்டான், தொடுத்தான், கண்டான், சொரிந்தான், so that the shooting is told at the speed of the act; it picks up கொண்டான் from the end of 807.
event: The archer looses a shower of arrows on the chariots, elephants, horses and kings.

reading: Laughing, he says that the herds of gold-caparisoned elephants, the masses of red-gold chariots and the sea-flood of the army are nothing but the leftovers of the arrows that travel from the lord's bow, and that there are no kings of gold ornament left at all.
nuance: நம்பன் is used of Civakan in 811; if the laughing speaker is his friend, he credits the rout to Civakan's bow even while he fights. The speaker is not named, and the verse could also be the narrator's report of the archer's taunt.
event: The archer mocks the enemy, saying their whole army is only what the lord's arrows have left.

tamil: ஒருவனே சிலையு மொன்றே யுடையதோர் களிற்றின் மேலா
னருவரை மார்பிற் சென்ற தறிந்தில னெஃக மின்னும்
பொருவரோ மன்ன ரென்றான் பொருசிலை மடக்கி யிட்டார்
வருகளி யானை மீட்டார் வாட்படை வாங்கிக் கொண்டார்.
reading: 'One man alone, one bow alone, on one elephant, and he did not even notice the spear that went into his mountain chest: will kings still fight?' said one, and they unstrung their bows, turned back their elephants and put up their swords.
nuance: The one who speaks is unnamed; the plural verbs that follow (மடக்கியிட்டார், மீட்டார்) make it a king among the attackers whose words turn the rest. வாட்படை வாங்கிக் கொண்டார் can mean they drew their swords or withdrew them; the unstrung bows favour withdrawal.
event: Struck by the lone fighter's disregard of a spear wound, the hostile kings give up the fight and turn back.

tamil: செங்கண்மா றெழிக்ப் பட்ட வலம்புரித் துருவங் கொண்ட
சங்குவாய் வைத்து நம்பன் றெழித்தலுந் தறுக ணாளி
பொங்கிய முழக்கின் வேழப் பேரினம் புலம்பி னாற்போற்
றங்குதார் மன்ன ரெல்லாந் தளர்ந்துகண் சாம்பி னாரே.
reading: When the lord set to his mouth a conch shaped like the right-whorled conch that red-eyed Mal sounds, and blew it, all the garlanded kings faltered and their eyes dimmed, like a great herd of elephants wailing at the roar of a fierce lion.
nuance: The conch is likened to Vishnu's, so the hero's blast borrows the god's; the verse wins the battle by sound rather than by a blow.
event: Civakan blows his conch and the enemy kings lose heart.

tamil: அருவரை நாகஞ் சுற்றி யாழியான் கடைய வன்று
கருவரை குடையப் பட்ட கடலெனக் கலங்கி வேந்தர்
திருவரை மார்பன் றிண்டேர் மஞ்ஞையே முருகன் தானென்
றொருவரோ டொருவர் கூடா வண்ணமே யுடைய லுற்றார்.
reading: Shaken like the sea when the one of the wheel churned it with the serpent wound round the mountain, the kings cried that the broad-chested one's chariot was the peacock and he was Murugan himself, and broke so that no two of them stayed together.
nuance: Two gods are borrowed in one verse: Vishnu churning the sea for the kings' turmoil, Murugan for the hero they think they see. The kings' cry is a mistake born of fear, not the poet's claim that Civakan is divine.
event: Taking Civakan for Murugan on his peacock, the hostile kings scatter in panic.

tamil: முளிமரக் காடு மேய்ந்த முழங்கழல் போன்று மைந்தன்
றெளிநலக் குமரர் கூற்றிற் றெழித்தனர் பகழி சிந்தி
யொளிநல வுப்புக் குன்ற மூர்புனற் குடைந்த தேபோற்
களிநல மன்னர் தங்கள் கடற்படை யுடைந்த தன்றே.
reading: Like a roaring fire that grazes through a forest of dry trees, the prince's companions of clear worth roared like Death and scattered arrows, and the sea-like army of the drunk-with-pride kings broke as a shining hill of salt crumbles in a flood.
nuance: The salt hill dissolving in water is an image of a mass that has no cohesion of its own: the kings' sea of soldiers is large but melts at the first flood.
event: Civakan's companions shower arrows and the kings' great army breaks up.

tamil: உறுபடை மன்னர் தம்மை யுடற்றியொன் றானு மின்றிச்
சிறுபடை யவர்கள் வென்று செகுப்பவோ வென்ன வேண்டா
செறியெயிற் றாளி வேழப் பேரினஞ் செகுத்த தன்றே
வுறுபுலி யொன்று தானே கலையின முடற்றிற் றன்றே.
reading: Do not ask whether a small band could beat kings with great armies and come away unharmed: a lion with close-set teeth kills a great herd of elephants, and a single tiger attacks a herd of deer.
nuance: The narrator turns to the listener (என்ன வேண்டா) to answer a doubt about the story's plausibility; the answer is from nature, and 815 then gives a moral cause as well.

tamil: நல்லவை புரியு மாந்தர் நாந்தகம் பிழைத்து வீழா
வல்லவை புரியு மாந்தர்க் கத்திர மொன்றும் வாயா
வெல்வதோ குணத்தின் மிக்கார் வெற்றிலை விடினும் வேலா
மில்லையே வென்றி தீமை யிடங்கொண்ட மனத்தி னார்க்கே.
reading: Those who do good are missed by the sword and do not fall, and for those who do evil no weapon finds its mark; those great in virtue win even if they throw a betel leaf, for it becomes a spear, and there is no victory for those in whose minds evil has made its home.
nuance: வெற்றிலை (betel leaf) puns on வெற்று இலை, a bare leaf: the weakest missile becomes a spear in a good man's hand. The verse does not say the virtuous never fight; it says the outcome of their fighting is decided by the state of the mind.

tamil: குழையுடை முகத்தி னாள்கண் கோணைப்போர் செய்த மன்னர்
மழையிடை மின்னி னொய்தா மறைந்தனர் விஞ்சை வேந்தர்
முழையிடை சிங்க மன்னான் மொய்யம ரேத்தி யார்த்தார்
விழவுடை வீதி மூதூர் விருப்பொடு மலிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The kings who had waged a war of envy over the eyes of the girl with earrings vanished faster than lightning in a cloud; the Vidyadhara kings praised the hard fighting of the one like a lion in its cave and shouted, and the old city of festive streets overflowed with joy.
nuance: கோணைப் போர் is a crooked or spiteful war; the poet names the kings' cause as envy over a girl's eyes, not a claim of right.
event: The hostile kings flee, the Vidyadhara kings cheer Civakan's fight, and the city rejoices.

tamil: பார்மிசை யுலக மேத்தும் படுகளங் கண்டு பற்றார்
போர்முகக் களிற்று வெண்கோ டுழதசெஞ் சால்கொண் மார்பின்
சீர்முகத் தோழர் சூழச் சீவகன் திருவின் சாயல்
வார்முக முலையி னாளை மனைவயிற் கொண்டு புக்கான்.
reading: Having seen the battlefield the world praises, Civakan, his chest scored with red furrows ploughed by the white tusks of the enemy war elephants, and surrounded by his companions, took the girl of fortune's grace and bound breasts into his house.
nuance: The tusk wounds are drawn as plough furrows (சால்) on his chest, so that the bridegroom enters the house bearing a field of war on his body.
event: Civakan, wounded, leads Gandharvadattai into his house with his companions around him.

tamil: நெய்க்கழி வைக்கப் பட்டார் நெய்ப்பத்தல் கிடத்தப் பட்டார்
புக்குழி யெஃக நாடி யிரும்பினாற் போழப் பட்டார்
மைக்கிழிந் தொழுகுங் கண்ணீர் மாநிலத் துகுக்கப் பட்டார்
கைக்கிழி கொடுக்கப் பட்டார் கலம்பல நல்கப் பட்டார்.
reading: Some were laid in troughs of ghee, some were stretched in ghee tubs, some had the spearheads sought out where they had entered and cut out with iron, some shed on the earth the tears that ran with their eye-black, some were given purses of coin, and some were given many ornaments.
nuance: The passive refrain (பட்டார்) lists the wounded only by what is done to them; healing and reward stand in one list, as if both were care owed to the fighters. Line 3 may describe the pain of the surgery or mourning for the dead; the verse does not say.
event: The wounded are treated with ghee and surgery, and rewarded with money and ornaments.

tamil: முதுமரப் பொந்து போல முழுமெயும் புண்க ளுற்றார்க்
கிதுமருந் தென்ன நல்லா ரிழுதுசேர் கவளம் வைத்துப்
பதுமுகன் பாவை மார்பி னெய்க்கிழி பயிலச் சேர்த்தி
நுதிமயிர்த் துகிற்குப் பாயம் புகுகென நூக்கி னானே.
reading: For those whose whole bodies were holed with wounds like the hollows of an old tree, the good women set balls of food with ghee, saying 'this is medicine', and Padumukan laid ghee-soaked cloths close on their chests and urged them off to beds of soft fur.
nuance: பதுமுகன் பாவை மார்பின் is hard to construe; பாவை may go with the women rather than with Padumukan, and the verse's single verb (நூக்கினான்) is his.
event: Padumukan and the women tend the wounded with ghee food and dressings and send them to rest.

tamil: பார்கெழு பைம்பொன் றன்னாற் பண்ணவ னுருவ மாக்கி
யூர்கெழு விழவு செய்தாங் குறுபொரு ளுவப்ப நல்கித்
தார்கெழு மின்னு வீசித் தனிவடந் திளைக்கு மார்பன்
போர்கெழு களத்துப் பாவம் புலம்பொடு போக்கி னானே.
reading: The lord whose chest gleams with garland and single chain made an image of the Holy One in green gold of the earth, held a festival through the town, gave wealth gladly, and with lament put away the sin of the battlefield.
nuance: The epic does not treat the victory as sinless because it was defensive: போர்கெழு களத்துப் பாவம் is named outright, and it is removed with புலம்பு, grief, not only with rite. பண்ணவன் is the Jina as the work's own Lord.
event: Civakan has a golden image of the Jina made, holds a festival and gives gifts to expiate the killing in battle.

tamil: செய்தவப் பாவ மெல்லாந் தீர்த்திடுந் தீர்த்தன் பாத
மெய்திய சேடங் கூலித் திறைஞ்சுபு தொழுது வாழ்த்தி
மையறு மணியிற் செய்த வலம்புரி யதனீர் கொண்டான்
வையக மளிக்க நீண்ட வலம்புரித் தடக்கை யானே.
reading: He of the long right-whorled-marked hand stretched out to protect the world took the remnant from the feet of the Tirthan who removes all sins committed, bowed, worshipped and praised, and took the water of the right-whorled conch made of flawless gem.
nuance: தீர்த்திடும் தீர்த்தன் puns on the Tirthan as the one who removes (தீர்). The claim of sin removed at the Jina's feet sits beside the work's teaching elsewhere (375) that deeds wear away on the path of knowledge. The word read as கூலித் in line 2 is doubtful.
event: Civakan worships at the Tirthankara's feet, receives the offering's remnant and takes the water from the jewelled conch.

reading: What is now told is the great wedding of the girl like a golden branch, round whose breasts, like a jewel casket set with dark gems and red rays, fine gems swing.
nuance: A short verse in a new metre opens the wedding section; the narrator announces the subject (பேசுகின்றதே) rather than telling an act.

reading: The guardian of the king's herds, lord of the shining spear, brought four hundred thousand pots filled fair with fine curd, milk and ghee, so that the town was amazed at the wedding feast.
nuance: வேள்வி here is the wedding as a feast, not a Vedic sacrifice. The herd chief is not named; கோன் தொறுக் காவலன் fits Nandagon, keeper of the king's herds.
event: Nandagon brings four hundred thousand pots of curd, milk and ghee for Civakan's wedding.

reading: On one side carts of white long-grained paddy rice, carts of countless sugar, carts of split pulses and carts of salt from sea-water stood crowded.
On another side, jackfruits heavy as drums on their branches, bananas and mangoes where the bees hum, tubers and vegetables of every kind carried by crowds left no room to stand.
On another side, bunches of tender areca green as emerald, ripe areca hung to ripen, and bundles of tender betel leaf were poured out like a sea with no room left.
nuance: The refrain ஒர்பால் (on one side) in 824 to 827 builds the wedding stores as a panorama, one heap per verse.

reading: On another side, crowds carrying loads of fragrant flowers, champak, tamanakam, tamala, jasmine, cool kazhuneer, kuvalai and lotus, with bees humming over them, made a splendid show.

title: காந்தருவதத்தையார் இலம்பகம் 828-850 (15/15)
theme: The last run of the Gandharvadattai ilampakam: the city throngs the wedding house with gifts, the feast and the fire rite are held, and Civakan, still called the merchant's son, marries the Vidyadhara princess and lives with her in pleasure. A letter from her father Kaluzhavegan recounts the vina contest and the war, offers his arms, and assures him that what destiny brings comes unsought; Civakan gives his bride her father's gifts as the poet turns to the city.
source_issues: 832: the four lines are printed out of order; lines 3-4 begin the sentence and the stray ர at the head of line 1 completes சீப்பவர் at the end of line 4 (read 3-4-1-2). The source also prints the verse with the number 833 (FLAG numbering).
834 line 3 (சொரிந்தனன் வீர னேற்றான்) breaks the second-letter rhyme in ன் shared by lines 1, 2 and 4 and repeats சொரி from line 2; it may be corrupt.
835 line 3, 837 line 1 and 845 line 1 carry repairs of TSCII slips (FLAG repaired); the repaired readings make sense.
838 and 839 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired).

cast.role: the hero, here called கந்துகன் சிறுவன், குருசில் and சாமி; husband of Gandharvadattai
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, won by Civakan at the vina and now his bride
the Vidyadhara king, Gandharvadattai's father, who writes to Civakan (கலுழன், 843)
the usurping minister; here very likely the கொடியான் who started the war over the bride
the Vidyadhara in Kaluzhavegan's service, who reported the contest and battle to him
the great crowd that throngs the wedding house
the people of the land who bring wedding gifts and wish for the hero's merit
those versed in the Veda who tend the wedding fire
the women who praise the couple and attend the bridal chamber (இளையவர், அரிவையர்)
the messenger who brings Kaluzhavegan's palm-leaf letter

reading: The narrator says the great crowd that mingled in the hero's rich house, like a dark sea, ringed it as spokes ring a hub and swarmed it like birds on a tree heavy with fruit.
nuance: அவன் has no named referent in the verse; the house is the hero's household of the wedding. The two similes do different work: the wheel puts the house at the centre of the town, the fruit tree makes the crowd its dependants.
event: Great crowds throng the house for the wedding.

reading: So many gifts came that those listing them wore out their hands and ran out of palm leaf, and the people of the land went away saying 'may the penance this man did come to us too'.
nuance: Line 2 (ஐயென விருப்பமற்று அன்னது ஆதலான்) is hard to construe: it may say the giving went on until desire itself was sated, or that the gifts were too many to want more; the reading of the wish in line 4 does not depend on it. The wish echoes the onlookers of 465 and 467, who ask where his mother did penance.
event: The people bring wedding gifts beyond counting and wish for the hero's merit.

reading: The red water in which the white rice was washed for the feast flowed into pools where horses and elephants sank, blue lilies and lotuses bloomed, bees hummed and herons dived.
nuance: Hyperbole of the feast's scale: the waste water of the kitchen becomes a landscape of tanks.

reading: Clothes, musk for rubbing, strung garlands, earrings and sandal paste dropped by those who gave and those who took lay heaped with jewels, lovelier than a sky in bloom with stars.
event: Gifts change hands so freely that what falls lies heaped on the ground.

reading: The clatter of vessels being washed, the anklet sounds of the women cooking fried dishes, and the tinkle of the gold bells of those sweeping away leftovers rose louder than the roaring salt sea.
nuance: The lines are printed out of order: lines 3 and 4 (கலங்கழும் அரவமும் ... மிச்சில் சீப்பவ) begin the sentence, and the stray ர at the head of line 1 is the end of சீப்பவர், so the verse reads 3-4-1-2.

tamil: மூழிவாய் முல்லை மாலை முருகுலாங் குழலி னாளு
மூழிவாய்த் தீயொ டொக்கு மொளிறுவாட் டடக்கை யானு
மாழிவாய் விரலிற் காம னம்பொடு சிலைகை யேந்தத்
தாழிவாய்க் குவளை வாட்கட் டையலார் பரவச் சார்ந்தார்.
reading: The bride with mullai garlands in her fragrant hair and the hero whose bright sword hand is like the fire of the world's end, like Kama holding bow and arrows in his ringed fingers, came to the wedding place while lily-eyed women praised them.
event: Civakan and Gandharvadattai come to the wedding place, praised by the women.

tamil: இன்னிய முழங்கி யார்ப்ப வீண்டெரி திகழ வேதந்
துன்னினர் பலாசிற் செய்த துடுப்பினெய் சொரிந்து வேட்ப
சொரிந்தனன் வீர னேற்றான் வலம்புரி யதனீர் கொண்டான்
முன்னுபு விளங்கு வெள்ளி முளைத்தெழ முருக னன்னான்.
reading: As instruments thundered and the fire blazed, those versed in the Veda poured ghee from palasa ladles in sacrifice; water was poured and the hero, like Murukan, received it from the right-whorled conch as Venus rose bright.
nuance: The Jain epic narrates a Vedic fire rite (வேதம், பலாசு ladle) without comment. Who pours the water (சொரிந்தனன்) is not named; the bride's guardian in the city is the likeliest. Line 3 breaks the second-letter rhyme (ன்) of the other three lines and repeats சொரி from line 2, so it may be corrupt.
event: The wedding fire is lit, ghee is offered, and Civakan receives the bride-giving water from the conch.

tamil: இட்டவுத் தரிய மின்னு மெரிமணிப் பருமுத் தார
மட்டவிழ் கோதை வெய்ய வருமுலை தாங்க லாற்றா
நெட்டிருங் கூந்த லாட னேர்வளை முன்கை பற்றிக்
கட்டழல் வலங்கொண் டாய்பொற் கட்டிறா னேறி னானே.
reading: Taking by the forearm the long-haired bride, whose shining upper cloth, string of great pearls and honeyed garland sat on breasts almost too heavy to bear, he circled the blazing fire to the right and stepped up onto the fine gold seat.
nuance: கட்டில் in line 4 may be a couch or the raised seat of the rite; the verse does not say which.
event: Civakan takes Gandharvadattai's hand, walks round the fire with her and mounts the gold seat.

tamil: மந்திரத் தரசன் காதன் மாதரம் பாவை தன்னைக்
கந்துகன் சிறுவன் வேட்ட கடிவினை நொடியின் மற்றோ
ரந்தர விசும்பிற் றேவர்க் கதிபதி யாய கோமா
னிந்திரன் றனக்கு மாகா தென்பது நடந்த தன்றே.
reading: The narrator declares that the wedding the merchant's son made in a moment with the Vidyadhara king's beloved daughter was one that even Indra, lord of the gods of the sky, could not have had.
nuance: Civakan is still named as Kantukkatan's son: the king's heir is hidden in the merchant's son, and the Vidyadhara princess is given to the supposed merchant.
event: The wedding is completed.

tamil: அடிமனை பவள மாக வரும்பொனா லலகு சேர்த்தி
முடிமணி யழுத்திச் செய்த மூரிக்காழ் நெற்றி மூழ்கக்
கடிமலர் மாலை நாற்றிக் கம்பல விதானங் கோலி
யிடுபுகை மஞ்சிற் சூழ மணவறை யியற்றி னாரே.
reading: They built the bridal chamber with a coral floor, gold-bound beams, gem-set pillars and great crossbeams, hung it with fragrant garlands, spread a woollen canopy and wrapped it in incense smoke like cloud.
nuance: The builders are not named (இயற்றினார்); the attendants are assumed.
event: The bridal chamber is built and decked.

tamil: ஐந்துமூன் றடுத்த செல்வத் தமளிமூன் றியற்றிப் பூம்பட்
டெந்திர வெழினி வாங்கி யின்முக வாசச் செப்புஞ்
சந்தனச் சாந்தச் செப்புந் தண்மலர் மாலை பெய்த
விந்திர நீலச் செப்பு மிளையவ ரேந்தி னாரே.
reading: They made three couches of manifold richness, drew a silk screen worked by machinery, and the young women held up a box of mouth-perfume, a box of sandal paste and a sapphire box of cool garlands.
nuance: ஐந்துமூன்று அடுத்த is literally 'five and three joined'; it may count layers of the couch or simply mean eightfold wealth.
event: The couches are made and the women bring perfumes and garlands.

tamil: கடைந்துபெய் மணிக்கைச் செம்பொற் காசறு தட்டிற் சூழ்ந்து
மிடைந்துபெய் மணிக்கட் பீலி மின்னுசாந் தாற்றி பொன்னா
ரடைந்துவீ சால வட்ட மரிவைய ரேந்தி யாற்றத்
தடங்கண்கள் குவளை பூப்பத் தையலோ டாடு மன்றே.
reading: The women held gold trays of jewel-handled peacock-feather fans, sandal-dryers and round fans, and fanned the pair, and he sported with the girl as her wide eyes bloomed like lilies.
event: Attended by fanning women, Civakan begins to sport with his bride.

tamil: பஞ்சுசூழ் பரவை யல்குற் பசுங்கதிர்க் கலாபம் வீங்கச்
செந்தளிர்க் கோதை சோரக் கிண்கிணி சிலம்பொ டேங்க
மைந்தருட் காம னன்னான் மகளிருட் டிருவ னாளை
யந்தரத் தமரர் பெற்ற வமிர்தெனப் பருகி னானே.
reading: The Kama among men drank the Lakshmi among women as the gods in the sky drank their nectar, while her girdle swelled, her garland slipped and her bells and anklets cried out.
event: Civakan and Gandharvadattai make love.

tamil: இளமுலை மணிக்கண் சேப்ப வெழுதுவிற் புருவ மேறக்
கிளைநரம் பனைய தீஞ்சொற் பவளவாய் திகழத் தேன்சோர்
வளமலர்க் கோதை தன்னை வாய்விடான் குழையப் புல்லி
யளமர லிலாத வின்பக் கடலகத் தழுந்தி னானே.
reading: Her young breasts reddening and her painted brows lifting, her coral mouth of words sweet as the strings shining, he held her close without parting from her mouth till she melted, and sank into a sea of untroubled joy.
nuance: கிளைநரம்பு (the lute's strings) ties her speech to the vina by which she was won.
event: Civakan embraces Gandharvadattai and is lost in joy.

tamil: இன்னண மொழுகு நாளு ளிளமரக் காவு காண்பான்
பொன்னணி மார்பன் சென்று புகுதலு மொருவன் றோன்றித்
துன்னியோ ரோலை நீட்டித் தொழுதனன் பெயர்ந்து நிற்ப
மன்னிய குருசில் கொண்டு மரபினால் நோக்கு கின்றான்.
reading: As days passed so, the gold-adorned hero went to see a grove of young trees; a man appeared, held out a palm-leaf letter, bowed and stood back, and the lord took it and read it in due form.
event: A messenger brings Civakan a letter in the grove, and he reads it.

reading: The letter opens: Kaluzhan of the thunder-bright spear sends this letter to the lord whose fame fills the world, whose parasol is rich with fortune, wishing him to fare well and wishing him dharma, pleasure and wealth.
nuance: The greeting names three of the four aims (அறன், இன்பம், பொருள்) and not release. Line 2 (பருமைக் குருப் பளிங்கில் புகழ்) is hard to construe; the reading of the fame image is a guess.
event: Kaluzhavegan's letter greets Civakan.

reading: The king writes that when the kings of the vina contended with Dattai and lost, and the master of the arts won the bud-breasted girl by music, the wicked one, his heart burning, declared she belonged to the strongest spear and stirred up war.
nuance: கொடியான் (the wicked one) is unnamed; the usurper Kattiyangaran is the likeliest, but the verse does not say so. The challenge 'she belongs to the strongest spear' sets the law of force against the law of the contest the king laid down.
event: The letter recounts the vina contest and the war started by the wicked one.

reading: He writes that he has also heard how the honey-garlanded lord, on his tall gold chariot, rained arrows from his thundering bow till elephants sank in hot blood, and played with the army of spears.
nuance: விளையாடியது: the king calls the battle play, the word the narrator uses for love in 839.
event: The letter recounts Civakan's victory in the battle.

reading: He writes that beyond this true account Dharan brought, he weighed fully what had been told before, and having known already the prowess of his lord of the leaping-horse chariot, he sent this letter.
nuance: முந்து அவன் மொழிந்த பொருள் may be what was foretold before (the astrologer's word that the destined husband lives in Rajamapuram, 539) or Dharan's earlier report; எந்தை here is a courteous title for the son-in-law rather than 'my father'. Both readings are open.

reading: He writes that, trusting his two arms that bring scorners low and praising the victory that raised his banner over the whole silver mountain, the hero should not slight the protection he offers, but only let him know what he has in mind; nothing else is needed.
nuance: Whose protection (காப்பு) is not to be slighted, and whether the boast of the silver mountain is the king's own or praise of the hero, are not plain. The offer looks forward to the war for Civakan's kingdom.
event: The king offers Civakan his armed support for whatever he intends.

reading: He writes that what is to come will come and none can undo it, and what is to go will go, such being the way of destiny; the sea does not go out to fetch fresh water, and the swelling river never needs to beg the rain.
nuance: பொறி (line 2) is destiny as an engraved mark. The images make fate a source of confidence, not resignation: the sea and the river receive without asking. In a letter that has just offered arms, this means Civakan's fortune will come to him, not that he should sit still.

reading: Bowing joyfully toward his great royal father-in-law's feet and sending off the loyal messenger, the lord gave the garlanded bride the things her king had sent, telling her these were made in the land of joy.
nuance: இன்ப நிலம் (the land of joy) names the Vidyadhara world as a realm of enjoyment.
event: Civakan honours his father-in-law, dismisses the messenger and gives Gandharvadattai her father's gifts.

reading: Painting creepers of saffron and sandal on her young breasts and playing as he went with his garlanded bride, the narrator says, he passed his days, and now the poem will tell what happened in that fair city.
nuance: The closing verse of the ilampakam, announcing (மொழிவாம்) the next part of the story.
event: Civakan lives in pleasure with his bride as the poet turns to events in the city.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 851-875 (1/13)
theme: Spring comes to Rajamapuram, and the whole city, likened to the Jina's walled assembly, pours out with litters, elephants, liquor, perfumes and powders to the water-play in the riverside groves; the women screen off a place in the grove, and Suramanjari and Gunamalai sit together until one holds out her powder, the start of the rivalry that opens the section.
source_issues: 851 line 2 (வடதிசை யயண ழன்னி) is garbled as written; the sense of the sun turning to its northern course (அயனம்) is a reading.
871 line 2 carries a stray dash (நுகர் - வேய்தலிற்) and the line is hard to construe.
852 line 2 has a full stop inside the verse (கொல்கி.); 863 lacks the final stop the other verses have.
860 lines 3-4 and 872 lines 2-4 are obscure as divided.

cast.role: the god of love, lord of the five arrows, who brings spring
the people of Rajamapuram
the women of Rajamapuram at the festival
a merchant's daughter of Rajamapuram, Gunamalai's rival in the powder contest
a merchant's daughter of Rajamapuram, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest

tamil: காசறு துறவின் மிக்க கடவுளர் சிந்தை போல
மாசறு விசும்பின் வெய்யோன் வடதிசை யயண ழன்னி
ஆசற நடக்கு நாளு ளைங்கணைக் கிழவன் வைகிப்
பாசறைப் பரிவு தீர்க்கும் பங்குனிப் பருவஞ் செய்தான்.
reading: When the sun, in a stainless sky like the minds of gods who excel in faultless renunciation, has turned to the northern course, the lord of the five arrows arrives and makes the season of Panguni that ends the longing of the war camp.
nuance: The section of a new marriage opens by likening the clear spring sky to the minds of renunciant gods: the season of desire is measured by the purity of those who have left it. பாசறைப் பரிவு may mean the war camp's hardship or the longing of those parted by it; the reading takes the second.
event: Spring (Panguni) comes, brought by the god of love.

tamil: தோடணி மகளிர் போன்ற துணர்மலர்க் கொம்பர் கொம்பி
னாடவர் போல வண்டு மடைந்தன வளியிற் கொல்கி.
யூடிய மகளிர் போல வொசிந்தன வூட றீர்க்குஞ்
சேடரிற் சென்று புல்லிச் சிறுபுறந் தழீஇய தும்பி.
reading: Flower-laden branches are like women wearing ear ornaments and the bees reach them like men; swaying in the wind the branches bend like sulking women, and the thumbi, like the go-between who ends a sulk, embraces them from behind.
nuance: The whole grove is cast as a scene of lovers' sulking and reconciliation, with a third party, the சேடர், ending the quarrel: the poem stages oodal before the women of the story arrive.

reading: The forest, fragrant like the bodies of brides bathed in perfumed oil and scented with eaglewood, received the spring god as a guest.
nuance: Spring is வேனிலான், a person, and the forest plays the bride's household welcoming a guest (விருந்து).

reading: With the cuckoo calling from the branches and the thumbi and bees playing the yazh over the bathing pools, the spring that longs with burning desire came and settled in the heights.
nuance: Line 4 (தும்பர் நீடுறக் கத்தியல் பொத்ததே) is obscure as divided; the reading of spring taking its place is a guess.

reading: The people of Rajamapuram, a city fragrant with fresh naga flowers and given wholly to pleasure, went for their enjoyment to the flowering groves beside the river.
event: The people of Rajamapuram go out to the riverside groves for the spring festival.

reading: Wanting the festival's water-play, the old city whose drums never sleep rose up and went out, like the ancient walled precinct of the faultless lord of kevala appearing for worship.
nuance: The simile is Jain: கேவலக் கிழவன் is the Jina possessed of kevala, perfect knowledge, and his மூதெயில் the walled assembly where he is worshipped. A pleasure festival is likened to the gathering round the Jina. தொழுவில் is taken as 'for worship'; it could be read otherwise.
event: The whole city sets out for the festival of water-play.

reading: The sandal paste that women with water-vessels rubbed on with their palms and scattered turned the ground to slush, the elephants slipped, and the conches in the flood of water roared.
event: Women scatter sandal paste in the water-play until elephants slip on the ground.

reading: Pearl-hung litters that seem to swim, curtained carts, gold palanquins glowing in the young sun, fine young elephants and herds of she-elephants with garlanded riders go out.
nuance: The line ends in a list with no verb; the poem lets the procession of vehicles stand as a catalogue.
event: The city's conveyances move out toward the grove.

reading: The cries of those calling 'mount, help them mount', the shouts, the ear ornaments that slip and fall, and the ring of anklets on the road combine like a roaring great sea.
The golden-shafted parasols, white umbrellas and peacock-feather fans crowd so that their light wanders as if at a loss, and the great city seems to have left its own circuit.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (என்செய் கோவென் றிரிந்த திழைநிலா) are hard as divided; the moonlight of jewels 'wondering what to do' is a reading.

reading: The waving chowries are like the broken waves of the clear sea, the eaglewood smoke like twisted garlands, and the spreading pollen like a canopy stretched across the sky.
Among the litters and carts, which are like waterfalls in the groves round a hill, the curtained elephants go like ranks of dark clouds.
Baskets of Vanga and Kalinga silk, jewel caskets for the men, poles slung with strong liquor, and garlands at every turn are carried in haste.
event: The people hurry to the grove carrying silks, jewels, liquor and garlands.

reading: Carrying scented butter, sandal paste that bees swarm on, bathing powder, food to eat and baskets of faultless pleasures, the great crowd pours into the gateway of the grove.
nuance: The bathing powder (சுண்ணம்) appears here among the stores; it becomes the object of the quarrel that starts the section's story.
event: The crowd enters the grove with its provisions.

reading: The sounds of song, of tuned music, of dancing, of shouting and of plated elephants trumpeting rise through and reach the high sky.
As though the golden heaven where the gods had played in flower-water had split the sky and dropped down whole as a great city, the sea-flood of people poured in there.
event: The crowd floods into the grove.

reading: Because the grove cooled the heat of the women with flashing sword-like eyes and warm breasts, they reached that grove of fresh flowers with no weariness at all.
nuance: The verse plays on வாட்டம் (withering, weariness) four times.
event: The women arrive at the flowering grove.

reading: On one side are pools crowded with lilies, stretches of water full of honeyed red lilies, and groves bright with fruit and birds.
On another side are red-skinned plantains, branches dripping honey, mangoes and jackfruit with long fleshy pods, all ripe.
Thieving monkeys, young black monkeys, leaping deer, herds of elephants, white swans and peacocks crowd the place and draw in the minds of those who look.
With the women whose eyes are like spears enjoying the grove, the great lotus pools seem as if a mass of lotuses had fallen into the grove.
nuance: The text carries a stray dash in line 2 and the construction is hard; the reading that the women's faces among the trees are like lotuses fallen there is a guess.

reading: The flowering grove so described, oozing honey and fragrant, with white sand under its shade, seemed as if it had gone down into a clear pond.
nuance: The image of the grove 'entering a clear pool' is obscure as divided; the reading is tentative.

reading: In the grove they ringed a space with curtain screens and, entering it like the women of the gods with their mynahs and parrots chattering, sat down in their fine silks.
event: The women screen off a space in the grove and settle there.

reading: There Suramanjari, like a coral creeper of the sea, with jasmine in her hair, sat free of care with Gunamalai of the kovvai-red lips, and said this.
nuance: The two sit together எவ்வம் தீர்ந்து, without grief, just before their powders set them against each other.
event: Suramanjari, seated with Gunamalai in the grove, begins to speak.

reading: She of the silk-clad waist scented with incense smoke, of the large garlanded spear-like eyes and the fair forehead bearing its mark, held out her bright powder that bears desire.
nuance: 874 ends with இது கூறினாள், but this verse describes, not speaks; the woman is named only by epithets. The reading takes her as Suramanjari, the one who has just begun to speak, but she may be Gunamalai or a maid.
event: One of the two women holds out her scented powder.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 876-900 (2/13)
theme: Suramanjari and Gunamalai quarrel over their scented powders and wager on them; their maids take the powders to Civakan, whose verdict for Gunamalai is challenged by Suramanjari's maid, until he proves it by letting the grove's bees choose; the defeated Suramanjari vows to wait until he comes humbled to her feet and withdraws into the maidens' mansion.
source_issues: Verse 883 line 3: வவ்வியி கண்ணியர் is probably for வவ்விய கண்ணியர் (women whose eyes have seized the sword).
Verse 885 line 2: முற்று நாயியுங் is hard to construe as printed; perhaps முற்றும் நாய்கனும் (all, and the merchant).
Verse 889 line 2 (வள்ள னீங்கப் பெறாய் வளைத்தேன்) and verse 890 line 4 (மண்ண னீக்கின்) are obscure as divided and may be corrupt.
Verse 899 line 4: நோற்ப னோற்றனை நீ is hard to divide; the sense of a vow is clear but the clause addressed to the maid is not.

cast.role: a merchant's daughter who loses the scented-powder contest and vows seclusion
a merchant's daughter, called Malai and Vannamalai, whose powder wins
the hero, who judges the powders
the women of the city, here the rivals and their circle who set the wager
Suramanjari's maid, who carries her powder and disputes the verdict
Gunamalai's maid, who carries her powder
the young men of the city, who send the maids on to Civakan
Civakan's companions
the four kinds of bee of the grove whom Civakan calls as witnesses
the maidens of the city who escort Suramanjari to the maidens' mansion
Suramanjari's mother

reading: Coming up to Gunamalai, Suramanjari laughs at her and asks whether this, carried under the name of powder, is what she thought would torment the waist of the one it adorns.
nuance: The speaker is named only by her loosened hair (சோர்குழல்); the scorn is taken as Suramanjari's because Malai, the one laughed at, is Gunamalai, and lines 2 to 3 are hard to construe.
event: Suramanjari mocks Gunamalai's scented powder.

reading: Seething, Gunamalai answers that if anything on earth, short of the golden heavens, matches her powder, her golden-statue-like rival should say so.
event: Gunamalai retorts that no powder on earth equals hers.

reading: The women bet that whoever loses at the powder gives up the water-play and pays the winner countless crores of gold, and lose all judgement over the fragrant stuff.
nuance: The closing phrase கண்ணற்றார் (they lost sight, lost discernment) is the narrator's verdict on the quarrel before it is judged: the contest is already a loss of measure on both sides.
event: The rival women fix the stakes: the loser forfeits the bathing festival and pays the winner gold.

reading: The spear-eyed women with jasmine-scented hair gather and, holding that the winning of this famous powder contest is a wager, send the powders out to be judged.
event: The women send the two powders out for a judgement that will settle the wager.

reading: Two slender maids, carrying golden trays covered with fine cloth, cross the long way with the powders.
event: The two maids carry the covered powders through the city.

reading: The maids show the powders, with jasmine garlands, to the young men of the city, who say that if they want the powders' worth known they must go to Civakan of the warlike, generous hand.
nuance: The townsmen defer to one judge rather than vote, which the maid will later turn against him (885) by citing what the whole city praised.
event: The young men decline to judge and send the maids to Civakan.

reading: Civakan sits ringed by young men whose learning is an ocean of books, like the cool moon among the stars.
The maids, whose eyes outdo the good sword with which Civakan has resolved to cut Kattiyangaran's shoulders, praise his feet and put their request.
nuance: The enmity with the usurper is slipped into a simile for the maids' eyes: in the middle of a contest of scents the poet reminds the reader that Civakan's sword already has a purpose.
event: The maids bow to Civakan and ask for his judgement.

reading: Asked to examine the powders and say which are good, Civakan looks and declares that these, from black-haired Vannamalai's side, are the good ones.
nuance: வண்ண மாலையி னீர் is taken as 'you of Vannamalai', a name for Gunamalai as in 876; the first two lines are the maids' request and the last two his verdict.
event: Civakan judges Gunamalai's powder the better at sight.

reading: Suramanjari's maid objects that every person of this great city, the merchant included, has seen these powders and praised them as fine, and asks whether the young lord learned his judgement along with them.
nuance: The appeal is to acclaim against judgement; the sarcastic last line also hints that a judge who sides with the crowd has learned nothing of his own. Whose powder 'these' are is inferred from the dispute that follows.
event: Suramanjari's maid challenges the verdict by appeal to the city's praise.

reading: With joined hands the women say they came to him because he knows: let him, ocean of learning, refine his scholarship, weigh closely and speak without falsehood.
event: The maids ask Civakan to judge again, closely and truly.

reading: Civakan answers that these powders are good, and if asked why the others fall a little short: they are not the fine flower-powder of the hot season but were made in the cold.
nuance: The verdict is grounded in the making, not in the smell at hand: quality is traced to the season, which the maid at once turns against him.
event: Civakan explains the lesser powder was made in the cold season.

reading: The maid with long spear-like eyes replies that when moist the bad becomes good and when wholly dried the good becomes bad, and asks whether that is not the way of the world.
nuance: She does not deny his season argument but generalises it until it cuts both ways, so that his reason can no longer settle which powder wins; this is why the dispute moves from argument to a test (889 to 894).
event: Suramanjari's maid answers that seasons change quality both ways.

reading: Civakan says she will not be let off until he has convinced her heart, and that if he brings a witness she must be settled in her mind.
nuance: வள்ள னீங்கப் பெறாய் வளைத்தேன் is hard to construe; the reading follows கரி (witness) and தெளிகென in lines 3 to 4.
event: Civakan offers to prove his verdict by a witness.

reading: The maid answers that neither men nor gods go beyond his word, and that if, with sweet-voiced birds and the like as witnesses, he removes the doubt, she will accept it.
nuance: மண்ண னீக்கின் is obscure; the sense of a condition accepted in advance is clear from ஒட்டுவல் யான் (I agree).
event: The maid agrees beforehand to abide by a witness.

reading: Civakan says four dwellers of the grove will go as witnesses, and the maid, joining her hands, answers that it shall be as her lord has said.
event: Civakan names the grove's four kinds of bee as witnesses and the maid accepts.

reading: Civakan calls on the bees, the honey-bees and the swarming insects that dart everywhere like the eyes and hearts of fine women and gorge on honey.
nuance: The four witnesses of 891 are named by four words for bee (சுரும்பு, வண்டு, தேன், ஞிமிறு), and they are likened to women's restless eyes and hearts, so the jury is itself a figure of desire.
event: Civakan summons the four kinds of bees.

reading: He tells them that the powder of Surama, the peahen of the grove, and that of Malai, the young peahen, are both very good, and bids them take the better as their delight and feed.
nuance: He praises both before the test, so that the outcome is left to the witnesses and not to his earlier verdict.
event: Civakan sets the two powders before the bees as judges.

reading: The lord of the bow throws the powders into the sky; Suramanjari's falls to the ground, and Malai's the bees seize and eat with their honey.
nuance: The proof needs no judge's word: the powder that the bees will not touch falls of its own weight, which answers the maid's argument of 888 without arguing.
event: Thrown in the air, Suramanjari's powder falls while the bees take Gunamalai's.

reading: He tells the coral-lipped maids, whose smiles are pearls set in coral, to look at whether this was fair and carry it so to their ladies.
nuance: ஒத்ததோ (was it equal, was it fitting) may ask whether the result matched his verdict or simply whether the test was fair.
event: Civakan sends the maids to report the result to their mistresses.

reading: A maid answers in praise of the spear-bearer, whose spear is like the eyes of her lady with brows arched as if painted in clear blue.
nuance: The verse does not say which maid speaks; praise linked to 'our lady's eyes' fits the winner's maid.
event: Gunamalai's maid praises Civakan.

tamil: சோலையஞ் சுரும்பிற் சுண்ணந் தேற்றிய தோன்ற றன்னை
வேலையம் படுத்த கண்ணார் தொழுதனர் விரைந்து போகி
மாலைக்கு வென்றி கூற மழையிடிப் புண்டோர் நாக
மாலையத் தழுங்கி யாங்கு மஞ்சரி யவல முற்றாள்.
reading: The spear-eyed maids bow to the prince who proved the powder by the bees and hurry off; they tell Malai of her victory, and Manjari grieves like a snake struck by thunder in its hole.
nuance: The thunder-struck snake is the image the patikam (27) uses for Civakan's dread of kingship before he renounces; here it marks the start of Suramanjari's withdrawal.
event: The maids report the result; Gunamalai hears of her victory and Suramanjari is stricken.

reading: Falling at her feet, a maid begs Suramanjari, who looks like a lotus crushed by the moon's rays, to speak to her quickly, there and then.
event: Suramanjari's maid falls at her feet and begs her to speak.

reading: Suramanjari answers her not a word, but says that since the generous one declared the powder she offered unacceptable, she will keep a vow until he comes defeated and worships her anklet-feet, and goes.
nuance: The vow makes the man who shamed her its condition of release: what looks like a refusal of men is a waiting for one man's surrender. நோற்பன் நோற்றனை நீ is hard to divide; the reading takes நோற்பன் as her vow.
event: Suramanjari vows to wait under a vow until Civakan comes humbled to worship her feet.

reading: Ringed by the maidens of the never-taken city, the maiden with eyes like new blue lilies reaches the maidens' mansion, and the maidens tell her mother what has befallen her.
nuance: கன்னி is rung eight times: the unconquered city, the maidens' house, the fresh flower, the girl herself and her companions, so that her chosen seclusion is set inside every sense of the word.
event: Suramanjari withdraws into the maidens' mansion and the girls tell her mother.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 901-925 (3/13)
theme: Suramanjari's mother tells her father of the girl's vow to see or hear of no man; the doting father buys a royal order with a priceless necklace so that men are barred and even statues made female, while Suramanjari vows to keep her nirai for Civakan alone. Gunamalai grieves that a game has cost her a friend and worships the Jina, the town gives to suppliants and the temple at the festival, and the water-play is shown scene by scene in a run of 'behold' verses as Civakan goes to watch.
source_issues: Verses 906, 917, 918, 919, 920 and 924 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the repair (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 907 line 3 prints ஏவ வாள்வழக் கற்ற, read here as ஏவ ஆள் வழக்கு அற்றது; division uncertain.
Verse 911 (மாசை மாக்கடல், மீசை நீள்விசும்பு) and verse 913 lines 3-4 (தவாவினை யடைகரை தயங்கு சிந்தை நீ ரவாவெனு முடை கடல்) are hard to divide and construe.
Verse 922 line 3 (நடலைந் நடுவின்) and verse 924 line 2 (ஓம்பு தாய்நீர் குடைய) are obscure as printed.
Verse 909 line 2 begins டுன்பக், a sandhi split carried over from விளையாட்டினுள் + துன்பக்.

cast.role: a merchant's daughter who loses the scented-powder contest and shuns men
Suramanjari's mother, who reports her vow to the father
Suramanjari's father, a rich merchant who buys a royal order to keep men from her
a merchant's daughter, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest, whom Civakan saves and marries
the hero, whose verdict in the powder contest shamed Suramanjari
Civakan's companions
the ruler of the city (the usurping minister), here only மன்னன் / மன்னவன்
the people of the city at the festival
the women of the city at the water-play
the companions of a woman at the water-play
the young men of the city at the water-play

reading: Thinking that grudges women take up do not leave them, even when bonds begun by the eyes would heal, the bright-eyed girl's mother speaks gently to her father.
nuance: The maxim is the mother's own judgment of her daughter (closed by என்று), not the narrator's; it prepares the father to take the vow seriously rather than as a sulk.
event: Suramanjari's mother goes to tell her husband what has happened to their daughter.

reading: The mother tells him that their daughter's resolve is like trying to bar the moon from the sky: she will not eat if she so much as sees or hears of men.
nuance: The vow is one of fasting tied to the senses (கண்ணின் ... காணினுங் கேட்பினும்): even hearing of a man would break it.
event: The mother reports Suramanjari's vow to refuse food if she sees or hears of men.

reading: She says that today at the water-play, over the difference that showed in the powders, the girl cried that she was undone, that it was death to her life, and stood shedding tears like pearls from her blue eyes.
nuance: இன்றேன் is read as 'I am no more'; the line division at 2-3 (வேறுபா / டின்றே னாவிக்கு) makes the exact construction uncertain.
event: The mother describes Suramanjari weeping after the powder contest at the water festival.

tamil: பட்டதென் னங்கைக் கென்னப் பாசிழைப் பசும்பொ னல்குன்
மட்டவிழ் கோதை சுண்ண மாலையோ டிகலித் தோற்றாள்
கட்டவிழ் கண்ணி நம்பி சீவகன் றிறத்திற் காய்ந்தா
ளட்டுந்தே னலங்கன் மார்ப வதுபட்ட தறிமோ வென்றாள்.
reading: Asked what has befallen his darling, she answers that the girl strove with Gunamalai over the powder and lost, and burns with anger at Civakan's verdict, and asks whether he knew it.
nuance: Line 1 is the father's question (பட்டதென் னங்கைக் கென்ன) folded into the mother's speech; the grievance is aimed at Civakan's judgment, not at Gunamalai alone.
event: The father asks what is wrong and the mother tells him of the lost contest and Suramanjari's anger at Civakan.

tamil: பள்ளிகொள் களிறு போலப் பரிவுவிட் டுயிர்த்தென் பாவை
யுள்ளிய பொருண்மற் றஃத லோபெரி துவப்பக் கேட்டேன்
வள்ளிதழ்க் கோதை மற்று நகரொடுங் கடியு மேனும்
வெள்ளநீ ணிதியி னின்னே வேண்டிய விளைப்ப லென்றான்.
reading: Sighing like a resting elephant, the father says he gladly hears what his girl has set her mind on, and that even if she would shut men out of the whole city he will bring it about with his flood of wealth.
event: The father agrees to carry out his daughter's wish with his wealth.

tamil: இன்னதோர் காலத் தின்னா னொருமக ளின்ன தொன்றிற்
கின்னதோ ரிடத்தி னெல்லை யாட்கடிந் தொழுகி னாள்போ
லின்னதோர் நகரி லென்றாங் கென்பெயர் நிற்க வேண்டு
மின்னதோ ராரந் தம்மோ வென்றுகொண் டேகி னானே.
reading: He wants his name to stand in story as the man whose daughter, at such a time and in such a city, kept men away to such a bound for such a cause, and he takes up a priceless necklace and goes.
nuance: The run of இன்னதோர் ('such a') mimics the shape of a told tale: the father wants the vow to become a story with his name in it, so his indulgence is also a bid for fame.
event: The father takes a priceless necklace and sets out, wishing to be remembered for his daughter's vow.

tamil: வையக மூன்றும் விற்கு மாமணி யார மேந்திச்
செய்கழன் மன்னற் குய்த்துத் தன்குறை செப்ப லோடு
மையென மன்ன னேவ வாள்வழக் கற்ற தென்ப
கைபுனை பாவை யெல்லாங் கதிர்முலை யாக்கி னானே.
reading: He gives the king a jewelled necklace worth the three worlds and states his request; the king orders it, men's coming and going in that place ceases, and he has every carved figure made into a woman with breasts.
nuance: வாள்வழக் கற்ற is read as ஆள் வழக்கு அற்றது, the traffic of men ending; the king is the ruler of the city in the story (Kattiyangaran), not named here. A private grief is turned into public law by a gift to the throne.
event: The father buys a royal order with a necklace; men are barred and even the carved figures are made female.

reading: Suramanjari resolves with a single mind that even if time runs out, if she is to be joined to Civakan's gold-bright chest let it be so, but otherwise no one shall break her self-containment, and she withdraws.
nuance: The vow against all men is not a refusal of love: the one man whose verdict shamed her is the one exception, so the vow is also a claim on him.
event: Suramanjari makes an exception of Civakan in her vow and shuts herself away.

reading: Thinking how a game meant to give joy had turned into a cause of sorrow that drove her friend away, Gunamalai wept in anguish out of love.
nuance: ஈர்மலர் மாலை is taken as Gunamalai (called மாலை in 904); துறப்பித்திடும் may mean that the game makes one give up a friend or that it makes Suramanjari renounce men, and the subject of தன் அன்பினால் is not explicit.
event: Gunamalai weeps over her friend's estrangement.

reading: Having bathed in the cool sweet water, she offers a thousand golden lotuses at the feet of the one under the pindi tree and bows.
nuance: பிண்டியினான், the one of the asoka (pindi) tree, is a Jain name for the Jina; the worshipper is taken to be Gunamalai continuing from 909, though the verse names no one.
event: Gunamalai, after bathing, worships the Jina with a thousand golden lotuses.

reading: When the king of the wide sea-girt land bathed and proclaimed that the needy and the Brahmins should take, the shout rose to the sky and the people carried off bright treasure.
nuance: மாசை (gold) and மீசை (above) are rare; the reading of the king's bath as the occasion of the gift is tentative.
event: At the festival bathing the king proclaims a free gift to the needy and Brahmins, and the people take the wealth.

reading: For the long temple-city of the peerless one who withered the god with the makara banner, walled in gold like fire-red peaks, the city gave eight crores.
nuance: The Jina is named only by his victory over Kama (மகர வெல்கொடி மைந்தனை வாட்டிய), a fitting epithet in a chapter about a vow against desire.
event: The city gives eight crores of gold to the Jina's temple.

reading: Those who from the new-moon day poured out their wealth to suppliants, gold piled to the lap and offered with joined hands, dammed the sea called craving, whose water is the wavering mind and whose shore is unfailing deed.
nuance: The metaphor's parts (தவாவினை, சிந்தை நீர், அவா கடல்) are clear but how they attach is hard to fix: தவாவினை may be the bank that holds the sea or the deed that gives way to it.
event: The townspeople give their wealth to suppliants through the festival.

reading: The peerless women with tinkling anklets on small feet and the men with sounding warrior anklets raise a roar in the golden water like a battlefield.
nuance: The water-play is figured as battle (போரரவக் களம்), as in the Paripadal's river festivals.
event: Men and women of the town plunge into the water-play.

reading: The water-play stands adorned as women like lightning playing in the clouds, with banded breasts, sport with garlanded young men in the swelling water.
Civakan, with the strength of a rutting tusker, goes to watch the women in flower-wreaths play, their young breasts pressing as bees drink.
event: Civakan goes to watch the women's water-play.

tamil: ஒன்றே யுயிரை யுடையீ ரொருவிப் போமி னிவள்க
ணன்றே கூற்ற மாகி யருளா தாவி போழ்வ
தென்றே கலையுஞ் சிலம்பு மிரங்க வினவண் டர்ப்பப்
பொன்றோய் கொடியி னடந்து புனல்சேர் பவளைக் காண்மின்.
reading: You who have only one life, keep away: look at her walking like a gold-touched creeper to the water, her girdle and anklets crying and bees humming that she has become Death itself, splitting lives without mercy.
nuance: No speech tag names the voice of the காண்மின் series (917-925); it is read here as Civakan, who has just gone to watch (916), pointing the scenes out to his companions, but it could be the poet addressing his hearers.
event: A young woman walks down to the water.

tamil: அழல்செய் தடத்துண் மலர்ந்த வலங்கன் மாலை யதனை
நிழல்செய் நீர்கொண் டீர்ப்ப நெடுங்கண் ணினையி னோக்கிக்
குழையும் பூணு நாணுங் கொழுந னுவப்ப வணிகென்
றிழைகொள் புனலுக் கீயு மிளையோ ணிலைமை காண்மின்.
reading: Look at the young woman who, seeing a garland of lotuses from the fiery pool drawn off by the water, gives her earrings, ornaments and string to the stream, telling it to wear them so its husband may rejoice.
nuance: She treats the stream as a bride whose husband must be pleased, the river's conventional marriage to the sea; same voice as 917.
event: A girl gives her jewels to the stream that took her garland.

tamil: கோல நெடுங்கண் மகளிர் கூந்தல் பரப்பி யிருப்பப்
பீலி மஞ்ஞை நோக்கிப் பேடை மயிலென் றெண்ணி
யாலிச் சென்று புல்லி யன்மை கண்டு நாணிச்
சோலை நோக்கி நடக்குந் தோகை வண்ணங் காண்மின்.
reading: Look at the peacock that took a woman's spread hair for a peahen, ran to embrace her, saw its mistake, and walks off ashamed to the grove.
nuance: Same voice as 917.
event: A peacock mistakes a woman's hair for a peahen and slinks away.

tamil: மின்னொப் புடைய பைம்பூ ணீருள் வீழக் காணா
ளன்னப் பெடையே தொழுதே னன்னை கொடியள் கண்டா
யென்னை யடிமை வேண்டி னாடித் தாவென் றிறைஞ்சிப்
பொன்னங் கொம்பி னின்றாள் பொலிவின் வண்ணங் காண்மின்.
reading: Look at the grace of the girl whose bright jewel fell unseen into the water: she begs the swan-hen, saying she worships it, that her mother is harsh, and that it should find the jewel and keep her as its servant.
nuance: The inset prayer (அன்னப் பெடையே தொழுதேன்) is a small comic vow: she offers herself as slave for the return of a jewel, set beside Suramanjari's grave vow earlier in the chapter. Same voice as 917.
event: A girl who has lost her jewel in the water pleads with a swan to find it.

tamil: தூமங் கமழுங் கோதை தொடுத்த துயரி முலையாத்
தேமென் கீதம் பாலாச் சுரந்து திறத்தி னூட்டிக்
காமக் குழவி வளர்ப்பக் கணவன் புனலு ணீங்கிப்
பூமென் பொழிலுக் கிவர்வான் புகற்சி காண்மி னினிதே.
reading: Look at the eagerness of the husband who leaves the water for the flowering grove while his wife, nursing the child of love with sweet songs as milk from her breasts, rears it.
nuance: காமக் குழவி, love as an infant fed on song, is the verse's own image; same voice as 917.
event: A husband leaves the water for the grove, drawn by his wife's songs.

tamil: கடலம் பவளம் மணையிற் கனபொற் கயிற்றிற் காய்பொன்
மடலங் கமுகி னூசன் மடந்தை யாட நுடங்கி
நடலைந் நடுவின் மகளிர் நூக்கப் பரிந்த காசு
reading: Look how, as a girl swings on a coral seat hung by gold ropes from areca stems and the women in the middle push her, the broken beads of her girdle flash and fall like lightning from the sky.
nuance: Same voice as 917; நடலைந் நடுவின் is obscure.
event: A girl swings and her girdle beads scatter.

tamil: நான நீரிற் கலந்து நலங்கொள் பூம்பட் டொளிப்ப
மேனி தோன்ற விளங்கி வெளிப்பட் டதற்கு நாணி
மான மகளிர் போல மணிமே கலைகள் பேசாத்
தானந் தழுவிக் கிடப்பச் செல்வோ டன்மை காண்மின்.
reading: Look at the girl walking on, her fine silk soaked with scented water so that her body shows through, ashamed of being exposed, while her jewelled girdle clings to its place and makes no sound, like proud women keeping silent.
nuance: Same voice as 917.
event: A girl in wet silk walks away in shame.

tamil: தீம்பாற் பசியி னிருந்த செவ்வாய்ச் சிறுபைங் கிளிதன்
ஓம்பு தாய்நீர் குடைய வொழிக்கும் வண்ண நாடிப்
பாம்பால் என்ன வெருவிப் பைம்பொற் றோடு கழலக்
காம்பேர் தோளி நடுங்கிக் கரைசேர் பவளைக் காண்மின்.
reading: Look at the bamboo-shouldered girl who, as the little parrot hungry for milk searched how its mother might be kept from the water, took fright thinking it a snake, lost her gold ear-ring and trembled her way to the bank.
nuance: Line 2 (ஓம்பு தாய்நீர் குடைய வொழிக்கும் வண்ண நாடி) is hard to construe; what frightened her is not clear. Same voice as 917.
event: A girl takes fright at something she thinks a snake and makes for the bank.

tamil: துணையி றோகை மஞ்ஞை யீயற் கிவரும் வகைபோன்
யிணையி றோழி மார்க ளிறுமா லிடையென் றிரங்க
வணியார் கோதை பூம்பந் தாடு மவளைக் காண்மின்.
reading: Look at her playing with the flower-ball, her bangled forearms thrown left and right like a lone peacock leaping at flying ants, while her friends grieve that her waist will break.
nuance: Same voice as 917.
event: A girl plays ball while her friends fear for her waist.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 926-949 (4/13)
theme: At the bathing festival the poet shows a run of pleasure sights (a mirror, dice, feasting, the ship of desire, swans and a doe fooled by jewels) and then the one Civakan saw: Brahmins beat a dog to death for touching their rice, a drunkard claims the dog and threatens them, Civakan drives him off, then weeps over the dying dog and whispers the five padas into its ear, and the dog is reborn at once as a god in a golden city.
source_issues: Verses 926-930 and 932 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 934 line 3 prints யெனக்கனக் றோடினர், probably for எனக் கனன்று ஓடினர் (ran in a rage); a letter seems lost or misread.
Verse 945 line 4 opens குதற்செய்கை, which does not construe clearly; the line may be corrupt.
Verse 936 ends with a comma and its sentence runs on into 937; lines 1-2 embed an unattributed speech.

cast.role: the hero, who saves the Brahmins and teaches the dying dog the five padas
the dog beaten to death by the Brahmins for touching their rice, reborn a god
the Brahmins (நான்மறை வல்லவர்) whose rice the dog seized and who beat it
the drunkard who claims the dog and threatens the Brahmins
the two maidens who carry the drunkard's toddy and serve it to him
Civakan's companions
the god the dog becomes, who later carries Civakan from prison (named in the epic's later telling, not here)
the women of the heavenly city who gather as the new god's retinue

tamil: திருவின் சாய லொருத்தி சேர்ந்த கோலங் காண்பான்
குருதித் துகிலி னுறையைக் கொழும்பொன் விரலி னீக்கி
அரவ முற்றும் விழுங்கி யுமிழும் பொழுதின் மதிபோன்
றுருவத் தெண்கண் ணாடி காண்மின் தோன்றும் வகையே.
reading: See how a woman graceful as Tiru draws the red cloth sheath off a clear mirror with her gold-ringed fingers to look at her adornment, the mirror showing like the moon spat out by the snake that swallowed it.
nuance: The verse is one of a run (926-932) of festival sights, each closing with காண்மின் ('see'), addressed to listeners; no character in the story is named as the one showing them. The eclipse image makes uncovering a mirror a small release of the moon from Rahu.

tamil: பலகை செம்பொன் னாகப் பளிங்கு நாயாப் பரப்பி
யலவ னாடும் வகைபோ லரும்பொன் கவறங் குருளக்
குலவும் பவழ வுழக்கிற் கோதை புரளப் பாடி
யிலவம் போதேர் செவ்வா யிளையோர் பொருவார்க் காண்மின்.
reading: See the young women with lips like silk-cotton buds playing dice on a gold board with crystal pieces, the gold dice rolling like crabs at play and their garlands slipping as they sing over coral cups.

tamil: தீம்பா லடிசி லமிர்தஞ் செம்பொன் வண்ணப் புழுக்க
லாம்பா லக்கா ரடலை யண்பன் னீரூ றமிர்தம்
தாம்பா லவரை நாடித் தந்தூட் டயர்வார் சொரிய
வோம்பா நறுநெய் வெள்ள மொழுகும் வண்ணங் காண்மின்.
reading: See how the servers seek out guests and press on them sweet milk rice, golden-coloured cooked grain, sugared dishes and rosewater nectar, until fragrant ghee runs like an unchecked flood.

tamil: அள்ளற் சேற்று ளலவ னடைந்தாங் கனைய மெய்யின்
கள்செய் கடலு ளிளமைக் கூம்பின் கடிசெய் மாலைத்
துள்ளு தூமக் கயிற்றிற் பாய்செய் துயரி நிதிய
முள்ளு காற்றா யுழலும் காமக் கலனும் காண்மின்.
reading: See too the ship of desire that wanders in the wind of the mind on a sea of toddy, with youth for its mast, garland and smoke for its ropes and sorrow for its sail, its bodies stuck like a crab in deep mud.
nuance: The allegory is dense and some of its parts (the crab in mud, துயரி நிதியம், the 'wind that is in the mind') can be construed more than one way; the reading of the ship as the pleasure-seekers' revel is my best construction. Among the festival sights this is the one that judges: it sets desire as a drifting ship, just before the scene where the Brahmins and the drunkard show the festival's darker side.

tamil: தாய்தன் கையின் மெல்லத் தண்ணென் குறங்கி னெறிய
வாய்பொன் னமளித் துஞ்சும் மணியார் குழவி போலத்
தோயுந் திரைக ளலைப்பத் தோடார் கமலப் பள்ளி
மேய வகையிற் றுஞ்சும் வெள்ளை அன்னங் காண்மின்.
reading: See the white swans sleeping on beds of petalled lotus as the lapping waves rock them, like a jewelled baby asleep on a gold cot while its mother pats its cool thighs.

tamil: நீலத் துகிலிற் கிடந்த நிழலார் தழலம் மணிகள்
கோலச் சுடர்விட் டுமிழக் குமரி யன்னங் குறுகிச்
சால நெருங்கிப் பூத்த தடந்தா மரைப்பூ வென்ன
வாலிச் சுடர்கள் கௌவி யழுங்கும் வண்ணங் காண்மின்.
reading: See how young swans, taking the flame-red gems lying shadowed on blue cloth for a thick bloom of lotuses, come close, peck at the bright rays and are dismayed.

tamil: வடிக்கண் மகளிர் வைத்த மரக தந்நன் மணிக
ளொடிக்கச் சுடர்விட் டுமிழ வுழையம் பிணையொன் றணுகிக்
கொடிப்புல் லென்று கறிப்பா னாவிற் குலவி வளைப்பத்
தொடிக்கட் பூவை நோக்கி நகுமா றெளிதோ காண்மின்.
reading: See how a doe, coming on the fine emeralds the women have set out shining, takes them for creeper-grass and curls its tongue to graze, and how easily the myna laughs to see it.
nuance: 931 and 932 make the same joke twice: creatures fooled by the city's jewels into taking them for nature.

tamil: இவையின் னனவும் பிறவு மெரிபொன் னார மார்பன்
கவிஞர் மதியி னகன்று காட்சிக் கினிய விழவின்
சுவையின் மிகுதி யுடைய சோர்வில் பொருளொன் றதுதா
னவையி னகல நோக்கி நயந்த வண்ண மொழிவாம்.
reading: Leaving these and other sights to the poets' fancy, the narrator says he will now tell one thing of the festival, of surpassing savour, that the hero with the gold chain looked on closely and with feeling.
nuance: The poet turns from the catalogue to the episode with மொழிவாம் ('we shall tell'); the 'thing of surpassing savour' at a festival of pleasures is the dying dog, an ironic choice of word.

reading: When a dog came and seized the heap of rice cooked for the Brahmins, those who saw it ran at it shouting that it would not escape now, men whose nature was like the fire that shone in their own minds.
nuance: தீயன நீரார் gives men who keep the sacred fire a mind of fire: the Vedic fire becomes their anger. Line 3 (யெனக்கனக் றோடினர்) looks damaged; 'ran in a rage' is the likely sense.
event: A dog snatches the rice cooked for the Brahmins, who chase it in anger.

reading: Holding stones and hard clubs they ran swifter than the wind, hemmed it in and set about killing it: it had fallen into the net of strong karma, which kills more surely than killing Death.
nuance: The narrator gives two causes at once: the men's fury, told in lines 1-3, and the dog's own வல்வினை in line 4. Karma does not excuse the men; the next verses call them brutes (மூர்க்கர்).
event: The Brahmins surround the dog with stones and clubs to beat it to death.

reading: Not heeding even the cry that the dog was someone's own, the brutes beat it at their feet, and it leapt into the long pond at the cool bathing steps and began to swim.
nuance: Lines 1-2 embed a speech (வேள்வியில் உண்டி விலக்கிய நீவிர்கள் ... ஆள் எனக்கு) whose speaker is not named: it may be a bystander's or the owner's protest, addressed to the men 'who keep food from the sacrifice', that the dog belongs to someone. The verse ends in a comma and runs on into 937.
event: Beaten, the dog leaps into the pond and swims.

reading: Then, with two maidens carrying toddy-pots of no clay but white as the moon, a drunken man appeared, so fearsome in his uncleanness that everyone trembled.
event: A drunkard appears with two maidens carrying pots of toddy.

reading: As the creeper-like women pressed silver cups of pure liquor to the mouth of the man with the wounding spear, they looked like two ray-spitting moons in a cave.
event: The maidens hold cups of liquor to the drunkard's mouth.

reading: Drinking flower-toddy that burns like fire until it rises in him, with rolling eyes, a slipping garland, anklets and a dark cloth belt, he spoke these words of abuse in slurred speech.
event: Drunk, the man turns on the Brahmins with abuse.

reading: 'You beat my dog and killed it, you drove its life out fast; if you want to fight, bear the strength of my big hands, or else I will smash my toddy-pot on you', he said.
nuance: The only voice raised for the dog's life is the drunkard's, and he speaks of it as property (என் நாய்). The poem gives the defence of the creature to the man it calls without merit, and the cruelty to the keepers of the Veda.
event: The drunkard claims the dog as his and threatens the Brahmins.

reading: Because that man with no good deed to his name was harrying the men learned in the four Vedas, Civakan, master of the bright spear, went quickly, drove off the trouble and ended their distress.
nuance: Civakan first protects the Brahmins, not the dog: the hero keeps the social order before he turns to the creature they have beaten. நல்வினை ஒன்றும் இலாதவன் (line 1) will return in 945 as நற்செய்கை ஒன்றும் இல்லார், said of the dog.
event: Civakan steps in and rescues the Brahmins from the drunkard.

reading: As the Brahmins went back, Civakan, bull-like, arriving with his gathered friends, saw the fine-toothed dog lying with no strength left, and wept.
event: Civakan finds the beaten dog dying and weeps.

reading: He tells the dog that, leaving its dog's body here, it will gain a god's body shining like the burning disc of the sun, if it will consent and think on the mantra of the path it goes to.
nuance: The school is assigned from 945-946, where the mantra is the ஐம்பதம் the Lord taught; this verse names it only செல்கதி மந்திரம். The promise is a better birth, not release.
event: Civakan speaks to the dying dog and urges it to fix its mind on the mantra.

reading: At this the dog pricked up its ears, looked at the noble one with tears running from both eyes, wagged its tail in joy within, and the mountain-like hero resolved to tell it the padas.
nuance: The poem takes care to show the dog's consent (தன்செவி ஓர்த்து, வால்குழைத்து): Civakan asked it to agree (நீ உடம்பட்டு, 943), and the mantra is given only once it does.
event: The dog shows it has heard, and Civakan resolves to teach it the padas.

tamil: நற்செய்கை யொன்று மில்லார் நாளுலக் கின்ற போழ்தின்
முற்செய்த வினையி னீங்கி நல்வினை விளைக்கும் வித்து
மற்செய்து வீங்கு தோளான் மந்திர மைந்து மாதோ
குதற்செய்கை தளிர்ப்பத் தாழ்ந்தாங் கதன்செவிச் செப்பு கின்றான்.
reading: The strong-shouldered hero bends low and whispers into its ear the five mantras, the seed that frees those with no good deed from their former karma at the hour their days run out and makes good karma grow.
nuance: Line 4 opens குதற்செய்கை, which I cannot construe with certainty; the bending (தாழ்ந்து) and whispering into the ear (செவிச் செப்புகின்றான்) are clear. The verse describes the mantra as a seed of new karma, so it works inside the economy of deeds rather than abolishing it.
event: Civakan whispers the five mantras into the dying dog's ear.

tamil: உறுதிமுன் செய்த தின்றி யொழுகினே னென்று நெஞ்சில்
மறுகனீ பற்றொ டார்வம் விட்டிடு மரண வச்சத்
பெறுதிநற் கதியை யென்று பெறுநவை யகற்றி னானே.
reading: 'Do not trouble your heart thinking you lived doing nothing good before; let go of attachment and longing; be firm against the fear of death; if you eat the nectar of the five padas the Lord spoke, you will reach a good state', and so he took away its harm.
nuance: நற்கதி is a good destination of birth; nothing in the verse speaks of release from birth. The five padas are named only as what இறைவன் spoke, so the Jain identification rests on the work's frame and the five-fold formula.
event: Civakan counsels the dog to give up attachment and the fear of death and take the five padas.

tamil: மனத்திடைச் செறும்பு நீக்கி மறவலை யாகி யைந்து
நினைத்திடு நின்க ணின்ற நீனிற வினையி னீங்கி
யெனைப்பக றோறும் விள்ளா வின்பமே பயக்கு மென்றாற்
கனைப்பத வமிர்த நெஞ்சி னயின்றுவிட் டகன்ற தன்றே.
reading: 'Put anger out of your mind, do not forget, and think on the five; freed of the dark karma lodged in you, it will give unbroken joy for as long as you say it', he said, and the dog swallowed the honeyed nectar of the padas in its heart and left its body.
nuance: செறும்பு நீக்கி asks the beaten dog to let go of anger at those who beat it: the dying creature is asked for the forgiveness its killers lacked. The narrator's last line closes the speech; நீனிற வினை colours karma dark, as in Jain teaching of karmic stain.
event: The dog takes the five padas to heart and dies.

reading: As the stage dancers gather on a high mountain top, make up their costume and, the curtain drawn back, appear dancing in the order of song, beat and opening, so he appeared at once as a god.
nuance: The god is not named here; I give him the id used for the god who later rescues Civakan (Sudanjanan, ch. 1-2 marks), on the story's identification, not this verse's. The simile is of the theatre: birth into heaven is instantaneous, like a dancer revealed when the screen is pulled away.
event: The dog is reborn and appears at once as a god.

reading: Through all the palace circle of the tall, battlemented golden city, women with fragrant hair and shoulders smooth as bamboo appeared, and the retinue gathered around him.
nuance: The verse does not name the city; that it is the new god's heaven follows from 948. Line 4 (ஆயினார் பரியாளம் அடைந்ததே) is compressed.
event: Heavenly women gather as the new god's retinue in his golden city.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 950-973 (5/13)
theme: The dog Civakan gave the five padas is reborn a god, Sudanjanan, lord of the yakshas; he comes back, is recognised by a god's signs, thanks Civakan as his father and promises to come whenever he is remembered, while the narrator defends the transformation by alchemy's iron turned to gold and declares worship only for the destroyer of the eight karmas and release as the harvest of the tilled body. The city then plays at war in the pool of the water festival, and as the crowd streams home the musth elephant Asanivegam breaks loose.
source_issues: Verse 958 line 4 prints an unmatched parenthesis in 'பிறவி (னென்றான்.'; the reading குறைவிலன் பிறவின் is uncertain.
Verses 951, 954-956, 959, 962-969 and 972 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 963 line 4 'மொய்த்திரள வன்ன' is hard to divide (மொய்த்து இரள் அன்னம்?); verse 957 line 4 (ஆடியுட் பாவை போனீ யணங்கிய தணங்க) is compressed and hard to construe.

cast.role: the hero, who gave the dying dog the five padas
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, now lord of the yakshas
the women of the city at the water festival
the young men of the city at the water festival
the warriors in the crowd returning from the festival
the musth state elephant that breaks loose

reading: The newly made god, lion-like, takes his delight among the celestial women with jewelled girdles, full breasts and lotus faces who have come to attend him.
nuance: The lion-like one is read as the reborn dog because 948-949 have just shown him appearing on a mountain top and the women of a golden palace gathering round; a reader coming to 950 alone might take the epithet for Civakan.
event: The dog reborn as a god rejoices among the heavenly women who attend him.

tamil: கற்றவைம் பதங்க ணீராக் கருவினை கழுவப் பட்டு
மற்றவன் றேவ னாகி வானிடு சிலையிற் றோன்றி
யிற்றத னுடம்பு மின்னா விடரொழித் தினிய னாகி
யுற்றத னிலையும் எல்லாம் ஓதியின் உணர்ந்து கொண்டான்.
reading: The five padas he learned served as water to wash off his black karma; he became a god, shining like a rainbow in the sky, free of the pain of his broken body, and by avadhi knowledge he understood all that had befallen him.
nuance: ஓதி here is the Jain avadhi, the knowledge of past and distant things given with a god's birth, not 'reciting'. The mantra does not end births: it turns the worst one into a better one, and the god still has a body and a station.
event: The dying dog, having heard the five padas, is reborn a god and knows his former life.

reading: As fire burns away iron's nature and makes it fine gold of its own colour, so the friend made him; longing for that dear friend, Sudanjanan with his bee-haunted garland swiftly appeared halting in the sky, it is said.
nuance: Civakan is the fire and the dog the iron: the image makes the teacher of the mantra, not the god it names, the agent of the change. என்பவே frames the arrival as told tradition.
event: Sudanjanan comes down out of the sky to find Civakan, the friend who transformed him.

reading: He appears with fragrant smoke spreading for a yojana around him, a body that glitters with moon-bright rays, a flawless jewelled crown hung with garlands, shining like the risen sun.
event: Sudanjanan appears before Civakan in a god's splendour.

tamil: குன்றெனத் திரண்ட தோளான் குறுகலுங் குமர னோக்கி
நின்றவ னெடுங்க ணொன்று மிமைப்பில நிழலில் யாக்கை
யன்றியுங் கண்ணி வாடா தமரனே யென்று தேறி
நன்றவன் வரவு கேட்பா னம்பி நீயாரை யென்றான்.
reading: When the hill-shouldered one draws near, the prince sees that his long eyes do not blink, his body casts no shadow and his garland does not wilt, concludes that he is a god, and asks him, 'Sir, who are you?'
nuance: Civakan reads the god by three bodily signs before he speaks, so the recognition is an inference, not a revelation; the question then lets the god tell his own story.
event: Civakan recognises the visitor as a god by his unblinking eyes, shadowless body and unfading garland, and asks who he is.

tamil: குங்குமக் குவட்டின் வீங்கிக் கோலம்வீற் றிருந்த தோளா
யிங்குநின் னருளிற் போகி யியக்கரு ளிறைவ னாகிச்
சங்கவெண் மலையின் மற்றுச் சந்திரோ தயத்தி னுச்சி
யங்கியா னுறைவ லெந்தை யறிகமற் றென்று சொன்னான்.
reading: The god tells him that by his grace he went on and became lord of the yakshas, and now dwells on the summit of Chandrodaya on the conch-white mountain, and asks his 'father' to know it.
nuance: He calls the young man எந்தை, my father: the one who gave the mantra is the giver of his new birth.
event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan he has become king of the yakshas on Mount Chandrodaya through Civakan's grace.

tamil: என்றவ னுரைப்பக் கேட்டே இமயமு நிகர்க்க லாற்றாப்
பொன்றரு மாரி வண்கைப் புரவலன் புகன்று நோக்கி
வென்றவர் உலகம் பெற்ற வேந்துடை யின்ப மெல்லா
