மின்றெனக் கெதிர்ந்த தென்றா னெரியுமிழ்ந் திலங்கும் வேலான்.
reading: Hearing this, the patron of the gold-raining hand looks at him gladly and says that all the joy of the kingship held in the world of the conquerors has come to him today.
nuance: வென்றவர் உலகம் may be the heaven won by those who conquer by merit, or the world of the Jinas; either way Civakan counts another's rise as his own highest pleasure.
event: Civakan rejoices to learn what has become of the dog.

tamil: சூடுறு கழலி னாற்குச் சுதஞ்சண னிதனைச் சொன்னான்
பாடல்வண் டரற்றும் பிண்டிப் பகவன திறைமை போல
மூடியிவ் வுலக மெல்லா நின்னடித் தருவ லின்னே
யாடியுட் பாவை போனீ யணங்கிய தணங்க வென்றான்.
reading: Sudanjanan tells him that, like the lordship of the Bhagavan of the pindi tree where bees hum, he will now bring the whole world covered to his feet, and that whatever afflicts him will afflict the god as a mirror's image follows its object.
nuance: The god measures what he offers by the Jina's sovereignty under the pindi (asoka) tree, so even the gift of the world is ranked below the Arhat's lordship. Line 4 (ஆடியுட் பாவை போல் நீ அணங்கியது அணங்க) is compressed and the sense of the mirror simile is a reading.
event: Sudanjanan promises Civakan the whole world at his feet and a share in every trouble.

tamil: வாளொடு வயவ ரீண்டி வாரணத் தொழுவின் முற்றி
மீளிமை செய்யின் வெய்ய நண்பநின் னினைப்ப தல்லால்
நாளொடு பக்கம் நைந்து வீழினும் வீழ்த லில்லாக்
reading: He goes on: should warriors with swords gather and close round him at the elephant stalls and do violence, he need only think of his friend; Civakan is like the bond of intimacy that does not fall even when days and fortnights wane, and the god lacks nothing in this birth.
nuance: The danger named, swordsmen closing round him by the elephant stalls, is the one the story is about to bring on: after Civakan masters the king's elephant he is seized and the god carries him off (patikam verse 15).
event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan to call him to mind if armed men ever besiege him.

tamil: இன்னிழ லிவரும் பூணா னிருவிசும் பிவர்த லுற்றப்
பொன்னெழு வனைய தோளாற் புல்லிக்கொண் டினைய கூறி
நின்னிழல் போல நீங்கே னிடவர்வரி னினைக்க வென்று
மின்னெழூஉப் பறப்ப தொத்து விசும்பிவர்ந் தமரன் சென்றான்.
reading: The god, wearing jewels of sweet light, about to rise into the sky, embraces him with shoulders like golden bars, says 'Like your shadow I will not leave you; if trouble comes, think of me', and rises into the sky like a flash of lightning.
nuance: The promise binds the god's help to Civakan's remembering (நினைக்க): the help is summoned by thought, as the dog's rise was won by holding the padas in mind.
event: Sudanjanan embraces Civakan, promises to come when remembered, and goes back to the sky.

tamil: சொல்லிய நன்மை யில்லாச் சுணங்கனிவ் வுடம்பு நீங்கி
யெல்லொளித் தேவ னாகிப் பிறக்குமோ வென்ன வேண்டா
கொல்லுலை யகத்திட் டூதிக் கூரிரும் பிரதங் குத்த
வெல்லையில் செம்பொ னாகி யெரிநிறம் பெற்ற தன்றே.
reading: The narrator tells the doubter not to ask whether this dog, with no good in it, could leave its body and be born a god of shining light: iron set in the smith's forge, blown upon and pierced with mercury becomes boundless red gold and takes the colour of fire.
nuance: The narrator answers an objection before it is put: the image is alchemical, mercury (இரதம்) piercing iron in the forge, so the change is presented as a work of a known art, not a miracle. The figure of 952 returns, with the mantra now in the place of the friend's fire.

tamil: தருமாலை யல்ல தியான் றலையிற் றாழ்ந்து பணிவேனோ.
reading: Let the gods who revel on the hot breasts of the women, wounded by Kama's killing arrows, keep their glory; the speaker will bow his head to none but the one who removes the eight karmas that come as a garland and makes a sea of bliss.
nuance: The first-person refusal has no speech tag. It reads as the poet's own confession closing the episode; it could also be the reborn god's vow, since he has just been among the heavenly women (950). The gods are not denied; they are set aside as still subject to Kama.

tamil: வென்றார் தம் வீட்டின்பம் விளைக்கும் விண்ணோ ருலகீன்றே.
reading: Yoke the plough of single-minded zeal, plough the field of the body, sow the red paddy of good vows, keep the water of conduct from failing and guard it with the fence of the five senses, and it will first yield the heavenly world and then the bliss of release of the conquerors.
nuance: The harvest comes in two crops: the gods' world is born (ஈன்று) on the way to the bliss of release, so heaven is a by-product, not the goal. Every stage is the practiser's own labour; no god tills the field.

tamil: இத்தலை யிவர்க ளேக விமயநட் டரவு சுற்றி
யத்தலை யலற முந்நீர் கடைந்தவ ரரவ மொப்ப
மைத்தலை நெடுங்க ணாரு மைந்தரு மறலி யாட
மொய்த்திரள வன்ன மார்க்கு மோட்டிரும் பொய்கை புக்கார்.
reading: While these two part, the dark-eyed women and the young men, with a roar like that of those who churned the ocean round the planted Himalaya with the snake, go into the great pool crowded with swans to fight in play.
nuance: The churning of the ocean is used only for its uproar; the poem pictures the mountain as the Himalaya.
event: The townswomen and young men plunge into the great pool for the water festival.

tamil: கலந்தெழு திரைநுண் ணாடைக் கடிக்கய மடந்தை காம
ரிலங்குபொற் கலாபத் தல்கு லிருகரைப் பரப்பு மாக
வலர்ந்ததண் கமலத் தம்போ தணிதக்க முகத்திற் கேற்ப
நலங்கெழு குவளை வாட்க ணன்னுத னலத்தை யுண்டார்.
reading: The pool is a bride whose fine garment is its mingling waves, whose two banks are her gold-girdled hips, whose lotus is her face and whose kuvalai are her eyes, and they enjoy her beauty.
event: The bathers take their pleasure in the pool.

tamil: தண்ணுமை முழவு மொந்தை தகுணிச்சம் பிறவு மோசை
யெண்ணிய விரலோ டங்கை புறங்கையி னிசைய வாக்கித்
திண்ணிதிற் றெறித்து மோவார் கொட்டியுங் குடைந்து மாடி
யொண்ணுதன் மகளிர் தம்மோ டுயர்மிசை யவர்க ளொத்தார்.
reading: Striking the water hard and without stopping with fingers, palms and the backs of their hands so that it sounds like the tannumai, muzhavu, montai and takunicham drums, diving and playing, the young men with the bright-browed women are like the gods above.
event: The bathers drum on the water with their hands and dive and play.

tamil: சிவிறியின் மாறு தூயுங் குங்கும மெறிந்துந் தேங்கொ
ளுவறுநீ ருழக்கி யோட்டி யுடைபுறங் கண்டு நக்குத்
தவறெனத் தாமம் பூட்டித் தருதிறை கொண்டு மின்பத்
திவறினார் காம வெள்ளத் தேத்தருந் தன்மை யாரே.
reading: Spraying each other with syringes, flinging saffron, churning the honeyed water and chasing, laughing when the other side turns its back, binding garlands on the loser as a fine and taking tribute, they swim in pleasure; who can praise them in that flood of desire?
nuance: The vocabulary is a campaign's: புறங்கண்டு (seeing the back), தவறு (offence), திறை (tribute). The last line can be wonder at a joy past praising or a dry aside on people lost in a flood of desire; the Tamil allows both.
event: The bathers play at war in the water, routing one another and exacting garland-fines and tribute.

tamil: சாந்தக நிறைந்த தோணி தண்மலர் மாலைத் தோணி
பூந்துகி லார்ந்த தோணி புனைகலம் பெய்த தோணி
கூந்தன்மா மகளிர் மைந்தர் கொண்டுகொண் டெறிய வோடித்
தாந்திரைக் கலங்கள் போலத் தாக்குபு திரியு மன்றே.
reading: Boats filled with sandal paste, boats of cool flower garlands, boats heaped with fine cloth and boats laden with jewels, pushed back and forth by the women and men, run and collide like ships on the waves.
event: The bathers drive little boats of paste, garlands, cloth and jewels at one another across the pool.

tamil: கலிவளர் களிறு கைந்நீர் சொரிவபோன் முத்த மாலை
பொலிவொடு திவண்டு பொங்கிப் பூஞ்சிகை யலமந் தாடக்
குலிகநீர் நிறைந்த பந்திற் கொம்பனா ரோச்ச மைந்தர்
மெலிவுகண் டுவந்து மாதோ விருப்பொடு மறலி னாரே.
reading: Pearl strings swaying like water sprayed from a rutting elephant's trunk and their flower tufts tossing, the creeper-like women hurl balls filled with vermilion water, and the young men, glad to see them tire, fight on with desire.
event: The women pelt the men with balls of vermilion water and the men press the play as the women tire.

tamil: வண்ணவொண் சுண்ணம் பட்டு மாலையுஞ் சாந்து மேந்தி
யெண்ணருந் திறத்து மைந்த ரெதிரெதி ரெறிய வோடி
விண்ணிடை நுடங்கு மின்னு மீன்களும் பொருவ போல
மண்ணிடை அமரர் கொண்ட மன்றலொத் திறந்த தன்றே.
reading: The countless young men run with coloured powder, silks, garlands and paste and throw them at each other face to face, like lightning and stars fighting in the sky, and it surpasses the wedding the gods held on earth.
nuance: Which wedding of the gods on earth is meant is not said.
event: The young men pelt each other with powder, silk, garlands and paste.

reading: Rubbed butter, bright fragrant powder, ground sandal, musk and garlands foam on the water, swarms of strong-winged bees hum, the water is churned, and the pleasure passes its bounds.
nuance: இன்பம் இறந்ததே may mean that the pleasure exceeded all measure, as இறந்தது does in 969, or that the bathing pleasure came to its end; the next verse turns to dressing after the bath.

tamil: கத்திகைக் கண்ணி நெற்றிக் கைதொழு கடவு ளன்ன
வித்தக விளைய ரெல்லாம் விழுமணிக் கலங்க டாங்கி
முத்தணிந் தாவி யூட்டி முகிழ் முலை கச்சின் வீக்கிப்
பித்திகைப் பிணையல் சூழ்ந்து பெண்கொடி பொலிந்த வன்றே.
reading: The skilled young men, like gods worshipped with joined hands, with kaththigai garlands on their brows, all bring jewelled ornaments; the women, decked with pearls, their hair dried in perfumed smoke, their budding breasts bound in bodices and wound with jasmine strings, shine like creepers.
event: After the bath the women are dressed and adorned, and the young men bring them jewels.

tamil: திருந்துபொற் றேருஞ் செம்பொற் சிவிகையு மிடைந்து தெற்றிக்
கருங்கயக் களிறு மாவுங் காலியற் பிடியு மீண்டி
நெருங்குபு மள்ளர் தொக்கு நெடுவரைத் தொடுத்த வெள்ளங்
கருங்கடற் கிவர்ந்த வண்ணங் கடிநகர்க் கெழுந்த வன்றே.
reading: Fine gold chariots and red-gold palanquins jostle and tangle, dark elephants, horses and swift cow-elephants gather, warriors throng, and the whole crowd rises toward the guarded city like a flood from a tall mountain rushing to the dark sea.
event: The festival crowd, with chariots, palanquins, elephants and horses, streams back toward the city.

reading: Like the sea, like the wind, like fierce-eyed Death, like the thunderbolt with angry body, like the fire of the world's end, breaking the chained post at its root, appears the musth elephant Asanivegam, hard to overcome.
nuance: The five similes run from nature (sea, wind) to Death and the end of the world; the elephant's name, Thunderbolt-speed, is held to the last word.
event: The musth elephant Asanivegam breaks its chained post and bursts out among the returning crowd.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 974-997 (6/13)
theme: A must elephant charges Gunamalai's palanquin; her bearers flee and her companion offers to die with her, and Civakan, judging death better than standing by, draws the beast on himself, escapes its trunk and drives it off, a deed the narrator measures by Krishna's. Taken home withered, Gunamalai turns from her kin like one who knows her births and, alone with her companions, confesses her love-sickness in images of Kama's archery, the sacrificial fire and the want of those who did no penance.
source_issues: Verses 974, 975, 976, 979, 980, 981, 983 and 985 were printed in eight half-lines and have been joined into four (FLAG repaired).
Verse 975 line 4 prints றோருங்குகை, which the sense requires as றொருங்கு கை (joining both hands); a misdivision or misprint.
Verse 978 line 4 prints ஆர்ததுமே, probably ஆர்த்து மேல் (shouting, upon it); a dropped letter.
Verse 990 line 1 prints மாலைபேற், probably மாலைபெற்; the line is hard to construe either way.
Verse 985 is in a longer metre than the verses around it and gives the number of Civakan's companions as ஐஞ்ஞாற்று நால்வர் (five hundred and four).

Gunamalai's companion, left with her before the elephant
Gunamalai's companions and attendants
Gunamalai's mother, wife of a great merchant
Gunamalai's loving kin, who take her home
the young men who bear Gunamalai's palanquin and flee
the must elephant that charges Gunamalai's palanquin
Civakan's companions
the crowds of Rajamapuram
Gunamalai's pet parrot

tamil: பொருதிழி யருவி போன்று பொழிதரு கடாத்த தாகிக்
குருதிகொண் மருப்பிற் றாகிக் குஞ்சரஞ் சிதைந்த தென்னக்
கருதிய திசைக ளெல்லாங் கண்மிசைக் கரந்த மாந்தர்
பருதியின் முன்னர்த் தோன்றா மறைந்தபன் மீன்க ளொத்தார்.
reading: The elephant, streaming must like a falling cascade and with blood on its tusks, breaks loose, and the people who had filled every quarter vanish from sight like the many stars that hide before the sun.
event: The must elephant runs amok and the crowds scatter out of sight.

tamil: கருந்தடங் கண்ணி தன்மேற் காமுக ருள்ளம் போல
விருங்களி றெய்த வோடச் சிவிகைவிட் டிளைய ரேக
வரும்பெற லவட்குத் தோழி யாடவ ரில்லை யோஎன்
றோருங்குகை யுச்சிக் கூப்பிக் களிற்றெதி ரிறைஞ்சி நின்றாள்.
reading: As the great tusker rushes on her as the hearts of lustful men rush on a dark-eyed woman, the bearers drop the palanquin and run, and the girl's companion, crying out whether there are no men, raises her joined hands above her head and bows before the elephant.
nuance: The simile of line 1 sets the elephant's charge beside men's desire for the woman, so that the danger and the courtship to come are drawn from one figure.
event: The bearers abandon Gunamalai's palanquin, and her companion bows to the elephant and calls for help.

tamil: என்னைக்கொன் றிவள்க ணோடு மெல்லையி லொருவன் றோன்றி
யின்னுயி ரிவளைக் காக்கு மன்றெனி லென்கண் மாய்ந்தாற்
பின்னைத்தான் ஆவ தாக வென்றெண்ணிப் பிணைக ணோக்கி
மின்னுப்போ னுடங்கி நின்றாள் வீததை பொற்கொம் பொப்பாள்.
reading: The companion resolves: let it kill me together with her, or let some man appear in time to save her dear life; if not, whatever comes after my eyes have closed may come; and she stands trembling like lightning, looking at the beast.
nuance: The thought (lines 1-3) is the companion's, closed by என்றெண்ணி; whether the one who stands trembling in line 4, likened to a flower-laden golden creeper, is the companion or Gunamalai herself the verse does not settle.
event: Gunamalai's companion resolves to die with her unless a rescuer comes.

tamil: மணியிரு தலையுஞ் சேர்த்தி வான்பொனி னியன்ற நாணா
லணியிருங் குஞ்சி யேறக் கட்டியிட் டலங்கல் சூழ்ந்து
தணிவருந் தோழர் சூழத் தாழ்குழை திருவில் வீசப்
பணிவருங் குருசில் செல்வான் பாவைய திடரைக் கண்டான்.
reading: Civakan, his hair bound up with a gold cord tipped with gems at both ends and wreathed with a garland, his ear-drops swinging and his loyal companions around him, is passing by when he sees the girl's peril.
event: Civakan, passing with his companions, sees the danger to the girl.

tamil: பெண்ணுயி ரவல நோக்கிப் பெருந்தகை வாழ்விற் சாத
லெண்ணின னெண்ணி நொய்தா வினமலர் மாலை சுற்றா
வண்ணப்பொற் கடக மேற்றா வார்கச்சிற் றானை வீக்கா
reading: Seeing a woman's life in danger, the noble one reckons death better than living on; at once he winds up his flower garland, pushes up his golden bracelet, binds his cloth with his belt, curses the elephant and runs at it shouting.
nuance: வாழ்வின் சாதல் எண்ணினன் is a judgment the narrator gives the hero at the moment of choice, before any thought of who the woman is: the rescue is first a matter of honour, and love comes after.
event: Civakan girds himself and runs at the elephant.

tamil: குண்டலங் குமரன் கொண்டு குன்றின்மேல் வீழு மின்போ
லொண்டிறற் களிற்றி னெற்றி யெறிந்துதோ டொலித்து வீழ
மண்டில முத்துந் தாரு மாலையுங் குழலும் பொங்க
விண்டலர் கண்ணி சிந்த மின்னிற்சென் றெய்தி னானே.
reading: The young man leaps like lightning falling on a hill and strikes the forehead of the mighty elephant with a clap of his arms, while his round pearls, chain, garland and hair fly and the open flowers of his wreath scatter.
event: Civakan leaps at the elephant and strikes its forehead.

tamil: படம்விரி நாகஞ் செற்றுப் பாய்ந்தரு கலுழன் போல
மடவர லவளைச் செற்று மதக்களி றிறைஞ்சும் போழ்திற்
குடவரை நெற்றி பாய்ந்த கோளரி போன்று வேழத்
துடல்சினங் கடவக் குப்புற் றுருமென வுரறி யார்த்தான்.
reading: Just as the must elephant bends to crush the girl, he springs at it like Garuda upon a hooded cobra, like a lion leaping on the brow of the western mountain, and roars like thunder so that the beast's rage turns on him.
nuance: The roar has a purpose the verse states: குப்புற்று ... உடல்சினங் கடவ, he turns the elephant's anger from the girl to himself.
event: Civakan springs at the elephant as it stoops over Gunamalai, drawing its fury to himself.

tamil: கூற்றென முழங்கிக் கையாற் கோட்டிடைப் புடைப்பக் காய்ந்து
காற்றென வுரறி நாகங் கடாம்பெய்து கனவிற் சீறி
யாற்றலங் குமரன் றன்மே லடுகளி றோட லஞ்சான்
கோற்றொடிப் பாவை தன்னைக் கொண்டுயப் போமின் என்றான்.
reading: The elephant roars like Death, beats at him between its tusks with its trunk, shrieks like the wind and pours must in fury; the strong youth, unafraid as it runs at him, tells those near to take the bangled girl and get her to safety.
event: As the elephant turns on him, Civakan orders the girl carried away to safety.

tamil: மதியினுக் கிவர்ந்த வேக மாமணி நாகம் வல்லே
பதியமை பருதி தன்மேற் படம்விரித் தோடி யாங்குப்
பொதியவிழ் கோதை தன்மேற் பொருகளி றகன்று பெற்றார்க்
கதியமை தோளி னானைக் கையகப் படுத்த தன்றே.
reading: As the great serpent that climbs to seize the moon spreads its hood and runs at the sun, the fighting elephant leaves the girl and seizes in its trunk the man whose shoulders were made for those who have no refuge.
nuance: The eclipse simile makes Civakan the sun (பருதி) and the elephant the serpent of eclipse; பெற்றார்க்கு அதியமை தோளினான் praises him as a refuge in the very line in which he is caught.
event: The elephant leaves Gunamalai and seizes Civakan in its trunk.

tamil: கையகப் படுத்த லோடுங் கார்மழை மின்னி னொய்தா
மொய்கொளப் பிறழ்ந்து முத்தார் மருப்பிடைக் குளித்துக் காற்கீ
ழையென வடங்கி வல்லா னாடிய மண்வட் டேய்ப்பச்
செய்கழற் குருசி லாங்கே கரந்துசே ணகற்றி னானே.
reading: The moment it seizes him he slips free quick as lightning from a rain cloud, dives between its pearl-tipped tusks, folds himself small beneath its feet like the clay ball an expert plays, and the anklet-wearing hero, keeping out of its reach there, drives it far away.
nuance: கரந்துசே ணகற்றினான் can be read as his hiding and driving the beast far off or as his vanishing far away himself; the next verse, in which the elephant withdraws, favours the first.
event: Civakan wriggles free, dodges between the tusks and under the feet, and drives the elephant off.

reading: The elephant was like the tusker that once ran to kill the gem-coloured lord of the wide waters, and Civakan was like that lord; and the elephant dripping triple must, as if a god were in it, gave way.
nuance: The simile is the story of Krishna and the elephant sent against him, told in one line without naming either; a Jain epic uses the Vaishnava deed as a measure of its hero without comment. தெய்வம்போல் may go with Civakan (godlike, he stood) or with the elephant (as if possessed); the line division favours the elephant.
event: The elephant gives way before Civakan.

tamil: ஒருகை யிருமருப்பின் மும்மதத்த தோங்கெழிற்குன் றனைய வேழந்
திருகு கனைகழற்காற் சீவகன்வென் றிளையாட்கு டைந்து தேனார்
முருகு கமழலங்கன் முத்திலங்கு மார்பினனைஞ் ஞாற்று நால்வ
ரருகு கழல்பரவத் தனியேபோ யுய்யான மடைந்தா னன்றே.
reading: Having beaten the one-trunked, two-tusked, triple-must elephant, tall as a fair hill, for the young girl, Civakan of the honey-scented garland and pearl-bright chest goes alone to the pleasure garden while his five hundred and four companions crowd round praising his feet.
nuance: ஐஞ்ஞாற்று நால்வர் reads as five hundred and four; the verse sets their praise beside தனியே போய், so 'alone' must mean apart from the girl and her people, not without his friends. The verse is in a longer metre than its neighbours.
event: Civakan, victorious, goes to the garden while his companions praise him.

reading: Her own people, whose love never slackens, take away the golden creeper whose distress the man of shoulders thick as a jewelled post had removed, telling her not to grieve.
event: Gunamalai's kin take her home and comfort her.

reading: The mother of the spear-eyed girl, beloved wife of the man who is a bull among the merchants with hands that give out great wealth from the roaring sea, sees her daughter wilted like a crushed garland and speaks.
event: Gunamalai's mother sees her wilted and speaks.

reading: 'What has come on my girl today, that she has withered and lost her golden colour like a hand-made garland thrust into a high ghee-fed flame?' she asks; and those who knew kept from telling, for wanting to come through safe.
nuance: The verse turns from the mother's question (lines 1-3) to the silence of those who know: the companions hide the danger, and with it the cause of her withering, out of fear for themselves.
event: The mother asks what has withered her daughter; the companions keep silent.

reading: Calling 'come', the mother wipes the tears from her daughter's bright eyes and embraces her, whose hair is full of mullai garlands drunk by bees and whose slender waist bends.
event: The mother calls her daughter to her, wipes her tears and embraces her.

reading: With the companions who never let go of her hand, the mother searches it out by her own understanding and finds that the girl's grief came upon her at the festive gathering.
nuance: Line 1 (கடம்பு சூடிய கன்னி மாலைபேற்) is hard to construe; it may tie the gathering to a rite of the kadambu-wearing god, and the text may be corrupt (மாலைபெற்).
event: The mother, questioning the companions, learns where the trouble began.

reading: They take off her heavy worked ornaments and put light ones on her body, set a soft garland on her and smear saffron over the creeper-like girl.
event: The women change Gunamalai's heavy jewels for light ones and anoint her.

reading: Her green parrot calls to the girl, 'go and fetch our sister who brings nectar in a golden cup', and our girl like a golden creeper goes.
nuance: Who is fetched and where the girl goes are not clear: the parrot's words may ask for its keeper, or may be a call the girl, lost in thought, answers by walking away. The verse ends in the voice of her own household (எம் பாவை).
event: Gunamalai's pet parrot calls out, and she goes.

reading: The girl whose red-lined eyes have stolen the power of the fat-smeared spear spurns all the talk of her kin, like those who have come to know their births, and wants nothing at all.
nuance: பிறப்பு உணர்ந்தவர் may mean those who recall their former births, the knowledge that in the epic's world turns a person to renunciation; the narrator lends the love-struck girl the renouncer's withdrawal, though her wanting nothing is wanting one man.
event: Gunamalai turns from her family's talk and from everything else.

reading: Finding a moment apart from her people, the girl like a creeper in a garland tells of her love for the youth, who is like the lord who appeared on the lotus to the gods' delight.
nuance: The lord born on the lotus to the gods' desire, called குமரன், reads as Murugan of the reed pool; the verse names Civakan only by the likeness.
event: Away from her kin, Gunamalai speaks of her love for Civakan.

reading: Gunamalai says that the cruel five-arrowed one practises his archery on her, making the time of union his school's hall, the space between her breasts his heap of target earth, and her life his mark.
nuance: Kama is an archer in training and she the butt: the conceit turns her pain into his practice, so that it will go on.

reading: 'Since even the earth could not bear it, my heart burns like the fire of a sacrifice: bring me quickly the man of the garlanded chest, Civaka Sami, who is Kama himself, ladies.'
nuance: The name சீவக சாமி, by which the invocation calls the hero, is here in the mouth of a girl who wants him as a lover.

reading: 'I speak with my hands and hear with my eyes; with a mind crowded with thought I have become a mute; like the small folk who did no penance, is there any door by which I can be saved?'
nuance: Speaking by hand and hearing by eye describes her silence before others: she cannot say her love aloud. The simile measures a lover's want by the want of those without the merit of past tapas.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 998-1021 (7/13)
theme: Lovesick Gunamalai, praising a woman's restraint yet thinking of the palmyra horse, sends her parrot to Civakan, who has painted her portrait and is embracing it; his wife Gandharvadattai comes upon the picture, sees through his excuse, scorns his appeasing words and leaves in a sulk, and the parrot, which waited hidden, comes down to his hand.
source_issues: 998 line 3: வெண்ணில் is doubtful (perhaps எண்ணில்); the reading of the line is uncertain.
1000 line 3: நைய னங்கையிற் நாட்டகத் shows an irregular junction (ற் before ந); perhaps நையல் நங்கை இந்நாட்டகத்து.
1012 line 2: பூங்கெடி is probably a misprint for பூங்கொடி.
1014 line 3: வேலினாற் கண்டு is odd as written; the sense needs the spear-bearer as object of கண்டு.

cast.role: the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant, now in love with him
Gunamalai's parrot, sent as her messenger
the hero, already married to Gandharvadattai
Civakan's wife, won at the vina contest

reading: Gunamalai says her eyes have lost their brightness, her bangles slip, and her heart cries out like a wound; a woman, though desire burns her, does not go forward, and nothing surpasses womanhood.
nuance: She praises the very restraint that is hurting her; the next verse shows how close it comes to breaking. The thought is the Kural's on women and the palmyra horse (1137) in other words, not a verbal echo.

reading: As her longing rises like the great sea, the girl with spear-like eyes thinks of riding the palmyra-stem horse with its hanging leaves.
nuance: The madal is a man's public threat; a heroine only thinking of it shows desire pressing past the rule she has just praised. She thinks of it but turns to the parrot instead.
event: Gunamalai, overcome by longing, considers riding the madal.

reading: Gunamalai begs her red-beaked parrot, whom she calls her only refuge, to tell her how she may live, and the parrot tells her not to waste away and to say without shame whom in the land she wants.
nuance: The closing என்றதே, a neuter verb, gives lines 3 and 4 to the parrot; the division of the speeches is my reading.
event: Gunamalai asks her parrot for help, and the parrot asks her to name the man.

reading: They say that she, matchless in radiance and grace even against the goddess on the lotus, helpless in heady desire, told her parrot her message and sent it as her envoy.
event: Gunamalai sends her parrot as messenger to Civakan.

reading: With her modesty, her family and her good name set beneath her longing, the dear green parrot flew through the sky to find the master of the vina.
nuance: Sending a go-between is itself counted as a loss of நாண், family standing and name: the price of the message is set before the message arrives.
event: The parrot flies off to find Civakan.

reading: Civakan blended and purified many coloured gems and painted on cloth the girl with the tilaka brow, as she was in look and trembling when she stood terrified before the rutting elephant.
nuance: He paints her not at ease but at the moment of terror: the danger that brought them together is the image he keeps.
event: Civakan paints Gunamalai's portrait on cloth as she stood before the elephant.

reading: Gazing and gazing at the painting, he strokes its slipping garment, falling hair, garland and the pearls on her young breasts, praises it, and clasps it to his shoulders.
event: Civakan caresses and embraces the portrait.

reading: Civakan says that the jewelled girdle on her broad hips, the ornaments on her breasts and the anklets on her lotus feet must all have done penance to be worn by her.
nuance: The verb நோற்ற, repeated three times, turns the language of the vow into a lover's compliment; the fancy assumes that good fortune is earned by austerity.

reading: While the prince lamented thus over her grace, the parrot of the girl of tormenting speech saw with delight Tattai, the prince's beloved, arriving.
nuance: The line puns on தத்தை, parrot and Gandharvadattai's short name: the parrot sees Tattai. The sense of மன்னணங் குறலொடு is doubtful.
event: As Civakan laments, the parrot sees Gandharvadattai approaching.

reading: On her hips, wide as a dancing snake's hood, the fine cloth wrapped over her girdle looked as if pale smoke of incense had gathered and curled about it.
The bright strands of pearl hanging over the tips of her rising breasts looked like young crescent moons drawn on a golden casket.
With an earring arching its light on one side and an ear-roll flashing on the other, the beauty of her face was like a full round moon.
The fine gold thread drawn through the dark hair at her forehead shone like lightning curved through a dark sky.
nuance: Which ornament நாணிற of line 3 names is not certain from the line alone.

reading: The jasmine garland trailing from her fragrant hair-knot looked like a koel bending on a swaying flowering creeper.
The parrot wonders who this wide-eyed woman can be, who walks with anklets and girdle chiming like a golden flowering creeper that has learned to walk while bees hum on it.
Saying that whoever she is, it will not go near on its errand until she has done what she came for and gone, the green parrot settles in a flowering champak.
nuance: The envoy keeps the go-between's rule of secrecy: the message is for him alone.
event: The parrot waits hidden in a champak tree.

reading: The honey-eyed woman, gold anklet-bells tinkling as she walked, came up to the man of the fierce spear, saw, and looked at him in a sulk.
event: Gandharvadattai comes upon Civakan with the portrait and sulks.

reading: Asked what the figure was, he called it a yakshi, and she answers that this is something new: since his garment and hair hang loose and that garlanded one so moves his mind, she must indeed be an iyakki.
nuance: The retort puns on இயக்கி, a yakshi and 'one who sets in motion'. Who asks and who answers in line 1 is my reading.
event: Civakan passes the portrait off as a yakshi, and Gandharvadattai turns the word against him.

reading: Sweat beaded on her face like pearls on a rising moon, her brows bent like a bow, and her eyes reddened like a cluster of water lilies.
event: Gandharvadattai shows her anger.

reading: Civakan pleads with her not to draw out her sulk: for him, a wretch, they are one life in two bodies, and would a swan that delighted in the flowering Ganges go near the white sand of a seep-well?
nuance: The Ganges and the well rank the two women: to soothe the wife he belittles the girl he has just embraced in paint.
event: Civakan tries to appease Gandharvadattai.

reading: Looking at the painted figure, she who flares at other women even by name felt her sulk toward her loving husband blaze like fire with ghee poured on it.
event: Gandharvadattai's anger grows as she looks at the portrait.

reading: Trembling like a creeper in her anger, anklets and girdle chiming, she set her flower-feet upon his garlanded head, turned with her earrings flashing, scattered her flowers and left.
nuance: Line 3 seems to have him bow and her feet touch his head; the gesture and who makes it are not plain.
event: Gandharvadattai leaves Civakan in anger.

reading: When his wife had gone with angry words, the parrot, saying that now there was no one else and it would come out, mixed sweet words and flew to the young man's feet.
event: The parrot comes down to Civakan once Gandharvadattai has gone.

reading: The parrot hails his anklet-feet and wishes him long life; he answers 'welcome, friend, come here', and the master of the yazh holds out his hand, his gem rings flashing.
nuance: The welcome is the borrowed word சுவாகதம், svāgatam, a courtly greeting.
event: Civakan welcomes the parrot onto his hand.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1022-1045 (8/13)
theme: Gunamalai's parrot carries her love-sickness to Civakan, who pledges marriage and sends back a sealed letter sworn in a warrior's self-curse; she divines with a sand circle, receives the letter with joy, and vows offerings to the gods that he keep his word.
source_issues: Verse 1042 line 2 ends with a stray opening bracket and word, (மென்றோட், and line 3 (வேட்டார்க்கு வேட்டனவே போன்றினிய வேய்) is short of a full line; a word seems displaced or lost between lines 2 and 3.
Verses 1039 and 1043 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joined lines read correctly.
Verse 1036 line 3 (குணமாலைக் காதகா தென்றுலக) is hard to divide; ஆ தகாது is one possible reading.
Verse 1030 line 1 (சென்ம ருந்துதந் தாய்) is divided in print against the likely sense சென்மருந்து தந்தாய்.

cast.role: the hero, who saved Gunamalai from the elephant
a merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant and who loves him
Gunamalai's green parrot, her messenger to Civakan

reading: The narrator tells that the parrot came ahead bearing the maiden's message, and Civakan, with a smiling look, asked it sweetly why it had come.
nuance: The message is called கன்னியர் தூது, the maidens' message, with an honorific plural; the sender is Gunamalai, whom the verse names only by her body.
event: Gunamalai's parrot arrives with her message and Civakan smilingly asks why it has come.

reading: The parrot answers that its mistress sent it to find the right moment with the famed lord who fought the maddened elephant and to come back, so it has come to see him.
nuance: செவ்வி கண்டு, 'having seen the moment', makes the go-between's skill one of timing; the elephant fight it recalls is the rescue from which Gunamalai's love began.
event: The parrot tells Civakan that Gunamalai sent it to him.

tamil: வெஞ்சின வேழ முண்ட வெள்ளிலின் வெறிய மாக
நெஞ்சமு நிறையு நீல நெடுங்கணாற் கவர்ந்த கள்வி
அஞ்சனத் துவலை யாடி நடுங்கினா ணிலைமை யென்னை
reading: The parrot reports that the girl who stole hearts and restraint with her long blue eyes, leaving them hollow like a wood-apple an elephant has swallowed, now trembles bathed in kohl-dark tears, and asks what her state is.
nuance: The thief who stole நிறை now has lost her own: the eyes that emptied others like the swallowed wood-apple are full of tears. Whose heart was stolen, and whether line 4 is the parrot's own question or Gunamalai's to her parrot, is not certain from the word order.
event: The parrot describes Gunamalai trembling in tears.

reading: The parrot goes on: she lies on her flower bed as on a fire, leans on a golden pillar like a carved doll, sighs again and again as if breath were flame, and softly sinks to sit on the ground.
event: Gunamalai, in the parrot's account, cannot rest on her bed and sinks to the ground.

reading: She no longer looks at her adornment, her ball or her young birds, does not play with gem jacks, her dark skin has paled, she has left the lute and her food, and sleep has left her eyes.
nuance: The list runs from a girl's games to the body's needs, so the account measures love-sickness by what the girlhood world has lost for her.
event: Gunamalai gives up play, music, food and sleep.

reading: She cries out to Civaka Saami of the shapely spear, laments that her conch bangles slip off, and begs him to come and hold her to his chest, she of grace like a flowering branch.
nuance: The parrot quotes her cries in the first person, so the girl's own appeal reaches the man only in the voice of the bird.
event: Gunamalai calls aloud on Civakan.

reading: The parrot says that maidens do not tell even those as dear as their eyes what ails them, out of shame, so it, who stays with her, cannot know her illness, and asks whether the prince himself knows it.
nuance: The parrot's ignorance is feigned: it has just described the illness and named its cause through her cries in 1027, so the question puts the diagnosis on the man.
event: The parrot asks Civakan whether he knows the cause of Gunamalai's illness.

reading: On hearing the bird's words, the spear-bearer, noble as the generous one who cut down the mango, felt as though he saw before him the long-eyed girl and her sweet words he had been thinking of.
nuance: மாத் தடிந்தான், 'he who cut down the mango', most likely names Murugan, who felled the demon standing as a mango tree; the comparison is the narrator's and the identification is a reading.
event: Hearing the parrot, Civakan feels Gunamalai is present before him.

reading: The parrot asks him, as the one who once gave her the medicine of life, to say what has settled in his mind, and says it seeks his bow-straightening shoulders as the sweet medicine for her.
nuance: சென்மருந்து தந்தாய் likely recalls the rescue from the elephant: the man who saved her life once is asked to save it again. The compound is hard to divide, so the sense is not fixed.
event: The parrot asks Civakan to declare himself and names him as her cure.

reading: Civakan replies that, were he offered a hill of gold or a town of paddy heaps ringed by flowering fields, he would still bring his rock-like shoulders to her and wed her without failing his word, and bids the parrot go and tell her.
nuance: சொல் குன்றா, 'without my word falling short', is the phrase Gunamalai will turn into her prayer in 1045 (சொற்குன்றான் ஆக).
event: Civakan pledges to marry Gunamalai and sends the parrot back with his word.

reading: The parrot says these things are hard for it to tell the fish-eyed girl and asks him to write a palm leaf; the garlanded hero gives one, and the parrot rises and flies off with the leaf and an ear of millet.
nuance: The bird asks for writing because speech is not enough: the pledge must reach her in a form she can hold, and the letter is read out in 1041 to 1043.
event: Civakan writes a palm-leaf letter, and the parrot flies off with it and a millet ear.

reading: Meanwhile the girl with well-dressed hair, small feet and fragrant body wrapped herself in the cover of the flowering pond and lay there, the dark-eyed doll, lovely in her waiting.
nuance: பூம்பொய்கைப் போர்வை, 'the covering of the flower pond', may be the pond's water or lotus leaves used to cool a fevered body; which is meant is not clear.
event: Gunamalai waits, lying by or in the flower pond.

reading: It is told that the spear-bearer of fierce bright spear went with his long anklets ringing and took his beloved's sulking away with his flower-crowned head, so that the long-eyed one's joy was full.
nuance: The verse ends என்பவே, 'they say', and reads as a told tale rather than an event of the story: probably the god with the spear ending his consort's sulk by bowing his head to her, set beside Gunamalai's waiting as the outcome she hopes for. Neither the god nor its place in the scene is named.

reading: Gunamalai frets whether the parrot has left its mate's company and found a lonely place to reach her beloved, whether it stayed, went or arrived, and whether it has said that this is the word of the girl who melts as she waits for his moment, and she sighs, alas.
nuance: The chain of questions with கொல், 'perhaps', follows the bird step by step, so the verse turns waiting into an imagined journey.
event: Gunamalai anxiously imagines the parrot's errand.

reading: She says that if the man the parrot went to gives one sweet word he gives her her life, and if he does not, while the world grieves that this is unfit for Gunamalai, she will strive and win him even by penance.
nuance: நோற்றானும் எய்துவனே makes தவம் a means to a husband: if this life fails, penance will bring him, presumably in a later birth. The division of காதகா தென்று (ஆ, தகாது?) is uncertain.
event: Gunamalai resolves that if he refuses she will win him by penance.

reading: Praying that if the errand of the one who went succeeds and the spear-warrior's adorned chest is to embrace her, it may come together without fail, the jewelled girl drew a circle on the long pearl-like sand.
nuance: The circle must close (கூடுக) for the omen to be good; the verse shows the rite as a girl's private divination, without a diviner.
event: Gunamalai draws a circle in the sand to divine whether she and Civakan will unite.

reading: As she thought that if the drawn line went wrong halfway her life would leave her, sinner that she was, the green parrot looked down from the sky, said that the maiden was there and it would go to her, and came down to her.
nuance: The bird arrives in the very moment of the drawing, so the answer to the divination comes as a messenger, not as the shape in the sand.
event: As Gunamalai fears the omen will fail, the parrot sees her from the sky and lands beside her.

reading: She saw it, sighed deeply, joined her hands in worship, took the millet ear and wore it in her hair, pressed the parrot to her breast till it hurt, heard the garlanded man's message from its beak and rejoiced through her body.
nuance: She worships the bird (கைதொழுதாள) and squeezes it till it hurts (நோவ): the messenger is honoured and embraced as a stand-in for the man.
event: Gunamalai greets the parrot, wears the millet ear and hears Civakan's message.

reading: She of bamboo-like shoulders fed the soft bird sweet milk, settled it to sleep in its gold and gem cage, touched the seal ring bearing his name, and read the clearly lettered leaf with care.
nuance: The ring with his name (மணிநாம மோதிரம்) seals the leaf, so the letter carries proof of its sender as well as words.
event: Gunamalai tends the parrot and opens Civakan's sealed letter.

reading: The letter begins: the leaf of the man of the curved bow, for Gunamalai to see; he who could not bear the burning grief inside has had his swelling sickness cured by the little parrot sent to comfort him, and may the long-eyed girl too have her sorrowful thoughts depart.
nuance: He says the bird, not the girl, cured him: love's medicine here is a message, received before any meeting.

reading: The letter goes on that, even giving away all his heaped treasure and the rich towns ringed by cool lily ponds, he will not fail to embrace the girl of bow-like brow, sweet to him as their desire to those who desire.
nuance: The verse repeats the wealth-weighing of 1031 in writing, now as the price he would pay rather than a gift he would refuse.

reading: He ends the letter by swearing that if he does not live with her to her joy, his garland marking her saffroned breasts and his presence quenching the fire in her mind with her tears, then let him be one who has thought of turning his weapon on men already beaten in sword battle.
nuance: The love-pledge takes the form of a warrior's self-curse: the penalty he names is the worst shame of the battlefield, even to have thought (நினைந்தேன்) of attacking the routed, so the oath measures his word by the code of war.

reading: She looked at the fine lines of the letters, laid like drawn thread, as if drinking sweet honey poured into milk, her fish-like eyes brimming with tears, and rejoiced through her body as though she had already embraced the chest of the man who had made her love-mad.
nuance: Reading is described as drinking and as embracing, so the written pledge gives her by anticipation the union 1043 promised.
event: Gunamalai reads the letter, weeps and rejoices.

reading: She vows to offer milk-rice, flowers, incense, sandal paste and gold lamps that no wind puts out, and to worship with joined hands, and asks those she addresses to watch, like the men of the learned assembly, that the man of the fierce bow does not fail his word.
nuance: Those addressed (நீங்கள்) are unnamed; the offerings point to household or temple deities. நூலவையார், the assembly versed in the books, makes them witnesses and judges of his oath, as an assembly hears a case.
event: Gunamalai promises offerings to the deities if they keep Civakan true to his word.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1046-1069 (9/13)
theme: Gunamalai's nurse sounds her with news of a match with a rich cousin; Gunamalai refuses, vowing death or penance unless she is given to the elephant-tamer, and the news passes from nurse to mother to father, who sends envoys to Kantukkatan; the match is agreed, the day fixed, the wedding held with a rich dowry, and Civakan and Gunamalai's union and his teasing close the run.
source_issues: Verses 1047 to 1053 and 1059 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 1055 is in the first person singular (வரப்பெற்றேன், சேர்ந்தேன்) but ends என நாய்கற் கவர்சொன்னார், the same close as 1056; the speaker is doubtful.
Verse 1057 line 1 repeats the epithet that names Kantukkatan in 1054 line 3, apparently for a different person.
Verse 1064 calls the giver of the dowry நாய்கன், the title used for Kantukkatan in 1054; the giver is probably the bride's father.

Verse 1053 divides the mother's name as வினையமா மாலை and 1059 line 3 prints பொன் கொம்பு அனையாளை unjoined, unlike the rest of the text; 1058 line 2 prints கைப்படுத் தான் போன் றிதுகூறக் with odd spacing.
Verses 1061 and 1069 lack the closing full stop the other verses carry.

cast.role: the hero, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan
the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant; here கிளவி, பாவை, குழலாள்
Gunamalai's nurse (also கைத்தாய்)
Gunamalai's mother, wife of Kuberamittiran
Gunamalai's father, a merchant chief
four learned men Kuberamittiran sends to Kantukkatan
the merchant who raised Civakan (நாய்கன், தாதை)
Kantukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother
the astrologers who fix the wedding day
Gunamalai's rival in the powder contest; only mentioned here

tamil: மவ்வலங் குழலி னாளை மதியுடம் படுக்க லுற்றுச்
செவ்வியுட் செவிலி சொல்லுஞ் சிலையிவர் நுதலி னாய்நின்
னவ்வைக்கு மூத்த மாம னொருமகற் கின்றுன் றாதை
நவ்வியம் பிணைகொ ணோக்கி நகைமுக விருந்து செய்தான்.
reading: Setting out to draw Gunamalai's mind into the open, her nurse tells her at a quiet moment that her father has today feasted the only son of her mother's elder brother.
nuance: மதியுடம்படுக்கலுற்று names the nurse's purpose: she is sounding the girl, so the news of a match that follows may be a test rather than a settled plan; the cousin is never mentioned again once Gunamalai answers.
event: Gunamalai's nurse tells her that her father has entertained her maternal cousin.

tamil: பண்டியாற் பண்டி செம்பொன் பல்வளை பரிய மாகக்
கொண்டுவந் தடிமை செய்வான் குறையுறு கின்ற தன்றிக்
கண்டவர் கடக்க லாற்றாக் கிழிமிசை யுருவ தீட்டி
வண்டிமிர் கோதை நின்னை வழிபடு நாளு மென்றாள்.
reading: The nurse goes on: the cousin begs to serve as her bondman, bringing cartloads of gold and bangles as bride-price, and daily worships a likeness of her painted on cloth that no one who sees it can pass by.
event: The nurse describes the cousin's bride-price and his worship of Gunamalai's painted portrait.

tamil: மைத்துனன் வனப்பின் மிக்கான் வளர்நிதிக் கிழவன் காளை
யுத்தம னுனது நாம மல்லதொன் றுரைத்த றேற்றா
னித்திறத் திவன்க ணின்னை யெண்ணினா ரென்ன லோடுந்
தத்தையங் கிளவி கையாற் செவிமுத லடைச்சிச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: The nurse praises the cousin as handsome, heir to growing wealth and speaking no name but hers, says the elders have fixed on him for her, and at this the parrot-voiced girl covers her ears with her hands and speaks.
nuance: Gunamalai's first answer is a gesture: she closes her ears before she says a word.
event: Told that her elders intend her for the cousin, Gunamalai covers her ears.

tamil: மணிமதக் களிறு வென்றான் வருத்தச்சொற் கூலி யாக
வணிமதக் களிற னானுக் கடிப்பணி செய்வ தல்லாற்
றுணிவதென் சுடுசொல் வாளாற் செவிமுத லீர லென்றாள்
பணிவரும் பவளப் பாவை பரிவுகொண் டனைய தொப்பாள்.
reading: Gunamalai says that, as wages for the toil of the man who conquered the rutting elephant, she can resolve on nothing but service at his feet, and asks the nurse not to cut her ears with the sword of burning words.
nuance: She frames her love as a debt (வருத்தச்சொற் கூலி, the wage of his pains), not as desire.
event: Gunamalai refuses the cousin and declares she will serve only Civakan.

tamil: கந்துகப் புடையிற் பொங்குங் கலினமா வல்லன் காளைக்
கெந்தையும் யாயு நேரா ராய்விடி னிறத்த லொன்றோ
சிந்தனை பிறிதொன் றாகிச் செய்தவ முயற லொன்றோ
வந்ததா னாளை யென்றாள் வடுவெனக் கிடந்த கண்ணாள்.
reading: She says that if her father and mother will not give her to the young horseman, tomorrow brings one of two things: death, or a mind turned elsewhere to the labour of penance.
nuance: The two alternatives are the epic's own exits for women, death and renunciation; she names them before any marriage, so the steadfastness usually asked of a wife is here a maiden's fixity on a man she has chosen.
event: Gunamalai declares that if her parents refuse Civakan she will die or take up penance.

tamil: தேனெய்போன் றினிய சொல்லாள் சிறுமுதுக் குறைமை கேட்டே
யூனைநைந் துருகிக் கைத்தா யுண்ணிறை யுவகை பொங்க
வானெய்பாற் கிவர்ந்த தொத்த தழேற்கவென் பாவை யென்று
தானையாற் றடங்க ணீரைத் துடைத்துமெய் தழுவிக் கொண்டாள்.
reading: Hearing the small girl's precocious wisdom, the nurse melts with joy, says it is like ghee climbing into milk, tells her not to weep, wipes her eyes with her garment and embraces her.
nuance: The nurse's joy confirms that the cousin story was a sounding: she wanted this refusal.
event: The nurse rejoices at Gunamalai's answer, comforts her and embraces her.

tamil: துகண்மனத் தின்றி நோற்ற தொல்வினைப் பயத்தி னன்றே
தகணிலாக் கேள்வி யான்கட் டங்கிய தென்று பின்னு
மகண்மனங் குளிர்ப்பக் கூறி மறுவலும் புல்லிக் கொண்டாங்
ககன்மனைத் தாய்க்குச் சொன்னா ளவளுந்தன் கேட்குச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: Saying that this man of flawless learning has come to her by the fruit of old deeds of penance done with a mind free of fault, the nurse embraces her again, then tells the girl's mother, who tells her husband.
nuance: Two things are joined: the nurse reads the match as karma ripening from former penance, and the news moves up the household in the order of akam disclosure, nurse to mother to father.
event: The nurse reports Gunamalai's choice to her mother, who reports it to her husband.

tamil: வினையமா மாலை கேள்வன் குபேரமித் திரற்குச் சொல்ல
வனையதே பட்ட தென்றா லையனே நங்கைக் கொத்தான்
வனையவே பட்ட போலு மணிமருண் முலையி னாளைப்
புனையவே பட்ட பொற்றார்ப் புண்ணியற் கீது மென்றான்.
reading: When Vinayamalai tells her husband Kuberamittiran, he says that if it has gone so, the lord is fit for the girl, the gold-garlanded man of merit suits her as though she were made for him.
event: Kuberamittiran hears his wife's report and approves Civakan as the girl's match.

reading: He sends four learned men skilled in speech and verse on a fine chariot; they go, and the merchant with the heated-gold anklet bids them come and receives them.
event: Kuberamittiran sends four learned envoys to Kantukkatan, who welcomes them.

reading: Kantukkatan gives them betel from a gem casket and they take it; then words are spoken to the merchant: 'You who are like the glowing kalpaka tree, I have been granted to come; today I have reached heaven.'
nuance: The speech is in the first person singular (வரப்பெற்றேன், சேர்ந்தேன்), which fits Kantukkatan's welcome, yet the closing words say it was said to the merchant, as in 1056; read here as the envoys' courtesy to their host, but the speaker is doubtful.
event: Kantukkatan offers the envoys betel, and they greet him with praise.

reading: The envoys tell the merchant that though no one offers a daughter with 'we give our girl, take her for your son', they have agreed today to give theirs to the one like a golden hill, on whose chest the lotus goddess dwells.
nuance: The bride's side breaking custom to offer the girl is itself the compliment: Civakan's worth justifies it.
event: The envoys formally offer Gunamalai in marriage to Civakan.

reading: The fragrant-garlanded merchant answers that he and the youth will do humble service to the strong-bowed man, and that he has been granted the favour of the creeper-like girl for the strong-shouldered one's son-in-law.
nuance: The phrase சுற்றார் வல்விற் சூடுறு செம்பொற் கழல் describes Kantukkatan in 1054 but here seems to name the bride's father; who is honoured by whom turns on that epithet.
event: Kantukkatan accepts the offer on Civakan's behalf.

tamil: கடல்சூழ் வையங் கைப்படுத் தான் போன் றிதுகூறக்
reading: As Civakan's father says this like one who has seized the sea-girt world, the envoys tell how Civakan conquered the elephant and what the girl's nature is.
event: Kantukkatan rejoices and the envoys recount the elephant fight and Gunamalai's virtues.

tamil: பொறையொன் றாற்றாப் போதணி பொன் கொம்பு அனையாளை
reading: Civakan's mother, of unfailing chastity like the flame of the Vedic sacrificial fire, gladly welcomes the girl as good.
nuance: The Jain epic compares a wife's chastity to the red flame of the mantra-fed Vedic sacrifice, an image of purity it borrows without comment.
event: Sunandai, Civakan's foster mother, approves the match.

reading: Having made the agreement firm, the envoys say they will go; told to leave, they depart on their bridled horses.
event: The envoys take their leave and ride home.

reading: They come back and tell the spear-bearing father what they have settled for the girl; he rejoices, and her mother, coming with anklets ringing, hears it and says it is fitting.
event: The envoys report to Kuberamittiran and his wife, who both approve.

reading: All agree that she is fit for the man fit for fortune, the astrologers fix the day, and they set out to end the pining of the girl who is nectar to drink.
event: The astrologers fix the wedding day.

reading: With the shout of a sea that breaks its shore, drums, mulavu and white conches, and crowds jostling, the Kama-like hero weds the girl of fragrant hair.
event: Civakan marries Gunamalai.

reading: With the girl, the merchant gives seven hundred adorned maidens, a crore of red gold and five old villages of sugarcane fields.
nuance: நாய்கன் named Kantukkatan in 1054, but a bride's father gives the dowry; Kuberamittiran, a merchant chief, is the likelier giver.
event: Gunamalai's father gives a dowry of maidens, gold and villages.

reading: The narrator praises her as a womanly nectar found neither in heaven nor on this earth, the nectar he has won.
While bees hum on the honey, her breasts press against him and his garland drips nectar: such is the pleasure they come to.
event: Civakan and Gunamalai enjoy their first union.

reading: He delights in her as if the sea's coral and pearl gave him nectar, while her kohl eyes and brows waver and her golden anklet-bells cry out.
event: The lovers' union continues.

reading: Civakan teases her: when the elephant threw all into turmoil she hid her long eyes in fear, and now the creeper that melts has melted for him, a strange thing and not the world's way.
nuance: The last line (வம்பே இது வையகத்தார் வழக்கு அன்றே) can be read as 'this is new, not the world's custom' or as a rhetorical 'is this not the world's custom?'; the tone of the teasing turns on it.

reading: He asks her to tell him today whether the harsh word spoken unguardedly about Suramanjari, who lost the powder contest at the water festival, is an arrow or nectar to him.
nuance: The harsh word is most likely his own verdict on the powders, which won him Gunamalai but drove Suramanjari to vow that he would come and worship her feet (899); whether அவள்கண் means 'about her' or 'to her' is not certain.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1070-1093 (10/13)
theme: Gunamalai's lovers' sulk is appeased and the two are joined in play, while the king's elephant, shamed since Civakan checked it, refuses food; the usurper Kattiyangaran, told the cause, sends his men to seize Civakan, who arms to fight but, recalling his teacher's word and at his foster parents' plea, lets himself be bound as the city wails and Sunandai falls in grief.
source_issues: 1071 line 1 prints தூமஞ் கமழ் where sandhi wants தூமங் கமழ்; a minor slip.
1079 line 1 prints நோககிக் for நோக்கிக், and line 2 கோக்குழர்ம் for கோக்குழாம் (TSCII slips).

1088 line 2 (கோளிழுக் குற்ற பின்றைக் வருகென வானி னுச்சி) repeats the words வருகென வானி னுச்சி of 1087 line 2 and breaks the second-letter rhyme in ளி of lines 1, 3 and 4; the line is corrupt, likely a copying error from the verse above.
1091 line 2 prints றோன்லுக் காண்மை, probably for (தோ)ன்றலுக் காண்மை with a letter lost.
1076 to 1091 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired).

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan
a merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant and married
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, the king of this chapter (வேந்தன், கொற்றவன்)
the king's war elephant that Civakan once checked when it charged Gunamalai
the mahout of the king's elephant
the swift young men the king sends to seize Civakan
the serving woman in Gunamalai's house who warns Civakan
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father (தாதை, தந்தை)
Kantukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother
the people of Rajamapuram

reading: Gunamalai, in a lovers' sulk, tells Civakan that he came to praise the beauty of another woman's powder, that he has forgotten her and that the other dwells in his heart, and bids him go, asking whether she is a simple woman who cannot see it plainly.
nuance: The verse never names the woman of fine shoulders (நற்றோள் அவள்) or whose powder (சுண்ணம்) is meant; the powder recalls the scented-powder contest between Gunamalai and Suramanjari that began this ilampakam, and the charge may be a feigned one turned on his own praise. Who is meant cannot be fixed from this verse alone.
event: Gunamalai sulks and sends Civakan away, accusing him of thinking of another woman.

reading: She leaves off her incense-scented silk, tears at her garland, rubs away the cool sandal, draws her bow-like brow tight, and with eyes like Kama's arrows reddening she sulks.
nuance: Every act undoes an adornment: the sulk is shown as a woman unmaking the toilette made for love.
event: Gunamalai strips off her ornaments and sulks with reddened eyes.

reading: Civakan falls at the feet of the lightning-waisted woman and pleads, his words pour like water on the fire of her anger, the tears leave her eyes, and she looks at him with joy and heady pride.
nuance: Line 2 is compressed (சொன்னீர் அவள் அழலுட் சொரிந்து ஆற்ற): his words are the water, her anger the fire, the image that the king's fire-like anger will answer a few verses later.
event: Civakan falls at Gunamalai's feet and pleads until her sulk gives way to joy.

reading: Civakan praises her as a golden creeper with soft shoulders like bamboo and young breasts under a gem ornament, saying that if the world were praised to its full worth it would only equal the price of her long bright eyes.
He clasps her in his arms, her coral lips and jewelled girdle gleaming, and desires the doll-like woman as nectar won on a lucky day.
event: Civakan embraces Gunamalai and they are reconciled in love.

reading: The narrator turns from the bright-faced, coral-mouthed woman of long painted eyes and her days of play with him to tell what befell the skilled one.
nuance: A hinge verse: the play is cut off by வித்தகற்கு உற்றது, what came upon him, announcing trouble without naming it.

tamil: அரும்பெறற் குருசிற் கஞ்ஞான் றோடிய நாக நாணிக்
கரும்பெறி கடிகை யோடு நெய்ம்மலி கவளங் கொள்ளா
திரும்புசெய் குழவித் திங்கண் மருப்பிடைத் தடக்கை நாற்றிச்
சுரும்பொடு வண்டு பாடச் சுளிவொடு நின்ற தன்றே.
reading: Ashamed since it fled from the prince that day, the elephant will not take its sugarcane and ghee-soaked balls of food, but stands sullen with its curved trunk hung between its moon-like tusks while bees hum about it.
nuance: The beast is given the lovers' own state: it stands with சுளிவு, sullen like a sulking woman, so the elephant's shame mirrors Gunamalai's ஊடல் in the verses just before.
event: The king's elephant, shamed by its defeat by Civakan, refuses its food.

tamil: பகைபுறங் கொடுத்த வேந்திற் பரிவொடு பகடு நிற்பத்
தகைநிறக் குழைக டாழ்ந்து சாந்தின்வாய் நக்கி மின்னப்
புகைநிறத் துகிலிற் பொன்னாண் டுயல்வரப் போந்து வேந்தன்
மிகைநிறக் களிற்றை நோக்கி வேழமென் னுற்ற தென்றான்.
reading: Like a king whose enemy has turned his back, the king comes out in his earrings and sandal, his gold thread swaying on smoke-coloured silk, looks at the elephant standing in distress and asks what has come over it.
event: The king sees his elephant off its food and asks what ails it.

tamil: கொற்றவன் குறிப்பு நோக்கிக் குஞ்சரப் பாகன் கூறு
மிற்றென வுரைத்த றேற்றே னிறைவநின் னருளி னாங்கொல்
செற்றமிக் குடைமை யாற்கொல் சீவக னின்ன நாளான்
மற்றிதற் குடற்சி செய்ய மதுமிது செறித்த தென்றான்.
reading: Reading the king's mind, the mahout says he cannot tell for certain whether it is by the lord's grace or from great enmity, but that some days ago Civakan, to anger it, checked its must and this has made it so.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard: the mahout's hedge (நின் அருளினாம் கொல், செற்றம் மிக்குடைமையாற் கொல்) may be his own doubt or a sly hint that Civakan acted from enmity to the king; the mahout reads the king's குறிப்பு and words his report to feed it.
event: The mahout tells the king that Civakan's checking of the elephant has broken its spirit.

tamil: ஈண்டழற் குட்டம் போல வெரியெழத் திருகி நோககிக்
கோண்டரு குறும்பர் வெம்போர் கோக்குழர்ம் வென்ற துள்ளி
மாண்டதில் செய்கை சூழ்ந்த வாணிகன் மகனை வல்லே
யாண்டிறங் களைவெ னோடிப் பற்றுபு தம்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Twisting like a blazing fire-pit and glaring, the king, recalling that Civakan had beaten the troop of hill-chiefs in fierce battle, orders his men to seize at once and bring the merchant's son who planned a deed beneath his station, saying he will root out his strength.
nuance: The elephant is only the occasion: the king remembers the earlier victory over the hill-raiders, so wounded pride over Civakan's rising fame drives the order. Calling him வாணிகன் மகன், the merchant's son, the usurper does not know whose son he has ordered taken. Lines 1 and 2 carry slips (நோககிக், கோக்குழர்ம்) and line 3 is obscure.
event: The king orders Civakan seized.

tamil: கன்றிய வெகுளி வேந்தன் கால்வலி யிளையர் காய்ந்து
கொன்றுயிர் கொணர வோடுங் கொழுங்குடர்க் கண்ணி மாலை
யொன்றிய வுதிரச் செச்சை யொண்ணிண மீக்கொ டானைத்
தென்றிசைக் கிறைவன் றூதிற் செம்மலைச் சென்று சேர்ந்தார்.
reading: At the angry king's command the swift-footed young men run to kill and bring his life, wearing garlands of guts, smeared with blood and topped with fat like messengers of the lord of the south, Death, and reach the noble one.
nuance: கொன்று உயிர் கொணர, 'kill and bring his life', is the king's order as the runners understand it; it exceeds the 'seize and bring' (பற்றுபு தம்மின்) of 1079, and the gore they wear makes them Death's envoys before any blow is struck.
event: The king's men run to take Civakan and reach him.

tamil: சண்பக மாலை வேய்ந்து சந்தனம் பளிதந் தீற்றி
விண்புக நாறு சாந்தின் விழுமுலைக் காம வல்லி
கொண்டெழுந் துருவு காட்டி முகத்திடைக் குளித்துத் தோண்மேல்
வண்டளி ரீன்று சுட்டி வாணுதல் பூப்ப வைத்தான்.
reading: Meanwhile he dresses her in a champak garland and sandal and camphor, draws with fragrant paste a love-creeper on her breasts that seems to climb to her face and put out tender leaves on her shoulders, and sets an ornament on her bright brow.
nuance: The order of the verses sets the lovers' toilette directly against the runners' garlands of guts in 1080: two kinds of adornment, one of love and one of death, converge on the same house.
event: Civakan paints and adorns Gunamalai.

tamil: பண்ணடி வீழுந் தீஞ்சொற் பாவைநின் வனப்பிற் கெல்லாங்
கண்ணடி கருங்க ணென்னு மம்பறாத் தூணி தன்னாற்
புண்ணுடை மாம்பத் தோவா தெய்தியா லெங்குப் பெற்றாய்
பெண்ணுடைப் பேதை யென்றோர் நாண்முற்றும் பிதற்றி னானே.
reading: Civakan babbles the whole day to her: doll whose sweet speech the very melody bows to, where did you get the never-empty quiver of your dark eyes, from which you shoot without pause at me already wounded, foolish girl?
nuance: பிதற்றினான், 'he babbled', is the narrator's word: the lover's talk is shown as delight that has lost its measure just as danger arrives.

tamil: திங்கள்சேர் முடியி னானுஞ் செல்வியும் போன்று செம்பொ
னிங்குவார் கழலி னானுங் கோதையு மிருந்த போழ்திற்
சிங்கவே றெள்ளிச் சூழ்ந்த சிறுநரிக் குழாத்திற் சூழ்ந்தா
ரங்கது கண்ட தாதி யையனுக் கின்ன தென்றாள்.
reading: While he of the golden anklet and his garlanded wife sat like the moon-crowned god and his consort, the king's men closed round like a pack of little jackals round a lion they despise, and the serving woman who saw it told the master.
event: The king's men surround the house and the maid warns Civakan.

tamil: என்றவ ளுரைப்பக் கேட்டே யிடிபட முழங்கிச் செந்தீ
நின்றெரி வதனை யொத்து நிண்முழைச் சிங்க வேறு
தன்றுணைப் பெட்டை யோடு தான்புறப் பட்ட தொத்தான்
குன்றிரண் டிருந்த போலுங் குங்குமக் குவவுத் தோளான்.
reading: Hearing her, the hero of shoulders like twin saffron-smeared hills rose roaring like thunder and blazing like fire, like a maned lion coming out of its cave with its mate.
nuance: The lion of 1083, scorned by jackals, now comes out with its mate: the simile keeps Gunamalai at his side even as he turns to fight.
event: Civakan rises in fury at the news.

tamil: பொன்னரி மாலை தாழப் போதணி கூந்த லேந்திப்
பன்னரு மாலை யாற்குப் பட்டதை யெவன்கொ லென்னாப்
பின்னரு மாலை யோராள் பெருநடுக் குற்று நின்றாண்
மன்னரு மாலை நாக மழையிடிப் புண்ட தொத்தாள்.
reading: Holding up her flower-decked hair, gold-strand garland hanging, she cried 'what has happened to my lord of the garland?', and, unable to grasp more, stood shaking hard, like a great serpent struck by thunder in the rain.
nuance: The four lines rhyme on மாலை in four senses (garland, the garlanded one, confusion, a garland-like serpent); the wordplay is the poet's, the terror hers.
event: Gunamalai stands trembling in terror for Civakan.

tamil: கடுகிய விளையர் நோக்குங் கண்ணிய பொருளு மெண்ணி
யடுசிலை யழல வேந்தி யாருயிர் பருகற் கொத்த
விடுகணை தெரிந்து தானை வீக்கற விசித்து வெய்தாத்
தொடுகழ னரல வீக்கிச் சொல்லுமின் வந்த தென்றான்.
reading: Weighing the look of the hurrying men and the purpose they had in mind, he took up his killing bow so that it seemed to blaze, chose arrows fit to drink life, girded his garment tight, bound on his anklet and said 'tell me why you have come'.
event: Civakan arms himself and demands the men's errand.

tamil: அடிநிழற் றருக வென்றெம் மாணைவேந் தருளிச் செய்தான்
வடிமலர்த் தாரி னாய்நீ வருகென வானி னுச்சி
யிடியுரு மேற்றிற் சீறி யிருநிலஞ் சுடுதற் கொத்த
கடிமதின் மூன்று மெய்த கடவுளிற் கனன்று சொன்னான்.
reading: The men say that their king of command has graciously ordered that he come to the shade of his feet, and bid him of the fine-flower garland come; at this he flared up like thunder from the height of the sky and, burning like the god who shot the three fortified cities that would scorch the earth, spoke.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are the men's words inside the narration; அடிநிழல் தருக, come to the shade of the feet, is the courtesy of a summons to a subject, which the hero hears as a demand for submission.
event: The men deliver the summons and Civakan blazes in anger.

tamil: வாளிழுக் குற்ற கண்ணாள் வருமுலை நயந்து வேந்தன்
கோளிழுக் குற்ற பின்றைக் வருகென வானி னுச்சி
னாளிழுக் குற்று வீழ்வ தின்றுகொ னந்த திண்டேர்
தோளிழுக் குற்ற மொய்ம்ப பண்ணெனச் சொல்லி னானே.
reading: Civakan says that after the king, desiring the breasts of a woman whose eyes outdo the sword, lost his hold, today may be the day this man's life slips and he falls, and bids a strong-armed companion harness the sturdy chariot.
nuance: Line 2 repeats words of 1087's line 2 (வருகென வானி னுச்சி) and is corrupt, so the sentence cannot be fixed. If the king of line 1 is Saccandan, who gave up rule for love of Vijayai, Civakan is naming his father's fall and the usurper's coming one; நந்த in line 3 may be a call to his brother Nandattan or a verb, 'to perish'.
event: Civakan calls for his chariot to go against the king.

tamil: வேந்தொடு மாறு கோடல் விளிகுற்றார் தொழில தாகுங்
காய்ந்திடு வெகுளி நீக்கிக் கைகட்டி யிவனை யுய்த்தா
லாய்ந்தடு மழற்சி நீங்கு மதுபொரு ளென்று நல்ல
சாந்துடை மார்பன் றாதை தன்மனத் திழைக்கின் றானே.
reading: The father of the sandal-chested hero reasons within himself that to contend with the king is the work of those bound to die, and that if they put off their burning anger, tie his hands and send him, the king's killing rage will cease; that is the wise course.
nuance: Kantukkatan's prudence assumes the king's anger (அழற்சி) can be appeased by surrender; it echoes in reverse the teacher's demand in 393 that Civakan bear no அழற்சி against the usurper for a year. The merchant counsels submission to the man who killed Civakan's real father.
event: Kantukkatan resolves to send Civakan bound to the king.

tamil: ஊன்பிறங் கொளிரும் வேலா னோர்த்துத்த னுவாத்தி சொல்லாற்
றான்புறங் கட்டப் பட்டுத் தன்சினந் தணிந்து நிற்பத்
தேன்பிறங் கலங்கன் மாலைச் சுநந்தையுந் துணைவன் றானுங்
கோன்புறங் காப்பச் சேறல் குணமெனக் கூறி னாரே.
reading: The hero of the bright spear, recalling his teacher's word, let his arms be bound behind him and stood with his anger quenched, while Sunandai and her husband said that going under the king's protection was the right course.
nuance: Two motives are given and kept apart: the parents' worldly counsel in line 4 and, decisively, the teacher's word (உவாத்தி சொல்) in line 1, the year's restraint promised in 393. Sunandai and Kantukkatan voice the claim together; voiced_by names him for both.
event: Remembering his teacher's word, Civakan lets himself be bound.

tamil: ஈன்றதாய் தந்தை வேண்ட விவ்விட ருற்ற தென்றாற்
றோன்லுக் காண்மை குன்றா தென்றசொல் லிமிழிற் பூட்டி
மூன்றனைத் துலக மெல்லா முட்டினு முருக்கு மாற்றல்
வான்றரு மாரி வண்கை மதவலி பிணிக்கப் பட்டான்.
reading: Because the mother who bore him and his father begged, saying this trouble had come, and bound him with the halter of the word that a noble one's manhood is not lessened by it, the mighty one, whose strength could crush the three worlds together and whose giving hand is like rain, was bound.
nuance: The verse calls Sunandai ஈன்றதாய், the mother who bore him, though she is his foster mother; it speaks as the household and the city know him. The real bond is the word (சொல் இமிழ்), not the cord. Line 2 (றோன்லுக் காண்மை) is corrupt, likely for தோன்றலுக்கு ஆண்மை.
event: At his foster parents' plea Civakan submits to being bound.

reading: As the warriors bound the twin shoulders of the long-haired prince with their belts, the old festive city wailed as if the serpent had seized the fiery god, the sun.
nuance: The eclipse simile makes the binding a cosmic and temporary darkening: the serpent swallows the sun only for a while, which forecasts his release.
event: The king's men bind Civakan's arms and the city laments.

reading: Scattering the pearls on her shoulders, the pearls of her breasts and the pearls of tears streaming from her eyes, his foster mother cried 'my young one, Nambi, Civaka Sami!' and fell like lightning into the long sea of unending grief.
nuance: She calls him சீவக சாமி, 'lord Civaka', the name the invocation gives him, and the triple pearls (ornament, breast, tears) make one shower of loss.
event: Sunandai falls in grief as Civakan is led away.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1094-1117 (11/13)
theme: Civakan, seized at Kattiyangaran's order and bound at his parents' word, tells the grieving women of his house that one who knows births and release does not grieve; the city's women run from their games and crafts to lament, blaming karma, their own want of penance, the king and the father; Kantukkatan forbids the weeping, boasts the house's firmness, and as his son goes like a lion bound with a spider's thread, sends twelve crores of gold to cool the king's anger.
source_issues: 1096, 1098, 1108, 1109, 1113-1117 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins look sound.
1106 line 1 (மாதரார்கள் கற்பினுக்கு உடைந்த) and 1110 line 3 (பாக்கயம், perhaps for பாக்கியம்) are hard to construe as written.
1114 line 2 (வேறிரு கூறு செய்வான் றுன்னினான்) runs words across the join and the first person of 1114-1115 makes the speaker uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, raised by Kantukkatan, seized and bound at the usurper's order (புலவலன், பூணான் here)
the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant
the women of Civakan's household, likened to goddesses of the house
the women of the city's streets and houses
the people of Rajamapuram, the old city
the merchant who raised Civakan, his father here (தாதை, கந்துகன்)
Kantukkatan's wife, who raised Civakan (named in 1109)
the usurping minister now ruling, who has ordered Civakan seized (not named in this run)

reading: Gunamalai, holding up her silk as the men lead Civakan away, cries twice that this is not fitting for her lord and is like a flower garland fallen into fire.
event: Gunamalai cries out that the arrest is not fitting for her lord and wilts in grief.

tamil: எரிதவழ் குன்றத் துச்சி யிரும்பொறிக் கலாப மஞ்ஞை
யிரிவன போன்று மாடத் தில்லுறை தெய்வ மன்னார்
பரிவுறு மனத்தி னோடிப் பட்டதை யுணர்ந்து பொற்றா
ரரியுறழ் மொய்ம்ப வோவென் றாகுலப் பூசல் செய்தார்.
reading: The women of the mansion, like goddesses of the house, run out like peacocks fleeing a burning hill, learn what has happened and raise a cry of lament to the lion-shouldered one.
event: The women of Civakan's house run out, learn of his arrest and lament aloud.

tamil: கங்கையின் சுழியிற் பட்ட காமரு பிணையின் மாழ்கி
யங்கவர்க் குற்ற துள்ளி யவலநீ ரழுந்து கின்ற
குங்குமக் கொடியோ டேந்திக் கோலம்வீற் றிருந்த கொம்மைப்
பொங்கிள முலையி னார்க்குப் புலவல னிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: To these women, sinking in grief like a doe caught in a whirlpool of the Ganges, the learned hero speaks the words that follow.
nuance: The narrator names him புலவலன், the one skilled in learning, at the moment he is bound: the title prepares the doctrinal consolation of the next verse rather than any warrior's answer.
event: Civakan turns to the grieving women of his house to speak to them.

tamil: கட்டுயி லனந்தர் போலக் கதிகளுட் டோன்று மாறும்
விட்டுயிர் போகு மாறும் வீடுபெற் றுயரு மாறு
முட்பட வுணர்ந்த யானே யுள்குழைந் துருகல் செல்லே
னெட்பக வனைத்து மார்வ மேதமே யிரங்கல் வேண்டா.
reading: Civakan says that he, who has understood within how souls appear in the states of birth as one wakes from heavy sleep, how life leaves, and how it gains release and rises, will not melt in grief; attachment even the size of a split sesame seed is a fault, so they must not grieve.
nuance: கதிகள் (the states of birth) and release as rising (வீடுபெற்று உயருமாறு) are the Jain frame the poem uses elsewhere; the school is the text's vocabulary, not a label added. The sesame measure (எட்பக அனைத்தும்) is the Kural's phrase for a small inner enmity (Kural 889, எட்பக வன்ன), but only two words match, so it is not marked as an echo.
event: Civakan, bound and led away, forbids his household to grieve.

tamil: நன்மணி யிழந்த நாகர் நல்லிளம் படியர் போல
வின்மணி யிழந்த சாம்பி யிருநில மிவர்க ளெய்த
மின்னணி மதியங் கோள்வாய் விசும்பிடை நடப்ப தேபோற்
கன்மணி யுமிழும் பூணான் கடைபல கடந்து சென்றான்.
reading: As the women, having lost their jewel, fall to the ground wilting like young naga women robbed of their gem, Civakan in gem-bright ornaments passes gate after gate like the moon moving across the sky in the mouth of the eclipse planet.
nuance: The eclipse image (மதியம் கோள்வாய்) makes the arrest a temporary swallowing: the moon in the planet's mouth still shines and will come out.
event: Civakan is led out through the many gates of the house while its women collapse.

reading: The young women of the city, crying that their hearts are burnt, leave their balls, dolls, play-stones and toy houses and run out with tinkling anklets to look.
event: Young girls of the city drop their games and run out to see Civakan led away.

reading: Women with jasmine garlands slipping and earrings flashing leave their vinas, breathe hot sighs and run till the street is full, anklets crying out.
event: Women leave their vinas and crowd the street.

reading: Women whose dark hair falls over their necks and whose breasts flush red throw down the balls that have made their palms ache, come there and are bewildered.
event: Women at ball-play leave it and come, dazed with grief.

reading: Garlanded women, their hearts melting, shed hot tears from kohl-lined eyes like the sea casting pearls and cry with great love, 'What can we do, O lord?'
event: Women weep and cry out to Civakan in helpless love.

reading: The dancing women, slender as lightning, run burning through the street with gold ear-rolls falling, jewels scattering and hair coming loose, asking what has befallen their beloved.
event: The dancing women of the city run through the street asking what has happened to him.

reading: Women with spear-long eyes brimming beat their bellies in grief, saying that if the garlanded one's beauty fades, the body will go and life itself will perish today.
nuance: நீயும் (line 2) addresses someone, perhaps a companion or the woman's own life; the line is read as a lament without fixing the addressee.
event: Women beat their bellies and say their lives will end if his beauty is harmed.

reading: Young women throw off their honeyed garlands and ornaments and come to look, asking whether he who was like the wish-granting creeper of desire has come to this, their slender waists aching as they run.
event: Women cast off their ornaments and run to look at him.

reading: Some women restring the gems of girdles that broke, others scatter them as they run, and the flower-like women come before the garlanded one, crying that this is not fit, and beat their bellies.
nuance: Line 1 (மாதரார்கள் கற்பினுக்கு உடைந்த மாமணிக்கலை) is hard to construe: the girdles may have broken in the women's haste, or the line may say that their steadfastness gave way at the sight of him; the reading leaves it open.
event: Women run before Civakan crying that his arrest is unjust and beat their bellies.

reading: Women who had been at their painting, with brush-box, board and fine colours, leave them, wilt like peacocks in distress, and with garlands scorched by their burning breath come and cling to the gateway.
event: Women leave their painting and cling to the gate to see him.

tamil: வினையது விளைவு காண்மி னென்றுகை விதிர்த்து நிற்பா
ரினையனாய்த் தெளியச் சென்றா லிடிக்குங்கொ லிவனை யென்பார்
புனைநல மழகு கல்வி பொன்றுமா லின்றொ டென்பார்
வனைகலத் திகிரி போல மறுகுமெம் மனங்க ளென்பார்.
reading: Some women shake their hands and say 'see the fruit of deeds', some fear that if he is taken in this state the king will strike him, some say that his beauty, grace and learning will end today, and some say their hearts whirl like a potter's wheel.
nuance: The karma explanation is one voice among several in a crowd; the next verse blames the father and the king in the same breath, so the poem gives the arrest more than one cause without settling which.
event: The city women speak their fears and griefs as Civakan is led away.

tamil: நோற்றிலர் மகளி ரென்பார் நோங்கண்டீர் தோள்க ளென்பார்
கூற்றத்தைக் கொம்மை கொட்டிக் குலத்தொடு முடியு மென்பா
ரேற்றதொன் றன்று தந்தை செய்தவிக் கொடுமை யென்பா
ராற்றலள் சுநந்தை யென்பா ராதகா தறனே யென்பார்.
reading: Some say the women did no penance to deserve him, some point to his hurt shoulders, some say the king has beckoned Death and will perish with his line, some that the father's act was a cruelty unfit to be done, some that Sunandai cannot bear it, and some cry out to dharma that it is not right.
nuance: Merit (நோற்றிலர்), the king's folly and the father's choice are all blamed here together, beside the previous verse's 'fruit of deeds'. The father's act was itself a decision to submit (verses 1089-1091), so the women condemn what the story has framed as prudence. கூற்றத்தைக் கொம்மை கொட்டி recalls Kural 894 (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால்) in sense, but only one word matches, so it is not marked as an echo.
event: The city women blame their own lack of merit, the king and Civakan's father for the arrest.

tamil: தூக்குமின் காளை சீறிற் றுற்றிவ னுளனோ வென்பார்
காக்குமால் வைய மெல்லாங் காவல னாகி யென்பார்
பாக்கயம் பெரிது மேகா ணிதுவுமோர் பான்மை யென்பார்
நோக்கன்மி னாணுங் கண்டீர் நுதிகொ ணாகரிக னென்பார்.
