reading: Some say, 'weigh it: if this bull raged, would the king survive?'; some say he would guard the whole world as its ruler; some say it is great luck and this too is a turn of fate; some say 'do not stare, he is ashamed, the keen and courtly one.'
nuance: The women's wish that he would guard the world as king is unknowing irony: he is the dead king's son, though no one here knows it. Line 3 (பாக்கயம் பெரிதுமே காண்) may mean the king's good fortune that Civakan does not resist, or the city's luck in such a man; the reading is not fixed.
event: The city women say Civakan could overpower the king and is fit to rule, and pity his shame.

tamil: பூவரம் பாய கோதைப் பொன்னனார் புலவி நீக்கி
நூபுரந் திருத்திச் சேந்த நுதிவிர னொந்த வென்பார்
யாவரும் புகழு மைய னழகுகெட் டொழியு மாயிற்
கோபுர மாட மூதூர் கூற்றுண விளிக வென்பார்.
reading: Some say the sharp fingers that, removing the sulks of golden women, set right their anklets and grew red are now hurt; some say that if the lord all praise loses his beauty, let the old city of towers and mansions perish as food for Death.
event: The city women lament his bound hands and curse the city if he is harmed.

tamil: கருஞ்சிலை மறவர் கொண்ட கணநிரை விடுக்க வல்ல
கருங்கட றுளுப்பிட் டாங்குக் கல்லெனக் கலங்கிக் காம
ரருங்கடி யரண மூதூ ராகுல மயங்கிற் றன்றே.
reading: Crying that this is unfit for the strong shoulders trained with the great bow that freed the herd seized by the black-bowed hunters, the old city behind its guarded walls is thrown into tumult like a dark sea churned by a mountain.
event: The whole city rises in grief and uproar at the arrest.

tamil: இங்கன மிவர்க ளேக வெரியகம் விளைக்கப் பட்ட
வெங்கணை விடலை தாதை வியனக ரவல மெய்தி
யங்கவ ருகுத்த கண்ணீ ரடித்துக ளவிப்ப நோக்கிப்
பொங்கம ருழக்கும் வேலான் புலம்புகொண் டழேற்க வென்றான்.
reading: As the crowds move thus, the father of the hero of the fire-hot arrows, seeing the great city's grief and the tears that laid the dust at their feet, tells them, as the spear-bearer who fights in war, not to weep.
nuance: பொங்கமர் உழக்கும் வேலான் (line 4) gives the merchant a warrior's epithet; it may refer to the son rather than the father, which would change who forbids the weeping.
event: Kantukkatan sees the city's grief and tells the people not to weep.

tamil: மின்னினான் மலையை யீர்ந்து வேறிரு கூறு செய்வான்
றுன்னினான் றுளங்கி னல்லாற் றுளங்கலம் மலையிற் குண்டே
யன்னதே துணிந்த நீதி யருநவை நமனு மாற்றா
னென்னைநேர் நின்று வாழ்த லிருநிலத் தாவ துண்டே.
reading: The speaker says that if one with lightning splits a mountain in two, it is the striker who shakes, not 'we', deeper than the mountain; such is the justice resolved, which even Yama cannot overturn; can anyone on the wide earth live standing against me?
nuance: The speech is most likely Kantukkatan's, following his 'do not weep' in 1113, but the first person (துளங்கலம், என்னை) could be the house speaking, or Civakan's words reported; the defiant tone sits oddly with the father who just reasoned that opposing a king is the deed of the doomed (1089).

tamil: வளைகடல் வலையிற் சூழ்ந்து மால்வரை வேலி கோலி
யுளையரி படுக்க லுற்றான் படுப்பினும் படுக்க மற்றென்
கிளையழ வென்னை வாள்வாய்க் கீண்டிட லுற்று நின்றான்
றளையவிழ் கண்ணி சிந்தத் தன்றலை நிலத்த தன்றே.
reading: The speaker says the king has set out to snare a maned lion by netting the curved sea and fencing it with mountains; let him snare it if he can, but if he stands ready to cleave me with the sword while my kin weep, his own head, its garland scattered, will lie on the ground.
nuance: The lion is Civakan, and the net of sea and mountains says the king's means are absurdly large and still too weak; who 'me' (என்னை) is, the father or the son, is not certain.

tamil: நீரகம் பொதிந்த மேக நீனிற நெடுநல் யானைப்
போரகத் தழலும் வாட்கைப் பொன்னெடுங் குன்ற மன்னா
னார்கலி யாணர் மூதூ ரழுதுபின் செல்லச் செல்வான்
சீருறு சிலம்பி நூலாற் சிமிழ்ப்புண்ட சிங்க மொத்தான்.
reading: Civakan, like a long golden hill, whose sword burns in war among dark cloud-coloured elephants, walks on while the festive old city follows weeping, like a lion bound with a spider's thread.
nuance: The spider's thread (சிலம்பி நூல்) makes the binding his own consent: the bond could not hold him, and what holds him is the word given to his parents (1091).
event: Civakan is led away bound while the city follows weeping.

tamil: மன்னர்தம் வெகுளி வெந்தீ மணிமுகில் காண மின்னிப்
பொன்மழை பொழியி னந்து மன்றெனிற் புகைந்து பொங்கித்
துன்னினார் தம்மை யெல்லாஞ் சுட்டிடு மென்று செம்பொன்
பன்னிரு கோடி யுய்த்துக் கந்துகன் பணிந்து சொன்னான்.
reading: Kantukkatan, reckoning that a king's anger is a hot fire that will die down if gold rains on it like lightning-lit cloud, and otherwise will smoke, flare and burn all who come near, sends twelve crores of red gold and speaks humbly to the king.
nuance: The merchant answers royal anger with money, the means of his own class, after the city's laments and his own defiant words; the plea itself begins in the next verse.
event: Kantukkatan sends twelve crores of gold to the king and pleads humbly for his son.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1118-1141 (12/13)
theme: Kantukkatan's plea for his son fails before Kattiyangaran, who swears to brand Civakan a thief; the father comforts Sunandai and Gunamalai with an ascetic's old prophecy that a famous son would come to them and that a yaksha would rescue him from the graceless king, while the friends learn that Civakan let his parents bind him and Buddhisenan plans to burn the city by night to free him.
source_issues: Every verse of 1118-1141 was printed in eight half-lines and has been joined into four by the build.
1125 line 4 has பட்டினிப பிரிவு, a missing pulli (பட்டினிப்); line 3 (ஆறும் மூன்றும் அமைந்த நால் அமிர்தம்) is obscure.
1139 line 2 has நோக்கிச சூழிமால், a missing pulli (நோக்கிச்).
1141 lines 3-4 are divided at விப்பர் / லாலைத்தீ, which looks like a misdivision (perhaps இப்பால் ஆலைத்தீ); the line's sense is uncertain.
1140 line 3 (இறைக்குற்றேல் செய்தல் இன்றி) and 1134 line 4 (ஒட்டியிஃ துணர லாமே) are hard to construe as written.

cast.role: the merchant who raised Civakan, called நாய்கன் and தந்தை here
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne and has Civakan bound
Kantukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother (தாய், மாமி)
the ascetic who once came to Kantukkatan's house when Sunandai's children had died and foretold Civakan's coming and his capture (கடவுள், அறவியான், விழுத்தவன்)
the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant, here grieving with Sunandai
the hero, called சீவக சாமி and மைந்தன் here
Civakan's companions
Civakan's friend
the spy the friends sent, who reports Civakan's binding
Kattiyangaran's warriors who surround Civakan's house
Civakan's companion who plans the night attack

tamil: மன்னவ வருளிக் கேண்மோ மடந்தையோர் கொடியை மூதூர்
நின்மதக் களிறு கொல்ல நினக்கது வடுவென் றெண்ணி
யென்மக னதனை நீக்கி யின்னுயி ரவளைக் காத்தா
னின்னதே குற்ற மாயிற் குணமினி யாது வேந்தே.
reading: Kantukkatan pleads with the king: when the king's own rutting elephant was about to kill a young woman of the old city, his son, thinking the death would be a stain on the king, drove it off and saved her life; if that is a fault, what then is a virtue?
nuance: The plea turns the charge round: the father argues that the rescue protected the king's name, since a killing by the royal elephant would have been the king's disgrace (வடு).
event: Kantukkatan pleads before Kattiyangaran for his son, who saved a girl from the king's elephant.

tamil: நாண்மெய்க்கொண் டீட்டப் பட்டார் நடுக்குறு நவையை நீக்க
லாண்மக்கள் கடனென் றெண்ணி யறிவின்மை துணிந்த குற்றம்
பூண்மெய்க்கொண் டகன்ற மார்ப பொறுமதி யென்று பின்னு
நீண்மைக்க ணின்று வந்த நிதியெலாந் தருவ லென்றான்.
reading: He goes on that it is the duty of men to remove the danger that makes those caught by fate tremble, asks the king to forgive the fault of a youth who acted without thinking, and offers all the wealth his line has gathered over long years.
nuance: The father both defends the act as a man's duty and calls it a fault of thoughtlessness (அறிவின்மை), conceding the king's frame while begging; the offer of wealth follows the twelve crores of 1117.
event: Kantukkatan asks the king's pardon and offers all his wealth.

tamil: வாழிய ரிறைவ தேற்றான் மாநிரை பெயர்த்த காளை
பீழைதான் பொறுக்க வென்னப் பிறங்கிண ரலங்கன் மாலை
சூழ்கதி ராரம் வீழ்நூல் பரிந்தற நிமிர்ந்து திண்டோ
ளூழ்பிணைந் துருமிற் சீறி யுடல்சினங் கடவச் சொன்னான்.
reading: When the merchant asks the lord to bear with the youth who brought back the king's herds, the king, his garland and pearl strings snapping as he swells with rage, speaks in a fury like thunder.
nuance: The father's last argument is service: the same youth had won back the royal herds from the raiders, which only sharpens the king's anger.
event: Kantukkatan reminds the king that his son recovered the king's cattle; the king flares into rage.

tamil: ஆய்களிற் றசனி வேக மதன்மருப் பூசி யாகச்
சீவக னகன்ற மார்ப மோலையாகத் திசைகள் கேட்பக்
காய்பவன் கள்வ ரென்ன வெழுதுவித் திடுவ லின்னே
நீபரி வொழிந்து போய்நின் னகம்புகு நினைய லென்றான்.
reading: The king says he will have the tusk of his elephant Asanivegam made the stylus and Civakan's broad chest the palm leaf, and have 'thief' written on it for all the quarters to hear; the merchant is to stop grieving, go home and think no more of it.
nuance: The punishment answers the rescue with the very beast Civakan subdued: the elephant's tusk is to write the sentence on his body. The charge 'thief' (கள்வர்) has no ground in the story; it is the usurper's word.
event: Kattiyangaran refuses the plea and threatens to brand Civakan a thief with the elephant's tusk.

tamil: நஞ்சனா னுரைப்பக் கேட்டே நாய்கனு நடுங்கி யுள்ளம்
வெஞ்சின வேழ முண்ட விளங்கனி போன்று நீங்கி
யெஞ்சினான் போல நின்றா னேத்தருந் தவத்தின் மிக்க
வஞ்சமில் கொள்கை யான்சொ லமிர்தினால் வற்புற் றானே.
reading: Hearing the venomous king speak, the merchant trembles and stands emptied like a wood-apple eaten hollow by the elephant disease, as if his life had gone, but he is held up by the nectar of the words of the ascetic of guileless doctrine, great in penance beyond praise.
nuance: The verse turns the plot from the court to memory: what saves the father is not his wealth or his plea but a prophecy, which the following verses tell.
event: Kantukkatan, crushed by the refusal, takes strength from an ascetic's earlier words.

tamil: மின்னிலங் கெஃகி னானைப் பெறுகலான் றந்தை மீண்டு
தன்னிலங் குறுக லோடுந் தாயழு தரற்று கின்றா
ளென்னிலை யைற் கென்ன யாவதுங் கவல வேண்டா
பொன்னலங் கொடிய னாயோர் பொருளுரை கேளி தென்றான்.
reading: Unable to win back his son of the shining spear, the father returns home, where the mother weeps and laments; he tells her not to grieve at all over their son's state, and to hear a true word.
event: Kantukkatan returns home and comforts the weeping Sunandai.

tamil: மதுமடை திறந்து தீந்தேன் வார்தரு கோதை நீமுன்
செதுமகப் பலவும் பெற்றுச் சிந்தைகூர் மனத்தை யாகி
யிதுமக வழியின் வாழே னிறப்பல்யா னென்னு மாங்கட்
கதுமெனக் கடவு டோன்றிக் கடைமுகங் குறுக வந்தான்.
reading: He reminds her that long ago, after bearing many children who died, she was sunk in grief and said she would not live but die, and at that moment a holy one appeared suddenly and came to their door.
nuance: The house's later fortune is rooted in a mother's despair over children born dead (செதுமகப் பலவும்), which the earlier narrative of the burning ground (325) presupposes.
event: Kantukkatan recalls how an ascetic came to their door when Sunandai, her children dead, wished to die.

tamil: கறவைகாண் கன்றின் வெஃகிக் கண்டடி பணிந்து காமர்
நறவயா வுயிர்க்கு மாலை நாற்றிய விடத்து ளேற்றி
யறவியாற் காறு மூன்று மமைந்தநா லமிர்த மேந்தப்
பறவைதா துண்ட வண்ணம் பட்டினிப பிரிவு தீர்த்தான்.
reading: Like a cow that sees its calf they longed for him, bowed at his feet, seated him in a place hung with fragrant garlands, and when the four kinds of food fit for the ascetic were set before him he broke his fast as a bird takes pollen.
nuance: Line 3 (ஆறும் மூன்றும் அமைந்த நால் அமிர்தம்) names a set of foods by number that the reading does not resolve; the bee-like eating marks the ascetic's restraint in taking alms.
event: The couple receive the ascetic, seat him and feed him.

tamil: ஆய்மணிப் பவளத் திண்ணை யரும்பெறற் கரகத் தங்கட்
டூய்மணி வாச நன்னீர் துளங்குபொற் கலத்து ளேற்று
வேய்மணித் தோளி நிற்ப விழுத்தவ னியம முற்றி
வாய்மணி முறுவ றோன்ற வந்தனை விதியிற் செய்தேன்.
reading: On the coral seat, with fragrant pure water poured from a rare pitcher into a golden vessel and she of the bamboo shoulders standing by, after the great ascetic had finished his rite, he says, he paid him homage with a smile according to the rule.
event: Kantukkatan washes the ascetic's feet and worships him after his observance.

tamil: ஆறெலாங் கடலுள் வைகு மருந்தவத் திறைவ னூலுள்
வேறெலாப் பொருளும் வைகும் விழுத்தவ வறிதி நீயே
யூறிலா வுணர்வி னோக்கி யுரைமதி யெவன்கொன் மக்கட்
பேறிலா ளல்லள் பெற்ற வுயிர்சென்று பிறக்கு மென்றேன்.
reading: He had said to the ascetic: as all rivers come to rest in the sea, all things rest in the scripture of the lord of great penance, and you know them; look with your unhindered knowledge and tell us why she is not blessed with children, for those she bears go on to be born again.
nuance: பெற்ற உயிர் சென்று பிறக்கும் puts the children's deaths in the language of rebirth: the lives she bears pass on to other births. The 'lord of great penance' (அருந்தவத்து இறைவன்) is the Jina, whose scripture the ascetic is credited with holding whole.
event: Kantukkatan asks the ascetic why their children die.

tamil: வம்பவிழ் கோதை தந்த வான்றுவர்க் காயை வீழ்த்தோர்
செம்பழுக் காயை வாங்கித் திருநிலத் தெடுத்துக் கொண்டாங்
கம்பழ நீண்ட வாட்க ணலமரு மணிசெ யம்பூங்
கொம்படு நுசுப்பி னாய்க்குத் தந்தனென் பேணிக் கொண்டாய்.
reading: He reminds her that she offered the ascetic an unripe areca nut, which he let fall, and that he picked a ripe red areca from the ground and gave it to her, and she took it with care.
nuance: The exchange of the unripe nut for a ripe one is told as the omen the next verse reads; that it figures the dead children replaced by a living son is a reading, not stated.
event: The ascetic drops the unripe areca Sunandai gives and hands her a ripe one.

tamil: பெற்றவந் நிமித்தத் தானும் பிறந்தசொல் வகையி னானு
மற்றமின் மணியை யங்கைக் கொண்டவர் கண்டு காட்டக்
கற்பகங் காம வல்லி யனையநீர் கேண்மி னென்று
முற்றுபு கனிந்த சொல்லான் முனிவரன் மொழியு மன்றே.
reading: From that omen and from the way the words had fallen, seeing as clearly as those who hold a flawless gem in the palm, the chief of sages spoke in ripe words, addressing them as like the wishing tree and the creeper of desire.
nuance: The sage's knowledge is presented as reading signs (நிமித்தம், the manner of speech) and as direct sight like a gem in the hand: omen and insight are joined.
event: The sage reads the omen and begins his prophecy.

tamil: ஒன்றுநீர் கவலல் வேண்டா வுலகெலா மாளுஞ் சீர்த்திப்
பொன்றிக ழுருவி னானோர் புண்ணியற் பெறுதி ரென்ன
நின்றநீ யுவந்து நீங்க நிகழ்பொரு ளெனக்குச் செப்பிப்
பின்றையு நிகழ்வ துண்டு பேசுவல் கேளி தென்றான்.
reading: The sage told them not to worry at all, for they would gain a meritorious son of golden form whose fame would rule the whole world; when she had gone off rejoicing, he told the merchant more of what would happen, and the merchant now says he will tell it.
nuance: The prophecy was split: the mother heard only the promise of a son, while the father alone kept the second part, the danger. That is why he can now comfort her with something she has never heard.
event: The sage foretells that they will gain a famous son, and tells Kantukkatan more in private.

tamil: நிலவுறழ் பூணி னானை நெடுநக ரிரங்கக் கையாத்
தலபல செய்து கொல்வா னருளிலான் கொண்ட போழ்திற்
குலவிய புகழி னானைக் கொண்டுபோ மியக்க னஞ்சல்
சிலபகல் கழிந்து காண்டி சிந்தியீ தென்று சொன்னான்.
reading: The sage had said that when the graceless one seizes the youth of moon-bright jewels to kill him, binding his hands with many torments while the great city mourns, a yaksha will carry off the famous one; they should not fear, for after some days they will see him again.
nuance: The usurper is named only as 'the one without grace' (அருளிலான்), the Jain lack that marks him; the rescuer is an இயக்கன், which the story will show to be Sudanjanan, the dog Civakan once helped.
event: Kantukkatan tells the rest of the prophecy: Civakan will be seized to be killed and rescued by a yaksha.

tamil: வசையற நிறைந்த கற்பின் மாலையு மாமி தானுந்
தசையற வுருகி வெந்து தம்முயிர் நீங்கு மாங்க
ணொசிதவன் சொற்க ளென்னு நோன்புணை தழுவி நெஞ்சிற்
கசிவெனுங் கடலை நீந்திக் கரையெனுங் காலை கண்டார்.
reading: Gunamalai of flawless chastity and her mother-in-law, melting as if their flesh dissolved and about to give up their lives, clung to the strong raft of the ascetic's words, swam the sea of grief in their hearts and saw the shore.
nuance: Gunamalai is already called the merchant's daughter-in-law's equal here: மாமி makes Sunandai her mother-in-law, so the household treats the betrothal as binding.
event: Gunamalai and Sunandai, near death with grief, are steadied by the prophecy.

tamil: திருக்குழன் மகளிர் நையச் சீவக சாமி திண்டோள்
வரிக்கச்சிற் பிணிக்கப் பட்டான் மன்னனா லென்னக் கேட்டே
தருக்குடை வேழம் வாளார் ஞாட்பினுட் டகைமை சான்ற
மருப்புட னிழந்த தொத்தார் மன்னுயிர்த் தோழன் மாரே.
reading: When the women of beautiful hair were wasting away and Civakan's dear friends heard that Civakasami's strong arms had been bound with a striped belt by the king, they were like a proud war elephant that has lost its tusks in the clash of swords.
event: Civakan's friends hear that the king has had him bound.

tamil: நட்டவற் குற்ற கேட்டே பதுமுக னக்கு மற்றோர்
குட்டியைத் தின்ன லாமே கோட்புலி புறத்த தாகக்
கட்டியங் கார னென்னுங் கழுதைநம் புலியைப் பாய
வொட்டியிஃ துணர லாமே யுரைவல்லை யறிக வென்றான்.
reading: Hearing what had befallen their friend, Padumukan laughs: can anyone eat the cub while the fierce tiger is outside? that donkey called Kattiyangaran leaping on our tiger, can such a thing be? you who are skilled in words, understand this.
nuance: The friends are the tiger outside the den; the usurper is the donkey. Line 4 (ஒட்டி இஃது உணரலாமே) is hard to construe and the reading of it is a guess.
event: Padumukan scorns the news, calling Kattiyangaran a donkey attacking a tiger.

tamil: சிலையொடு செல்வ னின்றாற் றேவரும் வணக்க லாற்றார்
முலையுடைத் தாயோ டெண்ணித் தந்தையிக் கொடுமை செய்தான்
கலைவல்லீ ரின்னுங் கேண்மி னின்னதென் றுரைக்கு மாங்கண்
விரைவொடு சென்ற வொற்றாள் விளைந்தவா பேசு கின்றான்.
reading: Padumukan says that if their lord stood with his bow even the gods could not bend him, so his father, taking counsel with the mother who nursed him, must have done this cruel thing; as he tells the learned friends to hear more, the spy who had gone quickly returns and tells what happened.
nuance: The friend reasons from Civakan's strength to the only power that could bind him: his own parents. கொடுமை is his word for their act, though the parents meant it to save him.
event: Padumukan guesses that Civakan's parents persuaded him to be bound; a spy arrives with the news.

tamil: இட்டிவேல் குந்தங் கூர்வா ளிருஞ்சிலை யிருப்புச் சுற்றார்
நெட்டிலைச் சூலம் வெய்ய முளைத்தண்டு நெருங்க வேந்தி
யெட்டெலாத் திசையு மீண்டி யெழாயிரத் திரட்டி மள்ளர்
கட்டழற் கதிரை யூர்கோள் வளைத்தவா வளைத்துக் கொண்டார்.
reading: The spy tells how fourteen thousand warriors, bearing lances, spears, sharp swords, great bows, iron discs, long-bladed tridents and fierce spiked clubs, gathered from all eight directions and ringed the house as a halo rings the blazing sun.
nuance: எழாயிரத்து இரட்டி is twice seven thousand.
event: Kattiyangaran's warriors surround Civakan's house.

tamil: பிடியொடு நின்ற வேழம் பெருவளைப் புண்ட வண்ணம்
வடிமலர்க் கோதை யோடும் வளைத்தலின் மைந்தன் சீறி
விடுகணை சிலையொ டேந்தி வெருவரத் தோன்ற லோடு
மடுபுலி கண்ட மான்போ லாறல வாயி னாரே.
reading: As an elephant standing with its mate is penned in, so the young man, hemmed in with his flower-garlanded lady, flared up, rose with bow and arrows ready and appeared so terrible that the warriors lost their way like deer that see a killing tiger.
nuance: The lady (வடிமலர்க் கோதை) is unnamed; in this section she is most likely Gunamalai.
event: Civakan takes up his bow and the besiegers scatter in fear.

tamil: சூழ்கழன் மள்ளர் பாறச் சூழ்ச்சியிற் றந்தை புல்லி
வீழ்தரு கண்ண டம்மோய் விளங்குதோள் பிணிப்ப மற்றென்
றோழரை வடுச்செய் திட்டே னென்றுதான் றுளங்கி நின்றா
னூழ்திரைப் பாம்பு சேர்ந்த வொளிமிகு பருதி யொத்தான்.
reading: As the warriors scattered, his father by a stratagem embraced him and his weeping mother bound his shining arms; saying 'I have brought disgrace on my friends', Civakan stood shaken, like the bright sun seized by the serpent of the eclipse.
nuance: The hero who routed fourteen thousand is bound by his parents' embrace; his shame is toward his friends, not his foe. Whether the mother's binding is literal or her arms hold him is not plain from line 2.
event: Kantukkatan and Sunandai hold and bind Civakan, who submits, ashamed before his friends.

tamil: ஒற்றன்வந்த துரைப்பக் கேட்டே யொத்ததோ வென்சொ லென்னாச்
சுற்றினார் முகத்தை நோக்கிச சூழிமால் யானை யன்னா
னுற்றவிவ் விடரைத் தீர்க்கு முபாயநீ ருரைமி னென்றான்
பொற்றிரட் குன்றம் போலப் பொலிவுகொண் டிருந்த தோளான்.
reading: When the spy had told it, Padumukan, elephant-like and with shoulders like a hill of gold, asked whether his word had not proved true, looked at the faces of those around him, and asked them to say how this danger might be ended.
event: Padumukan, his guess confirmed, asks the friends for a plan.

tamil: நிறைத்திங்க ளொளியொ டொப்பான் புத்திசே னினைந்து சொல்லு
மறைத்திங்க ணகரை வல்லே சுடுதுநாஞ் சுடுத லோடு
மிறைக்குற்றேல் செய்த லின்றி யெரியின்வாய்ச் சனங்க ணீங்கச்
சிறைக்குற்ற நீங்கச் செற்றாற் செகுத்துக்கொண் டெழுது மென்றான்.
reading: Buddhisenan, bright as the full moon, thinks and says: tonight we will quickly burn the city, and while it burns, doing no harm to the king's [people] and letting the people escape the fire's mouth, we will kill the enemy, end the imprisonment and carry him off.
nuance: The plan includes care that the townspeople escape the fire (சனங்கள் நீங்க). Line 3's இறைக்குற்றேல் செய்தல் இன்றி is obscure: it may mean without harming the king or without rendering him service; the reading leaves it open.
event: Buddhisenan proposes burning the city by night to free Civakan.

tamil: காலத்தீ நகரை மேயக் கடியரண் கடிந்த வம்பிற்
சாலத்தீச் சவரர் கோலஞ் செய்துநம் மறவ ரீண்டிக்
கோலத்தீ வேலி னானைக் கோயிலுள் வளைப்ப விப்பர்
லாலைத்தீ யிடங்க டோறு மாகுலஞ் செய்து மென்றான்.
reading: He continues: as the fire like the fire of the world's end feeds on the city, our warriors, gathered in the fierce guise of Savara hunters, will surround the king of the bright spear in his palace, and raise an uproar at every place the fire is lit.
nuance: The friends plan to fight disguised as hunters (சவரர்), so that the blame falls elsewhere. Lines 3 to 4 are divided oddly (விப்பர் / லாலைத்தீ) and their last part is a guess.
event: Buddhisenan lays out the disguise and the attack on the palace.

title: குணமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1142-1165 (13/13)
theme: Civakan's friends gather to free him from the usurper's prison by Padumukan's plan, and Gandharvadattai, able to free him by her spells, holds back because a husband saved by his wife would be shamed; Civakan too refuses her magic and calls on his friend, the god once a dog, who comes down in a storm and carries him off, while Madanan's men kill a stranger in his place and Kattiyangaran rewards the supposed murder.
source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1144 line 1 has சூழந்த, apparently for சூழ்ந்த.
1150 lines 1-3 and 1151 line 1 (புகழும் புழியும் மெழு நாளவை) are hard to construe as divided.
1153 line 4 குச்சென is obscure.
1165 line 2 நிண்பு looks like a misprint, perhaps for நண்பு.

cast.role: the hero, held prisoner by the usurper
Civakan's friend, author of the rescue plan, called தாமரை நாமன் in 1145
one of Civakan's companions
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Nabulan
Civakan's younger brother, called நந்தன் in 1144
Gunamalai's father, who joins the rescue with his sons
Civakan's companions
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife, mistress of spells
the armed powers of Gandharvadattai's spell-lore, called விண்ணோர் and எந்தைமார் in 1160
the god, once the dog Civakan gave the mantra to, who carries him out of captivity
the people of Rajamapuram
Kattiyangaran's brother-in-law, sent to execute Civakan
the warriors under Madanan
the usurping king

tamil: சிறைப்புறங் காத்துச் செல்லு மதனனைத் தெருவில் வீழப்
பிறைத்தலை யம்பிற் சென்னி பெருநிலத் திடுவ லிட்டான்
மறுக்குற்று மள்ளர் நீங்க மைந்தனைக் கொண்டு போகி
யறைத்தொழி லார்க்குஞ் செல்லா வருமிளை புகுமி னென்றான்.
reading: The plan goes on: when Madanan, who escorts the prisoner, comes down the street, the speaker will lay his head on the ground with a crescent-headed arrow, and as the warriors scatter in confusion the others are to take the young man and go into a thicket that even men of war cannot enter.
nuance: The speaker is not named here; 1145 calls the plan the policy told by the man named for the lotus (தாமரை நாமன்), Padumukan, so these two verses are read as his.

tamil: மாற்றவர் மலைப்பி னாங்கே வாட்கடாக் கொண்டு நொய்தா
வேற்றுல கேற்றி நும்பின் விரைதர்வே னுலகிற் கெல்லா
மாற்றிய நட்பு வல்லே வலிப்புறீஇ யிடுமி னென்றான்
கூற்றங்கள் பலவுந் தொக்க கூற்றத்திற் கூற்ற மொப்பான்.
reading: If the enemy fight there, they are to send them swiftly to the other world with their swords, and he will hurry after them; he bids them make firm at once the friendship that the whole world has proved, he who was like the death of all the deaths gathered together.
nuance: Line 3 (மாற்றிய நட்பு வல்லே வலிப்புறீஇ) is hard to construe; the reading takes it as a charge to hold fast to their friendship in the fight.

tamil: காலனைச் சூழந்த நோய்போ னபுலமா விபுலர் சூழ
வேலினை யேந்தி நந்தன் வெருவரத் தோன்ற லோடு
மாலைதன் றாதை தானு மக்களும் வந்து கூடிப்
பாலவர் பிறரு மீண்டிப் பாய்புலி யினத்திற் சூழ்ந்தார்.
reading: Like diseases round Death, Nabulan and Vipulan close round; Nandattan appears with his spear so that all fear him, and Gunamalai's father, his sons and others of their side gather and stand round like a pack of leaping tigers.
nuance: The bride's father joins his son-in-law's friends against the usurper: the new marriage has already made a kin party in the city.
event: Civakan's companions, his brother and Gunamalai's father and kin gather under arms for the rescue.

tamil: மட்டுவா யவிழ்ந்த தண்டார்த் தாமரை நாமன் சொன்ன
கட்டமை நீதி தன்மேற் காப்பமைந் திவர்க ணிற்பப்
பட்டுலாய்க் கிடந்த செம்பொற் கலையணி பரவை யல்கு
லிட்டிடைப் பவளச் செவ்வாய்த் தத்தையு மிதனைக் கேட்டாள்.
reading: While these stand on guard according to the plan Padumukan told, Gandharvadattai, of the silk-draped waist and coral mouth, hears of what has happened.
event: Gandharvadattai learns of Civakan's imprisonment.

tamil: மணியியல் யவனச் செப்பின் மங்கலத் துகிலை வாங்கிக்
கணைபுரை கண்ணி யேற்ப வுடுத்தபின் செம்பொற் செப்பிற்
பிணையலு நறிய சேர்த்திப் பெருவிலை யாரந் தாங்கித்
துணைவனுக் குற்ற துன்பஞ் சொல்லிய தொடங்கி னாளே.
reading: She takes an auspicious cloth from a gem-set Yavana casket and puts it on, sets fragrant garlands from a gold casket and a costly necklace on herself, and begins the rite for the trouble that has come upon her husband.
event: Gandharvadattai dresses in auspicious cloth and ornaments to begin a rite for her husband.

tamil: பொன்னணி மணிசெ யோடை நீரின்வெண் சாந்து பூசித்
தன்னுடை விஞ்ஞை யெல்லாந் தளிரிய லோத லோடு
மின்னடு வாளும் வேலுங் கல்லொடு தீயுங் காற்று
மன்னுட னேந்தித் தெய்வ மாதரைச் சூழ்ந்த வன்றே.
reading: Anointing herself with white paste and water from a gold vessel set with gems, the tender one recites all her spells, and the powers of her lore, bearing sword and spear, stone, fire and wind, come and surround the divine woman.
nuance: The princess of the Vidyadharas commands a war magic of her own: the rescue that the men are planning with arrows she could do alone, which is what the next verses weigh.
event: Gandharvadattai recites her Vidyadhara spells and their armed powers gather round her.

reading: She of the bamboo shoulders stands thinking that she could take away the hero's pain as fast as lightning, gently, and waits for the moment, and then she reflects that a lasting blame on earth would come of it to the noble one.
event: Gandharvadattai, ready to free Civakan by magic, hesitates for fear of the blame it would bring him.

reading: She asks the god what she is to do: if, while he is sunk in the king's prison as in the great sea, his wife comes to him and frees him, what then are his strength and learning worth, and how is the blame to be borne that would sweep the world for nothing?
nuance: The shame of a man rescued by a woman is voiced by the woman who could rescue him, and it holds her hand: the epic lets the wife carry the husband's honour code.

reading: She goes on: if it is said that Fortune herself freed the lord from prison there is no blame, as if there were no difference between Fortune and herself; but Fortune of the lotus is a woman common to all, while she, of the silver mountain, is a wife of family.
nuance: The word division of lines 1-3 is doubtful; the reading takes செய்யவள் as the goddess of fortune and வெள்ளிம்மலை as Gandharvadattai's Vidyadhara home set against the lotus. On that reading she refuses the cover story that his luck saved him, because the help of a wife, unlike the help of fortune, would be his shame.

reading: Saying 'let what must be, be; fame and blame last but seven days, and I will not seek them out among gods or men; ache, my heart', the peacock-gentle one stands gazing toward the prisoner like a cow newly calved toward her calf in the pen.
nuance: Line 1 (புகழும் புழியும் மெழு நாளவை) is read as fame and blame lasting seven days, which would be her setting reputation aside; the line is garbled as divided and the sense is not sure.
event: Gandharvadattai holds back her magic and stands watching over Civakan in his captivity.

tamil: மாநகர் சுடுத லொன்றோ மதனனை யழித்த லொன்றோ
வானிக ரில்லா மைந்தர் கருதிய ததுவு நிற்க
போயுயிர் வாழ்தல் வேண்டே னெனப்பொருள் சிந்திக் கின்றான்.
reading: Civakan ponders: burning the great city is one course, destroying Madanan another, and the plan of his matchless friends may stand, but he does not want to go on living set free by the spells of his bamboo-shouldered wife.
nuance: The husband reaches the same refusal as the wife (1149) without hearing her: both hold that his life is worth less than his name if she saves him.
event: Civakan, bound, rejects rescue by his wife's magic.

tamil: கச்சற நிமிர்ந்து மாந்தர்க் கடாவிடு களிறு போல
வுச்சியு மருங்கும் பற்றிப் பிளந்துயிர் பருகிக் கோண்மா
வச்சுற வழன்று சீறி யாட்டினம் புக்க தொப்பக்
குச்சென நிரைத்த யானைக் குழாமிரித் திடுவ லென்றான்.
reading: He says he will tear through the massed elephants as a must elephant loosed on men splits them, or as a raging lion leaps into a flock of goats, seizing crown and flank and drinking their lives.
nuance: குச்சென நிரைத்த (line 4) is obscure; the elephants are taken as ranked close like a thicket.

tamil: மின்னிலங் கெயிற்று வேழம் வேழத்தாற் புடைத்துத் திண்டேர்
பொன்னிலங் கிவுளித் தேராற் புடைத்துவெங் குருதி பொங்க
வின்னுயி ரவனை யுண்ணு மெல்லைநாள் வந்த தில்லை
யென்னையிக் கிருமி கொன்றென் றோழனை நினைப்ப லென்றான்.
reading: Striking elephant with elephant and chariot with chariot till hot blood surges, he could drink the life of that man, but the day of his end has not come; if this worm should kill him, he says, he will think of his friend.
nuance: இக்கிருமி, 'this worm', is Civakan's word for the usurper. எல்லைநாள் வந்ததில்லை makes the timing of the enemy's death a set limit, not his own choice; the 'friend' is the god who was the dog of the bathing festival.
event: Civakan resolves to call on his friend the god if the usurper moves to kill him.

tamil: தோழனுந் தேவி மார்தங் குழாத்துளான் றுளும்பு முந்நீ
ரேழ்தரு பருதி தன்மே லிளம்பிறை கிடந்த தேபோற்
றாழ்தகை யார மார்பிற் சீவகன் குணங்க டம்மை
reading: His friend the god sat among his goddesses beside a celestial dancer, shining on his chest like a young crescent on the sun rising from the sea, listening to them sing Civakan's virtues to the yazh.
nuance: The heaven he enjoys is the one his friend's mantra won him (947), and what its women sing there is the friend's praise.
event: Sudanjanan, in his heaven, listens to his goddesses sing Civakan's virtues.

reading: The bright god with the diamond crown felt his left lotus eye throb, thought of the one dear to him as life, saw what had befallen him by his far-seeing knowledge, and leaving a likeness for his peacock-like goddesses rose through the great sky.
nuance: ஓதி is read as the gods' far-seeing knowledge (avadhi); மயிலனார்க்குப் படி வைத்து is read as leaving a likeness or token for his consorts, which is doubtful. The throbbing eye works as an omen on a god as on a mortal.
event: Warned by an omen, Sudanjanan learns of Civakan's peril and sets out from heaven.

reading: Thunder, lightning and roaring filled the world as if the wind of the aeon's end were tearing out the mountains; the sun hid as though ashamed to see the distress, and rain poured down as if the sea had been lifted and thrown upon the land.
event: A storm and darkness fall on the city as the god comes down.

reading: With sky and earth indistinguishable, beasts and men robbed of sight and speech, and women and men crying 'see, the sea has taken it', the lord lifted the king's son Civakan, held him to his breast, and rose and went.
event: Under cover of the storm, Sudanjanan lifts Civakan and carries him away through the sky.

reading: As he rose carrying the hill-shouldered one, she of the fair brow blessed him, 'may good come', and with that blessing one thought rose in her: when will be the day her eyes see again the youth for whom her heart aches?
event: Gandharvadattai blesses the departing rescuer and longs to see Civakan again.

reading: In the fragrant ground strewn with garlands she praised the heavenly ones who had come, scattered flowers, and sent them away, saying 'my fathers, rise', she whose voice outdoes the parrot's.
nuance: The powers called up in 1147 go back unused: her restraint, not her magic, is what the episode records of her.
event: Gandharvadattai dismisses with worship the spell-powers she had summoned.

tamil: மலைத்தொகை யானை மன்னன் மைத்துனன் மதன னென்பான்
கொலைத்தொகை வேலி னானைக் கொல்லிய கொண்டு போந்தா
னலத்தகை யவனைக் காணா னஞ்சுயிர்த் தஞ்சி நோக்கிச்
சிலைத்தொழிற் றடக்கை மள்ளர்க் கிற்றெனச் செப்பு கின்றான்.
reading: Madanan, brother-in-law of the king of many elephants, who had brought the spear-bearing youth out to kill him, cannot find the handsome one; sighing and staring in fear, he speaks to the bowmen.
nuance: Madanan is the king's மைத்துனன் here, which ties the executioner to the usurper by marriage.
event: Madanan finds Civakan gone and turns in fear to his men.

tamil: மன்னனாற் சீறப் பட்ட மைந்தனைக் கொல்லப் போந்தா
மென்னினிச் சொல்லிச் சேறு மென்செய்தும் யாங்க ளெல்லா
மின்னது பட்ட தென்றா லெரிவிளக் குறுக்கு நம்மைத்
துன்னுபு சூழ்ந்து தோன்றச் சொல்லுமின் செய்வ தென்றான்.
reading: He says they came to kill the youth the king raged at, and asks what they will now say and do, for if it is known what has happened the king will burn them like lamp wicks; let them gather round and tell him what to do.
nuance: எரிவிளக் குறுக்கு நம்மை is read as the king burning them like lamps; the phrase is hard as divided. The fear of the tyrant, not loyalty, drives what follows.

tamil: வாழ்வதோ ருபாய நாடி மதியுடம் பட்டு வல்லே
சூழ்வினை யாள ராங்க ணொருவனைத் தொடர்ந்து பற்றிப்
யாழ்கல மாந்தர் போல வணிநக ரழுங்கிற் றன்றே.
reading: Seeking a way to save their lives, the plotters agreed, seized one man, split him with a sword and rolled his body over, and the fair city grieved like people on a sinking ship.
event: Madanan's men kill a bystander and pass his corpse off as Civakan's, and the city mourns.

tamil: காய்சின வெகுளி வேந்தே களிற்றொடும் பொருத காளை
மாசனம் பெரிது மொய்த்து மழையினோ டிருளுங் காற்றும்
பேசிற்றான் பெரிதுந் தோன்றப் பிழைத்துய்யப் போத லஞ்சி
வாசங்கொ டாரி னானை மார்புபோழ்ந் துருட்டி யிட்டேம்.
reading: Madanan tells the king: the youth who fought the elephant, with a great crowd thronging and rain, darkness and wind making escape likely, was in fear of losing him split open in the chest and rolled over.
nuance: The lie is built on the true storm: the god's darkness becomes the executioner's excuse.
event: Madanan falsely reports to Kattiyangaran that Civakan has been killed.

tamil: திருமலி யீகை போகந் திண்புகழ் நிண்பு சுற்ற
மொருவரிவ் வுலகில் யாரே சீவக னொக்கு நீரார்
பெரிதரி திவனைக் கொன்றாய் பெறுகெனச் சிறப்புச் செய்தான்.
reading: The king says no one in the world has Civakan's nature, his grace, strength, manliness, learning, beauty, wisdom, youth, zeal, giving, enjoyment, firm fame and kin, that it was very hard to kill such a man, and honours Madanan with a reward.
nuance: The usurper lists the very virtues that make Civakan fit to rule and rewards his murder for that reason: the praise is the measure of the threat.
event: Kattiyangaran praises the supposedly dead Civakan and rewards Madanan for killing him.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1166-1190 (1/10)
theme: The opening of Padumaiyar Ilampakam: freed from prison, Civakan meets both fortunes with equanimity as former deeds, is carried to the god Sudanjanan's mountain, bathed and renamed, hears the god explain that he is the dog Civakan once saved, declines the divine women's offer to win his kingdom for him, and asks to see the world; the god then maps the road ahead, past Jain ascetics washing their karma, a yakshi's welcome, elephant forests, life-drinking ghoul-women, the Pallava country and a burning desert where animals shelter their own.
source_issues: Verses 1166, 1167 and 1169 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 1176 line 4 prints கூறினாற் காற்றின தமைதி; the sense requires the division கூறினான் ஆற்றினது அமைதி (the nature of the way).
Verses 1179 and 1180 end line 1 with a full stop (காவதம். / தாமரை.) where the sentence runs on; the stops look like printing artefacts.
Verse 1189 line 4 (மடனாமய லார்மனம் வைப்பதுவே) is obscure and may be corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai; here renamed பவித்திர குமரன்
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison (called தேவன், விண்ணவன் here)
the god's queens and women (உரிமை, தெய்வ மகளிர்), who bathe Civakan and offer to win his kingdom

tamil: வீட்டருஞ் சிறையிற் றேவன் விடுத்துயக் கொள்ளப் பட்ட
கோட்டமில் குணத்தி னான்போ யென்செய்கின் றான்கொ லென்னிற்
கூட்டரக் கெறிந்த பஞ்சிற் கூடிய பளிங்கிற் றோன்றுந்
தீட்டரும் படிவ மன்னான் றிறங்கிளந் துரைத்து மன்றே.
reading: The poet turns to ask what the hero of flawless virtue did after the god set him free from the prison none escapes, and promises to tell the deeds of the one whose form, like a figure seen in crystal, no painter could draw.
nuance: The opening verse of Padumaiyar Ilampakam bridges the plot: the rescue (வீட்டரும் சிறையில் தேவன் விடுத்து உயக் கொள்ளப்பட்ட) was told at the end of the previous ilampakam, and the poet now resumes with the hero's travels.

tamil: விலங்கிவில் லுமிழும் பூணான் விழுச்சிறைப் பட்ட போழ்து
மலங்கலந் தாரி னான்வந் தருஞ்சிறை விடுத்த போழ்தும்
புலம்பலு மகிழ்வு நெஞ்சிற் பொலிதலு மின்றிப் பொன்னார்ந்
துலங்கலந் துயர்ந்த தோளா னூழ்வினை யென்று விட்டான்.
reading: Neither when he lay bound in the great prison nor when the garlanded god came and freed him did grief or joy rise in the hero's heart; he let both go, saying it was the working of former deeds.
nuance: The word is the hero's (ஊழ்வினை என்று விட்டான), and the narrator presents it as his virtue. The plot gives the karma a concrete face: the god who frees him is the dog he helped die well (943-948), as the god says in 1172, so the 'former deed' here is the hero's own act in this very life, not an unknown deed of a past birth. The verse names no school, so the claim is left general.
event: Civakan, freed from prison by the god, meets both captivity and release without grief or joy, ascribing them to former deeds.

tamil: வானர முகள நாக மலர்துதைந் தொழுக வஞ்சித்
தேனிரைத் தெழுந்து திங்க ளிறாலெனச் சென்று மொய்க்குங்
கானம ரருவிக் குன்றிற் காய்கதிர் சுமந்தோர் திங்கண்
மேனிமிர்ந் தேறி யாங்குத் தேவன்வெற் பேறி னானே.
reading: As a moon bearing the burning sun climbs high, so the god climbed his mountain carrying the hero, a mountain whose streams run thick with flowers, where monkeys and elephants roam and honeycombs hang like moons.
nuance: காய்கதிர் சுமந்து ஓர் திங்கள்: the god is the moon and the hero the sun he carries, which reverses rank and echoes the dog's promised body 'shining like the burning disc of the sun' (காய்கதிர் மண்டலம், 943).
event: The god carries Civakan up to his mountain.

tamil: திங்களைத் தெளித்திட் டன்ன பாற்கடற் றிரைசெய் தெண்ணீர்
வெங்கள்விட் டலர்ந்த கண்ணி விண்ணவ னுரிமை தன்னான்
மங்கல வகையி னாட்டி மணியணி கலங்கள் சேர்த்திப்
பங்கய நெடுங்க ணானைப் பவித்திர குமர னென்றான்.
reading: With clear water from the waves of the milk ocean, bright as moonlight, the god had his women bathe the hero in the auspicious way and deck him with jewels, and named the lotus-eyed youth the Holy Prince.
nuance: பவித்திர குமரன் (the pure or holy prince) is a new name given by the god, in the manner of a consecration bath; it marks the hero's passage from prison to divine favour.
event: The god's women bathe and adorn Civakan with milk-ocean water, and the god names him Pavittira Kumaran.

tamil: பொன்னணி காம்பு செய்த பொழிகதிர்த் திங்கள் போலும்
பின்னிய முத்த மாலைப் பிணையறாழ் குடையி னீழற்
கன்னியர் கவரி வீசக் கனமணிக் குழைவில் வீச
வின்னிசைக் கூத்து நோக்கி யிருந்தனன் றிலக மன்னான்.
reading: Under a parasol like the full moon on a golden staff, hung with strings of pearls, with maidens waving yak-tail whisks and gem earrings flashing, the hero sat watching the dance to sweet music.
event: Civakan sits in state on the god's mountain, fanned by maidens, watching dance and music.

tamil: இருமலர்க் குவளை யுண்க ணிமைப்பிலாப் பயத்தைப் பெற்ற
வரிமலர்த் தாரி னான்ற னழகுகண் டளிய வென்னாத்
திருமலர்க் கோதை யைம்பாற் றேவியர் தொடர்பு கேட்ப
வெரிமணிப் பூணி னானு மின்னண மியம்பி னானே.
reading: Seeing the beauty of the garlanded youth, the god's queens felt their unblinking eyes had found their reward, pitied him and asked how the god was bound to him, and the jewelled god answered thus.
nuance: இமைப்பிலாப் பயத்தைப் பெற்ற: gods do not blink, and the conceit is that their never-closing eyes are at last put to good use. அளிய (pitiable, dear) may be their pity for his sufferings or simply their tenderness; the verse does not say which.
event: The god's queens ask him what tie binds him to Civakan.

reading: The god tells them that when he was born among dogs this man removed his suffering, looked on him with grace and gave him this cooled and gracious body, and calls him a bull of countless virtues.
nuance: பிணிக்குலத்து அகவயின் is unusual for 'in the race of dogs'; the sense is clear from the story (941-948) but the wording is not a common name for dogs. The god gives the credit to the man (எனக்கு அருளி), not to the mantra Civakan whispered, so his rescue in 1167 is gratitude repaying a gift; the poem treats the debt of a benefit as the bond between god and man.
event: Sudanjanan tells his queens that Civakan freed him from his dog's birth and gave him his god's body.

reading: The divine women say that they will destroy the hard enmity of this youth, who is like the god with the shark banner, win him the wide earth, establish his marriage with a gentle maiden and give him all of it.
nuance: கடற்சுறவு உயரிய காளை is Kama, whose banner bears the makara; the offer is the whole programme of the rest of the epic (vengeance on Kattiyangaran, the throne, the marriages) handed over as a divine gift, and 1174 shows the hero declining to take it so.
event: The god's women offer to destroy Civakan's enemy, win him the land and marry him to a maiden.

reading: The hero answers that they need not plan how the earth may come to him by taking the enemy's life in battle; if they would give him the lordship of earth and the land of the gods, they are surely able to give it.
nuance: The sense of the reply turns on tone. எண்ணல் வேண்டுமோ may mean 'need you trouble to plan it' (he will win the land himself) or simply 'is there any need to think about it' (they can do it at once); the second half (தருகுந் தன்மையீர்) may be courtesy, or a polite deflection that their power could give even heaven, so earth is a small thing he will take on his own. Read with 1175, where he asks only to see the world, the first sense, a refusal of a gift he means to earn, is likelier.
event: Civakan answers the divine women's offer.

reading: He tells the god that he has one wish: to see the mountains and forests that lie on the earth, the lands and pools hard to reach, and the rivers that cool the eye and the mind.
event: Civakan asks the god's leave to go and see the lands of the earth.

reading: Those who are like fish living in a spring-fed well never set out to taste another land; 'Keep well, I shall go,' the hero said, and the god then told him plainly the nature of the road ahead.
nuance: Line 4 (காற்றின தமைதி) is best divided கூறினான் ஆற்றினது அமைதி, 'the nature of the way'; read as காற்றின் (of the wind) it makes poor sense. Lines 1-3 are the hero's speech and line 4 the narrator's; the god's directions fill 1177-1190.
event: Civakan takes leave of the god, who begins to describe the road.

tamil: இம்மலைக் கிரண்டு காத மிறந்தபி னிருண்டு தோன்று
மம்மலை யரண பாத மென்பதன் றாள்வாய்த் தோன்றுந்
தம்வினை கழுவு கின்றார் சாரணர் தரணி காவல்
வெம்மையி னகன்று போந்து விழைவறத் துறந்து விட்டார்.
reading: Two kathams beyond this mountain the god says a dark mountain called Aranapatham appears, and at its foot the Caranas wash away their own karma: men who left the cruelty of guarding the earth and renounced without desire.
nuance: சாரணர் are the Jain ascetics with the power of sky-going; the verse makes renunciation a king's turn from rule, which it calls cruelty (தரணி காவல் வெம்மை), and the cleansing is their own act (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்). The scene foreshadows the hero's own end in Mutti Ilampakam.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

tamil: சிந்தையிற் பருதி யன்னார் சேவடி யிறைஞ்ச லோடும்
வெந்திற லியக்கி தோன்றி விருந்தெதிர் கொண்டு பேணித்
தந்தவ ளமிர்த மூட்ட வுண்டவட் பிரிந்த காலைச்
சந்துடைச் சாரல் சேறி தரணிமேற் றிலக மன்னாய்.
reading: When the hero bows at the red feet of those whose minds are like the sun, the god says a yakshi of fierce power will appear, receive him as a guest and feed him nectar, and after leaving her he should go to the sandal-wood slopes.
nuance: The order matters: hospitality from the yakshi (இயக்கி) follows on worship of the ascetics; reverence opens the road.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Five kavathams on, the god says, lies a forest where herds of rutting elephants stay, which no one crosses alone, on the bank of the Ganga that looks like a sea.
nuance: கங்கை here may be the great river or a name for a local river; the route is a romance geography and the verse does not let one fix it.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Keeping on his right a great joyful pool where lotuses bloom as if fire crept over water and vaalai fish leap like swords, the hero is to go two kathams more.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Past two hills mixed with gems, diamonds and gold like the hero's own shoulders, the god says he will see a great ghoul forest that is decked like women in flowered cloth.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: There, says the god to the saffron-chested hero, ghouls like swaying gem-creepers will melt and pine, calling him the thief who stole their beauty by stealth.
nuance: The ghouls speak the language of a lovesick heroine (களவினின் அணி நலம் கவர்ந்த கள்வ); the deceit is that akam's own words are the lure.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Softening like ripe fruit and burning with desire, they come near saying this is the moment for an embrace, and when they embrace they wring out a man's life and drink it: they are ghouls.
nuance: The claim is put as a fact of this forest, but it carries the ethic of the warning against deceiving women; the final word (பேய்கள் ஆபவே) unmasks the lovers of 1182.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

tamil: கண்டபேய் நகரி னீங்கிக் காவதங் கடந்து தோன்றும்
வெண்டலைப் புணரி வீசிக் கிடந்தபொற் றீவிற் றாகிக்
கொண்டுலப் பரிய செந்நெல் கொடிக்கரும் புடுத்த வேலி
reading: Leaving the ghoul town and crossing a kavatham, the god says, a land appears beside a golden island washed by white-crested waves, fenced with red paddy and sugarcane, as sweet as coral and the fine-clothed waist of a woman.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

tamil: படுமழை பருவம் பொய்யாப் பல்லவ தேய மென்னுந்
தடமலர்க் குவளைப் பட்டந் தழுவிய யாணர் நன்னாட்
டிடைநெறி யசைவு தீர விருந்தவ ணேக லுற்றாற்
கடநெறி கடத்தற் கின்னாக் கல்லத ரத்த முண்டே.
reading: That good rich land is called the Pallava country, where the rains never fail their season and lily beds lie like a girdle; if he rests there to ease the toil of the road and then goes on, a stony desert path hard to cross awaits him.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: The god says the stones there are like the fine sharp spears of a fierce lord set out over the ground; none but those who know the way pass over them, and the very heat that dwells there would burn the mouth that told of it.
nuance: The metre changes here. விதி கண்டவர் அல்லது மீது செலார் can mean 'only those who know the rule of the road go over it' or 'only those whose fate has been seen (who are doomed) go there'; வெம்பரன் (a fierce lord, or a hot stone) is also open.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: In that heat, the god says, elephants hug their calves and bear the fire themselves lest the young faint, and cock birds fold their hens in their wings and ease their suffering.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Because there is no leaf shade there, the stag, fearing his doe will wither, stands and gives her the shade of his own body and himself melts in the scorching sun, he tells the strong hero.
nuance: 1187-1188 together are the three tender creatures of the palai tradition (the tusker, the bird with its wings, the stag giving its shadow); the Cintamani shifts the first from the mate to the calf.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: Where the must of rutting elephants has dripped on the ground, hooded snakes with bright gems, flashing like a waist-string or lightning, burn and writhe; this is the road, the god says, on which only those foolish in love would set their minds.
nuance: Line 4 (மடனாம் அயலார் மனம் வைப்பதுவே) is obscure; அயலார் may be strangers to the road or the deluded, and the construal of the snakes in lines 2-3 is also doubtful.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

reading: On that road, the god tells the spear-bearing hero, there are matted-haired tapasas who have weakened the hold of the senses and practise austerities, at whose sight those who falter on the road melt in heart.
nuance: பொறியில் தளர்வார் likely means those who have slackened the senses (ascetics) but could mean those weakened in body; the tapasas (தாபதர், with சடை) are forest ascetics, not the Jain Caranas of 1177, and the poem keeps the two apart.
event: Sudanjanan describes to Civakan the next stage of the way from his mountain.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1191-1215 (2/10)
theme: The god Sudanjanan continues to set out for Civakan the road ahead, hermitages, rivers, forests, hunters and wondrous pools, giving the route as a map of landmarks and closing with a prophecy of the king of the middle country, a marriage and the friends' return.
source_issues: Verse 1205 line 1 கையடு is flagged as possibly கையொடு with a lost vowel sign; both readings (bows that kill in hand, or bows in hand) give sense, and it is left as printed.
Verse 1200 ends mid-sentence (நீந்தினால) and its clause completes in 1201.
Verse 1204 lists the pools in a way that does not cleanly yield the four of 1203; the division around அமிர்த மல்லதொன் is doubtful.
Verse 1211 line 3 மரியவர் and மதன கீதம் do not construe clearly; the line may be corrupt.
Verse 1212 line 2 மாற்றரு மணநெறி மகளிர் is ambiguous (married women, or a scent figure).

cast.role: the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison and here describes his road
the hero, addressed by the god as காளை, மொய்ம்ப and other epithets
the king of the middle country who will receive Civakan, foretold in 1214-1215
Civakan's companions, foretold to rejoin him

reading: Beside the mountain river there are plantains with ripe clustered fruit, mango trees with sweet honeyed fruit, and jackfruit trees that have borne their thorny, nectar-filled fruit.
nuance: The god's route speech to Civakan, begun in the previous run, continues here; the abundance is a traveller's assurance of food on the way as much as praise of the place.

reading: Gold, long gems of bright lustre and land a yojana wide shine there: this is the cool Chitrakuta that the ascetics, never wearied, long for.
nuance: சித்திர கூடம் names a hill of hermitages; the verse sets the ascetics' desire on a place rather than on wealth, though the place is itself described as shining with gold and gems.

reading: The great river Anjana comes down roaring like drums and great cascades, dragging bamboo, sandalwood and diamonds and carrying away heaps of gems.

The god points out the hermitage, the snowy mountain, the river of clear sand and the grove ringed by surapunnai trees that brush the moon, and bids Civakan hold to his way without slackening his pace.
nuance: The deictic இது ... அது ('this is ... that is') makes the speech a map shown from above, fitting a god who has carried the hero through the sky.

reading: In the hermitage of the great ascetics who mortify themselves, the jasmine with sharp buds climbing the kurundu tree has the beauty of gold-like women clasping the side of the husbands they are joined to.
nuance: The image of the faithful wife embracing her husband is set inside the hermitage of those who have renounced: the poem keeps the householder's ideal and the ascetic's place side by side without comment.

reading: The wide land of the konrai and kura forest, where bees and honey-bees play the yazh to the songs of those who reap the millet with sickles, stretches twelve kaathams.
Beyond that boundary Civakan will see the beauty of a land of fitting renown, with strong toddy, gold pots filled with flowers, and fields ringed by the sweet sound of drums.
nuance: சீர்த்தக்க நாட்டு may name the Takka land, where the patikam (20) places Civakan's later marriage to a merchant's daughter, or simply mean 'a land of fitting excellence'; the division of the words does not settle it.

tamil: பாளைவாய்க் கமுகி னெற்றிப் படுபழ முதிர விண்டு
நீள்கழைக் கரும்பி னெற்றி நெய்ம்முதிர் தொடையல் கீறி
வாளைவா யுறைப்ப நக்கி வராலொடு மறலு மென்ப
காளைநீ கடந்து செல்லுங் காமரு கவின்கொ ணாடே.
reading: In the lovely land Civakan crosses, ripe areca fruit split from their spathes and tear the honey-heavy joints of the tall sugarcane, and the vaalai fish lick the drip and fight with the varaal.
nuance: Like the patikam's opening landscape of Emangadam (31), fruit falling on fruit is the stock sign of a rich land; the vocative காளை marks this as speech to the hero.

reading: On the way past that land a river will appear, covered with bunches of champak flowers, scented by the hair of the women of the land, with bees swarming down its whole length.
nuance: யங்கநாட் may be read அங்க நாட்டு, the Anga land, or as அங்கு அந் நாட்டு, 'of that land there'; the route's geography turns on it.

reading: That river, the god says, sweeps up many bright gems and, sharing its own excellence to feed the world, is a courtesan with a gold-girdled waist; if Civakan swims across it quickly,
nuance: The courtesan here is a figure of open-handed bounty: she shares her நலம் with the whole world as the river shares its gems. The sentence does not end in this verse; it runs into 1201.

reading: a forest will appear, ringed by the huts of the forest people, built of white elephant tusks, thatched with the white hair of the yak, and crammed with honey, meat, roots, unripe and ripe fruit.
nuance: The hunters' huts are rich in what the forest gives, meat among them, which prepares the harsher judgment on the forest people in 1205.

reading: Everywhere the sounds mingle and swell: the harsh drum, the voice of those churning toddy, the call of the long-trunked elephant, the long voice of the gem-bearing falls, and the cry of the frightened deer mixed with the roar of the killing tiger.
The god tells Civakan that there are four pools, set with fine gems, as hard to see as the virgin daughters of a gold-wheeled emperor, which will show themselves to him.
nuance: The comparison with a cakravartin's secluded daughters makes the pools a guarded treasure that appears only to one who is worthy, a promise to the hero more than a description.

reading: Of the pools, one is filled with red petals, one has a quickening water that turns dark iron to gold, one cures all diseases together, and one, beyond nectar or other than it, is a pool of opening blue water-lilies.
nuance: இரத நீர் is rasa-water, the alchemist's transmuting fluid; the verse lists it beside a healing water without remark. The count of four in 1203 does not fit the items cleanly: அமிர்தம் அல்லது ஒன்று may name a nectar pool and leave the lily pool as a fourth, or describe the lily pool as other than nectar.

reading: The forest dwellers with killing bows in hand, men of wretched bodies and forms of sin itself, show themselves suddenly, destroy travellers, and take their bodies, thinking escape impossible for them.
nuance: The judgment பாவ மூர்த்தியர், 'embodiments of sin', falls on the forest people as a class; the god names it as a danger of the road, not as a teaching, and the closing words (உய்வகை அரிதென) may be either the victims' plight or the killers' reasoning.

reading: If Civakan passes, with no thought for it, the pool on which men's eyes fasten as women's eyes fasten on a noble man, keeping it on his left, the bowmen will at once bow and gaze at him.
nuance: The instruction works like a charm: a ritual way of passing the pool turns the killers of 1205 into worshippers. What makes them bow is not said.

reading: Beyond, for five kaathams, the way runs sweetly, like the swaying grace of a dancing woman whose anklet-bells ring and whose girdle flashes as the bees play the yazh in her garland.
The straight red road, they say, lies on flower-pollen, strewn with fresh blossoms as if a garland had fallen, with jasmine and kaththigai, and is like the minds of chaste women.
nuance: The chaste woman's mind is the measure of a road that has no forks: karpu is figured as singleness of direction. Compare 1212, where women's hearts are the figure for a road that divides.

reading: The god bids Civakan see, as he goes, the great springs like jewelled bowls and, between them, the cool groves like flower baskets adorned with long gem-like blossoms.
On the right, like the moon, will appear Vanagiri, ringed by groves where falls cast down like nets roar, firmer than the chastity of high-born women with jewelled breasts and girdles of gold.
nuance: As in 1208, the chastity of women is the poem's standard of firmness, here for a mountain; the qualifier குலத்தலை மகளிர் ties that firmness to women of good family.

reading: They say it is a mountain where songs of love arose and wander, because those who live there keep without wavering the holy word of the Great One whose red feet the Dark One bowed his sacred crown upon.
nuance: கரியவன் 'the dark one' bowing to பெரியவன் 'the great one' is most naturally Krishna (or Vishnu) bowing to a Jina, a Jain ranking of gods; the verse does not name either. மரியவர் and மதன கீதம் are hard: the dwellers may be ascetics or celestials, and the link between their keeping the word and the songs of love is not clear.

reading: After he has passed the jewelled hill hard to climb, the road splits into many forks, like the hearts of women on the path of marriage that may not be changed, and the god says he will tell the true straight way so that Civakan may know it.
nuance: The phrase மாற்றரு மணநெறி மகளிர் is doubtful: if it means married women, the verse contradicts 1208's straight road like chaste women's minds; it may instead mean women of an unchanging scent-path, a garland figure.

reading: There is a spring ringed with blue lilies where bees swarm; beside it a round slab of gem-stone; there a vengai tree where bees hum with longing; and beside the vengai a red road has been laid out.
nuance: The chain of landmarks, each placed by the last (அச்சுனை மருங்கில், வேங்கையின் மருங்கில்), is the poem's way of making a route memorable.

tamil: கைம் மலர்த்த அனைய காந்தள் கடிமலர் நாறு கானம்
மொய்ம் மலர்க் குவளைக் கண்ணி மொய்ம்ப நீ முழுதும் நீந்தி
வைம் மலர்த்து இலங்கும் வெள்வேல் மத்திம தேயம் ஆளும்
கொய்ம் மலர்த் தாரினானைக் கண்ணுறு குணம் அது என்றான்.
reading: The god tells Civakan that when he has crossed the whole forest scented with kanthal like open hands, he will meet the king of the middle country with his bright spear and garland, and that this meeting is his good fortune.
nuance: குணம் அது, 'that is the good', sets the meeting as a fortune to be met rather than a deed; the god foretells what the patikam (21) summarizes as the king coming out to receive the hero.
event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan that after the kanthal forest he will meet the king of the middle country.

tamil: மண்ணகங் காவன் மன்னன் மாதரம் பாவை மாசி
லொண்ணுதன் மகளைத் தந்தீங் குறைகென வொழுகு நாளுள்
வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போற் புல்லென வெய்தி நின்ற
வண்ணனின் றோழ ரெல்லா மவ்வழி யடைய ரென்றான்.
reading: The god says that while Civakan lives there, after the king who guards the earth has given him his flawless daughter, all his friends, drooping like stars that have lost the white moon, will come to him there.
nuance: The prophecy names the marriage and the friends' reunion that the patikam (22-23) gives as events; the image of stars bereft of the moon, which the patikam gives to the younger brother, is here given to the friends.
event: Sudanjanan foretells Civakan's marriage to the middle country king's daughter and his friends' coming to him.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1216-1240 (3/10)
theme: Sudanjanan ends his account of the road, repays Civakan with three mantras, foretells in twelve months his reunion, kingship and final renunciation, and carries him down to earth; walking alone through a mourning forest, Civakan converts a hill hunter from meat, honey and toddy by setting hell against heaven, saves elephants from a forest fire, and reaches and circles a Jina temple on a mountain.
source_issues: 1220 line 2 'னாங்கெர் லெய்துவ' is corrupt; the sense 'shall I reach her there' is guessed.
1234 line 3 'சொல்லுங் தகள்ளொடூன்' has a stray letter; read as சொல்லும் கள்ளொடு ஊன்.
1219, 1220, 1224, 1225, 1227, 1231-1234, 1236 and 1240 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build.

cast.role: the hero, leaving the god's mountain to walk alone
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who gives him mantras and carries him to earth (called தேவன், வானவன், தோழன் here)
a hunter, chief of the hill kuravar (வேட்டுவன், குறவருள் தலைவன்), whom Civakan turns from meat and toddy
the hunter's wife, who comes with him

reading: Looking to his good, the god told him fully of the long roads, the matchless forests, the blocked narrow passes, the crowded hills, the friendly places, the lands and the pools on the way.
nuance: உறுதி நோக்கினான் closes the long road-map of the previous verses (1180s-1215): the description was given for the hero's welfare, not as display.
event: Sudanjanan finishes describing the route to Civakan.

reading: So that the fine prince who had whispered the mantra of the path to come into his ear might live and prosper, the able god told him to take three mantras, and explained what each would do.
nuance: Civakan is named here by his own earlier act: செல்கதி மந்திரம் செவியிற் செப்பிய recalls the five padas he whispered to the dying dog (943-947), now repaid with mantras by the god the dog became.
event: Sudanjanan gives Civakan three mantras and tells him their uses.

reading: He made it plain that one mantra gives a voice that even Kama with his flowered arrows would long for, one destroys the poison of snakes and other creatures and fierce diseases, and one gives whatever body is wished for.
nuance: These are worldly powers for the road, not the liberating formula of 945; the shape-changing mantra prepares the disguises of the later ilampakams.
event: Sudanjanan explains the three mantras: an enchanting voice, a cure for poison and disease, and a body of one's choosing.

tamil: கந்தடு களிறு கொல்லுங் கருவரை யுழுவை யன்னான்
மந்திர மூன்று மோதி வானவிற் புரையும் பைந்தா
ரிந்திரன் றன்னை நோக்கி யியக்கியர் குழாத்தை நோக்கிச்
சிந்தையிற் செல்வ லென்றான் றேவனுஞ் செலவு நேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The hero like a dark-hill tiger that kills the post-breaking elephant recited the three mantras, looked at the god, Indra-like in his rainbow garland, and at the throng of yakshi women, and said he would go as his mind was set; the god consented to his going.
nuance: இந்திரன் is read as a title for Sudanjanan as lord among the gods there, not the god Indra; சிந்தையிற் செல்வல் may also mean 'I will go in thought' (by the god's power), which 1224 would then fulfil.
event: Civakan learns the mantras and takes leave; Sudanjanan agrees to let him go.

tamil: மனைப்பெருங் கிழத்தி மாசின் மலைமக டன்னை யான்சென்
றெனைத்தொரு மதியி னாங்கெர் லெய்துவ தென்று நெஞ்சி
னினைத்தலுந் தோழ னக்கு நிழலுமிழ்ந் திலங்கு செம்பொற்
பனைத்திரண் டனைய தோளாய் பன்னிரு மதியி னென்றான்.
reading: When he only thought in his heart, 'in how many months shall I go and reach my faultless lady of the house, the mountain's daughter?', his friend smiled and answered, 'In twelve months, you whose shoulders are like gold palmyra trunks.'
nuance: The god answers a thought, not a question: நெஞ்சின் நினைத்தலும். மலைமகள் is read as Gandharvadattai, the Vidyadhara princess from the mountain and his first wife; the second line is corrupt (see source_issues), so the exact wording of the question is uncertain.
event: Sudanjanan answers Civakan's unspoken question: he will reach his wife in twelve months.

tamil: ஆறிரு மதியி னெய்தி யரட்டனை யடர்த்து மற்றுன்
வீறுயர் முடியுஞ் சூடி விழுநிலக் கிழமை பூண்டு
சாறயர்ந் திறைவற் பேணிச் சார்பறுத் துய்தி யென்று
reading: The god of the cool gem crown foretold that in twelve months he would arrive, crush the usurper, wear his own lofty crown, take the earth as his possession, hold festivals honouring the Lord, and then cut off attachment and be saved.
nuance: The whole remaining plot in one verse, ending not in kingship but in சார்பறுத்து உய்தி: rule and festival worship are set as stages before release. It is a prophecy, so no doctrinal claim is entered; the Lord (இறைவன்) is not named further.
event: Sudanjanan foretells Civakan's victory over the usurper, his kingship and his final renunciation.

tamil: சொற்றிறற் சூழ்ச்சி மிக்க சுதஞ்சணன் சுருங்க நாடி
விற்றிறற் குருசிற் கெல்லாம் வேறுவே றுரைப்பக் கேட்டே
சுற்றிய தோழி மாரை விடுத்தனன் றொழுது நின்றான்
கற்பக மரமுஞ் செம்பொன் மாரியுங் கடிந்த கையான்.
reading: Hearing Sudanjanan, mighty in word and counsel, tell the bow-strong prince each thing separately and briefly, the one whose hand outdid the wishing tree and the rain of red gold dismissed the companion women around him and stood with folded hands.
nuance: I take Civakan as subject of both விடுத்தனன் and தொழுது நின்றான்; Sudanjanan could instead be the one who dismisses the women. The hero worships the god who was once the dog he saved, so the debt now runs both ways.
event: Civakan, having heard the god's counsel, sends away the women attending him and stands in worship before the god.

reading: As though the flower goddess had set her brows as bows over her young red-carp eyes to guard them, the great sun rose from the waves like the tilaka on her fine forehead.
nuance: A dawn verse marking the morning of departure; the sun is the forehead-mark of the goddess Tiru.

reading: Thinking that the hero of the flowering garland could not cross this mountain on his anklet-bearing feet, the long-crowned god left the throng of sweet-voiced women, lifted him up, travelled by thought and came down to the earth.
event: Sudanjanan carries Civakan down from the mountain to the earth by the power of thought.

reading: In a broad grove of sandal, laurel and mango full of sweet fruit, the god embraced the spear-bearer who would rule the earth, saying 'may I see you again', and rose into the sky, and the prince set out on his way.
event: Sudanjanan embraces Civakan in a grove, takes leave and departs; Civakan sets out alone.

reading: Thinking that the war-bull had come alone, leaving behind his kin and fine land, the hills wept for the tiger-like hero, shedding long waterfalls as tears, crying out, their colour scorched and melting.
nuance: Nature mourns his solitude: the waterfalls are tears; the lament fixes the cost of the departure that the god's prophecy made sound easy.
event: The hills seem to weep as Civakan walks on alone.

reading: The honey-jasmine whose buds burst open like mean men who rejoice at the ruin of the great, the vengai, the kanthal that waved its hands like worthy men saying 'alas, this is wrong', and the many beasts and peacocks that gathered like kin all appeared and trembled.
nuance: The forest divides like society at a great man's fall: the laughing jasmine as the base who rejoice, the kanthal as the worthy who protest, the creatures as kin who crowd round.

reading: Saying to the jasmines that crept into the fields and thickets and smiled as if laughing at the lonely, 'we shall knock out your teeth', the bees fell on them, scattered their fresh petals, scorched their old colour and trampled them.
nuance: The bees punish the jasmine of the previous verse for its 'smile' at a lonely traveller: a comic revenge that continues the moral reading of the landscape.

reading: The hero with anklets on his feet crossed the flowering forest slope where she-elephants, like sulking women who say 'we want no flower garland, do not touch our hair, go to the proud women of your house', would not be won over though the tusked males tried to calm them.
event: Civakan crosses the forest slope.

tamil: காழக மூட்டப் பட்ட காரிருட் டுணியு மொப்பா
னாழளை யுடும்பு பற்றிப் பறித்துமார் பொடுங்கி யுள்ளான்
வாழ்மயிர்க் கரடி யொப்பான் வாய்க்கிலை யறித லில்லான்
மேழகக் குரலி னானோர் வேட்டுவன் றலைப்பட் டானே.
reading: A hunter came upon him, like a piece of darkness wrapped in black cloth, with a chest shrunk from dragging monitor lizards out of their deep holes, like a shaggy bear, knowing nothing of betel for his mouth, with a voice like a ram's.
nuance: The description is contemptuous, and the contempt prepares 1234, where the hunter's low birth is explained as the fruit of killing and eating flesh.
event: A hunter meets Civakan in the forest.

tamil: கொடிமுதிர் கிழங்கு தீந்தேன் கொழுந்தடி நறவொ டேந்திப்
பிடிமுதிர் முலையி னாடன் றழைத்துகிற் பெண்ணி னோடுந்
தொடுமரைத் தோலன் வில்லன் மரவுரி யுடையன் றோன்ற
வடிநுனை வேலி னான்கண் டெம்மலை யுறைவ தென்றான்.
reading: He came carrying ripe creeper tubers, sweet honey and fat meat with toddy, along with his woman whose breasts were like an old she-elephant's and who wore leaf garments, he himself in deer skin, with a bow and bark cloth; seeing him, the hero of the sharp spear asked on which mountain he lived.
event: The hunter appears with his wife and his provisions, and Civakan asks where he lives.

tamil: மாலைவெள் ளருவி சூடி மற்றிதா தோன்று கின்ற
சோலைசூழ் வரையி னெற்றிச் சூழ்கிளி சுமக்க லாற்றா
மாலையந் தினைகள் காய்க்கும் வண்புன மதற்குத் தென்மேன்
மூலையங் குவட்டுள் வாழுங் குறவருட் டலைவ னென்றான்
reading: The hunter answered that he is the chief of the kuravar who live in the south-western corner peak beyond the rich millet field on the ridge ringed with groves, there where white waterfalls hang like garlands, whose millet heads the parrots cannot carry.
event: The hunter tells Civakan he is chief of the hill kuravar.

tamil: ஊழினீ ருண்ப தென்னென் றுரைத்தலு முவந்து நோக்கி
மோழலம் பன்றி யோடு முளவுமாக் காதி யட்ட
போழ்நிணப் புழுக்க றேனெய் பொழிந்துகப் பெய்து மாந்தித்
தோழயாம் பெரிது முண்டுந் தொண்டிக்க ளிதனை யென்றான்.
reading: When Civakan asked what they eat as their custom, the chief looked at him gladly and said they cook boar and deer, pour honey-ghee over the sliced fat and eat it, and said, 'Friend, we eat plenty; take this, with the toddy'.
nuance: Line 1 is Civakan's question and lines 2-4 the chief's reply. ஊழின் is read as 'by your custom, in your way of life'; it is not the fate-sense of ஊழ். தொண்டிக்கள் is read as a kind of toddy, but the word is unclear to me. The offer is hospitality, and Civakan's refusal turns it into a sermon.
event: Civakan asks what the hill folk eat, and the chief describes their meat and offers him some with toddy.

tamil: ஊனொடு தேனுங் கள்ளு முண்டுயிர் கொன்ற பாவத்
தீனராய்ப் பிறந்த திங்ங னினியிவை யொழிமி னென்னக்
கானில்வாழ் குறவன் சொல்லுங் தகள்ளொடூன் றேன்கை விட்டா
லேனையெம் முடம்பு வாட்ட லெவன்பிழைத் துங்கொ லென்றான்.
reading: Civakan tells them that they have been born so low because of the sin of killing living beings and eating meat, honey and toddy, and bids them give these up; the forest-dwelling kuravan answers that if they let go of toddy, meat and honey their bodies will waste, and asks how they could survive.
nuance: The first claim makes social rank a karmic fruit: the hunter's birth is itself the punishment of former flesh-eating. The hunter's objection is answered at once in 1235, where Civakan reframes the wasting of the body as the price of a god's birth, and the hunter concedes; hence refuted. The school of the first claim is left general because the verse names no teaching; the Jain frame comes only in 1236.
event: Civakan tells the hunter to give up meat, honey and toddy; the hunter objects that without them they cannot live.

tamil: ஊன்சுவைத் துடம்பு வீக்கி நரகத்தி லுறைத னன்றோ
வூன்றினா துடம்பு வாட்டித் தேவரா யுரைத னன்றோ
வூன்றினா தொழிந்து புத்தே ளாவதே யுறுதி யென்றான்.
reading: Civakan asks him which is better, to fatten the body on the taste of meat and dwell in hell, or to waste the body by not eating meat and dwell as a god, and tells him to say which of the two is right; the hunter answers that giving up meat and becoming a god is right.
nuance: Civakan does not deny the hunter's premise that the body will waste; he accepts it and makes the wasting the price of heaven. The teaching is drawn out of the hunter himself as an answer, a question-and-answer conversion.
event: Civakan puts to the hunter the choice between hell and heaven, and the hunter chooses to give up meat.

tamil: உறுதிநீ யுணர்ந்து சொன்னா யுயர்கதிச் சேறி யேடா
குறுகினா யின்ப வெள்ளங் கிழங்குணக் காட்டு ளின்றே
யிறைவனூற் காட்சி கொல்லா வொழுக்கொடூன் றுறத்தல் கண்டா
யிறுதிக்க ணின்பந் தூங்கு மிருங்கனி யிவைகொ ளென்றான்.
reading: Civakan tells him that he has understood and spoken the right course and will go to a high state; today in this forest where he eats tubers he has come near a flood of joy; he has seen the vision of the Lord's scripture, the conduct of not killing and the renouncing of meat; and he bids him take these great fruits, in which bliss hangs at the end.
nuance: இறைவன் நூல் காட்சி and கொல்லா ஒழுக்கு name vision and conduct, the Jain pairing of right faith and right conduct; the school is assigned on these words. The 'great fruits' at the end are both the forest fruits he hands over and the fruit of the vow, and the hunter's diet is moved from meat to tubers and fruit.
event: Civakan blesses the hunter's choice and gives him fruits.

tamil: என்றலுந் தேனு மூனும் பிழியலு மிறுக நீக்கிச்
குன்றுறை குறவன் போகக் கூரெரி வளைக்கப் பட்ட
பஞ்சவர் போல நின்ற பகட்டினப் பரிவு தீர்த்தான்.
reading: At this the kuravan gave up honey, meat and toddy firmly, went and worshipped his feet, and left for his own mountain saying 'go well', and Civakan then relieved the distress of a herd of elephants that stood like the Pandavas when the fierce fire closed round them.
nuance: The convert's vow is followed at once by an act of compassion toward beasts, so the doctrine of not harming lives is shown being kept by the teacher. பகட்டினம் is read as a herd of elephants; how he relieved them is not said. The simile assumes the hearer knows the Pandavas' escape from the burning house.
event: The hunter renounces meat, honey and toddy, worships Civakan and goes home; Civakan saves a herd of elephants hemmed in by forest fire.

reading: The hero with a chest broad as a hill came to a long mountain whose peaks shone with emerald and gem-veins, poured out streams of gold, and where herds of deer and mountain goats leapt and played.
event: Civakan reaches a high mountain.

reading: He gladly reached the feet worshipped by the spotless great ascetics of mantra-true speech and by the Indras, whose long fame touches the vault of the sky and whose victorious light outshines burning pure gold.
nuance: I read அடி as the Lord's feet, that is the shrine on the mountain that 1240 names as a temple; it could also be the feet of the ascetics themselves.
event: Civakan reaches a shrine of the Lord worshipped by ascetics and gods.

tamil: முனிவரு முயன்று வான்கண் மூப்பிகந் திரிய வின்பக்
கனிகவர் கணனு மேத்தக் காதிகண் ணரிந்த காசி
றனிமுதிர் கடவுள் கோயி றான்வலங் கொண்டு செல்வான்
குனிதிரை முளைத்த வெய்யோன் குன்றுசூழ் வதனை யொத்தான்.
reading: As he went circling the temple of the flawless, supremely ancient god who cut away the ghati karmas, praised by the striving sages and by the host of the sky who enjoy the fruit of bliss free of age, he was like the sun risen from the curling waves circling the great mountain.
nuance: காதி names the obstructing (ghatiya) karmas that a Jina destroys to reach omniscience; the god is defined by what he cut away in himself, not by what he grants. The simile of the sun circling the mountain makes the pradakshina cosmic.
event: Civakan circumambulates the god's temple on the mountain.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1241-1265 (4/10)
theme: Civakan ends his worship at the hill temple with a hymn to the Jina as the one who crossed birth, ended karma and gave the world its teaching, then travels to Chandirapam in the Pallava country, where a dancer falls in love with him on stage and vows herself to him, and the prince, following her gaze, takes him as a friend.
source_issues: 1241, 1243, 1244, 1254, 1255, 1258, 1260, 1262: stanza printed in 8 half-lines, joined into 4 by the build.
1245 line 1: ஏதிதி is doubtful; perhaps ஏத்தி ('praising').
1252 line 3: அலர்கதிர் கரும்பிளை மடுப்ப வாய்நக. carries a stray full stop and is hard to construe.
1255 line 4: the verse ends without its final full stop, unlike its neighbours.
1256 line 4: வீடமை பசும்பொற் சாந்த is obscure as written.
1259 line 1: காண்ட லங்சி is probably a misprint for காண்டல் அஞ்சி.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai
