the Jina, the Omniscient, worshipped at the hill temple and addressed in Civakan's hymn (1241-1247)
the deity of the mountain, who feasts Civakan
the field-women of the Pallava country whom Civakan asks the way
the prince of Chandirapam in the Pallava country (இறைமகன் 1253, அரசன் 1262, இறைவன் 1264), who befriends Civakan; the name is traditional and not in these verses
the unnamed dancer of Chandirapam who falls in love with Civakan (அழகி 1254)
the audience at the dance

tamil: தண் கயம் குற்ற போதும் தாழ்சினை இளிந்த வீயும்
வண் கொடிக் கொய்த பூவும் வார்ந்து மட்டு உயிர்ப்ப ஏந்தித்
திண் புகழ் அறிவன் பாதம் திருந்து கைத் தலத்தின் ஏற்றிப்
பண்பு கொள் குணம் கொள் கீதம் பாணியில் பாடுகின்றான்.
reading: Civakan gathers flowers from the pond, fallen blossoms from low boughs and blooms from creepers, dripping honey, lays them with his own hands on the feet of the Omniscient of firm fame, and sings to the beat a song of the Lord's virtues.
nuance: Three sources of flowers (water, tree, creeper) make the offering complete; the god is named only as அறிவன், the Knower, the Jain title of the Jina, not by a personal name.
event: At the hill temple Civakan offers flowers at the Jina's feet and begins a hymn.

tamil: ஆதி வேதம் பயந்தோய்நீ யலர்பெய்ம் மாரி யமைந்தோய்நீ
நீதி நெறியை யுணர்ந்தோய்நீ நிகரில் காட்சிக் கிறையோய்நீ
நாத னென்னப் படுவோய்நீ நவைசெய் பிறவிக் கடலகத்துன்
பாத கமலந் தொழுவேங்கன் பசையாப் பவிழப் பணியாயே.
reading: Civakan hails the Lord as the one who gave the first Veda, who sat beneath the rain of blossoms, who knew the way of justice and is lord of peerless vision, and asks that the bonds of attachment of those who worship his lotus feet in the harmful sea of births be loosened.
nuance: 'The first Veda' (ஆதி வேதம்) is claimed for the Jina, not the Brahmins' Veda; the prayer asks not to be carried across the sea but for attachment (பசை) to come untied, the Jain account of what keeps one in it. The division பசை யாப்பு அவிழ is ours.

tamil: இன்னாப் பிறவி யிகந்தோய்நீ யிணையி லின்ப முடையோய்நீ
மன்னா வுலக மறுத்தோய்நீ வரம்பில் காட்சிக் கிறையோய்நீ
பொன்னா ரிஞ்சிப் புகழ்வேந்தே பொறியின் வேட்கைக் கடலழுந்தி
யொன்னா வினையி னுழல்வேங்க ளுயப்போம் வண்ண முரையாயே.
reading: He praises the Lord as one who has passed beyond painful birth, has bliss without equal, has rejected the unstable world and has boundless vision, and asks him to tell the way of rescue to those who sink in the sea of the senses' craving and wander in hostile karma.
nuance: What the worshipper asks for is speech, உரையாயே, 'tell': the Lord saves by teaching a way, which fits the hymn's figure of the Jina as the one who himself crossed (இகந்தோய்) rather than one who lifts others.

tamil: உலக மூன்று முடையோய்நீ யொண்பொ னிஞ்சி யெயிலோய்நீ
யலகை யில்லாக் குணக்கடலே யாரு மறியப் படாயாதி
கொலையி லாழி வலனுயர்த்த குளிர்முக் குடையி னிழலோய்நீ.
reading: He hails the Lord as owner of the three worlds, dweller within the bright golden wall, the foremost in strength, praised by the gods, an endless sea of virtues and the Primal one none can know, who raised the wheel that does not kill and sits in the shade of the cool triple umbrella.
nuance: The wheel of dominion, elsewhere the conqueror's sign, is here the wheel 'without killing' (கொலையில் ஆழி): the Jina's sovereignty is non-violence. The golden wall and triple umbrella are the marks of the Jina's preaching hall.

reading: In a question and answer, the hymn asks who it is that rose up to the crowned summit of the worlds while the worlds below praised him and showered blossoms, and answers that it is the Lord who destroyed the bonds of the three guarded fortresses.
nuance: The epithet of destroying three forts is the Saiva one of Siva and the three cities, taken over for the Jina; the word கட்டு ('bond', also 'fastening') suggests the forts are read as bonds, but the verse does not say which three. The 'crowned world' is the summit of the universe where the freed rest.

reading: The hymn asks who is the Real One who, having conquered the three worlds so that strife ceased, gave the Three on earth, and answers that it is the Lord, the Knower-Aran whose wheel is like the cool moon and who is the refuge of the world.
nuance: 'The Three' (மூன்று) are unnamed; in Jain teaching the triad given to the world would be right faith, knowledge and conduct, but that is our gloss. அரன் here is applied to the Jina, a second Saiva name taken over after the three forts of 1245.

reading: The hymn asks who is the Vaaman who ended karma that cannot be ended, discerned and handed on the sacred ford, and taught the state from which none return, and answers that it is the god of the blossoming asoka tree thick with flowers.
nuance: வாராக் கதி, 'the going from which none come back', names release as the end of return, not a heaven. Whose karma is ended is not stated; in the Jain frame (and 1240's temple of the one who cut the ghati karmas) it is first the Jina's own, which he then teaches others to end.

reading: Having bowed at the Jina temple on that hill and praised the golden-flowered red feet of the Lord, and having been feasted by the deity of the fierce mountain, the noble youth went on and reached the Pallava country.
event: The mountain deity feasts Civakan, and he leaves the hill and reaches the Pallava country.

reading: He asks two field-women, languid-eyed from drinking toddy, who pluck blue lilies in fields where striped varal fish leap, the way to the city and goes on ahead.
event: Civakan asks two field-women the way to the city.

reading: The city, ringed by moats of many lotuses where swans and makanril birds rest and by its ancient unbreached wall coiled like a serpent of green gold, shines like a lovely woman wearing the sea and adorned with gold.
nuance: கன்னி மூதெயில், 'the virgin ancient wall', is the wall never taken; the figure of the city as an adorned woman readies the scene of the dancer that follows.

reading: The young bull with the shining spear reaches Chandirapam, where flags on mansions fragrant with agil smoke cut through the clouds and shut out the daylight.
event: Civakan reaches the city Chandirapam.

reading: He went on while many praised his beauty and water was brought in flower-decked jewelled pots, and he entered the city like the one who measured the world.
nuance: Line 3 (அலர்கதிர் கரும்பு இளை மடுப்ப) is hard to construe; it may say that the sugarcane hedges took in the spreading rays. The comparison to உலகளந்தான் is the Vaishnava Trivikrama, used for the hero's stride into the city.
event: Civakan enters Chandirapam amid praise and ceremonial water.

tamil: சந்தனக் காவு சூழ்ந்து சண்பக மலர்ந்த சோலை
வந்துவீழ் மாலை நாற்றி மணியரங் கணிந்து வானத்
திந்திர குமரன் போல விறைமக னிருந்து காண
வந்தர மகளி ரன்னார் நாடக மியற்று கின்றார்.
reading: In a garden of sandal groves and blooming champak, with garlands hung and a jewelled stage adorned, women like the celestial maidens perform a drama while the king's son sits watching like Indra's son in heaven.
event: The prince of Chandirapam watches a dance-drama staged in the garden.

tamil: குழலெடுத் தியாத்து மட்டார் கோதையிற் பொலிந்து மின்னு
மழலவிர் செம்பொற் பட்டங் குண்டல மாரந் தாங்கி
நிழலவி ரல்குற் காசு சிலம்பொடு சிலம்ப நீடோ
ளழகிகூத் தாடு கின்றா ளரங்கின்மே லரம்பை யன்னாள்.
reading: Her hair tied up and bright with honeyed garlands, wearing a gleaming gold forehead band, earrings and a necklace, her girdle bells and anklets chiming together, the long-armed beauty like Rambha dances on the stage.
event: A dancer takes the stage.

tamil: தண்ணுமை முழவம் வீணை குழலொடு குயிலத் தண்பூங்
கண்ணொடு புருவங் கைகால் கலையல்கு னுசுப்புக் காம
ரொண்ணுதல் கொண்ட வாடற் றொட்டிமை யுருவ நோக்கி
வெண்ணெய்தீ யுற்ற வண்ண மாடவர் மெலிகின் றாரே
reading: To drum, muzhavu, vina and flute she dances with eyes, brows, hands, feet, garment, hips and waist, and the men who watch her form melt like butter touched by fire.
event: The dancer performs and the men watching are overcome.

tamil: பாடலொ டியைந்த வாடல் பண்ணமை கருவி மூன்றுங்
கூடுபு சிவணி நின்று குழைந்திழைந் தமிர்த மூற
வோடரி நெடுங்க ணம்பா லுளங்கிழிந் துருவ வெய்யா
வீடமை பசும்பொற் சாந்த மிலயமா வாடு கின்றாள்.
reading: Her dance is joined to the song, the three tuned instruments blend and flow like nectar, and as the arrows of her long streaked eyes tear into hearts she dances keeping the rhythm.
nuance: Line 4's வீடமை பசும்பொற் சாந்தம் is obscure as written; the image of fresh-gold sandal paste does not join clearly to the rest.

tamil: வாணுதற் பட்ட மின்ன வார்குழை திருவில் வீசப்
பூண்முலை பிறழப் பொற்றோ டிடவயி னுடங்க வொல்கி
மாணிழை வளைக்கை தம்மால் வட்டணை போக்கு கின்றாள்
காண்வரு குவளைக் கண்ணாற் காளைமே னோக்கி னாளே.
reading: With her forehead band flashing, her earrings throwing rainbows, her breasts trembling and her gold earring swaying on the left, she bends and circles her bangled hands, and with her blue-lily eyes she looks at the youth.
event: In the middle of the dance she looks at Civakan.

tamil: நோக்கினா ணெடுங்க ணென்னுங் குடங்கையா னொண்டு கொண்டு
வாக்கமை யுருவின் மிக்கான் வனப்பினைப் பருக விப்பா
லாக்கிய விலய நீங்கிற் றணங்கனா ணெடுங்கண் பில்கி
வீக்குவார் முலையி னெற்றி வெண்முத்தஞ் சொரிந்த வன்றே.
reading: She looked, and with her long eyes for a cupped palm she scooped up and drank the beauty of the finely formed youth; at that the rhythm she had kept left her, and her long eyes ran with tears that fell on her breasts like white pearls.
nuance: The art fails at the moment of desire: the dancer whose eyes were weapons in 1256 becomes the one who drinks through them, and loses the laya, the one thing the stage requires.
event: The dancer loses the rhythm and weeps.

tamil: செருக்கய னெடுங்க ணாளத் திருமகன் காண்ட லங்சி
நெருக்கித்தன் முலையின் மின்னு நிழன்மணி வடத்தை மாதர்
பொருக்குநூல் பரிந்து சிந்தாப் பூவெலாங் கரிந்து வாடத்
தரிக்கிலாள் காமச் செந்தீத் தலைக்கொளச் சாம்பி னாளே.
reading: The woman with proud kayal-fish eyes, shrinking from being seen as she looked at the noble son, pressed and broke the gleaming jewelled string on her breast so its thread snapped and scattered, and as all her flowers scorched and withered she could not bear it and languished in the red fire of desire.
nuance: The flowers withering on her body are the tradition's sign of love's fever. 'Shrinking from being seen' depends on reading காண்டல் அஞ்சி for the printed காண்ட லங்சி.
event: The dancer breaks her necklace and languishes with desire.

tamil: கன்னிமை கனிந்து முற்றிக் காமுறக் கமழுங் காமத்
தின்னறுங் கனியைத் துய்ப்பா னேந்தலே பிறர்க ளில்லை
பொன்னினா லுடையுங் கற்பென் றுரைத்தவர் பொய்யைச் சொன்னா
ரின்னிசை யிவற்க லாலென் னெஞ்சிட மில்லை யென்றாள்.
reading: She says that the sweet fruit of her ripened maidenhood, fragrant with desire, is for this lord alone and no other; those who said that chastity breaks for gold told a lie; there is no room in her heart for anyone but this sweet-voiced man.
nuance: A stage dancer, of the class the ethical books call women for hire, claims karpu for herself and calls the saying that gold breaks it a lie. The epic lets her speak it; whether the story bears her out is for later verses.
event: The dancer vows in her heart that she will belong to Civakan alone.

tamil: கருஞ்சிறைப் பறவை யூர்திக் காமரு காளை தான்கொ
லிருஞ்சுற வுயர்த்த தோன்ற லேத்தருங் குருசி றான்கொ
லரும்பெறற் குமர னென்றாங் கறிவயர் வுற்று நின்றா
டிருந்திழை யணங்கு மென்றோட் டேசிகப் பாவை யன்னாள்.
reading: Is he the lovely youth who rides the dark-winged bird, or the lord who raised the great shark banner, or the rare prince Kumaran, she wonders, and stands bewildered, the jewelled one like a lovely doll.
nuance: Her guesses are gods: the shark banner is Kama's; the bird-rider and Kumaran are less certain identifications (the bird may be Vishnu's Garuda or Murugan's peacock). Seeing the hero as a god in disguise is a recurring move of the poem.

tamil: போதெனக் கிடந்த வாட்கண் புடைபெயர்ந் திமைத்தல் செல்லா
தியாதிவள் கண்ட தென்றாங் கரசனு மமர்ந்து நோக்கி
மீதுவண் டரற்றுங் கண்ணி விடலையைத் தானுங் கண்டான்
காதலிற் களித்த துள்ளங் காளையைக் கொணர்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Her flower-like eyes turned aside and would not blink; wondering what she had seen, the king too looked carefully and saw the young man whose garland the bees hum over, and with his heart glad with affection he said, 'Bring the youth.'
nuance: The ruler reads the dancer's gaze as the usurper's ally did in 685, and draws the opposite conclusion: not a rival to resent but a man to meet.
event: Following the dancer's gaze, the prince sees Civakan and orders him brought.

reading: All who looked, in doubt, reasoned that if he were the god with the sugarcane bow he would have his bow and arrows, and since he has none he must be a king of the true Yakshas.

tamil: மந்திரம் மறந்து வீழ்ந்து மா நிலத்து இயங்கு கின்ற
அந்தர குமரன் என்று ஆங்கு யாவரும் அமர்ந்து நோக்கி
இந்திர திருவற்கு உய்த்தார்க்கு இறைவனும் எதிர் கொண்டு ஓம்பி
மைந்தனை மகிழ்வ கூறி மைத்துனத் தோழன் என்றான்.
reading: Everyone decided he was a heavenly prince who had forgotten his spell, fallen and was walking on the earth, and brought him to the prince of Indra's splendour; the lord received and honoured him, spoke to the young man with joy and called him his brother-in-law friend.
nuance: 'One who forgot his mantra and fell' is the lore of the Vidyadharas, whose flight depends on spells. மைத்துனத் தோழன் names a friend as close as a wife's brother; it may look ahead to a marriage tie the story has not yet made.
event: The crowd brings Civakan to the prince, who welcomes him and calls him a brother-in-law friend.

tamil: போதவிழ் தெரிய லானும் பூங்கழற் காலி னானுங்
காதலி னொருவ ராகிக் கலந்துட னிருந்த போழ்தி
னூதுவண் டுடுத்த மாலை யுணர்வுபெற் றிலயந் தாங்கிப்
போதுகண் டனைய வாட்கட் புருவத்தாற் கலக்கு கின்றாள்.
reading: When the prince of the flower garland and the youth of the anklet-feet sat together, one in affection, the dancer came back to herself, took up the rhythm again and troubled him with the brows of her flower-like eyes.
event: Civakan and the prince sit together as friends; the dancer recovers the rhythm and plays her glances at him.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1266-1290 (5/10)
theme: News comes that Padumai, reaching for a flower in her grove, has been bitten by a snake; the prince's mantras, a crowd of rival healers, seven thousand Brahmins and an astrologer all fail, until an omen points to a young man, the prince sends for Civakan, and he diagnoses the bite by its cause, smell and kind and cures her with a spell, so that her first look on reviving falls on him.
source_issues: 1271 line 4: திருமகள் named the princess in 1266 but here seems to be the queen the companion runs to; the referent is not certain.
1276 line 4: எனறுகே ளாதி தென்பார் has a misprint, probably என்று கேளாது இது என்பார் (என்று for எனறு).
1284: the verse names a speaker twice (நம்பி at line 1 and line 4, கொற்ற வேந்தன் at line 2), and who speaks to whom is not settled.
1286 and 1288: technical snake-lore terms (தட்டம், அதட்டம், பிளிற்று, மண்டலி) are rare and the division of the lines among them is uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called சீவகசாமி in the invocation
the princess of Chandrabham, bitten by a snake in her grove (named in 1273)
the king's son of Chandrabham, who has taken Civakan as friend (மன்னவன் சிறுவன் in 1282)
the king of Chandrabham, Padumai's father, who offers her hand to whoever cures her
the spear-bearing man who brings the prince news of the bite
the woman who runs to tell Padumai that her jasmine has flowered
Padumai's companion, who runs to the queen
the snake that bites Padumai
the poison-healers who give rival diagnoses and remedies
the seven thousand Brahmins versed in mantra and Veda who command the girl to rise
the astrologer who reads the hour of the bite
an unnamed reader of omens (here, at Chandrabham) who foretells Padumai's rescue; same id as the soothsayer type of 010, not the same person
the bangled women of Padumai's household who lie weeping

tamil: தேனுகுக் கின்ற கண்ணித் திருமக ளாட விப்பா
லூனுகுக் கின்ற வைவே லொருமக னுருமிற் றோன்றி
வானுகுக் கின்ற மீன்போன் மணிபரந் திமைக்கு மார்பிற்
கானுகுக் கின்ற பைந்தார்க் காவலற் றொழுது சொன்னான்
reading: While the princess, garlanded with dripping honey, was at play, a man bearing a spear that drips flesh appears as suddenly as thunder and, bowing, speaks to the prince whose chest glitters with gems like falling stars.
nuance: The verse holds back the news: the messenger's sudden coming (உருமின் தோன்றி) is the only sign of disaster, and the next six verses are his report.
event: A spear-bearing messenger rushes in and bows to the prince to speak.

tamil: கொய்தகைப் பொதியிற் சோலைக் குழவிய முல்லை மௌவல்
செய்யசந் திமயச் சாரற் கருப்புரக் கன்று தீம்பூக்
கைதரு மணியிற் றெண்ணீர் மதுக்கலந் தூட்டி மாலை
பெய்தொளி மறைத்து நங்கை பிறையென வளர்க்கின் றாளே.
reading: The messenger begins: in the grove of Pothiyil the lady has been rearing a young jasmine and a mauval creeper as one rears a crescent moon, watering them with clear water mixed with honey and screening them from the sun with garlands.
nuance: The care given to the plant is the care of a mother for a child (பிறையென வளர்க்கின்றாள்); the scene that follows turns on her delight in what she has raised.

tamil: பவழங்கொள் கோடு நாட்டிப் பைம்பொனால் வேலி கோலித்
தவழ்கதிர் முத்தம் பாய்த்தித் தன்கையாற் றீண்டி நன்னாட்
புகழ்கொடி நங்கை தன்பேர் பொறித்ததோர் கன்னி முல்லை
யகழ்கடற் றானை வேந்தே யணியெயி றீன்ற தன்றே.
reading: That maiden jasmine, staked on a coral pole, fenced in gold, strewn with pearls, touched by her own hand and inscribed with her name, has now put out buds like fine teeth, O king of the army wide as the moated sea.
nuance: The plant bears her name and is called a maiden (கன்னி முல்லை), so its first flowering mirrors her own coming of age.
event: Padumai's own jasmine comes into bud.

tamil: வலம்பலர் கோதை சிந்த மயிலென வொருத்தி யோடிக்
கொம்பலர் நங்கை பூத்தாள் பொலிகெனக் குனிந்த விற்கீ
ழம்பலர் கண்ணி யார நிதியறைந் தோகை போக்கிக்
கம்பலம் போர்த்த போலுங் கடிமலர்க் காவு புக்காள்.
reading: A woman ran like a peacock, garland scattering, crying that the creeper had flowered and wishing her prosperity; the lady rewarded the good news with treasure and entered the fragrant grove that seemed spread with a woollen cloth of blossoms.
nuance: ஓகை போக்கி is the custom of paying the bearer of glad news; the gift marks the joy just before the bite.
event: A woman brings word that the jasmine has flowered; Padumai rewards her and goes into the grove.

tamil: நறவிரி சோலை யாடி நாண்மலர்க் குரவம் பாவை
நிறையப்பூத் தணிந்து வண்டுந் தேன்களு நிழன்று பாட
விறைவளைத் தோளி மற்றென் றோழியீ தென்று சேர்ந்து
பெறலரும் பாவை கொள்வாள் பெரியதோ ணீட்டி னாளே.
reading: In the honey-dripping grove, where a kuravam tree had flowered into a doll and bees sang over it, the lady, calling it her companion, stretched out her long arm to take the rare flower-doll.
nuance: The kuravam's blossom cluster called பாவை, a doll, lets the girl treat the flower as a playmate (என் தோழி ஈது); the gesture of reaching is the moment of danger.
event: Padumai reaches out to pick the kuravam flower-doll.

tamil: நங்கைதன் முகத்தை நோக்கி நகைமதி யிதுவென் றெண்ணி
யங்குறை யரவு தீண்டி யௌவையோ வென்ற போகக்
கொங்கலர் கோதை நங்கை யடிகளோ வென்று கொம்பேர்
செங்கயற் கண்ணி தோழி திருமகட் சென்று சேர்ந்தாள்.
reading: A snake living there looked at her face, took it for the laughing moon and bit her; she cried out for her mother, and her carp-eyed companion ran, crying for the lady's elders, and reached the queen.
nuance: The bite is told as a praise of her face, the snake that seizes the moon of the eclipse turned on a girl. ஔவை here is 'mother'; திருமகள் in line 4 is most likely the queen, though the same word named the princess in 1266.
event: The snake bites Padumai, mistaking her face for the moon, and her companion runs to tell the queen.

tamil: அடிகளுக் கிறைஞ்சி யைய னடிகளைத் தொழுது நங்கை
யடிகளைப் புல்லி யாரத் தழுவிக்கொண் டௌவை மாரைத்
கொடியனா யென்னை நாளு நினையெனத் தழுவிக் கொண்டு
மிடை மின்னி னிலத்தைச் சேர்ந்தாள் வேந்தமற் றருளு கென்றான்.
reading: Bowing to the elders, worshipping her father's feet, clasping her mothers and asking them to think of her always though she has been cruel to them, she sank to the ground like lightning; 'O king, show grace,' the messenger ended.
nuance: Her farewell asks to be remembered as one who wronged them by dying (கொடியனாய்), the voice of a child who expects to die before her parents. Whose feet are meant by அடிகள் and ஐயன் in lines 1 and 2 is not certain.
event: Padumai takes leave of her parents as if dying and collapses.

tamil: பதுமையைப் பாம்பு தீண்டிற் றென்றலும் பையு ளெய்திக்
கொதிநுனை வேலி னாயிங் கிருக்கெனக் குருசி லேகிக்
கதுமெனச் சென்று நோக்கிக் காய்சினங் கடிதற் கொத்த
மதிமிகுத் தவல நீக்கு மந்திரம் பலவுஞ் செய்தான்.
reading: Hearing that a snake had bitten Padumai, the prince was stricken, told Civakan to stay where he was, went at once, looked, and worked many mantras fit to quench the burning venom and remove the grief.
nuance: The prince himself knows anti-venom mantras and fails; that he leaves his new friend behind sets up the later call for him (1282). Civakan is the one addressed by the spear epithet of line 2.
event: The prince leaves Civakan behind, goes to Padumai and tries many mantras on the venom.

tamil: ணுள்ளவ ரொன்ற லாத செயச்செய வூறு கேளா
தள்ளிலைப் பூணி னாளுக் காவியுண் டில்லை யென்ன
வெள்ளெயிற் றரவு கான்ற வேகமிக் கிட்ட தன்றே
reading: The noble prince tried all he knew, and those there tried every other remedy, but the girl heard nothing; asked whether life remained, they could not say, and the force of the white-fanged snake's venom rose higher.
event: Every remedy fails and the venom rises.

tamil: பைங்கதிர் மதிய மென்று பகையடு வெகுளி நாக
நங்கையைச் செற்ற தீங்குத் தீர்த்துநீர் கொண்மி னாடும்
வங்கமா நிதிய நல்கி மகட்டரு மணிசெய் மான்றே
ரெங்களுக் கிறைவ னென்றாங் கிடிமுர செருக்கி னானே.
reading: Proclaiming that whoever cures the lady of the harm the furious snake did her, taking her face for the moon, shall have the land, ships and great treasure and the daughter herself, the lord of the jewelled chariot had the thunder drum beaten.
nuance: The reward joins kingdom and bride, the formula of a svayamvara by deed; the Cintamani's marriages are won this way, by a feat rather than a match arranged for birth.
event: The king proclaims by drum that whoever cures Padumai will receive land, wealth and her hand.

tamil: மண்டலி மற்றி தென்பா ரிராசமா நாக மென்பார்
கொண்டது நாக மென்பார் குறைவளி பித்தொ டையிற்
பிண்டித்துப் பெருகிற் றென்பார் பெருநவை யறுக்கும் விஞ்சை
யெண்டவப் பலவுஞ் செய்தா மெனறுகே ளாதி தென்பார்.
reading: The healers argue: some say it is a மண்டலி snake, some a royal great snake, some that a naga has seized her, some that wind, bile and phlegm, out of balance, have clotted and grown; some say that though they have done many spells that cut great harm, she does not respond.
nuance: The scene is comic in its accumulation of என்பார்: each healer names a different snake or a humoral cause, and none agrees. The line on the three humours is the medical theory of the Kural's chapter on medicine, here applied to a bite.
event: The poison-healers give rival diagnoses and report their spells have failed.

tamil: சிரையைந்தும் விடுது மென்பார் தீற்றுதுஞ் சிருங்கி யென்பார்
குரைபுன லிடுது மென்பார் கொந்தழ லுறுத்து மென்பா
ரிரையென வருத்தக் கவ்வி யென்புறக் கடித்த தென்பா
ருரையன்மி னுதிர நீங்கிற் றுய்யல ணங்கை யென்பார்.
reading: Others say they will bleed her from the five veins, or feed her the drug சிருங்கி, or plunge her in rushing water, or apply fire; some say the snake bit to the bone as if seizing prey, and some say: speak no more, if the blood has left her the girl will not live.
nuance: The verse lists treatments without one being chosen; the remedies contradict each other (water and fire), which is the point. சிருங்கி is a rare word for a drug.
event: The healers propose bleeding, drugs, water and fire, and some give her up.

tamil: கையொடு கண்டங் கோப்பார் கனைசுட ருறுப்பின் வைப்பார்
தெய்வதம் பரவி யெல்லாத் திசைதொறுந் தொழுது நிற்பா
ருய்வகை யின்றி யின்னே யுலகுடன் கவிழு மென்பார்
மையலங் கோயின் மாக்கண் மடைதிறந் திட்ட தொத்தார்.
reading: Some bind her hand and neck, some lay bright flames to her limbs, some praise the gods and stand worshipping in every direction, some say the whole world will now topple without escape; the people of the bewildered palace were like a sluice thrown open.
nuance: Worship of the gods (தெய்வதம் பரவி) is listed among the failed remedies, beside cautery and binding, with no comment from the narrator.
event: Healers bind and burn her limbs, others pray, and the palace breaks into wailing.

tamil: வெந்தெரி செம்பொற் பூவும் விளங்குபொன் னூலும் பெற்றார்
மந்திர மறையும் வல்லா ரெழாயிரர் மறுவில் வாய்மை
யந்தரத் தறுவை வைப்பா ரந்தண ரங்கை கொட்டிப்
பைந்தொடிப் பாவை யின்னே பரிவொழிந் தெழுக வென்பார்.
reading: Seven thousand Brahmins, who had received gifts of fiery gold flowers and gleaming gold thread and were masters of mantra and Veda, set cloth aloft in the air with spotless truth, clapped their hands and said, 'Let the girl with green bangles rise now, her pain gone.'
nuance: The Brahmins are paid before they act (பெற்றார்), and their command fails; in a Jain epic the scene sets the Vedic ritualists' mantras beside the one that will work. The rite of setting cloth in the air (அந்தரத்து அறுவை வைப்பார்) is obscure.
event: Seven thousand paid Brahmins chant mantras and command her to rise, without effect.

tamil: பாம்பெழப் பாம்பு கொண்டாற் பகவற்கு மரிது தீர்த்த
றேம்பிழி கோதைக் கின்று பிறந்தநா டெளிமி னென்று
காம்பழி பிச்ச மாகக் கணியெடுத் துரைப்பக் கல்லென்
றூம்பழி குளத்திற் கண்ணீர் துகணிலத் திழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The astrologer, reading the stars, says that when a snake bites as the serpent rises, curing it is hard even for the Lord, and that today is the very day of the garlanded girl's birth star, so they must understand; at this the tears ran down to the dusty ground like water from a burst tank.
nuance: பாம்பு எழ may name the rising of an asterism or the serpent of the eclipse; either way the verdict rests on the hour, not on the venom. Whether the birth-star day aggravates or softens the verdict is not clear from the line, but the weeping shows how it was heard. The prediction is overturned in 1290.
event: The astrologer declares the bite nearly incurable by the stars, and all weep.

tamil: நங்கைக்கின் றிறத்த லில்லை நரபதி நீயுங் கேண்மோ
கொங்கலர் கோங்கி னெற்றிக் குவிமுகிழ் முகட்டி னங்கட்
டங்குதே னரவ யாழிற் றானிருந் தாந்தை பாடு
மிங்குநம் மிடரைத் தீர்ப்பா னிளையவ னுளன்மற் றென்றான்.
reading: Someone tells the king: the lady will not die today, O lord of men, listen: on the closed bud at the crown of the flowering kongu an owl sits and calls with a sound like a bee's yaal, and there is a young man here who will end our distress.
nuance: Against the astrologer's verdict a bird omen promises life and points to a rescuer not yet named; the verse makes divination itself split, one sign of death and one of help. Who speaks is not named (என்றான்), and reading ஆந்தை as an owl is likely but not certain.

tamil: பன்மணிக் கடகஞ் சிந்தப் பருப்புடைப் பவளத் தூண்மேன்
மன்னவன் சிறுவன் வண்கை புடைத்துமா ழாந்து சொன்னா
னின்னுமொன் றுண்டு சூழ்ச்சி யென்னொடங் கிருந்த நம்பி
தன்னைக்கூய்க் கொணர்மி னென்றான் றரவந்தாங் கவனுங் கண்டான்.
reading: Shaking the jewelled bracelets on his arm as he struck his hand on the coral pillar in his distress, the king's son said there was one more plan: 'Call and bring the young man who sat with me there'; they brought him, and Civakan saw the scene.
nuance: The omen of a young man (1281) is fulfilled by the prince's memory of his new friend, so the help comes through friendship rather than proclamation.
event: The prince remembers Civakan and has him fetched to Padumai.

tamil: பறவைமா நாகம் வீழ்ந்து பலவுடன் பதைப்ப போன்றுஞ்
சிறகுறப் பரப்பி மஞ்ஞை செருக்குபு கிடந்த போன்றுங்
கறவைகன் றிழந்த போன்றுங் கிடந்தழு கின்ற கண்ணா
ரிறைவளை யவரை நோக்கி யென்கொடி துற்ற தென்றான்.
reading: Seeing the bangled women lying and weeping, like great birds fallen and writhing together, like peacocks sprawled with spread wings, like cows that have lost their calves, Civakan asked what cruel thing had happened.
event: Civakan finds the women lamenting and asks what has befallen.

tamil: ஊறுகொள் சிங்கம் போல வுயக்கமோ டிருந்த நம்பி
கூறினான் கொற்ற வேந்தன் கொழுநிதி நிலத்து மற்றுன்
வீறுயர் புகழை வித்திக் கேண்மையை விளைத்தி யின்னே
நாறுபூங் கொம்ப னாளை நோக்கென நம்பி சொன்னான்.
reading: The one who sat in distress like a wounded lion spoke: 'Sow your towering fame in this victorious king's rich land, and reap kinship from it now; look at the girl who is like a fragrant flowering branch.'
nuance: The appeal is put in the language of farming: fame is the seed and kinship (கேண்மை) the harvest, a quiet repetition of the drum's promise of the bride (1275). The verse names the speaker twice, as நம்பி and as கொற்ற வேந்தன், and it is not clear whether the king or the prince speaks, or whether கொற்ற வேந்தன் is the one addressed.

tamil: புற்றிடை வெகுளி நாகம் போக்கறக் கொண்ட தேனு
மற்றிடை யூறு செய்வான் வானவர் வலித்த தேனும்
பொற்றொடிக் கிறத்த லில்லை புலம்புகொண் டழேற்க வென்றான்
கற்றடிப் படுத்த விஞ்சைக் காமரு காம னன்னான்.
reading: Civakan, master of learned spells and handsome as Kama, says: whether the furious snake from the anthill seized her past escape, or the gods willed it to do her harm, the girl with golden bangles will not die; do not weep in grief.
nuance: கற்று அடிப்படுத்த விஞ்சை calls his power a learned art mastered by practice, not a gift of the moment, though the story traced it to a god's teaching. He allows that the gods may have caused the bite and still promises life.
event: Civakan assures the household that Padumai will not die.

tamil: பொழிந்துநஞ் சுகுத்த லச்ச மிரைபெரு வெகுளி போகங்
கழிந்துமீ தாடல் காலம் பிழைப்பென வெட்டி னாகும்
பிழிந்துயி ருண்ணுந் தட்ட மதட்டமாம் பிளிற்றி னும்ப
ரொழிந்தெயி றூனஞ் செய்யுங் கோளென மற்றுஞ் சொன்னான்.
reading: He adds the lore of bites: a snake bites for eight causes, pouring out venom, fear, prey, great anger, after mating, being trodden on, the season, and by mistake; and he names the kinds of bite, the one that squeezes and drinks life and the others, by how the fangs strike.
nuance: Before any cure Civakan classifies: he names causes and kinds of bite as a physician names a disease, and that is what sets him apart from the healers of 1276-1279. Several terms (தட்டம், அதட்டம், பிளிற்று) are technical and their division is uncertain.

tamil: அந்தண னாறு மான்பா லவியினை யலர்ந்த காலை
நந்தியா வட்ட நாறு நகைமுடி யரச னாயிற்
றந்தியா முரைப்பிற் றாழைத் தடமலர் வணிக னாறும்
பந்தியாப் பழுப்பு நாறிற் சூத்திரன் பால தென்றான்.
reading: He says a bite smelling of the milk-and-ghee offering at dawn is from a Brahmin snake, one smelling of nandyavattam flowers from a royal snake, one smelling of the great screwpine from a merchant snake, and one smelling of decay from a Sudra snake.
nuance: Snakes are sorted into the four varnas, each known by a smell drawn from its varna's world (the sacrificial offering, the royal flower, the merchant's trade flower, decay). This is snake-poison lore, not a statement about people, but it carries the varna order into nature without question.

tamil: கன்னியைக் கடித்த நாகங் கன்னியே கன்னி நோக்க
மன்னதே யரசர் சாதி மூன்றெயி றழுந்தி யாழ்ந்த
கொன்னுமா நாகங் கொண்டாற் கொப்புளாம் விரலிற் றேய்த்தான்
மன்னிய தெண்மட் டாயின் மண்டலிப் பால தென்றான்.
reading: The snake that bit the maiden is itself a maiden, as the girl's look shows; it is of royal caste; and a great snake whose three fangs sink deep leaves blisters when the spot is rubbed with a finger, while one whose mark stays clear is of the மண்டலி kind.
nuance: The royal snake that bit a princess matches its victim, a symmetry the lore of 1287 makes possible. How lines 3 and 4 divide the tests is not certain.
event: Civakan diagnoses the bite as from a young female snake of royal caste.

tamil: குன்றிரண் டனைய தோளான் கொழுமலர்க் குவளைப் போதங்
கொன்றிரண் டுருவ மோதி யுறக்கிடை மயில னாடன்
சென்றிருண் டமைந்த கோலச் சிகழிகை யழுத்திச் செல்வ
னின்றிரண் டுருவ மோதி நேர்முக நோக்கி னானே.
reading: Civakan, his shoulders like twin hills, recited the mantra twice, pressed the girl's dark, well-dressed hair knot, and stood reciting it twice more as he looked straight into her face.
nuance: The cure is mantra and touch at the crown of the head, with the gaze into her face as part of the rite; the look that heals is also the first look between the two. இரண்டு உருவம் ஓதி most likely counts the repetitions (உரு) of the spell.
event: Civakan recites the mantra, pressing her hair knot and gazing into her face.

tamil: நெடுந்தகை நின்று நோக்க நீள்கடற் பிறந்த கோலக்
கடுங்கதிர்க் கனலி கோப்பக் காரிரு ளுடைந்த தேபோ
லுடம்பிடை நஞ்சு நீங்கிற் றொண்டொடி யுருவ மார்ந்து
குடங்கையி னெடிய கண்ணாற் குமரன்மே னோக்கி னாளே.
reading: As the noble one stood gazing, the venom left her body as darkness breaks when the bright sun born of the long sea gathers its rays; the girl regained her form and looked at the young man with long eyes cupped like a palm.
nuance: Her first act on returning to life is to look at Civakan (குமரன்மேல் நோக்கினாள்), so revival and falling in love are one moment; the drum's promise of 1275 has found its winner.
event: The venom leaves Padumai, she revives and her first look falls on Civakan.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1291-1315 (6/10)
theme: Padumai, revived, looks at her healer and falls at once into love's sickness; the palace honours Civakan with bath, meal and betel, the king tests and praises his learning, and the chapter closes on the two lovers' separate sleepless laments on the same night.
source_issues: Verses 1291, 1296, 1297, 1298, 1299 and 1303 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 1300 line 1 (ஏந்திய வேற்பத் தாங்கி) does not divide into clear words, and line 3 begins யாயந்தநன், probably for ஆய்ந்த நன்.
Verse 1303 line 1 reads செம்பெர் னடைப்பை, apparently a misprint for செம்பொன் அடைப்பை.
Verse 1312 line 3 ends மீட்டவ/ளிடைய (மீட்டவள்), feminine, where the sense seems to want the masculine; the line may be corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, who cured Padumai of the snakebite
the king's daughter, bitten by a snake in the garden and revived by Civakan
the king, Padumai's father (named in the verses only as மன்னன்)
Padumai's companions and nursing mothers
the palace serving women who attend Civakan at the king's order
the onlookers who watch Civakan revive Padumai
the women among the onlookers

tamil: நோக்கினா ணிறையு நாணு மாமையுங் கவினு நொய்திற்
போக்கினாள் வளையும் போர்த்தாள் பொன்னிறப் பசலை மூழ்கிற்
றாக்கினா ளநங்க னப்புத் தூணியை யமரு ளானா
தோக்கிய முருக னெஃக மோரிரண் டனைய கண்ணாள்.
reading: The narrator tells that Padumai, once she had looked at Civakan, at once lost her restraint, her modesty, her dark glow and her beauty, let her bangles slip, was covered over in a gold-coloured pallor, and made herself a quiver for Kama's arrows, she whose eyes were like the twin spears of Murugan raised in battle.
nuance: The first thing the cured girl does is look, and the look undoes in one line the whole list the akam books treat as a woman's defences (நிறை, நாண்) together with the signs the Kural gives to separation (slipping bangles, பசலை); here they come at the first sight, not after parting.
event: Padumai, revived from the snakebite, looks at Civakan and is at once overcome by love.

reading: The narrator says she was seized again by the snake of desire, whose fangs are the look of sword-like eyes and whose venom is a fierce fire, the snake that dwells within the anthill called the body, ruled by the master of the five senses.
nuance: மீட்டும் ('again') ties the figure to the plot: the girl has just been cured of a real snakebite, and the poet makes her love a second bite. The anthill of the body and the five senses (ஐம்பொறி) are the yogic and ascetic image of the body; whose eyes give the bite is not said, and வாட்கண் is usually a woman's epithet.
event: Padumai, just freed of the snake's poison, is struck anew by desire.

reading: As she swooned and sighed hotly, her companions and mothers, women with fragrant garlands, gathered round and told Civakan, whom they liken to an adorned elephant, that if he touched her the poison would go, and blessed him.
nuance: The women read the swoon of love as a return of the venom; the reader, told in 1292 that the second snake is desire, sees that their remedy (his touch) is the right one for the wrong reason.
event: Padumai faints again, and her companions and mothers beg Civakan to touch her and drive out the poison.

reading: Thinking that if she saw him, heard his firm words or felt his touch her life would hold, Civakan stroked the jewelled girl all over her body, as if spreading cool sandal paste on her.
nuance: The three channels he counts on (sight, speech, touch) are the senses through which love entered in 1291 and 1292; the cure goes in by the same doors as the sickness.
event: Civakan strokes Padumai's whole body to keep her alive.

reading: Then the girl of flawless, nectar-sweet speech, with a look of her wide sword-like eyes that looked as though it did not look, wound round the generous man and bound him fast.
nuance: உற்ற நோக்கம் உறாததொர் நோக்கு, a look that touches and seems not to, is the akam convention of the averted glance; here it is not a sign to be read but the cord that ties him.
event: Padumai binds Civakan with a covert glance.

tamil: விஞ்சையர் வீர னென்பார் விண்ணவர் குமர னென்பா
ரெஞ்சிய வுயிரை மீட்டா னிவனலா லில்லை யென்பார்
மஞ்சுசூ ழிஞ்சி மூதூர் மாமுடிக் குரிசி னாளை
நஞ்சுசூழ் வேலி னாற்கே நங்கையைக் கொடுக்கு மென்பார்.
reading: Some said he was a Vidyadhara hero, some that he was a prince of the gods, some that no one but he could have brought back a life that was ebbing away, and some that the great-crowned king of the old walled city would give the maiden this very day to the man with the deadly spear.
nuance: Each guess is introduced by என்பார், 'some say'; the crowd does not know who he is, and the hero keeps his identity hidden in this ilampakam.
event: Onlookers debate who Civakan is and foretell that the king will give him his daughter.

tamil: விளங்கொளி விசும்பில் வெண்கோட் டிளம்பிறை சூழ்ந்த மின்போல்
வளங்கெழு வடத்தைச் சூழ்ந்து வான்பொனாண் டிளைப்பச் சேந்த
விளங்கதிர் முலைக டம்மா லிவனைமார் பெழுதி வைகிற்
றுளங்குபெண் பிறப்புந் தோழி யினிதெனச் சொல்லி நிற்பார்.
reading: Other women stood saying to a friend that if one could lie with this man, having painted his chest with one's breasts, as lightning plays round the young white crescent in a bright sky and as gold chains play over a rich necklace, then even a woman's wavering birth would be sweet.
nuance: துளங்கு பெண் பிறப்பு, 'the trembling birth of a woman', is said in passing as common knowledge; the women do not argue it, they only name the one thing that would redeem it.

tamil: அருந்தவஞ் செய்து வந்த வாயிழை மகளிர் யார்கொல்
பெருந்தகை மார்பிற் றுஞ்சிப் பெண்மையாற் பிணிக்கு நீரார்
கருங்கணின் யாமுங் கண்டாங் காமனை யென்று சொல்லித்
திருந்தொளி முறுவற் செவ்வாய்த் தீஞ்சொலார் மயங்கி னாரே.
reading: Women of sweet speech and bright smiles were bewildered, asking who the jewelled women might be who, having done rare penance, would be born to sleep on this noble man's chest and bind him with their womanhood, and saying that with their own dark eyes they too had now seen Kama.
nuance: அருந்தவஞ் செய்து வந்த, 'who came having done rare penance', puts the marriage the story will bring under the law of merit from a past life; the speakers are bewildered onlookers, and the verse does not mark the claim as the poet's.

tamil: பன்மலர்ப் படலைக் கண்ணிக் குமரனைப் பாவை நல்லார்
மன்னவன் பணியின் வாழ்த்தி வாசநெய் பூசி நன்னீர்
துன்னின ராட்டிச் செம்பொற் செப்பினுட் டுகிலுஞ் சாந்து
மின்னறும் புகையும் பூவுங் கலத்தொடு மேந்தி னாரே.
reading: At the king's command the fair women praised the youth with his garland of many flowers, rubbed him with scented oil, bathed him in clear water, and brought in red-gold caskets clothes, sandal paste, sweet incense and flowers with their vessels.
event: By the king's order the palace women bathe and anoint Civakan and bring him clothes and perfumes.

tamil: ஏந்திய வேற்பத் தாங்கி யெரிமணிக் கொட்டை நெற்றி
வாய்ந்தபொன் குயிற்றிச் செய்த மரவடி யூர்ந்து போகி
யாயந்தநன் மாலை வேய்ந்த வரும்பெறற் கூடஞ் சேர்ந்தான்
பூந்தொடி மகளிர் போற்றிப் பொற்கலம் பரப்பி னாரே.
reading: Wearing wooden sandals inlaid with gold and with a gleaming gem knob at the front, he went and reached the rare hall decked with chosen garlands, where the women with flowered bangles honoured him and set out golden vessels.
nuance: Line 1 (ஏந்திய வேற்பத் தாங்கி) does not divide clearly; the reading of the opening phrase is a guess, and the sandals and the hall are the verse's sure content.
event: Civakan goes in jewelled sandals to the garlanded hall, where the women lay out golden dishes.

tamil: கன்னியர் கரக நீராற் றாமரை கழீஇய தொப்பப்
பொன்னடி கழீஇய பின்றைப் புரிந்துவாய் நன்கு பூசி
யின்மலர்த் தவிசி னுச்சி யிருந்தமிர் தினிதிற் கொண்டான்
reading: After maidens had washed his golden feet with water from pitchers, as one washes lotuses, he rinsed his mouth well, sat high on a seat of sweet flowers and ate the nectar-like food with pleasure, he who was the god of spring to spear-eyed women in bright jewels.
event: Civakan's feet are washed and he sits on a flower seat and eats.

tamil: வாசநற் பொடியு நீருங் காட்டிடக் கொண்டு வாய்ப்பப்
பூசறுத் தங்கை நீரை மும்முறை குடித்து முக்காற்
காசறத் துடைத்த பின்றைக் கைவிர லுறுப்புத் தீட்டி
தூசினா லங்கை நீவி யிருந்தனன் றோற்ற மிக்கான்.
reading: When fragrant powder and water were brought, he took them, washed off, sipped water from his palm three times, wiped his mouth three times so no stain was left, touched the parts of his face with his fingers, smoothed his palm with a cloth, and sat, splendid to see.
nuance: The poet slows the story for the full after-meal rite, three sips, three wipings and the fingers to the face, the very sequence a rule book of conduct sets out; the hero's correctness at table is part of what the king is watching before he tests his learning in 1303.
event: After the meal Civakan performs the mouth-rinsing in full.

tamil: சீர்கொளச் செய்த செம்பெர் னடைப்பையுட் பாகு செல்ல
வார்கழல் குருசிற் கொண்டு கவுளடுத் திருந்த வாங்கட்
போர்கொள்வேன் மன்ன னெல்லாக் கலைகளும் புகன்று கேட்டு
நீர்கொண்மாக் கடல னாற்கு நிகரில்லை நிலத்தி லென்றான்.
reading: When the hero with warrior's anklets had taken betel and areca from a well-made red-gold pouch and held it in his cheek, the king of the warring spear asked him about all the arts, heard his answers, and said that on earth there was no equal to this man who was like the great sea.
nuance: The king tests the stranger's learning only after he has been bathed, fed and given betel; the honour comes before the examination, and the verdict is spoken by the father whose daughter's hand is at stake.
event: The king questions Civakan on every art and declares him peerless on earth.

reading: The sun set, the long many-jewelled lamps were lit, instruments sounded, the prince climbed onto the soft couch heaped with cushions, and his thoughts grew intent.
nuance: கூர்ந்தது சிந்தையே closes the public day and opens the private night; what his thought turns to is left for the next verses to say.
event: At nightfall Civakan goes to his couch, his mind turning on Padumai.

reading: Her breasts, as if unable to bear his gaze there, swelled hot and rose, her waist gave way and wilted as if asking what this was, and her hips spread wider than men who keep no measure.
nuance: The verse has no first-person mark; it is read as the start of Civakan's night thoughts because 1306 and 1307 speak as 'I', but it may be the narrator's. The simile of line 4 (பாங்கிலாரின்) is a reading of a compressed phrase.

reading: Civakan says that the tender budding breasts of the girl with fragrant long hair, swelling in their nature, stand there to distress, her slender waist melts, and the side-glance of that painted doll torments his life.

Civakan says that the smoke-perfumed flower-cloth on her raised hips, the jewelled girdle and her thick hair where honeyed buds open have all turned enemy to wretched him and breed a spreading sickness.

Civakan asks whether it is her flower bow, her fighting spear-like eyes, her speech full of sweetness or her innocent look, says he cannot tell which, and concludes that it is desire itself that churns him through love for her who is like a goddess who afflicts.
nuance: After the list of 'or's he moves the cause from her to himself: the subject of கடைகின்றது is காமம், not any feature of hers.

reading: While the prince there suffered a sinking grief, the girl with the garland of bright flowers, there too, melted like butter set above hot embers and was barely alive.
nuance: The repeated அவ்வழி ('there', 'there too') sets the two nights side by side; the poet now turns from his lament to hers.
event: Civakan and Padumai, in separate rooms, both waste with longing.

reading: The girl with a waist like lightning flickering in rain and eyes like gleaming fish lay, while good women saluted her, in the soft bed made for her pleasure, like a doll fashioned by Maya.
nuance: மயன் இழைத்த பாவை, a doll made by the divine craftsman, gives her beauty and her stillness at once: she lies as lifeless as a figure.
event: Padumai lies motionless in her bed.

reading: Padumai asks her maidens whether the thief who clung to her heart and took her restraint is Kama with his bending bow and long arrows, or the young god of the dark hill on the fragrant flower, saying she does not know, and begs them to tell her.
nuance: நிறைகொண்ட கள்வன், 'the thief who took my restraint', names the loss of 1291 from inside. Which god மைவரை மைந்தன் means (perhaps Murugan) the verse does not settle.

reading: Padumai seems to say that her life, which has no one else, now lies with him who, as if he had embraced her fully with his lovely swelling shoulders like gate-posts, drew out the pain lodged in her breast.
nuance: Line 3 ends மீட்டவள் (feminine), where the sense seems to want the man who saved her; the verse may instead mean 'my life is in the waist of her who was saved', so the reading is tentative.

reading: Padumai says her heart is like the great sea whose water was churned and tossed when those seeking undying nectar gathered and, with knowledge, used the mountain as a churning stick.
nuance: The churning of the ocean for nectar is a Puranic story the Jain poet uses as plain ornament; the nectar sought points back to the life she has been given and the man who gave it.

reading: The laughing white moon, the anril in the palmyra frond, the low bell of the fine white bull, the hostile evening and the water-lily that brings grief all burn like a smokeless blazing fire.
nuance: The list is the akam evening of separation (the anril, the herd's bell, the moon); no first person marks the speaker, and it is read as Padumai's lament continuing from 1311 to 1313.

reading: The narrator says her sighs withered the round flower garlands strewn on her soft bed, and for the lovely girl, sick with the love her own eyes had given her, the length of the night passed like a year.
nuance: தன் கண் தரு காமநோய், 'the love-sickness her eyes gave', brings the chapter back to 1291, where the trouble began with her look.
event: Padumai spends a sleepless night of longing that seems a year long.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1316-1339 (7/10)
theme: Padumai's companions take the lovesick princess to the pleasure grove against the king's wish; Civakan, wounded by her look, follows, doubts whether she is a goddess, knows her by her human marks, and unites with her in a madhavi bower, praising her and pledging a love like the moon and its mark before hiding from her returning women; her father, knowing nothing of it, resolves to give her to the man who saved her life and bears the marks of a king.
source_issues: 1316 line 2: the word run மாதராடாதி divides as மாதராள் தாதி (nurse) or with ஆதி (eldest); the edition's division is unclear.
1324 line 4: நினையா can be read as 'thinking' or 'not thinking', and the sense of the line turns on it.
1331 and 1332 are printed with word division (கொடுங் குழை, பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்துப்) where the neighbouring verses run the words together in metrical units; the edition's two styles meet here.

cast.role: the hero, in the city of Padumai's father after curing her of snakebite, called வேலவன் and செல்வன் here
the princess whom Civakan cured, named பதுமை in 1327
Padumai's elder sister or elder kinswoman (அவ்வை in 1316, தவ்வை in 1337)
Padumai's companion
the company of girls who go with Padumai to the grove
the bees in Padumai's hair whom Civakan addresses
Padumai's father, the king of the city, unnamed in these verses

reading: The elder kinswoman and the dear companion of the girl whose prattle is like the yazh ask each other what they ought to do for the flower-haired one of golden grace.
nuance: The word run மாதராடாதி can be divided as மாதராள் தாதி (the girl's nurse) or read with ஆதி (the first, the eldest); 1337 calls the same woman தவ்வை, the elder sister. The verse does not say why she needs their help; the sequel shows it is her longing for Civakan.
event: Padumai's elder kinswoman and her companion take counsel over what to do for the lovesick girl.

reading: Her slender waist all but weeping under the weight, they cover her swelling breasts with saffron and pearls and then, reverently, set the garland and the chaplet on the young one who is like a painted creeper.
nuance: அழுது, weeping, is the poet's conceit for the waist that strains under the breasts; it is not a sign that Padumai weeps.
event: The two women adorn Padumai with saffron, pearls, garland and chaplet.

reading: Judging that it is right to go with the white-bangled band to the flowering grove and play there even if the king should be angry, the company gathers like peacocks and comes, and the grove shines with them.
nuance: வேந்து காயினும் admits that the outing is against the king's wish, so the grove where the lovers meet is reached by a small defiance of the father who in 1339 gives her away.
event: Padumai's companions decide, at the risk of the king's anger, to take her to the pleasure grove.

reading: Some string garlands, some pluck flowers, some call back to the echo off the hill, some leap together into the made pool and stir it, and some, for love, wed one bright doll to another.
nuance: The doll wedding (பாவை இருமணம்) is the girls' game, but it foreshadows the union that will take place in the same grove.
event: The girls of the company play in the grove.

reading: Women in long peacock-like garments swing, play at bright jacks, play with a ball held on a cord, and settle in every corner of the grove.
event: The girls swing and play jacks and ball through the grove.

reading: They say the man of the flaming spear, his heart torn open and burned within by the melting look of the fragrant-haired girl, went to see the grove where she was playing.
nuance: The longing is shared: the women's counsel in 1316 and Civakan's wound here make both lovers sick before the meeting. The look that wounds is hers (உருகு நோக்கம், a melting look), and the poet hedges with என்பவே, 'they say'.
event: Civakan, lovesick from Padumai's look, goes to the grove where she plays.

reading: Where the peacocks' dance, the monkeys' sulking and the koels' song all mingle, he comes to a bower of madhavi creeper with cool shade on white sand, out of the sun.
event: Civakan reaches a shaded madhavi bower in the grove.

reading: Her array: the ear ornament set at her ears, a cool blue water-lily heavy with pollen in her hand, a ring of pearls like the sea's and a cord of gold on her warm breasts.
Decked in white flowers that would hide the sky, in a dark grove that hides the eye, the girl with the champak garland stands alone, her fragrant body given over to thought of her beloved.
nuance: நினையா can be the verbal participle 'thinking' or the negative 'not thinking'; the reading here takes it as thinking of the friend (நண்பன்), the lover she has met before, but the line is not secure.
event: Padumai stands alone in the dark grove.

reading: As a flawless sapphire set in fresh milk breaks out in its colour and changes the milk's own nature, so her dark sheen tints the madhavi that hides her, and the noble one sees her with his mind.
nuance: The simile turns concealment into display: the leaves that hide her take on her colour, so he knows her presence before he sees her. சிந்தையின் நோக்கினான் may mean he looked intently, or that he saw her in thought; the reading keeps both.
event: Civakan glimpses Padumai through the madhavi bower.

reading: Is she the maiden of the mountain, the lady of the curving deep sea's waves, the woman of the honey lotus, or a famed yakshi? Who is this white-bangled one in fragrant array?
nuance: This is the lover's doubt (ஐயம்) of the Tamil code of secret love: he asks whether she is a goddess before he can approach her. The four candidates, Parvati of the mountain, the sea goddess, Lakshmi of the lotus and a yakshi, are a learned list where the Kural names only a goddess, a peahen or a woman.

reading: Her garland has withered, her sword-like eyes blink, her feet touch the earth: the one standing here is Padumai of the milk-sweet speech, with arms like the bamboo of the grove.
nuance: The doubt is settled by the three marks a goddess lacks: her garland fades, her eyes blink, her feet rest on the ground. It is the clearing (தெளிவு) that follows the doubt, and it ends with her name, for he has met her before.

reading: Because the sweet taste of the sweet verse that the Devar made is the true matter of southern Tamil, he resolves to enter the flowering grove of the girl with tender feet red as the kovam insect.
nuance: The verse grounds the hero's decision in literature: love is the மெய்ப்பொருள், the true subject, of Tamil poetry, so he follows it. தேவர் may be the gods or the poet's own name, Tiruttakkatevar; read as the poet, the line has the epic cite itself as the authority for kalavu. The reading is not secure.
event: Civakan resolves to go into the grove to Padumai.

reading: Between him and her, who is like the goddess of the lotus, the modesty that had held her fast fell away, and the great awareness of the stone-shouldered man passed its bounds: they were joined, it is said.
nuance: The union is told by what gives way, her naanam and his restraint, not by any rite; the father knows nothing of it when he decides on the marriage in 1339.
event: Civakan and Padumai unite in secret in the grove.

reading: Her eyes grow drunk, her white bangles clink and meet on her swelling bamboo-like arms, her dark sheen and the sprinkled powder are spoiled, and she shines in the flowered silk the saffron has stained.
nuance: A catalogue of the marks union leaves on the woman's body, which in the Tamil code of secret love is what the companions might read.

tamil: தவள மெல் இணர்த் தண் கொடி முல்லையே.
reading: Long may you live, red-spotted bees who flit in her hair where the curved earring meets the blue lily: say, has the white, soft-clustered cool jasmine creeper the beauty to put forth teeth as sharp as hers?
nuance: Civakan praises her (நலம் புனைந்துரைத்தல்) by asking the bees, the creatures who know flowers best, to judge whether the mullai can match her teeth.

tamil: பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்துப் பூங் கண்கள் போழ்ந்த புண்
இன்று இப் பூண் கொள் இள முலைச் சாந்து அலால்
reading: The wound her flower eyes cleft in my gold-resting chest, nothing can heal now but the sandal on these young adorned breasts: so he praised the woman's beauty.
She sets on the chaplet, dresses her dark hair, binds the coloured garland round the central tuft, wipes away the dust risen on her lovely anklets, and with all her skill gives the lord delight.
nuance: Putting the hair and anklets right is also hiding the marks of 1330 before her companions return.
event: Padumai restores her hair and dress after the union and pleases Civakan.

reading: Settling and making firm that their love is joined as the moon and its mark, he says: your people have come, girl of fragrant shining hair; I will hide here.
nuance: The pledge of permanence and the act of hiding come in one breath: secret love is sworn to last at the moment it has to conceal itself from her kin (நுமர், your people).
event: Civakan pledges his love to Padumai and, hearing her women come, says he will hide.

reading: Like a bright lightning that plunges into a cloud, the man of the fine spear plunged into the foliage, and the women with warm breasts that plunge through their jewels plunged through the vazhai trees and appeared.
nuance: The fourfold குளித்து, plunging, binds his vanishing and their arrival into one movement.
event: Civakan hides in the leaves as Padumai's companions come through the trees.

reading: Like a lightning moving nobly through the flowering grove, putting the swans to shame with her gait, she walked with anklets on her feet, stepping softly on soft flowers, the girl who had laid her goodness with him alone.
nuance: நன்னலம் அவற்கே வைத்த, 'who had placed her goodness with him alone', is the narrator's word that the secret union binds her as a wife.
event: Padumai walks out to meet her companions.

reading: Like the stars round the moon, her elder sister and companion reached the girl, and when the company had done service at her feet they sang her excellence out of love.
event: Padumai's sister, companion and company gather round her and praise her.

reading: Gathering the leaf skirts, chaplets and cool fragrant garlands they wanted, they went softly away, and the man like a roaring lion in a cave went, as was fitting, to his old friend.
nuance: Who the பழைய நண்பன் is the verse does not say; this chapter does not identify him.
event: The women leave the grove, and Civakan goes back to an old friend.

tamil: பூமியை யாடற் கொத்த பொறியின னாத லானு
மாமக ளுயிரை மீட்ட வலத்தின னாத லானு
நேமியான் சிறுவ னன்ன நெடுந்தகை நேரு மாயி
னாமவற் கழகி தாக நங்கையைக் கொடுத்து மென்றான்.
reading: Since he bears the marks fit to rule the earth and since he is the strong one who brought back my great daughter's life, if this lofty man like the son of the discus-bearer consents, we will give him the girl as is fitting, he said.
nuance: The speaker of என்றான் is not named; the story so far makes him Padumai's royal father. He gives two reasons, royal marks on the body and a debt for his daughter's life, and makes the gift wait on the hero's consent. நேமியான் சிறுவன், the son of the discus-bearer, is Kama, Vishnu's son, a figure for beauty.
event: Padumai's father resolves to give her to Civakan, if he will accept her.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1340-1363 (8/10)
theme: On the minister's counsel and the narrator's word that fate has ripened, the king gives Padumai, whom Civakan cured of snakebite, to Civakan; after the wedding rites and two months of love, which also bring him to Tesikappavai in the grove, he slips from his sleeping wife at night, and she wakes to search for him like a body for its life and to scold her parrot.
source_issues: 1341, 1342, 1343, 1345, 1352-1356 and 1360 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build; the joins read correctly.
1348 lines 1-2 are compressed and the sense is not secure.
1353 has no named speaker and line 3 is obscure; the speaker is a guess.

cast.role: the hero, called குமரன், வேலான், குருசில் in this chapter
the Pallava king's daughter, cured of snakebite by Civakan and married to him
the king of the city, Padumai's father
the queen, Padumai's mother
the king's minister, who counsels the marriage
the women who perform the wedding rites
the women who bathe and dress the bridegroom
the elders who perform the marriage
a young woman of the grove whom Civakan meets and joins
Padumai's green parrot

tamil: மதிதர னென்னு மாசின் மந்திர சொல்லக் கேட்டே
யுதிதர வுணர்வல் யானு மொப்பினு முருவி னானும்
விதிதர வந்த தொன்றே விளங்குபூண் முலையி னாளைக்
கொதிதரு வேலி னாற்கே கொடுப்பது கரும மென்றான்.
reading: The king says that, having heard the faultless counsel of his minister Mathidharan, he too sees it clearly: the young man matches her in looks and form, the thing has come as destiny brings it, and the right act is to give his jewelled daughter to the man of the burning spear.
nuance: The speaker is named only by the frame (he heard what Mathidharan said and answers with என்றான்); the narrator endorses his reading of fate two verses on, where the portion (பான்மை) is said to have ripened for the spearman (1342).
event: The king, after hearing Mathidharan's counsel, decides to give his daughter to Civakan.

tamil: உள்விரித் திதனை யெல்லா முரைக்கென மொழிந்து விட்டான்
றெள்ளிதிற் றெரியச் சென்றாங் குரைத்தலுங் குமரன் றேறி
வெள்ளிலை யணிந்த வேலான் வேண்டிய தாக வென்றா
னள்ளிலை வேல்கொண் மன்னற் கமைச்சனஃ தமைந்த தென்றான்.
reading: The king sends the minister to lay all this out plainly; the minister goes and tells it, the prince agrees that it be as the spear-bearing king wishes, and the minister returns to report that the matter is settled.
event: Mathidharan carries the offer to Civakan, who accepts, and reports the acceptance to the king.

tamil: பொன்றிய வுயிரை மீட்டான் பூஞ்சிகைப் போது வேய்ந்தா
னன்றியு மாமெய் தீண்டி யளித்தன னழகின் மிக்கா
னொன்றிய மகளிர் தாமே யுற்றவர்க் குரிய ரென்னா
வென்றிகொள் வேலி னாற்கே பான்மையும் விளைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The narrator gives the grounds: he brought back her departed life, set flowers in her hair, touched her body and saved her, and is surpassing in beauty; women who have been joined to a man belong to the one who touched them, and so the portion fated for the victorious spearman had ripened.
nuance: The touch was the physician's: in 1294 he strokes her whole body to keep her life in. The maxim at line 3 turns that healing touch into a claim on her, so the cure itself becomes the betrothal; the reading of ஒன்றிய and உற்றவர் as touching is the plainest sense of the line, but it is a compressed saying.

tamil: கோப்பெருந் தேவி கொற்றக் கோமக னிவைக ணாடி
யாப்புடைத் தையற் கின்றே நங்கையை யமைக்க வென்னத்
தூப்புரி முத்த மாலை தொடக்கொடு தூக்கி யெங்கும்
பூப்பரிந் தணிந்து கோயில் புதுவது புனைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The great queen and the victorious king, weighing these things, order that the girl be given that very day to the one bound to her, and the palace is newly dressed with hanging pearl garlands and flowers strewn everywhere.
event: The queen and king order the wedding for that day, and the palace is decorated.

tamil: கணிபுனைந் துரைத்த நாளாற் கண்ணிய கோயி றன்னுண்
மணிபுனை மகளிர் நல்லார் மங்கல மரபு கூறி
யணியுடைக் கமல மன்ன வங்கைசேர் முன்கை தன்மேற்
றுணிவுடைக் காப்புக் கட்டிச் சுற்றுபு தொழுது காத்தார்.
reading: On the day the astrologer fixed, inside the chosen palace, jewelled women recite the auspicious forms, tie the protective cord on the bride's wrist above her lotus hand, and stand round her in worship and guard.
event: On the fixed day the women tie the protective cord on Padumai's wrist.

tamil: மழகளிற் றெருத்திற் றந்த மணிக்குட மண்ணு நீரா
லழகனை மண்ணுப் பெய்தாங் கருங்கடிக் கொத்த கோலந்
தொழுதகத் தோன்றச் செய்தார் தூமணிப் பாவை யன்னார்
விழுமணிக் கொடிய னாளும் விண்ணவர் மடந்தை யொத்தாள்.
reading: Women like jewelled dolls bathe the handsome bridegroom with water from a gem pot brought on a young elephant's neck and dress him in the attire fit for the wedding, so that he seems worthy of worship; the bride, a gem-like creeper, looks like a maiden of the gods.
event: Civakan is bathed and dressed for the wedding, and Padumai is adorned.

reading: Elders of a dignity hard to praise perform the marriage of the carp-eyed bride and the Kama-like groom, and the two, free of confusion and of a love native to them, are joined.
nuance: இயற்கை அன்பு, a love by nature, presents the match as more than the king's arrangement, in line with the fate of 1340 and 1342.
event: Elders perform the marriage of Padumai and Civakan.

reading: The bride whose eyes have fought sword and spear and the warrior with the long anklet join shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot as if one form, and day after day share pleasure like the Nagas of the upper world.
event: Padumai and Civakan begin their married life together.

reading: Her hot breasts press against his garland until its buds open and it is crushed, and the poet asks what her pride can now do against such force.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the sense of தணிக்கும் தாமரையாள் நலம் and பிணிக்கும் பீடு is hard to fix; the reading follows line 3 and 4, where the crushing of the garland is plain.

reading: The signs of their love-play: garlands torn, saffron smeared, wreaths wilted, girdles snapped and the anklets sounding as the two, like bees parted from their kin, sport.
On a bed thick with the smoke of rich agil, morning and evening, the two whose love has come joined through seven births go on embracing without tiring.
nuance: எழுமையும் இயைந்து: the narrator treats the love as a bond carried over seven births, a phrase that will sit hard with the hero's departure ten verses on.

reading: Smelling and tasting, listening to the music of strings and watching cool dances, and pressed by her hot breasts, the spearman spends each day, they say.
nuance: The verse runs through the senses one by one, smell, taste, hearing, sight and touch, as the means of his pleasure; என்பவே marks it as report.

tamil: விரிகதிர் விளங்கு பன்மீன் கதிரொடு மிடைந்து திங்கட்
டெரிகதிர் திரட்டி வல்லான் றெரிந்துகோத் தணிந்த போலுஞ்
சொரிகதிர் முத்த மின்னுந் துணைமுலைத் தடத்தில் வீழ்ந்தான்
புரிகதிர்ப் பொன்செய் மாலைப் புகைநுதிப் புலவு வேலான்.
reading: The spearman with the gold garland and the smoke-tipped lance falls upon her breasts, where pearl strings shine as if a master had gathered the moon's rays and the many stars and strung them.

tamil: எழின்மாலை யென்னுயிரை யான்கண்டே னித்துணையே முலையிற் றாகிக்
குழன்மாலைக் கொம்பாகிக் கூரெயிறு நான்போழ்த லஞ்சி யஞ்சி
யுழன்மாலைத் தீங்கிளவி யொன்றிரண்டு தான்மிழற்று மொருநாட் காறு
நிழன்மாலை வேனாண நீண்டகண்ணே நெய்தோய்ந்த தளிரே மேனி.
reading: A voice praises her: I have seen my life, a creeper of a girl with breasts only this much grown, who lisps a sweet word or two as though afraid her sharp teeth might split it, her long eyes shaming a spear, her body a ghee-dipped sprout.
nuance: The speaker is not named. என் உயிரை யான் கண்டேன் fits the lover beholding his beloved, and the verse is read as Civakan's; but ஒருநாட்காறும் and the stress on how small she still is could belong to a nurse or mother recalling her growth, and the sense of line 3 is uncertain.

tamil: மாநீர் மணிமுகிலின் மின்னுக் கொடிநுசுப்பின் மயிலஞ் சாய
லேநீ ரிருபுருவ மேறி யிடைமுரிந்து நுடங்கப் புல்லித்
தூநீர் மலர்மார்பன் றொன்னலந் தான்பருகித் துளும்புந் தேறற்
றெனீர் மலர்மாலை தேன்றுளித்து மட்டுயிர்ப்பச் சூட்டி னானே.
reading: Embracing the lightning-waisted, peacock-gentle girl so that her two brows rise and her waist bends, the man of the flower-fresh chest drinks her beauty and crowns her with a honey-dripping garland.
event: Civakan embraces Padumai and puts a garland on her hair.

tamil: தேனடைந் திருந்த கண்ணித் தென்மட்டுத் துவலை மாலை
யூனடைந் திருந்த வேற்க ணொண்டொடி யுருவ வீணை
தானடைந் திருந்த காவிற் பாடினா டனிமை தீர்வான்
கூனடைந் திருந்த திங்கட் குளிர்முத்த முலையி னாளே.
reading: In the grove where she stays, a young woman with a honey-filled garland and spear-like eyes plays the vina to relieve her loneliness.
nuance: The woman is not named here. Since in the next verse Civakan enters the grove and meets the one called Tesikappavai, and 1358 speaks of two women, she is read as Tesikappavai rather than Padumai; the garland of line 1 could instead link her to 1354.
event: A young woman plays the vina alone in the grove.

tamil: வார்தளிர் ததைந்து போது மல்கிவண் டுறங்குங் காவிற்
சீர்கெழு குருசில் புக்கான் றேசிகப் பாவை யென்னுங்
கார்கெழு மின்னு வென்ற நுடங்கிடைக் கமழ்தண் கோதை
யேர்கெழு மயில னாளை யிடைவயி னெதிர்ப்பட் டானே.
reading: The prince enters the grove where tender leaves crowd, flowers abound and bees sleep, and comes face to face with the peacock-like woman called Tesikappavai, whose swaying waist outdoes the lightning of the rain cloud.
nuance: Whether தேசிகப் பாவை is a proper name or an epithet of beauty is not certain from this verse; என்னும் suggests a name, and 1358's two women support a second woman.
event: Civakan enters the grove and meets Tesikappavai.

tamil: சிலம்பெனும் வண்டு பாட மேகலைத் தேன்க ளார்ப்ப
நலங்கவின் போது பூத்த பூங்கொடி நடுங்கி நாணக்
கலந்தனன் காம மாலை கலையின தியல்பிற் சூட்டப்
புலம்புபோய்ச் சாய லென்னும் புதுத்தளி ரீன்ற தன்றே.
reading: With her anklets like humming bees and her girdle like sounding bees, the flower-creeper trembles in shame as he joins her and crowns her with a garland of love according to the art; her loneliness gone, her softness puts out a new sprout.
nuance: கலையினது இயல்பின் says the union follows the rule of an art, the poem's sign that love is treated as a learned discipline as well as a feeling.
event: Civakan unites with Tesikappavai in the grove.

tamil: சாந்திடைக் குளித்த வெங்கட் பணைமுலைத் தாம மாலைப்
பூந்தொடி யரிவை பொய்கைப் பூமக ளனைய பொற்பின்
வேந்தடு குருதி வேற்கண் விளங்கிழை யிவர்க ணாளு
மாய்ந்தடி பரவ வைகு மரிவையர்க் கநங்க னன்னான்.
reading: To these two women, the one with sandal-bathed breasts and flower bangles, lovely as the lady of the lotus pool, and the one with spear eyes red as if with kings' blood, who daily bow and praise his feet, he is like Ananga.

tamil: இங்ஙன மிரண்டு திங்க ளேகலு மேக வேலா
னங்ஙனம் புணர்ந்த வன்பி னவண்முலைப் போக நீக்கி
யெங்ஙன மெழுந்த துள்ள மிருளிடை யேக லுற்றான்
றங்கிய பொறியி னாக்கந் தனக்கொர்தே ராக நின்றான்.
reading: When two months had passed thus, the spearman put aside the pleasure of her breasts and the love in which they had joined; with his heart risen he set out into the darkness, and the fortune of his settled destiny stood as his chariot.
nuance: பொறி, fortune or destiny, is made his vehicle: the departure is his own resolve (எழுந்தது உள்ளம்) and his fate at once.
event: After two months Civakan leaves Padumai and goes out into the night.

tamil: தயங்கிணர்க் கோதை தன்மேற் றண்ணென வைத்த மென்றோள்
வயங்கிணர் மலிந்த தாரான் வருந்துறா வகையி னீக்கி
நயங்கிள ருடம்பு நீங்கி நல்லுயிர் போவ தேபோ
லியங்கிடை யறுத்த கங்கு லிருளிடை யேகி னானே.
reading: Gently, so that she is not hurt, he takes away his soft arm from where it lay across her garlanded body and goes out into the darkness of the night that has stopped all movement, as a good life goes when it leaves the body.
event: Civakan slips his arm from Padumai while she sleeps and leaves in the dark.

reading: When he left the dark-haired, bangled girl in her sleep, she woke behind him with her spear-like eyes, they say.
event: Padumai wakes after Civakan has gone.

reading: She is like a body that searches for the life that has left it and faints, and like a bird with flower eyes that searches its nest to find its mate.
nuance: The simile reverses the one in 1360: there he went as life leaves the body; here she is the body left behind, which in this image still feels and seeks.
event: Padumai searches the bed for Civakan.

reading: She reproaches the strong young man who, even when they embraced, would say 'it hurts if the jewel presses', and turns in anger on her fine green parrot too: you did not tell me he was leaving the house.
nuance: The tenderness she remembers (he feared even a jewel between them would hurt her) is turned into the charge against him: one so careful of her body left without a word.
event: Padumai rails at the absent Civakan and scolds her parrot for not warning her.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1364-1387 (9/10)
theme: Waking to find Civakan gone, Padumai laments to her myna, swan, peacock, lamp and mansion, strips off her ornaments, blames her eyes for sleeping, calls on bees, hills, gods and goddesses, reproaches the absent man whose grace failed her, and falls fainting like a hen-swan left at a dry pool, until her friend comes with words of comfort.
source_issues: 1370 line 4: வாடடினாள் looks miscopied (perhaps a form of வாட்டினாள்).
1377 lines 1-2: broken word division (உறைவீ ர்தனைத்) and an odd form மானிடார்ற்.
1378: lengthened vowels in புணார்வின், உணார்வீ ரமரார், கொணார்வீர் where the metre and sense want புணர்வின், உணர்வீர் அமரர், கொணர்வீர்.
1379 lines 3-4 corrupt: ளர்கோ lacks its first syllable (probably தளர்கோ), and line 3 does not construe.
1380 line 3: வுன்கண் breaks the metre of the run.
1385 and 1386 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build.

cast.role: princess of the Pallava city, Civakan's wife, whom he has left in the night
the hero, absent, addressed in Padumai's lament
Padumai's friend, who consoles her
the women who attend Padumai
Padumai's myna, addressed in her lament
the hen-swan of Padumai's house, addressed in her lament
the peacock, addressed in her lament
the bedroom lamp, addressed in her lament
the tall mansion, addressed in her lament
the bees on the flowers, addressed in her lament
the streams, hills, groves and moonlight called on together in 1376
the gods of heaven, addressed in 1377
the daughters of the gods, addressed in 1378

reading: Padumai reproaches her myna for not asking her lover whether it was right to leave the bed and go while their peerless doll lay distressed.
nuance: She scripts for the bird the words it should have said, calling herself 'our doll' (எம் பாவை) in its mouth, so her own grief is voiced through the household's pets.
event: Padumai, waking to find Civakan gone, laments to her myna.

reading: She chides the hen-swan for not going after the peerless one, bidding him go with their golden girl, and bringing him back close.
event: Padumai scolds the hen-swan for not stopping or fetching Civakan.

reading: Joining her hands, the carp-eyed girl begs the peacock, whose whole body is eyes that never close, to tell her truly where her lord went.
nuance: The peacock's eyed plumage is turned into a witness that cannot have slept, against her own eyes, which she later blames for sleeping (1373).
event: Padumai worships the peacock and asks it where Civakan has gone.

reading: She goes up to the bright flame and asks the lamp, nourished and pure, that shows great things, why it did not show her where her dear life, who played with her in love, has hidden.
nuance: Civakan is called her ஆருயிர், her dear life; the plea to find him is a plea to find her own life.
event: Padumai turns to the lamp and asks where Civakan is hidden.

reading: She sulks at the lamp: it drank the spreading dark, blackened and vomited it as soot, and stands trembling with its body burning, yet it will tell her nothing that concerns her.
nuance: The flame's flicker is read as guilty trembling, and the verb ஊடினாள் makes her complaint a lover's sulk directed at an object.
event: Padumai quarrels with the lamp for its silence.

reading: She promises the tall mansion that touches the clouds a crore of fine cloths, ornaments, bathing sandal and more if it will seek out her friend and reach him.
event: Padumai offers gifts to the mansion to send it after Civakan.

reading: Saying that these were at fault for keeping her from holding close the man with a chest like a mountain of gold, she strips the bracelets from her arms, long as gem pillars.
nuance: Line 4 reads வாடடினாள் as printed; the sense of removing or wasting the bracelets is clear from line 2, but the word looks miscopied.
event: Padumai pulls off her bracelets, blaming them for hindering her embrace.

reading: Saying that the man of the killing spear has left their union and asking what ornaments can do for her here, she smears mountain sandal over her mouth (or face) and scatters the great ornaments from her breasts.
event: Padumai throws off her breast ornaments.

reading: Asking her breasts what they will do in this body now that he has gone, she presses down the full breasts that weigh on her waist, her dark eyes reddening and troubled.
nuance: The breasts, praised throughout the love scenes, are addressed as useless parties once the lover is gone; the ornaments and body parts are dismissed in turn (1370 to 1373).
event: Padumai beats down her breasts in grief.

reading: She rages at her long eyes in her heart: she told them to keep from sleep so as to see the man with a chest like a cloud-girt mountain, yet they slept, so let them now deck themselves with collyrium.
event: Padumai blames her eyes for sleeping while Civakan left.

reading: As her lac-red lotus eyes are held back by the women who tend her, the girdle, as if afraid or thinking she was suffering, gives no sound, shakes and slips down.
nuance: The silenced, slipping girdle is the conventional sign of wasting in separation, given a feeling of its own.
event: Padumai's attendants restrain her, and her girdle falls silent and loosens.

reading: In a new metre she tells the bees lying on dewy flowers that she never did anything to cause a sulk; she is alone, a single woman's life is all she has, and she asks them to say whether she must now stay like this.
nuance: She denies having given cause (துனி), so the departure cannot be read as a lovers' quarrel she started.
event: Padumai protests her innocence to the bees.

reading: She calls on the rows of falling streams, the gold-pouring hills, the water, the plantain and leaves, the fragrant groves and the spreading moonlight to tell her where the guardian of her life is.
event: Padumai asks the hills, waters and moonlight where Civakan has gone.

reading: She turns to the gods who dwell in the golden heaven and know all: petty humans know nothing, the gods have no pity, so her spreading sickness grows and her life is hard to keep; she begs them for grace.
nuance: Line 1 is printed with a break (உறைவீ ர்தனைத்) and line 2 ends மானிடார்ற், so the exact construction is doubtful.
event: Padumai prays to the gods to pity her.

reading: She asks the daughters of the gods, who know that when a husband leaves even in the sweet hour of a lovers' sulk his wife's life slips from her hand, to be gracious and bring back the life of her, the cruel one.
nuance: She calls herself கொடியேன், the cruel one, taking the blame on herself while the next verses blame him.
event: Padumai begs the goddesses to bring her lover back.

reading: She addresses a garland or girdle-like woman and asks whether, if it has become her gem girdle, her breath will not linger, and whether she, who could sing his worth, must droop and droop.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are broken in the text (அகையா தெனதா விதழைக் குமெனத் / தகைபா டவலாய் ளர்கோ), and the addressee is unclear; only the closing cry of drooping is secure.

reading: Speaking to the absent man, she recalls how, when she said his garland pressed and bruised her, he cooled her burning jewelled breasts with his flower eyes and tended her, and now, without a thought, the great one has left her.
event: Padumai recalls Civakan's tenderness and reproaches his leaving.

reading: She calls him one who stands on the road of grace and speaks only dharma, flower-anklet wearer who has gained knowledge that seeks meaning, brother-in-law of the victorious lord of the tall chariot, and asks why he stands on a dark road and shows no grace to her who grieves.
nuance: The reproach turns on his own virtues: அருள் தேர் வழி against இருள் தேர் வழி in lines 1 and 3. Who the lord of the tall chariot is (line 4) is not fixed by the verse; it may be her brother, the king's son, which would make Civakan his மைத்துனன்.
event: Padumai reproaches Civakan for withholding grace.

reading: She asks whether she did some great wrong or whether his heart, taking no delight, grew sick of her, that he has done what is unfitting and left her in unending sorrow.
event: Padumai asks what fault of hers drove Civakan away.

reading: The narrator tells how the swan-gaited girl, unable to hold herself up, her gleaming golden garland crushed, falls to the ground like a flash of lightning.
nuance: Line 1 (குளிர்துன் னியபொன் னிலமே குதலாற்) is hard to construe; the fall itself is clear from lines 2 to 4.
