event: Padumai faints and falls to the floor.

reading: Crying 'strong youth, embrace me', faltering, rising, she lifts herself and walks seven steps, falls again to the ground, glimmers, melts and weeps, the jewelled one, overwhelmed.
event: Padumai rises, takes seven steps after him and falls weeping.

tamil: கரப்புநீர்க் கங்கை யங்கட் கடிமலர்க் கமலப் பள்ளித்
திருத்தகு திரைக டாக்கச் சேப்புழிச் சேவ னீங்கப்
பரற்றலை முரம்பிற் சின்னீர் வறுஞ்சுனைப் பற்று விட்ட
வரத்தவாய்ப் பவளச் செந்தாட் பெடையன்ன மழுவ தொத்தாள்.
reading: She is like a coral-footed hen-swan whose mate has left the lotus bed of the Ganges, its banks hidden by waves, and who weeps by a dry pool of little water on stony gravel.
nuance: Repaired from eight half-lines in the source.

tamil: மெழுகினாற் புனைந்த பாவை வெய்துறுத் தாங்கு மோவா
தழுதுநைந் துருகு கின்ற வாயிடைத் தோழி துன்னிக்
கெழீஇயினாள் கேள்வி நல்யாழ்க் கிளைநரம் பனைய சொல்லாள்
கழிபெருங் கவலை நீங்கக் காரண நீர சொன்னாள்.
reading: As she weeps and melts ceaselessly like a wax doll held to heat, her friend, whose speech is like the strings of a well-tuned yazh, comes close and speaks reasonable words to end her great grief.
event: Padumai's friend comes to console her.

tamil: தெள்ளறல் யாறு பாய்ந்த திரைதவழ் கடலின் வெஃகி
யள்ளுற வளிந்த காம மகமுறப் பிணித்த தேனு
முள்ளுற வெந்த செம்பொ னுற்றநீர்ப் புள்ளி யற்றாற்
கள்ளுற மலர்ந்த கோதாய் காதலர் காத லென்றாள்.
reading: The friend tells her that lovers' love is like the sea's craving for the clear river that flows into it, like honey that binds desire within, and like a drop of water fallen on gold heated through.
nuance: The point of the three comparisons is not fixed by this verse alone: they may say that a lover's love never has enough and so he will return, or that it vanishes as fast as water on hot gold; the next verses decide which.
event: The friend begins her consolation with sayings on lovers' love.

title: பதுமையார் இலம்பகம் 1388-1411 (10/10)
theme: The close of Padumaiyar Ilampakam: Padumai's friend consoles her for Civakan's night departure, first by belittling men's love, then by teaching the tree of suffering from ignorance to death and the impermanence of youth, wealth and union, and lastly by omens; her mother reads Civakan's veiled sayings as a promise to return, and Civakan, disguised, tells the king's searchers he will be back within ten months.
source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1391 line 4 and 1393 line 3 are hard to divide and construe.
1411 line 4 மைந்தனுக்கு (to the king's son) sits oddly with 1407, where the king himself sends the searchers.

cast.role: the princess whom Civakan married after curing her snakebite, and whom he leaves by night
Padumai's companion, who consoles her
Padumai's own mother, the king's queen (மாபெருந் தேவி)
Padumai's mothers, her mother and foster mothers
Padumai's father, the king
the men the king sends to find Civakan
the hero, called காளை and விடலை here, leaving Padumai in disguise

tamil: ஓடரி யொழுகி நீண்ட வொளிமலர் நெடுங்க ணாரைக்
கூடரி யுழுவை போல முயக்கிடைக் குழையப் புல்லி
யாடவ ரழுந்தி வீழ்ந்தும் பிரிவிடை யழுங்கல் செல்லார்
பீடழிந் துருகும் பெண்ணிற் பேதைய ரில்லை யென்றாள்.
reading: The friend goes on: men who clasp long-eyed women in close embrace, sinking into them like a striped tiger, still do not grieve when they part, and there are none so foolish as women who melt and lose their dignity over them.
nuance: The friend's consolation begins by belittling men's love (continuing 1387) before it turns, in 1389, to the nature of birth itself.

tamil: பேதைமை யென்னும் வித்திற் பிறந்துபின் வினைக ளென்னும்
வேதனை மரங்க ணாறி வேட்கைவேர் வீழ்த்து முற்றிக்
காதலுங் களிப்பு மென்னுங் கவடுவிட் டவலம் பூத்து
மாதுய ரிடும்பை காய்த்து மரணமே கனிந்து நிற்கும்.
reading: She sets out a tree of suffering: born from the seed of ignorance, it sprouts deeds as its trunks of pain, sends down desire as its root, branches into love and elation, flowers into sorrow, bears great affliction as fruit and ripens into death.
nuance: The verse names no school. Its order (ignorance, then deeds, then feeling and craving, ending in death) resembles the chain of dependent arising taught in Manimekalai 30, but it is cut down to one image and put in a friend's mouth to dry a lover's tears; love (காதல்) itself is one of the branches.

tamil: தேன்சென்ற நெறியுந் தெண்ணீர்ச் சிறுதிரைப் போர்வை போர்த்து
மீன்சென்ற நெறியும் போல விழித்திமைப் பவர்க்குந் தோன்றா
மான்சென்ற நோக்கின் மாதே மாய்ந்துபோ மக்கள் யாக்கை
யூன்சென்று தேயச் சிந்தித் துகுவதோ தகுவ தென்றாள்.
reading: As the path a bee has flown or a fish has swum under the rippled water leaves no trace even to those who watch unblinking, the human body passes away unseen, so she asks the doe-eyed princess whether it is fitting to waste her flesh in brooding.

tamil: பிரிந்தவற் கிரங்கிப் பேதுற் றழுதநங் கண்ணி னீர்கள்
சொரிந்தவை தொகுந்து நோக்கிற் றொடுகடல் வெள்ள மாற்றா
முரிந்தநம் பிறவி மேனாண் முற்றிழை யின்னு நோக்காய்
பரிந்தழு வதற்குப் பாவா யடியிட்ட வாறு கண்டாய்.
reading: If the tears we have wept, pining for those who left us in our former births, were gathered together, the sea would not hold them; look, she says, at how this weeping has only now taken its first step.
nuance: Line 4 (பரிந்தழு வதற்குப் பாவா யடியிட்ட வாறு கண்டாய்) is read as 'see how this weeping has set its first foot'; the sense of the half-line is not secure.

tamil: அன்பினி னவலித் தாற்றா தழுவது மெளிது நங்க
ளென்பினி னாவி நீங்க விறுவது மெளிது சேர்ந்த
துன்பத்தாற் றுகைக்கப் பட்டார் துகைத்தவத் துன்பந் தாங்கி
யின்பமென் றிருத்தல் போலு மரியதிவ் வுலகி லென்றாள்.
reading: To weep in love and be unable to bear it is easy, and easy too to let the life leave one's bones; what is hard in this world is to be crushed by sorrow and yet carry that sorrow and live as if it were joy.

tamil: மயற்கையிம் மக்கள் யோனிப் பிறத்தலும் பிறந்து வந்தீங்
கியற்கையே பிரிவு சாத லிமைப்பிடைப் படாத தொன்றாற்
கயற்கணி னளவுங் கொள்ளார் கவற்சியுட் கவற்சி கொண்டார்
செயற்கையம் பிறவி நச்சுக் கடலகத் தழுந்து கின்றார்.
reading: Born by delusion into the human womb, parting and death are by nature what comes here in less than a blink; those who will not grant it even the span of a fish-eyed glance take worry on worry and sink in the poison sea of births of their own making.
nuance: The play of மயற்கை, இயற்கை and செயற்கை (delusion, nature, what is made) carries the argument: birth comes from delusion, parting is its nature, and the drowning is self-made; the division of line 3 is doubtful.

tamil: இளமையின் மூப்புஞ் செல்வத் திடும்பையும் புணர்ச்சிப் போழ்திற்
கிளைநரிற் பிரிவு நோயில் காலத்து நோயு நோக்கி
விளைமதுக் கமழுங் கோதை வேலினும் வெய்ய கண்ணாய்
களைதுய ரவலம் வேண்டா கண்ணிமைப் பளவு மென்றாள்
reading: Seeing old age within youth, affliction within wealth, parting from kin within union and sickness within health, she tells the princess with eyes fiercer than a spear to put away grief even for the blink of an eye.

tamil: முத்திலங் காகந் தோய்ந்த மொய்ம்மலர்த் தாரி னானங்
கைத்தலத் தகன்ற பந்திற் கைப்படுங் கவல வேண்டா
பொத்திலத் துறையு மாந்தை புணர்ந்திருந் துரைக்கும் பொன்னே
நித்தில முறுவ லுண்டா னீங்கினா னல்லன் கண்டாய்.
reading: Do not grieve, she says: he will come back to your hand like a ball that has left it, for the owl that lives in the hollow calls in pairs, and the one who tasted your pearl smile has not left you.
nuance: The consolation turns from doctrine to omen: the owl's paired call is read as a sign of reunion.

tamil: வடிமலர்க் காவி னன்று வண்டளிர்ப் பிண்டி நீழன்
முடிபொருள் பறவை கூற முற்றிழை நின்னை நோக்கிக்
கடியதோர் கௌவை செய்யுங் கட்டெயிற் றரவி னென்றேன்
கொடியனாய் பிழைப்புக் கூறேன் குழையலென் றெடுத்துக் கொண்டாள்.
reading: She recalls that in the grove, under the shade of the asoka, when a bird spoke of what was to come, she looked at the princess and foretold a cruel trouble from a fanged snake; she, called cruel then, does not speak falsely now, and telling her not to droop she lifts her up.
nuance: கொடியனாய் பிழைப்புக் கூறேன் is read as the friend's 'I, whom you called cruel, do not speak amiss'; the earlier warning she cites is not traced here to a particular verse.
event: The friend reminds Padumai that her earlier omen of the snake came true and lifts her up.

tamil: அலங்கலுங் குழலுந் தோழி யங்கையி னடைச்சி யம்பூம்
பொலங்கலக் கொடிய னாடன் கண்பொழி கலுழி யொற்றிக்
கலந்தகி னாறு மல்குற் கவான்மிசைக் கொண்டி ருந்தாள்
புலர்ந்தது பொழுது நல்லா ணெஞ்சமும் புலர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: The friend gathers the princess's garland and hair in her hand, wipes the tears pouring from her eyes and holds her on her lap; the night ends, and with it the good woman's heart too grows dry.
nuance: புலர்ந்தது plays on dawn breaking and the heart drying of its tears.
event: The friend dries Padumai's tears and holds her in her lap until dawn.

tamil: பண்கனிந் தினிய பாடற் படுநரம் பிளகி யாங்குக்
கண்கனிந் தினிய காமச் செவ்வியுட் காளை நீங்கத்
தெண்பனி யனைய கண்ணீர்ச் சேயிழை தாய ரெல்லாந்
தண்பனி முருக்கப் பட்ட தாமரைக் காடு போன்றார்.
reading: As the string of a ripe, sweet song snaps in the middle, so the young man left her in the full ripeness of love, and the princess's mothers, their tears like clear dew, became like a lotus grove withered by frost.
event: Padumai's mothers learn that Civakan has gone and are stricken.

tamil: சில்லரிச் சிலம்பு சூழ்ந்த சீறடித் திருவி னற்றாய்
முல்லையங் குழலி னாய்நின் முலைமுதற் கொழுநன் மேனாட்
சொல்லியு மறிவ துண்டோ வெனக்குழைந் துருகி நைந்து
மெல்லியல் கங்குல் சொல்லிற் றிற்றென மிழற்று கின்றாள்.
reading: Her own mother, melting and worn, asks the jasmine-haired girl whether her husband ever said anything before, and the gentle girl murmurs what he said in the night.
event: Padumai's mother asks whether Civakan said anything beforehand, and Padumai repeats his night words.

reading: She reports that he said it is a man's duty to think of the hot wasteland and leave for deeds and for wealth, and a woman's duty, if he goes, to stay at home with dignity.
nuance: Civakan's words, given in his voice through Padumai's report, are the akam rule for the man's leaving; but he has not gone for work or wealth, and in hindsight the rule was a hint covering a secret departure.

reading: The broad-chested man, she says, also told her that though the royal swan that played on the scented lotus may rest elsewhere, it has no thought for the massed blue lilies.
nuance: A second veiled saying: away from the lotus, the swan will not turn to other flowers, a promise of faithfulness disguised as a remark about birds.

reading: As the girl of the gold-bearing breasts told this, she made her mother glad, as the asunam deer is gladdened on hearing the sweet voice of the lute.
event: Padumai's report of his words gladdens her mother.

reading: The king's great queen reads the riddle: he is the swan and you the lotus; he has left you but has not left you in love, and that is what he told you.
event: Padumai's mother interprets Civakan's saying as a promise to return.

tamil: சொரிபனி முருக்க நைந்து சுடர்முகம் பெற்ற போதே
பரிவுறு நலத்த வன்றே பங்கய மன்ன தேபோல்
வரிவளைத் தோளி கேள்வன் வருமென வலித்த சொல்லாற்
றிருநலம் பிறந்து சொன்னா டேனினு மினிய சொல்லாள்.
reading: As a lotus bruised by falling frost regains its beauty when it meets the radiant sun, so the bangled girl, at the firm word that her husband will come, regained her beauty, and she spoke with words sweeter than honey.
event: Padumai revives at the assurance that Civakan will return and speaks.

tamil: நஞ்சினை யமுத மென்று நக்கினு மமுத மாகா
தஞ்சிறைக் கலாப மஞ்ஞை யணங்கர வட்ட தேனு
மஞ்சிறைக் கலுழ னாகு மாட்சியொன் றானு மின்றே
வஞ்சனுக் கினைய நீரேன் வாடுவ தென்னை யென்றாள்.
reading: Poison does not become nectar because one licks it calling it nectar, and a peacock does not become Garuda though it kills a fearful snake; why then, she asks, should I, being such, wither for a deceiver?
nuance: The two proverbs can be read against him (he only seemed a Garuda when he cured her snakebite) or against her own grief (calling it sweet does not make it so); the turn from revived beauty in 1404 to 'deceiver' here is abrupt, and the reading is not secure.

tamil: பொய்கையுட் கமலத் தங்கட் புள்ளெனு முரச மார்ப்ப
வெய்யவன் கதிர்க ளென்னும் விளங்கொளித் தடக்கை நீட்டி
மையிருட் போர்வை நீக்கி மண்ணக மடந்தை கோலம்
பையவே பரந்து நோக்கிப் பனிவரை நெற்றி சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Dawn: the birds in the lotus pools sound like drums, the sun stretches out his rays as bright long hands, draws off the cover of black night, looks slowly over the adorned earth-woman and reaches the brow of the snowy mountain.

tamil: செவ்வழி யாழி னூறுந் தீஞ்சொலாட் குற்ற தெல்லா
மவ்வழி யரசற் குய்த்தார்க் கரசனு மவல மெய்தி
யெவ்வழி யானு நாடி யிமைப்பின தெல்லை யுள்ளே
reading: All that had befallen the girl of lute-sweet speech was carried to the king, and the king of horsed chariots, grieved, ordered them to search by every road and bring the man back within the blink of an eye.
event: The king hears of Padumai's grief and sends men to search for Civakan.

reading: Taking on a form born from within himself, as a lightning flash born inside lightning, the one bright as gold born from gold set his face to the north.
nuance: தன்னுளே பிறந்ததோர் வடிவு is read as a changed shape he assumes, a disguise; how he takes it is not said here.
event: Civakan takes on another form and heads north.

reading: He bound on his anklets, made his white cloth into two pieces, took off the many ornaments he wore and gave them to a man, and set out on the long road, bright as the full moon.
nuance: The putting off of ornaments and the plain white cloth look forward to renunciation, though here they are only a traveller's disguise.
event: Civakan puts off his ornaments, gives them away, dresses in two white cloths and sets out on the long road.

tamil: வேந்தனால் விடுக்கப் பட்டார் விடலையைக் கண்டு சொன்னா
ரேந்தலே பெரிது மொக்கு மிளமையும் வடிவு மிஃதே
போந்ததும் போய கங்குல் போம்வழிக் கண்ட துண்டேல்
யாந்தலைப் படுது மைய வறியினீங் குரைக்க வென்றார்.
reading: The men the king sent meet the young man and say: you closely resemble our lord, in youth and in form this is he; if on the way you saw anyone go by in the night just past, tell us, sir, and we will catch up with him.
nuance: The irony is the scene's point: they tell the man himself that he looks like the one they seek.
event: The king's searchers meet the disguised Civakan and ask him about the man they seek.

tamil: நெய்கனிந் திருண்ட வைம்பா னெடுங்கணாள் காத லானை
யையிரு திங்க ளெல்லை யகப்படக் காண்பி ரிப்பாற்
பொய்யுரை யன்று காணீர் போமினம் போகி நுங்கண்
மையலங் களிற்று வேந்தன் மைந்தனுக் குரைமி னென்றான்.
reading: He answers that within the limit of ten months they will see the beloved of the long-eyed girl, that this is no lie, and bids them go and tell it to the son of the king of the elephants in rut.
nuance: மைந்தனுக்கு (to the son) is unexpected, since the king himself sent them; it may name the king by his lineage or a prince of the house.
event: Civakan, unrecognized, sends the searchers back with word that Padumai's husband will return within ten months.

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1412-1436 (1/6)
theme: Civakan leaves Padumai, crosses the forest and mountain singing a hymn to the Jina on the fruit of deeds, the soul and the bond of love, and at a hermitage of Vaishnava forest ascetics answers their discourse by mocking their diet, fires, bathing and matted hair with the beasts that already live so, then sets out knowledge, right vision and right conduct as what ends deeds.
source_issues: 1414, 1415, 1418-1420, 1429-1431 and 1434-1436 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins read correctly.
1419 line 2 reads உண்டாய வ்வவுயிரே, apparently garbled for உண்டாய அவ்வுயிரே.
1420 line 3 திவண்டுலாங் looks like a misprint, perhaps for திவண்டு உலாம்; the sense is not affected.
1434 line 4 பறைக்குற்றாற் பறைக்கலாமே is hard to construe and may be corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, son of Vijayai, travelling alone after leaving Padumai
the Jina, Lord of the asoka tree, addressed in Civakan's hymn (1418-1420)
the forest ascetics of the hermitage, who keep the way of Kama's father and debate with Civakan

tamil: வானின் வழங்கும் வண்கை மணிசெய் யார மார்பிற்
ணானம் வழங்குங் கோதை நைய வெய்ய வாய
கானம் வழங்கன் மேவிக் காலின் னேகி னானே.
reading: Vijayai's son, whose generous hand gives like the rain cloud and whose fresh garland drips honey, leaves the woman of musk-scented hair to pine and takes on foot to the harsh forest.
nuance: The verb வழங்கும் returns in each line (the hand that gives, the garland that sheds honey, the hair that sheds musk, the forest he walks), so the line-by-line play binds his generosity, his finery and her grief to the walk into the wilds.
event: Civakan sets out alone on foot into the forest, leaving Padumai grieving.

tamil: சிலைகொ ணாணிற் றீராத் திருந்து கற்பின் னவர்த
மிலைகொள் பூந்தா ருழுத வின்ப வருத்த நீங்க
முலைகொள் கண்கள் கண்ணின் னெழுதி முள்கு மொய்ம்பன்
மலைகொள் கானம் முன்னி மகிழ்வோ டேகு கின்றான்.
reading: The strong hero, the weariness of love with women whose chastity holds like a string on a bow now passing, heads gladly for the mountain forest.
nuance: Line 3 (முலைகொள் கண்கள் கண்ணின் எழுதி முள்கும்) is hard to construe; it seems to recall his love-play with the wives, but the exact sense is not fixed. The bowstring simile praises the wives' karpu as something that never leaves them, even as he leaves.
event: Civakan, refreshed from the fatigue of love, presses on toward the hill forest.

tamil: கனிகொள் வாழைக் காட்டுட் கருமை மெழுகி யவைபோன்
றினிய வல்லா முகத்த முசுவுங் குரங்கு மிரியத்
துனிவு தீர நோக்கித் தோன்றல் செல்லு முன்னாற்
பனிவெண் டிரைசூழ் கடல்போற் பழுவந் தோன்றிற் றவணே.
reading: In a forest of fruiting plantains, as langurs and monkeys with faces like smeared black wax scatter, the prince looks about to ease his sorrow, and ahead of him a thicket appears like a sea ringed with cold white waves.
event: Civakan walks on through the plantain forest and sees a grove ahead.

tamil: பருகு வாரிற் புல்லிப் பயங்கண் மாறத் துறக்கு
முருகு விம்மு குழலார் போல மொய்கொ டும்பி
யுருவப் பூங்கொம் பொசியப் புல்லித் தீந்தேன் பருகி
யருகு வாய்விட் டார்ப்ப வண்ணன் மெல்லச் சென்றான்.
reading: Like women of fragrant hair who embrace their drinkers and cast them off when the gain runs out, the swarming bees cling to a flowering branch until it bends, drink its honey and drone nearby, while the noble one walks slowly on.
nuance: The landscape is read through a moral simile: the bees are the courtesans who leave a man once his wealth is gone.
event: Civakan walks slowly through the flowering grove.

tamil: செல்வர் மனத்தி னோங்கித் திருவின் மாந்தர் நெஞ்சி
னெல்லை யிருளிற் றாகிப் பூந்தா தினிதி னொழுகிக்
கொல்லும் மரவின் மயங்கிச் சிறியார் கொண்ட தொடர்பிற்
செல்லச் செல்ல வஃகு நெறிசேர் சிலம்பு சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: He reaches the mountain by a path that rises like the minds of the rich, is dark as the hearts of the wealthy, sheds pollen sweetly, winds like a deadly snake, and narrows the further one goes, like friendship with the small.
nuance: All four similes are moral: the pride and inner darkness of the rich and the dwindling friendship of petty men. The last is the didactic books' image of a bond that shrinks over time, set to a path.
event: Civakan climbs the narrowing path to the mountain.

tamil: சுனைகள் கண்க ளாகச் சூழ்ந்த குவளை விழியா
வனைய லாகா வுருவ நோக்கி மைந்தற் கிரங்கி
இனைவ போலும் வரையின் னருவி யினிதி னாடி
நனைகொள் போது வேய்ந்து நாதற் பாடு கின்றான்.
reading: The mountain, its pools as eyes and its kuvalai flowers as eyes, seems to pity the youth's matchless form and weep with its falls; he bathes gladly in the cascade, crowns himself with buds and sings to the Lord.
event: Civakan bathes in a mountain waterfall, garlands himself and begins a hymn to the Jina.

reading: Civakan praises the Lord of the cool flowering asoka for teaching that the fruit of the two kinds of deed travels to the one who did them and that no other receives it, and worships him if this is his word.
nuance: The refrain பூம்பிண்டிக் கோமான் names the Jina by the asoka (பிண்டி) under which he sits. The hymn's conditional form ('if this is the nature of your word') makes each doctrine the ground of worship, and the doctrine of the first verse is the one Civakan will use against the ascetics: no rite done by the body can carry off a deed's fruit.
event: Civakan sings the first verse of a hymn to the Jina of the asoka tree.

reading: He praises the Lord of the asoka, which spreads four kaathams bearing garlands loud with bees, for declaring that the soul exists, known by its own nature when one inquires, and that the soul is not from anything other than itself.
nuance: Line 2 is garbled in the text (உண்டாய வ்வவுயிரே); read as உண்டாய அவ்வுயிரே, it says the soul is not produced from another thing, which sets the hymn against those who make the soul a product of the elements.

reading: He praises the Lord of the asoka, over which honey drips and bees roam among the hanging garlands, for teaching both that by love the eight karmas pass and that, because it is still love, the eight karmas do not pass.
nuance: The verse is a deliberate paradox, and its sense turns on காதல், which may be love of the Jina or of the path, and on மறைதி, 'you declared' or 'you hid'. Read either way, even devotion is counted as a bond: the eight karmas (எண்வினை) are the Jain reckoning of the kinds of karma.

reading: Having praised thus sweetly and walked round in reverence, he goes on alone and comes upon a cool flowering grove where forest ascetics live, a sages' retreat like Chitrakuta.
nuance: முனிவர் சித்திர கூடம் முன்னாது may compare the grove to Chitrakuta, Rama's forest of sages, or say that he went on not thinking of it; the comparison is taken here.
event: Civakan circumambulates the shrine and reaches the ascetics' hermitage.

reading: He reaches the dwelling of those who eat only clean food: grass, lotus stamens, rice of the tall bamboo, wild grains grown in water, sweet fruits, green fruits and roots.
nuance: The list of foods is set out with care because Civakan will argue from it (1429, 1430): if such diet burned deeds, the beasts of the forest would be freed.
event: Civakan enters the hermitage of the forest ascetics.

reading: They are men of hard vows who stand amid the five fires to win release, whose tongues have recited the Veda at length, and whose minds are set on the fire rite without discernment.
nuance: The five fires (ஆரழல் ஐந்து) are the four fires round the ascetic and the sun above. தெரிவில் may be the narrator's judgment, 'without discernment', or mean only 'chosen'; if the first, the Jain poet has already weighed them before the debate.

reading: Those of generous heart bring him sweet nectar of the valli root and clear sweet fruit of the mountain plantain and, bidding the noble guest feast, tend him gladly.
event: The ascetics feed Civakan with roots and fruit as their guest.

reading: The great ascetics beside him, judging that this youth like the white moon is deep in learning and has heard the true doctrine, resolve to measure him too and recite one or two of their lofty discourses.
event: The ascetics test Civakan with a few discourses of their own.

reading: When the elders had spoken, the noble one answered that if a man who swims the sea with a mountain strapped to him could be saved, then all who are bound here by attachment would be saved as well.
nuance: தொடர்ப்பாடு (bond, attachment) is taken as the mountain on the swimmer's back; the image prepares the charge (1432 to 1434) that these ascetics have carried their households into the forest.
event: Civakan begins his reply to the ascetics with the image of a man swimming the sea under a mountain.

reading: Growing great matted hair in search of release, wrapping the body in cloth, carrying a white skull as a bowl and wearing bark: these, he says, are said to be seeds of a mean birth.
nuance: என்பவே ('so it is said') rests the judgment on authority rather than argument; the argument comes in 1429 to 1434. The verse does not say the marks are merely useless but that they seed a lowly birth.

reading: The ascetic replies: which is the safe good path? We too are resolved on that path of purity; young bull, if there is any evil in the way of Kama's father, tell it.
nuance: காமன் தாதை, Kama's father, is Vishnu, so the ascetics name their path as his, though their practices (the five fires, the Veda, the fire rite of 1423) are those of Vedic forest ascetics. The claim is refuted in Civakan's answer, 1429 to 1436, and the ascetics' conversion in 1437.
event: An ascetic challenges Civakan to show any fault in their Vaishnava way.

tamil: தூங்குறிக் கிடந்து காயும் பழங்களுந் துய்ப்ப நில்லா
பாங்கலா வினைக ளென்றார் பகவனா ரெங்கட் கென்னி
னோங்குநீண் மரத்திற் றூங்கு மொண்சிறை யொடுங்கல் வாவல்
பாங்கரிற் பழங்க டுய்ப்பப் பழவினை பரியு மன்றே.
reading: If, he says, the Lord told you that unfit deeds do not stay with those who eat the fruits that hang ripening from the trees, then the bat with its folded wings, hanging from tall trees and eating the fruit nearby, would shed its old deeds.
nuance: Each of the next verses has the same form: the ascetics' practice is stated as a conditional and answered with a forest creature that already lives that way. பகவனார் (the Lord) is the ascetics' god as Civakan quotes them.

tamil: அல்லியும் புல்லு முண்டாங் காரழ லைந்து ணின்று
சொல்லிய வகையி னோற்பத் துணியும்வெவ் வினைக ளென்னிற்
கல்லுண்டு கடிய வெம்புங் கானுறை புறவ மெல்லாம்
புல்லிய வினையை வென்று புறக்கொடை காணு மன்றே.
reading: If eating lotus stamens and grass and standing amid the five fires in the prescribed way cuts off cruel deeds, then all the forest doves, which eat grit and burn in the heat, would conquer their binding deeds and put them to flight.

tamil: நீட்டிய சடைய மாகி நீர்மூழ்கி நிலத்திற் சேர்ந்து
வாட்டிய வுடம்பின் யாங்கள் வரகதி விளைத்து மென்னிற்
காட்டிடைக் கரடி போகிக் கயமூழ்கிக் காட்டி னின்று
வீட்டினை விளைக்க வேண்டும் வெளிற்றுரை விடுமி னென்றான்.
reading: If, with long matted hair, plunging in water, lying on the ground and a wasted body, you would win the highest state, then the bear that roams the forest, plunges into pools and stands in the wild would have to win release; give up empty words, he says.

tamil: கலைவளர் கிளவி யார்தங் காமர்மென் சேக்கை நீங்கி
யிலைவளர் குரம்பை யங்க ணிருநிலஞ் சேக்கை யாக
முலைவள ராகந் தோய முழுவினை முரியு மாயின்
மலைவளர் குறவர்க் கம்மா வினைகளு மாயு மன்றே.
reading: If leaving the soft beds of women of artful speech for the bare ground of a leaf hut, while still embracing their breasts there, breaks all one's deeds, then, he says, the deeds of the hill kuravar would perish too.
nuance: The ascetics are householders in the forest: they have left the palace bed, not the wife. The kuravar, who live just so in leaf huts on the hill, make the point that a change of bed is not a change of life; 1437 has the converts put away their households.

tamil: வொண்ணிற வுதிரந் தன்னை யுதிரத்தா லொழிக்க லாமே
பண்ணிறக் கிளவி யார்தம் பசையினாற் பிறந்த பாவங்
கண்ணிற முலையி னார்தங் கலவியாற் கழிக்க லாமே.
reading: Can bright blood that has fallen on white cloth and stained it be washed out with blood? So can the sin born of clinging to sweet-voiced women be removed by union with women?
nuance: The image is of washing a stain with the same stuff that made it: the remedy must be other in kind than the fault.

tamil: நுண்டுகில் வேத லஞ்சி நெருப்பகம் பொதிந்து நோக்கிக்
கொண்டுபோய் மறைய வைத்தாற் கொந்தழல் சுடாது மாமே
கண்டத்தி னாவி யார்தங் கடிமனை துறந்து காட்டுட்
பண்டைச்செய் தொழிலிற் பாவம் பறைக்குற்றாற் பறைக்க லாமே.
reading: If one wraps fire in fine cloth for fear of its burning and hides it away, will the fierce flame not burn? So one who leaves the guarded house of women for the forest, but carries the sin of old deeds, cannot wear it away by wishing to.
nuance: Lines 2 and 4 are rhetorical questions in -ஆமே, and the second half of line 4 (பறைக்குற்றாற் பறைக்கலாமே) is hard to construe; it is read as 'can one wear it away merely by setting out to?'. The fire hidden in cloth is the old deed carried into the forest.

tamil: நோய்முதிர் குரங்கு போல நுகர்ச்சிநீர் நோக்கல் வேண்டா
காய்முதிர் கனியி னூழ்த்து வீழுமிவ் வியாக்கை யின்னே
வேய்முதிர் வனத்தின் வென்றா னுருவொடு விளங்க நோற்றுப்
போய்முதிர் துறக்கத் தின்பம் பருகுவ புரிமி னென்றான்.
reading: Do not gaze on pleasure like a sick old monkey, he says; this body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; practise austerity in the bamboo forest in the form of the Conqueror and go to drink the joy of the ripe heaven: strive for that.
nuance: Civakan does not reject austerity: he keeps it, in the Jina's form (வென்றான் உருவொடு), and promises heaven (துறக்கம்) rather than release, the nearer fruit; release comes only with the three jewels of 1436.

tamil: மெய்வகை தெரிதன் ஞானம் விளங்கிய பொருள்க டம்மைப்
பொய்வகை யின்றித் தேறல் காட்சியைம் பொறியும் வாட்டி
யுய்வகை யுயிரைத் தேயா தொழுகுத லொழுக்க மூன்று
மிவ்வகை நிறைந்த போழ்தே யிருவினை கழியு மென்றான்.
reading: Knowledge is discerning things as they truly are; right vision is trusting without falsehood the things so made clear; conduct is withering the five senses and living without wearing down any soul; when all three are full in this way, he says, both kinds of deed pass away.
nuance: These are the Jain three jewels, named here ஞானம், காட்சி and ஒழுக்கம். The weight falls on மூன்றும் and நிறைந்த: no one of them, and none in part, is enough. The answer to the ascetics is not less austerity but a different cause of release, in which conduct is defined by non-harm (உயிரைத் தேயாது).

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1437-1460 (2/6)
theme: The ascetics Civakan has argued with leave their households for the Jina, and he goes on to the Takka land and its city Kemamapuram, described as a goddess and a sea of wealth; there the merchant Subhadran's daughter Kemasari has waited twelve years under an astrologer's word that her husband is the man whose sight will shame her, while her father feeds a thousand and eight guests a day, and Civakan, meditating under a banyan outside the city, is met by the father, who begins to read his bodily marks.
source_issues: 1437, 1447, 1450, 1451, 1454 and 1456 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build.
1440 line 4 (தாங்கலா றக்கநா டாய தென்பவே) is divided obscurely; the first word cannot be fixed.
1449 line 2 has வேத வாணிகன், an unusual title for the merchant; perhaps a scribal form.
1458 line 3 (சேட்பட் டானரோ) is obscure as divided.
1444 line 2 has நாயில் for ஞாயில் (battlements), a variant spelling.

cast.role: the hero, travelling alone toward the Takka land
the forest ascetics whose austerities Civakan answers and who turn to the Jina (called பாகத்தார் in 1437)
the merchant's daughter of Kemamapuram in the Takka land
merchant of Kemamapuram, Kemasari's father
Kemasari's mother, Subhadran's wife
the astrologer who reads Kemasari's birth and names the sign of her husband

tamil: குன்ற னானுரைப்பக் கேட்டே பாகத்தார் குடும்ப நீக்கி
யின்றுகண் விடுக்கப் பட்டேம் யாமென வெழுந்து போகி
வென்றவன் பாதஞ் சேர்ந்து வீட்டுநன் னெறியைப் பெற்றார்
சென்றது பருதி வட்டஞ் செம்மலு மசைவு தீர்ந்தான்.
reading: Hearing what the hill-shouldered hero said, the ascetics of that side put away their households, saying that today their eyes had been opened, rose and went to the feet of the Conqueror and gained the good path of release; the sun went down and the noble one was rested.
nuance: Their words (இன்று கண் விடுக்கப்பட்டேம்) treat the conversion as the opening of eyes, so their earlier austerities are cast as blindness. That they now leave their families (குடும்ப நீக்கி) answers the jibe of 1432 that these ascetics still lay with women in their leaf huts. பாகத்தார் is taken as 'those on that side', the ascetics.
event: The forest ascetics, won over by Civakan's teaching, leave their families and take refuge with the Jina; night falls and Civakan rests.

reading: Rested, at dawn when the darkness thinned, he learned the direction and the river from the blameless converts who showed him the way, and went on, he whose body bore the true marks, with none above him.
nuance: மெய்ப்பொறி யாக்கையான், the man whose body bears the true marks, anticipates the reading of his bodily marks that begins at 1460; the construal of மிசையும் இல்லது in line 4 is not sure.
event: At dawn the converted ascetics show Civakan the road, and he sets out.

reading: He reached the border of the Takka land, a fitting country full of lotus ponds like a picture drawn on cloth, wide and sweet as the dark-gold skin of women with garlanded breasts.
event: Civakan reaches the border of the Takka country.

reading: The scent loosed from lotuses of the honeyed ponds, the sandal paste worn by flower-haired women and the fragrance of aghil smoke mingling everywhere make up the Takka land, they say.
nuance: Line 4 is divided as printed (தாங்கலா றக்கநா டாய தென்பவே); the reading takes it as naming the Takka land through sandhi, but the first word is unclear.

reading: Garlands of champak flowers, fragrant sandal, ripe areca with tender betel leaf, and food that fails no one: such is the look of that land of generous fame.
In the rich sugarcane-bordered fields the long red paddy lying across the lotuses at the bund looks like the forehead ornament of dancing women on the stage, with bees circling it.
nuance: The simile turns on இலம்பகம, the frontlet worn on the brow, the same word that names the epic's books.

reading: At the curving bee-haunted ghat the young vaalai fish, trembling as though a crab's claw had touched it, hides for shame and leaves its food; the poet turns to tell of the city ringed by a flowered moat fed by falling water.
nuance: The fish that flees in shame is a playful prelude to the heroine, whose sign is to be shame at the sight of the man (1451).

reading: The deep moat is the city goddess's silk, the snake-skin-smooth wall her famous girdle, the battlements her ornamented breasts, the gem-bright gate-tower her moon face, and the long flags her braided hair.
Since none who live there would leave it even if fed the nectar churned from the planted mountain, its shining golden wall is like a crest set upon the great city that holds heaped wealth.

With its flags held up like leaping sharks, mansions like mountains of rolling waves, great ships, women like the goddess Tiru and nectar, and its great roar, the rich city is a sounding sea, they say.

tamil: மதியக டுரிஞ்சுஞ் சென்னி மாடநீண் மறுகு தோறும்
பொதியவிழ் மாலை வீழ்ந்து பொன்செய்நன் கலன்கள் சிந்தி
நிதியறை திறந்து நோக்கி யன்னதோர் நீர்மை யெய்திப்
புதியவர்க் கியங்க லாகாப் பொற்பொடு பொலிந்த தன்றே.
reading: In every long street of mansions whose tops graze the moon, fallen opening garlands and dropped gold ornaments make it look like an opened treasure room, and it shines with a splendour strangers cannot walk through.
The golden city named Kemamapuram, of undying fame, is like a tilaka set on the earth, and its king, guardian of the land under a tall garlanded umbrella, is named Narapatidevan.
In that city lived a merchant like a king himself, matchless in person, bearing a well-made spear and fragrant garland, who passed his days beguiled by women with dark rain-cool eyes.
nuance: வேத வாணிகன் in line 2 is unusual for a merchant; it may be a scribal form, and the reading keeps only 'merchant'.

tamil: வார்சிலை வடிப்ப வீங்கி வரையெனத் திரண்ட தோளான்
சோர்புய றொலைத்த வண்கைச் சுபத்திரன் மனைவி பெற்ற
சீர்நலம் கடந்த கேம சரியெனத் திசைக ளெல்லாம்
பேர்நலம் பொறித்த பெண்மைப் பெருவிளக் காகி நின்றாள்.
reading: Subhadran, of shoulders swelled by the bow and massed like hills, whose giving hand outdid the pouring cloud, had by his wife a daughter Kemasari, beyond all praise, who stood as the great lamp of womanhood whose fame was written in every direction.
event: Kemasari is born to the merchant Subhadran and his wife.

tamil: மாசிலாள் பிறந்த ஞான்றே மதிவலான் விதியி னெண்ணிக்
காசிலாள் கண்ட போழ்தே கதுமென நாணப் பட்டான்
றூசுலா மல்கு லாட்குத் துணைவனாம் புணர்மி னென்று
பேசினா னன்று கொண்டு பெருவிருந் தோம்பு கின்றான்.
reading: On the day the stainless girl was born a man wise in reckoning worked it out by rule and said: the one at whose first sight she is suddenly overcome with shame will be her husband, so join them; and from that day the father keeps up a great feeding of guests.
nuance: The sign is the girl's own shame (நாண்), the virtue that normally keeps a maiden from a stranger's gaze; here it is made the test that marks the man. The feasting is the father's way of bringing men before her eyes.
event: An astrologer foretells that Kemasari's husband will be the man whose sight makes her feel shame, and her father begins daily feasts for guests.

tamil: தாழ்தரு பைம்பொன் மாலை தடமலர்த் தாம மாலை
வீழ்தரு மணிசெய் மாலை யிவற்றிடை மின்னி னின்று
சூழ்வளைத் தோளி செம்பொற் றூணையே சார்ந்து நோக்கு
மூழ்படு காத லானை யொருபிடி நுசுப்பி னாளே.
reading: Amid hanging garlands of gold, of broad flowers and of gems, the girl with bangled arms and waist a hand's span, shining like lightning, leans on a golden pillar and watches for the lover fate has appointed.
nuance: ஊழ்படு காதலான் makes the husband a matter of ūḻ, apportioned before she sees him.
event: Kemasari stands by a golden pillar watching the guests for her destined husband.

tamil: சேயிழை கணவ னாகுந் திருமகன் றிறத்து நாளு
மாயிரத் தெட்டு நேர்ந்த வாரமு தடிசி லூட்டி
யேயின வகையி னாலே யாறிரண் டெல்லை யாண்டு
போயின வென்ப மற்றப் பூங்கொடிச் சாய லாட்கே.
reading: For the sake of the fortunate man who will be the bride's husband, a thousand and eight guests were fed each day with nectar-like rice in fitting ways, and so twelve years passed for that flower-creeper of a girl.
event: For twelve years the household feeds a thousand and eight guests a day while Kemasari waits.

tamil: முருக்கிதழ் குலிக மூட்டி வைத்தன முறுவற் செவ்வாய்த்
திருக்கவி னிறைந்த வெங்கட் பணைமுலைத் தேம்பெய் கோதைப்
புரிக்குழற் பொன்செய் பைம்பூட் புனையிழை கோல நோக்கித்
தரிக்கிலா துருகி நையுந் தடமலர்க் கோதை நற்றாய்.
reading: Seeing the beauty of the girl, her smiling red lips as if dyed with vermilion over the murukku petal, her full breasts, honeyed garland, curled hair and golden ornaments, her own mother cannot bear it, and melts and wastes.
event: Kemasari's mother pines at seeing her daughter's beauty go unwed.

tamil: மாவடு மருட்டு நோக்கின் மதிமுக மழைக்கண் மாசில்
பூவொடு புரையுஞ் சாயல் புனைநலந் தனித்து வைக
வேவடு பிணையி னோக்கி யிறைவளை கழல நின்ற
தாய்படுந் துயர மெல்லாந் தாரவ னீக்கி னானே.
reading: As her daughter's beauty, eyes like the tender mango, moon face and flowerlike grace, stayed alone and unused, the mother looked on like a doe struck by an arrow, her bangles slipping, and the garlanded father took away all her grief.
event: Subhadran consoles his grieving wife.

tamil: போதுவாய் திறந்த போதே பூம்பொறி வண்டு சேர்ந்தாங்
கூதுமே மகளிர்க் கொத்த போகமு மன்ன தொன்றே
யாதுநீ கவல வேண்டா வாரழ குடைய நம்பி
காதலான் றவத்தின் மிக்கான் கண்ணுறு நாளை யென்றான்.
reading: He says that as the spotted bee comes to a bud the moment its mouth opens, so the pleasure fit for women comes in its season; she need not grieve, for a man of full beauty, a lover great in merit, will meet the girl's eyes tomorrow.
nuance: தவத்தின் மிக்கான் is read as 'great by the merit of former austerity', the Jain way of naming the good fortune that brings a husband; the 'tomorrow' (நாளை) is borne out at once in 1457.

reading: The prince with the warrior's anklet came near the town of the innocent wide-eyed girl, an unmatched flower creeper risen from golden ground, bright as lightning shot out, her hair braided like thick darkness.
event: Civakan comes near Kemasari's city.

reading: The father of the young girl with jasmine-scented hair, a man of jewels spreading many-rayed light, came upon the prince at some distance from the fine city.
nuance: சேட்பட் டானரோ is taken as சேண் படுதல், being far off; the line may instead mean that the father went out a long way to find him.
event: Kemasari's father meets Civakan outside the city.

reading: Like a fine red sun risen in the south and come round to the north, the man of the wedding-fit chest arrived and sat gladly in the shade of a banyan, meditating on the Lord.
nuance: The hero on his way to a marriage he does not know of is shown at meditation, not seeking a bride, so the match comes to him as the prophecy's work rather than his pursuit.
event: Civakan sits under a banyan tree in contemplation of the Jina.

reading: His fine crowned head was like a spread umbrella, his two feet had the shape of a tortoise's back, his rounded flanks curved with the grace of a bow, and his eyes were the colour of the fragrant lotus.
nuance: This opens a catalogue of auspicious bodily marks running to 1465, where the father reads them and decides that this is his daughter's husband; the marks are the second sign, beside the girl's shame.

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1461-1484 (3/6)
theme: The merchant Subhadran reads the auspicious marks on Civakan's body, decides he is his daughter's destined husband and brings him home; a hymn to the Jina is sung as they enter, Kemasari and Civakan fall in love at first sight, the house bathes and feasts him, and he lies lamenting the wounds of her beauty.
source_issues: 1461 and 1464: the physiognomic catalogue is compressed and several comparisons (குறங்கணி மயிலொடு, கெடிற்றழகு, மூக்கு ... தோட்டி) cannot be fixed with confidence from the verse alone.
1469 line 4 (ஓட்டிடுப வெண்குணனுங் கோட்பட் டுயிராவே): the construction, and so whose the eight qualities are, is uncertain.
1482 line 4 reads கொல்லுந் கொல்லுமே, with an unassimilated ந் before கொ; probably an edition or input slip for கொல்லுங் கொல்லுமே.

cast.role: the hero, a stranger arriving at Kemamapuram, read by the merchant as Kemasari's destined husband; called காளை, வள்ளல், செல்வன் here
the wealthy merchant of Kemamapuram, Kemasari's father (named at 1450), who reads Civakan's bodily marks and takes him home
Subhadran's daughter, destined to marry the man at whose sight she feels shy
the unnamed woman who garlands her vina and sings the hymn to the Jina as the chariot passes (1466-1469); possibly Kemasari
the unnamed woman likened to Rambha who hears the hymn and blesses the girl with a fitting husband (1470)
Kemasari's companions
the women of Subhadran's house who bathe, dress and feed Civakan

reading: The catalogue of the stranger's body goes on: his limbs are full and handsome, his neck is fit to be seen like a sounding gem drum, and his mouth has the colour of a fierce great tiger's.
nuance: This continues the head-to-foot survey begun at 1460 as the merchant looks the stranger over; each part is measured against a standard object, as a reader of bodily signs would measure it.

reading: On his hill-broad chest there are three lines, his tongue is flawless and gold-like, his shoulders are like hills, and his arms have the shape of the trunk of the king of the gods' elephant.
nuance: The three lines on the chest (வரியு மூன்று) and the elephant-trunk arms are marks to be read, not only praised: they are the kind of signs that let a father decide whom to give his daughter to (1465).

reading: The navel of this prince, who is like a shining golden hill, is like the seed-pod of a petalled lotus, deep and whorled to the right, and gives off a sweet scent.
nuance: The rightward whorl (வலஞ்சுழி) is the auspicious turn, as of the right-whorled conch; the description reads the body as a set of good omens.

reading: His wrists are thick and fitted to their measure, his calves outdo the kediru fish in beauty, his fingers are so close that not even a mustard seed can pass between them, and his nose is like a goad set with a rare gem.
nuance: Fingers that leave no gap (கடிப்பகை நுழைவற) are a sign of a hand that holds wealth; the survey keeps to the signs a merchant would value.

reading: Seeing a mouth set with long shining teeth like coral, and palms and feet like lotuses, the merchant concluded that this was the husband of Tirumagal, settled it, spoke with him and took him up onto his chariot.
nuance: திருமகள் கணவன் can be heard two ways: Lakshmi's lord, a man of royal fortune, and the husband of the merchant's own daughter, whom the house has been waiting for (1453 calls him திருமகன்). The decision is made by reading the body, not by asking the stranger's birth.
event: Subhadran, having read the marks on Civakan's body, decides he is the destined husband, speaks with him and takes him onto his chariot.

reading: As they rode the chariot, a creeper-like woman took a lovely garland, set it on her great-sounding vina, plucked with her sharp nail and sang of the god the world knows.
nuance: The text does not name the singer; she may be Kemasari herself or a woman of the house. Garlanding the instrument before playing is a worship of the vina.
event: As Subhadran and Civakan ride in, a woman garlands her vina and begins a hymn to the Jina.

reading: The singer says that those who do not scatter honeyed flowers and praise with their tongues the lord of the gods, sea-coloured, under the three umbrellas beneath the fragrant flowering pindi tree, will not reach the world of release.
nuance: The pindi (asoka) tree and the triple umbrella mark the Jina. The repeated half-line (தேவர் பெருமானைத் தேவர் பெருமானை) is the refrain form of a sung hymn, kept in all three stanzas.

reading: She sings that the sea-coloured one under the three umbrellas, lord of those who rose by slaying the mighty five senses, knew without flaw, and that those who do not sing his lotus feet without stain will not reach the world of the gods.
nuance: The refrain shifts from வீட்டுலகம் (1467, 1469) to வானுலகம் here: release and the heaven of the gods are not the same goal in Jain teaching, and the hymn names both as the reward of praise. காசின்று உணர்ந்தான் points to the Jina's faultless knowing.

reading: Those who do not praise, until their tongues are calloused, the sea-coloured one beneath the ever-flowering pindi will not reach the world of release; the thieves that are their deeds waylay them, and their souls, their eight qualities seized, are driven off.
nuance: On my reading of கோட்பட்டு, the eight qualities (எண்குணன்) here belong to the souls, plundered by deeds pictured as highway robbers (வினைக்கள்வர் ஆறலைப்ப), in keeping with the Jain teaching of eight karmas that cover the soul's eight qualities. The line is compressed and the construction is not certain.

reading: Hearing her sing the feet of the pearl-sea-coloured one whom the three worlds sing with devotion, a woman like Rambha rejoiced and said, 'May she now win a man of skill fit to match her.'
nuance: The wish is spoken as the destined husband enters the city, so it works as an auspicious word heard at the right moment. Who speaks and who இவள் is (the singer, or Kemasari) is not clear from the verse alone.
event: A woman who hears the hymn blesses the girl with a fitting husband, just as Civakan arrives.

reading: When they entered the long city, where treasure lay so thick the ground seemed to eat it, the gaze of the girl like a shining flowering creeper and the gaze of the man with mighty shoulders met as one.
nuance: நோக்கும் ஒத்த: the two looks are equal and simultaneous, the first-sight meeting of Tamil love poetry.
event: As Civakan enters the city with Subhadran, he and Kemasari see each other and their eyes meet.

reading: On seeing the young man, her bangles slipped down to the ground, her fair colour, her inner restraint and her modesty all broke, and desire kindled a bright fire in which she melted.
nuance: The signs of a separated woman's wasting (slipping bangles, lost colour) come here at the first instant of sight, before any separation.
event: At the sight of Civakan, Kemasari is overcome with desire.

reading: He who was master of the vina, whose lute was a goddess of speech, was pained as her glance became an afflicting goddess and sickened his mind; wondering whether she was a striking goddess or a mortal daughter, he sank down.
nuance: The word play runs on அணங்கு three times: வாக்கணங்கு (the lute as the goddess of speech), நோக்கணங்கு (her look as the goddess that afflicts), தாக்கணங்கு (the goddess who strikes). The vina-master who won Gandharvadattai by sound is here undone by sight.
event: Struck by Kemasari's look, Civakan wonders whether she is a goddess or a woman and is overcome.

reading: Saying that their mistress, whose face shamed the lotus and whose eyes were like killing spears, had melted, her companions spread the word and came and gathered round the strong-chested man.
nuance: The companions read her state from her body and act on it at once, the friend's role of Tamil love poetry turned into a crowd.
event: Kemasari's companions see she is in love and crowd round Civakan.

reading: Gazing at the beauty of the man of merit, like a bull among the herd, as if she had reached a long, full bliss beyond thought, the field-creeper girl with her grace looked once on his loveliness and turned her sword-like eyes away.
nuance: நிப்புதி is a rare word; it seems to be a loan of Prakrit nivvui (nirvrti), the bliss of release, used here as a simile for the joy of a lover's gaze. Turning her eyes away (வாட்கண் அகன்றாள்) is the shyness the astrologer named as the sign of the destined husband (1451).
event: Kemasari looks at Civakan in rapture and then turns her eyes away.

reading: They anointed the generous man with scented oil, bathed him with clear water poured from jewelled pots, dressed him in cloth that had drunk in sweet incense, and adorned him with a honey-dripping garland and ornaments.
event: The women of the house bathe Civakan, dress him and adorn him.

reading: After they had wiped on the auspicious white paste and drawn the pearls into place, the women with fragrant garlands took him inside and brought nectar-like food in bright golden vessels, and he ate it in proper style.
nuance: மங்கல வெள்ளை and முத்து ஈர்த்த are hard to fix; the sense of the second half, the meal, is clear.
event: The women lead Civakan in and serve him food in golden vessels, and he eats.

reading: Seated on a painted cushion upon a golden platform set with inlay rows, so that his dignity was honoured, the garlanded lord rinsed with water from a pitcher like pearl and gem and finished that rite.
event: Civakan washes after the meal, seated on a cushion on a golden platform.

reading: The areca pieces, scented with plump fruit and fragrant spice, came in a golden betel bag of Yavana workmanship, with crystal split and set, gold inlaid at its edges and pearls pressed along the rim.
nuance: The Yavana craftsmanship (யவனக் கைவினை) marks the merchant house as rich in foreign goods.
event: Betel and areca are brought to Civakan in a jewelled bag.

reading: He rolled the green leaves, chewed them, wiped his teeth till they shone, spat, and took the sweet fragrance into his mouth, while his gem earrings swung and shot their light aside, as they say.
event: Civakan chews betel after the meal.

reading: Civakan says: her girdle and fine cloth, spread over the broad hips of the girl whose speech is melody, pour out a fresh light from within and have captured the eyes and heart of wretched me.
nuance: The lament begins after the feast: the guest has been honoured in every way and is alone with longing. பாவியேன் is the lover's self-pity, not a confession of sin.

reading: He says the cruel girl binds his whole body with her fragrant hair, beats him with the strong bow of her brows bent at the middle, and, before her long flower eyes have even split his life, her young breasts kill and kill again.
nuance: Each feature is a weapon in a sequence of capture and execution: hair the rope, brow the bow, eyes the blade, breasts the death stroke. The doubled கொல்லும் is the climax.

reading: He says her hot breasts, cruel enough to be bound by a bodice, smeared with saffron, spread over with pearls on their sloping ground, destroy even the ground of her waist; what will they not do to me?
nuance: The bodice (கச்சு) is described as a restraint put on something dangerous, which the next verse repeats for the hair.

reading: He says her flower-decked hair, dark and fragrant within, is bound and coiled and thrown behind her; if it is like that, what will it not do? It bewilders like her large eyes, which are long and red-lined.
nuance: கட்டப் பட்டன is repeated from 1483: hair and breasts are both things that had to be bound, and still they overpower him.

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1485-1508 (4/6)
theme: Kemasari's concealed love is announced by her father, the marriage is held, and two months of bliss likened to the state beyond birth and death follow; then, on a night framed by a sunset told as a life's ageing, Civakan slips away while she sleeps, and she wakes to search for him like a serpent that has lost its gem.
source_issues: 1487: printed in 5 lines; lines 2 and 3 (ஊன்கறி கற்ற கால / னொண்மணித் தடக்கை வைவேல்) are one line of the stanza broken in two.
1500 line 1: வீணையுஞ் குழலும் has a nasal (ஞ்) that does not agree with the following க; the expected form is வீணையுங் குழலும், likely a typographical slip.
1501-1504 and 1506-1508: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build; the joins read correctly.
1502: the second half (துணைவண்டு துஞ்சின் நீயும் துஞ்சுவை ... பணிகொண்டது இன்மையால்) is hard to construe and may be corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, called காளை, மைந்தன், குருசில் and மார்பன் here; married to Kemasari and leaves her in secret
the merchant's daughter of the Takka land whom Civakan marries and leaves (not named in these verses)
Kemasari's father, the merchant, who announces the match to the king
Kemasari's kin and the townspeople who perform the wedding
the parrots of the millet slope
the bee at Kemasari's garland whom Civakan addresses

reading: Keeping her love shut inside her eyes, she makes the eye her messenger to tell him what she has resolved, and hides it so well that her kin find no fault; such a sword-eyed glance would outsell the sea's nectar and the whole world.
nuance: The verse turns on கரந்திட்ட: her love is real but concealed, and the concealment is itself praised because it spares her kin any blame (ஏதின்மை). It may be Civakan's thought rather than the narrator's; the speech of 1487 makes the point uncertain.

tamil: மிகுகொடா முத்தஞ் சூட்டி மீளிமை தீர்த்து மின்னு
நகுகொடா மணிக ணல்ல தெளித்துக்கொண் டெழுதி நன்பொன்
முகபடாம் வைப்ப வாட்செற் றழன்றுகண் கரிந்த முல்லைத்
தொகுகடாங் கோதை வெய்ய துணைமணி முலைக டாமே.
reading: Her breasts are figured as war-elephants: crowned with pearls, their fury cooled, decked with bright gems and given a face-cloth of fine gold, beside the garland of massed jasmine.
nuance: The elephant figure (முகபடாம், கடாம்) makes the beloved's body an armed force against the man who sees her, preparing Civakan's complaint in 1487 that her features are Death and Yama's noose.

tamil: தேன்கறி கற்ற கூழைச் செண்பக மாலை வேற்க
கூன்பிறை நுதலோர் கூற்றங் குவிமுலை நமன்கைப் பாசம்
யான்பிற னளியன் வாழ்வா னாசைப்பட் டிருக்கின் றேனே.
reading: Civakan says her hair has learned to feed on honey, her spear-eye on flesh, her curved brow is Death and her breasts are Yama's noose, and yet he, a pitiable stranger, sits longing to live.
nuance: The list of killers (கூற்றம், நமன்கைப் பாசம்) ends in the wish to live (வாழ்வான் ஆசைப்பட்டு): the lover desires the very thing he names as death. பிறன் marks him as an outsider in the Takka land.

reading: He tells the golden flower-creeper, a lamp to the beauty of goddesses wearing kalpaka garlands, that one woman's loveliness has made her an enemy to Murugan, to Kama, to himself and to the god of dense matted hair.
nuance: Setting himself beside Murugan, Anangan and the ascetic god of matted locks (மொய்சடை ஒருவன்) makes her beauty a rival even to the god who renounced and burned desire; how பகைத்தி is to be taken, as rivalry or as hostility, is not certain.

reading: While the youth who had passed beyond the many arts brooded on her beauty, the merchant told the king of the land, lord of musth elephants, by due custom, so that the people of the land should know.
nuance: The marriage moves at once from the glance of 1485 to a public act: the father's report to the king (நெறியிற் செப்பினான்) is what turns concealed love into an approved union.
event: Kemasari's father, the merchant, formally announces the match to the king and the land.

reading: With the many instruments of the flag-decked city roaring like the thunder-spitting surf, they held the wedding on an auspicious day and gave the flower-garlanded maiden to the young man, so it is told.
event: Kemasari is married to Civakan on an auspicious day amid the city's music.

reading: Such was the joy of the man with shoulders like gem-pots pressed close, who never let go of the woman whose beauty no astrologer could measure.
Her silk-clad breasts became the mountain, his twin shoulders the serpent, and the sea of her compassion, churned, gave him nectar, as they say.
nuance: The union is told as the churning of the ocean: she is mountain and sea, he the cord-serpent, and the nectar is what she gives; the borrowed myth makes the pleasure divine in kind.

reading: As the bangled girl's breasts plunged into the sandal mire and she leapt to him, the youth's garland was crushed and her anklets and girdle cried out with open mouths.

tamil: கோதையுங் குழலும் பொங்கக் குவிமுலைக் குழங்கன் மாலைப்
போதுகப் பொருது பூணும் பொருகடன் முத்து மூழ்கக்
காதலுங் களிப்பு மிக்குக் கங்குலும் பகலும் விள்ளார்
சாதலும் பிறப்பு மில்லாத் தன்மைபெற் றவர்க ளொத்தார்.
reading: Garlands and hair tumbling, pearls of the ornaments sinking as they struck, their love and delight swelling, they did not part night or day and were like those who have won the state with neither death nor birth.
nuance: சாதலும் பிறப்பும் இல்லாத் தன்மை is the language of release from rebirth, and the narrator gives it to two lovers in bed; it is a simile (ஒத்தார்), not a claim that pleasure frees, and the same night of 1504 ends it.
event: Civakan and Kemasari stay together without parting, night and day.

tamil: புனைமலர்த் தாரி னானும் போதணி கொம்ப னாளு
நனைமலர்க் காவு மந்தண் வாலியு நல்ல வாடிச்
சுனைமலர்க் குவளை குற்றுச் சூழ்மலர்க் கண்ணி சூட்டி
வினைநல நுகர்ந்து செல்வார் விதியினான் மிக்க நீரார்.
reading: The garlanded man and the woman like a flowering branch went through budding groves and cool clear streams, plucked lilies from the springs and crowned each other, enjoying the good of their deeds, people made eminent by fate.
nuance: வினைநலம் நுகர்ந்து and விதியினான் put the honeymoon in the book of karma: their delight is not earned in this life but eaten as the ripened good of earlier deeds.
event: The couple wander the pleasure groves and pools together.

tamil: பொழிந்துகு காதல் பூண்டு புல்லுகை விடாது செல்லக்
கழிந்தன விரண்டு திங்கள் காளையு மற்றோர் நாளாற்
பிழிந்துகொள் வனைய பெண்மைப் பெய்வளைத் தோளி தன்னோ
டழிந்துவீ ழருவிக் குன்றி லாய்மலர்க் காவு புக்கான்.
reading: As their overflowing love went on with no loosening of embrace, two months passed, and one day the youth went with the woman of pressed-out femininity into a grove of chosen flowers on a hill of falling cascades.
event: After two months of marriage, Civakan takes Kemasari to a flower grove on a hill with waterfalls.

tamil: காஞ்சனக் கமுகு காய்பொற் கனிக்குலை வாழை சூழ்ந்து
பூஞ்சினை நாகந் தீம்பூ மரக்கருப் பூரச் சோலை
மாஞ்சினை மயில்க ளாடச் சண்பக மலர்கள் சிந்துந்
தீஞ்சுனை யருவிக் குன்றஞ் சீர்பெற வேறி னானே.
reading: He climbed with splendour the hill of sweet springs and falls, ringed by golden areca, plantains with ripe clusters, flowering naga trees and camphor groves, where peacocks dance on mango boughs and champak drops its flowers.
event: Civakan climbs the wooded hill.

tamil: தினைவிளை சாரற் செவ்வாய்ச் சிறுகிளி மாத ரோப்பப்
புனைவளைத் தோளி சொல்லைக் கிளியெனக் கிள்ளை போகா
நனைவினை கோதை நாணிப் பொன்னரி மாலை யோச்சக்
கனைகழற் குருசி னண்ணிக் கவர்கிளி யோப்பி னானே.
reading: On the millet slope the little red-beaked parrots, taking the bangled woman's voice for a parrot's, would not fly off; ashamed, she waved her golden garland, and the hero with ringing anklets came near and drove the parrots away himself.
nuance: The scene is the akam scene of the girl guarding the millet field (தினை, கிளி ஓப்புதல்) moved into marriage; the joke that her voice is too parrot-like to frighten parrots makes her embarrassment (நாணி) the point.
event: Kemasari tries to scare the parrots from the millet; they take her voice for their own, and Civakan drives them off.

tamil: செந்தழை யலங்க லேந்திச் சீறடி பரவ வந்தே
னுய்ந்தினிப் பணிசெய் வேனோ வுடம் பொழித் தேகு வேனோ
பைந்தழை யல்குற் பாவாய் பணியெனப் பரவி னானே.
reading: He praised her: creeper who ate up my life with your spear-like eyes, I have come bearing a garland of red leaves to worship your small feet; shall I live on and serve you, or leave this body and go? Doll, command me.
nuance: The choice he puts to her, to live and serve or to leave the body and go (உடம்பு ஒழித்து ஏகுவேனோ), is a lover's hyperbole, but its verb of going returns as the plain event of 1505, when he leaves her without asking.
event: Civakan offers Kemasari a leaf garland and asks her to command him.

tamil: வீணையுஞ் குழலும் பாலு மமுதமுங் கரும்புந் தேனும்
பாணியாழ் கனியும் வென்ற பைங்கிளி மழலைத் தீஞ்சொல்
வாணிக மகளிர் தாமே வாணிகம் வல்ல ரென்னாப்
பூண்முலை பொதிர்ப்பப் புல்லிப் புனைநலம் பருகி னானே.
reading: Saying that merchants' daughters are the ones truly skilled in trade, since her parrot-sweet lisping speech outsold vina, flute, milk, nectar, sugarcane, honey and the music of the lute, he embraced her till her ornamented breasts swelled and drank her beauty.
nuance: The pun on வாணிகம் plays on her birth: a merchant's daughter who has 'sold' him sweetness outbidding every sweet thing; it is also the second time in the chapter (after விற்குமே in 1485) that her worth is put as a price.
event: Civakan praises Kemasari's speech and embraces her.

tamil: திங்களங் குழவி செவ்வா னிடைக்கிடந் திமைப்ப தேபோற்
குங்கும மார்பிற் பூண்ட மங்கையோ டிருந்த போழ்தோர்
வாளொளித் தடங்க ணீலம் மணிவண்டு கண்டு சொன்னான்
கங்குறா னீங்க லுற்றுக் கமழ்மல ரணிந்த தாரான்.
reading: As the young moon glimmers against the red sky, so she lay on his saffron chest; sitting with her, the man of fragrant garland, minded to leave in the night, saw a gem-bee at the lily of her bright wide eye and spoke.
nuance: கங்குல் தான் நீங்கல் உற்று is read here as his intent to leave by night, which makes the bee-speech that follows a covert farewell; it may instead mean only that night was passing.
event: Civakan, sitting with Kemasari, sees a bee near her eye and speaks to it.

tamil: மணிவண்டிம் மாதர் கோதை மதுவுண வந்த போழ்தங்
கிணைவண்டங் கிறந்து பாடின் றிருக்குமே யிரங்க லின்றாய்த்
துணைவண்டு துஞ்சி னீயுந் துஞ்சுவை யென்று நின்கட்
பணிகொண்ட தின்மை யாற்றான் பரிவொடு மிருக்கு மன்றே.
reading: He tells the gem-bee that when it came to drink honey from this lady's garland, its mate, left behind, would sit grieving without song, and that if its mate sleeps it too will sleep; so its partner stays on with tender grief.
nuance: Spoken to a bee in her presence, the verse seems to rehearse his own leaving: the one who goes for honey and the mate who stays behind grieving. The second half is hard to construe, and the sense of பணிகொண்டது இன்மை is not fixed.

tamil: குழவியாய்ப் பிறந்து வெய்யோன் குமரனாய் குறுகி யிப்பால்
விழைவுதீர் கிழவ னாகி விழுக்கதி ருலந்து வீழ
மழலைவண் டுழல நக்க மல்லிகை யலங்கல் சூட்டிக்
குழல்புரை கிளவி யோடுங் கொழும்புகை யமளி சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The sun, born an infant, grown a young man and then a desireless old man whose bright rays fade, fell; and he crowned the parrot-voiced woman with a jasmine garland where lisping bees wandered and went with her to the couch fragrant with smoke.
nuance: The sunset is told as a whole human life in a day (குழவி, குமரன், கிழவன்), and விழைவுதீர் gives the old sun the very loss of desire that the lovers do not yet feel; the image of impermanence frames the last night before he leaves.
event: At sunset Civakan garlands Kemasari and goes to bed with her.

tamil: திருத்துயில் பெற்ற மார்பன் றிருந்துதா ருழக்க வின்ப
வருத்தமுற் றசைந்த கோதை வாளொளித் தடங்க ணீலம்
பொருத்தலும் பொன்ன னாளைப் புறக்கணித் தெழுந்து போகிப்
பருச்சுடர்ப் பவழ நோன்றாழ்ப் பன்மணிக் கதவு சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: When the woman, wearied by the toil of pleasure after his garland had crushed her, closed her sword-bright lily eyes, he rose, turned from the golden one and went to the many-gemmed door with its strong coral bolt.
nuance: புறக்கணித்து, 'turning his back on', is a strong verb for a hero leaving a bride of two months; the verse gives no reason for the going.
event: While Kemasari sleeps, Civakan rises and goes to the door.

tamil: அல்லியுட் பாவை யன்னா ளறிவுறா வகையி னொற்றி
மெல்லவே திறந்து நீக்கி மின்னுவிட் டிலங்கு பைம்பூட்
கொல்சின மடங்க லன்னான் கொழுநிதி மாட நீந்திப்
பல்கதிர்ப் பரிதி போலப் பாயிரு ளேகி னானே.
reading: Pressing the door softly so that the lady like the doll in the lotus should not know, he opened it, and the man like a lion of killing rage crossed the treasure-filled mansion and went into the spreading dark like the many-rayed sun.
nuance: The simile of the sun going into darkness reverses the sun of 1503, which fell; here the hero is the light that leaves and the house is left dark. The secrecy (அறிவுறா வகையின்) is the centre of the verse.
event: Civakan opens the door secretly and leaves Kemasari's house in the dark.

tamil: தாளுடைத் தடங்கொள் செவ்வித் தாமரைப் போது போலும்
வாளுடை முகத்தி னாடன் வருமுலைத் தடத்தின் வைகி
நாளினும் பெருகு கின்ற நகைமதி யனைய காதற்
கேள்வனைக் கனவிற் காணாள் கிளர்மணிப் பூணி னாளே.
reading: The lotus-faced woman with bright ornaments, who had rested on his chest, does not see even in dream the husband whose love grew daily like the laughing moon.
nuance: கனவிற் காணாள: she does not see him even in dream, so the dream that in akam poetry consoles the separated woman is denied her; her sleep is unbroken while he goes.

tamil: அரந்தினப் பிறந்த பைம்பொ னரும்பிய முலையி னாளைக்
கரந்தவன் கங்கு னீங்கக் கதிர்வளை யணங்கு மென்றோள்
வரந்தரு தெய்வ மன்னாள் வைகிரு ளனந்த றேறிப்
பரந்தெலாத் திசையு நோக்கிப் பையவே பரிவு கொண்டாள்.
reading: When he had slipped away as night ended, she of gold-sprouting breasts, like a boon-giving goddess, woke from her heavy sleep, looked in every direction, and slowly grew distressed.
event: Kemasari wakes, finds Civakan gone, and searches with her eyes.

tamil: திருமணி குயின்ற செம்பொற் றிருந்துபூங் கொம்ப னாடன்
கருமணிப் பாவை யன்னான் கரந்துழிக் காண்டல் செல்லா
ளெரிமணி விளக்க மாடத் திருளறு காறு மோடி
யருமணி யிழந்தோர் நாக மலமரு கின்ற தொத்தாள்.
reading: Unable to find the man like the dark pupil of an eye where he had hidden, the woman like a flowering golden branch ran through the lamp-lit mansion until the dark lifted, like a serpent that has lost its rare gem.
nuance: Two images of loss meet: he is கருமணிப் பாவை, the pupil of her eye, so his going leaves her blind; and she is the serpent without its gem, a creature that in lore cannot see or live without the jewel it carries.
event: Kemasari runs through the mansion searching for Civakan.

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1509-1532 (5/6)
theme: Kemasari, waking to find that Civakan has left her in the night, laments to him, to the creatures and places around her, to her own eyes, shoulders, breasts and reflection; understanding at last the veiled words he spoke to the bee, she holds back her life for fear of harm to him and takes the bees as household gods, while a companion asks the house deity whether she can survive, and the morning star rises.
source_issues: 1527-1532: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1531 line 1: வங்சவாய்க் is very likely a misprint for வஞ்சவாய்க்.
1514 line 1, 1515 line 3, 1518 lines 3-4, 1521 lines 1-2, 1525 line 4: word division in the edition is unclear and the sense is uncertain.
1530 line 1: முகிழ்முலைத் தெய்வஞ் சேர is hard to construe.

cast.role: the merchant's daughter Civakan married and has left in the night
the hero, absent; addressed throughout
one of Kemasari's household, likely her companion, who speaks to the house deity (unnamed)
the deity of Kemasari's house
the bees of her garland, of which Civakan spoke before he left
Kemasari's own reflection, which she takes for a weeping friend
the creatures, places and her own limbs that she addresses in her lament

reading: Finding him gone, Kemasari cries out asking where her lord is, says she is afraid because her dear life strains to quit her body, confesses she has no restraint left, and begs the long-armed one to come back to her.
nuance: நிறையான் இலேன், 'I have no nirai', is her own admission that the self-containment a woman is meant to keep has gone; the narrator still calls her speech honey-sweet (தேனின் மிழற்றினாள்).
event: Kemasari wakes, finds Civakan gone, and calls out to him.

reading: She throws back at him his own saying that women are sweetest when ripe love mingles and two lives become one, and asks whether it is fitting that she, pale as the dewy moon, should now be alone.
nuance: Her argument turns his own doctrine of love, that the lovers' lives become one, into the charge against him: if their lives are one, his leaving her alone contradicts what he taught.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: Her heart slipping, her bangles loosening, her eyes wheeling and her body burning like heated gold, she says she cannot bear it and asks whether he has cast off even the love that should be as hard to shed as one's shadow.
nuance: The simile நிழலின் நீப்பருங் காதல், love as inseparable as a shadow, is taken up literally in 1524 and 1525, where the only thing that stays with her is her own reflection.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She calls him a deceiver who used to say that her slender waist suffered even under a jasmine garland, and asks whether he can now bear to see her scorched.
nuance: வஞ்ச நீ is the first time she names him a deceiver; his remembered tenderness is offered as evidence against him.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She recalls how he praised her coral lips and breasts, saying the gods would melt to see them, and says she did not grasp the meaning of what was said about the bee, he of the honey-dripping garland.
nuance: Line 3 looks back to 1501 and 1502, where Civakan, about to leave in the night, spoke to the bee on her garland of a bee whose mate stays on without grief; she now sees the words were a covert notice of his going. வண்டு கூறிய can be 'what the bee said' or 'what was said of (to) the bee'.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She recalls that if a thorn so much as touched her on the way he would bow his head to the ground and stroke her foot, says she is bewildered, and asks the master of the bow, the guardian of her life who has now shaken it, for grace.
nuance: She calls him என் உயிர் காவலனே, guardian of my life, in the same line that says he has shaken that life (உலைவித்தனை).
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She recalls him painting designs over every part of her pearl-strung breasts and living as one with her, and says that for one who cannot follow him, living on is mere folly.
nuance: Line 3 (உழைவார் அலனேன்) is hard to divide; the sense 'I am not one who can go where you are' is the likeliest but not certain.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: Because he had said she was one who would always have love, and no one had said her love would be cut off, she asks him to pity her as she wastes to the bone and to come near.
nuance: The verse plays பெறும் அன்பினள், she who receives love, against அறும் அன்பினள், she whose love is severed.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She quotes his words, 'if you walk your small feet will ache; you live within my life', tells him that he lied, and says he has gone alone and left her, the one of evil deeds.
nuance: வினையேன், 'I of (bad) deeds', is the usual self-name of one in grief, but it places a cause in her own past deeds in the same breath as she calls his word a lie (பொய்யுரைத்தனை): she blames both.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She says that, torn from his pearl-hung chest before her breasts had had their fill of it, she has been given two burnings, the blaze of desire and the burning of a spear wound in the breast.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure as divided; the two fires may be desire and grief rather than any literal wound.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She calls on the peacock of the field, the grove, the stream, the plantain, the hill and the waves, says she worships them, and asks whether through them she may find again the man of the fiery jewels.
event: Kemasari appeals to the creatures and places around her to help her find Civakan.

reading: She says her pain, crueller than an arrow, grows at midnight, the chariot of the long white moonlight does not move on, and she asks Virtue standing on the way to show her grace.
nuance: அறனே அருளாய் addresses Aram itself as a power that could end the night; she appeals not to a god but to virtue, which she implies her desertion has offended.
event: Kemasari, sleepless at midnight, appeals to Virtue.

reading: Turning to her flower-like eyes, which he once likened to kayal fish, she says that all he said of her innocence has come to nothing and asks them to tell her how she may survive.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to divide (கவிழ்ந்து கிடந்து, அயலேன் அறியாமை); the reading of what he said of her is not secure.
event: Kemasari, alone at dawn, laments to the absent Civakan.

reading: She asks her shoulders, on which he painted bangles and pearls and which he praised, which way the fragrant-garlanded one went, since they must know.
event: Kemasari questions her own shoulders about where Civakan went.

reading: She asks her breasts, which ploughed the chest of the young man of the bright spear, why they did not follow the bull when it left the diamond stall, and the jewelled one weeps.
nuance: Civakan is the bull (விடை) leaving its stall; the image makes his going a matter of nature as much as of fault.
event: Kemasari reproaches her breasts and weeps.

reading: Seeing her own reflection, its beauty wasted, shedding tears and weeping, she tells it not to grieve and not to weep, her dear friend, asking whether he could ever be an enemy.
nuance: She gives her image the consolation a friend would give her: அவரோ பகையாபவர், 'would he turn enemy?'. The hope she cannot hold for herself she offers to her reflection.
event: Kemasari takes her reflection for a weeping companion and comforts it.

reading: When the fallen garlands covered the floor and she could no longer see her reflection, she thought it had gone to search out the way he took, and waited long, saying it would come back now.
nuance: Line 4 (எறிவால் வளை கொண்டு வரும்) is obscure; it may say the reflection will come back bringing him, or her bangles.
event: Kemasari loses sight of her reflection under the fallen garlands and waits for it to return.

reading: She calls on the peahen, the cuckoo, the stately swan and the parrot who played with her, melting as she calls them her own, until her speech, sweet as the yazh, fails.
nuance: எனை அனை may be 'like me' or 'my mother'; either way she treats the birds as kin.
event: Kemasari calls on her pet birds until her voice fails.

tamil: மல்லுறை யலங்கன் மார்பன் பிரிவெனு மெரியுள் வீழ்ந்து
கல்லுறை நாகு வேய்த்தோட் கதிர்மணி முறுவற் செவ்வாய்
வில்லுறை புருவ மாதர் வெந்தனள் கிடப்ப மின்றோ
யில்லுறை தெய்வ நோக்கி யிரங்கிநின் றுரைக்கு மன்றே.
reading: As the woman, fallen into the fire of separation from the garlanded warrior, lies burnt, one of her household looks to the deity of the house and speaks in pity.
nuance: The verse does not name who speaks to the house deity (இல்லுறை தெய்வம்); a companion is the likeliest, and the speech follows in 1528 and 1529.
event: While Kemasari lies spent, someone of her household turns to the house deity and speaks.

tamil: புண்ணவாம் புலவு வாட்கைப் பொலன்கழற் புனைந்த பைந்தார்
கண்ணவாம் வனப்பி னானைக் காமனே கண்ட போழ்தும்
பண்ணவாம் பவளச் செவ்வாய்ப் படாமுலைப் பரவை யல்குற்
பெண்ணவா நிற்கு மென்றாற் பிணையனாட் குய்த லுண்டோ.
reading: The speaker asks the house deity whether, when even Kama seeing the warrior's beauty would long to become a woman, this doe-like girl can survive.
nuance: பெண் அவா நிற்கும்: Kama himself would long to be a woman for Civakan's sake, a hyperbole that makes her grief beyond blame.

tamil: கடத்திடைக் கவளந் தேனெய் கனியைத்தோய்த் தினிய துற்றத்
தடக்கையாற் கொடுத்துப் புல்லுந் தவழ்மதக் களிறு நீங்கின்
மடப்பிடிக் குய்த லுண்டோ வாலடிக் குஞ்சி சூட்டுங்
கொடைக்கையான் பிரிந்த பின்றைக் கோதையாட் குய்த லுண்டோ.
reading: The speaker asks whether a young cow elephant can live when the rutting bull who fed her honeyed morsels with his trunk has left her, and so whether the garlanded girl can live now that the generous-handed one has gone.

tamil: முயங்கினான் சொன்ன வண்டாய் முகிழ்முலைத் தெய்வஞ் சேர
வுயங்குவா ளுணர்ந்து கேள்வற் கூனமும் பிரிவு மஞ்சி
யியங்குவா னின்ற வாவி தாங்கின ளென்ப போலும்
வயங்குபொன் னீன்ற நீல மாமணி முலையி னாளே.
reading: The narrator says that, taking the bee as the one her lover had spoken of, the woman turned to the deity and, understanding, fearing both harm to her husband and their parting, held back the life that was leaving her.
nuance: She lives on for fear of harm (ஊனம்) to her husband, not only in hope of his return; the narrator hedges with என்ப போலும். முகிழ்முலைத் தெய்வம் சேர is hard to construe.
event: Kemasari understands Civakan's words about the bee and resolves to live.

tamil: வங்சவாய்க் காமன் சொன்ன மணிநிற வண்டு காணீர்
துஞ்சுவேன் றுயரந் தீரத் தொழுதகு தெய்வ மாவீர்
மஞ்சுதோய் செம்பொன் மாடத் தென்மனை தன்னு ளென்றாள்
பஞ்சிமேன் மிதிக்கும் போதும் பனிக்குஞ்சீ றடியி னாளே.
reading: She tells all to see the gem-coloured bee that the deceiving Kama spoke of, and asks the bees to be gods worthy of worship in her golden mansion so that her grief may end.
nuance: She calls Civakan காமன் and his mouth deceitful (வஞ்சவாய்), yet makes the bee he addressed an object of worship.
event: Kemasari takes the bees as household gods.

tamil: நொந்தெடுக் கலாது வீங்கும் வனமுலை நுசுப்பிற் றேய்ந்தோர்
பந்தெடுக் கலாத நங்கை பால்கடை வெண்ணெய்ப் பாவை
வெந்துடன் வெயிலுற் றாங்கு மெலிந்துக விளங்கும் வெள்ளி
வந்துவா னிட்ட சுட்டி வனப்பொடு முளைத்த தன்றே.
reading: The girl, so frail that a ball was too heavy for her, wasted like a butter doll left in the sun, and the morning star rose in the sky like a jewel on its brow.
event: As Kemasari wastes, the morning star rises and the night ends.

title: கேமசரியார் இலம்பகம் 1533-1556 (6/6)
theme: Kemasari's mother Nipputhi consoles her with karma and impermanence but cannot reach her; Civakan walks through the night, and at sunrise meets a wayfarer whose riddle of four wives and one son opens into a Jain sermon on the householder's giving, conduct, fasting and worship, on lust, drink and meat, and on women's beauty, after which Civakan gives him his ornaments and crosses the wilderness.
source_issues: 1534-1536, 1538, 1540-1541, 1543-1553, 1555-1556: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1544: three speeches run together without named speakers; attribution uncertain.
1549 line 3 (எட்டானும் பத்தானும் இல்லாதார்) and 1553 lines 1-3 are obscure and may be corrupt or proverbial.
1552 line 3 begins றறொழுகியமு, with a doubled ற that looks like a misprint (for றொழுகி).
1556: the subjects of நீட்டி, கூற and சென்றான் are not marked; whether Civakan or the wayfarer circles and leaves is uncertain.

cast.role: the merchant's daughter of the Takka land whom Civakan marries and leaves
Kemasari's mother, Subhadran's wife, named நிப்புதி in 1533
the hero, who leaves Kemasari and goes on alone (அண்ணல் 1542, காளை 1540)
