கொம்பு வெந்தீ யிடைப்பட்ட தொத்தாள் விரைசெய் கோதையே.
reading: The narrator says the moon-faced girl, whose long streaked eyes outdo Murugan's red spear and the flower arrows from Kama's bow, was like a flowering branch, fragrant and dripping honey, caught in a fierce fire.

tamil: மணிநிற மாமை சாயல் வளையொடு வண்டு மூசு
மணிநிறப் போர்வை யாய வரும்பெற னாணும் விற்றுப்
பணிநலம் புதிய துண்டான் பன்மலர் மாலை கொண்டேன்
பிணிநிறப் புறஞ்சொ லென்னும் பெருமிஞி றார்ப்ப வென்றாள்.
reading: She says she sold her dark gem-like colour, her softness, her bangles and the precious modesty that was her covering, and bought with them a garland of many flowers, while the great bee of slander hums about her.
nuance: Love is told as a bargain: modesty, called her mantle (போர்வை), is the price, and the gossip (புறஞ்சொல்) is its cost; the garland is all she has in return.

tamil: காதலான் காதல் போல வகன்று நீண் டலர்ந்தவாட்கட்
போதுலாங் கோதை மாதர் புனைந்தலர் தொடுத்த மாலை
யாதலா லலர தாகா தொழியுமே யழுங்க லென்று
மாதுலா மழலைச் செவ்வாய் மடக்கிளி மொழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: Her young parrot tells her not to grieve, since the garland was strung of flowers by a girl whose eyes spread wide as her lover's love, as though asking whether a thing made of flowers (அலர்) could fail to become talk (அலர்), and so comforts her.
nuance: The verse turns on அலர் as flower and as gossip; whether the parrot says the talk will cease or that it cannot be helped depends on how ஒழியுமே is taken, and who strung the garland (line 2) is unclear.
event: Kanakamalai's parrot speaks to comfort her.

tamil: என்னை யுள்ளம் பிணித்தென் னலங்க வர்ந்தவீர்ந் தாரினான்
றன்னை யானும் பிணிப்பே னெனத்தன் மணிச்செப் பினுண்
மன்னு மாலை கொடுத்தவனுக் குய்த்தீ யெனத்தொ ழுதுகொண்
டன்ன மென்னா வொதுங்கிச் சிலம்பரற் றச்சென் றணுகினாள்.
reading: She says that he has bound her heart and stolen her beauty and she too will bind him, gives the maid a lasting garland from her gem casket to take to him, and the maid takes it with joined hands and goes swan-like, anklets ringing, until she reaches him.
nuance: பிணித்து / பிணிப்பேன: the garland that bound her is to be answered by a garland that binds him, so the exchange of flowers is an exchange of bonds.
event: Kanakamalai sends her own garland to Civakan by the maid.

tamil: அணுகி முன்னின்ற வநங்க விலாசினி யங்கை கூப்பிப்
பிணைய னீட்டப் பெருந்தகை யஃதே லான்முக நோக்கலுந்
துணையி றோகை யென்னங் கைக்குத் தொங்கறொடுப் பாயுநீ
மணிசெய் மென்றோண் மருந்துநீ யாருயிரு நீயே லென்றாள்.
reading: Anangavilasini stands before him, joins her palms and holds out the garland, and when the noble one does not take it but looks at her face, she tells him that he strings garlands for her peerless peacock's hand, he is the medicine for her shoulders and her very life, so let him take it.
nuance: Civakan's hesitation is the first sign that taking the garland means more than a courtesy.
event: The maid offers Kanakamalai's garland; Civakan hesitates and she presses him.

tamil: மன்னர் கோயி லுறைவார் பொறிசெ றித்த மாண்பினரே
யென்ன வஞ்சி னாயென் றவனைநக் காட்கஃ தன்றுகோதா
யின்ன கொள்கை யேற்கேலா தென்ன விலங்கெ யிற்றினா
ளன்ன மன்ன நடையினா டான்வ ருந்து மெனநேர்ந்தான்.
reading: She laughs at him, asking why he fears when those who live in kings' palaces keep their seals of honour, and he answers that it is not that, but that such a course does not suit him; then, thinking that the swan-gaited girl will suffer, he agrees.
nuance: The split of the dialogue is my reading: the line on palace dwellers with sealed honour (பொறி செறித்த மாண்பினர்) may instead be his scruple and the laughter hers; கோதாய் addresses the maid. He yields from pity for her pain, not from desire.
event: Civakan, teased by the maid, says secret love is not his way but consents for the princess's sake.

tamil: குலிக மார்ந்த கொழுந்தா மரையன்ன வண்கை நீட்டி
யொலிய லேற்றா னிஃதூழ் வினையாலுள் ளஞ்சுடு மாலென்ன
விலைகொள் பைம்பூ ணிளமுலையாள் போகிக் கனக மாலை
மெலிய வெம்பி நைகின்றா ளுய்யும் வகைதொ டங்கினாள்.
reading: He holds out his lotus-like hand and takes the garland, saying it comes by former deed and burns the heart, and the maid goes off and begins the means by which Kanakamalai, wasting and fevered, may be saved.
nuance: Who says இஃது ஊழ்வினையால் உள்ளஞ் சுடும் is not clear: Civakan as he accepts, or the maid of the princess's fever; the claim is given to Civakan on the first reading. Either way the love is put down to ஊழ்வினை while Civakan's own consent was shown in 1669, so destiny and choice are both given.
event: Civakan accepts Kanakamalai's garland and the maid begins remedies for her.

tamil: நீர்செய் காந்த மணிகூந்த ளம்பா வைநீண் டழகியவோ?
செய் சாந்திற் கழுநீர் விரைகம ழும்பூக்கள் கோத்த
வார்செய் தண்டா மரைவளைய மைவரை யின்வெள் ளருவிநீர்
சீர்செய் கோமகளைச் சேர்த்தினாள் சீதஞ் செய்யா தொழிந்தனவே.
reading: She lays on the princess moonstone that sheds water, fragrant sandal, blossoms of kazhuneer, lotus bracelets on thongs and water from a white mountain waterfall, and none of them cool her.
nuance: Line 2 begins with a doubtful syllable in the edition (printed with a query), and the opening words of line 1 divide uncertainly.
event: The maid applies cooling things to Kanakamalai, without effect.

tamil: பவ்வத் தங்கட் பிறந்து பனிபெயர்க் குந்தண் ணூற்றதாகி
யெவ்வ மன்னர் படவுலகம் விற்கு மரும ணியினைச்
செவ்வ னூலிற் சித்திரிக்கப் பட்டதனைச் சேர்த்திப் பின்னு
மவ்வ னாறுங் குழலாட்கு மற்று மிவைக ணாடினாள்.
reading: She also fastens on her a rare gem born in the sea, cool and able to drive off heat, worth the world for which kings suffer, worked on a fine thread, and still more such things on the fragrant-haired girl.
nuance: பனிபெயர்க்கும் may mean the gem removes affliction or sheds coolness; the reading is uncertain.
event: The maid puts a cooling sea-gem on Kanakamalai.

tamil: களிசெய் கோசிக நீர்விழக் கடிமாலை மேற்றொ டர்ந்துகீழ்
நளிசெய் தண்பூஞ் சலஞ்சயன மாக்கி நன்னீர் பிலிற்றும்வாய்க்
குளிர்கொள் சாந்தாற்றி பொன்னால வட்டங்கொண் டேந்தி வீசச்
சளிகொள் சந்தின் கொழுஞ்சாந்த மாக முழுது மெழுகினாள்.
reading: She lets fragrant water fall over garlands, makes a cool flower couch below them, fans her with a moist fan and a golden round fan, and smears her whole body with rich cool sandal paste.
event: The maid makes Kanakamalai a flower bed, fans her and covers her in sandal.

tamil: கொம்மைவெம் முலையிற் சாந்தங் குளிர்செயா தாவி வாட்ட
வம்மென் மாலை முகங்கரிய நீர்துளும்ப நின்று நீடி
வெம்மை மிக்கது வீரன் றொடுத்த விளங்கு மாலை
பொம்ம லோதிக்குத் தானே துணையாம் புணையா யிற்றே.
reading: The sandal on her breasts does not cool them but withers her life, the soft garlands blacken and drip, and only the bright garland the hero strung becomes the companion and raft of the girl with heavy hair.
nuance: Every remedy fails and the only relief is the token of the one who causes the fever: the garland is both the sickness and its cure, as the maid called him her medicine in 1668.

tamil: வாச நீலங் கழுநீர் குவளை படைசாற் றிவந்
தோச னைக்க ணுடையு நெடுங்கட் கனக மாலை
தாசிதூ தாகத் தாமம் புணையாகச் செல்லு நாளுட்
காசில் கல்விக் கடலைக் கரைகண்டார் காளை மாரே.
reading: While long-eyed Kanakamalai passes her days with the maid as her messenger and the garland as her raft, the young men reach the farther shore of the faultless sea of learning.
nuance: One verse joins the two threads: her sea of night (1663) and the princes' sea of learning, both crossed, hers only with a raft of flowers.
event: Kanakamalai's love continues through the maid, and the princes complete their training under Civakan.

tamil: பொருசரஞ் சலாகை வெய்ய புகன்றனர் துரக்கு மாறும்
வருகணை விலக்கு மாறும் வாளமர் நீந்து மாறுங்
கருவியுட் கரக்கு மாறுங் கணைபுறங் காணு மாறும்
விரியமற் றவர்க்குக் காட்ட வீற்றிருந் தவருங் கற்றார்.
reading: Civakan shows them in full how to drive the fighting arrow and the dart, how to ward off a coming arrow, how to swim through sword battle, how to hide within armour and how to see an arrow's back, and even those who sat in state learned.
nuance: வீற்றிருந்தவரும் கற்றார் may mean the king and elders seated in state learned too, or that the princes learned while sitting at ease; கருவியுட் கரக்கும் ஆறு is read as hiding within one's gear.
event: The princes learn the arts of weapons from Civakan.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1677-1700 (6/14)
theme: Civakan finishes training the king's sons in arms; the delighted king, after a mock threat to fetter him, gives him his daughter Kanakamalai as a bride already fated to an archer, and the two are wed and enjoy each other; the narrator then turns to Rajamapuram, where Civakan's brother, searching for him, comes to Gandharvadattai as she sings three stanzas of a deserted woman's lament.
source_issues: 1683 line 3: பாபிந்து is not a word; read as பரிந்து (pitying).
1699 line 4: மணணார்வேற் looks like a misprint for மண்ணார்வேற்.
1699 line 3 has இனவளையும் where the parallel stanzas have நனிவளையும் and கோல்வளையும்; possibly a misprint.
1681: the princes' names run together and cannot be divided with confidence.
Many verses carry the flag 'stanza printed in 8 half-lines; joined into 4 lines'; the joins read correctly.

cast.role: the hero, teacher of arms to the king's sons and husband of Kanakamalai
the king of the city where Civakan teaches, father of Kanakamalai and the princes (called காவலன், மன்னன், வேந்தன் here; the name is traditional and not in these verses)
the king's sons, Civakan's pupils in arms (குமரர், மைந்தர்)
the king's daughter, whom Civakan marries (பாவை, நங்கை, கோதை here; the name is the ilampakam's title)
the people of the city who watch and misread the king's words
Civakan's younger brother (தம்பி)
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife in Rajamapuram, who sings of separation
Gandharvadattai's companion, addressed in her songs

tamil: வேலுடைத் தடக்கை யார்கள் வேழமேற் சென்ற போழ்திற்
காலிடைக் கரக்கு மாறுங் கையிடைத் திரியு மாறும்
வாலிடை மறியு மாறு மருப்பிடைக் குளிக்கு மாறு
நூலிடைக் கிடந்த வாறே நுனித்தவன் கொடுப்பக் கொண்டார்.
reading: The spear-handed princes, riding elephants, take from their keen teacher, exactly as the treatise lays it down, how to hide between the elephant's legs, wheel at its trunk, roll at its tail and plunge between its tusks.
nuance: நூலிடைக் கிடந்தவாறே, 'just as it lies in the book', makes the elephant craft a written science that Civakan transmits faithfully rather than a skill he invents.
event: Civakan teaches the king's sons the moves of fighting on and around the war elephant.

tamil: கொடிநெடுந் தேரின் போருங் குஞ்சரங் குறித்த போருங்
கடுநடைப் புரவிப் போருங் கரப்பறக் கற்று முற்றி
யிடனறிந் திலங்கும் வைவா ளிருஞ்சிலை குந்த மூன்று
முடனறிந் தும்ப ரார்க்கு முரைப்பருந் தகைய ரானார்.
reading: Learning without concealment the fighting of the tall-bannered chariot, of the elephant and of the fast horse, and knowing where each fits the sword, the great bow and the lance, they become warriors whose quality even the gods could hardly describe.
nuance: கரப்பற, 'with nothing held back', credits the teacher as much as the pupils: he kept no secret of his art from them.
event: The princes complete their training in chariot, elephant and horse combat and in sword, bow and lance.

tamil: தானையு ளன்றி நின்ற தனியிட மொற்றி மன்னர்
தானைமேற் சென்ற போழ்தும் வென்றியிற் றளர்த லின்றித்
தானையை யுடைக்கும் வெம்போர்த் தருக்கினார் மைந்த ரென்று
தானைசூழ் மன்னற் குய்த்தார் மன்னனுந் தருக வென்றான்.
reading: Reporting that the princes, proud in fierce war, can break an army, and do not flag in victory even when kings bear down on their force while they stand alone apart from their own lines, they bring them to the king ringed by his army, and he says 'bring them in'.
nuance: Who brings them is not named (உய்த்தார்); line 1, தனியிடம் ஒற்றி, may mean fighting alone apart from the army or something else, and the reading is offered tentatively.
event: The princes are presented to their father the king, who orders them brought before him.

tamil: மழையொடு சூழ்ந்து கொண்ட வான்றுகள் சிலையி னீக்கிக்
குழைமுக நெற்றி நக்கக் கோலவிற் பகழி வாங்கி
யிழைபக விமைப்பி னெய்திட் டெறிந்துமின் றிரிவ வேபோல்
விழைவுறு குமரர் புக்குச் சாரியை வியத்த ரானார்.
reading: Clearing from the bow the dust that gathers like a cloud, drawing the fine bow's arrow until it touches the earring at the brow, splitting a thread with a shot in the blink of an eye, the eager princes enter the arena and amaze all with their wheeling movements, darting like lightning.
nuance: Line 1 (மழையொடு சூழ்ந்து கொண்ட வான்துகள் சிலையின் நீக்கி) is hard to construe: it may be clearing dust or scattering a cloud of arrows; சாரியை names the formal circling movements of combat display.
event: The princes display their archery and their circling manoeuvres before the king.

tamil: விசயனே விசயன் விற்போர்க் கதம்பனே முருகன் வேற்போர்த்
திசையெலாம் வணக்கும் வாட்போர்க் கந்தணன் செம்பொ னாம
னசைவிலான் யானைத் தேர்ப்போர்க் கசலனே யசல கீர்த்தி
வசையிலான் புரவிச் சேனென் றியாவரும் புகழப் பட்டார்.
reading: Everyone praises them: in archery this one is Vijaya himself, in the lance another is Murugan, another in the sword bends all directions, one firm in elephant and chariot fighting is Achala of unmoving fame, and another without blemish is master of the horse.
nuance: The verse seems to name the princes (விசயன், perhaps அதம்பன் or கதம்பன், அசலன்) each with the arm he excels in, but the run-together script makes several names and their divisions uncertain; the comparisons to Vijaya (Arjuna) and Murugan are the clear part.

tamil: காவலன் மக்க ளாக்கங் கண்டுகண் குளிர்ந்து நோக்கி
யேவலா னரச னொன்றோ விருபிறப் பாள னல்லார்க்
காவதன் றின்ன மாட்சி யவனையா னிகளம் பெய்து
காவல்செய் திடுவல் வல்லே காளையைக் கொணர்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Seeing his sons' accomplishment the king gazes with cooled eyes and says that such excellence comes from no one but a king or one twice-born; he will put the youth in fetters and keep him under guard: bring the young bull at once.
nuance: The 'fetter' (நிகளம்) is a joke whose point 1684 reveals: he means to bind Civakan by marriage. His inference from skill to birth happens to be true, since Civakan is a king's son unknown to him, so the story neither confirms nor answers the claim as a rule.
event: The delighted king orders Civakan brought, saying he will fetter him and keep him.

tamil: கல்வியுங் கொடிது போலுங் காவலன் காளை தன்னை
யொல்லலன் சிறைசெய் கின்றா னென்றவன் கருதிற் றோரார்
பல்சனம் பாபிந்து நிற்பப் பார்த்திப குமரன் சோர்ந்தான்
வில்வலாற் கொண்டு வேந்தன் வேறிருந் திதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Not grasping what the king meant, the crowd thinks that learning too seems a cruel thing, since the king now cruelly imprisons the youth, and stands pitying him while the prince himself loses heart; the king takes the bowman aside and says this.
nuance: The crowd's maxim, கல்வியும் கொடிது போலும், is answered at once: 1684 shows the 'imprisonment' to be a reward, so the reflection stands as a misreading of the king's குறிப்பு. பாபிந்து in line 3 is read as பரிந்து.
event: The people and Civakan take the king's words for a real arrest, and the king draws Civakan aside to speak.

tamil: புண்முழு திறைஞ்சுங் கோட்டுப் பொருகளி றனைய தோன்றன்
மண்முழு தன்றி வானும் வந்துகை கூடத் தந்தாய்
கண்முழு துடம்பிற் பெற்றேன் காளைகைம் மாறு காணேன்
பண்முழு துடற்றுந் தீஞ்சொற் பாவைநின் பால ளென்றான்.
reading: The king tells the prince, like a fighting tusker whose tusks are wholly bowed in wounds, that he has put into his hands not the earth alone but heaven too; he feels he has eyes all over his body, sees no way to repay the young bull, and says the girl whose sweet words outdo all music is his.
nuance: The 'fetter' of 1682 turns out to be the bride: the joke depends on the king's word நிகளம் and the crowd's mistaking it. கண்முழுது உடம்பிற் பெற்றேன், 'I have got eyes over my whole body', says his joy needs more eyes to see his sons.
event: The king offers his daughter to Civakan in return for training his sons.

tamil: முடிகெழு மன்னன் சொல்ல மொய்கொள்வேற் குருசி றேற்றான்
வடிவமை மனனொன் றாக வாக்கொன்றா மறுத்த லோடுந்
தடிசுவைத் தொளிறும் வேலான் றன்கையான் முன்கை பற்றி
யிடிமுர சனைய சொல்லா லிற்றென விளம்பு கின்றான்.
reading: When the crowned king had spoken, the prince of the clustered spear, his mind of one shape and his word of another, declined; then the king, whose spear gleams having tasted flesh, took his forearm in his own hand and spoke with words like a thundering drum.
nuance: தேற்றான் at line 1 and the phrase மனனொன்றாக வாக்கொன்றா மறுத்தல் are read as the custom of a first refusal: his heart consents while his words decline. If தேற்றான் means 'reassured', the sense changes.
event: Civakan politely declines in words though willing at heart, and the king grasps his arm and presses the offer.

tamil: பூவியல் கோயில் கொண்ட பொன்னனா ளனைய நங்கை
காவியங் கண்ணி வந்து பிறத்தலுங் கண்க ளீண்டி
மூவிய றிரித லின்றிச் சாதக முறையிற் செய்தா
ரேவியல் சிலையி னாய்க்கே யுரியளென் றுரைப்ப நேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The king says that when the maiden like the golden lady of the lotus, with kaavi-flower eyes, was born, the wise gathered and cast her horoscope by rule without straying from the three, and declared her the due of the one whose bow speeds arrows; and Civakan consents.
nuance: The bride is promised not as a reward alone but as fated: the reckoning made her உரியள், 'rightfully belonging', to a master of the bow, and Civakan's archery training is the sign that fulfils it. மூவியல் is unclear (perhaps three factors of the reckoning).
event: The king cites the birth horoscope that destined his daughter for an archer, and Civakan agrees to the marriage.

tamil: வாருலா முலையி னாட்கும் வரிசிலைத் தடக்கை யாற்குஞ்
சீருலாங் கோலஞ் செய்தார் செப்பினார் வதுவை நன்னாட்
பாரெலா மறிய நின்று படாமுர சார்ப்பத் தீவேட்
டேருலாங் கோதை யின்பத் திளநலம் பருகு கின்றான்.
reading: They dress the girl with the bodice-bound breasts and the long-armed archer in festive finery, announce the good wedding day, and with the whole world knowing, drums sounding, he weds her by the fire and drinks the young delight of the garlanded one.
nuance: பாரெலாம் அறிய, 'with all the earth knowing', and the fire (தீவேட்டு) mark this as an open wedding, in contrast to the secret unions of some earlier ilampakams.
event: Civakan marries Kanakamalai by the fire rite, publicly, and they are united.

tamil: மோட்டிளங் குரும்பை யன்ன முலைக்கடாக் களிறு முத்தஞ்
சூட்டிய வோடை பொங்க நாணெனுந் தோட்டி மாற்றி
யாட்டிய சாந்த மென்னு முகபடா மழித்து வெம்போ
ரோட்டற வோட்டிப் பைந்தா ருழக்கியிட் டுவந்த வன்றே.
reading: Her breasts, like young swelling coconuts, become a musth elephant: the pearls are its forehead plate, it throws off the goad called shame, strips the face-cloth called sandal paste, drives the fierce fight to rout and tramples the fresh garland in its joy.
nuance: நாணெனுந் தோட்டி, 'the goad called shame', makes நாண் the control the elephant shakes off: in love her modesty is dropped, not lost.
event: The couple's lovemaking is told as the charge of an elephant.

tamil: ஒண்மணிக் குழைவில் வீச வொளிர்ந்துபொன் னோலை மின்ன
வண்ணமே கலைக ளார்ப்ப வான்சிலம் பொலிப்ப முத்துங்
கண்ணியும் பசும்பொ னாணுங் கதிர்முலை புடைப்பக் காம
ரண்ணலங் குமரன் றன்னொ டாயிழை யாடி னாளே.
reading: With jewelled earrings swinging, golden ear-rolls flashing, girdles jingling, anklets ringing and pearls, wreath and gold chain beating on her bright breasts, the woman sports with the lovely prince.
event: Kanakamalai and Civakan make love.

tamil: மூசுதேன் வாரி யல்குற் பட்டபின் முலைக ளென்னு
மாசறு கந்தின் மென்றோண் மணித்தொடர்க் கொளுத்தி வாட்க
ணாசறு வயிரத் தோட்டி நுதலணிந் தமுதச் செவ்வாய்
காசறு கவள மாகக் களிறுகோட் பட்ட தன்றே.
reading: After the bee-thronged ford of her hips, the elephant is captured: tied to the flawless posts of her breasts with the jewel-chain of her soft arms, goaded by the faultless diamond of her sword-eyes, the forehead ornament on her brow, and fed her nectared red mouth as its flawless mouthful.
nuance: The elephant figure of 1688 is turned round: there her breasts were the rampant elephant; here he is the elephant she captures and tames.
event: The lovemaking is told as the capture and taming of an elephant.

tamil: ஒப்பிணை தனக்கி லாதா னுறுவரை யகல மூழ்கிச்
கற்பக மரத்தைப் புல்லிக் கைவிடா தொழிந்து காமத்
துப்புர வுமிழுங் காம வல்லியின் றோற்ற மொத்தாள்.
reading: Sinking into the broad hill of the peerless one's chest, her red casket-like breasts reddening as they press, she looks like the desire-vine that clings to the wishing tree and never lets go, giving forth the riches of love.
nuance: கற்பக மரம் and காம வல்லி are the wish-granting tree and its creeper of the celestial world; the image makes the union a heavenly enjoyment, the fruit of merit.
event: Kanakamalai embraces Civakan.

tamil: காய்வுறு வேட்கை தன்னாற் கங்குலும் பகலும் விள்ளான்
வேய்வெறுத் தமைந்த தோளாள் விழுத்திரை யமுத மென்று
சேய்நலங் கடந்த செல்வன் றிருநலந் தெளித்திட் டாற்ற
வாய்விடாள் பருகி யிட்டாண் மடக்கிள்ளை மருட்டுஞ் சொல்லாள்.
reading: Burning with desire, never letting him go by night or day, the one with shoulders that shame the bamboo, whose speech beguiles the young parrot, drinks without taking her mouth away the beauty of the one who surpasses Murugan, as if it were the nectar of the great sea.
event: Kanakamalai delights in Civakan night and day.

tamil: திரையிடைக் கொண்ட வின்னீ ரமுதுயிர் பெற்ற தென்னு
முரையுடைக் கோதை மாத ரொளிநல நுகர்ந்து நாளும்
வரையுடை மார்ப னங்கண் வைகின னென்ப மாதோ
கரைகட லனைய தானைக் காவலன் காத லானே.
reading: They say that the beloved of the king whose army is like the shore-bound sea, the mountain-chested one, stayed there day after day enjoying the bright beauty of the garlanded woman, of whom it is said the sea's nectar had taken life.
nuance: என்ப, 'they say', puts the narrator at a distance from the scene just as he turns away from it.
event: Civakan stays on in the king's city with his bride.

tamil: வாளினான் மிடைந்த கண்ணாள் வருமுலைத் தடத்துள் வைகித்
தோளினான் மிடைந்து புல்லித் தொண்டைவா யமுத மாந்திக்
காளைசெல் கின்ற நாளுட் கட்டியங் காரன் மூதூர்
மீளிவேற் குருசிற் குற்றார்க் குற்றது விளம்ப லுற்றேன்.
reading: While the young bull lives on, lying among the swelling breasts of the sword-eyed one, clasping her with his arms and drinking the nectar of her coral mouth, I begin to tell what befell, in Kattiyankaran's old city, those who were close to the hero of the fierce spear.
nuance: The narrator's own first person (விளம்பல் உற்றேன்) marks the change of scene from Civakan's pleasures to the people he left behind in Rajamapuram.

tamil: வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போல் விடலைக்குத் தம்பி மாழாந்
தொண்மதிச் சூழ்ச்சி மிக்கா னுள்ளுழி யுணர்தல் செல்லான்
புண்மதித் துடைந்த போது பொழிந்துமட் டொழுகு நன்னாட்
டுண்மதி வருந்த நாடி யொளிநக ரெய்தி னானே.
reading: The hero's younger brother, desolate as the stars that have lost the white moon, unable to learn where the wise, counsel-rich one was, searched the good land of dripping honey with a grieving mind and came to the bright city.
nuance: Line 3 (புண்மதித்து உடைந்த போது) is obscure, and which city ஒளிநகர் means is not said here; the image of stars without the moon is the patikam's own (verse 23).
event: Nandattan, failing to find his brother, searches the land and comes to the city.

tamil: வெள்ளிவெண் மலைக்கு வேந்த னொருமகள் வேற்கட் பாவை
யொள்ளிழை யவளைக் கேட்பா னுறுவலி செல்லு மாங்கண்
வள்ளிதழ்க் கோதை தானே யிட்டதோர் வண்ணந் தன்னைக்
கொள்ளத்தான் முரல லுற்றுக் கோலமை வீணை கொண்டாள்.
reading: As the strong one goes to ask the only daughter of the king of the silver mountain, the spear-eyed doll in bright jewels, the woman with the thick-petalled garland takes her well-made vina to play a tune of her own setting.
nuance: Gandharvadattai is a Vidyadhara princess with arts beyond the human, which is why the brother comes to her; the song she sets herself (தானே இட்டதோர் வண்ணம்) comes first.
event: Nandattan goes to Gandharvadattai to ask after Civakan, and she takes up her vina.

tamil: ஆடகச் செம்பொ னாணி யானெய்வார்ந் தனைய திண்கோன்
மாடக நொண்டு கொண்டு மாத்திரை நிறைய வீக்கிச்
சூடக மணிந்த முன்கைத் தொகுவிரல் சேப்ப வெற்றித்
reading: Fixing the strings of red gold, firm as if poured from molten ghee, tightening the pegs to their full measure until the joined fingers of her bangled hand redden, the woman with the opening garland sings the song with resolve.
nuance: மாத்திரை names the measured pitch to which the strings are tightened, the technical vocabulary of the vina the poem has used since the vina contest.
event: Gandharvadattai tunes her vina and begins to sing.

reading: He who feared my slender waist would snap if I wore a flower, and scattered the fragrant flowers from his hand, does not come near; he has left me; as he leaves, my bangles leave my shoulders too and my eyes rain pearls without rest: friend, am I to pass away?
nuance: The verb துற runs through the stanza: the lover துறந்தார், and so the bangles துறப்ப; his old tenderness, fearing a flower too heavy for her, is set against his leaving. The plural forms (நண்ணார், துறந்தார்) are honorific.

reading: He who thought my fine waist could not bear the weight of a flower garland and would not hold, does not think of me; he has left me; as he leaves, my bangles leave my shoulders and my spear-eyes cannot sleep: friend, am I to be bewildered?
nuance: The second stanza of the set repeats the first's frame, changing the verb of his neglect (எண்ணார்) and of her suffering (மருள்வேனோ).

reading: He who, saying my waist ached when the bees buzzed, would wave the flower garland to drive them off, does not join me; he has left me; as he leaves, my rounded bangles leave my shoulders and my flower-eyes cannot sleep: friend, am I to grieve?
nuance: The third stanza closes the set: his care went as far as fanning bees from her waist, which makes the absence the sharper. The three stanzas move from death (கழிவேனோ) to bewilderment to grief.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1701-1724 (7/14)
theme: Gandharvadattai's spell shows Civakan to his grieving brother and carries Nandattan to Emamapuram, where Vijayan and Vasundari find a stranger in Civakan's likeness and the brothers meet.
source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1708 line 2 ends with a stray full stop (உள்ளான்.).
1712 line 4 பதிக்கட் டம்மென divides doubtfully.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, Civakan's wife, who stays behind in Rajamapuram
Civakan's younger brother
the hero, now at Emamapuram
the great deity that carries the sleeping Nandattan to Emamapuram
a prince of Emamapuram who learns the bow from Civakan and calls him brother-in-law
a woman of the Emamapuram palace who finds the stranger at the bow-practice ground

tamil: ஊன்றகர்த் தனைய போன்று மூடெரி முளைப்ப போன்றுந்
தோன்றுபூ விலவத் தங்கட் டொகையணி லனைய பைங்காய்
கான்றமென் பஞ்சி யார்ந்த மெல்லணை யாழ்கை நீக்கித்
தேன்றயங் கிணர்பெய் கோதை சிந்தையி னீட்டி னாளே.
reading: Pushing aside with her lute-playing hand the soft cushion stuffed with silk-cotton from pods red as torn flesh and green as squirrels, the garlanded woman lies long lost in thought.
nuance: The woman is not named; the yāḻ hand (யாழ்கை) and the next verses' visit of Civakan's younger brother identify her as Gandharvadattai, the vina player.
event: Gandharvadattai leaves her cushion and broods on the absent Civakan.

reading: Thinking of her lord, she sighs hot breaths, the beauty of her red mouth dulls and the sword-eyed woman wastes.
event: Gandharvadattai pines for Civakan.

reading: While she sits wondering when her young breasts will press the garlanded chest of her lord again, Civakan's younger brother comes to her.
event: Nandattan comes to Gandharvadattai as she longs for Civakan.

tamil: ஐவிலி னகல நின்றாங் கடிதொழு திறைஞ்சி னாற்கு
மைவிலை பெற்ற கண்ணாண் மைந்தனை மருண்டு நோக்கிக்
கைவிலுங் கணையு மில்லாக் காமன்போந் திருக்க வென்ன
மொய்வெல்லுங் குருதி வேலான் மூவிற்க ணிறைஞ்சி நின்றான்.
reading: He stands five bow-lengths away and bows at her feet; she looks at him in wonder and bids Kama without bow or arrow come and sit, and the spear-bearer bows again three times.
nuance: The distance kept (ஐவில் அகலம்) and the repeated bow mark the deference of a younger brother before his elder brother's wife.
event: Nandattan bows to Gandharvadattai from a distance and she bids him sit.

tamil: திங்கள்வாண் முகமு நோக்கான் றிருமுலைத் தடமு நோக்கா
னங்கதிர்க் கலாப மின்னு மணியல்குற் பரப்பு நோக்கான்
செங்கயற் கண்ணி னாடன் சீறடிச் சிலம்பு நோக்கி
யெங்குளா ரடிக ளென்னா வின்னண மியம்பி னானே.
reading: He looks neither at her moon face, nor her breasts, nor her girdled hips, but only at the anklet on her small foot, and asks where his lord is.
event: Nandattan, eyes on her anklet, asks Gandharvadattai where Civakan is.

tamil: பொறிகுலாய்க் கிடந்த மார்பிற் புண்ணியன் பொன்றி னானேல்
வெறிகுலாய்க் கிடந்த மாலை வெள்வளை முத்த நீக்கி
நெறியினா னோற்ற லொன்றோ நீளெரி புகுத லொன்றோ
வறியலென் கொழுநன் மாய்ந்தா லணிசுமந் திருப்ப தென்றான்.
reading: Nandattan reasons that if the meritorious one were dead she would have put off garland, bangles and pearls and taken either the path of penance or the long fire, for he knows of no wife who bears ornaments when her husband is gone.
nuance: The norm is not urged on anyone; it is used as evidence: her ornaments prove to him that his brother lives. The two courses are set side by side with ஒன்றோ ... ஒன்றோ, neither ranked above the other.

tamil: காய்தழல் கவரப் பட்ட கற்பக மரத்திற் கன்றி
யாய்கழற் குருசில் வாடி யற்புத்தீ யழலு ணிற்ப
வாய்மொழிந் துரைக்க லுற்றாள் வனைகுழற் கற்றை வண்டார்த்
தோய்பிழி துளிக்குங் கண்ணிச் சுரும்புசூழ் கொம்ப னாளே.
reading: As the prince withers like a wishing tree caught by fire and stands in the burning of his love for his brother, the bee-hung woman begins to speak.
event: Nandattan grieves for his brother and Gandharvadattai begins to answer.

tamil: மதுமுகத் தலர்ந்த கோதை மாற்றமைந் தற்கு ரைப்பாள்
கொதிமுகக் குருதி வைவேற் குருசிலோ நம்மை யுள்ளான்.
விதிமுக மணங்க ளெய்தி வீற்றிருந் தின்ப முய்ப்ப
மதிமுக மறியு நாமே வாடுவ தென்னை யென்றாள்.
reading: She answers that the prince with the spear does not think of them; he has gone to the marriages fate brings him and sits enjoying them, and asks why she, who knows it, should waste away.
nuance: The sense of மதிமுகம் அறியும் நாமே in line 4 is unclear: it may be 'we who know his ways' or refer to a moon-faced mirror of her lore; the bitterness about விதிமுக மணங்கள், marriages set by fate, is a wife's sulk, not a doctrine.

tamil: வேண்டிய தெமக்கு நேரின் வில்வலாய் நுமைய னாரைக்
காண்டியென் றுரைப்பக் காளை யெழுமையு மடிமை நேர
மாண்டதோர் விஞ்சை யோதி மதிமுகந் தைவந் திட்டா
ணீண்டது பெரிது மன்றி நினைத்துழி விளக்கிற் றன்றே.
reading: She says that if he grants what she asks he will see his brother; the youth agrees to be her servant for seven births, and she recites a fine spell and strokes a moon-like face, which lights up the far place he thinks of as if it were near.
nuance: What she strokes (மதிமுகம்) is doubtful: her own face, or a mirror-like surface on which the vision appears; the verse does not say what she asked in return.
event: Nandattan promises Gandharvadattai lifelong service, and her spell shows him the distant place.

tamil: பொற்புடை யமளி யங்கட் பூவணைப் பள்ளி மேலாற்
கற்பக மாலை வேய்ந்து கருங்குழற் கைசெய் வானை
முற்படக் கண்டு நோக்கி முறுவல்கொண் முகத்த னாகி
விற்படை நிமிர்ந்த தோளான் றொழுதுமெய் குளிர்ந்து நின்றான்.
reading: On a golden couch's flower bed he sees first his brother, crowned with a wishing-tree garland, dressing a woman's dark hair; he smiles, joins his hands and stands with his body cooled.
nuance: The woman whose hair Civakan dresses is not named; the ilampakam's story makes her Kanakamalai.
event: In the vision Nandattan sees Civakan dressing his new wife's hair, and worships.

reading: When the honey-voiced woman withdraws the spell, he, bewildered at heart since what he saw was only a seeming, bows and begs her grace that he may reach his lord's feet.
nuance: பொய்ய தன்மையின் (line 3) is read as the unreality of the image; it could also be a mark of his not lying.
event: Gandharvadattai ends the vision and Nandattan begs her to send him to Civakan.

reading: She orders garlands, sandal paste, a gold sword and a dagger, hair perfume and fine ornaments to be brought to the place.
nuance: The division பதிக்கட் டம்மென is doubtful; it is read here as an order to bring the things to the place.
event: Gandharvadattai has gifts and weapons brought for Nandattan's journey.

reading: The radiant youth puts on the many ornaments as she bids and goes in, and the garlanded woman then recites her spell.
event: Nandattan adorns himself and Gandharvadattai begins the spell.

reading: She smears the place with sandal, hangs garlands of chosen flowers, raises agil smoke, and withdraws with her young women.
event: Gandharvadattai prepares the chamber with rites and leaves.

reading: When the youth, like Kama's younger brother, has lain down on the smoke-scented couch, a great deity sets him down in Emamapuram, they say.
nuance: The verse names the deity's act and not Gandharvadattai's; the spell of 1713 is what binds them.
event: A great deity carries the sleeping Nandattan to Emamapuram.

reading: Shining like a wishing tree in flower with jewels and gold, the youth rises from sleep as the sun climbs the great hill.
event: Nandattan wakes at dawn in the new place.

tamil: செய்யவாய் நெடிய கண்ணாள் செல்கென விடுக்கப் பட்ட
வெய்யவாட் டடக்கை வீர னிருத்தலும் விசய னென்பான்
கையவாஞ் சிலையி னானைக் கண்டுவந் தருகு சேர்ந்தான்
பையவாய்ப் பரந்த வல்குற் பாவையர்க் கமிர்த மன்னான்.
reading: As the hero sent by the red-lipped woman sits there, Vijayan, bow in hand, sees him and comes near.
event: Vijayan finds the stranger and approaches him.

tamil: தெய்வமே கமழு மேனித் திருவொளி கலந்த மார்பி
னையநீ யாரை யென்றாற் கவனுரை கொடாது விட்டான்
பையவே பெயர்ந்து போகிப் பனிமலர்க் கோதை மார்பின்
மையலங் களிறு போலு மைத்துனற் கிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Asked who he is, the stranger with a god-fragrant body gives no answer, and Vijayan goes quietly back and tells it to his brother-in-law.
nuance: மைத்துனன் makes Civakan Vijayan's brother-in-law, through the marriage seen in 1710.
event: Nandattan does not answer Vijayan, who goes to tell Civakan.

tamil: சந்தனக் களியும் பூவுந் தமனியக் குடத்து ணீருங்
கெந்தநா றகிலு முத்துங் கிளரொளி விளக்கு மேந்தி
யந்தில்விற் பயிற்றுந் தானம் வழிபட வாங்குச் சென்றாண்
மந்திர மடந்தை யன்னாள் வசுந்தரி வந்து சொன்னாள்.
reading: Vijayan reports that Vasundari, carrying sandal paste, flowers, water in a gold pot, agil, pearls and a lamp to worship at the bow-practice ground, came and told him what she saw.
nuance: 1718 says Vijayan told 'this' to Civakan and 1722 closes with என்றான், so 1719 to 1722 are read as his speech, with Vasundari's words quoted inside it; the verse could also be the narrator's.
event: Vasundari goes to worship at the archery ground and reports a stranger.

tamil: ஆரகிற் சேக்கை நீங்கி வெறுநிலத் தடிக டாமே
நீரிதிற் கிடந்த தென்கொ லென்றியா னினைந்து போகிச்
சேர்துணை கழறச் சென்றேன் செல்வியோ டாங்குக் கண்டேன்
போர்பல கடந்த வேலோய் மாயங்கொல் போற்றி யென்றாள்.
reading: Vasundari tells how she wondered why their lord had left his agil couch to lie on the bare ground, went to tell her companion, and found him there with the princess, and she warns that it may be a magic.
nuance: Her அடிகள் is the stranger she took for Civakan; the likeness of the brothers drives the scene.
event: Vasundari finds the double of Civakan on the ground while Civakan is with his wife.

tamil: கணைகடி கண்ணி சொல்லக் காணிய யானுஞ் சென்றேன்
மணியிலங் கொண்பொன் வைவாள் கேடக மருங்கு வைத்த
விணைகடி சீய மன்னா னிளமையும் வனப்பு மேருந்
துணையமை வடிவுஞ் சொல்லி னிற்பொறி யொற்றிக் கொண்டான்.
reading: Vijayan says he went to see as she told him, and found a lion-like youth with sword and shield beside him whose youth, beauty, bearing and form are, in a word, stamped with Civakan's likeness.
nuance: சொல்லின் நிற்பொறி ஒற்றிக் கொண்டான் is read as 'he has taken your seal', that is, he looks like you; the image is not certain.
event: Vijayan goes to look at the stranger.

tamil: நீண்டதோ ணெடிய செங்க ணீலமாய்ச் சுரிந்த குஞ்சிப்
பூண்டதோ ரார மேனிப் பொன்னுரைத் திட்ட தொக்குங்
காண்டகு காதிற் றாழ்ந்த குண்டலங் குவளைப் பைந்தா
ராண்டகை யழகன் யார்கொ லறியல னவனை யென்றான்.
reading: He describes the stranger's long arms, red eyes, dark curled hair, necklace, gold-rubbed skin, hanging earrings and kuvalai garland, and says he does not know who the handsome man is.

tamil: இனத்திடை யேறு போலு மெறுழ்வலி யுரைத்த மாற்ற
மனத்திடை மகிழ்ந்து கேட்டு மைந்தனந் தட்ட னேயாம்
புனத்திடை மயில னாளாற் பொருளுரை பெற்று வந்தா
னெனத்தவி ராது சென்றாங் கெய்தின னென்ப வன்றே.
reading: Hearing the words gladly, Civakan knows that the youth is Nandattan, come with the message of the peacock-like woman, and goes without delay to where he is, they say.
event: Civakan recognises his brother from the description and goes to him.

tamil: கருமுகிற் பொடித்த வெய்யோன் கடலிடை நடப்ப தேபோற்
றிருமுகஞ் சுடர நோக்கிச் சீவகன் சென்று சேர்ந்தான்
றருமனை யரிதிற் கண்ட தனஞ்சயன் போலத் தம்பி
திருமலர்த் தடக்கை கூப்பிச் சேவடி தொழுது வீழ்ந்தான்.
reading: Like the sun breaking from a black cloud to walk on the sea, Civakan comes with shining face, and his younger brother, like Arjuna seeing Dharma after long, joins his hands and falls worshipping at his feet.
nuance: The simile of தனஞ்சயன் and தருமன் sets the brothers in the Pandava pattern of a younger brother's devotion to the eldest.
event: Nandattan falls at Civakan's feet as the brothers meet.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1725-1748 (8/14)
theme: Nandattan reaches Civakan in Kanakamalai's city by Gandharvadattai's spell; after the reunion and Kanakamalai's welcome he tells how the companions debated revenge, took an overheard song as a sign that Civakan lived, and scattered, and how he found Gunamalai wasting and Gandharvadattai sent him on; Civakan begins his own story.
source_issues: All verses except 1727 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
1737 lines 2-3 and 1741 lines 1-2 are hard to construe; 1746 line 2 (வெப்பரால் தட்பம் மாற்றி) is obscure.
1742 names the woman only as மாலை; the identification with Gunamalai rests on the story, not the verse.

cast.role: the hero, now in Kanakamalai's city
Civakan's younger brother, who arrives and tells what happened after Civakan vanished
Civakan's wife in this city, named only by epithets in these verses
Civakan's friend, who calls the companions to counsel
Civakan's companion, who calls for revenge
one of Civakan's companions, who urges inquiry first
merchant of Rajamapuram, friend of Civakan
Civakan's companions
an unnamed man whose song hailing Civakan the companions overhear
Civakan's wife in the old city, named here as மாலை (1742)
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife, called the mountain lady (மலைமகள்) here
Civakan's kin in the old city

tamil: தாமரைத் தடக்கை கூப்பித் தாண்முதற் கிடந்த தம்பி
தாமரைத் தடத்தை யொத்தான் றமையனும் பருதி யொத்தான்
றாமரைக் குணத்தி னானை மும்முறை தழுவிக் கொண்டு
தாமரைச் செங்க ணானுந் தன்னுறு பரிவு தீர்ந்தான்.
reading: The younger brother lies at Civakan's feet with joined hands; the elder, compared to the sun as the brother is to a lotus pool, embraces him three times and his own anguish ends.
nuance: The four lines all open on தாமரை: the brother is the lotus pool, his virtue lotus-like, the elder lotus-eyed and the sun that opens it, so the reunion is told as the sun meeting the lotus.
event: Nandattan falls at Civakan's feet and Civakan embraces him three times.

tamil: என்னுறு நிலைமை யோரா தெரியுறு தளிரின் வாடிப்
பொன்னுறு மேனி கன்றிப் போயினீர் பொறியி லாதேன்
முன்னுற விதனை யோரேன் மூரிப்பே ரொக்க லெல்லாம்
பின்னுறு பரிவு செய்தேன் பேதையேன் கவல லென்றான்.
reading: Civakan tells his brother that, not knowing his state, he has withered like a scorched shoot; he blames himself as luckless and foolish for not foreseeing this and for bringing grief on all their great kin, and bids him not to grieve.
event: Civakan blames himself for the grief his disappearance caused his kin.

tamil: ஆக்கமுங் கேடு முற்றீ ரடிகளே யல்லிர் மேலைப்
பூக்குலா மலங்கன் மாலைப் புட்கொடி யாற்கு முண்டே
வீக்குவார் முலையி னார்போல் வெய்துயிர்த் துருகி நைய
நோக்கினீ ரென்னை யென்றா னுதியழற் குட்ட மொப்பான்.
reading: Nandattan answers that gain and loss have come not to his lord alone, for even the god of the bird banner has had them, and asks why Civakan looked at him sighing and melting like a woman.
nuance: புட்கொடியான், the one with the bird (Garuda) banner, is Vishnu; the consolation sets the hero's fall beside a god's reverses. The speaker is named only as one like a pool of pointed fire, so taking him as Nandattan rests on அடிகளே, his word for his elder throughout this chapter.

tamil: குரவரைப் பேண லின்றிக் குறிப்பிகந் தாய பாவந்
தரவந்த பயத்தி னாலித் தாமரைப் பாத நீங்கிப்
பருவருந் துன்ப முற்றேன் பாவியே னென்று சென்னி
திருவடி மிசையின் வைத்துச் சிலம்பநொந் தழுதிட் டானே.
reading: Calling himself a sinner, he says that the fruit of the sin of failing to tend his elders and going against their wish parted him from these lotus feet and brought him hard suffering, and he lays his head on the holy feet and weeps aloud.
nuance: He reads the separation as his own deed bearing fruit (பாவம் தர வந்த பயம்), where Civakan in 1726 had blamed himself; each brother takes the cause on himself. Who the elders (குரவர்) are, and which wish he crossed, the verse does not say.
event: Nandattan lays his head on Civakan's feet and weeps.

tamil: பரிந்தழு கின்ற தம்பி பங்கய மனைய செங்கண்
பொருந்துபு துடைத்து வேண்டா புலம்புதல் காளை யென்று
மருந்தனா ளுறையுங் கோயின் மடுத்துடன் கொண்டு புக்கா
னருந்ததிக் கற்பி னாளை யடிபணிந் தவனுங் கண்டான்.
reading: Civakan wipes his weeping brother's lotus-red eyes, tells him there is no need to lament, and takes him into the palace where his nectar-like wife lives; the brother bows at the feet of the lady of Arundhati's chastity.
event: Civakan leads Nandattan into the palace, where he bows to Kanakamalai.

tamil: கொழுநனைக் குறிப்பி னாலே குமரன்யா ரென்று நோக்கக்
கழுமிய கற்பி னாய்நின் மைத்துன னைய னென்ன
வெழுமையும் பெறுக வின்ன விளங்கிளைச் சுற்ற மென்றாள்
கொழுமலர்த் தடங்கட் செவ்வாய்க் குவிமுலைக் கொம்ப னாளே.
reading: With a look Kanakamalai asks her husband who the youth is; told he is her brother-in-law, she says may they have such shining kin in all seven births.
nuance: Her question is asked by sign (குறிப்பினாலே) and only her blessing is spoken; the blessing reckons kinship across the seven births (எழுமையும்).
event: Kanakamalai asks by a glance who the youth is, and Civakan names him as her brother-in-law.

tamil: குடவரை யனைய மார்பிற் குங்கும மெழுதிக் கோல
வடவரை வைரச் சாதி வாலொளி கலந்த பைம்பூண்
டடவரை மார்பின் மின்னத் தம்பியோ டமிர்த முண்டான்
படவர வல்கு லாளும் பான்மையால் விருந்து செய்தாள்.
reading: Civakan, his saffron-painted chest gleaming with diamond ornaments, eats the feast with his brother, and his wife serves it as a guest's welcome in due form.
event: Kanakamalai serves a guest's feast to Civakan and Nandattan.

tamil: விருந்தவள் செய்த பின்றைத் தம்பியுந் தானும் வேறா
விருந்துழி யென்னைக் காணா துற்றதை யெவன்கொ லென்று
பொருந்தினார் செய்த தெல்லாம் புரைவிடுத் துரைமோ வென்னக்
கருங்கழற் செங்கட் பைந்தார்க் காளையீ துரைக்கின் றானே.
reading: After the feast, alone with his brother, Civakan asks what befell when they could not find him and bids him tell, holding nothing back, all that his companions did; the youth begins.
event: Civakan asks Nandattan what his companions did after he vanished.

tamil: புண்ணுமிழ் குருதி போர்த்த பொருகளம் போன்று தோன்றி
யண்ணலங் கதிரு மத்த மடைந்துசெவ் வான்கொ ளந்தித்
துண்ணெனக் களத்தி னீங்கித் தொன்னகர்ப் புறத்துத் தொக்கே
யெண்ணுமின் செய்வ தென்றான் பதுமுக னெரியும் வேலான்.
reading: Nandattan says that at evening, when the sun set and the red sky looked like a battlefield soaked in blood, the companions left the field in haste and gathered outside the old city, and Padumukan of the burning spear asked them to consider what to do.
nuance: The evening sky is likened to a battlefield (பொருகளம்) at the moment the companions are deciding whether to fight.
event: The companions gather outside the city at dusk and Padumukan asks what they should do.

tamil: மின்னென மிளிரும் பைம்பூட் புத்திசேன் வெகுண்டு வெய்ய
கன்னவி றோளி னானைக் காண்கலே மாயி னின்னே
மன்னனை வாளி னானே வானகங் காட்டி மூதூர்
தன்னையுஞ் சவட்டிப் போகிச் சாமியைச் சார்து மென்றான்.
reading: Buddhisenan, flaring up, says that if they cannot see their lord now, they will show the king the sky with their swords, trample the old city and go to join their master.
nuance: சாமியைச் சார்தும், 'we will reach the master', assumes Civakan is dead: the vow is to die after him once vengeance is taken.
event: Buddhisenan proposes to kill the king, wreck the city and follow Civakan in death.

tamil: சிலையொடு திரண்ட திண்டோட் டேவமா தத்த னென்பான்
மலையுடை யுருமிற் சீறி மாற்றல னுயிரை யுண்ட
லிலையுடைக் கண்ணி யீர்க்கிஃ தெளிதுநங் குருசி லுண்மை
யுலைவினோ டின்மை யாராய்ந் தொறுப்பதே துணிமி னென்றான்.
reading: Devadattan of the strong bow, raging like thunder on a hill, says that taking the enemy's life is easy for them, but they must first find out whether their lord is truly dead or not, and only then resolve on punishment.
event: Devadattan argues that they must learn whether Civakan is dead before taking revenge.

tamil: பவ்வத்துப் பிறந்த வெய்ய பருதிபோற் றிறலி னாற்குத்
தெவ்வரைக் கிழங்கி னோடுந் தின்றுநீ சொன்ன வாறே
யெவ்வத்தைத் தணித்து மென்றான் சீதத்த னென்ன லோடு
மவ்வல மணந்த தண்டார்ப் பதுமுக னிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Sridattan says that, as Buddhisenan has said, they will eat up the enemies root and all and so ease their grief; when he has spoken, Padumukan speaks what follows.
event: Sridattan backs the call for revenge and Padumukan rises to speak.

tamil: நம்பிநந் தட்டன் கேட்க நங்கட்குக் குரவ ருள்ளார்
தம்பரி வகற்றி யோம்பி நீர்க்கடன் மரபு தாங்கிக்
கம்பஞ்செய் பரிவு நீங்கிக் கற்பிப்பார்க் குவர்த்துச் சொல்லா
ரிம்பரிவ் வுலக மொப்பாய்க் கென்னையா னுரைப்ப தென்றான்.
reading: Padumukan, addressing Nandattan, says that the companions have elders who would bear their grief, care for them and keep the rites of water, and asks what he could advise one who is like the whole world to them.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are hard: the elders who keep the water rite (நீர்க்கடன்) seem to be the companions' parents, who will mourn them, so Padumukan leaves the final word to Civakan's own brother.

tamil: ஓம்படை சாற்றற் பால துள்ளவர்க் காகு மன்றே
யாம்புடை யென்க ணில்லை யங்கையென் கண்க ளாகத்
தேம்படு தாரி னீர்க்குஞ் செல்வற்குஞ் செய்வ செய்தேன்
காம்படு காட்டுத் தீயிற் கனன்றுட னெழுக வென்றேன்.
reading: Nandattan says he told them that charging others with protection is for those who have someone at their side; he has no one, has done for them and for the lord what was his to do, and bade them rise together blazing like a forest fire.
nuance: ஓம்படை, a solemn charge to protect, is what one leaves to those one leaves behind; he says he has no one left to charge, so the restraint Devadattan and Padumukan urged does not bind him.
event: Nandattan urges the companions to rise at once against the king.

tamil: கோட்டிளங் குழவித் திங்க ளிரண்டன்ன வெயிற்றுக் கோளே
வேட்டவோர் சிங்கஞ் சூழ்ந்த வேங்கையி னினத்தின் வெய்ய
வாட்படை யெழுந்து வாழ்க சீவக னென்னு மாங்கட்
பாட்டினை யொருவ னெங்கள் பரிவறப் பாடி னானே.
reading: Just then a man sang a song, 'long live Civakan, whose sword-army rose fiercer than a pack of tigers round a lion with tusks like two crescent moons', and their grief fell away.
event: A passer-by sings a song hailing Civakan, and the companions' grief lifts.

tamil: வருவர்நங் கேள்வ ரின்னே வாணுதற் பசலை தீர
வுருகிநைந் துடன்று முன்கை வளையுக மெலிய வேண்டா
வருவிமும் மதத்த யானை யதிர்ந்துழிக் காரென் றெண்ணித்
தெரிவில பேதை முல்லை பூத்தன தெளியி தென்றான்.
reading: The song tells a woman that her husband will come soon, that she need not melt and grieve till her bangles slip and her brow pales, for the foolish mullai, unable to tell, bloomed thinking the roar of the rutting elephant was the rain cloud.
nuance: The song is the old consolation of the friend who denies that the season has come: the flowers have been fooled, so he has not broken his word. Overheard, its 'our husband will come' is taken by the companions as a sign that Civakan lives.

tamil: பாட்டினைக் கேட்ட லோடும் பழம்பகை நட்பு மாமே
யோட்டியுங் கோறு மன்றே நம்பிதா னுண்மை பெற்றா
னாட்டிடம் பரந்து போகி நாடுது நாங்க ளென்னா
வீட்டமும் வேறு மாகி யிலைப்புரை கிளைத்திட் டேமே.
reading: On hearing the song they said old enmity could wait and the killing could come later, since their prince had surely survived; they would spread over the land and search, and so they gathered and parted, each his own way.
nuance: பழம்பகை நட்பும் ஆமே is obscure; it may mean that old enmity can turn to friendship, or that the feud can rest for now.
event: Taking the song as a sign that Civakan lives, the companions put off revenge and scatter to search for him.

tamil: மணிபொதி துகிலிற் றோன்று மஞ்சுசூழ் வரைக ணாடி
யணிநகர் யான்சென் றெய்தி மாலைதன் மனையைச் சேர்ந்தேன்
றுணைமலர்க் காந்த ளூழ்த்துச் சொரிவபோற் றோன்றி முன்கை
யணிவளை நலத்தோ டேக வங்ஙன மிருந்து நைவாள்.
reading: Crossing misty hills that seem like gems wrapped in cloth, he reached the fine city and came to Maalai's house, where she sat wasting, her bangles slipping from her forearms like falling kaanthal blossoms.
nuance: மாலை is taken as Gunamalai, Civakan's wife in the old city, since the mountain lady of 1745 is another.
event: Nandattan reaches the city and finds Gunamalai wasting in her house.

tamil: என்னைக்கண் டடிசி லாக்க வையர்க்கென் றவல நீங்கப்
பொன்னைக்கண் டனைய சாய லவர்புரிந் தடிசி லேந்தத்
துன்னிநோ யுற்ற மஞ்ஞைத் தோற்றம்போ லிருந்த நங்கை
பின்னைநாட் குவளை நீர்வீழ் பெற்றிய கண்ண ளாகி.
reading: Seeing him, she had food made for her guest so his sorrow might ease, and when the golden women brought it the lady, who had sat like an ailing peacock, then had eyes like kuvalai dropping water.
event: Gunamalai has a meal prepared for Nandattan and then breaks into tears.

tamil: அடிகளை யின்றி நீரே யுண்ணவும் வல்லீ ரானீர்
கடியிர்நீ ரைய னீரே யெனக்கசிந் துருகிக் காய்பொற்
கொடிதுக ளார்ந்த வண்ணங் குழைந்துமா நிலத்து வீழ்ந்த
பெடைமயிற் சாய லாடன் பேதுகண் டாங்கு மீண்டேன்.
reading: She cries that without their lord they can now eat by themselves and calls him hard, then melts and falls to the ground like a peahen; seeing her distress, he turned back.
nuance: Her reproach turns the meal she herself ordered into the charge: a brother who can eat has stopped grieving.
event: Gunamalai reproaches Nandattan for eating without Civakan and collapses; he leaves.

tamil: செல்வனை யின்று நாடிச் சேவடி தொழுத லொன்றோ
வல்லதிவ் வுடம்பு நீங்க வேற்றுல கடைத லொன்றோ
வெல்லையிவ் விரண்டி னொன்றை யிப்பகன் முடிப்ப லென்னா
மல்லிகைக் கோதை யைம்பான் மலைமகண் மனையைச் சேர்ந்தேன்.
reading: Resolving that this very day he would either find his lord and worship his red feet or leave this body and reach another world, he went to the house of the mountain lady with jasmine in her five-part hair.
nuance: மலைமகள், daughter of the mountain, is taken as Gandharvadattai, the Vidyadhara princess from the mountain; it is not Parvati.
event: Nandattan resolves to find Civakan or die that day, and goes to the mountain lady's house.

tamil: மணியொலி வீணை பண்ணி மாண்டகோ றடவ மாத
ரணிமுலைத் தடத்தி னொற்றி வெப்பராற் றட்ப மாற்றிப்
பிணைமலர்க் கோதை கீதம் பாடயான் பெரிதும் பேதுற்
றிணைமலர்க் கண்ணிக் கொவ்வா விளிவரு கிளவி சொன்னேன்.
reading: Her women played the jewel-voiced vina, stroking its fine frets, and cooled the heat with their hands, the garlanded lady sang, and he, much distraught, spoke to her words of reproach unfit for her.
nuance: Line 2's cooling (வெப்பரால் தட்பம் மாற்றி) is hard to place; the music seems to be her way of keeping calm while the brother breaks down.
event: Gandharvadattai sings to the vina, and Nandattan speaks harshly to her.

tamil: சொல்லிய வென்னை நோக்கித் துளங்கனும் மடிகள் பாதம்
புல்லயான் புணர்ப்ப லென்று பொழுதுபோய்ப் பட்ட பின்றை
யெல்லிருள் விஞ்சை யோதி யிவ்வழி யிடுவித் திட்டாள்
சொல்லுமி னடிக ணீரும் போந்தவா றெனக்கு மென்றான்.
reading: Looking at him, she told him not to tremble, for she would bring him to his lord's feet; when the day had gone she recited a spell in the deep dark and sent him by this way, and he asks his lord to tell him in turn how he came here.
nuance: விஞ்சை, the Vidyadhara's spell, carries a man across the land in a night; she promises reunion at the feet (பாதம் புல்ல), which is how 1725 opens.
event: Gandharvadattai sends Nandattan to Civakan by a spell, and Nandattan asks Civakan to tell his own story.

tamil: தாதையா ருவப்பச் செய்வான் றாழ்கச்சிற் பிணிப்புண் டைய
போதரா நின்ற போழ்திற் போர்ப்புலிக் குழாத்திற் சீறிக்
காதனஞ் சுற்ற மெல்லாங் கையிலங் கெஃக மேந்திச்
சாதலே புரிந்து தோன்றுந் தன்மையந் நகரிற் கண்டேன்.
reading: Civakan begins: when, to please his father, he was being led bound with a belt, he saw in that city all their dear kin raging like a troop of fighting tigers, spears raised, set on dying.
event: Civakan begins to tell how he was led bound from the city while his kin stood ready to die.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1749-1772 (9/14)
theme: Civakan finishes telling his brother Nandattan how he escaped and wandered, through the god's rescue, the rain on the burning forest, and his marriages to Padumai and Kemasari and the princess of the middle country, and says a brother is the one thing that cannot be gained; at home his four companions suspect Gandharvadattai's calm, learn from her that he is safe, worship her, take her sealed letter and set out with a host of horse.
source_issues: 1749-1760: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1749 line 1: கண்டபி னின்னைக் காண்பேன் is hard to construe as printed.
1755 line 1: அரிகுரற் கோழி நாமத் தரவவட் is obscure.
1756 line 1: வாவிப்புண் ணடையி னாளை is unclear.
1768 line 3 and 1770 line 1: word division unclear; sense uncertain.
1772 line 1: the number may be read as 1,020 or 20,000.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai
Civakan's younger brother
Civakan's companions, four of them in 1762
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, Civakan's wife (தத்தை 1762, வெள்ளி வெண்மலை வேந்தன் பாவை 1763)
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison (இயக்கன், வானவன் here)
the Pallava king, Padumai's father (named in 1754)
merchant of the Takka country, Kemasari's father
the king of the middle country who receives Civakan and gives him his daughter (இறைவன் 1758)
the horsemen and soldiers who set out with the companions (மள்ளர் 1772)

tamil: கண்டபி னின்னைக் காண்பேன் கருவரை புலம்பிப் பல்கால்
விண்டுவு முடைய வாலின் வெடித்துராய் வெகுண்டு நோக்கா
வெண்டிசை யோரு மெள்கக் குஞ்சர மிரியப் பாயு
மொண்டிறற் சிங்க மன்ன கதழொளி யுடற்சி கண்டேன்.
reading: Civakan, telling his brother how he came here, says that in the fight at his arrest he saw his brother's fury, like a lion of shining strength that leaps so that elephants scatter and even the guardians of the eight quarters quail.
nuance: Line 1 (கண்டபின் நின்னைக் காண்பேன்) is hard to construe as printed; the reading follows the second-person address and the lion simile of lines 3-4.
event: Civakan recalls seeing Nandattan rage like a lion in the fight when he was seized.

tamil: சினந்தலைப் பெருக்கித் தீக்கோ ளுறுப்பினைச் சுருக்கித் தீப்போ
லனன்றுநில் லாத கண்ணா னிறுத்தின செவியிற் றாகி
முனம்புக வடக்கிப் பின்போந் திருந்துபாய் வான மைந்த
வினந்தலைப் புலியோ டொக்குந் தோழர்நின் னிடத்திற் கண்டேன்.
reading: He goes on that he saw the companions at his brother's side like a pack of tigers, swelling their anger, drawing in their fiery limbs, ears pricked and eyes unblinking, crouching before they spring.
event: Civakan recalls his companions standing like tigers ready to spring.

tamil: கூடநீர் நின்ற பெற்றி கண்டிப்பா னோக்கு வேற்கொர்
கேடகம் வாளொ டேந்திக் கெடுகவிந் நகர மென்னா
மாடத்தி னுச்சி நின்ற மலைமக டன்மை கண்டே
யாடவர்க் குழுவை யொப்பா யஞ்சினே னதன்க ணென்றான்.
reading: Seeing how they all stood together, and seeing the mountain's daughter on the top of the mansion with shield and sword crying 'let this city perish', he says, he grew afraid at that.
nuance: What he fears is not the enemy but the slaughter and ruin his own side is ready for; the next verse turns that fear into his choice of death.
event: Civakan recalls Gandharvadattai on the mansion top, armed and cursing the city, and his fear at it.

tamil: பெண்ணிடர் விடுப்ப வாழ்விற் சாதலே பெரிது நன்றென்
றெண்ணினே னமர்கள் வீயு மியல்பினா னெருங்கப் பட்டுக்
கண்ணிநா னியக்கன் றன்னைச் சிந்தித்தேன் கடவுள் வாழ்த்தி
யண்ணல்வந் தழுங்கத் தோன்றி யாங்கென்னைக் கொண்டு போந்தான்.
reading: He says he judged death far better than living freed from distress by a woman, and, hemmed in as his people were about to die, thought of the yaksha and praised the god, and the lord appeared and carried him off.
nuance: பெண் இடர் விடுப்ப வாழ்வின் is taken as 'than a life in which a woman frees me from distress', which fits his earlier refusal to be freed by Gandharvadattai's spells; another division of line 1 is possible.
event: Civakan, choosing death over rescue by his wife's arts, thinks of the yaksha, who comes and carries him away.

tamil: மந்திர மூன்றுந் தந்து வானவன் விடுப்பச் செல்வேற்
கிந்திர திருவிற் சூழ்ந்த வினமழைக் குழாத்தின் வேழங்
கொந்தழற் காட்டுத் தீயால் வளைப்புண்ட குழாத்தை நோக்கிச்
சிந்தித்துக் கவன்று நிற்பத் திருமழை பொழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The god gave him three mantras and sent him off, and on the way he saw a herd of elephants like rain clouds under a rainbow ringed by forest fire, and as he stood anxious and grieving for them holy rain poured down.
nuance: In his own telling he does nothing but stand and worry; the rain is திருமழை, holy rain, and falls in answer to his compassion.
event: Civakan, given three mantras, sees a herd of elephants trapped by forest fire, and rain falls as he grieves for them.

tamil: வெல்களிற் றச்ச நீக்கி விரைவொடு வனத்தி னேகிப்
பல்லவ தேய நண்ணித் தனபதி யென்னு மன்ன
னல்வனப் புடைய தேவி திலோத்தமை பெற்ற நம்பி
செல்வன்மற் றுலோக பாலன் றிருமகள் பதுமை யென்பாள்.
reading: Having ended the elephants' fear he went swiftly through the forest into the Pallava country, where king Dhanapati's queen Tilottamai had borne the prince Lokapalan, whose sister was Padumai.
nuance: The names Dhanapati, Tilottamai and Lokapalan, absent from the verses that told this episode, are given here in Civakan's summary.
event: Civakan reaches the Pallava country of king Dhanapati.

tamil: அரிகுரற் கோழி நாமத் தரவவட் கடித்த தாகத்
திருவிழை யவளைத் தீர்த்தேன் றீர்விலா நண்பு வேண்டிப்
பொருகளி யானை மன்னன் புனையிழை யவளைத் தந்தா
னிருமதி கழிந்த பின்றை யிடையிராப் பொழுதிற் போந்தேன்.
reading: When a snake bit her he cured the jewelled girl; the king of fighting elephants, wanting a friendship without end, gave her to him, and after two months he left at midnight.
nuance: Line 1 (அரிகுரற் கோழி நாமத்து அரவு) seems to name the snake or the place of the bite in a way not fixed here.
event: Civakan recounts curing Padumai of the snakebite, marrying her, and leaving her at midnight after two months.

tamil: வாவிப்புண் ணடையி னாளை வஞ்சித்துத் தக்க நாட்டை
மேவியான் காண லுற்றுச் சார்தலு மிப்ப ருள்ளான்
றூவிப்பொன் மாட மூதூர்ச் சுபத்திர னென்னைக் கண்டே
யாவிக்க ணறிவு போல வளவளா யன்பு பட்டான்.
reading: Deceiving the woman, he set out to see the Takka country, and on his arrival Subhadran of the old town of gold-washed mansions saw him and loved him as the soul knows knowledge.
nuance: Civakan uses the word வஞ்சித்து of his own leaving; he does not excuse it. The phrase வாவிப்புண் அடையினாளை for Padumai is unclear.
event: Civakan recounts leaving Padumai by deceit and being welcomed by Subhadran in the Takka country.

tamil: பண்ணமை தேரி னேறி யவனொடியா னிருந்து போகி
விண்ணுயர் செம்பொன் மாடத் திழிந்தவண் விளங்கப் புக்கேன்
வெண்ணிலா முத்தஞ் சூழ்ந்த வெம்முலைத் தடங்க ணாளை
மண்ணெலாஞ் செல்ல நின்ற மகிழ்ச்சியின் மகிழ்ந்து தந்தான்.
reading: He rode with Subhadran in his chariot, entered his tall golden mansion, and the merchant, with a joy that spread over the whole earth, gave him his daughter with pearl-ringed breasts and wide eyes.
event: Civakan recounts Subhadran giving him his daughter Kemasari.

tamil: அவ்வழி யிரண்டு திங்கள் கழிந்தபி னவளி னீங்கி
யிவ்வழி நாடு காண்பான் வருதலு மிறைவன் கண்டே
செவ்வழி பாட ராகிச் சிலைத்தொழில் சிறுவர் கற்ப
மைவழி நெடுங்க ணாளைத் தந்தனன் மதலை யென்றான்.
reading: After two months there he left her and came this way to see the land, and the king here saw him, and so that his sons might learn archery in the right way gave him his long-eyed daughter, Civakan said, ending his account.
nuance: The marriage is tied to a service: the king's daughter comes with the teaching of the princes' bow-craft.
event: Civakan recounts leaving Kemasari and coming to the middle country, whose king gave him his daughter for teaching his sons archery.

tamil: தானுழந் துற்ற வெல்லாந் தம்பியை யுணரக் கூறித்
தேனுழந் தரற்றுந் தாரான் குரவரைச் சிந்தித் தாற்கு
வானிழிந் தாங்குக் கண்ணீர் மார்பக நனைப்பக் கையா
லூனுமிழ்ந் திலங்கும் வேலா னொற்றிமற் றிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: When he had told his brother all he had gone through, and the brother thought of their elders and wept so that his tears wet his chest like rain from the sky, the hero with the gleaming spear wiped them with his hand and said this.
nuance: The verse can also be read with Civakan as the one who thinks of the elders and weeps; the dative சிந்தித்தாற்கு is taken here as the brother.
event: Civakan finishes his story; Nandattan weeps at the thought of their elders, and Civakan wipes his tears.

tamil: திண்பொரு ளெய்த லாகுந் தெவ்வரைச் செகுக்க லாகு
நண்பொடு பெண்டிர் மக்கள் யாவையு நண்ண லாகு
மொண்பொரு ளாவ தையா வுடன்பிறப் பாக்க லாகா
வெம்பியை யீங்குப் பெற்றே னென்னெனக் கரிய தென்றான்.
reading: Firm wealth can be won, enemies can be destroyed, friends, wives and children can all be gained, he says, but a brother cannot be made; having got my brother here, what is there hard for me?
nuance: He puts his wives among the things that can be gained, in a book named for them; the one bond beyond acquisition is birth.

reading: The prince lived with his brother like milk mixed in honey while many days passed; meanwhile, back home, the companions, wasting like a hill in summer, their bodies withering, thought what they should do.
event: Civakan and Nandattan live together while the companions at home waste and take counsel.

reading: The four sat together and asked what they should do now, and said that the parrot-like Gandharvadattai, with the peacock's grace, shows no wasting of the body at all; could it be deceit?
nuance: They read her unwasted body by the convention that a parted wife pales and wastes, and take its absence for a sign of deceit.
event: The four companions take counsel and suspect Gandharvadattai because she does not waste.

reading: Saying 'if there is deceit we shall see it', they went gently and asked her, and the daughter of the king of the white silver mountain told them what had befallen the generous one and how he had gone hidden.
event: The companions question Gandharvadattai, who tells them what happened to Civakan and where he is hidden.

reading: Hearing her, the young men, like those who get back a life that had gone, felt their bodies cool with a gladness greater than that of the parents who bore her, and their grief left them since there was no danger.
nuance: பெற்ற மாந்தரின் is taken as her own parents' gladness; it may instead mean 'than those who gain (a treasure)'.
event: The companions are relieved to learn Civakan is safe.

reading: They set the anklets of the small feet of her, graceful as the goddess of fortune, on their tufted heads, their bodies swelling with melting hearts, and sang and danced with a love they drank in.
event: The companions place Gandharvadattai's feet on their heads and sing and dance for joy.

reading: They said that those who worship the form of this goddess of fortune, whose teeth are pearls like those the hooded snake spits out, will see every sorrow of theirs perish.
nuance: Praise turns into a formula of worship for the wife they had just suspected of deceit.

reading: 'We shall go to our lord there; lady, if you have any message, tell it quickly,' they said, and she with the garland on her arm wrote secretly with an inked stylus on a fine palm leaf.
event: The companions offer to carry a message, and Gandharvadattai secretly writes a letter on palm leaf.

reading: She put red lac on it, pressed her seal on it with her flower earring and held it out, and bowing, the honey-haired one said 'go with the sound of victory', and they set off toward him.
nuance: ஆடிசை செல்க is taken as a blessing, 'go with resounding fame'; the reading of line 3 is not secure.
event: Gandharvadattai seals the letter and sends the companions off with it.

reading: She sent them off crowned with garlands of honeyed flowers chosen by women whose dark eyes are like bows and arrows, with bees humming over them.
event: Gandharvadattai garlands the companions and sends them off.

reading: The steeds are described: they rise up and fill the ground, bear spotted whorls, leap as if spitting out their forelegs, and turn aside the arrows shot at them.
nuance: Line 1 (the white moon made hungry, அப்பகலே) is obscure.

reading: Through mire, sand, water and hard hills they run like the mind, never wavering in strength; in battle they wheel like a ring of fire so that the banners are drawn out; they are bred finer than those of the slopes of the great silver mountain.
Warriors mounted these horses, numbered in thousands and twenties, their harness bright, their garlands and bells jingling, chowries set on them, and the soldiers gathered and rose with a roar.
nuance: The number (ஈரைஞ்ஞாற்றினை இருபதின் முரணிய தொகைய) can be read as a thousand and twenty or as twenty thousand.
event: The companions' horsemen mount and set out with a roar.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1773-1796 (10/14)
theme: Civakan's companions ride out with a caravan, after reading the omens, through hill and field country to a hermitage, where they find a weeping woman ascetic worshipping the Jina; she is Vijayai, his mother, though no one names her, and when she will not tell her clan Devadattan answers with their city, their parents and their upbringing with the prince, and begins to tell his deeds.
source_issues: 1782 lines 1-2 (மாண்டிழகர், செய்கழகர் தாரரவர்) are divided obscurely; the reading 'young men' for the subject is a guess from context.
1790 line 3 (விளைத்திரும்பு மேய்ந்தொழிந்த மிச்சில்வரை மார்பன்) is obscure as divided.
1794 line 4 ends without a main verb; the construction runs on into 1795.
1796 ends with the name withheld (நாமம் எவன் என்னின் இது ஆம்); the name follows in 1797.

cast.role: Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage; unnamed in these verses
Civakan's companions, here the four who ride out and meet Vijayai without knowing her
the caravan and armed escort travelling with the companions
the men skilled in reading day, omens and hour who fix the departure
one of Civakan's companions, son of Vijayadattan and Piritimati, who speaks for the party
the hero, absent, whose deeds Devadattan recounts

reading: The narrator lists the party's train, trained horses, swift chariots and fierce camels, beasts that cover a hundred bow-lengths in a snap of the fingers, loaded with the goods they took.
nuance: ஒட்டகம், the camel, is a rare beast in this landscape; the verse piles up speed (நொடிப்பின் மாத்திரை நூற்றுவில்) rather than describing any one animal.
event: The companions' train is made ready with mounts and loaded goods.

reading: Four horses, swift of foot, coloured like the green parrot, with coral-like hooves and eye-catching looks, worth the price of the world, are saddled and the four mount them.
event: The four companions mount four saddled horses.

reading: Having had men skilled in the art examine the day, the bird omen, the good standing of the planets, the hour and the signs, they set out with the caravan, urging on with their feet.
nuance: Five separate reckonings are named (நாள், புள், கோள், ஓரை, நிமித்தம) and handed to specialists (ஆளும் மாந்தர்); the verse records the practice without saying it decides the outcome.
event: The companions have the day, omens and hour read and set out with the caravan.

reading: With drums and conches roaring all round, sheathed swords and bright spears flashing, the army sets out with a shout like red flood water that has broken its dam.
event: The armed escort sets out noisily.

reading: Along the way jasmine flowers shower onto the bent ears of ripe red paddy, and the swans and herons of the flooded fields scatter as the drums sound.
Elephants with winnow-like ears and hanging trunks, set swaying in the pepper forest where hens and cocks play under areca clusters and pepper vines swing, take fright and bolt.
nuance: The swing (ஊசல்) of pepper vines and the play of fowl are the settled hill country; the party's noise, not a hunt, is what startles the elephants (இளகப் பரிகொண்ட).

reading: Passing hills with waterfalls, dark-forested slopes, millet fields where sparrows rise crying, and the lands of those who have lost their fortune, the train comes and halts within the hermitage of the great ascetics.
nuance: திருவிற் றீர்ந்தவர் தேயம், 'the land of those parted from fortune', is set just before the hermitage where Vijayai, who lost her kingdom, lives; the poet lets the phrase stand ahead of the meeting.
event: The train passes through hill and field country and halts at a hermitage.

reading: The grove there, where bees sleep, cuckoos call and peacocks cry, where many flowers open and drip honey, branches bend under tender leaves and buds, is like the world of the gods.
Among pools full of kaavi, kazhuneer, kuvalai, aambal and fragrant lotus, with young herons, paired swans, old fish and bees, the people make camp between the tanks and the grove.
event: The party camps between the pools and the grove of the hermitage.

reading: In the hermitage where the ascetics dwell, the young men wander everywhere and, on a cool wooden bench in a bower of plucked flowers, they see a woman a little beyond Lakshmi herself.
nuance: The woman is Vijayai, Civakan's mother, though neither the verse nor the young men name her; the reader knows from 347-359 who lives in this hermitage. செய்யவள் is Lakshmi, and the line places her above the goddess even in her ascetic state.
event: The companions, wandering the hermitage, see a woman seated on a wooden bench.

reading: Her fine ochre-dyed cloth weighs on her hips, the fine red upper cloth weighs on her shoulder where it covers it, her little dark-haired son weighs on her mind, and her eyes, as if plucking at her, weigh on her as she weeps unable to bear it.
nuance: The four-fold வருத்த joins the ascetic's garments and the son in one list of burdens: the robe she took for him has not freed her from him. The 'little son' (சிறுவன்) is grown by now; she still thinks of him as the infant she left.
event: The woman sits in her ascetic's dress weeping for her son.

reading: Her five-plaited hair, dimmed with dirt and like threaded sapphire, hangs down her back unanointed and bound by its own neglect; laying fragrant flowers on the feet of the Jina in a hidden place, she recites praises in her mind that her fault may go, and sits worshipping.
nuance: வாமன் here is the Jina, the one whose feet receive the flowers; the worship is silent (மனத்து ஓதி) and private (மறைந்த வழி). The hair 'not anointed' (பூசுதலும் இன்றி) is the widow's mark of 349-354, kept now as a penance.
event: The woman worships at the feet of the Jina, reciting praises silently.

reading: Saying 'I will think now on my son's lot', she sits there while tears run from her long eyes and wet the cloth over her breasts; the young men come up to her, their hearts trembling, and bow with joy and great love.
nuance: Her thought for her son comes straight after the worship of 1784: the prayer does not end the grief but leads into it. The companions bow with love to a stranger; the reader alone knows she is their prince's mother.
event: The woman weeps thinking of her son, and the young men approach and bow to her.

reading: Seeing her dwelling in the hermitage girt by hills, they cannot tell whether she is the goddess with spear-long eyes who lives in the fragrant flower, the bright-browed goddess who lives on the tongue clothed in speech, or the sweet-voiced one clothed by the waves.
nuance: The three are Lakshmi of the lotus, Sarasvati of the tongue, and a third named only as clothed in waves (திரையுடுத்த), perhaps the sea-girt earth; the triple உடுத்த ('clothed') ties the three together.
event: The young men wonder which goddess she is.

reading: The young men ask her, 'You who are like the great goddess of fortune whose auspiciousness has died, what brings you here, and what is the lady's clan?', and she answers that her clan and her coming are not easy to tell if they would know them, and bids them tell their own clan and coming first.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are the young men's question and lines 3-4 her reply. மங்கலம் மடிந்த, 'whose auspiciousness has died', reads her as a widow from her dress. Her refusal keeps the secret of land and lineage the deity kept for her when she came (356).
event: The young men ask the woman her clan; she declines and asks theirs.

reading: Devadattan answers that their dwelling place is the city of Rajamapuram, famed for its watchfulness, where young vaalai fish crowding the old deep water sleep after fighting with the bow-shaped prawns.
nuance: The speaker of 1788-1796 is fixed only by 1792, where he names himself.
event: Devadattan names Rajamapuram as their city.

reading: He names the first of them: Sitattan, lion-like, with shoulders that make kings tremble, son of Kurudattai of long sword-like eyes, the wife worthy of Sagaran, the golden-chested minister of subtle understanding.
nuance: Each companion in 1789-1792 is named through both parents, the mother's beauty and the father's office or skill, so that the list is a list of lineages answering her question about clan. The father here is a minister (மந்திரி); whether this Sitattan is the merchant Sitattan of the sea voyage (493-580) the verses do not settle.

reading: Next is Buddhisenan, son of Achalan, master of the four Vedas beyond measure, and of Tilottamai, whose beauty matches the goddess of fortune; his chest is like a hill, and Devadattan says he would tire if he told his splendour.
nuance: Buddhisenan's father is a man of the four Vedas (நான்மறையினான்); the companions are of mixed birth, brahmin, minister's and merchant's sons, joined only by having been born on one day. Line 3 (விளைத்திரும்பு மேய்ந்தொழிந்த மிச்சில்) is obscure as divided.

reading: Then Padumukan, born to Pavittirai of bright brow and angry sword-like eyes, wife of the merchant Danapalan, whose honeyed chest bears the scars a musth elephant ploughed with its tusk.

Last he names himself: 'I, sir, am Devadattan, the loving son of Piritimati of unmatched chastity, who is the life's armour of Vijayadattan of bow-scarred shoulders, who won an emblem bearing the king's name in the golden city.'
nuance: His mother is called the 'life's armour' (உயிர்க் கவசம்) of his father, chastity praised as a protection to the husband, said to a woman who has outlived hers.
event: Devadattan names himself and his parents.

reading: He says that on the very day the king perished through their own ill deeds, they were born together with their prince, who is their life; they were given to the prince as his companions, and grew like the sun in beauty.
nuance: எங்கள் வினையால் takes the king's death as the companions' own karma, a humble formula the epic gives to several dependants (the deity as maid in 315). He tells this to the king's widow without knowing her.
event: Devadattan tells how the companions were born on the day of the king's death and given to the prince.

reading: When years had passed, Nandattan, the prince's younger brother, with Nabulan and Vipulan of noble qualities, grew up with them and reached the height of the raised seat, like the elephants of the quarters, with a heat none could touch.
nuance: Line 4 (தீண்டரிய வெம்மையொடு திக்கயங்கள் எனவே) ends the sentence on a simile without a main verb; the next verse completes the account.

reading: They all learned together archery, swordplay, the contest of the vina, wrestling, the work of the hide shield, the handling of elephants and the fine art of the horse, swimming across all the arts.
nuance: The vina is listed among the martial arts as a contest (வீணைபொரு தொழில்), which is how Civakan used it to win Gandharvadattai.

reading: And if she asks the name of the prince who rescued the herds from the hunters of cruel bows, won by vina contest the daughter of the Vidyadhara king who goes back to the sky, overcame the elephant and enjoyed Gunamalai's love, it is this.
nuance: Devadattan recounts Civakan's deeds in order (the cattle raid, the vina contest, the elephant and Gunamalai) to the one listener who most needs them and who has not yet been told whose they are; the name itself is held over to the next verse.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1797-1819 (11/14)
theme: Civakan's companions, searching for him, tell an ascetic mother in the hermitage that he was seized for death; her lament reveals that she is Vijayai, the dead king's queen, and Civakan his heir, and she charges them in secret to bring him to her, while they vow to crush the usurper.
source_issues: Most stanzas from 1799 on were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful (1802 line 3, 1804 line 1, 1807 line 2, 1811 lines 1-2, 1813 lines 2-3).
1798 line 4 ends with a stray full stop (வீழ்ந்தாள்.).
1812 line 3 சோந்தனந் looks like a misprint for சேர்ந்தனம்.
1816 line 3 செந் நில்லலா divides doubtfully (perhaps செந்நில்லா).

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised as Kantukkatan's son
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage
Civakan's companions, who have come to the hermitage in search of him
the women ascetics of the hermitage who sheltered Vijayai
the god who carried Civakan from the execution ground (named only as a deity here)
the merchant who took up and raised Civakan (mentioned)
Kantukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother (mentioned)
Civakan's father, the dead king (mentioned)
the usurper king, called கீழ்மகன் here (mentioned)

reading: A friend begins his report: Civakan, the strong-bowed first son taken up by Kantukkatan, the old merchant chief of the city, who ends the grief of all who think of him, was one day, for a fault, seized by the king.
nuance: The speaker calls Civakan என் தோழன் and names the foster father, not the true one: he does not yet know whose son he is talking to. Who the king is (Kattiyangaran) is left to the story so far; the fault (தவறு) is not named here.
event: Civakan's companion tells Vijayai that the king seized Civakan for an offence.

reading: The friend says the king had Civakan's bangled shoulders bound tight to be killed in the city of bannered mansions while the women wept, and the mother, stricken, falls like a hooded snake struck by thunder.
nuance: Line 4's வீழ்ந்தாள் shifts from the friend's report to the narrator's, so the verse carries both voices; the falling woman is named only in later verses.
event: Hearing that Civakan was bound to be put to death, Vijayai falls senseless.

tamil: மாதவப் பெருமை வண்ண மாநகர் நம்பிக் குற்ற
வேதத்தைக் கேட்ட லோடு மிருகணும் பிறழ்ந்து மாழ்கிக்
காதற்றம் மகனுக் குற்ற நவையெனக் கலங்கி வீழ்ந்தா
ராதலா னங்கை யாரே யருள்பெரி துடைய ரென்றார்.
reading: On hearing the harm that came to the young lord, the ascetic women of the great hermitage, their eyes rolling, are shaken as though it were harm to their own dear son and fall, and those present say that women indeed have great compassion.
nuance: Who falls and who speaks the closing words (என்றார்) is not stated; reading the fallers as the hermitage women and the speakers as the onlookers is a guess from line 1's மாதவப் பெருமை and line 3's தம் மகனுக்கு.
event: The ascetic women fall in grief as if Civakan were their own son.

tamil: மாழ்குபு மயங்கி வீழ்ந்த மாபெருந் தேவி தன்னை
யாழ்துய ரவித்தற் கொத்த வரும்பெறல் யோக நாடிக்
காழ்பரிந் தரைத்த சாந்தின் களிதரு நீரிற் றேற்ற
யாழ்புரை கிளவி யாற்றாண் மயங்கிவீழ்ந் தரற்று கின்றாள்.
