reading: They seek a fit remedy to quench the great queen's swoon and revive her with water thick with ground sandal, and she of the lute-like voice, unable to bear it, faints again and begins to lament.
nuance: The narrator gives her the title மாபெருந் தேவி, the queen's rank she has hidden in the hermitage, just before the friends learn it.
event: Vijayai is revived with sandal water, faints again and laments.

reading: Vijayai cries that when the guardian fell amid his sea-wide army and she rode the false peacock to the burning ground and fell there, he, her lord, appeared as her companion, and asks whether he now hides from her.
nuance: She calls the newborn எம்மானே and her companion (துணையாகி): the child born in the cremation ground is remembered as the one who stood by her there, and his reported death as his hiding from her (ஒளித்தியோ), the word the dead king's women used of him.
event: Vijayai recalls the king's death, her flight on the mechanical peacock and her son's birth at the burning ground.

reading: She laments that Kantukkatan, with his bright spear, carried the child off in joy and gave him to his wife, and that Sunandai who reared him without tiring is now struck by this harm, crying 'my lord' again and again because he has gone.
nuance: Line 3 நையாள் வளர்த்த சுநந்தை நவையுற வென் divides doubtfully; whether the harm is said to fall on Sunandai or on the speaker turns on it.
event: Vijayai recalls the merchant taking the child to his wife Sunandai, who raised him.

reading: She says the three dreams the spear-bearing king once spoke of were the raft on which she bore her life, and now her king has died without hearing her cry, and that raft has failed her.
nuance: முன்னுரைத்த points back to the king's reading of her dreams before Civakan's birth; she held to the promise of the son's crown and did not let herself weigh the falling tree he would not explain. என்னரசே here addresses the son, the king the dream promised.
event: Vijayai says the king's reading of her three dreams kept her alive and has now failed.

reading: She says that hoping to become the king's mother and see him guard the people under his umbrella, she has done only sin; she had thought that when her care was over he would bid her go and she would go, but he has gone before her.
nuance: Line 1 கோவமா வாகி is hard to divide (கோ அம்மா ஆகி, 'becoming the king's mother', is one guess), and the sense of the whole verse turns on it. The grief is the reversal of the order of deaths: a mother expected to be sent off by her son.

reading: She calls him son of the king, bull of war of the Kuru line, lord of Emamangatham, her dear life, a Kama, and says she has wrecked her ship in the sea, and asks whether he will go without seeing her tears.
nuance: In grief she says aloud what she has kept hidden: the titles கோமான் மகனே, குருகுலத்தார் போரேறே and ஏமாங்கதத்தார் இறைவா tell the listening friends that Civakan is the dead king's son.

reading: She says that hearing from those who came that the king's son was unharmed, she stayed hidden and grieved many times, and now she wastes away with this sorrow, crying 'alas, Aram, I cannot bear it'.
nuance: She addresses அறனே directly, as if the moral order owed her the son for whose sake she stayed hidden. Her concealment (மறைந்திருந்து) was the deity's counsel at the birth.
event: Vijayai tells how she lived hidden, content with reports of her son's safety.

reading: She says she once saw her son and her eyes were cooled, but the hope of seeing him once more has failed, and cries that no women like her should be born in this world; then the one with the gait of a hen-swan falls like a peacock.
nuance: Line 2 பிழைத்ததென் றேவிர்கா divides doubtfully; reading ஏவிர்காள் as a call to the women around her is a guess. The wish that no woman like her be born turns her grief into a judgement on her own birth.
event: Vijayai ends her lament and falls senseless again.

reading: Hearing the words of the queen of the garlanded king who shamed the battle elephants, the friends, hearts brimming, sigh hotly and look into one another's faces with eyes full of tears.
nuance: The recognition is wordless: they look at each other's faces. The narrator gives her the title பெருமாட்டி of the king, the knowledge they have just gained.
event: The friends realise from her lament that Vijayai is the dead king's queen and Civakan his son.

reading: Saying 'see how the deed has ripened', the friends wave their hands with bright bracelets and rise and dance for joy, saying that a life has come into being that will be Death to the base man who seized the sea-girt land.
nuance: கருமம் விளைந்தவாறு can be read as the usurper's deed ripening against him or as the fortune now ripening for Civakan; either way the friends read the queen's secret as fate's work. Their joy follows straight on her grief, since they know what she does not, that Civakan lives.
event: The friends rejoice that Civakan is the rightful heir who will destroy the usurper.

reading: As Vijayai lies fallen like a peacock, they bend over her and do many cooling things, and when she of wide spear-split eyes rises lamenting, they surround her, bow and worship and tell her how it stands with him.
nuance: They now bow and worship (தொழுது இறைஞ்சி) the woman they had addressed as a hermitage mother: the recognition changes their bearing before it changes their words.
event: The friends revive Vijayai, bow to her and begin to tell her what became of Civakan.

reading: The friends tell her that when he neared the execution ground a deity took him, saying 'this is a deity's station', and when it removed him he went, and the young man now rejoices like a tusker calf joined with a well-marked young she-elephant among the herds of the hills.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (கொண்டொர் தெய்வத / நிலைக்கள மிதுவென) divide doubtfully, so what the deity is said to have declared is unsure. The friends know only that a deity took him; the story told earlier, of the dog he once helped returning as a god, is not in their account.
event: The friends tell Vijayai that a deity carried Civakan from the execution ground and that he now lives happily with a wife.

reading: The friends say that the garlanded one, putting off his disguise, will now take on being the great son who owns the kingship, and that they have come and bowed at her red feet; she of the mango-slice eyes, rejoicing within, speaks.
nuance: போர்வை, 'the covering', is his life as a merchant's son: the friends treat the foster identity as a cloak to be thrown off now the birth is known.
event: The friends promise that Civakan will claim his kingship, and Vijayai, glad, begins to answer.

reading: Vijayai says that the guardian of the earth called Saccandan, born under Bharani, who stood unguarded against all his foes, met the end Hiranya met through the love he kept fixed on her.
nuance: பகை யாவையு / மரணி லானென்கட் divides doubtfully (அரண் இலான், 'without defence', is one reading). She blames her husband's death on his love for her, the cause the councillors had named. The comparison with இரணியன் draws on a Vaishnava story in a Jain epic, used only as a figure for a sudden violent death.
event: Vijayai tells the friends who Civakan's father was and how he died.

reading: She says that they should tell Nambi in order all the evil she, Vijayai, whose name went through the world and who is now without glory, suffered when her lord died through his attachment, and bring the young lord to her without fail.
nuance: பசையி னாற்றுஞ்சி may mean the king died of attachment or that she lay in it; the verse's account of her suffering turns on it.
event: Vijayai asks the friends to tell Civakan her story and bring him to her.

reading: She tells them to speak of this matter to no one but Nambi and to trust no one, and, since harm comes in such ways, not to talk with fools or with women.
nuance: A woman who has hidden her own rank for years bars women from the secret; the warning falls on her own sex.
event: Vijayai charges the friends to keep Civakan's birth secret.

reading: She says that the hearts of enemies, the track of a snake, the hearts of girdled women and lightning in the high cloud do not go straight, and tells the men of smoking spears to go on their way guarding themselves.
nuance: The list sets women's hearts among things whose course cannot be predicted, next to enemies and snakes; the speaker is the epic's model of the faithful wife, so the maxim is offered as prudence, not grievance.

tamil: வணக்கருஞ் சிலையி னானை யொருமதி யெல்லை நாளுட்
குணத்தொடு மலிந்த பாதங் குறுகயாங் கொணர்ந்த பின்றைப்
பணித்ததே செய்து பற்றார் பகைமுத லடர்த்து மென்றார்
மணிக்கொடி மாசுண் டன்னாண் மற்றதே துணிமி னென்றாள்.
reading: The friends promise that within one month they will bring the man of the unbending bow to her virtuous feet and then do as she commands and crush the enemy at the root, and she, like a jewelled creeper soiled, tells them to resolve on that.
nuance: The vow sets a term (ஒருமதி எல்லை) the story will have to keep, and the mother's command, not Civakan's, is to start the war on the usurper.
event: The friends vow to bring Civakan to his mother within a month, and Vijayai approves.

tamil: பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்றுப் புகரற நிறைந்த கொள்கைச்
செறிதவ விசயை பாதஞ் சென்னியின் வணங்கி மீண்டு
வெறிகமழ் சோலை நண்ணி வேண்டிய வடிசில் கைதொட்
டெறிபடை யெழுக வென்றார் வளையெழுந் தார்த்த வன்றே.
reading: Bowing their heads at the feet of Vijayai of close penance, who fasted with her senses held tight and kept a flawless rule of life, they return to the fragrant grove, eat the food they wish and order the army to rise, and the conches rise roaring.
nuance: பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று gives the widow's life in the hermitage the language of ascetic sense-restraint, in the verse that sends out an army at her command.
event: The friends take leave of Vijayai, eat in the grove and set the army marching.

tamil: பைந்துகின் மகளிர் தேன்சோர் பவளவாய் திகழ நாணிச்
சிந்தித்துக் கூந்தல் வாங்கிச் செவ்வணந் துடைப்ப தேபோ
லிந்திர கோபங் கௌவி யிறகுளர் கின்ற மஞ்ஞை
யந்தரத் திவர்ந்த பாய்மா வரும்பொற்றா ரரவத் தாலே.
reading: At the din of the golden bells of the horses leaping skyward, a peacock that had caught a red velvet-mite and was preening its feathers looks like silk-clad women who, abashed, their coral lips shining, draw back their hair and wipe away its redness.
nuance: The image of shy women wiping away red closes a chapter that has just warned against women's hearts.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1820-1842 (12/14)
theme: Civakan's friends reach the outskirts of Emamapuram and plan to raid the king's herd to draw him into battle, until Buddhisenan warns of the blame of retreat and the cost of blood; their three spies then report how Civakan tamed the king's must elephant Valaya Sundaram, rode it before the king, and was acclaimed as the one master of elephants.
structure_note: 1820-1823 the journey and the grove; 1824-1829 council (Padumukan proposes, Buddhisenan objects); 1830-1842 the spies' report of the elephant's taming.
source_issues: 1820 and 1821 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; word division in the joined lines is doubtful.
1822 line 4 தானையா is doubtful (perhaps தானையார் or தானையால்).
1830 lines 3-4 கேழரக் களைய divide doubtfully.
1834 line 1 அப்புதா தையென: word division doubtful.
1840 line 4 ends என்றதெ., probably for என்றதே.
1841 line 3 opens மௌளரும், not a Tamil word as printed (corrupt); line 2 has ஓய்யென where 1833 and 1838 have ஒய்யென.

cast.role: the hero, living under another name at Emamapuram as teacher of the princes
Civakan's friend, leader of the band that comes seeking him
Civakan's friend, called a man of the four Vedas (named புத்திசேன் in 1829)
Civakan's companions, the four friends and their force (நால்வர் in 1822 and 1829)
Padumukan's men, whom he rouses for the raid
the three spies the friends sent ahead to Emamapuram
the king of Emamapuram's elephant, which goes into must
king of Emamapuram (here only கொற்றவன்)
the royal assembly of Emamapuram, which acclaims Civakan
the great crowd watching the taming

tamil: சாந்தின்மேற் றொடுத்த தீந்தேன் றண்மதிக் கோடு போழப்
போந்துமட் டருவி வீழும் பொன்னெடுங் குன்று மந்த
ணேந்துபூங் காவு சூழ்ந்த விரும்புனல் யாறு நீந்தி
மாந்தரே மலிந்த நாடு மடுத்துடன் சென்ற தன்றே.
reading: Swimming the broad rivers ringed by flowering groves, past tall golden hills where honey hung on the sandal trees, split by the moon's horn, falls in streams of nectar, the company reached a land thick with people.
nuance: The verb சென்றது has no named subject; the next verses show it is the band of Civakan's friends travelling in search of him.
event: Civakan's companions and their force cross hills and rivers and reach a populous country.

tamil: மதுக்குலா மலங்கன் மாலை மங்கையர் வளர்த்த செந்தீப்
புதுக்கலத் தெழுந்த தீம்பாற் பொங்கலி னுரையிற் பொங்கிக்
கதிர்த்துவெண் மாடந் தோன்றுஞ் செவ்வெயிற் காத நான்கி
னதிக்கரை வந்து விட்டார் நச்செயிற் றரவோ டொப்பார்.
reading: Those who were like poison-fanged snakes came to a river bank four kaatham from the city whose white mansions rise like the foam of milk boiling over in new pots.
nuance: The companions are named only by a simile of menace, poison-fanged snakes, which prepares the plan of attack that follows.
event: The companions halt on a river bank four kaatham from Emamapuram.

reading: The four, with their force, came without delay to the white-sand bank of a forest river, a grove of honey where sunlight could not pierce, its curve like the waist of doe-eyed women.
event: The four friends reach a shaded grove on the river bank.

reading: Honey dripping, toddy breathing, flowers spread over the long sand and bees crowding the clustered blossoms above, the grove they entered had a nature hard to leave once one had come in.
event: The friends enter the grove.

reading: Seated in the rich shade, Padumukan, out of love, asks the others to say how they may reach the peerless-chested man with the honeyed garland.
event: Padumukan asks his fellows how they may reach Civakan.

reading: Padumukan proposes that once they have seized the bright herds of the glorious king's city, they will meet the mighty one face to face on the field, and no harm will come of it.
nuance: The raid is a lure: the friends count on Civakan riding out against cattle raiders as he did for the herdsmen of Rajamapuram, and on recognising him in the fight.
event: Padumukan proposes raiding the king's herds to draw Civakan out to battle.

reading: After they have traded bows, he says, if the fight comes to swords they can quickly bring him back, so rise eager; so the garlanded one told all his men.
nuance: மீட்கலாம் may mean that they can win Civakan back or that they can pull out of the fight; the sense of the plan turns on which.
event: Padumukan rouses his men for the raid.

reading: Buddhisenan objects that if, after they take the herd, the lord is not in the guarded city and the great army comes out, turning back will bring blame, and he has more to say.
nuance: The objection exposes the flaw in the lure: the plan depends on Civakan being in the city, which no one has checked.
event: Buddhisenan warns that the raid may bring the king's army and not Civakan.

reading: Like lightning flashing in a cloud-filled sky, the swords of honest warriors will flash and elephants will plunge in a flood of leaping blood, so, men of unfailing resolve, think and decide.
So spoke Buddhisenan of the four Vedas; as the four sat, agreeing that this was the point, the three spies they had sent ahead came together and announced what had happened that day.
nuance: நான்மறையினான் makes Buddhisenan a man of the four Vedas, a Brahmin counsellor among the friends. The three spies who come in agreement (ஒன்றி) recall the Kural's rule that three spies' concurring word is to be trusted, though ஒன்றி may instead go with the sending.
event: The friends accept Buddhisenan's counsel, and their three spies return with news.

reading: The spies tell of Valaya Sundaram, the king's elephant like a great mountain of collyrium, with pearl-filled tusks like the young crescent, the lord of five hundred young cow-elephants.
nuance: From here to 1842 the account follows the spies' announcement (இயம்புகின்றார்கள், 1829), and 1838's என்பவே and 1842's என்மரும் keep the voice of report; the passage may also be read as the poet's own narration. Line 3 to 4 (கேழரக் களைய) divides doubtfully.

reading: Raging in its fierce must and roaring like a rain cloud, it killed the mahouts who could not let it go, broke from its post and the cow-elephant, burst its bonds and at that hour went wild.
event: The king's elephant goes into must, kills its mahouts and breaks loose.

reading: Civakan subdued the noble elephant, whose skin seemed scorched by the fire its eyes spat and over which singing bees swarmed, and it grew meek as the minds of women in jewelled girdles.
nuance: The simile likens the tamed beast to the hearts of women won by the hero, the epic's recurring picture of Civakan as one who masters both.
event: Civakan subdues the raging elephant.

reading: Like a lion with shining teeth climbing a steep hill, the broad-chested man seized the rope and swiftly mounted the rare elephant, and the great crowd roared like the sea's waves.
event: Civakan mounts the elephant and the crowd roars.

reading: As the garlanded youth patted it with his palm, calling it fondly, the great elephant, swelling with joy, did with its trunk the trained responses it knew.
nuance: அப்புதா தையென is read here as fond calls to the beast (அப்பு, தாதை); the word division is doubtful.
event: Civakan calms the elephant with pats and it answers to his commands.

reading: He bound the neck rope doubled with its tassel knot, set the goad in his strong hand, tied on the two bells together and fastened the shining gold forehead plate, like lightning on a snowy hill.
event: Civakan harnesses the elephant with rope, goad, bells and forehead plate.

reading: He girded its belt, hung on the two sounding bells, set both his feet in the rope at its head and neck, and showed such strength that even the king above longed to see him.
event: Civakan finishes the harness and sits ready, admired by the king.

reading: When the victorious king, standing within the walled women's quarter, said 'let us see the lord's riding; bring it here', Civakan drove the elephant in like wind, like the sea, like thunder on a black hill, like Death.
nuance: The king is not named; he is presumably Tadamittan of Emamapuram, Civakan's host. கோற்றொடிப் புரிசை, the enclosure of the bangled women, puts the display before the palace women, among them Kanakamalai.
event: At the king's bidding Civakan rides the elephant into the palace court.

reading: They say he sat beyond any painter's power, like a young god flying lightly with a hill in his grasp, or a god riding a rain cloud.
nuance: Who the young god carrying a hill is (குழவியஞ் செல்வன்) is not clear from the verse; the image fits the hero high on the mountain-like beast.

reading: Like a potter's spinning wheel, or the wheel of time that runs over living beings with swift horses, he made it trace in a twinkling the circles, the straight courses and the rows that the art requires.
nuance: The second simile is காலசக்கரம், the wheel of time that passes over living lives: a reminder of mortality set inside a display of horsemanship.
event: Civakan puts the elephant through its circling and straight gaits.

reading: One man and one elephant looked like a hundred thousand wandering in every direction, and the discerning royal assembly declared there was no one else in the world who could own an elephant, and said no more.
event: The king's assembly proclaims Civakan the one true master of elephants.

reading: When he pressed its striped brow with the tip of his nail, the understanding elephant stood still at once, its two bells rang, and the flood-like crowd shook their hands in wonder.
nuance: Line 3's மௌளரும் is not a Tamil word as printed; the bells' sound is clear, the opening word is not.
event: At a touch of his nail the elephant halts and the crowd marvels.

reading: Some say that the good-minded elephant moved with the prince as if saying 'my mind and yours are not two', like one telling himself what is in his own heart.
nuance: The words of union, my mind and yours not two, are the lovers' and friends' language, here given to a rider and his beast; என்மரும் marks it as one view among those who saw.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1843-1865 (13/14)
theme: After the elephant's taming the city hails Civakan; his companions, guided by disguised spies, raid the king's herds dressed as hill raiders to draw him out, interrupting Nandattan just as he is about to tell the king their lineage; Civakan vows to bring the raiders captive, but Padumukan's arrow greets him as a crowned king's only son, and the friends bow at his feet and ride with him into the city.
source_issues: 1852-1862 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
திண்டோ (1858, 1859, 1860, 1862) and தோமேல் (1863) read as if for திண்டேர் and தேர்மேல்: the chariot word appears to have been mis-transcribed (ர read as ா), consistently across five verses.
1847 line 4 (அரணம் வீசினார்) and 1849 line 4 (ஆனிடை யழித்தபுள்) are hard to construe; 1863 line 3 (பின்முனா) is obscure.

cast.role: the hero, a guest at Tadamittan's court, called சீவக குமரன் in 1860
Civakan's younger brother, who drives his chariot
king of Hemamapuram, Kanakamalai's father (unnamed here: மன்னன், வேந்தன், கோ)
the king's sons, Civakan's pupils in arms (குமரர், மைந்தர்)
the people of the city who praise Civakan after he subdues the elephant
Civakan's friend, leader of the companions who stage the cattle raid
the spies the companions sent out, here in disguise
the warriors of Civakan's companions, dressed as hill raiders
Civakan's companions
the herdsmen of the king's cattle (கோவலர், ஆயர்)
Tadamittan's army sent to recover the herd

reading: Some in the crowd call the son a god in his beauty and good fortune, others say the girl must have done penance to win him, while the king and his sons look on his shoulders with cool delight, and the cry of the world rises high.
nuance: நோற்றனள் makes Kanakamalai's good match the fruit of her own austerity; the crowd's two sayings set the hero's worth beside the bride's merit, the usual pair of the Cintamani's wedding praises.
event: The city hails Civakan after he subdues the elephant, and the king and his sons gaze at him in delight.

reading: Those who saw it say they saw with their own eyes the man who bound the great elephant that eats balls of rice, with his younger brother, enter the palace while bards and heralds sang and the great city bowed.
event: Civakan and Nandattan enter the palace to the songs of bards as the city bows.

reading: At the word of his spies in disguise Padumukan, of matchless fame, joyfully gave them rich wealth, and his warriors, crowding like a shoal of sharks, took up bows, swords and shining spears.
nuance: படிவ ஒற்றாளர் are spies in a borrowed guise; the verse does not say whose. The scene shifts abruptly from the palace to the friends' camp, and the reader learns only from 1863 why armed men are gathering.
event: Padumukan rewards the disguised spies who found Civakan, and his men arm themselves.

reading: Men learned in refined treatises, whose horses had pressed their hooves on bee-swarmed elephants after breaching walls of spears and swords in fierce battle, laughed that rounding up a herd of cows was hardly a task, and harnessed their horses together.
nuance: The laugh is double: a cattle raid is trivial for warriors who have stormed fortresses, and this one is a feint meant only to draw Civakan out.
event: Padumukan's men laugh at the smallness of a cattle raid and ready their horses.

reading: They went to swallow up the herds with their bulls; small drums, tudi and white conches sounded, and the young warriors of killing arms, with clustered anklets, raised a din that rose to the sky and flung on their armour.
nuance: அரணம் வீசினார் is hard to fix: அரணம் may be armour or a defence, and வீசினார் may mean they put it on or threw it aside.
event: Padumukan's young warriors set out to seize the king's herds with drums and conches.

reading: They wore wreaths of fragrant kantal on their brows, carefully measured garments, quivers of split bamboo swinging on their backs, and bright axes on their shoulders.
nuance: Kantal wreaths, bamboo quivers and axes are the gear of hill raiders: the companions come dressed as the hunters of the first cattle raid, so the herdsmen take them for real raiders.

reading: The cowherds who keep the king's herds said that while they watched over the herd in the forest where bees hum over the honeyed flowers, a bird had spoiled things among the cattle.
nuance: ஆனிடை அழித்த புள் probably names an ill-omened bird, as in the herdsmen's warning before the first raid (420), but the line can also be read as a bird of prey among the cattle; whether the cowherds speak before or after the raid is unclear.
event: The king's cowherds speak of a bird that harmed the herd in the forest.

reading: The raiders scattered killing arrows from bows bright as hooded snakes, the white conches roared, and when the cowherds saw the swift horses charging they ran off at full speed.
event: The raiders shower arrows and the cowherds flee before the horses.

reading: Men like great tigers in their dens surrounded the fine herd; the hard-eyed herdsmen let out fearful cries, raised the alarm and ran to report it.
event: The raiders surround the herd and the herdsmen run crying to the city.

tamil: தோத்தொகைத் தானை மன்னன் சீவகற் கிளைய நம்பி
வார்த்தொகை முழவம் விம்ம மல்லுறழ் தோளி னானை
நீர்த்தொகைக் கழனி நாடு நெடுநகர்ப் பெயரு நுங்கள்
சீர்த்தொகைக் குலனு மெல்லாந் தெரிந்தெமக் குரைமோ வென்றான்.
reading: The king of the vast army said to Civakan's younger brother, of wrestler's shoulders, while the drums throbbed: tell us your country of watered fields, the name of your great city and the glory of your line.
nuance: The question is the one the whole ilampakam turns on: Civakan has come as a stranger and his birth as Saccandan's son is still hidden from his host.
event: Tadamittan asks Nandattan his country, city and lineage.

tamil: திருக்குறிப் பன்ன தாயிற் செப்புவ லடிகள் செம்பொ
னரித்தசும் பொழுகு குன்றத் தருவியின் வெரீஇய மஞ்ஞை
பரித்தவை பழன நாரைப் பார்ப்பொடு மருதிற் சேக்கு
முரைத்தகு நாடு மூருங் குலத்துட னுணர வென்றான்.
reading: Nandattan answers that if it please his lord he will tell the land, town and lineage: a land where peacocks frightened by the cascades of hills that spill red gold sleep on marutam trees beside the young of the paddy-field storks.
nuance: The peacock of the hills roosting among the marutam storks sets kurinji and marutam side by side: the land is praised as one where every region meets.
event: Nandattan begins to describe his homeland to the king.

tamil: பொருகய லுகளிப் பாயப் பூஞ்சிறைக் குமரி யன்னங்
குருகினோ டிரியச் செந்நெற் கொழுங்கதிர் குவளை யெற்ற
முருகுவிண் டிரியத் தீந்தேன் முழங்குநீர்க் கழனி நன்னா
டெரியுமிழ்ந் திலங்கும் வேலோ யேமமாங் கதம தென்றான்.
reading: He says the good land where carp leap, swans go with herons, the paddy ears strike the kuvalai flowers and honey spills into the sounding water of the fields is Emangatham, lord of the flaming spear.

tamil: பூந்துகிற் கொடுத்த தீந்தே னகிற்புகை பொன்ன னார்தங்
கூந்தலிற் குளித்த வண்டு கொப்புளித் திட்ட வாச
மாந்தர்மேற் றவழ்ந்து மாட மிருள்படப் புதையுஞ் செல்வத்
தேந்துபொன் னிஞ்சி மூதூ ரிராசமா புரம தென்றான்.
reading: He says the ancient city of golden walls, whose mansions are darkened by the scented smoke of honey and agil from women's hair, drifting over the people, is Rajamapuram.

tamil: எங்குல மடிகள் கேட்க வென்றலு மெழுந்தோர் பூசல்
பொங்குளைப் புரவி வெள்ளம் போக்கற வளைத்து முற்றி
யிங்குள நிரையை யெல்லாங் கவர்ந்ததென் றிட்ட போழ்தே
திங்கள் வெண்குடையி னான்றன் றிருச்செவிக் கிசைத்த தன்றே.
reading: As he said 'let my lord hear our lineage', an outcry broke out that a flood of horses with tossing manes had surrounded and carried off all the herds here, and it reached the ears of the king of the moon-white umbrella.
nuance: The interruption falls at the very word குலம்: the brother names land and city but never the line, so Civakan's birth stays hidden one scene longer, and the friends' raid, staged to find him, is what cuts the telling short.
event: The news of the raid interrupts Nandattan before he names his lineage, and reaches the king.

tamil: எரித்திறல் வென்றி வேந்தற் கிற்றென விசைப்பச் சீறி
மருப்புறக் கந்து பாய்ந்து முழங்குமால் களிறு போலத்
திருக்கிளர் மணிசெய் பொற்றூண் டீப்படப் புடைத்துச் செங்க
ணுருத்தெரி தவழ நோக்கி யுடல்சினங் கடவச் சொன்னான்.
reading: Told of it, the victorious king raged like a bull elephant that tusks its post and trumpets, struck a jewelled golden pillar till sparks flew, and with red eyes blazing and anger driving his body, spoke.
event: Tadamittan, enraged by the news, strikes a pillar and speaks.

tamil: நாற்கடற் பரப்பும் வந்து நன்னகர்க் கண்ணுற் றென்ன
வேற்கடற் றானை பாய்மா விளங்கொளி யிவுளித் திண்டோ
கூற்றென முழங்கு மோடைக் குஞ்சரக் குழாத்தோ டேகிப்
பாற்கடற் பரப்பின் வல்லே படுநிரை பெயர்க்க வென்றான்.
reading: He orders that, as if the four seas had come into the city, the sea of spears, the horses, the strong chariots and the herds of elephants roaring like death go out at once and drive back the seized herd.
event: Tadamittan orders his whole army out to recover the herd.

tamil: கண்ணகன் கடலங் கோடும் பறைகளு முழங்கி விம்ம
விண்ணகத் தியங்கு மேகக் குழாமென நிரைத்த வேழந்
திண்ணுகப் புரவித் திண்டோ விரைந்தன நிரந்த பாய்மா
மண்ணக மலிரக் காலாட் கடல்கிளர்ந் தெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: Drums and horns sounded over the broad moat, elephants ranged like herds of cloud in the sky, chariots with strong yokes and horses sped, and the foot soldiers rose like a sea till the earth shook.
event: The king's army marches out.

tamil: பானிறக் கவரி நெற்றிப் பசுங்கிளி நிறத்த பாய்மாத்
தானுறப் பண்ணித் திண்டோத் தம்பிகோல் கொள்ள வேறிக்
கூனிறக் குழவித் திங்கட் குளிர்கதி ரார மார்பிற்
றேனிறங் கொண்ட கண்ணிச் சீவக குமரன் சொன்னான்.
reading: Having his horses, green as parrots with milk-white plumes on their brows, yoked to the strong chariot, with his younger brother taking the reins, Civaka Kumaran, his chest hung with a pearl chain cool as the crescent moon, mounted and spoke.
event: Civakan mounts his chariot with Nandattan driving and speaks.

tamil: மன்னவ னிரைகொண் டாரை வளநகர்த் தந்து மன்னன்
பொன்னவிர் கழலிற் றங்கள் புனைமுடி யிடுவி யேனே
லின்னிசை யுலகந் தன்னு ளென்பெயர் சேற லின்றாய்க்
கன்னிய மகளிர் நெஞ்சிற் காமம்போற் கரக்க வென்றான்.
reading: Civakan vows that if he does not bring those who seized the king's herd to the city and make them lay their crowns at the king's golden anklets, let his name not go out in the world of sweet song but lie hidden like desire in the hearts of maidens.
nuance: The pledge is a self-curse on his fame, and its simile is love's: a name hidden like a maiden's unspoken longing. He is staking his reputation for a host king who does not yet know who he is.
event: Civakan vows to bring the raiders captive to Tadamittan.

tamil: பார்மலி பரவைத் தானைப் பரப்பிடைப் பறப்ப தேபோ
னீர்மலி கடாத்த கொண்மூ நெற்றிமேன் மின்னி னொய்தாத்
தார்மலி மார்பன் றிண்டோ தோன்றலுந் தறுகண் மைந்தன்
சீர்மலி பகழி யேந்திப் பதுமுகன் சிலைதொட் டானே.
reading: As the garlanded hero's strong chariot appeared in the midst of the army that spread over the earth, flying like lightning across a cloud heavy with rain, the bold youth Padumukan took up a fine arrow and set it to his bow.
event: Padumukan sees Civakan's chariot and fits an arrow to his bow.

tamil: குடைநிழற் கொற்ற வேந்த னொருமகற் காணக் குன்றா
வடிநிழ லுறைய வந்தே மடியம்யா மென்ன வெய்த
விடுகணை சென்று தோமேற் பின்முனா வீழ்த லோடுந்
தொடுகழற் குருசி னோக்கித் தூத்துகில் வீசி னானே.
reading: Padumukan's arrow, sent as if saying 'we your servants have come to see the only son of the victorious king of the shading umbrella and to dwell in the shade of his unfailing feet', flew and fell on the chariot, and the anklet-wearing prince looked at it and waved a white cloth.
nuance: என்ன leaves open whether the arrow bore a written message or only meant this; பின்முனா வீழ்தல் may say it fell butt first, a sign it was not shot to harm. The greeting names Civakan as the only son of a crowned king, the lineage his brother had just failed to tell.
event: Padumukan's arrow carries the companions' greeting to Civakan, who answers by waving a white cloth.

tamil: சேந்தன கண்ணி னாலுந் திண்ணெழிற் றோளி னாலும்
வாய்ந்தவின் சொல்லி னாலு மாலைதாழ் முடியி னாலு
மாய்ந்தவன் சிறப்புச் செய்தா னவலநோ யவருந் தீர்ந்தார்.
reading: All the companions fell worshipping at the hero's feet, and with his reddened eyes, strong shoulders, fitting sweet words and garlanded crown he honoured them, and their grief was ended.
nuance: The four instruments of honour, eyes, shoulders, words and crown, mean a look, an embrace, a greeting and a bow of the head; அவலநோய் names the grief that had made them plan revenge and death.
event: The companions fall at Civakan's feet, he honours them, and their grief ends.

tamil: கழலவாய்க் கிடந்த நோன்றாட் காளைதன் காத லாரை
நிழலவா யிறைஞ்சி நீங்கா நெடுங்களிற் றெருத்த மேற்றி
யழலவாய்க் கிடந்த வைவே லரசிளங் குமரர் சூழக்
குழலவாய்க் கிடந்த கோதை தாதையூர் கொண்டு புக்கான்.
reading: The young bull of strong anklet-bound legs set his dear friends, who bowed in his shade, on the necks of tall elephants, and with the young princes of fiery spears around him entered the city of the garlanded lady's father.
event: Civakan brings his companions on elephants into Kanakamalai's father's city.

title: கனகமாலையார் இலம்பகம் 1866-1888 (14/14)
theme: The companions arrive at Kanakamalai's city, are received by the king and feasted by the princess; Civakan reads Gandharvadattai's sulking letter, with its gifts, its cover-story to the Vidyadharas and its report of Gunamalai's wasting; he hears that his mother lives as an ascetic, weeps, the companions declare his Kuru birth to the king, and he takes leave of Kanakamalai and rides out.
source_issues: 1880-1888 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
1870 line 1 (தழுமுற்றும்), 1875 lines 1-2, 1879 line 4 and 1887 line 4 (புள்ளாவிச் செங்கழுநீர்க் குவளை செய்தாள்) are hard to construe as printed.
1867 line 4 reads புறகக் களற்றான், probably for கழற்றான் (the anklet-wearer); 1869 line 4 ஓமின்னு may be a mis-division of தோமின்னு or similar.
The verses name neither the letter-bearer of 1872 nor the king; both identifications rest on the story.

cast.role: the hero, called சீவக சாமி in 1872, about to leave Kanakamalai's city
Civakan's companions, come from his mother to fetch him
Civakan's brahmin companion (நான்மறையினான் in 1829), taken here as the bearer of the letter
the king of the city, Kanakamalai's father (called மன்னன், வேந்தன், நரதேவன் here; the name is not in these verses)
the king's sons, Civakan's pupils (சிறுவர் in 1888)
Civakan's wife in this city, named only by epithets in these verses
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife, who writes the letter and signs as தத்தை
Vidyadhara king, Gandharvadattai's father, who sends gifts (எம் மன்னன் in 1874)
the Vidyadhara of Kaluzhavegan's service, to whom Gandharvadattai gives a covering account
Civakan's wife in the old city, whose wasting Gandharvadattai reports

reading: In the old city of mansions whose flags wave in the sky, the companions, like lions come down from a herd of elephants, dismount while the women of the mansions, with sweet speech and doe-like eyes, worship them and the young men praise them.
event: Civakan's companions dismount from their elephants in Kanakamalai's city amid the townspeople's welcome.

reading: Watched with longing by the long-eyed women, they enter the palace whose red gold outshines the young sun, come in by the king's grace, and bow at the feet of the gold-anklet king.
event: The companions enter the palace and bow at the king's feet.

reading: As the king, his broad chest bright with his jewels, looks at his son-in-law's face, Civakan tells him that all these young men are his friends, dear as his own life.
nuance: Civakan addresses his father-in-law as அடிகள், and the king is seen looking at him as மருமான், his son-in-law: the scene places the companions inside a family before it places them in a court.
event: Civakan presents the companions to the king as his dearest friends.

reading: The king of the diamond crown and jewelled anklets graciously bids them go and see the lady whose waist flickers like lightning in a cloud, and they bow and go.
nuance: Line 4 opens ஓமின்னு தாரான், which the stanza join leaves hard to divide; the sense that the king bids them go is clear from காண்க சென்று என்று.
event: The king sends the companions to meet Kanakamalai.

reading: In the palace hung with garlands she stands like a lamp that lights the whole house by itself, a jewelled creeper; the companions bow to her, she looks at them knowing who they are, and affection wells up in the bright-bangled lady.
nuance: The opening word தழுமுற்றும் is obscure as printed.
event: Kanakamalai receives the companions, who bow to her.

reading: The princess of the old city they call heaven itself laughs, 'Are these the thieves who drove off the herd? These are the men to be punished,' and having teased them, feasts them as lavishly as a rich man's daughter.
nuance: The joke has a ground: the companions had just seized the king's herd to draw Civakan out to battle (1845-1863), so the 'thieves' she would punish are her husband's friends, now her guests. The phrase வெறுக்கைக் கிழவன் மகள் may also glance at Civakan's upbringing in a merchant's house.
event: Kanakamalai teases the companions as the cattle thieves and then feasts them.

reading: The companion who keeps only the hard fire-rites and expounds all the Vedas as a feast gives a palm-leaf letter to Civaka Sami, who sits apart, and Civakan, removing the seal pressed by the bright earring, looks into it.
nuance: The letter-bearer is named only by his rites; Buddhisenan is the companion called நான்மறையினான் in 1829, so the identification rests on the story. எரி குண்டலத்தால் may name the earring that made the seal (1768) or the earrings Civakan wears.
event: A brahmin companion hands Civakan Gandharvadattai's sealed letter and he breaks the seal.

reading: The letter opens: let the lord see and grant it; under his flower feet his little servant Tattai falls at his feet, and she prays that the protections she has set within for his feet, his food and his bath may keep him well, and falls at his feet again.
nuance: Three times in four lines the Vidyadhara princess falls at his feet (அடிவீழ்ச்சி, அடிவீழ்ந்தேன்): the letter's courtesy is a wife's self-abasement written out, which makes the sulking at its end sharper.
event: Gandharvadattai's letter opens with her obeisance and the protective charms she sends.

reading: She lists what her king has sent: diamond and jewelled ornaments, a fragrant garland of the wish-granting tree, a heady drink, a staff and robes, flawless sandal paste, bow and arrows, a jewelled lance and a sword, and a cloak of the hair-rat's fur.
nuance: The gifts mix a bridegroom's finery with arms; மயிர் எலியின் போர்வை is the fabled cloak of a rat's hair, a Vidyadhara wonder.
event: Gandharvadattai's letter lists the gifts her father the Vidyadhara king sends Civakan.

reading: She writes that when the one who came was brought in secret so that no one knew, and Taran asked, she told him that this was the lord's own resolve: that the jewel of men was there with his kin and would stay there to the term of five months.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 (வந்தவனை ... தந்து) is hard to fix, and who 'the one who came' is, Nandattan or Taran, is not certain; the sense that she answered Taran's question with a story of a planned absence is carried on by 1876.
event: Gandharvadattai tells Civakan she gave Taran a covering account of his absence.

reading: Fearing that the blame he had fallen into would spread over the Silver Mountain, she sent Taran off with another message; for what can come from a woman with a blossoming garland except to guard against blame that has fallen and spread fame?
nuance: The duty she names is served by a falsehood: what she told Taran (1875) was not what had happened, and she says so to her husband without apology. The blame (பழி) is the disgrace of a Vidyadhara's son-in-law vanishing after his arrest.
event: Gandharvadattai sends Taran away with a false message to keep Civakan's disappearance from her father's people.

reading: Besides, she writes, her younger sister Gunamalai cannot bear it: seeing the moon move she says 'day, you are short', looking at the many-rayed sun she says 'moon, you are long'; the delicate one cannot tell whether it is morning or not.
nuance: Gandharvadattai calls her co-wife எங்கை, my younger sister, and pleads her case to their husband: the co-wives are allied in his absence. The confusion of sun and moon is the lovesick woman's loss of the day's order.

reading: Her wide mound like a cobra's hood lies on the ground, the bright girdle like a rainbow has slipped from her, and brow, moon-face, praised shoulders and close-set breasts have lost their form; your servant cannot tell whether she still lives.
nuance: அடிச்சி may be Gandharvadattai speaking of herself (your servant does not know) or the subject of the doubt (whether your servant Gunamalai lives); both read.

reading: Told 'he comes tomorrow, do not grieve', she is glad, and laughing she says to her parrot, 'Is the day called tomorrow near, or very far? Tell me when tomorrow is'; every day of this lady's grief is such a day.
nuance: The four lines each begin with நாள், and the promise of 'tomorrow' becomes a riddle the girl puts to her parrot, so the comfort itself measures how long the waiting is. Line 4 is hard to construe.

tamil: நோக்கவே தளிர்த்து நோக்கா திமைப்பினு நுணுகு நல்லார்
பூக்கம ழமளிச் சேக்கும் புதுமண வாள னார்தா
நீப்பிலார் நெஞ்சி னுள்ளா ராதலா னினைத்தல் செய்யேன்
போக்குவல் பொழுதுந் தாந்தம் பொன்னடி போற்றி யென்றாள்.
reading: Of the women who flourish when he looks at them and waste if he does not look even for a blink, she says: the new bridegroom who lies on flower-scented beds dwells in the hearts of those who never leave him, so she will not need to remember him, and will pass her days praising his golden feet.
nuance: புதுமணவாளனார், 'the new bridegroom', is the reproach: he has married again in this city. The pledge of worship is the sulk (புலவி, 1881) in its politest form.
event: Gandharvadattai closes her letter with a sulking pledge of devotion.

tamil: இலவம்பூ வாக்குண் டன்ன பஞ்சிமெல் லடியி னாடன்
புலவிச்சொற் பொறித்த வோலை திருமுடி துளக்கி நோக்கித்
தலைவைத்த காப்பு விஞ்சை கொண்டபின் றாமஞ் சூழ்ந்து
கொலைவைத்த குருதி வேலான் றோழரைக் குறுகி னானே.
reading: Having read with a shake of his crowned head the letter in which the lady of feet soft as silk-cotton had inscribed her sulking words, and having taken the protective spell set for his head, the garlanded hero of the bloodied spear goes over to his companions.
nuance: The verse names the letter's tone itself, புலவிச்சொல்: the narrator reads the courteous letter as a lover's sulk.
event: Civakan reads the letter, takes up the protective spell it carries and goes to his companions.

reading: When he asks where they heard of his affairs, they tell him that they met the beloved great queen of the king of the just sceptre, who has taken the form of unceasing penance and lives guarded in the Dandaka forest, and learned it from her.
nuance: They name Vijayai only as the queen of a king of செங்கோல், and the dead Saccandan is still given the just sceptre that was taken from him.
event: The companions tell Civakan they found his mother living as an ascetic in the Dandaka forest.

reading: Eagerly asking 'What? What is it you said?', he hears them tell it all again in order as before, and tears from his lotus eyes pour over his golden chest like scattered gems, and he grieves.
event: Civakan, hearing of his mother, weeps.

reading: He asks whether his lady mother is then alive; told this is how she has lived, he cries that to those who bore him there is no sorrow that does not come, asks where, where she is, turns to face that way, worships her feet in anguish and goes to the king's palace.
nuance: என்னைப் பெறவல்லார்க்கு எய்தா இடருளவே: he counts his mother's sufferings as the cost of having borne him, taking the blame on himself rather than on her fate or her enemies.
event: Civakan learns his mother lives, worships toward her and goes to the king.

tamil: கலைவிரவு தீஞ்சொல் லார்காம னென்றார் கமழ் தாரார்.
reading: The king, wanting to know the hero's clan, looks to the young man's friends, and the garlanded men answer that the prince of the murderous spear is of the Kuru clan, a Kama to the sweet-voiced women.
event: The companions tell the king that Civakan is of the Kuru clan.

reading: Saying that if the lord is of the Kuru clan then what he had guessed before is so, and that the young man who hid it has come out, the king embraces his golden chest, takes counsel with ministers of subtle learning, sends him on by the proper way, and enters his palace.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are the king's words without a verb of speech, and விடுத்தான் may mean he dismissed the companions or sent Civakan on; the run of the story favours Civakan's leave-taking.
event: The king, his guess at Civakan's birth confirmed, embraces him, consults his ministers and lets him go.

reading: 'Beloved young daughter of the king of broad unyielding shoulders, lady of fragrant flowers that bubble with honey, you are the life within my heart; you are not left behind,' he says, and the jewelled lady ... with the red water-lily in her hand.
nuance: Line 4, புள்ளாவிச் செங்கழுநீர்க் குவளை செய்தாள், is not secure: it may say that her hot breath withered the red lily in her hand, a sign of grief at parting, but the reading cannot be fixed.
event: Civakan takes leave of Kanakamalai, telling her she is the life in his heart.

reading: Embracing her so that the lady of bangled bamboo-like arms is glad at heart and her tearful eyes are cooled, the long-armed one leaves her, embraces the broad chests of the king's sons, mounts his horse, and the conches sound.
event: Civakan embraces Kanakamalai and her brothers and rides out to the sound of conches.

title: விமலையார் இலம்பகம் 1889-1910 (1/5)
theme: Leaving Kanakamalai's city, Civakan hears his brother's counsel against trust and poison, crosses rich mountains to the hermitage, and is reunited with his mother Vijayai, now an ascetic.
source_issues: Most verses of 1889-1910 (except 1896-1905, 1909) were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1890 line 4 has a stray letter: புல்லாள்ட்.
1892 line 2 அரிறபத் திமிரி reads corruptly.
1899 line 3 விண்ணுளு வுண்டென is doubtful.
1900 line 1 கிலுத்தமற் றவற்றியற் divides doubtfully and may be corrupt.
1909 line 3 சோந்து looks corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, on his way from Kanakamalai's city to his mother
Civakan's younger brother (தம்பி), who counsels him and gives orders for his safety
Civakan's friend, charged with guarding him and sent to his mother
Civakan's companions
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, now living as an ascetic in the hermitage (தேவி, அடிகள்)
those who say a tree has no life, mocked in 1907

tamil: முருகுகொப் புளிக்குங் கண்ணி முறிமிடை படலை மாலைக்
குருதிகொப் புளிக்கும் வேலான் கூந்தன்மா விவர்ந்து செல்ல
வுருவவெஞ் சிலையி னாற்குத் தம்பியிஃ துரைக்கு மொண்பொற்
பருகுபைங் கழலி னாருட் பதுமுகன் கேட்க வென்றே.
reading: As Civakan, his spear dripping blood and his garland woven of fragrant flowers and tender leaves, rides off on the maned horse, his younger brother speaks to him so that Padumukan among the gold-anklet warriors may hear.
nuance: The bowman (சிலையினான்) is Civakan and the speaker is his தம்பி, Nandattan, who came to him in the last ilampakam; the advice of the next verses is meant for Padumukan, who will carry it out.
event: Civakan rides out from Kanakamalai's city and his younger brother begins to speak to him in Padumukan's hearing.

tamil: விழுமணி மாசு மூழ்கிக் கிடந்ததிவ் வுலகம் விற்பக்
கழுவினீர் பொதிந்து சிக்கக் கதிரொளி மறையக் காப்பிற்
றழுவினீ ருலக மெல்லாந் தாமரை யுறையுஞ் செய்யாள்
வழுவினார் தம்மைப் புல்லாள்ட் வாழ்கநுங் கண்ணி மாதோ.
reading: The brother blesses Civakan: this world lies like a fine gem sunk in grime, waiting to be washed and to shine again, and the lady of the lotus does not embrace those who slip, so long may his garland flourish.
nuance: The gem in grime is most likely the kingdom under the usurper, which Civakan must wash clean; lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe, and line 4 has a stray letter (புல்லாள்ட்).

tamil: தொழுததங் கையி னுள்ளுந் துறுமுடி யகத்துஞ் சோர
வழுதகண் ணீரி னுள்ளு மணிகலத் தகத்து மாய்ந்து
பழுதுகண் ணரிந்து கொல்லும் படையுட னெடுங்கும் பற்றா
தொழிகயார் கண்ணுந் தேற்றந் தெளிகுற்றார் விளிகுற் றாரே.
reading: He warns that weapons lie hidden in hands joined in worship, in a crown of hair, in weeping tears and in jewelled vessels, and kill when a fault is found, so trust no one's eyes: those who trusted have died.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 take up the wording of Kural 828 (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் ... அழுதகண் ணீரும்) with words inserted between (தொழுத தம் கையினுள்ளும், அழுத கண்ணீரினுள்ளும்), so it is not marked as an echo under the four-word rule, but the debt is plain. The epic extends the couplet's list to hair and jewel caskets, and closes on a judgment the couplet leaves unsaid: those who trusted are dead.

tamil: தோய்தகை மகளிர்த் தோயின் மெய்யணி நீக்கித் தூய்நீ
ராய்முது மகளிர் தம்மா லரிறபத் திமிரி யாட்டி
வேய்நிறத் தோளி னார்க்கு வெண்டுகின் மாலை சாந்தந்
தானல கலங்கள் சேர்த்தித் தடமுலை தோய்க வென்றான்.
reading: He orders that any women who are to touch the prince first be stripped of their ornaments, bathed in pure water and rubbed down by old women, then given white silk, garlands, sandal and fresh good ornaments, and only then let them embrace him.
nuance: The danger is poison carried on a woman's body or jewels; line 2 (அரிறபத் திமிரி) reads corruptly.

tamil: வண்ணப்பூ மாலை சாந்தம் வாலணி கலன்க ளாடை
கண்முகத் துறுத்தித் தூய்மை கண்டலாற் கொள்ள வேண்டா
வண்ணலம் புள்ளோ டல்லா வாயிரம் பேடைச் சேவ
லுண்ணுநீ ரமிழ்தங் காக்க யூகமோ டாய்க வென்றான்.
reading: Garlands, sandal, ornaments and clothes are not to be taken until their purity has been seen with the eyes, and the water and food he takes are to be guarded and tested with birds, the noble swan and the cock with its many hens.
nuance: Line 3 and the close of line 4 (யூகமோ டாய்க) are hard to fix: the birds seem to be poison-testers, and யூகம் may be judgment or a name.

tamil: அஞ்சனக் கோலி னாற்றா நாகமோ ரருவிக் குன்றிற்
குஞ்சாம் புலம்பி வீழக் கூர்நுதி யெயிற்றிற் கொல்லும்
பஞ்சியின் மெல்லி தேனும் பகைசிறி தென்ன வேண்டா
வஞ்சித்தற் காத்தல் வேண்டு மரும்பொரு ளாக வென்றான்.
reading: As a snake no thicker than a collyrium stick, on a hill of waterfalls, kills an elephant with its sharp fang so that it falls bellowing, so no enemy should be called small, even one softer than cotton; one must guard against deceit as against the loss of a precious thing.

tamil: பொருந்தலாற் பல்லி போன்றும் போற்றலாற் றாய ரொத்து
மருந்தவர் போன்று காத்து மடங்கலா லாமை போன்றுந்
திருந்துவேற் றெவ்வர் போலத் தீதற வெறிந்து மின்ப
மருந்தினான் மனைவி யொத்து மதலையைக் காமி னென்றான்.
reading: He bids them guard the one in their charge like a lizard in clinging close, like mothers in care, like great ascetics, like a tortoise in drawing in, like spear-bearing foes in cutting away harm, and like a wife in giving him delight.
nuance: மதலை may mean the child (here Civakan, cherished like a son) or the prop of the house; the sense of the ascetics' simile (மருந்தவர்) is not certain.

tamil: பூந்துகின் மாலை சாந்தம் புனைகலம் பஞ்ச வாச
மாய்ந்தளந் தியற்றப் பட்ட படிசினீ ரின்ன வெல்லா
மாந்தரின் மடங்க லாற்றற் பதுமுகன் காக்க வென்றாங்
கேந்துபூண் மார்ப னேவ வின்னண மியற்றி னானே.
reading: Clothes, garlands, sandal, ornaments, the five scents and the measured prepared water, all these Padumukan, a lion among men, is to guard; so the broad-chested one commanded, and Padumukan did as told.
nuance: The one who commands (ஏந்துபூண் மார்பன்) is taken to be the brother who has been speaking since 1889, but the epithet could fit Civakan.
event: Nandattan puts Padumukan in charge of everything that touches Civakan, and Padumukan carries out the order.

reading: On the way, a herd of small-eyed elephants tires, monkeys leap about not knowing a rock from what they take, and a yak, struck by fragrant sandal pieces, shrinks and spreads its hair.
nuance: The mountain description opens; the order of who throws what at whom is hard to fix from the joined words.

reading: On the famed hilltop, many-haired rats bigger than cats and red as coral dig up vermilion and pour it on the collyrium-dark hill, like the face-cloth on the brow of an elephant.
Where mountain goats leap on the peak, bright gems break and fall as dust, and every broad tree beneath looks like a wishing tree of heaven.
nuance: Line 3 (விண்ணுளு வுண்டென) is doubtful; it may compare the falling dust to something in the sky.

reading: Trees ripen near the deer, pythons lie sleeping in the forest like fallen palms, and when they wake the lion in its gold cave roars.
nuance: Line 1 (கிலுத்தமற் றவற்றியற்) is hard to divide and probably corrupt.

reading: On the slope, among timisu and sandal, the sweet-scented trees, takkolam, clove, camphor and musk spread their fragrance for a yojana.
Herds of large-eyed beasts stare at the young men, elephants in musth graze the sandal, deer scatter through the leafy woods and lions with lashing tails are everywhere.
Monkeys leap from jackfruit to jackfruit, gold flows down the hills like a rainbow fallen to earth, and the glow of gems climbs and splits the sky.
On that hard mountain slope the snow-rocks melt in the hot sun and flow like butter and honey, and the sandal wind through cloud-wrapped groves brings deep sorrow.
nuance: The sorrow the sandal breeze brings is the separated lover's, a stock pain set into a landscape the hero crosses to reach his mother.

reading: Through owls, costus and saffron spread over the hard land, the party lodges, rises and goes on, and comes with delight to a fine grove of naga trees where peacocks and swans cry together.
event: Civakan's party crosses the hills and halts in a grove of naga trees.

tamil: பூத்தகி றவழும் போர்வை பூசுசாந் தாற்றி பொன்னூற்
கோத்துநீர் பிலிற்றுங் காந்தங் குங்கும வைரப் பொற்கோய்
சாத்துறி பவழக் கன்னல் சந்தன வால வட்ட
நீத்தவ ரிடத்து நாற்றி நிழன்மணி யுலகஞ் செய்தார்.
reading: There they spread cloth and covering, set out sandal, a gold thread-hung moonstone that drips water, saffron and diamond-set gold vessels, coral sugar, sandal fans, and in the place of the renouncers made a world of shining gems.
nuance: நீத்தவர் இடத்து, 'in the place of those who have renounced', sets the luxury beside the hermitage where Civakan's mother lives as an ascetic.
event: The companions furnish a camp near the ascetics' grove.

tamil: நித்தில முலையி னார்த நெடுங்கணா னோக்கப் பெற்றுங்
கைத்தலந் தீண்டப் பெற்றுங் கனிந்தன மலர்ந்த காண்க
வைத்தலர் கொய்யத் தாழ்ந்த மரமுயி ரில்லை யென்பார்
பித்தல ராயிற் பேய்க ளென்றவாற் பேச லாமோ.
reading: The narrator asks: see how the trees ripen and flower when the pearl-breasted women look at them with long eyes and touch them, and bow down to be plucked; can those who say a tree has no life be anything but madmen or ghouls?
nuance: The flowering of trees at a woman's glance or touch is a poetic convention; here it is turned into an argument that plants live, a teaching Jains hold, though the verse names no school. The claim it mocks is answered in the same verse, so it is refuted here.

tamil: பொறிமயி லிழியும் பொற்றார் முருகனிற் பொலிந்து மாவி
னெறிமையி னிழிந்து மைந்தன் மணிக்கைமத் திகையை நீக்கி
வெறுமையி னவரைப் போக்கி வெள்ளிடைப் படாத நீரா
லறிமயி லகவுங் கோயி லடிகளைச் செவ்வி யென்றான்.
reading: Civakan, more splendid than Murugan of the peacock, dismounts from his horse, lays aside the jewelled whip, sends his men away to go plainly and unseen, and says: tell the lady of the temple where peacocks call that it is time to receive me.
nuance: He calls his mother அடிகள், the title of an ascetic: the queen he comes to meet is now a renouncer, and he puts off the signs of rank to approach her.
event: Civakan dismounts, dismisses his retinue and sends to ask an audience of the ascetic lady at the shrine.

tamil: எல்லிருட் கனவிற் கண்டேன் கண்ணிட னாடு மின்னே
பல்லியும் பட்ட பாங்கர் வருங்கொலோ நம்பி யென்று
சொல்லின டேவி நிற்பப் பதுமுகன் றொழுது சோந்து
நல்லடி பணிந்து நம்பி வந்தன னடிக ளென்றான்.
reading: The queen says to a woman beside her that she saw a dream in the dark night, her eye throbs on the good side and a lizard has sounded there too: will her son come? Padumukan bows, falls at her good feet and says: lady, the prince has come.
nuance: டேவி is தேவி after சொல்லினள் by sandhi; the queen is still called தேவி though she wears the ascetic's robe. Padumukan speaks the last line. In 1909 line 3 சோந்து looks corrupt.
event: Vijayai reads a dream, a throbbing eye and a lizard's call as signs of her son's coming, and Padumukan announces that he has come.

tamil: எங்கணா னைய னென்றாட் கடியன்யா னடிக ளென்னாப்
பொங்கிவில் லுமிழ்ந்து மின்னும் புனைமணிக் கடக மார்ந்த
தங்கொளித் தடக்கை கூப்பித் தொழுதடி தழுவி வீழ்ந்தா
னங்கிரண் டற்பு முன்னீ ரலைகடல் கலந்த தொத்தார்.
reading: When she asks where her lord's son is, he says 'I am your servant, lady', joins his bright bangled hands, worships and falls clasping her feet, and the two are like two seas of love mingling.
nuance: Vijayai asks the question (ஐயன், the lord, here her son), and Civakan answers it himself with அடியன், 'your servant', the word of a worshipper to an ascetic as well as a son to a mother.
event: Civakan falls at his mother Vijayai's feet and they embrace for the first time since his birth.

title: விமலையார் இலம்பகம் 1911-1931 (2/5)
theme: Civakan finds his mother Vijayai in the hermitage: she weeps and nurses him in her embrace, both take the family's ruin on themselves, and she yields her motherhood to Sunandai and Kandukkatan and claims Nandattan as her own; after six days she teaches him kingcraft (marriage alliances, just wealth, spies, divide and rule, wealth that buys army and land), measures their exile against it, and when Civakan and his friends answer with lion-like confidence in force, she answers with the crow that killed the owls and the lion caught in a net, and sends him to his maternal uncle.
source_issues: 1911, 1914, 1915, 1916, 1925 to 1929: stanzas printed in half-lines and joined by the build (text flags).
1911 line 2: stray space in 'வ னமுலை' (வனமுலை).
1912 lines 3-4: 'தாளையா ... றோளையாத் தீர்ந்த' hard to divide; the sense is uncertain.
1914 line 3: 'விடைமகன்' doubtful (இடைமகன்?); the figure of the baleful tree is not fixed.
1915 line 4: 'மகிழ்ச்' appears to be a misprint for மகிழச்.
1919 line 4: 'நோபவே' doubtful; the closing verb is unclear.
1922 line 4: 'பொன்றுஞ் சாகத்தினாய்' read as பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்தினாய்.
1930 line 2: 'சோந்த' appears to be a misprint for சேர்ந்த; line 3 obscure.
1931 line 2: 'றோதோன்ற' appears to be a misprint for (வெய்யோன்) தேர் தோன்ற, and 'மலருஞ்செம்மனின்' for மலரும் செம்மல் நின்.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by Kandukkatan
Saccandan's widowed queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage
Civakan's younger (foster) brother, Sunandai's son, called நந்தன் here
Civakan's companions, called குமரர் and மைந்தர் here
Civakan's friend, one of the companions

tamil: திருவடி தொழுது வீழ்ந்த சிறுவனைக் கண்ட போழ்தே
வருபனி சுமந்து வாட்கண் வ னமுலை பொழிந்த தீம்பான்
முருகுடை மார்பிற் பாய்ந்து முழுமெயு நனைப்ப மாதர்
வருகவென் களிறென் றேத்தி வாங்குபு தழுவிக் கொண்டாள்.
reading: The moment she sees the boy who has fallen at her holy feet, the mother's eyes fill with tears and sweet milk spills from her breasts over his chest, and crying 'come, my elephant' she draws him into her arms.
nuance: The milk that flows on sight of a grown son is the epic's sign of recognised motherhood; it answers the burning-ground birth, where she could not nurse him and gave him up.
event: Civakan falls at Vijayai's feet; she weeps, her milk flows, and she embraces him.

tamil: காளையாம் பருவ மோராள் காதன்மீக் கூர்த லாலே
வாளையா நெடிய கண்ணான் மகனைமார் பொடுங்கப் புல்லித்
தாளையா முன்பு செய்த தவத்தது விளைவி லாதேன்
றோளையாத் தீர்ந்த தென்றா டொழுதகு தெய்வ மன்னாள்.
reading: Forgetting in her love that he is now a grown youth, the woman like a goddess to be worshipped clasps her son tight to her breast and says that her arms' long ache is over, she who had thought her former penance had borne no fruit.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (தாளையா ... றோளையாத் தீர்ந்த) are hard to divide; the sense that her penance had seemed fruitless and that her arms' longing is now ended is a reading, not a certainty.
event: Vijayai holds Civakan to her breast like a child and speaks of her grief ended.

tamil: வாட்டிறற் குருசி றன்னை வாளம ரகத்து ணீத்துக்
காட்டகத் தும்மை நீத்த கயத்தியேற் காண வந்தீர்
சேட்டிளம் பருதி மார்பிற் சீவக சாமி யீரே
யூட்டரக் குண்ட செந்தா மரையடி நோவ வென்றாள்.
reading: She calls herself the base woman who left the king in the sword-fight and left him in the burning forest, and marvels that Civakan Saami, with a chest like the young sun, has come to see her on lotus feet that may be hurt.
nuance: கயத்தியேன் is strong self-blame: the story told her flight as the king's command and the child's leaving as forced, but the mother judges herself by the result, not the necessity.
event: Vijayai reproaches herself for abandoning husband and child and greets Civakan.

tamil: கெடலருங் குரைய கொற்றங் கெடப்பிறந் ததுவு மன்றி
நடலையு ளடிகள் வைக நட்புடை யவர்க ணைய
விடைமகன் கொன்ற வின்னா மரத்தினேன் றந்த துன்பக்
கடலகத் தழுந்த வேண்டா களைகவிக் கவலை யென்றான்.
reading: Civakan answers that he was born only to see an unperishing victory perish, while his lady mother lived in misery and her well-wishers grieved; he is the baleful tree of the proverb, and she should not sink in the sea of sorrow he has caused, but put away this care.
nuance: Mother and son each take the blame on themselves in successive verses. The figure in line 3 (விடைமகன் கொன்ற இன்னா மரத்தினேன், a tree of ill that killed a herdsman?) turns on a doubtful word and a story not told here.
event: Civakan blames his own birth for the family's ruin and asks his mother to cast off her grief.

tamil: யானல னௌவை யாவாள் சுநந்தையே யையற் கென்றுங்
கோனலன் றந்தை கந்துக் கடனெனக் குணத்தின் மிக்க
பானிலத் துறையுந் தீந்தே னனையவா யமிர்த மூற
மானலங் கொண்ட நோக்கி மகன்மன மகிழ்ச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: With eyes like a deer's and words sweet as honey from a mountain hive, Vijayai says, to gladden her son, that she is not his mother: his mother is Sunandai, always, and his father is not the king but Kandukkatan, great in virtue.
nuance: The birth mother and queen gives up both her own claim and the dead king's to the merchant couple who reared him; the verse says she says it so that her son may rejoice, which makes it a gift of gratitude rather than a denial.
event: Vijayai tells Civakan that his foster parents, Sunandai and Kandukkatan, are his true mother and father.

tamil: எனக்குயிர்ச் சிறுவ னாவா னந்தனே யைய னல்லை
வனப்புடைக் குமர னிங்கே வருகென மருங்கு சோத்திப்
ரினத்திடை யேற னானுக் கின்னளி விருந்து செய்தாள்.
reading: She goes on that her life's own son is Nandan, not he, and calling 'come here, handsome prince' draws Nandattan to her side, sets his garland and flowered hair right, and gives the bull among his foes a feast of tender love.
nuance: The exchange is symmetrical: having given Civakan to his foster mother, she takes the foster mother's own son as hers, so that the two brothers are each other's mother's child.
event: Vijayai claims Nandattan as her own son, draws him close and tends him.

tamil: சிறகராற் பார்ப்புப் புல்லித் திருமயி லிருந்த தேபோ
லிறைவிதன் சிறுவர் தம்மை யிருகையி னாலும் புல்லி
முறைமுறை குமரர்க் கெல்லா மொழியமை முகமன் கூறி
யறுசுவை யமிர்த மூட்டி யறுபகல் கழிந்த பின்னாள்.
reading: As a peahen sits gathering her chicks under her wings, the queen holds her sons with both arms, gives each of the youths in turn fitting words of welcome, and feeds them six-flavoured nectar until six days have passed.
event: Vijayai embraces her sons, welcomes Civakan's companions and feeds them for six days.

reading: In a flowering grove of maravam, nagam, fragrant champak, kuravam, kongam and vazhai, sitting apart, the lady speaks on the matter she has weighed, as the next verses give it.
nuance: The ascetic mother, in a hermitage grove, gives not a sermon but a lesson in kingcraft; the setting and the matter pull against each other.
event: After six days Vijayai sits apart with Civakan in a grove and begins her counsel.

reading: She says it is the custom of kings whose rule stands firm to take as wives the daughters of the chiefs who live by the hills and forests, and the daughters of the mighty of the earth.
nuance: The verse ends in a doubtful word (நோபவே); the sense 'they hold this to be kings' custom' is taken from the run of the counsel. It forecasts Civakan's many marriages as policy as well as love.

reading: She lists what is approved: gathering treasure by justice and right, fixing which is the first and gravest enemy, using a thorn to find out the thorn of enmity, and splitting foes by sowing bewilderment among them.
nuance: Just acquisition and divide-and-rule stand in one breath; the verse sees no conflict between அறம் in getting wealth and stratagem in breaking enemies.

reading: Testing spies by other spies, taking learned men as one's eyes, and enlarging the circle of kin around one: these, they say, are the marks of victory for a king who means to win.
Wealth, she tells the son on whose chest fortune sleeps, makes victory, makes eminence, makes the diminished into mountains, and makes beauty along with learning.
nuance: பொன்றுஞ் சாகத்தினாய் is best divided பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்தினாய், an address to Civakan; the 'diminished' of line 2 are, as 1924 makes plain, the speaker and her son.

reading: From gold comes a fighting army, from that army the land, from the land in turn great wealth, and when that wealth is gathered there is nothing that does not come.

She sets out their state: driven from their land, worn down in treasure, fallen from the standing of their line, and with no learned counsellors here, and asks the young bull what he has resolved; and the generous one replies.
nuance: Each item answers a maxim just given: no land for the army-and-land chain of 1923, no treasure for 1922, no learned eyes for 1921. The counsel was a measure of what they lack.
event: Vijayai lists their losses and asks Civakan what he has decided; he begins to answer.

tamil: எரியொடு நிகர்க்கு மாற்ற லிடிக்குரற் சிங்க மாங்கோர்
நரியொடு பொருவ தென்றாற் சூழ்ச்சிநற் றுணையொ டென்னாம்
பரிவொடு கவல வேண்டா பாம்பவன் கலுழ னாகுஞ்
சொரிமதுச் சுரும்புண் கண்ணிச் சூழ்கழ னந்த னென்றான்.
reading: Civakan answers that when a thunder-voiced lion with strength like fire fights a jackal, what need is there of strategy and good allies; she should not grieve, for the enemy is a snake and Nandan of the honeyed garland and warrior's anklet is Garuda.
nuance: The claim is answered at once: 1927 restores the weighing of time and place, and 1928 has the lion that leaps without thought caught in a net. The young hero repeats in brave words the trust in force over counsel that undid his father.
event: Civakan dismisses the need for strategy against Kattiyangaran and names Nandattan as the Garuda to the enemy's snake.

tamil: கெலுழனோ நந்த னென்னாக் கிளரொளி வனப்பு னானைக்
கலுழத்தன் கையாற் றீண்டிக் காதலிற் களித்து நோக்கி
வலிகெழு வயிரத் தூண்போற் றிரண்டுநீண் டமைந்த திண்டோள்
கலிகெழு நிலத்தைக் காவா தொழியுமோ காளைக் கென்றாள்.
reading: 'Is Nandan a Garuda, then?' she says, and weeping, touches the bright and handsome youth with her hand, gazes at him in love and delight, and asks whether shoulders thick and long as diamond pillars could fail to guard the clamorous earth.
nuance: Whether the youth she touches is Nandattan, just named, or Civakan the காளை of line 4, the Tamil does not settle; கலுழ may also be read of the one touched rather than of her.
event: Vijayai touches and praises the youth whose shoulders she says will surely guard the earth.

tamil: இடத்தொடு பொழுது நாடி யெவ்வினைக் கண்ணு மஞ்சார்
மடப்பட லின்றிச் சூழ மதிவல்லார்க் கரிய துண்டோ
கடத்திடைக் காக்கை யொன்றே யாயிரங் கோடி கூகை
யிடத்திடை யழுங்கச் சென்றாங் கின்னுயிர் செகுத்த தன்றே.
reading: For those strong in judgment who weigh place and time, fear no undertaking and plan without folly, is anything too hard? In the wilderness a single crow went among the owls in their own place and, while they lay helpless, took the lives of a thousand crore.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the verse answers Civakan's 1925 and reads as the mother's. The crow among the owls is a fable known also from the Sanskrit tale collections; here it puts weakness plus judgment above strength.

tamil: இழைபொறை யாற்ற கில்லா திட்டிடை தளர நின்ற
குழைநிற முகத்தி னார்போற் குறித்ததே துணிந்து செய்யார்
முழையுறை சிங்கம் பொங்கி முழங்கிமேற் பாய்ந்து மைதோய்
வழையுறை வனத்து வன்க ணரிவலைப் பட்ட தன்றே.
reading: Men who do not resolve and carry through what they intend are like women whose waists sag under the weight of their jewels; and the lion of the cave, swelling and roaring and leaping upon its prey, fell into the net of hard-eyed men in the dark forest.
nuance: The lion is Civakan's own image from 1925, turned against him. Lines 1 and 2 are a hard simile; whether they blame the timid or the rash is not certain.

tamil: ஊழிவாய்த் தீயொ டொப்பான் பதுமுக னுரைக்கு மொன்னா
ராழிவாய்த் துஞ்ச மற்றெம் மாற்றலா னெருங்கி வென்று
மாழைநீ ணிதியந் துஞ்சு மாநிலக் கிழமை யெய்தும்
பாழியாற் பிறரை வேண்டேம் பணிப்பதே பாணி யென்றான்.
reading: Padumukan, like the fire at the world's end, says that the foes will sleep on the battlefield, that pressing on by their own strength they will win and gain lordship of the great earth where gold lies stored, that they need no others for the fight, and that the lord has only to command.
nuance: After the mother's case for allies and stratagem, the friend repeats Civakan's confidence; the verse sets the two counsels side by side without deciding here.
event: Padumukan vows that the companions alone will win the kingdom and asks only for orders.

tamil: பொருவருங் குரைய மைந்தர் பொம்மென வுரறி மற்றித்
திருவிருந் தகன்ற மார்பன் சேவடி சோந்த யாங்க
ளெரியிருந் தயரு நீர்மை யிருங்கதி ரேற்ற தெவ்வர்
வருபனி யிருளு மாக மதிக்க வெம் மடிக ளென்றார்.
reading: The peerless youths roar out together that they who have come to the red feet of this broad-chested lord of fortune hold the enemies to be no more than the dew and darkness that come before the great-rayed sun, and their lady should reckon them so.
nuance: Line 3 (எரியிருந் தயரு நீர்மை) is obscure; the sun-and-dew figure of line 4 carries the sense.
event: Civakan's companions shout their loyalty and scorn for the enemy.

reading: As mullai blooms when the rain-cloud appears and the lotus when the sun's chariot appears, so, she says, his maternal uncle will bloom when Civakan's glory appears; he should go to him and, with his word, destroy the enemy who stands open on the earth.
nuance: Her last word reinstates what Civakan and his friends set aside: the ally (the uncle) and his counsel (சொல்லினோடே) come before the fight.
event: Vijayai sends Civakan to his maternal uncle, to strike the enemy with the uncle's counsel.

title: விமலையார் இலம்பகம் 1932-1952 (3/5)
theme: Civakan answers his mother, travels with his company through forest to a river country, is feasted, sung to and loved at a grove halt, worships the Jina at dawn, and enters the city, where the women cannot tell him from Murugan or Kama and a maiden is playing ball.
source_issues: 1950 and 1951 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
1932 line 2 (எமர்க்கேயேன துண்மை) has a doubtful word division; the sense 'show the truth to our people' is clear, the verb is not.
1933 line 2 நூற்றைவர் can be read as a hundred and five or five hundred.
1952 line 2 (நிழன்மலிந்த நோவடந்நி ழற்படப்ப டைத்தர) is broken by the printed division and hard to construe.

cast.role: the hero, travelling to the city where Vimalai lives
Civakan's mother, whose counsel he answers in 1932
the young men of Civakan's company
the women who cook, serve and sing for Civakan at the halt
the women of the city who throng to see Civakan
the maiden playing ball, not named in these verses

reading: Civakan accepts his mother's counsel: he will go next day to that city, show his own people the truth, and come back the same day, and he asks her to go ahead to the one of the victorious elephant.
nuance: அடிகள் is his address to his mother; the one of the victorious elephant (வென்றிக் களிற்றுன்) is most likely the maternal uncle (மாமன்) she named in 1931, but the verse does not name him.
event: Civakan tells Vijayai he will go to the city to show his kin the truth and asks her to go to her brother.

tamil: காற்றிற் பரிக்குங் கலிமான் மிசைக் காவ லோம்பி
reading: The young man of the strong bow set out toward the forest hot as spear-points, walking with his band, his road guarded by riders on wind-swift horses and an army fit for the journey.
nuance: நூற்றைவர் gives the size of his band, a hundred and five or five hundred depending on how the compound is read.
event: Civakan sets out through the hot forest with his company and a guard of horsemen.

reading: Crossing hills where falls never cease and rivers ringed with cool tanks, the hero of the gem-mountain chest reached a river country of fields and groves.
event: Civakan reaches a fertile river country.

reading: The scent of flowers opening on the groves, the breath of lotuses in the pools and the sandal the women wore met the newcomer at every turn as feast after feast.
nuance: The land itself plays host: the fragrances are said to make விருந்து, the guest's welcome, before any person greets him.

reading: He of the gold-wrought gem ornaments halted in a divine flower grove where bees, drunk on honey dripping from comb into lotuses, hummed like a tuned yaazh.
event: Civakan halts in a flowering grove.

reading: The pack beasts were unloaded, the young men of gem anklets were rid of their weariness, and the women of fragrant garlands made the four kinds of food of six tastes for the lord of the famed spear.
event: The company rests and the women prepare a meal for Civakan.

reading: Nosebags were filled with jaggery rice, boiled pulse and horse-gram for the horses, while the other beasts grazed tall cane and red paddy, drank, and rested in the rich shade.
event: The horses and other beasts are fed and rested.

reading: Only after the man like a musth elephant had eaten the sweet food served by the women with dripping garlands did the backwater lotuses, open like eyes, close for the evening.
nuance: The closing of the lotuses waits on his meal, so evening is timed to the guest.
event: Civakan eats the meal the women serve as evening falls.

reading: Gem lamps glimmered, sweet smoke rose, strings sounded, flutes sang, and the drum and gold cymbals made a pleasant din.
After the women of red mouths and rain-dark fish eyes had kindled desire with songs sweeter than nectar, he went to the soft bed.
nuance: வேனலான் அளித்த பின் in line 3 is hard to place: it may name the spring god Kama as the giver, or a song of the hot season.
event: The women sing to Civakan and he retires to bed.

reading: Shoulders strong enough to crush sweet cane and swelling lovely shoulders entwined, hot breasts pressed against his cool garland till its gold dust fell, and so he swam across the dark night.
nuance: The verse does not name his partner; the context of 1941 makes it the singing women. The Jain epic tells the hero's night of pleasure without a word of reproach and moves straight to his dawn worship of the Jina.
event: Civakan spends the night in love.

reading: When the sun opened its eye at dawn, the hero like Murugan washed his radiant face with a hand like a budding lotus, showered flowers and bowed to the Lord (முனைவன்).
nuance: முனைவன் is the Jain name for the Jina; the morning rite follows the night of 1942 with no sense of conflict between them.
event: At dawn Civakan washes and worships the Lord.

reading: His daily duties done, the hero of the famed spear went quickly, in a form that bangled women desire, to see the wealth of the sword-guarded city.
event: Civakan goes into the city to see its riches.

reading: The long city's wealth never runs short: lac paste slipping from feet, ornaments cast off in lovers' sulks, golden petals strewn by garlands that trail along the ground.
nuance: The wealth is proved by what is wasted: ornaments thrown off in புலத்தல், the lovers' quarrel, lie in the street as litter.

reading: The sandal-painted breasts of the women whose garlands smell of the kazhuneer lily turn even those whose minds run toward release (சித்தி) back in this direction.
nuance: சித்தி here is the final attainment of the Jain path, not yogic power; the verse is praise of the city's women, and the seekers' lapse is its measure.

reading: Within the circle of the walls there is no room for anything but crowds of women whose waists shame the vanji creeper, with dyed feet and anklets, and young men in crowned locks.
The women like golden creepers lament: is he the tall Vel of the long kadamba, or the son of the five arrows and the long bow? We cannot tell; tell us.
event: The city's women, seeing Civakan, cry out that they cannot tell whether he is Murugan or Kama.

reading: His true form, like a youth of the heavens, seizes and devours all the long eyes of the women, as a bird of the backwater takes fish.
nuance: The usual figure is reversed: elsewhere women's eyes are the fish or the arrows; here his beauty is the bird that eats their eyes.

tamil: புலாத்தலைத் திகழும் வைவேற் பூங்கழற் காலி னானை
நிலாத்தலைத் திகழும் பைம்பூ ணிழன்மணி வடத்தோ டேந்திக்
குலாய்த்தலைக் கிடந்து மின்னுங் குவிமுலை பாய வெய்தாய்க்
கலாய்த்தொலைப் பருகு வார்போற் கன்னியர் துவன்றி னாரே.
reading: Maidens crowded upon the man of the flesh-tipped spear, holding up garlands with gem strands, their breasts thrusting, as if they would drink him with their eyes.
event: Young women crowd round Civakan with garlands.

tamil: வேனெடுங் கண்க ளம்பா விற்படை சாற்றி யெங்குந்
தேனெடுங் கோதை நல்லார் மைந்தனைத் தெருவி லெய்ய
மானெடு மழைக்க ணோக்கி வானவர் மகளு மொப்பாள்
பானெடுந் தீஞ்சொ லாளோர் பாவைபந் தாடு கின்றாள்.
reading: While the women everywhere aim their eye-arrows at the young man in the street, a girl like a daughter of the gods, with eyes like a doe's and speech sweet as milk, is playing ball.
nuance: The girl is not named here; the ilampakam's title makes her Vimalai. She is absorbed in her game while every other woman is looking at him.
event: A maiden is playing ball in the street where Civakan walks.

reading: Her garland bounces, her hot breasts and pearl strings shift, her gem earrings swing like bows, her gold ear-leaf flashes, and her girdle and anklets ring as she dances at the ball.
nuance: The verse changes to a quick சந்தம் rhythm that moves with the ball.
event: Vimalai plays ball.

title: விமலையார் இலம்பகம் 1953-1973 (4/5)
theme: A merchant's daughter plays with five balls; one falls in the street before Civakan, she sees him, turns pale and laments that her modesty and restraint are stolen and that desire has no cure, while he, struck by her glance, sits lovesick on her father's step and laments her eyes as Death, and at that moment her father's long-unsold goods sell.
