source_issues: 1955 line 3 மணிடி லம்வ ரப்புடைத்தன் is garbled as printed (likely மண்டிலம், 'a circle'); 1955, 1957, 1958 and 1970 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined.
1958 line 2 கின்னெகிழ்ந்து is likely a misprint (perhaps கண் or கச்சு நெகிழ்ந்து); the sense 'loosening' is clear, the noun is not.
1970 line 2 போகொடுத்தார் is likely a misprint of பேர்கொடுத்தார்; line 4 விந்நகரை நீத்திட டொழியாரோ has a doubled syllable.
1971 line 2 முகத்திலங்க்ச் carries a stray virama (for முகத்திலங்கச்).
1960 lines 1-2 (நீர்தங்கு திங்கண் மணிநீணிலம், கங்கைத் திருநீர்த் துவலை மாந்தி) are obscure as divided; the moonstone-terrace reading is a guess.

cast.role: the hero, here in the merchants' street of Rajamapuram, unnamed in these verses
the merchant Sagaradattan's daughter, who sees Civakan while playing ball; named in 1975, not in these verses
the merchant, Vimalai's father, whose goods sell when Civakan sits at his step

reading: Five balls rest in the palm of the maiden's hand; as she plays they rise together like bees circling a garland and go up without scattering, and her red-carp eyes and brows travel with their shapes.
nuance: The game is ஐந்து பந்து, five balls kept in the air at once; the verse already makes her eyes follow the balls, the eyes that will soon follow Civakan.
event: Vimalai plays with five balls.

reading: The narrator follows the balls as they hide in her garland and come back to her hand, pass behind her fragrant hair and before her bright face, by a waist thin as thread and at the garland on her crown, and drop back to her fingers.
event: Vimalai keeps the balls moving round her body.

reading: The figures of the game are named, catching and letting go, garlanding, rising in the eight directions, circling in rows, leaping like a peacock, while bees sing, and so the woman plays her five balls.
nuance: The verse is a list of technical moves of the game (கொண்டு நீங்கல், கோதை வேய்தல், எண்டிசையும் ஏற்றல்); some of their exact sense is not recoverable from the words.
event: Vimalai plays through the named figures of the ball game.

reading: As she plays, the saffron on her breasts, the gold powder sprinkled over her and the sandal of the mark on her forehead run down with sweat between her breasts and fall like the rainbow melting.
event: Vimalai sweats as she plays, and her cosmetics run.

reading: With her anklets and girdle-bells laughing, one ball of the gold-garlanded girl leaps out past her jasmine garland, bounds away and falls in the street before the man of the bright spear.
nuance: The narrator gives the ball, not the girl, the move that brings the two together; no one is said to aim it.
event: One of Vimalai's balls flies out and falls in the street before Civakan.

reading: The slender-waisted girl hurries after the fallen ball, her girdle showing, her hair loosening and her garland tumbling onto her breasts, and comes and looks out with wide eyes like a flowering creeper.
event: Vimalai runs out for the ball and looks out into the street.

reading: Crowned with mandara flowers, while drunken bees hum in the gandhara mode, she stands longing for the ball with her lily eyes spread wide, standing like Tiru on the red lotus.
nuance: பந்தார்வம் is longing for the ball; the line keeps her desire on the game a moment before she sees him.
event: Vimalai stands at the doorway looking out.

reading: The creeper on the moonstone terrace, as though fed on cool spray of the Ganga, no sooner sees the young bull than she becomes another, pale as the unopened peerkku flower.
nuance: பீர் (the yellow ridge-gourd flower) is the old sign of the pallor of love; here it comes at first sight, not in separation, which is where the akam poems put it.
event: Vimalai sees Civakan and turns pale.

reading: She says the thief who stole her modesty that never left her, her firm restraint, her beautiful dark skin and grace, the beauty of her eyes and her bangles, is the son of the five-flower-arrowed god come down to earth.
nuance: She lists what a woman's virtue is made of (நாண், நிறை) beside her skin and bangles, as goods a thief has carried off; the loss is put on him, not on her.

reading: She thinks: such is this desire that even if one dies of it, it cannot be told even to one's dearest; it is hard, a hot fire that burns and melts one inside, the one sickness in the world that has no medicine.
nuance: Two silences are joined: the sickness cannot be spoken even to the dearest, and it has no cure; the first is shame (naanam), the second her despair.

reading: She says there is no restraint at all where desire that burns like fire exists, and where restraint is whole there is not a kunri seed of desire; the pallor beats it out like a drum, she says, and wilting she stands while desire wide as the roaring sea tosses her.
nuance: The claim is put as an either-or, and the very next verse shows her holding herself with நிறை while desire takes her, so the story does not bear out the rule she states.

reading: Her heart shaken, she stood steadying herself with restraint; but the look of his guileless eyes on her moon-bright face of red-lily eyes gave refuge to desire, and its hot fire took hold of her.
nuance: Whose eyes look at whose face in lines 2-3 is not fixed by the words; the reading here takes the look as his, falling on her face.
event: Vimalai tries to compose herself as Civakan's look falls on her, and desire takes her.

reading: As the flower-eyed girl bent her brow-bows and shot, he asked what medicine there could be for the wound in his scorched heart, looked back at the doe-eyed maiden, and the spear-bearing lord melted and lost his strength.
nuance: His question (என்கொல், line 2) answers her statement two verses back that there is no medicine; the two have now said the same thing without speaking to each other.
event: Civakan, struck by Vimalai's glance, looks back at her and is overcome.

reading: With the fierce fever of desire around him, burning together with this pyre called the body, he could not bear the burning and sat lamenting on the flower-strewn step of the house of the girl's father.
nuance: The body is named a pyre (ஈமம்) that burns with the fire of desire; the image is the renouncer's, used here for a lover. Sitting on the father's step (கடை) is, as 1977 will reveal, the sign that fulfils the girl's horoscope.
event: Civakan sits down, lovesick, at the step of Vimalai's father's shop.

reading: Civakan laments that he does not know who the goddess is that pains his life, she whose hair shames musk and whose carp eyes shame the blue lily, and that there is no one who will come close and bring him word to end his sickness.
He asks whether the womanliness that showed the nature of honeyed lily eyes, and with one look stole all his inner nature that was wide as the sea, knew him already in an earlier birth.
nuance: மேனாள் பிறந்தும் அறியுமோ: the lover reaches for a former birth to explain how one look could take so much; it is asked, not asserted.

reading: He says her dark hair, red mouth, flower eyes, ears and jewelled breasts are Death to the dear life of men, she looks at those who come as guests and leaves them empty bodies, and asks whose daughter this woman of great fortune is and what her name is.

He says that those who named the girl of the strap-bound breasts and bee-swarmed garland called her a woman; had they called her Death, would not garlanded men who wanted their lives have left this sea-girt city?
nuance: போகொடுத்தார் in line 2 is read as பேர் கொடுத்தார், 'those who gave her a name'; the joke turns on that reading.

reading: He says the look she cast with her neck turned, her makara earrings and ear-rolls shining on her moon face, her red mouth and teeth shining and her honeyed hair hanging, appears wherever he looks.
He asks whether her eyes are swords of her bright moon face, or split mango, red lily, blue lily or lotus, long spears, arrows, carp, or long eyes, or Death come full that has begun to kill.
nuance: The list runs through the stock likenesses of eyes and ends on Death that has begun to kill (கொல்வான் தொடங்கின), so the last guess is the one that wins.

reading: As the conqueror sat lamenting and thinking how he could win the girl's beauty, at that very moment the cool Sagaradattan sold, without any loss, six crores' worth of gold-bright goods that had long lain unsold.
nuance: The narrator gives the sale without saying why; the cause, a sign written at Vimalai's birth, is told only by the merchant in 1976-1977.
event: While Civakan sits at his step, the merchant Sagaradattan sells six crores' worth of goods at once.

title: விமலையார் இலம்பகம் 1974-1994 (5/5)
theme: The close of the Vimalaiyar ilampakam: the merchant Sagaradattan tells Civakan that a prophecy made at his daughter's birth, that her husband would make the unsold cargo sell, is fulfilled, gives him Vimalai, and the chapter follows their union through one night to the dawn when Civakan, promising a quick return, leaves her in tears.
source_issues: 1976 line 3 (தும்பியாது மில்லாக் குளம்போன்றதென் றோமில் பண்டங்) is obscure as divided, and the vocative in line 4 (கூம்பாத செல்வக் கொடியே) fits Civakan badly.
1978 line 1 (ஏழாண்டின் மேலு மிரண்டாண்டிரண் டெய்தி) gives Vimalai's age in a form that can be summed more than one way.
1979 line 1 (ஏற்ற கைத்தொடி வீழ்ந்தென) and the subject of தேற்றினான் in line 2 are unclear.
1982 line 2 (கலவங் கண்புதை யாது கனற்றலி) is compressed; the sense of the burning is uncertain.
1989 line 2 (அயிர்ப்பதென் பணிசெய் வேனுக் கருளிற்றுப் பொருள தென்ன) is divided obscurely.
1974 line 4 runs இல் and மாமனொடு together (நிலமாமனொ); read as இல் மாமனொடு.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, here married to Vimalai; called மைந்தன், காளை, வேலினான் in these verses
the merchant, Vimalai's father, named in 1973; called நாய்கன் here
Sagaradattan's daughter by Kamalai, whom Civakan marries
the women of Vimalai's house who play the dawn music

reading: The merchant greets Civakan as Fortune itself come to his house, tells the warrior of the spear that this place is his, and the youth goes up into the red-gold house with the man who is to be his father-in-law.
nuance: The narrator already calls the merchant மாமன் (line 4, as divided இல் மாமனொடு) before any word of marriage is spoken: the match is settled in the telling before it is offered.
event: Sagaradattan welcomes Civakan as Fortune come in person and takes him up into his golden house.

reading: The merchant asks Civakan to listen a moment: living in this fair golden city, he had by his wife Kamalai a steadfast daughter named Vimalai, whose colour outshines red gold and whose nature is like Fortune's.
nuance: கம்பம் இலாதாள் (line 3), 'one without trembling', praises her steadiness before her beauty; the name விமலை, 'the stainless', is set beside her mother's name கமலை.
event: Sagaradattan tells Civakan of his daughter Vimalai, born to his wife Kamalai.

reading: He goes on: when this flower-doll was born, those who know what is to come wrote her fortune that very day, and he bids his hearer listen to what they said of the house and its goods.
nuance: Line 3 (தும்பியாதும் இல்லாக் குளம் போன்றது என்று ஓம் இல் பண்டம்) seems to compare the house's stock to a pond, but the construction is obscure as divided; the vocative கூம்பாத செல்வக் கொடியே in line 4 is odd addressed to Civakan and may belong to the quoted prophecy.
event: Sagaradattan recalls that at Vimalai's birth the astrologers wrote down her fortune.

reading: The prophecy, as he reports it: the man fit for the girl will come up onto the shop, and when he does the ship-borne goods and stored wealth will all be taken at once; and the chest of that peerless man will be the maiden's fragrant flower-bed.
nuance: The sign of the destined husband is a commercial one, fitted to a merchant's house: not a feat of arms or a contest, but goods that would not sell selling the moment he climbs onto the shop.
event: Sagaradattan repeats the astrologers' sign: the destined husband will sit at the shop and its unsold cargo will sell at once.

reading: Vimalai is now past seven years and two and two more; the wealth that would not sell has sold all at once for the master of the bow; it has come about as fated, so let him take the beauty of the girl with the slender waist and garlanded breasts, the merchant says.
nuance: ஊழாயிற்று (line 3) makes the offer of the daughter an act of compliance with destiny rather than the father's choice. The age in line 1 (ஏழாண்டின் மேலும் இரண்டாண்டு இரண்டு) can be summed more than one way.
event: Sagaradattan declares the prophecy fulfilled and offers Vimalai to Civakan.

reading: As if a bangle had dropped into an outstretched hand, the merchant duly assured the prince of the girl's great beauty, and the lady, seeing the prince, eased her pain and held on to her life.
nuance: The simile in line 1 (ஏற்ற கைத்தொடி வீழ்ந்தென) and the subject of தேற்றினான் are unclear; the reading takes the merchant as the one who reassures.
event: Civakan accepts the match, and Vimalai, seeing him, recovers from her lovesickness.

reading: For the woman like a golden branch and the man like a red-gold hill with warrior anklets, the many instruments of the golden city sounded and the people made a joy unmatched on earth.
event: Civakan and Vimalai are married amid the music of the whole city.

reading: The handsome youth who mounted the bed and the lady of the honey-dripping garland never left each other, and so, joined, they became one life in two bodies.
nuance: The oneness is given a cause, விட்டு நீங்குதல் இன்மையின், 'because they never parted': the formula holds only while they stay together, which the chapter's end tests.
event: Civakan and Vimalai live together as one.

reading: The fine cloth like white moonlight and the jewels did not hide her eyes for the burning, and they say the pleasure of the breasts of the woman with spear-like eyes is worth the three worlds.
nuance: The valuation is hedged as hearsay (என்பவே, line 3). Line 2 (கலவங் கண்புதையாது கனற்றலின்) is compressed and the sense of the burning is uncertain.

reading: The lady with the honey-scented garland and the youth with the spear that pierces enemies' flesh stayed on the soft bed fragrant as a forest, in the manner of the gods.
event: Civakan and Vimalai spend their days in pleasure on the bridal bed.

tamil: வெண்மதி நெற்றி தேய்த்து விழுத்தழும் பிருப்ப நீண்ட
வண்ணனன் மாடத் தங்க ணகிற்புகை யமளி யேறிப்
பண்ணமை மகர வீணை நரம்புரீஇப் பாவை பாட
மண்ணமை முழவுத் தோளான் மகிழ்ச்சியுண் மயங்கி னானே.
reading: In the long fine mansion whose walls bear the scars of rubbing against the white moon, mounting the couch in agil smoke, the doll-like girl tuned the strings of the makara vina and sang, and the man with drum-like shoulders was lost in delight.
nuance: Civakan won Gandharvadattai by the vina; here the bride plays and he only listens.
event: Vimalai plays the vina and sings for Civakan.

tamil: இன்னரிச் சிலம்பொ டேங்கிக் கிண்கிணி யிகலி யார்ப்பப்
பொன்னரி மாலை தாழப் பூஞ்சிகை யவிழ்ந்து சோர
மின்னிருங் கலாபம் வீங்கி மிளிர்ந்துகண் ணிரங்க வெம்பித்
துன்னருங் களிகொள் காமக் கொழுங்கனி சுவைத்து விள்ளான்.
reading: With her anklets and girdle-bells crying out against each other, her gold garland hanging, her flowered tresses loosened, her jewelled belt swelling and her eyes melting, he tasted the rich ripe fruit of desire and would not let go.
event: Civakan and Vimalai make love.

tamil: தொழித்துவண் டிமிருங் கோதை துணைமுலை முள்கப் பூம்பட்
டழித்துமட் டொழுகுந் தாரான் மணிவள்ளத் தாய்ந்த தேற
லெழிற்பொலி மாதர்க் கேந்த வினிதினி னுகர்ந்து காமக்
கொழித்திரை கடலுண் மூழ்கிக் கோதைகண் டுயின்ற வன்றே.
reading: Her garland crushed against his breast and her silk disordered, the man of the honey-dripping garland held up wine in a jewelled cup to the lovely lady, who drank it sweetly and, plunged in the sea of desire, fell asleep.
nuance: The epic, Jain by tradition, narrates the drinking of தேறல் in the bridal chamber without comment; no claim about drink is made here.
event: Civakan offers Vimalai wine from a jewelled cup; she drinks and falls asleep.

tamil: பாசிலை சுருட்டி மைந்தன் கொடுக்கிய பரந்து மின்னும்
தூசுலா மல்கு றீண்டத் துயிற்கண்கள் விழித்த தோற்றம்
வாசவான் குவளை மெல்ல வாய்விடா நின்ற தொக்கு
மேசுவ தொன்று மில்லா விணைவட முலையி னாட்கே.
reading: When the youth, rolling betel leaves for her, touched the silk at her waist, the sleepy eyes of the girl with faultless breasts opened slowly, like a fragrant blue lily opening its mouth.
event: Civakan wakes Vimalai with betel and a touch.

tamil: கங்குற்பாற் புகுந்த கள்வ னிவனெனக் கதுப்பிற் றாழ்ந்த
தொங்கலான் முன்கை யாத்துச் சொல்லுநீ வந்த தென்ன
நங்கையான் பசித்து வந்தே னெப்பொரு ணயப்ப தென்றாட்
கங்கலுழ் மேனி யாய்நின் னணிநல வமிழ்த மென்றான்.
reading: Calling him a thief who has crept in by night, she binds his forearm with the garland hanging from her hair and asks why he has come; he says he came hungry, and when she asks what he craves, he answers: the nectar of your beauty.
nuance: The arrest is play: the garland is the rope, and the 'thief' confesses a hunger that is a compliment.
event: Vimalai playfully binds Civakan as a night thief and questions him, and he answers that he hungers for her.

tamil: செயிர்த்தவள் சிவந்து நோக்கிச் சீறடி சென்னி சோத்தி
யயிர்ப்பதென் பணிசெய் வேனுக் கருளிற்றுப் பொருள தென்ன
வுயிர்ப்பது மோம்பி யொன்று முரையலை யாகி மற்றிப்
பயிர்ப்பில்பூம் பள்ளி வைகு பகட்டெழின் மார்ப வென்றாள்.
reading: Feigning anger, she reddens and stares; he sets her small feet on his head and asks why she doubts and what grace she grants her servant; she tells the broad-chested one to hold his breath, say nothing, and stay on the flower-bed.
nuance: Line 2 (அயிர்ப்பதென் பணிசெய்வேனுக்கு அருளிற்றுப் பொருளது) is divided obscurely; the reading takes it as Civakan's plea.
event: Vimalai feigns anger, Civakan bows to her feet, and she bids him be silent and stay.

tamil: உள்ளிழு துடைய வெம்பி யுற்பல வுருவு கொண்ட
வெள்ளியிற் புனைந்த கோல விளக்கொளி வெறுவி தாக
வள்ளிதழ்க் கோதை வல்லான் வட்டிகை நுதியின் வாங்கிப்
பள்ளிமே லெழுதப் பட்ட பாவைபோ லாயி னாளே.
reading: As the ghee within burned down and the light of the lovely lotus-shaped silver lamp grew faint, she became like a figure painted on the bed by a master's brush.
nuance: The lamp running dry marks the end of the night that the next verse confirms.
event: As the lamp burns low, Vimalai lies still as a painted picture.

reading: The marutham-mode lute and flute the women played seemed to grieve that this prince would leave the lady today, so that all were troubled; the night went by and the morning's duties were done.
nuance: The music knows what neither lover has said: the parting is announced first by the dawn melody (மருதம்), before Civakan speaks in 1993.
event: At dawn the women's music sounds, as if lamenting that Civakan will leave Vimalai.

reading: The man of the garlanded spear arranged her raised flower garlands, painted her young breasts with sandal so they shone, took her kanthal-bud fingers in his hand, and spoke to her.
event: Civakan adorns Vimalai and takes her hand to speak to her.

reading: He tells the woman of flower-hung tresses and body like mango shoots that he will go to the grove to see his friends and come back quicker than an arrow loosed from the bow.
nuance: The promise of a return quicker than an arrow is made, but this chapter, the last of the ilampakam, does not show it kept.
event: Civakan tells Vimalai he will go to see his companions in the grove and return at once.

reading: When he said this, the pupils of her painted eyes swam in standing tears; he comforted the fragrant woman, and the man like a great jewel-hill went, while she, a creeper, drooped.
event: Vimalai weeps; Civakan consoles her and leaves.

title: சுரமஞ்சரியார் இலம்பகம் 1995-2016 (1/5)
theme: Returning from Vimalai, Civakan is teased by his companions that his brides came by their parents' giving, and dared by a Brahmin companion to win Suramanjari, who shuns men; he swears to do it, disguises himself as a decrepit Brahmin, begs his way past the gatekeepers, and is surrounded by her armed women, some of whom hold back for fear of the sin of harming a Brahmin.
source_issues: 1995, 1997, 2002, 2003: stanzas printed in eight half-lines in the source and joined into four lines by the build.
1997: spellings டைய்ய, னைய்ய, ரவ்வர், ரவ்வ double consonants as written; the speaker word அந்தணன் is split across lines 1 and 2 (வந்தண / னம்பு).
2003 line 3 (நீல முண்டது காற்றி யாண்பே ரூட்டுவல்) is obscure as divided.
2007 line 3 (இவ் வகுளி லாணலங்) does not divide cleanly.
2013 line 4 has irregular word spacing (தொய்யின் முலை யவர்கள் கடைத் தோன்றனனி புக்கான்) unlike the other lines.

cast.role: the hero, who takes up his companions' dare and enters Suramanjari's house disguised as an old Brahmin
Civakan's companions, who meet him in the grove
a Brahmin among Civakan's companions, wearer of the sacred thread, who teases him and dares him to win Suramanjari
Civakan's newest bride, named only
the merchant's daughter who vowed to shun men after the powder contest; described, not present
the gatekeepers of Suramanjari's mansion
Suramanjari's maids and armed women attendants

tamil: வாளி ரண்டு மாறு வைத்த போன்ம ழைக்கண் மாதரார்
நாளி ரண்டு சென்ற வென்று நைய மொய்கொள் காவினுட்
டோளி ரண்டு மன்ன தோழர் தோன்ற லைப்பு ணாந்தபின்
றாளி ரண்டு மேத்தி நின்று தைய னாமம் வேண்டினார்.
reading: After two days away, while his brides pined, Civakan meets his companions in the dense grove; they embrace him, praise his feet and ask the name of the woman he has taken.
nuance: The opening line's women whose eyes are like two swords set crosswise are the brides who count the two days of his absence, so the ilampakam opens on the cost to the women left behind before it turns to the next one to be won.
event: Civakan's companions embrace him in the grove and ask the name of his new bride.

tamil: வீடு பெற்ற வரும் வீழும் வெம்மு லைவி மலையென்
றாடு வான ணிந்த சீர ரம்பை யன்ன வாணுத
லூடி னும்பு ணாந்த தொத்தி னியவளு ளாளரோ.
reading: Civakan names Vimalai, whose breasts would make even the released fall and who is like Rambha dancing in heaven, and asks whether any woman is sweeter, one who is sweet to join even in a lovers' quarrel.
nuance: வீடு பெற்றவரும் வீழும், that even those who have won release would fall for her, is a lover's hyperbole that borrows the language of liberation; the speaker is not named and is taken to be Civakan answering the question of 1995.
event: Civakan tells his companions his new bride is Vimalai and boasts of her.

tamil: அம்பொ ரைந்து டைய்ய காம னைய்ய னென்ன வந்தண
னம்பு நீர ரல்லர் நன்கு ரங்கு நீர ராயினுந்
தங்கு ரவ்வர் தாங்கொ டுப்பி னெஞ்சு நோந்து தாழ்வர்தாம்
பொங்க ரவ்வ வல்கு லாரெ னப்பு கன்று சொல்லினான்.
reading: A Brahmin companion, granting that the lord is Kama with his five arrows, teases that women are not won by trust: whatever their own strength of mind, when their elders give them away they yield, aching at heart.
nuance: The speaker is fixed by அந்தணன் at the join of lines 1 and 2 (written வந்தண / னம்பு) and by the sacred thread Civakan names in 2002; the tease deflates the boast of 1996 by crediting the brides' parents rather than the hero.
event: The Brahmin companion teases Civakan that his brides married him only because their elders gave them.

tamil: அற்று மன்று கன்னி யம்ம டந்தை மார ணிநலம்
முற்றி னாரை நீடு வைப்பின் மூள்கும் வந்து பாவமுங்
குற்ற மற்று மாகு மென்று கோதை சூழ்ந்து கூறினார்க்
குற்ற டுத்த யாவு யிர்த்தொழிதல் யார்க்கு மொக்குமே.
reading: Nor is that all, he goes on: parents, saying that sin and fault come upon those who keep a grown maiden long at home, plan her garland and give her, and for anyone so given, to sigh and accept what befalls is the common lot.
nuance: பாவம் here is the guardians' sin of delay, not the girl's; the companion uses a household rule to say the hero's eight conquests owed more to custom than to charm.

reading: The companion says Civakan joins in new marriage with honey-garlanded women in every town he enters, but here in the great city, in its streets, is one moon-faced maiden.
nuance: விதிக்கிடை காணலாம் is hard to fix: either that what is fated can be seen in the city's streets or that the streets are laid out by rule; the turn from teasing to challenge is clear either way.

reading: If men so much as pass near her quarters, or she hears their names asked after, she rages as though her life would leave her; she goes about with maids attending her as on a goddess.
nuance: The companion's account of Suramanjari's horror of men's names restates the vow she made after the powder contest, now become city talk.

reading: Even if Kama himself came she would flare up and not look, saying her body would burn; if you frighten that bamboo-shouldered girl and enjoy her beauty, all of us will hail our lord as Ananga-mathilakan, the crown of Kama.
nuance: ஏமுறுத்து, to frighten or overpower, makes the dare one of conquest rather than courtship, and the title offered, அநங்கமா திலகன், puts the prize in renown among the companions.

tamil: தாசியர் முலைக டாக்கத் தளையவிழ்ந் துடைந்த தண்டார்
வாசங்கொண் டிலங்கு முந்நூல் வலம்படக் கிடந்த மார்ப
பேசிய பெயரி னாளைப் பேதுறா தொழிவே னாகி
னாசுமன் பிலாத புன்பெண் கூந்தல்யா னணைவ லென்றான்.
reading: Civakan answers the companion whose chest bears the sacred thread among the garlands crushed by courtesans' breasts: if he does not bewilder the girl of the name just spoken, may he touch the hair of a base woman without love.
nuance: The oath's penalty is a self-curse of disgrace: to have to touch a loveless low woman's hair. The addressee's முந்நூல் (sacred thread) is what marks the teasing companion as a Brahmin.
event: Civakan swears to win Suramanjari, staking his honour on it.

tamil: வண்டுதேன் சிலைகொ ணாணா மாந்தளிர் மலர்க ளம்பாக்
கொண்டவன் கோட்டந் தன்னுட் கொடியினைக் கொணர்ந்து நீல
முண்டது காற்றி யாண்பே ரூட்டுவ லுருவக் காமன்
கண்டபொற் படிவஞ் சார்ந்து கரந்திரு நாளை யென்றான்.
reading: He tells them to bring the creeper-like girl into the shrine of Kama, whose bow is cane strung with bees and whose arrows are mango shoots and flowers, where he will make her take in a man's name, hiding tomorrow beside the golden image of Kama.
nuance: ஆண்பேர் ஊட்டுவல, 'I will feed her a man's name', answers her refusal to hear men's names (2000); line 3's நீலம் உண்டது காற்றி is obscure, and whether he or the friends are to hide (கரந்திரு) is not certain.
event: Civakan lays a plan to meet Suramanjari at the shrine of Kama.

reading: Strong as a maned lion in its cave, he told his keen-eyed friends his intent and rose to go, meaning to bring love-sickness on the rain-eyed maiden of the jewelled breasts and slender waist.
event: Civakan leaves his companions to set his plan in motion.

reading: Civakan feels his mind rise in turmoil, longing to bathe coolly in the breasts and chest, hung with pearl strings, of the swooning beauty Suramanjari.
nuance: The hunter is already caught: the verse turns from the dare to his own unrest before he has seen her.

reading: He pictures her breasts swelling like burnished gold caskets beneath their chains and her blue-lily eyes, longer than a cupped palm, as things now dwelling in his mind.
Her dark flower-crowned hair, bound behind with a jasmine garland, rouses his male beauty and stirs his mind.
nuance: Line 3's இவ் வகுளில் is not clear as written; the sense of a beauty that agitates him is secure.

reading: He reckons that the way to the gate of her beauty is easy: he, lord of distress, will go as a Brahmin.
nuance: அல்லலங் கிழவன், the lord of distress, is his self-mocking name for a man in love; the disguise borrows the one status her ban does not fear.
event: Civakan resolves to disguise himself as a Brahmin to enter Suramanjari's house.

reading: He appears with skin like a snake's slough, body bent like a bowed strong bow, a tangled thread across his chest, as if he had studied a great book and written old age out of it.
nuance: The image of old age copied out from a book makes the disguise an act of learning: the youth reproduces decay by rule.
event: Civakan takes on the guise of a decrepit old Brahmin.

reading: White-haired and blotched, with trembling flesh and dimmed gaze, carrying an umbrella and leaning on a staff, he became even a ghost for love of a woman's beauty.
nuance: The narrator's பேயும் ஆயினான் is comic, but it names the price: the hero's own beauty is given up for desire.
event: Civakan completes his old man's guise with umbrella and staff.

reading: As a mahout who would tame the elephant of her beauty with the goad of his lute-like throat, hidden under the face-cloth of old age, the young bull reached her guarded, rich mansion.
nuance: Old age is a முகபடாம், the cloth over an elephant's face, so the disguise is itself an elephant's trapping while she is the elephant to be goaded by song: the elephant image is used on both sides.
event: Civakan in disguise reaches Suramanjari's guarded house.

reading: Leaning on his staff, sinking and panting, seen and rebuked by the gatekeepers, he looks into their faces and says that in his youth he loved milk-rice and today he longs for what kindly people give.
nuance: The plea is double: the old man's craving for milk-rice stands for the young man's craving for the girl.
event: The disguised Civakan begs the gatekeepers for milk-rice.

tamil: தொய்யின் முலை யவர்கள் கடைத் தோன்றனனி புக்கான்
reading: Those who saluted him with joined hands passed on; deaf with age, he talked like a madman as his mind moved him, and the guards, pitying his hunger, let him go with 'walk slowly', and he entered the women's gate.
nuance: The ban on men is undone by the guards' own compassion for hunger; feigned deafness lets him ignore their rebukes.
event: The gatekeepers, pitying the old Brahmin's hunger, let him into the women's quarters.

reading: The women run up, hair loosened under garlands with bees buzzing, pearl strings and ornaments swinging, crying that this is a fault and he must go; he gives no answer and stands swaying as if about to fall.
nuance: ஊதவுகு தன்மையின், as if he would drop at a breath, is the guise kept up under pressure; the exact sense of the phrase is not certain.
event: Suramanjari's women rush out to drive off the intruder, who stands silent and swaying.

reading: The women, breasts bound in bodices, take up jewelled swords, sharp spears, arrows and bows that tremble in their hands, and, turning their sweet words sour and hot to frighten him, surround him.
nuance: The weapons tremble (நடுங்க) in the women's hands, so the threat is half display; the image of sweetness turned sour (அமது புளித்தாங்கு) is of milk going off.
event: Suramanjari's armed women surround the old man and threaten him.

reading: Some of them say: this is sin, do not speak to hurt him; old Brahmins die if they are touched; let us learn the command of our lady, beyond compare with the painters' dolls, about what we have seen.
nuance: The Brahmin's protected status, the very thing Civakan chose the guise for (2008), now works as planned: it turns the guards' anger into scruple and carries the decision to Suramanjari herself.
event: Some of the women restrain the rest and resolve to ask Suramanjari what to do with the old Brahmin.

title: சுரமஞ்சரியார் இலம்பகம் 2017-2038 (2/5)
theme: Civakan, disguised as a destitute old brahmin, is received by Suramanjari, who had vowed to look on no man: she laughs at his wish to bathe at Kumari and be young again, feeds, dresses and lodges him in her mansion, and at nightfall, while the city's lovers come together, his singing bewilders her women and reminds them of the youth she keeps in her mind.
source_issues: 2017 lines 1-2: the run of epithets may describe the maid or the lady she addresses; the speaker is read from context.
2021 line 4 (கறிதிர்பிற நீவிரென) is obscure as divided; perhaps காண்டிர் was meant.
2028 line 4 (தன்னஞ்சிறி தேதுயின்று தாழவவ ணக்காள்) is hard to divide; the sense of feigned sleep is a guess from context.
2032 line 3 கொழுமெனறும் is probably கொழுமென் நறும் with a letter lost.
2034 line 4 சோந்தார் is probably a misprint for சோர்ந்தார்.
2035 line 4 (கின்னமிர்த மாகவிளை யாருமது கேட்டார்) is obscure as divided.
2036 and 2037 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.

cast.role: the hero, here in the guise of an aged brahmin (பார்ப்பான், சாமி)
a merchant's daughter who lost the scented-powder contest and vowed to see no man
Suramanjari's maid, who announces the brahmin
the women of Suramanjari's mansion who cook, serve and hear the song
the women of the city's streets and houses
the men of the city, husbands and lovers, in the night scene

reading: A maid tells the lady that a brahmin with no means of living has come, brought by fate in extreme old age, and urges her to rise and come, saying it is easy to grant what he asks.
nuance: The brahmin is Civakan in the old man's guise taken in the previous verses; the maid's ஊழின் (line 3), 'by fate', makes his age and poverty his lot, the first of many words in the scene that are true of the disguise and false of the man. The epithets of line 1 to 2 may describe the maid or the lady addressed, so who speaks to whom is a reading from context.
event: A maid announces to Suramanjari that an aged brahmin has come to the house.

reading: Garlanded, dripping honey, her breasts smeared with agil and thick sandal paste, speaking with the lisp of a jewelled lute in the paalai mode, she comes down from the golden upper floor like a peahen descending a mountain grove.
nuance: She has kept to the upper storey since her vow to look on no man; this descent toward a male visitor is the first breach of the seclusion, made safe in her eyes by his age.
event: Suramanjari descends from the upper floor of her mansion.

reading: Her small feet's anklet bells and anklets chiming, her girdles murmuring softly, bees singing over her garland, she comes as if a fragrant flowering branch were learning to walk.
event: Suramanjari walks out to meet the visitor.

reading: She asks why he has come; he tells the sword-eyed maiden that he means to bathe in the sacred waters of Kumari, which trouble his mind, and when she asks what gain comes of it he says, the end of the old age that afflicts him.
nuance: The verse is a dialogue (her என்றாள் line 3, his என்றான் line 4). The claim is feigned: a youth asks to be cured of an age he does not have, and the story laughs at it through Suramanjari in the next two verses rather than refuting it in argument.
event: Suramanjari asks the old brahmin his errand, and he says he is going to bathe at Kumari to be rid of old age.

reading: The lady with honey-scented hair laughs aloud and asks him to say truly whether there are others who have gained this, and he says that among those who know the ford, go there, worship and bathe, they will see others, without doubt.
nuance: Her laugh (பெரிது நக்கு, line 1) is the hinge of the trick: once the old man is ridiculous he is harmless, and the woman who vowed to see no man will now serve him with her own hands.
event: Suramanjari laughs and asks if anyone has been made young by the bath; he insists that some have.

reading: Thinking that those who say a dead tree swarmed by rain will sprout again are mad, and that she will at least cure the ailment this man has, she goes up to the jewelled mansion whose crowded gems shrink the sun's bright rays.
nuance: Her scepticism is sound common sense, and it is the reason the disguise holds: what she is sure cannot happen is exactly what, in the story's terms, is about to happen before her eyes.
event: Suramanjari dismisses the hope of youth regained and resolves to relieve the old man's present want.

reading: She says that this is his form and his old age is pitiable, notes the coral-creeper mouth and the lotus hue of eyes and feet, says he is cruelly hungry, and tells the bangled maids to make food quickly and bring it here.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 list a red mouth and lotus-coloured eyes and feet in a man just called pitifully old: the youth shows through the disguise, and she sees it without reading it.
event: Suramanjari orders her maids to cook food at once for the hungry old man.

reading: Rubbing him with fragrant powder and bathing him in scented water, the sweet-voiced one gives him a gleaming white cloth, a sacred thread of fine gold and the darbha ring, and he sits down at ease on the seat set for him.
nuance: The gifts are the marks of the brahmin (நூல், பவித்திரம்): her hospitality completes the disguise she is taken in by.
event: The old brahmin is bathed, dressed in white with thread and ring, and seated.

reading: Spreading many golden vessels bright as the stars about the moon, the women bring sweet food like nectar, and the great worthy one eats, saying there is no such taste anywhere.
nuance: மிகு சான்றோன் (line 3) is said with a smile: the honour paid to an old man of learning falls on a young lover in disguise.
event: The guest is served on golden vessels and eats with praise for the food.

reading: Women whose grace is entwined with Tamil hold a vessel pouring pure flower-water; the strong one sits and rinses, and when they show him betel leaf with the five fragrances prepared like nectar he takes it into his cheek.
nuance: தமிழ் தழிய சாயலவர் (line 1), women whose softness embraces Tamil, uses the language's name as a word for sweetness; உரவோன், 'the strong one', slips past the old man's frailty to the hero underneath.
event: After the meal the guest rinses his mouth and is given betel.

reading: She asks what he is skilled in; he says he is master of the Veda; asked how far, he says to the meaning and the very end; asked how long he studied, he tells the honey-voiced, parrot-speaking maiden that he does not remember.
nuance: The last answer is the joke: the man who claims the Veda to its end has no years of study to show, because the years are false.
event: Suramanjari questions the brahmin about his learning, and he claims the whole Veda but cannot say when he learned it.

reading: Marvelling that there are no such men on earth, she praises him and sits gazing, and he, thinking that she will next speak of his leaving, nods off a little and droops.
nuance: Line 4 is hard to divide; the sense that his sleep is feigned to forestall dismissal follows from line 3 (போகு திறம் பேசும் என எண்ணி) and the next verse.
event: Suramanjari praises the old man; he feigns drowsiness so as not to be sent away.

reading: Looking at the maiden of the lily eyes, the very old master says his legs ache badly and his eyes are heavy with sleep, and asks the lady of the cardamom-scented garland what she will do for it.
nuance: சாமி, 'master', is the title the epic gives Civakan himself (சீவகசாமி); applied to the old brahmin it is a quiet signal of who he is.
event: The old brahmin complains of weariness and asks her for a place to rest.

reading: The lady of the honey-dripping garland tells him to rest without care on the couch spread with silk; he lies down gently on the bed laid for him, and begins to churn an ocean of desire that burns like fierce fire.
nuance: Line 4 tears the disguise for the reader: the frail guest in the woman's own chambers is a lover, and the house she guarded against men now has one inside it by her own leave.
event: Suramanjari gives the old man a silk couch in her mansion, and he lies on it burning with desire.

reading: The day sinks, the sun sets in gloom, evening comes, the moon rises and joy with it, and the spear-eyed women join their beloved husbands, painting their strong shoulders with their breasts.
event: Night falls over the city and the women go to their husbands.

reading: Agil smoke raised on flowered beds, the scented smoke breathing from wilted garlands, the agil smoke of hair and the fragrant smoke of perfumed cloth all rise from mansions taller than cloud-capped hills.
nuance: Four kinds of smoke (புகை) in four lines: the night's lovemaking given by scent alone.

reading: Having eaten a little of the faultless milk-food, wearing light garlands, ear ornaments, fine cloth and fragrant sandal, the spotless maidens pluck the strings of the jewelled vina.
event: The young women of the city eat lightly, dress, and play the vina.

reading: Peerless men with garland-crowned hair smear their strong shoulders and broad chests with fragrance, drink the nectar of coral lips sweet as sugarcane, and swoon as their rich garlands are crushed.
event: The city's men lie with their women through the night.

reading: On the flower couch in the golden chamber he, to bring on first the wedding he intends, hums a melody sweetly, and all who hear it take it as nectar.
nuance: முன்னிய தன் மன்றல் (line 2): the song is a means to the marriage. The city's night of lovers (2031 to 2034) frames a house where the one man present is still playing the old man.
event: At night the old brahmin sings softly in the mansion, and the household listens.

tamil: மன்ம தன்ம ணிக்கு ரன்ம ருட்டு மென்று மால்கொள்வா
ரின்ன தின்றி யக்க ரின்னி யக்க வந்த தென்றுதம்
பின்னு முன்னு நோக்கு வார் பேது சால வெய்துவார்
கன்னி தன்ம னத்தி ழைத்த காளை நாமம் வாழ்த்துவார்.
reading: Wondering whether it is the voice of the god of love's jewel bell, that nothing like it exists, whether it is the music of the yakshas, they look behind and before, are deeply bewildered, and praise the name of the youth the maiden has wrought into her mind.
nuance: கன்னி தன் மனத்து இழைத்த காளை (line 4): the youth she has fashioned in her mind is Civakan, for whom alone she said she would break her seclusion; the song is recognised by its likeness to him before anyone guesses that it is him.
event: The women of the house, bewildered by the song, are reminded of Civakan and praise his name.

tamil: கொம்பி னொத்தொ துங்கி யுங்கு ழங்கன் மாலை தாங்கியு
மம்பி னொத்த கண்ணி னார டிக்க லம்ம ரற்றவுந்
நம்பி தந்த கீதமேந யந்து காண வோடினார்
வெம்பு வேட்கை வேனி லானின் வேற லானு மாயினான்.
reading: Shrinking like branches, wearing curled garlands, the arrow-eyed women run to see, their anklets crying out, longing for the song the noble one gave, and he becomes none other than the god of spring whose desire burns.
event: The women run toward the singer, and the old man seems to them the god of love.

tamil: தாம மாலை வார்கு ழற்ற டங்க ணார்க்கி டங்கழி
காம னன்ன காளை தன்க ருத்தொ டொத்த தாகலான்
சாம கீத மற்று மொன்று சாமி நன்கு பாடினான்.
reading: Because it matched the thought of the long-eyed women with garlanded hair, the youth like Kama, the master, sang well another Sama chant that lay in his jewelled throat.
nuance: சாம கீதம் (line 4): the song of the brahmin's own Veda keeps up the disguise while doing the lover's work; the verse calls the singer காமன் அன்ன காளை and சாமி in one breath.
event: The disguised Civakan sings a second Sama melody for the women.

title: சுரமஞ்சரியார் இலம்பகம் 2039-2059 (3/5)
theme: Disguised as a very old Brahmin, Civakan draws Suramanjari and her maidens with song, learns from them that her hatred of men is anger at his own verdict, and sings an evening-song of a woman's longing that undoes her vow; next morning she prays at Kama's temple to be joined to Civakan, and his hidden companion answers in the god's voice.
source_issues: Every verse but 2039 and 2049-2051 was printed in eight half-lines and has been joined into four by the build; the joins look right.
2049 line 4 மழூங்குவிக்கு looks like a misprint of அழுங்குவிக்கும் (with sandhi), as 2051 line 4 has மழுங்குவிக்கு.
2043 line 4 (ஆய்ந்தன மைய னுய்ந்தா னறிந்தன மதனை) and 2045 line 3 (பொன்றெட்டேம்) are obscure as divided.
2044 turns on தத்தை (parrot / Gandharvadattai) and its speaker and sense are unsure.

cast.role: the hero, here disguised as a very old Brahmin singer
a merchant's daughter who lost the powder contest and vowed to shun men
Suramanjari's maid, who disputed Civakan's powder verdict
Suramanjari's maidens and attendants in her mansion
the god of love (also அநங்கன்), at whose temple Suramanjari prays
Civakan's companion; here the 'king's friend' (வேந்தன் தோழன்) who speaks as the god

tamil: கள்ள மூப்பி னந்த ணன்க னிந்தகீத வீதியே
வள்ளி வென்ற நுண்ணி டைம ழைம லர்த்த டங்கணார்
புள்ளு வம்ம திம்ம கன்புணர்த்த வோசை மேற்புகன்
றுள்ளம் வைத்த மாம யிற்கு ழாத்தி னோடி யெய்தினார்.
reading: Hearing the ripe song that the falsely aged Brahmin sends down the street, the wide-eyed maidens of Suramanjari's mansion run to it like a flock of peacocks, their hearts set on the sound.
nuance: The narrator names the disguise at the outset (கள்ள மூப்பு, a false old age) and calls the singer's art புள்ளுவம், trickery, so the reader is never in doubt that the music is bait.
event: Suramanjari's maidens run toward the disguised Civakan's singing.

tamil: இனிச்சிறி தெழுந்து வீங்கி யிட்டிடை கோறு நாங்க
ளெனக்கொறு கொறுப்ப போலு மிளமுலைப் பரவை யல்குற்
கனிப்பொறை மலிந்த காமர் கற்பக மணிக்கொம் பொப்பாள்
பனிப்பிறைப் பூணி னான்றன் பாண்வலைச் சென்று பட்டாள்.
reading: Suramanjari herself, a gem-branch of the wishing tree whose young breasts seem to grumble that a little more swelling will break her slender waist, goes and falls into the singer's net of song.
nuance: பாண்வலை, the net of song, makes the woman who shut out men the quarry of a hunt; she goes to it on her own feet.
event: Suramanjari is drawn to the singer.

tamil: அடிக்கல மரற்ற வல்குற் கலைகலந் தொலிப்ப வந்து
முடிப்பதென் பெரிது மூத்தேன் முற்றிழை யரிவை யென்ன
வடிக்கணா ணக்கு நாணித் தோழியை மறைந்து மின்னுக்
கொடிக்குழாத் திடையோர் கோலக் குளிர்மணிக் கொம்பி னின்றாள்.
reading: She comes with anklets crying and girdle sounding, and when the old man says that he is very old and can do nothing, she laughs, is ashamed, and hides behind her maid among the throng of women.
nuance: The disclaimer முடிப்பதென் பெரிது மூத்தேன் is the disguise talking: by protesting his age he lets her come near a man without breaking her vow in her own eyes.
event: Suramanjari arrives; the old man disclaims his age, and she laughs and hides behind her maid.

tamil: இளையவற் காணின் மன்னோ வென்செய்வீர் நீவி ரென்ன
விளைமதுக் கண்ணி மைந்தர் விளிகெனத் தோழி கூற
முலையெயிற் றிவளை யாரு மொழிந்தன ரில்லை யென்றோ
வுளைவது பிறிது முண்டோ வொண்டொடி மாதர்க் கென்றான்.
reading: The old man asks what they would do if they saw a young man; the maid answers 'may honey-garlanded young men perish!'; and he asks whether the lady grieves because no one has spoken to her, or for some other cause.
nuance: His second question offers the lady a softer cause for her grief, that no one has courted her, in place of the anger she professes: he is testing whether the hatred is wounded pride.
event: The disguised Civakan probes the maid about the lady's hatred of men, and the maid curses young men.

tamil: வாய்ந்தவிம் மாதர் சுண்ணஞ் சீவகன் பழித்த பின்றைக்
காய்ந்தன ளென்று கூறக் காளைமற் றிவட்குத் தீயான்
மாய்ந்தனன் போலு மென்ன மாதரா ரொருங்கு வாழ்த்தி
யாய்ந்தன மைய னுய்ந்தா னறிந்தன மதனை யென்றார்.
reading: The maid explains that the lady has been angry ever since Civakan disparaged her powder; the old man says that young man must be as good as dead to her; and the women bless him together, saying they have weighed it and know the lord came through.
nuance: Civakan, unrecognised, pronounces his own sentence (தீயான் மாய்ந்தனன் போலும்). Line 4 (ஆய்ந்தன மைய னுய்ந்தா னறிந்தன மதனை) is hard to construe; whether ஐயன் is the old man or Civakan, and in what sense he 'escaped', is a guess.
event: The maid names the powder verdict as the cause of the lady's anger, and the disguised Civakan condemns the young man who gave it.

tamil: காலுற்ற காம வல்லிக் கொடியெனக் கலங்கி நங்கை
மாலுற்று மயங்க யாங்கண் மடக்கிளி தூது விட்டேஞ்
சேலுற்ற நெடுங்கட் செவ்வாய்த் தத்தைதன் செல்வங் கண்டே
பாலுற்ற பவளச் செவ்வாய்த் தத்தையாற் பரிவு தீர்ந்தேம்.
reading: The maids say that when their lady was shaken like a love-creeper in the wind and bewildered, they sent a young parrot as messenger, and that by a parrot-mouthed one, having seen Tattai's good fortune, their distress was eased.
nuance: தத்தை means both a parrot and Gandharvadattai, Civakan's first bride; the verse plays on both and I cannot fix who sent which messenger or whose distress ended. It may glance at Gunamalai's parrot messenger to Civakan earlier in the book.

tamil: அன்பொட்டி யெமக்கோர் கீதம் பாடுமி னடித்தி யாரு
முன்பட்ட தொழிந்து நுங்கண் மூகவியர் முனிவு தீர்ந்தார்
பொன்றெட்டேம் யாமு நும்மைப் போகொட்டோம் பாடல் கேளா
தென்பட்டு விடினு மென்றா ரிலங்குபூங் கொம்பொ டொப்பார்.
reading: The flower-branch women beg the old man to sing them a song out of kindness, saying the serving women have forgotten what passed and dropped their anger, and that whatever happens they will not let him go without hearing it.
nuance: பொன்றெட்டேம் (line 3) is obscure as divided; the reading of it is left open. The women who shut men out now refuse to let a man leave.
event: The women press the old man to sing.

tamil: பாடுதும் பாவை பொற்பே பற்றிமற் றெமக்கு நல்கி
னாடமைத் தோளி னீரஃ தொட்டுமேற் கேண்மி னென்ன
நாடியார் பேயைக் காண்பார் நங்கைகா ளிதுவு மாமே
யாடுவ தொன்று மன்றிவ் வாண்மக னுரைப்ப தென்றார்.
reading: The old man says he will sing if the lady grants him something touching her beauty, and bids them agree before they listen; the women ask one another who would go looking to see a demon, and say this man's words are no game.
nuance: What he asks (பாவை பொற்பே பற்றி) is veiled; the women's reply about seeking out a பேய் shows they hear a demand on the lady herself behind the old man's words.
event: The old man sets a condition for his song, and the women are alarmed by it.

tamil: பட்டுலாய்க் கிடந்த செம்பொன் பவளமோ டிமைக்கு மல்கு
லொட்டினா ளதனை யோரோ துலம்பொரு தோளி னானும்
பட்டவா ணுதலி னாய்க்குப் பாடுவல் காமன் றந்த
தொட்டிமை யுடைய வீணைச் செவிச்சுமை யமிர்த மென்றான்.
reading: She of the silk-clad waist agrees to it, and the strong-shouldered one says he will sing for her of the bright forehead the nectar that burdens the ear, from the vina that Kama gave.
nuance: She binds herself to an unknown condition for the sake of a song: the pledge will be called in when he is revealed.
event: Suramanjari accepts the condition, and Civakan agrees to sing.

tamil: வயிரவில் லுமிலும் பைம்பூண் வனமுலை மகளிர் தம்மு
ளுயிர்பெற வெழுதப் பட்ட வோலியப் பாவை யொப்பாள்
செயிரில்வாண் முகத்தை நோக்கித் தேன்பொதிந் தமுத மூறப்
பயிரிலா நரம்பிற் கீதம் பாடிய தொடங்கி னானே.
reading: Looking at her flawless face, she like a painted doll come to life among the women, he begins to sing on faultless strings a song that drips honey and flows with nectar.
event: Civakan begins his song, looking at Suramanjari.

reading: In the first stanza of his song, evening comes, making bangles slip from the arms and rain pour from long eyes onto the breasts, and wears down the longing heart of women like us.
nuance: The song speaks as a woman in separation (நந்திறத்தது, 'of our kind'), so the man who has come to win the lady sings her the lament of a woman who already loves; the refrain repeats line 2's close at the head of line 3.

reading: In the second stanza evening, laying the hips low and turning breath to fire, makes the hand slip and press the ground while tears beat on the cheeks, and enters like a spear into a running wound.
nuance: புண்ணீரும் வேலிற் புகுந்ததால்: evening is not a fresh blow but a spear pushed into a wound already open.

reading: In the third stanza, with the flower garland loosened on the breast and golden pallor blooming on the budding breasts while pearls of tears gather in the fish-like eyes, evening wears down the heart melting in love.

tamil: பாடினான் றேவ கீதம் பண்ணினுக் கரசன் பாடச்
சூடக மகளிர் சோர்ந்து செருக்கிய மஞ்ஞை யொத்தா
ராடகச் செம்பொற் பாவை யந்தணற் புகழ்ந்து செம்பொன்
மாடம்புக் கநங்கற் பேணி வரங்கொள்வ னாளை யென்றாள்.
reading: He sang the divine song, a king of melody, and the bangled women swooned like proud peacocks; the golden doll praised the Brahmin and said that tomorrow she would enter the golden temple, worship Anangan and win a boon.
nuance: She does not say what boon; the evening-song has done its work, and the next verses show it is Civakan.
event: The women swoon at the song, and Suramanjari resolves to pray to Kama for a boon the next day.

tamil: மடலணி பெண்ணை யீன்ற மணிமருள் குரும்பை மான
வுடலணி யாவி நைய வுருத்தெழு முலையி னாளு
மடலணி தோழி மாரு மார்வத்திற் கழும விப்பாற்
கடலணி திலகம் போலக் கதிர்திரை முளைத்த தன்றே.
reading: While she with breasts like the gem-bright young fruit of the palmyra, her life wasting in her body, and her friends were all consumed with longing, the sun rose from the sea like its forehead mark.
event: Night passes in longing and the sun rises.

tamil: பொன்னியன் மணியுந் தாருங் கண்ணியும் புனைந்து செம்பொன்
மின்னியற் பட்டஞ் சோத்தி யானெய்பால் வெறுப்ப வூட்டி
மன்னியற் பாண்டில் பண்ணி மடந்தைகோல் கொள்ள வைய
மின்னியற் பாவை யேற்பத் தோழியோ டேறி னாளே.
reading: The bulls are dressed with gem bells, garlands and gold forehead plates and fed full with ghee and milk, the carriage is made ready, a woman takes the goad, and Suramanjari climbs into it with her maid.
event: Suramanjari sets out in her bullock carriage with her maid.

tamil: ஆடவ ரிரிய வேகி யஞ்சொல்லார் சூழக் காமன்
மாடத்து ளிழிந்து மற்றவ் வள்ளலை மறைய வைத்துச்
சூடமை மாலை சாந்தம் விளக்கொடு தூப மேந்திச்
சேடியர் தொழுது நிற்பத் திருமகள் பரவு மன்றே.
reading: Men scatter from her path as she goes ringed by sweet-voiced women; she alights at Kama's temple, where the generous one has been hidden, and while her attendants stand worshipping with garlands, sandal, lamp and incense, she prays.
nuance: ஆடவர் இரிய: the royal order her father bought still clears men from her road even as she goes to pray for one. The line does not say who hid Civakan.
event: Suramanjari reaches Kama's temple, where Civakan lies hidden, and begins to worship.

tamil: பொன்னிலஞ் சென்னி புல்ல விடமுழந் தாளை யூன்றி
மின்னவிர் மாலை மென்பூங் குழல்வலத் தோளின் வீழக்
கன்னியங் கமுகின் கண்போற் கலனணி யெருத்தங் கோட்டித்
தன்னிரு கையுங் கூப்பித் தையலீ துரைக்கு மன்றே.
reading: Her head touching the golden floor, her left knee planted, her soft garlanded hair falling on her right shoulder and her neck bent, the maiden joins both hands and speaks.
event: Suramanjari prostrates herself before Kama.

tamil: தாமரைச் செங்கட் செவ்வாய்த் தமனியக் குழையி னாயோர்
காமமிங் குடையேன் காளை சீவக னகலஞ் சோத்தின்
மாமணி மகர மம்பு வண்சிலைக் கரும்பு மான்றேர்
பூமலி மார்ப வீவ லூரொடும் பொலிய வென்றாள்.
reading: She prays to the lotus-eyed god with golden earrings that she has one desire, and that if she may join the chest of the young bull Civakan she will give him a makara banner, arrows, a sugarcane bow and a horse chariot, so that he shines with his whole town.
nuance: The offerings are Kama's own emblems (மகரம், அம்பு, கரும்புச் சிலை): she promises to arm the god who has just conquered her.
event: Suramanjari vows offerings to Kama if she may marry Civakan.

tamil: மட்டவிழ் கோதை பெற்றாய் மனமகிழ் காத லானை
யிட்டிடை நோவ நில்லா தெழுகென வேந்த றோழன்
பட்டிமை யுரைத்த தோராள் பரவிய தெய்வந் தான்வாய்
விட்டுரைத் திட்ட தென்றே வேற்கணாள் பரவி மீண்டாள்.
reading: 'You have won the beloved who gladdens your heart; rise, do not stand so that your slender waist aches': the king's friend spoke this trick, and the spear-eyed one, not knowing it, took it that the god she worshipped had spoken with its own mouth, and praised it and went home.
nuance: The text names only வேந்தன் தோழன்; that this is Buddhisenan is from the story, not the verse. The narrator calls the oracle பட்டிமை, a deceit, and says outright that she did not see through it.
event: Civakan's companion, hidden in the shrine, answers her prayer in the god's voice, and she leaves believing Kama has spoken.

tamil: அடியிறை கொண்ட செம்பொ னாடகச் சிலம்பி னாளக்
கடியறை மருங்கி னின்ற மைந்தனைக் கண்டு நாணி
வடியுறு கடைக்க ணோக்க நெஞ்சுதுட் கென்ன வார்பூங்
கொடியுற வொசிந்து நின்றாள் குழைமுகத் திருவோ டொப்பாள்.
reading: She of the golden anklets, seeing the young man standing by the fragrant chamber, is ashamed; when her sidelong glance meets him her heart starts, and she stands bending like a long creeper, like Tiru herself.
event: Suramanjari sees Civakan in the temple and stands abashed.

title: சுரமஞ்சரியார் இலம்பகம் 2060-2080 (4/5)
theme: Civakan and Suramanjari unite in secret in Kama's shrine; he swears to wed her next day, she discloses the union through friend, foster mother and mother to her father Kuberadattan, who gives her to Civakan before the fire with a great dowry.
source_issues: 2060-2062, 2064-2067, 2070, 2072, 2073, 2075-2077 and 2079 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2065 and 2066 are in a longer metre than the verses around them (lines of seven to eight feet).
The print gives ோ where the sense needs ேர்: சோந்து (2062, for சோர்ந்து), சோத்தி (2074, for சேர்த்தி), நோந்தேன் (2079, for நேர்ந்தேன்).
2077 line 2 பெருவளைப் பிட்டுக் காத்த is obscure.
2079 line 3-4 (கோடி மூன்று ரெரியழன்) is divided across the line break; read as கோடி, மூன்று ஊர், எரியழல்.
2070 line 3 காமதிலகன் may be a name or an epithet.

cast.role: the hero, in disguise in Suramanjari's city, called வேலான் and காமதிலகன் here
the merchant's daughter who had vowed to shun men, now united with and wed to Civakan
Civakan's friends, who ask for Suramanjari in marriage
Suramanjari's maid and friend, to whom she discloses the union
Suramanjari's foster mother
Suramanjari's mother, named Sumati in 2075
Suramanjari's father, the merchant Kuberadattan (named in 2076)

tamil: இலங்குபொன் னோலை மின்ன வின்முகஞ் சிறிது கோட்டி
யலங்கலுங் குழலுந் தாழ வருமணிக் குழையோர் காதிற்
கலந்தொளி கான்று நின்று கதிர்விடு திருவில் வீச
நலங்கனிந் துருகி நின்றா ணாமவேற் காமர் கண்ணாள்.
reading: Suramanjari stands before Civakan with her face a little turned, garland and hair hanging, one gem earring throwing light like a rainbow, melting with love.
event: Suramanjari stands melting before Civakan in Kama's shrine.

tamil: எரிமணிக் கலாபத் திட்ட விந்திர நீல மென்னு
மொருமணி யுந்தி நேரே யொருகதி ருமிழ்வ தேபோ
லருமணிப் பூணி னாட னவ்வயி றணிந்த கோலத்
திருமயி ரொழுக்கம் வந்தென் றிண்ணிறை கவர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: Civakan says the line of fine hair rising from her jewelled navel, like a single ray shot upward from a sapphire, came and carried off his firm restraint.
nuance: The restraint that is lost here is the man's own (என் திண்ணிறை), in the chapter whose heroine had vowed that no one would break hers.

tamil: தேறினேன் றெய்வ மென்றே தீண்டிலே னாயி னுய்யேன்
சீறடி பரவ வந்தே னருளெனத் தொழுது சோந்து
நாறிருங் குழலி னாளை நாகணை விடையிற் புல்லிக்
கோறொடுத் தநங்க னெய்யக் குழைந்துதார் திவண்ட தன்றே.
reading: Saying that he took her for a goddess, that he will not live unless he touches her, and that he came to worship her small feet and begs her grace, Civakan bows, faints with love and embraces her on the couch while Anangan shoots his arrows.
nuance: தேறினேன் தெய்வம் என்றே may also mean that she trusted the god's answer of 2058, which was his friend's trick; either way the worship she offered Kama for him is now offered by him to her.
event: Civakan worships Suramanjari as a goddess and embraces her.

tamil: கலைபுறஞ் சூழ்ந்த வல்குற் கார்மயிற் சாய லாளு
மலைபுறங் கண்ட மார்பின் வாங்குவிற் றடக்கை யானு
மிலைபுறங் கண்ட கண்ணி யின்றமி ழியற்கை யின்ப
நிலைபெற நெறியிற் றுய்த்தார் நிகர்தமக் கிலாத நீரார்.
reading: The woman of the peacock's grace and the man of the hill-defeating chest, matchless both, enjoyed by the proper way the pleasure of the natural union of sweet Tamil so that it would last.
nuance: இன்றமிழ் இயற்கை இன்பம் names the Tamil grammar of love: the first secret union (இயற்கைப் புணர்ச்சி) of the akam poems, and நெறியின் claims the union keeps that rule.
event: Civakan and Suramanjari are united in secret.

tamil: குங்குமங் குயின்ற கொம்மைக் குவிமுலை குளிர்ப்பத் தைவந்
தங்கலுழ் மேனி யல்குற் காசுடன் றிருத்தி யம்பொற்
பொங்குபூஞ் சிலம்பிற் போர்த்த பூந்துக ளவித்து மாதர்
கொங்கலர் கோதை சூட்டிக் குழனலந் திருத்தி னானே.
reading: Afterwards he strokes her saffron-painted breasts to cool them, sets right the beads of her girdle, brushes the pollen from her anklets, crowns her with a garland and arranges her hair.
event: Civakan adorns Suramanjari again after their union.

tamil: வானார்கமழ் மதுவுஞ் சாந்து மேந்தி மதுத்துளித்து வண்டுஞ் சுரும்பு மூசுந்
தேனார்பூங் கோதாய் நினக்குக் காமன் சிலையிரண்டுஞ் செவ்வனே கோலித் தந்தான்
றானாரப் பண்ணித் தடறு நீக்கித் தண்குருதி தோய்த்துத் தகைமை சான்ற
வூனார்ந்த வோரிணை யம்புந் தந்தா னென்னை யுளனாக வேண்டி னானே.
reading: Civakan tells her that Kama bent both his bows straight and gave them to her as brows, and gave her a pair of flesh-fed arrows dipped in cool blood as eyes, because he wanted him to live.
nuance: The closing என்னை உளனாக வேண்டினானே is turned: the weapons that wound him are said to be given so that he may stay alive, which is the lover's paradox and may also mean that Kama wanted him to exist only as her captive.

tamil: கண்ணக்க கண்ணிக் கமழ்பூங் குழற்க ரும்போ தீஞ்சொ லாள்கதிர் முலைகளின்
வண்ணக்கு வானு நிலனுமெல் லாம்விலை யேமழை மின்னு நுசுப்பி னாளைப்
பெண்ணுக் கணியாக வேண்டி மேலைப் பெரியோர் பெருமான் படைத்தா னென்று
புண்ணக்க வேலான் புகழ நாணிப் பூநோக்கிப் பூக்கொசிந்த கொம்பொத் தாளே.
reading: When Civakan praises her, saying that sky and earth together are the price of her breasts and that the lord of the ancient great ones made her as an ornament for womankind, she is shy, looks down at the flowers and bends like a branch heavy with blossom.
event: Civakan praises Suramanjari and she bows her head in shyness.

tamil: இறங்கிய மாதர் தன்னை யெரிமணிக் கடகக் கையாற்
குறங்கின்மேற் றழுவி வைத்துக் கோதையங் குருதி வேலா
னறந்தலை நீங்கக் காக்கு மரசன்யா னாக நாளைச்
சிறந்தநின் னலத்தைச் சேரே னாய்விடிற் செல்க வென்றான்.
reading: Taking the bowed girl on his thigh, Civakan swears that if he does not join her beauty tomorrow he may become a king whose guarding lets dharma leave, and bids her go.
nuance: The oath is a self-curse, and the penalty he names is a king's failure, though he passes as a merchant's son: the hidden prince swears by the sceptre he has not yet regained. நாளை promises marriage, which 2078 keeps. The reading of அறந்தலை நீங்கக் காக்கும் as 'guarding so that dharma departs' is the plainest the words allow but is not certain.
event: Civakan swears an oath to wed Suramanjari the next day and sends her away.

tamil: வில்லிடு மணிசெ யாழி மெல்விரல் விதியிற் கூப்பி
நல்லடி பணிந்து நிற்ப நங்கைநீ நடுங்க வேண்டா
செல்கெனச் சிலம்பு செம்பொற் கிண்கிணி மிழற்ற வொல்கி
யல்குற்கா சொலிப்ப வாயம் பாவைசென் றெய்தி னாளே.
reading: She folds her ringed fingers in due form and bows at his feet; told not to tremble but to go, she sways away with anklets and girdle chiming and reaches her company.
event: Suramanjari bows to Civakan, leaves him and rejoins her companions.

tamil: பருமணிப் படங்கொ ணாகப் பையெனப் பரந்த வல்கு
லெரிமணிப் பூணி னானுக் கின்னல மொழிய வேகித்
திருமணிச் சிவிகை யேறிச் செம்பொனீண் மாடம் புக்காள்
விரிமணி விளங்கு மாலை வெம்முலை வேற்க ணாளே.
reading: Leaving her sweetness with the jewelled man, the girl of the spear-like eyes mounts the gem palanquin and enters her golden mansion.
event: Suramanjari returns home in her palanquin.

tamil: திருவிற்றான் மாரி கற்பான் றுவலைநாட் செய்வ தேபோ
லுருவிற்றாய்த் துளிக்குந் தேற லோங்குதார் மார்பன் றோழர்
பொருவிற்றா நம்பி காம திலகனென் றிருந்த போழ்திற்
செருவிற்றாழ் நுதலி னாள்கண் மணத்திறஞ் செப்பு கின்றார்.
reading: While Civakan, his garland dripping honey like a rainbow that learns to rain, sits as the peerless prince Kamatilakan, his friends go to speak of marriage for the girl of the bow-like brows.
nuance: காமதிலகன் may be a name under which the friends present him, as he is in disguise in this ilampakam, or only an epithet; the verse does not settle it.
event: Civakan's friends go to ask for Suramanjari in marriage.

tamil: புனைகொடி பூத்த தேபோற் பொறுக்கலா நுசுப்பிற் பாவை
நனைகுடைந் துண்டு தேக்கி நன்மணி வண்டு பாடும்
புனைகடி மாலை மாதர் திறத்திது மொழிந்து விட்டார்.
reading: They make their proposal concerning the girl, a flowering creeper painted with the sea's nectar and honey, whose waist can hardly bear her, wearing a garland where bees sing.
event: Civakan's friends ask for Suramanjari in marriage.

tamil: ஐயற்கென் றுரைத்த மாற்றங் கேட்டலு மலங்க னாய்கன்
வெய்யதேன் வாய்க்கொண் டாற்போல் விழுங்கலோ டுமிழ்த றேற்றான்
செய்வதெ னோற்றி லாதே னோற்றிலா டிறத்தி னென்று
மையல்கொண் டிருப்ப வப்பாற் குமரிதன் மதியிற் சூழ்ந்தாள்.
reading: Hearing that she is asked for the master, the merchant, like a man with hot honey in his mouth, can neither swallow nor spit, and grieves that he and his daughter alike have done no penance, while the girl turns the matter over in her own mind.
nuance: The father who bought a royal order to keep men from her (907) is caught between the offer and her vow; he blames neither the suitor nor her but their lack of earlier penance (நோற்றிலாதேன் நோற்றிலாள்).
event: Suramanjari's father hears the proposal and cannot decide, while she deliberates.

tamil: பொற்பமை தாமக் கந்து பொருந்திய மின்னுப் போல
வெற்பக வெரியு மாலைப் பவளத்தூண் பொருந்தி யின்னீர்க்
கற்பெனு மாலை வீசி நாணெனுங் களிவண் டோப்பிச்
சொற்புக ரின்றித் தோழிக் கறத்தினோ டரிவை நின்றாள்.
reading: Leaning on a coral pillar like lightning on a garlanded post, waving the garland of chastity and driving off the drunken bee of shame, she stands before her friend and tells her, with no flaw in her words, as dharma requires.
nuance: அறத்தினோடு நின்றாள் is the akam convention அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், disclosing a secret union so that it may end in marriage; the image sets chastity above shame, since she must put shame away for chastity's sake.
event: Suramanjari discloses her union with Civakan to her friend.

tamil: வழிவளர் மயிலஞ் சாயற் பவளப்பூம் பாவை யன்ன
கழிவளர் கயற்க ணங்கை கற்பினை யறிந்து தோழி
யழிமது மாலை சோத்தி யடிபணிந் தார வாழ்த்திப்
பொழிமதுப் புயலைங் கூந்தற் செவிலியைப் பொருந்திச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: Knowing her chastity, the friend puts a garland on her, bows at her feet, blesses her and goes to tell the foster mother.
event: Suramanjari's friend tells the foster mother.

tamil: நனைவளர் கோதை நற்றாய் நங்கைக்கீ துள்ள மென்று
சுனைவளர் குவளை யுண்கட் சுமதிக்குச் செவிலி செப்பக்
கனயிருட் கனவிற் கண்டேன் காமர்பூம் பொய்கை வற்ற
வனையதாங் கன்னி நீரின் றற்றதா நங்கைக் கென்றாள்.
reading: The foster mother tells Sumati, the girl's mother, that this is the girl's heart, and the mother says she saw in a dream in the thick dark a lovely flower pond run dry, and that so today the girl's maidenhood has gone.
nuance: Who speaks the dream is not marked: கண்டேன் ... என்றாள் follows the foster mother's report and is most naturally the mother's answer, but it may continue the foster mother's words.
event: The foster mother tells Sumati, who recalls a dream that foretold the loss of the girl's maidenhood.

tamil: கெண்டையுஞ் சிலையுந் திங்க ளிளமையுங் கிடந்து தேங்கொ
டொண்டையங் கனியு முத்துந் தொழதக வணிந்து தூங்குங்
குண்டல முடைய திங்க ளிதுவெனு முகத்தி தாதை
வண்புகழ்க் குபேர தத்தன் கேட்டனன் மனைவி சொன்னாள்.
reading: The wife tells Kuberadattan of great fame, father of the girl whose face is a moon with fish, bow, coral, pearls and earrings in it.
event: Sumati tells Kuberadattan of their daughter's union.

tamil: செருவிளைத் தனலும் வேலோய் சிறுமுதுக் குறைவி தானே
பெருவளைப் பிட்டுக் காத்த கற்பிது போலு மையன்
கரிவிளைத் தாய்ந்த சுண்ணம் வாட்டின னென்று கண்டாய்
திருவிளை தேம்பெய் மாரி பாற்கடற் பெய்த தென்றாள்.
reading: She tells him that their small, too-wise daughter kept this chastity of hers against all, and that the very man who made her powder lose has won her: the honey rain of fortune has fallen into the sea of milk.
nuance: The mother turns the girl's grievance into proof: the vow taken in anger at Civakan's verdict (904, 908) is read as chastity kept for Civakan. பெருவளைப் பிட்டுக் காத்த is obscure.

tamil: கேட்பது விரும்பி நாய்கன் கிளைக்கெலா முணர்த்தி யார்க்கும்
வேட்பன வடிசி லாடை விழுக்கலன் மாலை சாந்தங்
கோட்குறை வின்றி யாக்கிக் குழுமியங் கறங்கி யார்ப்ப
நாட்கடி மாலை யாற்கு நங்கையை நல்கி னானே.
reading: Glad of what he hears, the merchant tells all his kin, prepares food, cloth, jewels, garlands and sandal for everyone without lack, and with drums sounding gives his daughter to the man of the fresh garland.
event: Kuberadattan gives Suramanjari to Civakan in marriage.

tamil: பரியகஞ் சிலம்பு பைம்பொற் கிண்கிணி யார்ந்த பாதத்
தரிவைய ராடன் மிக்கா ரருமணி வீணை வல்லா
ருரியநூற் றெண்மர் செம்பொ னொன்றரைக் கோடி மூன்று
ரெரியழன் முன்னர் நோந்தே னென்மகட் கென்று சொன்னான்.
reading: He says that before the fire he has given his daughter a hundred and eight women with anklets, skilled in dance and the vina, one and a half crore of red gold, and three villages.
nuance: The bride is given before the fire (எரியழல் முன்னர்), and with her a dowry the father declares himself.
event: Kuberadattan declares the dowry given with his daughter before the fire.

tamil: மாசறு மணியு முத்தும் வயிரமு மொளிரு மேனி
யாசறு செம்பொ னார்ந்த வலங்கலங் குன்ற னானுந்
தூசுறு பரவை யல்குற் றூமணிக் கொம்ப னாளுங்
காசறக் கலந்த வின்பக் கடலகத் தழுந்தி னாரே.
reading: He with jewel-bright body and a chest like a garlanded hill, and she like a gem-hung branch, sink into a sea of pleasure mingled without flaw.
event: Civakan and Suramanjari live in wedded pleasure.

title: சுரமஞ்சரியார் இலம்பகம் 2081-2101 (5/5)
theme: The close of Suramanjari's ilampakam: the first nights of Civakan and Suramanjari, her jealous sulk over the painted figure ended when he lays his head on her anklets as her old vow required, his leave-taking, and his secret homecoming to his foster parents and wives, Gunamalai blaming her own deeds and he crediting her penance, before he leaves the city again as a merchant.
source_issues: Every verse except 2084 was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2087 line 3 ஓரூ ரிரண்டஃக மாயிற் is obscure as divided; the sense of the proverb is not certain.
2097 line 1 கந்துகண் கழற is read as Kantukkatan's name in short form; the division is not certain.
2089 line 1 prints னழிழ்துறழ், apparently a misprint for னமிழ்துறழ் (அமிழ்து உறழ், like nectar).

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called சீவகசாமி in the invocation
a merchant's daughter who loses the scented-powder contest and shuns men, now Civakan's wife
the god of love, lord of the five arrows, who brings spring
Civakan's companions
Kandukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother (named in 365)
Civakan's kin in the old city
the merchant who takes up and raises the newborn Civakan
the merchant's kinsfolk
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina; his wife, called தத்தை
a merchant's daughter, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest, whom Civakan saves and marries

tamil: பொன்வரை பொருத யானைப் புணர்மருப் பனைய வாகித்
தென்வரைச் சாந்து மூழ்கித் திரள்வடஞ் சுமந்து வீங்கி
மின்வளர் மருங்குல் செற்ற வெம்முலை மணிக்கண் சேப்பத்
தொன்னலம் பருகித் தோன்ற றுறக்கம்புக் கவர்க ளொத்தான்.
reading: Her hot breasts, like the joined tusks of an elephant that has battered a golden hill, steeped in southern sandal and swelling under their strings of pearls, redden at their gem tips as he drinks her old beauty, and he is like those who have entered heaven.
nuance: The beauty he drinks is தொன்னலம், her beauty of long standing: the woman who had vowed to look on no man has kept it unspent until now.
event: Civakan and Suramanjari come together on their first night.

tamil: வரிக்கழற் குருசின் மார்பு மடந்தைவெம் முலையுந் தம்முட்
செருச்செய்து திளைத்துப் போரிற் சிலம்பொலி கலந்த பாணி
யரிப்பறை யனுங்க வார்க்கு மேகலைக் குரலோ டீண்டிப்
புரிக்குழல் புலம்ப வைகிப் பூவணை விடுக்க லானே.
reading: The hero's chest and the girl's breasts make war and revel; the beat of the anklets, the clinking girdle and the drum-like rhythm mingle, her braided hair moans, and he lingers so that he cannot leave the flower bed.
nuance: Love-making is told in the vocabulary of battle (செரு, போர்), with the ornaments as the war-drums.

tamil: மணியியல் வள்ளத் தேந்த மதுமகிழ்ந் தனந்தர் கூர
வணிமலர்க் குவளைப் பைம்போ தொருகையி னருளி யம்பொற்
பிணையனா ளருகு சேரிற் பேதுறு நுசுப்பென் றெண்ணித்
துணையமை தோள்க டம்மாற் றோன்றறான் புல்லி னானே.
reading: Drinking wine from a gem cup until drowsiness came on, he gave her a fresh blue lily with one hand, and thinking that if the golden doe came close her slender waist would be hurt, he held her with his two shoulders.
event: Civakan gives Suramanjari a lily and embraces her.

tamil: மல்லலங் கங்கை போலும் பலர்முயங் கார மார்பிற்
புல்லன்மின் போமின் வேண்டா வென்றவள் புலந்து நீங்க
முல்லையங் கோதை யொன்றும் பிழைப்பிலேன் முனிய னீயென்
றல்லலுற் றரத்த மார்ந்த சீறடி தொழுதிட் டானே.
reading: She sulks and pulls away, telling him not to embrace her with a chest that many embrace as they do the broad Ganges; he, in distress, saying he has done no wrong and asking the jasmine-garlanded one not to be angry, worships her small red-dyed feet.
nuance: The charge has a literal base in this epic: by this ilampakam the hero has already married several wives, so her figure of the river all may bathe in is a complaint as well as a lover's pretext.
event: Suramanjari, jealous, refuses Civakan's embrace, and he bows to her feet.

tamil: வட்டிகைப் பாவை நோக்கி மகிழ்ந்திருந் திலிரோ வென்னாத்
தொட்டிமை யுருவந் தோன்றச் சுவரையே பொருந்தி நின்றாய்
கட்டழ குடைய நங்கை நீயெனக் கருதிக் கண்ணா
னொட்டியா னோக்கிற் றென்றா னொருபிடி நுசுப்பி னாட்கே.
reading: She asks whether he was not delighting in gazing at the painted figure, and he answers the slim-waisted one that she stood pressed to the wall so that her form showed on it, and his eye, taking it for her, the beautiful maid, clung to it.
nuance: The construal of line 2 is uncertain: it may be his excuse (she leaned on the wall and her likeness showed there) or part of her charge (he stood fixed at the wall); the reading here takes it as his reply, closed by என்றான்.
event: Suramanjari accuses Civakan of gazing at a painted figure; he says he took it for her.

tamil: நுண்டுகி னெகிழ்ந்த வல்குன் மணிபரந் திமைப்ப நொந்து
கண்களை யிடுகக் கோட்டிக் காமத்திற் செயிர்த்து நோக்கிக்
குண்டல மிலங்கக் கோதை கூந்தலோ டவிழ்ந்து சோர
வொண்டொடி யூடி நின்றா ளொளிமணிப் பூங்கொம் பொப்பாள்.
reading: Her fine silk slipping and the gems on her waist flashing, hurt, she narrowed her eyes, glared at him in love's anger, and with earrings shining and her garland coming loose with her hair, the bright-bangled one stood sulking like a flowering branch of bright gems.
event: Suramanjari stands apart in her sulk.

tamil: கிழவனாய்ப் பாடி வந்தென் கீழ்ச்சிறை யிருப்பக் கண்டே
னெழுதிய பாவை நோக்கி யிமையவித் திருப்பக் கண்டே
னொழிகவிக் காம மோரூ ரிரண்டஃக மாயிற் றென்றாங்
கழுதகண் ணீர்கண் மைந்த னாவிபோழ்ந் திட்ட வன்றே.
reading: She says she saw him come as an old man singing and sit in her lower chamber, and saw him sit unblinking gazing at the painted figure, and cries away with this love, the one town has become two; and the tears she wept split the young man's life.
nuance: She now knows the old singer who sat in her chamber was Civakan in disguise. The phrase ஓரூர் இரண்டஃகமாயிற்று (the one town has become two, or two measures) seems proverbial for a divided love, but its exact sense is not clear from the verse.
event: Suramanjari recalls Civakan's disguise as an old man and his gazing at the painting, and weeps.

tamil: அலங்கறா தவிழ வஞ்செஞ் சீறடி யணிந்த வம்பூஞ்
சிலம்பின்மேற் சென்னி சோத்திச் சிறியவர் செய்த தீமை
புலம்பலர் பொறுப்ப ரன்றே பெரியவ ரென்று கூறி
யிலங்குவேற் கண்ணி யூட லிளையவ னீக்கி னானே.
reading: Setting his head on the anklets of her small red feet so that his garland came undone, and saying that the great bear without complaint the wrongs the small have done, the young man ended the sulk of the woman with spear-bright eyes.
nuance: He has just said he did no wrong (2084), yet he pleads as the small one who erred, making her the great one who forgives: the maxim is used as a lover's tactic. The gesture also completes her vow of 899, that she would keep apart until he came defeated and worshipped her anklet feet.
event: Civakan lays his head on Suramanjari's anklets and ends her sulk.

tamil: யாழ்கொன்ற கிளவி யாட னழிழ்துறழ் புலவி நீக்கிக்
காழின்றிக் கனிந்த காமக் கொழுங்கனி நுகர்ந்து காதற்
றாழ்கின்ற தாம மார்பன் றையலோ டாடி விள்ளா
னூழ்சென்ற மதியம் வெய்யோ னொட்டியொன் றாய தொத்தான்.
reading: Ending the sulk of her whose speech outdoes the yal and is sweeter than nectar, and tasting the ripe fruit of love that has no hard stone, the man with the hanging garland did not leave his play with the girl, and was like the moon and sun joined in one when their time comes round.
nuance: ஊழ் here is the turn of time that brings sun and moon together at the new moon, not deeds of a former birth.
event: After the quarrel Civakan and Suramanjari are reunited in love.

tamil: பச்சிலைப் பட்டு முத்தும் பவளமு மிமைக்கு மல்கு
னச்சிலை வேற்கண் மாதர் நகைமுக முறுவன் மாந்தி
யிச்சையுங் குறிப்பு நோக்கி யெய்வதே கரும மாகக்
கைச்சிலை கணையோ டேந்திக் காமனிக் கடையைக் காப்பான்.
reading: Kama, holding bow and arrow, guards this doorway, drinking the laughing face and smile of the woman whose waist shines with green silk, pearls and coral, and watching for desire and signs, his only work to shoot.
nuance: The god of love is posted as doorkeeper of their chamber, where earlier her father's guards had kept men out.

tamil: கடிப்பிணை காது சோத்திச் சிகழிகை காத நாறத்
தொடுத்தலர் மாலை சூட்டிக் கிம்புரி முத்த மென்றோ
ளடுத்தணிந் தாகஞ் சாந்தி னணிபெற வெழுதி யல்கு
லுடுத்தபொற் கலாபந் தைவந் தொளிவளை திருத்தி னானே.
reading: He set ornaments in her ears, crowned her braid with a strung garland whose scent carried far, put pearl-tipped bands on her soft arms, painted her body with sandal, stroked the gold girdle on her waist and set her bright bangles right.
event: Civakan adorns Suramanjari.

tamil: இலங்குவெள் ளருவிக் குன்றத் தெழுந்ததண் டகரச் செந்தீ
நலங்கிள ரகிலுந் தேனுங் கட்டியு நன்கு கூட்டிப்
புலம்பற வளர்த்த வம்மென் பூம்புகை யமளி யங்கண்
விலங்கர சனைய காளை வெள்வளைக் கிதனைச் சொன்னான்.
reading: On the couch fragrant with soft smoke from tagara wood of the hill of white falls, with fine agil, honey and sugar mixed and burned to end loneliness, the youth like a king of beasts said this to the white-bangled girl.
event: Civakan prepares to speak to Suramanjari on the couch.

tamil: கருமநீ கவல வேண்டா கயற்கணாய் பிரிவல் சின்னா
ளருமைநின் கவினைத் தாங்க லதுபொரு ளென்று கூறப்
பெருமநீ வேண்டிற் றல்லால் வேண்டுவ பிறிதொன் றுண்டோ
வொருமைநின் மனத்திற் சென்றே னுவப்பதே யுவப்ப தென்றாள்.
reading: He tells the carp-eyed girl not to worry about his business, for he will be parted from her only a few days and her duty is to bear her rare beauty; she answers that she wants nothing but what he wants, that she has gone with one mind into his heart, and what pleases him is what pleases her.
nuance: The verse holds both voices: lines 1 and 2 are his, lines 3 and 4 hers. The woman who had sworn to shun all men now defines her will as his.
event: Civakan tells Suramanjari he must leave for a few days, and she consents.

tamil: நாணொடு மிடைந்த தேங்கொ ணடுக்குறு கிளவி கேட்டே
பூண்வடுப் பொறிப்பப் புல்லிப் புனைநலம் புலம்ப வைகேன்
றேன்மிடை கோதை யென்று திருமக னெழுந்து போகி
வாண்மிடை தோழர் சூழத் தன்மனை மகிழ்ந்து புக்கான்.
reading: Hearing her honey-sweet words woven with modesty, he embraced her so that his ornaments left their marks, told the honey-garlanded one not to pine and let her beauty fade, rose, and went with his sword-bearing friends round him gladly into his own house.
event: Civakan leaves Suramanjari and goes with his friends to his foster father's house.

tamil: புரவியுங் களிறு நோக்கிப் பொன்னெடுந் தேரு நோக்கி
யிரவினும் பகலு மோவா தென்மகன் யாண்டை யானென்
றழுதகண் ணீரி னாலே கைகழீஇ யவலிக் கின்ற
மெழுகெரி முகந்த தொக்குந் தாய்மெலி வகற்றி னானே.
reading: He ended the wasting of his mother, who, looking at horses, elephants and tall golden chariots, never ceasing night or day to cry where is my son, had washed her hands in the tears she wept and grieved like a wax figure taken by fire.
nuance: The mother scans the horses, elephants and chariots, the things her son rode, as if they could tell her where he is.
event: Civakan returns to his foster mother and ends her grief.

tamil: ஒற்றரு முணர்த லின்றி யுரையவித் துறுப்பி னாலே
சுற்றத்தார்க் குரைப்ப வேண்டித் தொக்குடன் றழுவிக் கொள்வா
