ரெற்றுவா ரினைந்து சோர்வார் நம்பியோ நம்பி யென்னா
வுற்றுடன் றழுத கண்ணீர் காலலைத் தொழுகிற் றன்றே.
reading: So that not even spies should know, they silenced their speech and wanted to tell the kin by gestures; the kin gathered and embraced him, beat themselves, wilted, and crying Nambi, o Nambi, wept tears that ran down and washed his feet.
nuance: His return must stay hidden from Kattiyangaran's spies: even the reunion is held in signs.
event: Civakan's kin greet him in secret, weeping, without words.

tamil: கந்துகண் கழறக் கல்லென் கடற்றிரை யவிந்த வண்ணம்
வந்தவர் புலம்பு நீங்க மறைபுறப் படுமென் றெண்ணி
யெந்தைதா னிறந்த நாளின் றெனநக ரியம்பி யாரு
மந்தமி லுவகை தன்னா லகங்குளிர்ப் பெய்தி னாரே.
reading: When Kandukkan rebuked them the uproar fell still like the waves of the roaring sea, and thinking the secret would get out, he proclaimed in the city that today was the day his father died, and all were cooled within by a joy without end.
nuance: The weeping of joy is given out as mourning so that no spy guesses its cause. The verse is read here with கந்துகண் as Kantukkatan and எந்தை as his father; both are the likeliest readings, not certain.
event: Kantukkatan quiets the kin and announces a death anniversary to explain the weeping.

tamil: செங்கயன் மழைக்கட் செவ்வாய்த் தத்தையு மகிழ்ந்து தீஞ்சொ
லெங்கையைச் சென்று காண்மி னடிகளென் றிரந்து கூற
மங்கல வகையிற் சோந்து மதுத்துளி யறாத மாலை
கொங்கலர் கண்ணி சோத்திக் குங்கும மெழுதி னானே.
reading: Tattai of the red carp-like eyes, rejoicing, begged him in sweet words to go and see her younger sister, and in auspicious fashion he set a garland of unceasing honey and a fragrant wreath on her and painted her with saffron.
nuance: எங்கை, my younger sister, is Gunamalai, called so by her co-wife. Whether the woman he adorns in lines 3 and 4 is Tattai, before he goes, or Gunamalai on his arrival is not clear from the verse.
event: Gandharvadattai sends Civakan to see Gunamalai, and he adorns a wife with garland and saffron.

tamil: தீவினை யுடைய வென்னைத் தீண்டன்மி னடிகள் வேண்டா
பாவியே னென்று நொந்து பரிந்தழு துருகி நையக்
காவியங் கண்ணி யொன்றுங் கவலல்யா னுய்ந்த தெல்லா
நாவியே நாறு மேனி நங்கைநின் றவத்தி னென்றான்.
reading: Gunamalai cries do not touch sinful me, lord, there is no need, I am a wrongdoer, and grieves, weeps and melts; he tells the girl with lily eyes not to grieve at all, for all his survival came from her penance, the girl whose body smells of musk.
nuance: She calls herself தீவினை உடைய, one with evil deeds, because his seizure followed his rescue of her from the elephant; he turns her guilt into merit. The verse does not name a school for the power of தவம்.
event: Gunamalai blames herself for Civakan's danger; he says her penance saved him.

tamil: அன்னமென் னடையு நோக்குஞ் சாயலு மணியு மேரு
மின்னினுண் ணுசுப்பும் வெய்ய முலைகளு முகமுந் தோன்ற
வென்மனத் தெழுதப் பட்டா யாயினு மரிவை கேளா
யுன்னையான் பிரிந்த நாளோ ரூழியே போன்ற தென்றான்.
reading: He tells her that though her soft gait like a swan's, her look, her grace, her jewels, her beauty, her lightning-slim waist, her breasts and her face were painted in his mind, the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
nuance: Her image painted in his mind did not make the parting short: memory is set against absence and loses.

tamil: இளையவண் மகிழ்வ கூறி யின்றுயி லமர்ந்து பின்னாள்
விளைபொரு ளாய வெல்லாந் தாதைக்கே வேறு கூறிக்
கிளையவர் சூழ வாமான் வாணிக னாகிக் கேடி
றளையவிழ் தாம மார்பன் றன்னகர் நீங்கி னானே.
reading: Telling the young woman things to delight her, he slept, and the next day he gave all the wealth he had gained to his father, and with his kin around him, as a merchant on a fine horse, the man of the flawless garland left his city.
nuance: வாமான் வாணிகனாகி may mean he went as a horse-trader or simply rode as a merchant; either way he leaves in disguise, still hidden from the usurper.
event: Civakan gives his gains to Kantukkatan and leaves the city in a merchant's guise.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2102-2126 (1/9)
theme: Civakan and his company cross the five landscapes in turn, the desert in a single day, reach Videham and send word to its king, who orders a welcome; the city throngs to see him, hails him with the names of Kama and Murugan, and its women plead with his elephants to walk slowly.
source_issues: 2102-2111 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2123 lines 3-4 are flagged for a possible lost vowel sign (துடியடு, வடியடு); both read well as அடு 'defeat' and are best left unrepaired.
2120 line 2 அமா குமரனின் is probably a corruption of அமர் குமரனின்.
2118 lines 1-3 are divided across words (அல்கு/ல், தொ/றோட) by the printed line breaks.
2126 line 4 (உயிர்கா வலற்கொண் டுதவநில்) is hard to construe; 2109 line 3 and 2106 line 4 are also obscure.

cast.role: the hero, travelling to Videham and welcomed into its city
the young men of Civakan's company (திறலார், தீதிலார், இளையவர்)
the king of Videham (விதையம்), who orders the welcome; not named in these verses
the king's people of Videham, who meet the guest with gifts
the crowds of the city of Videham, who gather and hail Civakan (நகரம், ஏனையவர்)
the women of the towns and city of Videham, who praise, gaze at and bless Civakan
the elephants of Civakan's entry, the she-elephant (இரும்பிடி) and the tusker (சிறுபிடி கேள்வன்) the women address

tamil: குடம்புரை செருத்தற் குவளைமேய் கயவாய்க் குவிமுலைப் படர்மருப் பெருமை
நடந்தவா யெல்லா நறுமலர் மரையி னாகிலைச் சொரிந்தவந் தீம்பா
றடஞ்சிறை யன்னங் குருகொடு நாரைப் பார்ப்பின மோம்புதண் மருத
மடங்கல்போற் றிறலார் மாமணி கறங்க வளவயற் புள்ளெனக் கழிந்தார்.
reading: Civakan's company, strong as lions, passes through the marutam fields, where a buffalo with udders like pots grazes the kuvalai and its sweet milk, spilled wherever it walks, feeds the young of swans, herons and storks, and their great bells ring as they go.
nuance: The verse opens a journey through all five landscapes in order: marutam (2102), neytal (2103), mullai (2104), kurinji (2105) and palai (2106-2107).
event: Civakan and his company pass through the farm country of the marutam fields.

tamil: புரிவளை யலறிப் பூசலிட் டீன்ற பொழிகதிர் நிலத்தில் முழக்கி
வரிவளை சூழும் வலம்புரி யினத்துட் சலஞ்சல மேய்வன நோக்கி
யரிதுண ரன்னம் பெடையெனத் தழுவி யன்மையி னலமர லெய்தித்
திரிதரு நோக்கந் தீதிலார் நோக்கி நெய்தலுங் கைவலத் தொழிந்தார்.
reading: Watching a swan that, among the conches circling a right-whorled conch on the shore, embraces one as its mate and then reels in distress to find it is not, the faultless travellers leave the neytal shore on their right.
nuance: The swan's mistake of a conch for its mate is a small figure of desire deceived by likeness, set in the landscape the travellers merely pass.
event: The company passes the seashore of the neytal country.

tamil: கோட்டிளங் கலையுங் கூடுமென் பிணையுங் கொழுங்கதிர் மணிவிளக் கெறிப்பச்
சேட்டிளங் கொன்றைத் திருநிழற் றுஞ்சச் செம்பொறி வண்டவற் றயலே
நாட்டிளம் படியார் நகைமுகம் பருகு நல்லவர் போன்மலர் பருகு
மோட்டிள முல்லை மொய்ம்மலர்க் கான முருகுவந் தெதிர்கொள நடந்தார்.
reading: Where the buck and doe sleep under the konrai and bees drink the flowers as good men drink the smiling faces of the country's young women, the mullai forest comes out to meet them with its fragrance as they walk.
event: The company walks through the mullai forest.

tamil: குழவிவெண் டிங்கட் கோட்டின்மேற் பாயக் குளிர்புனல் சடைவிரித் தேற்கு
மழலவிர் சூலத் தண்ணலே போல வருவிநீர் மருப்பினி னெறியக்
கழைவளர் குன்றிற் களிறுநின் றாடுங் கடிநறுஞ் சந்தனச் சார
லிழைவளர் முலையார் சாயல்போற் றோகை யிறைகொள்பூங் குறிஞ்சியு மிறந்தார்.
reading: They cross the kurinji, where on the bamboo hill a tusker stands and plays with a stream falling on its tusks, like the lord of the bright trident who takes cold water on his spread matted hair with the young white moon, and where peacocks gather like women in their grace.
nuance: The elephant under the waterfall is likened to the trident-bearer receiving the river on his matted hair with the crescent, Siva's image used as ornament in a Jain epic, with no claim about the god.
event: The company crosses the hill country.

tamil: ஊன்றலைப் பொடித்தாங் கனையசெஞ் சூட்டி னெளிமயிர் வாரண மொருங்கே
கான்றபூங் கடம்பின் கவட்டிடை வளைவாய்ப் பருந்தொடு கவர்குரல் பயிற்று
மான்றவெம் பாலை யழன்மிதித் தன்ன வருஞ்சுரஞ் சுடர்மறை பொழுதி
னூன்றினார் பாய்மா வொளிமதிக் கதிர்போற் சந்தன மொருங்குமெய் புதைத்தே.
reading: At sunset they mount their leaping horses for the hard desert track, hot as if one trod on fire, where red-combed jungle fowl call among the kadamba with the hooked-beaked kites, their bodies covered with sandal like moonbeams.
nuance: They take the desert by night and against the heat cover themselves with sandal paste.
event: At nightfall the company rides into the palai desert.

tamil: நிலையிலா வுலகி னின்றவண் புகழை வேட்டவ னிதியமே போன்று
மிலைகுலாம் பைம்பூ ணிளமுலைத் தூதி னின்கனித் தொண்டையந் துவர்வாய்க்
கலைவலார் நெஞ்சிற் காமமே போன்றுங் கடவுளர் வெகுளியே போன்று
முலைவிலார் நில்லா தொருபக லுள்ளே யுருப்பவிர் வெஞ்சுரங் கடந்தார்.
reading: Not stopping, they cross the burning desert within a single day, as quickly as the wealth of one who seeks the generous fame that stands in an unstable world goes from him, as desire goes from the hearts of the learned when a young woman's messenger comes, and as the anger of the holy passes.
nuance: The three similes are three things that do not stay, and each is praise: the fame-seeker's wealth leaves because he gives it away, the learned man's desire leaves because he masters it, the anger of the holy leaves because it is brief. கடவுளர் may mean gods or the holy ascetics; the second simile's line (தூதின் ... கலைவலார் நெஞ்சிற் காமம்) is compressed and its sense is my best construal.
event: The company crosses the desert in one day.

tamil: புதுக்கலம் போலும் பூங்கனி யாலும் பொன்னிணர்ப் பிண்டியும் பொருந்தி
மதுக்கலந் தூழ்த்துச் சிலம்பிவீழ் வனபோன் மலர்சொரி வகுளமு மயங்கிக்
கதிர்த்ததண் பூணி கம்புடாழ் பீலிக் கனைகுர னாரைவண் டான
மெதிர்த்ததண் புனல்சூ ழின்னதிக் கரைமே லிளையவ ரயாவுயிர்த் தெழுந்தார்.
reading: On the bank of this river, ringed by cool water where bakula trees shed flowers as if honey dripped from them and the hum of herons and bees meets the stream, the young men breathe out their weariness and rise.
event: The young men rest on a river bank after the desert and set out again.

tamil: அள்ளிலைப் பலவி னளிந்து வீழ் சுளையுங் கனிந்துவீழ் வாழையின் பழனும்
புள்ளிவா ழலவன் பொறிவரிக் கமஞ்சூன் ஞெண்டினுக் குய்த்துநோய் தணிப்பான்
பள்ளிவாய் நந்து மாமையும் பணித்துப் பன்மலர் வழிபடக் குறைக்கும்
வெள்ளநீர்ப் படப்பை விதையம்வந் தடைந்தே வேந்தனுக் குணர்த்தமுன் விடுத்தார்.
reading: Reaching the water-rich groves of Videham, where the spotted crab carries fallen jackfruit and banana to ease the craving of its pregnant mate, they send men ahead to tell the king.
nuance: The crab feeding its pregnant mate is the last of the journey's small domestic scenes before the human welcome begins. The third line, on the snail and the turtle, is hard to construe.
event: The company reaches Videham and sends word ahead to its king.

tamil: வீட்டிடந் தோறும் வில்லக விரல்போற் பொருந்திநின் றொருங்கெதிர் கொள்கென்
றேட்டின்மேற் றீட்டித் திருவெழுத் திட்டாங் கிறைவனுந் தமர்களைப் பணிப்ப
நாட்டகத் தமிர்து நளிகட லமிர்து நல்வரை யமிர்தமு மல்லாக்
காட்டகத் தமிர்துங் காண்வரக் குவவிக் கண்ணகன் புறவெதிர் கொண்டார்.
reading: The king writes his order on the palm-leaf in the royal hand, that his people in every house should stand close together like the fingers in a bow-guard and receive the guest as one, and they heap up the nectars of the land, the sea, the hills and the forest and go out to meet him on the wide outskirts.
nuance: The four nectars (land, sea, hill, forest) gather the landscapes the company has just crossed into the welcome itself.
event: The king of Videham orders his people by written decree to receive Civakan, and they meet him with the produce of all four lands.

tamil: பொருமத யானைப் புணர்மருப் பேய்ப்பப் பொன்சுமந் தேந்திய முலையா
ரெரிமலர்ச் செவ்வாய் திறந்துதே னூற வேத்துவார் பூக்கடூய்த் தொழுவார்
வருகுலைக் கமுகும் வாழையு நடுவார் வரையுமி ழாவிபோன் மாடத்
தருநறும் புகையு மேந்துவா ரூர்தோ றமரர்த முலகமொத் ததுவே.
reading: Women with gold-laden breasts open their red mouths in praise, strew flowers and bow, plant fruiting areca and plantain, and carry fragrant smoke like a mountain's mist, so that every town is like the world of the gods.
event: The women of the towns line the road, praising and worshipping the guest.

reading: The gates and temples, the halls, theatres and avenues of the mansioned city, like a great mountain loud with falls, all gather to see the noble one.
event: The whole city gathers to see Civakan.

reading: On one side the bright golden bands tied on the brows of beautiful women, decked with many-rayed necklaces and ornaments, their young breasts fierce as tusks, shine.
On one side is the beauty of the women who come out in throngs to see the lord, scattering powder and wreaths, their long hair and the anklets on their feet sounding as they rise.
event: The women run out in crowds to see Civakan.

reading: On one side the bright women, whose grace mocks the flowering creeper, run on each other's heels, pearls heaving on their young breasts and their tinkling anklet bells ringing.
On one side the well-jewelled women who have crowded the cloud-touching mansions, breasts bound tight in bodices and waists sagging, let their large eyes roam.
On one side, women with flashing earrings and garlands fill the golden mansions until they are hidden, gathered like a flock of spotted peacocks, rich in their fixed array.

On one side the singing women and the dancing women with many-stranded girdles run through every market street, and the ornaments that fall and break from them split the long darkness with their light.
nuance: The printed line division cuts words across lines (அல்கு/ல், தொ/றோட); read across, the sense is clear.

reading: With women of curved earrings and men alike crowding the street and the terraces above to see, garlands tangle with garlands and the pollen of the flowers makes every place like a spread carpet.
event: Men and women crowd the street and the roofs.

reading: Seeing the lord on the elephant's neck, like the young war god, in the midst of a sea of army while yak-tail whisks drive the bees from him, the others too rejoice and cry out.
nuance: அமா குமரனின் is probably for அமர் குமரனின், Kumaran of battle, that is Murugan.
event: Civakan rides into the city on an elephant amid his army, and the crowd raises a cry.

reading: Let fortune enter, with lovely eyes of honeyed flowers; let the bridegroom of the great flower garland enter; let Kama enter, let the bull among men enter; let the famed and handsome Nambi of the Vidyadharas enter.
nuance: Each title recalls something told earlier: the bridegroom of the marriages, the Kama the women took him for, the one bound to the Vidyadharas through Gandharvadattai's marriage. திருவே may hail him as fortune itself or as the one who has fortune.
event: The crowd hails Civakan as he enters, giving him one title after another.

reading: Let the one of the spear who slew the lightning-touching mountain enter; let the Yaksha of the sweet-honeyed garland enter; let the victor enter, let the hero enter: so the city came out to meet him.
nuance: The spear-bearer who slew the mountain is Murugan who split the Krauncha; the Yaksha likely recalls Sudanjanan, the yaksha god who befriended him. The acclaim gives Civakan the god's names without the epic claiming he is the god.
event: The city welcomes Civakan with acclaim.

reading: Scattering fragrant pounded powder on every side and showering scented garlands and wreaths, women with waists that shame the drum, red mouths like the tondai fruit and eyes that shame the blade stand blessing him.
nuance: துடியடு and வடியடு are best read with அடு, 'to defeat' (a waist that outdoes the drum's narrow middle, eyes that outdo the blade), not as lost -யொடு.
event: The women shower Civakan with powder and garlands and bless him.

reading: Holding out bee-swarmed garlands in worship, the women say: great she-elephant, we learned our gait from you; if you love us, walk slowly, so that we may see Kama with our dark eyes.
nuance: The conventional figure that women walk like a she-elephant becomes a claim of kinship on the beast: having taught us our gait, she owes us a slow one.
event: The women beg the elephant carrying Civakan to walk slowly so they can look at him longer.

reading: Others sulk, their ornaments shifting and breasts heaving: you have not understood that a gentle gait is the beauty of womanhood; you have learned a rough gait; you will lose your husband; you are no she-elephant, you wretch.
nuance: The rule of womanly gait is put playfully in the mouths of women who are themselves running in the streets after a stranger; the epic neither endorses nor answers it here.
event: Some of the women scold the elephant for carrying Civakan past too fast.

reading: And others say to the tusker, husband of the small she-elephant with hairy mouth, small eyes, large ears and great feet, who vies with Airavata: carry the lord who guards our lives and stand and help us.
nuance: The address turns from the she-elephant of 2124-2125 to her mate; which beast Civakan rides the verses leave unclear. The last line (உயிர்கா வலற்கொண் டுதவநில்) is hard to construe: 'the guardian of life' may be Civakan, guardian of their lives, or the elephant asked to guard his.
event: Women ask the tusker to halt with Civakan.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2127-2151 (2/9)
theme: Civakan enters his maternal uncle Govindan's city and palace, is received with tears, and exchanges first looks with the uncle's daughter; then Govindan in council hears Kattiyankaran's lying letter, which blames Saccandan's death on an elephant, and resolves to answer guile with guile, proclaiming a false alliance while mustering his army.
source_issues: Most verses of this run (2129-2133, 2138, 2140-2144, 2146-2151) were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2137 line 3 மலாபுர்த் is garbled; the sense 'over the flowers' (perhaps மலர்ப்புறத்து) is clear from context.
2141 is hard to construe: who sets Sitattan in rule and over which city is not fixed by the line division.
2135 line 4 செய்பூங் கழலைக் has a doubled consonant before தொழுதான் (கழலைத் expected).
2144 line 1 விதையத்தார் stands for the Videha people; 2147 lines 2-3 (இருநிலக் கிழமை வேண்டி நினைத்துத்தா னெடிதல் செல்லா) are of uncertain construction.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called சீவகசாமி in the invocation
king of Videham (விதையம்), Vijayai's elder brother and Civakan's maternal uncle; named in these verses only as வேந்தன், மன்னன், காவலன்
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother
Govindan's daughter, the maternal uncle's daughter Civakan is to marry; unnamed in these verses (நங்கை)
the young she-elephant Civakan rides into the city
the women of the city's streets and houses
the women of Govindan's palace
Govindan's crowned queens
the whole household of Govindan's palace
Govindan's ministers, addressed as நூல்வலீர்
merchant's son who sails for wealth and is shipwrecked; here set to guard the city
Civakan's companions
the man at Govindan's court who breaks the seal and reads Kattiyankaran's letter
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne and imprisons Civakan
king of Emangatham, Civakan's father, who loses his kingdom to a plot
the musth state elephant that breaks loose
the drummer who beats out Govindan's proclamation in the old city

reading: The women of the street call to Civakan's young she-elephant: bring the king of rare beauty to our street tomorrow, and we will give you balls of rice.
nuance: The women bargain with the elephant, not the man: desire speaks through a bribe of food (கருனைக் கவளம்) to his mount, as if the beast decides where the prince goes.
event: The women of the street ask Civakan's she-elephant to bring him to their street the next day.

reading: On every side women in gem girdles, gold anklets and bright earrings praise the prince in the street and rejoice.
event: The adorned women of the city praise the prince as he passes.

tamil: விளங்குபாற் கடலிற் பொங்கி வெண்டிரை யெழுவ வேபோற்
றுளங்கொளி மாடத் துச்சித் துகிற்கொடி நுடங்கும் வீதி
யுளங்கழித் துருவப் பைந்தார் மன்னவன் கோயில் சேர்ந்தா
னிளங்கதிர்ப் பருதி பௌவத் திறுவரை யிருந்த தொத்தான்.
reading: Through the street where cloth flags wave on the bright mansions like white surf on the milk sea, Civakan reaches the king's palace, like the young sun resting on the mountain at the sea's edge.
event: Civakan passes through the bannered street and reaches the king's palace.

tamil: இழையொளி பரந்த கோயி லினமலர்க் குவளைப் பொற்பூ
விழைதகு கமல வட்டத் திடைவிராய்ப் பூத்த வேபோற்
குழையொளி முகமுங் கோலக் கொழுங்கயற் கண்ணுந் தோன்ற
மழைமின்னுக் குழாத்தின் மாலை மங்கையர் மயங்கி நின்றார்.
reading: In the palace bright with jewels, the women stand dazed in clusters like lightning in a cloud, their faces and carp-like eyes showing like blue lilies set among lotuses.
event: The palace women stand gazing at Civakan, bewildered.

tamil: எரிக்குழாஞ் சுடரும் வையே லேந்தலைக் கண்டு கோயிற்
றிருக்குழா மனைய பட்டத் தேவியர் மகிழ்ந்து செய்ய
வரிக்குழா நெடுங்க ணாரக் கொப்புளித் துமிழ வம்பூ
விரைக்குழா மாலைத் தேனும் வண்டுமுண் டொழுக நின்றார்.
reading: Seeing the bearer of the flaming spear, the crowned queens, like a host of goddesses of fortune, rejoice and stand, their streaked eyes brimming as if spilling over, honey and bees flowing from their garlands.
event: The king's queens look on Civakan with joy.

tamil: அலங்கறா தவிழ்ந்து சோர வல்குற்பொற் றோரை மின்னச்
சிலம்பின்மேற் பஞ்சி யார்ந்த சீறடி வலத்த தூன்றி
நலந்துறை போய நங்கை தோழியைப் புல்லி நின்றா
ளிலங்கொளி மணித்தொத் தீன்ற வேந்துபொற் கொடியோ டொப்பாள்.
reading: Her garland loosening and slipping, her girdle flashing, the maiden accomplished in beauty stands embracing her friend, her small foot set on her anklet, like a golden creeper that has put out clusters of gems.
nuance: The verse names her only as நங்கை; that she is the king's daughter Ilakkanai, the bride the patikam promised, is known from the story, not from this verse. Leaning on the friend is the shy girl's stance at first sight.
event: A maiden of the palace stands leaning on her friend as Civakan arrives.

tamil: தாமரைப் போதிற் பூத்த தண்ணறுங் குவளைப் பூப்போற்
காமரு முகத்திற் பூத்த கருமழைத் தடங்கண் டம்மாற்
றேமலர் மார்பி னானை நோக்கினாள் செல்வன் மற்றப்
பூமலர்க் கோதை நெஞ்ச மூழ்கிப்புக் கொளித்திட் டானே.
reading: Her dark rain-cloud eyes, flowering in her face like blue lilies in a lotus, look at the man of the honeyed chest, and the prosperous one plunges into the heart of the flower-garlanded girl and hides there.
nuance: The look is hers and the entering is his: her eyes act, but it is he who is said to sink in and hide (ஒளித்திட்டான்), so the first-sight love is told as his capture by her glance.
event: The maiden looks at Civakan and he enters her heart.

reading: Her breasts swelling so that even those who travel the sky are troubled, and as he looks on them, the girl like gold plunges into the heart of the one of the wounding spear, who is like Kama of the five arrows.
nuance: With 2133 the entering is made mutual: he sinks into her heart, then she into his, the same verb மூழ்கு used both ways.
event: The maiden in turn enters Civakan's heart.

reading: Like a tiger coming down from a dark mountain, the young man gets down from the garlanded she-elephant, goes and bows, his head lowered, at the king's anklet that is rubbed bright by the crowns of kings.
event: Civakan dismounts and bows at the king's feet.

reading: The king of strong shoulders, rejoicing, embraces his nephew without letting go, and as his love swells, tears like pearls from his red lotus eyes wet the young man's fragrant jewelled chest.
nuance: மருமான் is the sister's son: the welcome is the mother's kin receiving the child of the sister whose husband was killed, and the tears carry that past, though the verse names only love (அன்பு).
event: Govindan embraces his nephew and weeps over him.

reading: When the king wept unceasingly, the whole palace, losing itself, wept too, the rain of tears pouring over flower garlands, like a flock of peacocks crying on a mountain.
event: The whole palace weeps with the king.

tamil: வகைநலம் வாடி யெங்கு மழுகுரன் மயங்கி முந்நீ
ரகமடை திறந்த தேபோ லலறக்கோக் கிளைய நங்கை
மிகைநலத் தேவி தானே விலாவணை நீக்கி னாளே.
reading: Grief spread through the golden palace where no music was heard, the cries mingling like the sea breaking its dam, until the king's younger sister, the queen of surpassing grace, herself put an end to the lament.
nuance: கோக்கு இளைய நங்கை is the king's younger sister, Vijayai, who had gone ahead to her brother (1932): the one with most cause to weep is the one who ends the weeping.
event: Vijayai stops the palace's lament.

tamil: பல்கதிர் மணியும் பொன்னும் பவழமுங் குயிற்றிச் செய்த
செல்வப்பொற் கிடுகு சூழ்ந்த சித்திர கூட மெங்கு
மல்குபூந் தாமந் தாழ்ந்து மணிபுகை கமழ வேந்தன்
வெல்புகழ் பரவ மாதோ விதியுள யெய்தி னானே.
reading: Into the painted hall ringed with gold panels inlaid with gems, gold and coral, hung with garlands and fragrant with incense, the king went in due form while his victorious fame was praised.
event: The king enters the painted hall in state.

tamil: எரிமணி யடைப்பை செம்பொற் படியக மிலங்கு பொன்வாள்
கருமணி முகடு வேய்ந்த கஞ்சனை கவரி கொண்ட
வருமுலை மகளிர் வைத்து வான்றவி சடுத்து நீங்கப்
பெருமக னெண்ணங் கொள்வா னமைச்சரோ டேறி னானே.
reading: When the women had set down the gem betel pouch, the gold vessel, the shining sword, the casket and the whisk, laid out the high seat and withdrawn, the great one went up with his ministers to take counsel.
event: Govindan goes up with his ministers to take counsel.

tamil: உலந்தநா ளவர்க்குத் தோன்றா தொளிக்குமீன் குளிக்குங் கற்பிற்
புலந்தவே னெடுங்கட் செவ்வாய்ப் புதவிநாட் பயந்த நம்பி
சிலம்புநீர்க் கடலந் தானைச் சீதத்தற் கரசு நாட்டிக்
குலந்தரு கொற்ற வேலான் கொடிநகர் காக்க வென்றான்.
reading: The king of the lineage-given spear names Civakan the son born of a woman whose chastity outshines the star that hides from those whose days are ended, and orders that Sitattan of the sea-like army be set in rule to guard the bannered city.
nuance: The star unseen by the dying is Arundhati, the emblem of a wife's chastity; Vijayai's karpu is said to make it hide. Who is set in rule and over which city is not certain: the line can be read as Civakan setting up Sitattan, or as the king's own order.
event: Govindan orders that Sitattan be put in charge to guard the city.

tamil: மாற்றவ னொற்ற ரொற்றா வகையினின் மறைய நம்பிக்
காற்றின் தோழர்க் கெல்லா மணிகல மடிசி லாடை
வேற்றுமை யின்றி வேண்டுட் டமைத்தன னருளி யிப்பா
லேற்றுரி முரச நாண வெறிதிரை முழக்கிற் சொன்னான்.
reading: So that the enemy's spies could not single them out, the king gave all Civakan's companions jewels, food and clothing as he wished, without any distinction from his own, and then spoke in a voice like the roaring sea that shamed the bull-hide drum.
nuance: The gifts are a disguise: honouring the guests exactly as his own men makes them invisible to Kattiyankaran's spies.
event: Govindan provides for Civakan's companions as for his own people so that spies cannot pick them out.

tamil: கட்டியங் கார னம்மைக் காண்பதே கரும மாக
வொட்டித் தான் விடுத்த வோலை யுளபொரு ளுரைமி னென்னத்
தொட்டுமேற் பொறியை நீக்கி மன்னனைத் தொழுது தோன்ற
விட்டலர் நாகப் பைந்தார் விரிசிகன் கூறு மன்றே.
reading: The king bids them tell what is in the letter Kattiyankaran sent, with a pledge, aiming at a meeting; Virisikan of the naga-flower garland breaks the seal, bows to the king and reads it out.
event: Virisikan opens Kattiyankaran's letter and reads it to the king.

tamil: விதையத்தார் வேந்தன் காண்க கட்டியங் கார னோலை
புதையவிப் பொழிலைப் போர்த்தோர் பொய்ப்பழி பரந்த தென்மேற்
கதையெனக் கருதல் செய்யான் மெய்யெனத் தானுங் கொண்டான்
சிதையவென் னெஞ்சம் போழ்ந்து தெளிப்பினுந் தெளிநர் யாரே.
reading: The letter begins: let the king of Videham see this letter of Kattiyankaran; a false blame covering this world has spread over me, people took it as truth and not as a tale, and even if I split my heart to show it, who would be convinced?
nuance: The blame he calls false is the killing of Saccandan, which the narration told plainly (290). The letter's voice is the usurper's own; the reader knows it lies.
event: In his letter Kattiyankaran protests that the blame laid on him is false.

tamil: படுமணிப் பைம்பொற் சூழிப் பகட்டின மிரியப் பாய்ந்து
கொடிநெடுந் தோக ணூறிக் கொய்யுளை மாக்கள் குத்தி
யிடுகொடி யணிந்த மார்ப ரிருவிசும் பேறச் சீறி
யடுகளிற் றசனி வேக மலமர வதனை நோனான்.
reading: The letter goes on: the killing elephant Asanivegam charged, scattering the herds of belled tuskers, smashing the tall-bannered chariots, goring the plumed horses and hurling warriors to the sky, and he could not bear it.
event: Kattiyankaran's letter tells that the elephant Asanivegam ran amok and the king could not bear it.

tamil: நூற்றுவர் பாகர் தம்மைப் பிளந்துயி ருண்ட தென்னு
மாற்றத்தைக் கேட்டுச் சென்று மதக்களி றடக்கி மேற்கொண்
டாற்றலங் கந்து சோத்தி யாப்புற வீக்கும் போழ்திற்
கூற்றென முழங்கி வீழ்த்துக் கொல்லக்கோ லிளகிற் றன்றே.
reading: Hearing that it had torn apart a hundred mahouts and eaten their lives, he went, subdued the musth elephant and mounted it, and as he was binding it fast to the post, it roared like Death, threw him down and killed him, and so the sceptre slackened.
nuance: This is the usurper's cover story. The letter never names the king; the killed one is Saccandan by the story. கோல் இளகிற்று, 'the sceptre slackened', turns a regicide into an accident of the royal stable.
event: Kattiyankaran's letter claims the king was killed by the elephant he tried to tame.

tamil: தனக்கியா னுயிரு மீவேன் றான்வரப் பழியு நீங்கு
மெனக்கினி யிறைவன் றானே யிருநிலக் கிழமை வேண்டி
நினைத்துத்தா னெடிதல் செல்லா தென்சொலே தெளிந்து நொய்தாச்
சினக்களி யானை மன்னன் வருகெனச் செப்பி னானே.
reading: For him I would give even my life; if he comes, the blame will go; henceforth he alone is my lord; not lingering to think of claim to the wide earth, trusting my word, let the king of angry elephants come quickly, the letter says.
nuance: The pledge of life and the owning of a new lord repeat the bow Kattiyankaran made to Saccandan when he took the rule (203); the letter is bait to draw the king into reach.
event: Kattiyankaran's letter invites Govindan to come quickly and promises him loyalty.

tamil: ஓலையுட் பொருளைக் கேட்டே யொள்ளெயி றிலங்க நக்குக்
காலனை யளியன் றானே கையினால் விளிக்கு மென்னா
நூல்வலீ ரிவனைக் கொல்லு நுண்மதிச் சூழ்ச்சி யீதே
போல்வதொன் றில்லை யென்றான் புனைமணிப் பொன்செய் பூணான்.
reading: Hearing what the letter held, the king of gem-set gold ornaments laughed, his bright teeth showing, and said: the wretch calls Death with his own hand; you learned in the books, there is no subtle scheme for killing him like this.
event: Govindan laughs at the letter and tells his ministers it gives the means to kill Kattiyankaran.

tamil: கள்ளத்தா னம்மைக் கொல்லக் கருதினா னாமுந் தன்னைக்
கள்ளத்தா லுயிரை யுண்ணக் கருதினே மிதனை யாரு
முள்ளத்தா லுமிழ வேண்டா வுறுபடை வந்து கூட
வள்ளுவார் முரச மூதூ ரறைகென வருளி னானே.
reading: He thought to kill us by guile; we too have resolved to take his life by guile; let none of you let it out of your heart; let the drum of the old city proclaim that the great army gather, the king commanded.
nuance: The counter-deceit is a king's policy stated in council, not a maxim the narrator endorses; the verse also orders secrecy (உள்ளத்தால் உமிழ வேண்டா).
event: Govindan resolves to meet Kattiyankaran's guile with guile and orders the army gathered.

tamil: கட்டியங் கார னோடு காவல னொருவ னானான்
விட்டுநீர் நெல்லும் பொன்னும் வழங்குமின் விளைவ கூறி
னொட்டல னிறைவன் சொன்னீர் நாநும வல்ல வென்னக்
கொட்டினான் றடங்கண் வள்வார்க் குளிறிடி முரச மன்றே.
reading: The drummer beat the thundering drum: the guardian has become one with Kattiyankaran; give out paddy and gold freely; if you speak of what will come of it, the lord will not allow it; if you speak, your tongues are not your own.
nuance: The public face of the plot: a feast of alliance and a threat against anyone who guesses aloud what it is for. விட்டுநீர் is read as 'freely'; the word division is not sure.
event: The drum proclaims in the city that the king has made alliance with Kattiyankaran and forbids talk of it.

tamil: விண்டவ ருடலங் கீறிச் சுளித்துநின் றழலும் வேழ
மொண்கொடி யுருவத் திண்டே ரொளிமயிர்ப் புரவி பண்ணி
வண்கழ லணிந்து மள்ளர் வாள்வலம் பிடித்து நாளைத்
தெண்டிரைப் பரப்பு நாணத் திருநகர்த் தொகுக வென்றான்.
reading: Tomorrow let the musth elephants that rip the bodies of foes, the bannered chariots and the bright-maned horses be made ready, and the warriors in hero-anklets, swords in hand, gather in the city so that the sea is put to shame, he said.
event: Govindan orders the elephants, chariots, horses and warriors to gather in the city the next day.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2152-2176 (3/9)
theme: The Videha king musters and reviews a vast army of elephants, horses, chariots and foot, marches under good omens into the Emangatha country and camps near the usurper's city, while ill omens fill Kattiyangaran's palace; the usurper, unaware, exchanges gifts with the king who means to kill him by feigned friendship.
source_issues: 2152-2158 and 2173-2176 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2155 and 2157: the army's counts are compounds whose grouping is not certain (அறுபதிற்றறுபது, இராயிரத்தைஞ்ஞூறு, ஆறாயிரத் திரட்டி).
2160 line 1 பார சூரவம் பல்லவம்: the division of the horse-country names is doubtful.
2162 line 1 இயறோ and lines 2-3 வெண் மதியத் தன்னை யூர்கொண்ட are hard to construe; 2163 line 1 நொச்சி மாமலர் நிறத்தன has no clear subject.
2164 line 3 துயிற்றியபல் கேள்வியினர் is obscure.
2172 line 2 has a doubtful division (இசையோவாவேமாங் கதநாட்டெய்தியபி); the place name ஏமாங்கதம் is read from it.

cast.role: king of the Videhas, Civakan's maternal uncle, who feigns alliance with the usurper (விதையத்தார் வென்றி வேந்தன் 2153, விதையத் தார்கோன் 2176; not named in these verses)
the Videha king's army (சேனை 2169)
the one who shows the army to the king in 2167, perhaps its commander
the usurping minister now ruling Civakan's father's city
the pleasure women of the usurper's palace
the world the narrator addresses in 2176

tamil: ஏற்றுரி போர்த்த வள்வா ரிடிமுர சறைந்த பின்னாட்
காற்றெறி கடலிற் சங்கு முழவமு முரசு மார்ப்பக்
கூற்றுடன் றனைய தானை கொழுநில நெளிய வீண்டிப்
பாற்கடற் பரப்பின் வெள்வாட் சுடரொளி பரந்த வன்றே.
reading: The day after the strapped, bull-hide drum had proclaimed the muster, conches, muzhavus and drums roared like a wind-beaten sea, and an army fierce as angry Death massed until the rich earth sagged, the gleam of its white swords spreading like the milk ocean.
nuance: பின்னாள் ties the muster to the drum of 2150 and 2151, which announced the king's false alliance with the usurper.
event: The day after the proclamation, the Videha king's army musters to the noise of conch and drum.

tamil: புதையிரு ளிரியப் பொங்கிக் குங்குமக் கதிர்க ளோக்கி
யுதையத்தி னெற்றி சோந்த வொண்சுடர்ப் பருதி போலச்
சுதையொளி மாடத் துச்சி வெண்குடை நீழற் றோன்றி
விதையத்தார் வென்றி வேந்தன் விழுப்படை காணு மன்றே.
reading: Like the bright sun that rises on the brow of the eastern mountain scattering the thick dark with saffron rays, the victorious king of the Videhas appears under a white umbrella on top of his lime-white mansion and looks over his fine army.
event: The Videha king reviews his army from the roof of his palace.

tamil: அரும்பனைத் தடக்கை யபரகாத் திரம்வாய் வாலெயி றைந்தினுங் கொல்வ
கருங்கடற் சங்குங் கறந்தவான் பாலுங் கனற்றிய காலுகி ருடைய
பெரும்புலி முழக்கின் மாறெதிர் முழங்கிப் பெருவரை கீண்டிடுந் திறல
திருந்தியே ழுறுப்புந் திண்ணிலந் தோய்வ தீயுமிழ் தறுகணிற் சிறந்த.
reading: The war elephants are described: trunks like palm trunks, killing with all five of their weapons, white as sea conch and fresh milk, roaring back at the great tiger's roar, strong enough to tear a mountain, their seven limbs well formed and touching the firm ground, and unmatched in fire-spitting fury.
nuance: ஏழுறுப்புந் திண்ணிலந் தோய்வ names the mark of a fine elephant, seven parts reaching the ground; which five parts kill (ஐந்தினுங் கொல்வ) the verse does not list.

tamil: கவிழ்மணிப் புடைய கண்ணிழ னாறிற் கனன்றுதந் நிழலொடு மலைவ
வவிழ்புயன் மேக மனையமம் மதத்த வறுபதிற் றறுபதா நாகம்
புகழ்பருந் தார்ப்பப் பூமதம் பொழிவா னின்றன விராயிரங் கவுள்வண்
டிகழ்மதஞ் செறித்த விராயிரத் தைஞ்ஞா றிளையவு மத்துணைக் களிறே.
reading: The elephants hung with bells on both flanks rage and fight their own shadows when they catch its scent, dark as loosening rain clouds and running with must, and the poet gives their numbers by the thousand: herds that pour must while kites cry over them, young ones, and as many tuskers.
nuance: The counts are built from compounds (அறுபதிற்றறுபது, இராயிரம், இராயிரத்தைஞ்ஞூறு) whose grouping is not certain, so the total cannot be fixed.

tamil: குந்தமே யயில்வாள் குனிசிலை மூன்றுங் குறைவிலார் கூற்றொடும் பொருவா
ரந்தர மாறா யானைகொண் டேறப் பறக்கெனிற் பறந்திடுந் திறலார்
முந்தமர் தம்முண் முழுமெயு மிரும்பு மேய்ந்திட வெஞ்சமம் விளைத்தார்
கொந்தழ லஞ்சாக் குஞ்சர மிவர்ந்தார் கோடியே விருத்தியா வுடையார்.
reading: The elephant riders are masters of lance, sword and bow who would fight Death itself, men who could make their mounts fly at a word, whose whole bodies iron had bitten in earlier battles, who ride elephants unafraid of blazing fire, a crore of them living by this work.
nuance: கோடியே விருத்தியா வுடையார் makes them a standing force living by war, not levies.

tamil: குங்கும நறுநீர் பந்திநின் றாடுங் குதிரையா றாயிரத் திரட்டி
பொங்குவெண் மயிர்சூழ் பொற்படை பொலிந்த வறுபதி னாயிரம் புரவி
வெங்கணை தவிர்ப்ப வெள்ளிவெண் படைய வாய்விடி னிலவரை நில்லாப்
பைங்கதிர்க் கொட்டைக் கவரிசூழ்ந் தணிந்த பகரினத் தொகையன பாய்மா.
reading: The horses are counted: twice six thousand that bathe in saffron water in their stalls, sixty thousand with white plumes and gold trappings, armoured in silver against arrows, that would not stay on the ground if let go, and a host past telling hung with green-rayed chowries.
nuance: ஆறாயிரத் திரட்டி may be twice six thousand or a doubled troop of six thousand.

tamil: வேய்நிறக் கரும்பின் வெண்ணிறப் பூம்போன் மிடைந்தொளிர் குந்தமும் வாளுந்
தோநிலை யரவின் றோற்றமே போலுஞ் சிலைகளும் பிறகளுந் துறைபோ
யூனமொன் றில்லா ருயர்குடிப் பிறந்தா ராயிர மடுகளங் கண்டார்
பானிலாப் பூணார் படைத்தொழிற் கலிமாப் பண்ணுறுத் தேறினா ரவரே.
reading: The horsemen, skilled to the end in gleaming lance, sword, bows curved like a snake shedding its skin and other arms, flawless men of high birth who have seen a thousand battlefields and wear moon-white ornaments, mount their harnessed war horses.
event: The cavalry mount their harnessed horses.

reading: Some of the horses are lotus-coloured and fierce, with flawless hooves, from Malava; others, perfect in form, coloured like the fruit of a full-branched jambu and dancing to the drum, come from the banks of the cool Sindhu.
nuance: Whether the verse names one breed or two (Malava and the Sindhu) depends on how its four lines are grouped.

reading: Horses born in lands called Parasa, Suravam and Pallava, heroic in strength and coloured like strong ripe toddy, would think it a great disgrace to walk on the earth and, ashamed, leap into the sky so that the long rain clouds shake.
nuance: பார சூரவம் பல்லவம் is a list of foreign horse countries whose division into names is not secure.

reading: Horses beautiful as the peacock's neck, from the Maratta country, with bodies coloured like young parrots and hooves like sea coral, came down from ships that sail the battling sea.

tamil: பொன்னும் வெள்ளியு மணியினும் பொலிந்து வெண் மதியத்
reading: Chariots of fine make, harnessed to such full-maned horses, shine with gold, silver and gems as if they had taken the white moon for their home, and their number is twenty thousand and six hundred.
nuance: இயறோ is read as இயல் தேர், and the count as twenty thousand ending in six hundred; வெண் மதியத் தன்னை யூர்கொண்ட is hard to construe.

reading: The chariot warriors, with swords that burn like the sun at noon over the sea and practised in thrown weapons beyond the sword, feed their enemies to Death every day.

The foot soldiers are like tigers striking with their teeth, trained in bow, sword and spear alike, hearers of much instruction, picked out from many, and able with sharp weapons to cut down the fury of rutting elephants.
nuance: துயிற்றியபல் கேள்வியினர் is obscure; it may mean men whose much learning has settled, or something else.

reading: They are like Death with its train of fierce diseases, able to fill the roaring sea and dig up mountains, renowned in manly work, four lakhs in number, who have besides won a place of special trust.
nuance: மேலும் நுமரால் addresses someone as 'your people'; the addressee is not clear from the verse.

reading: Lion-skin shields, swords, spears and bows spread out together and flashed like lightning, moon and sun among clouds, so that even Death of the fierce eye took to a fortress.
nuance: கூற்றுமரண் சேர is read as Death itself seeking shelter in fear; it could instead say the army spread to reach the enemy's fort.
event: The armed host spreads out its shields and weapons.

reading: The one who wore the ring of fresh gold showed the army to the king of kings, the bright-anklet king mounted his Airavata of an elephant till it grew hot, and the host cheered 'may he win'.
nuance: Who ஆழி தொட்டான் is, the commander or another, the verse does not say; அயிராவணம் names the elephant after Indra's.
event: The army is presented to the king, who mounts his elephant amid cries of victory.

reading: Small white conches sounded, strong drums roared like the sea and the rain cloud, birds and other signs favoured the road, and the king's right eye throbbed in accord.
nuance: The right eye's throb is a good sign here for a man; 2173 gives the same throb to the usurper's women as an ill one.
event: Good omens attend the king's setting out.

reading: With the ringing bells of the great elephants, the clatter of the five-gaited horses, the shout and the flashing swords like lightning, the army moved like a great sea.
event: The army marches.

reading: Under white umbrellas like the evening moon and the cool shade of peacock-feather parasols, with the three musts of the elephants pouring down like a grove's rain, the land the army crossed turned from desert into fertile field.
nuance: The hyperbole makes the army a giver of water: பாலை போய் மருதம் பயந்திட்டது turns a march into a change of tinai.

reading: Peacocks of the commons rose screaming, herds of deer with their fawns scattered, and fearing the victorious spear-army it looked as if the hills and their forests were moving away.

tamil: படுகண் முழவி னிமிழருவி வரையுங் காடும் பலபோகி
னெடுவெண் ணிலவி னெற்றிதோய் நிழலார் செம்பொற் புரிசையே
கடிமண் காவல் கருதினான் கோயி லாகக் கருதினான்.
reading: Passing many hills and forests whose falling streams sounded like drums, after reaching the Emangatha country, the king took a golden walled place whose top touched the moonlight as the guard of his camp and as his palace.
nuance: கடிமண் காவல் and கோயிலாகக் கருதினான் are read as camp and palace; the doubled கருதினான் is unusual.
event: The army reaches the Emangatha country and the king makes camp in a walled enclosure.

tamil: போக மகளிர் வலக்கண்க டுடித்த பொல்லாக் கனாக்கண்டா
ராக மன்னற் கொளிமழுங்கிற் றஞ்சத் தக்க குரலினாற்
கூகை கோயிற் பகற்குழறக் கொற்ற முரசம் பாடவிந்து
மாக நெய்த்தோர் சொரிந்தெங்கு மண்ணும் விண்ணு மதிர்ந்தவே.
reading: In the usurper's palace the pleasure women's right eyes throbbed and they saw evil dreams, the king's body lost its lustre, owls hooted by day in the palace with dreadful cries, the victory drum lost its voice, blood rained from the sky, and earth and sky shook.
nuance: Each sign reverses one of 2168's: the throbbing right eye, the drum that now falls silent, the birds; the verse states the portents and does not say what they portend.
event: Ill omens fill Kattiyangaran's palace.

tamil: கூற்றம் வந்து புறத்திறுத்த தறியான் கொழும்பொ னுலகாள்வான்
வீற்றிங் கிருந்தே னெனமகிழ்ந்து வென்றி வேழ மிருநூறுங்
காற்றிற் பரிக்குந் தோநூறுங் கடுங்கா லிவுளி யாயிரமும்
போற்றி விடுத்தான் புனைசெம்பொற் படையே யணிந்து புனைபூணான்.
reading: Not knowing that Death had come and camped outside, the ruler of the rich land rejoiced that he sat there in splendour and with care sent two hundred victorious elephants, a hundred wind-swift chariots and a thousand fierce horses, decked in red-gold armour.
nuance: கூற்றம் is the camped army itself; the narrator's word makes the guest Death before the host knows it.
event: Kattiyangaran sends elephants, chariots and horses as gifts to the Videha king, whose army is camped near his city.

tamil: மன்ன னாங்கோர் மதவேழம் வாரி மணாள னென்பதூஉ
மின்னங் கொடித்தோ விசயமும் புரவி பவன வேகமும்
பொன்னிற புனைந்து தான்போக்க நிகழ்வ தோரான் மகிழ்வெய்தி
முன்யான் விட்ட வினக்களிற்றி னிரட்டி விடுத்தா னெனப்புகழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The king there sent back, decked in gold, one rutting elephant called Vari Manalan, the chariot Vijayam with its lightning banner and the horse Pavana Vegam, and the usurper, not seeing what was coming, was delighted and praised him for returning twice the elephants he had sent.
nuance: நிகழ்வது ஓரான் gives the narrator's view; the usurper reads three named mounts as more than his hundreds, a measure of worth he does not see is bait.
event: The Videha king returns named gifts, and Kattiyangaran, deceived, praises his generosity.

tamil: வீங்குநீர் விதையத் தார்கோன் கட்டியங் காரன் றன்னோ
டாங்கவ னொருவ னாகி யன்பெனு மயில்கொள் வாளால்
வாங்கிக்கொண் டுயிரை யுண்பான் வஞ்சத்தாற் சூழ்ந்த வண்ண
மோங்குநீ ரோத வேலிக் குணரயா முரைத்து மன்றே.
reading: The narrator announces that he will now tell the world how the Videha king, making himself one with Kattiyangaran, plotted by deceit to seize and devour his life with the sharp sword called love.
nuance: அன்பெனு மயில்கொள் வாள் names the false friendship as the weapon, and வஞ்சம் is the narrator's own word for the hero's side's plan.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2177-2201 (4/9)
theme: At Govindan's boar contest, staged as a trap for Kattiyangaran, a catalogue of crowned suitors fails one by one, thrown by the machine or shamed by bow and arrow, and after six days Civakan rises, mounts his elephant, terrifies Kattiyangaran, who laments that his victim escaped, and waits a whole day before the machine while the failed kings mock him.
source_issues: 2179 to 2201 (all but 2181, 2184 and 2194): stanza printed in eight half-lines; joined into four by the build.
2181 line 2 செம்போற் is probably செம்பொற்.
2191 line 2 சோந்தாங் is probably சேர்ந்தாங்; line 4 விற்றுவின் is obscure and may be corrupt.
2200 line 1 to 2 பன்றி மூன்று and நெடுந்தகை மூன்று are hard to construe; the number three may be a corruption or a detail of the machine not explained in the verse.

cast.role: king of Videha, who holds the boar contest for his daughter (named in 2205)
kings who came seeking the princess
the king of Vinitai, a suitor
king of the elephant city, Hastinapuram, a suitor
king of Kampili, a suitor
the lord of Kosala, a suitor
the crowned king of Avanti, a suitor
the king of Magadha, a suitor
the lord of the Kalingas, a suitor
king of Varanavasi, a suitor
the king of Pothanapuram, a suitor
the southern (Pandya) king, a suitor
a suitor king called Vijayan, famed as a bowman; not Civakan's companion of Hemamapuram
the hero, who comes to the contest to take on his enemy
the usurper of Saccandan's throne, who comes to the contest
the women of the city who hail Civakan

tamil: பெருமகன் காதற் பாவைப் பித்திகைப் பிணையன் மாலை
யொருமக ணோக்கி னாரை யுயிரோடும் போக டாத
திருமக ளவட்குப் பாலா னருந்திரி பன்றி யெய்த
வருமக னாகு மென்றாங் கணிமுர சறைவித் தானே.
reading: The great king has the drum proclaim that whoever shoots the hard-turning boar will be the husband of his beloved only daughter, a goddess of fortune who lets no man who looks at her go away with his life.
nuance: The previous verse (2176) has just said that the Videha king made himself one with Kattiyangaran in friendship so as to take his life by deceit; read after it, the bride-contest is the lure. The king is not named here; he is named கோவிந்தன் in 2205. The daughter is praised, not named.
event: Govindan has the drum proclaim that the man who shoots the revolving boar shall marry his daughter.

tamil: ஆய்மதக் களிறு திண்டே ரணிமணிப் புரவி யம்பொற்
காய்கதிர்ச் சிவிகை செற்றிக் கலந்த வைநுரைக ளாகத்
லாய்முடி யரச வெள்ள மணிநக ரீண்டிற் றன்றே.
reading: Rutting elephants, sturdy chariots, jewelled horses and gold palanquins crowd together like foam on a flood, and a flood of crowned kings gathers in the fair city as the waters of the world's rain gather in the old town.
event: Crowned kings with their elephants, chariots, horses and palanquins flood into the city for the contest.

tamil: நல்லவள் வனப்பு வாங்க நகைமணி மாலை மார்பர்
வில்லன்றே யுவனிப் பாரும் வெங்கணை திருத்து வாரும்
சொல்லுமி னெமக்கு மாங்கோர் சிலைதொட நாளென் பாரும்
பல்சரம் வழங்கு வாரும் பரிவுகொள் பவரு மானார்.
reading: Drawn by the girl's beauty, the garlanded kings busy themselves: some peer at the bow, some straighten their fierce arrows, some ask when the day to touch the bow is, some loose many shafts, and some fret.
event: The suitor kings prepare their bows and arrows and ask when they may try.

tamil: பிறையெயிற் றெரிகட் பேழ்வாய்ப் பெருமயிர்ப் பைம்பொற் பன்றி
யறையெனத் திரியு மாய்பொற் பூமியி னிறைந்து மன்ன
ருறுகணை யொன்றும் வில்லு முடன்பிடித் துருவ நேமிப்
பொறிதிரி வதனை நோக்கிப் பூமுடி துளக்கி நின்றார்.
reading: A gold boar with crescent tusks, burning eyes, gaping mouth and thick bristles turns as if it were proclaiming itself on the golden ground, and the kings, each holding one arrow and the bow, look at the machine turning on its wheel and stand shaking their flowered crowns.
nuance: Each king is allowed one arrow (உறுகணை ஒன்றும் வில்லும்); that is the rule the following verses test, one failure to a verse.
event: The kings stand with bow and one arrow, staring at the boar machine turning on its wheel.

tamil: ஏந்தெழி லாகஞ் சாந்தி னிடுகொடி யெழுதிக் காதிற்
காய்ந்தெரி செம்போற் றோடுங் கனமணிக் குழையு மின்ன
வேந்தருள் வினிதை வேந்தன் வெஞ்சிலை தளர வாங்கி
யாய்ந்தபொற் பன்றி நெற்றி யருந்துக ளார்ப்ப வெய்தான்.
reading: The king of Vinitai, sandal creepers painted on his chest and gold and jewelled rings flashing at his ears, bends the fierce bow till it slackens and shoots, but only raises the fine dust about the gold boar's forehead.
nuance: நெற்றி அருந்துகள் ஆர்ப்ப may mean the arrow grazed the boar's brow or fell short and kicked up dust; either way the boar is not brought down. The list of failed kings is a comic catalogue, each failure with its own image.
event: The king of Vinitai shoots and his arrow only stirs the dust at the boar's forehead.

tamil: குடர்தொடர் குருதிக் கோட்டுக் குஞ்சர நகரத் தார்கோன்
சுடர்நுதற் பட்ட மின்னச் சுரும்பிமிர் கண்ணி சிந்த
வடர்கதிர்ப் பைம்பொற் பூணு மாரமு மகலத் தொல்கப்
படர்சிலை குழைய வாங்கிப் பன்றியைப் பதைப்ப வெய்தான்.
reading: The lord of the elephant city, his frontlet flashing and his bee-swarmed garland scattering, his jewels sliding off his chest, bends the spreading bow till it sags and shoots, and the boar only shudders.
nuance: குஞ்சர நகரம், the elephant city, is taken here as Hastinapura, whose king was among the suitors at Gandharvadattai's contest; the verse does not use that name.
event: The king of the elephant city shoots and makes the boar quiver but does not fell it.

tamil: வார்மதுத் துளிக்கு மாலை மணிமுடித் தொடுத்து நாலக்
கார்மதங் கடந்த வண்கைக் காம்பிலிக் காவன் மன்ன
னோமதக் கேழ லெய்வா னேறலும் பொறியி னேறுண்
டார்மதக் களிற்று வேந்தர்க் கருநகை யாக வீழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The open-handed guardian king of Kampili, honeyed garland on his jewelled crown, climbs to shoot the boar, is struck by the machine and falls, to the great laughter of the elephant-riding kings.
nuance: To shoot, a king must mount the wheel (ஏறலும்); the machine itself throws the unskilled. The laughter of the other kings makes the contest a public shaming as well as a test.
event: The king of Kampili climbs the machine to shoot, is thrown by it and falls while the other kings laugh.

tamil: முலைவட்டப் பூணு முத்து முள்கலிற் கிழிந்து பொல்லா
விலைவட்டத் தாம மார்பிற் கோசலத் திறைவ னெய்த
குலைவட்டக் கருதி யம்பு வானின்மேற் பூச லுய்ப்பான்
சிலைவட்ட நீங்கி விண்மேற் செவ்வனே யெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: The lord of Kosala, his breast-ornaments and pearls torn by the press of embraces, shoots, and his arrow, as if bent on making war on the sky, leaves the bow's curve and rises straight up into the heavens.
event: The king of Kosala's arrow flies straight up into the sky instead of at the boar.

tamil: ஊடிய மடந்தை போல வுறுசிலை வாங்க வாரா
தாடெழு வனைய திண்டோ ளவந்திய னதனை நோனா
னாடெழுந் தார்ப்ப மற்றந் நன்சிலை முறித்திட் டம்பை
வாடினன் பிடித்து நின்றான் மண்மகன் போல நின்றான்.
reading: The king of Avanti, shoulders like a bolt, cannot bear that the bow, like a sulking woman, will not bend to him; as the people roar he breaks the good bow and stands holding the arrow, wilted, like a man of clay.
nuance: மண்மகன் போல நின்றான் (line 4), 'stood like a man of clay', plays on the section's name, மண்மகள் இலம்பகம். The bow that will not come like a sulking woman (ஊடிய மடந்தை) joins the contest's two prizes, the bow and the bride.
event: The king of Avanti cannot bend the bow, breaks it in anger and stands holding his arrow.

tamil: பில்கித்தே னொழுகுங் கோதைப் பிறர்மனை யாள்கட் சென்ற
வுள்ளத்தை யுணர்வின் மிக்கா னொழித்திடப் பெயர்ந்த தேபோன்
மல்லனீர் மகத ராசன் றுரந்தகோன் மருள வோடிப்
புல்லியப் பொறியை மோந்து புறக்கொடுத் திட்ட தன்றே.
reading: As a wise man draws back a heart that has gone out to another man's wife, so the arrow shot by the king of Magadha runs, sniffs at the machine and turns its back.
nuance: The simile is double-edged: it gives the retreating arrow the dignity of restraint while it mocks the king whose arrow it is. The rule it assumes is that the heart may go toward another's wife and the wise man's work is to call it back (ஒழித்திடப் பெயர்ந்தது).
event: The king of Magadha's arrow reaches the machine and turns back.

tamil: தென்வரை பொதியி லார மகிலொடு தேய்த்த தேய்வை
மன்வரை யகலத் தப்பி மணிவடந் திருவில் வீச
மின்னென் விட்ட கோலை விழுங்கக்கண் டழுங்கி வேர்த்துக்
கன்மலிந் திலங்கு திண்டோட் கலிங்கர்கோன் மெலிந்து மீண்டான்.
reading: The Kalinga lord, his chest daubed with southern Pothiyil sandal and agil, his jewelled chains flashing like a rainbow, sees the arrow he loosed like lightning swallowed up, and sweating and dismayed he turns back weakened.
nuance: What swallows the arrow is not named; it may be the sky or the turning machine.
event: The Kalinga king's arrow vanishes and he withdraws in dismay.

tamil: மன்னுயி ரின்று காக்கும் வாரண வாசி மன்னன்
மின்னிழை சுடர வாங்கி விட்டகோ லுற்று றாதாய்
மன்னுயிர் நடுங்க நாணி மண்புக்கு மறைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The king of Varanavasi, who once lifted the golden hill against the rain of stones and saved the herds and now protects living beings, bends the bow so that his jewels blaze, but his arrow does not reach; ashamed, while all creatures tremble, it enters the earth and hides.
nuance: Lines 1 to 2 give this king the deed of lifting the hill to shelter the herds, the deed of the dark god of the cowherds; whether the verse means he is of that line or ironically lends him the god's deed cannot be settled from the verse. It is the arrow, not the king, that is said to hide for shame.
event: The Varanavasi king's arrow falls short and buries itself in the ground.

tamil: எரிகதிர்ப் பைம்பொற் சுண்ண மிலங்கமெய்ம் முழுது மப்பிப்
புரிகழ லணிந்த நோன்றாட் போதன புரத்து வேந்த
னரிதினிற் றிகிரி யேறித் திரிந்துகண் சுழன்று சோர்ந்து
விரிகதிர்க் கடவுள் போல வெறுநிலத் தொலிப்ப வீழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The king of Pothanapuram, his body smeared all over with shining gold powder and warrior anklets on his strong feet, with difficulty mounts the wheel, spins round, his eyes reeling, and faints and falls crashing on the bare ground like the rayed sun.
event: The king of Pothanapuram mounts the wheel, grows dizzy and falls to the ground.

tamil: மலையச்செஞ் சாந்து முந்நீர் வலம்புரி யீன்ற முத்து
மிலைவைத்த கோதை நல்லா ரிளமுலைப் பொறியு மார்ந்து
சிலைவைத்த மார்பிற் றென்னன் றிருமணிப் பன்றி நோக்கித்
தலைவைத்த தம்பு தானுந் தரணிமேற் பாதம் வைத்தான்.
reading: The southern king, his bow-scarred chest marked with Malaya sandal, sea-conch pearls and the prints of young women's breasts, looks at the jewelled boar, and the arrow he had set to the bow sets its own foot on the earth.
nuance: தென்னன் is the usual name of the Pandya; nothing in the verse ties him to any king of the Sangam poems. The chest marked by women's breasts is the courtly lover who fails as an archer, a contrast the catalogue keeps making.
event: The southern king's arrow drops to the ground.

tamil: விற்றிறல் விசய னென்பான் வெங்கணை செவிட்டி நோக்கி
யொற்றுபு திருத்திக் கைம்மே லுருட்டுபு நேமி சோந்தாங்
குற்றதன் சிலையின் வாய்ப்பெய் துடுவமை பகழி வாங்க
விற்றுவின் முறிந்து போயிற் றிமைப்பினி னிலங்கித் திட்டான்.
reading: One called Vijayan, mighty with the bow, eyes his fierce arrow, straightens it, rolls it on his hand, comes up to the wheel and sets the star-feathered arrow to his bow, and in the blink of an eye the bow snaps.
nuance: This Vijayan, named as a renowned bowman (விற்றிறல் விசயன்), is one of the suitor kings; the verses do not make him the Hemamapuram prince who was Civakan's pupil, and the name is also the epithet of Arjuna. Line 4 விற்றுவின் is obscure.
event: A king named Vijayan readies his arrow at the wheel and his bow breaks.

tamil: குண்டல மிலங்க வாங்கிக் குனிசிலை யுறையி னீக்கிக்
கொண்டவன் கொழும்பொற் றாரு மாரமு மிளிர வேறிக்
கண்டுகோ னிறைய வாங்கிக் காதுற மறித லோடும்
விண்டுநா ணற்ற தாங்கே விசயனும் வீக்க மற்றான்.
reading: His earrings flashing, Vijayan draws the curved bow from its case, mounts with his gold garland and chains glinting, draws the arrow full to the ear, and at that moment the string parts and his swagger is gone.
event: Vijayan tries again with another bow; the string snaps and he gives up.

tamil: உளைவனப் பிருந்த மான்றே ரொளிமுடி மன்ன ரெல்லாம்
வலைவனப் பிருந்த தோளாள் வருமுலைப் போகம் வேண்டி
விளைதவப் பெருமை யோரார் விற்றிறன் மயங்கி யாருங்
களைகலார் பொறியை யாங்கோ ராறுநாள் கழிந்த வன்றே.
reading: All the bright-crowned kings of the swift chariots, wanting the pleasure of the girl with bangled shoulders, do not understand the greatness of austerity come to fruit; bewildered in their archery, none can bring down the machine, and six days go by.
nuance: விளைதவப் பெருமை ஓரார (line 3) is the narrator's explanation of six days of failure: the kings bring desire (போகம் வேண்டி) and the bow, and lack the merit of past austerity that alone wins her. The verse does not name a school; the ripening of past tapas into present fortune is the epic's way of telling Civakan's successes.
event: Six days pass and no king has brought down the boar machine.

tamil: பனைக்கை யானை மன்னர் பணியப் பைம்பொன் முடியிற்
கனைக்குஞ் சுரும்பார் மாலை கமழ மதுவுந் தேனு
நனைக்குங் கழலோன் சிறுவ னாம வெள்வேல் வலவ
னினைக்க லாகா வகையா னேரா ருயிர்மே லெழுந்தான்.
reading: While kings with palm-trunked elephants bow so that the bees hum on the garlands of their gold crowns and honey wets the hero's anklets, the son of that anklet-wearer, master of the terrible white spear, rises against the lives of his foes in a way no one could have foreseen.
nuance: The verse does not name Civakan; the son (சிறுவன்) of the anklet-wearer whom kings bow to is read as Civakan from 2196 to 2202. நேரார் உயிர்மேல் எழுந்தான் makes his rising an attack on his enemies' lives, not a suit for the bride.
event: Civakan rises to take up the contest against his enemies.

tamil: காரின் முழங்குங் களிறுங் கடலின் முழங்குந் தேரும்
போரின் முழங்கும் புரவிக் கடலும் புகைவாட் கடலுஞ்
சீரின் முழங்கு முரசு மலறுஞ் சிறுவெண் சங்கு
நீரின் முழங்க முழங்கு நீல யானை யிவர்ந்தான்.
reading: He mounts the blue elephant that trumpets amid elephants roaring like cloud, chariots roaring like sea, a sea of war-horses, a sea of smoking swords, drums thundering in rhythm and small white conches crying like water.
event: Civakan mounts a blue elephant amid the din of his army.

tamil: கல்லார் மணிப்பூண் மார்பிற் காம னிவனே யென்ன
வில்லார் கடலந் தானை வேந்தர் குழாத்துட் டோன்றப்
புல்லான் கண்ணி னோக்கிப் புலிகாண் கலையிற் புலம்பி
யொல்லா னொல்லா னாகி யுயிர்போ யிருந்தான் மாதோ.
reading: As the hero appears among the kings with their sea of bow-bearing armies, so that men say this is Kama himself with jewelled ornaments on his chest, the base one looks at him with his eyes, cries out like a deer that has seen a tiger, and sits as if his life had left him.
nuance: புல்லான், 'the base one', is the narrator's name for Kattiyangaran here; the man who once had Civakan led out to be killed now sees him alive. Who says காமன் இவனே is not stated, probably the onlookers.
event: Kattiyangaran sees Civakan alive in the assembly and is struck with terror.

tamil: புலியாப் புறுத்திக் கொண்டேன் போக்கி விட்ட பிழைப்பும்
வலியார் திரடோண் மதனன் னவனைப் பிழைத்த பிழைப்பு
கலியு மென்னை நலியு மென்னக் களிற்றி னுச்சி
யிலையார் கடகத் தடக்கை புடைத்து மெய்சோர்ந் திருந்தான்.
reading: Saying 'the blunder of letting go the tiger I had caught and bound, and the blunder of strong-shouldered Madanan who failed to kill him: this trouble will crush me', he beats the top of the elephant's head with his hand bearing the leaf-patterned bracelet and sits slumped.
nuance: He names two blunders, his own release of the bound 'tiger' and Madanan's failure, and does not name the deed itself, the order to kill, as his wrong; his regret is that the killing failed. Madanan had reported Civakan killed (1164) and been rewarded for it.
event: Kattiyangaran laments that Civakan escaped him and Madanan, and beats his elephant's head in despair.

tamil: மைபூத் தலர்ந்த மழைக்கண் மாழை மானோ நோக்கிற்
கொய்பூங் கோதை மடவார் கொற்றங் கொள்கென் றேத்தப்
பெய்பூங் கழலான் வேழத் திழிந்து பிறைபோற் குலாய
செய்பூண் சிலைநா ணெறிந்தான் சேரார் நாளுக் கனவே.
reading: As women with dark rain-cool eyes and deer glances, wearing plucked flower garlands, cry 'take victory', the hero of the flower anklets comes down from the elephant and twangs the string of his crescent-curved, ornamented bow, a nightmare to the days of his enemies.
nuance: சேரார் நாளுக்கு அனவே, 'a dream to the days of the foes', makes the twang a foreboding of death for Kattiyangaran's side; the bride is not mentioned.
event: Civakan dismounts and twangs his bowstring while the women hail his victory.

tamil: கனிபடு மொழியி னாடன் காரிகை கவற்ற வந்து
குனிசிலை தோற்ற மன்னர் கொங்குகொப் புளிக்கு நீலப்
பனிமலர்க் காடு போன்றார் படர்சிலை தொடாத வேந்த
ரினிதினின் மலர்ந்த வேரார் தாமரைக் காடு போன்றார்.
reading: The kings who came because the girl of fruit-sweet speech troubled their hearts and were beaten by the curved bow are like a grove of blue lilies dripping honey, and the kings who never touched the bow are like a lotus grove sweetly in bloom.
nuance: The two groves read the faces: the defeated darkened and drooping like blue lilies, those who stayed out bright like lotuses. Not trying is here safer than trying and failing.

tamil: போர்த்தகல் விசும்பில் வந்து பொறித்திரி பன்றி மூன்று
நீர்த்தகப் புணர்ந்த போதி னெடுந்தகை மூன்று மற்றுச்
சூர்த்துடன் வீழ நோக்கிச் சுடுசரஞ் சிதற வல்லா
னோர்த்தொன்றே புணர்ப்ப நாடி யொருபகல் காறு நின்றான்.
reading: When the three revolving boars come rightly together in the wide sky, the noble one skilled in scattering burning arrows watches for the three to fall together, and studying how to bring them into one, stands a whole day.
nuance: பன்றி மூன்று (line 1) and நெடுந்தகை மூன்று are obscure: the machine may carry three boars, or a boar and its images, which must line up for one shot to bring all down. That the waiting archer is Civakan is a reading from நெடுந்தகை and from 2202, where he mounts the wheel.
event: Civakan studies the turning machine for a whole day, waiting for the moment to shoot.

tamil: பொறியின்மே லேற றேற்றா னாணினாற் போதல் செய்யா
னெறியின்வில் லூன்றி நிற்ப நிழன்மணிப் பன்றி யற்று
மறியுமோ வென்று முன்னே மணிமுடி சிதறி வீழ்ந்த
செறிகழன் மன்னர் நக்குத் தீயத்தீ விளைத்துக் கொண்டார்.
reading: Seeing him not yet daring to mount the machine and yet out of pride not going away, but standing leaning his bow on the path, the kings whose jewelled crowns had fallen earlier laugh, 'will the shadowed jewel boar break and fall of itself?', and so kindle a fire that will burn them.
nuance: The verse reads as the narrator's irony: the mockers' laughter (நக்கு) is the fire they light against themselves (தீயத் தீ விளைத்துக் கொண்டார்), as 2204 will show. Whether the one who stands is Civakan or another hesitant suitor is not certain.
event: The kings who failed mock Civakan as he stands waiting by the machine.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2202-2226 (5/9)
theme: Civakan shoots the boar target on its revolving wheel at Videham, King Govindan proclaims his lineage, a voice from the sky foretells that he will kill Kattiyangaran, Madanan musters the usurper's army, and the poet sets out the two hosts and the opening of the battle, naming its cost in widows, dead beasts and a grieving Earth.
source_issues: 2202-2206 and 2220 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins read correctly.
2204 line 3 இருந்தவன் பொறியும் is obscure; the reading of what device fell is uncertain.
2207 names no speaker; the attribution to Kattiyangaran rests on context.
2221 line 4 புலமகன் is unexpected and may be a corruption; the agent of the raging spear is uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, who shoots the boar target at Videham (நம்பன் in 2202)
the king of Videham, who holds the boar contest and proclaims Civakan's lineage; named கோவிந்தன் in 2205
the army assembled at the contest, which roars when the boar falls
the figure who appears in the sky and foretells Kattiyangaran's death
the usurping minister, Civakan's enemy, whose army is counted in 2220
Kattiyangaran's ally, who musters the fourfold army
the hundred spear-bearing sons who gather to the usurper's army
the charioteers
the young warriors who harness the horses and take up arms
the Mleccha horsemen
the foot soldiers (தறுகணாளர்)
the 'learned one' whose spear rages in 2221, probably Civakan
the archers of the two armies
the lancers and swordsmen of the two armies

tamil: சிரற்றலை மணிகள் வேய்ந்த திருந்துபொற் றிகிரிச் செம்பொ
னுரற்றலை யுருவப் பன்றி யிடம்வலந் திரிய நம்பன்
விரற்றலைப் புட்டில் வீக்கி வெஞ்சிலை கணையோ டேந்திக்
குரற்றலை வண்டு பொங்கக் குப்புற்று நேமி சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The boar figure stands on a mortar-shaped head above a turning wheel of red gold set with gems, swinging left and right, and the lord binds the finger-guard, takes up the bow with its arrow, and, the bees in his hair rising, closes on the wheel.
nuance: The target is a machine: a boar image on a post that swings to either side above a revolving wheel, so the feat is aiming at a moving mark. குப்புற்று (line 4) may mean he leapt or that he bent low; the sense of his approach turns on it.
event: Civakan arms himself and goes up to the revolving wheel that carries the boar target.

tamil: ஒள்ளழல் வைரப் பூணு மொளிர்மணிக் குழையு மின்ன
வொள்ளழற் கொள்ளி வட்டம் போற்குலாய்ச் சுழலப் பொன்ஞா
ணொள்ளழ னேமி நக்க மண்டல மாக நின்றா
னொள்ளழற் பருதி மேலோர் பருதிநின் றதனை யொத்தான்.
reading: His diamond ornaments and gem earrings flashing, he wheels round like a whirled firebrand, his gold cord making a circle with the blazing wheel, so that he stands like one sun set upon another.
nuance: Each line opens with ஒள்ளழல், 'bright fire', and the verse builds a single figure out of the repetition: the hero, his ornaments and the wheel all become circles of fire, ending in the doubled sun.
event: Civakan circles with the turning wheel as he takes aim.

tamil: அருந்தவக் கிழமை போல விறாதவில் லறாத நாண்வாய்த்
திருந்தினார் சிந்தை போலுந் திண்சரஞ் சுருக்கி மாறா
யிருந்தவன் பொறியும் பன்றி யியற்றரும் பொறியு மற்றாங்
கொருங்குட னுதிர வெய்தா னூழித்தீ யுருமோ டொப்பான்.
reading: With a bow that never breaks, like the rare virtue of penance, a string that never parts, and arrows straight like the minds of the refined, he shoots so that the mechanism and the hard-wrought boar device fall shattered together, he himself like the fire of the world's end joined with thunder.
nuance: The similes borrow from ascetic and moral life: the bow is unbreakable as penance is, the arrows straight as a refined mind. The feat that wins the contest is praised in the language of virtue just before it opens a war. இருந்தவன் பொறியும் (line 3) is obscure; it may name the device on which the boar was mounted.
event: Civakan's arrow strikes the target and shatters both the boar and the machine that moved it.

tamil: இலங்கெயிற் றேன மேவுண் டிருநிலத் திடித்து வீழக்
கலங்குதெண் டிரையுங் காருங் கடுவளி முழக்கு மொப்ப
உலம்புபு முரசங் கொட்டி யொய்யெனச் சேனை யார்ப்பக்
குலம்பகர்ந் தறைந்து கோமான் கோவிந்தன் கூறி னானே.
reading: The bright-tusked boar takes the arrow and crashes to the ground, the drums are beaten with a roar like the troubled sea, the cloud and the gale, the army shouts, and the lord Govindan proclaims the hero's lineage by drum.
nuance: This is the turn of the ilampakam: the contest's winner is named as the dispossessed king's son, so the proclamation of birth is also a declaration of war on the usurper.
event: The boar falls, and King Govindan has Civakan's lineage proclaimed before the assembled host.

tamil: வானிடை யொருவன் றோன்றி மழையென முழங்கிச் சொல்லுந்
தேனுடை யலங்கல் வெள்வேற் சீவக னென்னுஞ் சிங்கங்
வேன்மிடை சோலை வேழத் தின்னுயிர் விழுங்கு மென்றான்.
reading: A figure appears in the sky and, thundering like a rain cloud, declares that the lion called Civakan, of the honeyed garland and white spear, will swallow the sweet life of the elephant called Kattiyangaran, of the garlanded chest.
nuance: The prophecy is cast as a beast image, lion against elephant, the old figure of the smaller, fiercer animal killing the larger; the next verses give the usurper the larger army.
event: A voice from the sky foretells that Civakan will kill Kattiyangaran.

reading: A speaker scorns the threat: shall he fear because the other has come bringing the fierce army of the Vidyadharas? The other does not know his strength; if it comes to fierce battle, let him cut down that pride and end the deceit, with him.
nuance: No speaker is named. The mention of the Vidyadhara army suits a word aimed at Civakan's side, and the next verse has Madanan blaze up on hearing the 'famed one', so this is read as Kattiyangaran's answer; the closing clause, who is to cut whose pride and whose deceit is meant, can be read either way.

reading: As the sunstone pours out fire on seeing the sun, so Madanan, hearing the word of the far-famed one, blazes up like the thunder of a raining cloud.
nuance: The sunstone makes the anger borrowed: Madanan's fire is kindled by another's words, as the stone's fire is the sun's. Who the பேரிசையான் is depends on the reading of the previous verse.
event: Madanan flares into rage on hearing the words.

reading: In an instant he readies foot soldiers, elephants, horses and chariots and gathers the fourfold army, and a hundred warrior sons with poisoned-leaf spears assemble.
nuance: Whose sons the hundred are is not said in the verse; the usurper's side is meant.
event: Madanan musters the fourfold army, and a hundred spear-bearing sons gather to it.

reading: The poet announces that he will tell all that befell those who met in the sword battle between the fierce army of the master of the bow and the army of the one who rose up in wrath.
nuance: A rare first-person turn by the narrator (உரைக்குற்றேன், line 4), marking the set battle-piece that follows.

reading: The armoured elephants are drawn up in rows, like great jewelled mountains, with forehead plates, rut streaming like falls down their brows, and pearl-bearing tusks that split the front.
As men with curved bows and bloody weapons mount the elephants, the bright flags crowded in the dark sky look like a forest of banners struck by the wind.
The charioteers, with fine cloth on their heads, ready the chariots, beautiful under their parasols, guarded with shields, with raised gold seats and quivers fitted to the footboard.
event: The charioteers make the chariots ready.

reading: They bind the strong yokes with fitted ropes on the trimmed-maned horses and set the goads, and the young men check the bows and other weapons and take them in hand.
event: The young warriors harness the horses and take up their weapons.

reading: The horses, proud and quick as flight, wheel like spinning tops in the wide battle, plumed at the brow, and bear marks on their thighs by which those learned in the great treatises may know where they were bred.
nuance: Line 3 to 4 refer to a learned lore of horses (பெரிய நூலவர்): the breed and country of a horse read from marks on its body.

reading: As Mlecchas mount with deadly-tipped lances, bows and lightning-leaf swords, the horses throng, with gold-meshed caparisons and garlands bounding, raging forward with a roar.
nuance: Foreign (மிலேச்சர்) horsemen in the army, as in the Sangam memory of Yavana guards; the verse does not say on whose side.
event: Mleccha horsemen mount and the cavalry surges forward.

reading: The fierce-eyed foot soldiers have garlands and chaplets on their heads, ringing anklets on their feet, short swords gripped hard in their hands, and mail on their bodies.
The host with its hair-tufted shields, hide shields, long screens, staves and wooden boards in ranks looks like a sea of tigers that has entered the face of battle.

tamil: பார்நனை மதத்த பல்பேய் பருந்தொடு பரவச் செல்லும்
போர்மதக் களிறு பொற்றேர் நான்கரைக் கச்ச மாகு
மோமணிப் புரவி யேழா மிலக்கமேழ் தேவ கோடி
கார்மலி கடலங் காலாள் கற்பகத் தாரி னாற்கே.
reading: For the one of the kalpaka garland there are war elephants in rut, attended by crowds of spirits and kites, and golden chariots, four and a half kaccham, horses seven lakh, and foot soldiers seven deva-koti, a sea swelling like a rain cloud.
nuance: The verse counts Civakan's army; read with the next it sets the two hosts side by side. The units (கச்சம், இலக்கம், தேவ கோடி) are traditional large numbers and their values are not fixed here.

tamil: நிழன்மணிப் புரவித் திண்டேர் நிழறுழாய்க் குனிந்து குத்து
மழறிகழ் கதத்த யானை யைந்தரைக் கச்ச மாகு
மெழின்மணிப் புரவி யேழா மிலக்கமேழ் தேவ கோடி
கழன்மலிந் திலங்குங் காலாள் கட்டியங் காரற் கன்றே.
reading: For Kattiyangaran, then, there were strong chariots with shining-maned horses and fire-wrathful elephants that stoop and gore, five and a half kaccham, horses seven lakh, and foot soldiers seven deva-koti, bright with anklets.
nuance: Against 2219 the usurper's elephants and chariots are one kaccham more, the rest equal: the poem gives the wrongful side the larger force.

reading: So that the women of noble houses put off their adornment, the tossing-maned horses and the elephants die, and the Earth-woman beats her breast with her hand and pines, the learned one raged, and his spear smoked.
nuance: The verse states the war's cost before its glory: widowhood (the noble women's adornment put off), slaughter, and the Earth herself mourning, in an ilampakam named for the Earth-woman (மண்மகள்). Who the புலமகன் is, Civakan or another, the verse does not fix.
event: The fighting begins, its cost foretold in widowed women, dead beasts and a grieving Earth.

reading: Struck with drumsticks, the war drums roar, the white conches and the kettledrums spread their sound, the pampai drums throb, the tall peacock-feather standards rise everywhere, and the din of the front is like the roar of the sea.

The crowned kings are like the rising sun, the massed elephants like great ships breaking the waves, and the flashing swords like killing sharks, so that the clash looks like a time when two seas met in wrath.
event: The two armies meet.

reading: Warriors in dark anklets, with quivers packed with arrows tossing on their broad backs and tight girdles, set arrows to their black bows and pour a rain of shafts until the sky is filled.
event: The archers loose a rain of arrows.

reading: Driving their dark arrows into fat-swollen chests, shoulders and foreheads, they fought a tangled battle like men struggling in a fragrant oncoming flood; such was its nature.
nuance: The simile of line 3 sets the slaughter beside the festival play of men and women in scented flood water, a scene the epic elsewhere describes for pleasure.
event: The armies fight at close quarters with arrows.

reading: They drew their burning swords; eyes smoked and burned and lids were scorched; they roared like Death, opened chests and destroyed sweet lives, and the lancers' din grew.
event: The sword fight kills many.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2227-2251 (6/9)
theme: The great battle of the Earth-lady ilampakam: the clash of horses, chariots and elephants, the arrows that darken the sky, the Earth veiling her eyes in a blanket of blood, the slain bridegrooms feasted on by ghouls and jackals, and the duels in which Vijayan's fight ends Madanan, Buddhisenan seizes kings by the hair, Devadattan routs the Magadha king and Sridattan kills the Kalinga king.
source_issues: Verses 2235, 2236, 2238 and 2242 to 2251 were printed in eight half-lines and have been joined into four.
Verse 2230 line 2 prints கொம்மை கொட்வே, apparently for கொட்டவே.
Verse 2246 calls the warrior மன்மதன் where 2245 has மதனன்; they are read as one man.

cast.role: the Earth goddess, who in the battle-poetry veils her eyes from the slaughter
the ghouls of the battlefield
Kattiyangaran's ally who urges force; killed in the final war (called மன்மதன் in 2246)
prince of Hemamapuram, Civakan's friend, who fights in his war
the war elephant Manmathan climbs in 2248
Civakan's companion, a Brahmin (நான்மறையாளன்), a fighter in the war (written புத்திமா சேனன் in 2249)
one of Civakan's companions (written தேவமா தத்தன் in 2250)
the king of the Magadhas, fighting on Kattiyangaran's side, who flees
merchant of Rajamapuram, Civakan's friend, a fighter in the war
the king of the Kalingas, fighting on Kattiyangaran's side, killed by Sridattan

reading: The narrator says the severed heads of warriors falling with their precious garlands on the field looked like dark ripe palmyra fruit shaken down when the wind strikes a palm grove.
event: Warriors' heads are struck off and fall on the field.

reading: The narrator describes the war horses, impatient of the stable, golden-garlanded, plumed on the forehead with yak-tail, swift enough to outrun arrows, young and evenly paired, as they go into the fight with their riders.
event: The cavalry rides into the battle.

reading: The narrator describes the chariots, their hubs shaped by the sharp chisel, gold-rimmed and flashing like lightning from a cloud, as they close wheel to wheel with the best of the enemy's chariots.
event: The chariots close with one another.

reading: The narrator describes the war elephants, painted with collyrium and fed on rice balls, their drums beating like Death's, looking like mountains with wings, clashing like cloud-climbed hills.
event: The war elephants clash.

reading: The royal elephants crash into one another so that fire flies, like great sea ships that have snapped their ropes in a contrary wind and run together with no way out.
event: The royal elephants collide.

reading: The loosed arrows crowd the sky until the sun's rays are hidden and darkness spreads, and in that darkness the gleam of killing spears and the gems on kings' crowns burn like sunlight.
event: Arrows darken the sky over the field.

reading: The narrator says that the Earth goddess, with jewelled breasts, saying she cannot look with her eyes at such cruel things, covered herself with a single red blanket, that is, the blood that now covers the field.
