nuance: The conceit turns the reddened ground into a modesty: Earth, the bride the hero is to win in this ilampakam of the Earth-lady (மண்மகள்), veils her eyes from the war fought for her. Her words are reported speech inside the narration (எனா).
event: The field is covered in blood, which the poet makes the Earth's red veil.

reading: Men whose broad garlanded chests had been ploughed by the jewelled breasts of women with earrings are now ploughed by the killing tusks of rutting elephants, and bathe in blood.
nuance: The verb உழப்பட்ட is used twice, once for love and once for the tusk, so the same chest is worked over first by pleasure and then by death.
event: Warriors are gored by elephants and lie in blood.

reading: Warriors whose dark hair had worn the wedding garlands their brides strung with soft fingers, now washed by blood, wear garlands of entrails and make a great feast for the corpse-garlanded ghoul-woman.
nuance: The verse runs four garlands in a row (மணமாலை, இணர்மாலை, நிணமாலை, பிணமாலை): the bride's garland gives way to the entrail-garland, so the wedding becomes the ghoul's banquet.
event: Slain warriors lie in blood, a feast for the ghouls.

reading: The ankleted feet of kings who never lost a battle, cut off with their anklets by flashing swords as they raised their bangled arms and spat fire at one another, writhe in the blood like sharks in the dark sea.
event: Kings' feet are cut off in the sword fight.

reading: Elephants whose armour has been pierced and who are swarmed with arrows, maddened, crush the bannered chariots and rise carrying the rolling wheels on them, spreading like hills the sun has reached.
event: Wounded elephants crush the chariots.

reading: The cut trunks of rutting elephants lying under tall garlanded parasols in thick blood look like the white moon of the high sky pulled down to earth together with a dark serpent.
nuance: The white parasol is the moon and the dark trunk the eclipse serpent; the image of a fallen light swallowed by a serpent returns in 2245 and 2251 for the fallen captains.
event: Elephants' trunks are cut off and lie under the fallen parasols.

reading: The elephants, their black colour lost under a cloak of blood, look like vermilion mountains, and the blood that bubbles out where they charge looks like vermilion falls on every side.

Men lie with an elephant for a pillow at the head and a maned horse at the feet, having paid off the debt of the red rice, still gripping their angry swords on the cloth they wore, their waist cords glinting, while jackals come up in fear and howl over them.
nuance: செஞ்சோற்றுக் கடன் names the fighter's death as repayment of a debt, not as glory; the only mourners in the verse are jackals.
event: The dead lie on the field and jackals gather and howl.

reading: Warriors bite down their lips, the coral mouths that gave nectar to their lovers, as if saying they will not give them to alien birds to eat, and lie with gold ear-studs and earrings gleaming, broad-chested, like sleeping Vidyadharas.
nuance: The bitten lip is the warrior's fury at death; the poet reads it as a lover's refusal to let the mouth his beloved kissed be eaten by birds.
event: The fallen warriors lie with lips bitten.

reading: Small jackals dragging entrails through the mire of fat and flesh look like fierce dogs pulling at chains, and birds rising with bangled arms look like Garuda rising with hooded snakes.
event: Jackals and birds feed on the slain.

reading: Like lions rolling on the ground when thunder strikes the hill, the royal elephants, with flawless gold face-plates, fight in a rising cloud of dust, are destroyed and sink with their kings into the killing field.
nuance: Line 2's நிரையுளை அரிநன்மா may be maned lions (the simile) or fine maned horses; read as the simile, it keeps the verse's subject the royal elephants of line 4.
event: Royal elephants fall with their kings on the field.

reading: The chest that women with kuvalai eyes and long hair had embraced, sandal-smeared, chains tangling, is now embraced by the sword, and the jewel lying in the flowing blood looks like a young crescent in a wide red sky.
nuance: புல்லிய and புல்ல repeat the verb of embrace: the sword takes the women's place on the same chest.
event: A warrior lies slain in his own blood.

tamil: காளமா கிருளைப் போழ்ந்து கதிர்சொரி கடவுட் டிங்கள்
கோளரா விழுங்க முந்நீர்க் கொழுந்திரைக் குளித்த தேபோ
னீளம ருழக்கி யானை நெற்றிமேற் றத்தி வெய்ய
வாளின்வாய் மதனன் பட்டான் விசயன்போர் விசயம் பெற்றான்.
reading: Like the moon that splits black darkness, swallowed by Rahu and plunging into the sea's waves, Madanan, after churning the long battle and leaping onto an elephant's forehead, falls at the mouth of a fierce sword, and Vijayan wins the victory of the fight.
nuance: The syntax leaves open whether Madanan or Vijayan leaps onto the elephant's forehead; the next three verses tell the fight at length and end it on the elephant's tusk, not a sword, so 2245 reads as the summary and 2246 to 2248 as its telling.
event: Madanan falls by the sword and Vijayan wins the fight.

tamil: மன்மத னென்னுங் காளை மணியொலிப் புரவித் தேர்மேல்
வின்மழை சொரிந்து கூற்றிற் றெழித்தனன் றலைப்பெய் தார்ப்பக்
கொன்மலி மார்பன் பொற்றேர் கொடுஞ்சிலை யறுப்பச் சீறிய
பொன்வரைப் புலியிற் பாய்ந்து பூமிமேற் றோன்றி னானே.
reading: The youth called Manmathan, on his chariot drawn by bell-ringing horses, rains arrows and roars like Death; when the death-dealing hero cuts the bow on his golden chariot, he leaps down like an angry lion from a golden hill and stands on the ground.
nuance: மன்மதன் is taken as the same man as 2245's மதனன் (both are names of Kama), and the bow-cutter as Vijayan; the verse names neither identification.
event: Manmathan fights from his chariot; when his bow is cut he leaps down to fight on foot.

tamil: நெற்றிமேற் கோல்கண் மூன்று நெருப்புமிழ்ந் தழுந்த வெய்யச்
சுற்றுபு மாலை போலத் தோன்றறன் னுதலிற் சூடிப்
பொற்றதோர் பவழந் தன்மேற் புனைமணி யழுத்தி யாங்குச்
செற்றெயி றழுந்தச் செவ்வாய் கௌவிவா ளுரீஇ னானே.
reading: Three arrows sink spitting fire into his forehead and he wears them on his brow like a garland, like gems set on coral; pressing his teeth into his red lip, he draws his sword.
event: Struck in the forehead by three arrows, Manmathan bites his lip and draws his sword.

tamil: தோளினா லெஃக மேந்தித் தும்பிமே லிவரக் கையா
னீளமாப் புடைப்பப் பொங்கி நிலத்தவன் கவிழ்ந்து வீழக்
கீளிரண் டாகக் குத்தி யெடுத்திடக் கிளர்பொன் மார்பன்
வாளினாற் றிருகி வீசி மருப்பின்மேற் றுஞ்சி னானே.
reading: Lifting his blade on his shoulder he climbs onto the elephant; it strikes him with its long trunk so that he falls face down on the ground, gores him and lifts him torn in two, and the gold-chested warrior, twisting, swings his sword and dies upon the tusk.
nuance: Whose elephant it is, and whether the one who dies on the tusk is Manmathan or the elephant's rider, the verse does not say; this reading follows the run of 2246 to 2247.
event: Manmathan climbs the elephant, is thrown and gored, strikes with his sword and dies on its tusk.

tamil: நனைகலந் திழியும் பைந்தார் நான்மறை யாளன் பைம்பொற்
புனைகலக் குப்பை யொப்பான் புத்திமா சேனன் பொங்கி
வனைகலத் திகிரித் தோமேன் மன்னரைக் குடுமி கொண்டான்
கனையெரி யழலம் பெய்த கண்ணுதன் மூர்த்தி யொத்தான்.
reading: Buddhisenan, the man of the four Vedas, with honey-dripping garland, like a heap of wrought gold ornaments, surges up and from his chariot with wheels like a potter's seizes kings by their tufts, like the forehead-eyed god who loosed the blazing fire-arrow.
nuance: The companion is called நான்மறையாளன், a Brahmin, and the Jain epic likens his fury to Siva burning the three cities with a fiery arrow, using the Saiva myth purely as a simile of rage.
event: Buddhisenan drives his chariot through the kings and seizes them by the hair.

tamil: செண்பகப் பூங்குன் றொப்பான் றேவமா தத்தன் வெய்தா
விண்புக வுயிரைப் பெய்வான் வீழ்தரு கடாத்த வேழ
மண்பக விடிக்குஞ் சிங்க மெனக்கடாய் மகதர் கோமான்
றெண்கடற் றானை யோட நாணிவேல் செறித்திட் டானே.
reading: Devamathattan, like a hill of campaka flowers, fiercely sending lives into the sky, charges like a lion that strikes a rutting elephant so that the earth splits, and the Magadha king, seeing his sea-like army flee, in shame sheathes his spear.
nuance: The Magadha king's shame ends in sheathing the spear, not in death: the verse lets the defeated king withdraw.
event: Devadattan routs the Magadha army, and its king, ashamed, sheathes his spear.

tamil: சின்னப்பூ வணிந்த குஞ்சிச் சீதத்தன் சினவு பொன்வாண்
மன்னருட் கலிங்கர் கோமான் மத்தகத் திறுப்ப மன்னன்
பொன்னவிர் குழையும் பூணு மாரமுஞ் சுடர வீழ்வான்
மின்னவிர் பருதி முந்நீர்க் கோளொடும் வீழ்வ தொத்தான்.
reading: Sridattan, with small flowers in his hair, strikes his angry golden sword into the forehead of the Kalinga king among the kings, and the king falls, his earrings, ornaments and necklace blazing, like the bright sun falling into the sea together with a planet.
event: Sridattan kills the Kalinga king with his sword.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2252-2276 (7/9)
theme: The battle of the Manmagal ilampakam at its height: Govindan, Ulokapalan, Nabulan, Vipulan and Padumukan kill or rout the allied kings, Nabulan and Vipulan refuse to strike the frightened, the weaponless, the wounded, the young and the old, and Vipulan's single duel ends with the slain challenger received into heaven.
source_issues: 2252 line 1 உழவன மான்றேர் is probably உழவன் மான்றேர் (or உழவன் அமான்றேர்) with a letter misdivided.
2258 line 1 ஏந்தறன் is read as ஏந்தல் தன்.
2260 line 4 (கண்காவல கழுகோம்புவ துயராநனி வினவும்) is hard to construe.
2275 lines 2-4: உடு and வயிரம் are doubtful, and the elephant's part is unclear.
2276 line 4 (பத்திரக் கடிப்பு மின்னப் பகடு போர்த்தான்) is a foot short and repeats the opening of 2277; the end of 2276 may be lost or misplaced.
2252-2259 and 2262-2275 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.

cast.role: the king who leads Civakan's war (கோவிந்த னென்னுஞ் சிங்கம் 2252; hailed கோவிந்தன் வாழ்க in 2277)
a king on the enemy side, killed with his elephant by Govindan
the prince of Chandirapam in the Pallava country, Civakan's friend; named உலோக பாலன் in 2255 and பல்லவ தேச மன்னன் in 2253
the king of Kampili, fighting on the enemy side and killed by Ulokapalan
one of Civakan's companions
the king of Magadha, on the enemy side, whom Nabulan spares
an unarmed young warrior on the enemy side who claps and shouts a challenge at Nabulan
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Nabulan
the kings fighting on the enemy side, whom Vipulan challenges
the warrior who challenges Vipulan to single combat and is killed
the celestial women who receive warriors slain in battle
Civakan's friend, fighting from an elephant
a warrior on the enemy side, killed by Padumukan
a warrior on the enemy side who charges to avenge Kamukan
the fighting men of the armies
a boasting prince on the enemy side killed by Padumukan's arrow
a named war elephant whose tusks break in the charge

tamil: கொடுஞ்சிலை யுழவன மான்றேர்க் கோவிந்த னென்னுஞ் சிங்க
மடங்கருஞ் சீற்றத் துப்பின் மாரட்ட னென்னும் பொற்குன்
றிடத்துபொற் றூளி பொங்கக் களிற்றொடு மிறங்கி வீழ
வடர்ந்தெரி பொன்செ யம்பி னழன்றிடித் திட்ட தன்றே.
reading: Govindan, a lion among chariot-bowmen, strikes with blazing gold-worked arrows until the king called Marattan, a mountain of gold, comes down and falls with his elephant in a cloud of gold dust.
nuance: The fallen king is likened to a gold hill, so the dust of his fall is gold dust: the praise of the enemy's splendour measures the victor's arrows.
event: Govindan's arrows bring down the Maratta king together with his elephant.

tamil: கோங்குபூத் துதிர்ந்த குன்றிற் பொன்னணி புளகம் வேய்ந்த
பாங்கமை பரும யானைப் பல்லவ தேச மன்னன்
றேங்கமழ் தெரியற் றீம்பூந் தாரவ னூர்ந்த வேழங்
காம்பிலிக் கிறைவ னூர்ந்த களிற்றொடு மலைந்த தன்றே.
reading: The elephant ridden by the king of the Pallava country, on whose trappings gold lies like kongu flowers shed on a hill, closes with the tusker ridden by the lord of Kampili.
nuance: The Pallava king is named Ulokapalan only in 2255 (மற்றவ னுலோக பாலன்); the identification of the two is a reading of that line.
event: The Pallava king's elephant and the Kampili king's elephant clash.

tamil: கொந்தழல் பிறப்பத் தாக்கிக் கோடுகண் மிடைந்த தீயால்
வெந்தன விலையி லாத சாமரை வீர மன்ன
னந்தரம் புதைய வில்வா யருஞ்சரம் பெய்த மாரி
குந்தத்தால் விலக்கி வெய்ய கூற்றென முழங்கி னானே.
reading: The tusks strike so hard that fire leaps from them and burns the priceless yak-tail whisks, and the heroic king beats back with his lance the rain of arrows that hides the sky and roars like Death.
nuance: Which king wards off the arrows is not said; the next verse's மற்றவன் ('the other one') for Ulokapalan suggests this one is the Kampili king.
event: The Kampili king wards off a rain of arrows with his lance.

tamil: மற்றவ னுலோக பாலன் வயங்குபொற் பட்ட மார்ந்த
நெற்றிமே லெய்த கோலைப் பறித்திட வுமிழ்ந்த நெய்த்தோ
ருற்றவன் களிற்றிற் பாயத் தோன்றுவா னுதயத் துச்சி
யொற்றைமாக் கதிரை நீட்டி யொண்சுட ரிகுந்த தொத்தான்.
reading: The other, Ulokapalan, pulls out the arrow shot into his gold-banded forehead, and the blood that gushes onto the foe's elephant makes him look like the rising sun stretching out a single great ray.
nuance: The wound is turned into ornament: the jet of blood becomes the sun's first ray, so the verse makes the hurt a sign of glory rather than of danger.
event: Ulokapalan plucks an arrow from his own forehead and fights on.

tamil: கொடுமரங் குழைய வாங்கிக் கொற்றவ னெய்த கோல்க
ணெடுமொழி மகளிர் கோல நிழன்மணி முலைக ணோபட்
டுடனுழ வுவந்த மார்ப மூழ்கலிற் சிங்கம் போலக்
கடன்மருள் சேனை சிந்தக் காம்பிலி மன்னன் வீழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The conqueror bends his bow until it bows, and his arrows sink into the chest that the breasts of soft-spoken women once ploughed, so that the Kampili king falls like a lion while his sea-like army scatters.
nuance: The arrows enter exactly where the women's breasts lay: love's marks on the chest become the place of death, an image the chapter repeats (2273).
event: Ulokapalan's arrows kill the king of Kampili, and his army breaks.

tamil: பொன்னிறக் கோங்கம் பொற்பூங் குன்றெனப் பொலிந்த மேனி
நன்னிற மாலின் மேலா நலங்கொடார் நபுல னென்பான்
மின்னிற வெஃக மேந்தி வீங்குநீர் மகதை யார்கோன்
கொன்னிறக் களிற்றி னெற்றிக் கூந்தன்மாப் பாய்வித் தானே.
reading: Nabulan, whose body glows like a hill of golden kongu blossom and whose beauty passes even Mal's, raises a lightning-bright spear and makes his maned horse leap onto the brow of the Magadha king's elephant.
event: Nabulan rides his horse up onto the Magadha king's war elephant.

tamil: ஏந்தறன் கண்கள் வெய்ய விமைத்திட வெறித லோம்பி
நாந்தக வுழவ னாணி நக்குநீ யஞ்சல் கண்டாய்
காய்ந்திலே னென்று வல்லே கலினமாக் குன்றிற் பொங்கிப்
பாய்ந்ததோர் புலியின் மற்றோர் பகட்டின்மேற் பாய்வித் தானே.
reading: When the lord's eyes flicker in fear, the swordsman, ashamed, holds back his blow, laughs, tells him not to be afraid since he is not angry, and swiftly makes his horse spring like a tiger onto another elephant.
nuance: The shame (நாணி) is the victor's, not the loser's: to strike a man who flinches would dishonour the striker. ஏந்தறன் (line 1) is read as ஏந்தல் தன், the lord's.
event: Nabulan spares the frightened Magadha king, reassures him, and turns to another elephant.

tamil: கைப்படை யொன்று மின்றிக் கைகொட்டிக் குமர னார்ப்ப
மெய்ப்படை வீழ்ந்த நாணி வேழமு மெறிதல் செல்லான்
மைப்பட நெடுங்கண் மாலை மகளிர்தம் வனப்பிற சூழ்ந்து
கைப்படு பொருளி லாதான் காமம்போற் காளை மீண்டான்.
reading: When a youth with no weapon in his hand claps and shouts, the young man, ashamed because his foe's arms have fallen, will not strike even his elephant, and turns back like the desire of a man with no money who hovers round the beauty of dark-eyed women.
nuance: The simile is unexpected and exact: the warrior who meets no fit foe is like a penniless lover who can only look at courtesans, a desire with nothing to spend itself on. The young man who claps is read as an enemy youth; that he is the same as Nabulan is unlikely since line 4 names the one who turns back காளை.
event: Nabulan refuses to fight a weaponless youth who challenges him, and withdraws.

reading: Vipulan asks the enemy: is there among you anyone who, finding no joy in guarding the earth, would rather guard heaven and leave his fame behind here; and his spear, flashing like lightning in dark night, raised high where the vultures wait, puts the question too.
nuance: The taunt is courteous in form, an offer of heaven; line 4 (கண்காவல கழுகோம்புவது) is hard to construe, and the reading that the vultures guard the spear's point is a guess.
event: Vipulan challenges the enemy kings to come and die.

reading: The spear-ploughman does not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction; nor a wounded man, even an equal, since he is another's leavings; nor the young, since without a match valour withers; nor the old, since they lack strength.
nuance: Every reason is the striker's honour, not the victim's need: the wounded are refused as leftovers (மிச்சில்), the young because valour would wither, so the restraint is pride as much as mercy. The next verse (2262) at once qualifies the first rule: he will take on elephants if they fall many to one blow.

reading: Asking whether there are rutting elephants, one or many, worth felling in a single stroke, the angry spearman goes like a tiger cub of the golden slopes, bees humming in his garland, and a thousand hostile elephants flee.
event: Vipulan seeks out elephants, and a thousand of them flee before him.

reading: A man with long earrings, a gold ear-leaf, a waist-string and a shining sword comes up and says 'strike, you who have no equal'; the hero laughs 'is that so?' and, glowing with manly beauty, says 'here at last is my match'.
nuance: The speakers of the two short speeches are not named; the challenger is read as the ஒருவன் of line 2 and the one who laughs as Vipulan.
event: A warrior challenges Vipulan to single combat and Vipulan accepts him as a match.

reading: Like two young suns at war on the waves of sweet water, whirling with lightning between them as if at play, the two, with gold bowstrings, matchless bows, shields and killing swords, garlands and banner-marked chests, circle each other.
event: Vipulan and his challenger circle each other in the duel.

reading: 'You are my guest; strike', says one, offering his fragrant chest, and the other strikes and breaks his dark ornament; 'now it is your turn', and the blazing spear cleaves the challenger through the middle so that he stands unaware of it; the celestial women shower flowers and bow, and he reaches heaven.
nuance: ஊழ் in line 2 (நினதூழினி) means 'turn', not fate. The duel is framed as hospitality: the first blow is the guest's portion. Heaven goes to the man who loses, not the victor. Who says which line is a reading.
event: Vipulan lets the challenger strike first, then kills him with one blow, and the dead man is received into heaven.

tamil: நித்திலக் குப்பை போல நிழலுமிழ்ந் திலங்கு மேனிப்
பத்திப்பூ ணணிந்த மார்பிற் பதுமுகன் பைம்பொற் சூழி
மொய்த்தெறி யோடை நெற்றி மும்மதக் களிற்றின் மேலான்
கைத்தலத் தெஃக மேந்திக் காமுகற் கண்டு காய்ந்தான்.
reading: Padumukan, his body glowing like a heap of pearls and his chest hung with rows of ornaments, mounted on a triple-rutting elephant with a gold forehead plate, raises his spear and blazes with anger on seeing Kamukan.
event: Padumukan sights Kamukan and moves against him in anger.

tamil: மாற்றவன் சேனை தாக்கித் தளர்ந்தபின் வன்கண் மள்ள
ராற்றலொ டாண்மை தோன்ற வாருயிர் வழங்கி வீழ்ந்தார்
காற்றினாற் புடைக்கப் பட்டுக் கடலுடைந் தோடக் காம
ரேற்றிளஞ் சுறாக்க ளெங்குங் கிடந்தவை போல வொத்தார்.
reading: After the enemy army attacked and tired, the hard-eyed fighting men, showing strength and manhood, gave up their lives and fell, lying everywhere like young sharks cast up when the wind beats the sea and it breaks.
nuance: Which army's men fall is unclear; மாற்றவன் சேனை may be the subject of தாக்கி or its object.
event: Warriors of both sides fall in numbers on the field.

tamil: தூசுலாம் பரவை யல்குற் றுணைமுலை மகளி ராடு
மூசல்போற் சேனை யோடப் பதுமுகன் களிற்றை யுந்தி
மாசில்சீர் மழையி னெற்றி மாமதி நுழைவ தேபோற்
காய்சினக் களிற்றி னெற்றி யாழிகொண் டழுத்தி னானே.
reading: As the army sways and runs like the swing of women at play, Padumukan drives his elephant and, as the full moon enters the brow of a cloud, drives a discus into the brow of the furious elephant.
nuance: ஆழி is read as a discus or wheel-weapon; the brow it enters is read as Kamukan's elephant's.
event: Padumukan drives a weapon into the forehead of Kamukan's elephant.

tamil: பெருவலி யதனை நோனான் பிண்டிபா லத்தை யேந்தி
யருவரை நெற்றிப் பாய்ந்த வாய்மயிற் றோகை போலச்
சொரிமதக் களிற்றின் கும்பத் தழுத்தலிற் றோன்றல் சீறிக்
கருவலித் தடக்கை வாளிற் காளையை வெளவி னானே.
reading: Unable to bear that great strength, Kamukan raises a javelin, and as it sinks into the temple of the rutting elephant like a peacock's tail on a mountain's brow, the lord, enraged, takes the young man with his sword.
nuance: Read with 2270, the young man taken (காளையை வெளவினான்) is Kamukan, who falls in the next verse; the verse names neither.
event: Kamukan wounds Padumukan's elephant with a javelin, and Padumukan kills him with his sword.

tamil: தீமுகத் துமிழும் வேற்கட் சில்லரிச் சிலம்பி னார்தங்
காமுகன் களத்து வீழக் கைவிர னுதியிற் சுட்டிப்
பூமுக மாலை மார்பன் பொன்னணி கவச மின்னக்
கோமுகன் கொலைவல் யானை கூற்றெனக் கடாயி னானே.
reading: When Kamukan, lover of the anklet-wearing women whose spear-like eyes spit fire, falls on the field, Komukan, his armour flashing and garland on his chest, points with his fingertip and drives his killing elephant on like Death.
nuance: The name Kamukan is played on: he is the காமுகன், the lover, of the women with anklets, so his fall is also their loss.
event: Kamukan falls, and Komukan charges Padumukan to avenge him.

tamil: சாரிகை திரியும் யானை யுழக்கலிற் றரணி தன்மே
லார்கலிக் குருதி வெள்ள மருந்துகள் கழுமி யெங்கும்
வீரியக் காற்றிற் பொங்கி விசும்புபோர்த் தெழுதப் பட்ட
போர்நிலைக் களத்தை யொப்பக் குருதிவான் போர்த்த தன்றே.
reading: The elephants wheel and churn the field, the roaring flood of blood on the earth mixes with the dust, rises on a mighty wind and covers the sky, so the heavens are hung with blood like a painted battle scene.
nuance: The simile reverses art and life: the real field is compared to a painting of a field, so the slaughter is seen as a spectacle.

tamil: சென்றது தடக்கை தூணி சேந்தகண் புருவங் கோலி
நின்றவிற் குனிந்த தம்பு நிமிர்ந்தன நீங்கிற் றாவி
வென்றிகொள் சரங்கண் மூழ்கி மெய்ம்மறைத் திட்டு மின்றோய்
குன்றின்மேற் பவழம் போலக் கோமுகன் றோன்றி னானே.
reading: His hand goes to the quiver, his eyes redden and brows arch, the bent bow sends the arrows straight and lives depart; then victorious arrows sink in and cover his body, and Komukan appears like coral on a lightning-touched hill.
nuance: Whether lines 1 to 2 describe Komukan shooting or Padumukan shooting him is not clear; the coral image means he is red with blood, and the verse does not say he dies.
event: Komukan shoots and kills, then is himself covered with arrows.

tamil: பனிவரை முளைத்த கோலப் பருப்புடைப் பவழம் போலக்
குனிமருப் புதிரந் தோய்ந்த குஞ்சரங் கொள்ள வுந்திக்
கனிபடு கிளவி யார்தங் கதிர்முலை பொருது சேந்த
துனிவரை மார்பன் சீறிச் சுடுசரஞ் சிதறி னானே.
reading: Like a beautiful coral branch growing on a snow mountain, the elephant whose curved tusks are dipped in blood is driven in to seize him, and the man whose chest is flushed from pressing women's bright breasts rages and scatters burning arrows.
nuance: The two images of red (coral, the flushed chest) join love and slaughter in one figure; who is described is not named, and he is read as Padumukan.
event: A warrior on an elephant presses the attack, shooting burning arrows.

tamil: பன்னலம் பஞ்சிக் குன்றம் படரெரி முகந்த தொப்பத்
தன்னிரு கையி னாலுந் தடக்கைமால் யானை யாலு
மின்னுயிர் பருகிச் சேனை யெடுத்துக்கொண் டிரிய வோட்டிக்
கொன்முரண் டோன்ற வெம்பிக் கொலைக்களிற் றுழவ னார்த்தான்.
reading: Like fire spreading over a hill of cotton, with both his hands and with his great-trunked elephant he drinks the sweet lives of the army, routs and drives it, and the elephant-rider, his fierce strength showing, roars.
event: Padumukan routs the enemy army and roars in triumph.

tamil: தருக்கொடு குமர னார்ப்பத் தன்சிலை வளைய வாங்கி
யொருக்கவன் கையும் வாயு முளங்கிழித் துடுவந் தோன்றச்
சுருக்குக்கொண் டிட்ட வண்ணந் தோன்றலெய் திடுத லோடு
மருப்பிறக் களிறு குத்தி வயிரந்தான் கழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: As a prince roars in pride, the lord bends his bow and with one arrow tears through his hand, his mouth and his heart so that the feathered end shows; and as the lord shoots, the elephant, its tusk breaking, gores and its strength is spent.
nuance: உடு is read as the arrow's feathered butt and வயிரம் as the elephant's hardness or fury; both are doubtful, and the elephant's part in lines 3 to 4 is unclear.
event: Padumukan kills a boasting prince with a single arrow, and the prince's elephant is broken.

tamil: நித்தில மணிவண் டென்னு நெடுமதக் களிறு பாய
முத்துடை மருப்பு வல்லே யுடைந்துமுத் தொழுகு குன்றின்
மத்தக யானை வீழ்ந்து வயிரங்கொண் டொழிந்த தாங்குப்
reading: When the long-rutting elephant called Nittilamanivandu charges, its pearl-bearing tusks break at once, as an elephant falls on a hill that flows with pearls and its fury ends there; the last line, with ear ornaments flashing, is broken.
nuance: Line 4 is a foot short and its first words repeat the opening of 2277 (பத்திரக் கடிப்பு மின்ன), so the end of the verse may be lost.
event: The elephant Nittilamanivandu charges and breaks its tusks.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2277-2301 (8/9)
theme: In the battle for the earth (மண்மகள் இலம்பகம்), champions of both armies fight: men hailing Govindan, Nandan and Civakan stand alone, pluck spears from their bodies and laugh, and die so their lord may take the land; Civakan then mounts his chariot and his arrows send a river of blood over the kings' regalia, and Arichandan tries to stop the rout by shaming the fleeing.
source_issues: 2277, 2278, 2288, 2290, 2292, 2294, 2296, 2297 and 2299 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.
2285 line 1 alludes to a sage who received spear-eyed women in a sacrifice; the story is not told and the line's link to the rest of the verse is unclear.
2291 line 4 கானெறி is hard to divide (கான் நெறி or கால் நெறி).
2293 line 2 (வான் புண்ணுள் நீட்டி) and 2299 line 2 (நீடெரி நிலைக்கண்ணாடி) are obscure as divided.
2295 line 4 மான்றோ is read as மான்தேர்.

cast.role: the hero, fighting to recover his father's kingdom
the king who leads Civakan's war against Kattiyangaran, hailed in the war cries
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, Civakan's enemy
Civakan's younger brother (taken to be the நந்தன் of 2288)
a young warrior of Govindan's side who stands alone (2277)
a champion in the service of the Pallava king
an archer in the battle
a young warrior who swears loyalty to Kattiyangaran and is shot down (2282 to 2287)
an archer of Govindan's side who shoots the boasting warrior
a warrior hailing Nandan who holds the kings back and takes their spears
a champion of the enemy army who throws only at elephants
the kings of Kattiyangaran's side
a warrior of Civakan's side who dies standing
Civakan's warriors
a captain who rallies the fleeing warriors
the routed young warriors Arichandan addresses

tamil: பத்திரக் கடிப்பு மின்னப் பங்கியை வம்பிற் கட்டிக்
கொத்தலர்த் தும்பை சூடிக் கோவிந்தன் வாழ்க வென்னாக்
கைத்தலத் தெஃக மேந்திக் காளைபோய் வேறு நின்றான்
மத்தக யானை மன்னர் வயிறெரி தவழ்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: A young warrior binds his hair, wears thumbai, cries long life to Govindan, takes his spear and stands apart, and the kings of the rutting elephants burn inwardly.
nuance: The thumbai (line 2) is the battle flower; standing apart (வேறு நின்றான்) marks the champion who seeks single combat, and the enemy's burning belly (line 4) is the first effect of the challenge, before any blow.
event: A warrior of Govindan's side, hailing his king, takes his stand alone before the enemy kings.

tamil: மேகலைப் பரவை யல்குல் வெள்வளை மகளிர் செஞ்சாந்
தாகத்தைக் கவர்ந்து கொண்ட வணிமுலைத் தடத்து வைகிப்
பாகத்தைப் படாத நெஞ்சிற் பல்லவ தேய மன்னன்
சேவகன் சிங்க நாதன் செருக்களங் குறுகி னானே.
reading: Simhanadan, warrior of the Pallava king, who had lain on the breasts of women whose paste he had taken, approaches the battlefield with a heart that knows no half-measures.
nuance: The verse joins the lover and the fighter in one man: the sandal paste his chest took from women's breasts is the same chest that now goes to war, a pairing the whole run repeats. பாகத்தைப் படாத நெஞ்சு (line 3) may mean a heart that does not share itself (undivided) or one that does not yield; read as undivided resolve.
event: Simhanadan, a champion of the Pallava king, comes up to the field.

tamil: புனைகதிர் மருப்புத் தாடி மோதிரஞ் செறித்துப் பொன்செய்
கனைகதிர் வாளை யேந்திக் கால்கழ லணிந்து நம்மை
யினையன பட்ட ஞான்றா லிறைவர்க ணினைப்ப தென்றே
முனையழன் முளிபுற் கான மேய்ந்தென நீந்தி னானே.
reading: A warrior rings his tusk-like beard, takes his gold-bright sword and binds on his anklets, saying that it is for a day like this that lords keep men like him, and swims through the enemy like fire through a dry grass forest.
nuance: The speech (lines 2 to 3, closed by என்றே) is the warrior's own account of the bond between lord and fighter: the king's care is a debt that falls due in battle. Who speaks is not named; read as Simhanadan of the verse before.
event: The champion arms himself and drives through the enemy ranks like wildfire.

tamil: தாரணி பரவை மார்பிற் குங்கும மெழுதித் தாழ்ந்த
வாரமும் பூணு மின்ன வருவிலைப் பட்டி னங்க
ளோபடக் கிடந்த பொன்ஞா ணிருள்கெட விழிப்ப வெய்ய
பூரண சேனன் வண்கைப் பொருசிலை யேந்தி னானே.
reading: Poornasenan, sandal painted on his broad garlanded chest and his gold cords and silks flashing until the dark is dispelled, takes up his fighting bow.
nuance: Which army Poornasenan fights for is not said in the verse.
event: Poornasenan takes up his bow for the fight.

tamil: ஊனமர் குறடு போல விரும்புண்டு மிகுத்த மார்பிற்
றேனமர் மாலை தாழச் சிலைகுலாய்க் குனிந்த தாங்கண்
மானமர் நோக்கி னாரு மைந்தருங் குழீஇய போருட்
கானமர் காம னெய்த கணையெனச் சிதறி னானே.
reading: With his iron-hard chest like a meat-block, garland swaying and bow bent, he scatters arrows through the battle where doe-eyed women and young men had gathered, like the arrows Kama shoots.
nuance: The simile turns war arrows into love's arrows: those hit fall as lovers fall to Kama, an inversion the poet keeps returning to in this run. The women in the battle (line 3) may be those watching, or the image may carry over from the festival crowds Kama shoots at.
event: Poornasenan shoots arrows thick through the battle.

tamil: வண்டலை மாலை தாழ மதுவுண்டு களித்து வண்கைப்
புண்டலை வேலை யேந்திப் போர்க்களங் குறுகி வாழ்த்திக்
கண்படு காறு மெந்தை கட்டியங் கார னென்றே
யுண்டொலை யார்க வேலென் றுறுவலி தாக்கி னானே.
reading: A warrior, drunk on toddy and garlanded, takes his wound-headed spear and comes to the field, swearing that until his eyes close his lord is Kattiyangaran, and bids his spear eat its fill as he charges.
nuance: The usual warrior's oath of faith to the lord is sworn here to the usurper who killed Civakan's father; the epic gives the enemy's men the same loyalty and courage as its hero's, without comment.
event: A fighter of Kattiyangaran's side vows lifelong loyalty to the usurper and attacks.

tamil: கூற்றென வேழம் வீழாக் கொடிநெடுந் தோக ணூறா
வேற்றவர் தம்மைச் சீறா வேந்திர நூழில் செய்யா
வாற்றலங் குமரன் செல்வா னலைகடற் றிரையி னெற்றி
யேற்றுமீ னிரியப் பாய்ந்த வெறிசுறா வேறு போன்றான்.
reading: The strong young man goes on without felling elephants like Death, cutting down their banners or raging at lesser foes, like a fierce shark leaping through the sea so that the fish flee.
nuance: His refusal to strike what lies in his path is a point of pride: valour is measured by the foe chosen. That this குமரன் is the drinker of 2282 is a reading from the run; the verse does not name his side.
event: The young warrior passes over lesser foes looking for one worthy of him.

tamil: மாலைக்க ணாம்பல் போல மகளிர்தங் குழாத்திற் பட்டார்
கோலவாட் போருட் பட்டாற் குறுமுயற் கூடு கண்டு
சாலத்தாம் பனிக்கும் பொய்கைத் தாமரை நீர ராயின்
ஞாலத்தா ராண்மை யென்னா மெனநகா வருகின் றானே.
reading: He comes on laughing and saying: if men who are captured among women's crowds like lilies opening at evening tremble in sword-battle like pond lotuses at the moon, what becomes of the manliness of the world?
nuance: குறுமுயல் கூடு (line 2), the small hare's house, is the moon, at whose sight the lotus closes; the lily that opens at evening and the lotus that shuts at moonrise set the lover's eagerness against the coward's shrinking.
event: The warrior advances laughing and taunting the fearful.

tamil: முடிச்சடை முனிவ னன்று வேள்வியிற் கொண்ட வேற்கண்
மடத்தகை மகளிர் கோல வருமுலை யுழக்கச் சேந்து
கொடிப்பல வணிந்த மார்பிற் கோவிந்தன் வாழ்க வென்று
நடத்துவா னவனை நோக்கி நகாச்சிலை பாரித் தானே.
reading: Seeing a warrior striding with a chest flushed from women's breasts, who cries long life to Govindan, the other draws his bow without a smile.
nuance: Line 1 (the matted-haired sage who once received in sacrifice the spear-eyed women) is an allusion whose story the verse does not tell. Who looks at whom and who draws the bow turns on நடத்துவான் அவனை நோக்கி (line 4); read as Govindan's man drawing on the laughing one, whose laughter is answered by நகா, the unsmiling bow.
event: A fighter of Govindan's side faces the laughing warrior and bends his bow.

tamil: போர்த்தநெய்த் தோர னாகிப் புலாற்பருந் தார்ப்பச் செல்வான்
சீர்த்தகை யவனைக் கண்டென் சினவுவே லின்னு மார்ந்தின்
றூர்த்துயி ருன்னை யுண்ணக் குறைவயி றாரு மென்றாங்
கார்த்தவாய் நிறைய வெய்தா னம்புபெய் தூணி யொத்தான்.
reading: Covered in blood, with kites screaming over him, the young warrior tells his worthy foe that his angry spear is still unfed and will fill its belly today on his life; the other shoots arrows into his shouting mouth until he looks like a quiver.
nuance: The boast about the spear's hunger is cut off by arrows filling the mouth that makes it: the verse punishes the speech in the organ of speech. Who is shot is read from context.
event: The boasting warrior is shot full of arrows as he shouts his threat.

tamil: மொய்ப்படு சரங்கண் மூழ்க முனையெயிற் றாளி போல
வப்பணைக் கிடந்த மைந்த னருமணித் திருவில் வீசுஞ்
செப்பிள முலையி னார்கண் சென்றுலாய்ப் பிறழச் சிந்திக்
கைப்பட வெடுத்திட் டாடும் பொலங்கழற் காயு மொத்தான்.
reading: Pierced by thronging arrows, the warrior lies on that bed like a sharp-toothed yali, and is like the gold ball that women with breasts like caskets toss and catch in play.
nuance: Two similes in one verse: the beast of the first keeps his fierceness in death, and the women's ball of the second makes the arrow-studded body a plaything, the run's habit of seeing war through the women's world.
event: The fallen warrior lies on a bed of arrows.

tamil: புனைகதிர்ப் பொன்செய் நாணிற் குஞ்சியைக் கட்டி நெய்த்தோர்
நனைகதி ரெஃக மேந்தி நந்தன்வாழ் கென்ன நின்ற
வினையொளிர் காளை வேலைக் கடக்கலார் வேந்தர் நின்றார்
கனைகடல் வேலை யெல்லை கடக்கலா வண்ண நின்றார்.
reading: A youth binds his hair with a gold cord, raises his blood-wet spear and stands crying long life to Nandan, and the kings cannot pass his spear, standing as the roaring sea stands at its shore.
nuance: Nandan is taken as Nandattan, Civakan's brother, fighting on his side; the verse gives only the name. The play on வேலை, spear and shore (lines 3 to 4), makes one man's spear a coast the sea of kings cannot cross.
event: A warrior hailing Nandan holds the enemy kings at bay by himself.

tamil: நின்றவப் படையு ளானே யொருமக னீலக் குஞ்சி
மன்றல மாலை நெற்றி மழகளி றன்றி வீழான்
வென்றியங் கொளிறும் வெள்வேன் மின்னென வெகுண்டு விட்டான்
சென்றவேல் விருந்து செங்கண் மறவனக் கெதிர்கொண் டானே.
reading: One man of that standing army, blue-haired and garlanded, who would not throw at anything but a young elephant, angrily hurls his shining spear like lightning, and the red-eyed warrior receives the spear as a guest.
nuance: Two courtesies of war in one verse: the thrower honours the youth by spending on him a spear kept for elephants, and the youth honours the spear by welcoming it as a guest (விருந்து எதிர்கொண்டான்), the host's word for meeting a visitor.
event: An enemy champion throws his spear at the warrior, who meets it.

tamil: மான்வயி றார்ந்து நோக்கும் வெருவுறு மருளி னோக்கிற்
றேன்வயி றார்ந்த கோதைத் தீஞ்சொலார் கண்கள் போலு
மூன்வயி றார்ந்த வெள்வே லொய்யெனப் பறித்து நக்கான்
கான்வயி றார்ந்து தேக்கிக் களிவண்டு கனைக்குந் தாரான்.
reading: The warrior, whose garland hums with drunken bees, plucks out in one pull the white spear that had fed on his flesh, like the frightened, darting eyes of sweet-voiced women, and laughs.
nuance: Line 3 (ஊன்வயிறு ஆர்ந்த வெள்வேல் ஒய்யெனப் பறித்து நக்கான்) is the deed of Kural 774 in other words; the spear is likened to women's eyes, which also wound.
event: The wounded warrior pulls the spear from his body and laughs.

tamil: விட்டழல் சிந்தி வெள்வேல் விசும்பின்வீழ் மின்னி னொய்தாக்
கட்டழ னெடுங்கண் யாது மிமைத்திலன் மகளி ரோச்சு
மட்டவிழ் மாலை போல மகிழ்ந்துபூண் மார்பத் தேற்றுக்
கட்டழ லெஃகஞ் செல்லக் கானெறி யாயி னானே.
reading: As the white spear flies like lightning falling from the sky, he does not blink his fierce long eyes at all, but receives it gladly on his ornamented chest like a garland that women throw, and as the fiery spear passes through, he becomes a path for it.
nuance: இமைத்திலன் (line 2) is the unblinking eye of Kural 775. கானெறி ஆயினான் (line 4) is hard: perhaps he became a road for the spear (கால்நெறி), perhaps he went the forest way, that is, died; it is taken as his fall. Whether this spear is the one of 2289 or a second is unclear.
event: Another spear comes; the warrior takes it on his chest without blinking and falls.

tamil: கவிமதங் கடந்து காமர் வனப்புவீற் றிருந்த கண்ணார்
குவிமுலை நெற்றித் தீந்தேன் கொப்புளித் திட்ட பைந்தார்ச்
செவிமதக் கடலங் கேள்விச் சீவகன் கழல்கள் வாழ்த்திச்
சவிமதுத் தாம மார்பிற் சலநிதி தாக்கி னானே.
reading: Salanidhi, learned and broad of hearing as a sea, his garland drenched with honey from the breasts of beautiful women, praises Civakan's feet and attacks.
nuance: Line 1 (கவிமதம் கடந்து) may praise beauty past what poets can describe, belonging to the women, or Salanidhi's mastery beyond poets; read as the women's.
event: Salanidhi, a man of Civakan's side, praises his lord and charges.

tamil: குஞ்சரங் குனிய நூறித் தடாயின குருதி வாடன்
வெஞ்சம நோக்கி நின்று மிறைக்கொளி திருத்து வாற்கண்
டஞ்சிமற் றரசர் யானைக் குழாத்தொடு மிரிந்திட் டாரே.
reading: His sword bent from crushing elephants and red with blood, he pulls out the spear that had entered his heart, holds it over the great wound and stands watching the fierce battle while he straightens his sword in a bend, and the kings, afraid, flee with their elephant herds.
nuance: மிறைக்கொளீஇ திருத்துவான் (line 3), setting the bent blade in a lever to straighten it, is the image of Purananuru 284, where a warrior straightens his twisted sword on the tusk of the elephant he killed. What he does with the pulled spear (வான் புண்ணுள் நீட்டி, line 2) is unclear.
event: Salanidhi, wounded, pulls out the spear and straightens his bent sword, and the enemy kings flee.

tamil: தோட்டுவண் டொலியன் மாலைத் துடியிடை மகளி ராய்ந்த
மோட்டுவெண் முத்த மின்னு முகிழ்முலை யுழுது சாந்தம்
கோட்டுமண் கொண்ட மார்பங் கோதைவாள் குளித்து மூழ்கிக்
கோட்டுமண் கொள்ள நின்றான் குருசின்மண் கொள்ள நின்றான்.
reading: His chest, which had ploughed the bud-like breasts of slender women wearing pearls and taken their paste, now takes the plunge of swords, and he stands to take the tusk's earth, stands so that his lord may take the earth.
nuance: The last line turns on மண் கொள்ள twice: the warrior's chest takes the earth dug up by tusks (the warrior's marking, or the elephant's blow), and his lord takes the earth, the kingdom, the மண்மகள் of the ilampakam's name. The warrior's body is spent for the lord's land.
event: Salanidhi stands under the swords so that his lord may win the land.

tamil: எரிமணிக் குப்பை போல விருளற விளங்கு மேனித்
திருமணிச் செம்பொன் மார்பிற் சீவகன் சிலைகை யேந்தி
யருமணி யரச ராவி யழலம்பிற் கொள்ளை சாற்றி
விரிமணி விளங்கு மான்றோ விண்டொழ வேறி னானே.
reading: Civakan, his body bright as a heap of glowing gems that drives away the dark, takes his bow in hand, proclaims that he will plunder the lives of the jewelled kings with his fire-arrows, and mounts his jewelled chariot as the gods worship.
nuance: Until now the run has shown only his men dying for him; here the lord himself enters. மான்றோ (line 4) is read as மான்தேர், the horse-drawn chariot.
event: Civakan takes his bow and mounts his chariot to enter the battle.

tamil: கருவளி முழக்குங் காருங் கனைகட லொலியுங் கூடி
யருவலிச் சிங்க வார்ப்பு மாங்குடன் கூடிற் றென்னச்
செருவிளை கழனி மள்ள ரார்ப்போடு சிவணிச் செம்பொற்
புரிவளை முரச மார்ப்பப் போர்த்தொழி றொடங்கி னானே.
reading: As if the roar of the black wind, the thundercloud, the roaring sea and the lion had all joined, the shouts of the field-reaping warriors and the twisted conch and drum sound together, and he begins the work of war.
nuance: செருவிளை கழனி மள்ளர் (line 3) makes the battlefield a crop field and the warriors its reapers.
event: Civakan opens battle to the noise of his warriors, conches and drums.

tamil: அரசர்த முடியும் பூணு மாரமும் வரன்றி யார்க்கு
முரசமுங் குடையுந் தாரும் பிச்சமுஞ் சுமந்து மாவும்
விரைபரித் தேரு மீர்த்து வேழங்கொண் டொழுகி வெள்ளக்
குரைபுனற் குருதி செல்லக் குமரன்விற் குனிந்த தன்றே.
reading: As the prince's bow bends, a roaring flood of blood flows, sweeping kings' crowns, jewels and pearl strings, carrying drums, parasols, garlands and peacock-plume fans, dragging horses and swift chariots and bearing off elephants.
nuance: The river carries off exactly the signs of royalty (crown, drum, parasol), so the flood is the end of the kings' rule as well as of their men.
event: Civakan's archery fills the field with a river of blood that carries away the enemy kings' regalia.

tamil: கேழ்கிள ரெரிகட் பேழ்வாய்க் கிளர்பெரும் பாம்பி னோடுஞ்
சூழ்கதிர்க் குழவித் திங்க டுறுவரை வீழ்வ தேபோற்
றாழிருந் தடக்கை யோடுந் தடமருப் பிரண்டு மற்று
வீழ்தரப் பரந்த வப்பு நிழலிற்போர் மயங்கி னாரே.
reading: Great trunks and tusks fall together, as if a fiery-eyed gaping serpent and the young crescent moon fell together from a mountain, and in the shade of the spreading arrows the fighters are bewildered.
nuance: Trunk as serpent and curved tusk as crescent: the image is of an eclipse falling from a hill, the arrows thick enough to cast shade.
event: Elephants' trunks and tusks are cut down and the fighters lose their way under the arrows.

tamil: ஆடவ ராண்மை தோற்று மணிகிளர் பவழத் திண்கை
நீடெரி நிலைக்கண் ணாடிப் போர்க்களத் துடைந்த மைந்தர்
காடெரி கவரக் கலலென் கவரிமா விரிந்த வண்ண
மோடக்கண் டுருவப் பைந்தா ரரிச்சந்த னுரைக்கின் றானே.
reading: Seeing the routed young men of the battle, whose coral-strong hands had shamed other men's manliness, flee like yaks scattering from a forest fire, Arichandan of the garland speaks.
nuance: Arichandan's side is not named; since those fleeing are the ones Civakan has just broken, he is read as a captain of the opposing army trying to stop a rout. Line 2 (நீடெரி நிலைக்கண்ணாடி) is obscure.
event: Arichandan sees the broken warriors fleeing and addresses them.

tamil: மஞ்சிவர் மின்ன னார்தம் வாலரிச் சிலம்பு சூழ்ந்து
பஞ்சிகொண் டெழுதப் பட்ட சீறடிப் பாய்த லுண்ட
குஞ்சியங் குமரர் தங்கண் மறம்பிறர் கவர்ந்து கொள்ள
வஞ்சியிட் டோடிப் போகி னாண்மையார் கண்ண தம்மா.
reading: Arichandan says: if young men whose tufted heads have been kicked by the small feet of lightning-like women, painted with lac and ringed with anklets, let others take their valour and run in fear, where then is manliness?
nuance: A lover kicked by his beloved in a quarrel is a stock image of the man who submits to a woman; Arichandan's taunt is that men who bear that should not bear defeat, the same argument the laughing warrior made in 2284.
event: Arichandan shames the fleeing warriors.

tamil: உழையின முச்சிக் கோடு கலங்குத லுற்ற போதே
விழைவற விதிர்த்து வீசி விட்டெறிந் திடுவ தொப்பக்
கழலவ ருள்ள மஞ்சிக் கலங்குமே லதனை வல்லே
மழைமினி னீக்கி யிட்டு வன்கண்ண ராப வன்றே.
reading: He goes on: as deer, when the horns on their heads trouble them, shake and throw them off, so the brave, when their hearts waver in fear, cast it off at once like lightning and become fierce-eyed again.
nuance: The speech grants what the taunt denied: fear touches the brave too, and courage is the speed with which it is thrown off. The deer simile in lines 1 to 2 is hard to fix (shedding antlers, or tossing the head); that it continues Arichandan's speech is a reading.

title: மண்மகள் இலம்பகம் 2302-2326 (9/9)
theme: The end of the war of மண்மகள் இலம்பகம்: Ariccandan's rally fails, Civakan kills the usurper's sons and then Kattiyangaran, who meets his death speaking of karma and fate and vowing on his honour, and the Earth goddess passes to Civakan.
source_issues: Nine stanzas (2308, 2309, 2311, 2316, 2318, 2323, 2324, 2325, 2326) were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build.
2304 line 2 சோந்து and 2306 line 1 சோவபோல் appear to have lost an r (சோர்ந்து, சோர்வபோல்); 2306 and 2309 line 4 தோமிசை likewise for தேர்மிசை.
2309 line 4 ends இஞ்சினார், not a word as printed (perhaps துஞ்சினார்); line 3 நெஞ்சம looks truncated.
2313 line 2 செறித்திட்டு டஞ்சி has a doubled syllable.
2315 line 4 சந்து மாலியும் is obscure as divided.
2322 line 3 வெகுவத்துவர் is obscure as divided.
2323 line 4 விட்டமு தவன்கண் ஆர்வம் can be divided more than one way, changing whether the Earth puts away grief or gives her love.
2325 line 2 சூழாத்தின் for குழாத்தின் (cf. line 1).

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called குமரன், காளை, சீவக சாமி here
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, killed by Civakan in this run
a warrior on Kattiyangaran's side who rallies the routed men (named at 2299)
the army Kattiyangaran leads against Civakan
the sons of the king who ride out against Civakan and die
the warriors on Civakan's side
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother
the Earth goddess (பூமி தேவி), figured as the bride Civakan wins

tamil: தற்புறந் தந்து வைத்த தலைமகற் குதவி வீந்தாற்
கற்பக மாலை சூட்டிக் கடியர மகளிர்த் தோய்வர்
பொற்றசொன் மாலை சூட்டிப் புலவர்கள் புகழக் கன்மே
னிற்பர்தம் வீரந் தோன்ற நெடும்புகழ் பரப்பி யென்றான்.
reading: Ariccandan ends his rallying speech: men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them are garlanded with karpaka flowers and embrace the women of heaven, are crowned with poets' garlands of praise, and stand on the hero-stone with their valour shown and their fame spread wide.
nuance: Three rewards are stacked, one in each world: heaven (கற்பக மாலை, அரமகளிர்), the poets' word, and the stone on earth. The speaker is named in 2299 (அரிச்சந்தன்); this verse names him only by என்றான், and the next verse shows the men he rallied going down before Civakan's arrows.
event: Ariccandan finishes urging the routed men back to the fight.

tamil: பச்சிரும் பெஃகிட் டாங்குப் படையைக்கூர்ப் பிடுத லோடுங்
கச்சையுங் கழலும் வீக்கிக் காஞ்சனத் தளிவம் வாய்க்கிட்
டச்சுற முழங்கி யாரா வண்ணலங் குமரன் கையு
ணச்செயிற் றம்பு தின்ன நாளிரை யாக லுற்றார்.
reading: The men sharpen their weapons as one thrusts a spear into green bamboo, bind on belts and anklets, put gold into their mouths, roar to strike fear, and become the day's food for the arrows in the young prince's hand.
nuance: Putting gold in the mouth (காஞ்சனத் தளிவம் வாய்க்கிட்டு) is the warrior's preparation for death; the speech of 2302 is answered at once by the slaughter.
event: Rallied, the enemy warriors arm and charge, and Civakan's arrows cut them down.

tamil: வடதிசை யெழுந்த மேகம் வலனுராய் மின்னுச் சூடிக்
குடதிசைச் சோந்து மாரி குளிறுபு சொரிவ தேபோற்
படர்கதிர்ப் பைம்பொற் றிண்டோ பாங்குற விமைப்பி னூர்ந்தா
னடர்சிலை யப்பு மாரி தாரைநின் றிட்ட தன்றே.
reading: As a cloud rising in the north sweeps rightward wreathed in lightning and pours thundering rain on the west, Civakan drove his chariot in a flash with gold-armoured shoulders, and the rain of arrows from his bow stood like a falling stream.
event: Civakan drives into the enemy and pours arrows on them.

tamil: அற்றுவீழ் தலைகள் யானை யுடலின்மே லழுந்தி நின்ற
பொற்றதிண் சரத்திற் கோத்த பொருசரந் தாள்க ளாகத்
தெற்றிமேற் பூத்த செந்தா மரைமலர் போன்ற செங்கண்
மற்றத்தா துரிஞ்சி யுண்ணும் வண்டின் மொத்த வன்றே.
reading: Severed heads lodged on the elephants' bodies, held up on the arrows driven through them as on stalks, looked like red lotuses on a terrace, and their red eyes like bees crowded to sip the pollen.
nuance: A battlefield-as-garden figure; it prepares the fuller lotus-pond allegory of 2311.

tamil: திங்க ளோடுடன் குன்றெலாந் துளங்கி மாநிலஞ் சோவபோற்
சங்க மத்தகத் தலமரத் தரணி மேற்களி றழியவும்
பொங்கு மாநிரை புரளவும் பொலங்கொ டோபல முறியவுஞ்
சிங்கம் போற்றொழித் தார்த்தவன் சிறுவர் தோமிசைத் தோன்றினார்.
reading: As if the moon and all the hills shook and the great earth gave way, with conches wailing, elephants falling, horses rolling and gold banners snapping, the sons of the king appeared on their chariots roaring like lions.
nuance: அவன் சிறுவர் says only 'his sons'; that they are Kattiyangaran's is read from 2311, where the king's children are the stamens round the king.
event: The usurper's sons ride out in their chariots against Civakan.

tamil: சந்த னஞ்சொரி தண்கதிர்த் திங்க ளந்தொகை தாம்பல
குங்கு மக்கதிர்க் குழவியஞ் செல்வ னோடுடன் பொருவபோன்
மங்குன் மின்னென வள்ளறேர் மைந்தர் தேரொடு மயங்கலின்
வெங்கண் வில்லுமிழ் வெஞ்சர மிடைந்து வெங்கதிர் மறைந்ததே.
reading: As when the cool moon with its crowd of stars wrestles with the young sun of saffron rays, the sons' chariots tangled with the generous hero's in a flash like lightning in cloud, and the hot arrows from their bows crowded so thick that they hid the sun.
event: The sons close with Civakan's chariot and their arrows darken the sky.

tamil: குருதி வாளொளி யரவினாற் கொள்ளப் பட்டவெண் டிங்கள்போற்
றிருவ நீர்த்திகழ் வலம்புரி வாய்வைத் தாங்கவன் றெழித்தலும்
பொருவில் கீழ்வளி முழக்கினாற் பூமி மேற்சன நடுங்கிற்றே
யரவ வெஞ்சிலை வளைந்ததே யண்ணல் கண்ணழ லுமிழ்ந்ததே.
reading: Like the white moon seized by a serpent, the hero, red with the blade's light, set the right-whorled conch to his mouth and blew; the earth's people trembled as at the roar of the east wind, his serpent-fierce bow bent, and the lord's eyes spat fire.
event: Civakan blows his conch and draws his bow in anger.

tamil: கங்கை மாக்கடற் பாய்வதே போன்று காளைதன் கார்முக
மைந்த ரார்த்தவர் வாயெலா நிறைய வெஞ்சரங் கான்றபி
னெஞ்சம போழ்ந்தழ லம்புண நீங்கி னாருயிர் நீண்முழைச்
சிங்க வேறுகள் கிடந்தபோற் சிறுவர் தோமிசைத் இஞ்சினார்.
reading: As the Ganga rushes into the sea, the young bull's bow poured hot arrows till they filled the mouths of the youths who had roared, and pierced through the chest they lay dead on their chariots like lions in a long cave.
nuance: The last word, printed இஞ்சினார், is read as 'lay dead' only from the simile; the line is likely corrupt.
event: Civakan's arrows kill the usurper's sons on their chariots.

tamil: நிவந்த வெண்குடை வீழவும் வேந்தர் நீள்விசும் பேறவு
முவந்து பேய்க்கண மாடவு மோரி கொள்ளைகொண் டுண்ணவுங்
கவந்த மெங்கணு மாடவுங் களிறு மாவொடு கவிழவுஞ்
சிவந்த சீவக சாமிகண் புருவ மும்முரி முரிந்தவே.
reading: White umbrellas fell, kings rose to the far sky, hosts of ghouls danced, jackals feasted, headless trunks danced everywhere, elephants and horses toppled, and the red-eyed Civakasami's brows curved in wrath.
nuance: Kings 'climbing the sky' (நீள்விசும்பு ஏற) is the battlefield death 2302 promised as heaven, now told of the enemy.
event: The field fills with the dead as Civakan's anger mounts.

tamil: பொய்கை போர்க்களம் புறவிதழ் புலவு வாட்படை புல்லித
ழைய கொல்களி றகவித ழரச ரல்லிதன் மக்களா
மையில் கொட்டையம் மன்னனா மலர்ந்த தாமரை வரிசையாற்
பைய வுண்டபின் கொட்டைமேற் பவித்திரத் தும்பி பறந்ததே.
reading: The battlefield is a lotus pond: the swords are the outer petals, the elephants the inner petals, the kings the stamens, the king's sons the inner ring, and the king himself the seed-pod; and having slowly fed on the flower in order, the holy bee flew up onto the pod.
nuance: The allegory turns the slaughter into a bee's orderly feeding from the outside in, so the order of the battle is also the order of a hierarchy, ending at its centre; the bee is called பவித்திரம், holy.
event: Having destroyed the army and the sons, Civakan turns on the king himself.

tamil: கலைமுத்தங் கொள்ளு மல்குற் கார்மழை மின்ன னார்த
முலைமுத்தங் கொள்ளச் சாந்த மழிந்துதார் முருகு விம்மு
மலைமுத்தங் கொள்ளு மார்பின் மன்னனுங் கண்டு காய்ந்தான்
சிலைமுத்தங் கொள்ளுந் திண்டோட் செம்மலுந் தீயிற் சேந்தான்.
reading: The king, whose mountainous chest is kissed by the pearls of women's breasts, saw it and burned with rage, and the noble one, whose strong shoulders the bow kisses, reddened like fire.
nuance: The fourfold முத்தம் pun (pearl and kiss) sets the lover's chest of the king against the archer's shoulders of the hero.
event: Kattiyangaran and Civakan face each other in fury.

tamil: தன்மதந் திவண்ட வண்டு தங்கிய காட்டுள் வேழம்
பின்மதஞ் செறித்திட்டு டஞ்சிப் பிடிமறந் திரிந்து போகும்
வென்மதக் களிற்று வெய்ய வசனிவே கத்தின் மேலான்
மின்னுமிழ் மாலை வேந்தன் வீரற்கு விளம்பி னானே.
reading: Seated on the fierce elephant Asanivegam, at whose musk a wild tusker swallows its own must, fears and runs leaving its mate, the king of the flashing garland spoke to the hero.
event: Kattiyangaran, mounted on his war elephant, addresses Civakan.

tamil: நல்வினை யுடைய நீரார் நஞ்சுணி னமுத மாகு
மில்லையே லமுது நஞ்சா மின்னதால் வினையி னாக்கங்
கொல்வல்யா னிவனை யென்று மிவன்கொல்லு மென்னை யென்று
மல்லன நினைத்தல் செல்லா ரறிவினாற் பெரிய நீரார்.
reading: Kattiyangaran says that for those with good deeds poison drunk becomes nectar, and for those without, nectar becomes poison, such is the working of deeds; so the truly wise never think 'I can kill him' or 'he will kill me'.
nuance: The usurper, about to die, gives the whole outcome to deeds and none to his own seizure of the throne. The story has given another cause: Dharmadattan warned at 245 that Fortune would turn from him if he seized the king. Here karma and the ruler's fault are both on the page, in different mouths.

tamil: அகப்படு பொறியி னாரை யாக்குவா ரியாவ ரம்மா
மிகப்படு பொறியி னாரை வெறியராச் செய்ய லாமோ
பகைக்கதிர்ப் பருதி சந்து மாலியும் பயத்த லுண்டே.
reading: He goes on: who can ruin those whose fortune is in their grasp, and can those of great fortune be made empty? the cool-rayed moon may scorch till men tremble, and the hostile sun may yield coolness.
nuance: பொறி is fortune as allotted; the reversed moon and sun of lines 3-4 can be read as what fortune can do, or as his own fall. The end of line 4 (சந்து மாலியும்) is unclear as divided.

tamil: புரிமுத்த மாலைப் பொற்கோல் விளக்கினுட் பெய்த நெய்யுந்
திரியுஞ்சென் றற்ற போழ்தே திருச்சுடர் தேம்பி னல்லா
லெரிமொய்த்துப் பெருக லுண்டோ விருவினை சென்று தேய்ந்தாற்
பரிவுற்றுக் கெடாமற் செல்வம் பற்றியா ரதனை வைப்பார்.
reading: A lamp of pearl-strung gold stand does not flare up after its ghee and its wick are spent; its flame only dwindles; so when the two kinds of deed have worn away, who can keep wealth from perishing, however anxiously he guards it?
nuance: இருவினை, both good and bad deeds, makes the fuel of wealth all of one's karma, not only merit; the usurper reads his own lost throne as a lamp that has burnt out rather than one taken from its owner.

tamil: நல்லொளிப் பவளச் செவ்வாய் நன்மணி யெயிறு கோலி
வில்லிட நக்கு வீர னஞ்சினா யென்ன வேந்தன்
வெல்வது விதியி னாகும் வேல்வரி னிமைப்பே னாயிற்
சொல்லிநீ நகவும் பெற்றாய் தோன்றன்மற் றென்னை யென்றான்.
reading: The hero, baring his jewel-like teeth, laughed so they flashed and said 'you are afraid'; the king answered that victory comes by fate, but if he blinked when a spear came, then the hero might say so and laugh, and bade him come at him.
nuance: Civakan's mockery reads the fate speech of 2314 to 2316 as cowardice; the king separates the two, granting the outcome to fate while keeping courage, the unblinking eye, as his own.
event: Civakan mocks Kattiyangaran's talk of fate as fear, and Kattiyangaran challenges him.

tamil: பஞ்சிமெல் லடியி னார்தம் பாடகந் திருத்திச் சேந்து
நெஞ்சுநொந் தழுத கண்ணீர் துடைத்தலி னிறைந்த கோல
வஞ்சனக் கலுழி யஞ்சே றாடிய கடக வண்கை
வெஞ்சிலை கொண்டு வெய்ய வுருமென முழங்கிச் சொன்னான்.
reading: With the bangled generous hand that had set right the anklets of soft-footed women, wiped the tears they wept when hurt and so been smeared with their collyrium, he seized the cruel bow and spoke roaring like thunder.
nuance: The hand is a lover's before it is a warrior's; the next verse's elephant shows it is the king's, and the image echoes 2312's lover's chest.
event: Kattiyangaran takes up his bow and speaks.

reading: He vows that if he loses in valour he may become a base man of a heart that fears his wife and kills the face of the guest, and fuming he split through the press of bow and sword, glared, drove his killing elephant forward and fitted one last arrow.
nuance: The self-curse names faults of the house, not the field: the worst he can imagine becoming is a henpecked man who shames a guest. The vow is in the first person (தோற்பின்), while the description around it is the narrator's.
event: Kattiyangaran vows, charges on his elephant and sets an arrow to his bow.

reading: Before he could draw and loose the arrow he had fitted, the hero of the sharp white spear and diamond ornaments shot with a bright crescent-headed arrow and cut the arrow, the bow and its string so that they fell.
event: Civakan cuts Kattiyangaran's arrow, bow and bowstring with one crescent arrow.

reading: Blazing that his arrow and bow were cut, he gripped his gold sword in fury and leapt at the hero's chariot crying 'let the gold-crowned one fall', like a god descending from the golden world.
event: Disarmed, Kattiyangaran leaps sword in hand onto Civakan's chariot.

reading: The red one's golden arrows went into the chest that had been a battlefield for the breasts of women, and with them his life went; eyes burning, lips bitten, he fell like the moon falling from the dark sky.
nuance: The lover's chest of 2312 and 2318 becomes the target; the moon-fall answers 2308 and 2324, where Civakan is the moon in the serpent's mouth and then the sun freed from it.
event: Civakan's arrows pierce Kattiyangaran's chest and he falls dead.

tamil: கட்டியங் கார னென்னுங் கலியர சழிந்த தாங்குப்
பட்டவிப் பகைமை நீங்கிப் படைத்தொழி லொழிக வென்னாக்
கொட்டினர் முரச மள்ள ரார்த்தனர் குருதிக் கண்ணீர்
விட்டமு தவன்க ணார்வ மண்மக ணீக்கி னாளே.
reading: As if the Kali-rule called Kattiyangaran had perished, the warriors beat the drums proclaiming that the enmity was over and the work of arms should cease, and roared; and the Earth goddess, shedding tears of blood, gave her longing to him.
nuance: கலியரசு names the usurper's reign as the age of Kali, a rule against order rather than a single wrong. Line 4 (விட்டமு தவன்கண் ஆர்வம் மண்மகள் நீக்கினாள்) can be divided so that the Earth puts away her grief or turns her love to Civakan; the ilampakam's name rests on it.
event: With Kattiyangaran dead, Civakan's warriors proclaim the war's end.

tamil: ஒல்லைநீ ருலக மஞ்ச வொளியுமிழ் பருதி தன்னைக்
கல்லெனக் கடலி னெற்றிக் கவுட்படுத் திட்டு நாகம்
பல்பகல் கழிந்த பின்றைப் பன்மணி நாகந் தன்னை
வல்லைவாய் போழ்ந்து போந்தொர் மழகதிர் நின்ற தொத்தான்.
reading: Civakan was like the young sun that a serpent had seized in the forehead of the sea and held in its cheek while the world trembled, standing forth after many days when it had split open the jewelled serpent's mouth.
nuance: The 'many days' (பல்பகல்) under the serpent are the years of the usurpation since his father's death; the victory is figured as release from an eclipse, not a conquest.

tamil: கோட்டுமீன் குழாத்தின் மள்ள ரீண்டினர் மன்னர் சூழ்ந்தார்
மோட்டுமீன் சூழாத்தி னெங்குந் தீவிகை மொய்த்த முத்த
மாட்டுநீர்க் கடலி னார்த்த தணிநகர் வென்றி மாலை
கேட்டுநீர் நிறைந்து கேடில் விசயைகண் குளிர்ந்த வன்றே.
reading: The warriors gathered like the hosts of stars round the moon, kings surrounded him, the city roared like the sea, its lamps thronged like stars; and hearing the victory garland proclaimed, the faultless Vijayai's eyes filled with tears and grew cool.
nuance: Vijayai's cooled eyes close the grief that began when she left the city on the peacock machine; கேடில் (faultless, without ruin) is said of her at the moment her ruin is reversed.
event: The army and kings gather round Civakan, and Vijayai hears of his victory and weeps for joy.

tamil: அணிமுடி யரசர் மாலை யழனுதி வாள்க ளென்னு
மணிபுனை குடத்தி னெய்த்தோர் மண்ணுநீர் மருள வாட்டிப்
பணைமுலைப் பைம்பொன் மாலைப் பாசிழைப் பூமி தேவி
யிணைமுலை யேக மாக நுகரிய வெய்தி னானே.
reading: With the crowned kings' garlands and fire-edged swords as jewelled pots and their blood standing for the bathing water, he was bathed as for anointing, and came to enjoy as one the paired breasts of the Earth goddess of gold garlands and fine jewels.
nuance: The coronation bath (மண்ணுநீர்) is made of the battlefield, and the winning of the kingdom is told as a marriage, the hero's last bride after his eight wives: this is the ilampakam's மண்மகள்.
event: Civakan, as if anointed in the enemy's blood, takes the earth as his bride.

title: பூமகள் இலம்பகம் 2327-2343 (1/3)
theme: Civakan enters his father's city in triumph: the women crowd the mansions to praise and worship him and pale with longing as he passes, while his warriors drive the dead usurper's women out of the palace barefoot onto the hot ground, and the question of which of them was queen meets the answer that the king and his sons lie dead.
source_issues: 2330 line 3: 'சிந்நி' looks like a misprint for 'சிந்தி'.
2343 line 2: 'யாவ னென்ன' asks 'which one' with a masculine யாவன் of the woman who wore the fillet (அணிந்தாள்); யாவள் would be expected.

cast.role: the hero, returning victorious to his father's city
the women of the city who watch and praise Civakan's entry
the warriors in the procession who praise Civakan's strength
kings related to Civakan by marriage, riding beside him
Civakan's warriors who take the fallen usurper's palace
the women of the fallen usurper Kattiyangaran's palace

reading: Having won the field and finished the rites of victory, the hero of the fragrant chest enters the ancient city, whose garlands the bees drink, while its people worship him with joined hands.
nuance: The verse is a மடக்கு: every line opens with கண்ணாடி in a different sense (a mirror for the chest in line 1, the bees drinking in line 3), and the sense of the word in lines 2 and 4 (a foe's eye, a battle, a kind of elephant) can only be guessed. The opening of the ilampakam named for பூமகள், the goddess of fortune, is his return to his father's city.
event: Civakan, victorious, enters the old capital as its people worship him.

reading: Praising the one who set his killing spear on the wasting of his foes like a tiger or a lion of the cave, the garlanded young women crowd the high mansions like peacocks.
nuance: Again a மடக்கு on கூடார் / கூடாரம்: the enemies (கூடார், those who do not join) and the women's tent-shaped breasts and mansions share one sound.
event: The city's women gather on the mansions, praising Civakan.

reading: Women with flower-like hair say that this man with his sharp arrows has destroyed the deluded one together with all his sons, and others say that today the blame that would not die has died.
nuance: மாயாப் பழி, the blame that does not perish, is said to have perished (மாய்ந்தது): the women speak as if the regicide's stain lay on the city, or on the son who had not yet avenged it, until this day. The Tamil does not say whose blame it was.

reading: The young women look like the maidens of the gods' world, as the city's elephants with jewelled forehead-plates, its flowering trees and its hill-streams scattering gems all play on the one word நாகம்.
nuance: Each line opens with நாகம் in a different sense (mountain or serpent, elephant, the naga tree, the heavenly world); which sense governs which line is a guess.

reading: Some dress the tall mansions, like ships with high masts, with banners of new silk, and others, jewels flashing like golden creepers, go to the front to worship the victor king.
event: The city is hung with new silk banners, and women press forward to worship Civakan.

reading: As warriors with bows and anklets praise his strength, the women ask who here could equal him once he takes up the bow, and bid one another to see their lord and worship him with joined hands.
event: Warriors praise Civakan and the women urge each other to worship him.

reading: As the long-eyed women climb the gem mansions to scatter flowers and his kinsmen kings ride round him on great elephants, he looks like the dark gem-coloured god among his kin.
nuance: மைத்துன runs through all four lines; in line 4 the dark god surrounded by his மைத்துனர் is most likely Krishna among his cousins and brothers-in-law, so the procession of kin is likened to the god's.
event: Women shower flowers from the mansions while Civakan rides ringed by his kinsmen kings.

reading: Lotuses where bees hum and blue waterlilies seem to have bloomed together filling the street, for the women's faces, with their flashing spear-eyes, have opened like flowers.
Seeing the swelling shoulders of the master of the vina who slew the king, the women's breasts with their jewels and garlands break into gold, and the rich city looks like Amaravati, the gods' city.
nuance: பொன் பூத்து is the gold-coloured pallor of longing spreading over the women, set beside the gold of their ornaments; the epithet வீணை வித்தகன் recalls how he won Gandharvadattai, so the musician and the king-slayer are one man in the women's eyes.

reading: When he of the wishing-tree garland comes near, the beauty of the crowds of garlanded women on the walls wastes away, like a forest of waterlilies that closes when the moon wanes and the sun is seen.
nuance: The women are the night-flowering ambal and he the sun: the same arrival that makes the city bloom in 2334 makes these women close.
event: The women on the walls wilt with longing as Civakan passes.

tamil: தோகைம் மடவார் துவர்வாய் துடித் தஞ்ச வெம்பா
reading: Like jewelled snakes trembling at thunder in the sky, the warriors burst into the usurper's wide palace, and while the peacock-like women's coral lips quiver in fear, they order them fiercely to leave at once without looking back.
nuance: The command in line 4 (விழியாத்தொழித் தேகுகென்றார்) is hard to divide: either 'go without looking' or 'leave everything and go'. The palace is not named as Kattiyangaran's; it is the one the victors now take.
event: Civakan's warriors enter Kattiyangaran's palace and drive out its women.

tamil: செய்பாவை யன்னார் சிலம்பார்க்கு மென் சீற டியார்
reading: The doll-like women with anklets on soft small feet, who had never walked except on made flower-cushions, go out sobbing onto the bare hot ground, kohl-dark tears running over their jewelled breasts.
nuance: The verse names no fault of the women and no doctrine: the reversal from cushion to scorching earth is left to speak for itself.
event: The usurper's women leave the palace on foot across the bare ground.

reading: Their feet redden as if the earth they smelled were fire, blisters rise like the ripe fruit of the marul plant, their gold anklets seem to cry out their pain, and they go on, their cotton-soft feet aching.
event: The women walk on with blistered feet.

reading: Among them go women whose jewelled breasts, risen as if to learn fierce war, have seen the battlefield and turned from it, and others whose stance gives way, with chains laid on their breasts.
nuance: The sentence runs into 2341, which lists more groups of women and gives the verb. Lines 1 and 4 (பொருகோட்டை யழித்து, நெற்றிந் நிறுத்து வடம்வைத்த) are obscure; my reading of who these women are is a guess.
event: The palace women leave in their several groups.

reading: Women holding red-footed infants, women near their time whose breasts run with milk, and women laden with gold coins, pearls and coral, all crowd into the royal forecourt and fill it.
nuance: Infants and women about to give birth are among the expelled: the fall of the usurper's house takes in children who did nothing, as Civakan himself was born in the burning ground after his father's fall.
event: The expelled women, with infants and the pregnant among them, fill the palace forecourt.

reading: Their gold-strung garlands slipping from oiled hair, the bangled women, flashing like flower-creepers in lightning from a cloud that has not rained, tremble in unwasting grief like does that see a tiger before them.
nuance: The tiger (புலி) is the victor before their eyes, and the women his prey, the same figure the city's women used of Civakan in praise in 2328.

reading: When it is asked which among these was the one who won the favour of the garlanded king and wore the queen's golden fillet, the answer is that he and his sons have fallen in battle, ringed by golden crowns.
nuance: Who asks and who answers is not said (என்ன ... என்றார்). The answer does not name a queen: with the king and his heirs dead, the fillet has no wearer, and the question of rank among his women has become empty.

title: பூமகள் இலம்பகம் 2344-2360 (2/3)
theme: After the usurper's fall his queen dies of the news, and Civakan spares his women with a choice of maintenance or gold; he takes the palace, has the wounded tended, sleeps through a night of grief and triumph, worships the Jina at dawn, and holds court among his kin, friends and allied kings.
source_issues: 2354-2360 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2358 line 3 கமுநீர் is probably a misprint for கழுநீர் (as in 2346 line 3).
2351 line 1 (முலையீன்ற பெண்ணைத் திரடாமங்க டாழ்ந்து) and 2356 line 3 (முப்பழநீர்ப் பளிங்களைஇ) are hard to construe.
2357 lines 2-3, the collyrium as விளக்கு of the victory adornment, are obscure.

cast.role: the hero, now victor over the usurper
Kattiyangaran's chief queen, who dies on hearing of his death (named only by the gold fillet in 2343)
the women of the dead usurper's household, whom Civakan spares
the army on Civakan's side
the palace women who bathe, attend and praise Civakan
Civakan's maternal uncle, king of Videham, who led the allied chariots
the allied kings who fought on Civakan's side
Civakan's companions
Civakan's younger brother
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father

reading: Told that the bull-like usurper and his sons have fallen, his queen cries 'has it come to that?', sinks like a doe struck by a spear, her red eyes rolling up and sinking like carp in shallow water, and dies.
nuance: The question in 2343 asks which of the women wore the gold fillet the usurper gave her; this verse follows on with her answer in death, so she is taken as his chief queen, though the verse never names her.
event: Kattiyangaran's queen hears that he and his sons died in the battle, faints and dies.

reading: Civakan tells the usurper's women that his fiery anger, hissing like the five-hooded snake, was let go when the cruel man breathed his last, and that they need not melt in fear like dark serpents caught in Garuda's beak.
nuance: The anger is said to have been spent on the one enemy (வெய்யோன் உயிர்ப்பின் விடுத்தேன்): the victor draws a line between the usurper and his household.
event: Civakan assures the dead usurper's women that his anger ended with the usurper.

reading: He goes on: women of waists fine as a thread through a gem, of speech like song, he will do them no harm, and they should not let their long eyes rain tears like the red water-lily spilling pearls.
event: Civakan promises the women he will not harm them and bids them stop weeping.

reading: The broad-shouldered hero says they have nothing to fear from him: he will give them a living here to live on, or they may take gold and go and live elsewhere.
nuance: The choice to stay or leave with gold is the epic's picture of a just conqueror's treatment of the fallen enemy's household; nothing is taken from them.
event: Civakan offers the usurper's women maintenance in the city or gold to leave with.

reading: Hearing the spear-bearer's words like the thunder of the sky, the women, whose small feet flinch from a red cushion as from fire, go off like a flock of young peahens to their own towns ringed with coconut and cane.
event: The usurper's women leave the palace for their home towns.

reading: Calling them a burden, they put off their ear-rings, sea-conch bangles, saffron and the weight of their flower garlands, roll pearl tears from their kuvalai eyes and sob, and grow pale like the ash of the champak.
nuance: The putting off of ornaments is the mark of widowhood; the scene repeats, on the usurper's side, what Saccandan's women did at his death.
event: The widowed women strip off their ornaments and weep.

reading: When his soldiers, carrying bright lamps in their hands, have quickly searched every gold-walled hall and treasure chamber of the palace, he worships the goddess of the red lotus and goes in.
nuance: The goddess of the lotus is Fortune (பூமகள், the ilampakam's name); entering the palace only after the search and her worship marks the taking of the kingdom.
event: Civakan's soldiers search the palace, and he worships the lotus goddess and enters it.

reading: Women of polished speech take watch over the scented flower bed made ready for the hero, with garlands of palm-like strands hanging down and fragrant smoke rising like mist from a hill.
event: The palace women prepare and guard Civakan's bed.

reading: He puts off his battle dress, is bathed by women with breasts painted in gold, and, his garland gleaming, bows to his uncle, lord of the host of chariots, and speaks.
event: Civakan bathes, takes off his armour and bows to his uncle to speak.

reading: He asks that the men whose chests the iron fouled in the battle have their wounds tended and be cared for, and then, while sweet-voiced women stroke his feet, the conqueror lies at rest like the lord on the serpent bed.
event: Civakan charges his uncle with the care of the wounded and lies down to rest.

tamil: வாள்க ளாலே துகைப்புண்டு வரைபுண் கூர்ந்த போல்வேழ
நீள்கால் விசைய நேமித்தே ரிமைத்தார் நிலத்திற் காண்கலாத்
தாள்வல் புரவி பண்ணவிழ்த்த யானை யாவித் தாங்கன்ன
கோள்வா யெஃக மிடம்படுத்த கொழும்புண் மார்ப ரயாவுயிர்த்தார்.
reading: Elephants slashed by swords like hills full of wounds, the swift chariots, the horses unsaddled and the tuskers unharnessed, and the warriors with gaping spear wounds in their chests all breathe out in relief.
event: The wounded army, its elephants and horses unharnessed, rests after the battle.

tamil: கொழுவாய் விழுப்புண் குரைப்பொலியுங் கூந்தன் மகளிர் குழைசிதறி
யழுவா ரழுகைக் குரலொலியு மதிர்கண் முரசின் முழக்கொலியுங்
குழவாய்ச் சங்கின் குரலொலியுங் கொலைவல் யானைச் செவிப்புடையு
மெழுவார் யாழு மேத்தொலியு மிறைவன் கேளாத் துயிலேற்றான்.
reading: Amid the noise of deep wounds, the cries of weeping women scattering their ear-rings, the roll of drums, the conches, the flapping ears of elephants, the lutes and the songs of praise, the lord sleeps as if he heard none of it.
nuance: The grief and the triumph of the night are heard together in one list, and the king's sleep is the still centre of it.
event: Civakan sleeps through the night's noise of wounds, mourning and celebration.

tamil: தொடித்தோண் மகளி ரொருசாரார் துயரக் கடலு ளவர்நீந்த
வடிக்கண் மகளி ரொருசாரார் வரம்பி லின்பக் கடனீந்தப்
பொடித்தான் கதிரோன் றிரைநெற்றிப் புகழ்முப் பழநீர்ப் பளிங்களைஇக்
கடிப்பூ மாலை யவரேந்தக் கமழ்தா மரைக்கண் கழீஇயினான்.
reading: While one group of bangled women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a boundless sea of joy, the sun rises, and as women hold up fragrant garlands he washes his lotus eyes in clear water.
nuance: Line 3's முப்பழநீர் is obscure, and which women grieve and which rejoice is left to the reader: the usurper's household against the victor's.
event: At sunrise Civakan washes his face while some women grieve and others rejoice.

tamil: முனைவற் றொழுது முடிதுளக்கி முகந்து செம்பொன் கொளவீசி
நினைய லாகா நெடுவாழ்க்கை வென்றிக் கோல விளக்காகப்
புனையப் பட்ட வஞ்சனத்தைப் புகழ வெழுதிப் புனைபூணான்
கனைவண் டார்க்கு மலங்கலுங் கலனு மேற்பத் தாங்கினான்.
reading: He bows his crowned head to the Lord, flings out red gold by the handful, has collyrium put on as the lamp of the triumphal adornment for a long life beyond thought, and takes up the bee-loud garland and his ornaments.
nuance: முனைவன் is the Jina in this work's usage; worship and a gift come first in the morning order, before the king puts on his ornaments.
event: Civakan worships the Jina, gives gold and puts on collyrium, garland and ornaments.

tamil: முறிந்த கோல முகிழ்முலையார் பரவ மொய்யார் மணிச்செப்பி
லுறைந்த வெண்பட் டுடுத்தொளிசேர் பஞ்ச வாசங் கவுட்கொண்டு
செறிந்த கமுநீர்ப் பூப்பிடித்துச் சேக்கை மரீஇய சிங்கம்போ
லறிந்தார் தமக்கு மநங்கனா யண்ணல் செம்மாந் திருந்தானே.
reading: Praised by women, he puts on white silk kept in a gem casket, holds the five scents in his cheek, takes a kazhuneer flower in hand and sits like a lion on its couch, the noble one proud and a Kama even to the wise.
event: Civakan dresses in white silk and sits in state.

tamil: வார்மீ தாடி வடஞ்சூடிப் பொற்பார்ந் திருந்த வனமுலையா
ரேர்மீ தாடிச் சாந்தெழுதி யிலங்கு முந்நீர் வலம்புரிபோற்
கார்மீ தாடிக் கலம்பொழியுங் கடகத் தடக்கைக் கழலோனைப்
போர்மீ தாடிப் புறங்கண்ட புலால்வேன் மன்னர் புடைசூழ்ந்தார்.
reading: The kings with flesh-smelling spears, who had seen the enemy's backs in battle, gather round the hero whose large hand, bright with bracelets, pours out wealth like a cloud.
event: The victorious kings gather round Civakan.

reading: His four kinds of old companions, his younger brother, his uncle, the hero's father, the rich city and the fertile country all gather quickly together in the palace.
nuance: The father here (செல்வன் தாதை) can only be Kantukkatan, the foster father, since Saccandan is dead; the court that forms round the new king is his household of old, not the usurper's.
event: Civakan's companions, brother, uncle, father, the city and the country assemble in the palace.

title: பூமகள் இலம்பகம் 2361-2377 (3/3)
theme: The Vidyadhara kings and the gods gather for Civakan's crowning; he is bathed, crowned and seated on the lion throne, and his first orders as king, given through his brother and the royal drum, restore the temples' and Brahmins' lands, remit dues, and promise help to the hungry, the sick and the abandoned before the narrator turns to the next ilampakam.
source_issues: 2361-2377 were printed in eight half-lines in most verses and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2375 line 1 பதிளை யாண்டைக் குறுகடன் is obscure; 'sixteen years' is taken from பதிளை and is not certain.
2368 line 4 and 2362 lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

cast.role: the hero, now crowned
Civakan's younger brother (தம்பி), who carries out the king's orders
the Vidyadhara kings who gather for the crowning
the god who descends and crowns Civakan
the heavenly women who descend and sing
the beings who appear in the sky (taken as gods)
the guardian kings allied to Civakan
the people of the land who live under Civakan

reading: The Vidyadhara kings of the silver mountain leave it and gather in Civakan's city in such numbers that they look like the moon's scattered rays drawn together.
event: The Vidyadhara kings come down from Vellimalai and assemble in the city.

reading: Someone urges that there is nothing more to consider, that he should resolve to put on the fine crown and that the lord and the assembly should come, while a crown set with gems is made ready on the god-like hero's head.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are an exhortation in the imperative, but the verse does not name who speaks or who கண்ணனார் is; lines 3-4 are hard to construe.
event: The assembled kings press Civakan to be crowned and a gem-set crown is prepared.
