reading: A god with a flowing garland, a shining crown and a jewelled chest-ornament swaying descends, trembling like a golden hill.
nuance: Which god is meant is not said; the Cintamani's gods who attend Civakan are not named here.
event: A god comes down from the sky for the crowning.

reading: Heavenly women with full breasts, bright jewelled strings and soft hair come down like flashes of lightning from a rain-cloud.
event: Celestial women descend in a procession.

reading: Fierce-looking beings arrive in the sky in splendour, bringing a scent of the divine city that drowns the scent of the rutting elephants of the king's city.
nuance: வெய்யர் (the fierce or hot ones) is taken to be the gods of the sky; the verse does not say so.
event: More heavenly beings arrive in the sky above the city.

reading: The citizens, frightened, clap in wonder; with rains of flowers and gold he bathes Civakan with a hundred and eight pots of water from the milk sea and places the bright gold crown on him, worshipping.
nuance: The subject of கவித்தனன் is not named; it is taken to be the god who came down in 2363. The crown is given by heavenly hands, not by a priest or an elder king.
event: A god bathes Civakan with water from the milk sea and sets the golden crown on his head.

reading: Divine drums sound to announce it to the gods, apsaras praise with the vina's sound and smoke and powder rise, and the guardian kings and the assembly do what is due.
event: The apsaras sing and the kings and assembly carry out the rites of the crowning.

reading: A white umbrella rises like the full moon over a pole of gems, and the god who has risen to bless is joined with the matchless Earth-goddess, the king who now guards the sea-girt land.
nuance: The verse is built from similes and its last line, where the god rises and joins பூமகள், is ambiguous: it may mean Civakan taking the land as his bride or the god's blessing on it. The ilampakam is named for பூமகள்.
event: Civakan, crowned, is joined to the goddess of earth as ruler of the land.

tamil: மின்னுங் கடற்றிரையின் மாமணிக்கை வெண்கவரி விரிந்து வீசப்
பொன்னங் குடைநிழற்றப் பொன்மயமா முழைக்கலங்கள் பொலிந்து தோன்ற
மன்னர் முடியிறைஞ்சி மாமணியங் கழலேந்தி யடியீ டேத்தச்
சின்ன மலர்க்கோதைத் தீஞ்சொலார் போற்றிசைப்பத் திருமால் போந்தான்.
reading: With white fly-whisks waving, a golden umbrella shading him and kings bowing to take his feet, he goes forth in state, praised by women of sweet speech, like Vishnu.
event: Civakan goes in procession to the throne hall, with kings bowing to his feet.

tamil: மந்தார மாமாலை மேற்றொடர்ந்து தழுவவராத் தாம மல்கி
யந்தோவென் றஞ்சிறைவண் டேக்கறவின் புகைபோய்க் கழுமி யாய்பொற்
செந்தா மரைமகளே யல்லதுபெண் சாராத திருவின் மிக்க
சிந்தா மணியேய்ந்த சித்திரமா மண்டபத்துச் செல்வன் புக்கான்.
reading: He enters the picture-hall, set with the gem called cintamani, a hall that only the lotus goddess of fortune, and no other woman, has entered.
event: Civakan enters the painted hall of the throne.

tamil: பைங்க ணுளையெருத்திற் பன்மணி வாளெயிற்றுப் பவள நாவிற்
சிங்கா சனத்தின்மேற் சிங்கம்போற் றேர்மன்னர் முடிகள் சூழ
செங்கட் கமழ்பைந்தார்ச் செஞ்சுடர்போற் றேர்மன்ன னிருந்தா னன்றே.
reading: He sits on the lion throne, among kings in their crowns, like a lion, with his earrings flashing, like the sun shining from a dark cloud.
event: Civakan takes his seat on the lion throne in the midst of the kings.

tamil: வார்பிணி முரச நாண வானதிர் முழக்க மேய்ப்பத்
தார்பிணி தாம மார்பன் றம்பியை முகத்து ணோக்கி
யூர்பிணி கோட்டஞ் சீப்பித் துறாதவ னாண்ட நாட்டைப்
பார்பிணி கறையி னீங்கப் படாமுர சறைவி யென்றான்.
reading: Looking at his younger brother, Civakan bids him clear the afflictions of the towns and the districts and have the war-drum proclaim that the land his enemy ruled is rid of the stain of its burden.
nuance: The enemy's land is described by பிணி (bond or disease) in each half-line; the drum is the royal drum used for orders. The pun is not fixed.
event: Civakan orders his brother to relieve the towns of their afflictions and to proclaim it by drum.

tamil: கடவுள ரிடனுங் காசில் கணிபெறு நிலனுங் காமர்
தடவளர் முழங்குஞ் செந்தீ நான்மறை யாளர் தங்க
ளிடவிய நிலத்தோ டெல்லா மிழந்தவர்க் கிரட்டி யாக
வுடனவை விடுமி னென்றா னொளிநிலா வுமிழும் பூணான்.
reading: He commands that the lands of the temples, the lands of the learned who read the stars, and the fire-places and fields of the four-Veda Brahmins, taken from them, be given back twofold.
nuance: The seizure is not told in these verses; the 'losers' are the gods' shrines, the astrologers and the Brahmins, so the order is also the work's picture of whom a Jain king should protect.
event: Civakan orders land taken from temples and Brahmins to be restored at double.

tamil: என்றலுந் தொழுது சென்னி நிலனுறீஇ யெழுந்து போகி
வென்றதிர் முரசம் யானை வீங்கெருத் தேற்றிப் பைம்பொற்
குன்றுகண் டனைய கோலக் கொடிநெடு மாட மூதூர்ச்
சென்றிசை முழங்கச் செல்வன் றிருமுர சறைவிக் கின்றான்.
reading: Hearing him, the brother bows, touches the ground with his head, has the victorious drum set on a tall elephant and, through the old city of flagged mansions, has the drum of the lord proclaimed.
event: Nandattan has the royal drum carried on an elephant through the city to proclaim the orders.

tamil: ஒன்றுடைப் பதிளை யாண்டைக் குறுகட னிறைவன் விட்டா
னின்றுளீ ருலகத் தென்று முடனுளீ ராகி வாழ்மின்
பொன்றுக பசியு நோயும் பொருந்தலில் பகையு மென்ன
மன்றல மறுகு தோறு மணிமுர சார்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: The drum announces that the king has remitted the dues for sixteen years and that those who are alive should live together, and that hunger, disease and enmity should perish.
nuance: பதிளை யாண்டை is read as sixteen years; the number is not certain, and the reading of குறுகடன் as 'dues' is a guess.
event: The drum proclaims remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.

tamil: நோக்கொழிந் தொடுங்கி னீர்க்கு நோய்கொளச் சாம்பி னீர்க்கும்
பூக்குழன் மகளிர்க் கொண்டான் புறக்கணித் திடப்பட் டீர்க்கும்
கோத்தரு நிதியம் வாழக் கொற்றவ னகரோ டென்ன
வீக்குவார் முரசங் கொட்டி விழுநக ரறைவித் தானே.
reading: The drum goes on to those blind, wasted with disease, women left by the husbands who married them, and others cast out, that the stored wealth will be given so that they may live, and the king has it sounded through the city.
event: The king has the drum proclaim that his wealth will support the blind, the sick, abandoned wives and the cast out.

tamil: திருமக னருளப் பெற்றுத் திருநிலத் துறையு மாந்த
ரொருவனுக் கொருத்தி போல வுளமகிழ்ந் தொளியின் வைகிப்
பருவரு பகையு நோயும் பசியுங்கெட் டொழிய விப்பாற்
பெருவிறல் வேந்தர் வேந்தற் குற்றது பேச லுற்றேன்.
reading: The narrator says that, by the grace of Civakan the people live in gladness like one wife to one man, with enemies, disease and hunger gone, and that he will now tell what befell the king of kings.
nuance: The last line turns from the praise of Civakan's rule to the next ilampakam; the story it opens ends in the king's renunciation, as the patikam (verse 27) says.
event: The people live at ease and the narrator moves on to what happened to the king of kings.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2378-2402 (1/9)
theme: The women are brought back across the wasteland and rejoined with the hero in tears and joy; the poet turns to the wedding of Ilakkanai, where an astrologer names the days, a hundred and eight elephants are readied, a herald-drum orders feasting and decking, and the city keeps the days in music, flowers and gifts.
source_issues: 2378-2384: the verses carry no name for the hero or the women; they continue from the last verses of the preceding chapter.
2390 line 1 பிள்ளை வெண்பிறைச் சிறுநுதற் பெரும்பிட்ட மணிமின் is hard to construe (பிட்டம்).
2397 line 1-2 is obscure.

cast.role: the hero, never named in this chapter's verses
the women, joined with the hero before, brought back across the wasteland
the astrologer who lays out the days
the king for whom the astrologer lays out the days, called elephant-lord
the drummer-heralds seated on the battle elephant
the people of the city who dress, decorate and give

reading: The hero with the saffron-smeared mountain chest bids that the women who were joined with him be brought, and they are fetched through the lonely wasteland and handed over with grace.
nuance: The verse names neither the hero nor the women; they are the ones he asked for in the preceding verses, which this chapter's first verse cannot show.
event: At the hero's word the women are brought across the desert and given back to him.

reading: The women, like peacocks, step down from the guarded jewelled palanquin, lightning-slender, as if they had seen release, in a place where bees and birds that never saw the sun or the moon tremble.
nuance: The simile of those who have seen release (வீடு கண்டவர்) is for their relief and not a doctrinal statement.
event: The women alight from the palanquin.

reading: Withered in body, in the garlands and sandal of the day before, yet with no loss of gold ornament, they fall at their beloved's lotus feet while pearls of joy drop from their blue-lily eyes.
event: The women fall at their lord's feet and weep with joy.

reading: As he lifts and embraces them against his mountain-like chest, their long eyes, bearing tears and trembling, dart like a pair of carp in stirred water.
event: The hero embraces the women, who weep and tremble.

reading: Like forest jasmine buds scorched in the summer and then meeting the rain clouds, the proud women lose their pining and grief at the touch of their husband's honeyed chest, and shine.
event: The women's grief ends in their husband's embrace.

reading: The fish-eyed women set right their anklets and brow marks, wear fragrant garlands, paint the saffron creeper on their breasts and put on bamboo-bright shoulder pearls.
event: The women adorn themselves.

reading: Their wide eyes, bright like fish that have fed on poison, roll and glance; as the jewelled girdles slip and spill, the slender-waisted ones shine, and he stayed with them.
nuance: மாதோ at the end ends the scene; he who stayed is the hero, never named here.
event: Civakan passes the time with the women.

reading: The poet turns from these women to a new bride, Ilakkanai, whose gold-ringed small feet, narrow waist and bright jewelled girdle he describes, and says he will now tell her wedding rite.
nuance: The line 'we shall tell' makes the poet speak in the first person plural, as the poets of the Cintamani do when opening a new tale.
event: The poet announces the story of Ilakkanai's wedding.

reading: A learned king, who finishes coming deeds in their due hour even apart from fate, owner of crowned elephants and a golden litter, has a great astrologer set out the days for the elephant-lord.
nuance: Line 2 says he brings about a coming deed in its hour even apart from fate (ஊழின் அன்றியும்); the text does not say whether this places hour above karma.
event: The astrologer lays out the auspicious days for the king.

reading: On the great day the astrologer named for the king, a hundred and eight rutting elephants are made ready, wearing garlands and brow marks, white as silver hills.
event: A hundred and eight elephants are dressed for the day.

reading: They dress the proclaimers in white cloth and sandal, hang ear-rings and flowers and pearls on them and seat them on a battle elephant so that they can beat the wedding drum.
event: Drummers are set on an elephant to proclaim the wedding.

reading: The proclaimer cries: listen, wear pearl strings and sandal, bear the flower crest though the waist ache, put on fine cloth.
event: The drum announces that all must dress in finery for the wedding.

reading: Adorn the children and the whole body with jewels, he says; for seven days none may eat anything but the milk-nectar made by the generous lord's word, whatever the heart wants.
nuance: The first half of line 1, and what பிட்டம் means, turn on a rare word; the sense of the command is clear.
event: The drum commands feasting only on milk-nectar for seven days.

reading: Plant plantain and fruit-laden areca, hang garlands, spread pots of aloe smoke, make lute-song and dance in every place, raise many golden flags like a cloven sky.
event: The drum orders the city to be decked.

reading: For the seven days of the king's wedding the ill-behaved rutting elephants are to be kept away, and the drum thundered out its order that the great city by the dark sea live.
nuance: The king (மன்னவன்) whose wedding it is is not named; it is the king of the earlier verses, not necessarily the hero.
event: The drum is beaten and the city is told to keep the wedding days.

reading: After the drum six days passed, and everywhere white bangles swelled; lutes, flutes, drums and the thannumai sounded like thunder in the sky.
Women with parrot-sweet speech scattered flower dust like sky-lamps, sandal that lit the eyes, and flowers for the bali, brightening the earth.
event: Women sprinkle flowers and sandal for the offering.

reading: The steam of the milk boiling in pots rose in the mansions like thin silk shrouding them from the outside.
The red lac paint with which fair women, bowing, anointed the soles of the small feet spread over the ground like red sky at dusk.
The dressers' lamps, looking into the mirror, held the bees at dusk in the gaze of the garlands as moons held in a hand.
nuance: The simile of line 1 is hard to follow; the verse's own subject is the mirrors in which dressers see themselves.

reading: Golden gates rose through the clouds, garlands hung from the banners, and rows of pots lined the streets of the cloud-high city.
Dancers' anklets, songs, lutes and drums rang together so that the mansion city was like a great sea.
The dust of flowers and sandal and the smoke of incense seemed as if Indra's city had come to hold a festival here.
They poured sugar and ghee in rivers, gave milk-nectar to all who begged, and bade them take away fine cloth and jewels, even carrying them for them.
event: The people feed and give to all who come.

reading: They filled coconuts with jackfruit, plantain and mango fruit, pressed juices and sugarcane juice, and gave them to drink.
event: The people give fruit drinks to all.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2403-2427 (2/9)
theme: At the wedding of the Ilakkanaiyar ilampakam the city is heaped with goods and decked with flags and pots, the astrologer fixes the hour, the king is bathed by elephant-borne water and anointed with ghee amid blessings, then dressed, perfumed and fanned by countless fly-whisks.
source_issues: 2414-2417 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2405 line 3 மண்மகண் is probably a misprint for மண்மகள்; line 1 வழுவின் may stand for வழுவில்.
2407 lines 3-4 (தடிநிலம் பெறாததோர்) are hard to construe.
2411 line 2 வேறலு is unclear (perhaps ஏறலு).
2421 line 4 கேந்தினார் is unclear.
2427 line 4 இவரித் தொகை is unclear.

cast.role: the hero, bridegroom of the Ilakkanaiyar ilampakam
the bride of the ilampakam (named only in its title)
the astrologer who fixes the auspicious hour
the women who attend, bathe, anoint and bless
the kings who attend the rite
the townspeople who lay out the festival
the thousand and eight who raise fly-whisks
the guards who wave the fly-whisks
the earth-maiden of a figure

reading: The city heaps up areca bunches, tender betel leaves, camphor and the rest in such quantity that the great earth can scarcely bear them, for people to take freely and eat.
nuance: The lavishness is the point: the goods are laid out as plunder (கொள்ளை) to be taken, so the wedding feast is open to all.
event: The townspeople pile up areca, betel and camphor for all to take.

reading: Heaps of incense-smoking luxuries, held up as good fortune, make the fine city look as if the golden wish-trees and the wish-creeper had taken it as their ground.
The earth-maiden, unable to bear the crowd of people and cattle, is imagined opening her whole mouth and weeping, her tears turning into ghee and milk.
nuance: A conceit of plenty: the earth's weight of people and herds becomes a flood of ghee and milk. This is the poet's figure, not a doctrinal claim about the earth.

reading: At the palace gates the banners rise, areca and plantain put out their spathes, and mirrors, silks and full auspicious pots stand in bloom.
nuance: The auspicious objects (flags, pots full of water, mirrors, areca and plantain) are named as the marks of a wedding house; the verse gives no event.

reading: In the palace where women's anklets and bells ring, a wealth is said to have filled the place that the umbrella-shaded kings had not found on earth.
nuance: The last two lines (கோதைத் தாதுவேய்த் தடிநிலம் பெறாததோர் செல்வம்) are hard to construe; the sense of 'wealth the kings did not find on earth' is the likeliest.

reading: Ear-ornaments, studs, powder, aloe paste and flowers, with gem ornaments and necklaces throwing young rays, shine so that they make the upper world seem to be spurned.
nuance: The hyperbole (the heaven-dwellers' world made loathsome beside this display) is the epic's habitual way of praising a festival.

reading: The city, built like the waist of the goddess of the golden lotus and roofed like a sky blossomed with gem-dust, is made ready as the garlanded people set the great auspicious seat.
nuance: தவிசு is read as the seat on which the rite is done; the verse does not say who will sit on it.
event: The garlanded people set up the great auspicious seat.

reading: Gold, gems and conch pearls are heaped as auspicious offerings, lamps burn and sweet smoke rises, and one thousand and eight attendants raise fly-whisks.
event: Attendants raise fly-whisks among the heaped auspicious wealth.

reading: After the great astrologer fixes the hour, the auspicious king mounts, rice grains are sprinkled, auspicious instruments sound before him, and he is blessed with true words.
nuance: Line 2's வேறலு is not clear (perhaps ஏறலு, 'on mounting'); the whole verse is read as the beginning of the rite at the hour the astrologer set.
event: The astrologer's hour is fixed, and the king is blessed with rice grains and music.

reading: As auspicious instruments sound with a sweet roar, women with plump carp-like eyes take golden vessels and go down to the bath for the sacred hair, while rows of fly-whisks gleam and conchs boom.
nuance: திருமயிர் is taken as the hair of the one to be bathed; whether it is the bridegroom's or the bride's is not said in this verse.
event: Carp-eyed women go down with golden vessels to the bath as instruments sound.

reading: The gold-garlanded woman, bright like a coral creeper sprung from the milk-sea, is given her day's fragrant hair-dressing so that the goddess who dwells in the golden lotus is left to lament.
nuance: The woman is taken to be Lakshanai, the bride of the ilampakam's title, though she is not named; the closing figure says her beauty leaves the lotus-goddess grieving.
event: Attendants dress the bride's hair.

tamil: விரைத்தலை மாலை சூட்டி மின்னனா ரங்கை சேப்ப
வரைத்தசாந் தணிந்த கோட்ட வாயிரத் தெட்டு வேழ
நிரைத்தன மண்ணு நீர்க்கு முரசொடு முழவம் விம்ம
வரைத்தலைத் துவலை போன்று மதநில நனைப்ப வன்றே.
reading: Garlands are set on, the women's palms redden, and one thousand and eight elephants, their tusks smeared with ground sandal, are lined up for the bathing water, drums booming and rut-water wetting the ground like mountain spray.
event: A thousand and eight sandal-marked elephants are drawn up for the bathing water amid drums.

tamil: கான்முகம் புதைத்த தெண்ணீர் கவர்ந்துபொற் குடங்க ளார்த்தி
யூன்முகம் புதைத்த வேற்கண் ணவர்களிற் றுச்சி யேற்றி
வான்முகம் புதைத்த பன்மீன் மதியென மருண்டு நோக்கத்
தேன்முகம் புதைத்த மாலைக் குடைநிழற் றிருவிற் றந்தார்.
reading: Spear-eyed women raise golden pots of clear water onto the elephants' heads while the people stare as at a moon among confused stars, and fortune is given under the garlanded umbrella's shade.
nuance: The last line (குடைநிழற் றிருவிற் றந்தார்) can be read as the giving of fortune under the umbrella or as a naming of the pots; I take the first.
event: Women lift the golden pots of bathing water onto the elephants' heads.

tamil: இழைத்தபொன் னகரின் வெள்ளி யிடுமணை மன்ன ரேத்தக்
குழைப்பொலிந் திலங்கு காதிற் கொற்றவ னிருந்த பின்றை
மழைக்கலின் றெழுந்த வார்கொண் மணிநிற வறுகை நெய்தோய்த்
தெழிற்குழை திருவில் வீச மகளிர்நெய் யேற்று கின்றார்.
reading: When the king, ear-rings flashing, has sat on the silver seat while kings praise him, women dip durva grass in ghee and anoint him with it.
event: The king sits on a silver seat and women anoint him with ghee on durva.

tamil: மின்னுமிழ் வைரக் கோட்டு விளங்கொளி யிமய மென்னும்
பொன்னெடுங் குன்றம் போலப் பூமிமே னிலவி வைய
நின்னடி நிழலின் வைக நேமியஞ் செல்வ னாகி
மன்னுவாய் திருவோ டென்று வாழ்த்திநெய் யேற்றி னாரே.
reading: Women bless him as they pour ghee: may he shine on earth like the Himalaya of diamond peaks, may the world lie in the shade of his feet, and may he be lord of the wheel and abide with Fortune.
nuance: The blessing wishes sovereignty over the whole earth (நேமியஞ் செல்வன்), a wish, not a fact in the story; it is spoken to the bridegroom, not to a king already crowned.
event: Women bless the king as they anoint him with ghee.

reading: The women like lightning rub and bathe him with water of gems and with perfumed waters, and instruments sound together.
event: Women rub and bathe the king amid music.

reading: The water the chariot-kings pour from silver pots over the fortunate king's head looks like the moon's sweet rays pouring down when the sun's light is hidden.
nuance: The kings serve the bridegroom with the water of the bath, so the vassal kings of the earlier chapters now do him honour in the rite.
event: The chariot-kings pour water from silver pots over the king's head.

reading: A pavilion of gem is raised on four shining gem pillars, silver-roofed and ringed with garlands, so that it looks like the young sun resting there.
event: Attendants set up a gem pavilion on four pillars with a silver roof.

reading: A rug of golden milk-white wool is spread on the white-gold dais under a pearl canopy, and the seat is made ready for him.
nuance: Line 4 (கேந்தினார் அணி ஏந்தும் நீர்மையால்) is unclear in the printed text.

reading: When the damp has been dried, his hair, from which the dark gem-light spreads shadow, is scented with aloe smoke until it looks painted.
event: Attendants dry and scent his hair with aloe smoke.

reading: He anoints himself with matchless sandal and puts on a bee-loud garland whose pure flowers seem to have won release that day.
nuance: வீடு பெற்றன is a figure for flowers that are lucky to be worn; it makes no claim about release and is not a doctrinal use of veedu.
event: He anoints himself with sandal and puts on a garland.

reading: On his broad chest the necklace casts a rainbow, as if the wishing tree had blossomed, and he wears gold ornaments.
event: He puts on his gold ornaments and necklace.

reading: In hair-silk and with flashing ear-rings and a garland like Indra's bow, he becomes Kama himself to the women of fragrant hair.
event: He dresses in silk and ornaments and looks like Kama to the women.

reading: After the hanging garlands shine and water and rice grains are sprinkled, they wave incense smoke and show the unwavering fierce lamps.
event: Attendants sprinkle rice and water and wave incense and lamps.

reading: The guards wave so many white whisks, like the sea's foam-white waves, that the count of them is lost.
nuance: The last line (இவரித் தொகை என்பது இன்றி ஆயினார்) is taken to mean that the whisks passed counting.
event: Guards wave countless white fly-whisks.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2428-2452 (3/9)
theme: At Lakkanai's wedding the king's daughter is blessed, bathed and seated in a pearl hall, and a skilled dresser does her hair, brow, eyes, ears, wrists, breasts, girdle, feet and hands, until her beauty disarms Kama and bewilders onlookers, and the household hides her with fans and a parasol.
source_issues: 2437-2447 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2446 line 3 வலத்தகம் is probably a misprint for அலத்தகம்.
2443 line 1 நாண்சுமக்கலாத, 2445 lines 3-4 and 2435 விலாசி are hard to construe.
2448 lines 3-4 இருளிலார் and அருளிலார் can be read more than one way.

cast.role: the king's daughter, Lakkanai, the bride being adorned
the bride's women attendants (கதிர்முலையவர், வளைத்தோளினார்)
the skilled woman who dresses the bride's hair and body
the many who bless the bride at the wedding
Kama, the god of love

reading: Water scented with white durva flowers washes the lord's red feet, the faultless auspicious light that was lifted is shown, and the wedding fills with finely worked decoration.
nuance: இறைவன் may be the king giving the bride or the Jina; the verse does not say, so who is honoured is left open.
event: The rite of washing the lord's feet and showing the auspicious light opens the wedding.

reading: Many bless the girl, whose lily eyes are like bright swords drawn from the sheath and who is like the goddess of wealth, and set her on a silver stool and then on a jewelled couch.
event: Many bless the bride and seat her on a silver stool, then a jewelled couch.

reading: They hail her as gold grown on the mountain, a single right-whorled conch-gem, nectar of the waves and the object of Lakshmi's wish, and the fine women put durva grass in ghee on her to the sound of bangles, drums and conches.
event: Women praise the bride and anoint her with ghee and durva grass.

reading: They bathe the king's daughter with clear bathing water brought in a fine jewelled pot on a white musth elephant, and she looks like Lakshmi on a flower.
nuance: The syntax of ஏற்றி (raised, carried) leaves open whether the pot rides the elephant or the girl is lifted to it; the sense of an elephant-borne bath pot matches Gandharvadattai's bath in 623.
event: The bride is given the ceremonial bath with water from a jewelled pot carried on an elephant.

reading: The bath water flows on with flower foam, with gems it does not spill, with scented powder and saffron mixed into mud on the young sand banks, and with bees singing over it.
They seat her in a hall of pearl pillars set with coral under a golden canopy hung with pearl strings, where rays shine like the moon's.
event: The bride is seated under a golden canopy in a pearl hall.

reading: Women with garland-wreathed hair stand about the bride bearing ornaments, garlands and bright cloth, as she sits shaded like a creeper.
event: The attendants gather round the bride with ornaments, garlands and cloth.

reading: The women begin to adorn the soft-voiced girl with bangles, an anklet, the eye-ornament called விலாசி and garlands for the wrist and body.
nuance: விலாசி is a rare word whose sense (an ornament for the eye or brow) is a guess.
event: The attendants begin to dress the bride in ornaments.

reading: Her dresser draws from its sheath, as the moon from cloud, the auspicious comb made from the right tusk of the lord of elephants, set with gold and gems.
event: The dresser takes the ivory comb out of its case.

tamil: மைந்நூற் றனைய மாவீ ழோதி வகுத்துந் தொகுத்தும் விரித்துங்
கைந்நூற் றிறத்திற் கலப்ப வாரிக் கமழு நானக் கலவை
யைந்நூற் றிறத்தின் னகிலின் னாவி யளைந்து கமழ வூட்டி
யெந்நூற் றிறமு முணர்வா ளெழிலேற் றிமிலின் னேற்ப முடித்தாள்.
reading: A woman who knows every treatise parts, gathers and spreads her dark hair according to the hand-books, steeps it in musk paste and agil smoke, and ties it in a knot as handsome as a bull's hump.
nuance: The dresser is named only by her skill in the manuals (கைந்நூல், நூல்); dressing the hair is told as a learned art, as Civakan's dressing of the dancer is in 673.
event: The dresser combs, perfumes and knots the bride's hair by the rules of the craft.

tamil: கரும்புந் தேனும் மமிழ்தும் பாலுங் கலந்த தீஞ்சொன் மடவாட்
கரும்பும் மிலையு மயக்கி யாய்ந்த முல்லைச் சூட்டு மிலைச்சித்
திருந்து திங்கள் சூழ்ந்த மின்னிற் செம்பொற் பட்டஞ் சேர்த்தி
விரும்பும் முத்தம் மாலை நான்ற விழுப்பொன் மகரஞ் செறிந்தாள்.
reading: The sweet-worded dresser fastens jasmine and white-flower garlands, sets a gold band like the moon among lightning on the bride's brow, and ties on a golden makara hung with pearls.
event: The dresser sets the flower garlands, forehead band and makara ornament on the bride.

tamil: கள்ளுந் தேனும் மொழுகுங் குவளைக் கமழ்பூ நெரித்து வாங்கிக்
கிள்ளை வளைவா ருகிரிற் கிள்ளித் திலகந் திகழப் பொறித்துத்
தெள்ளும் மணிசெய் சுண்ணம் மிலங்கத் திருநீர் நுதலின் னப்பி
யுள்ளம் பருகி மதர்த்த வாட்கண் ணுருவம் மையிற் புனைந்தாள்.
reading: She crushes honey-dripping kuvalai flowers, nips them with her curved nail to print the forehead mark, spreads bright powder on the brow and draws the bride's long heart-drinking eyes in collyrium.
nuance: The finger-and-nail setting of the mark is what Vijayai undoes in 350.
event: The dresser prints the tilaka and paints the eyes with collyrium.

tamil: நாகம் மருப்பி னியன்ற தோடுந் நலங்கொள் கறவுக் குழையும்
போக நீக்கிப் பொருவிஃ றிருவில் லுமிழ்ந்து மின்னுப் பொழியு
மேக மாகி யெரியும் மணியின் னியன்ற கடிப்பு வாங்கி
மேக விசும்பிற் றேவர் விழைய விளங்கச் சேர்த்தி னாளே.
reading: She takes off the bride's ear-studs of tusk and the plain ear-rings and sets in their place gem ear-ornaments that burn like a cloud pouring lightning, so bright that the gods in the sky desire her.
event: The dresser changes the bride's plain ear-ornaments for the gem wedding ear-rings.

tamil: விலங்கரம் பொருத சங்கின் வெள்வளை தெளிர்க்கு முன்கை
நலங்கிளர் பவள நன்பொன் விரன்மணி யாழி மின்னக்
கலந்தின்று பணைத்த தோளுங் கவின்வளர் கழுத்து மார்ந்த
வலம்புரி யீன்ற மூத்த மணிநிலா நக்க வன்றே.
reading: Bangles of conch ring on her forearms, coral and gold finger-rings flash, and a pearl from a right-whorled conch on her neck and full shoulders shines like moonlight.
event: The dresser puts bangles, rings and the pearl necklace on the bride.

tamil: மாமணி முகடு வேய்ந்த மரகத மணிச்செப் பன்ன
தூமணி முலைக டம்மைத் தொழுதகக் கமழுஞ் சாந்திற்
காமரு காம வல்லிக் கொடிகவின் கொண்டு பூத்துத்
தூமணிக் கொழுந்து மென்றோட் டுயல்வர வெழுதி னாளே.
reading: On breasts like emerald caskets roofed with gems she draws in sandal paste the creeper of desire, flowering and trembling, down her soft shoulders.
nuance: The pattern is called காம வல்லி, the creeper of desire; the poet names the art by the god it serves.
event: The dresser paints the sandal-paste creeper on the bride's breasts and shoulders.

tamil: நாண்சுமக் கலாத நங்கை நகைமின்னு நுசுப்பு நோவப்
பூண்சுமக் கலாத பொன்ஞாண் வடத்தொடு புரள நோக்கிப்
பாண்குலாய் வண்டு பாடும் படுகணை மறந்து காமன்
காண்கிலேன் கடிய வென்னா வுருகிமெய் கரந்திட் டானே.
reading: Seeing her waist ache under its smiling lightning and the gold chain roll free of its weight, Kama forgets his bee-song bow and arrows, says he cannot bear to look, melts and hides his body.
nuance: நாண்சுமக்கலாத is hard (she who bears no shame or no bow-string); the sense that her beauty disarms the love-god is clear either way.
event: Kama, seeing the adorned bride, forgets his arrows and hides himself.

tamil: அவாக்கிடந் தகன்ற வல்கு லணிகிளர் திருவிற் பூப்பத்
தவாக்கதிர்க் காசு கண்டா ராவியைத் தளரச் சூட்டிக்
கவாய்க்கிடந் தணங்கு நாறுங் கண்கொளாப் பட்டு டுத்தா
ளுவாக்கதிர்க் திங்க ளம்மென் கதிர்விரித் துடுத்த தொத்தாள்.
reading: She puts on a girdle of gems whose rays loosen the life of those who look, and a silk their eyes cannot hold, so that she looks like the full moon wearing its own soft rays.
event: The dresser girdles the bride and clothes her in fine silk.

tamil: இடைச்செறி குறங்கு கௌவிக் கிம்புரி யிளக மின்னும்
புடைச்சிறு பரடு புல்லிக் கிண்கிணி சிலம்போ டார்ப்ப
நடைச்சிறு பாதங் கோல மணிவிர லணிந்து நாகத்
துடைச்சிறு நாவிற் றோகை யிரீஇயினண் மாலை சேர்ந்தாள்.
reading: Thigh-bands, tinkling anklets and gem toe-rings go on, and she is made to sit among garlands.
nuance: Lines 3-4 (நாகத் துடைச் சிறு நாவில் தோகை) are hard to construe and the last clause is a guess.
event: The dresser puts thigh, ankle and toe ornaments on the bride and seats her among garlands.

tamil: அம்மல ரடியுங் கையு மணிகிளர் பவழ வாயுஞ்
செம்மலர் நுதலு நாவுந் திருந்தொளி யுகிரோ டங்கேழ்
விம்மிதப் பட்டு வீழ வலத்தக மெழுதி யிட்டா
ளம்மலர்க் கண்ட முள்ளிட் டரிவையைத் தெரிவை தானே.
reading: The dresser paints the soft feet, hands and mouth of the girl with red lac and finishes the bride.
nuance: வலத்தகம் is probably a misprint for அலத்தகம், the red lac.
event: The dresser paints the bride's hands and feet with lac.

tamil: வாண்மதர் மழைக்க ணோக்கி வருமுலைத் தடமு நோக்கிக்
காண்வர வகன்ற வல்குற் கண்விருப் புற்று நோக்கிப்
பாணுவண் டாற்றுங் கோலச் சிகழிகைப் படியு நோக்கி
யாண்விருப் புற்று நின்றா ரவ்வளைத் தோளி னாரே.
reading: The bangled women look at her bright eyes, her breasts, her hips and the knot of her hair in turn and stand with a man's longing for her.
nuance: The women, not men, are said to feel ஆண்விருப்பு; the poem lets the dressing itself show how great the beauty is.
event: The attendants stand gazing at the bride with longing.

reading: The narrator says that even her maker, if he saw her, would be bewildered, and even the unbewildered would reel, so how could those in the sickness of delusion escape; such was how the graceless ones adorned her beauty.
nuance: இருளிலார் and அருளிலார் in lines 3-4 can be read in more than one way (those free of darkness, those without compassion); the narrator's point is the overpowering of the heart by beauty.

reading: Fully adorned she stands like a gem branch of the wishing tree blossoming in gold, her body shining with lightning, as though the lotus-goddess had left the opened lotus in a sulk, her eyes red.
Her flowered hair looks as if a skilled maker of jasmine garlands had strung it with cuts of darkness between the flowers and gathered scrolls of white moonlight in one place.
Death has come in the form of the king's daughter, and her girdle, anklet and bells cry with their own mouths to the onlookers to go while they can, keeping their lives and guarding their hearts.
nuance: The warning is spoken by her ornaments, the same cry that onlookers put in the ornaments' mouths for Gandharvadattai in 637.

reading: Fearing that even the graceless, though like Hara, would reel and make the world roll today, the chowries, sandal fans and white parasol hide the girl.
nuance: The sense of அருளிலார் இவடம் அரன்னராயினும் is uncertain; the plain act, fans and parasol screening her, is clear.
event: The attendants shade the bride with fans and a parasol to hide her.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2453-2477 (4/9)
theme: At the wedding of Civakan and his uncle Govindan's daughter Ilakkanai, the attendants praise the bride and the rival kings burn with envy; the priests kindle the fire and Civakan takes the gift-water and circles the fire; the women prepare the bridal bed, and the night is told in the figure of a rain-cloud filling a tank.
source_issues: Verses 2457 to 2466, 2468 to 2470, 2473, 2474, 2476 and 2477 were printed in eight half-lines and the build joined them into four lines.
2457 and 2469 contain words (உத்தராசங்கம், அயினி) whose sense is not fixed, so the rites they name are not certain.
The bride is named only in the section title; no verse of this run names her.

cast.role: the hero, bridegroom
Govindan's daughter, the bride; never named in the verses of this run
the bride's father, Civakan's maternal uncle, king of Videha
the women of the wedding hall who attend the bride and make the bridal bed
the umbrella kings who watch the wedding, some of them losing suitors
the nurses who brought up the bride
the priests who kindle the wedding fire
the fire god, who rises from the sacrificial fire

reading: A string of loving names (sugar-cane, honey, nectar, jewelled vina, swan, peahen, koel, doe) is poured on the king's daughter, addressed as the doll of the jewel-wearing king.
nuance: The verse names no speaker; the women of the wedding hall are taken as the speakers from the verses that follow, and 'the king's doll' is Govindan's daughter by the chapter's title.

reading: The bride steps aside while her attendants cry that they will lay down a bed softer than anicham flowers and swan down, which she would not tread for fear of its heat, and praise her feet.
nuance: The syntax of lines 2 to 4 is hard (whose feet are praised, and who lays what); the reading follows the plain order of the words.
event: The bride, praised by her attendants, steps aside from a flower-soft path.

reading: The bride comes into the cool wedding pavilion, with a thousand gold pillars and a hundred gem pillars and wreaths of flowers, like a daughter of the celestials.
event: The bride arrives at the pavilion.

reading: Seeing the form of the king's daughter, whose moon-face and doe-like grace outdo Kaman's bow and arrows, the umbrella kings are scorched in the eyes as by fire and cannot rest.
nuance: The kings' pain is the pain of the losing suitors; it makes the bride's worth the measure of what Civakan wins.
event: The assembled kings, seeing the bride, burn with longing and grief.

tamil: வண்டலர் கோதை வாட்கண் வனமுலை வளர்த்த தாயர்
கண்டுயி ருண்ணுங் கூற்றங் கயிறுரீஇக் காட்டி யிட்டா
ருண்டுயிர் சிலர்கண் வாழ்கென் றுத்தரா சங்கம் வைத்தார்
தெண்டிரை வேலி யெங்குந் தீதின தாக மாதோ.
reading: The nurses who reared the bride, seeing her eyes as Death that drinks lives, pull out the cord and show it, and the verse closes with a wish that evil be across the whole sea-ringed land.
nuance: The lines on the nurses' act and the word உத்தராசங்கம் are obscure; the verse closes with the same refrain as 2466 and may be a ward against the evil eye, which the Tamil does not state.
event: The bride's nurses show a cord at the sight of her death-dealing eyes.

tamil: கண்ணினா லின்று கண்டாங் கூற்றினைக் காமர் செவ்வா
யொண்ணுத லுருவக் கோலத் தொருபிடி நுசுப்பிற் றீஞ்சொல்
வண்ணித்த லாவ தில்லா வருமுலை மதர்வை நோக்கிற்
பெண்ணுடைப் பேதை நீர்மைப் பெருந்தடங் கண்ணிற் றம்மா.
reading: The onlookers say that today they saw Death with their own eyes: it is the great wide eyes of a woman with a waist like an elephant cow's, whose breasts no praise can describe.
nuance: No speaker is named; the kings of 2456 and 2459 are taken, though any watcher could be meant.

tamil: அரத்தக மருளிச் செய்த சீறடி யளிய தம்மாற்
குரற்சிலம் பொலிப்பச் சென்னிக் குஞ்சிமேன் மிதிப்ப நோற்றான்
றிருக்குவாய்க் கிடந்த மார்பிற் சீவக னாங்க ளெல்லாந்
தரித்திலந் தவத்தை யென்று தார்மன்ன ரேமுற் றாரே.
reading: The kings, seeing the bride's soft reddened feet, say that Civakan, on whose head-tuft she will tread with sounding anklets, must have done penance, which they themselves could not bear, and fall into grief.
nuance: The kings give the win to Civakan's earlier tavam, which the verse does not specify; the Jain epic lets the losers name deeds as the cause of his luck.
event: The rival kings lament that Civakan has won the bride.

tamil: கோவிந்த னென்னுஞ் செம்பொற் குன்றின்மேற் பிறந்து கூர்வேற்
சீவக னென்னுஞ் செந்நீர்ப் பவளமா கடலுட் பாய்வான்
பூவுந்தி யமுத யாறு பூங்கொடி நுடங்கப் போந்து
தாவிரி வேள்விச் சாலை மடுவினுட் டாழ்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: The nectar river of the bride flows down from the golden mountain Govindan toward the coral sea that is Civakan, but sinks into the pond of the sacrificial hall.
nuance: Govindan, the bride's father and Civakan's uncle, is the mountain; the wedding is that of cousins and the sacrificial hall is the bride's place of marriage.
event: Govindan's daughter is brought to the sacrificial hall to be given to Civakan.

tamil: சாணிடை நெடிய வாட்கண் டளையவிழ் குவளை பூப்பப்
பூணுடை முலையின் பாரம் பொறுக்கலாச் சுளிவின் மேலு
நாணட நடுங்கிக் கையா னகைமுகம் புதைத்த தோற்றஞ்
சேணிடை யரவு சேர்ந்த திங்களை யொத்த தன்றே.
reading: The bride, her fish-long eyes opening like flowers and weighed down by her breasts, trembles with shame and hides her smiling face with her hand, like the moon in the sky caught by a serpent.
event: The bride covers her face in shyness.

tamil: முத்துமிழ் திரைக ளங்க மொய்கொள் பா தால முத்தீ
யொத்தன வேலை வேள்வி யொலிகட னான்கு நாண
வைத்தநான் மறையு நீந்தி வான் குண மென்னுஞ் சாலி
வித்திமே லுலகத் தின்பம் விளைத்து மெய் கண்டநீரார்.
reading: The verse likens the sacrifice's sound to the sea and says the truth-seers who have crossed the four Vedas sow the paddy of virtue and bring about the world's joy.
nuance: A Jain work describes a Vedic wedding rite without answering it here; the verse leaves open whether the narrator holds the claim or only describes the priests' belief.
event: The marriage priests begin the sacrifice.

tamil: தருமணற் றருப்பை யார்ந்த சமிதையிம் மூன்றி னானும்
விரிமல ரணிந்த கோல வேதிகை யியற்றி யானெ
யொருமணி யகலுட் பெய்தோர் பொன்னக லார்ந்த தூப
மிருமணி யகலு ணீர்பெய் திடவயி னிரீஇயி னாரே.
reading: The priests build the altar with fine sand, darbha and three sorts of fuel, adorned with flowers, and set incense in one jewel-bowl and water in another.
event: The priests make the altar and set out the vessels.

tamil: நெற்பொரி நிறையப் பெய்து நிழலுமிழ் செம்பொன் மூழிக்
கற்புரி கடவு ளான்பா லவியொடு கலப்ப வைத்து
மூற்பெரி யானை யாகத் தருப்பையான் முடிந்து மூன்று
பொற்புரி வரையும் பொய்தீர் சமிதைக ளிரண்டும் வைத்தார்.
reading: They fill a gold vessel with parched rice, set it with the ghee for the god of fire, tie it with darbha and lay out the three gold-ringed bars and two pure sticks.
event: The priests lay out the offerings.

tamil: மந்திர விதியின் மாண்ட சிறுவிரற் றருப்பை சூழ்ந்து
முந்துநா மொழிந்த நெய்யை முனைமுதிர் தருப்பை தன்னான்
மந்திரித் தமைய முக்கான் மண்ணிமற் றதனை நீக்கிச்
சிந்தித்து மறையிற் செந்தீத் தண்டிலத் தங்கண் வைத்தார்.
reading: By the rule of the mantras they take darbha, purify the ghee with it three times, remove it and place it, thinking it over, in the fire-bed.
event: The priests consecrate the ghee and place it on the fire.

tamil: தண்டிலத் தகத்திற் சாண்மே லெண்விரற் சமிதை நானான்
கெண்டிசை யவரு மேத்தத் துடுப்புநெய் சொரித லோடுங்
கொண்டழற் கடவுள் பொங்கி வலஞ்சுழன் றெழுந்த தென்ப
தெண்டிரை வேலி யெங்குந் திருவிளை யாட மாதோ.
reading: As the spoon pours ghee on the eight-finger sticks and the quarters bless, the fire god is said to rise turning right, that fortune may play across the whole sea-ringed land.
nuance: The words 'they say' (என்ப) mark the omen as hearsay; the verse does not endorse the rite.
event: The fire rises on the pouring of the ghee.

tamil: கரையுடைத் துகிலிற் றோன்றுங் காஞ்சன வட்டின் முந்நீர்த்
திரையிடை வியாழந் தோன்றத் திண்பிணி முழுவுஞ் சங்கு
முரசொடு முழங்கி யார்ப்ப மொய்கொள்வேன் மன்ன ரார்ப்ப
வரசரு ளரச னாய்பொற் கலசநீ ரங்கை யேற்றான்.
reading: With gold pot water in the shape of the sea and Jupiter showing, drums, conches and kings roaring, Civakan, king of kings, takes the water into his palm.
nuance: The pouring of water into the groom's palm is the sign of giving the bride; the verse does not name the giver, taken as Govindan.
event: Civakan receives the gift-water that gives him the bride.

tamil: குளிர்மதி கொண்ட நாகங் கோளைவிடுக் கின்ற தேபோற்
றளிர்புரை கோதை மாதர் தாமரை முகத்தைச் சேர்ந்த
வொளிர்வளைக் கையைச் செல்வன் விடுத்தவ ளிடக்கை பற்றி
வளரெரி வலங்கொண் டாய்பொற் கட்டிறா னேறி னானே.
reading: As the serpent lets go the moon, Civakan takes the bangled hand of the lotus-faced bride in his left, goes round the fire, and mounts the gold bed.
event: Civakan takes the bride's hand, circles the fire and sits her on the couch.

tamil: விளங்கொளி விசும்பிற் பூத்த வருந்ததி காட்டி யான்பால்
வளங்கொளப் பூத்த கோல மலரடி கழீஇய பின்றை
யிளங்கதிர்க் கலத்தி னேந்த வயினிகண் டமர்ந்தி ருந்தான்
றுளங்கெயிற் றழுவை தொல்சீர்த் தோகையோ டிருந்த தொத்தான்.
reading: After the star Arundhati is shown, her feet are washed with milk; he sits looking at the ceremonial offering, like a fanged tiger beside a peahen.
nuance: The word அயினி and the person who washes the feet are obscure, so which rites are meant here is not certain.
event: The couple are shown Arundhati and Civakan sits down with her.

tamil: பொன்னங் காழிற் பொலிந்த முத்து விதானம் புணர்ந்துதேன்
மன்னு மாலை பலதாழ்ந்து மணப்புகை விம்மி மல்கிய
வன்னத் தூவி யடர்பஞ்சி யவிர்மயி ராதி யாகப்
பன்னிச் சொன்ன பதினைந்தும் படுத்தார் பாவை மார்களே.
reading: The maids arrange the fifteen things named for the bed, among them a pearl canopy, garlands, swan down and soft cotton, with scented smoke filling the room.
event: The women prepare the bridal bed.

reading: The slim women put the bed's coverings of cool soft cotton and down, hang a curtain, and draw it.
event: The women dress the bed and draw the curtain.

reading: The girls, whose eyes are like two drawn spears, set gem-eared lamps and silver-gold mirrors on both sides of the bed.
nuance: The words மணிச்செவி and படியகம் are rare; the objects are read as vessels and mirrors but are not certain.
event: The women set out lamps and mirrors by the bed.

tamil: அங்கருங் காலி சீவி யூறவைத் தமைக்கப் பட்ட
செங்களி விராய காயுஞ் செம்பழுக் காயுந் தீந்தே
னெங்கணுங் குளிர்த்த வின்னீ ரிளம்பசுங் காயு மூன்றுந்
தங்களி செய்யக் கூட்டித் தையலார் கைசெய் தாரே.
reading: The women prepare a pleasurable mix of the soft, ripe, red-sap and tender cool-water fruits with sweet honey.
event: The women prepare the mixed fruit and betel items.

tamil: கைசெய்து கமழு நூறுங் காழ்க்கும்வெள் ளிலையுங் காம
மெய்தநன் குணர்ந்த நீரா ரின்முக வாச மூட்டிப்
பெய்தபொற் செப்பு மாலைப் பெருமணிச் செப்புஞ் சுண்ணந்
தொய்யறப் பெய்த தூநீர்த் தொடுகடற் பவளச் செப்பும்.
reading: They add the scented lime, the bitter white leaf, and the cool liquid scents that give the breath a sweet smell, in gold, gem and coral caskets filled with powder.
event: The women stock the caskets with betel and scent.

tamil: தாமணி நானச் செப்புஞ் சலஞ்சலக் கலன்பெய் செப்புந்
தூமணித் துகில்க ளார்ந்த வலம்புரித் துலங்கு செப்புங்
காமநீர்க் காம வல்லி கவின்கொண்டு வளர்ந்த தேபோ
னாமவே னெடுங்கட் பாவை நயப்பன வேந்தி னாரே.
reading: The long-eyed girls carry in caskets of musk, vessels of scent, a conch casket of fine cloth, like the creeper of desire growing in the water of love.
event: The women bring in the caskets of scent and cloth.

tamil: விரிகதி ரார மின்னித் தாரெனுந் திருவில் வீசிக்
குரிசின்மா மேகம் பெய்த கொழும்புயற் காம மாரி
யரிவைதன் னெஞ்ச மென்னு மகன்குள நிறைந்து வாட்கட்
கரியமை சேறு சிந்திக் கலிங்குக டிறந்த வன்றே.
reading: Civakan the great cloud lets fall a rain of desire, with pearl strings for lightning and the garland for a rainbow, which fills the tank of the bride's heart, and her kohl runs as mud when the sluices open.
nuance: The consummation is told wholly by the figure of a rain-cloud filling a tank; no act is described.
event: Civakan and the bride come together.

tamil: தோக்கையந் துகிலி னாடன் றுணைமுலை பொருது சேந்த
வேக்கொசி விலாத வில்லா னிடுகொடி யகல மின்றேன்
றேக்கிவண் டிமிருங் கோதை செல்வன்றா ருழக்க நைந்து
பூக்கொய்து துவண்ட கொம்பின் பொற்பின ளாயி னாளே.
reading: After the bride's close embrace, her cloth dishevelled, breasts reddened, her bee-humming wreath crushed by her husband's garland, she is left like a creeper wilted by the flower-plucking.
event: The bride, after the night, lies drained.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2478-2502 (5/9)
theme: The wedding of Civakan and Ilakkanai: the bride is fanned and arrayed, her ornaments jest at the groom, the pavilion and emblems are set out, Civakan and the bride sit together, the groomer is introduced and shaves Civakan, and the pair bathe and dress.
source_issues: 2478-2481 are fine, but 2491, 2492, 2493, 2494, 2495, 2496, 2501 and 2502 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly except 2494.
2494 line 1 (நச்செயிற் றரவி னோக்கின் யொளிமுடிச் சிதறி னானே) reads as the end of the sentence that line 4 begins; lines are out of order or corrupt.
2489 lines 2-3 (இருந்தவலிர் பஞ்சி; திருநோக்கும் வார முறைக் கருவி) are obscure.
2491 ஆவிதன் and 2497 கூற்றனான் are doubtful words.
2478-2502 contain no verse that names the groomer's trade; he is inferred from the scene.

cast.role: the hero, now being wed to his maternal uncle's daughter
Govindan's daughter, the bride
the women appointed to attend and fan the bride and to sing for her
the bride's anklet, girdle and bells, personified as complainants
the workmen and men who raise the pavilion and set out the offerings
the women who stand at the corners of the pavilion with the auspicious emblems and swords
the skilled groomer who shaves and trims Civakan (his trade is not named in the verses)
the allied kings who attend and pour the bathing water

tamil: அணித்தகு பவள மேற்பக் கடைந்துமுத் தழுத்தி யம்பொன்
றுணித்தடி விளிம்பு சேர்த்தித் தொழுதகச் செய்த வண்கை
மணிச்சிரற் சிறகு நாண வகுத்தசாந் தால வட்டம்
பணித்தகு மகளிர் வீசிப் பாவையைக் குளிர்ப்பித் தாரே.
reading: The women appointed for the task fan the bride, the living doll, with sandal-wood palm fans framed in coral and pearl and edged with gold, and so cool her.
event: Appointed women fan the bride to cool her.

reading: Her lotus-red eyes and breasts are painted and sandal is smoothed over her, fine flowers are chosen to crown her, and he joins his hands to her in salutation.
nuance: The verse names no one but the pronoun in 'அவன் அஞ்சலி செய்தான்'; that he is the groom, and that the painted figure is the bride and not an image, is read from the scene around it.
event: The bride is painted with sandal and crowned with flowers, and the groom salutes her.

reading: The bride drinks in the song the garlanded women sing to the jewelled lute, the soft flute and the drum, and looks like a coral creeper that has blossomed in gems and pearls.
event: The bride listens to the women's songs and music.

reading: Her water-ringing anklet, her girdle and the croaking little bells together raise a clamour, as if crying that the girl has sown distress among the women.
nuance: The ornaments are given a voice as petitioners; the verse leaves the 'women' of line 2 unspecified, so the complaint is a conceit about the bride's rivals or her own band.
event: Her anklet, girdle and bells jangle together as if in complaint.

reading: The ornaments fall silent once the sandal-breasted bride embraces the groom, saying that the king of kings has turned cruel-sceptred and will not even look into, or heed, the clamour they raised together.
nuance: A lovers' jest cast in the language of petition and a bent sceptre (கொடுங்கோல்); the 'cruel king' is the bridegroom whose embrace silences the complaint, and no real injustice is told.
event: The bride embraces Civakan, and her jangling ornaments fall silent.

reading: The narrator announces that he will now tell how the groom, whose mountain-like chest is hung with garlands and who sports with his garlanded bride as people sport in a world full of bliss, has the grown hair removed.
nuance: வீடுமலி உலகினவர் is read as the dwellers of a world rich in bliss, to which the sport of the pair is likened; whether வீடு means the Jain release or the heaven of the gods is not settled by the verse.

reading: Workmen mark out and raise tall, mature, solid pillars, then spread over them an embroidered canopy like the serpent-world of the poison-jewelled nagas.
nuance: The first two lines are hard to construe; the pillars are an inference from உயர்திண்காழ் and ஊன்றி.
event: Workmen raise pillars and spread a canopy over the wedding pavilion.

reading: They lay out the pavilion floor eight arm-lengths across with figures of tusker-heads and of the goddess of fortune, and complete the pattern with threads of fine gold dust.
event: Workmen draw the auspicious figures on the pavilion floor.

reading: Spear-bearing men set out, in the proper way, offerings of black gram, green gram, rice-cakes and pastries, fill a thousand measures with red rice, and trim the tender tips of arugu grass.
event: Men prepare the food offerings and the grass tips for the rite.

reading: Fine-eyed women stand in the south-east holding, set in gems, the eight auspicious emblems: the pair of red fish, the sign of fortune, lamps, mirror, banner, drum, goad and pot.
nuance: The list is read from the compressed words of lines 1 to 3 and the identification of each emblem is partly inferred; the verse itself says only that the eight are held.
event: Women stand in the south-east holding the eight auspicious emblems.

reading: Two women stand in the north-east with drawn swords bright as lightning, while garlanded women in the south-west, their hearts melting as they gaze, hold up vessels of black gram and stand with joined hands.
nuance: உழுத்தகலும் is read as a vessel of gram; the reading is uncertain.
event: Sword-bearing women and hand-joined women take their places at two corners of the pavilion.

reading: In the west stand gem plates brimming with hill-rice flowers, water and arugu grass hung with pearl strings; in the north, cotton and the instruments lie ready in proper turn.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (இருந்தவலிர் பஞ்சி, திருநோக்கும் வார முறைக் கருவி) are obscure; the cotton and instruments are inferred.

reading: Civakan, great king beneath the sky-high umbrella, sits gently beside the spear-eyed bride on the couch, like the sun come to rest with the moon, their rays scattering.
event: Civakan and the bride sit together on the wedding couch.

reading: The poet turns to a man who lived in a forest of fruit-groves and mango-boughs with a matted-haired sage, and who, leaving that kin, became by a rising curse a being in his own right.
nuance: ஆவிதன் is the doubtful word; the verse is read as the origin of the groomer who appears from 2492, but it does not name his trade.
event: A sage's curse sends a man away from his kin in the forest.

reading: Born in the line that sprouted from the sage's foot, he learned deeply, showed his skill in adornment, was given by the king the honour of riding an elephant to town, and was fit for the great palanquin.
nuance: கால்முளை (the foot's sprout) is the only mark of his caste; the verse does not call him a barber, and the king here is the unnamed ruler of the city.
event: The groomer is honoured by the king with an elephant ride and a palanquin.

tamil: நித்தில வடமும் பூணு மாரமு நிழன்று தாழ
வொத்தொளிர் குழைகள் காதி னான்றுபொன் னூச லாடப்
பைத்தர வல்குற் பாவை கரகநீர் சொரியப் பாங்கின்
வித்தகன் பூசி வெள்வேல் வேந்தனுக் கிறைஞ்சி னானே.
reading: Hung with pearl strings and ornaments, his ear-rings swinging like golden swings, the skilled man has a doll-like woman pour water from a pitcher, anoints himself and bows to the white-speared king.
nuance: The king is not named; he is taken as the king who presides at the wedding.
event: The groomer is poured water, anoints himself and bows to the king before his work.

tamil: நச்செயிற் றரவி னோக்கின் யொளிமுடிச் சிதறி னானே.
வச்சிர வண்ணன் காப்ப மன்னரை நடுங்க நோக்கி
வச்சுதங் கொண்டு மன்ன வாழிய ரூழி யென்னா
யுச்சிவண் டிமிரு மாலை னடிமுடித் தெளித்து நங்கை
reading: With Vajravannan as guard, the skilled man glares until the kings tremble, wishes the king life for ages, sprinkles water at the feet and loosens the groom's shining hair-knot.
nuance: Line 1 reads as the end of the sentence that line 4 begins; the verse is out of order or corrupt here and its sense is partly guessed.
event: The groomer loosens the groom's hair-knot after wishing the king long life.

tamil: வாக்கினிற் செய்த பொன்வாண் மங்கல விதியி னேந்தி
யாக்கிய மூர்த்தத் தண்ணல் வலக்கவு ளுறுத்தி யார்ந்த
தேக்கணின் னகிலி னாவி தேக்கிடுங் குழலி னாளை
நோக்கல னுனித்து நொய்தா விடக்கவு ளுறுத்தி னானே.
reading: At the auspicious moment the lord takes the golden razor by rule, presses the groom's right cheek without so much as a glance at the fragrant-haired bride, and then presses his left.
nuance: The 'lord' of line 2 is the groom being shaved; the pressing of the cheek is the shaver's hand on it.
event: The groomer begins to shave Civakan, right cheek first, then left.

tamil: ஆய்ந்தபொன் வாளை நீக்கி யவிர்மதிப் பாகக் கன்மேற்
காய்ந்தவாள் கலப்பத் தேய்த்துப் பூநிறீஇக் காமர் பொன்ஞாண்
டோய்ந்ததன் குறங்கில் வைத்துத் துகிலினிற் றுடைத்துத் தூய்தா
வாய்ந்தகைப் புரட்டி மாதோ மருடகப் பற்றி னானே.
reading: He sets down the golden razor, whets another on the stone, wipes it clean on his cloth, lays the gold-corded thing across his thigh, and takes the groom's hand with a turning grip.
nuance: The thigh-laid gold cord (பொன்ஞாண்) is hard to place; the verse is read as the razor's preparation.
event: The groomer whets and wipes the razor and takes up his work.

reading: Working up and down and pressing in between, as one applies sandal, he dresses the face, which shines like the red sun rising out of the sea.
nuance: கூற்றனான் முகம் is hard to read and is left out of the sense given here.
event: The groomer trims the groom's face until it shines.

reading: Weighed down by the garland, held back by her shyness and by the shame of looking at the face of a man new to her, the bride, eyes on his feet, slowly and without fault lifts her moon-face.
event: The bride lifts her face slowly to look at the groom.

reading: As he shapes the brows into a rainbow, the twin fish-red eyes seem frightened birds about to flee into the sky.
nuance: The eyes belong to the groom under the razor, though the simile of frightened fish and birds could also be taken of the bride's glance.
event: The groomer trims the groom's brows.

reading: Having removed the hair and finished the fine scissor-work, washed in water, the garlanded man praises the feet and withdraws.
nuance: The garlanded man (தாரன் மாலைக் கண்ணியான்) may be the groomer or the groom; I take him as the groomer.
event: The groomer finishes, washes, praises the feet and withdraws.

reading: The swan-gaited bride and the spear-bearing warrior, whose garland makes kings' umbrellas tremble, bathe from shining gem pitchers lifted by kings and dress in flowers, cloth and sandal.
event: Civakan and the bride bathe in water poured by kings and dress.

reading: The pearl necklace that took over her whole body, heedless of its own kin, lived under her breasts and dried up (grew limp) where it touched the waist's bodice, and so adorned the spear-eyed doll.
nuance: The conceit gives the necklace a will and a family; the grammar of lines 2 and 3 is hard.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2503-2526 (6/9)
theme: After the lovers' quarrel in which Ilakkanai mistakes Civakan's tears for thoughts of other women, the parrot's mock death ends it and the wedding days pass; Civakan then rides the elephant Culamani in state through the city.
source_issues: 2503, 2506-2509, 2511-2517, 2522-2526: stanzas printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build.
2504, 2512, 2518-2520: lines garbled or corrupt in the edition's printing; readings marked uncertain.
2511: தத்தை addresses the parrots, but the edition's wording may mean the speaker is a woman named Tattai; read as parrots.
2520: last line corrupt.

cast.role: the hero, now a king, wedding Ilakkanai; called Sunandai's son in 2521
Govindan's daughter, Civakan's new bride; unnamed in these verses
the household parrot that threatens to hang itself to end the quarrel
the myna and parrot of the household, who plead for Civakan
the women of Ilakkanai's household, who scold the birds
the kings and armies who accompany Civakan in procession

reading: The bridegroom, whose body smells of ghee and whose chest is a flower, sinks into a sea of desire as the bed of flowers delights.
nuance: The first half-lines (a smoke-scented, ghee-touched young body) are hard to join, so the sense of the opening is taken from the closing line, where the man sinks in the sea of desire.
event: Civakan and his bride, on a flower couch, give themselves to love.

reading: The bride, clinging to the garlanded chest as lightning clings to the cloud that swallows it, is spent and lies like a vine that has dropped away.
nuance: Line 2 is obscure and the simile is read from lines 3 and 4 only.
event: The bride lies clasped to Civakan's chest and then goes slack.

reading: The garlanded man and the girl, not knowing it is wrong, delight in each other and lie on a silk bed on which incense smokes, drunk on the wine of love.
nuance: The words in line 2 (எய் உணர் வாமி தென்று அறியாது) could mean they do not know how the night passes or that they do not heed what is forbidden; the reading takes the first.
event: The pair lie together on the silk bed, drunk with desire.

tamil: மாதர்தன் வனப்பு நோக்கி மகிழ்ந்துகண் ணிமைத்தல் செல்லான்
காதலித் திருப்பக் கண்கள் கரிந்துநீர் வரக்கண் டம்ம
பேதைமை பிறரை யுள்ளி யழுபவர்ச் சேர்த வென்றாள்
வேதனை பெருகி வேற்கண் டீயுமிழ்ந் திட்ட வன்றே.
reading: Civakan gazes at her beauty without blinking until his eyes smart and water; she takes the tears for tears shed thinking of other women, says 'let this folly join those who weep for others', and her spear eyes spit fire in anguish.
nuance: Her accusation rests on a misreading: the tears come from not blinking at her, so the sulk is a lovers' quarrel the verse itself shows to be groundless.
event: Civakan's tears of rapt gazing make Ilakkanai suspect he is thinking of other women, and she flares in a sulk.

tamil: நாறுசாந் தழித்து மாலை பரிந்துநன் கலன்கள் சிந்திச்
சீறுபு செம்பொ னாழி மணிவிர னெரித்து விம்மா
வேறியு மிழிந்து மூழுழ் புருவங்கண் முரிய நொந்து
தேறுநீர் பூத்த செந்தா மரைமுகம் வியர்த்து நின்றாள்.
reading: Angry, she wipes off the sandal, snaps her garland, scatters her jewels, wrings the gold ring on her gem-like finger, sobs, lets her brows crinkle and stands with her lotus face sweating.
event: Ilakkanai tears off her ornaments in her sulk and stands sobbing.

tamil: இற்றதென் னாவி யென்னா வெரிமணி யிமைக்கும் பஞ்சிச்
சிற்றடிப் போது புல்லித் திருமகன் கிடப்பச் சேந்து
பொற்றதா மரையிற் போந்து கருமுத்தம் பொழிப் வேபோ
லுற்றுமை கலந்து கண்கள் வெம்பணி யுகுத்த வன்றே.
reading: The prince lies clasping her tender feet while her eyes, red as lamps, shed tears like black pearls, and she, her life as if broken, weeps with him.
nuance: The simile of tears like black pearls rests on a doubtful word in line 3 (பொழிப் வே).
event: Civakan falls at Ilakkanai's feet while she weeps.

tamil: கொண்டபூ ணின்னைச் சார்ந்து குலாய்க்கொழுந் தீன்ற கொம்பே
கண்டுகண் கரிந்து நீரா யுகுவது கரக்க லாமே
பண்டியான் செய்த பாவப் பயத்தையார்க் குரைப்பென் றேன்காள்
வண்டுகாள் வருடி நங்கை வரந்தர மொழிமி னென்றான்.
reading: Seeing the bough that bore the sprout weep from burning eyes, he asks whom he can tell the fruit of his old sin, and bids the bees stroke her and ask her to give him the boon.
nuance: The karma claim is a lover's figure of speech for an undeserved quarrel, not a teaching; and it is the husband, not the narrator, who blames an old deed for a wrong he has not done.
event: Civakan, unable to hide her tears, begs the bees to plead with her for forgiveness.

tamil: பூவையுங் கிளியுங் கேட்டுப் புழைமுகம் வைத்து நோக்கிக்
காவலன் மடந்தை யுள்ளங் கற்கொலோ விரும்பு கொல்லோ
சாவம்யா முருகி யொன்றுந் தவறில னருளு நங்கை
பாவையென் றிரத்து மென்ற பறவைக டம்முட் டாமே.
reading: The myna and the parrot, hearing, look through the cage-holes and say among themselves: is the king's daughter's heart stone or does it relent; we melt and the prince is faultless; let us beg our gracious lady.
nuance: In line 3 the words சாவம் யாம் உருகி are doubtful; the sense of pleading for the faultless man is taken from the whole verse.
event: The household parrot and myna, watching the quarrel, decide to plead for Civakan.

tamil: பெற்றகூ ழுண்டு நாளும் பிணியழந் திருத்தும் பேதாய்
முற்றிமை சொல்லி னங்கை மூன்றுநா ளடிசில் காட்டாள்
பொற்றொடி தத்தை யீரே பொத்துநும் வாயை யென்றே
கற்பித்தார் பூவை யார்தங் காரணக் கிளவி தம்மால்,
reading: The women, 'myna-like' with their reasoned words, scold the birds: you eat the food she gives every day and still dare to speak; if you say more she will show you no food for three days, so shut your mouths.
nuance: The speaker is taken to be the household women (பூவையார்); the word may instead denote the myna, so the speaker is not certain. The birds are addressed as தத்தை (parrot).
event: The women of the house silence the parrot and myna with the threat of withheld food.

tamil: பழியொடு மிடைந்த தேனுஞ் சீறடி பரவி னாற்கு
வழிபடு தெய்வ மாகி வரங்கொடுத் தருளல் வேண்டு
மொழிபடைக் களிறு போல வுயங்கவு முருகி நோக்காப்
பிழிசடு கோதை போலாம் பெண்டிரைக் கெடப்பி றந்தாள்.
reading: A speech that, though stained with blame, he who has worshipped her small feet asks that she become the goddess he serves and grant the boon, and that she cease to be like a tied elephant that melts and does not look back.
nuance: Line 4 (பிழிசடு கோதை போலாம் பெண்டிரைக் கெடப் பிறந்தாள்) does not parse and the speaker is inferred from the plea; the sense is not settled.
event: Civakan pleads with Ilakkanai in the language of worship.

tamil: ஈன்றதா யானு மாக விதனைக்கண் டுயிரை வாழே
னான்றியான் சாவ லென்றே நலக்கிளி நூலின் யாப்ப
மான்றவண் மருண்டு நக்காள் வாழிய வரம்பெற் றேனென்
றான்றவ னாரப் புல்லி யணிநலம் பரவி னானே.
reading: The parrot cries that even were it the bride's own mother it would not live to see this, and it will die, and ties itself with a thread; she, bewildered, laughs; he cries 'live long, I have won the boon', embraces her and praises her ornaments.
nuance: The sulk ends only when a third party, the pet, stages a death; neither of the lovers yields first.
event: The parrot's mock hanging breaks Ilakkanai's sulk and Civakan embraces her.

tamil: நிறையோத நீர்நின்று நீடவமே செய்யினும் வாழி நீல
மறையோ விரிவை வரிநெடுங்க ணொக்கிலையால் வாழி நீலங்
வண்ண மிதுவோ மதுவுண்பார் சேரியையோ வாழி நீலம்.
reading: Addressing the blue lily, he says it does not match her long dark eyes even if it stays in the flood in long penance, and asks whether its laughing colour is that, or the street of the wine-drinkers; long may the lily live.
nuance: The refrain வாழி நீலம் can be taken as a blessing to the lily or as a name; the verse is read as his praise of her eyes against the flower.

tamil: பாண்குலாய்ப் படுக்கல் வேண்டா பைங்கிளி பூவை யென்னு
மாண்பிலா தாரை வைத்தா ரென்னுறா ரென்று நக்கு
நாண்குலாய்க் கிடந்த நங்கை நகைமுக வமுத மீந்தாள்
பூண்குலாய்க் கிடந்த மார்பிற் பொன்னெடுங் குன்ற னாற்கே.
reading: The shy girl, laughing that the parrot and myna have blamed the faultless, gives the golden-chested lord the nectar of her smiling face, and no lute-song is needed to lay the quarrel to rest.
nuance: Line 1 (பாண் குலாய்ப் படுக்கல் வேண்டா) is obscure and is read as 'no song need be sung to soothe her'.
event: Ilakkanai laughs at the birds' scene and ends the sulk with a smile for Civakan.

tamil: நலங்குவித் தனைய மாதர் நன்னல மாய வெல்லாம்
புலம்புவித் தருளி னீங்கிப் பகைப்புலம் புக்க வேந்திற்
கலங்குவித் தனைய நம்பி கவர்ந்திடக் கலாப மேங்கச்
சிலம்புநொந் திரங்கத் தேன்றார் பரிந்துதே னெழுந்த தன்றே.
reading: Like a king who enters the hostile land and shakes it, the man shakes her beauty away; the peacock-like plume droops, her anklets weep and the honey-garland snaps so that honey runs.
nuance: The conquering-king simile in line 2 and 3 casts lovemaking as invasion of a foe; it is the poet's, and it sits oddly beside the sulk just ended.
event: Civakan and Ilakkanai make love, her garland and anklets breaking.

tamil: திருநிறக் காம வல்வி திருக்கவின் கொண்டு பூத்துப்
பெருநிறங் கவினி யார்ந்த கற்பகம் பிணைந்த தேபோ
லருநிறக் குருசின் மார்பத் தசைந்தன ளலங்கல் வேலு
நெரிபுறத் தடற்று வாளு நீலமு நிகர்த்த கண்ணாள்.
reading: Her eyes like spear, sword and blue lily, she clings to his broad chest as the kalpaka tree entwines the creeper of love that has flowered and grown lovely.
event: Ilakkanai clings to Civakan's chest after the reconciliation.

reading: The peacock-like woman and the lion-like king, bound by love and twined together, let the seven appointed days go by.
nuance: Line 2 (மணிக்கந் தன்னதோள்) is garbled in the edition; the seven days are clear from line 4.
event: The couple spend the seven days of the wedding together.

reading: They are anointed with sandal and powder and adorned with garland, gold thread and earrings, the pearl strings set about them.
nuance: The edition prints strange forms here (மோட்டி, மோட்டு) and the subject of the plural verb is taken to be the two.
event: The pair dress for the wedding ceremony after the seven days.

reading: He wears green silk, the garland on his chest and the line of ornaments, and to the deer-eyed women with their wondering look he becomes one who consumes their flesh and life together.
nuance: The last line (ஊனு யிருணு மொருவ னாயினான்) is corrupt; the sense given is only a guess.
event: Civakan dresses and is seen by the women.

reading: Sunandai's son, the bees drinking from the rutting streams of an elephant of three musths, mounts it while the bowed yak-tail fans and the conches sound.
nuance: Civakan is named as Sunandai's son, the foster mother who raised him, in the very verse in which he rides as a king.
event: Civakan mounts a state elephant with fans and conches.

tamil: இரும்பிடி நூறு சூழ விறுவரை நின்ற தேபோற்
கரும்பொடு காய்நெற் றுற்றிக் கருப்புரக் கந்தி னின்ற
சுரும்புசூழ் மதத்த சூளா மணியெனுஞ் சூழி யானைப்
பெருந்தகைப் பிணையன் மன்னர் முடிமிதித் தேறி னானே.
reading: On the elephant called Culamani, among a hundred cow elephants, laden with sugarcane and paddy, the garlanded king mounts treading on the crowns of kings.
nuance: The phrase மன்னர் முடிமிதித்தேறினான் may mean the kings bow so that he mounts over their crowns, or that he rides over them; it is read as a figure for their submission.
event: Civakan rides the elephant Culamani, the other kings' crowns beneath him.

tamil: சட்டகம் பொன்னிற் செய்து தண்கதிர் வெள்ளி வேய்ந்து
வட்டநல் வைரம் வாய்ப்ப நிறைத்துமேன் மணிகள் சேர்த்திச்
சுட்டுதற் கரிய முத்தின் றொத்துவாய் நாற்ற முந்நீர்ப்
பட்டவான் பவளக் காம்பின் குடைநிழற் பருதி யொத்தான்.
reading: His umbrella of gold, silver, diamond and pearl hung with coral stems makes him look like the sun in its shade.

tamil: மடற்பனைக் குழாத்திற் பிச்ச நிரைத்தன மன்னர் சூழ்ந்து
புடைக்களி றேறித் திங்கட் பொழிகதிர்க் குப்பை யன்ன
வெடுத்தெறி கவரி வீச வியம்பல முழங்கி யார்ப்பக்
கடற்படை வெள்ளஞ் சூழக் காவலன் வீதி சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: The kings crowd round with whisks while he rides an elephant like the moon pouring beams, with drums and shouts, and the king enters the street with his sea of troops.
event: Civakan, with the kings about him, enters the street in procession.

tamil: அடிநில முறுத னாணி யருவருத் தமரி னாலித்
திடுமயிர் சிறக ராக வெழுந்துமேற் பறப்ப போலப்
படுமழைத் துளியிற் பாய்மாப் பரந்தன நிரந்த பொற்றே
ரிடைநில மின்றி வேழ மீண்டின மள்ளர் தொக்கார்.
reading: Horses spread like rain, golden chariots fill the ground and elephants and warriors crowd without a gap.
nuance: Line 1-2, with the horse's hooves shamed by the ground and the hair flying like wings, is a stock simile and its grammar is loose.

tamil: கொழுமடற் பெண்ணை யீன்ற குரும்பையுஞ் செப்புங் கொன்ற
விழைமுலைத் தடத்தி னாடன் கணவனைக் காண வேகிக்
கழுமொலி யரவ வானங் கனைபெயல் கடற்பெய் தன்ன
குழுமொலி யரவ மீண்டிக் கொடிநகர் பொலிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The city of banners is loud like the sea that takes the rain as the women who have killed the palmyra's shoots with their breasts go to see her husband.
nuance: The subject in lines 1 and 2 is difficult and the identity of the woman who is said to go to see her husband is not settled.
event: The people go to see the bridegroom as the city roars.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2527-2550 (7/9)
theme: The city's women crowd the streets, jewelled, bewildered and shamed, to watch Civakan pass in procession, and in the last verses throw powder and flowers, praise him as Murugan's brother and Kama, and beg him with their eyes.
source_issues: 2527-2531, 2533-2546 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2538 line 2 போவான் has no named subject; 2541 line 1 and 2549 lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

cast.role: the hero, whom the city's women watch
the women of the city who throng to see Civakan
the young girls among the watchers
the maidens who dress before mirrors

tamil: ஒள்ளிலைச் சூலந் தெண்ணீ ருலாமுகில் கிழிக்கு மாடக்
கொள்கொடிக் குழாத்தி னாலுங் கொழுநறும் புகையி னாலுந்
தெள்ளுறு சுண்ணத் தாலுந் தேமலர்த் துகளி னாலும்
புள்ளினம் பொழுது காணா புலம்பிக்கூ டடைந்த வன்றே.
reading: The street is so thick with banner-staffs, perfumed smoke, fine powder and flower-pollen that the birds can no longer tell the time of day and gather in distress.
nuance: The scene opens the crowding of the city around the wedding day; nothing here names who is coming, so it is setting only.

tamil: பைந்தொடி மகளிர் பாங்கர் பரிந்துநூல் சொரிந்த காசு
சிந்தின தழலென் றஞ்சிச் சிறையன்ன நிலத்தைச் சேரா
விந்திர கோப மாமென் றிளமயில் குனிந்து குத்திச்
சிந்தையிற் றேம்பத் தாமே திருமணி நக்க வன்றே.
reading: Gems fall from the coin-strings the bangled women have loosed, and a young peahen, taking them for fire or for red velvet mites, shrinks from the ground and pecks at them till the jewels seem to laugh at her.
nuance: The peahen's mistake is the poet's proof of how much jewellery has been scattered: loss of ornament is shown as a bird's confusion, not a woman's grief.

tamil: வெள்ளைமை கலந்த நோக்கிற கிண்கிணி மிழற்றி யார்ப்பப்
பிள்ளைமை காதல் கூரப் பிறழ்ந்துபொற் றோடு வீழத்
துள்ளுபு செலபுஇய தோற்றந் தொடுகழற் காமன் காமத்
துள்ளுயி ரறியப் பெண்ணாய்ப் பிறந்ததோர் தோற்ற மொத்தார்.
reading: Girls with childish, innocent looks, anklets ringing and gold ear-ornaments slipping as they run, seem Kama himself born as a woman so that his heart could know desire.
nuance: The simile makes the girls the god of love's own experiment: he becomes female in order to feel what his arrows cause.

tamil: தன்னெறி வளரக் காமன் றான்முலை யிரண்டு மாகி
முன்னரே வளர்கின் றாற்போன் முகிழ்முலை முத்த மேந்திப்
பொன்னெறி மணியிற் பொங்கிக் குழல்புறம் புடைப்ப வோடிப்
பின்னிறீஇ வைத்த போலப் பெதும்பையர் விதும்பி நின்றார்.
reading: The budding girls, their pearl-strung young breasts swelling as though Kama himself were growing them, stand hurrying forward, their hair bulging behind, as if set there for show.
event: The young girls of the city press forward to see.

tamil: அணிநிலா வீசு மாலை யரங்குபுல் லென்னப் போகித்
துணிநிலா வீசு மாலைப் பிறைநுதற் றோழி சேர்ந்து
மணிநிலா வீசு மாலை மங்கையர் மயங்கி நின்றார்
பணிநிலா வீசும் பைம்பொற் கொடிமணி மலர்ந்த தொத்தார்.
reading: The long evening, with its moonlight, leaves the stage empty; the women, joined by friends with crescent brows, stand bewildered in the jewel-lit dusk like a golden creeper hung with bright gems.
nuance: Mayakkam (bewilderment) here is the desire the sight is about to cause; the verse prepares for the women's eager speeches in the last four verses.
event: Women gather in the evening, bewildered, to see the procession.

tamil: வள்ளுகிர் வரித்த சாந்தின் வனமுலை நோக்கி னாரை
யுள்ளுயி ருண்ணுங் கூற்றி னுடன்றுகண் கரிந்து பொங்கக்
கள்ளுயி ருண்ணு மாலைக் கதுப்பொரு கையி னேந்தி
நள்ளிருள் விளக்கிட் டன்ன நங்கைமார் மல்கி னாரே.
reading: Women with nail-marked sandal-paste on their breasts, their eyes burning and darkening at those who look at them, hold their wreathed hair aside with one hand and fill the street like lamps lit in the middle of the night.
nuance: The hostile figure of Death eating life, borrowed for their glance, turns an angry eye into an erotic one, as the Kural does for a woman's eyes.
event: Women crowd the street, lit with jewels.

tamil: மட்டொளித் துண்ணு மாந்தர் மாண்புபோன் மறைந்து வண்ணப்
பட்டொளித் தொழிய வல்குற் பசுங்கதிர்க் கலாபந் தோன்றக்
குட்டநீர்க் குவளைக் கண்கள் விருந்துண விரும்பி நின்றா
ரட்டுந்தே னணிந்த மாலைப் பவளக்கொம் பணிந்த தொத்தார்.
reading: Women hide their silk and show their jewelled girdles as drinkers hide their cups, and stand eager to give their blue-lily eyes a feast of the sight, like a coral branch hung with honeyed garlands.
event: Women wait with eyes ready for the sight.

tamil: பெரும்பொரு ணீதிச் செங்கோற் பெருமக னாக்கம் போலப்
பரந்திட மின்றி மேலாற் படாமுலை குவிந்த கீழா
லரும்பொரு ணீதி கேளா வரசனிற் சுருங்கி நந்து
மருங்குநொந் தொழிய வீதி மடந்தைய ரிடங்கொண் டாரே.
reading: The women make room in the street by stepping back, their breasts firm and not sagging, like the wealth of a just ruler that has no free space above and shrinks below, or like a king who will not hear justice.
nuance: The sceptre doctrine is not the subject; it is the measure of a breast's firmness. The line shows a poet could assume a just king and an unjust king as a common yardstick for shape.
event: Women step back and take places along the street.

tamil: செல்வர்க்கே சிறப்புச் செய்யுந் திருந்துநீர் மாந்தர் போல
வல்குற்கு முலைக்கு மீந்தா ரணிகல மாய வெல்லா
நல்கூர்ந்தார்க் கில்லை சுற்ற மென்றுநுண் ணுசுப்பு நைய
வொல்கிப்போய் மாடஞ் சேர்ந்தா ரொருதடங் குடங்கைக் கண்ணார்.
reading: As people honour only the rich, the women give their jewels only to hips and breasts, saying the poor have no kin, and withdraw with waists worn thin into the houses, a pair of big-eyed women among them.
nuance: The world's partiality towards wealth is used as a simile for the way the body's rich parts take the jewels while the waist is neglected.
event: Women return to their houses, leaving the waist unadorned.

tamil: கார்வளர் மின்னு வீசுங் குண்டலங் காய்பொ னோலை
யேர்வளர் பட்ட மேற்ப வணிந்திருள் சுமந்து திங்க
ணீர்வளர் நீலம் பூத்து நிரைத்தபோ னிரைத்த மேலால்
வார்வளர் முலையி னார்த மாழைவாண் முகங்கண் மாதோ.
reading: Ear-rings bright as cloud-lightning, gold ear-leaves and a forehead ornament frame the faces of the full-breasted women, who look like a moon bearing darkness with blue lilies in a pool set in rows above.

tamil: குறையணி கொண்ட வாறே கோதைகா றொடர வோடிச்
சிறையழி செம்பொ னுந்தித் தேன்பொழிந் தொழுக வேந்திப்
பறையிசை வண்டு பாடப் பாகமே மறைய நின்றார்
பிறையணி கொண்ட வண்ணல் பெண்ணொர்பால் கொண்ட தொத்தார்.
reading: With their garlands dragging, wreaths half arranged, honey pouring from gold-edged buds as bees drone, the women stand half hidden, like the crescent-crowned god taking a woman into one half of himself.
nuance: Civakan's own faith is Jain; the simile uses the Saiva Ardhanarisvara figure, a poet's image without doctrinal claim.
event: Women stand half-hidden behind the crowd.

tamil: பொன்னரி மாலை பூண்டு பூஞ்சிகை குலாவி முன்கை
மின்னரிச் சிலம்பு தொட்டு விருப்பொடு விரைந்து போவான்
கன்னிய ராடி நோக்கித் தம்மைத்தாங் கண்டு நாணிப்
பின்னவை யணிந்து செல்வா ரிடம்பெறா தொழிந்து போனார்.
reading: A man hurrying forward with his gold-streaked garland, flower-topped hair and anklets is watched by maidens who, after looking at themselves in mirrors, grow ashamed, put on more adornments, and fail to find a place.
nuance: The hurrying man is probably Civakan himself, but the verse does not name him; the sense of who is seen by whom turns on the unclear subject of போவான்.
event: Maidens look in mirrors, grow ashamed, and put on more jewels, but find no room in the crowd.

tamil: முத்துலாய் நடந்த கோல முலைமுதன் முற்ற மெல்லாம்
வித்திய வேங்கை வீயும் விழுப்பொனும் விளங்கக் காமத்
தொத்துநின் றெரிந்து கண்டார் கண்சுடச் சுடர்ந்து நின்றா
ரொத்தொளிர் காம வல்லி யொருங்குபூத் துதிர்ந்த தொத்தார்.
reading: Pearls swinging on their breasts, the courtyards before their houses strewn with gold, and the women glowing so that the sight burns the eyes of those who see them, like a desire-creeper flowering all at once and shedding.
event: Women stand blazing with jewels in the courtyards.

tamil: உகிர்வினை செய்து பஞ்சி யொள்ளொளி யரத்த மூட்டி
யகில்கம ழங்கை சேப்ப வரிவைய ரலங்க றாங்கி
வகிர்படு மழைக்கண் சின்னீர் மாக்கய லெதிர்ந்த வேபோன்
முகில்கிழி மின்னி னோக்கி முரிந்திடை குழைந்து நின்றார்.
reading: Women with nails reddened with lac and fingers glowing, arms perfumed with aloe, stand bending at the waist under their jewels, their eyes looking like carp glancing at the lightning in the cloud.
event: Women stand dressed, waists bent, looking.

tamil: முனித்தலைக் கண்ணி நெற்றிச் சிறார்முலை முழாலிற் பில்கிப்
புனிற்றுப்பால் பிலிற்றித் தேமா வடுவிறுத் தாங்குப் பாய
நுனிந்துக்கண் ணரக்கி நோக்கா தொசிந்துநின் றார்க ளன்றே
கனிப்பொறை மலிந்து நின்ற கற்பகப் பூங்கொம் பொத்தார்
reading: Girls with milk still springing from their breasts, as a mango's juice springs from a broken unripe fruit, stand with narrowed painted eyes, not looking, bent like a wishing-tree branch heavy with fruit.
nuance: The verse's picture of milk springing from the girls' breasts is obscure in line 1; the sense is of fullness, not nursing in a plot sense.
event: Women stand bent, not looking straight.

tamil: அவிரிழை சுடர முல்லை யலங்கலங் கூந்தல் சோரத்
தவிர்வெய்ய காமந் தாங்கித் தடமுலைக் கால்கள் சாய
விவர்தரு பிறவி யெல்லா மின்னமா கென்று நின்றார்
சுவர்செய்தாங் கெழுதப் பட்ட துகிலிகைப் பாவை யொத்தார்.
