reading: With bright ornaments flashing, jasmine garlands slipping from their hair and their full breasts sinking under the load of desire, the women stand wishing that all their births to come be like this, like painted dolls on a wall.
nuance: The wish for all births to be as this one treats rebirth as given and wants to repeat it, not to escape it, the opposite of the work's Jain end in release.
event: Women, overcome by desire, wish for the same lot in every birth.

tamil: வேரிநா றலங்கன் மாலை மின்னிழை மயங்கி யெங்கும்
பூரித்துப் புதவந் தோறுங் குவளையு மரையும் பூத்துப்
மாரிமா மயில னாரு மைந்தரு மயங்கி னாரே.
reading: Women with bright garlands and fine peacock-like looks, and young men, are all in confusion together, as if a golden world of nagas had fallen here, blossoming blue lilies and red lotuses in every gate.
event: Women and young men mingle, confused.

tamil: கோதைதாழ் குடையி னீழற் கொற்றவன் பருதி யாக
மாதரார் முகங்க ளென்னுந் தாமரை மலர்ந்த தெண்ணீர்க்
காதநான் ககன்ற பொய்கைக் கடிநகர் குவளை பூத்துப்
பேதுறு கின்ற போன்ற பெருமழைக் கண்கண் மாதோ.
reading: With the king who wears a hanging-garland umbrella as the sun, the women's faces open like lotuses in a clear pond four leagues wide, and the great eyes seem like blue lilies dazed in the fortress-city.
nuance: The king as sun making women's faces open is a court image of the king as the one who causes the city to bloom.

tamil: மாந்தரு மாவுஞ் செல்ல மயங்கிமே லெழுந்த நீறு
தேந்தரு கோதை யார்தந் தெண்மட்டுத் துவலை மாற்ற
வாய்ந்தபொன் னகர மெங்கு மணிகல வொளியி னாலே
காய்ந்துகண் கலக்கப் பூத்த கற்பக மொத்த தன்றே
reading: Dust raised by men and elephants moving in confusion is laid by the honey-drops from the women's garlands, and the golden city, glittering with jewels, seems to flower like a wishing tree.
event: The women's garland-drops lay the dust of the passing procession.

tamil: பெண்பெற்ற பொலிசை பெற்றார் பிணையனார் பெரிய யாமுங்
கண்பெற்ற பொலிசை பெற்றா மின்றெனக் கரைந்து முந்நீர்
மண்பெற்ற வாயுள் பெற்று மன்னுவாய் மன்ன வென்னாப்
புண்பெற்ற வேலி னான்மேற் பூமழை தூவி னாரே.
reading: The women say that Pinaiyanar has gained a daughter's wealth and that they themselves have gained eyes this day, and shower flowers on the spear-wounded hero, wishing him a life long as the sea-girt earth.
nuance: Who Pinaiyanar is - the bride's father or another - the verse does not say; it is a doubtful name for a speaker or object of praise.
event: The women bless Civakan and shower flowers on him as he passes.

reading: The women pour powder over him, bow and drop garlands, throw balls full of sandal water and honey, hurl garlands that are tied into wreaths, and sprinkle scented water as he passes.
event: The women pelt Civakan with powder, balls and garlands as a mark of welcome.

reading: The women say he is Murugan's younger brother, Anangan with five arrows, a lion fed by Kandukkan; they are glad in their hearts, their long eyes fixed on him.
nuance: The comparison with Murugan echoes the kings' battle cry in 812, but then it was fear of the one who beat them; here it is longing.
event: The women name him in praise as Murugan's brother, Kama and a reared lion.

reading: With turbans and silks slipping so they hang as ropes, and flowers and garlands falling, the women speak a flawless desire and beg him with their eyes.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe: தேசிகம் and பாசம் may name the headdress and ropes of cloth; the begging with the eyes is clear.
event: The women beg Civakan with their eyes, their clothes slipping.

reading: After seeing the garlanded one's looks, they say they have lost their own bloom with their bangles, and live seeing his form, praising the women who were born as women as great.
event: The women declare that they have lost their bloom and bangles, and live by gazing at him.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2551-2574 (8/9)
theme: The women and people of the city praise Civakan and argue for tapas; he worships the Jina in his temple with hymns and an endowment, then sits among kings and pays out his debts of land, rule and wealth to brother, friends, nurses, kin and uncle, and builds a golden memorial for the friend who saved him.
source_issues: 2573 line 1 reads corrupt: நீக்கிப் யாய is short and the word பயாய is not a word as printed.
2551-2554, 2558-2560, 2567-2572 and 2573-2574 print as 8 half-lines joined into 4 (the tool's repair).
2561-2563 repeat the second line's words in the third; this is the stanza form, not doubling.

cast.role: the hero, now victor and king
the women of the city who praise Civakan
the people of the city, here arguing for tapas
Civakan's younger brother
Civakan's companions
kings related to Civakan by marriage
king of Videham, Civakan's maternal uncle
the nurses who brought up Civakan

tamil: கொழித்திரை யோத வேலிக் குமரனைப் பயந்த நங்கை
விழுத்தவ முலக மெல்லாம் விளக்கிநின் றிட்ட தென்பார்
பிழிப்பொலி கோதை போலாம் பெண்டிரிற் பெரிய ணோற்றாள்
கழித்துநின் றறாத கற்பிற் சுநந்தையே யாக வென்பார்.
reading: The women of the city say that the woman who bore the prince has by her great austerity lit up the whole world, and that the greatest vow among women must be Sunandai's, whose chastity never broke.
nuance: The verse echoes the street talk in 465, where the people ask what penance Civakan's mother did. Whether the first woman (the one who bore him) and Sunandai (who raised him) are one or two is not settled by the words, so the praise may belong to either.

tamil: சாந்தகங் கிழிய மாலைத் தடமுலை ஞெமுங்கப் புல்லிச்
சேர்ந்தெழு நங்கை மாரே திருநங்கை மார்க ளல்லார்
கூந்தலு முலையு முத்துங் கோதையுஞ் சுமந்து நைவான்
போந்தவந் நங்கை மார்கள் பொய்ந்நங்கை மார்க ளென்பார்.
reading: The women say that those women who press against him, crushing their sandalled breasts and garlands as they cling, are not truly fortunate women but false ones, bearing hair, breasts, pearls and garlands only to waste away.
nuance: It is unclear whether the speakers mock rival women or pity them; the sense of the last two lines (போந்த அந்நங்கைமார்கள் பொய்ந்நங்கைமார்கள்) turns on that.

tamil: இடம்பட வகன்று நீண்ட விருமலர்த் தடங்க ணென்னுங்
குடங்கையி னொண்டு கொண்டு பருகுவார் குவளைக் கொம்பி
னுடம்பெலாங் கண்க ளாயி னொருவர்க்கு மின்றி யேற்ப
வடங்கவாய் வைத்திட் டாரப் பருகியிட் டீமி னென்பார்.
reading: The women urge one another to drink in his beauty, their wide dark eyes cupped like palms, each taking her fill so that none is left out.
nuance: The third line sets a vine-woman whose whole body became eyes against the sharing; the exact turn of the thought is hard to fix.

tamil: முலைமுத றுறத்த வன்றே மூரித்தா ளாளி யானைத்
தலைநிலம் புரள வெண்கோ டுண்டதே போன்று தன்கைச்
சிலையிடம் பிடித்த ஞான்றே தெவ்வரைச் செகுத்த நம்பி
நிலவுமிழ் குடையி னீழற் றுஞ்சுக வைய மென்பார்.
reading: The women say that from the day he left the breast, as a lion tears the tusks from the head of a fallen elephant, he slew his foes the moment he took up the bow, and that the world may now sleep in the shade of his moon-bright umbrella.

They say that anyone who sees how he was born in this city's burning ground, how he grew up as a matchless merchant's son, and how kings have come to worship him must ask why one should live heedless instead of doing penance.
nuance: Civakan's rise from the burning ground (304) is made here into an argument for tapas, in the epic's own mouth, before the last ilampakam where he does take it up. The subject of the last line (the city folk, or each hearer, or Civakan himself) is not fixed by the verse.

tamil: மொரு முழமுஞ் சேறலில ரேனும் பொரு ளூர்க்கே
reading: The speakers say that, however a man crosses roaring seas and mountains and suffers sickness, wealth does not come without fortune's favour, while it may come home to those who go not a cubit; so let tapas be taken up with effort.
nuance: The Tamil of lines 3 and 4 (the words after ஒருமுழமும் சேறலிலரேனும்) is hard, and the verse's speaker is taken from the neighbouring verses; read it as a loose argument from fortune to tapas.

reading: They say that one strong in tapas takes no harm even from poison and escapes even from between a mighty elephant's tusks, whereas once tapas is spent no hiding in fear saves; so the fearless, with dharma as their refuge, are those rich in tapas.
nuance: The words ஆணில்லை and களைகண் are rare, and both the grammar of line 2 and the sense of the closing phrase are read from the whole stanza.

tamil: முரல்வாய சூற்சங்க முடமுட் டாழை முகைவிம் முங்
reading: Passing through the city amid its praise, the lord of the shore goes to the temple of the king of the flowering pindi tree, which the verse sets round with pearl-bearing conches and screwpine on the sea's edge.
nuance: The one who goes is called கடற்சேர்ப்பன் (lord of the shore), an unusual title for Civakan; he is taken as Civakan because the next verses show him worship and endow the temple. The pindi (asoka) tree is the Jina's tree.
event: Civakan goes in procession to the Jina's temple.

reading: In the flowery grove, where peacocks dance, swans cry and koels call, he puts aside his weapons and arrives at the golden temple of the one with the twisted, resounding anklet.
nuance: The verse does not say why he lays down arms; the step before the shrine reads as a mark of reverence.
event: Civakan sets aside his guard and reaches the golden temple.

reading: Circling the gem-doored shrine thick with aloe smoke, the king of kings says that he has been born, will not be born again, and has found the one who is not born; then bows, shakes his head in praise and worships with his hands.
nuance: The claim is made by the hero in worship and rests on reaching the unborn one; the verse does not say the Jina acts to free him.
event: Civakan circles the Jina's shrine and worships, declaring that his births end.

reading: They hymn the one with the sacred mark on his chest and the three-umbrella crest, father of the sages who bear the rare scripture, and say they worship his fire-bright lotus feet.
nuance: The stanza is built by repeating its second line's words in the third (as 2562 and 2563 do), a hymn form and not a text fault; the 'we' (தொழுதும்) leaves it open whether Civakan sings alone or with his company.

reading: They hymn the god who knows the world, of fearful might, whose path is unequalled in its moon-bright ornament, and worship his lotus feet.
nuance: Built like 2561, with the second line's words repeated in the third.

reading: They hymn the one who understood without fault, the wheel that removes stain, the lord of merit who set bounds to the senses, and worship his fragrant lotus feet.
nuance: Built like 2561, with the second line's words repeated in the third.

tamil: நொந்தார்க் கடந்தான் கொடுத்தான் பின்னை நூறு மூதூர்
reading: Civakan lays at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus an endowment of four crore, a hundred old towns, rutting tuskers and a hundred flagged chariots, that the lamp which never fails may be kept.
nuance: The opening of line 2 (நொந்தார்க் கடந்தான் கொடுத்தான்) can be read as a gift to the afflicted or as a clause about the foe-conqueror; and 'புறம்' for the lamp is read as its endowment.
event: Civakan endows the Jina's temple with gold, towns, elephants and chariots.

reading: He offers garlands that never fade, of gems, gold, pearl and coral, hung so that they fall like streams, then the foe-conqueror circles the shrine and goes on to his own place.
event: Civakan offers garlands, circles the shrine and goes on.

tamil: உலமரு நெஞ்சி னொட்டா மன்னவ ரூர்ந்த யானை
வலமருப் பீர்ந்து செய்த மணிகிளர் கட்டி லேறி
நிலமகள் கணவன் வேந்தர் குழாத்திடை நிவந்தி ருந்தான்
புலமகள் புகழப் பொய்தீர் பூமகட் புணர்ந்து மாதோ.
reading: Seated on a couch of gems made from the right tusks of the elephants his enemies rode, the lord of the earth sits raised among the kings, praised by the goddess of learning and joined to faultless Fortune.
nuance: The couch turns the defeated kings' own elephants into his seat.
event: Civakan sits among the kings on a couch made of the enemy's elephant tusks.

tamil: எத்துணைத் தவஞ்செய் தான்கொ லென்றெழுந் துலக மேத்த
வித்திய புகழி னாற்கு விருந்தர சியற்றி நாடு
மொத்தன னல்கித் தன்னை யுழந்தனள் வளர்த்த தாய்க்குச்
சித்திரத் தேவிப் பட்டந் திருமக னல்கி னானே.
reading: While the world rises to ask what penance the man must have done, he gives a feast of rule and a share of land to the one of famed repute, and gives the Chittiratevi title to the mother who toiled to raise him.
nuance: The world's cry 'what penance did he do!' recalls the Kural's phrase for a son's repayment to his father (kural:70), but with different words; the verse does not name who receives the feast or which mother is meant (Sunandai is the nurse named in 2551).
event: Civakan gives land and rule to the famed one and the queen's title to the mother who raised him.

tamil: இனக்களி யானை மன்ன ரிளவுடை யானென் றேத்தத்
தனக்கிளை யானை நாட்டித் தான்றனக் கென்று கூறிச்
சினக்களி யானை மன்னர் மகளிரைச் சேர்த்தி நம்பன்
மனக்கினி துறைக வென்று வளங்கெழு நாடு மீந்தான்.
reading: At the kings' praise he installs his younger brother as the heir, calls him his own, joins him to kings' daughters and gives him a rich land, bidding him live as he pleases.
nuance: The title இளவுடையான் is read as heir or the younger one; the brother is Nandattan only by inference from the story.
event: Civakan sets up his younger brother with a kingdom and royal brides.

tamil: ஆழ்கடல் வையத் தில்லா வருநிதி யரசு நல்ல
சூழ்மணி யாழி செம்பொற் சூட்டொடு கண்ணி காதற்
றோழர்கட் கருளித் தொல்லை யுழந்தவர் தம்மைத் தோன்ற
வாழ்கென நிதியு நாடு மன்னவன் கொடுப்பித் தானே.
reading: The king gives his dear friends, who suffered long with him, a rule and treasure unmatched on earth, with gem ring, gold crest and garland, and bids them live.
event: Civakan gives his companions treasure and a country.

tamil: வளர்த்தகைத் தாயர் தம்மை வருகென வருளித் தங்கள்
கிளைக்கெலாஞ் சிறப்புச் செய்து கேட்டவர் மருள வைந்தூர்
விளைத்துள கெடாத வைக லாயிர மிறுப்புத் தண்டக்
கொளக்கொடுத் தயா வுயிர்த்தான் கொற்றவ னென்ப வன்றே.
reading: He calls the nurses who reared him, honours their kin, and to the amazement of the hearers gives five villages and a thousand days of produce with the right to levy dues, and the king breathes easy.
nuance: The last two lines turn on இறுப்புத் தண்டக் கொள; the grant is read as the right to collect dues.
event: Civakan rewards the nurses and their families with villages and dues.

tamil: கைத்தல மந்தி கொண்ட கைமகப் போன்று தன்கட்
பத்திமை விடாது மேனாட் படைக்கல நவின்ற பொற்றேர்
மைத்துன மன்னர்க் கெல்லாம் வளநிதி மணிசெய் மான்றேர்
தத்துநீர் மிசைச்சென் மாவுந் தவழ்மதக் களிறு மீந்தான்.
reading: To the kings of his marriage-kin, who clung to him in devotion like the young held by a monkey and had trained with him in arms, he gives gold chariots, wealth, gem-wrought horse chariots, sea-going horses and rutting elephants.
event: Civakan gives chariots, horses and elephants to his kinsmen kings.

tamil: கோமகன் கோல மான்றேர்க் கோவிந்த னென்னுங் கொய்தார்
மாமற்கு மடங்க லாற்றற் கட்டியங் கார னென்ற
தீமக னுடைய வெல்லாந் தேர்ந்தனன் கொடுத்துச் செல்வ
னோவலில் கறவை யொத்தா னுலோகபா லற்கு மாதோ.
reading: Having picked out all that belonged to Kattiyangaran, the wicked son of lion-like strength, he gives it to his uncle Govindan, king of fine chariots, and stays like an inexhaustible cow even to the guardian of the world.
event: Civakan gives the usurper's goods to his uncle Govindan.

tamil: கோரிடஞ் செய்து பொன்னா லவனுரு வியற்றி யூரும்
பாரிடம் பரவ நாட்டி யவனது சரிதை யெல்லாந்
தாருடை மார்பன் கூத்துத் தான்செய்து நடாயி னானே.
reading: For the friend who lifted a great trouble from him he makes a place, has his likeness wrought in gold and set up so that the city and the land praise it, and himself has the friend's whole story made into a dance.
nuance: The first line reads corrupt (நீக்கிப் யாய). The friend is taken as Sudanjanan, the god who was once the dog Civakan helped (945) and who carried him from trouble, but the verse never names him.
event: Civakan sets up a golden image and a dance of his friend's story.

tamil: ஊன்விளை யாடும் வைவே லுறுவலி சிந்தித் தேற்பத்
தான்விளை யாடி மேனா ளிருந்ததோர் தகைநல் லாலைத்
தேன்விளை யாடு மாலை யணிந்துபொற் பீடஞ் சேர்த்தி
யான்விளை யாடு மைந்தூ ரதன்புற மாக்கி னானே.
reading: Thinking of the strength of his sharp spear, he decks with honey-dripping garlands the fine place where he used to play, sets a golden seat there, and makes five villages its surround.
nuance: The noun ஆலை is read as a hall or workplace and not a mill, and what the place was is not fixed by this verse.
event: Civakan adorns the place of his old play and endows it with five villages.

title: இலக்கணையார் இலம்பகம் 2575-2598 (9/9)
theme: The eight wives are crowned and the land flourishes under Civakan's single umbrella; then the dancer Anangamalai, whom the usurper once seized, comes to the king with a letter that recalls her devotion, and he receives her, enjoys her dance and takes her to bed.
source_issues: 2582-2583 and 2584-2598 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2587 lines 3-4 (கந்து கற்குச் சிறுவயானிப் படிய னல்காய்) are hard to construe, and 2590 line 3 (வந்தவென் றோழி வாமலேகை) leaves the reason for the friend's naming unclear.
2593 line 2 (தெருளலான்) and 2594 line 4 (அறியுநாடகங் கண்டான்) are doubtful in sense, and 2594 line 2 (நெறியின்வட்டித்து) is obscure.
2582 line 1 (செருநாடு ... திருநாடு) reads as names or epithets of lands; the sense is not fixed.

cast.role: the hero, now king
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina
the dancer who loves Civakan, once seized by the usurper; named அநங்க மாலை in 2584
Civakan's eight wives, here crowned
the kings subject to Civakan
the women who bring sandal, garlands and incense to the couple
the dead usurper, recalled in Anangamalai's letter as the cruel spearman (2587)

reading: The eight women with swollen breasts like lotus buds and honey-dripping garlands reach the rank of crowned queens, and the world bows to them.
nuance: The verse does not name the eight; they are read as the wives Civakan has won in the earlier ilampakams, the last being Ilakkanai.
event: Civakan's eight wives attain the crowned rank and are honoured by all.

reading: Women with soft hair and bud-opening garlands fall at the small feet of the Vidyadhara's daughter.
nuance: Neither the bowing women nor the Vidyadhara's daughter is named. She is taken to be Gandharvadattai, whom the poem has called a Vidyadhara's daughter, set first among the wives; the bowers may be the other wives or her maids.
event: The women of the household bow at the feet of the Vidyadhara's daughter.

reading: Civakan settles on the wives an unfailing income of five and a half crore, with a thousand a day, so that bathing, sandal and cooking are provided for.
nuance: The sum and the line about daily provision (ஆயிர நாடொறு) are hard to fix: the verse may count a yearly revenue, or an endowment paid daily. Only the fact of a settled provision is certain.
event: Civakan assigns the women a fixed endowment for their daily needs.

reading: The forests where elephants once ran in rut now ring with deer-eyed women drinking, and the scorched lands the white chariot crossed are flooded with milk-rice.
nuance: The verse says only that wild and dry lands turned to plenty and pleasure under the king; the cause is left to the surrounding verses on his rule.

reading: With rain abundant the earth-woman brims past her bounds, and ghee-rich food lies in lakes everywhere.
nuance: The last line is closed with என்பவே, 'they say': the poet gives the plenty as report, not as sight.

reading: Under his single white umbrella the cool shade of his grace reaches the sea, so that the lands of effortless enjoyment, the golden land and the serpents' world are ashamed and withdraw.
nuance: போக பூமி is the Jain cosmos's land of enjoyment without labour. The verse uses it as a measure for praise; it does not teach cosmology here.

reading: Fish-eyed women and their husbands eat, grow old and travel without hindrance, so the earth is as full as in the first age.
nuance: பண்டை யூழி, 'the ancient age', is the poet's name for a golden age; the verse does not say which.

reading: Lords of battle lands and prosperous lands cannot get audience and find no room for the rare ornaments they carry as tribute; the kings of single lands bow, and the able lord's victory stands high.
nuance: The names in line 1 (செருநாடு, திருநாடு) may be regions or epithets of kings; the verse is a figure of crowded homage either way.
event: Subject kings queue with tribute for an audience with Civakan.

tamil: வலையவர் முன்றிற் பொங்கி வாளென வாளை பாயச்
நிலைதிரிந் தூழி நீங்கி யுத்தர குருவு மாகிக்
கொலைகடிந் திவற வின்றிக் கோத்தொழி னடத்து மன்றே.
reading: As fish leap in the fishers' yards and deer fatten on the hunters' ground, the age turns, becomes like Uttarakuru, banishes killing and miserliness, and goes on under one ruler.
nuance: Uttarakuru is a land of effortless enjoyment in Jain and Buddhist cosmology. The poet sets the king's peace beside it; he does not say that the cosmic age itself has changed.

tamil: கதங்கனல் யானை நெற்றிக் கட்டிய பட்ட மேபோன்
மதங்கமழ் கோதை யல்குன் மனாக்கிடந் திமைத்துக் காமப்
பதம்பல பார்க்குஞ் சாயற் பாவைமற் றநங்க மாலை
விதம்படக் கருதி மாதர் விளைத்தது விளம்ப லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet says he will tell what the doll-like dancer Anangamalai brought about, whose hair lies on her hip like the gold fillet bound on a rutting elephant's brow and who watches for the moments of love.
nuance: This is the poet's turn from praise of the reign to the dancer's story, in the first person (உற்றேன்).

tamil: றார்ந்த செந்தா மரைமுகத்தினா ளடிகள்வந்தீங் ககன்கடை யுளாள்
சார்ந்த சாயற் றடமாமுலைத் தையல்வல்லே வருகென் றான்
சேர்ந்து மன்னர் முடிவைரவிற் றிளைக்குஞ் செம்பொற் செறிகழலினான்.
reading: Civakan, whose gold anklets are rubbed by the diamonds of kings' crowns, calls to the lotus-faced young woman who said she would reach her lord's feet and now stands at the outer gate, to come quickly.
nuance: The verse never names the woman; she is Anangamalai because the letter that follows is hers (2586-2590) and 2584 has just announced her.
event: Civakan has Anangamalai, waiting at the gate, called in.

tamil: விரவி யென்ன விளங்குமொளி யிறைவன் கொண்டாங் கதுநோக்குமே.
reading: Anangamalai, ashamed like a swan, slips in, bows at the king's feet, folds her slender hands and hands over a letter in the proper manner; he takes it and reads.
event: Anangamalai presents Civakan with a written letter and he reads it.

tamil: கடிசெய் பைந்தார்க் கமழ்மாலைவேற் கந்து கற்குச் சிறுவயானிப்
reading: The letter asks the lord to see it and be pleased, and recalls that, after she had once bowed to him and the cruel spearman in rage had thrown her out of the stage and put her under guard in the temple, she, a girl bound to Kantukkatan, is asked to be granted a favour.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are not fully construable: whether கந்து கற்கு (Kantukkatan's) is the girl's foster-bond, and what is asked, remain unsettled. Line 2 is read as the usurper's anger after her glance at Civakan (685).
event: Anangamalai's letter recalls her bowing to Civakan and the usurper's punishment of her.

tamil: தன்னந் துஞ்சு மடிக்குடிலினுள் ளன்றியான் கொண்ட நாடகத்தினைத்
மன்னர் மன்ன மதிதோய்குடையாய் மகளிர்காம மறைத்தொழி தியோ.
reading: The letter goes on that, released because he could no longer bear her crying, she kept to a thatched hut among crowing birds, painted Civakan's image, garlanded and worshipped it; and it asks the king of kings whether he will hide women's love.
nuance: The letter is her own account; the poem has shown her devotion only through her letter. The verse's last clause is a plea, not a proven wrong.
event: Anangamalai writes that she worshipped a painted image of Civakan and asks him not to ignore her.

tamil: பண்கொள் சொல்லார் மாமைநீங்கிப் பைம்பொன் போர்த்த படாமுலைகளு
reading: She asks whether the world is to be told that the king lacks friendship, whether women are to give up their lives, and whether those who reach the friendship of the great go away.
nuance: The first three lines describe her wasting: sleepless eyes, loosened bangles and anklets, lost sheen of the body. They are the cost she lays before him, not a narrative.

reading: Standing under the umbrella that gives the world the shade of dharma, she asks whether she is outside it, and begs the king of kings to grant release now, so that the standing of her friend Vamalekai, who came with her, may not be ruined.
nuance: The claim is her appeal, not the narrator's. What is to be released, and why Vamalekai is named, is unclear: the verse says only that the friend's standing depends on it.
event: Anangamalai petitions Civakan under the figure of his umbrella.

reading: On a gold bed made by a skilled craftsman while birds, lute and flute sound, Civakan holds the flower-creeper whose sweet words take the lute's voice, his shoulders swelling and his ear-ornament swinging.
nuance: The woman is not named; she is Anangamalai from the sequence of the letter.
event: Civakan embraces Anangamalai on the royal bed.

reading: Women bring sandal ground on coral stones, flower garlands, thick scented smoke and five-fold perfumes to the garland-chested king and to the woman.
nuance: The attendants and the couple are known only from the context.
event: Attendants bring Civakan and Anangamalai perfumes, sandal and garlands.

reading: Civakan says to Anangamalai that in the delight of wealth he said confused words that measured her mind, and asks how he could forget her; the woman with rolling pearl breasts shows her joy.
nuance: The verse is hard to divide: the question in line 1 and the confession of lines 2-3 are read as the king's, but the speaker is not named.
event: Civakan assures Anangamalai that he has not forgotten her, and she rejoices.

reading: With her moon-like smile, her bent brows, her darting long eyes, and the sounds of her anklets and girdle in time with the music, the dancer plays before the king, who watches the play, his garland opening and her charm melting.
nuance: The king's name வேந்தன் is split across lines 3 and 4, so the agent is tagged by the verb கண்டான்.
event: Anangamalai dances before Civakan, who watches.

reading: Like a four-tusked rutting elephant playing with a lotus-lady, Civakan takes the beauty of the Fortune-like woman while the spear-eyed women praise, and so goes on, the lord of jewels without equal in heaven or on earth.
event: Civakan lives in pleasure with Anangamalai, praised by the women.

tamil: நரம்புமீ திறத்தல் செல்லா நல்லிசை முழவும் யாழு
மிரங்குதீங் குழலு மேங்கக் கிண்கிணி சிலம்பொ டார்ப்பப
பரந்தவா ணெடுங்கட் செவ்வாய்த் தேசிகப் பாவை கோல
வரங்கின்மே லாடல் காட்டி யரசனை மகிழ்வித் தாளே.
reading: To the sound of the lute, drum and flute, the foreign dancing-doll, her wide eyes and red mouth bright, dances on the stage and pleases the king.
nuance: தேசிகப் பாவை, 'the doll of the regional style', is the poet's name for her dancing; the verse does not say she came from elsewhere.
event: Anangamalai dances and pleases Civakan.

tamil: கடற்படை மன்னர் தம்மைக் காதலின் விடுத்துக் காமன்
றொடுத்தகோன் மார்பிற் றங்கத் தூமலர்க் கொம்ப னாளை
reading: After lovingly releasing the sea-army kings, Civakan drinks the woman like nectar, she who is like a gold shoot on the arrow-wounded king's chest, and she quivers like a tender shoot that the bee drinks.
nuance: கடற்படை மன்னர் is read as the kings with the 'sea-wide army' who fought for him in the last war.
event: Civakan sends the allied kings home and takes Anangamalai to bed.

reading: She, the field of youth ploughed and fenced with gold, her soft shoulders the ridges, bears the seed of beauty; the lord of the lute dwells enjoying the sweet harvest that love ripened from the music and dance.
nuance: The field figure turns the woman's body into land worked and harvested; the verse presents it as praise and does not weigh the cost, a point where the Siddhar texts differ.
event: Civakan enjoys the fruit of love with Anangamalai.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2599-2623 (1/22)
theme: The last ilampakam opens with a Jina temple and festival; Vijayai repays those who helped her in her wretchedness, receives the eight wives, and then retells the old king's fall through pleasure and warns her son, in a run of exhortations, that life is short and giving and penance must come first.
source_issues: Verses 2602, 2604-2607, 2609-2618 and 2623 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2611 line 2 ends with a full stop in the print, though its sentence runs on into line 3.
2603, 2609, 2613, 2614, 2617, 2618 and 2621-2623 are hard to construe in places (see their nuance); the speaker of 2609-2614 is taken as Vijayai without any word naming her after 2609 line 1.
Verses 2621 line 1 புத்தச்சொன்று and 2618 line 3 அத்தை are uncertain readings.

cast.role: Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother
the hero, now an old king
Kandukkatan's wife, Civakan's foster mother
Civakan's maternal uncle, king of Videham
Civakan's eight wives, who renounce with him
Civakan's father, the old king who fell to the usurper
the old king's ministers who failed to rouse him
the usurper who overthrew Saccandan
the townspeople, women among them, who hold the festival

reading: The poet opens the last ilampakam: the king of the famed spear, with war-drums booming and gold ornaments scattered in gifts, goes about the earth, and what befell on one of those days is now to be told.
nuance: The verse names no one; that the spear-bearing king is Civakan is taken from the chapter's place at the end of the work.
event: The poet announces the closing episode of Civakan's reign.

reading: A temple rises for the one who has gone beyond the eight qualities, set in a grove of asoka trees where striped bees and honey-bees sing, its towers touching the sky.
nuance: The asoka (பிண்டி) grove marks the Jina's temple, as elsewhere in the epic; the eight qualities are named only as 'eight' (எண்பால்).

tamil: அடிசிற் கலங் கழீஇக் கருனை யார்ந்த வினவாளை
நெடுநீர்க் கழனிசூழ் நியமஞ் சேர்த்தி விழவ யர்ந்து
reading: The townsfolk, after washing the feasting vessels, hold a festival in a town ringed by watered fields, with women's dance and song arranged.
event: The townspeople hold a festival with dance and song.

reading: Vijayai, the archer-king's lady, gives every delight to those who relieved her woe with lily seeds, wild fruit and roots, saying that no return could ever repay them.
nuance: The helpers are not named; the foods (lily stamens, wild fruit, roots) are those of a woman living rough, so the verse looks back to her days in the burning ground and the forest.
event: Vijayai rewards with every pleasure those who sustained her in her distress.

reading: Vijayai grants a lovely town to the sweet-voiced woman who sheltered her when she fell alone in the burning ground and gives her peacock-machine its due, and has the scene painted on her high mansion so she can always see it.
nuance: The text does not name the 'fruit-voiced one'; the foster mother Sunandai is the likeliest, but the verse leaves it open. Reading of 'மயிற்கு' as the peacock machine is a guess.
event: Vijayai gives a town to her rescuer and has the story of her rescue painted on a mansion wall.

reading: Vijayai recalls how the hero, once born, was reared: five hundred nurses gave him milk and Govindan had butter melted and poured out like a flood to feed him, and she, who had borne the garlanded king, lost her grief.
event: Govindan has Civakan fed with melted butter in a flood while five hundred nurses suckle him.

reading: Sunandai comes and worships; Vijayai embraces her, saying she has borne the great boy, and with many shaming words of praise makes the woman who lit the Kuru line shine in her turn.
nuance: 'Shame-making words' (நாண மொழிகள்) are words of praise too large for her to accept.
event: Sunandai worships Vijayai, who embraces and praises her.

reading: The eight wives, eyes long and wide as an axe, fall at the lady's feet; she lifts and embraces them and tells them that, as mothers of the sons who will rule the world, they should trust the king.
nuance: The speaker is Vijayai by the story, not by a word naming her in these lines.
event: The eight queens bow to Vijayai, who embraces them and urges them to trust their lord.

reading: Vijayai tells them they came into the night's dream as a crown of eight garlands on the king's jewelled crown and begs them never to part; then, eyes wide, she bids the king come.
event: Vijayai tells the queens of her dream of the eight garlands and calls Civakan to come.

reading: Civakan, walking like a lion, has flowers strewn and many bless him; he marks his lord-mother's feet on his head, asks what she commands without fear, and sits on the seat set for him, like a bull in battle.
event: Civakan comes, worships his mother, and sits at her bidding.

tamil: மிற்றென வுரைப்பக் கேண்மோ விலங்குபூ ணலங்கன் மார்பிற்
செற்றவர்ச் செகுத்த வைவேற் சீவக சாமி யென்றாள்.
reading: Vijayai turns to her son and says that if he has learned his king's fault from others, she will tell it herself: it is the one who slew his foes with the five-pointed spear, Civaka Swami.
nuance: The pronouns are ambiguous: 'your king' (நுங்கோ) may be Saccandan, and the closing address to Civaka Swami may be the poet's or hers. The sense is taken as the opening of a retelling.
event: Vijayai begins to tell her son the story of his father's fall.

tamil: நாகத்தால் விழுங்கப் பட்ட நகைமதிக் கடவுள் போலப்
போகத்தால் விழுங்கப் பட்டுப் புறப்படான் புன்சொ னாணா
னாகத்தா னமைச்சர் நுண்ணூற் றோட்டியா லழுத்தி வெல்லும்
பாகர்க்குந் தொடக்க நில்லாப் பகடுபோற் பொங்கி யிட்டான்.
reading: Swallowed by pleasure as the shining moon-god is swallowed by the serpent, the old king would not come out, was not ashamed of base talk, and, when his ministers pressed him with fine counsel, he rose up like an elephant that will not be mastered by its drivers.
nuance: Saccandan is not named here; the identification rests on the earlier telling of his fall in 261.
event: The king, sunk in pleasure, brushes off his ministers' counsel.

tamil: நுண்மதி போன்று தோன்றா நுணுகிய நுசுப்பி னார்தங்
கண்வலைப் பட்ட போழ்தே கடுநவை யரவோ டொக்கும்.
பெண்மையைப் பெண்மை யென்னார் பேருணர் வுடைய நீரா
ரண்ணலைத் தெருட்ட றேற்றா தமைச்சரு மகன்று விட்டார்.
reading: Once caught in the net of slender-waisted women's eyes, a man is like one with a deadly snake; the wise count womanhood no womanhood, and the ministers gave up trying to rouse the lord.
nuance: Line 2 is closed with a full stop in the print; the sense carries to line 3, whose meaning ('the wise do not call womanhood womanhood') is hard.
event: The ministers fail to rouse the king and leave him.

tamil: கற்சிறை யழித்து வெள்ளங் கடற்கவா யாங்குக் கற்றோர்
சொற்சிறை யழித்து வேந்தன் றுணைமுலை துறத்தல் செல்லான்
விற்சிறை கொண்ட போலும் புருவத்து விளங்கு வேற்க
reading: As flood breaks the stone dam into the sea, the king breaks the dam of the learned men's words, cannot bear to leave the breasts of his queen, and, caught in the prison of her spear-bent brows, leaves land and city unguarded.
event: The king abandons the guard of the land to stay with his queen.

tamil: பிளிறுவார் முரசத் தானைப் பெருமகன் பிழைப்பு நாடிக்
களிறுமென் றுமிழப் பட்ட கவழம்போற் றகர்ந்து நில்லா
தொளிறுவேற் சுற்ற மெல்லா முடைந்தபி னொருவ னானான்
வெளிறுமுன் வித்திப் பின்னை வச்சிரம் விளைத்த லாமோ.
reading: The great lord of the roaring drum and army, seeking to save himself, crumbles like a quid spat by an elephant, and when all his kin have broken away he stands alone; sowing the seed late cannot bring a diamond.
nuance: 'வெளிறு முன் வித்தி' in line 4 is obscure; the sense of a late remedy is a reading, not fixed.
event: The king is left alone when his kin and army break away.

tamil: வனைகலக் குயவ னாணின் மன்னரை யறுத்து முற்றிக்
கனைகுர லுருமி னார்ப்பக் காவல னின்னை வேண்டி
வினைமயிற் பொறியி னென்னைப் போக்கிவிண் விரும்பப் புக்கான்
புனைமுடி வேந்த போவல் போற்றென மயங்கி வீழ்ந்தான்.
reading: The speaker, in the king's own words, says that the potter-like Kattiyangaran conquered the kings and, roaring like thunder, sent her away by the deed-peacock machine while he himself went up to the sky; the king fell swooning as he called 'I go, protect'.
nuance: The calling of the usurper 'one who makes pots' and the order of speakers are uncertain; the line 3 phrase வினைமயில் (deed's peacock) may be an image for the machine as fate's instrument.
event: The king sends the queen away on the peacock machine and falls fainting as he takes leave.

tamil: சீதநீர் தெளித்துச் செம்பொற் றிருந்துசாந் தாற்றி தம்மான்
மாதரார் பலரும் வீச வளர்ந்தெழு சிங்கம் போலப்
போதொடு கலங்கள் சோர வெழுந்துபொன் னார மார்பன்
யாதெனக் கடிகண் முன்னே யருளிய தென்னச் சொன்னாள்.
reading: Women sprinkle cold water and fan him with sandal; he rises like a growing lion, flowers and ornaments slipping, and asks what it was that had been said; she tells him all.
nuance: The women who fan him are not named; the speaker of the last line is taken as Vijayai.
event: Civakan, roused from a faint by his women, asks to be told and Vijayai tells him.

tamil: பிறந்துநாம் பெற்ற வாணா ளித்துணை யென்ப தொன்று
மறிந்திலம் வாழ்து மென்னு மவாவினு ளழுந்து கின்றாங்
கறந்துகூற் றுண்ணு ஞான்று கண்புதைத் திரங்கி னல்லா
reading: Vijayai says that we are born without even knowing how many days we have and sink in the longing to live; only when the cow is milked do we cover our eyes and weep, but who can bring back the days that are gone?
nuance: Her speech is a mother's urging to renounce; the milked cow stands for life being drawn off while one weeps only at the end.

tamil: சுமைத்தயிர் வேய்ந்த சோற்றிற் றுய்த்தினி தாக நம்மை
யமைத்தநா ளென்னு நாகம் விழுங்கப்பட்ட டன்ன தங்க
ணிமைத்தகண் விழித்த லின்றி யிறந்துபா டெய்து கின்றா
முமைத்துழிச் சொறியப் பெற்றா மூதியம் பெரிதும் பெற்றாம்.
reading: The days fixed for us are a serpent swallowing us like sweet curd-sprinkled rice; we die with no wink of the eye, but we are glad of an itch scratched when we blink, as if we had gained a great gift.
nuance: Line 1 first half and line 4 (the itch and the blink) are hard; the translation of the closing image is tentative.

tamil: கடுவளி புடைக்கப் பட்ட கணமழைக் குழாத்தி னாமும்
விடுவினை புடைக்கப் பாறி வீற்றுவீற் றாயி னல்லா
லுடனுறை பழக்க மில்லை யொழிமதி யத்தை காதல்
வடுவுடைத் தென்று பின்னு மாபெருந் தேவி சொன்னாள்.
reading: As clouds struck by a hard wind are scattered in all directions, so we, struck by the force of deeds, are parted, and have no lasting companionship; she says to give up love for the 'aththai', since love has a flaw.
nuance: The word 'அத்தை' in line 3 may be a form of address ('father'/'dear') or the sense of 'those who are with us'; it is not fixed. The school tag 'jain' is given because the claim states the deed's force parting people, in the work's own frame, not because the verse names a school.
event: The great queen tells her son that kin are scattered by the force of deeds and bids him give up attachment.

reading: Before bright-toothed youth in the women's street drinks the toddy of youth without seeing its lapse, before black heads turn white, she says, do hard penance and give.
nuance: From here the addressees broaden from her son to all who listen, and it is unclear whether the speaker is still Vijayai.

reading: The fire of disease burns the body, with life poured in as ghee and awareness as oil; before Death, who drinks us up, leaves the house, she says to give, eat and do good.

Many who could not teach themselves to drive the cart of the word of the Buddha-wise were lost; before that cart's axle breaks and it sinks in the river of sorrow, drivers, take good conduct as fare and drive it.
nuance: 'புத்தச் சொன்று' in line 1 is obscure and may not name the Buddha at all; no school is given from it.

reading: All who are born are greedy and great; they give up and never seek fame, and they never give a handful to the poor; she says that if people know nothing about virtue being hard and far, then let go of the empty wealth.
nuance: Lines 2-3 are tangled; 'துற்ற விழு மீயார்' is taken as 'those who do not give a handful'.

tamil: முல்லை முகைசொரிந்தாற் போன்றினிய பாலடிசின் மகளி ரேந்த
நல்ல கருனையா னாள்வாயும் பொற்கலத்து நயந்துண் டார்க
ளல்ல லடைய வடகிடுமி னோட்டகத்தென் றயில்வார்க் கண்டுஞ்
செல்வ நமரங்கா ணினையன்மின் செய்தவமே நினைமின் கண்டீர்.
reading: Seeing those who eat sweet milk-rice, served by women in gold bowls, she says do not pity those who starve and do not think we are rich: think of austerity, which alone is what we have done.
nuance: Line 3 'அடகிடுமின்' and 'ஓட்டகத்து' are hard; the meaning of feeding the poor rather than rich diners is a reading.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2624-2648 (2/22)
theme: The women take the Jain vow: three sights of fallen wealth, cloth and youth turn Sunandai and Civakan to renunciation, the matrons go in palanquins to Pammai's nunnery, are washed, bound, stripped, shorn and filled with virtue while the king bows at their feet, and he and Nandattan protest and are answered.
source_issues: 2624-2627 and 2642-2648 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2628 line 2 prints அங் கௌவை மார்கடாஞ், read as அங்கு ஔவைமார்தாம் (the matrons).
2629 line 1 (நன்மயிற் பொறியின்மேற் போயா நாளினும்) and the words மன்னனி லாகுலம் in line 4 are hard to construe.
2635 line 3 (தானுரலாய்த் தடமுலை முற்றம் சூழ்ந்தரோ) is hard to construe.
2639 line 2 prints எற்புடம்பெண்ணிலாக்; பெண்ணிலாக் may be a misprint for எண்ணிலாக்.
2642-2648: who speaks and who is addressed is not named, and is inferred from the sequence.

cast.role: the unnamed voice of the three sights of 2624-2626, probably the nun-teacher; nothing in the verses names the speaker
the hero, now king, left behind by the women who renounce
Kantukkatan's wife, who reared Civakan and is Nandattan's mother; she takes the vow
the two matrons who leave in palanquins to renounce (probably Vijayai and Sunandai; the verse names neither)
the women who go to Pammai's nunnery and take the vow
the head nun, whose nunnery the women reach and who teaches and answers
the matron who has taken the vow, silent before the king in 2642 and the lady ascetic of 2648
a thousand maidens who catch the shorn hair on gold trays
Civakan's army that carries flowers behind him
the women ascetics of the nunnery
the great queens, whom the nuns send to speak kindly to Civakan
Civakan's younger brother and Sunandai's son

tamil: அம்பொற் கலத்து ளடுபா லமர்ந்துண்ணா வரிவை யந்தோ
வெம்பிப் பசிநலிய வெவ்வினையின் வேறாயோ ரகல்கை யேந்திக்
கொம்பிற் கொளவொசிந்து பிச்சை யெனக்கூறி நிற்பாட் கண்டு
நம்பன்மின் செல்வ நமரங்கா ணல்லறமே நினைமின் கண்டீர்.
reading: The sermon points to a woman who once drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now, worn by hunger and cut off from her fortune by cruel deeds, stands bent like a creeper with a wide bowl held out, crying 'alms'; seeing her, the rich are told not to trust their wealth and to think on good dharma.
nuance: The fall is put to வெவ்வினை (cruel deeds), so the picture is an instance of karma ripening and not mere chance. The same closing refrain, நல்லறமே நினைமின் கண்டீர், ends 2625 and 2626, so the three verses are three sights under one refrain: food, cloth, youth. The verse does not name the speaker or the hearers; the refrain addresses the rich (செல்வ).

tamil: வண்ணத் துகிலுடுப்பின் வாய்விட் டழுவதுபோல் வருந்து மல்கு
னண்ணாச் சிறுகூறை பாகமோர் கைபாக முடுத்து நாளு
மண்ணாந் தடகுரீஇ யந்தோ வினையேயென் றழுவாட் கண்டு
நண்ணன்மின் செல்வ நமரங்கா ணல்லறமே நினைமின் கண்டீர்.
reading: A second sight: a woman once in bright silk, now in a small torn cloth that she wears half and holds half, who weeps day by day 'alas, my deeds'; the rich are told not to cling to wealth and to think on good dharma.
nuance: She herself cries அந்தோ வினையே ('alas, my deeds'), so the sermon takes karma from the sufferer's own mouth. The simile in line 3 (அண்ணாந்த தடகுரீஇ) is hard to construe and is left out of the reading.

tamil: மைதிரண்ட வார்குழன்மேல் வண்டார்ப்ப மல்லிகைமென் மாலை சூடிக்
கைதிரண்ட வேலேந்திக் காமன்போற் காரிகையார் மருளச் சென்றா
ரைதிரண்டு கண்டங் குரைப்பவோர் தண்டூன்றி யறிவிற் றள்ளி
நெய்திரண்டாற் போலுமிழ்ந்து நிற்கு மிளமையோ நிலையா தேகாண்.
reading: A third sight: a youth in a jasmine garland, spear in hand, whom women gazed at as at Kama, comes to lean on a staff, his understanding thrust out by the phlegm that rattles in his throat, and he stands drooling like melted ghee: youth does not last.
nuance: The verse turns on a single person shown before and after, so the loss is felt as one life's, not as a general remark; the refrain here reads நிலையாதே காண் (it does not stay) in place of the refrain of 2624-2625.

tamil: என்றலுஞ் சுநந்தை சொல்லு மிறைவிதான் கண்ட தையா
நன்றுமஃ தாக வன்றே யாயினு மாக யானு
மொன்றினன் றுறப்ப லென்ன வொள்ளெரி தவழ்ந்த வெண்ணெய்க்
குன்றுபோல் யாது மின்றிக் குழைந்துமெய்ம் மறந்து நின்றான்.
reading: Sunandai answers that the lady has seen it herself, and whether it be so or not she too has joined in and will renounce; at that Civakan stands melted like a hill of butter over a bright fire, with no hold on himself and unmindful of his body.
nuance: That இறைவி means the nun who has just told the three sights, and that the one who melts in line 4 is Civakan, are inferred from this verse alone; the speaker of யானும் ஒன்றினன் துறப்பல் could also be read as Civakan.
event: Sunandai declares that she too will renounce, and Civakan stands melted and unmindful of his body.

reading: As if two bodies were going and leaving one life behind, the matrons go in palanquins to their noble renunciation and the noble one is left, and the eyes of the women stream like rain.
nuance: ஆரியன் is taken as Civakan, the one the two matrons leave, and the matrons as Vijayai and Sunandai; the verse names neither. In line 2 the matrons are written அங் கௌவை மார்கடாம், read here as அங்கு ஔவைமார்.
event: The two matrons go in palanquins to take the vow, leaving Civakan behind, while the women weep.

reading: The city is told to be thrown into uproar like a sea struck by the wind, with weeping voices mingling and flowers torn off.
nuance: Line 1 (நன்மயிற் பொறியின்மேற் போயா நாளினும்) and the words மன்னனி லாகுலம் in line 4 are hard to construe; the reading keeps only the simile and the weeping.

reading: After weeping, she goes through the decked city among a thousand worshipful palanquins and comes to the nunnery of Pammai of unblemished fame.
nuance: The singular அன்னவள் is left unnamed; whether she is one of the matrons or a queen is not said.
event: A woman, followed by a thousand palanquins, goes to Pammai's nunnery.

reading: As Pammai sits like a creeper among a throng of creeper-like women ascetics and tells the dharma, the long-eyed woman comes down, joins her hands in worship and begs the lady to take them all in and save them.
nuance: The one who asks is not named, and எமை (us) shows she speaks for more than herself.
event: A woman alights before Pammai, worships, and asks to be taken in with the others.

tamil: ஆரழன் முளரி யன்ன வருந்தவ மரிது தானஞ்
சீர்கெழு நிலத்து வித்திச் சீலநீர் கொடுப்பிற் றீந்தேன்
பார்கெழு நிலத்து ணாறிப் பல்புக ழீன்று பின்னாற்
reading: Pammai tells her that penance is as hard as a lotus in a fierce fire, but that a gift sown in good ground and watered with virtue (சீலநீர்) grows sweet on the earth, gives many kinds of fame and afterwards gives the pleasures of the garlanded gods.
nuance: The reward named is fame and heaven, not release: the nun sets the gift of the householder below the rare penance she is about to grant, in the epic's own order of fruit. The speaker is known only by the closing என்றாள் and the situation.
event: Pammai tells the woman the reward of a gift sown with virtue, and that penance is harder.

tamil: துறவுதந் தருளு கென்னத் தூநக ரிழைத்து மேலா
னறவிரி தாம நாற்றி வானகம் விதானித் தாய்ந்து
திறவிதிற் றவிசு தூபந் திருச்சுடர் விளக்கிட் டாரே.
reading: Having heard the dharma again, they ask the lady to grant them renunciation quickly; then they raise a pure hall, hang fragrant garlands, spread a canopy like the sky, and set a seat, incense and bright lamps.
event: The women ask for renunciation and prepare the hall of ordination.

reading: They wash her small feet with milk and, by the rule, bind fine white cloth woven of thread round her breasts, as if blindfolding Death.
nuance: The simile காலனைக் கண்புதைத்தாங்கு makes the binding a way of blinding Death; who binds and who is bound is not named.
event: The women's feet are washed with milk and white cloth is bound on them by rule.

reading: They scatter garlands and ornaments, wrap their breasts' broad court in soft cloth pale as moonlight, and so sow white thorns on the road by which Kama, lord of spring, would come.
nuance: Line 3 (தானுரலாய்த் தடமுலை முற்றம் சூழ்ந்தரோ) is hard to construe; the reading follows its general sense.
event: The women throw off garlands and ornaments and put on plain white cloth.

reading: Facing east, the women sit on seats of fine blooms and let fall their hair like many peahens shedding feathers.
event: The women sit facing east and shed their hair.

reading: The matrons, their dark hair reddened by the jewelled comb, pluck it out themselves without a flinch, and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the book the Lord spoke.
nuance: Only பரமன் is said; that he is the Jina is the work's setting, not this verse's words. The women pull their own hair out, which the verse presents as done without flinching (பணிவிலர்).
event: The matrons pluck out their own hair and take the vow.

reading: A thousand maidens like golden creepers carry gold trays and catch the golden hair so that it does not touch the good ground, and the women who shed their old hair look like dancing peahens.
event: A thousand maidens catch the women's hair on gold trays.

reading: As if pouring jewels into gold pots, they fill the bone-body with virtues, spread and guard compassion over every living thing, and turn their thought to the nectar of the one who knows all.
nuance: எற்புடம்பு names the body as bones, a frame to be filled with virtues where the preceding verses took ornaments off it. Line 2 prints பெண்ணிலாக் (womanless), which sits oddly with எண்ணிலாக் (countless); the reading keeps the plain sense of a full body of virtues.
event: The new nuns fill themselves with virtues and compassion and look to the nectar of the all-knowing.

reading: Neither glad at praise nor pitying scorn, having dug into the Anga books and packed their hearts with the rare meanings, they became the tilaka of the order, shining like a burning lamp.
event: The new nuns study the Anga books and shine as the order's ornament.

tamil: அலைமணிக் கவரி மான்றே ரடுகளி யானை பாய்மா
நிலநெளி கடலந் தானை நிரந்துபூச் சுமப்ப மன்னன்
சிலமலர் தானு மேந்திச் சென்றுசீர் பெருக வாழ்த்தி
யிலமலர்ப் பஞ்சிப் பாதத் தெழின்முடி தீட்டி னானே.
reading: With elephants, chariots, horses and the sea-like army carrying flowers, the king himself bears a few blooms, goes and praises them richly, and touches his beautiful crown to the feet that are dyed red like cotton and lac.
nuance: Whose feet they are is not said; the new nuns of 2636-2640 are the natural referent.
event: Civakan and his army carry flowers to the new nuns, and he bows his crowned head at their feet.

tamil: கடியவை முன்பு செய்தேன் கண்ணினாற் காணச் சின்னா
லடிகளிந் நகரி னுள்ளே யுறைகென வண்ணல் கூற
முடிகெழு மன்னற் கொன்று மறுமொழி கொடாது தேவி
படிமம்போன் றிருப்ப நோக்கிப் பம்மைதான் சொல்லி னாளே.
reading: The lord says he did harsh things before and asks that the lady stay a few days in the city so that he may see her with his own eyes; she gives the crowned king no word, standing like an image, and seeing it Pammai replies.
nuance: That the lord is Civakan and that தேவி is a matron now ordained (not a queen of his house) are inferred from the sequence; the verse gives neither a name.
event: Civakan asks the lady to stay a few days; she is silent and Pammai answers for her.

tamil: காதல னல்லை நீயுங் காவல நினக்கி யாமு
மேதில மென்று கண்டா யிருந்தது நங்கை யென்னத்
தாதலர் தாம மார்ப னுரிமையுந் தானு மாதோ
போதவிழ் கண்ணி யீர்த்துப் புனல்வரப் புலம்பி னானே.
reading: Pammai tells the king that he is no longer her lover and that she and the others are strangers to him; and the garlanded man, undone of his claim and himself, wrenches at his flower wreath and laments as his tears pour.
nuance: Which side of the break lines 1-2 name (the lady's, or the nuns') is hard to fix; உரிமையுந் தானுமாதோ is read as the king losing both his right and himself.
event: Pammai tells him he has no more claim on her, and Civakan weeps and laments.

tamil: ஏதில னாயி னாலு மிறைவர்தம் மறத்தை நோக்கக்
காதல னடிக ளென்னக் கண்கனிந் துருகிக் காசின்
மாதவ மகளி ரெல்லா மாபெருந் தேவி யாரை
யேதமொன் றில்லை நம்பிக் கின்னுரை கொடுமி னென்றார்.
reading: The nuns, moved by the Lords' dharma, say that though he is a stranger to them he is dear to the order, and tell the great queens to give the king gentle words, for he has done no wrong.
nuance: The line-by-line sense of lines 1-2 is uncertain and the reading gives only its general turn.
event: The nuns urge the great queens to speak kindly to Civakan.

tamil: திரைவள ரிப்பி யீன்ற திருமணி யார மார்பின்
வரைவளர் சாந்த மார்ந்த வைரக்குன் றனைய திண்டோள்
விரைவளர் கோதை வேலோய் வேண்டிய வேண்டி னேமென்
றுரைவிளைத் துரைப்பக் காளை யுள்ளகங் குளிர்ந்து சொன்னான்.
reading: Addressing him as the spear-bearer with the diamond-hill shoulders and the garland, they say they have asked what they wished; his heart cools and he speaks.
nuance: Who the speakers are is taken from the preceding verse, which sends the nuns' message to the great queens.
event: The queens tell Civakan they have asked what they wished, and he answers with a cool heart.

tamil: அடிகளோ துறக்க வொன்று முற்றவர் யாது மல்லர்
சுடுதுய ரென்கட் செய்தாய் சுநந்தைநீ யௌவை யல்லை
கொடியைநீ கொடியை செய்தாய் கொடியையோ கொடியை யென்னா
விடருற்றோர் சிங்கந் தாய்மு னிருந்தழு கின்ற தொத்தான்.
reading: Crying that the lady may go but that the rest who joined are nothing to him, he cries to Sunandai that she has given him a burning grief and is no mother, and calls her cruel again and again, like a lion in distress crying before its mother.
nuance: The speaker is taken as Nandattan, Sunandai's son, because the simile has a lion crying before its mother and 2648 answers Nandattan; Civakan, her foster son, is possible.
event: He rebukes Sunandai for leaving, calling her no mother.

tamil: சென்றதோ செல்க விப்பாற் றிருமக ளனைய நங்கை
யின்றிவ டுறப்ப யானின் னரசுவந் திருப்பே னாயி
னென்றெனக் கொழியு மம்மா பழியென விளங்கு செம்பொற்
குன்றனான் குளிர்ப்பக் கூறிக் கோயில்புக் கருளு கென்றாள்.
reading: A woman answers that what has gone is gone: if, now that this lady has renounced today, she herself sat on in the king's realm, the blame would never leave her; and with these words to cool the golden-hill-like hero she bids him go in to the palace.
nuance: Whether இவள் is the speaker herself or the lady who has renounced, and who the speaker is, cannot be fixed from this verse.
event: She consoles him and asks him to return to the palace.

tamil: பந்தட்ட விலலி னார்தம் படாமுலை கிழித்த பைந்தார்
நந்தட்டன் றன்னை நோக்கி நங்கையா ரடிகள் சொன்னார்
நொந்திட்டு முனிய வேண்டா துறந்தில நும்மை யென்னக்
கந்தட்ட திணிதிண் டோளான் கற்பக மலர்ந்த தொத்தான்.
reading: The lady ascetic tells Nandattan, whose garland tore the bosoms of ball-playing women, that he need not be hurt and angry, for they have not given him up; and the strong-shouldered man opens like a wish-tree in bloom.
nuance: நங்கையார் அடிகள் is read as the matron who has taken the vow, Nandattan's mother Sunandai; the verse does not name her.
event: The lady ascetic comforts Nandattan that she has not forsaken him.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2649-2673 (3/22)
theme: The hero worships the renounced women and a queen of the court gives up pleasure for austerity; the ministers, afraid he will follow, fill a pool for a water-battle in which the women are beaten by the king, and the chapter closes in the pleasures of the couch, the last enjoyment before his own turning away.
source_issues: 2649-2650: the speaker and the women are not named in the verses and the subjects are inferred; கந்தி in 2649 may be a word for a nun.
2663: lines 1-2 are obscure.
2665-2666: the verses' pronouns are hard to fix.
2668-2673: the metre changes to short lines; 2668 ends with என்பவே.

cast.role: the hero, here the king, unnamed in these verses
Civakan's wife, who sprays and fights on in the water-war
the ministers who build the pool to keep the king from renouncing
the king's honoured lady who gives up pleasure for austerity
the daughter of the mountain king who takes the enemy's part in the game
the women of the court who play and lose the water-war
the slender woman who takes the king's garland and loses her silk
the saffron-vined women who ride in procession to the palace
the mothers-in-law who send the women off

tamil: துறந்த விந்நங்கை மார்தந் தூம லரனைய பாத
முறைந்தவென் சென்னிப் போதின் மிசையவென் றொப்ப வேத்திக்
கறந்தபா லனைய கந்திக் கொம்படுத் துருவப் பைம்பூண்
பிறங்குதார் மார்பன் போந்து பெருமணக் கோயில் புக்கான்.
reading: Having praised the feet of the women who renounced as flowers resting on his head, the garlanded hero goes and enters the great fragrant temple.
nuance: The nun-like figure behind கந்தி and the antecedent of the pronouns are not given in the verse.
event: The hero worships the renounced women's feet and enters the temple.

tamil: வடிநிரை நெடிய கண்ணார் மாமிமார் விடுப்ப வேகிக்
கடிநிரை சிவிகை யேறிக் கதிர்மணிக் குடைபின் செல்ல
வுடைதிரைப் பரவை யன்ன வொளிறுவேன் மறவர் காப்பக்
கொடிநிரைக் கோயில் புக்கார் குங்குமக் கொடிய னாரே.
reading: Sent off by the mothers-in-law, the saffron-vined women ride a gem-canopied palanquin guarded by spearmen and enter the flag-lined palace.
nuance: Whether these are the women of the preceding verse or the hero's wives cannot be fixed from the verse.
event: The women, dismissed by their mothers-in-law, go in procession to the palace.

reading: The king's honoured lady, like a doll of pure gem, gives up pleasure that is like a rain-bubble, puts away desire and takes up the austerity of her line, living like a goddess.
nuance: The poem shows renunciation by a woman of the court before the hero turns to it himself, and gives the bubble image as the reason.
event: The king's lady gives up enjoyment and takes to austerity.

tamil: உடைதிரை முத்தஞ் சிந்த வோசனிக் கின்ற வன்னம்
படர்கதிர்த் திங்க ளாகப் பரந்துவான் பூத்த தென்னா
வடர்பிணி யவிழு மாம்ப லலைகடற் கானற் சேர்ப்பன்
குடைகெழு வேந்தற் கிப்பா லுற்றது கூற லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet of the sea-shore, with its swans and lilies, says he will now tell what befell the umbrella-king.
nuance: A poet's turn to a new matter, in the narrator's own voice.

tamil: துறவின்பாற் படர்த லஞ்சித் தொத்தொளி முத்துத் தாம
முறைகின்ற வுருவக் கோலச் சிகழிகை மகளி ரின்பத்
திறைவனை மகிழ்ச்சி செய்து மயங்குவா னமைச்ச ரெண்ணி
நிறையநீர் வாவி சாந்தங் கலந்துடன் பூரித் தாரே.
reading: Fearing that the king will turn towards renunciation, the ministers work to keep him in the pleasure of the women and fill a water-tank with scented water.
nuance: The ministers' fear (துறவின்பாற் படர்தல் அஞ்சி) states the cause of the whole water-sport: it is a device against his leaving.
event: The ministers, fearing his turn to renunciation, prepare a pleasure-pond to hold the king.

tamil: நீரணி மாட வாவி நேர்ம்புணை நிறைத்து நீணீர்ப்
போரணி மாலை சாந்தம் புனைமணிச் சிவிறி சுண்ணம்
வாரணி முலையி னார்க்கு மன்னற்கும் வகுத்து வாவி
யேரணி கொண்ட விந்நீ ரிறைவகண் டருளு கென்றார்.
reading: The ministers fill the tank with floats, garlands, sandal paste, gem syringes and powders for the women and the king, and ask the lord to come and see it.
event: The ministers equip the pool and invite the king to come and see it.

tamil: கணமலை யரசன் மங்கை கட்டியங் கார னாகப்
பணைமுலை மகளி ரெல்லாம் பவித்திரன் படைய தாக
விணைமலர் மாலை சுண்ண மெரிமணிச் சிவிறி யேந்திப்
புணைபுறந் தழுவித் தூநீர்ப் போர்த்தொழி றொடங்கி னாரே.
reading: The women are drawn into two armies, with the mountain king's daughter taking the enemy general's part and the rest the king's host, and they open a water-war with garlands, powder and syringes.
nuance: கட்டியங்காரன் here is a role in the game, not the usurping minister of the story; the mountain-king's daughter is not named.
event: The women divide into the king's army and the mock enemy and begin the water-battle.

tamil: தூமலர் மாலை வாளாச் சுரும்பெழப் புடைத்துந் தேன்சோர்
தாமரைச் சதங்கை மாலை சக்கர மென்ன வீழ்த்துங்
காமரு கணைய மாகக் கண்ணிக ளொழுக விட்டுந்
தோமர மாகத் தொங்கல் சிதறுபு மயங்கி னாரே.
reading: The women strike with flower garlands that scatter bees, hurl lotus chains of bells like discs and let garlands fall like arrows, so that the tangle of garlands is their weapon.
event: The women fight with flower garlands used as arms.

tamil: அரக்குநீர்ச் சிவிறி யேந்தி யாயிரந் தாரை செல்லப்
பரப்பினாள் பாவை தத்தை பைந்தொடி மகளி ரெல்லாந்
தரிக்கிலா ராகித் தாழ்ந்து தடமுகிற் குளிக்கு மின்போற்
செருக்கிய நெடுங்கண் சேப்பச் சீதநீர் மூழ்கி னாரே.
reading: Gandharvadattai takes up a syringe of red water and sends a thousand streams, and the women, unable to bear it, plunge like lightning into a cloud, with their eyes reddened by the cold water.
event: Gandharvadattai sprays the women, who dive into the water.

tamil: தானக மாட மேறித் தையலார் ததும்பப் பாய்வார்
வானகத் திழியுந் தோகை மடமயிற் குழாங்க ளொத்தார்
தேனின மிரியத் தெண்ணீர்க் குளித்தெழுந் திருவி னன்னார்
பான்மிசை சொரியுந் திங்கள் பனிக்கடன் முளைத்த தொத்தார்.
reading: The women climb the pool's pavilion and leap in like peacocks coming down from the sky, and rise from the clear water like lakshmis or like a moon newly risen on the dewy sea.
event: The women leap from the pavilion into the pool.

tamil: கண்ணிகொண் டெறிய வஞ்சிக் காறளர்ந் தசைந்து சோர்வார்
சுண்ணமுஞ் சாந்தும் வீழத் தொழுதன ரிரந்து நிற்பா
ரொண்மலர் மாலை யோச்ச வொசிந்துகண் பிறழ வொல்கி
வெண்ணெயிற் குழைந்து நிற்பார் வேற்கணா ராயி னாரே.
reading: Struck with garlands the women sag and falter, beg with powder and sandal falling, bend to the thrown garlands and melt like butter.
event: The women, struck with garlands, melt and plead for mercy.

tamil: கூந்தலை யொருகை யேந்திக் குங்குமத் தாரை பாயப்
பூந்துகி லொருகை யேந்திப் புகுமிடங் காண்டல் செல்லார்
வேந்தனைச் சரணென் றெய்த விம்முறு துயர நோக்கிக்
காய்ந்துபொற் சிவிறி யேந்திக் கார்மழை பொழிவ தொத்தான்.
reading: The women with their hair in one hand and their silk in the other, unable to watch where they step, run to the king for refuge, and he, seeing their distress, takes up a golden syringe and pours like a rain-cloud.
nuance: The king's anger is playful: காய்ந்து is the word for it, set against a pour compared to rain.
event: The women flee to the king, who answers with his own syringe.

tamil: வீக்கினான் றாரை வெய்தாச் சந்தனத் தளிர்நன் மாலை
யோக்கினார் கண்ணி சுண்ண முடற்றினா ருருவச் சாந்திற்
பூக்கமழ் துகிலுந் தோடு மாலையுஞ் சொரியப் போர்தோற்
றாக்கிய வநங்கன் சேனை யாறலா றாயிற் றன்றே.
reading: The king looses streams, the women let their garlands and powder and perfumed cloths fall, and the army of the love-god, defeated in the war, is routed.
nuance: The battle names the love-god's army as the women's, and it is the women who lose; Kama's army is beaten by the king in play.
event: The king's streams win; the women's garlands and cloth fall and the love-god's army is routed.

tamil: அன்னங்க ளாகி யம்பூந் தாமரை யல்லி மேய்வார்
பொன்மயி லாகிக் கூந்தல் போர்த்தனர் குனிந்து நிற்பா
ரின்மலர்க் கமல மாகிப் பூமுகம் பொருந்த வைப்பார்
மின்னுமே கலையுந் தோடுங் கொடுத்தடி தொழுது நிற்பார்.
reading: The beaten women turn into swans among lotuses, peacocks hiding in their hair, lotuses laying faces on his, and give up their girdles and earrings and bow to touch his feet.
event: The defeated women submit, giving girdles and earrings and touching his feet.

tamil: பண்ணுரை மகளிர் மாலை பைந்துகில் கவர்ந்து கொள்ளக்
கண்ணுரை மகளிர் சோர்ந்து காரிருட் டிவளு மின்போற்
பெண்ணுரைப் பிடிக்கைக் கூந்தற் பொன்னரி மாலை தாழ
வெண்ணுரை யுடுத்து நின்றார் வேந்தனோக் குண்ண நின்றார்.
reading: The women who have lost their garlands and silk stand wrapped only in a white foam, their lightning-like bodies shaking, looking to the king.
nuance: The first two lines compare the women's eyes and the snatching of garlands in a way the verse does not make clear.
event: The women, stripped of garlands and silk by the sport, stand looking at the king.

tamil: தன்படை யுடையத் தத்தை சந்தனத் தாரை வீக்கி
யொன்பது முகத்தி னோடி யுறுவலி யகலம் பாயப்
பொன்படு சுணங்கு போர்த்த பொங்கிள முலையிற் றூவான்
முன்படு குலிகத் தாரை முழுவலி முறுக்க லுற்றான்.
reading: Her ranks broken, Gandharvadattai binds on a stream of sandal and, running with nine jets, sprays red powder over the king's wide chest and begins to twist its force against him.
nuance: Gandharvadattai is named in 2657 and again here, the one wife who stays to fight on.
event: Gandharvadattai, her side broken, turns a nine-jet stream of red powder on the king's chest.

tamil: மெய்ப்படு தாரை வீழி னோமிவட் கென்ன வஞ்சிக்
கைப்படை மன்ன னிற்பக் கதுப்பயன் மாலை வாங்கிச்
செப்பட முன்கை யாப்பத் திருமகன் றொலைந்து நின்றான்
பைப்புடை யல்கு லாளைப் பாழியாற் படுக்க லுற்றே.
reading: A slender woman with a hand-weapon stands before the king and takes his garland; he, undone, stands helpless as she tries to bind and throw the other woman by force.
nuance: The pronouns of the last two lines are hard to fix; I read the king as the one who stands helpless.
event: A woman disarms the king of his garland and the game turns on him.

tamil: அடுத்தசாந் தலங்கல் சுண்ண மரும்புனல் கவர வஞ்சி
யுடுத்தபட் டொளிப்ப வொண்பொன் மேகலை யொன்றும் பேசா
கிடப்பமற் றரச னோக்கிக் கெட்டதுன் றுகின்மற் றென்ன
மடத்தகை நாணிப் புல்லி மின்னுச்சேர் பருதி யொத்தான்.
reading: The sandal and powder are carried off by the water, and the slender woman's silk is lost and her gold girdle lies silent; looking at the king she asks what has fallen, and shy, embraces him like the sun joined with lightning.
event: A woman loses her silk to the water and, ashamed, embraces the king.

tamil: விம்மகிற் புகையின் மேவி யுடம்பினை வேது செய்து
கொம்மென நாவி நாறுங் கூந்தலை யுலர்த்தி நொய்ய
வம்மல ருரோமப் பூம்பட் டுடுத்தபி னனிச்ச மாலை
செம்மலர்த் திருவி னன்னார் சிகழிகைச் சேர்த்தி னாரே.
reading: After the sport the women steam their bodies with agil smoke, dry their fragrant hair, put on fine silk and set anicham garlands in their tresses.
event: The women dry and dress themselves after the water-sport.

reading: They say the women, with bright garlands, enjoyed the grace of the man with mountain-like shoulders whose body the water had heated.
nuance: The metre changes here; the opening lines are hard to read exactly and the verse is closed with என்பவே, 'they say'.
event: The women enjoy the king's company after the water-sport.

reading: In the heat of summer the king lies on a couch cooled by sandal paste and moon-rays, staying on the breasts of the woman who lies with him.
event: The king rests with a woman on a sandal-cooled couch.

reading: Her gem ornaments seem to weep pearls, her brow like a vine bends in worship and the flowers of her hair sink as if she were tired with the whole body's pleasure.
event: A woman gives her whole body to pleasure with the king.

reading: The women, like coral boughs of the wishing-tree, know writing, song and dance, and the king, in their company, is the very love-god of the five-arrow love-god.
nuance: The compliment makes the king the love-god of the love-god, setting him above the god he has just defeated in the water-war of 2661.

reading: Frightened by the thunder of the clouds, the women with their hair like a rain-cloud's shadow embrace the king and gain the beauty of boughs clinging to a tree.
event: The women, frightened by thunder, cling to the king.

reading: The women descend to the low agil-scented couch, their sandal paste wiped off, their breasts bruised by garlands, and their girdles and anklets sounding as they fall apart.
event: The women lie with the king on the low couch, their paste and girdles undone.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2674-2698 (4/22)
theme: Through the cold and dewy seasons the women of Civakan's household drink, dress and revel; Gunamalai's sulk at the moon in her cup is ended by his flattery, and as spring comes the groves become a stage and the women adorn themselves for the spring sport.
source_issues: 2690-2698 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2674 lines 2-3 and 2689 line 3 are hard to construe; 2694 line 3 has irregular word spacing; 2678 and 2685 end without a full stop.

cast.role: the hero, never named in this chapter's verses
Civakan's wife, who sulks at the moon in her cup
the women who dress and revel in the cold and spring seasons

reading: The verse praises tender, doe-eyed women, said to be like does that have been startled; its middle lines are too obscure to construe with confidence.
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (யான றாமுலைப் பாலமுது, ஒன்றானும் மேவலர்) do not yield a certain sentence, so only the frame of praise is recorded.

reading: When the cold season has come and moves about, the dark-lily-eyed women take to warm sandal paste for their full breasts, hot wine, opening-flower garlands, incense smoke and powder.
nuance: The season is felt through what the women reach for: warmth and scent stand for the cold.
event: The women, in the cold season, take to warming pastes, wine, garlands and incense.

reading: Women in bee-humming garlands put out their beauty like buds, and the earth's king, thinking them sea-nectar, longs for them while the five arrows of spring's king press upon him.
nuance: The one pressed by the arrows is called the earth's king (தரணி மன்னன்) without a name; the context makes Civakan likely, but the verse does not say so.

reading: A woman tilts a cup of fire-coloured wine at her left side, sees the moon in it, and drinks it down as if to destroy a rival's shadow, then sulks as she looks at the sky.
nuance: The sulk is aimed at the moon reflected in the wine, not at a person; who she is the verse does not say, though the next verse names Gunamalai.
event: A woman sees the moon in her wine cup, drinks it and sulks.

reading: Saying to the moon that she has drunk it and it hid and wasted with pallor yet lingers, Gunamalai sulks with eyes gone red, and he sets out to drive the sulk away by holding her close.
nuance: The sulk is built on the moon-face conceit: she treats the reflected moon as a rival who has paled before her. The final line is left open and runs on into the next verse.
event: Gunamalai sulks at the moon in her cup, and Civakan sets out to end the sulk by embracing her.

reading: He tells her that the moon has darkened within and wasted in beauty before the light of her face, bids her not grieve in her heart, and takes her in his arms.
nuance: The quarrel is ended by turning her own moon conceit into praise; he does not argue the sulk but flatters it away.
event: Civakan consoles Gunamalai by saying the moon pales before her face, and embraces her.

reading: As the dewy season that wilts the lotus arrives, the garlanded women wrap themselves in a cloak of fragrant rising smoke.
nuance: The lotus's enemy is the cold season; the women answer it with smoke as a wrap.
event: The women wrap themselves in incense smoke against the dewy season.

reading: With smoke in their hair, sandal on their soft breasts, tamala garlands and serpent-like girdles, the women angrily scatter pearls.
nuance: The scattering of pearls from a girdle is the poet's sign of lovers' passion or haste; the verse does not say who angers them.
event: The women scatter pearls from their girdles.

reading: The women, delighted, drink fruit wine and rice liquor and wear champak and jasmine garlands.
event: The women drink fruit wine and rice liquor and put on champak and jasmine.

reading: Garlands strike the women's eyes and their pearled breasts ache; anklets give a tired sound as hands are lifted, and desire sinks.
nuance: The last clause, காமந் தாழ்ந்ததே, can be read as desire lowered or as passion grown heavy; the verse leaves it open.

reading: The early dewy season passes entirely and the late dewy season comes to be tended, as the beauty of the women is dressed for it.
nuance: The verse marks the turn of the cold seasons, early dew to late dew, and so places the chapter in the months leading to spring.

reading: The women are described in white silk and white flower garlands, with red hips and jewelled ornaments gleaming like fire.
Kings give the women red blankets of fine fur warmed at the fire, which the women take gladly, and they are called peerless.
nuance: The kings' gift is a cold-season comfort; the verse presents the women as receivers of royal gifts.
event: Kings give the women fire-warmed red blankets, which they gladly take.

reading: Daily the women live happily in the lower storey of a golden mansion that rubs the moon, delighting in dance and drinking the sound of song.
event: The women pass their days in the golden mansion with dance and song.

reading: In the lovers' battle between the curl-haired women and the heroes of the fine anklets, small drums, anklets, bells and girdles sound like the instruments of war.
nuance: Lovemaking is figured as a battle, with the ornaments' sound as the war music.

reading: The innocent women have bow-like brows and saffron on their breasts; bees settle on the paste in swarms, so that it seems laid down like brick, and it shines like the women's flower-hued bodies.
nuance: The middle lines, வாய்ச்சியா லிட்டிகை செத்து, are hard to construe.

tamil: குரவம் பாவை கொப்புளித்துக் குளிர்சங் கீர்ந்த துகளேபோன்
மரவம் பாவை வயிறாரப் பருகி வாடை யதுநடப்ப
விரவித் தென்றல் விடுதூதா வேனி லாற்கு விருந்தேந்தி
வரவு நோக்கி வயாமரங்க ளிலையூழ்த் திணாபுன் றலர்ந்தனவே.
reading: As the north wind goes and the southern breeze is sent as envoy, the trees bring out new leaves and flowers to welcome the coming of the spring king.
nuance: The coming of spring is told as a guest's arrival: the breeze is the envoy and the trees prepare the welcome.
event: The south breeze goes as envoy and the trees put out leaves and flowers to greet spring.

tamil: இளிவாய்ப் பிரசம் யாழாக விருங்கட் டும்பி குழலாகக்
களிவாய்க் குயில்கண் முழவாகக் கடிபூம் பொழில்க ளரங்காகத்
விளியாக் கொண்டிங் கிளவேனில் விருந்தா வாட றொடக்கினான்.
reading: Bees are the lute, dark beetles the flute, cuckoos the drum and the scented groves the stage, and spring begins his feast-dance, taking as his call the loosened bangles and pallor of women whom lovers have left.
nuance: The celebration is paid for by the parted women: their wasted wrists are what spring takes up as his song.
event: Spring begins a feast-dance in the groves, with the bangles and pallor of forsaken women for his call.

tamil: வேனி லாடும் விருப்பினால் வியன்காய் நெல்லிச் சாந்தரைத்து
நான வெண்ணெய் கதுப்புரைத்து நறுநீ ராடி யமிர்துயிர்க்குந்
தேனா ரகிலின் புகைசேர்த்தி வகுத்து நாவிக் குழம்புறீஇ
யானாப் பளித நறுஞ்சுண்ண முகிரி னுழுதாங் கணிந்தாரே.
reading: Out of desire for spring sport the women grind nelli-fruit paste, rub civet-butter into their hair, bathe in scented water, perfume themselves with agil smoke, and put on fragrant powders.
event: The women bathe, perfume and powder themselves for the spring sport.

tamil: முத்தார் மருப்பி னிடைவளைத்த முரண்கொள் யானைத் தடக்கையி
னொத்தே ருடைய மல்லிகையி னொலியன் மாலை யுறுப்படக்கி
வைத்தார் மணிநூற் றனவைம்பால் வளைய முடித்து வான்கழுநீ
ருய்த்தாங் கதனுட் கொளவழுத்திக் குவளைச் செவித்தா துறுத்தாரே.
reading: The women gather jasmine garlands over their long plaits and set blue water-lilies in their ears.
event: The women put jasmine garlands in their plaits and lilies in their ears.

tamil: புகையார் வண்ணப் பட்டுடுத்துப் பொன்னங் கலைகள் புறஞ்சூழ்ந்து
நகையார் கவுள கிண்கிணியுஞ் சிலம்பு நாய்நாச் சீறடிமேற்
பகைகொண் டார்போற் சுமாஅய்க்கண்பின் பரூஉக்காம் பனைய கணைக் கால் சூழ்ந்
தகையார்ந் திலக்கும் பரியகந் தாமே கவினச் சேர்த்தினார்.
reading: The women put on smoke-coloured silk, golden girdles and ringing anklets, and adorn their calves and ankles.
nuance: Line 3 has an odd spacing (சுமாஅய்க்கண்பின் பரூஉக்காம் பனைய கணைக் கால் சூழ்ந்) that makes the words hard to divide.

tamil: பிடிக்கை வென்று கடைந்தனபோற் பஞ்சி யார்ந்த திரள் குறங்கு
கடித்துக் கிடந்து கவின்வளருங் காய்பொன் மகரங் கதிர்முலைமே
லுடுத்த சாந்தின் மிசைச்செக்க ரொளிகொண் முந்நாட் பிறையேய்ப்பத்
துடிக்குங் குதிர் சேர் துணைமுத்தந் திருவில் லுமிழ்ந்து சுடர்ந்தனவே.
reading: Thighs, golden makara ornaments and pearl strings on the breasts are described, with the pearls compared to a three-day crescent that gives off light like a rainbow.

tamil: குழியப் பெரிய கோன்முன்கை மணியார் காந்தட் குவிவிரன்மேற்
கழியப் பெரிய வருவிலைய சிறிய மணிமோ திரங்கனலத்
தழியப் பெரிய தடமென்றோட் சலாகை மின்னத் தாழ்ந்திலங்கும்
விழிகண் மகர குண்டலமுந் தோடுங் காதின் மிளிர்ந்தனவே.
reading: The women's ears gleam with makara-shaped earrings and studs that outweigh their size in price.
nuance: The gems are said to be small in size and very great in value.

tamil: நாணுள் ளிட்டுச் சுடர்வீசு நன்மா ணிக்க நகுதாலி
பேணி நல்லார் கழுத்தணிந்து பெருங்கண் கருமை விருந்தூட்டி
நீணீர் முத்த நிரைமுறுவல் கடுச்சுட் டுரிஞ்சக் கதிருமிழ்ந்து
தோணீர்க் கடலுட் பவளவாய்த் தொண்டைக் கனிக டொழுதனவே.
reading: Bright gem necklaces on the women's necks, large eyes feasting on darkness, pearl-bright teeth and coral lips like fruits all shine and bow.
nuance: The last clause is hard to read; the pearl-and-coral figures are plain.

tamil: மாலை மகளி ரணிந்ததற்பின் பஞ்ச வாசங் கவுட்கொண்டு
சோலை மஞ்ஞைத் தொழுதிபோற் றோகை செம்பொ னிலந்திவளக்
காலிற் சிலம்புங் கிண்கிணியுங் கலையு மேங்கக் கதிர்வேலு
நீலக் குவளை நிரையும்போற் கண்ணார் காவி லிருந்தாரே.
reading: When evening has come and the women have dressed, they keep five-scent pastes in their cheeks and sit in the grove like flocks of peacocks, with anklets, bells and girdles sounding and their eyes like spear and blue lilies.
event: The dressed women sit in the garden at evening.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2699-2723 (5/22)
theme: Civakan's last pleasures: women playing in paddy and wine, the birth, naming and schooling of eight sons, the spring outing, and a male monkey's secret tryst, his mate's rebuke and their making up.
source_issues: 2699-2709 and 2711-2723 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2719 line 2 has a stray space in 'சு ரும்புண' (for சுரும்புண).
2701 line 2 repeats 2700 line 2 word for word.
2720 'கடுகன்' is probably கடுவன் (male monkey); 2722-2723 speakers are not marked in the text.

cast.role: the hero, the king, at the last of his pleasures
Civakan's wives and women, who play with him in garden and field
the nurses and carers who shape the infants (not named in the verse)
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who comes as the king's divine friend
the woman with a jasmine garland who brings the spring's tribute
the maidens who guard the king in the garden with raised blades
the male monkey of the jackfruit grove
the male monkey's own mate, who sees him with another female

tamil: மணிவண் டொன்றெ நலம்பருக மலர்ந்த செந்தா மரைத்தடம்போ
லணிவேன் மன்ன னலம்பருக வலர்ந்த வம்பார் மழைக்கண்ணார்
பணியார் பண்ணுப் பிடியூர்ந்து பரூஉக்காற் செந்நெற் கதிர்சூடித்
தணியார் கழனி விளையாடித் தகைபா ராட்டத் தங்கினார்.
reading: The king and his bright-eyed women, drunk on one another's beauty like a bee on a red lotus, ride she-elephants, wear sprays of ripe paddy and play in the fields until they stop to praise one another.
nuance: Nothing names the king; he is the lord of the preceding verses (the wives' pleasure outing of the closing ilampakam) and is known only from the story so far.
event: Civakan and his women play in the paddy fields and halt there, praising each other.

tamil: எண்ணற் கரிய குங்குமச்சேற் றெழுந்து நான நீர்வளர்ந்து
வண்ணக் குவளை மலரளைஇ மணிக்கோல் வள்ளத் தவனேந்த
வுண்ணற் கினிய மதுமகிழ்ந்தா ரொலியன் மாலை புறந்தாழக்
கண்ணக் கழுநீர் மெல்விரலாற் கிழித்து மோந்தார் கனிவாயார்.
