reading: One day the king of kings sees the party at the lotus pool, asks who has separated them, hears from his attendants that it is the young prince, and orders the spear-bearer brought.
nuance: The Tamil asks who 'separated' them without saying whom; read as the swans and their young.
event: The king sees the prince's party at the pool, asks who has done this, and has the prince summoned.

reading: As drums and lutes sound and the slim-waisted women dance, the attendants tell the seated prince that the lord has sent for him, and he goes and bows at his feet.
event: The prince is told of the summons and goes, hands joined, to his father.

reading: Holding his right shoulder with the left hand and keeping fingers from his mouth, the prince, wearing the ring and bowing his head, bows to the old king.
event: The prince makes the bow of a son before the king.

reading: While women of the bangled hands fan him with whisks, the king, jewelled ear-rings blazing, tells him: if he would hear of the two pains of parting from kin, he must stay and be the seed that grew them.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 is difficult; the speaker and the seed image are read from the last line, where 'the king' ends the sentence, and the sense of 'two kinds of parting' is a best reading.
event: The king begins his lesson to the prince while the women fan him.

reading: The king tells him that when virtue is great and the heart turns to wrong, the dire deeds that swell run and strike, and the killing of life most of all brings great suffering, so he must not kill.
nuance: The verse is the first of five that run on: killing, lying, theft, another's wife, and wealth got by deceit; the same four are named as sins the ascetic guards against at 2824. Here they are taught to a layman prince.

reading: He says that the towers of the upper world rise for the one who speaks true and are lasting, while the towers of the great hell are for the lie; so the prince is bidden to throw lying out.

He says that kings torture a thief, tearing him with the tusks of the lotus-faced elephant, and that the great unseen misery drops him into a fallen birth, so theft and the gambler's trade must be given up.
nuance: The last line pairs theft with gambling (சூது); the reading takes both as to be given up. The lines are hard in parts.

reading: He says that one who goes to others' wives, who is like a bright sword over his own neck, falls into heavy suffering, and that to put down such unsteady desire is good.
He says that wealth which, once it is clear, would not take one to the heavenly world is no wealth: gold laughs, the senses laugh, and so does all that earns it.
nuance: The verse was printed in eight half-lines and joined; the lines on laughing gold and senses are read loosely and the argument may be a different one.

reading: He ends by telling the prince to abandon wealth-greed tangled with lies, the dust of deeds, the crooked path, deceit, and the dice cunningly played.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2874-2898 (12/22)
theme: The elder's sermon to the young prince Asodharan, with caged birds, karma that follows like a thread and the dread of rebirth, ends in the prince's freeing of a cygnet, his father's order to rule first, his argument that kin are strangers and his leaving with his wives; the chapter then returns to the king hearing the great ascetic, the Charanas' departure and the grief of the women at his announced renunciation.
source_issues: Verses 2876, 2878-2884, 2886-2888, 2897 and 2898 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.

The speakers of 2874-2879 and 2889-2890 are not named; 'elder' is a working id. Whether 2889-2890 address the prince now a god or Civakan hearing his earlier birth, and whether 2891 onward is Civakan, is inferred from the story and not fixed by the Tamil.
2877, 2878, 2881, 2887 and 2897 have similes whose syntax is hard to parse; their readings are marked uncertain.

cast.role: the unnamed elder who preaches to the prince
the young prince of Bhumi Tilakam who renounces
the prince's father, the king of kings
the prince's wives who also take the vow
the hero, now an old king, who hears the great ascetic
the great ascetic who preaches to the king
the sky-going ascetics who rise away
the king's women who weep at his vow

reading: The speaker says that people ruled by desire, anger and greed, those who deck themselves with garlands and sandal, and those who eat only from hunger are not a refuge, and bids the hearer bow to no feet but those of the lord who has none of these.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the verse follows a sermon that begins at 2867 and is taken here as the same voice. வாமன் is read as a title of the passionless lord, not a name.
event: The elder tells the prince to worship only the lord free of passion.

reading: Parrots, mynas, peacocks, swans and many other birds cry out when they are torn from their kin and shut under guard; the speaker tells the renowned prince that those who do this will themselves be parted from their kin, and that the keeping of them is unseemly.
nuance: This answers the scene at 2864, where the birds are found taken from the pond. The verse says the captors will leave their kin; it does not say when or by what mechanism.
event: The elder rebukes the prince for keeping caged birds away from their flocks.

tamil: அல்லித்தா ளற்ற போது மறாதநூ லதனைப் போலத்
தொல்லைத்தம் முடம்பு நீங்கத் தீவினை தொடர்ந்து நீங்காப்
புல்லிக்கொண் டுயிரைச் சூழ்ந்து புக்குழிப் புக்குப் பின்னின்
றெல்லையி றுன்ப வெந்தீச் சுட்டெரித் திடுங்க ளன்றே.
reading: As the thread in a lotus stalk does not break when the stalk is torn, so the deed of earlier lives does not leave when the body leaves: it clings to the soul, enters whatever body it enters, follows behind and burns it with the fierce fire of endless suffering.
nuance: The thread image makes karma a continuous strand that outlasts each body; the verse names no way to cut it, so its remedy has to come from the verses that follow.

tamil: அறவிய மனத்த ராகி யாருயிர்க் கருளைச் செய்யிற்
பறவையு நிழலும் போலப் பழவினை யுயிரோ டாடி
மறவியொன் றானு மின்றி மனத்ததே சுரக்கும் பால
கறவையிற் கறக்குந் தம்மாற் காமுறப் பட்ட வெல்லாம்.
reading: If one turns the mind to kindness toward living souls, the old deed plays with the soul as a bird plays with its own shadow, and without a lapse yields from the mind whatever one desires, as a cow gives milk to the milker.
nuance: The cow and the bird with its shadow are the two comparisons; the syntax of lines 2-4 is hard and the comparison of the second is read loosely.

tamil: நெடுமணி யூபத் திட்ட தவழ்நடை யாமை நீணீர்த்
தொடுமணிக் குவளைப் பட்டந் துணையொடு நினைப்ப தேபோற்
கடுமணிக் கயற்க ணல்லார் காமமும் பொருளுஞ் சிந்தித்
தடுமணி யாவி நீப்பா ரறிவினாற் சிறிய நீரார்.
reading: A tortoise set on a jewelled post in deep water thinks of its mate in the blue lily bed, and so women with keen fish-like eyes who dwell on desire and wealth lose their lives, being small in understanding.
nuance: The grammar of lines 3-4 is hard, so who is said to give up life (the women, or the men who think of them) is not fixed; the simile is read as one of longing that does not release.

tamil: வீறழி வினைசெய் காலன் வைரவாள் வலையிற் பட்டாற்
சாறழி குவளை மாலை யவரையுந் தனமு நீக்கி
யாறிழி வரையிற் றோன்று மறநனி நினைப்பர் செம்பொ
னேறெழி னெறியி னேறி யிருவிசும் பாளு நீரார்.
reading: When Death, who ruins all splendour, catches a man in his diamond net, the wise leave garlanded women and wealth and think only of dharma, which shows itself like a river coming down a mountain, and so climb a golden way to rule the two heavens.

tamil: துன்னிமற் றறத்தைக் கேட்டே துகினெருப் புற்ற தேபொன்
மின்னுத்தார் மார்பன் மெய்வெந் தாலியி னுருகிப் பெண்பா
லன்னப்பார்ப் பன்று கொண்ட தடத்திடை விடுவித் திட்டான்
பின்னைத்தன் கிளைகள் கூட்டம் பெருந்தகை வித்தி னானே.
reading: Having listened to dharma, the prince melts like cloth touched by fire, lets the female cygnet he had taken go free in the pool, and then does something with the gathering of its kin that the last word leaves unclear.
nuance: The last word வித்தினான் ('sowed') is read here as bringing the flock together again; the verse does not say so.
event: Asodharan releases the cygnet he had captured into the pond and rejoins it to its flock.

tamil: மெய்ப்படு முதுபுண் டீர்ப்பான் மேவிய முயற்சி போல
வொப்புடைக் காமந் தன்னை யுவர்ப்பினோ டொழித்துப் பாவ
மிப்படித் திதுவென் றஞ்சிப் பிறவிநோய் வெருவி னாலே
மைப்படு மழைக்க ணல்லார் வாய்க்கொண்ட வமுத மொப்பான்.
reading: Like effort to cure an old wound, the prince casts out matching desire with disgust, fearing that this is sin and dreading the disease of birth, and is like one holding nectar in his mouth.
nuance: The last line's comparison to nectar in the mouths of dark-eyed women is hard to place and may refer to the prince's earlier pleasure.
event: Asodharan gives up desire out of fear of sin and rebirth.

tamil: ஆளியாற் பாயப் பட்ட வடுகளி யானை போல
வாளிவிற் றடக்கை மைந்தன் வாய்விட்டுப் புலம்பிக் காம
நாளினு நஞ்சு துய்த்தே னச்சறை யாக நன்பொற்
றோளியர்த் துறந்து தூய்தாத் தவஞ்செய்வ லடிக ளென்றான்.
reading: Like a spotted elephant sprung on by a lion, the bowman cries aloud that he has tasted desire's poison day after day, and will leave the golden-armed women and do pure tapas, lord.
nuance: The speaker is read as the prince and the addressee அடிகள் as his father, since the next verse has a king answer the youth.
event: Asodharan cries out that he will give up the women and do tapas.

tamil: சிறுவன்வாய் மொழியைக் கேட்டே தேர்மன்னன் றானுஞ் சொன்னா
னுறுகளிற் றுழவ மற்றுன் னொளிமுடித் தாய மெய்தி
யறைகடல் வேலி காத்துன் னலங்கல்வேற் றாய மெல்லாம்
பெறுதகு புதல்வற் கீந்து பின்னைநீ துறத்தி யென்றான்.
reading: Hearing the youth, the chariot-king answers that he should first take his bright-crowned share, guard the kingdom bounded by the roaring sea, give all to a worthy son and only then renounce.
nuance: Whether the chariot-king is the father is not said; the verse answers a youth's vow with the order of duties, and the story that follows does not wait for a son.
event: The king tells the prince to rule and pass on the kingdom before he renounces.

tamil: கொலைச்சிறை யுய்ந்து போகு மொருவனைக் குறுக வோடி
யலைத்தனர் கொண்டு பற்றி யருஞ்சிறை யழுத்து கின்றார்
தொலைப்பருஞ் சுற்றத் தாரோ பகைவரோ வடிக ளென்ன
விலைப்பெரு மணியை முந்நீர் நடுக்கடல் வீழ்த்த தொத்தான்.
reading: Like a man who has escaped the prison of killing and is run down, seized and thrust into a hard cell again, he asks whether these kin he cannot shake off are kin or enemies, and is like one who throws a priceless gem into mid-ocean.
nuance: The question is in the youth's mouth and the gem comparison may be the narrator's; the next verse gives his answer.

tamil: காதல மல்ல மேனாட் கழிந்தநம் பிறவி தம்மு
மாதலாற் சுற்ற மில்லை யதுபட்ட வாறென் றம்பூந்
தாதலர் மார்ப னற்புத் தளையறப் பரிந்திட் டானே.
reading: He reasons that those about him are not his own, since in past births they were strangers and in the bodies to come they will be strangers again, so there is no kin; and the garlanded one cuts the bond of affection through.
event: Asodharan reasons that no one is truly kin and cuts the bonds of affection.

tamil: நற்பொறி குயிற்றி வல்லான் செய்ததோர் நன்பொற் பாவை
பொற்பொறி கழல வெல்லாப் பொறிகளுங் கழல்வ தேபோற்
சொற்பொறி சோர வெல்லாப் பொறிகளுஞ் சோர்ந்து நம்ப
னிற்பொறி யின்ப நீக்கி யிராயிரர் சூழச் சென்றான்.
reading: As a jointed doll made by a master falls apart in every joint when its pins are loosed, so every sense fails when the joint of speech fails; the prince leaves the delight of the senses and goes surrounded by two thousand.
nuance: The doll image describes the body's failing as a mechanism; the verse then turns to the prince's leaving without saying that his leaving is this failing.
event: Asodharan leaves his pleasures and goes out with two thousand companions.

tamil: தணக்கிறப் பறித்த போதுந் தானளை விடுத்தல் செல்லா
நிணப்புடை யுடும்ப னாரை யாதினா னீக்க லாகு
மணப்புடை மாலை மார்ப னொருசொலே யேது வாகக்
கணைக்கவி னழித்த கண்ணார்த் துறந்துபோய்க் கடவு ளானான்.
reading: As the flesh-smelling monitor lizard that clings to its hole when a plank is torn away can be moved by some means, so on the cause of a single word the garlanded prince left the women with arrow-bright eyes and became a holy man.
nuance: கடவுளானான் is read as 'became a holy one', one who has taken the vow, not as becoming a deity. The details of the lizard simile are not fully clear.
event: Asodharan abandons the women and becomes an ascetic after one word.

tamil: தூமமார்ந் தணங்கு நாறுஞ் சுரும்புசூழ் தாரி னானுந்
தாமமா ரொலிய லைம்பாற் சயமதித் திருவு மார்ந்த
காமமா சுண்ட காதற் கதிர்வளைத் தோளி னாரு
நாமநாற் கதியு மஞ்சி நற்றவத் துச்சி கொண்டார்.
reading: The prince and the women with shining bangles and garlanded hair, fearing the dreaded four states of birth, took the summit of fine tapas.
nuance: நாற்கதி is the four courses of rebirth (hell, beast, human, god) of Jain teaching; the verse does not list them.
event: Asodharan and his wives take the vow of tapas.

tamil: ஆசார நாணத் தவஞ்செய் தலர்க் கற்ப கத்தார்ச்
reading: A speaker greets one who by tapas done in regard for conduct and shame became a bright god, lord of the Kalpa-dwellers called Sasaran, and has come ruling a jewelled sky-world.
nuance: Neither speaker nor addressee is named; the addressee may be Civakan, whose earlier birth the sermon tells, or the prince now a god. The last line is hard.

reading: The speaker tells the garlanded king that in earlier days he parted others and so seems to have been shut in a prison himself, and the speaker's words are medicine for the disease of woeful births.
nuance: This returns to the cage of 2875 and puts the repayment in the same form; who is addressed is not fixed.

reading: At the words of the great ascetic, mountain-like and full of a sinless sermon, the king with the poison-spitting spear sits in fear and trembles as though an arrow had fallen.
nuance: The king is read as Civakan; the verse names neither. The sermon's content is not given here.
event: The king trembles at the ascetic's sermon.

reading: The king, ringed by peacock-like women, bows his jewelled crown and praises the glorious feet of the ascetics.
event: The king bows his crown at the ascetics' feet and praises them.

reading: The Charanas, high in great tapas, rise like the sun and moon, and the sky grows bright as they go.
nuance: The Charanas are the sky-going ascetics of Jain tradition; the verse reports their rising and does not teach how it is done.
event: The Charanas ascend through the sky.

reading: When the Charanas have gone, the eyes of the vine-slender women with sandal-pasted breasts, bright as spears, brim over like blue lilies filled with water.
event: The women weep after the Charanas leave.

reading: The king, his chest bright with southern sandal like a golden mountain under the moon, gives the slender women no kind word and goes to the banner-hung palace.
event: The king leaves the women without a word and goes to the palace.

reading: On a soft cotton couch the women with sea-wide hips lie with their cloud-dark moon faces dimmed, their beauty withered by sighs of poison.
event: The women lie wasting on their couch.

tamil: வெள்ளெயிற் றரவு மேய்ந்த மிச்சிலின் மெலிந்து மேகப்
புள்வயிற் பிறந்த புட்போ லொன்றலா துரைத்த றேற்றார்
கள்வயிற் றலர்ந்த கோதைக் கலாபவில் லுமிழு மல்கு
லொள்ளெயிற் றவர்கள் பொன்பூத் தொளிமணி யுருவ நீத்தார்.
reading: The women, who thin like what the white-fanged snake has eaten and leaves, who can say nothing but one thing like the cloud-bird, lose their golden pallor and the colour of their bright gems.
nuance: The two comparisons (the snake's leavings and the bird of the cloud) are hard to place; the sense of loss is clear but the figure is not.
event: The women lose their colour and ornament in grief.

tamil: கிளிச்சொலி னினிய சொல்லார் கிண்கிணி சிலம்பொ டேங்கக்
குளித்துநீ ரிரண்டு கோலக் கொழுங்கயல் பிறழ்ப வேபோற்
களித்துநீர் சுமந்து வாட்கண் கலாஅய்ப்பிறழ்ந் தலமந் தாட
வளித்ததா ரலங்க லாழி யவன்றுற வுரைத்து மன்றே.
reading: The women with parrot-sweet speech, their anklets crying out, weep and toss like carp in water, because the king in his garland and ring has told them of his renunciation.
nuance: The verse says only that he spoke of renunciation; his words are not given.
event: The women weep because the king has told them he will renounce.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2899-2923 (13/22)
theme: Civakan offers the kingdom to Nandan, who refuses even heaven and release for his brother's feet; the king then instructs his eldest son on rule, crowns his heirs and gives away treasure, and goes to his women, who wither when they read that he means to leave.
source_issues: 2899, 2901-2908, 2910-2916, 2918 and 2923 are printed in eight half-lines in the source and were joined into four lines; the line splits are the editor's.
2900 (the cobra and drum simile), 2904 lines 2-3, 2910 (நாந்தக உழவர்), 2917 line 4 and 2920 line 3 are obscure or loosely constructed.
2912 and 2914 do not name the youth crowned or the giver; the identities here are inferred from 2905 and 2913.

cast.role: the hero, now the old king, who makes over the kingdom
Civakan's younger brother (நந்தன்), who refuses the throne
the eldest of the young princes, Gandharvadattai's son, whom the king instructs
the youth, a lady's son, whom the king makes crown prince in 2912
Ilakkanai's son, the lion-like boy decreed great lord
Civakan's wives, brought to hear his intent

tamil: புனைமருப் பழுந்தக் குத்திப் புலியொடு பொருது வென்ற
கனைகுர லுருமுச் சீற்றக் கதழ்விடை யுரிவை போர்த்த
துனைகுரன் முரசத் தானைத் தோன்றலைத் தம்மி னென்றா
னனைமல ரலங்கற் கண்ணி நந்தனுந் தொழுது சேர்ந்தான்.
reading: Civakan sends for the lord of the drum-sounding army, and Nandan, in a wreath of wet flowers, bows and comes up to him.
nuance: The verb 'said' has no named subject and 'the lord of the army' is not named; Civakan and Nandan are read from 2903, where the younger brother is called Nandan.
event: Civakan orders Nandan to be brought, and Nandan bows and approaches.

tamil: கொடியணி யலங்கன் மார்பிற் குங்குமக் குன்ற மன்னா
னடிபணிந் தருளு வாழி யரசரு ளரச வென்னப்
படுசின வெகுளி நாகப் பைத்தலை பனித்து மாழ்க
விடியுமிழ் முரச நாண வின்னண மியம்பி னானே.
reading: Nandan, bowing at his feet, begs him to be gracious as king of kings, and his voice is likened to thunder that shames the drum and makes the angry cobra's hood shake.
nuance: Lines 2-3 are a simile of a loud voice that the cobra and the drum cannot match; the grammar linking the cobra clause to the speech is loose.
event: Nandan bows at Civakan's feet and asks for his grace.

tamil: ஊனுடைக் கோட்டு நாகான் சுரிமுக வேற்றை யூர்ந்து
தேனுடைக் குவளைச் செங்கேழ் நாகிளந் தேரை புல்லிக்
கானுடைக் கழனிச் செந்நெற் கதிரணைத் துஞ்சு நாடு
வேன்மிடை தானைத் தாயம் வீற்றிருந் தாண்மோ வென்றான்.
reading: Civakan tells Nandan to sit enthroned and rule the inheritance of the spear-crowded army, in a land where creatures sleep on the ears of red rice.
event: Civakan offers Nandan the kingdom.

tamil: கரும்பலாற் காடொன் றில்லாக் கழனிசூழ் பழன நாடுஞ்
சுரும்புலாங் கண்ணி விண்ணோர் துறக்கமும் வீடும் வேண்டே
னரும்புலா யலர்ந்த வம்மென் றாமரை யனைய பாதம்
விரும்பியான் வழிபட் டன்றோ வாழ்வதென் வாழ்க்கை யென்றான்.
reading: Nandan turns down the rich land of cane fields, the heaven of the bee-haunted gods and release alike, and asks whether his life is not to live worshipping the lotus-like feet he loves.
nuance: Naming வீடு beside country and heaven makes the refusal total. The verse does not name whose feet are meant; the context of the offer in 2901 reads them as Civakan's.
event: Nandan refuses the kingdom and says he wants only to serve his brother.

tamil: குன்றென மருண்டு கோல மணிவண்டுங் குழாங்கொ டேனுஞ்
சென்றுமொய்த் திமிரும் யானைச் சீவகற் கிளைய நம்பி
மன்றல்வீற் றிருந்து மின்னு மணிக்குவ டனைய தோளா
னொன்றுமற் றரசு வேண்டா னுவப்பதே வேண்டி னானே.
reading: The younger brother, shoulders like a bright blue lily, wants no kingdom at all and asks only for what delights him.
nuance: What 'delights' him is left open; read after 2902 it is the service of his brother.
event: Nandan declines any kingdom.

tamil: பொலிவுடைத் தாகு மேனும் பொள்ளலிவ் வுடம்பென் றெண்ணீ
வலியுடை மருப்பி னல்லால் வாரணந் தடக்கை வையா
தொலியுடை யுருமுப் போன்று நிலப்படா தூன்றின் வைவேற்
கலிகடிந் துலகங் காக்குங் காளையைக் கொணர்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Reasoning that the body, however handsome, is hollow, Civakan tells his men to bring the youth who will guard the world, as an elephant lays its trunk on nothing but its strong tusk.
nuance: Opening on the body's hollowness before naming an heir makes the choice of successor follow from seeing the body as unreliable. Lines 2-3 (the elephant's trunk resting on its tusk, thunder not falling to earth) are two obscure similes; I take them to mean resting weight on a sound support.
event: Civakan orders the youth who will protect the world to be brought.

tamil: கழுமணி யார மார்பிற் காவலன் மக்கள் காய்பொ
னெழுவளர்ந் தனைய திண்டோ ளிளையவர் தம்முண் மூத்த
தழுமலர்க் கொம்பு போலுந் தத்தைநாட் பயந்த நம்பி
விழுமணிப் பூணி னானை வீற்றிரீஇ விதியிற் சொன்னான்.
reading: The king seats the eldest of the young princes, the jewelled son of Gandharvadattai, and instructs him by rule.
nuance: Gandharvadattai is the Tattai of line 3, as in the earlier ilampakams; 2906-2911 read as the instruction that begins here.
event: Civakan seats his eldest son and begins to instruct him.

tamil: பால்வளை பரந்து மேயும் படுகடல் வளாக மெல்லாங்
கோல்வளை யாமற் காத்துன் குடைநிழற் றுஞ்ச நோக்கி
நூல்விளைந் தனைய நுண்சொற் புலவரோ டறத்தை யோம்பின்
மேல்விளை யாத வின்பம் வேந்தமற் றில்லை கண்டாய்.
reading: Civakan tells the heir that if he guards the sea-ringed earth under his umbrella with the sceptre unbent and keeps dharma with poets whose fine words are ripe as treatises, a king has no higher joy.
nuance: The joy of kingship is ranked highest by a king who is about to give it up; the claim is for the heir, not for Civakan's own last aim.

tamil: வாய்ப்படுங் கேடு மின்றாம் வரிசையி னரிந்து நாளுங்
காய்த்தநெற் கவளந் தீற்றிற் களிறுதான் கழனி மேயின்
வாய்ப்பட லின்றிப் பொன்றும் வல்லனாய் மன்னன் கொள்ளி
னீத்தநீர் ஞால மெல்லா நிதிநின்று சுரக்கு மன்றே.
reading: A ruler who takes his revenue in measure, as an elephant is fed balls of ripe paddy cut each day, loses nothing, whereas the elephant that grazes the field itself perishes; the land he has watered then pours out wealth.

tamil: நெல்லுயிர் மாந்தர்க் கெல்லா நீருயி ரிரண்டுஞ் செப்பிற்
புல்லுயிர் புகைந்து பொங்கு முழங்கழ விலங்கு வாட்கை
மல்லலங் களிற்று மாலை வெண்குடை மன்னர் கண்டாய்
நல்லுயிர் ஞாலந் தன்னு ணாமவே னம்பி யென்றான்.
reading: Of rice and water, both called the life of men, he says the king with blazing spear, white umbrella and elephants is the good life of the earth that people dread.

tamil: ஆர்வலஞ் சூழ்ந்த வாழி யலைமணித் தேரை வல்லா
மூர்நில மறித றேற்றா தூருமேன் முறிந்து வீழுந்
தார்நில மார்ப வேந்தர் தன்மையு மன்ன தாமே.
reading: A driver who knows his chariot can run it long on a ploughed field, but if he drives without learning the ground it breaks and falls; kings are the same, he warns.

tamil: காய்ந்தெறி கடுங்கற் றன்னைக் கவுட்கொண்ட களிறு போல
வாய்ந்தறி வுடைய ராகி யருளொடு வெகுளி மாற்றி
வேந்தர்தாம் விழைப வெல்லாம் வெளிப்படார் மறைத்தல் கண்டாய்
நாந்தக வுழவ ரேறே நன்பொரு ளாவ தென்றான்.
reading: Like an elephant that holds a hurled stone in its cheek, learned kings put away anger with mercy and keep what they desire hidden, which he calls the real wealth, addressing the heir as a bull among swordsmen.
nuance: நாந்தக உழவர் is read as the warriors of the nandaka sword; the compound is rare.

tamil: குடிபழி யாமை யோம்பிற் கொற்றவேன் மன்னர் மற்று
னடிவழிப் படுவர் கண்டா யரும்புகழ் கெடுத லஞ்சி
நொடியலோ ரெழுத்தும் பொய்யை நுண்கலை நீத்த நீந்திக்
கொடியெடுத் தவர்க்கு நல்கு கொழித்துணர் குமர வென்றான்.
reading: If he guards his people from blame, other kings will follow his path; fearing the loss of fame he should not speak even one false syllable, and he should give to those who have crossed the arts and raised their banner.

tamil: சேனடந் தாங்கு மோடிச் சென்றுலாய்ப் பிறழும் வாட்கண்
மான்மட நோக்கின் மாதர் மாலைநாட் பயந்த மைந்தன்
கானடந் தனைய மான்றேர்க் காளையைக் காவன் மன்னன்
றானுட னணிந்து தன்போ லிளவர சாக்கி னானே.
reading: The king himself dresses a youth, son of a doe-eyed lady and splendid as a forest of deer-drawn chariots, and makes him crown prince like himself.
nuance: The verse does not say whether this youth is the prince of 2905 or another son.
event: Civakan makes a youth crown prince.

tamil: கூரெயி றணிந்த கொவ்வைக் கொழுங்கனிக் கோலச் செவ்வா
யேரணி மயிலஞ் சாய லிலக்கணை யீன்ற சிங்கஞ்
சீருடைச் செம்பொற் கண்ணிச் சிறுவனைச் செம்பொன் மாரி
பேரறைந் துலக முண்ணப் பெருநம்பி யாக வென்றான்.
reading: He decrees that the lion-like boy whom Ilakkanai bore, in a gold garland, shall become the great lord while a shower of gold is announced for the world to enjoy.
nuance: பொன் மாரி is a lavish public gift; the golden shower comes from the king's treasure, not from the heavens.
event: Civakan orders his son by Ilakkanai made great lord and a golden shower proclaimed.

tamil: தன்கழ றொழாத மன்னர் தாஞ்சுமந் தேந்தி நின்ற
பொன்றிக ழுருவிற் றம்பி புதல்வனைத் தந்து போற்றி
மின்றிகழ் முடியுஞ் சூட்டி வீற்றிரீஇ வேந்து செய்தான்
குன்றினங் குழீஇய போலுங் குஞ்சரக் குழாத்தி னானே.
reading: The younger of golden form, whom kings who never worshipped his anklets raised aloft, hands over the boy, honours him, crowns him with a lightning-bright crown and sets him on the throne among elephants massed like hills.
nuance: Who is the 'younger' of golden form is not stated. Nandan, who has just refused the kingdom, is the likelier giver and Civakan the one who crowns, but the verse does not separate them.
event: The boy is given over, honoured, crowned and enthroned.

tamil: நிலஞ்செதி ளெடுக்கு மான்றேர் நித்திலம் விளைந்து முற்றி
நலஞ்செய்த வைரக் கோட்ட நாறுமும் மதத்த நாகங்
குலஞ்செய்த குமரர்க் கெல்லாம் கொடுத்தன னிதியு நாடு
முலஞ்செய்த வைரக் குன்ற மோரிரண்ட டனைய தோளான்.
reading: The king, whose shoulders are like two diamond hills, gives all the princes of the line elephants whose tusks bear pearls, and the treasure and the country.
event: Civakan gives treasure, country and elephants to the princes.

tamil: நூற்கிடங் கொடுத்த கேள்வி நுண்செவி மண்கொண் ஞாட்பில்
வேற்கிடங் கொடுத்த மார்பின் வில்வலான் றோழர் மக்க
ணாற்கடல் வளாகங் காக்கு நம்பிதன் கண்க ளாகப்
பாற்கடற் கேள்வி யாரைப் பழிப்பற நாட்டி னானே.
reading: He sets the learned and blameless sons of his bowman comrades as the eyes of the young lord who will guard the four-sea earth.
nuance: 'Eyes' for counsellors is an old figure for a king's advisers; the comrades' sons inherit their fathers' place beside the throne.
event: Civakan appoints his comrades' sons as the young king's counsellors.

tamil: காவல ரகல மென்னுங் கழனியு ளுழுது காமர்
மாவலம் விளைத்த கோட்டு மழகளிற் றரச னன்னான்
பூவலர் கொடிய னாரை விடுக்கிய கோயில் புக்கான்
றூவல ரொலிய லார்தம் வலக்கண்க டுடித்த வன்றே.
reading: The king, who ploughed the field of kings' chests and reaped elephants, enters the palace to release his women, whose right eyes begin to throb.
nuance: The throbbing of the right eye is told as an omen; the verse does not call it ill, and the closing phrase of line 4 is obscure.
event: Civakan goes to the women's palace to release them, and their right eyes throb.

tamil: செம்பொனாற் செறிய வேய்ந்து திருமணி முகடு கொண்ட
வெம்புநீள் சுடருஞ் சென்னி விலங்கிய மாட மெய்தி
யம்பொனாற் றெளிந்த பாவை யனையவர்த் தம்மி னென்றான்
பைம்பொனால் வளர்க்கப் பட்ட பனைதிரண் டனைய தோளான்.
reading: In a mansion roofed with gold and jewels whose peak the sun's fire grazes, the king tells his people to bring the gold-doll women.
event: Civakan orders his wives brought to the mansion.

reading: Garlands are listed one after another, of crystal, strung flowers, fragrant flowers, gold, pearls and jewels, hanging in masses.
nuance: The verse is a list with no verb; it runs into 2920.

reading: Among long garlands, in incense smoke rising like foam, the women whose breasts could buy three worlds lie on soft beds laid in jewelled rooms.
nuance: The picture of luxury is set just before the women are told of the king's intent.

reading: As the young women hail it as grace, bees hum, slim waists ache under shining girdles and gold anklets ring, the women stand before the king, bow at his feet and cry 'live long'.
event: The women come before Civakan and bow at his feet.

reading: Civakan addresses the women, with hair like peacock tails and moon-bright girdles, and bids them hold the wandering mind steady and hear the lasting good, which he calls nectar.
event: Civakan asks his wives to listen to what is lastingly good.

tamil: வாயழ லுயிர்க்கு மாழி மன்னவன் குறிப்பு நோக்கி
வேயழத் திரண்ட மென்றோள் வெம்முலைப் பரவை யல்குற்
றோய்பிழி யலங்க லார்தந் தொன்னலந் தொலைந்து வாடிக்
காயழற் கொடியைச் சேர்ந்த கற்பக மாலை யொத்தார்.
reading: Reading the wheel-king's sign, the garlanded women lose their old beauty and fade like kalpaka garlands laid on a vine of burning fire.
nuance: வாயழல் உயிர்க்கும் may be the women's hot sighs or a figure for the king's wheel; I take it as sighs, which makes the simile one of grief.
event: The women read Civakan's intent and wither.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2924-2948 (14/22)
theme: In the last ilampakam Civakan preaches to his eight wives on giving, the foulness and fading of the body, and the fear of Death, and, when he tells them they are now strangers, they weep, fall at his feet and ask what fault they committed.
source_issues: Verses 2924-2927, 2938-2940 and 2944-2948 were printed in eight half-lines in the source and joined into four lines (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2924 lines 3-4, 2926, 2930 lines 1-2, 2932 lines 3-4, 2937 lines 1-2 and 2942 are hard to parse; readings are marked uncertain.
The speaker of 2941, 2942, 2947 and 2948 is not named in the Tamil and is inferred from context.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who preaches renunciation to his wives
Civakan's eight wives, who hear him and weep

tamil: கருங்கடற் பிறப்பி னல்லால் வலம்புரி காணுங் காலைப்
பெருங்குளத் தென்றுந் தோன்றா பிறைநுதற் பிணைய னீரே.
யருங்கொடைத் தான மாய்ந்த வருந்தவந் தெரியின் மண்மேன்
மருங்குடை யவர்கட் கல்லான் மற்றையர்க் காவ துண்டே.
reading: As the conch and pearl are found only in the dark sea and never in a big pool, so the rare austerity that ripens from giving is found in few on earth, though lesser folk may share some of it.
nuance: The last two lines turn on a doubtful syntax (மருங்குடை யவர்கட் கல்லான்); the contrast between the few and the rest is read from the sense, not fixed.

tamil: அட்டுநீ ரருவிக் குன்றத் தல்லது வைரந் தோன்றா
குட்டநீர்க் குளத்தி னல்லாற் குப்பைமேற் குவளை பூவா
விட்டுநீர் வினவிக் கேண்மின் விழுத்தகை யவர்க ளல்லாற்
பட்டது பகுத்துண் பாரிப் பார்மிசை யில்லை கண்டீர்.
reading: As diamonds come only from the hill of the pouring stream and the blue lily blooms only in clear water, so only the noble share what they have; listen and ask, he says, for none else on earth does it.

tamil: நரம்பொலி பரந்த கோயி னன்னுதன் மகளிர் தூவும்
பெரும்பலிச் சோற்றி னீதல் பெரிதரி தாகு மேனுஞ்
சுரும்பொலி கோதை யார்த மனைவயிற் றூண்டோ றூட்டு
மரும்பலி யனைத்து மீயி னதுபொருட் குன்று கண்டீர்.
reading: Though giving out of the offering-rice that women scatter in the temple is hard, one who gives the rare alms at every house-pillar of the women's homes gains a mountain of wealth.
nuance: The picture of feeding at each pillar of a household is hard to place and the sense of 'offering' (பலி) is uncertain.

tamil: அற்றவர் வருத்த நீக்கி யாருயிர் கொண்டு நிற்குந்
துற்றவி ழீதல் செம்பொற் றுறக்கத்திற் கேணி யாகு
முற்றுயி ரோம்பித் தீந்தே னூனொடு துறப்பின் யார்க்கு
மற்றுரை யில்லை மண்ணும் விண்ணுநும் மடிய வன்றே.
reading: Food given to the hungry that removes their distress and keeps their life is a well in the golden heaven, and one who guards every life and gives up honey and flesh has nothing to be said against him: earth and sky are his servants.
Kings who rule the world, after playing in the garden with bangled girls, are those who guard the habit of not drinking liquor, a small service.
nuance: The verse names the cause only by hint (சிற்றுபகாரம், 'small help'); the later-birth reading is supplied from the sermon's frame.

reading: Those who never ate after giving stand shrinking in Masi-month cold, in cloth stitched from thorn-torn rags, begging 'a morsel' with the hand held out.
nuance: The cause (never giving) is stated in the last line only; karma is implied, not named.
event: Civakan shows his wives a beggar shivering in rags with an outstretched hand, who never gave.

reading: Death is shown as a hunter driving a great deer in the forest, who, if we have no shelter, will mix up our lives and drink them like a ripened liquor he has laid by.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to parse (காட்டகத் தொருமகன் துரக்கும் மாக்கலை; ஓட்டுடைத் தாமெனின்) and the simile is read tentatively.

reading: Even from the hands of fowlers some birds escape; he bids the women look, and not dismiss with 'what' the word of a wise man, but learn the way of dharma.
nuance: The addressee is the women; the bird image is read as an escape that dharma gives.

reading: The moon tells of dying, birth, growth and waning; to be angry with good dharma when it fails is what belongs to fools.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure (வாய்புகப் பெய்யினும் வழுக்கின்); the sense that scorn of dharma is folly is the best fit.

reading: A drop of water falls, grows within foul flesh and appears in a place; if the great virtue is thought of, the hut of flesh will be escaped and will yield only the pleasure of floods, so they say.
nuance: Line 4's 'flood-water pleasure' is obscure; the verse is reported hearsay (என்பவே).

reading: Drops of milk and coral-water swell into flesh, it escapes by a narrow channel, then sinks in a pool of muddy water and, having no provision for the road, weeps and falls.
nuance: 'Provision for the journey' (கால்துணா, line 4) is read as stored good deeds; the word is not explained in the verse.

reading: Good dharma is a golden wishing-tree that blossoms with wealth and pleasure, so though they are troubled, the women should not forget the way of dharma.
Without charm and medicine no one would touch a five-headed snake; without the garland of bees, men would not come near women.
nuance: The snake simile for desire is the sermon's; the verse's logic (adornments make desire) is inferred from the paired lines.

reading: He tells the golden women that they shall give nothing but sweet liquid, and asks them to sit beside him and hear a few words, for they are worthy to win.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (தருதும் பாகுநீர் தின்றலாற்); the speaker and the offer are read from the context.

tamil: மெய்ப்படு சாந்தும் பூவு மிகநனி கமழு மேனுங்
கைப்படு சாந்தும் பூவுங் கொண்டலாற் கலக்க லாகா
வைப்படு பித்து நெய்த்தோ ரசும்புசோ ரழுகற் புன்றோற்
பொய்ப்பட வுரைத்த துண்டோ பொன்னனீர் நம்மு ணாமால்.
reading: Though the body smells strongly of sandal and flower, the sandal and flower are only what was put on by hand; underneath are fat, blood, oozing pus and soiled skin, and he asks if there is any lie in that.

tamil: அனிச்சத்தம் போது போலத் தொடுப்பவே குழைந்து மாழ்கி
யினிச்செத்தாம் பிறந்த போழ்தே யென்றுநா மிதனை யெண்ணித்
தனிச்சித்தம் வைத்த றேற்றாந் தளர்ந்துகண் பரப்பி நோக்கிப்
பனித்துமென் றுற்ற போழ்தே பழுதிலா வறிவி னென்னாம்.
reading: Like the anichcham flower they droop as soon as they are touched; we think 'we die from the day we are born', and what use is clear knowledge when, shaking and gazing about, one says 'we shall tremble'?
nuance: The last two lines compress an argument; the sense that knowledge should be used before the shaking of death is read from the simile.

tamil: நீனிறங் கொண்ட வைம்பா னிழன்மணி யுருவ நீங்கிப்
பானிறங் கொண்டு வெய்ய படாமுலை யையிற் றூங்கி
வேனிற மழைக்கண் டாமு மிமைகுறைந் தழுகி மேனி
தானிறங் கரக்குங் காலந் தையலீர் மெய்ய தன்றே.
reading: The blue colour of the five-part hair leaves, the breasts hang pale and sagging, the eyes lose their lustre and the body hides its colour: this, women, is not the body's true state.
The speaker, who ate rich food scented with ghee, fears the alms that must be begged in the great city, and says he will renounce but has no desire.
nuance: Whether the fear of begging is the wives' answer to the sermon or part of Civakan's own argument is not settled; the verb துறப்பல் (I will renounce) and ஆர்வமில்லையே (there is no desire) may be read as a refusal.

reading: Two who join in anger against one will break the strength of that one, he says to the slender-waisted, gem-adorned women.
nuance: The argument is incomplete; the verse looks like an introduction to the renunciation announcement but the logic of two against one is not clear.

reading: When the word that from the day love is gone they are strangers reached the women's ears, tears from their wide eyes poured down on their flowered breasts.
event: The wives hear Civakan say that they are now strangers to him, and they weep.

reading: The tears of the spear-eyed women, whose spear-like looks fed on flesh and killed kings, fall across the jewelled chains and gather in a pool, then pour down like a waterfall on their breasts.
nuance: The simile of the waterfall is the narrator's; the opening 'ate flesh and killed kings' refers to the spear, not to the women.
event: The wives weep until their tears flood their jewelled chests.

reading: Like flowers fallen on the ground after a thunderbolt of harsh words, the garlanded women fall at the feet, fill a vessel with their tears and cry as their hair sways.
event: The wives fall at Civakan's feet and weep.

tamil: குலிகவஞ் சேற்று ணாறிக் குங்கும நீரு ளோங்கிப்
பொலிகென வண்டு பாடப் பூத்ததா மரைகள் போலு
மொலிகழ லடிக ணுங்ககீழ்ப் பிழைத்ததென் னுரைமி னென்னப்
புலிநிழற் பட்ட மான்போற் போழுயி ராகி நின்றார்.
reading: They stand like a deer in the shadow of a tiger, their lives split, and ask what fault they committed under his feet, whose feet are like lotuses growing in red paste.
event: The wives ask what wrong they did, and stand in terror.

tamil: பெருந்தகு குறங்கு காணீர் பெண்ணுயி ரளிய தாமே
வருந்துமா லென்று நோக்கீர் வாடுமா லாவி யென்னீர்
reading: The women say: see the thighs that bore us as a rare couch; do not think the women's lives will be pitiful and pained; look at the empty bodies when you stand like guests.
nuance: The Tamil of lines 1-3 is dense; the sense of an appeal against the king's coldness is read from the whole.
event: The wives appeal to Civakan to look at what is left of them as he stands like a guest.

tamil: கோதையுந் துகிலு மேந்திக் குங்கும மெழுதிக் கொய்பூந்
தாதுகொண் டளகத் தப்பித் தடமுலை வருடிச் சேர்ந்து
காதல்கொண் டிருந்த காமர் கைவிர லளிய நீரு
மேதில லாகிக் கோமா னெண்ணமே யெண்ணி னீரே.
reading: Holding garland and cloth, applying kunkumam, putting pollen in their hair and stroking their breasts, those lovers' fingers are pitiable; you too became strangers and thought only of the king's mind.
nuance: The speaker and the addressee are doubtful: the verse may be the wives' own reproach or the narrator's comment on them.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2949-2973 (15/22)
theme: At the start of Civakan's departure for the ascetic's life, his wives weep and reproach his shoulders, chest, tongue, eyes and crown and recall the loves that brought him to them, and the palace and city fall into a silence of grief.
source_issues: Verses 2949-2955 and 2967-2973 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2956-2963 do not name their speakers and several wives are named only as the lovers recalled, so speakers are given as the wives as a group.
Many lines of 2949-2955 are hard to parse and are marked uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, now preparing to renounce his kingdom
the wives of Civakan, who lament his leaving; individual speakers are not named in the Tamil

tamil: பஞ்சிகொண் டெழுதி யார்ந்த சீறடி பனித்த லஞ்சிக்
குஞ்சிமே லேற்ற கோமான் கொப்புளித் திட்ட வெம்மை
வஞ்சித்தீர் மணிசெய் தோள்காள் வாங்குபு தழுவிக் கொள்ளீர்
நெஞ்சநீர் வலியீ ராகி நிற்பிரோ நீரு மென்பார்.
reading: The wives, speaking to the jewelled shoulders of their lord, recall the favour he showed their painted feet and ask whether the shoulders will now embrace them or stand hard of heart.
nuance: They address his body parts, not him; the lament runs through shoulders, chest, tongue, eyes and crown in the verses that follow. The sense of the second line is hard to fix.
event: Civakan's wives reproach his shoulders as he prepares to leave them.

tamil: முட்டுவட் டனைய கோல முத்துலாய்க் கிடந்து மின்ன
மட்டுவிட் டலர்ந்த கோதை மதுவொடு மயங்கி நாளு
மொட்டியிட் டுறைய வெங்கட் குயரணை யாய மார்ப
நட்புவிட் டொழியு மாயி னன்மையார் கண்ண தம்மா.
reading: Speaking to the chest where pearls and wreaths lay, the wives say that if the old friendship is dropped, that chest is no longer the refuge it was.
event: The wives reproach his chest.

tamil: மாக்கவின் வளரத் தீண்டி மணிநகை நக்கு நாளும்
பூக்கவி னார்ந்த பைந்தார் புனைமதுத் தேனொ டேந்தித்
தாக்கியெம் முலைக டம்மை நெருங்கினாய் தரணி மன்னி
னீக்கிநீ யெம்மை நோக்காய் நீத்தியோ நீயு மென்பார்.
reading: The wives remind the chest that it pressed their breasts in love and ask whether he will now cast them off and not look at them once he rules the earth.
event: The wives accuse him of leaving them for his rule.

tamil: அன்னமே தோகை நல்யா ழமுதமே யாய்ந்த தீந்தே
னின்னரே நங்கை மாரென் றேத்திய பவளச் செந்நா
வென்னைநீ கண்ட தெம்மை யிரண்டுநா வாயி னாயே
மன்னன்போ லீர மின்றி வலித்தனை வாழி யென்பார்.
reading: The wives say the tongue that praised them as swan, peacock, lute and nectar has shown two tongues, and call him, like a king, pitiless and hard.
event: The wives reproach his tongue for its broken praise.

tamil: பூணினா னெருங்க நொந்து பொதிர்த்தன வெம்பி யென்று
நாணினால் வருத்தந் தீர்ப்பா னன்முலைக் கண்க டம்மைப்
பேணிநீ ரெழுதி யோம்பிப் பேரின்பங் கொண்டு தந்தீர்
காண்மினோ வின்றெம் வண்ணங் கண்ணிலீர் கண்க ளென்பார்.
reading: The wives tell his eyes that they cared for their breasts and gave them great joy, and now, eyeless, do not see the state they are in.
event: The wives reproach his eyes.

tamil: சென்னிமேன் மிதித்த வஞ்செஞ் சீறடித் திருவில் வீச
மின்னிவா ளாரஞ் சிந்த வெறுநிலத் துறைந்து நீயெ
மின்னகை முறுவல் பார்த்தா யின்றெம தாவி பார்த்தாய்
மன்னிய மாலை வண்டார் மணிமுடி வாழி யென்பார்.
reading: The wives tell the jewelled crown that it looked on their smiles and now looks on the loss of their lives, and bid it 'live long' in bitter irony.
nuance: The 'long life' is an irony; the crown that once took their feet now sees them destroyed.
event: The wives reproach his crown with bitter blessing.

tamil: வீங்குபாற் கடலு நஞ்சாய் விளைந்ததால் விரிந்த வெய்யோன்
பாங்கிலா விருளை யீன்று பார்மறைத் திட்ட தாலோ
தீங்கதிர்த் திங்கள் செந்தீச் சொரிந்ததாற் றிசைக ளெல்லாந்
தாங்குமா றென்னை யாவி தரிக்கிலேந் தேவிர் காளோ.
reading: The wives cry that the sea of milk has turned to poison, the sun has borne darkness and the moon pours fire, and ask how they can hold their lives, calling on the gods.
event: The wives cry out that the world has turned against them.

reading: The speaker asks whether the woman of the long eyes, named Gandharvadattai, is a heavenly maid or a Vidyadhara girl, and asks who will now take up the music she knew.
nuance: The addressees and speaker are not fixed by the Tamil; the verse may be a wife's plea about Gandharvadattai or Gandharvadattai's own.
event: One wife turns her lament to Gandharvadattai and the music they shared.

reading: A wife promises to kill the long-eyed Gunamalai, who was caught by the elephant and was rescued when he killed it and embraced her, and asks whether she too is of that kind now.
nuance: The verse reminds him of the rescue to show what he owes; the threat to kill is more likely a cry of despair than a plan.
event: A wife recalls the elephant's attack on Gunamalai and his rescue.

reading: A wife recalls Padumai, whom the snake bit and who revived when he took her coral mouth as nectar, and asks whether the venom has now come back on them.
event: A wife recalls the cure of Padumai.

reading: A wife reminds him that her eyes pierced his chest through the sandal paste and asks whether he will let that joy, once gained, go.
event: A wife recalls their first love and asks him not to leave it.

reading: A wife says that he who raved over their eyes, lips and bodies, and showed his bow, now gives them up like a rag laid on a wound, and asks if renouncing is worth anything.
nuance: Here the wives put renunciation as a question of what is fitting; the Naladiyar and Kural praise it as the best course.
event: A wife questions the worth of his renunciation.

reading: A wife says that those who entered the golden city's street and were caught in the net of a dancing woman's long eyes now find that the light has gone and ask whether the wreath is a pain.
event: A wife recalls how he was caught in love's net.

reading: A wife says that he who delighted in the one like a lotus, guarded by women, and joined her as a brahmin with music, is wrong to give them up, and asks if renouncing is fitting.
nuance: It recalls the episode in which Civakan came as a brahmin; the wife it names is not fixed by the Tamil.
event: A wife recalls his stay as a brahmin and asks if renouncing is fitting.

reading: A wife says that he, strong-shouldered and the killer of enemies, drank and danced with Lakshmanai before all, and asks whether he will leave in affection while others tremble.
event: A wife recalls how Civakan danced with Lakshmanai.

reading: The palace, with sobbing women worshipping him and weeping in every direction, becomes like a deep sea, as even stones and trees melt.
nuance: The verse moves from the wives' own words to the narrator's sight of the whole palace in grief.
event: The women of the palace weep and worship him as he prepares to go.

reading: Some women beat their golden bangles, scatter garlands and tremble like caught does, asking whether the king will guard their lives or leave them unguarded.
event: The women strip off ornaments and weep as the king departs.

reading: The women, weeping with faces like water-lilies, are like jewelled flags on a mast that tremble and cry.
event: The women cry out in grief.

tamil: பண்ணார் பணைமுழவம் பாடவிந்து பன்மணியாழ் மழலை நீங்கிப்
புண்ணார் புனைகுழலு மேங்கா புனைபாண்டி லிரங்கா வான்பூங்
கண்ணா ரொலிகவுள கிண்கிணியு மஞ்சிலம்புங் கலையு மாரா
மண்ணார் வலம்புரியும் வாய்மடங்கிக் கோன்கோயின் மடிந்த தன்றே.
reading: The drums, the lutes, the flutes and the tinkling anklets all fall silent, and the king's palace is as if dead.

tamil: அணியார் மணியரக்கு வட்டழுத்தி வைத்தனைய செங்கண் மாத்தாட்
பிணியார் பெருந்துருத்தி யன்ன பெருங்கடவுள பிறையேர் கோட்ட
பணியார் கமழ்கடாத் தண்ண லரசுவாப் பண்ணார் பாய்மா
விணையாது மில்லாத கண்ணீர்வீழ்த் துண்ணாநின் றினைந்த தாமே.
reading: Great tuskers, war-horses and the rest stand silent and shed tears, taking no food, in the palace of the departing king.

tamil: கழித்த கடிப்பிணையுங் கைவளையு மாலையுங் களைந்து முத்துந்
தொழித்த நறுஞ்சாந்துஞ் சுண்ணமும் பன்மணியுங் கலனுஞ் சிந்தி
விழித்து வியன்கோயில் பன்மீன் பரந்திமைக்கும் பனியார் வானம்
பழித்துப் பசும்பொன் னுலகு குடிபோயிற் றொத்த தன்றே.
reading: Women, having cast off earrings, bangles, wreaths, sandal and jewels, make the palace look like a sky robbed of stars, as if the golden world had moved out.

tamil: அழலார் சுரையெயிற்று வெஞ்சினவைந் தலைசுமந்த வெகுளி நாக
நிழலார் திருமணியுந் தேவர் திருமுடிமே னிலவி வீசுஞ்
சுழலார் பசும்பொன்னும் வேய்ந்து சொரிகதிர்மென் பஞ்சி யார்ந்த
கழலா னகர மமுது கடைகடல்போற் கலங்கிற் றன்றே.
reading: The king's city, rich in jewels and gold, is stirred like the sea churned for nectar.

tamil: நீர்நிறை குளத்து மாரி சொரிந்தென நறுநெய் துள்ளு
நேர்நிறை பொரியுங் குய்யும் வறைகளு நிவந்த வாசம்
பார்நிறை யடிசிற் பள்ளி தளியொடு சாலை யெல்லா
மூர்நிறை யுயிர்த்த லின்றி யுயிர்சென்ற போன்ற வன்றே.
reading: The kitchens, almshouses and halls, once rich in ghee, rice and savoury, now stand as if every living breath had gone from the town.

tamil: கோட்புலிச் சுழல்கண் ணன்ன கொழுஞ்சுவைக் கருனை முல்லை
மோட்டிள முகையின் மொய்கொள் கொக்குகிர் நிமிரல் வெண்சோ
றூட்டுறு கறிகொ டேமாங் கனிசுவைத் தயிரோ டேந்தி
வேட்டவர்ப் பெறாது வீதி வெறுநிலங் கிடந்த வன்றே.
reading: The costly rice, the sweet dishes and the curd lie wasted on the empty street, since those who wanted them are not there.

tamil: மைந்தர்தம் வண்கை யான்முன் மணிவள்ளத் தெடுத்த தேறல்
பைந்துகின் மகளிர் மேவார் பாசிழை பசும்பொன் மாலை
சிந்தியே கரந்தார் சொற்போன் மெய்யின்கட் சேர்த லின்றாய்ச்
சந்தனச் சாந்தொ டாரந் தாங்கவி னிழந்த வன்றே.
reading: The cup of wine in the youth's hand is untouched, the maids leave their jewels and garlands, and sandal and pearls lose their beauty.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2974-2998 (16/22)
theme: The last farewell: the palace falls silent as Civakan prepares to renounce, he teaches the weeping wives that wealth ends at the burning ground and that even the fruit of good deeds binds, they take off their ornaments and choose penance, and after giving away all he has he worships his mother and is carried off by the gods.
source_issues: 2974, 2975, 2976, 2979, 2983, 2984, 2985, 2986, 2988, 2991, 2993 and 2998 and other stanzas were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines in the core file.
2979 line 4, 2981, 2983, 2984, 2986, 2989, 2993 and 2996 carry rare words or syntax that cannot be fixed; the readings are marked uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who hears the sage
Civakan's eight wives, who renounce with him
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother
the gods who carry Civakan's palanquin

tamil: தாழிவாய் மறைக்குந் தண்ணென் றடம்பெருங் குவளைக் கண்ணார்
மூழிவாய் முல்லை மாலை முலைமுக முரிந்து நக்க
யாழின்வாய் முழவம் விம்ம வாட்டொழிந் தயர்ந்து தீந்தே
னூழிவாய்க் கொண்ட தொக்கும் பாடலு மொழிந்த தன்றே.
reading: In the palace the lute, the drum and the women's song fall silent, the women's jasmine garlands crushed at their breasts, and the singing that was like sweet honey is gone.
nuance: The verse gives no cause for the silence; the following verses supply it, the king's coming departure.

tamil: அருங்கல நிறைந்த வம்பூம் பவளக்கா றிகழம் பைம்பொற்
பெருங்கிடு கென்னுங் கோலப் பேரிமை பொருந்தி மெல்ல
வொருங்குட னகர மெல்லா முரங்குவ தொத்த தொல்லென்
கருட்கடல் கல்லென் சும்மை கரந்தது மொத்த தன்றே.
reading: The whole city falls hushed as if asleep, and the roar like a dark sea that filled it is hidden.

tamil: கலையுலாய் நிமிர்ந்த வல்குற் கடல்விளை யமுத மன்னார்
முலையுலாய் நிமிர்ந்த மொய்தார் முழவுமுத் துரிஞ்சி மின்னச்
சிலையுலாய் நிமிர்ந்த மார்பன் றிருநகர் தெருள்க லாதாய்
நிலையிலா வுலகின் றன்மை நீர்மைமீக் கூறிற் றன்றே.
reading: The palace of the bowman-chested king, with its women and its drums, can teach what the unsteady world is like to anyone who has not yet understood it.
nuance: The line 3 phrase தெருள்கலாதாய் is read here as 'to one who has not yet understood'; the verse turns the palace's splendour into a lesson.

reading: The smoke of hair-incense, of oblations, of lifted cloth and of garlands is gone, vanished like the fame of misers who give nothing of what they have gathered.
nuance: வேள்விக் கொழும்புகை may be oblation smoke of a household rite; the verse does not name a school for it and uses it only as one of the things that vanish.

reading: The neighing of the grass-eating horses, the cries of the conch-cutters and the herons, the careless laughter of young boys and the trumpet of the killer elephant and the conch all cease.

Flowers, garlands, sandal and ornaments, and the drink of honey that the women guarded, lose their hold and are no longer wanted, as the words of a text lose their sense for those who do not value it.
nuance: Line 4's simile (சொற்பொருள்போல்) is hard: the sense may be that things are dropped like words of no concern; the reading here is a best guess.

reading: The parrot forgets the sweet milk, the gods' offerings stop, the elephants no longer eat sugarcane, speech halts and all become strangers, and the city turns to a forest in the dark of night.
As the king prepares to renounce before the great lord, the wealth of the land that rolled like the roaring sea passes to the young ones and the city and country come to the feet of the strong one.
nuance: Who is 'the great lord' (திருமால்) and who 'the strong one' (உரவோன்) is not fixed in the Tamil; the reading takes the first as Civakan and the second as his heir. The sons are not named.

reading: With eyes red and long like spearheads set in the forge's flame, the women weep in grief, and the king speaks to them.
nuance: The last line introduces the speech that fills the next verses.
event: Civakan speaks to the weeping wives, beginning his teaching to them.

tamil: நற்றவம் பரவை ஞால நாமுட னிறுப்பின் வைய
மற்றமி றவத்திற் கென்று மையவி யனைத்து மாற்றா
திற்றென வுணர்ந்து நிற்பிற் றிருமக ளென்று நீங்காள்
பற்றொடே நிற்பி னென்றுந் திருமகள் பற்றல் செல்லாள்.
reading: The king tells them that if the whole earth and sea were set against good penance they would not equal it, and that Fortune, who never leaves the one who knows that even a world of wealth is short of that and so lets go, will never reach the one who holds on with attachment.
nuance: The Tamil of lines 1 to 4 is dense and the logic of 'never leaves' against 'never clings' reads as a paradox: wealth comes to the unattached. In the first ilampakam Fortune had left the clinging king (232).
event: Civakan teaches the wives the worth of penance over wealth.

tamil: உப்பிலிப் புழுக்கல் காட்டுட் புலைமக னுகுப்ப வேகக்
கைப்பலி யுண்டி யானும் வெள்ளின்மேற் கவிழ நீரு
மைப்பொலி கண்ணி னீரான் மனையக மெழுகி வாழ
விப்பொருள் வேண்டு கின்றீ ரிதனைநீர் கேண்மி னென்றான்.
reading: Civakan asks if they want wealth that ends with unsalted rice poured by an outcaste in the burning ground, a rice-ball overturned on the bier and a wife smearing the house with her eye-black tears, and bids them listen.
nuance: வெள்ளின் in line 2 is read as the bier-frame; the picture of the funeral is pieced together from rare words and cannot be fixed exactly.
event: Civakan sets before the wives the funeral to which wealth leads and asks them to hear him.

tamil: கொல்சின யானை பார்க்குங் கூருகிர்த் தறுக ணாளி
யில்லெலி பார்த்து நோக்கி யிறப்பின்கீ ழிருந்த லுண்டே
பல்வினை வெள்ள நீந்திப் பகாவின்பம் பருகி னல்லா
னல்வினை விளையு ளென்னு நஞ்சினுட் குளித்த லுண்டே.
reading: Civakan says that even the lion that looks at the elephant may at the end sit beneath death, and that unless one crosses the flood of many deeds and drinks undivided bliss, one is bathing in the poison called the fruit of good deeds.
nuance: The Jain view that merit as well as sin binds is stated strongly: நல்வினை விளையுள் is poison. Compare the sermon at 2846 where release is freedom from deeds.
event: Civakan teaches that even good deeds have a fruit that binds.

tamil: ஆற்றிய மக்க ளென்னு மருந்தவ மிலார்க ளாகிற்
போற்றிய மணியும் பொன்னும் பின்செலா பொன்ன னீரே
வேற்றுவ ரென்று நில்லா விழுப்பொருள் பரவை ஞால
நோற்பவர்க் குரிய வாகு நோன்மின் நீரு மேன்றான்.
reading: Civakan says that if their children lack the great penance the guarded gems and gold will not follow them, and that the wealth of the sea-girt earth belongs to those who do penance, so they should do it.
nuance: Line 1 is hard: ஆற்றிய மக்கள் என்னும் அருந்தவம் is read as 'the great penance called children'; the sense may be otherwise.
event: Civakan urges the golden-adorned wives to take up penance.

tamil: காதலஞ் சேற்றுட் பாய்ந்த மதியெனுங் கலங்க னீரை
யூதுவண் டுடுத்த தாரா னுவர்ப்பினி னுரிஞ்சித் தேற்ற
மாதரார் நெஞ்சந் தேறி மாதவஞ் செய்து மென்றார்
காதலான் காத லென்னு நிகளத்தா னெடுங்க ணாரே.
reading: The long-eyed women's hearts, muddied by the clay of love, are cleared when the garlanded king stirs and settles them with disgust, and they say they will do great penance, though still held by the fetter of love for him.
nuance: The verse's own image is of muddy water cleared by a stirrer; love for the husband is named the fetter that still binds the women as they decide.
event: Civakan's teaching clears the wives' minds and they decide to take up penance.

tamil: தூமஞ்சால் கோதை யீரே தொல்வினை நீத்த நீந்தி
நாமஞ்சால் கதியி னீங்கி நன்பொன்மே லுலகி னுச்சி
யேமஞ்சா லின்பம் வேண்டி னென்னோடும் வம்மி னென்றான்
காமஞ்சாய்த் தடர்த்து வென்ற காஞ்சனக் குன்ற மன்னான்.
reading: Civakan calls the wives to cross the old deeds, leave the famed rebirth and come with him if they want the secure bliss at the top of the golden world above.
nuance: The summit of the world above is the Jain siddha abode; the verse says nothing of a god who grants it.
event: Civakan invites the wives to renounce with him and reach release.

tamil: நாடக நயந்து காண்பார் நலங்கிளர் கண்கள் சூன்று
மாடகக் கலத்து ளான்பா லமிர்தினை நயந்துண் பாரை
நீடகம் வெகுண்டுங் கையாற் பிடித்துநீ றட்டி யிட்டேங்
கோடக மணிந்த கோல முடியினாய் துறத்து மென்றார்.
reading: The wives answer that to cling to pleasure now would be like gouging out one's eyes to watch a dance or throwing nectar from a jewelled vessel into the ash, and tell the crowned one that they will renounce.
nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are hard: the images of gouged eyes and ash-covered nectar are read as the wives' own comparison, but the Tamil is unclear on who does these things.
event: The wives accept Civakan's call and declare they will renounce.

reading: The wives bow to the king whose hair they used to serve with flowers and ask him not to be angry when they come in the world he reaches to serve him as today.
event: The wives bow to Civakan and ask to serve him in the world he goes to.

tamil: தெண்டிரை நீத்த நீந்தித் தீங்கதிர் சுமந்து திங்கள்
விண்படர்ந் தனைய மாலை வெண்குடை வேந்தர் வேந்தன்
கண்டிரண் முத்த மாலைக் கதிர்முலை நங்கை மாரை
வெண்டிரை வியக்குங் கேள்வி விசயைகண் ணபயம் வைத்தான்.
reading: The king of kings, having crossed the clear flood of the sea of learning, sees the pearl-garlanded women and entrusts them to the care of Vijayai, wise in lore.
nuance: 'Care' is read from அபயம் வைத்தான், which can also mean he gave them a promise of safety; the verse does not state that they join her order, though the story elsewhere has her renounce.
event: Civakan places his wives under his mother Vijayai's protection.

tamil: கடிமலர் நிறைந்து பூத்த கற்பகக் கொம்புங் காமர்
வடிமலர் மலர்ந்த காம வல்லியுந் தம்மைத் தாமே
யுடைமலர் கொய்து போக வுகுத்திடு கின்ற தொத்தார்
படைமலர் நெடுங்க ணல்லார் பாசிழை நீக்கு கின்றார்.
reading: The wives lay aside their jewelled ornaments, like the wishing-tree branch and the vine of desire shedding the flowers that they themselves strip.
nuance: The vine of desire (காமவல்லி) is the image: what had been the plant of desire is shown shedding its own flowers.
event: The wives remove their ornaments.

tamil: தழுமலர்த் தாம நான்று சந்தகின் மணந்து விம்முஞ்
செழுமணி நிலத்துச் செம்பொற் றிருமுத்த விதான நீழ
லெழுமையும் பெறுக வென்னு மெழின்முலை நெற்றி சூழ்ந்தார்
கழுமிய துகிலிற் காமன் கண்புடைத் திரங்க மாதோ.
reading: Under the pearl canopy on the gem floor the garlanded women, wishing that this may be theirs for seven births, wrap their breasts and brows in cloth while the god of love is said to beat his eyes and grieve.
nuance: The last two lines are obscure and the reading is tentative: it may be the women wishing 'may we have this for seven births' or the jewels falling away.
event: The wives put on the renunciant's cloth as the god of love mourns.

tamil: நறும்புகை நான நாவிக் குழம்பொடு பளிதச் சுண்ண
மறிந்தவ ராய்ந்த மாலை யணிந்தபைங் கூந்த லாய்பொ
னிறந்தரு கொம்பு நீலக் கதிர்க்கற்றை யுமிழ்வ வேபோற்
செறிந்திருந் துகுத்துச் செம்பொற் குணக்கொடி யாயி னாரே.
reading: With perfume smoke, musk and powders put aside and the fragrant garlands of their hair taken off, the women become golden vines of virtue.
nuance: The vine image (குணக்கொடி) turns the women into plants of virtue as they strip themselves of the scents of desire.
event: The wives strip off their perfumes and garlands and become renunciants.

reading: The king's bangled hands pour out the gifts to those who ask because they are in great want, as if two gold conches were pouring gems.
nuance: The giving here is the last act before renunciation, with nothing to be had in return for it.
event: Civakan gives gifts to beggars before he leaves.

reading: His generous hands pour out white vessels like gold-showering lotuses, so that the world may eat its fill.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (என்பரிந்து எரிதலை): the reading takes them as the plea of the world in hunger.
event: Civakan gives out vessels of food and gold to all the world.

reading: The king gives away the fine clothes, ornaments, garlands and sandal that the world enjoys with delight and becomes a grove of wishing trees that rain gems.
event: Civakan gives his clothes, ornaments and garlands to the world.

tamil: தேய்பிறை யுருவக் கேணித் தேறுநீர் மலர்ந்த தேனா
ராய்நிறக் குவளை யஞ்சிக் குறுவிழிக் கொள்ளும் வாட்கண்
வேய்நிறை யழித்த மென்றோள் விசயையைத் தொழுது வாழ்த்திச்
சேய்நிறச் சிவிகை சேர்ந்தான் றேவர்கொண் டேகி னாரே.
reading: Civakan worships and blesses Vijayai, whose tender arms put the bamboo to shame, and boards the red palanquin that the gods then lift and carry away.
nuance: The palanquin that had carried the mothers to renunciation (2628) now carries the son, and the gods, not men, bear it.
event: Civakan bows to his mother, boards the palanquin and is carried off by the gods.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 2999-3023 (17/22)
theme: In the last ilampakam Civakan comes to the assembly of the Jina, with its festival, tree and gods' whisks, bows and circles, hears that a king's renunciation is the excellent course, and the hymns to the Jina's feet place the freedom from deeds in worship and the Jina's word.
source_issues: Verses 3017-3021 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
3007 and 3015 do not say plainly who descends or who bows.
3013 line 2 has a misprint (றோன்னினா for தோன்றினான்).
3021 line 4 has a corrupt word (னருவாய்) and repeats the first half of 3020 line 4.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who comes to the Jina's assembly
the Jina, the lord of the three umbrellas and the pindi tree, who has shed his deeds
the gods who hold whisks and rain flowers at the Jina's assembly
the unnamed singer who hymns the Jina in the second person (3017-3021), taken as a worshipper in the host or the king

reading: The lutes and flutes sound softly, the drums answer in a guest's welcome, and the bright gem-set instruments are said to pour out their sound as the festival begins.
nuance: The last line reports the sound as hearsay (என்பவே), a poet's formula for scenes he did not see.

reading: Aloe smoke, wish-tree garlands and heaped flowers make earth and sky look like a red-gemmed casket.
Many praise, sing and dance at the city of the lord of the three umbrellas, and the massed instruments sound like a flood of the world roaring.
nuance: The 'lord of the three umbrellas' (முக்குடைச் செல்வன்) is the Jina, whose city is the assembly Civakan is approaching.

reading: Groves, lotus tanks, bee-filled gardens, tall golden walls and white banners are said to spread as if they had joined the sky.
The raised pinnacles, the trident-topped gate-towers and the golden hill-like heights look as if time had brought all the earth together for the eye to see.
nuance: Line 4 (காலமுற்றுடன் கண்ணுற்ற போன்றவே) is hard to parse; the comparison is read loosely.

reading: Gate arches hung with wish-tree garlands, spread over the walls, are said to outshine Indra's golden city while aloe smoke veils the sun.
White birds on the lotus tops look like a white lotus of glory opening in a red lotus, and the poet adds that one could doubt whether they were real.
nuance: Line 3 (ஐயஞ்செய்தடுபா னிறப்புள்ளின) is hard to parse, so the poet's doubt is only partly clear.

reading: The moat like a great sea and the temple with its roaring birds are so fine that, the verse says, heaven would be sweet only if this did not exist on earth.
nuance: The construction of line 3-4 (இல்லை யேற்றுறக்கம் இனிதென்பவே) can be read two ways, as a boast that heaven is lesser or as 'heaven would be sweet if there were no such place'.

reading: A radiant figure comes down from the sky, worships and draws near, and the lord appears like a young sun over the milk-sea on a gem mountain.
nuance: It is not clear whether the one who descends is Civakan, a god, or the one who appears; line 4 names the lord (இறைவன்) as the one who shows himself, and I read him as the Jina.
event: A radiant figure descends, worships and approaches, and the lord appears.

reading: The one who has shed his deeds sits with his hand placed, his face like the sun and the lotus opened at its rising.
nuance: வினையுதிர்த்தவர் (those who shed deeds) is the verse's own name for the liberated, a Jain sense that the narrator holds rather than argues.

reading: At the sight the king's hair stands up, tears pour, and with love he praises, scatters flowers like rain and circles to the right.
nuance: Line 1 (இரிந்தன விருவினை) may mean the deeds flee at his seeing or that his hairs stand; the claim is taken as the first.
event: Civakan praises with tears, scatters flowers and walks round the Jina keeping him on his right.

reading: Pearl garlands, gem clusters, golden and coral wreaths and flower strings hang down in profusion.
The gods hold up whisks as if the sea waves had met a gem mountain, and the sweet rays of the three umbrellas drink the dark.
nuance: The whisks and the three umbrellas are the marks of the Jina's assembly; the verse does not say so in words, and the sense is from the scene.
event: The gods fan the Jina with whisks under the three umbrellas.

reading: The Jina's pindi tree opens its flowers, bees gather, and the cuckoo calls as if keeping a festival.
nuance: வீரன் பிண்டியே names the tree as the hero's, the ashoka that marks the Jina.

reading: In the pindi's thick shade, to end the disease of birth, the hero appears and drums announce that all should eat the nectar of dharma.
nuance: Line 2 has a misprint (றோன்னினா for தோன்றினான்); the sense is that he appeared.
event: The Jina appears under the pindi tree and the drums call all to eat the nectar of dharma.

reading: The gods rain flowers and the king reaches the faultless lord whose red feet sit on a honeyed lotus, the one who ends the births of ascetics.
event: Civakan reaches the Jina's feet while the gods rain flowers.

reading: The one who bows touches his gem crown to the ground and praises, saying that the scion of Civakan's line and the Kasyapa lord may live, while jewelled lutes ring out.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to parse: the names சீவக குமரன் and காசிப அடிகள் stand in a run of titles and it is not clear whether the praise is of the Jina or the king's own line, and the word மருகலில் is unclear.
event: Civakan bows with his crown to the ground and praises the Kasyapa lord.

reading: The lord's sweet word, that a king's renunciation is the excellent thing, falls like a rain-cloud's thunder out of his mouth, like gold hill opened.
nuance: The word of the Jina is given as a narrated report in the poet's words, not in direct speech, and the sense of the second line (the hill opening its mouth) is a simile for the voice.
event: The Jina tells Civakan that the king's renunciation is the excellent course.

tamil: காய்களிற்றி னிடைமருப்பிற் கவளம்போன் றேமாராக் கதியுட் டோன்றி
யாங்களிய வெவ்வினையி னல்லாப்புற் றஞ்சினே னறிந்தார் கோவே
வேய்களிய வண்டறைய விரிந்தலர்ந்த தாமரையின் விரைசேர் போதின்
வாயொளியே பெறநடந்த மலரடியை வலங்கொண்டார் வருந்தார் போலும்.
reading: Speaking to the lord of the knowers, the singer says he was born in the unsafe course like a morsel between an elephant's tusks and feared his deeds, and that those who circle the lotus-treading feet seem not to suffer.
nuance: The speaker is not named; the 'I' who feared is read as Civakan or as a worshipper in the host. Lines 3-4 are hard to parse. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

reading: In praise to the lord whose garland never fades under the pindi, the singer says that the world does not sing of those who do not sing his virtues and that those who do not wear the flowers of his feet are not worn by the gods.
nuance: The second half of the stanza is hard to parse (பாடாதாரைப் பாடாது உலகம், சூடார்மலை ...), so the claim is a loose reading. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

tamil: வைய மூன்று முடனேத்த வளருந் திங்கள் வாளெயிற்
றைய வரிமான் மணியணைமே லமாந்தோய் நின்னை யமராதார்
வெய்ய வெந்நோய் வினையுதைப்ப வீழ்ந்து துன்பக் கடலழுந்தி
நெய்யு நுண்ணூ னாழிகையி னிரம்பா நின்று சுழல்வரே.
reading: The singer says that those who do not reach the lord on his gem seat, praised by all three worlds, are kicked by their fierce deeds, fall into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread in a weaver's spool.
nuance: The comparison in line 4 is of a thread wound on the shuttle (நெய்யும் நுண்ணூல் நாழிகையில் நிரம்பா நின்று): the same thread goes round without end. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

tamil: தொழுதிப் பன்மீன் குழாஞ்சூழத் துளும்பா திருந்த திங்கள்போன்
முழுதும் வைய முடனேத்த முதுவாய் வலவை யாயிருந்
தழுது வினைக ளல்லாப்ப வறைந்தோய் நின்சொ லறைந்தார்கள்
பழுதி னறுநெய்க் கடற்சுடர்போற் பல்லாண் டெல்லாம் பரியாரே.
reading: The singer addresses the lord, calm as a moon among stars, who sat as the ancient master and spoke while beings wept under their deeds, and says that those who say his word will not suffer for countless years.
nuance: Line 2 (முதுவாய் வலவையாயிருந்து) is hard to parse; வலவை reads as a skilled speaker. Line 4's first half is repeated at the start of 3021's last line, which suggests a refrain or a copyist's slip. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

tamil: செழும்பொன் வேய்ந்து மணியழுத்தித் திருவார் வைர நிரைத்ததனுட்
கொழுந்து மலருங் கொளக்குயிற்றிக் குலாய சிங்கா தனத்தின்மே
லெழுந்த பருதி யிருந்தாற்போ யழுந்தேன் வந்துன் னடியடைந்தே
பழுதி னறுநெய்க் கடற்சுடர்போற் னருவாய்ப் போத லழகிதோ.
reading: The singer says he sank in the sea of birth, came to the lord's feet on a golden throne of gems, and asks whether it would be fair to go again.
nuance: The word னருவாய் in line 4 is corrupt and the question's sense cannot be fixed. The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and joined into four.

reading: The king bows with his gem crown, with his ear-rings, gold bands, garland of pearls and flower cluster shining on the ground, to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees.
nuance: The lotus under the walking feet is the Jina's own seat among the lotuses in the assembly; the verse names no person, and the 'king' is taken from the crown.
event: Civakan bows with his crown to the Jina's feet.

reading: The lord of the jewel crown bows, while the sky wonders, to the sea of countless virtues, the wheel of dharma that guards life and clears the world's darkness of hunger, hatred and disease, and whose limit is wisdom.
nuance: The verse names both அறவாழி (wheel of dharma) and குணக்கடல் (sea of virtues): the same Tamil element ஆழி/கடல் is both a wheel and a sea here.
event: Civakan bows to the Jina with the gods wondering.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 3024-3048 (18/22)
theme: Civakan, having praised the Jina, strips off his ornaments and plucks his hair in the grove, the gods carry the hair to the milk sea, the god Sutanjanan praises him, his followers take the ascetic's vows, and the narrative turns to the Magadha king Senikan, who prepares to feast the Jina's feet.
source_issues: Verses 3024, 3042-3044 and 3047-3048 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
3045 lines 1-2 are corrupt as printed and cannot be parsed.
3032-3034 and 3036 are hard to parse in places; marked uncertain.

cast.role: the hero, now renouncing
the gods who attend the Jina and carry off the hair
the bees of the grove, who speak after the tonsure
the god who was once the dog Civakan helped
Civakan's kin and followers who renounce with him, as the story has it
king of Magadha at Rajagriha who prepares a feast for the Jina's feet

reading: Having praised the Jina, a sea of virtues and the limit of all joy, Civakan rises from his seat resolved to renounce.
event: Civakan hymns and bows to the Jina and rises, resolved to renounce.

reading: Gods with crowns and women bow around the sage, and his golden city blooms like wishing trees tangled with love-vines.
nuance: The two kinds of onlooker, gods and women, are the verse's only actors; they bow and do nothing else, so it is scene-setting for the renunciation.

reading: Circling the glorious golden city of the wise Jina, Civakan goes on to the painted grove like a mass of hair.
nuance: 'செல்வன்' as Civakan is read from the story; the verse names no one, and the hair simile in line 3 is hard to place.
event: Civakan circles the Jina's city and reaches the pleasure grove where he will cast off his state.

reading: Counting the sea-ringed world as a mere drop of milk, the spear-bearing king puts off his fine ornaments and fragrant garlands, as if Kama were stripping off his gear.
event: Civakan strips off his jewels and garlands.

reading: He takes off the silk of royal state like a gem from its sheath, and stands like the sun risen from the milk sea, an earthly tilaka.
event: Civakan removes his royal garments.

reading: He puts off garlands, coloured cloth and gem-set ornaments as burdens he was tired of carrying, and shines like a wishing tree.
event: Civakan lays aside the last garlands and ornaments.

reading: Facing east, bright-chested, he seems a roaring lion shaking off its mane as he tears out his hair.
nuance: The plucking of the hair (the Jain way of tonsure) is put by simile alone; the verb 'துறப்பது' carries both leaving and shedding.
event: Civakan faces east and pulls out his hair.

reading: Prince Civakan lets the plucked hair fall from his lotus hand into a white tray, like pouring dark rays into the moon.
event: Civakan drops his plucked hair into a white tray.

reading: The hair set aside, the bees of the grove, like a kalpaka tree dropping jewelled leaves at dawn, bow to the king and speak.
nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are hard to parse; the bees as speakers are what the last line gives.
event: The bees of the grove bow to the king after his tonsure and speak.

reading: The bees complain that he has cut off his hair and garland, which they lived by, and ask where they are to go now.
nuance: The bees' lament is a poet's device for what the lord's former life lost; the verse does not argue against renunciation.

reading: The bees, grieving, go with the garland's swarm and, bowing to the king's golden hair, circle it and depart.
nuance: The sense of 'என்றன தேனினம்' and the second line is uncertain.
event: The bees circle the cast-off hair and leave.

reading: Gods lift the golden tray with its kalpaka-garland, cry 'homage to him who crossed the four seas,' and let it fall like the moon into the milk sea.
nuance: The cry 'நமோ' is the homage-word of the Jain mantra; the verse does not itself say which.
event: The gods carry off Civakan's hair, cry homage, and lay it in the milk sea.

reading: Whoever whispers these unstrung-gem words into the ears of the dying becomes, at that hour, a deathless god adorned with pearls.
nuance: 'ஏவா இருந்த அடிகள்' is hard to place and the speaker may be a charge from the god Sutanjanan; the claim recalls verse 945, where Civakan gave the dog the mantra.

reading: The god, having praised Civakan the crest-jewel of an old line at his feet, enters his own shrine.
nuance: The subject 'புக்கானே' is read as Sutanjanan from the next verse.
event: Sutanjanan, after praising Civakan's feet, goes into his own palace.

reading: Sutanjanan enters with his consorts like a crowd of golden lotus maidens, and sings and dances the virtue of the lord until his palace overflows like a sea of sweet milk.
event: Sutanjanan and his women sing and dance in praise of Civakan's virtue.

reading: All of them, dropping attachment and hatred like a snake's skin, become ascetics, shed the milk of kindness on every life, and set a gem lamp so that darkness does not reach the mind.
nuance: 'எல்லாரும்' is the queens, kin and followers by the story; the verse does not list them.
event: Civakan's kin and followers renounce and become ascetics.

reading: Following the lord like elephants, they reach the Jina's temple, praise his feet, bathe in the sea of virtue and enter like a right-turned conch among ordinary shells.
event: They worship at the Jina's feet and enter the order.

reading: As the lotus feet of the lord of the flowering pindi tree shine like a sun on thick dark, the poet turns to praise what then happened.
nuance: A link verse that turns from Civakan's renunciation to the closing account of the work.

tamil: கயலின முகளிப் பாய முல்லையம் பொதும்பிற் காமர்
புயலின மொக்குள் வன்கட் குறுமுயல் புலம்பிக் குன்றத்
தயல்வளர் கின்ற வாமான் குழவியோ டிரிந்து செந்நெல்
வயல்வளர் கரும்பிற் பாயு மகதநா டென்ப துண்டே.
reading: A land called Magadha lies where fish leap, mullai groves bloom and deer graze by paddy fields and cane.

tamil: இரும்பிடி தழீஇய யானை யிழிமதங் கலந்து சேறாய்ச்
சுரும்பொடு மணிவண் டார்க்குந் துகிற்கொடி மாட வீதிப்
பெருங்கடி நகரம் பேசி னிராசமா கிருக மென்ப
ரருங்கடி யமரர் கோமா னணிநக ராய தொன்றே.
reading: Its chief city, Rajagriha, with rutting elephants, flag-hung mansions and bright streets, is said to be a match for the city of the king of the gods.

tamil: எரிமிடைந் தனைய மாலை யினமணி திருவில் வீசுந்
திருமுடி யார மார்பிற் சேணிக னென்ப நாம
மருமுடி மன்னர் சூழ வலரணி பிண்டி வேந்தன்
றிருவடி விருந்து செய்வான் றிரண்முர சறைவித் தானே.
reading: Senikan, whose crown and garlands flash like fire, orders the drum beaten for a feast in honour of the Jina's feet while kings throng.
event: King Senikan has the drum proclaim a feast for the feet of the Jina, lord of the pindi tree.

reading: The king, having cleaned his mouth with scented water, spits it out before going to worship.
nuance: The first two lines are corrupt as printed and cannot be parsed; the sense of rinsing the mouth rests on line 3 alone.
event: Senikan rinses his mouth with scented water.

reading: Dressed in milk-white silk, sandalled, garlanded and with his hair bound, he mounts a white elephant like a lotus mountain.
event: Senikan dresses and mounts his elephant to go to the Jina.

tamil: எறிசுரும் பரற்று மாலை யெரிமணிச் செப்பு வெள்ளம்
பொறிவரி வண்டு பாடும் பூஞ்சுண்ண நிறைந்த பொற்செப்
பறிவரி துணர்வு நாணித் தலைபணித் தஞ்சுஞ் சாந்தஞ்
செறியிரும் பவழச் செப்புத் தெண்கடற் றிரையி னேரே.
reading: Caskets of fragrant flower-dust, loaded with bees, are carried as offerings, each like a wave of the clear sea.
nuance: The verse is a list of offerings carried; line 3's 'தலைபணித்தஞ்சும்' is hard to place.

tamil: வந்துதேன் மயங்கி மூசு மலயச்செஞ் சாந்த மார்ந்த
சந்தனச் செப்புங் கங்கை தருமண லலகை யாற்றாச்
சுந்தரம் பெய்த யானைத் தூமருப் பியன்ற வெண்செப்
பந்தரத் தலர்ந்த பன்மீ னெனைத்துள வனைத்து மாதோ.
reading: Caskets of sandal paste and ivory, as many as the stars in the sky, are likewise carried.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 3049-3073 (19/22)
theme: At the Lord's assembly the king and the gods bow, a radiant god beside the Lord is named Civakan, and Sudharman tells how Civakan on the sandalwood hill cut the eight karmas and stood through summer heat, rain and cold to the end of his austerity.
source_issues: Verses 3049-3051, 3053-3054, 3058, 3062 and 3070-3073 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
3066 and 3069 are cut short at the end of line 4 in the source.
3065-3066 and 3072 are hard to parse; readings marked uncertain.
The ilampakam heading says 19/22, so the chapter ends mid-ilampakam; 3073 does not close the story.

cast.role: the king of the assembly who bows to the Lord, sees the god and asks Sudharman for the ascetic's story
the teacher, named in 3061, who answers the king and tells Civakan's story
the hero, now an ascetic on the hill
the radiant god seated beside the Lord, who 3058 names as Civakan
Civakan's wives, who come with the sons to see him
the kings who come to the assembly
the king's army
the guards of the hill fields

tamil: மைபொதி குவளை வாட்கண் மல்லிகைக் கோதை நல்லார்
நெய்பொதி நெஞ்சின் மன்னர் நிலம்பிறக் கிடுவ போலுங்
கொய்சுவற் புரவி மான்றேர் குழுமணி யோடை யானை
மெய்பொதிந் துயர்ந்த கோமான் விரைப்பலி சுமந்த வன்றே.
