reading: The lord of the land, with women of lotus eyes, horses, chariots and elephants in his train, comes carrying fragrant offerings to the Lord's assembly.
nuance: The Tamil never names the king; the next verses and the question in 3059 point to the king who hears Sudharman. Lines 2-3 compare the horses and chariots to something that gives out land, which is hard to parse.
event: The king comes in state to the Lord's assembly carrying the fragrant offering (bali).

tamil: கொடிக்குழாங் குஞ்சி பிச்சக் குழாநிறை கோல மாலை
முடிக்குழா மூரி வானம் பால்சொரி கின்ற தொக்குங்
குடைக்குழா மிவற்றின் பாங்கர்க் குளித்தது குளிர்சங் கார்க்கும்
படைக்குழாம் பாரிற் செல்லும் பாற்கடல் பழித்த வன்றே.
reading: The king's host of banners, crests, garlands, crowns, umbrellas and troops fills the earth like a milk-sea poured out, outdoing the sea of milk itself.

tamil: கனைகடல் கவரச் செல்லுங் கணமழைத் தொழுதி போலு
நனைமலர்ப் பிண்டி நாத னல்லறங் கொள்ளை சாற்றிப்
புனைமுடி மன்ன ரீண்டிப் பொன்னெயிற் புறத்து விட்டார்
வினையுடைத் தின்ப வெள்ளம் விரும்பிய வேட்கை யானே.
reading: Kings who gathered to hear the Lord of the pindi tree proclaim his good dharma freely left their retinues outside the golden rampart, out of longing for the flood of bliss.
nuance: Line 4, வினையுடைத் தின்ப வெள்ளம், can be read as the bliss of those with karma or as bliss that belongs to the one without it; the sense is not fixed.
event: Kings assemble to hear the Lord's dharma and leave their retinues outside the golden wall.

reading: The king carries the bee-ringed flower offering, circles the Lord to the right, bows and praises the Lord's feet until the dwellers of the eight quarters marvel.
event: The king circles the Lord, worships his feet and praises him before the whole assembly.

tamil: பகல்வளர் பவழச் செந்தீப் பருதிமுற் பட்ட தேபோ
லிகல்வினை யெறிந்த கோமா னிணையடி யொளியிற் றோன்றா
தகல்விசும் புறையுந் தேவ ரொளியவிந் திருப்ப மன்னன்
முகிழ்கிழி மதியம் போலு முனிக்குழா நோக்கி னானே.
reading: Like a coral-red fire in front of the sun, the lights of the sky-dwelling gods dim before the glow of the feet of the Lord who cut down his hostile karma, and the king looks on the crowd of sages.
event: The king looks over the assembly of sages while the gods' lights fade beside the Lord's feet.

tamil: கண்வெறி போக வாங்கோர் கடுந்தவ னுருவ நோக்கி
யொண்ணெறி யொருவிக் கோமா ணொளிதிரண் டிருந்த தாங்கொல்
விண்ணெறி வழுவி வீழ்ந்த விண்ணவ னொருவன் கொல்லென்
றெண்ணெறி யாது மோரா திருந்திது கூறி னானே
reading: Dazzled and taking a stern ascetic's shape for a god fallen from his path, the king speaks hastily without weighing what he sees.
nuance: Who is the 'lord' of line 2 and who speaks the question is not settled by the Tamil; this reading takes the king as the one who 'says this' in line 4 and the 'unweighed' guess as his. The next verses answer it.
event: The king, seeing a radiant ascetic, wonders aloud whether a god has fallen from the sky.

reading: The speaker reports seeing a god descend in bright light and sit renouncing like a young sun, trembling at the word of the Lord of the three umbrellas, and bowing to him.
nuance: The speaker is probably the king putting his question to Sudharman, but line 4 sounds like the narrator; the one who bows may be the god Civakan of 3057-3058, which the Tamil does not yet say.
event: A god comes down from the sky, sits as an ascetic and bows to the Lord.

reading: Sudharman tells the king that the dwellers of heaven, in the golden wishing-tree land of enjoyment, renounce nothing, and that nothing is seen except as the Lord's word has said.
nuance: That Sudharman is the speaker comes from 3059-3061; in this verse only the address to the king shows a teacher is speaking.

reading: Beside the Lord sits a lotus-eyed god whose very form seems to speak without his opening his mouth, and whose unfailing light is fearsome to look at.
nuance: The verse does not name the god; 3058 does.

tamil: திருவி னோடகன்ற மார்பிற் சீவக சாமி யென்பா
னுருவினோ டொளியு நோக்கி னொப்புமை யுலகி னில்லை
மருவினா ரிமைத்து நோக்கின் மனம்பிறி தாகி நிற்பா
ரரிதிவன் முகத்து நோக்க லழகொளி யன்ன வென்றான்.
reading: The speaker says of Civakan, whose chest is parted from Fortune, that his form and light have no equal on earth and that those who gaze on him with unblinking eyes find their minds changed.
nuance: Naming the god Civakan Swami here answers the king's guess in 3054: the radiant figure is the hero, now seen as a god. Who says 'என்றான்' is read as Sudharman.

reading: The king bows and asks Sudharman to tell, without fault, the history of the great ascetic and how he gave up his life.
event: The king bows and asks Sudharman to tell the ascetic's story and his renunciation.

reading: The great sage's words rain from the cloud over the ocean of unmatched complete knowledge, and the world drinks the nectar of the unfailing dharma.
nuance: The rain-cloud picture is the narrator's praise of the sage; whether the 'great sage' here is Sudharman or the Lord is not fixed by the Tamil.
event: Sudharman speaks and the world takes in his teaching.

reading: The gathered hosts, with the king first, praise Sudharman, the sinless teacher, saying that they would be of Civakan's company.
event: The assembly praises Sudharman and wishes to share Civakan's fortune.

tamil: முல்லைசூழ் முல்லை வேலி முயலொடு கவரி மேயுங்
கொல்லைசூழ் குன்றத் துச்சிக் குருசினோற் றுயர்ந்த வாறும்
வில்லுமிழ்ந் திலங்கு மேனி விழுத்தவ நங்கை மார்கண்
மல்லலங் குமரர் வான்மேற் சென்றதும் வகுக்க லுற்றேன்.
reading: The poet announces that he will tell how Civakan suffered on the hill-top and how the young princes and the ascetic women went up to heaven.
nuance: The 'I will tell' voice may be the narrator's or Sudharman's; verse 3063 onward is read as the telling.

reading: Civakan goes to the sandalwood hills dripping with honey from the jack-fruit groves, so that the hill trembles with his coming.
nuance: The speaker's closing 'என்பவே' (they say) marks this as reported story.
event: Civakan reaches the sandalwood hill.

reading: With a will that cuts the eight karmas into pieces, he becomes like gem set on gem and a sun that cannot be approached.
nuance: Karma is destroyed here by the ascetic's own strength of mind, not by grace or by a god.
event: Civakan cuts the eight karmas by the firmness of his mind.

reading: The sound of waterfalls on the hill goes out in every direction and seems to call all to come, while on one side of the mountain he stands above.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to parse (a call 'come, fill up'); the waterfall as voice is my reading.

reading: On one side of the hill, guards of the golden-bound millet fields drive back rutting elephants, and flung gems fly through the air like stars.
nuance: The last half-line is cut off in the source, and the Tamil is hard to parse.

reading: On another side elephants bathe in saffron, drink from honey-flowing springs, and dance with their mates and calves, without harm.
On another side striped tigers with their cubs sleep in gold caves lit by serpent-gems, while the kinnaras sing and show their forms.
nuance: The peace between beasts is described, not explained; the verse does not say it comes from the ascetic.

reading: On another side monkeys leave fallen jack, plantain and mango fruit, dance in the revel, and bathe in the honey-spoiled spring.
nuance: The last half-line is cut off in the source.

tamil: நளிசிலம் பதனி னுச்சி நாட்டிய பொன்செய் கந்தி
னொளியொடு சுடர வெம்பி யுருத்தெழு கனலி வட்டந்
தெளிகடல் சுடுவ தொத்துத் தீயுமிழ் திங்க ணான்கும்
விளிவரு குரைய ஞான வேழமேற் கொண்டு நின்றான்.
reading: In the four months of the sun's burning ring, as if it would scorch the sea, he stands on the elephant of knowledge beside a gold post, unmoved by the heat that spits fire.
nuance: This is the first of three four-month seasons, summer (70), rains (71) and cold (72).
event: Civakan endures the four hot months standing in tapas.

tamil: பார்க்கடல் பருகி மேகம் பாம்பினம் பதைப்ப மின்னி
வார்ப்பிணி முரசி னார்த்து மண்பக விடித்து வான
நீர்த்திரள் பளிக்குத் தூணி சொரிந்திட நின்று வென்றான்.
மூர்த்தியாய் முனிவ ரேத்து முனிக்களி றனைய கோமான்.
reading: Like a sage-elephant, he overcomes the rains: clouds drink the sea, lightning frightens snakes, thunder breaks the ground, and sheets of water pour down while he stands.
nuance: Line 3 ends with a full stop in the source and line 4 gives the subject: the subject carries over from 3070.
event: Civakan stands through the four months of rain and storm.

tamil: திங்கணான் கவையு நீங்கத் திசைச்செல்வார் மடிந்து தேங்கொள்
பங்கயப் பகைவந் தென்னப் பனிவரை யுருவி வீசு
மங்குல்சூழ் வாடைக் கொல்கான் வெள்ளிடை வதிந்து மாதோ
விங்குநான் காய திங்க ளின்னுயி ரோம்பி னானே.
reading: When the four months of the cold north wind and mist have passed, he lived in the open field, and in these four months he guarded sweet life.
nuance: 'இன்னுயிர் ஓம்பினான்' may mean he protected creatures' lives (ahimsa in the rains-retreat) or his own; the Tamil leaves both open. Line 1 and 2 are hard to parse.
event: Civakan stays out in the open through the four cold months.

tamil: வடிமலர் நெடுங்க ணாரு மைந்தரும் வரவு பார்த்தங்
கடிமலர் பரவ வேறி யாரமிர் தரிதிற் கொள்வான்
கடிமலர்க் கமலத் தன்ன கையினை மறித்துக் கொள்ளான்
முடிதவக் கடலை நீந்தி யின்னண முற்றி னானே.
reading: His wives and sons come to watch for him and worship his feet, and he, who would take the nectar-like food with difficulty, holds back the lotus hand and takes none; thus he crosses the sea of austerity and ends.
nuance: The ending of the verse (அரிதிற் கொள்வான் ... கையினை மறித்துக் கொள்ளான்) can be read as a refusal of food that leads to his end, or as a gesture of withdrawal; the Tamil does not use the word for death by fasting, so I do not tag it.
event: His family comes to him; he refuses food and completes his austerity.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 3074-3097 (20/22)
theme: Civakan's last war: the hero, as an ascetic, destroys the passions and the four destroying karmas with the arrows of meditation, attains omniscience, and the gods, kings and nuns come and sing hymns to the Lord.
source_issues: Stanzas 3074-3086 and 3088-3090 print in 8 half-lines in the edition and have been joined into 4 lines.
3077 line 2 has a stray full stop inside the line.
3087 line 4 contains அரசுவா, which I cannot read; the stanza may be corrupt.
3091-3097 are in a different, shorter metre from the verses before them; 3095-3097 read as a closing benediction and may be a later addition or a separate hymn.

cast.role: the hero, now a Jain ascetic who conquers his inner foes
the four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors
the gods who worship the Lord
the Vidyadhara kings who come to worship
kings of the earth who come to worship
the god, Civakan's friend from earlier, who dances
the congregation that sings the hymn to the Lord
the nuns of penance who join the hymn

tamil: ஒளிறுதேர் ஞானம் பாய்மா வின்னுயி ரோம்ப லோடைக்
களிறுநற் சிந்தை காலாள் கருணையாங் கவசஞ் சீலம்
வெளிறில்வாள் விளங்கு செம்பொன் வட்டமெய்ப் பொருள்க ளாகப்
பிளிறுசெய் கருமத் தெவ்வர் பெருமதின் முற்றி னானே.
reading: The hero besieges the great walled fort of his foes, with knowledge as his chariot, protecting life as his horses, thought as his rutting elephant, mercy as armour, virtue as a flawless sword and the true things as the golden discs.
nuance: The whole passage, 3074 to 3082, is an allegory: the army is the ascetic's virtues, the foes are the passions and the karmas that bind. The text does not say so in a plain sentence, it simply lets the war language carry it; the siege is a siege of karma.
event: Civakan lays siege to the fortress of his enemies, armed with the inner qualities named as an army.

tamil: உறக்கெனு மோடை யானை யூணெனு முருவத் திண்டேர்
மறப்பெனும் புரவி வெள்ளம் வந்தடை பிணிசெய் காலாட்
டிறப்படப் பண்ணிப் பொல்லாச் சிந்தனை வாயில் போந்து
சுறக்கட லனைய தானை துளங்கப்போர் செய்த தன்றே.
reading: Sleep as a rutting elephant, food as a firm chariot, forgetfulness as a flood of horses, and disease as foot-soldiers come against him; he kills them and the sea-like host of bad thought, which had come in at the gate, is shaken.
nuance: The four-fold army of the foe mirrors the king's own army of 3074: elephant, chariot, horse, foot; the epic fits the ascetic's war to the shape of the royal war it has told many times before.
event: The enemy host of sleep, appetite, forgetfulness and disease, with the thoughts that let them in, is broken in battle.

tamil: தெளிவறுத் தெழுவர் பட்டா ரீரெண்மர் திளைத்து வீழ்ந்தார்
களிறுகா லுதைப்ப வெண்மர் கவிழ்ந்தனர் களத்தி னுள்ளே
பிளிறிவீழ் பேடி பெண்ணோ யறுவகைத் துவர்ப்பும் பேசி
னளிபடு சிந்தை யென்னு மாழிவாய் வீழ்ந்த வன்றே.
reading: Seven and sixteen of the foes fall, eight are trampled by elephants, the neuter, the woman and the sick are named with the six 'astringent' things, and all are swallowed in the whirl of the thought named 'pity'.
nuance: The numbers (seven, sixteen, eight) and the neuter, woman and sickness read as the Jain lists of the lesser passions and the three sexes of desire; this is my reading of a list the verse names without saying what it counts, and the half-lines are corrupt in places.
event: Groups of the enemy fall in the field one after another.

tamil: மயக்கப்போர் மன்னன் மக்கண் மந்திரி யவரும் வீழ
வியப்புறு வேத வில்வாய். வேட்கையம் பெடுத்திட் டெய்யக்
கலக்கமி லசுப மென்னுங் குந்தத்தாற் கணைபெய்ம் மாரி
விலக்கித்திண் வெறுப்பு வாளால் விரைந்துயி ரவனை யுண்டான்.
reading: With the sons and the minister of the king named 'delusion' fallen, the bow of the Veda-desires shoots a rain of arrows, but he wards it off with the spear called 'impurity' and quickly takes the king's life with the sword of dislike.
nuance: Line 2 has a full stop in the middle and a corrupt word division. மயக்கப்போர் மன்னன் is the king of confusion (the delusion-karma), and வேத here is the three drives of sex, not the scripture; this is the Jain use, and the verse leaves it for the reader to know.
event: Civakan kills the king Delusion after his sons and minister have fallen.

tamil: கரும்பெறி கடிகை போன்றுங் கதலிகைப் போழ்கள் போன்று
மரும்பொறிப் பகைவர் தம்மை யுறுப்பறத் துணித்து மீர்ந்து
மருந்தெறி பிணியைக் கொல்லு மருத்துவன் போன்று மாதோ
விருந்தெறிந் தெறியு மூவர் மேற்படை யியற்றி னானே.
reading: As a hunter cuts the sugarcane, as a physician cuts out a disease with medicine, he cuts the enemies limb from limb and throws a weapon against the three guests.
nuance: The simile of a physician who kills the disease is the verse's own account of what the cutting is: not cruelty but cure. The three that remain are unnamed here and the rest of the passage does not say what they are.
event: Civakan cuts down his enemies and turns on the remaining three.

tamil: செழுமல ராவி நீங்கு மெல்லையிற் செறிந்து காயங்
கழுமிய வுதிரம் போல விமைப்பினுட் கரந்து நீங்கக்
கொழுமலர்க் குவளைக் கண்ணிக் கூற்றுயி ருண்பதே போல்
விழுமிய தெவ்வர் வாணாள் வீழ்ந்துக வெம்பி னானே.
reading: As the spirit leaves a body and the blood dries within the wound, the lives of the foes pour away in a blink and fall; Death, in a garland of kuvalai, seems to drink their lives, and he is angry.
nuance: The image of Death garlanded with flowers and drinking lives makes the ascetic himself Death to the karmas; it is the opposite of the Jain horror at killing a living being, and the verse can use it only because the foes are not living things.
event: The enemies' lives leave them at once as Civakan strikes.

tamil: குரோதனே மானன் மாயன் கூர்ப்புடை யுலோப னென்பார்
விரோதித்து விரலிற் சுட்டி வெருவரத் தாக்க வீர
னிரோதனை யம்பிற் கொன்றா னித்தைநீள் பசலைப் பேரோர்
விராகெனும் வேலின் வீழ வெகுண்டன னவரும் வீழ்ந்தார்.
reading: The four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, rise against him and point at him with their fingers; the hero kills one, Nirodhanai, with an arrow, and Pride and the rest fall to the spear called 'Viraagam', each of them dying in anger.
nuance: Kural 360 names three roots of all pain (desire, anger, confusion); here the Jain list is of four (anger, pride, deceit, greed), the same four that the Jain tradition calls the kasayas. The text gives the spear its name only in the single word விராகு, which I read as the Sanskrit-derived 'virāga', dispassion.
event: Civakan kills the four passions in turn, with arrow and spear.

tamil: புணரிபோற் சிறுபுண் கேள்விப் படையொடு புகைந்து பொங்கி
யுணர்வொடு காட்சி பேறென் றிடையுறு கோக்க ளேற்றா
ரிணரெரி முழக்க மன்ன சுக்கிலத் தியான மென்னுங்
கணையெறிந் துகைப்ப வீழ்ந்து காற்படை சூழப் பட்டார்.
reading: Like the sea his lesser foes rise in a mist of petty learning, and the feeble lords who stand between knowledge, sight and attainment cannot hold; he fires the arrow named the pure meditation, like a roar of blazing fire, and they fall and are surrounded by his foot-soldiers.
nuance: சுக்கிலத் தியானம் is the named Jain 'white' meditation, the last of the four meditations; the verse gives it as a weapon. The 'feeble lords of knowledge, sight and attainment' are the obstructing karmas, which I read from the Jain scheme rather than from the verse.
event: Civakan fires the arrow of pure meditation and the remaining foes fall.

tamil: காதிப்போர் மன்னர் வீழக் கணையெரி சிதறி வெய்யோ
னோதிய வகையி னொன்றி யுலகுச்சி முளைத்த தேபோல்
வீதிபோ யுலக மூன்றும் விழுங்கியிட் டலோக நுங்கி
யாதியந் தகன்ற நான்மைக் கொடியெடுத் திறைமை கொண்டான்.
reading: When the four destroying kings have fallen, he sprouts like the sun at the world's summit, the fire of his arrows spreading, swallows the three worlds and then the world of non-world, and lifts the banner of the fourfold infinite, taking sovereignty.
nuance: காதிப்போர் மன்னர் are the four ghati karmas, those that obscure knowledge, sight, bliss and power; the verse's 'fourfold' (நான்மை) is the four infinites listed in 2847. The second line is difficult and I read it as the sun rising from the world's top; it is the moment the work calls attaining the supreme knowledge.
event: Civakan destroys the four destroying karmas and attains omniscience, taking sovereignty over the three worlds.

tamil: பசும்பொனி னுலகிற் றேவர் பயிர்வளை முரச மார்ப்ப
வசும்புசேர் களிறு திண்டே ரலைமணிப் புரவி வேங்கை
விசும்பியங் கரியோ டாளி விடைமயி லன்ன நாக
நயந்தவை பிறவு மூர்ந்து நாதன்றாள் கோயில் கொண்டார்.
reading: The gods in the golden world beat the drums that roar, bringing elephants, chariots, horses, lions, peacocks and nagas, and take their place in the temple of the lord's feet.
event: The gods bring their mounts and gather at the Lord's temple to worship.

tamil: நறுமலர் மாலை சாந்தம் பரூஉத்துளித் துவலை நன்னீர்க்
கறைமுகில் சொரியக் காய்பொற் கற்பக மாலை யேந்திச்
சிறகுறப் பரப்பி யன்னம் பறப்பன போல வீண்டி
நிறைகடல் விஞ்சை வேந்தர் நீணில மன்னர் சேர்ந்தார்.
reading: Vidyadhara kings and kings of the earth come, as swans spread their wings, bearing fragrant flowers, garlands, sandal, and bright water from dark clouds, and the heavenly wishing-tree garlands.
event: The Vidyadhara and earth kings arrive with offerings.

tamil: விண்ணியங் கருக்கன் வீழ்ந்து மீனிலங் கொள்வ தேபோன்
மண்ணெலாம் பைம்பொன் மாரி மலர்மழை சொரிந்து வாழ்த்தி
யெண்ணிலாத் தொழில்க டோற்றி யிந்திரர் மருள வாடிக்
கண்முழு துடம்பிற் றோன்றிச் சுதஞ்சணன் களிப்புற் றானே.
reading: Like the sun falling from the sky to take the earth, the god Sudanjanan scatters a rain of gold and flowers, blesses, shows endless dances to make the Indras marvel, and is glad, his body full of eyes.
nuance: Sudanjanan is the god who in earlier ilampakams had been the yaksha rescued by Civakan and acted as his friend and helper; the verse does not say so and the reader must carry that from earlier. The body of eyes is my reading of கண் முழுது உடம்பிற் றோன்றி.
event: The god Sudanjanan, once Civakan's friend, rains gold and dances before the Lord.

tamil: குளித்தெழு வயிர முத்தத் தொத்தெரி கொண்டு மின்ன
வளித்துல கோம்பு மாலை யகன்குடை கவித்த தாங்கு
வளிப்பொர வுளருந் திங்கட் கதிரெனக் கவரி பொங்கத்
தெளித்துவில் லுமிழுஞ் செம்பொ னாசனஞ் சேர்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: The golden seat comes with the umbrella shining like a jewelled canopy, the fans flowing like moonlight; the seat that pours its brightness is reached.
nuance: The umbrella, fans and seat are the royal insignia given to the Arhat; the preacher is thus given the royal regalia of the king that he put off, which the verse accepts without comment.
event: The Lord's golden seat, with umbrella and fans, is set up in the assembly.

reading: The scent of his jewelled hair, of the gods' incense and the Kalpaka garland that had wandered away is surpassed by the scent of the one who cut the deeds that could not be cut; if the royal ... does not tell it, who will?
nuance: The last line is corrupt, the word அரசுவா is not a word I can read, and the sense of the closing rhetorical question is a guess.
event: The scent of the Lord's body surpasses all heavenly perfumes.

reading: The Lord's shining teeth, coral lips and the sound of his voice outshine the Mandara tree; his scent is known as that of the one who hates the deeds, and the green-eyed one (a lion or elephant) of the golden hill cannot say it.
nuance: The last line names a 'green-eyed great one' (பைங்கண்மா) whom I read as a beast of the golden mountain; the sense is the rhetorical question again, that even the best of beasts cannot speak of it.
event: The splendour of the Lord's body is praised above the heavenly trees.

reading: His whole body gives out light too bright to perceive, like a hill made of the sun and the moon gathered in; he who shook off the two deeds can be described, but is not the dark iron in a blazing fire black no longer?
nuance: The last line is difficult. கறுப்பொழிந்த ... கரியன்றே I read as the comparison of iron which has lost its black in the fire; if so the Lord's colour is the glow of burnt-out karma.
event: The Lord's body is shown shining beyond description.

tamil: கனார் பிண்டிக் கமழ் தாமங் கறையார் முகிலி னிறங்காட்டுந்
தேனார் புகைக ளிவையெல்லாந் திகைப்பத் திகைகண் மணநாறி
reading: The flowers that the gods rain down, the coloured sandal, the flower dust, the pindi garlands and the incense that shows the colour of dark clouds fill the quarters with scent, and the gods wear the Lord's fragrance on their crowns.
event: The gods rain flowers and perfumes and wear the Lord's fragrance on their heads.

reading: The worshippers, with the god who bears the fish banner and Death slain, give up all other thought, pray 'let our birth end', and wearing flowers, sweeping the floor with sandal, worship the feet of the Lord of the path of renunciation with incense.
nuance: சுறவுக்கொடிக் கடவுள் is Kaman, the god of desire whose banner is the fish; the Lord is praised for having destroyed him and Death, which makes the Arhat's victory a defeat of desire and mortality together. The verse is in a different metre from those before it, and 3091 to 3097 read as the worshippers' hymn.
event: The worshippers pray for the end of birth and worship the Lord's feet.

reading: We worship the Lord who cut the four deeds at once, whose pure thought blazes, who knew the three times together, and whose feet are flowers, ends the four-fold ...
nuance: Here the hymn first speaks as 'we' (தொழுதும் யாம்), a change of voice from the narrator of 3074 to 3091; I read the speaker as the congregation of worshippers. The line 'நான்மைவரம்பாகி' I read as 'become the limit of the fourfold', the four infinites.
event: A hymn in the first person praises the Lord's feet.

reading: Like the sun risen from the roaring sea, you rose against the wailing deeds, swallowing the three worlds without casting them out, the seed of qualities, and we praise your faultless feet.
nuance: The 'swallowing the three worlds' repeats the image of 3082, now as praise: where the narrator told it as a victory, the hymn tells it as a quality of the Lord.
event: The worshippers praise the Lord for having risen like the sun over the deeds.

reading: The gods stand and worship the Lord, praising him with tongues that grow numb, and the nuns of penance come and sing hymns to wash off the dust of the eyes, praising the one who has left the unpraiseable qualities beyond limit.
nuance: The nuns of penance appear here in the same assembly as the gods; the verse gives women a place in the hymn of the Lord, which earlier ilampakams had also done by sending the queens to the nun's life.
event: Gods and nuns praise the Lord with hymns.

reading: Worship of the Lord's lotus feet, with no doubt that the doer of penance gets the deed's fruit, and the speaker salutes with pure flowers, 'the king who spoke of the true world'.
nuance: The line 'செய்தவனே வினை சேரும் அதற்கு' reads as 'the doer is reached by the deed for it'; the whole verse is a salutation closing in the form of a later benediction, and its metre differs from the narrative verses.
event: A worshipper salutes the Lord's feet and states the law of deeds.

reading: The petty lords who seek out only the unsound as good, and speak what is not good, have borne the mother who bears many deeds; speak, Sugata, of what they say.
nuance: சுகதா (Sugata) is a name the Buddhists use for the Buddha; here a Jain hymn addresses it to the Lord, and either the title is common to all the teachers who have reached release or the verse is borrowed. The line 'பல்வினைக்கும்முலைத் தாய்பயந்தாரவர்' is difficult.
event: A worshipper asks the Lord to speak against the false teachers.

reading: Having praised the feet of the one whose virtue the mind cannot know, those who worship the unbroken praise bow, filled like a treasure house, so that the heroes know the fate that does not fall.
nuance: The last verse of the ilampakam as numbered here closes in praise; the grammar of the last two lines is hard and I give only the gist.
event: The worshippers conclude their praise and bow.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 3098-3121 (21/22)
theme: The wives praise the Lord and hear the king's sermon on desire, harm and release, the Lord is released and cremated by the gods, and Civakan, embracing the maiden Kevala, and the women, who see their bodies as dirt, take up austerity and reach heaven.
source_issues: Many stanzas are printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four lines by the edition.
3118 line 2 'இன்றேன்' looks corrupt.
3117 and 3118 leave the king's identity open between the Lord and Civakan.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who has heard the sage and preaches to his wives
Civakan's wives who sing, hear the sermon and take up austerity
the Lord, the Jina, whose feet are praised and who is released
the gods who honour the Lord's passing
the maiden Kevala, a figure of omniscient knowledge

tamil: தீவினைக் குழவி செற்ற மெனும்பெயர்ச் செவிலி கையுள்
வீவினை யின்றிக் காம முலையுண்டு வளர்ந்து வீங்கித்
தாவினை யின்றி வெந்நோய்க் கதிகளுட் டவழு மென்ற
கோவினை யன்றி யெந்நாக் கோதையர்க் கூற லுண்டே
reading: The women say that the bad deed is a child handed to a nurse named anger, which drinks the breast of desire, grows, and crawls among the painful states of rebirth, and that they have no word of their own beyond the king who told it so.
nuance: Stanza printed in eight half-lines and joined by the edition; the last line's grammar is hard and the speaker is inferred from the 'we' of the next verse.
event: The wives repeat the king's parable of the bad-deed child and its nurse.

tamil: நல்வினைக் குழவி நன்னீர்த் தயாவெனுஞ் செவிலி நாளும்
புல்லிக்கொண் டெடுப்பப் பொம்மென் மணிமுலை கவர்ந்து வீங்கிச்
செல்லுமாற் றேவர் கோவா யெனுமிருள் கழிந்த சொல்லா
வல்லிமே னடந்த கோவே யச்சத்து ணீங்கி னோமே.
reading: The good deed is a child nursed by the nurse called compassion, who embraces and raises it, and the women say that, freed from the darkness of 'be our king among the gods', they have gone beyond fear.
nuance: The pairing of two nurses, anger and compassion, makes the two kinds of deed two upbringings rather than two amounts; the verse does not say how one becomes the other's nurse.
event: The wives answer the parable with its counterpart of the good-deed child and declare themselves free of fear.

reading: Beyond the light a gem gives and the cool scent a flower gives, the feet are said to give shelter to the dense gnat-swarm of the crowd, and the verse addresses the Lord's red feet that gave this.
nuance: The addressee is not named in the verse; 'the Lord of wealth' is read as the Jina from the surrounding hymn.

reading: The Lord's feet, like the sun that rises bearing the day to break the dark at its root, are a spear that cuts the hard-gathered deeds.
nuance: The feet are a weapon rather than a giver of grace: they cut karma as a spear cuts, which differs from a god who forgives it.

reading: The slender women of moon faces and parrot voices are told to sing the Lord's qualities, for the deeds that fell on them have been stopped and do not stay.
event: The women sing the qualities of the Lord and their karma ceases to settle.

reading: As the night-lily opens drinking the moon's rays and drips honey, so those who hail the qualities of the one of perfect knowledge, with no wavering mind, are said to leave their shaking hearts behind.
Having worshipped the feet of the Lord of fullness in company with the ascetic heroes, the women ask to worship the light that cuts the dark, and the king gives his answer like a rain of nectar.
event: The wives ask to worship the Lord and the king answers them.

tamil: இன்பமற் றென்னும் பேரா னெழுந்தபுற் கற்றை தீற்றித்
துன்பத்தைச் சுரக்கு நான்கு கதியெனுந் தொழுவிற் றோன்றி
நின்றபற் றார்வ நீக்கி நிருமலன் பாதஞ் சேரி
னன்புவிற் றுண்டு போகிச் சிவகதி யடைய லாமே.
reading: The king says that desire is a bundle of grass that tempts souls into the four states of rebirth, a pen that yields suffering, and that to give up clinging and reach the stainless one's feet is to sell love for the road to the state of release.
nuance: The four states (gods, humans, animals and hell) are not listed in the verse; they are supplied from the Jain scheme the word implies.

tamil: வாட்கையம் மைந்த ராயும் வனமுலை மகளி ராயும்
வேட்கையை மிகுத்து வித்திப் பிறவிநோய் விளைத்து வீயாத்
தேட்கையிற் கொண்ட தொக்கு நிச்சநோய்ச் செற்றப் புன்றோற்
பூட்கையை முனியின் வாமன் பொன்னடி தொழுமி னென்றான்.
reading: The king tells them to worship the golden feet and to hate the strong young men and the full-breasted women who sow desire and reap the disease of birth, since the body so kept is a skin that holds disease.
nuance: The king speaks as a ruler who has just given up many wives; the 'hate the women' language is the sermon's, addressed to women who are about to renounce.

reading: If a person protects living beings every day as he guards his own life, he will be born lord of sweet lives, an image of joy, a golden soul that rises beyond.
nuance: The reward is rank in a later birth, which makes non-injury a ladder rather than an end; Kural 327 sets the same rule against the loss of one's own life.

reading: If a person makes fire a life for food and does harm, the two deeds kick him down and the fire of the world draws him in, roasts him and sends him into burning flame.
nuance: The first two lines are hard (the nouns turn on a word 'நெருப்புயிர்'); the sense of harm for food is taken from the verbs, so the image of harm by fire is the better-supported reading.

reading: The teaching under the pindi tree is like a rare gem got by one who escaped the great sea of roaring waves, and the good law has taken refuge in a shaded grove of sandal.
One who lives in the shade of the wishing-tree will not seek another to give to him, and one who has eaten the nectar under the pindi will not set his mind on the wealth of others.

The king grades souls by metals, from gem and gold through silver and copper to iron, and says he has told this to the end of disease, and urges them to decide, whereupon the women worship and bless him.
nuance: The metal grades are given as a list of ranks; the verse does not say which deeds put a soul at which rank.
event: The king ends the sermon and the women bow and bless him.

reading: Flowers rain from the sky, a full moon seems to pour milk, and honey blossoms seem to walk on the earth as the Lord walks and grants his sight.
event: The Lord walks the earth and the heavens shower flowers on him.

tamil: பான்மிடை யமிர்து போன்று பருகலாம் பயத்த வாகி
வானிடை முழக்கிற் கூறி வாலற வமிர்த மூட்டித்
தேனுடை மலர்கள் சிந்தித் திசைதொழச் சென்ற பின்னாட்
டானுடை யுலகங் கொள்ளச் சாமிநாள் சார்ந்த தன்றே.
reading: The Lord's teaching, like milk and nectar, sounded in the sky and fed the pure nectar, and flowers were scattered and the directions bowed, and then the day came for him to take the world he had earned.
nuance: 'சாமிநாள்' is read as the day of final release from the line that follows it; the verse itself does not say the word for death.
event: After his last sermon the Lord reaches the day of his passing.

tamil: உழவித்தி யுறுதி கொள்வார் கொண்டுய்யப் போகல் வேண்டித்
தொழுவித்தி யறத்தை வைத்துத் துளங்கிமி லேறு சேர்ந்த
குழவித்தண் டிங்க ளன்ன விருக்கைய னாகிக் கோமான்
விழவித்தாய் வீடு பெற்றான் விளங்கிநால் வினையும் வென்றே.
reading: To make those who want gain take their lasting good, the lord set virtue and sat, like the young cool moon, on a seat of his own, and having conquered the four karmas he reached release in festival.
nuance: 'Four karmas' is read as the four that remain after the omniscient one has gone; the verse does not name them. The subject 'kōmān' is the Lord and not Civakan, who comes next.
event: The Lord, having conquered four karmas, reaches release.

tamil: துந்துபி கறங்க வார்த்துத் துகிற்கொடி நுடங்க வேந்தி
யந்தரம் விளங்க வெங்கு மணிகமூர்ந் தமர ரீண்டி
வந்துபொன் மாரி சிந்தி மலர்மழை சொரிந்து சாந்துங்
கெந்தநா றகிலுங் கூட்டிக் கிளர்முடி யுறுத்தி னாரே.
reading: Gods gather with drums beating and cloth banners waving, pour a golden rain and flowers, mix sandal and aloe fragrance and crown the Lord.
event: The gods honour the Lord's passing with rain of gold, flowers and perfume.

tamil: முளைத்தெழு பருதி மொய்கொண் முழங்கழற் குளித்த தேபோற்
றிளைத்தெழு கொடிகள் செந்தீத் திருமணி யுடம்பு நுங்க
விளைத்தபின் விண்ணு மண்ணு மங்கலம் வகையிற் செய்து
வளைப்பொலி கடலி னார்த்து வலங்கொண்டு நடந்த வன்றே.
reading: The flags seem to be swallowed by the red flame, as the rising sun is by the fire, as the bright jewelled body is burnt, and then gods and earth do their auspicious rites, circle the pyre and move away like a shell-loud sea.
nuance: The verse does not say whose body it is; the context of the Lord's release in 3114 supports the Lord.
event: The jewel-bright body of the Lord burns in the flame, and the gods circle it and go away.

tamil: கேவல மடந்தை யென்னுங் கேழ்கிளர் நெடிய வாட்கட்
பூவலர் முல்லைக் கண்ணிப் பொன்னொரு பாக மாகக்
காவலன் றானொர் கூறாக் கண்ணிமை யாது புல்லி
மூவுல குச்சி யின்பக் கடலினுண் மூழ்கி னானே.
reading: The king, whose bright eyes are those of a maiden named Kevala, the knowledge that sees all, embraces her with unblinking eyes, the garland of jasmine on one side and gold on the other, and sinks into a sea of pleasure at the peak of the three worlds.
nuance: The grammar makes the king's identity open: he could be the Lord or Civakan; the book's last ilampakam and 3118 let the reader take Civakan. The maiden is a figure of knowledge and no real woman.
event: The king, now omniscient, embraces the maiden Kevala and sinks in the sea of joy at the top of the three worlds.

tamil: பிரிதலும் பிணியு மூப்புஞ் சாதலும் பிறப்பு மில்லா
வரிவையைப் புல்லி யம்பொ னணிகிளர் மாடத் தின்றேன்
சொரிமது மாலை சாந்தங் குங்குமஞ் சுண்ணந் தேம்பாய்
விரிபுகை விளக்கு விண்ணோ ரேந்தமற் றுறையு மன்றே.
reading: Embracing the woman who has no parting, disease, old age, death or birth, he lives in a tall gold mansion where gods carry wine, garlands, sandal, saffron, powder, smoke and lamps.
nuance: The verse mixes heaven's service (wine, garlands) with release; it does not separate the god's heaven from the freed soul's state, and 'இன்றேன்' in line 2 looks corrupt.
event: He lives with the maiden free of ageing and death, served by gods.

tamil: வல்லவன் வடித்த வேல்போன் மலர்ந்துநீண் டகன்ற வாட்கண்
மெல்லவே யுறவி யோம்பி யொதுங்கியு மிருந்து நின்று
முல்லையஞ் சூட்டு வேயின் முரிந்துபோ நுசுப்பி னல்லார்
மல்லற்குன் றேந்தி யன்ன மாதவ முற்றி னாரே.
reading: The women of spear-bright wide eyes, who walked softly, sat and stood like jasmine crests, with bending waists, reached the great austerity, like one holding up a mountain.
event: The women take up great austerity.

reading: Looking at the bodies they had adorned, as one looks at a green bracelet clinging to a gold doll, the women see the dirt on them and think how to crush the poor birth of woman.
nuance: The poem presents this as the women's own thought, but the narrator's phrase 'ஏழைப் பெண்பிறப்பு' (the poor birth of woman) passes the verdict on women's birth as the work's own.
event: The women see the stain on their own bodies and resolve to end birth as women.

reading: Without desire, love or doubt, the women, who did their austerity until the sound of the world ate it, cast off the despised state of woman, became Indras, pure knowledge, and reached heaven.
nuance: Heaven (துறக்கம்) is the end named, not release; the poem's women reach the gods' world, one step below the state the king reached in 3117-3118.
event: The women, having shed their womanhood by austerity, are reborn as Indras and reach heaven.

title: முத்தி இலம்பகம் 3122-3145 (22/22)
theme: In the close of the last ilampakam the poem sets the court's lovemaking beside the ascetics' penance, which ends in death on a mountain and rebirth as gods in heavenly pleasure, then ends with the poet's praise of the three-umbrella Lord's feet and of the work's hearers.
source_issues: Verses 3136 to 3138, 3142, 3143 and 3145 print in eight half-lines and were joined into four; the joins are the build's.
Verses 3142 to 3145 are the poet's closing praise and sit outside the story; the identification of the Lord in 3144 is from context, not from a naming word.

cast.role: the lovers of the pleasure scene, women and men named only as groups
the youth Nandan, who with his companions takes up penance
the companions who share the penance
the ascetics reborn as gods who enjoy heaven's pleasure
the poet speaking in the first person at the end of the work

reading: Men embrace the long-haired women as wishing-trees are wrapped in creepers of desire, and reach the pleasure that is the comfort of their breasts.
nuance: The verse names no one; that these are the hero's household is carried from the ilampakam, not from the words. The simile of the heavenly wishing-tree already puts the bed in the language of paradise.
event: The lovers of the court lie in each other's arms and take their pleasure.

reading: The fruit of the pleasure of union is the lovers' quarrel; the wet-eyed glances of the golden-boughed women pierce the hearts of the men in their leaf-patterned jewels.
nuance: Union and sulking are set as seed and fruit, so the quarrel is a part of the pleasure and not its break.
event: The women sulk and their glances pierce the men's hearts.

reading: The lily-eyed women cast reproachful side-glances while their anklets ring and the men's hair is stirred; the play of the lovers' quarrel goes on.
nuance: The first two lines turn on a clause (பெண்பெயர் நிவிற்றினீர்) that I cannot parse with confidence; the reading rests on lines 3 and 4 only.
event: The women reproach the men in play, with glances and sounding anklets.

reading: A soft-footed, flower-browed woman fears that the flowers set in the man's hair have pained the lady's heart, and the verse calls such fear a fault of its own.
nuance: Who is meant by 'the lady' and whose fault the last line names are not fixed by the words.
event: A woman frets that she has hurt another's feelings with the flowers in a man's hair.

reading: The lovers fasten the white anklet strings, praise the lily-eyed beauty and set a honeyed wreath on her, asking whether eyes that saw her could ever blink.
nuance: The sentence is carried by three participles and ends in verse 3127, so the last line is read as an offering of the wreath; this is the less certain half.
event: The men dress the women and praise their eyes.

reading: The women, bright as lightning, put on girdles of many gems, settle them, brush pollen powder over their golden breasts, and their two gem earrings seem to laugh.
event: The women adorn themselves after love.

reading: The earrings of the dark-haired woman, shaking, seem to laugh so that all feel shame, as if saying that those who did the deed and those it was done to will each come to know everything.
nuance: The saying ascribed to the earrings echoes a wording of deed and its object (செய்த, செயப்பட்டார்), which a reader may take as a faint hint at karma; the verse does not draw the doctrine out.
event: The woman's earrings shake in laughter and shame those present.

reading: The anklets sound, the jasmine garlands scatter, the worn wreaths roll about, and the girdles on the women's hips gape and gasp in the heat of love.
event: The lovers' union breaks the women's ornaments.

reading: The slender women take up, as if it were a drink named desire mixed with toddy, a gem cup and drink, trembling and wilting.
nuance: Desire is given the name of the drink itself; the drink is a figure for the lovers' pleasure and is not a separate scene of drinking.
event: The women drink from gem cups and tremble.

reading: After the women of soft speech have drunk to the full the honeyed nectar of heat and lived on rejoicing, the narrator turns to tell what befell the righteous ascetics.
nuance: The turn from the bed to the ascetics (செம்மை மாதவர்) is the hinge of the chapter: the poet gives no argument, he lays the two lives side by side.
event: The narrator closes the scene of pleasure and turns to the ascetics.

reading: Like the white moon on a full-moon day, the youth Nandan and his companions, while each day others tremble, pile up good penance by their own effort and gain themselves.
nuance: That 'the youth' (காளை) is Civakan and not a second person cannot be told from the words; Nandan is named, and the group is read as ascetics only from the next verse.
event: Nandan and his companions practise penance.

reading: With meditation and fasting, which wash off evil deeds, and by reverence to the Teacher (தீர்த்தன்), the righteous move like bees on flowers and fear even the tongue's craving as they fear poison.
nuance: தீர்த்தன் may be the Tirthankara or a bathing-place figure; the epic's Jain setting makes the first likelier.
event: The ascetics fast and meditate and fear the craving of the tongue.

reading: When the time bound in the womb at conception came, the five of them ended their lives on a mountain that rises like a white crescent horn, and became gods, as splendid as the appearance of Tiru.
nuance: The ascetics' penance here ends in heaven, not yet in release; the verses after it spend seven stanzas on heavenly pleasure, which is a reward that the Jain scheme counts below release.
event: The five ascetics die on a mountain and are reborn as gods.

reading: The gods who once burned in penance against the god of love now enjoy the dark-eyed, peacock-like women as bull elephants enjoy the herds of cow elephants.
nuance: The first line is read as a reversal: those who fought desire through penance now live in it. The identification of the gods with the ascetics is from the sequence of verses, not from a word in this one.
event: The new gods take their pleasure with the heavenly women.

tamil: காதணிந்த தோடொருபான் மின்னு வீசக் குழையொருபாற் றிருவில் வீசத்
தாதணிந்த தாமங்க ளொருபாற் சோரத் தாமரைக்கண் டாமிரங்கப் புருவு மாட
மாதணிந்த நோக்கினா ரல்குற் காசு மணிமழலைக் கிண்கிணியுஞ் சிலம்பு மேங்கப்
போதணிந்த தாருடையப் பொருது பொங்கிப் புணர்முலைகள் போர்க்களந்தாங் கண்ட வன்றே.
reading: The heavenly women's earrings, bows of brows and garlands tremble and fall, their girdles and anklets ring, and the breasts meet like armies on the field of love.
nuance: The battle of the breasts is the same figure that verse 3140 pursues with a weapon of sulking.
event: The gods and the women join in love-play, imagined as a battle.

tamil: முழுதார மின்னுமுலைக் குவட்டினான்மொய்ம் மார்பிற்குங் குமச்சே றிழுக்கிவீழ
வுழுதார்வம் வித்தி யுலப்பிலாத நுகர்ச்சிவிளைத் தலர்ந்தகற் பகத்தின்கீ
ழெழுதார் மணிக்குவளைக் கண்வலையுட்பட் டிமையார்கள் காமமறு சுழியுளாழ்ந்
திழுதார்மென் பள்ளிப்பூந் தாதுபொங்க விருவர் பலராகி யின்புறுபவே.
reading: Saffron paste rubs off the breasts and chests, a plough of eager love sows a harvest of endless enjoyment, and the immortals sink in the whirlpool of desire, two becoming many in their pleasure.
nuance: The gods are said to be caught in a net of desire and a whirlpool, images that elsewhere in the work belong to bondage.
event: The gods lose themselves in love.

tamil: மண்கனிந்த பொன்முழவ மழையின் விம்ம மாமணியாழ் தீங்குழல்க ளிரங்கப் பாண்டில்
பண்கனியப் பாவைமார் பைம்பொற் றோடுங் குண்டலமுந் தாம்பதைப்ப விருந்துபாட
விண்கனியக் கிண்கிணியுஞ் சிலம்பு மார்ப்ப முரிவுருவ வேனெடுங்கண் விருந்து செய்யக்
கண்கனிய நாடகங்கண் டமரர்காமக் கொழுந்தீன்று தந்தவந்தா மகிழ்ந்தா ரன்றே.
reading: To the beat of drums, the lute, the flute and the dance, the gods feast their eyes on the women and take joy in the garden of desire.
event: The gods watch dance and music and are feasted by the women.

reading: The women with flowers in their hair and pearls on their shoulders pierce the men's hearts with sidelong looks, and the men fall on their breasts, smearing the sandal paste.
event: The gods are pierced by glances and fall on the women's breasts.

reading: The women's spear-bright eyes, with the hand of love as messenger, join in the sulking-war, and by their play the heaven of the gods shines.
nuance: Love is a war here in which sulking is the arms and the hand is the messenger, a figure that borrows the vocabulary of kings.
event: The gods and women quarrel and make up in the play of love.

reading: Drinking the honey of desire in the bodies of the slender-waisted women, the gods sink in a sea of senses beyond rival.
nuance: The sinking (ஆழ்ந்தார்) is praise in the poet's mouth, but the sea of senses recalls the image of birth as a sea that the last verses name as a thing to cross.
event: The gods drink their fill of pleasure and sink in the sea of sense.

tamil: முகடு மணியழுத்தி முள்வைர முள்வேய்ந்து முத்தம் வாய்ச்சூழ்ந்
தகடு பசுமணியார்ந் தங்காந் திருள்பருகி யடுபால் விம்மிப்
பகடு படவடுக்கிப் பண்ணவனார் தம்மொளிமே னின்றாற் போலுந்
தகடு படுசெம்பொன் முக்குடையான் றாளிணையென் றலைவைத் தேனே.
reading: The poet compares the Arhat's feet, set upon a gem-studded pedestal bright as the Lord's own radiance, and places them on his head.
nuance: முக்குடையான் is the Arhat, the three umbrellas being his sign in Jain worship; the rest is a long simile for his golden pedestal.
event: The poet bows his head to the feet of the three-umbrella Lord.

tamil: முந்நீர் வலம்புரி சோர்ந்தசைந்து வாய்முரன்று முழங்கி யீன்ற
மெய்ந்நீர்த் திருமுத் திருபத்தேழ் கோத்துமிழ்ந்து திருவில் வீசுஞ்
செந்நீர்த் திரள்வடம்போற் சிந்தா மணியோதி யுணர்ந்தார் கேட்டா
ரிந்நீர ராயுயர்வ ரேந்துபூந் தாமரையாள் காப்பா ளாமே.
reading: Those who read and understand the Cintamani, which is like the pearls a conch gave up from the sea strung into a fine rope, and those who hear it, will rise in this way, and the lotus goddess will guard them.
nuance: The fruit named is worldly, since Tiru, the lotus goddess of fortune, guards the hearers; the epic's last ilampakam is called release, but its closing blessing is of prosperity.
event: The poet states the fruit of reading and hearing his work.

reading: Having sung the feet of the Lord on whose chest the lotus goddess dwells, the poet says that he has scattered the story of the Cintamani, and that the wise gain an undying lamp and good gem.
nuance: The Lord with Tiru on his chest is a figure the Vaishnava tradition also uses; here the three-umbrella Arhat is meant by the context of the closing verses, which is the less certain of two readings.
event: The poet ends the telling of the story with praise of the Lord's feet.

tamil: செய்வினை யென்னு முந்நீர்த் திரையிடை முளைத்துத் தேங்கொண்
மைவினை மறுவி லாத மதியெனுந் திங்கண் மாதோ
மொய்வினை யிருள்கண் போழு முக்குடை மூர்த்தி பாதங்
கைவினை செய்த சொற்பூக் கைதொழு தேத்தி னேனே.
reading: The poet, raising his hands, praises with the flowers of his words the feet of the three-umbrella Lord, a spotless moon that rises from the sea of deeds and breaks the dark of deeds' binding.
nuance: The sea is of deeds (செய்வினை), not of births, so the work ends on the figure of karma as the water to be crossed, and gives its closing act to a hymn.
event: The poet offers his poem as a flower at the Lord's feet and ends the work.

title: kundalakesi
theme: The nineteen surviving fragments, in the editor's order, open with an invocation to a lord defined by labour for others and an apology that excuses the poet's slips by the worth of his subject; most of the rest argue a renouncer's case: bodily austerities are mere words, desire is not quenched by enjoyment, death is a daily march to execution, the body is carrion that cannot be called 'mine', a fault stays a fault even in a god, and the wise meet pardon and death alike as the fruit of deeds. Two verses praise an unnamed king.
source_issues: The core file carries no quoted_in for any of the 19 verses, though the brief says the fragments record the work that preserved each; the source of each fragment cannot be checked here.
Verses 10 and 17 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins read correctly.
Verse 4 line 3 (சார்த்தரிடு) and line 4 (மடிந்தொழுக) admit more than one division and sense.
Verse 14 line 2 (றினைப்பெய்த புன்கத்தைப் போலச்) is obscure as divided; the simile cannot be fixed.
Verse 16 lines 3 and 4 (தடு மாற்றத்துத் தோற்றம்) are obscure.
The order of the fragments is the editor's; links between them (2 and 17, 7 and 9, 18 and 19) rest on their content, not on any story sequence.

cast.role: the unnamed man whose words verse 4 reports; the fragment does not say who he is
the unnamed king praised in verses 15 and 16
the unnamed king of verse 19 who orders a man released
the unnamed man of verse 19 who stays unmoved by pardon and a plot against his life

reading: The invocation takes as lord and refuge the one who stood in greatness from the first, who until he reached the end thought only good and spoke only virtue, kept nothing for himself and laboured only for the good of others.
nuance: The lord is not named; he is defined by a career (முன் ... முடிவு எய்து காறு, from the beginning until the end was reached) spent wholly for others (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்), not by creation or omniscience. That selfless career across a long course is the mark of the Buddha-to-be, and the claim is tagged Buddhist on that mark; the verse itself does not say Buddha.

reading: As the sick do not weigh the taste of medicine and those who need fire do not reckon the harm of its smoke, the poet says, so for one praising the fame of him who cut away the three faults, the slips of his own speech are no slips.
nuance: The apology does not ask pardon; it argues that the worth of the object cancels the fault of the words, using two images in which a lesser harm is accepted for a greater need. The three faults (குற்றம் மூன்றும்) are named only by number.

reading: As a well-built ship is made with an eye to the wind and a life is lived with an eye to its span, so all purity looks to the pure one who has not even the thought that leans toward evil deeds.
nuance: துப்புரவு may mean purity or, as often in older Tamil, the means of living and enjoyment; on the second reading the verse says all that sustains us depends on the pure one. The two similes, ship to wind and life to lifespan, make the dependence one of guidance rather than creation.

reading: An unnamed speaker lists wrapping the body or stripping it bare, smearing it with dust, enduring biting cold, bathing and standing in fire, living on alms and wearing matted hair, and says these are mere words: the tapas to practise is to live subdued.
nuance: The list takes in practices of several orders at once: going naked was the mark of one Jain order, ash and matted hair of Saiva and Vedic ascetics, standing in fire of the five-fires penance. The reading of the last line (வார்த்தை இவை; செய்தவம் மடிந்து ஒழுகல்) as 'these are talk; tapas is to live restrained' is mine; மடிந்து could also mean 'as one already dead'. சார்த்தர் (line 3) may be caravan merchants who give the alms.

tamil: வகையெழிற் றோள்க ளென்றும் மணிநிறக் குஞ்சி யென்றும்
புகழெழ விகற்பிக் கின்ற பொருளில் காமத்தை மற்றோர்
தொகையெழுங் காத றன்னாற் றுய்த்தியாந் துடைத்து மென்பா
ரகையழ லழுவந் தன்னை நெய்யினா லவிக்க லாமோ.
reading: Some say they will wipe out the senseless desire that is dressed up in praise of shapely shoulders and gem-dark hair by enjoying it with love; the verse asks whether a blazing pit of fire can be put out with ghee.
nuance: The body praised is a man's: குஞ்சி is a man's tuft of hair and the shoulders are the hero's. The verse also blames the praise itself (புகழ் எழ விகற்பிக்கின்ற), the poetic convention that inflates desire.

tamil: அனலென நினைப்பிற் பொத்தி யகந்தலைக் கொண்ட காமக்
கனலினை யுவர்ப்பு நீராற் கடையற வவித்து மென்னார்
நினைவிலாப் புணர்ச்சி தன்னா னீக்குது மென்று நிற்பார்
reading: Those who will not put out the fire of desire, lodged within like a flame, with the water of revulsion, and insist they will remove it by thoughtless union, are like one who would stop a flood with more flood.
nuance: உவர்ப்பு names the remedy: revulsion, the deliberate turning against the body that verses 11 to 14 then practise. The verse pairs with 5: there the wrong remedy is fuel on fire, here water on water.

tamil: போதர வுயிர்த்த வாவி புகவுயிர்க் கின்ற தேனு
மூதிய மென்று கொள்வ ருணர்வினான் மிக்க நீரா
ராதலா லழிதன் மாலைப் பொருள்களுக் கழிதல் வேண்டா
காதலா னழுது மென்பார் கண்ணனி களைய லுற்றார்.
reading: Those of surpassing understanding count it gain each time a breath that went out comes back in; so for things whose nature is to perish their perishing need not be mourned, and those who say they weep from love are only stripping their own eyes.
nuance: The argument inverts ordinary reckoning: life is not a possession that death takes away but a run of returned breaths, each a windfall. The sense of the last half-line (கண் அணி களையல் உற்றார்) is not certain; it may mean they ruin their eyes with weeping or lose the eye of understanding.

tamil: அரவின மரக்க ராளி யவைகளுஞ் சிறிது தம்மை
மருவினாற் றீய வாகா வரம்பில்கா லத்து ளென்றும்
பிரிவில மாகித் தன்சொற் பேணியே யொழுகு நங்கட்
கொருபொழு திரங்க மாட்டாக் கூற்றின்யா ருய்து மென்பார்.
reading: Even snakes, demons and lions do no harm to those who stay near them a little while; but from Death, who will not pity for one moment us who through boundless time have never left him and have lived obeying his word, who can escape?
nuance: வரம்பில் காலத்துள் (through limitless time) assumes the round of births: we have been Death's servants life after life, and long service earns no mercy.

tamil: பாளையாந் தன்மை செத்தும் பாலனாந் தன்மை செத்தும்
காளையாந் தன்மை செத்துங் காமுறு மிளமை செத்தும்
மீளுமிவ் வியல்பு மின்னே மேல்வரு மூப்பு மாகி
நாளுநாட் சாகின் றாமா னமக்குநா மழாத தென்னோ.
reading: The foetus has died, the child has died, the youth has died, the desiring young adult has died; this same course now brings old age, so we die day by day, and the verse asks why we do not weep for ourselves.
nuance: Each stage of life is spoken of as a death (செத்தும), so death is not one event at the end but the steady form of living.

tamil: மீளினு மீளக் காண்டு மீட்சியொன் றானு மில்லா
நாளடி யிடுத றோன்று நம்முயிர் பருகுங் கூற்றின்
வாளின்வாய்த் தலைவைப் பாக்குச் செல்கின்றோம் வாழ்கின் றோமோ.
reading: Caught in the net and led to the killing ground, one might yet see a return; but each day's step has no return, and we walk to set our heads at the edge of the sword of Death that drinks our life: is this living?
nuance: The image is of a condemned prisoner led to execution: ordinary life is that walk, only with no chance of reprieve.

tamil: நன்கன நாறுமி தென்றிவ் வுடம்பு நயக்கின்ற தாயி
னென்பது வாயில்க டோறு முண்ணின் றழுக்குச் சொரியத்
தின்பதொர் நாயு மிழுப்பத் திசைதொறுஞ் சீப்பில்கு போழ்தி
னின்பநன் னாற்ற மிதன்க ணெவ்வகை யாற்கொள்ள லாமே.
reading: If one loves this body thinking it smells sweet, when filth pours from every opening, a dog drags it about to eat and it rots in every direction, the verse asks how any fragrance can be found in it.

tamil: மாறுகொள் மந்தர மென்று மரகத வீங்கெழு வென்றும்
தேறிடத் தோள்க டிறத்தே திறத்துளிக் காமுற்ற தாயிற்
பாறொடு நாய்க ளசிப்பப் பறிப்பறிப் பற்றிய போழ்தி
reading: If one desires shoulders praised as rivals of Mount Mandara and as swelling emerald bars, the verse asks what delight there is in that flesh when vultures and dogs tear and pluck at it.
nuance: Again the praised body is a man's: Mandara and the bar (எழு) are the stock similes for a hero's shoulders, so the contemplation of foulness is aimed at desire for a man.

tamil: உறுப்புக் கடாமுடன் கூடி யொன்றா யிருந்த பெரும்பை
மறைப்பில் விழைவிற்குச் சார்வாய் மயக்குவ தேலிவ் வுறுப்புக்
குறைத்தன போல வழுகிக் குறைந்து குறைந்து சொரிய
வெறுப்பிற் கிடந்த பொழுதின் வேண்டப் படுவது முண்டோ.
reading: If the great bag in which the limbs and their fluids are bound into one, hidden and serving as a prop for longing, deludes us, the verse asks whether anything will be wanted of it when its limbs rot away as if cut and it lies loathsome.

tamil: எனதெனச் சிந்தித்த லான்மற் றிவ்வுடம் பின்பத்துக் காமேற்
றினைப்பெய்த புன்கத்தைப் போலச் சிறியவு மூத்தவு மாகி
நுனைய புழுக்குலந் தம்மா னுகரவும் வாழவும் பட்ட
வினைய வுடம்பினைப் பாவி யானென தென்னலு மாமே.
reading: Because one thinks of it as 'mine', this body is taken for pleasure; yet it is a body made by deeds, where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live, and the verse asks whether a sinner can call it 'I' and 'mine'.
nuance: The denial is argued from the body's other tenants: the worms already live off it, so the claim 'mine' is false on its face. வினைய உடம்பு makes the body itself a product of past deeds. Line 2 (இனைப் பெய்த புன்கத்தைப் போல) is obscure.

reading: The king of the moon-white umbrella, the sceptre that holds to dharma and the elephant in triple must is praised as an embodied form, born to bring together all the good qualities that are hard to attain.
nuance: The sense of இறந்த (line 1), 'surpassing' or 'gone away', changes whether the king gathers rare virtues or restores lost ones.

reading: Having crushed anger and put away falsehood, warding off death with his sceptre, the king spoke no word but 'give', and appeared so that even the bewildered longed for the sight of him.
nuance: கூற்றம் காய்ந்து may mean that his rule kept death from his subjects or that he gave up putting men to death. The last line's தடுமாற்றத்துத் தோற்றம் is obscure.

tamil: மண்ணுளார் தம்மைப் போல்வார் மாட்டதே யன்று வாய்மை
நண்ணினார் திறத்துங் குற்றங் குற்றமே நல்ல வாகா
விண்ணுளார் புகழ்தற் கொத்த விழுமியோ னெற்றி போழ்ந்த
கண்ணுளான் கண்டந் தன்மேற் கறையையார் கறையன் றென்பார்.
reading: Not only in earthly people like us but in those who have reached truth, a fault stays a fault and does not turn good: who would say the stain on the throat of the exalted one praised by the gods, whose forehead is split by an eye, is not a stain?
nuance: The example is the Saiva god, named by his forehead eye and stained throat; the verse uses the mark that Saiva praise treats as a sign of his grace as proof that even a god carries a fault. It stands against the poet's own plea in 2.

reading: What turns back will turn back, what swells will swell, what is to be gained is gained and what is to be lost is lost; those who know this neither grieve nor exult, and it is good to say that what is to come will come.
nuance: The verse names no agent of the outcome, neither god nor deed; equanimity rests only on the certainty that what is due arrives. Verse 19 supplies the cause as deeds (வினை).

reading: Both when the king of the fragrant garland said 'let him go' and after a death was plotted against him in an unbearable way, the man stood with no swelling or wilting, able to say that all that had unfolded was the fruit of deeds.
nuance: The verse tells an event but not whose: the man is unnamed, and who plotted the killing (கொலை சூழ்ந்த) is not stated; it may be the same king. The fragment does not let the story be rebuilt.
event: A king orders a man released, and later his killing is plotted; through both the man stays unmoved.

title: பதிகம்
theme: The patikam tells how Puhar got its two names, from the goddess Champa and from the Kaveri released by Agastya, then runs through the whole story from the festival and the prince's pursuit to the bowl, the prison made a house of charity, the hearing of the schools and Manimekalai's vow in Kanchi to end rebirth; its colophon has Saathan recite the thirty songs of her renunciation to a listening Ilango.
source_issues: Line 71 had a leftover HTML quote mark and line 78 an old-font vowel sign; both repaired in the core file, sense unaffected.
Lines 10 (கஞ்ச வேட்கையின் காந்த மன்) and 17 (ஆணு விசும்பின்) read oddly; the sense of the Kaveri's welcome at 17-18 is not certain.
