the immortal sage who overturned his water-pot to release the Kaveri
the Chola king of the sun's line whose request brought the Kaveri
Madhavi's mother, a courtesan of Puhar
Madhavi's attendant
the dancer of Puhar, Manimekalai's mother, now a Buddhist renunciant
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, who renounces and becomes a Buddhist ascetic
the Chola prince of Puhar who pursues Manimekalai
the sea goddess, Kovalan's family deity, who carries Manimekalai to Manipallavam
Manimekalai's companion, left asleep in the Uvavanam garden
the guardian goddess of the island Manipallavam, who gives Manimekalai the bowl
the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, later in Kanchi
the earlier owner of the bowl, reborn as king of a land across the sea
the goddess who gave the bowl to Aputhiran
the chaste wife of Puhar (named Aathirai later in the epic) who puts the first food in the bowl
a vidyadhara woman cursed with an insatiable hunger (ஆனைத்தீ)
Kayachandigai's vidyadhara husband, who kills the prince
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
the queen, Udayakumaran's mother, to whom Manimekalai teaches dharma
the Chera prince-poet of the Silappathikaram, here the listener
the grain merchant (கூல வாணிகன்), poet of the Manimekalai

tamil: பொன் திகழ் நெடு வரை உச்சித் தோன்றி
தென் திசைப் பெயர்ந்த இத் தீவத் தெய்வதம்
மா நில மடந்தைக்கு வரும் துயர் கேட்டு
வெந் திறல் அரக்கர்க்கு வெம் பகை நோற்ற
செங் குணக்கு ஒழுகி அச் சம்பாபதி அயல்
ஆங்கு இனிது இருந்த அருந் தவ முதியோள்
ஓங்கு நீர்ப் பாவையை உவந்து எதிர்கொண்டு ஆங்கு
reading: The narrator tells how Champa, the shining goddess of this island who came south from the golden mountain and did austerity against the asuras for the sake of the suffering earth, dwelt under the jambu tree at Champapati, and how, when a Chola king of the sun's line asked for water, Agastya overturned his pot and the Kaveri flowed east to that city, where the old ascetic goddess welcomed her as a lamp come to quench a long desire.
nuance: The patikam opens not with the heroine but with the founding of Puhar's two names, so the city of the epic is first a goddess's seat. Lines 10 (கஞ்ச வேட்கையின்) and 17-18 (ஆணு விசும்பின் ஆகாயகங்கை வேணவாத் தீர்த்த விளக்கே) are hard: whether the Ganga of the sky is the one whose desire is quenched or a title given to the Kaveri is not clear from the words.
event: Agastya, at a Chola king's request, overturns his water-pot; the Kaveri flows to Champapati and the goddess Champa welcomes her.

tamil: பின்னிலை முனியாப் பெருந் தவன் கேட்டு ஈங்கு
தான் நிலை திரியாத் தண் தமிழ்ப் பாவை
என் பெயர்ப் படுத்த இவ் விரும் பெயர் மூதூர்
நின் பெயர்ப் படுத்தேன் நீ வாழிய! என
reading: Agastya bids the river bow to the old ascetic goddess; the Kaveri, the Chola banner who never fails her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens, bows, and Champa takes her to her lap and gives the old city, named for herself since Brahma's creation, the river's name as well.
nuance: This is how the patikam accounts for the city's two names (இரு பால் பெயரிய, line 32): Champapati and the Kaveri's city. The river is called the daughter of the Cholas of the unbending sceptre, so the land's fertility is tied to the dynasty's justice from the first page.
event: At Agastya's word the Kaveri bows to Champa, who takes her on her lap and names the city after her.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the core units 1-18, 19-34 and 35-50 are recut here to 19-31 and 32-50, since the welcome scene closes with Champa's blessing நீ வாழிய! என at line 31, and line 32 opens the catalogue of the story's events (-ததும்) that runs to the end.

tamil: இரு பால் பெயரிய உரு கெழு மூதூர்
ஆங்கு அப் பூம்பொழில் அரசு இளங் குமரனைப்
ஆங்கு அத் தீவகத்து ஆய் இழை நல்லாள்
தான் துயில் உணர்ந்து தனித் துயர் உழந்ததும்
உழந்தோள் ஆங்கண் ஓர் ஒளி மணிப் பீடிகைப்
reading: The patikam begins its summary of the story: Indra's festival is proclaimed in the twice-named city; Chitrapathi, stung that the town's gossip grows, sends word to Madhavi through Vasantamalai; Manimekalai goes to the garden for flowers, sees the prince, hides in the crystal chamber, and he leaves troubled; the goddess Manimekala carries her to Manipallavam and wakes Sutamati; alone on the island she grieves, and at a shining jewel seat she comes to know all her former births.
nuance: The summary names the jewel seat (மணிப் பீடிகை) only by its light; that it is the Buddha's seat is left to kaathai 9 onward. The knowledge of former births (பழம் பிறப்பு) is given as an event, not argued, and it is the turn on which the whole renunciation rests.
event: Manimekalai flees the prince into the crystal chamber, is carried by the goddess to Manipallavam, and there learns her former births at the jewel seat.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 34/35 to 31/32: the core unit 35-50 began in mid-sentence (பெருகியது அலர் என at 34 is the thought of சித்திராபதி at 35). This unit runs from the festival announcement at 32 to the knowledge of former births at 50, closed by உணர்ந்ததும்.

tamil: பிச்சைக்கு அவ் ஊர்ப் பெருந் தெரு அடைந்ததும்
கொங்கு அலர் நறுந் தார்க் கோமகன் சென்றதும்
reading: The summary continues: the goddess gives her a mantra and bids her cease grieving; Deepatilakai gives her the great bowl; with her mothers she bows to the teacher Aravanar, who tells her of Aputhiran and of how Chinta Devi gave him the bowl; she carries it into the city's street for alms, a chaste wife puts the first food in it, she ends Kayachandigai's elephant-fire hunger, and when she goes to the public hall the prince follows.
nuance: The bowl passes from goddess to Aputhiran to Manimekalai, and its first food comes from a பத்தினி (line 64), so the epic's charity starts from a chaste wife's gift; the heroine who renounced the courtesan's life receives first from the epic's figure of wifely virtue. The begging renunciant is the one who ends another's hunger.
event: Manimekalai receives the bowl, hears its history from Aravanar, begs in Puhar, is first fed by a chaste wife, and ends Kayachandigai's hunger.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 67/68 to 68/69: line 67 (அம்பலம் அடைந்தனள் ஆய் இழை என்றே) is the report that brings the prince at line 68 (கோமகன் சென்றதும்), so the sentence ends at 68.

tamil: ஐ அரி உண் கண் அவன் துயர் பொறாஅள்
நறு மலர்க் கோதைக்கு நல் அறம் உரைத்து ஆங்கு
உற்றவள் ஆங்கு ஓர் உயர் தவன் வடிவு ஆய்
reading: The summary goes on: in Kayachandigai's form Manimekalai turns the king's prison into a house of charity; Kanchanan, taking her for his wife, kills the prince with his sword; she, grieving, is calmed by a divine voice; the king orders her imprisoned and then freed; she teaches dharma to the queen, goes to Aputhiran's land and with him to Manipallavam, takes an ascetic's form in Vanji, and asks the schools' reckoners to state the truth.
nuance: Line 72 sets the epic's justice theme in one turn: a prison of the war-making king (மறம் செய் வேலோன்) becomes a house of dharma (அறம் செய் கோட்டம்). Whom she teaches at line 81 is not named: நறு மலர்க் கோதை is read here as the queen, since 58 used the same phrase for Manimekalai as hearer and here she is the teller. The patikam says she heard (கேட்டதும்) the schools, not that she refuted them.
event: Manimekalai frees the prison, Kanchanan kills the prince, the king jails and releases her, and she travels to Aputhiran's land, Manipallavam and Vanji, where she hears the schools.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 87/88 to 88/89: line 87 ('நவை அறு நன்பொருள் உரைமினோ' என) is her request to the schools and line 88 (சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்டதும்) completes it.

tamil: புக்கு அவள் கொண்ட பொய் உருக் களைந்து
மா வண் தமிழ்த் திறம் மணிமேகலை துறவு
ஆறு ஐம் பாட்டினுள் அறிய வைத்தனன் என்
reading: The summary ends: with her mothers she seeks out Aravanar and enters Kanchi, casts off her borrowed form and bows at his feet, takes up the ascetic life, hears the dharma and vows that the round of becoming be cut; and the colophon says that Saathan, the grain merchant, with Ilango the prince graciously listening, set out Manimekalai's renunciation in thirty songs.
nuance: The epic's title theme is given at line 97 as மணிமேகலை துறவு, and its count as ஆறு ஐம் பாட்டு (thirty). The roles of the Silappathikaram's patikam are reversed: there Ilango composes and Saathan hears; here Saathan composes and Ilango hears. Whether this colophon is the poet's own or a later frame the text does not say.
event: Manimekalai finds Aravanar in Kanchi, bows to him, takes up austerity and vows to end rebirth; Saathan recites the work before Ilango.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 87/88 to 88/89 (see 69-88); the unit begins with the journey to Aravanar in Kanchi.

title: விழாவறை காதை
theme: The opening kaathai tells how Puhar's festival of Indra was founded at a sage's word by the hanging-fort Chola, why it must not be forgotten (the guardian spirit's anger), and gives the hereditary drummer's proclamation: the gods will come down, the city is to be adorned, every god worshipped by its own rite, the schools are to debate without enmity, and hunger, disease and enmity are to leave. The warning about a forgotten festival is the seed of Puhar's later loss to the sea.
source_issues: Lines 39-41 (மன்னன் கரிகால்வளவன் நீங்கிய நாள் இந் நகர் போல்வதோர் இயல்பினது ஆகி) are syntactically obscure: it is unclear whether Karikalan's leaving is his death or a departure, and how the comparison of heaven with the city runs.
Lines 9-10: whether அது நேர்ந்தது closes the founding story or runs on into கவராக் கேள்வியோர் கடவார் ஆகலின் is not settled by the text; the boundary at 9 is a sense break, not a full stop.

cast.role: the great ascetic of the Malaya hill (Agastya by tradition; the kaathai does not name him) at whose word the festival was founded
a Chola of the past, the destroyer of the hanging fort, who asked Indra to dwell in Puhar for the festival
Indra, king of the gods, the thousand-eyed, whose festival Puhar holds
the king's five great assemblies
the eight groups of royal attendants, acting together at the festival
the drummer of the old hereditary house who beats the festival drum and proclaims the festival
the guardian spirit sent by Indra to remove the Chola king's distress

tamil: உலகம் திரியா ஓங்கு உயர் விழுச் சீர்ப்
ஓங்கு உயர் மலயத்து அருந் தவன் உரைப்ப
தூங்கு எயில் எறிந்த தொடித் தோள் செம்பியன்
நால் ஏழ் நாளினும் நன்கு இனிது உறைக' என
reading: To raise the old city's renown, at the word of the great ascetic of the Malaya hill, the Chola of braceleted arms who destroyed the hanging fort bowed before the king of the gods and asked him to dwell in his city through the twenty-eight days of the festival the worthy desire, and the king of the gods agreed.
nuance: The festival is given a charter, not a date: a sage's counsel, a king's request and a god's consent. The founder is identified only by his feat (தூங்கு எயில் எறிந்த), the hanging fort that the Purananuru also gives to a Chola ancestor; the kaathai does not name the sage, whom tradition takes for Agastya.
event: At the Malaya sage's word the hanging-fort Chola asks Indra to dwell in his city for the twenty-eight days of the festival, and Indra agrees.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 9: line 9 (அமரர் தலைவன் ஆங்கு அது நேர்ந்தது) closes the founding story, and lines 10-18 are one sentence naming the gatherers and their verb (குழீஇ, 18), which the core cut at 16 split from its list.

tamil: மெய்த் திறம் வழக்கு நன்பொருள் வீடு எனும்
இத் திறம் தம் தம் இயல்பினின் காட்டும்
மடித்த செவ் வாய் வல் எயிறு இலங்க
ஏற்று உரி போர்த்த இடி உறு முழக்கின்
reading: Because the learned do not neglect what is due, the reckoners of the schools who each show truth, method, the good end and release, the reckoners of times, gods in disguise, speakers of many tongues, the five great assemblies and the eight groups gather and say that if the festival is forgotten the spirit that removed the king's distress will roar and torment the city and the spirit that beats and eats the wicked bound in its noose will be displeased, so let the festival of the thousand-eyed begin; the drum is taken from the Vajra temple onto an elephant's neck, and its hereditary drummer hails the city and wishes it three rains a year and a king whose rule does not let the planets leave their course.
nuance: The festival is kept out of fear as much as joy: the assemblies' reason is the guardian spirit's anger if it is forgotten, a threat the epic later fulfils, though by another hand (Manimekala deity's curse, kaathai 25). Line 34 can be read as a king whose sceptre keeps the planets in their places, so that rain and just rule are wished for in one breath; the reading of கோள் நிலை திரியா as qualifying the king's rod is mine. The schools' reckoners are listed among the festival's guests, the first sign of the debating hall of line 61.
event: The schools, the guests and the king's assemblies gather and call for the festival to begin; the drum is mounted on an elephant and the hereditary drummer begins the proclamation.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 9 at the start (see manimekalai:1:1-9); the unit now runs from the gatherers' list (10) through the assemblies' warning to the drummer's first blessing, ending at the sentence close கோலோன் ஆகுக! (34).

tamil: பால் வேறு தேவரும் இப் பதிப் படர்ந்து
பழ மணல் மாற்றுமின் புது மணல் பரப்புமின்
reading: The drummer proclaims that on the good day of the island's rite of peace the thousand-eyed and the gods of four kinds and many classes will come to this city, leaving the golden city of heaven empty, as those who know the ancient order hold for certain, and he bids the people set up arches, golden pots, sprouts in golden trays and lamp-bearing images, plant areca, plantain, vanchi, flowering creepers and sugarcane, hang pearl strings on the gold pillars, and in the streets and squares change the old sand for new.
nuance: Lines 39 to 41 are hard: heaven, emptied by the gods' coming, becomes 'like this city on the day king Karikal Valavan left it', which seems to measure heaven's emptiness by Puhar's desolation at the loss of Karikalan, whether at his death or his going away the line does not say. The phrase தீவகச் சாந்தி returns in kaathai 24, where the day it is not performed is the day the city enters the sea.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 51: line 50 (விழவு மலி மூதூர் வீதியும் மன்றமும்) is the object of மாற்றுமின் and பரப்புமின் in line 51, which closes the sentence.

tamil: பதி வாழ் சதுக்கத்துத் தெய்வம் ஈறு ஆக
வெண் மணல் குன்றமும் விரி பூஞ் சோலையும்
தண் மணல் துருத்தியும் தாழ் பூந் துறைகளும்
நால் ஏழ் நாளினும் நன்கு அறிந்தீர் என
அணி விழா அறைந்தனன் அகநகர் மருங்கு என்
reading: The drummer bids them raise flags and banners on the mansions and gates, have those who know the proper rites worship every god in its own way from the brow-eyed lord to the deity of the crossroads, bids those who know the good word of merit take their seats in the sand pavilions and halls and the debaters of the schools mount the debating hall, and part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not share their view, for gods and men will roam together through the twenty-eight days; then, amid swordsmen, chariots, horses and elephants, he beats the drum, wishes that hunger, disease and enmity leave and rain and plenty overflow, and so proclaims the festival through the inner city.
nuance: The proclamation makes room for every cult, Saiva and local alike, and sets the schools' debate inside a civic festival under a rule of civility: dispute is allowed, enmity is not. The closing wish names hunger first, the ill the heroine's begging bowl will later answer. The ills of line 70 are those Kural 734 excludes from a land, but in other words, so there is no echo.
event: The drummer finishes his commands, beats the drum among the troops and proclaims the festival through the inner city.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 51 at the start (see manimekalai:1:35-51); the unit now begins with the flags of line 52 and runs to the end of the kaathai.

title: ஊரலர் உரைத்த காதை
theme: On the day of Puhar's festival, Chithirapathi, grieved that Madhavi and Manimekalai stay away, sends Vayantamalai to tell Madhavi that the town calls an accomplished dancer's turn to tapas shameful. Madhavi answers that she lost her shame when she outlived the news of her lover's suffering, that Kannaki fits none of the known kinds of pathini, that Manimekalai as Kannaki's daughter will go to tapas and never to the courtesan's trade, and that the Buddhist teacher Aravanar has taught her that birth is suffering born of attachment and given her the five precepts.

cast.role: Madhavi's mother, a senior courtesan of Puhar
Madhavi's attendant and companion, the Silappathikaram's வசந்தமாலை
the courtesan dancer, Kovalan's lover and Manimekalai's mother, now turned to tapas
the many of Puhar who talk about Madhavi's renunciation
Kovalan's wife, the great pathini who burned Madurai, named here only by that title
the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, later in Kanchi, in whose dwelling Madhavi has taken refuge

tamil: தத்து அரி நெடுங் கண் தன் மகள் தோழி
'பயம் கெழு மா நகர் அலர் எடுத்து உரை' என
reading: On the festival day of the island's peace rite for the king of the gods, Chithirapathi, pained that Madhavi and Manimekalai have not come, calls her daughter's friend Vayantamalai and tells her to go and tell them what the town is saying; Vayantamalai, herself wasted by Madhavi's renunciation, goes to the flower hall where the two sit, grieves at the dancer's worn body, and begins to speak.
nuance: Chithirapathi does not plead; she sends the town's gossip (அலர்) as her argument, so public talk is the pressure brought to bear on a renunciant. Both women who come to Madhavi are wasted by her choice (அயர்ந்து, மெய் வாடிய; வாடிய மேனி), the friend in grief and Madhavi in austerity.
event: Chithirapathi, grieved that Madhavi stays away from the festival, sends Vayantamalai to tell her the town's talk, and Vayantamalai comes to Madhavi in the flower hall.

tamil: உன்னோடு இவ் ஊர் உற்றது ஒன்று உண்டுகொல்?
ஓவியச் செந் நூல் உரை நூல் கிடக்கையும்
நல் தவம் புரிந்தது நாண் உடைத்து" என்றே
reading: Vayantamalai reports what the town says of Madhavi: that a woman who learned and mastered every art laid down for dancing women, the court and common styles of dance and song, the lute, drum and flute, the arts of the ball, cookery, perfume, bathing, the bed, the seasons, the body, reading intent, speech, cipher, painting, garlands, adornment, the reckoning of time and the treatises, should have taken up tapas is a shame.
nuance: The list is the town's argument, not an ornament: every accomplishment named is a reason, in its eyes, that the dancer belongs to her trade. நல் தவம் (33) is the town's own phrase, so it grants the tapas is good and calls it shameful for her. Several items (கரந்து உறை கணக்கு, வட்டிகைச் செய்தி, கோவையின் கோப்பு) are rare names of arts and are taken here only as items of the list. The claim is answered at once: Vayantamalai herself sets it down to the talk of the many (34-36), and Madhavi replies to it in 38-57, which is why its stance is refuted.
event: Vayantamalai tells Madhavi that the town says her turning to tapas, after mastering the dancer's arts, is shameful.

tamil: பலர் தொகுபு உரைக்கும் பண்பு இல் வாய்மொழி
reading: Vayantamalai sets the words, 'there is no good in it, it is shameful', down to the ill-bred talk of the many rather than the worthy elders of the old city, and Madhavi answers that she, who stayed alive on hearing of her lover's cruel suffering, already lost the town's good word and gave up her shame.
nuance: Madhavi turns the town's charge: the shame is not in her tapas but in her having outlived Kovalan's death (போதல்செய்யா உயிரொடு நின்றே), so renunciation is her answer to a shame already incurred. Whether lines 34 to 36 are Vayantamalai's own gloss on the town's words or part of the report is not certain; the reading takes them as hers, since 37 names her as the one who spoke.
event: Vayantamalai disowns the town's talk as the many's, and Madhavi replies that she gave up shame when she survived the news of her lover's suffering.
unit_note: The core unit 34-56 is split at 41, where Madhavi's first sentence closes on நாணுத் துறந்தேன்; 42 opens her account of the kinds of pathini.

tamil: ஊது உலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்து அகத்து அடங்காது
நல் நீர்ப் பொய்கையின் நளி எரி புகுவர்
உடன் உறை வாழ்க்கைக்கு நோற்று உடம்பு அடுவர்
அத் திறத்தாளும் அல்லள் எம் ஆய் இழை
கணவற்கு உற்ற கடுந் துயர் பொறா அள்
கண்ணீர் ஆடிய கதிர் இள வன முலை
காவலன் பேர் ஊர் கனை எரி ஊட்டிய
reading: Madhavi says that pathini women of the wide world, when their husbands die, give up their lives with sighs like a smith's bellows, or else enter the blazing fire as if a cool pool, or else wear down the body in vows to live again with the beloved, but that Kannaki was of none of these kinds: unable to bear her husband's suffering she twisted off her breast and set the king's city aflame, and Manimekalai, the daughter of that great pathini, will be brought to tapas and never to the evil trade of unreformed conduct.
nuance: Madhavi calls Manimekalai the daughter (மகள்) of the great pathini, not her own, so the courtesan's daughter is given Kannaki's lineage and with it a claim to be kept from the courtesan's trade (தீத் தொழில்). The three kinds are ranked by the word ஆயின் (if not), each a fallback from the one before; the third does not say in which life the couple will live together. Madhavi herself fits none of the three either, having lived on, which is the point of her opening in 38 to 41. The second kind, who enters the fire as if it were a cool pool (45), uses the figure of Purananuru 246, and the third, who wears the body down in vows, is the widow's austerity that the queen of that poem refuses.
event: Madhavi tells Vayantamalai the kinds of pathini, sets Kannaki apart from them, and says Manimekalai will be given to tapas.
unit_note: Starts at 42 after the split at 41, and runs to 57, where the sentence begun at 55 (மணிமேகலை அருந் தவப் படுத்தல் அல்லது) closes on படாஅள்; the core unit 57-75 began mid-sentence.

tamil: மற வணம் நீத்த மாசு அறு கேள்வி
மா பெருந் துன்பம் கொண்டு உளம் மயங்கி
"உய் வகை இவை கொள்" என்று உரவோன் அருளினன்
மைத் தடங் கண்ணார் தமக்கும் எற் பயந்த
ஆங்கு அவள் உரை கேட்டு அரும் பெறல் மா மணி
ஓங்கு திரைப் பெருங் கடல் வீழ்த்தோர் போன்று
reading: Madhavi tells how she came to this dwelling of ascetics and fell at the feet of the teacher Aravanar, told him her lover's suffering, and was taught that the born meet ever-growing suffering and the unborn the greatest bliss, that the one comes of attachment and the other to those who are free of it, and was shown the five precepts as the way to be saved; she bids Vayantamalai tell this to the courtesans and to Chithirapathi, and Vayantamalai leaves helpless, like one who has dropped a rare gem into the sea.
nuance: The teaching answers grief, not a question of doctrine: Madhavi brings Aravanar her lover's suffering and is given the cause of all suffering. ஐவகைச் சீலம் are the five lay precepts of the Buddhists, offered as உய் வகை, a way of survival, before any word of release. The closing simile makes Madhavi, lost to the courtesans, the gem dropped in the sea.
event: Madhavi tells how Aravanar taught her the cause of suffering and the five precepts and sends word to Chithirapathi; Vayantamalai goes away in despair.
unit_note: Starts at 58 (ஆங்கனம் அன்றியும், 'besides that') after the boundary moved from 56/57 to 57/58.

title: மலர்வனம் புக்க காதை
theme: Manimekalai's tears for her parents spoil Madhavi's garland, and she must fetch fresh flowers; Sudhamathi, herself once carried off from a garden by a sky-being, rules out every garden but the Buddha's Uvavanam, whose crystal pavilion and lotus seat she describes, the seat built to prove that a deed without intention bears no fruit. Walking through the festival street past a drunk pleading with a naked ascetic, a raving man in ash, a eunuch dancer and the start of Murugan's procession, the girl is surrounded by a crowd that blames her mother for her tapas, and enters the grove.
source_issues: Line 100 (தெளிந்து) was repaired by the build from an old-font ௌ for ெள; the reading is secure.
Line 101 கையுதிர்க்கொணம் is a rare form; the drunk's last clause is read as 'you may cast us off', which is uncertain.

The automatic cut split speeches at lines 24/25, 155/156, and ran the crowd list across units; eight units were re-cut to sense breaks (see unit_note). The sentence of 3:42-51 ends at line 52, left in place because other chapters link to 3:52-68.

cast.role: the courtesan dancer, Kovalan's lover and Manimekalai's mother, now turned to tapas
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, the heroine
Manimekalai's companion, a brahmin's daughter from Champai abandoned in Puhar by a vidyadhara
the vidyadhara who carried off Sudhamathi and left her in Puhar
the divine builder who made the Uvavanam's lotus seat
a naked fasting ascetic of the Jain dwelling met in the festival street
a drunk who begs the ascetic to drink toddy
a crazed man smeared with ash raving in the street
a street performer of Kama's eunuch dance
the women who set their boys on the festival elephant
the many of Puhar who talk about Madhavi's renunciation; here the festival crowd

tamil: மாதர் செங் கண் வரி வனப்பு அழித்து
புலம்பு நீர் உருட்டிப் பொதி அவிழ் நறு மலர்
மது மலர்க் குழலியொடு மா மலர் தொடுக்கும்
அணி திகழ் நீலத்து ஆய் மலர் ஒட்டிய
கடை மணி உகு நீர் கண்டனன் ஆயின்
reading: As Madhavi tells Vayantamalai of the suffering of Manimekalai's father and mother, the girl, hearing it, weeps onto the flower garland she is stringing; Madhavi wipes her tears and says the garland, wet with them, has lost its purity, so she must fetch fresh flowers herself, and Sudhamathi, stringing flowers beside her, answers in grief that no man who saw tears falling from the girl's eyes could turn away from one before whom Kama himself would lay down his bow, unless he were no man.
nuance: The whole errand to the grove, and so the prince's pursuit, starts from a garland spoiled by tears for Kovalan and Kannaki: Madhavi's word தூத்தகை இழந்தது (14) makes grief a pollution of an offering. Sudhamathi's warning (23-25) is that the renunciant's grief makes her more desirable, not less. The unit was extended by one line, from 24 to 25, because line 25 (பேடியர் அன்றோ ...) ends the question begun at 23.
event: Manimekalai weeps on hearing of her parents' suffering and spoils the garland; Madhavi sends her to gather fresh flowers, and Sudhamathi objects that men will not leave such a girl alone.
unit_note: Lower boundary moved from 24 to 25: Sudhamathi's question runs from line 23 to line 25 (பேடியர் அன்றோ பெற்றியின் நின்றிடின்?).

tamil: ஈங்கு இந் நகரத்து யான் வரும் காரணம்
ஆங்கு அவன் ஈங்கு எனை அகன்று கண்மாறி
reading: Sudhamathi tells Madhavi why she is in Puhar: she is the only daughter of Kausikan, a twice-born man of Champai, and while she gathered flowers alone and unafraid in a garden, the vidyadhara Marutavegan, coming in garlands and gold to see the great festival held for the king of the gods, seized her, rose into the sky, lay with her, made her his, and then left her here and went off to his own far city.
nuance: Her own story is the argument: a girl who picks flowers alone (ஒரு தனி, 31) at festival time can be carried off, and so Manimekalai must not go alone (43). The sky-being comes to the very festival now running, so the danger is present, not past. She tells her abandonment flatly, with no blame word for him.
event: Sudhamathi tells how the vidyadhara Marutavegan carried her off from a garden in Champai, made her his and abandoned her in Puhar.
unit_note: Upper boundary moved from 25 to 26 to follow the change in 3:1-25.

tamil: பல் மலர் அடுக்கிய நல் மரப் பந்தர்
விண்ணவர் கோமான் விழாக் கொள் நல் நாள்
பாடு வண்டு இமிரா பல் மரம் யாவையும்
reading: Sudhamathi says Manimekalai is not one to gather flowers alone, and goes through the gardens: beyond the wall the Ilavanthikai garden is full of the king's men, and on Indra's festival day men of earth do not seek out the gardens the gods take, whose trees hang unfading garlands and no bee hums in them, so knowing people keep away from the royal park, saying a spirit with a noose in its hand guards it.
nuance: The gardens are ruled out one by one for different dangers: the king's men, the gods' claim on the festival day, and a guarding spirit. Unfading garlands and silent bees are the signs of the gods' presence. The sentence that begins at 51 ends at 52 (உய்யானத்திடை உணர்ந்தோர் செல்லார்), in the next unit; the boundary was left in place because other chapters already link to 3:52-68.

tamil: தவா நீர்க் காவிரிப் பாவை தன் தாதை
மூப்பு உடை முதுமைய தாக்கு அணங்கு உடைய
உவவனம் என்பது ஒன்று உண்டு அதன் உள்ளது
தூ நிற மா மணிச் சுடர் ஒளி விரிந்த
தாமரைப் பீடிகை தான் உண்டு ஆங்கு இடின்
சுரும்பு இனம் மூசா தொல் யாண்டு கழியினும்
reading: Sudhamathi goes on: the knowing do not enter the Champati grove where the vulture Champati, who lost his wings to the sun's heat, once sat, nor the Kavera grove where Kaveran, father of the Kaveri maiden, sat, for both are known to hold old striking spirits; but there is the Uvavanam, where many trees flower by the command of the Bhagavan, whose unfailing vow was grace, love and the great resolve to guard all life, and in it a crystal pavilion that lets no sound out but shows the body outside, with a lotus seat of shining gem where buds laid on it open and flowers never fade and are never swarmed by bees though years pass.
nuance: The one safe grove is safe because it belongs to the Buddha (பகவன்), set against two groves of old local spirits; the epic's first Buddhist place in Puhar is introduced as a refuge from anangu. The crystal pavilion that shows the body but keeps sound in is the device the next kaathai uses to shut Manimekalai away from the prince while he can see her. Line 52 finishes the sentence of 3:42-51.

tamil: கடம் பூண்டு ஓர் தெய்வம் கருத்திடை வைத்தோர்
ஆங்கு அவர் அடிக்கு இடின் அவர் அடி தான் உறும்
மயன் பண்டு இழைத்த மரபினது அது தான்
அவ் வனம் அல்லது அணி இழை! நின் மகள்
reading: Sudhamathi adds what she had forgotten: if those who have taken a vow and hold a god in mind lay flowers on the seat, the flowers reach that god's feet, but if they are laid without any thought, they stay where they are; Maya made the seat so of old, showing it with flowers, to grieve the fierce ascetics who say a deed done even without intention reaches its doer, and to be proof for those who say a deed without intention comes to nothing; and other than that grove, she says, there is no fit place for Madhavi's daughter to go.
nuance: This is the epic's first doctrinal claim, made by a device rather than an argument: the seat settles a debate by showing it. The losing side is named only as வெந் திறல் நோன்பிகள், 'vow-keepers of fierce strength' (75); I tag them Jain because the view that an unintended act still binds is theirs and because the next unit's naked, fasting ascetic is called by the same word, உண்ணா நோன்பி (90, 102), but the unit does not name the school. The winning view, that the deed lies in the intention (சிந்தை), is the Buddhist one, and the seat stands in the Buddha's grove (61).
unit_note: Split from 3:69-93: Sudhamathi's speech ends at line 81 (செவ்வனம் செல்லும் செம்மை தான் இலள்), and line 82 begins the walk to the grove.

tamil: அணி இழை நல்லாய்! யானும் போவல்' என்று
எம் தம் அடிகள்! எம் உரை கேண்மோ
அழுக்கு உடை யாக்கையில் புகுந்த நும் உயிர்
தன் வயின் தரூஉம் என் தலைமகன் உரைத்தது
உண்டு தெளிந்து இவ் யோகத்து உறு பயன்
reading: Saying she too will go with Manimekalai to gather flowers, Sudhamathi sets out with her down the street of chariots, where a naked ascetic of the Jain dwelling, with a water pot in a sling and a cane staff, who has left shame and clothing, grieves even for lives he cannot see and goes unwashed under a vow of fasting, is followed by a drunk who bows to his feet and pleads that the master's soul, lodged in a filthy body, should not suffer like a prisoner in a stinking cell, that his own master said toddy brings this world, the next and endless joy, that there is no killing in coconut toddy, and that if the ascetic drinks and sees the fruit of this yoga he may then cast them off.
nuance: The drunk argues on the ascetic's own ground: the Jain rule is not to harm life, and he answers that toddy kills nothing (98), so it should be allowed; he even calls drinking a yoga (100). The ascetic's practice is described without mockery (care for unseen lives, 89), and the comedy falls on the drunk who swears and begs him. Who the drunk's தலைமகன் (97) is, a teacher or a god of drink, the unit does not say; கையுதிர்க்கொணம் (101) is a rare form I read as 'you may cast us off'.
event: Sudhamathi and Manimekalai walk through the festival street, where a drunk begs a naked Jain ascetic to drink toddy.
unit_note: New unit 82-103, from lines 82-93 of 3:69-93 and 94-103 of 3:94-109: the first item of the crowd list (the drunk's followers) ends at line 103 (களிமகன் பின்னரும்).

tamil: சிதவல் துணியொடு சேண் ஓங்கு நெடுஞ் சினைத்
வெண் பலி சாந்தம் மெய்ம் முழுது உரீஇப்
பண்பு இல் கிளவி பலரொடும் உரைத்து ஆங்கு
reading: Others stand grieving behind a crazed man who wears oleander and erukku garlands, a rag and broken twigs for clothing, white ash smeared over his whole body, babbles senseless words to all, weeps, falls, wails, shouts, worships, rises, whirls, runs, hides in a corner, stretches out and fights his own shadow, and they watch his helpless suffering.
nuance: Ash and erukku are marks the Saiva ascetic wore, and worship (தொழூஉம், 111) is among his acts, so the figure may be a god-possessed devotee seen from outside; but the narrator calls him only மையல் உற்ற மகன் (114), and the crowd's response is pity. The heaped verbs with lengthened vowels (110-113) make the line itself reel.
event: A crazed man smeared with ash raves and whirls in the street while people watch him in pity.
unit_note: New unit from lines 104-109 of 3:94-109 and 110-115 of 3:110-125: the madman's description ends at line 115 (கண்டு நிற்குநரும்).

tamil: சுரியல் தாடி மருள் படு பூங் குழல்
பவளச் செவ் வாய் தவள வாள் நகை
ஒள் அரி நெடுங் கண் வெள்ளி வெண் தோட்டு
கருங் கொடிப் புருவத்து மருங்கு வளை பிறை நுதல்
காந்தள் அம் செங் கை ஏந்து இள வன முலை
நீள் நிலம் அளந்தோன் மகன் முன் ஆடிய
reading: Others watch a performer in the eunuch dance, with curled beard, braided hair, coral lips, white teeth, long eyes, white ear-rolls, a brow like the crescent, red hands, young breasts, wide hips and a painted costume, the dance that the son of the one who measured the earth danced in the street of Bana's great city.
nuance: The costume is a man's beard over a woman's body, the 'turned' figure of the பேடி. The legend (Kama, Vishnu's son, dancing in Bana's city) is the one the Silappathikaram gives among Madhavi's eleven dances, so Madhavi's art is here a street show the renunciant daughter passes by.
event: A street performer dances Kama's eunuch dance before a watching crowd.
unit_note: New unit 116-125, cut from 3:110-125 at the start of the eunuch-dance item (116).

tamil: விழவு ஆற்றுப் படுத்த கழி பெரு வீதியில்
பொன் நாண் கோத்த நன் மணிக் கோவை
மயிர்ப் புறம் சுற்றிய கயிற்கடை முக் காழ்
பொலம் பிறைச் சென்னி நலம் பெறத் தாழ
செவ் வாய்க் குதலை மெய் பெறா மழலை
அற்றம் காவாச் சுற்று உடைப் பூந் துகில்
தளர் நடை தாங்காக் கிளர் பூண் புதல்வரை
பொலந் தேர் மீமிசைப் புகர் முக வேழத்து
இலங்கு தொடி நல்லார் சிலர் நின்று ஏற்றி
reading: In the old city loud with strangers, others stand before the paintings that skilled painters made on the white plaster of every tall brick house, likenesses of every kind of being from the spotless gods down; and in the great festival street, women lift little boys, babbling and drooling on their five-weapon amulets, decked in gold chains, beads and loose silk, onto an elephant on a golden car, saying 'see the opening of the festival of the son of the one under the banyan', and stand watching.
nuance: The festival for Indra also holds a procession for the son of Siva (ஆல் அமர் செல்வன் மகன், 144), as the first kaathai bade every god be worshipped. The infants, unable to hold their walk or their speech, stand against the girl in robes who passes them.
event: Women set their small boys on an elephant to watch the start of Murugan's festival while others gaze at the painted houses.

tamil: விராடன் பேர் ஊர் விசயன் ஆம் பேடியைக்
தாயோ கொடியள் தகவு இலள் ஈங்கு இவள்
மா மலர் கொய்ய மலர்வனம் தான் புகின்
நல் இள அன்னம் நாணாது ஆங்கு உள
மா மயில் ஆங்கு உள வந்து முன் நிற்பன
பைங் கிளி தாம் உள பாவை தன் கிளவிக்கு
reading: Like the noisy crowd that gathered round Vijaya in his eunuch's guise in Virata's city, all these people gather round Manimekalai and say that the mother who put one so lovely into hard tapas is cruel and without decency, and ask whether, if she enters the grove, the swans there could match her walk, the peacocks learn her grace or the parrots equal her speech, and say it is not fitting.
nuance: The crowd's simile casts Manimekalai as Arjuna in disguise, a figure whose true nature is hidden under an assumed form, and so, unintended by the speakers, sees the robe as a costume. Their blame of Madhavi repeats on the street what Chithirapathi sent to her as the town's talk in the last kaathai.
event: The festival crowd surrounds Manimekalai and blames her mother for putting her to tapas.
unit_note: Lower boundary moved from 155 to 157: the crowd's speech runs to line 157 (இசையுந அல்ல').

tamil: என்று இவை சொல்லி யாவரும் இனைந்து உக
செந் தளிர்ச் சேவடி நிலம் வடு உறாமல்
எரி மலர் இலவமும் விரி மலர் பரப்பி
reading: As all who said these things grieve, the grove appears as if covered by a painted cloth that skilled hands had made, its kuravam, maravam, kurunthu, konrai, tilakam, vakulam, vetchi, narantham, nagam, punnai, pidavam, thalavam, thazhai, kudasam, bamboo, asoka, serunthi, vengai, sanbakam and ilavam spreading their flowers so that her soft feet should not be marked by the ground; bowing to the Uvavanam that Sudhamathi has shown her, Manimekalai enters it with her to gather flowers.
nuance: The list of flowers of every land is a carpet laid for her feet, so the grove receives her as the street did not. She bows (தொழுதனள், 170) before entering: the grove is a shrine, as 3:52-68 said.
event: Manimekalai bows to the Uvavanam and enters it with Sudhamathi to gather flowers.
unit_note: Upper boundary moved from 156 to 158 to follow the change in 3:146-157.

title: பளிக்கறை புக்ககாதை
theme: In the grove Manimekalai's companion Sudhamathi shows her its beauties; Udayakumaran, fresh from taming his maddened elephant, hears from a musician that she is there and comes for her; Sudhamathi locks her in the crystal pavilion and answers the prince's questions with a sermon on the body born of deeds, which the sight of the girl through the crystal outruns.
source_issues: Line 97: a closing quotation mark stands after முலை in the middle of the prince's speech, which runs on to உரை? என at 104, where no closing mark appears.
Line 1 opens with a quotation mark for Sudhamathi's speech carried over from the previous kaathai, with no speaker named until line 25.
Line 125 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, newly turned from the courtesan's life
Manimekalai's companion in the grove
the Chola king's son, who desires Manimekalai
a merchant's son of Puhar, a yal player in the dancers' street
the prince's elephant, maddened by musth

tamil: வெயில் நுழைபு அறியா குயில் நுழை பொதும்பர்
மயில் ஆடு அரங்கில் மந்தி காண்பன காண்!
மாசு அறத் தெளிந்த மணி நீர் இலஞ்சி
பாசடைப் பரப்பில் பல் மலர் இடை நின்று
ஒரு தனி ஓங்கிய விரை மலர்த் தாமரை
கரை நின்று ஆலும் ஒரு மயில் தனக்கு

கோடு உடை தாழைக் கொழு மடல் அவிழ்ந்த
வால் வெண் சுண்ணம் ஆடியது இது காண்!
reading: Sudhamathi points out the grove to Manimekalai as a stage: bees and beetles make music while a monkey watches a peacock dance, a royal swan sits on a lone lotus in a clear pool while a waterhen drums and a koel calls to another peacock, and a screw-pine's white pollen dusts a lotus as street dust dims the girl's own face.
nuance: The grove is described as a theatre (அரங்கு, முழவு, யாழ்), which keeps the courtesan's art in view at the moment Manimekalai has turned from it; the comparison at 15 (a lotus dulled by the dust of chariot streets like your face) quietly notes the grief that has worn her beauty, which Ettikumaran will also see.

tamil: மாதர் நின் கண் போது எனச் சேர்ந்து
தாது உண் வண்டு இனம் மீது கடி செங் கையின்
செங் கயல் பாய்ந்து பிறழ்வன கண்டு ஆங்கு
எறிந்து அது பெறா அது இரை இழந்து வருந்தி
மறிந்து நீங்கும் மணிச் சிரல் காண்!' எனப்
reading: Sudhamathi ends her tour with bees that mistake the girl's eyes for flowers and a kingfisher that dives at carp in a lotus pool and comes up hungry, and Manimekalai looks over the flowering garden.
nuance: The kingfisher that strikes and loses its prey (23 to 24) is set just before the prince enters the story; whether it is meant as a sign of his failed pursuit is a reading, not something the lines say.
event: Sudhamathi shows Manimekalai the grove and the pool, and Manimekalai looks at the garden.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 26: Sudhamathi's showing of the grove closes with காண்பழி at 26; lines 27 to 34 open the long sentence of the prince's elephant, which the core unit split from its main verb.

tamil: கூம்பு முதல் முறிய வீங்கு பிணி அவிழ்ந்து
கயிறு கால் பரிய வயிறு பாழ்பட்டு ஆங்கு
இதை சிதைந்து ஆர்ப்ப திரை பொரு முந்நீர்
இரு பால் பெயரிய ஒரு கெழு மூதூர்
ஒரு பால் படாஅது ஒரு வழித் தங்காது
விடு பரிக் குதிரையின் விரைந்து சென்று எய்தி
reading: The mount of the king's son Udayakumaran, the elephant Kalavegam, goes mad with musth, breaks free of its keepers like a storm-tossed ship that has lost mast and ropes, runs through the cowherds' street, the chariot street and the market and throws all Puhar into uproar, until the prince rides it down on a swift horse and quells its frenzy.
nuance: The syntax of 28 to 29 (உதயகுமரன் உரு கெழு மீது ஊர் மீயான்) is read here as the rider of the prince's own fearsome mount, so the elephant is his; the simile of the wrecked ship runs eight lines and the main verb comes only at 46. The deed echoes Kovalan's taming of a rogue elephant in the Silappathikaram.
event: The prince's elephant Kalavegam breaks loose in musth and rampages through Puhar; Udayakumaran overtakes it on horseback and subdues it.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 26 at the start and from 59 to 46 at the end: the elephant's rampage begins at 27 and its subduing ends with அடக்கி at 46, before the prince's chariot arrival at 47.

tamil: அணித் தேர்த் தானையொடு அரசு இளங் குமரன்
சாளரம் பொளித்த கால் போகு பெரு வழி
வீதி மருங்கு இயன்ற பூ அணைப் பள்ளி
reading: Holding the rail of his jewelled chariot, wearing the aar garland that alone shows he is not Murugan, the prince drives into the dancers' street and finds the merchant's son Ettikumaran lying with a woman on a flower bed by a window, his yal in his arms, still as a painted figure, and asks what trouble has struck him.
nuance: The ஆர் (aar) garland is the Chola emblem; the line makes the prince's beauty godlike and his lineage the only mark that tells him from the god. Ettikumaran's stillness is the courtesan quarter's music stopped.
event: Udayakumaran drives into the dancers' street and asks Ettikumaran, who sits frozen beside a woman with his yal, what has troubled him.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 35 to 47 at the start and from 59 to 60 at the end: the prince's question begun at 59 closes with என்றலும் at 60.

ஆங்கு அவன் தேர் ஒலி போலும் ஆய் இழை!
ஈங்கு என் செவிமுதல் இசைத்தது என் செய்கு?' என
reading: Ettikumaran bows and says that seeing Manimekalai, Madhavi's daughter, entering the grove with her beauty faded like a flower kept in a casket, brought back the cruel grief of Kovalan, so that his hand slipped onto a jarring string; glad at the news, the prince says he will bring her back in his chariot and drives to the grove gate, and Manimekalai, hearing the chariot, recalls Vasanthamaalai telling Madhavi that Udayakumaran, through Chithirapathi, had set his heart on her, and asks what she should do.
nuance: Three voices meet here: Ettikumaran (65 to 71), the prince (73 to 74) and Manimekalai (79 to 84). The same sight moves the musician to grief for Kovalan and the prince to gladness; the merchant reads her faded beauty as mourning, the prince as a chance. Line 61 (வீங்கு இள முலையொடு) is read as Ettikumaran rising with the woman beside him; 69 to 70 (நீர்மையை நீக்கி வெம் பகை நரம்பின்) as grief driving the music out of his hand, and neither is sure.
event: Ettikumaran tells the prince that the sight of Manimekalai in the grove, recalling Kovalan's fate, threw his playing off; the prince drives to the grove to carry her off, and Manimekalai, hearing his chariot, asks Sudhamathi what to do.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 60 to 61 at the start and from 83 to 84 at the end: Manimekalai's speech begun at 79 closes with என் செய்கு?' என at 84.

tamil: அமுது உறு தீம் சொல் ஆய் இழை உரைத்தலும்
ஒளித்து அறை தாழ் கோத்து உள்ளகத்து இரீஇ
ஆங்கு அது தனக்கு ஓர் ஐ விலின் கிடக்கை
பல் மலர்ப் பூம்பொழில் பகல் முளைத்தது போல்
அரசு இளங் குமரன் 'ஆரும் இல் ஒரு சிறை
ஒரு தனி நின்றாய்! உன் திறம் அறிந்தேன்
வளர் இள வன முலை' மடந்தை மெல் இயல்
செங் கயல் நெடுங் கண் செவி மருங்கு ஓடி
வெங் கணை நெடு வேள் வியப்பு உரைக்கும்கொல்?
தானே தமியள் இங்கு எய்தியது உரை? எனப்
reading: Trembling like a peacock, Sudhamathi bids Manimekalai enter the crystal pavilion, bolts it with her inside and stands five bow-lengths off; the prince halts his chariot, sweeps the grove with his eyes and, finding her alone, asks whether the girl has grown to know her slender waist, whether her lisping speech has ripened and her teeth come in like pearls, whether her long eyes now speak of Kama, and why she has left the ascetics' dwelling to come here alone.
nuance: The prince's questions are a catalogue of a girl's coming of age in the stock images of love poetry, asked of a girl who has taken to the ascetics; his last question names exactly the change he does not accept (மாதவர் உறைவிடம் ஒரீஇ). Lines 89 to 90 (ஐ விலின் கிடக்கை) are read as Sudhamathi standing five bow-lengths from the pavilion, and 96 (உன் திறம் அறிந்தேன்) as the prince saying he knows who she is; both are doubtful.
event: Sudhamathi locks Manimekalai inside the crystal pavilion; the prince arrives and questions Sudhamathi about the girl's ripening and why she is there.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 84 to 85 at the start and from 98 to 104 at the end: the prince's questions run from 95 to உரை? என at 104, across the core break at 98.

tamil: பொதி அறைப் பட்டோர் போன்று உளம் வருந்தி
வினை விளங்கு தடக் கை விறலோய்! கேட்டி
மூப்பு விளிவு உடையது தீப் பிணி இருக்கை
என்று அவள் உரைத்த இசை படு தீம் சொல்
reading: Distressed as one shut in a closed room, Sudhamathi asks whether women must teach knowledge, worth and royal custom to the heir of the strong one who, ashamed of his youth, put on old age to give a verdict, and then tells him one thing: this human body is born of deeds and is the field where deeds ripen, flesh to be cast out once its finery is gone, bound to age and die, a seat of disease, a hold for attachment, a vessel of faults, a bed of anger like a snake in its anthill, holding sorrow, care, helplessness, lament and a restless mind; knowing it so, he should turn from it; but before her words reach his heart, the girl appears before him through the crystal like a coral doll.
nuance: The sermon is answered at once by the story: before it can reach him (123), the hiding place shows her body through the crystal, the very body she has just called flesh. Her opening is a modesty formula that is also a rebuke: the Chola who judged in youth (108) was wise without being told. The run of sorrows at 118 (அவலம் கவலை கையாறு அழுங்கல்) reads like the Buddhist list of griefs, but the unit names no school, so its claims are tagged general.
event: Sudhamathi tells the prince that the body is a karma-born thing of flesh, sickness and faults and urges him to turn from it; before her words take hold, Manimekalai's form shows through the crystal wall.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 99 to 105 at the start; the unit keeps Sudhamathi's whole answer (107 to 121) with the narration that frames it.

title: மணிமேகலா தெய்வம் வந்து தோன்றிய காதை
theme: Through the crystal the prince sees Manimekalai, brushes off Sudhamathi's warning of the girl's fated austerity, and hears Sudhamathi's story of how Jain monks turned away her gored Brahmin father and a Buddhist monk carried him to safety; he leaves trusting Chithirapathi to deliver the girl, Manimekalai confesses her heart has followed him and curses desire, and the goddess Manimekala arrives to praise the Buddha's seat as evening falls on Puhar.
source_issues: Line 13 puts quotation marks around the epithet குருகு பெயர்க் குன்றம் கொன்றோன் inside Sudhamathi's speech, as if it were a separate quotation; it reads as an epithet for Murugan in her own sentence.
Lines 86 to 87 are quoted as the prince's words, but he says nothing of the kind in this kaathai or the last; the quotation marks frame Manimekalai's reading of his scorn.
Line 141 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, as in kaathai 4.

tamil: விரை மலர் ஐங் கணை மீன விலோதனத்து
தாழ் ஒளி மண்டபம் தன் கையின் தடைஇச்
எத் திறத்தாள் நின் இளங்கொடி? உரை' என
reading: Through the crystal screen the prince sees the girl as if a painted image of Lakshmi stood there to stir Kama, wonders at what the painter must have imagined, then grasps that it is the dark-eyed girl herself, feels along the pavilion with his hand, and asks Sudhamathi what sort of girl hers is; she replies that even if the girl will not drink in his Murugan-like beauty with her eyes, she is one whose austerity comes by fate, whose curse is an arrow, and whose truthfulness has passed beyond Kama.
nuance: Lines 1 to 8 are dense: the prince first takes the figure behind the crystal for a painting, and only at 8 does he see a living girl, which keeps the crystal room's double nature (it hides and shows) in play. Sudhamathi's three epithets at 16 to 17 claim for Manimekalai an ascetic's powers she has only just begun to seek: the austerity is called ஊழ் தரு, given by fate, so destiny and not yet her own practice is named as its source.
event: Udayakumaran sees Manimekalai through the crystal, tries the pavilion with his hand and asks Sudhamathi about her; Sudhamathi warns that the girl's austerity can curse.

tamil: செவ்வியள் ஆயின் என்? செவ்வியள் ஆக!' என
ஆங்கு அவர் உறைவிடம் நீங்கி ஆய் இழை!
ஈங்கு இவள் தன்னோடு எய்தியது உரை' என
தீ நெறிப் படரா நெஞ்சினை ஆகு மதி!
reading: The prince retorts that no dam holds a swollen flood and no restraint holds once desire takes root, so let her be as ripe as she likes, and, turning away with a twisted heart, asks Sudhamathi, whom the city says a vidyadhara carried off, why she left her people's place to come here with this girl; she blesses him, prays that his heart not take the evil path, and begs the ruler of the sea-girt earth to hear her reason.
nuance: The prince's maxim at 19 to 20 makes desire an irresistible force and so excuses in advance whatever he does; Sudhamathi's answer at 29 treats his heart as still able to choose. The word அராந்தாணம் at 23, the place where the vidyadhara left her, is rare and its sense here is not fixed.
event: Udayakumaran brushes off Sudhamathi's warning and asks how she came to be with Manimekalai; Sudhamathi begins her account.

tamil: யாப்பு உடை உள்ளத்து எம் அனை இழந்தோன்
பழ வினைப் பயத்தான் பிழை மணம் எய்திய
குரங்கு செய் கடல் குமரி அம் பெருந் துறைப்
கடல் மண்டு பெருந் துறைக் காவிரி ஆடிய
reading: Sudhamathi tells that her father, an old Brahmin of firm mind who had lost her mother, kept the ritual food rules and tended the fire that brings rain, grieved when through the fruit of old deeds she fell into a wrong union, searched for her among the crowds at the Kumari bathing ghat, and on his way back, coming with Sanskrit-speakers who had bathed in the Kaveri, found her here and asked how she had come.
nuance: Sudhamathi gives her abduction two causes in one line (35): the fruit of former deeds and the wrong union itself, without blaming the vidyadhara. Her father's fire is credited with bringing rain (34), a claim the story then sets beside his ruin.
event: Sudhamathi tells how her Brahmin father searched for her after her abduction and found her in Puhar.

tamil: தாங்காக் கண்ணீர் என் தலை உதிர்த்து ஆங்கு
இரந்து ஊண் தலைக்கொண்டு இந் நகர் மருங்கில்
பரந்து படு மனைதொறும் திரிவோன் ஒரு நாள்
நிணம் நீடு பெருங் குடர் கை அகத்து ஏந்தி
மை அறு படிவத்து மாதவர் புறத்து எமைக்
கதிர் சுடும் அமயத்துப் பனி மதி முகத்தோன்
தன் கைப் பாத்திரம் என் கைத் தந்து ஆங்கு
reading: Weeping over her, her father would not abandon her though she was no longer fit for the learned Brahmins, and lived by begging from house to house in the city, until one day a cow with a new calf gored him; holding his gut in his hands like a red garland he staggered into the place where she lived and begged the Jain monks for refuge, but they, angry with her too, said he was not one of them and drove them out, and as the two cried in the street whether any righteous people were left, a monk with a bowl in his palm and a golden robe, his face like a cool moon at noon, asked what had befallen them, cooled their hearts with kind words and put his bowl into her hand.
nuance: The scene runs through three refusals and one answer: her father's own Brahmins (43), the Jain ascetics of spotless form (54), and then the street, where the cry அறவோர் உளீரோ (56) is answered by a monk of a third order. The Jains reject the dying man as not of their faith, so the episode sets the Buddhist's compassion against a refuge limited to one's own; that is the Buddhist work's framing, not a Jain account.
event: Gored by a cow, Sudhamathi's father seeks refuge with the Jain monks, who turn him and his daughter away; a Buddhist monk with a begging bowl stops to help them.

tamil: சா துயர் நீங்கிய தலைவன் தவ முனி
எம் கோன் இயல் குணன் ஏதம் இல் குணப் பொருள்
மிகை நா இல்லேன் வேந்தே வாழ்க!' என
'அம் சொல் ஆய் இழை! இன் திறம் அறிந்தேன்
அப் பொழில் ஆங்கு அவன் அயர்ந்து போய பின்
"கற்புத் தான் இலள் நல் தவ உணர்வு இலள்
வருணக் காப்பு இலள் பொருள் விலையாட்டி" என்று
reading: Sudhamathi finishes: the monk lifted her father onto his head, carried him to the dwelling of the ascetics, and this Sangadharuman, who freed him from the grief of death, taught them the nature of their lord, who lives not for himself but for others, turned the wheel of dharma out of compassion so that all beings might reach bliss, and passed beyond Kama, and she has no tongue for anything but his feet; the prince says he knows her case now and that Manimekalai may yet come to him through Chithirapathi, and leaves; Manimekalai opens the crystal room and confesses that though he scorned her as a woman without chastity, without austerity, without caste protection, one who sells herself, her heart went after the stranger, and asks whether this is the nature of desire.
nuance: The monk is called மறையோன் at 68, a word for one who knows the sacred lore, and is then named Sangadharuman; the lines read most simply as one person, but whether the bowl-bearer and the teacher are the same is not certain. The words Manimekalai puts in the prince's mouth at 86 to 87 are not spoken by him in this kaathai or the last; she reads his scorn from his manner. Her question is the first crack in her renunciation, and she answers it herself at 91.
event: Sudhamathi ends her story of the monk Sangadharuman; Udayakumaran leaves vowing to win Manimekalai through Chithirapathi; Manimekalai comes out and admits her heart has followed him.

tamil: மணி அறைப் பீடிகை வலம் கொண்டு ஓங்கி
தீ நெறிக் கடும் பகை கடிந்தோய் என்கோ!
ஆயிர ஆரத்து ஆழி அம் திருந்து அடி
நா ஆயிரம் இலேன் ஏத்துவது எவன்?' என்று
reading: Manimekalai cries that if this is desire, let its power perish; as she stands with Sudhamathi, the goddess Manimekala, who comes to see the adorned festival of Indra, takes the form of a woman of the city, circles the jewelled seat and praises the Buddha as the wise one, the ford-maker, the meritorious, the ancient, highest in vows for the world, who destroyed fault and curbed hatred, the first who knew fully, who passed beyond Kama, who is refuge and who drove off the fierce enemy of the evil path, ending that she lacks a thousand tongues to praise his wheel-marked feet.
nuance: The goddess's first epithets answer Manimekalai's curse on desire: காமற் கடந்தோய் (102) is the epithet Sudhamathi gave the girl at 17 and the Buddha at 77, so the one quality the girl has just failed to hold is the one the praise returns to. The jewelled seat (பீடிகை) is the Buddha's seat in the grove, worshipped in his absence.
event: Manimekalai curses the power of desire; the goddess Manimekala, disguised as a city woman, circles the Buddha's seat in the grove and praises him.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 103 to 105: the goddess's praise of the Buddha begun at 98 closes with என்று at 105; the core unit cut it after the second of three என்கோ clauses.

பல் மலர் சிறந்த நல் நீர் அகழிப்
புள் ஒலி சிறந்த தெள் அரிச் சிலம்பு அடி
வாயில் மருங்கு இயன்ற வான் பணைத் தோளி
எதிர் எதிர் ஓங்கிய கதிர் இள வன முலை
ஆர் புனை வேந்தற்குப் பேர் அளவு இயற்றி

வெள்ளி வெண் தோட்டொடு பொன் தோடு ஆக
reading: The narrator turns to evening on Puhar, pictured as a flowering creeper of a woman: its moat her girdle and anklets, its walls and gates her jewelled belt and arms, its two tall temple towers her breasts, its great temple her face, and the rising full moon in the east and the setting sun in the west her silver and gold earrings.
nuance: The figure maps the city part by part onto a woman's body and ornaments, and one of the ornaments is named மேகலை (112), the girl's own name; several mappings (108 to 109, 114 to 116) are compressed and their exact correspondences are a reading.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 104 to 106 at the start and from 119 to 122 at the end: the praise ends at 105, and the figure of Puhar as a woman adorned with moon and sun for earrings closes with பெய்தலும் at 122.

tamil: பூம் பொதி சிதையக் கிழித்துப் பெடை கொண்டு
ஓங்கு இருந் தெங்கின் உயர் மடல் ஏற
முலை பொழி தீம் பால் எழு துகள் அவிப்ப
கன்று நினை குரல மன்று வழிப் படர
பைந் தொடி மகளிர் பலர் விளக்கு எடுப்ப
தமர் அகம் புகூஉம் ஒரு மகள் போல
வந்து இறுத்தனளால் மா நகர் மருங்கு என்
reading: Evening's signs follow: a swan tears open a lotus that has shut on its mate and carries her to a coconut frond, the anril hen calls her mate at sunset, cows that grazed on lilies return lowing for their calves with milk dripping, Brahmins tend the evening fire, women bring lamps, lute players strum the marutham mode and cowherds take up the mullai flute, and evening comes to the great city with pale skin and grief like a woman who has lost her husband in battle going back to her kin's house.
nuance: The closing simile (137 to 140) makes evening a war widow returning to her own people, a figure of loss that falls on the day Manimekalai has confessed her heart's going after the prince; the swan that frees its mate from the closed lotus (123 to 126) may glance at the girl shut in the crystal, but the lines do not say so.
event: Evening falls on Puhar.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 120 to 123: the unit now begins with the evening's events after the earrings of moon and sun are set at 122.

title: சக்கரவாளக் கோட்டம் உரைத்த காதை
theme: Manimekala, disguised as a townswoman, sends Sudhamathi and Manimekalai into the Chakravala Kottam beside Puhar's burning ground and explains its name: she describes the cemetery that teaches death spares no one, and tells how the Brahmin boy Sarngalan died of fright there, how the goddess Champapathi told his mother Gotami that his own deed and not a demon took him, refused her life in exchange, and had every god of the cosmos confirm that none can give back a life; on that spot Maya modelled the whole world-system. Then the goddess carries the sleeping girl to Manipallavam.
source_issues: Line 71: a leftover HTML quote mark at the start of the line was removed by the build (show's repair flag).

Lines 34 to 36: the goddess's answer opens with a quotation mark placed mid-line before இந், after நேர் இழை கூறும், and her speech, which contains the quoted speeches of Gotami and Champapathi, closes only at line 205 (இதன் வரவு இது'); the nested quotations at 128 to 130 and 132 to 138 use double marks inside it.
Line 214 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
Line 172: ஊழி முதல்வன், whose giving of life Champapathi excepts, is not identified in the unit; the sense of lines 172 to 174 is uncertain.

வெள்ளி வெண் குடத்துப் பால் சொரிவது போல்
கள் அவிழ் பூம் பொழில் இடைஇடைச் சொரிய
reading: After the evening has passed the moon rises, its spot showing in the clear sky as a fault shows plainly in the worthy, pouring light over the grove like milk from a silver pot; the goddess Manimekala, a body bright as lightning given form, bows and praises the seat of the first lord who turns the wheel of dharma, takes the shape of a woman of the town and asks Sudhamathi why they are standing there.
nuance: The simile at lines 3 to 5 runs the Kural's comparison backwards: the couplet compares the fault of the high-born to the moon's spot, and here the moon's spot is compared to the fault of the worthy, as if the moral were the better-known term. The lord of the wheel of dharma whose foot-seat she worships (11 to 12) is the Buddha by the epic's usage; the unit does not name him.
event: Manimekala comes to the grove at moonrise, worships at the Buddha's seat and, disguised as a townswoman, asks Sudhamathi why she stands there.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவள் ஆங்கு அவன் கூறியது உரைத்தலும்
'அரசு இளங் குமரன் ஆய் இழை தன் மேல்
பெருந் தெரு ஒழித்து இப்பெரு வனம் சூழ்ந்த
திருந்து எயில் குடபால் சிறு புழை போகி
அங்கு நீர் போம்' என்று அருந் தெய்வம் உரைப்ப
reading: When Sudhamathi tells what the prince said, the goddess warns that he has not given up his gaze on the girl and, though he left calling the grove the ascetics' wood, will keep haunting the outer streets, so they should leave by the small western gate into the Chakravala Kottam, where great ascetics live, and come to no harm though the night passes; Sudhamathi answers that apart from the trickster vidyadhara Maruthavegan and the goddess herself everyone in the city calls the place only the cremation-ground shrine, and asks why she gives it another name.
nuance: The goddess judges that Sudhamathi's sermon in the previous kaathai has not worked: the prince's look is unabated (தணியா நோக்கம்), and the answer now is refuge in place rather than argument. Sudhamathi's question sets up the whole kaathai as an explanation of a name: what the city calls the burning ground's shrine, the goddess calls by the name of the cosmos.
event: The goddess tells Sudhamathi to take Manimekalai by the west gate into the Chakravala Kottam; Sudhamathi asks why it bears that name when the city calls it the burning-ground shrine.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 31|32 to 33|34: Sudhamathi's question begun at line 27 runs to ஈங்கு இதன் காரணம் என்னையோ? என at line 33; line 34 (ஆங்கு அதன் காரணம் அறியக் கூறுவன்) begins the goddess's answer.

tamil: நீ கேள்' என்றே நேர் இழை கூறும் 'இந்
reading: The goddess says she will tell the reason, even if deep night comes upon Madhavi's daughter, and begins: beside this place lies the cremation ground that arose with the famous city itself, with four gates, one painted with a chariot that is never driven where the gods enter, one painted with paddy, cane, water and groves, one of plain white plaster with no figure inside, and one where a tall clay figure stands with folded red lips, fierce eyes, noose and trident.
nuance: The cemetery is as old as the city (37 to 38): the city of festivals in the earlier kaathais and the place of the dead are founded together. The fourth gate's figure with noose and trident reads as Death's guardian, though the unit does not name him.
event: The goddess begins to explain the shrine's name by describing the four gates of the old cremation ground beside it.
unit_note: Starts at line 34 after the boundary moved from 31|32 to 33|34 (see manimekalai:6:16-33); the end at 47 is unchanged.

tamil: காப்பு உடை இஞ்சிக் கடி வழங்கு ஆர் இடை
தலை தூங்கு நெடு மரம் தாழ்ந்து புறம் சுற்றி
காடு அமர் செல்வி கழி பெருங் கோட்டமும்
நால் வேறு வருணப் பால் வேறு காட்டி
அருந் திறல் கடவுள் திருந்து பலிக் கந்தமும்
நிறைக் கல் தெற்றியும் மிறைக் களச் சந்தியும்
reading: Within the guarded wall stand the great shrine of the goddess who dwells in the forest, where the heads of those who with unwavering heart paid life's debt hang from a tall tree; tall shrines of burnt brick, short and high like hills, raised by the eminent for the dead, whether ascetics, kings or women who died together with their husbands, kept apart by the four varnas; altars of offering to fierce gods, stone platforms, and the huts where guards with staff and skull-bowl eat and sleep.
nuance: The cemetery keeps distinctions the dead no longer have: memorials are sorted by varna (56), and ascetics, kings and women who died with their husbands each get their own. The heads hung at the forest goddess's shrine (50 to 51) are of those who offered their own lives; the goddess describes them without comment here, but her account later (164 to 166) bears on what such offerings achieve. Taking உயிர்க் கடன் இறுத்தோர் (50) as those who offered their own heads is the plain sense, not a certain one.

tamil: நீள் முக நரியின் தீ விளிக் கூவும்
reading: Smoke-flags, flaming arches and funeral pandals are everywhere; those who burn, who lay out, who put in dug pits, who shut in vaults and who cover with urns come and go night and day without pause; the dirge drum that shakes the heart, the cry of worship when an ascetic dies and the wailing when others die, the jackal's howl, the owl that calls the dying, and the cries of the flesh-eating kural and the horned owl fill it.
nuance: Lines 66 and 67 list five ways of disposing of the dead side by side, burning, exposure, pit burial, vault and urn, with no one way set above another. Lines 72 and 73 set the ascetic's death, greeted with worship, against the ordinary death, greeted with weeping: the only difference the cemetery records between the renouncer and the rest.

வெண் நிணம் தடியொடு மாந்தி மகிழ் சிறந்து
விரத யாக்கையர் உடை தலை தொகுத்து ஆங்கு

அழல் பெய் குழிசியும் புழல் பெய் மண்டையும்
reading: An unpleasant noise like the roar of the sea never ceases there; thanri, oduvai and ulinjil trees rise and thorn and cactus crowd, bands of starving demons gather, and there are the halls under the vaagai, the vilam where birds feast on fat, the vanni where the cremation-ground vow-keepers light fires with steady hearts, the iratthi where those vowed in body gather skulls, and the open hall where corpse-eaters feast from pots of fat, with fire pots, skull-bowls, bier poles and shrouds lying about.
nuance: The ascetics of the burning ground, the சுடலை நோன்பிகள் and விரத யாக்கையர், are listed among the cemetery's sights beside the corpse-eaters, not apart from them; the Buddhist goddess describes them without praise.

tamil: தவத் துறை மாக்கள் மிகப் பெருஞ் செல்வர்
reading: Over the wide field lie torn garlands, broken pots, paddy, puffed rice and grains of offering; and the goddess asks whether, seeing the cruel worker Death kill and heap up ascetics, the very rich, young mothers just delivered, helpless infants, old and young without distinction, for this fiery burning ground to eat, there can be greater fools than people who revel in wealth and drink and live without desiring dharma.
nuance: The list of the dead (97 to 99) puts the ascetic first and the infant beside the rich man: tapas, wealth and youth buy no exemption. The conclusion is aram, not fame or giving; the next unit tells of one who saw the same sights and died of them.

அலத்தகம் ஊட்டிய அடி நரி வாய்க் கொண்டு
கலைப் புற அல்குல் கழுகு குடைந்து உண்டு
சாந்தம் தோய்ந்த ஏந்து இள வன முலை
காய்ந்த பசி எருவை கவர்ந்து ஊண் ஓதையும்
மண் கணை முழவம் ஆக ஆங்கு ஓர்
கருந் தலை வாங்கி கை அகத்து ஏந்தி
இரும் பேர் உவகையின் எழுந்து ஓர் பேய் மகள்
கண் தொட்டு உண்டு கவை அடி பெயர்த்து
வெம் முது பேய்க்கு என் உயிர் கொடுத்தேன்" என
தம் அனை தன் முன் வீழ்ந்து மெய் வைத்தலும்
reading: A Brahmin youth named Sarngalan, going alone and taking the place for a guarded city, comes among sights that proclaim to the attached that the body is bone, flesh and blood: a jackal howling with a lac-dyed foot torn from a worm-ridden lump, a vulture tearing the girdled hips, a dog crunching a braceleted hand, a starving vulture eating sandal-smeared breasts, and a demon woman who lifts a dark head on the ash-white stage, scoops out and eats its eyes without stopping to ask whether hair or cloud, eye or carp, lip or flower, tooth or pearl, and dances; terrified, he flees crying to his mother that he has given his life to the old demon of the burning ground, falls before her and lays down his body.
nuance: The demon woman's 'cloud or hair? carp or eye?' (122 to 124) is the lover's comparison of love poetry taken apart limb by limb: what the poems doubt between, she eats without asking. The parts eaten are the parts a lover praises: dyed foot, girdled hips, braceleted hand, sandal-smeared breast. Who 'proclaims' at 107 to 108 is not plain; the sights are read here as the subject. The boy sees exactly what is meant to teach detachment and dies of fear.
event: Sarngalan wanders into the burning ground at night, sees a demon woman eating a corpse's eyes and dancing, runs home in terror, and dies before his mother.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 122|123 to 131|132, merging the old units 105-122 and 123-135 up to line 131: the demon woman's dance begun at 118 runs into line 126, and Sarngalan's flight and death close at 131 (மெய் வைத்தலும்); line 132 begins his mother's lament.

tamil: மகன் மெய் யாக்கையை மார்பு உறத் தழீஇ
இடை இருள் யாமத்து என்னை ஈங்கு அழைத்தனை
ஊழ்வினை வந்து இவன் உயிர் உண்டு கழிந்தது
மா பெருந் துன்பம் நீ ஒழிவாய்" என்றலும்
reading: His mother Gotami, a woman who lives with a blind Brahmin and has no one else, clasps her son's body at the burning ground's outer gate and cries to Champapathi, guardian of the ghats, halls, old trees, dwellings and shrines, asking whether a demon or a spirit has eaten his life and whether she has no justice; the golden goddess appears asking why she is called at midnight, hears that the helpless boy lies as if asleep, and answers that neither spirits nor demons eat lives: with the Brahmin boy's terror as its occasion, his own former deed came, ate his life and went, so she should give up her grief.
nuance: Champapathi denies that a spirit or demon kills and gives the deed (ஊழ்வினை) as the cause, with fright only as its occasion (பேது கந்தாக, 151): the cemetery's demon, so vivid in the previous unit, is reduced to an occasion. Gotami's word for herself, தீத்தொழிலாட்டியேன் (133), blames her own past deeds before the goddess does.
event: Gotami carries her dead son to the burning-ground gate and calls on Champapathi, who appears and tells her that his former deed, not a demon, took his life.
unit_note: Starts at line 132 after the boundary moved from 122|123 to 131|132 (see manimekalai:6:105-131); ends at line 153, where Champapathi's first answer closes (என்றலும்), instead of 159; lines 154 to 159 begin Gotami's offer and the goddess's reply, which runs to 167.

tamil: "என் உயிர் கொண்டு இவன் உயிர் தந்தருளில் என்
கண் இல் கணவனை இவன் காத்து ஓம்பிடும்
இவன் உயிர் தந்து என் உயிர் வாங்கு என்றலும்
ஆங்கு அது கொணர்ந்து நின் ஆர் இடர் நீக்குதல்
ஈங்கு எனக்கு ஆவது ஒன்று அன்று நீ இரங்கல்
அவலப் படிற்று உரை ஆங்கு அது மடவாய்
நிரயக் கொடு மொழி நீ ஒழிக" என்றலும்
reading: Gotami begs the goddess to take her life and give back his, so that he may look after her blind husband; the old goddess, pitying her, answers that once a life has gone it surely goes by its deeds into another birth, that bringing it back is not in her power, that the offer is like the false and wretched saying of those whose trade holds that killing is dharma, and asks whether there have not been those who gave their lives for the world's kings, and yet in this burning ground stand a thousand shrines for kings; she bids her leave such hell-bound words.
nuance: Champapathi counts a mother's offer of her own life in exchange as killing, and so as the same error as the claim that killing is dharma (162 to 163); 'those whose trade' it is are not named, and the unit does not say whether sacrificers or others are meant. Lines 164 to 166 answer the offer from the cemetery itself: lives given for kings did not keep the kings alive. Reading 164 as 'give their lives in place of the kings' lives' is the plainer sense but not certain.
event: Gotami offers her life for her son's; Champapathi refuses, saying a departed life goes on by its deeds and that a life given for another saves no one.
unit_note: Starts at line 154 after the boundary moved from 159|160 to 153|154 and ends at 167 (என்றலும்), where Champapathi's reply closes, instead of 175; line 168 begins Gotami's appeal to the Brahmins' books.

tamil: யானோ காவேன் என் உயிர் ஈங்கு" என
பல் வகை அசுரரும் படு துயர் உறூஉம்
எண் வகை நரகரும் இரு விசும்பு இயங்கும்
வரம் தரற்கு உரியோர் தமை முன் நிறுத்தி
"அரந்தை கெடும் இவள் அருந் துயர் இது" எனச்
reading: Gotami says that the Brahmins of the four Vedas declare in their books that the gods grant boons, and that if the great goddess will not grant one she will not keep her own life; Champapathi answers that unless the first one of the aeon gives life, if those who move within the ring of the world can give it she will too, and to show her power she sets before Gotami all who can grant boons in the Chakravala, the four classes of formless Brahmas, the sixteen of Brahmas with form, the two lights, the six kinds of gods, the many asuras, the eight kinds of beings in hell, the stars and planets, and asks them to end her sorrow, and every god there says just what Champapathi said.
nuance: Gotami's appeal to the Veda's promise of boons is answered by assembling every god of the cosmos to deny it; the gods here are beings within the world-system, not above it. The ranks named, formless and form Brahmas in four and sixteen kinds within a Chakravala, are the Buddhist cosmology, which is the ground for tagging the claim Buddhist. Who 'the first one of the aeon' (172) is, whose giving Champapathi excepts, the unit does not say.
event: Gotami cites the Vedas' promise of boons; Champapathi summons every boon-giving god of the Chakravala, and all confirm that none can give back the boy's life.
unit_note: Starts at line 168 after the boundary moved from 159|160 to 153|154 and from 175|176 to 167|168; the end at 187 is unchanged.

reading: Her grief gone, Gotami places her son in the burning ground and dies; then, to show Champapathi's power, in the place where all the gods had gathered the great Maya modelled in clay the ring-mountain bounded by the sea, Meru standing at the centre, the seven ranges around it, the four great continents, the two thousand small islands and all their regions, with the beings that live in each, so that the order of things could be known; this is the Chakravala Kottam, and because it lies outside the wall of the shrine of the dead, people call it only the cremation-ground shrine; that, says the goddess, is its origin.
nuance: Gotami's grief ends because the gods' confession convinced her, and she dies of her own accord (189): the tale does not call it suicide or praise it. The cosmos model stands on the spot where every god admitted he could not undo a death, so the shrine teaches the order of the world from the place of that admission; the name the city uses forgets it.
event: Gotami lays her son in the burning ground and dies; Maya models the whole cosmos in clay on the gods' meeting place, and this becomes the Chakravala Kottam.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 199|200 to 205|206: the description of the model runs from line 192 through காண் at 202 to the goddess's closing words at 205 (இதன் வரவு இது' என்று இருந் தெய்வம் உரைக்க); lines 206 to 214 turn back to Sudhamathi and Manimekalai.

reading: As the goddess tells of the life of those who are born, Sudhamathi, her simple heart overcome by sorrow, falls asleep in the deep midnight; the goddess embraces Manimekalai, carries her thirty yojanas south through the sky to Manipallavam, girded by waves, sets her down there and departs.
nuance: The goddess's story of Gotami is called the life of those who are born (பிறந்தோர் வாழ்க்கை, 207), a summary of birth itself; it puts Sudhamathi to sleep and leaves Manimekalai to wake alone on the island of her former births.
event: Sudhamathi falls asleep, and the goddess carries Manimekalai through the sky to Manipallavam and leaves her there.
unit_note: Starts at line 206 after the boundary moved from 199|200 to 205|206 (see manimekalai:6:188-205).

title: துயிலெழுப்பிய காதை
theme: In the Thuyilezhuppiya Kaathai the goddess Manimekala, having hidden the girl on Manipallavam, warns the prince that a swerving sceptre ruins planets, rain and life, and wakes Sudhamathi with the news that a ripened cause has set Manimekalai on the Buddha's path; through a sleeping city Sudhamathi goes to the hall of the Chakravala kottam, where the painted pillar image reveals the two women's former births, and at dawn she tells Madhavi, who sits stricken at her daughter's absence.
source_issues: The core unit boundaries at 24/25, 37/38, 99/100 and 115/116 fall inside sentences or speeches; the units are re-cut at 14, 25, 39, 97 and 109.

Lines 117-124 are paired lines that repeat a sound with a different sense (ஆர்கைப் / ஆர் கைப், பண் இயம் / பண்ணியம்); the word division of 119-120 in this text decides the pun and may differ in other editions.
Line 134 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
Line 114 புலம் புரிச் சங்கம் is obscure: the conch of the learned, or a play on வலம்புரிச் சங்கம் in 113.

அவத் திறம் ஒழிக' என்று அவன்வயின் உரைத்த பின்
reading: Having left Manimekalai on Manipallavam, the goddess Manimekala appears before the sleepless prince Udayakumaran, who expects to have the girl in his hands by morning, and warns him that if the sceptre swerves the planets swerve, rain fails and no life is left, so that the king can no longer be called the life of all beings; he must drop the wrongful intent he has set on one who has taken up tapas.
nuance: The goddess treats a prince's desire for a renouncer as a swerving of the sceptre itself, though he is only the heir and has judged no case; the fault is private desire, and the stakes she names are cosmic. Lines 11-12 can be read either as all beings calling the king their life or as all beings being the king's own life; on either reading the title lapses because the beings it rests on are gone.
event: The goddess Manimekala appears to the sleepless prince Udayakumaran and warns him to give up his designs on Manimekalai.
unit_note: The core unit 1-24 is split at line 14, where the speech to the prince closes with ஒழிக' என்று and the goddess turns to Sudhamathi.

tamil: உவவனம் புகுந்து ஆங்கு உறு துயில் கொள்ளும்
