இன்று ஏழ் நாளில் இந் நகர் மருங்கே
reading: The goddess then enters the Uvavanam, wakes Sudhamathi, tells her not to fear because she is Manimekala come to see the city's Indra festival, and says that since the cause for the young girl to enter the great sage's path of dharma has ripened, she has carried her by magic to Manipallavam, from where, having come to know her former birth, the girl will appear near the city in seven days.
nuance: The goddess does not say she chose to act: she acts because a cause (ஏது) has ripened, so the rescue is the working-out of a condition, not a divine decision. Her self-announcement வந்தேன் அஞ்சல் மணிமேகலை யான் is word for word the formula she spoke to Kovalan's shipwrecked ancestor in the Silappathikaram (15, line 33).
event: The goddess wakes Sudhamathi in the Uvavanam and tells her she has carried Manimekalai to Manipallavam, from where the girl will return in seven days knowing her former birth.
unit_note: Starts at line 15, where the goddess leaves the prince for the grove; the core boundary after line 24 is moved to line 25, which closes the sentence begun at 23 (வந்து தோன்றும் மடக்கொடி நல்லாள்).

reading: The goddess adds that the girl, even if she enters the city in a changed form, will not hide herself from Sudhamathi, that many things are caused to happen here on the day she comes, and bids her tell Madhavi of this visit, for Madhavi will know her: on the night Kovalan, saying there is a goddess in the sea, gave the child her name, she told Madhavi in a dream as vivid as waking that she had borne a great creeper of tapas who would cut the cruel harm and leave Kama helpless.
nuance: The naming that the Silappathikaram tells as gratitude for a rescue at sea is given here a second, hidden meaning: the same night the goddess marked the infant for tapas. The forecast that she will come in another form (ஒளித்து உரு எய்தினும்) points ahead to her disguise as Kayasandigai.
event: The goddess bids Sudhamathi tell Madhavi of her visit, recalling the dream she gave Madhavi on the night Kovalan named the child Manimekalai.
unit_note: Starts at line 26 (the core unit began at 25, which ends the preceding sentence) and ends at line 39, where the goddess's speech closes with உரை' என்று, instead of at 37.

reading: The goddess rises into the sky and leaves; Sudhamathi gets up in burning grief in a city fast asleep, where the drums and lutes of the dancing halls have fallen silent, women who cannot bear their lovers' straying sleep sulking and will not be soothed, and others sleep embracing their lovers on fragrant beds.
nuance: The night catalogue that begins here (to line 86) is one long sentence whose subject is Sudhamathi, awake and alone among sleepers; the sleepers' loves and sulks are the courtesan quarter's life that Madhavi and her daughter have left.
event: The goddess departs into the sky, and Sudhamathi rises in grief in the sleeping city.
unit_note: Starts at line 40, where the narration resumes after the goddess's speech closes at 39; the core unit began at 38, inside her speech.

reading: The sleeping city goes on: small boys worn out with pulling toy carts sleep wearing the five-weapon amulet while their nurses throw mustard against harm and wave incense, the birds of eaves, waters and groves are hushed, the festival's revelry and drums are still; and at midnight come the praises of the palace watch who keep the hours by the water-clock, the long cry of a starving elephant that has broken its restraint in its stall, and the drums of the town watchmen in the streets and lanes.

reading: More night sounds reach Sudhamathi: the drowsy songs of shipwrights drunk on toddy at the harbour, the bathing of women freed from the impurity of childbirth amid smoke of mustard and snake-repelling herbs, the thunderous cry of warriors like tigers at the crossroads of the bhuta offering bali for the victory of the king of the bannered chariot, and the mantra-men who cure new mothers, infants, pregnant women and the wounded calling on the demoness of the common hall to come and take the offering.
nuance: The warriors' cry at 79-80 repeats the Silappathikaram's festival formula for the offering at the bhuta's altar (கொற்றம் கொள்க, உருமுக் குரல்/இடிக் குரல்), here heard as one noise among many in the night. The sense of தீர் வினை மகளிர் (76), women whose task is done or women freed of the birth-pollution, is not certain.

reading: Troubled by all these mingled cries, Sudhamathi leaves the grove in thick darkness by the small gate in the western wall, goes to the Chakravala kottam that the goddess had praised, and sits at one side of the world's hall of charity whose wide gate stands open to all; there, as she is bewildered and afraid, the wondrous image painted on the tall pillar speaks with a divine voice.
nuance: Sudhamathi takes refuge not in a temple of a god but in the open hall of charity of the burning-ground enclosure, where the speaking image is a painting; the help comes from a figure that shows causes (காரணம் காட்டிய, 94).
event: Sudhamathi goes by night to the Chakravala kottam and sits in its hall of charity, where the painted image on the pillar begins to speak.
unit_note: The core unit 85-99 is cut at line 97, where the narration ends with தெய்வக் கிளவியின் and the image's speech begins at 98.

இன்று ஏழ் நாளில் இடை இருள் யாமத்து
தன் பிறப்பு அதனொடு நின் பிறப்பு உணர்ந்து ஈங்கு
அஞ்சல்' என்று உரைத்தது அவ் உரை கேட்டு
reading: The image addresses Sudhamathi by her former and present births, as the daughter of Ravivarman and queen of Thuchayan of the horse army who, bewildered at Tarai's death, gave up her life before an elephant, and as the daughter of Kausikan of Champai who came to this city with Marutavegan, Virai joined with her elder sister Tarai, now Sudhamathi, and tells her that in seven days at midnight her younger sister, who was Lakshmi, will come knowing both their births, so she should not fear.
nuance: The image is first to reveal that the companions are sisters across births; it names only Sudhamathi's past and leaves Madhavi's (Tarai) implicit, which Manimekalai will supply when she repeats the same address in kaathai 11. Which of the sisters died first and how is told only here in passing, so the story behind 100-101 cannot be fixed from this unit.
event: The pillar image tells Sudhamathi her former birth as Virai and foretells that Manimekalai, once Lakshmi, will come in seven days knowing both their births.
unit_note: Spans the image's whole speech, from its first word at 98 to அஞ்சல்' என்று உரைத்தது at 109; the core units broke at 99 and 115.

குயிலுவர் கடைதொறும் பண் இயம் பரந்து எழக்
ஏ உறு மஞ்ஞையின் இனைந்து அடி வருந்த
நல் மணி இழந்த நாகம் போன்று அவள்
தன் மகள் வாராத் தனித் துயர் உழப்ப
reading: Shaken by the words, Sudhamathi waits as the watchmen sleep and the city wakes, conches sounding, elephants and cocks crying, horses and birds rising, flower offerings laid at the gods' altars and the traders' stalls, music and food spread at every door, until the sun rises from the sea; then, aching like a peacock struck by an arrow, she walks through the streets and tells Madhavi everything that happened in the night, and Madhavi, grieving alone that her daughter has not come, sits like a cobra that has lost its gem, like a body that has lost its life.
nuance: The dawn is built of paired lines that repeat a sound with a new sense (பணை நிலைப் புரவி / புள், பூம்பொழில் ஆர்கை / பூங்கொடியார் கை, பண் இயம் / பண்ணியம்), so the whole city's waking is staged as a doubled music against which Madhavi alone does not stir. Madhavi has renounced and been taught that attachment breeds suffering, yet her grief for her child is drawn in the strongest terms of loss. The sense of புலம் புரிச் சங்கம் (114) is not clear.
event: At dawn Sudhamathi tells Madhavi all that happened in the night, and Madhavi sits stricken at her daughter's absence.
unit_note: Starts at line 110, after the image's speech closes at 109, and runs to the kaathai's end; the core boundary at 115/116 fell inside the dawn catalogue, which is one sentence from 110 to 130.

title: மணிபல்லவத்துத் துயருற்ற காதை
theme: Manimekalai wakes alone on the island of Manipallavam, knowing neither the place nor whether she dreams, calls for Sudhamathi and suspects the goddess who brought her of deceit, then, wandering the shore, laments her father, whose death by the sword in a foreign land she lays to a cruel deed come to ripeness. Before her appears the Dharma seat placed by the king of the gods, over which two Naga kings once warred, each calling it 'ours', until the great sage stopped the war by calling it 'ours' and preached dharma from it.
source_issues: The printed unit 20-34 breaks in mid-sentence (break score 1): line 19 opens Manimekalai's speech that runs to line 27, and the sentence of her search runs from 28 to காணாள் at 35; the units were re-cut at 18, 35 and 43.
Line 63 ends தோன்றியது ஆங்கு என்: the closing என் is the kaathai-ending particle, not part of the sentence.

reading: While Manimekalai is thus carried off, on Manipallavam, an island girdled by the sea where conches plough the shore, pearls grow in the fields with red coral and pools of lily and kuvalai lie under shading punnai and screw-pine, the girl wakes on a bed of flowers in the moon-white sand and, like a life born in another place, sees neither her kin nor her town but only things she never saw, the long blue sea and the morning sun spreading its rays.
nuance: The simile at line 14, வேறு இடத்துப் பிறந்த உயிரே போன்று, compares her waking to a rebirth in a strange place, before the next kaathai makes her recover her real former birth on this very island; the waking is already shaped as a birth that has forgotten what came before. The island is drawn as a lush shore (neythal things: conch, pearl, coral, punnai, screw-pine), so her fear is not of a wasteland but of an unknown beauty.
event: Manimekalai wakes on the sands of Manipallavam at sunrise and finds neither her companions nor her town.
unit_note: The end of the printed unit 1-19 moved back one line to 18: line 18 closes the description of what she sees at sunrise, and her cry opens at line 19, so the speech is kept whole in the next unit.

tamil: ஒரு தனி அஞ்சுவென் திருவே வா!' எனத்
திரை தவழ் பறவையும் விரி சிறைப் பறவையும்
எழுந்து வீழ் சில்லையும் ஒடுங்கு சிறை முழுவலும்
பல் நிறப் புள் இனம் பரந்து ஒருங்கு ஈண்டி
வீசு நீர்ப் பரப்பின் எதிர் எதிர் இருக்கும்
துறையும் துறை சூழ் நெடு மணல் குன்றமும்
reading: Manimekalai cries out asking whether this is some spot beside the Uvavanam grove, reproaches Sudhamathi for hiding and causing her pain, says she cannot tell waking from dream and begs for an answer, calls on her friend to come since the night is over and Madhavi will be distraught, wonders whether the shining woman who appeared by sorcery has tricked her, and says she fears being all alone; then she wanders everywhere over the shore and dunes, where flocks of many-coloured birds with the swan as their king gather facing one another like kings in a war camp, and finds none of her companions.
nuance: She suspects the goddess who saved her, விஞ்சையின் தோன்றிய விளங்கு இழை மடவாள் (25), of வஞ்சம்: the rescue that the story treats as providence feels to the rescued girl like a betrayal. The bird simile at 30 to 33 (a swan king, flocks massed like kings' encampments, பாசறை மன்னர் பாடி) prepares, in miniature and harmlessly, the war of the two Naga kings over the seat told at the end of the kaathai.
event: Manimekalai calls for Sudhamathi, asks whether she is dreaming, suspects the goddess of a trick, and searches the shore for her companions in vain.
unit_note: Both boundaries moved: the unit now starts at line 19, where her quoted cry begins, and ends at line 35, where காணாள் completes the sentence of her fruitless search begun at line 28 (the printed unit ended at 34 in mid-sentence, break score 1).

tamil: குரல் தலைக் கூந்தல் குலைந்து பின் வீழ

reading: Her hair coming loose and falling behind, she wails, calls aloud and weeps, and in her deep grief thinks of her father: the cruel deed that casts us into this misery ripened, so that he went to a foreign land with the woman of the round bangles and his jewelled chest suffered the sharp sword, and she cries 'O father!'
nuance: Her lament names no king, no goldsmith and no guard: the sword stroke is set down wholly to the ripening of a cruel deed (வெவ் வினை உருப்ப, 40), where the Silappathikaram gives both the bent sceptre and the former deed as causes. And the deed is one that afflicts 'us' (எம், 40): she counts her own abandonment on the island and her father's death as one ripening, though the text does not say whose deed it was. Kannaki is not named and not called mother, only the woman of the round bangles (கோல் தொடி மாதர், 41), though in kaathai 2 Madhavi calls Manimekalai the great pathini's daughter.
event: Wandering the shore, Manimekalai weeps and laments her father Kovalan, killed by the sword in a foreign land.
unit_note: New unit cut from the printed units 35-49 and 50-63: it begins at line 36, after காணாள் ends the search, and ends at line 43, where her lament closes with ஐயாவோ என்று; line 43's அழுவோள் முன்னர் leads into the apparition of the seat that fills lines 44 to 63.

கீழ் நில மருங்கின் நாக நாடு ஆளும்
தம் பெருஞ் சேனையொடு வெஞ் சமம் புரி நாள்
பெருந் தவ முனிவன் இருந்து அறம் உரைக்கும்
reading: Before her as she weeps there appears the Dharma seat: a jewelled seat spreading bright rays, three cubits high and nine cubits across on every side, its circle laid out by rule and topped with a lotus square, called the seat made for the virtuous one, on which trees let fall only fragrant flowers and near which birds do not beat their wings, set there by the king of the gods, a seat of dharma on which births shine clear; over it two kings of one line who rule the Naga land below, each saying 'this is ours', could neither lift it nor let go of their great attachment and with red eyes and smoking hearts made fierce war with their armies, until the great sage of tapas, saying 'cease this great war, this is ours', sat on it and preached dharma, and the noble praise it.
nuance: The kings' claim and the sage's are the same words, எமது ஈது (56, 60): the war is ended not by the sage's refusing to own but by a counter-claim made for dharma by one without attachment, which the kings' own attachment (பெரும் பற்று, 57) could not answer. The seat's peace (no fruit falls on it, no wings beat near it) is set against their red eyes and smoking hearts. பிறப்பு விளங்கு (53) is read here as 'on which births shine clear', which the next kaathai bears out when Manimekalai, worshipping at it, knows her former birth; it could also be read as praise of the seat's own origin.
event: The Dharma seat set by Indra appears before the weeping Manimekalai; the narrator tells how two Naga kings warred over it until the great sage stopped the war and preached dharma from it.
unit_note: The start of the printed unit 50-63 moved back to line 44: lines 44 to 63 are one sentence describing the seat, whose finite verb is தோன்றியது at line 63, so the seat's description is kept whole.

title: பீடிகை கண்டு பிறப்புணர்ந்த காதை
theme: At the jewel seat on Manipallavam Manimekalai weeps, falls and rises knowing her former birth, and tells it aloud to the absent sage Brahmadharma: his warning that King Attipathi's city Idavayam would sink, the king's evacuation and the city's fall on the foretold day, her birth as Lakshmi and marriage to Attipathi's son Rahulan, and the sage's prophecy that Rahulan would die of a glance-poison snake, that she would enter his pyre, be reborn in Puhar, be carried by Manimekala to an island and there know her birth at the seat. She ends asking for the deity who was to show her husband's new birth.
source_issues: Line 64: the edition's தௌிவாய் was repaired to தெளிவாய் (old fonts drew ௌ and ெள alike).
Default unit boundaries at lines 25/26 and 38/39 fell inside sentences (the second split the phrase அசோதரம் ஆளும் இரவிவன்மன்); three units were adjusted to 16-30, 31-41 and 42-57.
Line 48: எட்டு இரு நாள் is read as sixteen days; it could be ten.

tamil: ஆங்கு அது கண்ட ஆய் இழை அறியாள்
காந்தள் அம் செங் கை தலை மேல் குவிந்தன

இறு நுசுப்பு அலச வெறு நிலம் சேர்ந்து ஆங்கு
reading: Seeing the seat, Manimekalai joins her hands above her head, weeps, circles it three times and falls like a lightning-creeper with its cloud, and rising with her former birth known without error, she hails the sage Brahmadharma, brother-in-law of King Attipathi of Gandhara, and says that all he spoke on the bank of the Kayangarai she now knows to have come true.
nuance: Lines 1 to 8 are narration and line 9 begins her speech, which runs to line 70. She speaks to Brahmadharma as if present, though only the seat is before her: the recognition of the birth and the confirmation of the sage's word (வாயே ஆகுதல், 11) arrive together, so the seat's first gift is proof that a prophecy held.
event: Manimekalai worships the jewel seat, falls to the ground, rises knowing her former birth and addresses the sage Brahmadharma.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவன் தன்பால் அணைந்து அறன் உரைப்போய்

நின்று நடுக்கு எய்த நீள் நில வேந்தே!
இதன்பால் ஒழிக" என இரு நில வேந்தனும்
மா பெரும் பேர் ஊர் மக்கட்கு எல்லாம்
வட வயின் அவந்தி மா நகர்ச் செல்வோன்
சேய் உயர் பூம்பொழில் பாடி யெய்து இருப்ப
reading: Manimekalai recalls that the sage went to King Attipathi and warned him that in seven days an earthquake would sink his city four hundred yojanas into the Naga underworld, and that the king had the drum proclaim that all should leave with their cattle and horses, left Idavayam with his army for Avanti in the north, and camped in a flowering grove on the bank of the Kayangarai.
nuance: The sage gives no cause for the city's fall: no fault of the king and no curse, only the warning, and the king acts on it at once. Set against the later fall of Puhar, which the epic ties to a forgotten festival and a goddess's anger, this first drowned city is the case of a warning heeded.
event: Brahmadharma warns Attipathi that Idavayam will sink in seven days; the king proclaims an evacuation, leaves the city and camps on the bank of the Kayangarai.
unit_note: Boundary moved from after line 25 to after line 30: line 25 ends with என்றே and the proclamation runs on into line 26 (பறையின் சாற்றி), and the clause of the king's journey closes with இருப்ப at line 30.

tamil: எம் கோன் நீ ஆங்கு உரைத்த அந் நாளிடைத்
தங்காது அந் நகர் வீழ்ந்து கேடு எய்தலும்

உலகு துயர் கெடுப்ப அருளிய அந் நாள்
reading: On the day the sage had named the city fell, and the king and all the people gathered round his feet and praised him while he, bound to the dharma of compassion, taught to end the world's suffering; at that time, she says, she had been born as Lakshmi, daughter of Queen Amuthapathi and King Ravivarman of sea-loud Asotharam.
nuance: The sentence ties her birth to 'that day' (அந் நாள், 37), which most naturally means she was living as Lakshmi at the time, not born that day. Her memory of the camp at Kayangarai is all worship and teaching; kaathai 21 will add what she does not say here, that on the same visit her husband killed the cook.
event: Idavayam sinks on the foretold day; the king and people worship Brahmadharma, who teaches them; Manimekalai names her former birth as Lakshmi of Asotharam.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit began at line 26 and ended at line 38, which split the phrase அசோதரம் ஆளும் / இரவிவன்மன் across lines 38 and 39. It now begins at line 31 (எம் கோன், a new clause after இருப்ப at 30) and ends at line 41, where பிறந்தேன் closes the sentence.

tamil: தவாக் களி மூதூர்ச் சென்று பிறப்பு எய்துதி
அணி இழை! நினக்கு ஓர் அருந் துயர் வரு நாள்
அன்று அப் பதியில் ஆர் இருள் எடுத்து
தென் திசை மருங்கில் ஓர் தீவிடை வைத்தலும்
reading: As Lakshmi she married Rahulan, son of Attipathi and Queen Neelapathi, and when she bowed with him at the sage's feet he foretold that within sixteen days Rahulan would die of a snake whose glance is poison and she would sink into his fire, and that since the cause for her awakening had not come to pass there, she would be born in the city named for the Kaveri, and on a day of great sorrow the goddess Manimekala would carry her by night to an island in the south.
nuance: The sage foretells the pyre as plainly as the death, with no word of praise or blame for it; the reason he gives for her rebirth in Puhar is that the ripening cause (ஏது நிகழ்ச்சி, 51) is absent 'here', a term the epic will use again for the conditions that must mature before release. Rahulan is the sage's nephew (Attipathi's son, and the sage is Attipathi's மைத்துனன், line 15). எட்டு இரு நாள் (48) is read as sixteen days (eight times two); ten is grammatically possible.
event: Lakshmi marries Rahulan; when the two bow to Brahmadharma he foretells Rahulan's death by a glance-poison snake, her death in his fire, her rebirth in Puhar and her carrying by Manimekala to a southern island.
unit_note: Begins at line 42 instead of 39, since lines 39 to 41 now close the sentence of the previous unit (பிறந்தேன், 41); ends at 57 as before.

ஈங்கு இவன்' என்னும்" என்று எடுத்து ஓதினை
reading: The prophecy goes on: on that island she was to worship the bright seat where the physician of the disease of birth sat and taught dharma, where the Naga kings put away the stain of anger and of mind and opened the ear of dharma and closed the ear of war, and that same day know her birth and see his words were clear; she, faint at the news of death, had asked to be shown her lover's next birth, and he had said the goddess who brought her would appear and say 'this is your husband'; will that goddess not come, she asks, and weeps.
nuance: The Buddha is not named: he is the physician of the disease of birth (பிறவிப் பிணி மருத்துவன், 61) and the seat is where he sat. Lakshmi's one question to the sage after hearing her husband would die was not about release but about finding him again, and Manimekalai repeats it now as her first wish after recovering the birth: the attachment the sage foresaw is still at work.
event: Manimekalai recalls the sage's promise that at the seat she would know her birth and that a goddess would show her her husband, and weeps asking why that goddess has not come.

title: மந்திரம் கொடுத்த காதை
theme: At the Buddha's seat on Manipallavam the Manimekala goddess descends, praises the Buddha, and tells Manimekalai her former birth: as Lakshmi she fed a sky-roaming sage, a gift that will end her births; the prince who pursues her is her husband of that birth, Rahulan, and her sisters then are Madhavi and Sudhamathi now, reborn beside her for worshipping the Buddha's footprints; the goddess gives her a mantra to change form and fly, for hearing the false words of other schools, and one against hunger, since the body is a lump of food.
source_issues: Line 40 carries the line mark 110-040 with kaathai number 110; read as 10-040.
Line 7 opens the hymn with a single quotation mark and line 15 closes it with a double one; the speaker is not named.
Line 87 has a quotation mark before பதிப் புகுவாய் inside a speech opened at 83, leaving the goddess's quoted speech unbalanced.
Line 93 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.

tamil: பொரு அறு பூங் கொடி பூமியில் பொலிந்தென
பொருள் வழங்கு செவித் துளை தூர்ந்து அறிவு இழந்த
வறம் தலை உலகத்து அறம் பாடு சிறக்கச்
நீயே ஆகி நிற்கு அமைந்த இவ் ஆசனம்
reading: Knowing that the girl has recovered her former birth at the Buddha's seat, the Manimekala goddess comes down through the sky with fragrant flowers and, while Manimekalai stands listening, praises the Buddha as a young sun that rose when the world had lost its understanding and dharma's light had failed, bows to the seat as his own presence, and asks that her grief end.
nuance: The hymn (7 to 15) is read here as the goddess's, since she has just descended and the next unit has her circling the seat; the Tamil does not name the singer, and it could be Manimekalai's own prayer heard by the goddess. The seat is worshipped as the Buddha himself (நீயே ஆகி நிற்கு அமைந்த இவ் ஆசனம்): no image, only the place where he sat. Lines 1 and 2 seem to be the goddess's own thought before she descends.
event: The Manimekala goddess descends to Manipallavam and sings praise of the Buddha before his seat as Manimekalai listens.

tamil: என் பெருங் கணவன் யாங்கு உளன்?' என்றலும்
மடந்தை மெல் இயல் மலர் அடி வணங்குழி
தெரு மரல் ஒழித்து ஆங்கு இரத்தினத் தீவத்துத்
விரா மலர்க் கூந்தல்! அவன் வாய் புதையா
பகை அறு பாத்தியன் பாதம் பணிந்து ஆங்கு
reading: As the goddess circles and bows to the seat, Manimekalai falls at her feet, thanks her for the knowledge of her birth and asks where her husband is; the goddess recalls how Lakshmi, sulking with Rahulan in a grove, saw the sky-roaming sage Saadhusakkaran come down at noon from turning the wheel of dharma in Ratnadvipa, bowed in awe, silenced her angry husband for not bowing, and with him offered the sage water and food, which he accepted.
nuance: The scene is a lovers' quarrel (புலத்தகை, இடங்கழி காமம்) broken into by a holy man: Lakshmi turns from her husband's pleading at her feet to the sage's feet, and it is she, not Rahulan, who knows whom to honour. The sage calls her எம் அனை, 'my mother', as he accepts.
event: Manimekalai asks the goddess where her former husband is; the goddess tells how Lakshmi and Rahulan once fed the sage Saadhusakkaran in a grove.

tamil: அந் நாள் அவன் உண்டருளிய அவ் அறம்
வெந்து உகு வெங் களர் வீழ்வது போன்ம் என
அறத்தின் வித்து ஆங்கு ஆகிய உன்னை ஓர்
reading: The goddess says that the charity the sage ate that day will not stay idle but will cut off Lakshmi's births, that Udayakumaran who came to her in the Uvavanam grove is that same Rahulan, and that because her heart too still clings to him, she carried her away, a seed of dharma about to fall like fine paddy seed on scorched saline ground, to set her on the right path.
nuance: This explains Manimekalai's own pull toward the prince and the goddess's taking her to the island: the gift's merit is secure, but a love that survives rebirth threatens to waste it. The goddess does not condemn the love as sin; she calls it the wrong ground for the seed.
event: The goddess reveals that Udayakumaran is Manimekalai's former husband Rahulan and that she carried her off to save the merit of her past gift.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 51 to 49: the goddess's account of the gift and the prince closes with செய்தேன் at 49; lines 50 and 51 open the sentence about Lakshmi's sisters, which runs to கொண்டனன் at 54.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவர் தம்மை அங்க நாட்டு அகவயின்
அவருடன் ஆங்கு அவன் அகல் மலை ஆடி
மற வணம் நீத்த மாசு அறு கேள்வி
உடங்கு உயிர் வாழ்க என்று உள்ளம் கசிந்து உக
தொழுது வலம் கொள்ள வந்தேன் ஈங்கு இப்
பழுது இல் காட்சியீர்! நீயிரும் தொழும்" என
reading: The goddess goes on: Lakshmi's elder sisters Tharai and Veerai were taken by Thuchayan, king of Kachchayam in Anga, and as he sported with them by the Ganga the flawless sage Aravanan came by; asked who he was, the sage said he had come to circle and worship the hill named for the lotus feet of the first lord of the dharma wheel, who once stood there and taught dharma with a melting heart so that people's sorrow and even the beasts' fear of one another might end, and he bade them worship too.
nuance: The goddess quotes Aravanan's speech inside her own, so 61 to 70 is a report two removes deep. The footprints are said to destroy faults (குற்றம் கெடுக்கும், 66) by lying there, which gives the place, not a living teacher, the power. Whether this Aravanan is the Aravana Adigal of Puhar in the story's present the unit does not say.
event: King Thuchayan, sporting with Tharai and Veerai by the Ganga, meets the sage Aravanan, who bids them worship the hill of the Buddha's footprints.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 52 to 50: the sentence naming Lakshmi's sisters begins at 50 (இன்னும் கேளாய் இலக்குமி) and reaches its verb at 54.

பல் வேறு சமயப் படிற்று உரை எல்லாம்
அல்லி அம் கோதை! கேட்குறும் அந் நாள்
விளை பொருள் உரையார் வேற்று உரு எய்தவும்
அந்தரம் திரியவும் ஆக்கும் இவ் அருந் திறல்
பொது அறிவு இகழ்ந்து புலம் உறு மாதவன்
திருவறம் எய்துதல் சித்தம் என்று உணர் நீ
இப் பெரு மந்திரம் இரும் பசி அறுக்கும்' என்று
ஆங்கு அது கொடுத்து ஆங்கு அந்தரம் எழுந்து
நீங்கியது ஆங்கு நெடுந் தெய்வம் தான் என்
reading: Because the two sisters heeded the sage and worshipped at the hill, the goddess says, they have been reborn with Manimekalai as Madhavi and Sudhamathi; now that she knows her birth and dharma's worth she will hear the false teachings of many schools, and since no one will tell a young girl the truth, she gives her a mantra to change form and travel the sky, foretells the great sage's day on the full moon, tells her to worship the seat and go home, then turns back for something forgotten: the human body is a lump of food, and this second mantra cuts off hunger; then she rises and is gone.
nuance: Two mantras are given: one for changing form and flying, for hearing the schools in disguise (fulfilled in kaathai 27), and one against hunger, added as an afterthought (மறந்ததும் உண்டு). The goddess calls the other schools' teachings படிற்று உரை, false or deceitful words, before Manimekalai has heard them. Lines 83 to 85 are obscure: the full-moon day on which the great sage 'attains holy dharma' may be the Buddha's festival or a prophecy about Manimekalai's own path.
event: The goddess tells Manimekalai that her sisters of the former birth are Madhavi and Sudhamathi, gives her a mantra for changing form and flying and another against hunger, and departs into the sky.

title: பாத்திரம் பெற்ற காதை
theme: On Manipallavam the guardian goddess Deepathilakai meets Manimekalai, who answers 'who are you?' with her two births; the bowl Amudhasurabhi rises into her hand on the Buddha's day, Deepathilakai preaches that those who feed the hungry give life, Manimekalai names the bowl as the fruit of a meal she gave a holy man in her former life, and she flies home to name Madhavi and Sudhamathi as her sisters of that life.
source_issues: The core unit boundary at 129/130 has break score 0 and splits Madhavi's cry (128-130); moved in this file.
Lines 40-43 give the day of the bowl's rising in compressed calendrical terms (எரி கதிர் இடபத்து, ஒருபதின் மேலும் ஒருமூன்று, மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து) that I cannot fix.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, in her former birth Lakshmi, wife of Rahulan
the guardian goddess of the jewel seat on Manipallavam, set there by Indra
the Buddha, the Lord of the Bodhi tree, praised and addressed but not present
Manimekalai's mother, in a former birth her elder sister Tharai
Manimekalai's companion, in a former birth her elder sister Veerai

tamil: இலங்கு தொடி நல்லாய்! யார் நீ?' என்றலும்
reading: Left alone on Manipallavam after the goddess has gone, Manimekalai looks over its white sand hills, groves and pools and wanders a kaatham, until Deepathilakai appears in a deity's form and asks who she is, come here like a woman cast up from a wrecked ship.
nuance: The question 'who are you?' (யார் நீ, 8) is the hinge of the kaathai: Manimekalai will answer it with two births, not one name.
event: Manimekalai wanders the island and the goddess Deepathilakai appears and asks who she is.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 10 to 8: Deepathilakai's question closes with என்றலும் at 8; Manimekalai's answer begins at 9 and the core unit 11-20 cut it after its first two lines.

tamil: இராகுலன் மனை யான் இலக்குமி என் பேர்
என் பெயர்த் தெய்வம் ஈங்கு எனைக் கொணர இம்
மன் பெரும் பீடிகை என் பிறப்பு உணர்ந்தேன்
ஈங்கு என் வரவு இது ஈங்கு எய்திய பயன் இது
பூங் கொடி அன்னாய் யார் நீ?' என்றலும்
ஆய் இழை தன் பிறப்பு அறிந்தமை அறிந்த
reading: Manimekalai answers by asking in which birth the question is meant: in the birth gone by she was Lakshmi, wife of the prince Rahulan, and in this one she is Manimekalai, Madhavi's daughter, brought here by the goddess of her name to know her birth at the jewel seat; then she asks Deepathilakai the same question.
nuance: Her reply turns a request for identity into a doctrine of identity: the self who answers spans two lives (போய பிறவியில் ... ஆய பிறவியில், 11, 13), and she names the coming and its use (வரவு, பயன், 17) as if reporting an errand completed.
event: Manimekalai tells Deepathilakai she was Lakshmi, Rahulan's wife, in her former birth and is now Madhavi's daughter, and asks who Deepathilakai is.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 10 to 8 at the start: the unit now opens with Manimekalai's answer at 9 and keeps its original end at 20, where the narration turns to Deepathilakai.

tamil: பழுது இல் காட்சி இந் நல் மணிப் பீடிகை
ஆங்கனம் ஆகிய அணி இழை! இது கேள்
reading: Deepathilakai says she has come from worshipping the feet of the Lord of dharma on the peak of Samantam in the Jewel Island, feet that are a ship of dharma across the great sea of births, and that she guards this jewel seat at the command of the king of the gods; those who keep unswervingly the vow of the dharma the Lord taught, on seeing and worshipping it, come to know their former births, and such people are rare.
nuance: The gods are put in service to the Buddha's seat: Indra (தேவர் கோன், 28) assigns the guard, and the guardian goddess herself is a pilgrim to the footprint. Lines 34-35 are compressed: the word of dharma is said to be fitting in the world for those rare ones, which may mean that only they are fit to receive teaching.
event: Deepathilakai names herself as the seat's guardian, set there by Indra, newly come from worshipping the Buddha's feet on Samantam.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 43 to 36: Deepathilakai's account of herself and of who may see the seat closes with இது கேள் at 36; the description of the Gomukhi pool and the bowl that follows begins at 37 and runs into the core unit 44-58.

tamil: ஈங்கு இப் பெரும் பெயர்ப் பீடிகை முன்னது
அந் நாள் இந் நாள் அப் பொழுது இப் பொழுது
நறு மலர்க் கோதை! நின் ஊர் ஆங்கண்
எழுந்து வலம் புரிந்த இளங்கொடி செங் கையில்
reading: Deepathilakai tells of the pool Gomukhi before the seat, where each year on the day the Lord of the Bodhi appeared the great bowl Amudhasurabhi of Aputhiran rises, and says that day and hour have come round now as if for her; the life-medicine put in it never fails and only tires the hands of those who take, and Aravanan in her town will tell her its nature; Manimekalai worships the seat, circles the pool with the goddess, and the bowl comes into her hand.
nuance: Lines 40-43 fix the day by season and stars (spring, the sun in Taurus, a count of thirteen days, the middle star); the reckoning is compressed and I cannot fix it, beyond its tie to the Buddha's day (போதித் தலைவனொடு பொருந்தித் தோன்றும், 43). The food is called ஆருயிர்மருந்து, medicine for dear life, and the only limit on the bowl is the tiredness of the receivers' hands (49), so scarcity moves from the giver to the taker.
event: Deepathilakai tells of Aputhiran's bowl rising from the Gomukhi pool; Manimekalai worships and circles the pool, and the bowl rises into her hand.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 43 to 36 at the start: the unit now opens on the Gomukhi pool at 37 and keeps its original end at 58, where the bowl enters Manimekalai's hand.

tamil: தீ நெறிக் கடும் பகை கடிந்தோய்! நின் அடி
பிறர்க்கு அறம் முயலும் பெரியோய்! நின் அடி
எண் பிறக்கு ஒழிய இறந்தோய்! நின் அடி
கண் பிறர்க்கு அளிக்கும் கண்ணோய்! நின் அடி
தீ மொழிக்கு அடைத்த செவியோய்! நின் அடி
நரகர் துயர் கெட நடப்போய்! நின் அடி
reading: Overjoyed at receiving the bowl, Manimekalai praises the Buddha's feet line by line, as the hero who conquered Mara, who drove off the enmity of evil ways, who strives for others' dharma, who did not want heaven, who went beyond reckoning, who gives others sight, whose ears are shut to evil words and whose tongue excels in truth, who walks to end the pain of the hell-dwellers and the serpents, and says her tongue can only bow, not praise; Deepathilakai praises the same feet and turns to speak.
nuance: The praise is a litany with the refrain நின் அடி closing ten lines; its first item, மாரனை வெல்லும் வீர (61), names desire's god as the one enemy, and துறக்கம் வேண்டாத் (64) sets the Buddha against the heaven that Vedic and Jain merit aims at. The gift of the bowl is answered not by thanks to the goddess but by praise of the teacher.
event: Manimekalai, holding the bowl, praises the Buddha's feet, and Deepathilakai praises them and begins to speak to her.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 73 to 75: the sentence that begins with என்ற ஆய் இழை முன்னர் at 72 runs through the Lord who appears in the Bodhi's shade (73-74) to its verb உரைக்கும் at 75; the core unit cut it at 73.

tamil: நாண் அணி களையும் மாண் எழில் சிதைக்கும்
பசிப் பிணி என்னும் பாவி அது தீர்த்தோர்
இசைச் சொல் அளவைக்கு என் நா நிமிராது
புல் மரம் புகையப் புகை அழல் பொங்கி
மழை வளம் தருதலின் மன் உயிர் ஓங்கி
கயக்கு அறு நல் அறம் கண்டனை என்றலும்
reading: Deepathilakai says her tongue cannot rise to praise those who cure the sinner hunger, which destroys high birth, kills dignity, drops the raft of learning, strips modesty and beauty and leaves a man standing at others' gates with his wife; she recalls a drought in which a Brahmin of the Veda, wandering, was about to eat dog's flesh until the god appeared and gave rain; those who give to the able sell dharma, the world's true way belongs to those who end the hunger of the helpless, those who give food give life, and Manimekalai, having taken up that gift of life, has seen flawless dharma.
nuance: Line 96 is Purananuru 18's உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே, a king's counsel to build tanks, here made the creed of an alms-bowl; and kaathai 10:90 has already lent the same poem's உணவின் பிண்டம். The famine tale (82-91) is compressed: அரசு தலைநீங்கிய (84) may be a Brahmin who had left kingship or a land without a king, and the one who performs Indra's rite (88) may be that Brahmin; I read it as the old tale of a hungry sage at a dog's flesh, but the lines do not name him. Line 92 classes gifts to those who can repay as trade in dharma.
event: Deepathilakai tells Manimekalai that those who cure hunger are beyond praise and that in taking the bowl she has seen true dharma.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 74 to 76 at the start and from 91 to 98 at the end: Deepathilakai's speech begins at 76 after உரைக்கும் (75) and runs to கண்டனை என்றலும் at 98; the core unit 92-115 cut it before its maxim.

tamil: ஆங்கு அதன் பயனே ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து ஆய்
ஈங்கு இப் பாத்திரம் என் கைப் புகுந்தது
வித்தி நல் அறம் விளைந்த அதன் பயன்
துய்ப்போர் தம் மனை துணிச் சிதர் உடுத்து
வயிறு காய் பெரும் பசி அலைத்தற்கு இரங்கி
வெயில் என முனியாது புயல் என மடியாது
தீம் பால் சுரப்போள் தன் முலை போன்றே
முகம் கண்டு சுரத்தல் காண்டல் வேட்கையேன்' என
மறந்தேன் அதன் திறம் நீ எடுத்து உரைத்தனை
ஈங்கு நின்று எழுவாய்' என்று அவள் உரைப்பத்
reading: Manimekalai says that in the birth she left, when her husband was dying of the sight-venom and she was about to burn with him, she fell into a dream-like daze like the hour she fed Saathusakkaran, and that deed's fruit has now come to her hand as this bowl; she longs to see its food flow, like a mother's breast at the face of her newborn, for the many who stand ragged at the gates of those enjoying the fruit of dharma sown in this land; Deepathilakai says she herself had forgotten that nature, that the bowl flows truly only for the excellent who feed out of compassion with dharma as witness, and bids her rise.
nuance: Karma is on both sides of the gate: the prosperous enjoy the fruit of dharma sown (108-109), and those outside are, on one reading of 112-113, those who did not stand by dharma before; yet the speaker's response to this is the mother's milk, not a verdict. Line 101 (உயிரொடு வேவேன்) and the run 111-113 are compressed and my reading of them is not secure. The bowl's condition (120-121) is the condition Aputhiran set when he let it go (14:93-94).
event: Manimekalai tells that the bowl is the fruit of her feeding Saathusakkaran in her former birth and longs to feed the hungry with it; Deepathilakai says it flows only for the compassionate and bids her rise.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 92 to 99 at the start and from 115 to 123 at the end: Manimekalai's reply runs from 99 to வேட்கையேன் என at 118, and Deepathilakai's answer closes with என்று அவள் உரைப்ப at 123; the core units broke her reply at 115 in the middle of its simile.

tamil: மா பெரும் பாத்திரம் மலர்க் கையின் ஏந்திக்
எழு நாள் வந்தது என் மகள் வாராள்!
தீவினை அறுக்கும் செய் தவம் நுமக்கு ஈங்கு
செறி தொடி நல்லீர்! உம் பிறப்பு ஈங்கு இஃது
மா பெரும் பாத்திரம் நீயிரும் தொழும்!' என
எழுக' என எழுந்தனள் இளங்கொடி தான் என்
reading: Manimekalai bows at Deepathilakai's feet, takes the bowl, worships the seat and rises through the sky, appearing before Madhavi just as she cries that the seventh day the true goddess promised has come and her daughter has not; she clears their bewilderment, hails Madhavi and Sudhamathi as Tharai and Veerai, her elder sisters in the birth when all three were born of Amudhapathi, who have now become her mothers, bids them seek from Aravana Adigal the austerity that cuts evil deeds in this human body, and has them worship the bowl, and they set out for the teacher.
nuance: The recognition reverses kinship: her elder sisters of the last birth are her mothers in this one (அவ்வையர் ஆயினீர், 137). The human body is named as the place where austerity can cut evil deeds (138-139), the first time in the kaathai the bowl's dharma of feeding is joined to a path of release.
event: Manimekalai flies home with the bowl, finds Madhavi grieving at the seventh day, tells her and Sudhamathi they were her sisters Tharai and Veerai, has them worship the bowl, and they set out for Aravana Adigal.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 129 to 123 at the start: the narration of Manimekalai's departure starts at 124 and the core unit 116-129 broke Madhavi's cry (128-130) across two units at a break score of 0. The unit ends at the kaathai's close, 146.

title: அறவணர்த் தொழுத கதை
theme: Manimekalai finds Aravana Adigal and tells him all that has happened; he tells how Tarai and Virai, Madhavi and Sudhamathi in their former birth, died, laments the decline of the Buddha's dharma and foretells the next Buddha's coming, defers his own teaching until events have run their course, and gives her the dharma of ending hunger, at which she takes up the bowl.
source_issues: The kaathai title prints அறவணர்த் தொழுத கதை, not காதை as in the other titles.
Line 55 reads பிறவியும் அறவியும்; அறவி is a rare form and the line's sense is not certain.
Line 121 ends with the closing mark என், as the kaathais do.

tamil: மைம் மலர்க் குழலி மாதவன் திருந்து அடி
களிக் கயல் நெடுங் கண் கடவுளின் பெற்றதும்
reading: With her two companions Manimekalai asks where Aravana Adigal lives, comes to the dwelling of the white-haired elder whose tongue never falters, bows three times at his feet, praises him, and begins to tell him of the grove, Udayakumaran's words, the goddess carrying her to Manipallavam, the Buddha's seat showing her the birth she had left, and her learning from the goddess of the husband of that birth.
nuance: Her story is given as a list of clauses ending in -ததும் and -வண்ணமும், so the poet retells eleven kaathais in a breath without letting her speak in direct words; the seat is called அறவோன் ஆசனம், the virtuous one's seat, without naming the Buddha.
event: Manimekalai seeks out Aravana Adigal, bows at his feet and begins to recount what has happened to her since the grove.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 14: Manimekalai's reported account of her own doings closes with பெற்றதும் at 14; line 15 opens the goddess's quoted words about Tarai and Virai, which run to 20.

tamil: வெவ் வினை உருப்ப விளிந்து கேடு எய்தி
ஆங்கு அவர் தம் திறம் அறவணன் தன்பால்
பூங் கொடி நல்லாய்! கேள்' என்று உரைத்ததும்
கேள்' என்று உரைத்து கிளர் ஒளி மா தெய்வம்
reading: Her report goes on: the goddess told her that her elder sisters of that birth, Tarai and Virai, died when a cruel deed ripened and were reborn as Madhavi and Sudhamathi to be with her, and that she should hear their story from Aravanan; the goddess gave her three mantras and left; Deepathilakai appeared with grace, gave her Aaputhiran's bowl in truth and sent her to hear Aaputhiran's story from the same teacher; and all this she told the ascetic, bowing.
nuance: Both divine speakers send her to Aravanar for the stories behind what they reveal, so the unit sets up the elder as the keeper of the past lives the goddesses only name; the deaths of 16 are blamed on a ripened deed before 43 to 48 say how they happened.
event: Manimekalai tells Aravanar how the goddess revealed Tarai and Virai's rebirth and gave her three mantras, and how Deepathilakai gave her Aaputhiran's bowl and sent her to him.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 14 at the start: the unit now opens with the goddess's quoted words at 15 and ends with உரைத்தலும் at 30, which closes the whole report begun at 7.

tamil: உற்று உணர்வாய் நீ இவர் திறம் உரைக்கேன்
நின் நெடுந் தெய்வம் நினக்கு எடுத்து உரைத்த
அந் நாள் அன்றியும் அரு வினை கழூஉம்
துச்சயன் தன்னை ஓர் சூழ் பொழில் கண்டேன்
reading: Hearing her, the great ascetic is filled with joy upon joy, promises to tell her the two women's story, and begins: besides the day her goddess told of, when he was going to worship the Padapankaya hill, the twin feet of the First Lord that wash away hard deeds, he met Duchayan, king of Kachchayam, in a grove and asked whether all was well with him and his queens.
nuance: ஆதி முதல்வன், the First Lord, is here the Buddha, whose footprints give the hill its name (kaathai 10, 61 to 68); the Kural's first couplet uses a near phrase (ஆதி பகவன்) for its own unnamed first being. Aravanar speaks of the earlier visit as something the goddess already told, so his account adds a second meeting.
event: Aravanar, delighted, begins to tell how on a later pilgrimage to the Padapankaya hill he met King Duchayan and asked after him and his queens.

tamil: ஆங்கு அது கேட்டு ஓர் அரமியம் ஏறி
"பழ வினைப் பயன் நீ பரியல்" என்று எழுந்தேன்
reading: The king, broken, told him that Virai, dazed with drink, went heedlessly before a newly captured elephant and was killed, and that Tarai, hearing it, climbed a terrace and fell to her death; Aravanar told him not to grieve over the fruit of old deeds and rose to leave, and now he asks the two women whether they have come back in another costume, like dancers.
nuance: Karma and the women's own acts are both given: line 16 calls the deaths a cruel deed ripening, while 46 names the drink and 48 the leap; Aravanar's consolation at 50 lets the first explain the second without excusing it. The closing image of dancers changing costume (51 to 52) fits Madhavi, a dancer, and makes rebirth a change of dress.
event: Duchayan tells Aravanar that Virai was killed by an elephant while drunk and Tarai threw herself from a terrace; Aravanar consoles him and leaves.

tamil: இறுதி இல் நல் கதி செல்லும் பெரு வழி
செயிர் வழங்கு தீக் கதி திறந்து கல்லென்று
உயிர் வழங்கு பெரு நெறி ஒரு திறம் பட்டது
உலா நீர்ப் பெருங் கடல் ஓடாது ஆயினும்
ஆங்கு அத் துளை வழி உகு நீர் போல
ஈங்கு நல் அறம் எய்தலும் உண்டு எனச்
reading: Not content with the women's story, Aravanar tells Manimekalai that the dharma the Lord of Dharma taught no longer flourishes: the great road to the endless good state is choked with grass and thorns while the road to the evil states stands open, the dharma is known to exist only as a sun swallowed by mist is known, and as sea water still seeps through a needle-bored hole in a gem, good dharma can still be reached here, though people will not credit him when he says so.
nuance: Line 55 பிறவியும் அறவியும் is hard: read here as 'birth and dharma' that she has come to know, but அறவி is a rare form. The two similes grade the loss: the mist hides the sun without destroying it, and the hole lets in only a trickle, so decline is not extinction.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 68 to 70: the needle-hole simile begun at 66 completes its sense with உண்டு எனச் சொல்லலும் உண்டு at 69 to 70 and the clause யான் சொல்லுதல் தேற்றார் at 70.

tamil: இருள் பரந்து கிடந்த மலர் தலை உலகத்து
பெருங் குள மருங்கில் சுருங்கைச் சிறு வழி
அளவாச் சிறு செவி அளப்பு அரு நல் அறம்
உளம் மலி உவகையோடு உயிர் கொளப் புகூஉம்
reading: Because worldly people will not grasp it, all the gods of the cosmic circle gathered in Tushita and fell begging at the feet of the Great One, so that in one thousand six hundred and sixteen years the great wise one will appear like the sun over a dark world, and after that the measureless dharma will pour gladly into small ears as a great flood enters a tank through a narrow sluice.
nuance: ஈர் எண்ணூற்றோடு ஈர் எட்டு (77) is read as two eight-hundreds and two eights, 1616 years; the text does not say from what point the years are counted. The sluice simile (79 to 82) answers the needle-hole simile of 66 to 68: the same small opening, but now with a flood behind it.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 69-80 to 71-82: the unit now opens with the clause on worldly people at 71 that leads into the gods' entreaty, and ends with புகூஉம் at 82, which completes the tank-and-sluice simile begun at 79.

tamil: மைத்து இருள் கூர்ந்த மன மாசு தீரப்
ஊன் உடை உயிர்கள் உறு துயர் காணா
நளி இரு முந்நீர் நலம் பல தரூஉம்
கறவை கன்று ஆர்த்தி கலம் நிறை பொழியும்
அந் நாள் பிறந்து அவன் அருளறம் கேட்டோர்
reading: When the Buddha-sun rises to clear the dark stain of minds, Aravanar says, sun and moon will shine unharmed, the stars keep their course, the rain will not fail, the earth, winds and sea will yield, cows will feed their calves and fill the pails, beasts and men will lose their fear of each other, the beings of hell and the ghosts will be freed of torment, and no creature will be born hunchbacked, dwarfed, dumb, deaf or deluded; those born then who hear his dharma of grace will pass beyond painful birth, and so he will not forget, in any birth, to praise the feet of the Lord of the Bodhi tree.
nuance: The blessings of 87 to 98 are the old Tamil signs of a just king's reign (unfailing rain, full udders) moved to a Buddha's coming. Aravanar does not expect to escape birth himself before then: his vow is to keep worshipping through every birth until the age of hearing comes.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 81 to 83: lines 81 and 82 complete the sluice simile of the unit before; this unit opens with the gem-and-sunrise simile at 83 and ends with the vow at 103.

tamil: ஓங்கு உயர் போதி உரவோன் திருந்து அடி
தொழுது வலம் கொண்டு தொடர் வினை நீங்கிப்
பழுது இல் நல் நெறிப் படர்குவர் காணாய்
ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து ஆம் அமுதசுரபி எனும்
தவப் பெரு நல் அறம் சாற்றினர் ஆதலின்
மடுத்த தீக் கொளிய மன் உயிர்ப் பசி கெட
reading: Aravanar tells her that many events will happen in the city because of her and that she will not take up the teaching until they have; that Madhavi and Sudhamathi, having worshipped the Padapankaya hill, will with her worship the Bodhi sage's feet, shed their deeds and go the faultless way; and that since she now holds the great bowl Amudhasurabhi, he gives her one dharma alike in its end for men and gods, ending the disease of hunger; and the girl takes up the bowl to quench the burning hunger of all lives.
nuance: பொருளுரை பொருந்தாய் (107) is read as a deferral: the doctrine will come after the events, and the epic keeps it back until kaathai 29. Feeding the hungry is given first to a renunciant, not to a householder or king, and is called தவப் பெரு நல் அறம், the great good dharma of tapas.
event: Aravanar defers his teaching, foretells Madhavi's and Sudhamathi's release, and gives Manimekalai the dharma of ending hunger; she takes up the bowl.

title: ஆபுத்திரன் திறம் அறிவித்த காதை
theme: Aravana Adigal tells Manimekalai the early life of Aputtiran, first holder of her bowl: abandoned by his brahmin mother, nursed by a cow and adopted by a brahmin, he steals a cow from a sacrifice, answers the brahmins' contempt for his birth with their own seers' animal and courtesan births, and is driven out to live in Madurai as a beggar who feeds the helpless.
source_issues: Line 1 opens a quotation for Aravana Adigal's speech that is not closed within the kaathai; it continues into kaathai 14.
Lines 93-98: Aputtiran's reply opens with a double quotation mark at 93 and closes with a single mark after தவறு? at 98.
Line 115 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut off in this text.
Unit boundaries at 44/45, 68/69 and 93/94 fell inside sentences (the last with break score 0); they were moved to 48/49, 69/70 and 91/92.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher who tells Manimekalai the bowl's history
Madhavi's daughter, who has received the bowl
the cow-nursed foundling, first holder of the bowl
Abanjikan's wife, Aputtiran's mother
Veda teacher of Varanasi, Saali's husband
the cow that nursed the abandoned infant
brahmin of Vayanangodu who adopts Aputtiran
Ilampoothi's wife
the cow led to the sacrifice and stolen by Aputtiran
the brahmins who pursue and revile Aputtiran
the brahmins' teacher, gored by the cow
the brahmin who reports Saali's confession

tamil: சூல் முதிர் பருவத்து துஞ்சு இருள் இயவிடை
தாய் இல் தூவாக் குழவித் துயர் கேட்டு ஓர்
ஆ வந்து அணைந்து ஆங்கு அதன் துயர் தீர
reading: Aravana Adigal begins Aputtiran's story for Manimekalai: Saali, wife of the Varanasi Veda teacher Abanjikan, having wronged her husband and fled his punishment, bears a child on her way back from bathing at Kumari and leaves it in a hidden grove; a cow licks and suckles it and guards it seven days, until the brahmin Ilampoothi of Vayanangodu hears it cry, weeps, and claims it as his own son, not a cow's.
nuance: The unit sets the human mother who 'did not pity' the child (இரங்காள் ஆகி, 9) against the cow that comes to end its sorrow (அதன் துயர் தீர, 12); Ilampoothi's first words, 'not a cow's son but my son' (19), anticipate the insult the brahmins will later throw at the boy.
event: Saali abandons her newborn in a grove near the road; a cow nurses and guards it for seven days, and the brahmin Ilampoothi finds the child and takes it as his son.

tamil: நாத் தொலைவு இன்றி நன்கனம் அறிந்த பின்
அப் பதி தன்னுள் ஓர் அந்தணன் மனைவயின்
வெரூஉப் பகை அஞ்சி வெய்து உயிர்த்துப் புலம்பிக்
அஞ்சி நின்று அழைக்கும் ஆத் துயர் கண்டு
உள்ளம் கரந்து ஆங்கு ஒரு புடை ஒதுங்கி
அல்லிடை ஆக் கொண்டு அப் பதி அகன்றோன்
காட்டிடை நல் ஆக் கதழ்ந்து கிளர்ந்து ஓட
reading: Ilampoothi and his wife take the boy home and rejoice in a son, and he masters the brahmins' learning before his thread ceremony; entering a brahmin's house where a flesh-ringed sacrifice is prepared, he sees a garlanded cow trembling like a deer in a net, steals it away by night, and is caught on the desert road by the brahmins, who call him no son of theirs but a base boy and beat him with sticks until the cow gores their teacher and runs off into the forest.
nuance: The narrator names the rite புலை சூழ் வேள்வி (28), a sacrifice surrounded by what is foul, and the boy's own aim is to end the cow's suffering from 'stealthy work' (கள்ள வினை, 35), so the theft is framed as rescue before the brahmins name it theft. The cow that kills the teacher (46-47) makes the rescued victim the cause of a death, a cost the narration states without comment. Boundary moved: see unit_note.
event: The boy steals the cow meant for a sacrifice, is caught and beaten by the brahmins, and the cow gores their teacher to death and escapes.
unit_note: The boundary between this unit and the next was moved from 44/45 to 48/49: the sentence that begins at 40 with the brahmins' capture runs through the beating (45) and the cow's flight (48), and Aputtiran's speech opens at 49.

tamil: விடு நில மருங்கில் படு புல் ஆர்ந்து
பிறந்த நாள் தொட்டும் சிறந்த தன் தீம் பால்
அறம் தரு நெஞ்சோடு அருள் சுரந்து ஊட்டும்
reading: Aputtiran tells the brahmins not to do hurtful things and to hear him: the cow eats the grass of the waste lands and from the day of their birth feeds all people its sweet milk with a heart that gives virtue and overflowing kindness, so what enmity do they have with it?
nuance: He defends the cow by what it gives, not by any sanctity of its kind: it eats what no one owns (விடு நில மருங்கின் படு புல், 51) and nourishes everyone, so the brahmins' claim on it as a victim is answered with a claim of debt.
event: Aputtiran asks the brahmins why they bear enmity to a cow that feeds all people.
unit_note: Starts at 49 instead of 45; see the note on 20-48. Ends at 56 as before.

tamil: "பொன் அணி நேமி வலம் கொள் சக்கரக் கை
மன் உயிர் முதல்வன் மகன் எமக்கு அருளிய
அரு மறை நல் நூல் அறியாது இகழ்ந்தனை
நீ மகன் அல்லாய் கேள்" என இகழ்தலும்
ஈங்கு இவர் நும் குலத்து இருடி கணங்கள் என்று
ஓங்கு உயர் பெருஞ் சிறப்பு உரைத்தலும் உண்டால்
நான்மறை மாக்காள் நல் நூல் அகத்து?" என
reading: The brahmins scorn him as one who despised the Veda that Brahma, son of the discus-bearing lord of life, gave them, a small-minded boy fit to be a cow's son and no son of theirs; Aputtiran answers that their own tradition praises the seers Asalan, son of a cow, Sringi, son of a deer, Virinchi, son of a tiger, and Kesakambalan, son of a jackal, as sages of their line, and asks whether the good books of the four Vedas know any lineage ruined by birth from a cow.
nuance: The brahmins' insult turns the boy's history into a verdict (ஆ மகன் ஆதற்கு ஒத்தனை, 61); Aputtiran does not reject the Veda but argues from within it. The names at 63-65 are rare and their legends are not told here, so whose tradition supplies them is not clear from the Tamil.
event: The brahmins revile Aputtiran as a cow's son ignorant of the Veda, and he replies with seers of their tradition born of animals.
unit_note: The boundary with the next unit was moved from 68/69 to 69/70: Aputtiran's question that begins at 68 (ஆவொடு வந்த அழி குலம் உண்டோ) ends at 69 with என, and the brahmin's new speech opens at 70.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவர் தம்முள் ஓர் அந்தணன் உரைக்கும்
"ஈங்கு இவன் தன் பிறப்பு யான் அறிகுவன்" என
'யாது நின் ஊர்? ஈங்கு என் வரவு?' என
ஆரண உவாத்தி அரும் பெறல் மனைவி யான்
பொன் தேர்ச் செழியன் கொற்கை அம் பேர் ஊர்க்
அல்லல் உற்று அழுத அவள் மகன் ஈங்கு இவன்
புல்லல் ஓம்பன்மின் புலை மகன் இவன்" என
reading: One of the brahmins says he knows the boy's birth: he met Saali, worn by the road, worshipping at Kumari, and when he asked her town and errand she told him she was the wife of the Varanasi Veda teacher, had behaved unlike a brahmin woman and slighted her husband, had fled in fear of punishment, and on her way back had left her newborn in a grove beyond Korkai, asking whether a sinner like her had any good course left; this boy is her son, so they must not touch him, for he is an outcaste.
nuance: Saali's confession (78-88) repeats the narrator's account at 3-10 almost word for word, now inside a hostile witness's speech, so the same facts are used once to explain the child and once to condemn him. The brahmin judges the son by the mother's conduct; Aputtiran answers that verdict in the next unit (92-98).
event: A brahmin reports Saali's confession of her lapse and her abandonment of the child, and declares Aputtiran her son and an outcaste.
unit_note: Starts at 70 instead of 69 (see the note on 57-69) and ends at 91 instead of 93: the brahmin's speech closes at 91 with என, and 92-93 introduce Aputtiran's reply.

tamil: புரி நூல் மார்பீர்! பொய் உரை ஆமோ?
தங்கினன் வதிந்து அத் தக்கணப் பேர் ஊர்
யாவரும் வருக' என்று இசைத்து உடன் ஊட்டி
உண்டு ஒழி மிச்சில் உண்டு ஓடு தலை மடுத்து
reading: Aputtiran laughs and tells the brahmins to hear the birth of their own line: the two first brahmin seers of the ancient Veda were the beloved sons of a heavenly courtesan, so what fault has Saali? He is then cast out by his father Poothi as unfit to study among brahmins, stones are dropped in his begging bowl in every brahmin village as 'the cow-stealing thief', and he goes to southern Madurai, lodges in the hall before the temple of Chinthadevi, begs from house to house, calls the blind, the deaf, the lame, the unprotected and the sick to eat, eats what is left and sleeps with his bowl for a pillow.
nuance: The tradition names the two seers born of a heavenly courtesan as Vasishtha and Agastya; the Tamil here does not name them. The narrator calls the outcast beggar காவலன் (115), protector, the word for a king, and the begging bowl (கடிஞை, 103, 109) stoned in the villages is the one he will soon exchange for the divine bowl (Manimekalai 14).
event: Aputtiran mocks the brahmins' pride of birth, is disowned by Ilampoothi and driven from the brahmin villages, and settles in Madurai begging to feed the helpless.
unit_note: Starts at 92 instead of 94; see the note on 70-91.

title: பாத்திர மரபு கூறிய காதை
theme: Aravana Adigal goes on telling Manimekalai the bowl's history: the goddess Chintadevi gives Aputhiran the never-failing bowl in the Madurai rest hall; his feeding shakes Indra's seat, and when Indra comes offering a reward he laughs at a heaven where no one gives; Indra answers with rain so plentiful that no one needs the bowl, the hall falls to idlers, and Aputhiran, sailing to famine-struck Savakam, is left on empty Manipallavam, where he gives the bowl to the Gomukhi pool for some compassionate hand, starves himself to death, and is born again in Savakam to sustain its people.
source_issues: Line 1 opens with a quotation mark (') that is not closed in this kaathai: Aravana Adigal's narration runs on from kaathai 13 and into kaathai 15 (which opens 'இன்னும் கேளாய்').
Lines 103-104 (சாவகம் ஆளும் தலைத் தாள் வேந்தன் / ஆ வயிற்று உதித்தனன்) are hard to construe; தலைத் தாள் is obscure, and the kaathai ends on the closing particle என் that runs into kaathai 15.
Line 57 வசித் தொழில் is a rare expression; read here as the work of rain.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher, who tells Manimekalai the history of the bowl and its first owner
Madhavi's daughter, who now holds the bowl and hears its story
the outcast brahmin's son who feeds the poor from the rest hall in southern Madurai, the bowl's first owner
the goddess of the temple of learning in Madurai, who gives Aputhiran the bowl
Indra, king of the gods, the thousand-eyed
travellers worn by the road who come to the rest hall hungry on a night of rain
the rakes, profligates and idlers who take over the empty rest hall
the men of a ship from Savakam who tell Aputhiran of its famine and leave him on Manipallavam

tamil: மாரி நடு நாள் வல் இருள் மயக்கத்து
"கேள் இது மாதோ கெடுக நின் தீது" என
நாடு வறம் கூரினும் இவ் ஓடு வறம் கூராது
reading: Aravana Adigal tells Manimekalai how, on a night of heavy rain, road-worn travellers came to the rest hall where Aputhiran slept and begged him to ease their hunger, and he, who had no food but what he begged, grieved at finding no means, until the goddess Chintadevi of the temple of learning appeared and bade him take a bowl that would not run dry though the land did, whose food would fail only as the hands of the takers tired.
nuance: The gift answers Aputhiran's grief at being unable to feed others (8, ஆற்றுவது காணான்), not his own hunger; the goddess's words at 13 to 15 are repeated almost exactly by Deepatilakai when Manimekalai receives the bowl (11:49-50), so the bowl carries the same warrant from its first owner to its second.
event: Hungry travellers beg Aputhiran for food on a rainy night; Chintadevi appears and offers him an inexhaustible bowl.

tamil: தன் கைப் பாத்திரம் அவன் கைக் கொடுத்தலும்
ஆங்கு அவர் பசி தீர்த்து அந் நாள் தொட்டு
வாங்கு கை வருந்த மன் உயிர் ஓம்பலின்
மா இரு ஞாலத்து மன் உயிர் ஓம்பும்
ஆர் உயிர் முதல்வன் தன் முன் தோன்றி
உன் பெரும் தானத்து உறு பயன் கொள்க" என
reading: The goddess puts the bowl in his hand; he praises her as the undying lamp of the temple of learning, queen of the gods and first of those on earth, feeds the travellers, and from that day feeds every creature until men, beasts and birds crowd round him with a noise like birds in a fruiting tree, so that his deeds shake Indra's white throne and Indra comes before him as a bent old brahmin with a staff, names himself, and bids him take the fruit of his great giving.
nuance: Indra's seat is shaken not by austerity but by feeding (28 to 29), and the god comes disguised as a brahmin to the man whom brahmins had driven out (kaathai 13); the offer of a reward for giving (35) sets up the refusal that follows.
event: Aputhiran takes the bowl, praises the goddess and feeds all creatures; Indra's throne trembles and Indra comes in a brahmin's form to offer him the reward of his giving.

tamil: வெள்ளை மகன் போல் விலா இற நக்கு ஈங்கு
நல் தவம் செய்வோர் பற்று அற முயல்வோர்
வருந்தி வந்தோர் அரும் பசி களைந்து அவர்
திருந்து முகம் காட்டும் என் தெய்வக் கடிஞை
reading: Aputhiran laughs till his ribs ache, says 'Go', and asks the king of a heaven where deeds done here are only enjoyed, where there is no one who does dharma, protects others, does good austerity or strives to cut attachment, what he could give here: food, clothes, women or attendants, to one whose divine bowl takes away the hunger of all who come and brightens their faces.
nuance: The scorn is precise: heaven is a place for consuming merit, not for making it, so a reward there would end the giving that earned it. 'வெள்ளை மகன் போல்' (36) is read as 'like a simpleton', laughing without restraint before a god.
event: Aputhiran laughs at Indra's offer and asks what a god of heaven could give him.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 47 to 48: Aputhiran's question to Indra closes with தேவர்கோன்? என்றலும் at 48; the core unit cut it off before its last line.

tamil: நிரப்பு இன்று எய்திய நீள் நிலம் அடங்கலும்
பரப்பு நீரால் பல் வளம் சுரக்க!" என
ஓங்கு உயர் பெருஞ் சிறப்பு உலகோர்க்கு அளித்தலும்
மன் உயிர் மடிய மழை வளம் இழந்தது
வசித் தொழில் உதவ மா நிலம் கொழுப்பப்
reading: Indra wills that the protector's bowl, still brimming with food, should sit idle for want of beggars, and that the whole land should overflow with plenty from spreading rain; so for Aputhiran's sake the thousand-eyed gives the world great abundance, the Pandya land that had lost its rain for twelve years grows rich and knows no hunger, and the hall's noise of eating falls silent, left to rakes, idlers and wayfarers who laugh, play dice and gamble there.
nuance: Indra's answer is a reward in form and a defeat in fact: plenty does not refute Aputhiran's scorn of heaven but takes away the hunger on which his giving depends. The sense of வசித் தொழில் (57) and whether the twelve-year drought (55 to 56) ended with this rain or preceded it are not certain; the same twelve-year formula returns for Savakam's famine at 25:101-102.
event: Indra sends abundant rain so that no one needs Aputhiran's food, and the rest hall falls silent and becomes a haunt of gamblers and idlers.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 48 to 49 at the start and from 63 to 64 at the end: Indra's wish opens at 49, and the account of the idle hall ends with முறைமையது ஆக at 64, before Aputhiran leaves it at 65.

tamil: அங்கு அந் நாட்டுப் புகுவது என் கருத்து" என
reading: Aputhiran leaves the hall and goes from town to town asking for anyone who will eat, mocked by all with 'who is this?', alone like a rich man whose fortune the sea has taken, until men from a ship bow to him and tell him that in Savakam the rain has failed and creatures are dying, and he resolves to carry there the bowl that, by the king of the gods' command, has found no eaters and grown old unused.
nuance: The giver is now the beggar of beggars, asking for someone to take food; குமரி மூத்த (77), 'grown old a maiden', pictures the bowl as a girl who never married for want of a taker.
event: Aputhiran wanders finding no one to feed; shipmen tell him of famine in Savakam, and he decides to go there with the bowl.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 64 to 65: line 64 closes the description of the idle hall, and Aputhiran's departure begins with ஆபுத்திரன் at 65.

வழங்கு நீர் வங்கம் வல் இருள் போதலும்
வங்கம் போய பின் வருந்து துயர் எய்தி
"மன் உயிர் ஓம்பும் இம் மா பெரும் பாத்திரம்
தவம் தீர் மருங்கின் தனித் துயர் உழந்தேன்
"ஓர் யாண்டு ஒரு நாள் தோன்று" என விடுவோன்
"அருள் அறம் பூண்டு ஆங்கு ஆர் உயிர் ஓம்புநர்
உளர்எனில் அவர் கைப் புகுவாய்" என்று ஆங்கு
reading: He sails gladly with the shipmen, but a gale drives the ship to Manipallavam, where he goes ashore; the crew, thinking he has re-embarked, sail off in the dark, and alone on the uninhabited island he says he will not use the great bowl that sustains all lives to sustain his own, that he has suffered lone sorrow where his merit ran out, and with folded hands lets it go into the Gomukhi pool, bidding it rise one day each year and enter the hands of any who wear compassion and dharma and sustain lives.
nuance: The bowl is refused to its owner because it is for others; Aputhiran's release sets a condition (93 to 94) that Deepatilakai later applies to Manimekalai. தவம் தீர் மருங்கின் (89) is read as the exhausting of his merit, which he gives as the cause of his plight; the unit does not say whether the work agrees.
event: Stranded on Manipallavam by the departing ship, Aputhiran consigns the bowl to the Gomukhi pool for a compassionate owner.

tamil: அந் நாள் ஆங்கு அவன் தன்பால் சென்றேன்
தன் உற்றன பல தான் எடுத்து உரைத்தனன்
குண திசைத் தோன்றி கார் இருள் சீத்துக்
ஆ வயிற்று உதித்தனன் ஆங்கு அவன்தான் என்
reading: As Aputhiran was giving up his life by the vow of not eating, Aravana Adigal went to him and asked what had befallen him, heard his many troubles, and saw him, like the sun that rises in the east, clears the dark and sets in the west, leave his body on Manipallavam with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives, and be born from a cow's womb to rule Savakam.
nuance: The narrator is himself a witness: he was on the island at the death (96 to 98). The birth is shaped by the purpose held at death (102), and he is born in the very land whose famine he had set out to relieve. How சாவகம் ஆளும் தலைத் தாள் வேந்தன் (103) attaches to ஆ வயிற்று உதித்தனன் is not clear; kaathai 15 (15:15-30) confirms the birth from a cow, and 25:64-76 says the childless king took him up.
event: Aputhiran dies by fasting on Manipallavam, watched by Aravana Adigal, and is reborn from a cow in Savakam.

title: பாத்திரம் கொண்டு பிச்சை புக்க காதை
theme: Aravanar finishes Aputhiran's story, his rebirth from the cow's womb in Savakam and his rise to kingship, and charges Manimekalai not to lay aside the hunger-ending bowl; she enters Puhar's street in a nun's garb, and on her word that a chaste wife's alms are worthiest, the cursed and hungry Kayasandigai sends her to Athirai's house.
source_issues: Lines 51 and 81: the build removed a leftover HTML quote mark at the start of the line; the Tamil otherwise reads cleanly.
The break score of 3 after line 46 falls inside a rhetorical pair (46-47, துய்ப்பிலன்கொல்லோ? / அருளிலன்கொல்லோ); the units were recut at 45 and 54.
The kaathai ends at line 86 with காரிகை தான் என், the closing particle, after the speaker's name has been held back from என்றனள் at line 80.
Line 25 (மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து அகவையின்) is obscure in this text, and the date it gives cannot be fixed from it.

tamil: அந் நாள் அவனை ஓம்பிய நல் ஆத்
தன் நலம் பிறர் தொழத் தான் சென்று எய்தி
தான் முலை சுரந்து தன் பால் ஊட்டலும்
மழை வளம் சுரப்பவும் மன் உயிர் ஓம்பவும்
reading: Aravanar goes on with Aputhiran's story: the good cow that once sheltered him, golden-horned and golden-hoofed, came to the great sage Manmukhan by the white mountain of Savakam and, before it had ever calved, gave its milk to every creature, and the sage who knew the three times foretold that from its womb would come a protector of lives to make the rain abound, born not with the cord about him but within a golden egg.
nuance: The cow nurses all creatures before calving (ஈனாமுன்னம்), so its gift of milk precedes and announces the birth; and the prophecy names the newborn's work as bringing rain and guarding lives (11-12), the very want that drove Aputhiran from Madurai toward rainless Savakam in the previous kaathai.
event: In Savakam a golden-horned cow gives its milk to all creatures before calving, and the sage Manmukhan foretells that a protector of lives will be born from its womb in a golden egg.

tamil: பிணி நோய் இன்றியும் பிறந்து அறம் செய்ய
ஆங்கு அவ் ஆ வயிற்று அமரர் கணம் உவப்பத்
தீம் கனி நாவல் ஓங்கும் இத் தீவினுக்கு
ஒரு தான் ஆகி உலகு தொழத் தோன்றினன்
reading: Aravanar says that the one who gave up his life on Manipallavam, because his steady heart never let go of the cow that had once guarded and fed him, was born from that cow's womb to the gods' delight, one alone for this jambu island, and he tells the season of the birth, a day of spring fixed to the Bodhi lord's own, when a rain of holy water and flowers fell over the whole earth without a cloud.
nuance: The cause given for the womb he is born from is a bond of the mind: he 'did not let go' of the cow with an unwavering heart (17-18), which reads as gratitude carried through death; kaathai 14 had given his dying intent to sustain lives as the cause of the birth itself. The date at 23-26 is reckoned by the season, the sun in Taurus and the Buddha's day; line 25 (மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து அகவையின்) is obscure, and the reading does not rest on it.
event: Aputhiran, who died on Manipallavam, is born from the cow's womb in Savakam in spring, and holy water and flowers rain over the earth without clouds.
unit_note: End moved from line 30 to 28: line 28 (சொரிந்தது) closes the account of the rain, and the quotation at 29-30 belongs with its speakers, the ascetics named at 31-32.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவன் தன் திறம் அறவணன் அறியும்" என்று
ஈங்கு என் நாவை வருத்தியது இது கேள்
நிரை தார் வேந்தன் ஆயினன் அவன் தான்
reading: The ascetics of the Chakravala kottam, marvelling that such wonders were seen though it was not the time of a Buddha's coming, went through the thick dark to ask the image a god had painted on the pillar, which told them that the one who died on Manipallavam had arisen in Savakam to save lives and that Aravanan knew his story; that, Aravanar says, is what set his tongue to telling it; and the king of Savakam, bowing at Manmukhan's feet and saying that he had no child and had gained a son by the sage's grace, raised the boy, who became king since the wealth of rule was his.
nuance: Aravanar names the pillar image as the source that sends the knowledge to him (36-39), so his account of a rebirth across the sea is given a witness; the childless king takes the egg-born child as a gift of a sage's grace (42-43), and the poem passes over how a foundling took the throne with the bare remark that the wealth of kingship was his (44).
event: The pillar image tells the ascetics of the Chakravala kottam that Aputhiran is reborn in Savakam, and the childless king of Savakam takes him from the sage Manmukhan as a son, and he becomes king.
unit_note: Start moved from line 31 to 29 so that the ascetics' quoted marvel (29-30, ending என) sits with their naming at 31-32; end moved from line 46 to 45, where ஆயினன் அவன் தான் closes the account of his kingship, since line 46 opens a rhetorical pair completed at 47.

tamil: வறன் ஓடு உலகின் வான் துயர் கெடுக்கும்
அறன் ஓடு ஒழித்தல் ஆய் இழை! தகாது' என
reading: Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven lacks his share or the king of the just sceptre lacks grace, observes that though the Kaveri swells and spreads its water a season of want has come on every living thing, and tells Manimekalai that to put away the bowl that ends the world's great hunger, as the gods put away the leftover nectar the white waves gave them, is not fitting.
nuance: The two questions (46-47) seem to clear both the god of rain and the just king, so the want of 48-50 is given no culprit; the sense of துய்ப்பிலன் is uncertain. The comparison at 51-52 turns the gods' nectar, saved and kept after they had eaten, into the type of a hoard withheld from the hungry.
event: Aravanar tells Manimekalai that want has come despite the flowing Kaveri and that she must not lay the bowl aside.
unit_note: Units 31-46 and 47-60 were recut: this unit starts at 46, where the rhetorical pair begins, and ends at 54, where தகாது' என closes Aravanar's speech.

reading: When the sage has spoken, Manimekalai bows with her mothers, takes up the divine bowl and goes in a bhikkhuni's garb into the great street, and the town's little folk, rakes and libertines crowd round with noise, pitying her as men once pitied Yugi the Brahmin of Ujjain in a sickness unsuited to his form, when he freed the Vatsa king of Kosambi from his bonds, and they grieve that the honey-haired girl Udayakumaran had set his heart on has come carrying a begging bowl.
nuance: The crowd sees disgrace in the bowl (சிந்தை நோய் கூர), while the simile likens her garb to Yugi's feigned disease, a guise that hid a plan to free a king from prison; the onlookers are the same 'rakes and libertines' (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும்) who in kaathai 14 idled in Aputhiran's hall once plenty made his bowl useless. Udayakumaran is only named, not present.
event: Manimekalai bows with her mothers and goes into the great street in a nun's garb with the bowl, and the townsfolk crowd round, grieving that the girl the prince loved now carries a begging bowl.
unit_note: Start moved from line 61 to 55, where மாதவன் உரைத்தலும் opens the narration after Aravanar's speech; end moved from 74 to 70, where சிந்தை நோய் கூர closes the crowd's sentence begun at 59, before Manimekalai speaks at 71.

tamil: அணி மலர்ப் பூங் கொம்பு 'அகம் மலி உவகையின்
பிச்சை ஏற்றல் பெருந் தகவு உடைத்து' எனக்
ஆதிரை நல்லாள்? அவள் மனை இம் மனை
வட திசை விஞ்சை மா நகர்த் தோன்றித்
தென் திசைப் பொதியில் ஓர் சிற்றியாற்று அடைகரை
வீவு இல் வெம் பசி வேட்கையொடு திரிதரும்
reading: The flowering branch Madhavi bore says with full gladness that to receive the alms good chaste wives give is a thing of great worth, and Kayasandigai, a woman of the northern vidyadhara city who, her harsh deed ripening through a sage's curse by a stream on southern Pothiyil, wanders in unending fierce hunger, tells her that Athirai stands alone among the house-dwelling wives whose chastity gives rain, like one lotus risen above the rest in a pool, and that this is her house, which she should enter.
nuance: The nun's first choice is of a giver, not of food: the bowl is to take its first alms from a pathini, and the one who points the way is herself a woman suffering the fruit of her own deed. Manimekalai is named here as Madhavi's child (மாதவி ஈன்ற) just as she seeks a chaste wife's alms, and Kayasandigai's praise of Athirai's rain-giving karpu (77) answers her claim at once.
event: Manimekalai says that alms from a chaste wife are worthiest, and Kayasandigai, a vidyadhara woman cursed to endless hunger, tells her to enter Athirai's house.
unit_note: Start moved from line 75 to 71, so that Manimekalai's claim (71-74, ending எனக்) stands with the reply it prompts; the unit runs to the kaathai's end.

title: ஆதிரை பிச்சையிட்ட காதை
theme: Kayasandigai tells Manimekalai why Aathirai's house should give the first alms: Aathirai's husband Saathuvan, ruined by a courtesan and dice, was wrecked at sea and reported dead; Aathirai entered a funeral fire that would not burn her, and a heavenly voice promised his return; on the island of the naked cannibal Nagas Saathuvan, knowing their language, refused their woman, liquor and meat, argued for rebirth from the corpse and the dream, gave their chief a dharma he could keep, and came home with treasure. Aathirai then fills the bowl Amudasurabi, praying that hunger leave the whole earth.
source_issues: Line 105: the edition's ௌ before a vowel sign was read as ெள (தௌி repaired to தெளி); the repair fits the sense 'know clearly'.
