tamil: நளி இரு முந்நீர் வளி கலன் வௌவ
ஒடி மரம் பற்றி ஊர் திரை உதைப்ப
"இடை இருள் யாமத்து எறி திரைப் பெருங் கடல்
உடை கலப் பட்டு ஆங்கு ஒழிந்தோர் தம்முடன்
reading: Kayasandigai begins Aathirai's story for Manimekalai: her husband Saathuvan, lacking worth, left her for a courtesan who fed him, squandered his wealth on dice and gaming, was cast off by the courtesan as a man without a coin once his wealth was gone, sailed off with merchants in restless desire, was wrecked, clung to a broken spar and was washed to the hill of the naked Nagas, while the men who escaped the wreck reported that he had died with the others in the dark sea.
nuance: The tale is told as a lesson attached to a house: Kayasandigai sends Manimekalai to Aathirai's door and then explains why it is the right first door, and she begins not with Aathirai's virtue but with her husband's fault (தகவு இலன், line 4). Line 16 tells the reader ahead of time that he came to belong to the Nagas (அவர் பான்மையன் ஆயினன்), so the survivors' report of his death at line 21 is known to be false before Aathirai hears it.
event: Saathuvan leaves Aathirai for a courtesan, loses his wealth at dice, is cast off, sails with merchants and is shipwrecked; survivors report him dead.

tamil: ஆதிரை நல்லாள் ஆங்கு அது தான் கேட்டு
உடுத்த கூறையும் ஒள் எரி உறா அது
விரை மலர்த் தாமரை ஒரு தனி இருந்த
ஊர் திரை கொண்டு ஆங்கு உய்ப்பப் போகி
நின் பெருந் துன்பம் ஒழிவாய் நீ" என
reading: Hearing the report, Aathirai calls on the townsfolk to give her a funeral pyre, digs a pit in the burning ground, lights a fire of dry wood and enters it saying she will go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire touches neither her bed, her cloth, her sandal paste nor the garland in her hair, so that she sits in it unharmed like Lakshmi alone on a lotus, and when she cries that she is a woman of evil deeds whom even fire will not kill, a voice tells her that her husband reached the Naga hill and will come back on the ship of the merchant Chandradattan.
nuance: Aathirai reads the miracle backwards: the fire's refusal, which the story offers as proof of her virtue, she takes as proof of her own bad karma (தீயும் கொல்லாத் தீவினையாட்டியேன், line 35). Her reason for entering the fire is also karmic and not only grief: she means to follow her husband into whatever birth his deeds have led him (வினைப் பயன் உய்ப்ப, line 27). The lotus and the goddess on it (lines 33-34) echo the image by which Kayasandigai praised her at the close of the previous kaathai.
event: Aathirai enters a funeral fire for her husband; it does not burn her, and a voice from the sky tells her he lives and will return.

tamil: ஐ அரி உண் கண் அழு துயர் நீங்கி
கண் மணி அனையான் கடிது ஈங்கு உறுக!" என
ஓங்கு உயர் பிறங்கல் ஒரு மர நீழல்
மஞ்சு உடை மால் கடல் உழந்த நோய் கூர்ந்து
துஞ்சு துயில்கொள்ள அச் சூர் மலை வாழும்
ஊன் உடை இவ் உடம்பு உணவு" என்று எழுப்பலும்
reading: When the bodiless voice has spoken from the sky, Aathirai's tears cease, she goes home untroubled like a woman coming back from a bath in a pool and prays for her husband's quick return, becoming one whom even the chaste wives who never fail in merit and bring down the rain revere; meanwhile her husband, worn out by the sea, sleeps in a tree's shade on the shore of the high hill, and the unkind naked Nagas who live there find him and rouse him, saying that this lone, pitiable man come by himself is a body of flesh fit for food.
nuance: The rank given here goes beyond the rain-bringing wife: the women whose word brings rain themselves worship Aathirai (lines 49-51), so the test by fire sets her above the very standard of chastity. The simile at line 46, a woman returning from bathing in a pool, turns the pyre she has just left into water. The scene then cuts from a wife whose fire would not burn her body to a husband whose body is about to be eaten.
event: Aathirai goes home comforted; on the island the naked Nagas find the sleeping Saathuvan and mean to eat him.

tamil: மற்று அவர் பாடை மயக்கு அறு மரபின்
கள் அடு குழிசியும் கழி முடை நாற்றமும்
கோடு உயர் மர நிழல் குளிர்ந்த பின் அவன்
ஆங்கு அவற்கு அலை கடல் உற்றதை உரைத்தலும்
வெங் களும் ஊனும் வேண்டுவ கொடும்" என
reading: Because Saathuvan had learned their language well, the fierce men stop, bow and talk with him and lead him to their chief, whom he finds sitting with his woman like a bear with its mate in a place full of liquor pots, a reek of rotting flesh and white bones drying; bound to him by the shared tongue, the chief asks in the cool of a tree why he came, hears of his sufferings at sea, and orders his people to give the starving man a young woman, strong liquor and meat.
nuance: Saathuvan is saved by learning, not by virtue: knowing the Nagas' speech (பாடை, lines 60 and 70) turns him from food into a guest. The chief's welcome is generous by his own lights, offering what he holds most valuable, which sets up the coming debate as a clash of goods rather than of kindness and cruelty.
event: Saathuvan speaks to the Nagas in their language and is led to their chief, who orders a woman, liquor and meat to be given to him.

tamil: அல் அறம் செய்வோர் அரு நரகு அடைதலும்
reading: Saathuvan, dismayed, says he has heard a cruel word and wants none of it; the chief, provoked to anger, asks what use there is for men in the world without women and food and bids him show it if there is any; Saathuvan answers that the faultless have forbidden deluding liquor and the killing of living beings, because dying and being born are like sleeping and waking, and the doers of good reach a good world and the doers of ill a hard hell.
nuance: The man who lost everything to a courtesan and to dice now refuses a woman and liquor offered as hospitality, so the refusal reads as the reversal of his fall in the first unit. His reason for abstaining is not disgust but a world-view: abstinence follows from rebirth and its fruits. Line 86-87 puts the sleep-and-waking simile of Kural 339 in other words (உறங்கலும் விழித்தலும்), too far from the couplet's wording to count as an echo. The sentence runs on into line 90.
event: Saathuvan refuses the woman, liquor and meat; the angry chief challenges him and Saathuvan explains why the wise forbid liquor and killing.

tamil: கண்டனை ஆக!" என கடு நகை எய்தி
"உடம்பு விட்டு ஓடும் உயிர் உருக் கொண்டு ஓர்
இடம் புகும் என்றே எமக்கு ஈங்கு உரைத்தாய்
அவ் உயிர் எவ்வணம் போய்ப் புகும், அவ் வகை
உடம்பிடைப் போனது ஒன்று உண்டு என உணர் நீ
போனார் தமக்கு ஓர் புக்கில் உண்டு என்பது
உடம்பு ஈண்டு ஒழிய உயிர் பல காவதம்
ஆங்கனம் போகி அவ் உயிர் செய் வினை
என்று அவன் உரைத்தலும் எரி விழி நாகனும்
reading: Saathuvan ends that the wise gave these things up because they understood this; the chief laughs harshly and demands to be told plainly how a life that runs out of the body takes on a form and enters another place; Saathuvan, without anger, argues that the body feels while life dwells in it, but once life leaves, the body feels nothing though it is cut and burned, so something has gone out of it; that the departed have a dwelling everyone knows, not he alone; that in dreams the life goes many leagues while the body stays here; and that, going so, the life enters the body its own deeds have put on.
nuance: Saathuvan answers a request for a mechanism with two proofs by inference: the corpse's insensibility (lines 96-99) and the dream journey (lines 102-103), each leading to the conclusion that something leaves the body. It is a lay merchant's argument, not a monk's, and it speaks of a life (உயிர்) that travels and enters a new body, which the Buddhist teaching later in the epic would put differently; the text names no school for it. The chief had already granted the soul in his question (line 92 repeats what he was told), so the argument persuades him without his ever conceding the premise in words.
event: The chief mockingly asks how a life can pass into another body, and Saathuvan answers him with the corpse and the dream.

tamil: நன்று அறி செட்டி நல் அடி வீழ்ந்து
உள் உறை வாழ் உயிர் ஓம்புதல் ஆற்றேன்
எமக்கு ஆம் நல் அறம் எடுத்து உரை" என்றலும்
உன் தனக்கு ஒல்லும் நெறி அறம் உரைத்தேன்
உடை கல மாக்கள் உயிர் உய்ந்து ஈங்கு உறின்
அடு தொழில் ஒழிந்து அவர் ஆர் உயிர் ஓம்பி
மூத்து விளி மா ஒழித்து எவ் உயிர்மாட்டும்
reading: The chief falls at the feet of the merchant who knows the good and says that if he gives up liquor and meat he cannot keep alive the life within this body, so he asks to be told a good dharma that suits them until they die in their own way; Saathuvan praises the request, says he will tell the dharma within his reach, and bids him, if shipwrecked men come here alive, to stop killing and protect their lives, and, leaving aside the beasts that die of old age, to give up harm toward every living thing.
nuance: Saathuvan does not ask the Nagas for the full abstinence he practises; he scales dharma to what they can bear (உன் தனக்கு ஒல்லும் நெறி அறம், line 113). The sense of line 116 is not certain: மூத்து விளி மா ஒழித்து seems to set aside animals that die of age as the one flesh still allowed, flesh that needs no killing, but it may instead belong with the prohibition. The command closes at line 117.
event: The chief, persuaded, asks for a dharma he can keep, and Saathuvan gives him a lesser rule: spare the shipwrecked and harm no living thing.

விரை மரம் மென் துகில் விழு நிதிக் குப்பையோடு
இவை இவை கொள்க" என எடுத்தனன் கொணர்ந்து
இந் நகர் புகுந்து ஈங்கு இவளொடு வாழ்ந்து
தன் மனை நன் பல தானமும் செய்தனன்
பூங் கொடி நல்லாய்! பிச்சை பெறுக!" என
தொழுது வலம் கொண்டு துயர் அறு கிளவியோடு
reading: The chief promises to keep this dharma and bids Saathuvan take the precious goods fit for him, the fragrant wood, fine cloth and heaps of treasure of men from wrecked ships whom they had eaten before; Saathuvan boards Chandradattan's ship when it comes, returns to this city, lives with Aathirai and gives many gifts from his house; Kayasandigai bids Manimekalai take alms from such an Aathirai's hand, and when Manimekalai enters and stands like an unadorned picture, Aathirai bows, circles her and fills the wide bowl Amudasurabi, saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth', and gives the food that is medicine for precious life.
nuance: The wealth that ends the story is the plunder of men the Nagas ate, now given as a teacher's fee and spent on charity at home; the cannibal's hoard becomes the merchant's alms. The voice's prophecy is fulfilled in a single line (line 124). Kayasandigai's speech ends at line 129, and lines 130-135 are the poet's narration. Aathirai's wish at line 134 turns one gift into a vow for the whole earth, and line 135 names the food ஆருயிர்மருந்து, a name the bowl's story uses elsewhere.
event: Saathuvan returns home rich on Chandradattan's ship; Aathirai puts the first alms into Manimekalai's bowl.

title: உலக அறவி புக்க காதை
theme: Manimekalai feeds the crowd from the bowl a chaste wife first filled and cures Kayasandigai's insatiable 'elephant-fire' hunger; Kayasandigai tells how, as her evil deed ripened, she crushed the twelve-yearly fruit of the fasting sage Viruchikan and was cursed with hunger and the loss of her sky mantra, then sends Manimekalai to the public hall (உலக அறவி) where the hungry and the friendless sick wait, and Manimekalai, holding up Aputhiran's bowl, calls all who would receive.
source_issues: Line 72 (பின் வரும் யாண்டு அவன் எண்ணினன் கழியும்) does not construe cleanly: whether the vidyadhara counts the coming years and departs, or the counted years of the curse are now passing, cannot be fixed from the line; the unit is marked uncertain.
Line 48 (இந் நாள் போலும் இளங்கொடி! கெடுத்தனை!) is elliptical: it may say the curse's term falls today or that Manimekalai has ended it before its term.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, now carrying the Amudhasurabhi bowl
a vidyadhara woman cursed with an insatiable hunger (ஆனைத்தீ)
Kayachandigai's vidyadhara husband (called விஞ்சையன் here, not named)
an ascetic by the Pothiyil forest river who eats one fruit in twelve years and curses Kayasandigai
the earlier owner of the bowl, named in Manimekalai's call

tamil: வாங்கு கை வருந்த மன் உயிர்க்கு அளித்துத்
குரங்கு கொணர்ந்து எறிந்த நெடு மலை எல்லாம்
இட்டது ஆற்றாக் கட்டு அழல் கடும் பசிப்
பட்டேன் என் தன் பழ வினைப் பயத்தால்
அன்னை கேள் நீ ஆர் உயிர் மருத்துவி
reading: The narrator likens the bowl, whose first food a chaste wife gave, to wealth won by dharma that flows the way of the virtuous: Manimekalai gives to living beings till the receivers' hands ache and it never runs low, and Kayasandigai, who carries the elephant-fire disease in her belly, bows and asks her, as physician of life, to cure a hunger that swallows whatever is given as the sea swallowed the hills the monkeys threw when the Tall One bridged it, a hunger she says came from her old deeds.
nuance: Two causes meet in one sentence of Kayasandigai's: the hunger is a disease (நோய், 7 and 16) and the fruit of old deeds (பழ வினைப் பயத்தால், 14), so the cure she seeks is food from another's hand, not merit of her own. The epic names Vishnu's descent as Rama with the word மயங்கி (9), 'bewildered' or 'having taken on confusion', a casual Buddhist touch on a Vaishnava story that the line does not develop. She calls Manimekalai ஆர் உயிர் மருத்துவி, the Sangam title of the giver as physician of hunger turned feminine.
event: Manimekalai feeds many from the alms bowl, and Kayasandigai, bowing, begs her to cure her insatiable hunger.

tamil: வயிறு காய் பெரும் பசி நீங்கி மற்று அவள்
காசு இல் காஞ்சனபுரக் கடி நகர் உள்ளேன்
விஞ்சையன் தன்னொடு என் வெவ் வினை உருப்பத்
இடு மணல் கான் யாற்று இயைந்து ஒருங்கு இருந்தேன்
புரி நூல் மார்பின் திரி புரி வார் சடை
பெருங் குலைப் பெண்ணைக் கருங் கனி அனையது ஓர்
இருங் கனி நாவல் பழம் ஒன்று ஏந்தி
தேக்கு இலை வைத்துச் சேண் நாறு பரப்பின்
reading: Manimekalai puts food from the bowl into Kayasandigai's hand, her burning hunger and grief leave her, and she begins her story: she lived in Kanchanapuram on the northern ridge of the vidyadharas, came south with her vidyadhara to see Pothiyil as her cruel deed was ripening, and stayed by a forest river where Viruchikan, a sage with the sacred thread, twisted matted locks and bark clothes, set a great jambu fruit like a palm fruit on a teak leaf and went to bathe in a lotus pool.
nuance: The journey itself is credited to the ripening deed (என் வெவ் வினை உருப்ப, 23) before anything wrong is done: karma here moves the traveller to the place of the offence. Viruchikan's marks (thread, matted hair, bark) are those of a Brahmin forest ascetic, not a Buddhist monk.
event: Kayasandigai, fed, tells how she came south with her vidyadhara and how the sage Viruchikan left his fruit on a leaf to bathe.

tamil: ஈர் ஆறு ஆண்டில் ஒரு கனி தருவது
அக் கனி உண்டோர் ஆறு ஈர் ஆண்டு
முந்நால் ஆண்டில் முதிர் கனி நான் ஈங்கு
உண்ணும் நாள் உன் உறு பசி களைக!" என
அந் நாள் ஆங்கு அவன் இட்ட சாபம்
reading: Driven by her ripening evil deed she went proudly and crushed the fruit with her foot; Viruchikan, coming to eat, saw it and cursed her: the divine jambu gives one fruit in twelve years that frees a human body from hunger for twelve years, he fasts but one day in twelve years, and since she crushed his food she shall lose her sky-travelling mantra and suffer alone the elephant-fire until, twelve years on, he eats a ripe fruit here; and she tells Manimekalai that the curse of that day seems to end today, for she has destroyed it.
nuance: The curse is measured exactly against the sage's loss: he must now fast twelve more years, and she must hunger until he eats. Her own account puts the cause first in her deed (தீவினை உருத்தலின், 33) and only then in her pride (செருக்கு). Line 48 may mean the term falls today or that Manimekalai's food has ended it early.
event: Kayasandigai crushes Viruchikan's fruit, and he curses her with ceaseless hunger and the loss of her sky mantra for twelve years.

நோற்றோர் உறைவது ஓர் நோன் நகர் உண்டால்
அப் பதிப் புகுக" என்று அவன் அருள்செய்ய
இப் பதிப் புகுந்து ஈங்கு யான் உறைகின்றேன்
இந்திர கோடணை விழவு அணி வரு நாள்
வந்து தோன்றி இம் மா நகர் மருங்கே
reading: When the sage, himself left to wasting hunger, had gone, the vidyadhara who had fled in fear of her rash act came back grieving, told her she suffered without cause at the hands of a terrible ascetic and bade her rise into the sky, but she had forgotten the mantra; the fruits, roots and vegetables he fetched could not satisfy her, and, unable to leave her, he told her kindly of a strong city in the Tamil land of Jambudvipa where unshaken rich men help those who cannot help themselves and ascetics dwell, and bade her go there by land, so she came to this city.
nuance: Her husband calls the curse causeless (காரணம் இன்றியும், 54) where she has just named her own deed as its cause: the unit keeps both views without settling them. Puhar is introduced by its charity, ஆற்றா மாக்கட்கு ஆற்றும் துணை (64), which plays on the verb ஆற்று as Kural 225 does.
event: The vidyadhara returns, finds she has lost her sky mantra and cannot be fed, and sends her on foot to Puhar, the Tamil city of givers.

tamil: என் உறு பெரும் பசி கண்டனன் இரங்கி
பின் வரும் யாண்டு அவன் எண்ணினன் கழியும்
தணிவு இல் வெம் பசி தவிர்த்தனை வணங்கினேன்
பலர் புகத் திறந்த பகு வாய் வாயில்
வடு வாழ் கூந்தல்! அதன்பால் போக' என்று
reading: On the day of Indra's festival the vidyadhara comes to the city, sees her hunger and pities her, counting the years to come; she bows to Manimekalai for removing her unabating hunger, says she will now go to her sky city, and tells her of the public hall in the Chakravala kottam of the stainless ascetics, with a wide gate open to all, where the hungry of every town and the sick who have no one wait, choosing their givers, and bids her go there.
nuance: The hall is described from the side of the receivers: they wait and choose who will give (இடுவோர்த் தேர்ந்து, 81), not the givers choosing whom to feed. Line 72 is unclear (see source_issues).
event: Kayasandigai thanks Manimekalai, prepares to return to her sky city, and directs her to the public hall where the hungry and friendless sick wait.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவள் போகிய பின்னர் ஆய் இழை
வல முறை மும் முறை வந்தனை செய்து அவ்
கந்து உடை நெடு நிலைக் காரணம் காட்டிய
தம் துணைப் பாவையைத் தான் தொழுது ஏத்தி
வெயில் சுட வெம்பிய வேய் கரி கானத்துக்
யாணர்ப் பேர் ஊர் அம்பல மருங்கு என்
reading: When Kayasandigai has gone, Manimekalai steps aside in the high street, circles the public hall three times, enters it, worships the shrine of the old goddess whom the townsfolk praise and the pillar image that showed her the cause, and like a rain cloud over a sun-scorched bamboo forest appears with the Amudhasurabhi before the hunger-wasted, calling that this is Aputhiran's bowl and all who would receive should come, and the noise of eating rises by the hall of the rich city.
nuance: The closing ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி (97) and யாணர் (98) are the words of Purananuru 173's feast at a patron's house; here the feast has no patron, and the giver names the bowl's former owner rather than herself.
event: Manimekalai worships at the public hall and, holding up Aputhiran's bowl, calls all the hungry to come, and they eat.

title: உதயகுமரன் அம்பலம் புக்க காதை
theme: Chithirapathi, the courtesan grandmother, vows to drag Manimekalai back to the dancers' life and urges Prince Udayakumaran to seize her as royal custom allows; the prince, ignoring the goddess's warning, confronts Manimekalai in the public hall, where she bows to him as her husband of a former birth but answers that the body is a vessel of suffering, then hides from him in Kaayasandigai's form in the old goddess's shrine, where he vows to stay until she is given to him.
source_issues: Line 62 reads பாழ்ம்ம் பறந்தலை with a doubled ம்; probably a typing error for பாழ்ம் or பாழ் பறந்தலை.
The unit boundary at 156/157 falls inside the prince's speech to the goddess (153-172), which runs across both units with no sentence close at 156.
Lines 55-63 and 64-76 contain two speakers (Chithirapathi, then the prince) in one unit; the division rests on the quotatives at 63 and 65.

cast.role: Madhavi's mother, a courtesan of Puhar
the dancing women of Chithirapathi's house, to whom she makes her vow
the Chola prince of Puhar who pursues Manimekalai; Rahula of her former birth
Madhavi's daughter, now a Buddhist ascetic feeding the hungry from her bowl
the sea goddess who warned the prince at midnight
the old goddess of the shrine beside the public hall, petitioned by Manimekalai and the prince

tamil: ஆங்கு அது கேட்டு ஆங்கு அரும் புண் அகவயின்
தீத் துறு செங் கோல் சென்று சுட்டாங்குக்
இது தக்கு என்போர்க்கு எள் உரை ஆயது!
முளி எரிப் புகூஉம் முது குடிப் பிறந்த
reading: Burning with anger at the news of Manimekalai's begging, Chithirapathi vows to end 'this dharma' and tells the dancing women that Madhavi's retreat to the monks' house after Kovalan's death has made the city laugh, since women of their house are not pathini wives of old families who, unable to outlive a husband, enter fire as if bathing in a pool, but live on the hands of many.
nuance: Chithirapathi reuses Madhavi's own words from kaathai 2: 'staying alive though the lover died' (போதல்செய்யா உயிரொடு, 12) and the widow who enters fire as a pool (13-14). Madhavi used them to confess her shame; her mother uses them to argue that a courtesan owes no widow's grief at all.
event: Hearing that Manimekalai begs in the public hall, Chithirapathi resolves to end her daughter's and granddaughter's renunciation and addresses the dancing women.

tamil: பாண் மகன் பட்டுழிப் படூஉம் பான்மை இல்
நறுந் தாது உண்டு நயன் இல் காலை
reading: Chithirapathi goes on that courtesans are not like a lute that dies with its bard but like bees that leave a drained flower, and like Fortune herself leave a man when his merit runs out, so that their taking an ascetic's dress is a joke; and she swears that unless she has Udayakumaran show Manimekalai's begging bowl to the beggars and carry her off in his golden car, she will be paraded round the stage carrying burnt brick like a disgraced dancer and never enter a dancer's house again.
nuance: She names her own penalty in the form of a vow (the next unit calls it வஞ்சினம், 37), with a professional disgrace as the forfeit. Her picture of courtesans as bees on a drained flower (19-20) is the moralists' charge made from inside the profession, and offered as its rule.
event: Chithirapathi swears before the dancing women that she will have the prince carry Manimekalai off or suffer a courtesan's public disgrace.

tamil: செறி வளை நல்லார் சிலர் புறம் சூழக்
குறு வியர் பொடித்த கோல வாள் முகத்தள்
தரு மணல் ஞெமிரிய திரு நாறு ஒரு சிறைப்
பவழத் தூணத்து பசும் பொன் செஞ் சுவர்த்
விளங்கு ஒளி பரந்த பளிங்கு செய் மண்டபத்து
துளங்கும் மான் ஊர்தித் தூ மலர்ப் பள்ளி
வெண் திரை விரிந்த வெண் நிறச் சாமரை
இருந்தோன் திருந்து அடி பொருந்தி நின்று ஏத்தித்
திருந்து எயிறு இலங்கச் செவ்வியின் நக்கு அவன்
reading: Having sworn her vow and chosen deceitful words, Chithirapathi walks through the chariot street with a few bangled women to the young prince, who lies in a crystal hall on a couch with women fanning him, bows at his feet, and when she smiles he asks whether the ascetic dress Madhavi took with Manimekalai is still unbroken.
nuance: The splendour of the prince's hall (43-50) is set between the courtesan's sweat-beaded face and her lie: she comes on foot along a chariot road to a man who has not moved. The question at 53-54 is the prince's, sounding out the vow before she makes her offer.
event: Chithirapathi goes to Udayakumaran's palace, bows to him, and he asks after Madhavi's and Manimekalai's ascetic vow.

tamil: ஒரு தனி ஓங்கிய திரு மணிக் காஞ்சி
வாழ்க நின் கண்ணி! வாய் வாள் வேந்து!' என
வான் புணை பெற்றென மற்று அவட்கு உரைப்போன்
காந்தள் அம் செங் கை தளை பிணி விடாஅ
ஏந்து இள வன முலை இறை நெரித்ததூஉம்
மா இதழ்க் குவளை மலர் புறத்து ஓட்டிக்
காய் வேல் வென்ற கருங் கயல் நெடுங் கண்
reading: Chithirapathi answers that the flower has opened for the bee called Udayakumaran and now stands in the ruined public hall, and the prince, like a shipwrecked man given a raft, tells her how he dismissed the girl in the crystal pavilion as a painted image until her hands, breasts, smile and eyes told him she had already guessed his mind.
nuance: Lines 55-63 are Chithirapathi's answer and 64-76 the prince's reply; the opening image of the jewelled kanchi where the heron breeds and the flower blooms for Bharata's dance (55-59) is obscure, and the speaker division rests on the quotative என at 63 and 65.
event: Chithirapathi tells the prince that Manimekalai is in the public hall, and he recounts seeing her in the crystal pavilion.

tamil: உளம் கொண்டு ஒளித்தாள் உயிர்க் காப்பிட்டு" என்று
அங்கு அவள் தன் திறம் அயர்ப்பாய்" என்றனள்
எய்யா மையலேன் யான்! என்று அவன் சொலச்
reading: The prince ends that the coral doll in the crystal stole his heart, and that at midnight a golden woman appeared, showed him a sceptre and told him to forget the girl who has taken up austerity, so that he cannot tell whether it was a god or a vision; Chithirapathi laughs and tells him to let it go, since even gods are confused in the drunken play of desire.
nuance: The goddess's warning in kaathai 7 was an argument about the sceptre, rain and the people's lives; the prince remembers only a sceptre shown and an order, and treats it as a riddle (84-85), which lets the courtesan dissolve it with a laugh.
event: Udayakumaran tells Chithirapathi of the goddess who warned him at midnight with a sceptre, and Chithirapathi laughs it off.

tamil: ஆயிரம் செங் கண் அமரர் கோன் பெற்றதும்
அருந் திறல் முனிவர்க்கு ஆர் அணங்கு ஆகிய
reading: Chithirapathi gives her examples: the king of the gods who got a thousand eyes for his longing after a sage's wife, and the fire god's wife who took the forms of the sages' wives at the lake on Meru to quench his desire for them.
nuance: She draws on stories of gods to make the prince's desire seem natural; the second story turns on the wife of Agni (அங்கி மனையாள்) assuming other women's forms, which anticipates Manimekalai taking another woman's form later in the kaathai.
unit_note: Lower boundary moved from line 99 to line 97: the sentence 'கேட்டும் அறிதியோ வாள் திறல் குருசில்?' closes at 97, and 98-102 begin a new sentence that ends at பிறந்தாள் அல்லள் (102).

tamil: சுருப்பு நாண் கருப்பு வில் அருப்புக் கணை தூவச்
செருக் கயல் நெடுங் கண் சுருக்கு வலைப் படுத்துக்
பண் தேர் மொழியின் பயன் பல வாங்கி
விரை பரி நெடுந் தேர்மேல் சென்று ஏறி
காடு அமர் செல்வி கடிப் பசி களைய
தீப் பசி மாக்கட்குச் செழுஞ் சோறு ஈத்துப்
reading: Chithirapathi argues that Manimekalai is not born of the families whose women guard themselves as maiden, wife and widow and worship no god but the man who took them, but of dancers who capture men with art and leave them like bees, so binding such a woman and silencing her false talk is a prince's right; inflamed, the prince drives to the hall, sees her feeding the hungry like the forest goddess feeding with a skull bowl, and asks himself why the thief of his heart has taken up begging.
nuance: The definition of the chaste family at 101 (கொண்டோன் அல்லது தெய்வமும் பேணா) is the Kural 55 ideal in other words; here it serves to exclude Manimekalai from the protection chastity gives. The goddess's speech in kaathai 7 (7:1-14) had already told the prince the opposite of 'கோன்முறை' (111): that wronging a woman under austerity bends the sceptre. The work does not answer Chithirapathi in this unit.
event: Chithirapathi urges the prince to seize Manimekalai as royal custom allows; he drives to the public hall and sees her feeding the hungry from her bowl.
unit_note: Upper boundary moved from line 100 to line 98, to keep the sentence of 98-102 in one unit (see manimekalai:18:90-97).

tamil: தன் அடி தொழுதலும் தகவு!' என வணங்கி
இறை வளை முன்கை ஈங்கு இவன் பற்றினும்
தோட்ட செவியை நீ ஆகுவை ஆம் எனின்
reading: The prince asks her why she has taken up austerity; Manimekalai, knowing him for her husband Rahula of a former birth, bows to him, admits her heart goes out to him, and, since it is wrong to refuse a former husband's word, answers that she has understood the human body to be a vessel of suffering that is born, ages, sickens and dies, and so chose the higher dharma, adds that warriors do not heed women's wisdom, and tells him to do as he likes.
nuance: She keeps the former-birth rule (132-133) by answering exactly the question he asked, and makes the answer a refusal. Her words at 136-138 repeat Sudhamathi's lesson to the same prince in kaathai 4 (மக்கள் யாக்கை இது என உணர்ந்து). The jab at 140-141 expects the teaching to fail.
event: Udayakumaran questions Manimekalai in the hall; she bows to him as her former husband and tells him why she renounced.
unit_note: Lower boundary moved from line 141 to line 142: her speech closes at 'வேட்டது செய்க!' என (142), and 143 begins the narration of her leaving.

tamil: குச்சரக் குடிகை தன் அகம் புக்கு ஆங்கு
ஈங்கு இம் மண்ணீட்டு யார் என உணர்கேன்?
reading: Leaving the prince, Manimekalai enters the Gujarat-built shrine where the old first goddess sits, prays to her that none can know what men will do, recites the illusion-mantra and takes the form of Kaayasandigai; the prince comes in, approaches the goddess and demands to know how, with Kaayasandigai showing her begging bowl, he can tell which is Manimekalai hidden by illusion.
nuance: The 'old one' (முதியாள், 144) and 'the maiden of the shrine' (குமரி, 152) are taken here as the shrine's goddess, whom the prince addresses as a clay image at 156; the unit does not name her, and her identity with the city goddess Champapati is not stated here.
event: Manimekalai hides in the old goddess's shrine and takes Kaayasandigai's form by a mantra; the prince follows and questions the goddess.
unit_note: Upper boundary moved from line 142 to line 143 (see manimekalai:18:124-142).

tamil: ஆங்கு அவள் இவள் என்று அருளாய் ஆயிடின்
பவளச் செவ் வாய்த் தவள வாள் நகையும்
அஞ்சனம் சேராச் செங் கயல் நெடுங் கணும்
முரிந்து கடை நெரிய வரிந்த சிலைப் புருவமும்
குவி முள் கருவியும் கோணமும் கூர் நுனைக்
இது குறை' என்றனன் இறைமகன் தான் என்
reading: The prince tells the goddess that unless she shows him which one is Manimekalai he will lie at her shrine for many days, describes how the girl's lips, eyes and brows worked on him like an elephant-keeper's goads while she quoted old wisdom to tame him as a newly caught elephant, and swears by the goddess's feet that he will not leave without her.
nuance: He casts her teaching as a capture: her sayings (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி, 167) are one more instrument of the elephant hunt, so the sermon on the body is heard as seduction. The same phrase returns in kaathai 20 when Kaanchanan watches her speak to him.
event: Udayakumaran vows at the goddess's feet to stay at the shrine until he is given Manimekalai.

title: சிறைக்கோட்டம் அறக்கோட்டம் ஆக்கிய காதை
theme: Rebuked by a deity and pursued by his own desire, the prince withdraws; Manimekalai, to escape him, takes Kayachandigai's form and feeds the king's prisoners from the bowl, and while the king plays in his grove the guard reports her, and at her request he turns the prison into a house of dharma.
source_issues: Line 63 reads இரு சிறைக் விரித்து, with a doubled க் before வி; line 64 has the expected ஒரு சிறைக் கண்டு. Probably இரு சிறை விரித்து.
Line 109 reads வினைஞ்அர், a typing error for வினைஞர்.
Line 1 opens mid-scene: முதியாள் and the prince's வஞ்சினம் continue the previous kaathai.
Quotation marks are unbalanced: line 3 opens a single quote, line 9 a double, and line 16 closes with a single quote after அறிவாம்.
Line 162 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle.

Unit boundaries at 16/17 (break score 0), 49/50, 65/66, 77/78, 93/94, 108/109, 127/128 and 143/144 fell inside sentences or speeches; the chapter was recut into nine units: 1-28, 29-50, 51-66, 67-78, 79-92, 93-106, 107-116, 117-138, 139-162.

cast.role: the Chola king's son, who desires Manimekalai
a deity speaking from a crafted image in the old goddess's shrine, who rebukes the prince
the young men of the city playing lutes with their women at nightfall
Madhavi's daughter, here in Kayachandigai's form
the guards of the king's prison, one of whom reports to the king
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
the Chola queen, Udayakumaran's mother, of Mavali's line
the women skilled in dance, music and adornment who sport with the king
the craftsmen of Magadha, Maratha, Avanti, the Yavanas and the Tamil land who built the pavilion

tamil: பொதி அறைப் பட்டோர் போன்று மெய் வருந்தி
பை அரவு அல்குல் பலர் பசி களையக்
அகல் வாய் ஞாலம் ஆர் இருள் உண்ண
பகல் அரசு ஓட்டி பணை எழுந்து ஆர்ப்ப
காமர் செங் கை நீட்டி வண்டு படு
பூ நாறு கடாஅம் செருக்கி கால் கிளர்ந்து
இளி புணர் இன் சீர் எஃகு உளம் கிழிப்பப்
பறாஅக் குருகின் உயிர்த்து அவன் போய பின்
reading: After the prince bows three times at the old goddess's feet and swears his vow, a deity in a crafted image rebukes him for speaking rashly before 'our lady'; shaken, he counts three wonders (the deity who showed him the sceptre and told him to forget her, the bowl she carries to end many people's hunger, and the image's charge that he wronged the 'first lady' of old) and resolves to learn their meaning from the girl's later deeds, and he goes off as evening, pictured as a riderless musth elephant with the crescent for its tusk, hounds him and the city youths' lute music tears his heart.
nuance: Whom the image means by எம் கோமகள் (3) and முத்தை முதல்வி (13) is not settled by this unit: the old goddess of the shrine, or Manimekalai as his wife of a former birth (kaathai 10 told her the prince was Rahulan). The prince does not yield; he defers (பின் அறிவாம், 16). Evening comes 'with an aspect that destroys restraint' (நிறை அழி தோற்றமொடு, 23), so the loss of nirai is cast as something that pursues him from outside.
event: Rebuked by a deity speaking from a crafted image, Udayakumaran, shaken, decides to learn more from the girl's deeds and leaves the shrine at nightfall in torment.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 16/17 to 28/29: line 16 ('பின் அறிவாம்' எனப் பெயர்வோன் தன்னை) leaves the prince as the object of a sentence that ends only at line 28 (அவன் போய பின்).

reading: Inside the shrine's chamber Manimekalai reasons that if she goes about the hall as Madhavi's daughter the prince will not let her be, so she takes the form of Kayachandigai, known to the whole city as a woman of burning hunger, citing the learned that for an alms-seeker taking and giving are both duty but going to the needy to give is the finer thing; she takes the Amudhasurabhi from the goddess's shrine, enters the king's prison for those who offended him, and with a sigh feeds the hungry there until her hand aches, and the guards, marvelling that one bowl fed them all, go to report the gift and the girl to the king.
nuance: The disguise has two motives in one breath: to escape the prince (31-32) and to serve the helpless (35). Kayachandigai's known insatiable hunger makes the borrowed body a fitting carrier for a bowl that never empties. She enters the prison 'with desire' (விருப்பொடும், 44): the prison is chosen, not stumbled on.
event: Manimekalai takes Kayachandigai's form, carries the bowl into the king's prison and feeds the prisoners, and the guards go to tell the king.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 49/50 to 50/51: the guards' words begun at 48 (கோமகன் தனக்கு இப் பாத்திர தானமும் பைந்தொடி செய்தியும்) end only at line 50 (இசைத்தும்' என்று ஏகி).

tamil: நெடியோன் குறள் உரு ஆகி நிமிர்ந்து தன்
மாவலி மருமான் சீர் கெழு திரு மகள்
வரிக் குயில் பாட மா மயில் ஆடும்
விரைப் பூம் பந்தர் கண்டு உளம் சிறந்தும்
இரு சிறைக் விரித்து ஆங்கு எழுந்து உடன் கொட்பன
ஒரு சிறைக் கண்டு ஆங்கு உள் மகிழ்வு எய்தி
ஆடிய குரவை இஃது ஆம்' என நோக்கியும்
reading: Meanwhile the king, with Queen Seerthi, daughter of the line of Mavali who poured the gift-water when the tall god took a dwarf's form and measured the earth, enters a flowering grove where bees, beetles, koels and peacocks make a concert, and seeing peahens, peacocks and a mateless swan whirl together he says it is the kuravai that the gem-coloured god, his elder brother and Pinnai danced.
nuance: The queen's line is traced to Mavali, the king who lost the earth by his gift to the dwarf, while the king amuses himself; the grove scene runs alongside Manimekalai's prison feeding, which the guards are on their way to report.
event: The Chola king enters a pleasure grove with his queen and reads the birds' whirling as the divine kuravai.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 65/66 to 66/67: line 65 opens the king's exclamation ('மாமணி வண்ணனும் தம்முனும் பிஞ்ஞையும்) and line 66 closes it (ஆடிய குரவை இஃது ஆம்' என நோக்கியும்).

tamil: செம் பொன் தட்டில் தீம் பால் ஏந்திப்
பைங் கிளி ஊட்டும் ஓர் பாவை ஆம்' என்றும்
பிணவுக் குரங்கு ஏற்றி பெரு மதர் மழைக் கண்
தொடி சேர் செங் கையின் தொழுது நின்று ஏத்தியும்
reading: The king goes on finding pictures in the grove: a peacock beside a mango and kongu blossom is a doll feeding milk from a gold plate to a parrot, a male monkey swinging a female on the jewelled swing made for women makes him laugh, and green bamboo standing by white-flowered maraam is the tall god standing with his elder brother, to which he joins bangled hands in worship.
nuance: The bangled hand (தொடி சேர் செங் கை, 78) could be the queen's, but the run of participles (நோக்கியும், நகை எய்தியும், ஏத்தியும்) keeps the king as subject.
event: The king sees likenesses in the grove, laughs at the monkeys on the swing and worships a bamboo and maraam pair as Krishna and his brother.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 77/78 to 78/79: line 77 (நெடியோன் முன்னொடு நின்றனன் ஆம் என) is completed by line 78 (தொழுது நின்று ஏத்தியும்).

tamil: பண் யாழ் நரம்பில் பண்ணு முறை நிறுப்போர்
நல் நெடுங் கூந்தல் நறு விரை குடைவோர்
ஆங்கு அவர் தம்மோடு அகல் இரு வானத்து
reading: With women who know dance and gesture, who know the drama-poems, set the modes on the lute, beat the drum, keep time with flute and voice, string pearls, rub on sandal, paint saffron on their breasts, braid lilies, perfume their hair and stand before golden mirrors, the king plays like the king of the wide sky.
event: The king sports in the grove with women skilled in dance, music and adornment.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 93/94 (unit 78-93) to 92/93: line 92 (வேந்தனின் சென்று விளையாட்டு அயர்ந்து) closes the clause of the women and their sport; line 93 begins the flowering shrubs.

tamil: குறுங் கால் நகுலமும் நெடுஞ் செவி முயலும்
பிறழ்ந்து பாய் மானும் இறும்பு அகலா வெறியும்
வந்து வீழ் அருவியும் மலர்ப் பூம் பந்தரும்
பரப்பு நீர்ப் பொய்கையும் கரப்பு நீர்க் கேணியும்
reading: Standing among kurunthu, jasmine and other shrubs, the king smiles and calls a mongoose, a hare, a leaping deer and a lurking creature to come, beckoning with his hand beside his beloved companion, and with Kama, spring and the young south wind as his fellows he wanders and plays among machine-wells, built hills, falls, ponds, hidden pools, hiding places and crystal chambers.
nuance: Kama, spring and the breeze are named as the king's companions (100-101), so the king's play is drawn as a festival of desire at the hour his son is being turned back by a goddess.
event: The king plays with animals and wanders through the grove's artificial wells, hills, pools and crystal rooms.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 108/109 (unit 94-108) to 106/107: line 106 (யாங்கணும் திரிந்து தாழ்ந்து விளையாடி) ends the king's wandering; line 107 begins the craftsmen who built the pavilion.

tamil: கொண்டு இனிது இயற்றிய கண் கவர் செய்வினைப்
பவளத் திரள் கால் பல் மணிப் போதிகைத்
பைஞ் சேறு மெழுகாப் பசும் பொன் மண்டபத்து
reading: The king, Indra-like, mounts a pavilion of green gold that Magadha artisans, Maratha smiths, Avanti metalworkers and Yavana carpenters made with Tamil craftsmen, with coral pillars, jewelled capitals, hanging strings of pearl and a gold-sheathed canopy.
nuance: The list of foreign craftsmen working with Tamil ones (107-109) is a picture of Puhar's reach through trade.
event: The king ascends the golden pavilion built by craftsmen from many lands.
unit_note: New unit from the redrawn 109-127: it begins at 107 where the craftsmen enter and ends at 116 (இனிது ஏறலும), where the king's long sentence of play closes before the guard's approach at 117.

tamil: எஞ்சா மண் நசை இகல் உளம் துரப்ப
மறம் கெழு நெடு வாள் வயவரும் மிடைந்த
சிலைக் கயல் நெடுங் கொடி செரு வேல் தடக் கை
கேள் இது மன்னோ! கெடுக நின் பகைஞர்
யானைத்தீ நோய்க்கு அயர்ந்து மெய் வாடி இம்
மா நகர்த் திரியும் ஓர் வம்ப மாதர்
பெரும் பெயர் மன்ன! நின் பெயர் வாழ்த்தி
மொய் கொள் மாக்கள் மொசிக்க ஊண் சுரந்தனள்
reading: Announced at the gate and admitted by the king's grace, the prison guard bows and praises Maavankilli, whose protecting umbrella was won at Kaariyaaru by the young prince over the bow-and-fish banners that came out of Vanji wearing the vanji flower in hunger for land, and then reports that a stranger woman, wasted by the elephant-fire disease, entered the prison, blessed the king's name, and with one begging bowl made food flow for the crowding prisoners.
nuance: The bow and fish of 124 are the Chera and Pandya emblems, so the enemies who came from Vanji appear to be their alliance; whether the young prince (இளங்கோன், 125) is Udayakumaran is not said. The guard frames the prisoners' feeding as a blessing on the king's name (134), before the king has done anything.
event: The prison guard is admitted, praises the king's victory at Kaariyaaru and reports the stranger woman who feeds the prisoners from one bowl.
unit_note: The original units 109-127 and 128-143 were redrawn as 107-116, 117-138 and 139-162: line 117 (வாயிலுக்கு இசைத்து) begins the guard's approach, and line 138 (வாழி எம் கோ மன்னவ!' என்றலும்) ends his speech.

tamil: யாங்கு ஆகியது இவ் ஏந்திய கடிஞை?' என்று
விஞ்சை மகள் யான் விழவு அணி மூதூர்
ஊன் உடை மாக்கட்கு உயிர் மருந்து இது' என
அருஞ் சிறை விட்டு ஆங்கு ஆய் இழை உரைத்த
பெருந் தவர் தம்மால் பெரும் பொருள் எய்த
அறவோர்க்கு ஆக்கினன் அரசு ஆள் வேந்து என்
reading: The king graciously summons her; she comes and blesses him, and asked who she is and how she came by the bowl, she says she is a vidyadhara woman who has wandered the festive old city in disguise, blesses rain, earth and the prince, and says a deity near the hall gave the bowl, which became divine, ended her elephant-fire hunger and is life-medicine for embodied beings; when the king asks what he should do for her, she asks him to clear the prison and make it a house for those who do dharma, and he releases the prisoners and makes the prison into such a house.
nuance: Her self-account is true and false at once: she calls herself a vidyadhara woman (விஞ்சை மகள், 147), which is Kayachandigai's identity, while saying she has wandered the city in வஞ்சம் (148), which names her disguise. Her blessing 'no harm to the prince' (150) comes just before the prince is killed because of that disguise. The king does not punish or pardon one offender; he abolishes the prison as an institution at a beggar's request. Line 160 (through the great ascetics, great wealth gained) is compressed: whether the ascetics are given the building, or the king gains merit through them, is not clear.
event: Manimekalai, in Kayachandigai's form, tells the king of the bowl and asks him to turn the prison into a house of dharma, and he frees the prisoners and does so.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 143/144 to 138/139: the king's question begins at 143 (தவத்தோய் நீ யார்?) and ends at 144 (என்று), so the dialogue is kept whole from the king's summons at 139.

title: உதயகுமரனைக் காஞ்சனன் வாளால் எறிந்த காதை
theme: Kanchanan, come to Puhar for his wife Kayasandikai at the end of her curse, takes Manimekalai in her form for his wife and, seeing her teach Udayakumaran the body's decay by pointing to an old woman, judges the prince her lover; when the prince comes to the hall at midnight Kanchanan kills him, and the pillar goddess tells him that his wife died over the Vindhya, that the prince died by his own former deed, and that the killing will still cling to Kanchanan.
source_issues: Line 23 reads பழப் வினைப் பயத்தான், with a stray ப் after பழ; the sense is பழவினைப் பயத்தான் (the fruit of an old deed).
Line 80 carries a malformed line mark (20-0810) in the source; the line text itself is sound.
Line 91 reads வான்தேர்ப் பாகனைப் மீன், with an unexpected ப் before மீன்.
Line 118 reads போவார் உளர்அனின், which looks corrupt for உளர் எனின் ('if there are any who go').
Chapter 21 of the tool is kaathai 20 (உதயகுமரனைக் காஞ்சனன் வாளால் எறிந்த காதை); unit ids use the kaathai number.

tamil: தீப் பிறப்பு உழந்தோர் செய் வினைப் பயத்தான்
யாப்பு உடை நல் பிறப்பு எய்தினர் போலப்
கட்டு உடைச் செல்வக் களிப்பு உடைத்து ஆக
ஆய் இழை சென்றதூஉம் ஆங்கு அவள் தனக்கு
பற்றினன் கொண்டு என் பொன் தேர் ஏற்றி
கற்று அறி விச்சையும் கேட்டு அவள் உரைக்கும்
reading: The narrator recalls that the prison, freed of its hellish cruelty by the king's order and Manimekalai's compassion, has become a place of temple, monks' dwelling, kitchen and dining hall; hearing all this, Udayakumaran resolves that, whatever the wise say and however the king rages, he will seize her when she leaves the hall, set her in his golden chariot and hear her learning and her wise old sayings.
nuance: The opening simile (3-4) compares the changed prison to those who, after suffering evil births, reach a good birth through the fruit of their deeds, so the chapter that ends on a killing paid for by deeds opens with deeds as a means of rising. The prince's resolve names the two checks he will override, the wise (மதியோர்) and the king (மன்னவன்), the very sceptre whose order made the hall.
event: Udayakumaran hears that Manimekalai has turned the prison into a house of charity by the king's leave and resolves to carry her off in his chariot.

tamil: மதுக் கமழ் தாரோன் மனம் கொண்டு எழுந்து
பலர் பசி களைய பாவை தான் ஒதுங்கிய
கழை வளர் கான் யாற்று பழப் வினைப் பயத்தான்
தேர்ந்தனன் திரிவோன் ஏந்து இள வன முலை
மாந்தர் பசி நோய் மாற்றக் கண்டு ஆங்கு
reading: The prince sets out for the public alms-hall where Manimekalai feeds the hungry; meanwhile Kanchanan, the vidyadhara husband of Kayasandikai, despairing that the twelve years of the sage's curse are over and she has not returned, comes down into the old city, searches its squares, groves, hermitages and halls, and sees the girl relieving people's hunger.
nuance: Kanchanan's lament (22-26) attributes the curse itself to the fruit of an old deed (பழ வினைப் பயத்தான், 23), so even before he acts the chapter frames his story in deeds. What he sees is Manimekalai in Kayasandikai's form, and the narration lets the reader know this while he does not.
event: Udayakumaran heads for the alms-hall while Kanchanan, come to fetch his wife at the end of her curse, searches Puhar and finds Manimekalai, in his wife's form, feeding the hungry.

tamil: குமிழ் மூக்கு இவை காண் உமிழ் சீ ஒழுக்குவ
reading: Kanchanan greets her fondly, asking whether the gods have ended her elephant-fire hunger now that one bowl in her hand feeds many; unmoved, she leaves him, goes to Udayakumaran, points to a grey-haired old woman and begins to show him, feature by feature, how hair, brow, eyebrows, eyes and nose have turned from their praised likenesses into decay.
nuance: Each feature is first named by its lover's simile (dark sand of the stream, crescent brow, bow, kazhuneer flower, kumizh bud) and then shown in the old woman as its opposite (white sand, wrinkled skin, dried prawn, running water, dripping matter), so the lesson is made out of the love poets' own catalogue. The one who gives it is the desired girl herself, disguised as another man's wife, and the unit opens with that husband's tenderness, which she leaves unanswered.
event: Manimekalai turns away from Kanchanan, who takes her for his wife, and shows Udayakumaran an old woman's face as a lesson on the body.

tamil: இலவு இதழ்ச் செவ் வாய் காணாயோ நீ
வள்ளைத் தாள் போல் வடி காது இவை காண்
தாழ்ந்து ஓசி தெங்கின் மடல் போல் திரங்கி
நரம்பொடு விடு தோல் உகிர்த் தொடர் கழன்று
முளி முதிர் தெங்கின் உதிர் காய் உணங்கல்
reading: Manimekalai carries the lesson down the old woman's body, teeth, lips, ears, breasts, shoulders, fingers, thighs, calves and feet, each now withered, and ends by telling the prince that he fails to see the deceit those of old set up when they hid the flesh and its smell under flowers, sandal paste, cloth and jewels.
nuance: The closing charge (67-69) blames the deceit not on the woman but on custom, தொல்லோர் வகுத்த வஞ்சம், the dress and ornament handed down by those of old. Her teaching works by showing a living body in time rather than a corpse, and it is the prince's own seeing that she calls at fault (தெரியாய்).
event: Manimekalai finishes showing the prince the old woman's decayed body and tells him its adornment is a deceit.

tamil: பிறன் பின் செல்லும் பிறன் போல் நோக்கும்
ஈங்கு இவன் காதலன் ஆதலின் ஏந்து இழை
ஈங்கு ஒழிந்தனள்' என இகல் எரி பொத்தி
புற்று அடங்கு அரவின் புக்கு ஒளித்து அடங்கினன்
reading: When she has spoken thus as the vidyadhara woman, Kanchanan, reading her refusal of his praise, her following of another man, her looking at him as a stranger and her wise talk and smiling eyes for the prince, concludes that the prince is her lover and the reason she stayed on earth, and burning with rage he slips into the hall where she lodges and hides like a snake in its anthill.
nuance: Every sign Kanchanan reads is real (she does ignore him, does go to the prince, does speak to him with care) and every inference is false, because the woman is not his wife and her talk is a lesson against desire. The snake simile (80) begins an image the chapter repeats when he strikes (104-105).
event: Kanchanan decides that the prince is his wife's lover and hides in the hall in anger.
unit_note: End moved from 84 to 81: line 81 (காஞ்சனன் என்னும் கதிர் வாள் விஞ்சையன்) completes the sentence of his hiding, and line 82 begins the prince's part.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவள் உரைத்த அரசு இளங் குமரனும்
வம்பலன் தன்னொடு இவ் வைகு இருள் ஒழியாள்
இங்கு இவள் செய்தி இடை இருள் யாமத்து
வந்து அறிகுவன்' என மனம் கொண்டு எழுந்து
ஊர் துஞ்சு யாமத்து ஒரு தனி எழுந்து
வேழம் வேட்டு எழும் வெம் புலி போல
போகு உயர் புற்று அளை புகுவான் போல
ஆங்கு முன் இருந்த அலர் தார் விஞ்சையன்
reading: The prince, his desire unspent, tells himself that Manimekalai has taken Kayasandikai's form and bowl to bewitch minds and will not leave the stranger she lectured in the hall tonight, so he will come at midnight to learn what she does; with Kama as his companion he leaves the palace when the town sleeps, like a tiger stalking an elephant, and steps slowly into the hall as if entering a cobra's hole, while the vidyadhara waiting there says, 'here he has come to her'.
nuance: The prince also misreads: he suspects her with the stranger (வம்பலன், 88), so each man takes the other for her lover. The narrator's two similes split his part: he goes as a tiger to prey (95) and enters as one going into a hole where a fiery serpent lies (98-99), the hunter already the prey.
event: Udayakumaran, suspecting Manimekalai of a night with a stranger, goes alone at midnight to the hall where Kanchanan lies in wait.
unit_note: Start moved from 85 to 82: line 81 closes Kanchanan's hiding, and the prince's sentence and speech begin at line 82 (ஆங்கு அவள் உரைத்த அரசு இளங் குமரனும்).

tamil: வெஞ் சின அரவம் நஞ்சு எயிறு அரும்பத்
தன் பெரு வெகுளியின் எழுந்து பை விரித்தென
இருந்தோன் எழுந்து பெரும் பின் சென்று அவன்
சுரும்பு அறை மணித் தோள் துணிய வீசி
reading: Rising like an enraged cobra with poison in its fangs, Kanchanan follows the prince and cuts through his shoulder with his sword, then moves toward the girl to carry 'Kayasandikai' into the sky, when the image of a goddess painted on a pillar of the hall speaks: 'Do not come near, Kanchana! She is Manimekalai in a hidden form; hear how Kayasandikai, freed of her hunger, went: those who fly through the sky do not pass over the Vindhya where the goddess dwells, and any who do are seized by their shadow and put in her belly.'
nuance: The pillar image, which the narrator says a god drew (கடவுள் எழுதிய பாவை, 111), stops the second wrong before it happens and corrects the first too late. Kayasandikai, released by Manimekalai's food to fly home, was lost on the way, so the husband who came for her end of curse kills over a likeness of a wife who no longer lives.
event: Kanchanan kills Udayakumaran with his sword and turns to take Manimekalai, but the pillar image tells him who she is and that his wife died over the Vindhya.

tamil: அம் மலைமிசைப் போய் அவள் வயிற்று அடங்கினள்
அவ் வினை நின்னையும் அகலாது ஆங்கு உறும்'
கன்றிய நெஞ்சில் கடு வினை உருத்து எழ
விஞ்சையன் போயினன் விலங்கு விண் படர்ந்து என்
reading: The image finishes: Vindha, the guardian of the Vindhya, took Kayasandikai into her belly; do not grieve, Kanchana; though it was the prince's own ripened former deed that came here and took his life, you did not know that, and you have done a cruel deed that will not leave you either; and the vidyadhara, the hard deed rising in his scorched heart, goes off into the sky.
nuance: The pillar gives two causes at once and keeps both: the prince died by his own ஊழ்வினை (123), and Kanchanan's killing is still his own வெவ் வினை (125) that will cling to him. That he 'did not know' (அறியாய்) excuses nothing; it is the reason he cannot claim to have been fate's instrument. கைம்மை கொள்ளேல் (122) is read here as 'do not take on mourning'; the word can also name rashness, and the line is not certain.
event: The pillar goddess tells Kanchanan that the prince died by his own former deed but that the killing will cling to him, and Kanchanan flies away.

title: கந்திற்பாவை வருவது உரைத்த காதை
theme: Waking in Champapati's shrine after the prince's killing, Manimekalai casts off her borrowed form and mourns him; the deity of the pillar image, Thuvathikan, forbids her grief, traces the prince's violent deaths to a cook he killed in anger in a former birth, and foretells her imprisonment and release, her voyage, the schools of Vanji, the famine of Kanchi, her teaching by Aravanar, and her release births later as the Buddha's chief disciple.
source_issues: The chapter's units carry the kaathai number 21 (manimekalai:21:...) while the book's chapter number is 22, because the patikam is chapter 1.
Line 184 was repaired for the old-font ௌ / ெள confusion (தெளிந்தே).

Quotation marks are unbalanced at 106 to 111 (a quote closes after நகுதி and new ones open at 107 and 109) and at 145, where a closing mark after துவதிகன் உரைக்கும் leaves the speaker of 145 to 146 unclear.
Lines 5 to 8 say Manimekalai heard the pillar image's words to Kanchanan (kaathai 20, 110 to 126) though she lay senseless; the text gives no means.

tamil: கந்து உடை நெடு நிலைக் கடவுள் பாவை
கட்டு அழல் ஈமத்து என் உயிர் சுட்டேன்
உன் பிறப்பு எல்லாம் ஒழிவு இன்று உரைத்தலின்
அறம் தரு சால்பும் மறம் தரு துன்பமும்
யான் நினக்கு உரைத்து நின் இடர் வினை ஒழிக்கக்
reading: Waking in Champapati's shrine beside the pillar carved with a god, Manimekalai learns what the vidyadhara did, what befell the prince and what the pillar image told the killer; crying 'perish this form', she casts off her borrowed shape and laments to the dead prince that she burned herself on his pyre in the birth when he died of the snake's poison glance, that the goddess carried her to Manipallavam where she learned her own and all his births, and that she took Kayachandigai's form only to teach him birth and death and the fruits of dharma and wrong and so end his evil karma.
nuance: Her disguise is given a purpose here that the earlier kaathais did not state: it was a teaching form, meant to save him, and it became the cause of his death, since Kanchanan struck him for approaching 'Kayachandigai'. The pillar image's words to Kanchanan (kaathai 20, lines 110 to 126) are what she 'hears' at lines 5 to 8; the text does not say how a woman lying dazed heard them.
event: Manimekalai wakes in Champapati's shrine, learns of the prince's killing, throws off Kayachandigai's form and laments over him.

tamil: வை வாள் விஞ்சையன் மயக்கு உறு வெகுளியின்
reading: Manimekalai asks whether he died by the deluded wrath of the vidyadhara's sword as his cruel karma ripened, weeps and rises to go to him; the pillar deity stops her, saying that he has been her son and she his daughter, in birth after birth, that the birth she has seen is not the only one, and that one striving to leave the low round of wandering births should not grieve.
nuance: The deity's argument against grief is not that the dead are well but that kinship itself is unstable across births: the husband of one life was a son in another, so the bond she mourns is one turn among many. The unit's speaker changes at 27; the deity is named only at 35.
event: Manimekalai weeps and rises to go to the prince's body, and the pillar deity forbids her to go.

tamil: என்று இவை சொல்லி, இருந் தெய்வம் உரைத்தலும்
விட்ட பிறப்பின் வெய்து உயிர்த்து ஈங்கு இவன்
நெஞ்சு நடுங்கி நெடுந் துயர் கூர யான்
பெறுவேன் தில்ல நின் பேர் அருள் ஈங்கு!' என
reading: Manimekalai turns to the voice, asks whether it is the deity of unfailing tongue who dwells in this hall, worships its feet, and asks whether it knows why the prince died by the snake's poison glance in the birth left behind and now by the vidyadhara's sword, begging its grace to be told.
nuance: Her question pairs two deaths across two births and asks for one cause; the deity's answer will give the second death a cause in the first life, not the snake.
event: Manimekalai worships the pillar deity and asks it why the prince died twice by violence.

tamil: 'ஐ அரி நெடுங் கண் ஆய் இழை! கேள்' எனத்
மாயம் இல் மாதவன் வரு பொருள் உரைத்து
மருள் உடை மாக்கள் மன மாசு கழூஉம்
நடைத் திறத்து இழுக்கி நல் அடி தளர்ந்து
reading: The deity answers that in the former birth, on the bank of the Kayangarai, she and Rahulan served the sage Brahmadharman and offered to cook him a special meal at dawn; when the cook, coming at daybreak, slipped and fell and broke the vessels, Rahulan, angry that the meal for the ascetic had failed of its hour, cut him through with the sword so that shoulder and head came apart: that was the cruel deed.
nuance: The murder is set inside an act of piety: the anger rises because the gift to the sage is spoiled. The cook's fall is an accident (நடைத் திறத்து இழுக்கி), so the whole weight of the deed lies on the anger.
event: The deity tells how Rahulan, in his former birth, killed with his sword a cook who stumbled and spoilt the meal prepared for Brahmadharman.

tamil: விரா மலர்க் கூந்தல் மெல் இயல் நின்னோடு
மறம் செய்துளது எனின் வல் வினை ஒழியாது
தீங்கு உறும் உயிரே செய் வினை மருங்கின்
ஆங்கு அவ் வினை காண் ஆய் இழை கணவனை
ஈங்கு வந்து இவ் இடர் செய்து ஒழிந்தது
reading: The deity draws the lesson: those who say a grievous deed done for one's master is shielded by that master do not know; though done from love of doing dharma, if it is violence its strong karma does not leave, and when it draws near it returns on the life in a later birth; it is that deed which came here and did this harm to her husband.
nuance: The deity names and rejects a defence, that the one served answers for a deed done in his service; intention to serve dharma does not change a killing's fruit. Lines 61 to 62 and 67 to 69 are compressed and the exact construction is unclear, though the sense of 66 and 70 to 71 is plain. Kaathai 20 has the same deity tell the killer Kanchanan that his deed too will not leave him (20:120-129): the prince's karma ripens through a new wrong that is itself accountable.

reading: The deity foretells her near future: the king, grieving his son and hearing the ascetics' true report, will imprison her; the queen, set on keeping her near, will take her from the prison; Madhavi, bowing at the great sage's feet and telling him the trouble, will come with him, and on his word the queen will free her; she will go to Aputtiran, now ruling a kingdom, agree with him in true teaching and sail with him to the island of Manipallavam.
nuance: The queen's motive is given in one word, கொட்பினள், which can mean scheming or set on a purpose; the following kaathais show her tormenting Manimekalai before she relents, which the prophecy passes over.
event: The deity foretells Manimekalai's imprisonment, her release by the queen at the sage's word, and her voyage with Aputtiran.

tamil: சாவக மன்னன் தன் நாடு அடைந்த பின்
ஆங்கு அத் தீவம் விட்டு அருந் தவன் வடிவு ஆய்
பூங் கொடி வஞ்சி மா நகர் புகுவை
ஆங்கு அந் நகரத்து அறி பொருள் வினாவும்
பல் வேறு சமயப் படிற்று உரை எல்லாம்
அல்லி அம் கோதை! கேட்குறும் அந் நாள்
எள்ளினை போலும் இவ் உரை கேட்டு! இங்கு
ஒள்ளியது உரை!" என உன் பிறப்பு உணர்த்துவை
காம்பு அன தோளி! கனா மயக்கு உற்றனை"
என்று அவன் உரைக்கும் இளங் கொடி நல்லாய்!
reading: The deity goes on: after the Javaka king learns his own story from Deepatilakai and returns home, she will leave the island in an ascetic's form and enter Vanji, where learned men will set out the schools' false words: that God our lord made all lives in order, that the formless one who makes other forms is God, that painful austerity cuts this bondage and seats one at the top of the world of bliss, that all is a combining of the elements; and when one declares there is no God, the dead are not reborn and dharma is pointless, she who knows birth and dharma will laugh at him, tell him her former birth, and hear him say a deity deluded her and she was deceived by a dream.
nuance: The four views at 94 to 100 are not named by school; the creator god may be the Brahma-vadin's and the formless maker the Saiva's of kaathai 27, the austerity that seats the soul at the top of the world reads as Jain, and the combining of elements is the materialist's. The prophecy calls them all படிற்று உரை, false talk, but answers only the materialist. Even his rejoinder is foretold: the epic anticipates the objection that knowledge of past births is a dream sent by a god, and the deity's own role in carrying her off makes it pointed. The two materialist claims are marked refuted because the work answers them: here Manimekalai's laugh and her account of her birth (106 to 108), and in kaathai 27 her argument that he knows even his own parents only by inference (27:284-289). The speakers of 107 to 110 are not marked and are read from the sense.
event: The deity foretells Manimekalai's going to Vanji in an ascetic's form, hearing the schools, and mocking the materialist.

tamil: முது மர இடங்களும் முது நீர்த் துறைகளும்
காப்பு உடை மா நகர்க் காவலும் கண்ணி
ஆங்கு அத் தெய்வதம் அவ் இடம் நீங்கா
என் திறம் கேட்டியோ இளங் கொடி நல்லாய்!
reading: The deity tells her not to falter before the materialist but to affirm that evil deeds reach their doer and the dead are reborn; then it explains its own speech: wood, earth, stone and painted images do not speak, but the wise, planning the protection of a guarded city, have craftsmen shape the deities they intend in clay, stone, wood and wall at its streets, temples, old trees, ghats and halls, and those deities never leave their places and tell men of fleshly eyes what will befall.
nuance: The deity concedes the sceptic's premise, that an image as material does not speak, and relocates the voice in a deity bound to the place by the city's founders; the image is a seat, not the speaker. The two halves of the unit go together: the materialist will call her knowledge a god's trick, and the deity's account of how gods speak through images is the apparatus he will deny.

tamil: நீங்கேன் யான் என் நிலை அது கேளாய்
அவனுடன் யான் சென்று ஆடு இடம் எல்லாம்
நா நனி வருந்த என் நலம் பாராட்டலின்
துணிவுடன் உரைத்தேன் என் சொல் தேறு' என
reading: The deity names itself Thuvathikan, one of the great divine host, who never leaves the image Mayan carved in its likeness on the ancient pillar; it speaks of its close companion Oviyachenan, whom the city paints beside it wherever the two went to play, honouring it with flowers and incense, and bids Manimekalai trust its word; she says she does not doubt and asks for its divine words to the end, and it promises to tell what is to come.
nuance: Line 134, 'what men know the gods do not know', and line 136, 'who told this city what he is?', are hard to place in the argument; they may mean that the townspeople's worship knows the deity better than it knows itself, but that is a guess. The closing quotation mark at 145 sits oddly, so whether 145 to 146 are narrator or deity is unclear.
event: The pillar deity tells its name and its bond to the image, and Manimekalai asks it to tell her future to the end.

tamil: மன் உயிர் நீங்க மழை வளம் கரந்து
பொன் எயில் காஞ்சி நகர் கவின் அழிய
ஆங்கு அது கேட்டே ஆர் உயிர் மருந்தாய்
செறி தொடி! காஞ்சி மா நகர் சேர்குவை
அறவணன் அருளால் ஆய் தொடி! அவ் ஊர்ப்
பிற வணம் ஒழிந்து நின் பெற்றியை ஆகி
அறன் ஓடு ஏந்தி ஆர் உயிர் ஓம்புவை
ஆய் தொடிக்கு அவ் ஊர் அறனொடு தோன்றும்
அறவணன் தனக்கு நீ உரைத்த அந் நாள்
"மற இருள் இரிய மன் உயிர் ஏம் உற
அற வெயில் விரித்து ஆங்கு அளப்பு இல் இருத்தியொடு
reading: Thuvathikan foretells that when rain is withheld and Kanchi of the golden walls loses its beauty as lives perish, she will take the divine vessel kept in this shrine as medicine for lives, go with her mothers to Kanchi where Aravanar also is, cast off her borrowed form there by his grace, and bearing the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world protect its people; when she tells Aravanar the doctrines of the other schools, he will teach her austerity, dharma, dependent arising and the path that ends becoming, and vow that, dying and being born, he will guard the true doctrine and not leave that place until the Buddha-sun rises.
nuance: The bowl is set against drought itself: அறன் ஓடு, 'the bowl of dharma', gives the plenty that rain would give (157 to 158). Aravanar's vow to keep dying and being born until the next Buddha appears is a vow to stay in the round of births for the teaching's sake, which the same kaathai otherwise urges Manimekalai to escape.
event: Thuvathikan foretells Manimekalai's journey to famine-struck Kanchi with the bowl, and Aravanar's teaching and vow there.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவன் உரைத்தலும் அவன் மொழி பிழையாய்
பாங்கு இயல் நல் அறம் பலவும் செய்த பின்
வலை ஒழி மஞ்ஞையின் மன மயக்கு ஒழிதலும்
உலகு துயில் எழுப்பினன் மலர் கதிரோன் என்
reading: Thuvathikan foretells that after many deeds of dharma her life will end in Kanchi, and that in every birth after it in northern Magadha she will be born a man, never leave the dharma of compassion, clear away delusion, and become chief disciple of the great one who gives dharma to others, cutting dependence and so being saved; it adds that the Manimekala goddess, who once lifted her ancestor from the waves, came to her in the grove and bore her to Manipallavam because she had fed the sage Sadhuchakkaran; hearing this, Manimekalai leaves her sea of grief like a peacock freed from a net, and the sun wakes the world.
nuance: Release is placed several births away and in a male body: the epic's prophecy makes rebirth as a man a step before discipleship, which is the epic's view, stated without comment. The closing simile, a peacock freed from the net, answers the unit's opening grief; what frees her is knowing her births, not any change in the facts.
event: Thuvathikan foretells Manimekalai's future births and release and explains why the goddess saved her, and Manimekalai's grief leaves her at dawn.

title: சிறை செய் காதை
theme: The ascetics bring the Chola king news of his son's death indirectly, through old stories of Kakandi in which men who desired chaste women were punished by the spirit's warning or by Kakandhan's own sword, and through a tale of lifelong chastity and charity; asked for the present case, they tell how the prince's ripened deed killed him, and the king calls the killing his own duty done by another, orders the body burned in secret and Manimekalai put under guard.
source_issues: Line 95: the edition's text had ௌ for the vowel sign ெள (தெளித்திலேன்); repaired in the core.
Line 191: a leftover HTML quote mark at the start of the line was removed in the core.
Line 209: a stray backtick was removed in the core.
The core's units 1-16 through 193-215 broke mid-sentence in several places (16, 57, 68, 116, 131, 151, 175, 192); all twelve units were moved to sense breaks, keeping twelve units.
