tamil: ஆங்கு அவள் தன்னை ஆர் உயிர் நீங்கிய
நிவந்து ஓங்கு வெண்குடை மண்ணகம் நிழல் செய!
தீது இன்று உருள்க நீ ஏந்திய திகிரி!
reading: At dawn the worshippers at the old woman's shrine tell the ascetics of the Chakravala shrine what happened to Udayakumaran; the ascetics ask Manimekalai, who tells them unshaken, and then, hiding her with the prince's body, they go to the palace, have themselves announced, and bless the king's umbrella, spear, sceptre, wheel and years.
nuance: The ascetics come to the king with a death in which he is implicated, yet open only with blessing; the news itself is withheld for two hundred lines. Lines 11-12 (கோயில் மன்னனைக் குறுகினர் சென்று) use the formula with which Kannaki is brought before the Pandya in Silappathikaram 20.
event: The ascetics of the Chakravala shrine learn of the prince's death, hear Manimekalai's account, hide her with the body, and go to the palace to bless the king.
unit_note: End moved from line 16 to line 18: the blessing that begins at line 13 closes with வாழிய வேந்தே at line 18.

tamil: தன் முன் தோன்றல் தகாது ஒழி நீ" எனக்
துயர் நீங்கு கிளவியின் யான் தோன்று அளவும்
இயைந்த நாமம் இப் பதிக்கு இட்டு ஈங்கு
reading: One ascetic tells the king that not only today but of old men who, drunk with lust, approached chaste wives or sent their hearts after women of penance have died when their evil deed ripened, and begins with old Kakandi: King Kanthan, told by the virgin goddess to keep out of Parasurama's sight, called Kakandhan, his son by the city's courtesan, to guard the town, since one with no right to rule would not draw Parasurama, and the town was named Kakandi.
nuance: The general claim is made before any example, and widened from the chaste wife to the woman of penance (நல் தவப் பெண்டிர், 22), which is where Udayakumaran stands. The Kanthan story explains the town's name and introduces Kakandhan, whose lack of a right to rule (33) is what protects him; who the virgin goddess (கன்னி, 27) is, the unit does not say.
event: King Kanthan, to hide from Parasurama, leaves the city in the keeping of Kakandhan, his courtesan's son, and names it Kakandi.
unit_note: Start moved from line 17 to 19 (the blessing ends at 18) and end from 37 to 38, where the naming of the town (இயைந்த நாமம் இப் பதிக்கு இட்டு) completes Kanthan's speech; line 39 still links Kanthan's departure to the next story.

tamil: உள்வரிக் கொண்டு அவ் உரவோன் பெயர் நாள்
புக்கேன் பிறன் உளம் புரி நூல் மார்பன்
முத் தீப் பேணும் முறை எனக்கு இல்" என
reading: Kakandhan's son, seeing the brahmin wife Maruthi returning alone from her Kaveri bath, calls her to him; she reasons that rain-bringing wives never enter another man's heart, so having entered his she is no longer fit to tend her husband's three fires, will not go home, and at the Bhuta's crossroads protests that she did no wrong against her husband, kept the household chastity that brings rain, and does not know her fault, and asks whether the god there is false.
nuance: Maruthi condemns herself for something that happened only in the youth's mind (கண்டோன் நெஞ்சில் கரப்பு எளிதாயினேன், 52): the fault she cannot name is not an act but having been desirable, and the rule that excludes her from the fire rite is one she applies to herself before anyone accuses her.
event: Kakandhan's son calls the brahmin wife Maruthi to him at the river; distraught, she goes not home but to the Bhuta's crossroads and accuses its god.
unit_note: Start moved from 38 to 39 and end from 57 to 56: Maruthi's lament closes with அரற்றலும் at 56; line 57 begins the Bhuta's appearance and speech.

tamil: நீ கேள்" என்றே நேர் இழைக்கு உரைக்கும்
பெய் எனப் பெய்யும் பெரு மழை" என்ற அப்
விசி பிணி முழவின் விழாக் கோள் விரும்பி
ஆங்கு அவை ஒழிகுவை ஆயின் ஆய் இழை!
ஓங்கு இரு வானத்து மழையும் நின் மொழியது
கட்டாது உன்னை என் கடுந் தொழில் பாசம்
மன் முறை எழு நாள் வைத்து அவன் வழூஉம்
reading: The great Bhuta appears and tells Maruthi that she has not trusted the poet who never lies on the wife who worships her husband rather than a god, that her love of riddles, gossip and drum-loud festivals and her duty to worship gods have cost her the power to command rain and to scorch the hearts of others as steadfast women do, that if she gives these up the rain will obey her, that its noose will not bind her as it binds straying wives, and that its own justice comes only after the king's seven days, within which Kakandhan will cut down the youth; on the day it named, the youth is killed by his father's sword.
nuance: The Bhuta does not blame her for the youth's desire; it blames her worship of gods, festivals and talk, taking the couplet's தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally. It also sets an order of justice: the king's punishment first, the spirit's only if the king fails within seven days (72-73), and the king does not fail.
event: The Bhuta appears to Maruthi, explains her lost power and foretells the youth's punishment; within the seven days his father kills him with the sword.
unit_note: Start moved from 58 to 57 so the Bhuta's appearance and speech stay together; end moved from 68 (mid-speech) to 79, where the narrator reports the youth's death; 80-81 open the next story.

tamil: பெரு மதர் மழைக் கண் விசாகையும் பேணித்
ஒத்தனர்" என்றே ஊர் முழுது அலர் எழ
உலகர் பெரும் பழி ஒழிப்பாய் நீ" என
reading: The ascetic goes on: the cousins Dharmadattan and Visakai were so beautiful that the whole town said they were fit for a lovers' marriage; Visakai left her house, climbed into the Ulaka Aravi hall, asked the image painted on its pillar to clear the slander, and when the speaking image told the city that she is a woman who brings rain, vowed that, since only a god's word could clear the town's mind, she would be her cousin's wife in her next birth and not join him in this one.
nuance: The image clears her by naming her a rain-bringer (மழை தரும் இவள், 93), the very power Maruthi lost; yet Visakai answers vindication with renunciation, as if the god's word cleared her name but not the occasion for talk.
event: Slandered with her cousin, Visakai goes to the pillar image in the Ulaka Aravi, which proclaims her chaste, and vows not to marry him in this birth.
unit_note: Start moved from 82 to 80: lines 80-81 (இன்னும் கேளாய் ... மன்னவர் ஏறே) address the king to open this second story.

tamil: மற்று அவள் கன்னி மாடத்து அடைந்த பின்
நா உடைப் பாவையை நலம் பல ஏத்தி
தக்கண மதுரை தான் சென்று அடைந்த பின்
விரி தரு பூங் குழல் விசாகையை அல்லது
பெண்டிரைப் பேணேன் இப் பிறப்பு ஒழிக!" எனக்
நீள் நிதிச் செல்வன் ஆய் நீள் நில வேந்தனின்
எட்டிப் பூப் பெற்று இரு முப்பதிற்று யாண்டு
reading: Visakai tells her mother and shuts herself in the maidens' chamber; Dharmadattan and his parents leave the city praising the image and settle in southern Madurai, where he vows to cherish no woman but Visakai and to let this birth go, and grows so rich in trade that the king gives him the etti flower, until he has reached sixty.
nuance: His vow mirrors hers from the other side: she refuses him in this birth, he refuses every other woman, so both give up this birth's marriage and keep the bond.
event: Visakai enters the maidens' chamber; Dharmadattan leaves with his parents for southern Madurai, vows to love no other woman, and grows rich and honoured until old age.
unit_note: End moved from 116 to 114: the brahmin's speech beginning at 115 runs to 120.

tamil: இப் பதிப் புகுந்தனன் இரு நில வேந்தே!
மற்று அவன் இவ் ஊர் வந்தமை கேட்டு
reading: A brahmin asks the rich Dharmadattan what he has done with his life, whether he has heard that those without a chaste wife do not enter the world of the gods however many good deeds they do, and bids him go home at once; he leaves Madurai and returns, and Visakai, hearing of it, comes out of her house and, unashamed before the crowd, goes to him.
nuance: The brahmin's saying makes a wife a man's condition for heaven; the next unit has Visakai answer it, putting virtue alone in that place (137-138). The school tag follows the speaker, a brahmin quoting a maxim; the unit names no text.
event: A brahmin sends the aged Dharmadattan home to marry, and Visakai goes out before the crowd to meet him.
unit_note: Start moved from 117 to 115 (the brahmin's speech begins there) and end from 131 to 126, before Visakai's speech starts at 127.

tamil: ஆறு ஐந்து இரட்டி யாண்டு உனக்கு ஆயது என்
இப் பிறப்பு ஆயின் யான் நின் அடி அடையேன்
அப் பிறப்பு யான் நின் அடித்தொழில் கேட்குவன்
ஆங்கு அவன் அவளுடன் செய்த நல் அறம்
reading: Visakai tells Dharmadattan that they never knew each other, asks where the beauty that bewildered them has hidden now that he is sixty and his hair is grey, says she will not come to his feet in this birth but will serve him in the next, reminds him that youth, body and wealth do not last and that sons do not give heaven, only great virtue being a true companion, and bids him give; he shows her his wealth, and the good they did together outnumbers the stars.
nuance: She addresses him as a householder without a wife (உளன் இல்லாள, 132), granting the brahmin's premise only to answer it: not a wife and not sons but virtue is the companion, and the two do their charity together while keeping her vow apart. The narrator's count (more than the stars) endorses her.
event: Visakai refuses marriage in this birth but turns the aged Dharmadattan to charity, which they practise together.
unit_note: Start moved from 132 to 127, where Visakai's speech begins, and end from 151 to 142, where the narration of their shared charity closes; 143 begins the elder son's story.

tamil: குமரி மூத்த அக் கொடுங் குழை நல்லாள்
சுரி இரும் பித்தை சூழ்ந்து புறந் தாழ்ந்த
கடுஞ் சினம் திருகி மகன் துயர் நோக்கான்
reading: As the aged virgin, cleared of slander by the god's grace, walks the bannered street, Kakandhan's elder son, whose brother died over Maruthi, burns with desire, takes the garland from her hair saying this is the marriage the ancients spoke of, and lifts it to wear; his raised hand will not come away from his hair, and Kakandhan, hearing it was for this woman, in fierce anger and without regard for his grief as a father, strikes his son with his sword.
nuance: The second son repeats the first son's offence against a woman now old, and claims an ancient form of marriage for it; the miracle answers him before the father does. Kakandhan, himself only a keeper of the city with no right to rule, twice executes his own son, which is the example the ascetic is preparing for the king. Whose head the hand sticks to turns on குஞ்சி (154), usually a man's hair, and on what இடுவான் (152) takes as object; the reading here takes it as his own.
event: Kakandhan's elder son seizes the aged Visakai's garland as a token of marriage, his hand sticks fast, and his father kills him with the sword.
unit_note: Start moved from 152 to 143 and end from 175 to 158: the elder son's story runs from 143 to his death at 158; 159 returns to the frame.

tamil: நன்று அறி மாதவிர்! நலம் பல காட்டினிர்
இன்றும் உளதோ இவ் வினை? உரைம்' என
ஆங்கு அது கடிந்தோர் அல்லவை கடிந்தோர்" என
reading: The ascetic closes with a blessing; the king, catching his 'not only today', asks whether such a deed has happened today too, and the ascetic answers that those who know the final truth name five things to be shunned, toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust, of which lust is hardest to throw off; ascetics renounce it as the shunning of all evil, and those who do not renounce it suffer in unbearable hell.
nuance: The king himself asks for the present case, so the verdict that follows comes from his mouth. The five match the Buddhist precepts, but the unit attributes them only to those who know the final truth (முடி பொருள் உணர்ந்தோர், 169), so the claims are tagged general.
event: The king asks whether such a deed has happened today, and an ascetic begins his answer with the five things to be shunned.
unit_note: Start moved from 176 back to 159 and end set at 176: the sentence that begins நீங்கார் அன்றே (175) ends with உழப்போர் at 176.

tamil: சே அரி நெடுங் கண் சித்திராபதி மகள்
மதி மருள் வெண்குடை மன்ன! நின் மகன்
ஓங்கு இருள் யாமத்து இவனை ஆங்கு உய்த்து
ஆங்கு அவன் தன் கை வாளால் அம்பலத்து
ஈங்கு இவன் தன்னை எறிந்தது" என்று ஏத்தி
reading: The ascetic tells the king that Madhavi, unable to bear her lover's suffering, entered the monks' dwelling, that her young daughter Manimekalai, resolved on penance, begged from house to house and came to the hall, that the prince nevertheless followed her like a shadow and, fearless of the dark, came to the hall for her, where she had taken Kayachandikai's form; and that since his evil deed had ripened it brought her to the hall, led him there at midnight, called Kayachandikai's husband, deceived his mind with 'he came for the vidyadhara's wife', and cut the prince down by that man's sword.
nuance: The grammatical subject of the killing (எறிந்தது, 203) is the ripened evil deed of 193, not the vidyadhara, whose hand is only its instrument; the ascetic thus tells the father his son's death without naming a human culprit. Whether one ascetic or several speak (161, 168, 204) the text leaves open.
event: The ascetic tells the king how his son, pursuing Manimekalai to the hall by night, was killed by Kayachandikai's vidyadhara husband.
unit_note: The original units 176-192 and 193-215 broke mid-sentence; this unit runs from 177 to the closing மாதவன் உரைத்தலும் at 204, and the king's reply (205-215) is its own unit.

tamil: அணி கிளர் நெடு முடி அரசு ஆள் வேந்து என்
reading: The king turns to his general Chozhika Enathi and says that the vidyadhara did to the prince what the king himself should have done, that without a guardian's guarding there can be neither ascetics' vows nor women's chastity, and orders that before other kings hear that an evil-doer was born in the line of the king who did justice on his own son, the prince be put on the pyre and the courtesan's daughter be put under guard.
nuance: The king takes the ascetics' examples as meant, but his justice is half concealment: the body is to be burned before the story reaches other kings, and the girl, whom the stories have shown blameless, is imprisoned. தகவு இலன் (207) may say the vidyadhara is not at fault or that he lacked the standing to act; either way he goes unpunished. The ancestor 'who did justice on his son' (210) is the Chola of the calf whom Kannaki cites in Silappathikaram 20.
event: The king declares the vidyadhara's killing of his son a just act, orders the body burned and Manimekalai put under guard.
unit_note: Split from the original 193-215 at line 205, where the king's speech begins.

title: சிறை விடு காதை
theme: The Chola queen, grieving her son, has Manimekalai released into her keeping and tries to destroy her by drug, slander and starvation; each trick fails by the knowledge and mantras Manimekalai has gained, and when the queen repents Manimekalai teaches her that grief for a body is idle, that the prince died by his own past deed, and that lust, killing, drink, falsehood and theft must be renounced, until the queen's grief is quenched and the two bow to each other.
source_issues: Line 140 carries the kaathai number 223 in its line mark; read as 23-140 (flagged by show).
Lines 51, 89, 138 and 142 had ௌ for ெள, repaired in the core (flagged by show).
Lines 31 to 36: the saying in 31 to 32 is hard to construe, and the change of speaker between the queen and the king (34, இறை சொல; 35 to 36) is not marked.
Lines 98 to 100: whether சென்ற பிறவியில் belongs with 'I did not set my mind on' or with காதலற் பயந்தோய் is unclear; and காருக மடந்தை (105) is a rare expression.

the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
Madhavi's daughter, the Buddhist ascetic held in the palace

tamil: கலங்கு அஞ்அர் ஒழியக் கடிது சென்று எய்தி
அழுது அடி வீழாது ஆய் இழை தன்னைத்
reading: By the king's leave the old woman Vasanthavai, whose counsel soothes king, prince and queen alike, goes to the grieving queen Rajamadevi, bows to her without weeping at her feet, and reminds her that in this conquering line even a king who dies old is laid on darbha grass and cut with a sword so that he may go where battle-loving kings go, since a quiet death is a shame to the house.
nuance: Her consolation is a rebuke: she does not weep with the queen (9, அழுது அடி வீழாது) and offers the warrior code's rite for a non-heroic death, the rite Purananuru 93 describes, as the measure by which the prince's death is to be judged.
event: Vasanthavai goes to the grieving queen, bows, and tells her of the rite by which kings of this line who die old are cut with a sword on darbha grass.

tamil: தன் மண் காத்தன்று பிறர் மண் கொண்டன்று
என் எனப் படுமோ நின் மகன் மடிந்தது?
துன்பம் கொள்ளேல்' என்று அவள் போய பின்
அம் சில் ஓதி அரசனுக்கு ஒரு நாள்
கரும்பு உடைத் தடக் கைக் காமன் கையற
செறிந்த சிறை நோய் தீர்க்க' என்று இறை சொல
தன் ஓடு எடுப்பினும் தகைக்குநர் இல்' என்று
அங்கு அவள் தனைக் கூஉய் அவள் தன்னோடு
கொங்கு அவிழ் குழலாள் கோயிலுள் புக்கு ஆங்கு
reading: Vasanthavai ends by asking what the prince's death can be called, since he died neither guarding his own land nor taking another's, and bids the queen not grieve before the king; the queen hides her grief, resolves to deceive Manimekalai, and tells the king that the prince had lost his wits and his kingly conduct while the girl who has risen to wisdom does not deserve prison, so the king lets her take Manimekalai into her palace, where the queen privately vows to turn the girl's mind and make her a spectacle for the city.
nuance: The queen's plea for release is true in content and false in aim: the narrator frames it with her hidden grief and false conduct (21 to 23) and her private vow (39 to 40). Lines 31 to 34 quote a saying on whom kings should honour and whom set aside, and who speaks 31 to 36 is not plain: the queen may continue to 34 and the king answer at 35 to 36, or the king may speak from 31. The words கையாற்று and பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம் (21 to 22) return in Manimekalai's teaching at 124 to 125.
event: The queen, concealing her grief and intent, persuades the king to release Manimekalai from prison into her keeping and takes her into the palace.

tamil: மயல் பகை ஊட்ட மறு பிறப்பு உணர்ந்தாள்
இணை வளர் இள முலை ஏந்து எழில் ஆகத்துப்
ஆங்கு அவன் சென்று அவ் ஆய் இழை இருந்த
நிரயக் கொடு மகள் நினைப்பு அறியேன்' என்று
reading: The queen feeds Manimekalai a drug meant to derange her, but having known her former birth she stays clear-minded; the queen then pays an unlettered youth a handful of coins to go to her, make marks of lovemaking on her body and tell everyone she has lain with him, and when he comes to her room Manimekalai, seeing the queen's trick, chants her mantra and sits in a man's form, so that the youth, finding a man in the royal women's quarters, flees in fear, calling the queen a woman fit for hell.
nuance: The trick aims at the one thing an ascetic woman's standing rests on, report (46 to 47, பலர்க்கு உரை); the mantra of changing form given her in kaathai 10 answers it, and the hired youth, not the narrator, is the first to name the queen's cruelty (56).
event: The queen drugs Manimekalai and hires a youth to dishonour her; Manimekalai stays clear-minded and takes a man's form by a mantra, and the youth flees.

tamil: பொன் நேர் அனையாய்! பொறுக்க" என்று அவள் தொழ
விழித்தல் ஆற்றேன் என் உயிர் சுடு நாள்
reading: Asking why she should keep the one who brought ruin on her son, the queen gives out that Manimekalai has stopped eating from an incurable illness and shuts her in a stifling cell, but the mantra that does away with food keeps her unharmed; the queen trembles, bows and begs forgiveness for wronging an ascetic out of grief for her son, and Manimekalai begins her answer by asking where the queen was weeping on the day the serpent with fiery eyes took the life of Rahulan, son of Neelapathi, and she herself, unable to bear it, burned her own life.
nuance: The false illness (59, ஊண் ஒழிந்தனள்) is made literally true by the mantra (61, ஊண் ஒழி மந்திரம்) without harm, so the lie defeats itself. Manimekalai's question turns on the same life having died before: the queen did not weep for Rahulan, and weeps now for Udayakumaran, who is that Rahulan reborn.
event: The queen starves Manimekalai in a closed cell under a pretended illness; the mantra keeps her well, and the queen repents and begs her forgiveness.

tamil: அவ் உயிர்க்கு அன்பினை ஆயின் ஆய் தொடி!
உடல் துணிசெய்து ஆங்கு உருத்து எழும் வல் வினை
நஞ்சு விழி அரவின் நல் உயிர் வாங்கி
reading: Manimekalai tells the queen she has done what is unfitting and asks whether she weeps for the body or the life: if for the body, who but the mourners cast her son into the burning ground, and if for the life, where it enters next is set by its deeds and hard to know, so that one who loves that life should pity every life; and she tells her that the thief who killed her son was his own violent deed, the cutting down of a cook who fell and broke the serving vessels, which rose in wrath, took his life once by a serpent and ended it now by the vidyadhara's sword.
nuance: The 'thief' (கள்வன், 81) who killed the prince is the deed itself, not Kanchanan, whose sword is only its instrument (85); the deed is said to 'rise in wrath' (83, உருத்து எழும்), the verb of the Silappathikaram's moral of karma. Manimekalai speaks of a life (உயிர்) entering a dwelling (புக்கில், 76) by its deeds; the text puts the Buddhist teaching in these words without raising the question of a lasting self.
event: Manimekalai answers the queen's grief and tells her that the prince's death was the fruit of his killing of a cook in a former birth.

tamil: பூங் கொடி நல்லாய்! புகுந்தது இது என
கல்லாக் கயவன் கார் இருள் தான் வர
reading: Saying that if the queen asks how she knows this she will tell, Manimekalai recounts everything from entering the flowering grove to grasping the deity's words, and then says that because the queen's drug found her already knowing her former birth she was not deluded, that when the unlettered lout came in the dark she held a man's form, and that it was her mantra against hunger that made the queen's deceit fail.
nuance: Lines 92 to 94 repeat lines 41 to 43 almost word for word, with the narrator's third person turned into her first: she tells the queen her own plot, so that the confession the queen made in 64 to 66 is met with full knowledge, not with discovery.
event: Manimekalai tells the queen her story from the grove onward and how each of the queen's tricks failed.

tamil: எய்யா மையல் தீர்ந்து இன் உரை கேளாய்
மான்று ஓர் திசை போய் வரையாள் வாழ்வுழி
புதல்வன் தன்னை ஓர் புரி நூல் மார்பன்
ஆங்கு அப் புதல்வன் அவள் திறம் அறியான்
தான் புணர்ந்து அறிந்து பின் தன் உயிர் நீத்ததும்
நீர் நசை வேட்கையின் நெடுங் கடம் உழலும்
reading: Manimekalai says she did not set her mind on flying off or changing her form to escape, but stayed so as to remove the grief of the queen who bore her beloved of the former birth and to end her evil deed, and bids her hear sweet words: in a land thrown into turmoil by its rulers, a weaver's wife abandoned by her husband and parted from her infant went off and lived as a woman without bounds, and the son, raised by a brahmin without the townsfolk knowing whose he was, lay with her unknowing and, learning the truth, gave up his life.
nuance: The stories that follow (104 to 123) answer, one by one, to unchaste desire, killing, drink, falsehood and theft, which 126 to 129 gather as 'these' to be renounced; the text does not name the set. Whether 98 to 99 means she refrained from using her powers against the queen, or that she lacked them in her former birth, turns on where 'சென்ற பிறவியில்' attaches; காருக மடந்தை is read as a weaver's wife.
event: Manimekalai tells the queen of a son who unknowingly lay with his abandoned mother and gave up his life on learning it.

tamil: சூல் முதிர் மட மான் வயிறு கிழித்து ஓடக்
மான் மறி விழுந்தது கண்டு மனம் மயங்கி
பயிர்க் குரல் கேட்டு அதன் பான்மையன் ஆகி
உயிர்ப்பொடு செங் கண் உகுத்த நீர் கண்டு
விடாஅது சென்று அதன் வெண் கோட்டு வீழ்வது
இள வேய்த் தோளாய்க்கு இது' என வேண்டா
மன் பேர் உலகத்து வாழ்வோர்க்கு இங்கு இவை
reading: She goes on: a forest hunter shot a doe big with young so that the fawn fell from her torn belly, and seeing the tears in her red eye he gave up his life; drunkards who go before a rutting elephant are gored on its white tusk, such is the pride of toddy; those who take the way of falsehood as their gain never pass beyond helpless grief; and the queen should not tell herself that such sufferings belong to thieves alone, for to all who live in this great world these bring sorrow and must be renounced, and learning that is merely learned is not learning.
nuance: 124 to 125 turn on the queen the very words the narrator used of her at 21 to 22 (கையாற்று, பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம்): the general lesson is aimed at her own conduct. Line 130 runs into the next unit's definition of true learning.
event: Manimekalai tells of a hunter who died of remorse at a dying doe's tears and of drunkards gored by an elephant, and urges the queen to renounce such ways.

tamil: திருந்து ஏர் எல் வளை! செல் உலகு அறிந்தோர்
மகன் துயர் நெருப்பா மனம் விறகு ஆக
அகம் சுடு வெந் தீ ஆய் இழை அவிப்ப
தேறு படு சில் நீர் போலத் தெளிந்து
ஆங்கு அவள் தொழுதலும் ஆய் இழை பொறாஅள்
reading: Manimekalai ends that the truly learned are those who have curbed hatred and understood fully, who supply what the suffering lack, who know the world to come, who end the hunger of those who come wearied, who grasp the firm truth that cuts off sorrow, and whose love for all creatures never ceases; so she pours the clear water of wisdom into the queen's ear and quenches the fire of grief that had her mind for fuel, and the queen, cleared like water settled by the clearing-nut and no longer hostile, bows to her, but Manimekalai cannot bear it, bows and praises her in return, saying she has done what is not fitting, for she is the mother of her beloved and the king's great queen.
nuance: The queen's bow (144) would set the ascetic above the queen; Manimekalai's returned bow (147) restores the order of kinship from her former birth, so the reconciliation is completed in family terms as well as doctrinal ones. The grief-as-fire image (140 to 141) and the clearing-nut image (142) make the teaching a medicine rather than a refutation.
event: The queen's grief is quenched by Manimekalai's teaching; she bows to Manimekalai, who bows to her in return.

title: ஆபுத்திரன் நாடு அடைந்த காதை
theme: After the prince's death Chithirapathi begs the queen to release Manimekalai, warning through the old story of Killi and the Naga princess that the city's fate hangs on Indra's festival and on the goddess whose name the girl bears; the queen refuses the courtesan house, Aravanar comes and, answering the queen's wish for his long life, teaches that ageing and death are nature and sets out the twelve links and the ten evil deeds; Manimekalai takes leave and flies to Nagapuram, where Aputhiran is reborn as a king under whom rain never fails.
source_issues: Line 176 (அகை மலர்ப் பூம்பொழில் அருந் தவன் தான் என்) ends on என், a sentence that runs on into kaathai 25.
Line 66 (ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்) is hard to construe: which two cities are meant is not clear from the unit.
Lines 85 and 114 carry the repaired ௌ/ெள font flag (தெளியா, தெளிதல); the repaired readings make sense.

tamil: தொல் முது கணிகை தன் சூழ்ச்சியில் போயவன்
மாதவி மகள் தனை வான் சிறை நீக்கக்
ஆங்கு அவன் புதல்வனோடு அருந் தவன் முனிந்த
திருக் கிளர் மணி முடித் தேவர் கோன் தன் முன்
ஒன்று கடை நின்ற ஆறு இருபதின்மர் இத்
தோன்று படு மா நகர்த் தோன்றிய நாள் முதல்
reading: Shaken to hear that the prince, drawn by her scheme, has died by the vidyadhara's sword, the old courtesan falls at the queen's feet to get Madhavi's daughter out of prison, and laments that of all the hundred and twenty-one heavenly dancers cursed down to earth since the city arose, her line included, none suffered as she has: when the man who paid the flower-price died, Madhavi went into the monks' abode and the stage dancer took a bowl from house to house, a thing people only laugh at in courtesans; and besides the prince, she warns, the city faces a calamity through a woman.
nuance: The count adds up: eleven given to Indra, five born on earth for a slip in gesture, a hundred and four cursed with Indra's son, and Urvasi of her own line make the ஒன்று கடை நின்ற ஆறு இருபதின்மர் (6 x 20 + 1) of line 15. Chithirapathi measures disgrace by the courtesan line's own heavenly charter, not by any law of conduct; and her own scheme set the prince on the road to his death (lines 1-3), which she does not mention to the queen. Whose woman threatens the city (மாதரால், 25) is left open here; the story that follows is of Pilivalai, but lines 72-73 point at Manimekalai. The claim is answered by the queen at 77-82, who calls the courtesan's life itself base.
event: Hearing of the prince's death, Chithirapathi falls at the queen's feet to have Manimekalai released and laments Madhavi's turn to the begging bowl.
unit_note: End moved from 19 to 26: the sentence of line 19 (பொன்றினன் என்று) runs on into 20-22, and Chithirapathi's complaint closes at இடுக்கணும் உண்டால் (26), before the Killi story begins at 27.

tamil: உம்பளம் தழீஇய உயர் மணல் நெடுங் கோட்டு
பொங்கு திரை உலாவும் புன்னை அம் கானல்
பூ நாறு சோலை யாரும் இல் ஒரு சிறை
உற்று உணர் உடம்பினும் வெற்றிச் சிலைக் காமன்
பொரு அறு பூங்கொடி போயின அந் நாள்
reading: Chithirapathi tells how the Chola Nedumudi Killi, in a lonely flowering grove of the seaside punnai shore in early spring, met a girl alone, was overcome by love through all five senses under Kama's flower-arrows, served her for a month without learning who she was, and, when she vanished, searched for her until a sky-walking sage appeared and the king bowed and asked him if he had seen her.
nuance: The king who 'saw the backs of many' and 'slew kings' (41, 45) is made to bow and serve; the five senses of 35-37 (seen, heard, eaten, breathed, touched) are the same five gates the Buddhist sermon of 101-122 will count among the links of birth, though Chithirapathi tells it as a love story.
event: In Chithirapathi's story, King Killi loves an unknown girl in a seaside grove for a month, loses her, and asks a sky-walking sage where she is.
unit_note: Moved: starts at 27, where the Killi story opens after Chithirapathi's warning, and ends at 51, where the king's question to the sage closes with அவன் உரைப்பான்; the core break at 44 fell mid-sentence (என்றே).

காவல் மா நகர் கடல் வயிறு புகூஉம்
ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்
வேந்தரை அட்டோய்! மெய் எனக் கொண்டு இக்
காசு இல் மா நகர் கடல் வயிறு புகாமல்
மாதவன் போயின அந் நாள் தொட்டும் இக்
மன் பெருந் தெய்வம் வருதலும் உண்டு என
reading: Chithirapathi gives the sage's answer: the girl is Pilivalai, daughter of the Naga king Valaivanan, of whom it was foretold at her birth that she would unite with one of the sun's line and return with child, so she will not come back except with that son; and on the day the island's peace rite is not kept, Puhar will enter the sea, which the Manimekala goddess's word cannot stop because Indra's curse stands, so the king must never forget Vasava's festival; since then, she says, the city has never been free of dread, and she fears the great goddess may come if the girl who bears her name is harmed.
nuance: Chithirapathi's real argument is the last two lines: Manimekalai was named after the goddess, so harming her may bring the goddess, and the city's sinking is the threat behind her plea. The sage's warning is conditional, a rite to keep, unlike the fixed date given by the Buddhist sage of kaathai 9. Line 66 (ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்) is hard to place: 'that city' and 'this city' may be the Naga city and Puhar, or two moments of Puhar.
event: In Chithirapathi's story the sage names Pilivalai, foretells her son's coming, and warns that Puhar will sink into the sea if Indra's festival is ever neglected; Chithirapathi says she fears the goddess's coming.
unit_note: Moved: starts at 52 with the sage's answer and ends at 74, where Chithirapathi's whole speech closes with அஞ்சினேன் அரசன் தேவி! என்று ஏத்தி; the core break at 69 split the sage's warning from her fear that follows from it.

tamil: தலைமையாக் கொண்ட நின் தலைமை இல் வாழ்க்கை
என்னொடு இருக்கும்' என்று ஈங்கு இவை சொல்வுழி
துணி கயம் துகள் படத் துளங்கிய அதுபோல்

மற வேல் மன்னவன் தேவி தன்பால் வரத்
reading: Chithirapathi asks for the dancer whose mind has turned good to be given to her house, and the queen refuses: the girl fled the life of drink, lying, lust, killing and deceit that the wise renounce and that Chithirapathi's house takes as its chief, fearing it base, and she will stay with the queen; Madhavi, hearing of her daughter, troubled like a stirred pool and shaking like a wind-tossed branch, tells Sudhamathi, falls at Aravanar's feet and comes with him to the queen.
nuance: The queen, who had imprisoned Manimekalai, now speaks the renouncer's list against the courtesan's house; the five she names (கள், பொய், காமம், கொலை, உள்ளக் களவு) are close to the Buddhist precepts, but the unit attributes them only to உரவோர், 'the strong', so the claim is tagged general. நல் மனம் பிறந்த (75) is Chithirapathi's own phrase, used to win the girl back.
event: The queen refuses to hand Manimekalai to Chithirapathi; Madhavi, alarmed, brings Aravanar to the queen.
unit_note: Moved: starts at 75 with Chithirapathi's request, after her speech closes at 74, and ends at 88 (தன்பால் வர), with Madhavi and Aravanar arriving before the queen; the core break at 89 split the list of those present (தேவியும் ஆயமும் சித்திராபதியும் / மாதவி மகளும்).

tamil: எழுந்து எதிர்சென்று ஆங்கு இணை வளைக் கையால்
திருந்து அடி விளக்கிச் சிறப்புச் செய்த பின்
"யாண்டு பல புக்க நும் இணை அடி வருந்த என்
மூத்த இவ் யாக்கை வாழ்க பல்லாண்டு!' என
reading: Seeing the sage, the queen, her women, Chithirapathi and Manimekalai rise and go to meet him and bow at his feet; he blesses them with 'may wisdom arise', and the queen seats him, washes his feet, honours him, and says her good deeds have brought him after many years and wishes his tired, aged body long life, though his tongue has not failed.
nuance: Even Chithirapathi rises and bows. The sage's blessing is for wisdom, the queen's for the body's long life; the next unit answers her wish.
event: All rise and bow to Aravanar, who blesses them; the queen washes his feet and wishes him long life.
unit_note: Start moved from 90 to 89 so that the list of those who rise (தேவியும் ஆயமும் சித்திராபதியும் / மாதவி மகளும்) is not split; the end at 100 is the core's.

tamil: இற்று என வகுத்த இயல்பு ஈர் ஆறும்
அலகு இல பல் உயிர் அறு வகைத்து ஆகும்
reading: Aravanar answers that though he lives in a body given to austerity he is like the setting sun, for to be born, grow old, fall ill and die is the nature of things, and he teaches the twelve links from ignorance through action, consciousness, name and form, the six gates, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming and birth to the fruit of deeds, saying that those who know them gain the great reward and those who don't go down to hell; ignorance is failing to know these, forgetting what is seen in the nature of things and trusting hearsay that a hare has horns; and living beings are of six kinds, born by good and bad deeds and shown joy and sorrow when the deeds ripen.
nuance: The queen's wish for long life is turned without rebuke into the first lesson: ageing is nature (இயல்பே, 104), not a misfortune to be wished away. The list of twelve ends with வினைப் பயன் where the old age and death of the usual list would be, and those come back as the opening sentence. Ignorance is defined epistemically, as trusting what one heard over what one saw (113-114), which kaathai 29's means of knowledge will develop.
event: Aravanar answers the queen's blessing and begins to teach the twelve links of dependent arising and the six kinds of beings.
unit_note: End moved from 118 to 122: the six kinds of beings (115-118) are the subject of the sentence that runs to காட்டும் at 122, where they are born of good and bad deeds and taste joy and sorrow.

tamil: ஆய் தொடி நல்லாய்! ஆங்கு அது கேளாய்
பொய்யே குறளை கடுஞ் சொல் பயன் இல்
மேல் என வகுத்த ஒரு மூன்று திறத்து
reading: Aravanar defines evil deeds as ten: killing, theft and lustful desire of the body; lying, slander, harsh speech and idle speech of the tongue; and covetousness, anger and wrong view of the mind; the wise do not walk this way, and those who do are born as animals, ghosts and beings of hell in a troubled mind; good deeds are leaving these ten, keeping the precepts and standing first in giving, and those who do them are born as gods, humans and Brahmas and enjoy the fruit.
nuance: Good deeds here win only the higher births of the six, gods, humans and Brahmas; they do not end birth, which the previous unit ties to knowing the twelve links. The ten are counted by the door they come through (body, speech, mind), so wrong view (பொல்லாக் காட்சி) is itself a deed.
unit_note: Moved: starts at 123 with the question on evil deeds, after the account of births closes at 122, and ends at 140, where the fruit of good deeds is eaten; the core break at 141 put the address to the queen (அரைசன் தேவியொடு ஆய் இழை நல்லீர்!) in this unit, apart from the கேண்மின் at 142 it belongs to.

tamil: புரை தீர் நல் அறம் போற்றிக் கேண்மின்
பிற அறம் கேட்ட பின் நாள் வந்து உனக்கு
நன்று அறி மாதவன் நல் அடி வணங்கி
இந் நகர் மருங்கின் யான் உறைவேன் ஆயின்
ஆபுத்திரன் நாடு அடைந்து அதன் பின் நாள்
reading: Aravanar bids the queen and the women hold to this dharma, and tells Manimekalai, who knows her former birth, that after she has heard the other doctrines he will tell her all of it in full; he rises, and she bows at his feet and tells the queen, the women and Chithirapathi not to forget his words, saying that if she stays they will call her death to the king's son, so she will go to Aputhiran's land, then worship at Manipallavam, then enter Vanji and do good deeds everywhere for the great pathini, and they need not grieve for her.
nuance: Aravanar's order is a method: Manimekalai is to hear the rival doctrines first and be taught the full dharma after (144), which is the shape of kaathais 27 to 30. Her own itinerary (153-156) names the next stages of the epic, and the pathini of Vanji is Kannaki, her father's wife.
event: Aravanar promises to teach Manimekalai fully later; she bows, takes leave of the queen and Chithirapathi, and says she will go to Aputhiran's land, Manipallavam and Vanji.
unit_note: Moved: starts at 141 with Aravanar's address to the queen and her women, and ends at 158, where Manimekalai's farewell closes with அவரையும் வணங்கி; the core unit 142-161 cut the address from its verb and ran into the list of shrines (161-162).

reading: At dusk Manimekalai circles and praises the world's charity hall, the old woman's shrine and the shining pillar, flies through the sky and comes down in a flower grove outside the great city of Indra's descendant, bows to an ascetic there and asks the city's name and king, and he tells her it is Nagapuram, ruled by Punniyarajan, son of Bhumichandran, since whose birth rain has never failed, earth and trees have yielded plenty and no wasting disease has touched living beings.
nuance: Punniyarajan is the reborn Aputhiran (the land she named at 153), and the city is called that of Indra's descendant (164): the plenty Indra once sent to idle Aputhiran's bowl now marks his birth as a king. The ascetic credits the rain to the king's birth, not to his rule.
event: Manimekalai flies from Puhar to a grove outside Nagapuram, where an ascetic tells her the city is ruled by Punniyarajan.
unit_note: Start moved from 162 to 159 so that the list of shrines she circles (உலக அறவியும் முதியாள் குடிகையும் / இலகு ஒளிக் கந்தமும்) is not split; the end at 176 is the kaathai's.

title: ஆபுத்திரனோடு மணிபல்லவம் அடைந்த காதை
theme: Manimekalai wakes the king of Savakam, Aputhiran reborn, to his former birth: he hears his birth story, resolves to renounce, is argued back to his duty by his minister, sails to Manipallavam where the dharma seat shows him his past, and is shown by the island's goddess the bones of his former body and of those who died following his fast; the goddess tells Manimekalai how Puhar was cursed into the sea, and Manimekalai sends the king home to rule, telling him a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all lives.
source_issues: Line 31 had a leftover HTML quote mark, removed in the core file.
Line 93 தெளிந்த was repaired from an old-font ௌ.

Line 37 opens a quotation inside Manimekalai's speech that runs to line 67 with further nested quotations (41-50, 54-57, 58-65); the nesting is hard to follow and the speaker of 54-57 (Manimekalai in her former birth) is inferred.
Lines 55-57: கரியவன் as the one who placed the seat is unclear (line 182 says the king of the gods set it), and மன் பெரும் பீடிகை மாய்ந்து உயிர் நீங்கிய is hard to construe.
Line 118 ஒர்ந்தனை is probably ஓர்ந்தனை.
Line 170 அன்பு உடை ஆர் உயிர் அரசற்கு அருளிய is obscure.
Lines 207-212 are compressed and the referents of 'the guardian of the sea' and 'your lord of lives' are inferred.
The kaathai ends on என் (239), running into kaathai 26; the last unit has break score 0.

tamil: இங்கு இணை இல்லாள் இவள் யார்?' என்ன
ஆங்கு அவள் இவள்! அவ் அகல் நகர் நீங்கி
reading: The king of Savakam enters the grove with his household, worships the teacher Dharmasavakan and hears from him dharma and its opposite, the impermanent and the permanent, suffering, the passage of lives, dependent arising and release by cutting it; seeing a peerless woman with a bowl in her hand listening to dharma, he asks who she is, the chamberlain tells him she is the girl whose birth Aravanan revealed in Puhar, and Manimekalai tells the king that his bowl has come into her hand and asks what he has done, bewildered by wealth, not knowing even this birth of his from a cow's womb.
nuance: The teaching the king hears (3 to 6) is a list of Buddhist headings, ending with dependent arising and release by cutting it (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி), but it has not woken him; it takes Manimekalai's reproach to do that. Her charge is not that he has forgotten a former life, which few remember, but that wealth has hidden from him even the present one (23 to 24), the cow's womb he was born from.
event: The king of Savakam hears dharma from Dharmasavakan, asks who the woman with the bowl is, and Manimekalai tells him his bowl is now in her hand and reproaches him for not knowing his birth.

tamil: ஆங்கு வருவாய் அரச! நீ' என்று அப்
வான் நின்று இழிந்து மறி திரை உலாவும்
தொழுது வலம் கொள்ள அத் தூ மணிப்பீடிகைப்
பழுது இல் காட்சி தன் பிறப்பு உணர்த்த
மாயம் இல் மாதவன் தன் அடி பணிந்து
reading: Manimekalai tells the king he will not know the nature of bound birth unless he circles Manipallavam and bids him come there, then rises into the clear sky, comes down before sunset on the island's flowered shore, circles it, sees the jewelled seat of the bond-free great ascetic and, as she worships and circles it, the seat's flawless sight makes her know her birth again, and she begins to speak of how on the Kayankarai bank she bowed to the sage, heard dharma and praised him.
event: Manimekalai summons the king to Manipallavam, flies there herself, circles the dharma seat and recalls again her former birth.

tamil: அந் நாள் அவன் அறம் கேட்டோர் அல்லது
நாக் கடிப்பு ஆக வாய்ப் பறை அறைந்தீர்
அவ் உரை கேட்டு நும் அடி தொழுது ஏத்த
மன் பெரும் பீடிகை மாய்ந்து உயிர் நீங்கிய
என் பிறப்பு உணர்த்தலும் என்?" என்று யான் தொழ
reading: Manimekalai, speaking as if to the sage of her former birth, recalls his proclamation to all who went with him: put away the evil deeds that make men beasts, hell-beings and ghosts, and you become gods, men and Brahmas, so keep up good deeds unwearied; an all-knowing one will appear to save the world, and none but those who hear his dharma escape painful birth, so practise dharma before death comes; and she recalls that after his harsh word to her she asked why the seat had been placed before the Great One's coming and why it shows her birth, and he answered that it bears none but the all-knowing first one, that the god will not worship it until it has borne him, and that the god set it for him and bade it declare the births of those born.
nuance: The 'harsh word' (வெவ் உரை, 53) is the sage's prophecy in kaathai 9 that Rahulan would die within sixteen days and she would enter his pyre; here she places in the same hearing her question about the seat, so the seat's power was explained to her in the life she lost. Good deeds earn better births (43 to 44), but only hearing the coming Buddha's dharma ends birth (47 to 48): the sermon keeps those two apart. Who கரியவன் (55) is, who placed the seat, is not clear; at 182 the seat is said to have been set by the king of the gods. Lines 56 to 57 (மன் பெரும் பீடிகை மாய்ந்து உயிர் நீங்கிய என் பிறப்பு) are hard to construe.
event: Manimekalai recalls the sage's sermon on deeds and rebirth and his explanation of why the dharma seat reveals births.

tamil: இருள் அறக் காட்டும்" என்று எடுத்து உரைத்தது
இன்று எனக்கு' என்றே ஏத்தி வலம் கொண்டு
ஆங்கு அப் பொழில் விட்டு அகநகர் புக்கு
குடர்த் தொடர் மாலை சூழாது ஆங்கு ஓர்
reading: The sage's answer ends: because the god so ordained, the seat will show her births too, clearing the dark; Manimekalai says the word the sage spoke that day has come true for her today, praises and circles the seat; meanwhile the king leaves the grove for the inner city and learns of the birth in which a sage was his father and a cow his mother, how by the sage's grace he lay in a golden egg without the cord of the gut, and how childless Bhumichandran took him, hearing it from his mother Amarasundari.
nuance: The king learns his former birth twice: from his foster mother in the palace (70 to 77) before the seat shows it to him (134 to 138). The golden egg 'not wound in the gut-chain' (72 to 73) marks this birth as unsoiled by the womb.
event: Manimekalai says the sage's word is fulfilled; the king returns to the city and hears from his mother the story of his birth from a cow and his adoption.

tamil: தாய் வாய்க் கேட்டு தாழ் துயர் எய்தி
அம் கையில் துறு மலர் சுரி குழல் சூட்டி
நறு முகை அமிழ்து உறூஉம் திரு நகை அருந்தி
மதி முகக் கருங் கண் செங் கடை கலக்கக்
தூ அறத் துறத்தல் நன்று' எனச் சாற்றி
reading: Grieving at what he hears, the king thinks of what his mother did in the life he lost and of the nature of the birth he now has, and declares that it is good to renounce wholly the intoxicating game of desire that kingship is, with its throne before which kings wait, its dancing and music, its waiting on queens' sulks, painting saffron on their breasts and drinking their smiles under the sugarcane bow's arrows; the seed the clear-sighted lord sowed in his ear, he says, has ripened today without fault, with Manimekalai as its cause.
nuance: 'What the mother did' (78) is the abandonment of the newborn Aputhiran by Saali in his former birth. The king does not renounce kingship as a burden but as a drunkenness of pleasure (காமக் கள்ளாட்டு, 91): his catalogue is the life of a pleasure-king, not of a protector. The 'clear lord' who sowed the seed (93) is most likely Dharmasavakan, whose teaching he had just heard in the grove. His claim is answered: the minister calls it a wrong judgment by the Buddha's own example (115 to 118), and Manimekalai sends him back to rule with the dharma of grace (226 to 231).
event: Hearing his birth story, the king grieves and declares he will give up kingship and its pleasures for renunciation.

tamil: அணி மணி நீள் முடி அரசன் கூற
நும் கோன் உன்னைப் பெறுவதன் முன் நாள்
பன்னீராண்டு இப் பதி கெழு நல் நாடு
மன் உயிர் மடிய மழை வளம் கரந்து ஈங்கு
ஊன் உடை உயிர்கள் உறு பசி அறியா
துயர் நிலை உலகம் காத்தல் இன்றி நீ
reading: Seeing the king's mind changed, the minister Janamitran bows and tells him that before his father had him, this land had no rain for twelve years, so that creatures died and a mother would eat alone without pity for her infant; he appeared like a raincloud in a burning summer, and since then the sky has not failed nor the earth its yield, and no creature has known hunger; if he goes, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone, and if he seeks the higher world without guarding this suffering one, then even as lives perish, lord,
nuance: The minister ties the rain not to the king's rule but to his birth (105 to 109): the merit that returns the rain is Aputhiran's giving in his former life, carried into this one (kaathai 14, 95 to 104). The mother eating alone in the famine (103 to 104) is the reversal of the bowl's ethic of feeding others first. The unit ends mid-sentence; the minister's argument completes at 115 to 118.
event: The minister Janamitran tells the king of the twelve-year famine that ended at his birth and warns that his land will be orphaned if he leaves.

tamil: தன் உயிர்க்கு இரங்கான் பிற உயிர் ஓம்பும்
மன் உயிர் முதல்வன் அறமும் ஈது அன்றால்
ஒரு மதி எல்லை காத்தல் நின் கடன்' என
இலங்கு நீர்ப் புணரி எறி கரை எய்தி
தங்காது அக் கலம் சென்று சார்ந்து இறுத்தலும்
அரைசன் கலம் என்று அகம் மகிழ்வு எய்தி
தே மலர்ச் சோலைத் தீவகம் வலம் செய்து
தென் தமிழ் மதுரைச் செழுங் கலைப் பாவாய்!
reading: you would gain what you desire, the minister says, yet the dharma of the Buddha, first of all lives, who does not pity his own life and protects the lives of others, is not this, and the king has judged wrongly; the king answers that the unquenchable longing to circle Manipallavam is hard to quiet, charges the minister to guard kingdom, queens and city for one month, summons shipwrights, sails, and reaches the island, where Manimekalai, glad to see the king's ship, circles it with him and shows him the dharma seat, which, as he circles and praises it, shows him his ended birth like a clear mirror held to a face, and he cries that he knows his birth and his grief is ended, hailing the image of the arts of Tamil Madurai.
nuance: The minister turns the Buddha's own example against the king's renunciation: the Buddha's mark is that he does not pity his own life (116 to 117), and seeking a higher world for oneself while one's people suffer is pity for oneself. The king does not answer the argument; he asks only for a month to circle the island. Line 118 ஒர்ந்தனை is read as ஓர்ந்தனை.
event: The minister appeals to the Buddha's example; the king leaves him to guard the realm for a month, sails to Manipallavam, and the dharma seat shows him his former birth.

tamil: மாரி நடு நாள் வயிறு காய் பசியால்
ஆர் இருள் அஞ்சாது அம்பலம் அணைந்து ஆங்கு
"நாடு வறம் கூரினும் இவ் ஓடு வறம் கூராது
ஏடா! அழியல் எழுந்து இது கொள்க" என
மணி திகழ் அவிர் ஒளி மடந்தை! நின் அடி
reading: The king recalls to the goddess of Madurai how, when hungry beggars came to him in the rest hall in the middle of a rainy night and he grieved with no food to give, she put Amudasurabi in his palm saying the bowl would not fail though the land did, and so cut off his round of becoming; he hails her, who rises in the mind and makes the meaning of words known, and begins to praise her feet, which even gods and Brahmas worship.
nuance: The goddess's words at 144 to 145 repeat almost word for word those Aravanar gave her in kaathai 14 (12 to 13): the king's own memory now agrees with the teacher's account. பவம் அறுவித்த (147) is read as 'who cut off my becoming'; it may mean only that she ended his misery.
event: The king, knowing his former birth, recalls and praises Chintadevi's gift of the bowl.

tamil: நா மாசு கழூஉம் நலம் கிளர் திருந்து அடி
தூ மலர்ப் புன்னைத் துறை நிழல் இருப்ப
பெருந் துயர் தீர்த்த அப் பெரியோய்! வந்தனை
பின் நாள் வந்து நின் பெற்றிமை நோக்கி
நின் குறி இருந்து தம் உயிர் நீத்தோர்
ஒன்பது செட்டிகள் உடல் என்பு இவை காண்
ஆங்கு அவர் இட உண்டு அவருடன் வந்தோர்
ஏங்கி மெய் வைத்தோர் என்பும் இவை காண்
ஊர் திரை தொகுத்த உயர் மணல் புதைப்ப
ஆய் மலர்ப் புன்னை அணி நிழல் கீழால்
அன்பு உடை ஆர் உயிர் அரசற்கு அருளிய
நின் உயிர் கொன்றாய் நின் உயிர்க்கு இரங்கிப்
பின் நாள் வந்த பிறர் உயிர் கொன்றாய்
reading: Praising her feet, which wash the stain of the tongue, the king vows never to forget them in any birth, then goes with Manimekalai southwest to the Gomukhi pool and sits in the shade of a punnai; the island's guardian goddess, glad to see Aputhiran there, comes and tells him: you who held in your palm the medicine that saves life and ended great suffering, you have come; those who forgot you that day came back later, saw what you had done and gave up their lives where you had lain: see the bones of the nine merchants and of those who ate from their hands and died grieving; see your own bony frame under the sand by the punnai; you killed your own life, and, pitying your life, the others who came later killed theirs: are you not a killer? you have become a king.
nuance: The goddess's charge reckons self-starvation as killing (நின் உயிர் கொன்றாய், 172) and lays the later deaths of the merchants and their company on Aputhiran, who set the example; then she turns the charge with a play of sound, கொலைவன் against கொற்றவன் (174): the 'killer' has become a king. Whether this is reproach or wonder is not settled by the Tamil. Line 170 (அன்பு உடை ஆர் உயிர் அரசற்கு அருளிய) is hard: read as the body that, by the loving life it gave up, gave the king his kingship.
event: At the Gomukhi pool the island's guardian goddess shows the king the bones of the nine merchants who died where he had died and calls him a killer who has become a king.

tamil: மடவரல் நல்லாய்! நின் தன் மா நகர்
நாக நல் நாடு ஆள்வோன் தன் மகள்
புனிற்று இளங் குழவியொடு பூங்கொடி பொருந்தி இத்
தீவகம் வலம் செய்து தேவர் கோன் இட்ட
மா பெரும் பீடிகை வலம் கொண்டு ஏத்துழி
அங்கு அவன்பால் சென்று அவன் திறம் அறிந்து
கலம் கொண்டு பெயர்ந்த அன்றே கார் இருள்
இலங்கு நீர் அடைகரை அக் கலம் கெட்டது
வானவன் விழாக் கோள் மா நகர் ஒழிந்தது
"அணி நகர் தன்னை அலை கடல் கொள்க" என
reading: Turning to Manimekalai, the goddess tells her why her great city went into the sea: Pilivalai, daughter of the Naga king, came with her newborn son by the Chola of the sun's line, circled the island and the seat Indra set, and gave the boy to the merchant Kambalan, whose ship had put in, as the king's son; he took the child with joy, but that night the ship was wrecked on the shore and the boy lost; the Chola, told of it, searched beach, sea and shore like a cobra that has lost its gem, the city's Indra festival lapsed, and the goddess Manimekala, unable to bear that, cried 'let the sea take the city'.
nuance: The city's ruin has a chain of causes with no evil intent in it: a mother's gift, a shipwreck, a father's grief, a festival forgotten in that grief, and a goddess's anger at the lapse. The king's search 'like a cobra that has lost its gem' (195) recalls the Naga line of the lost child.
event: The guardian goddess tells how the Chola's infant son by Pilivalai was lost in a shipwreck, the grieving king neglected the Indra festival, and Manimekala cursed Puhar to be taken by the sea.

tamil: கடவுள் மா நகர் கடல் கொள பெயர்ந்த
வடி வேல் தடக் கை வானவன் போல
அருந் தவன் தன்னுடன் ஆய் இழை தாயரும்
பரப்பு நீர்ப் பௌவம் பலர் தொழ காப்போள்
முன் நாள் எடுத்ததும் அந் நாள் ஆங்கு அவன்
அந்தரத் தீவகத்து அருந் தெய்வம் போய பின்
ஊன் பிணி அவிழவும் உடல் என்பு ஒடுங்கித்
வெண் சுதை வேய்ந்து அவண் இருக்கையின் இருந்த
reading: The goddess ends: the curse was laid and came to pass; as the waves swallowed the city, its king went off alone like Indra leaving his drowned city, and the sage went safely with Manimekalai's mothers to Vanji; if she would hear how Manimekala once rescued her lord of all lives from the sea and how he then ruled as a king of dharma, she will hear it from Aravanan in Vanji; the goddess departs, and the king, grieving, digs the sand with Manimekalai and uncovers his former body, the flesh fallen away but the bones still holding together, seated as if coated in white lime, and the king is bewildered at the sight until Manimekalai rises and asks him what has befallen him.
nuance: The skeleton is kept whole (216 to 217): the flesh's bonds have loosened but the bones' have not, and it sits in the posture of the faster as if plastered for a shrine. The sight that might teach the body's impermanence instead bewilders the king (220). Lines 207 to 212 are compressed: 'the guardian of the wide sea' (207) is read as Manimekala, and 'your lord of lives' (209) as the Buddha in a former birth whom she saved from the sea.
event: The goddess tells of Puhar's drowning and the flight of Manimekalai's mothers to Vanji and departs; the king digs up his own former skeleton and is bewildered.

மன்னா! நின் தன் மறு பிறப்பு உணர்த்தி

நல் நுதல்! உரைத்த நல் அறம் செய்கேன்
என் பிறப்பு உணர்த்தி என்னை நீ படைத்தனை
மன் பெரு நல் நாடு வாய் எடுத்து அழைக்கும்
அந்தரத்து எழுந்தனள் அணி இழை தான் என்
reading: Manimekalai tells the king that she came to his land and called him here to show him his former birth so that his name would stand on this island and on the great continent; if kings who rule the wide earth take up the dharma of grace, nothing else is needed to remove faults, and if he asks what dharma is, he should remember that for all living beings it is nothing but food, clothing and shelter; the king vows to do this good dharma in his own land and in others', says she has made him anew by revealing his birth and that he cannot bear to part from her, and she bids him not grieve, for his land calls him back, to go by ship while she goes to Vanji, and rises into the sky.
nuance: Manimekalai does not take the king's offered renunciation; she sends him back to rule and defines his dharma as material provision for every life (230), the bowl's work made a king's duty. His reply widens it at once beyond his own kingdom (232). The kaathai ends on என் running into the next.
event: Manimekalai tells the king that a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all, he vows to practise it, and she sends him home by ship and flies to Vanji.

title: வஞ்சி மாநகர் புக்க காதை
theme: Manimekalai flies to the shrine of her parents' image, and Kannaki, speaking as the pathini goddess, retells Mathurapathi's word that Kovalan's death was the fruit of a killing in a former birth, confesses that she burned Madurai in anger after hearing that truth and must suffer its fruit once her heavenly merit is spent, foretells her and Kovalan's release on hearing the Buddha, and sends her daughter to hear the schools and find them false; Manimekalai takes an ascetic's form and enters Senguttuvan's Vanchi.

tamil: கற்புக் கடன் பூண்டு நும் கடன் முடித்தது
அருளல் வேண்டும்' என்று அழுது முன் நிற்ப
ஒரு பெரும் பத்தினிக் கடவுள் ஆங்கு உரைப்போள்
வெம்மையின் மதுரை வெவ் அழல் படு நாள்
reading: Manimekalai rises through the sky, enters the shrine to see the image in which her mother Kannaki and her father Kovalan are figured as deities, bows, praises them and weeps that her mother, neither holding to the debt of love nor taking the way of penance, took on the debt of chastity and so discharged what she owed, and asks for her grace; the great pathini goddess there begins to answer by recalling the day Madurai burned and the word of its goddess Mathurapathi.
nuance: Manimekalai's two refusals (அற்புக் கடன் நில்லாது, நல் தவம் படராது, 7) answer Madhavi's list in kaathai 2 of what pathinis do when a husband dies: die of grief, enter the fire, or wear the body down in vows; the daughter, like the mother, places Kannaki outside all three. The image is of both parents (தாய் கண்ணகியையும் ... தாதை கோவலன் தன்னையும், 2-3), and Kovalan is called கொடை கெழு, open-handed. கடவுள் எழுதிய படிமம் (4) may mean an image drawn as deities or one a god made; the line does not settle which, and it does not say this is the shrine Senguttuvan built.
event: Manimekalai flies to the shrine of Kannaki and Kovalan, worships their image and begs her mother's grace, and the pathini goddess begins to answer.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 13: Kannaki's speech opens at 10 and names Mathurapathi as subject at 13; the goddess's own quoted word begins at 14 (இது நீர் முன் செய் வினையின் பயனால்) and closes at 32.

tamil: காசு இல் பூம்பொழில் கலிங்க நல் நாட்டுத்
அங்கு ஆள்கின்றோர் அடல் செரு உறு நாள்
உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல் ஒழியாது" எனும்
reading: Kannaki repeats what Mathurapathi told her: in Kalinga, when the kinsmen kings Vasu of Singapuram and Kumaran of Kapilai were at war and no one crossed the land between, the merchant Sangaman came secretly with his wife to Haripuram to sell his goods, and Kovalan in a former birth, Bharatan, a man in the king's service, seized him as a spy and had the faultless man killed; his wife Neeli, wailing, climbed a hill and cursed, and that curse has now bound them, for a former deed rising in wrath does not fail to come.
nuance: The line that closes the goddess's word (உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல் ஒழியாது, 32) is the Silappathikaram's own phrase (உம்மை வினைவந் துருத்த காலை, 23:171), now heard from Kannaki's mouth: the wife confirms her husband's old crime herself. The Manimekalai calls Bharatan தீத் தொழிலாளன், a doer of evil work (26), and Sangaman குற்றம் இலோன், faultless (28), the very word Kannaki used of herself when she burned Madurai (குற்றமிலேன், Silappathikaram 21:42). Kapilai here (17) is the Kalinga town, not the Buddha's Kapilai of line 44, though the epic lets the one name serve both the city of the old killing and the city of the teacher.
event: Mathurapathi's account, as Kannaki retells it: Bharatan, Kovalan in a former birth, has the merchant Sangaman killed as a spy, and Sangaman's widow Neeli curses those who caused her grief.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 17 to 14 at the start: Mathurapathi's quoted word runs from 14 to its close at 32 (ஒழியாது எனும்), so the unit is that word whole.

tamil: மேற் செய் நல் வினையின் விண்ணவர்ச் சென்றேம்
அவ் வினை இறுதியின் அடு சினப் பாவம்
உம்பர் இல் வழி இம்பரில் பல் பிறப்பு
யாங்கணும் இரு வினை உய்த்து உமைப் போல
reading: Kannaki confesses that even after the goddess had spoken that true word she destroyed the rich city in anger; by good deeds done before, she and Kovalan went to the heavens, but when that merit is spent the sin of murderous anger will reach them by some way, and, with no heaven left to them, they will be driven by their two kinds of deeds through many births here, swimming the sea of births that is hard to leave, being born and dying.
nuance: This reverses the Silappathikaram, where Kannaki raged at the city as one without fault (குற்றமிலேன், 21:42) and the fire spared the good at her command: here she calls the same act sin (அடு சினப் பாவம், 36) and says she did it after hearing the truth (மெய்ம்மைக் கிளவி விளம்பிய பின்னும், 33), so her anger was not ignorance. Heaven is a reward that runs out (அவ் வினை இறுதியின், 36), not an end. Two causes stand together: the old deed brought the loss, and her own anger is a new deed with its own fruit.
event: Kannaki tells Manimekalai that she burned Madurai in anger after hearing the truth, went to heaven by former merit, and must yet suffer that anger's fruit in further births.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 49 to 41: Kannaki's account of her own anger and its fruit closes with உழல்வோம் at 41; at 42 a new sentence begins with the land of Magadha and the Buddha's coming.

tamil: ஒரு பெருந் திலகம்" என்று உரவோர் உரைக்கும்
கரவு அரும் பெருமைக் கபிலை அம் பதியின்
அளப்பு அரும் பாரமிதை அளவு இன்று நிறைத்து
தீது அறு நால் வகை வாய்மையும் தெரிந்து
இற்று என இயம்பி குற்ற வீடு எய்தி
அன்பு உறு மனத்தோடு அவன் அறம் கேட்டு
reading: Kannaki foretells that in Kapilai of Magadha, the land where rain never fails, the Buddha will appear like a sun, fill the perfections beyond measure, sit at the Bodhi tree, know the four truths and the arising of the twelve links and how they all cease, declare them and reach release from fault; when he spreads the rays of his dharma through the world-systems, she and Kovalan, because they praised the seven Indra viharas of the Lord, will not be born into a state of suffering, will hear his dharma with loving minds, gain the mind of renunciation and leave birth behind, though for a long age before that they will work wonders for people of every kind; and she turns to tell her daughter what she too must do in this old city.
nuance: The pathini goddess of the Silappathikaram is kept as a goddess, still giving help to all who ask (இருத்தியும் செய்குவம், 61, a word for wonder-working power), but her release is postponed to a future birth and made to depend on hearing the Buddha, not on her chastity. What saves her from a bad birth is not her karpu but her and Kovalan's worship at the seven Indra viharas (இந்திர விகாரம் ஏழும், 55). இருத்தி and the exact count of the viharas are read from the words alone.
event: Kannaki foretells the Buddha's birth and awakening and her and Kovalan's future release on hearing his dharma.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 42: the sentence on the Buddha's coming begins at 42 (மறந்தும் மழை மறா மகத நல் நாட்டுக்கு) and its verb of knowing runs through 48 to 51, so it cannot be cut at 49; Kannaki's charge to Manimekalai begins at 62 and the unit keeps its first two lines, as the received boundary at 64 is kept.

tamil: இன்னது இவ் இயல்பு' எனத் தாய் எடுத்து உரைத்தலும்
விளை பொருள் உரையார் வேற்று உருக் கொள்க" என
மந்திரம் ஓதி ஓர் மாதவன் வடிவு ஆய்
நல் நெறி காணிய தொல் நூல் புலவரும்
நில நாடு எல்லை தன் மலை நாடென்ன
reading: Kannaki closes her counsel: Manimekalai is to hear from each school what it holds, and when its lack of truth is plain to her she will not stray from the great one's Pitaka path; remembering the goddess's warning that no one would tell a young girl the truth, Manimekalai chants the mantra the deity gave and takes the form of an ascetic, and comes to the dwellings outside the walls, full of temples, platforms, monasteries, groves and pools, ascetics, the learned and old scholars seeking the good way, in the city of Senguttuvan, the king of the just sceptre who wore the vanji of war.
nuance: Lines 68 and 69 are, almost word for word, the Manimekala goddess's own warning in kaathai 10 (79-80), set in quotation as Manimekalai recalls it; the speaker here is the narrator, and Kannaki's voice ends at 67. The order of study is fixed in advance: the schools are to be heard so that their falseness may show, which makes kaathai 27's survey a planned stage, not an open inquiry. Kannaki, a goddess of a Tamil cult, is the one who sends her daughter to the Pitakas.
event: Kannaki ends her counsel; Manimekalai takes an ascetic's form by the goddess's mantra and comes to the outskirts of Senguttuvan's Vanchi.

tamil: கார் மயங்கு கடலின் கலி கொளக் கடைஇ
கங்கை அம் பேர் யாற்று அடைகரைத் தங்கி
அனைவரை வென்று அவர் அம் பொன் முடி மிசை
வில் திறல் வெய்யோன் தன் புகழ் விளங்க
பொன் கொடிப் பெயர்ப் படூஉம் பொன் நகர்ப் பொலிந்தனள்
reading: The narrator praises Senguttuvan, who drove his army like a roaring sea, camped on the bank of the Ganga, crossed it northward by boat, defeated Kanaka, Vijaya and many kings, set the divine stone of the Himalaya on their golden crowns and the vaagai of victory on his own, and says that Manimekalai shone in his golden city named for the golden creeper, for the good cause had ripened that would make the four truths plain to her.
nuance: The Chera's northern campaign, two long kaathais of the Silappathikaram, is folded into an epithet of the city, and its prize, the stone for Kannaki's image, is named only as a token of his victory (தெய்வக் கல், 89), though Kannaki has just spoken from her shrine. The last lines (93-94) turn from the king to the cause that is ripening in Manimekalai and run on, as the epic's kaathais do, into the next.
event: Manimekalai, in disguise, enters Vanchi, the city of Senguttuvan, conqueror of Kanaka and Vijaya.

title: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
theme: In an ascetic's borrowed form Manimekalai hears the schools of Vanji one by one: the Vedic logician's means of knowledge and their fallacies, the Saiva, Brahma, Vaishnava and Vedic accounts of God and scripture, the Ajivika's atoms and fixed fate, the Jain categories and release by exhausting deeds, Sankhya's nature and person, the Vaisheshika categories, and the materialist's denial of any next world, which alone she answers, turning his trust in perception against his knowledge of his own parents. Every school is given in a Buddhist work's account and set aside on the way to the Buddhist teaching of kaathai 29.
source_issues: Line 190: the source's line mark reads 227-190, carrying the kaathai number; read as 27-190.
Lines 50, 59, 67, 207-212, 221 and 223 were repaired for the old-font ௌ / ெள confusion (தெளிதல், வெளிப்பட்டு).
Line 36 opens a quotation ("இது மழை பெய்யும்) that is never closed in the text as printed.
Lines 151-152 print பசும்ம், செம்ம், பொன்ன், வெண்ண் with a doubled final consonant, presumably for metre.
Lines 9-12 name what reads as eleven means of knowledge though line 7 implies ten; the descriptions at 14-56 cover ten (மீட்சி ஒழிவறிவு appears to be one item).
Line 184 prints அநித்தயம் for அநித்தியம்; line 90 prints யாக்கையுமய்க்.
