the Vedic logician who sets out the means of valid knowledge
the debater for the Saiva view of God
the debater who holds the world to be an egg laid by one god
the reciter of the purana of the sea-coloured god, for Narayana as protector
the Vedic brahmin who holds the Veda to be without beginning or end
the Ajivika teacher, versed in the book of Makkali
the Jain (Nigantha) debater
the debater for the Sankhya
the debater for the Vaisheshika
the materialist (Lokayata) debater

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: ஏதம் இல் சைமினி எனும் இவ் ஆசிரியர்
எய்தி உண்டாம் நெறி என்று இவை தம்மால்
மருள் இல் காட்சி ஐ வகை ஆகும்
இவை இவை கண்டு கேட்டு உயிர்த்து உண்டு உற்று
துக்கமும் சுகமும் எனத் துயக்கு அற அறிந்து
பயில் ஒளியொடு பொருள் இடம் பழுது இன்றி
reading: Manimekalai goes among the schools' reckoners and asks the Vedic logician his doctrine; he names the teachers who counted ten, eight and six means of knowledge, lists the ten, and defines perception as fivefold sense-knowledge that, free of indefiniteness, error and doubt, grasps a thing's place, name, class, quality and action.
nuance: The logician is called வைதிக மார்க்கத்து அளவை வாதி, and his authorities are Vyasa, Kritakoti and Jaimini, so the school is Vedic without being one darsana; the chapter does not tie him to Nyaya or Mimamsa. Lines 9 to 12 name what reads as eleven items for the ten promised (மீட்சி ஒழிவறிவு may be one item, and உண்டாம் நெறி is the உள்ள நெறி of line 55). The account is given by a Buddhist work and is answered in kaathai 29, where perception is stripped of name, class, quality and action.
event: Manimekalai comes to the Vedic logician and asks him to state his doctrine; he begins to set out the means of knowledge.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 24: the definition of perception that begins at 14 runs to அறிவது ஆகும் at line 24; the core unit 1-15 broke it mid-list.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: மூ வகை உற்று அது பொது எச்சம் முதல் ஆம்
கடம் திகழ் யானைக் கான ஒலி கேட்டோன்
உடங்கு "எழில் யானை அங்கு உண்டு" என உணர்தல்
நிச்சயித்து அத் தலை மழை நிகழ்வு உரைத்தல்
முதல் என மொழிவது கருக்கொள் முகில் கண்டு
reading: The logician defines inference as knowing the inferable through a mark, in three kinds, and gives an example of each: the unseen elephant known by its sound, rain upstream known by the flood, rain to come known from pregnant clouds; a sound reason, tied to one of the three times and free of fault, knows the unseen through the seen.
nuance: The three kinds (பொது, எச்சம், முதல்) run from present sign, from effect back to cause, and from cause forward to effect. Lines 29 and 30, on the general kind holding even without concomitance (அந்நுவயம் இன்றாய் இருந்தும்), are hard to construe and the reading here is tentative.
unit_note: Starts at 25 where the definition of inference (கருத்து அளவு ஆவது) opens, and ends at 40, which closes the account of inference before உவமம் at 41.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: எய்தியது ஓர் பேய் உண்டு" எனத் தெளிதல்
தவாது அவ் இடத்துத் தான் இலை" என்றல்
reading: The logician gives the remaining means with an example each: comparison (the wild gavaya is like a cow), scripture (from the knower's book, that a world of enjoyment exists), presumption (a village 'on the Ganga' must be on its bank), aptness (the man on the elephant asking for a goad is handed the goad), tradition (a ghost haunts this tree), absence, implication (Rama won, so Ravana lost), and possibility (what turns an iron rod is a magnet).
nuance: Scripture counts as its own means here, and its example is an unseen world (போக புவனம்): the logician needs it for exactly what perception and inference cannot reach, which is where the Lokayata at the chapter's end will refuse to follow.
unit_note: Runs from உவமம் at 41 to line 56, where the last of the ten means (உள்ள நெறி) closes with எனக் கூறல்; the core units broke at 53, inside the example of மீட்சி.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: விரி கதிர் இப்பியை வெள்ளி என்று உணர்தல்
கண்டு உணராமை கடு மாப் புலி ஒன்று
புணர்ந்திடல் மருந்து எனப் புலம் கொள நினைத்தல்
பிறர் சொலக் கருதல் இப் பெற்றிய அளவைகள்
reading: The logician lists eight false semblances of knowledge, each with an example (bare awareness that something is there, shell taken for silver, 'post or man?', a post taken for a man without looking, failing to know a tiger seen, the hare's horn, knowing the known, and taking on others' word that these are your parents), then pairs six schools with their teachers and closes that six means of knowledge are current now.
nuance: The list at 78 to 85 sets six schools against six teachers and six means, and is most simply read cumulatively: Lokayata with perception alone, the Buddhists with inference added, and so on to Mimamsa with absence. சினன் (Jina) is here the Buddhists' teacher, as ஆதி சினேந்திரன் is the Buddha at 29:47; it is not the Jain Tirthankara. The parents example at 75 to 77, filed here as a fallacy, is the one Manimekalai turns on the materialist at 284.
unit_note: Joins the core units 54-76 (from 57) and 77-89 (to 85): the eight fallacies run from 57 to the middle of 77, and the same sentence goes on (இப் பெற்றிய அளவைகள்) into the list of schools, which ends at 85 before the narrator turns to the Saiva at 86. Lines 54-56 go with the unit before.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
reading: Leaving the logician, Manimekalai asks the Saiva debater what his god is like; he answers that the Lord is the one who is the eight (the two lights, the sacrificer and the five elements), who binds soul and body, whose form is the arts, who creates and plays, who wipes away sorrow, and who has nothing other than himself.
nuance: இரு சுடரோடு இயமானன் ஐம் பூதம் is the eight-formed god, in the oldest form of the list. தன்னில் வேறு தான் ஒன்று இலோன், the one with nothing other than himself, can be read as sole being or as one beyond any second; the line does not settle which.
event: Manimekalai leaves the logician and asks the Saiva debater what his god is like, and he describes Siva.
unit_note: The core unit 77-89 is split: 86 opens with the narrator leaving the logician for the Saiva, and 95 closes the Saiva's speech with என்று உரைத்தனன்.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: ஆதி அந்தம் இல்லை அது நெறி' எனும்
எத் திறத்தினும் இசையாது இவர் உரை' என
reading: In quick succession the Brahma-vadin says the whole world is an egg laid by one god, a devotee recites the purana of the sea-coloured god and says Narayana protects, and the Vedic brahmin says the Veda, with its six limbs as hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose and face, arises from no cause and has no beginning or end; Manimekalai judges that none of their words agrees with any way of truth.
nuance: The Veda is called சார்பின் தோன்றா, not arising from dependence: in a Buddhist work, whose own teaching is that everything arises by சார்பு, this is the phrase most open to attack. Manimekalai's verdict at 106 to 107 covers the whole group heard since 86 (இவர் உரை), not only the brahmin.
event: The Brahma-vadin, a Vaishnava reciter and a Vedic brahmin state their views, and Manimekalai rejects them all.
unit_note: The core unit 90-107 is cut at 96, where the Brahma-vadin's speech begins after the Saiva's என்று உரைத்தனன் at 95.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: 'பேசும் நின் இறை யார்? நூற்பொருள் யாது?' என
வரம்பு இல் அறிவன் இறை நூற்பொருள்கள் ஐந்து
உரம் தரும் உயிரோடு ஒரு நால் வகை அணு
நிலம் நீர் தீ காற்று என நால் வகையின
மலை மரம் உடம்பு எனத் திரள்வதும் செய்யும்
அவ் வகை அறிவது உயிர் எனப் படுமே
reading: Manimekalai asks Puranan, who knows the Ajivika book, for his god and his categories; he says the god is the knower without limit, present in all things at all times, and the categories are five, the soul and four kinds of atom, which touch, are seen, combine into mountain, tree and body and part again, while the soul is what knows.
nuance: புராணன் may be the teacher's name (an Ajivika teacher Purana is known from other traditions) or a description, one learned in the old book; the line allows either. Four kinds of atom without a fifth for space is part of the account as given.
event: Manimekalai asks the Ajivika teacher for his god and his doctrine, and he begins.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: இழினென நிலம் சேர்ந்து ஆழ்வது நீர் தீத்
தெறுதலும் மேல் சேர் இயல்பும் உடைத்து ஆம்
முது நீர் அணு நில அணுவாய்த் திரியா
தேயா மதி போல் செழு நில வரைப்பு ஆம்
ஒன்று முக்கால் அரை கால் ஆய் உறும்
reading: The Ajivika gives each element's nature (earth hard and low, water cool and sinking, fire burning and rising, wind moving) and says the atoms are without beginning, never destroyed, never newly born, never entering one another or turning into another kind, never splitting or spreading, yet they move, sink and rise, mass into mountains and diamonds, part again, and in a compound are named for the element that predominates.
nuance: The proportions at 140 (one, three quarters, half, quarter) give a rule for naming mixtures by the larger share; the images of bamboo and the unwaning moon at 136 and 137 are examples of what massed atoms become, and their exact sense is not secure.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: இக் குணத்து அடைந்தால் அல்லது நிலன் ஆய்ச்
கழி வெண் பிறப்பில் கலந்து வீடு அணைகுவர்
reading: The Ajivika says atoms act as earth, water, fire or wind only in these qualities; a single atom is seen only by those with divine eyes, as a single hair is not seen at dusk though a mass of hair is; and beings born through six births in order, black, dark blue, green, red, golden and white, reach release in the last white birth, a straight course they cannot fail to reach, while straying from it is the circling round.
nuance: The six colour-births are the Ajivika's own scheme as this account gives it. கருமம் பிறப்பு at 150 is read as the dark birth; பசும்ம், செம்ம், பொன்ன், வெண்ண் have an added consonant as printed. அழியல் வேண்டார் அது உறற்பாலார் says those in the course need not perish and are bound to reach it: release here comes by a fixed course, not by effort.
unit_note: Ends at 158 instead of 157: the sentence இது தப்பும் அது மண்டலம் என்று அறியல் வேண்டும் runs over 157 into 158.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: உறும் இடத்து எய்தலும் துக்க சுகம் உறுதலும்
இன்பமும் துன்பமும் இவையும் அணு எனத் தகும்
reading: The Ajivika ends that gain and loss, hindrance, pleasure and pain, parting, birth and death are all mixed in at the moment of conception, that pleasure and pain are themselves atoms, and that the fate laid down before makes what comes after, which is the doctrine of Makkali's book; Manimekalai leaves this tangle of words and asks the Jain debater for his lord, his categories, how they occur, and bondage and release.
nuance: This is the chapter's strongest statement of fate, and it is put in a rival's mouth: everything a life meets is fixed at conception, with no room for deed or effort. The Buddhist narrator's word for it, சொல் தடுமாற்றத் தொடர்ச்சி, is a dismissal, not an argument.
event: The Ajivika finishes; Manimekalai leaves him and asks the Jain debater to state his doctrine.
unit_note: Moved to 159-170 from the core 158-180: 158 closes the colour-births, 165 closes the Ajivika's speech (மற்கலி நூலின் வகை இது), and 170 closes Manimekalai's question to the Jain, whose answer begins at 171.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
reading: The Jain says his lord is the one the Indras worship, and the categories he gave are dharma, adharma, time, space, the faultless soul, atoms, good and bad deeds, the bondage they cause, and release; each thing has its own nature and a nature from what it depends on, is both lasting and passing, and in every moment takes on origination, persistence and destruction.
nuance: Dharma and adharma here are not merit and demerit but the media of motion and rest (as 187 to 190 make clear); merit and demerit are named separately at 175. A thing both lasting and passing is the Jain many-sided view of substance and its modes.
unit_note: The core unit 158-180 is cut at 171, where the Jain's answer begins, and ends at 182, where the sentence on origination, persistence and destruction closes with ஆக்கலும் உரித்தாம்.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: தா இல் சுவை முதலிய புலன்களை நுகரும்
ஓர் அணு புற்கலம் புற உரு ஆகும்
reading: The Jain illustrates with the sprouting neem and with gram cooked into a dish (the kind persists while the form passes), says dharma pervades all and makes things move, adharma makes them stay, time is the instant and the aeon, space gives room to all, the soul joins a body and enjoys the senses, the atom is matter's outward form, and release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and wear out the fruit of past deeds by living it through.
nuance: Release needs no grace and no god here: it is the stopping of new deeds and the exhausting of old ones. Both good and bad deeds bind (இரண்டையும் மாற்றி). Line 190's number in the source carries the kaathai number (227-190).
unit_note: Runs from 183, where the examples begin, to 201, where the Jain's speech ends with வீடு ஆகும் என்றனன்; the core units broke at 196 and 197, inside the account of the soul and of release.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: மன நிகழ்வு இன்றி மாண்பு அமை பொதுவாய்
தங்கிய அப்பில் வாய் சுவை எனும் விகாரமும்
வாக்கு பாணி பாதம் பாயுரு உபத்தம் என
அந்தம் இல் பிரளயம் ஆய் இறும் அளவும்
reading: The Sankhya speaker says primal nature is hard to know, made of the three qualities, without mind, the common ground from which all things appear; from it in turn appear intellect, space, wind, fire, water, earth, mind and the sense of self, then the senses and their objects from each element and the five organs of action, and from the elements the world of mountains and trees, which returns the way it came into dissolution while primal nature stays one, pervading and eternal.
nuance: The order given (intellect, then the elements, then mind and the sense of self) is not the order of the classical Sankhya texts, where the sense of self comes before the senses and elements; the Tamil account should not be taken as the school's own sequence. No creator is named: nature unfolds and withdraws by itself.
unit_note: Runs from 202, where the Sankhya speaker begins, to 226, where the account of primal nature closes (ஒன்றாய் எங்கும் பரந்து நித்தியம் ஆம்) before the account of purusha at 227; the core units broke at 220 and 221, inside the list of the organs of action.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: மெய் வாய் கண் மூக்கு செவி தாமே
உறு சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்மே
உயிர் எனும் ஆன்மா ஒன்றொடும் ஆம்' எனச்
reading: The Sankhya speaker says the person (purusha) is unlike nature: not of the three qualities, not the ground of things, but the awareness that knows them all, one, pervading and eternal; the principles are twenty-five, the five elements, five sense organs, five objects, five organs of action, mind, intellect, the sense of self, thought, and the soul.
nuance: The count of twenty-five here lists thought (சித்தம்) among the inner organs and ends with the soul, without naming primal nature in the list, so the twenty-five are not quite the classical list. அறிதற்கு எளிதாய் at 227 sets purusha against nature, which was hard to know at 203.
unit_note: Runs from 227, where the account of purusha begins, to 240, which closes the Sankhya section (செப்பிய திறமும் கேட்டு) before the Vaisheshika is addressed at 241.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: ஆம் ஆறு கூறு ஆம் அதில் பொருள் என்பது
பொருளுக்கும் ஏது ஆம் அப் பொருள் ஒன்பான்
ஞாலம் நீர் தீ வளி ஆகாயம் திசை
ஒலி ஊறு நிறம் சுவை நாற்றமொடு ஐந்தும்
சுவை முதல் ஒரோ குணம் அவை குறைவு உடைய
ஒன்று அணு கூட்டம் குணமும் குணியும்' என்று
reading: Asked for his doctrine, the Vaisheshika says there are six categories, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence; substance bears quality and action and is the cause of all compounds, and is ninefold (earth, water, fire, wind, space, direction, time, self, mind); earth has all five qualities and the other elements fewer; and generality is the common being that lets substance and quality act.
nuance: Line 249 gives earth sound among its five qualities; the Vaisheshika's own texts give sound to space alone, so this may be the account's slip or a different count. Lines 257 to 261 on generality are compressed and their sense is tentative.
event: Manimekalai asks the Vaisheshika for his doctrine and he sets it out.
unit_note: Runs from 241, where the Vaisheshika is addressed, to 262, where the narrator closes his speech (ஒன்றிய வாதியும் உரைத்தனன்); the core units broke at 261 and 262.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: அவ் உணர்வு அவ் அப் பூதத்து அழிவுகளின்
வெவ் வேறு பிரியும் பறை ஓசையின் கெடும்
அவ் அப் பூத வழி அவை பிறக்கும்
மெய் வகை இதுவே வேறு உரை விகற்பமும்
reading: The materialist says that as intoxication arises when dhataki flowers and jaggery are mixed, awareness arises in the combined elements and is lost when they part, like the sound of a drum dying away; beings with and without awareness both come from the elements; perception alone is valid and inference fails; this life and its fruits are all there is, and a next world where deeds are eaten is a lie.
nuance: The intoxication simile is the materialist's emblem in Tamil polemic: the Jain Neelakesi puts the same image in his mouth. Line 273 makes the materialist's own understanding the measure of truth, which is the point Manimekalai will press.
event: Manimekalai calls on the materialist, and he sets out his doctrine.
unit_note: Runs from 263, where the materialist is called on, to 276, which ends his speech (வினை துய்த்தல்'); the core units broke at 275 and 276, mid-sentence.

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: மையல் உறுவார் மனம் வேறு ஆம் வகை
reading: Having heard every path, Manimekalai says that though they are not good she will not answer them, and laughing asks whether there are not those who have come to know a birth before this one; the materialist replies that the minds of those deluded by a god or by dreams are changed, and such knowledge is nothing but doubt.
nuance: The speakers of 278 to 283 are not named and are fixed here from the sense: the laughing question suits Manimekalai, who learnt her own former birth in kaathai 9, and the rejoinder suits the materialist. His answer names the very means of her knowledge: a deity carried her off and she woke at the Buddha's seat.
event: Manimekalai, having heard all the schools, asks the materialist whether no one knows a former birth, and he dismisses such knowledge as delusion.
unit_note: The core unit 276-289 is split: 277 opens with Manimekalai's reply after all the schools, and 283 ends the materialist's rejoinder (ஐயம் அன்றி இல்லை' என்றலும்), before her answer at 283-284 (நின் / தந்தை).

section: சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்ட காதை
tamil: மெய்யுணர்வு இன்றி மெய்ப் பொருள் உணர்வு அரிய
ஐயம் அல்லது இது சொல்லப் பெறாய்' என
reading: Manimekalai answers that he knows his own father and mother only by inference, that without true understanding the true nature of things is hard to know, and that on his terms his own claim can be stated only as doubt; so, speaking in her assumed form, she learned the five kinds of religion.
nuance: The answer turns the materialist's rule on itself: a man who accepts perception alone cannot know his own parents, so his denial of past births is no firmer than the knowledge he calls doubt. The parents example was a fallacy of memory in the logician's list (75 to 77); here it is an inference no one can do without. ஐவகைச் சமயம் counts five where the chapter heard more speakers; which five is not said.
event: Manimekalai refutes the materialist and, having heard them all, comes to know the five kinds of religion.
unit_note: The last six lines of the core unit 276-289: Manimekalai's answer from 284 (தந்தை தாயரை) to the narrator's close at 289.

title: கச்சி மாநகர் புக்க காதை
theme: Leaving the schools of Vanji, Manimekalai finds Kovalan's father as a Buddhist ascetic there, hears how the Chera kings and her own ancestor took up the Buddha's teaching, that Kovalan's heaven still owes its evil deed and his release waits for the Buddha at Kapilai, and that drought-stricken Kanchi is her charge; she flies there, where the king, unable to tell whether his sceptre, austerity or women's chastity has failed, has built a copy of Manipallavam on a deity's word, and her bowl feeds every creature and brings back the rain before she casts off her disguise at Aravanar's feet.
source_issues: Line 148 (நின்னது தன்மை அந் நெடு நிலைக் கந்தில் துன்னிய) is longer than an akaval line and may join two lines of the edition.
Line 181 had a stray HTML mark removed by the core build (flag printed by show).

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, a Buddhist renunciant, still in an ascetic's borrowed form until the last line
Kovalan's father, the Puhar merchant now a Buddhist ascetic in Vanji (named here only as கோவலன் தாதை)
a Chera king of old, carver of the bow on the mountain, who fed the Dharma charanas in the Vanji grove
sky-going Buddhist sages returning from circling Samanoli in Lanka
Kovalan's namesake ancestor nine generations back, the Chera king's friend, who renounced and built a caitya in Vanji
the far-seeing ascetics of the Vanji caitya who foretell Puhar's drowning and Kovalan's release
the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, now in Kanchi
Manimekalai's mother, a Buddhist renunciant
Manimekalai's companion, counted with Madhavi as her mothers (தாயர்)
the chamberlain of the Kanchi king
the Chola Ilangkilli, ally (துணை) of Killi, builder of the Bodhi caitya in Kanchi; taken here as the king of Kanchi, whom the Tamil calls மன்னன் and வேந்தன்
the great deity who appeared to the Kanchi king in the drought and foretold the maiden with the bowl
the hungry people of eighteen tongues and the beasts who gather at the bowl

tamil: தம் தமில் ஆடிய சாந்து கழி நீரும்
புவி காவலன் தன் புண்ணிய நல் நாள்
சீல உபாசகர் செங் கை நறு நீரும்
அறம் செய் மாக்கள் அகில் முதல் புகைத்து
செறித்து அரைப்போர் தம் செழு மனை நீரும்
reading: Seeking her mothers and Aravanar, Manimekalai leaves the schools' hall and passes through the outer quarters that ring the Chera's Vanji like besieging kings, where the waters of many uses all run together: hair-wash from the houses, the spent sandal water of the pleasure tanks, the scented sprays of the king's birthday, the water lay devotees pour on the monks' feet, the rain from charity pandals and the perfume-grinders' wash.
nuance: The list sets the monks' foot-washing (lines 11 and 12) among the city's ordinary waters: Vanji is shown as a city where lay Buddhist practice is already part of the daily scene, which prepares for the monastery she finds at line 72.
event: Manimekalai, looking for her mothers and Aravanar, passes the outer quarters of Vanji.

tamil: இந்திர தனு என இலங்கு அகழ் உடுத்து
வந்து எறி பொறிகள் வகை மாண்பு உடைய
பசு மிளை பரந்து பல் தொழில் நிறைந்த
reading: Those mingled waters flow into the moat so that its crocodiles and fish lose their stink of flesh and its lotuses and lilies hum with bees, and beyond the moat girdling the city like a rainbow and the walls fitted with engines she reaches the bannered gate and goes in among the guards to the broad crowded street.
event: Manimekalai crosses the moat and walls of Vanji and enters by its gate.

tamil: பல் மீன் விலைஞர் வெள் உப்புப் பகருநர்
பாணர் என்று இவர் பல் வகை மறுகும்
reading: The narrator lists the streets of Vanji's trades: fish-sellers, salt-sellers, toddy-women, cake-makers, meat-sellers, potters, copper-, brass- and goldsmiths, carpenters, clay-modellers, painters, leather-workers, tailors, garland-makers, astrologers, bards who show the modes on the lute, and the shell-cutters and gem-workers.

tamil: வேத்தியல் பொது இயல் என்று இவ் இரண்டின்
பால் வேறு ஆக எண் வகைப் பட்ட
பொன் உரை காண்போர் நல் மனை மறுகும்

reading: The catalogue goes on to the streets of the dancers who know both court and common styles, of the eight kinds of grain, of bards and panegyrists, of herders, weavers of fine cloth, gold-assayers and gem-sellers, the Brahmins' street, the streets of the king's and ministers' households, the halls, squares and crossroads, and the avenues where new elephants and horses are trained.

தீவகம் விட்டு இத் திரு நகர் புகுந்ததும்
reading: Past artificial hills, groves and pools that the gods might leave heaven for, Manimekalai enters a monastery of the Buddha's preachers, fair as an Indra vihara where sky-walkers delight to dwell, bows at the feet of Kovalan's father, now a great ascetic, and recounts her life since the bowl: the gift of the bowl, her former birth shown by the seat, the goddess's comfort, her coming to Vanji after the sea took Puhar, and hearing the schools in a false form and finding none of them straight.
nuance: Lines 74 to 90 are a summary of kaathais 11 to 27 in her own report. The monastery is likened to an இந்திர விகாரம் with அந்தர சாரிகள் (69 to 70), the very words the Silappathikaram uses for the place where Kovalan's father renounced in Puhar. Line 85 keeps her in the பொய் உரு she took to hear the schools; she drops it only at line 245.
event: Manimekalai enters a Buddhist monastery in Vanji, bows to Kovalan's father, now an ascetic, and tells him her story.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 85 to 90: the list of what Manimekalai tells the ascetic, which begins at line 74, runs to வந்த வண்ணமும் at line 90 and is closed by சொல்லினள் at 91; the core unit 62-85 cut it mid-list.

reading: Manimekalai asks the pure one whether seeing him is the fruit of her good deeds, and he answers that when he heard her father and mother had died in sorrow as their evil deeds ruined the city, he, fit for the loving dharma of the Sugata, knew household life for an illusion and wealth and body for things that do not last a moment, and took up the great austerity of unshaken dharma.
nuance: Her mother Madhavi is alive, so the தாய் who died with her father must be Kannaki, counted here as Manimekalai's mother. The Silappathikaram gives grief and a great gift as the cause of his renunciation; here he gives the reason in doctrine, that home is மாயம் and wealth and body do not stand, and he makes his fitness for the Sugata's dharma part of the cause.
event: Manimekalai asks the ascetic whether meeting him is her good deeds' fruit; he tells her he renounced on hearing of her parents' deaths.
unit_note: Units 86-99 and 100-119 replaced by 62-90, 91-100 and 101-119: the ascetic's sentence that begins at 93 ends only with மா தவம் புரிந்தேன் at line 100, which the core boundary at 99 split.

tamil: புரிந்த யான் இப் பூங் கொடிப் பெயர்ப் படூஉம்
விடர்ச் சிலை பொறித்த வேந்தன் முன் நாள்
துப்பு அடு செவ் வாய்த் துடி இடையாரொடும்
இப் பொழில் புகுந்து ஆங்கு இருந்த எல்லையுள்
அங்கு அவர்க்கு அறு சுவை நால் வகை அமிழ்தம்
reading: He tells her how he came to Vanji: long ago a Chera king of the Kuttuvar, who carved the bow on the mountain cleft, was in this grove with his women when Dharma charanas, sky-going sages returning from circling the peak Samanoli in Lanka, came down and sat on its rock; the king, by austerity done before, praised them, washed their lotus feet, fed them the six-flavoured food of four kinds from a vessel and bowed to them with his court.
nuance: The king is named only by his line and the epithet விடர்ச் சிலை பொறித்த வேந்தன், the bow carved in the cleft; the Tamil does not name him. The sages are தரும சாரணர், Buddhist counterparts of the Jain charanas of the Silappathikaram, and Samanoli (the peak now called Adam's Peak) is their place of worship. The king's welcome, feet washed and six tastes served, is the pattern Manimekalai follows at lines 239 to 243.
event: A Chera king of old meets sky-going Dharma charanas descending into this grove, washes their feet, feeds them and worships them.
unit_note: Starts at 101 instead of 100 (see 91-100); ends at 119 as in the core.

tamil: நின் பெருந் தாதைக்கு ஒன்பது வழி முறை
வான் ஓங்கு சிமையத்து வால் ஒளிச் சயித்தம்
கண்டு தொழுது ஏத்தும் காதலின் வந்து இத்
தூ உரை கேட்டுத் துணிந்து இவண் இருந்தது
reading: The charanas poured the Buddha's truth, the suffering of birth and the bliss of no birth, into the king's ear; Kovalan, the king's dear friend and Manimekalai's ancestor nine generations back, heard it too, gave away in seven days the crores he had earned himself, beyond his inheritance, became an ascetic and built a towering white caitya to the Sugata for the relief of all who come after; Kovalan's father came to worship it, heard its ascetics foretell that the sea would take Kaveripattinam, and stayed here.
nuance: This Kovalan is a namesake ancestor (ஒன்பது வழி முறை முன்னோன்), not Manimekalai's father; the epic gives the family a Buddhist past in Vanji. The distinction at lines 127 to 128 is exact: he gave away what he had earned, not what the ancestors had laid up. The prophecy of the flood (line 135) is why the ascetic is in Vanji and not in drowned Puhar.
event: Kovalan's ancestor hears the charanas, gives away his wealth, renounces and builds a caitya; Kovalan's father, come to worship there, is told Puhar will be drowned and stays in Vanji.

tamil: நாதன் நல் அறம் கேட்டு வீடு எய்தும்" என்று
அந் நாள் ஆங்கு அவன் அற நெறி கேட்குவன்
நின்னது தன்மை அந் நெடு நிலைக் கந்தில் துன்னிய
reading: He gives the seers' word: her father, who went where his evil deed ripened, has appeared among the gods by the fruit of former austerity, yet must still eat that evil deed, and by the austerity he bore under the Bodhi of the earlier Buddha he will take up austerity again and with his beloved reach release by hearing the Lord's dharma at Kapilai; understanding this, the ascetic resolves to hear that dharma on that day too, and asks whether she did not learn her own nature from Thuvathikan in the pillar.
nuance: Merit and evil deed run side by side here: heaven is earned and the evil deed is not cancelled by it, only deferred. Lines 141 to 142 are compressed (முன்னவன் போதியில் நல் அறம் தாங்கிய தவத்தால் தான் தவம் தாங்கி), and whose earlier Bodhi is meant is not fixed. Line 148 carries more words than an akaval line and may join two lines.
event: The ascetic reports the seers' prophecy of Kovalan's heaven, remaining karma and future release at Kapilai, and vows to hear the Buddha then himself.

tamil: ஆங்கு அவன் தானும் நின் அறத்திற்கு ஏது

பொன் தொடி தாயரும் அப் பதிப் படர்ந்தனர்

மன் உயிர் மடிய மழை வளம் கரத்தலின்

கார் எனத் தோன்றிக் காத்தல் நின் கடன்' என
reading: He tells her that Aravanar declared Kanchi the ground of her dharma and went there, her mothers following, and that because the Kanchi country has lost its rain and its people are dying, its ascetics, finding none to give them alms, have come to Vanji; so it is her duty, medicine of lives, to appear in that land like a rain cloud and save it.
nuance: The drought is told first through its effect on the monks: with no givers left, even austerity must migrate. The charge repeats Thuvathikan's foretelling in kaathai 21 almost line for line (பொன் எயில் காஞ்சி, மழை வளம் கர).
event: The ascetic tells Manimekalai that Aravanar and her mothers have gone to drought-struck Kanchi and charges her to go and save it.

reading: Manimekalai bows, takes the bowl, rises west of Vanji and flies north to Kanchi, which lies desolate though rich as Indra's city fallen to earth; heart melting, she circles its walls, comes down in the city's centre, worships the caitya that Ilangkilli, ally of Killi, made for the Lord of the Bodhi, and goes to a grove to the south-west; a chamberlain tells the king that Kovalan's daughter, keeper of the virtuous vows, has appeared in the Dharmadavanam with the Amudhasurabhi like a great rain cloud.
nuance: The chamberlain names her by her father (கோவலன் மடந்தை) and her vows (குணவதம்), not by her courtesan mother. The Tamil names Ilangkilli as the builder of the caitya; it does not here name the reigning king of Kanchi, though the epic's tradition makes him that king.
event: Manimekalai flies to drought-stricken Kanchi with the bowl, worships at Ilangkilli's caitya, and a chamberlain reports her arrival to the king.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 182 to 183: the chamberlain's report that begins at 179 ends with மா மழை போல்' என at line 183.

பொய்கையும் பொழிலும் புனைமின்" என்று அறைந்து அத்

இவ் இடம்" என்றே அவ் இடம் காட்ட அத்
reading: The king and his counsellors, saying the pillar image's words have all come true, go to her, and he tells her that, not knowing whether his sceptre had bent, austerity had failed, or women's chastity had fallen short, so that the whole land was in want, he was bewildered when a great deity appeared and told him not to grieve: by his own high austerity a maiden would come, her great bowl would save the land, at her grace Indra would send rain, and he should build a pool and grove as if Manipallavam with its Gomukhi pool had come here; this, he says, showing her the place, is what they made.
nuance: The king tries the three causes the tradition gives for failed rain, the bent sceptre, failed austerity and failed chastity, and the deity answers none of them: it does not say which was at fault but points to a remedy, the renunciant's bowl, and credits the king's own austerity for bringing her. The words அலத்தல்காலை ஆகியது and நலத்தகை repeat Aravanar's lament over Puhar's famine in kaathai 15. How the king knows the pillar image's words (185) is not told here.
event: The Kanchi king goes to Manimekalai and tells how a deity, in the drought, foretold her coming and bade him build a replica of Manipallavam's pool and grove, which he shows her.
unit_note: Units 183-203 and 204-219 replaced by 184-206 and 207-219: the king's speech, which begins at 187, quotes the deity to புனைமின் at 204 and ends with அவ் இடம் காட்ட at 206; the core boundary at 203 cut the deity's words.

tamil: அங்கு அப் பீடிகை இது என' அறவோன்
பங்கயப் பீடிகை பசிப் பிணி மருந்து எனும்
reading: Seeing the grove like the island, she rejoices and takes it for the seat that showed her former birth; a lotus seat of the Virtuous One is laid out in due form, a fitting shrine is made for Deepathilakai and the great goddess Manimekala to be worshipped, the king holds festival, and she worships, sets the Amudhasurabhi, medicine for the disease of hunger, on the lotus seat, and calls, let all living beings come.
nuance: Who lays out the seat at lines 210 to 211 is not clear: அறவோன் may be the Buddha whose seat it is, with the king as the builder, or the builder himself. On Manipallavam the bowl rose from the pool once a year into a fit hand; here it is set on the replica seat and offered to every creature.
event: A replica of the Buddha's seat and a shrine to the two goddesses are made in the Kanchi grove; Manimekalai sets the bowl on the seat and calls all beings to come.
unit_note: Starts at 207 instead of 204 (see 184-206).

tamil: பைத்து அரவு அல்குல் பாவை தன் கிளவியின்
மன் உயிர் அடங்கலும் வந்து ஒருங்கு ஈண்டி
அருந்தியோர்க்கு எல்லாம் ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து ஆய்
பெருந் தவர் கைப் பெய் பிச்சையின் பயனும்
வசித் தொழில் உதவி வளம் தந்தது என
reading: At her word the peoples of the eighteen tongues, the blind, deaf and lame, the uncared-for, the mute and the sick, the vow-keeping ascetics, the hungry and the destitute, with countless herds of beasts, all gather, and the bowl becomes life's medicine to all who eat, its plenty swelling like the fruit of alms laid in great ascetics' hands and like seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools, until the rain's work too brings abundance.
nuance: The list gives the disabled, the ascetics and the animals alike; the bowl makes no distinction of birth or species. Two images of increase are set side by side: the merit of alms given to ascetics and the harvest of well-sown seed, both depending on conditions. வசித் தொழில் at line 233 is a rare word; read as the work of rain, it fulfils the deity's promise at lines 196 to 197.
event: All the hungry people and animals of the land gather and eat from the bowl, and rain returns.

tamil: ஆசனத்து ஏற்றி அறு சுவை நால் வகைப்
reading: As the people go praising the maiden who cured the disease of hunger, her mothers and Aravana Adigal, who drives away what is not right, come to the hall of charity of the city's mother of lives; she bows at his feet, washes them, seats him, serves the six-flavoured food of four kinds in its hour, offers betel and camphor, prays that the dharma in her heart may come true, and, casting off her illusory form, bows down.
nuance: மாயை விட்டு is the dropping of the borrowed ascetic's form she took to hear the schools (பொய் உரு, line 85; the patikam's பொய் உருக் களைந்து). Her prayer வாய்வது ஆக என் மனப்பாட்டு அறம் turns into her own vow the blessing Aravanar is foretold to give in kaathai 21. She honours her teacher as a lay giver before she takes vows in kaathai 29.
event: Aravanar and her mothers arrive at the hall of charity; Manimekalai washes their feet, feeds them, prays for her dharma and casts off her disguise.

title: தவத்திறம் பூண்டு தருமம் கேட்ட காதை (1/2)
theme: In Kanchi Aravanar first tells Manimekalai why she bears the goddess's name and why Puhar fell to the sea, and then, when she asks for the true doctrine after rejecting the five schools, begins the Buddhist account of knowledge: two means only, perception as bare awareness and inference, with the forms of a valid proof and a catalogue of false theses and false reasons, many of whose examples are the doctrines of the schools she heard in kaathai 27.
source_issues: Line 90 prints புகஈ for புகை.
Line 94 (பகைத்திருப்ப) and line 92 (ஊர்த்தச் சாமம் கௌடிலச் சாமம்) are obscure as printed.
Line 77 prints அநன்னுவயத்தில் where the sense calls for the reason from non-appearance; the word may be corrupt.
Line 203 names the doubtful reason சித்த அசித்தம், though its definition (204-206) is of a reason in doubt; the name may be corrupt.
Lines 189 (அவன்ன்) and 192 (விருத்தம்ம்) print a doubled final consonant.
Line 131 reads ஆ அகாசம், with a stray ஆ.
Lines 113, 114 and 201 were repaired for the old-font ௌ / ெள confusion.
The core unit breaks at 16 and 42 fall inside sentences: Aravanar's account runs from line 1 to 37 as one sentence.

tamil: தனிக் கலக் கம்பளச் செட்டி கைத் தரலும்
கொணர்ந்திடும் அந் நாள் கூர் இருள் யாமத்து
நின் உயிர்த் தந்தை நெடுங் குலத்து உதித்த
reading: Blessing the girl who bows to him, Aravanar begins a long account: the Naga king's daughter Pilivalai bore Killi's son on the island and handed the infant to the merchant Kambala Chetti, whose ship broke up near the shore that night; told the child was lost, the grieving king searched for him and forgot Indra's festival, and because his festival lapsed the lord of the gods...
nuance: The sentence that begins here runs on to line 34, where the lord of the gods named at line 13 lays the curse; lines 14 to 33 are an inset about Manimekalai's ancestor. The unit tells as past what kaathai 1 gave as a warning: that a lapsed festival brings ruin on the city.
event: Aravanar tells how Killi's infant son by Pilivalai was lost when the merchant's ship sank, and how the grieving king forgot Indra's festival.

tamil: எழு நாள் எல்லை இடுக்கண் வந்து எய்தா
எவ்வம் உற்றான் தனது எவ்வம் தீர்" எனப்
அற அரசு ஆளவும் அற ஆழி உருட்டவும்
reading: The inset: when the ship of her father's ancestor, the first among living beings, sank, he struggled in the sea for seven days without harm because of his unfailing virtue, until Indra saw his pale stone seat tremble and bade the goddess relieve the one who would become the lord at the root of the Bodhi tree, and she lifted him from the sea, being one who helps him in every birth to complete the perfections, rule the kingdom of dharma and turn its wheel.
nuance: The ancestor of Kovalan's line is named only as a future Buddha (போதி மூலத்து நாதன் ஆவோன்), so the epic makes Manimekalai's own family the family of a Bodhisattva. The image of line 17 likens the man in the sea to a gold needle stitched into a green blanket. Indra's throne that trembles at a good man's distress is a story pattern the unit takes for granted.
event: Aravanar tells how the founder of her father's line, shipwrecked, endured seven days in the sea until Indra's seat trembled and the sea goddess lifted him out.

நகர் கடல் கொள்ள நின் தாயரும் யானும்
நூல் துறைச் சமய நுண் பொருள் கேட்டே
reading: Because the sky-going sages told the reason, her father named her after the goddess for that help; the goddess Manimekala had announced her renunciation in a dream that night, and by the curse laid in accord with her the sea took the city, so her mothers and Aravanar came to Kanchi for her sake; Manimekalai bows and answers that Deepathilakai of the Buddha seat told her this, and so, in a borrowed form, she heard the subtle doctrines of the schools in that city...
nuance: Two speakers share the unit: Aravanar to line 37, Manimekalai from 38. The phrase என்பவட்கு ஒப்ப அவன் இடு சாபத்து leaves open how far the curse is Indra's and how far the goddess's; the epic elsewhere has the goddess carry out the punishment. The naming and the dream were first told by the goddess herself in kaathai 7; here the reason behind the naming is given.
event: Aravanar tells that her father named her after the goddess and that a curse let the sea take Puhar, so he and her mothers came to Kanchi; Manimekalai bows and says she heard the schools in Vanji in a borrowed form.

tamil: அவ் உரு என்ன ஐ வகைச் சமயமும்
ஏதம் இல் பிரத்தியம் கருத்து அளவு என்னச்
reading: Manimekalai says that because the five kinds of schools were not right she kept none of them in mind, and asks for the true doctrine; Aravanar says the first Jina taught only two means of knowledge, perception and inference: perception is bare awareness that leaves out name, class, quality and action, which belong to inference, and of inference from cause, from effect and from co-presence only that from effect, as smoke to fire, cannot err.
nuance: ஆதி சினேந்திரன் is the Buddha under a title the Jains also use. The definition answers kaathai 27's logician point for point: he put name, class, quality and action inside perception, and this teacher puts them outside. The rejection of the schools is Manimekalai's own judgment, made before any teaching; the teacher then gives a method, not a verdict on each school.
event: Manimekalai asks Aravanar for the true doctrine, and he begins to teach the two means of knowledge.

reading: All other means of knowledge are inference; an inference has five members, thesis, reason, example, application and conclusion, shown on 'this hill has fire, because it has smoke, like a kitchen', with the counter-example 'what has no fire has no smoke, like water'; the pure reasons are of effect and of own nature, as in 'sound is impermanent' with 'because it is made' stated of the subject.
nuance: The other means named in kaathai 27 (comparison, scripture, presumption and the rest) are not refuted one by one but absorbed into inference by a single line (55-56). The five-member form is given here only to be cut to three at line 109.

reading: The positive example states 'whatever is made is impermanent, like a pot' and the negative 'whatever is not impermanent is not made, like space'; for the reason from non-appearance, 'there is no pot in this open place, because none appears', with 'we do not see the hare's horn, because it is not' and 'whatever exists comes to appear, like a gooseberry in the hand'.
nuance: With the effect reason and the own-nature reason of line 68, this gives three kinds of valid reason, the third proving absence. The word naming it, அநன்னுவயத்தில் (77), is doubtful as printed.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 87 to 84: the non-appearance example ends at ஏற்ற விபக்கத்து உரை எனல் ஆகும் (84); line 85 begins the question of how a reason proves.

tamil: இலா இடத்துப் புகை இலை எனல் நேர் அத்
reading: Asked how smoke proves fire, the teacher denies that bare co-presence or co-absence does it: the smoke itself, rising and dark as fire's effect, must prove it; if co-presence proved, a man who once saw a donkey with a courtesan would have to infer the courtesan whenever he saw the donkey, and if co-absence proved, a donkey's neck bare of both dog's tail and jackal's tail would let one infer the one tail from the other.
nuance: The two jokes carry the argument: a reason proves because it is tied to what it proves by nature (here as effect to cause), not because the two were once seen together or apart. Lines 92 and 94 (ஊர்த்தச் சாமம் கௌடிலச் சாமம், பகைத்திருப்ப) are obscure as printed, so the description of the smoke is uncertain.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 88 and 98 to 85 and 108: the question begins at இவ்வகை ஏது பொருள் சாதிப்பன (85) and the second objection closes at அதனால் அதுவும் ஆகாது (108).

tamil: நன்கு என் பக்கம் என நாட்டுக அது தான்
reading: Application and conclusion fold into the example, leaving thesis, reason and example, each of which may be good or bad; the thesis is to be set out as what joins an evident subject with an evident property to be proved, marked off from other things.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 99 and 113 to 109 and 117: line 108 ends the argument on co-presence, and the definition of the thesis that begins at 111 ends at நன்கு என் பக்கம் என நாட்டுக (117).

reading: In 'sound is impermanent' the subject is sound and the property to be proved is impermanence; a good reason has three marks, resting in the subject, found among similar cases and wholly absent from dissimilar ones, as 'being made' and 'arising from effort' are found in sound and in pots and never in space.
nuance: The test case throughout is the impermanence of sound, which matters to a Buddhist teacher because everything made is impermanent; the logic is taught on a doctrine of the school.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 114 and 138 to 118 and 135: the worked example begins at 118 and closes at விளங்கிற்று என்க (135).

reading: The example is of two kinds, by likeness and by difference, and these belong to a sound proof; their bad counterparts are the false thesis, false reason and false example, and the false thesis is of nine kinds, which the teacher names.
nuance: The nine are the contradictions of perception, of inference, of one's own words, of common usage and of scripture, and four kinds of term the opponent does not accept. Kaathai 27's logician also listed false appearances, but of knowing; these are false steps in arguing before an opponent.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 139 and 153 to 136 (153 unchanged): the account of the example begins at ஏதம் இல் திட்டாந்தம் இரு வகைய (136).

tamil: சுவசன விருத்தம் தன் சொல் மாறி இயம்பல்
ஆகம விருத்தம் தன் நூல் மாறு அறைதல்
reading: The teacher gives an example of each false thesis: 'sound is not heard by the ear' goes against perception, 'the pot is eternal' against inference, 'my mother is barren' against one's own words, 'the moon is not the moon' against common usage, a Vaisheshika calling the impermanent eternal against his own scripture, and a Buddhist telling a Sankhya that sound perishes uses a predicate the Sankhya does not accept.
nuance: The rival schools enter as test cases, not as opponents to be beaten: the Vaisheshika is called அநித்த வாதி and the Sankhya அவிநாசவாதி, and the rule is that a thesis must be put in terms the hearer grants. Line 163 turns on மதி and சந்திரன், two words for the moon.

reading: A Sankhya telling a Buddhist 'the soul has consciousness' names a subject the Buddhist, who denies a soul, does not accept; a Vaisheshika telling a Buddhist 'the soul is the cause of pleasure and the rest' uses subject and predicate both unaccepted; and telling a Buddhist 'sound is impermanent' proves what he already holds, which needs no proof.
nuance: The Buddhist's denial of the soul (அநான்ம வாதி, 177) is stated in passing, as a fact a debater must allow for, not argued. The rule makes a debate depend on what the other side grants.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 192 to 190: the false theses end at வேறு சாதிக்க வேண்டாது ஆகும் (190); 191 begins the false reasons.

reading: False reasons are of three kinds, unestablished, inconclusive and contradictory; the unestablished are four: unaccepted by both sides ('sound is impermanent because seen by the eye'), unaccepted by one ('because produced', to a Sankhya for whom things are manifested, not produced), doubtful (declaring fire on seeing what may be mist or steam), and lacking a subject.
nuance: The doubtful kind is named சித்த அசித்தம் (203), though the definition (ஏது சங்கயமாய்) describes a reason in doubt; the name may be corrupt. The Sankhya example matches kaathai 27, where the Sankhya speaker describes every stage of the world as வெளிப்பட்டு, becoming manifest.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 193 and 205 to 191 and 206: the false reasons begin at ஏதுப் போலி ஓதின் (191), and the example of the doubtful reason ends at துணிதல் (206).

reading: The reason lacking a subject is shown by 'space is a substance because it has the quality of sound', said to one who denies that space is a substance; the inconclusive reasons are six, and the first, the too general, belongs to both similar and dissimilar cases, as 'sound is impermanent because knowable' leaves open whether sound is known like a pot or like space.
nuance: The example thesis about space is the Vaisheshika's (space is among his nine substances and sound among the qualities in kaathai 27); who denies it is not said.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 206 and 221 to 207 and 222: the reason lacking a subject begins at 207, and the question about knowability closes at நித்தத்து அறிவோ? (222).

reading: The too narrow reason belongs to the subject alone and to neither similar nor dissimilar cases, as 'sound is eternal because it is heard' leaves doubt, since only sound is heard; the next kind is the reason found in part of the similar cases and throughout the dissimilar ones.
nuance: The kaathai's account of false reasons runs on past this chapter's end at 233.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 222 to 223: line 223 opens with the closing word of the previous example (என்னல்) and then begins the too narrow reason.

title: தவத்திறம் பூண்டு தருமம் கேட்ட காதை (2/2)
theme: Aravanar completes his account of faulty inference for Manimekalai: the inconclusive reasons, the four contradictory reasons (two of them turned against Sankhya and Vaisheshika proofs), and the ten faulty examples, ending with the charge to examine and know true from false without doubt. The teacher's examples mostly defend the rival thesis that sound is eternal, and the whole is the method he gives before the doctrine of kaathai 30.
source_issues: manimekalai:29 line 296: இந்தியங்களியும் reads as a slip for the senses in the accusative (இந்திரியங்களையும்); 298 has இந்தியத்துக்கும் for the same word.
manimekalai:29 lines 333 to 335: words are broken across lines (விபரீதான் / னுவயம், திட் / டாந்த), and 336 to 337, 345 and 354 are very short lines.
manimekalai:29 lines 443 to 444: the dissimilar example lacks the negation the sense needs after அநித்தம், and 444 has the misprint அன்ன்று.
manimekalai:29 line 463: என்றால் என்று நின்ற இடத்து reads awkwardly and may be corrupt.
manimekalai:29 lines 234 to 472: most core unit boundaries fall mid-definition (break score 0 or 1); thirteen adjusted units follow the fallacy definitions.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, now in Kanchi, who teaches Manimekalai the means of knowledge and the dharma
Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist renunciant, here Aravanar's pupil

reading: Aravanar finishes the reason found in some similar cases and in every dissimilar one, with sound said not to arise from effort because it is impermanent (lightning arises without effort, space never shows it, the pot does), then gives its mirror, the reason found in every similar case and some dissimilar ones, with sound said to arise from effort because impermanent.
nuance: The two fallacies are built on one example turned round, which is why each ends in a pair of questions (240 to 242, 251 to 253): 'like the pot, or like the lightning?'. The teacher's point is that an inconclusive reason leaves the hearer with a question, not a verdict.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 248 to 253: the second fallacy, defined at 243 to 245, has its example and its closing questions to எனல் at line 253; the core unit broke it at 248.

reading: The reason found in only part of the similar and part of the dissimilar cases: sound is eternal because incorporeal, where incorporeality is in space but not the corporeal atom, and in pleasure but not the pot, so the hearer can ask whether sound is eternal like space or impermanent like pleasure.
nuance: Both the eternal atom (259 to 261) and pleasure as incorporeal and passing (262 to 263) are taken as granted for the example; the teacher does not say here whether he holds them.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 254 and 266: the fallacy is named at 254 and its example closes with எனல் at 266.

reading: The last inconclusive reason is the one that admits a contrary reason: 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort' meets 'sound is eternal because it is heard, like soundness', both proofs stand and both end in doubt; then the contradictory reason is announced in four kinds.
nuance: This is the one fallacy that no single proof shows: it appears only when two arguments meet, so it names the stalemate of a debate hall. சங்கயம் and ஏகாந்தம் அல்ல (274) set doubt against one-sided certainty in borrowed Sanskrit; the eternal-sound proof is a rival's, though no school is named here.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 267 and 280: the fallacy is defined from 267, and the four kinds of contradiction close with என்ன நான்கு வகையது ஆகும் at 280; the core unit ran on into the first kind.

reading: The contradictory reason proves the opposite of the property ('sound is eternal because it is made', when the made is impermanent) or destroys its intended character: the argument that the eye and other senses serve another because they are aggregates, like beds and seats, proves that other to be composite, like the user of a bed, and so undoes the partless self it set out to prove.
nuance: The text does not name the school at 291 to 302, but the argument from aggregates serving another and the partless self (நிர் அவயவமாயுள்ள ஆன்மா, 299 to 300) are the Sankhya's, whose purusha kaathai 27 describes; the reply turns the Sankhya proof against its own conclusion rather than denying a self outright. Line 296 இந்தியங்களியும் reads as a slip for the senses in the accusative.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 281 and 302: the first kind of contradiction is defined from அத் தன்மச் சொரூப விபரீத சாதனம் at 281, and the second ends with விபரீதம் at 302; the core units broke both mid-sentence.

tamil: குணமும் அன்று எத் திரவியம் ஆம் எக்
reading: The reason can also undo the subject itself: the argument that existence is not substance, quality or action because it differs from them, like generality and particularity, takes away the common being of all three and leaves existence nothing, turning being into non-being; and the same reason undoes existence's specific character as what gives the notion 'it is'.
nuance: Substance, quality, action, generality and particularity are the Vaisheshika's categories, and பொருளும் குணமும் கருமமும் with உண்மை (310 to 311) repeats the wording of the Vaisheshika's own account at 27:257 to 258; the school is not named here. Lines 321 to 325, on the fourth kind, are compressed, and the sense of கருத்தாவுடைய கிரியையும் குணமும் (322 to 323) is tentative.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 303 and 325: the third kind begins at 303 and the fourth ends with கெடுத்தது in line 325, which also opens the faulty examples (தீய எடுத்துக்காட்டு ஆவன); the core unit broke at 321.

tamil: திட்டாந்தம் இரு வகைப் படும் என்று முன்
reading: Faulty examples are the semblances of the example, of two kinds as the example was: five by similarity (lacking the reason, lacking the property, lacking both, without the connection, with the connection reversed) and five by difference (not excluding the property, not excluding the reason, excluding neither, without the exclusion, with the exclusion reversed).
nuance: The list is a mirror: each failing of a similar example has a counterpart in the dissimilar one, so the teacher can define the second five by reversing the first. Lines 333 to 335 break words across lines (விபரீதான் / னுவயம், திட் / டாந்த), and 336 to 337 are unusually short.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 326 and 339: the faulty examples are introduced at 325 to 326 and the two lists of five end with என்ன இவற்றுள் at 339.

reading: An example by similarity may lack the reason (sound is eternal because incorporeal, like the atom, which is eternal but has form) or lack the property to be proved (like cognition, which is incorporeal but passing).
nuance: Both examples defend 'sound is eternal', so the teacher's faulty examples are all on the rival thesis; the eternal, formed atom and the passing cognition (புத்தி) are taken as granted for the lesson.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 340 and 358: the first kind of faulty example is defined at 340, and the second closes with சாத்திய நித்தத்துவம் குறையும் at 358; the core units broke at 356.

tamil: என்று இரு வகையாம் இவற்றுள் சன்னா உள
reading: An example may lack both properties, and this is of two kinds, of an existing thing or a non-existent one; of an existing thing: sound is eternal because incorporeal, like a pot, which came into being and has form, so has neither.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 357 to 359: line 358 ends the previous kind, and the definition of lacking both begins at 359.

reading: Of a non-existent thing: sound is impermanent because it has form, like space; for one who says space is unreal it has neither property, and for one who says it is real, space is eternal and formless, so it lacks both for him too.
nuance: The teacher settles nothing about space: the example fails on either view (381 to 384), so the logic can be taught without deciding the ontology the schools dispute. Who holds 'space is unreal' (ஆகாசம் அசத்து) is not said.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 373 and 384: the non-existent kind is defined from 373 and its verdict ends at குறையும் at 384; ananvaya begins at 385.

tamil: யாதொன்று யாதொன்று கிருத்தம் அது அநித்தம்" எனும்
reading: Without the connection is to show the reason and property together in a pot without stating 'whatever is made is impermanent'; with the connection reversed is to say 'whatever is impermanent is made', running from the wider to the narrower, which fails because the wider occurs without the narrower.
nuance: The correct rule, கிருத்தம் அது அநித்தம், is the Buddhist teaching that whatever is made passes; the teacher states it only as the model of a well-formed connection, and the reversed form fails because some impermanent things are not made, as the lightning of 238 to 241 showed.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 385 and 401: ananvaya is defined from 385 and the reversed connection ends with விபரீதம் ஆம் at 401; the core units broke at 386 and 398.

reading: An example by difference may fail to exclude the property (sound is eternal because incorporeal: 'whatever is not eternal is not incorporeal, like the atom', which is eternal and formed) or fail to exclude the reason ('like action', which is incorporeal and passing).
nuance: Action (கன்மம், 418 to 421) is the incorporeal but passing thing here, a category from the Vaisheshika list; it is not karma in the moral sense.
unit_note: Boundaries moved to 402 and 423: the dissimilar examples begin at 402 and the second kind ends with சாதனமான அமூர்த்தம் மீளாது at 423; the core units broke at 414.

reading: An example by difference may exclude neither property, again of an existing or a non-existent thing: for one who holds space a real thing, space is eternal and formless and so excludes neither; for one who says space is no thing, it has no being, so nothing is excluded or kept.
nuance: Space is again judged by both views (437, 446), as at 381 to 384. Line 443 lacks a negative the sense needs (whatever is not impermanent), and 444 has அன்ன்று; the lines read as corrupt.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 426/427 to 424 and 449: the third dissimilar kind is named at 424 and its non-existent case closes with இலையாகும் at 449; avyatireka begins at 450.

tamil: ஐயம் இன்றி அறிந்து கொள் ஆய்ந்து என்
reading: Without the exclusion is to show the pot made and passing without stating that where the property is absent the reason is absent; with the exclusion reversed is to deny the reason before the property; and Aravanar closes by bidding Manimekalai learn by these rules, having examined, to know without doubt what is true and false in the semblances of inference.
nuance: The lesson that began with the true means of knowledge ends with false inference, and its last word is a method for the hearer (ஆய்ந்து அறிந்து கொள்), not a doctrine to accept. Line 463 (என்றால் என்று நின்ற இடத்து) reads awkwardly and may be corrupt.
event: Aravanar ends his account of faulty inference and tells Manimekalai to examine and know true from false by these rules.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 456 to 450: avyatireka is defined from 450, and the four closing lines (469 to 472) cannot stand as a unit; the core unit 445-455 broke the definition at 455.

title: பவத்திறம் அறுகெனப் பாவை நோற்ற காதை
theme: Manimekalai takes refuge in the three jewels and her teacher expounds dependent arising: the twelve links forward and in reverse, with their four sections, three junctions, three times, the four truths, the five aggregates, the modes of speech, the four nayas and the four ways of answering, ending in the claim that bondage and release have their own causes and no giver, and in a remedy for each of desire, anger and delusion; hearing it, she vows to end the round of becoming. The kaathai is the Buddhist doctrine the debates of kaathai 27 were set aside for.
source_issues: Line 54: the core's repair of ௌ read as ெள (தெளிதல்) is accepted.
Line 106 spells அரூரு where lines 45, 84, 102, 107, 121, 138, 163, 172 and 179 have அருஉரு; a spelling variant, not a different link.

Lines 45-47 list twelve links ending in தோற்றம், வினைப்பயன், but the reverse chain (lines 127-130) runs கருமத் தொகுதி, தோற்றம், பிறப்பு as separate steps, which gives thirteen; a link may be doubled in the text.
Short lines at 18, 183, 235 and 241 break the akaval line length and may mark loss or a displaced half-line.
Lines 159-169: each time-label stands before its list; read the other way the present links would be future. I have read label-before-list throughout.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, now a Buddhist renunciant hearing the doctrine
the Buddhist teacher who expounds the doctrine; named in this kaathai only as மொழிவோன்
the Buddha, whose descent, awakening and teaching the discourse recounts

reading: Manimekalai, who has known what she entered into in her former birth by holding to giving and keeping the precepts, bows three times to the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha and goes to them for refuge, and the teacher begins to speak the form of dharma.
nuance: தானம் and சீலம் (line 1) are the two practices she held in her former birth, and the same pair returns at line 78 as what makes a good birth: the teacher's doctrine of good deeds is first shown in the hearer. The teacher is only மொழிவோன், 'the one who speaks'; the story so far makes him Aravana Adigal.
event: Manimekalai takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, and the teacher begins his discourse.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 17 to 6: lines 1-6 are the narrator's frame, closing on மொழிவோன் (line 6); the teacher's speech opens at line 7, and the core unit 1-17 ran the frame into the middle of the speech.

tamil: ஈர் அறு பொருளின் ஈந்த நெறி உடைத்தாய்ச்
reading: The teacher says that when the world's knowledge had run dry the Buddha came down from the Tushita heaven at the gods' entreaty, sat at the Bodhi tree, conquered Mara and taught, as countless past Buddhas taught, the twelvefold teaching of arising by dependence: where this is not that is not, where this is that is, with four sections, three junctions, three modes and three times, the ground of the four truths and the account of the five aggregates.
nuance: Lines 21-22 (ஈங்கு இது இல்லாவழி இல்லாகி / ஈங்கு இது உள்ளவழி உண்டு ஆகலின்) give the general formula of dependence before any of the twelve is named. The long run of ஆகி and உடைத்தாய் from line 16 is a table of contents for the whole kaathai: each item (sections, junctions, times, truths, aggregates, modes of speech, nayas, kinds of answer) is expounded later in this order.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 17/18 to 6/7: the speech that begins at line 7 is now one unit up to the core boundary at 33, ending on the list of the chain's properties.

tamil: மெய் வகை ஆறு வழக்கு முகம் எய்தி
இற்று என வகுத்த இயல்பு ஈர் ஆறும்
அலகு இல பல் உயிர் அறு வகைத்து ஆகும்
reading: The teacher says the chain has no maker and is not made, has no I and no mine, no going and no coming, and is itself deed, fruit, birth and release; he names the twelve links, ignorance, action, consciousness, name-and-form, the six gates, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth and the fruit of deeds, says that those who know them gain the great reward and those who do not know hell, and defines ignorance as forgetting what reasoning has shown and trusting the report that a hare has horns, before naming the six kinds of beings.
nuance: Line 37 (நின்மதி இன்றி ஊழ்பாடு இன்றி) is compressed: I read it as 'without a governing mind and without fixed fate', but நின்மதி may be read otherwise, and the tension link to the Ajivika rests on ஊழ்பாடு. Ignorance is defined not as plain not-knowing but as preferring hearsay (கேட்டது) to what has been established (கண்டது), with the hare's horn (முயற்கோடு) as the stock example of a non-thing; the same example returns at lines 208 and 216.

tamil: ஆய் தொடி நல்லாய்! ஆங்கு அது கேளாய்
reading: The teacher says that beings enter the womb by good or bad deeds and that the deed's fruit gives them joy or sorrow; he names the ten bad deeds (killing, theft and lust of the body; lying, slander, harsh and idle words of speech; coveting, anger and wrong view of the mind), says those who do them are born as animals, ghosts and hell-beings, and those who avoid them, keep the precepts and give are born as gods, humans and Brahmas; then he defines consciousness as awareness like a sleeper's, without intention or grasp of objects.
nuance: The ten are sorted by where they arise: the body, speech and the mind (உள்ளம் தன்னின் உருப்பன, line 71), so coveting, anger and wrong view count as deeds before any act. Lines 82-83 begin the definitions of the twelve links in the middle of the unit; the address ஆய் தொடி நல்லாய் (line 65) is the teacher's only word to his hearer in the doctrinal part.

tamil: தரும் முறை இது எனத் தாம்தாம் சார்தல்
reading: The teacher defines the rest of the links: name-and-form as the life and body that go with consciousness, the six gates as the place where contact happens, contact as mind and gate meeting objects, feeling as tasting them, craving as unsated wanting, clinging as sticky knowing, becoming as the heap of karma, birth as appearing in a destiny by that karma, and sickness, aging and death; then he begins the forward chain, each link arising with the one before as its support.
nuance: Death is defined as the name-and-form vanishing like the setting sun (lines 102-103), with யாக்கை as the body that falls: no self passes on. Line 106 spells the link அரூரு where every other line has அருஉரு.

reading: The teacher completes the forward chain (contact gives feeling, feeling craving, craving clinging, clinging the heap of karma, and that the next birth, from which come aging, sickness, death, grief, lament, care and despair, an unending sorrow) and then turns to the reverse: as ignorance ceases, action ceases, and so on link by link.
nuance: Line 118 calls the round ஊழின் மண்டிலம், the circle of ஊழ்: the word that elsewhere names fate here names the turning of the chain itself, which line 37 said has no fixed fate.

tamil: கையாறு என்று இக் கடை இல் துன்பம்
reading: The teacher finishes the reverse chain, in which birth and all its sorrow cease, and then begins the four sections: the first is this cessation, the second ignorance and action as the causes, and the third begins with consciousness.
nuance: The reverse chain has தோற்றம் and பிறப்பு as two steps (lines 129-130), where the list at lines 45-47 has twelve links with தோற்றம் as the eleventh; the edition's text may double a link here.

tamil: என இவை பிறப்பில் உழக்கு பயன் ஆதலின்
reading: The teacher completes the four sections (consciousness to feeling, as results of what went before; craving, clinging and becoming, as fault and deed; birth, sickness, aging and death, as the suffering birth brings) and names three junctions: the first awareness of a birth, the knowing of feeling joined with desire, and the karma-heap moving toward the next birth; then he begins the three kinds of birth.
nuance: The junctions (சந்தி) at lines 148-152 are the hinges between the sections, but lines 149-150 (புகர்ச்சி இன்று அறிவது) and 154 are hard to construe, and I cannot fix the second junction's sense beyond the joining of feeling and desire.

reading: The teacher gives three kinds of birth (appearing with awareness alone, as form with awareness hidden, and with awareness and form together as humans, gods and animals) and then the three times: ignorance and action belong to the past, consciousness through becoming to the present, and birth with its sorrows to the future; the last line introduces fault.
nuance: Each time-label stands before its list: இறந்த காலம் (160) before ignorance and action, நிகழ்ந்த காலம் (162) before consciousness to becoming, எதிர்காலம் (166) before birth and its sorrows; read the other way, the present links would become future. Line 169's குற்றம் opens the next list rather than closing this one. The three births (155-158) are obscure, and line 155's தோன்றல் வீடு எனத் துணிந்து is a reading I cannot fix.

tamil: புனையும் அடை பவமும் வினை செயல் ஆகும்
நுகர்ச்சி பிறப்பு மூப்புப் பிணி சாவு இவை
இப்படி உணரும் இவை வீட்டு இயல்பு ஆம்
reading: The teacher sorts the links into fault (craving, clinging, ignorance), deed (becoming and action) and fruit (consciousness to feeling, birth, aging, sickness, death); seeing that these are sorrow, unstable, and that no thing has a self, is the nature of release; and he names the links from consciousness to despair as the disease.
nuance: எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை (line 177) is the chapter's one plain statement of no-self, and it is placed as what is to be seen for release, not argued against a rival here. Line 182 begins the four truths with நோய், the disease, the medical frame that runs through the epic's name for the Buddha as the physician of birth.

reading: The teacher gives the four truths (the disease, its cause in ignorance, action, craving, clinging and becoming, sorrow caused by birth and clinging, and joy that is release caused by not clinging), names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness), and begins the six modes of speech.
nuance: Line 187 (இன்பம் வீடே பற்றிலி காரணம்) names release as joy, so the third and fourth truths are put as a cause and its result, parallel to the first two. The four truths are called வாய்மை, but they are not the virtue of truthfulness, so I have not tagged vaaimai.

tamil: சொல்லிய தொகைத் திறம் உடம்பு நீர் நாடு
தொடர்ச்சி வித்து முளை தாள் என்று இந்
சொல் எனத் தோற்றும் பல நாள் கூடிய
உள் வழக்கு உணர்வு இல் வழக்கு முயற்கோடு
reading: The teacher explains the modes of speech by example: the collective name (the body; water; a country), the continuity name (seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy), the name stressing one stage (it perishes, it arose, it aged), the joined name (letters together as a word, days together as a month), and four modes of affirming and denying what exists and what does not, as consciousness, the hare's horn and the mind that flashes up like lightning.
nuance: The point of the modes is that names like paddy or month are conventions for collections and continuities, not things in themselves. The examples for the four existence-modes at lines 208-213 are terse, and which example belongs to which mode is my best construal.

tamil: நெல் வித்து அகத்துள் நெல் முளை தோற்றும் எனல்
நல்ல இயல்பு நயம் இவற்றில் நாம் கொள்பயன்
தொக்க பொருள் அலது ஒன்று இல்லை என்றும்
reading: The teacher ends the modes of speech (an effect without a cause is the mode of denial resting on what is not, as there is no arising for a hare's horn) and gives the four nayas: oneness (cause and effect seen as one), difference (each felt apart), non-agency (no mind in the cause that intends its effect) and own-nature (paddy seed gives paddy sprout), and begins what is gained from them: that there is nothing but aggregated things.
nuance: The non-agency naya (lines 223-226) says the cause has no intention of producing the effect, which applies the chain's 'no maker' (line 39) to every cause and effect.

tamil: அதுவும் அன்று அது அலாததும் அன்று என்றும்
reading: The teacher completes what the four nayas yield (no clinging to things, no doer apart from the doing, effects come from causes, and the middle that is neither this nor not-this) and names the four ways of answering a question, illustrating two: 'what has arisen will perish' is the definite answer, and a question whether the dead man will be reborn is answered by asking whether he was free of clinging.
nuance: The rebirth question (lines 240-242) is not answered yes or no but turned to the condition: whether one is reborn depends on whether clinging has ended, which is the chain applied to a person.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 244 to 243: the illustration of the analytic answer ends at விளம்புவர் (line 243), and the example of setting a question aside begins at line 244.

tamil: இந் நால் வகையான் மனத்திருள் நீங்கு!' என்று
'பவத் திறம் அறுக!' எனப் பாவை நோற்றனள் என்
reading: The teacher illustrates the last two kinds of answer (the question whether egg or palmyra came first set aside by asking 'which egg, which palmyra?', and silence before a question about the age of a sky-flower), says bondage and release have their own causes and no one can grant them, names desire, anger and delusion as the cause of all he has taught, and prescribes a remedy for each: seeing impermanence, sorrow, no-self and impurity to cut clinging, friendliness, compassion and sympathetic joy to end hatred, and hearing, reflecting, cultivating and seeing to drive off delusion; the narrator says that, the lamp of knowledge shown, Manimekalai took up austerity and vowed to cut the round of becoming.
nuance: Lines 250-251 (கட்டும் வீடும் அதன் காரணத்தது / ஒட்டித் தருதற்கு உரியோர் இல்லை) deny any giver of bondage or release. Line 253's காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் is the same triad, in the same order, as Kural 360; three words fall short of an echo, so it is a link. Line 263 (தவத் திறம் பூண்டு தருமம் கேட்டு) repeats the title of kaathai 29, and line 264 gives this kaathai its title.
event: Having heard the teaching, Manimekalai takes up austerity and vows to end the round of births.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 244/245 to 243/244: line 244 begins the example of setting a question aside (the egg and the palmyra), which runs to 246.

title: பதிகம்
theme: The patikam frames the epic: hill folk report a one-breasted woman taken to heaven, Saathan tells Ilango the story of Kovalan's death and Kannaki's burning of Madurai and its cause in a curse from a former birth, and Ilango sets down the poem's three morals, the death of an erring king by dharma, the praise of the pathini and the inevitability of the past deed, before the thirty kaathais are listed.

cast.role: the Chera prince who gave up kingship and lives at the eastern-gate shrine; the patikam names him as the poet
the grain merchant of Madurai (கூல வாணிகன்), Tamil poet, who tells Ilango the story and hears the poem
the hill-dwelling kuravar who saw the one-breasted woman taken to heaven
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived
the royal goldsmith of Madurai who accused Kovalan of theft
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as வேம்பன், பாண்டியன்)
the Pandya's guards who carry out the killing
the guardian goddess of Madurai who tells Kannaki the cause from a former birth

reading: The hill kuravar gather before Ilango, the Chera prince who gave up the throne and lives at the shrine of the eastern gate, and tell him that under a flowering vengai they saw a great pathini who had lost one breast taken up to heaven, with her beloved husband shown to her, by the retinue of the king of the gods; they ask him to find out what this wonder means, and Saathan, sitting beside him, says he knows how it came about.
nuance: The epic opens from the outside: the witnesses are hill folk who do not know the woman's name, and the frame puts the story in the mouth of a merchant-poet told to a renouncer prince. The poet himself is introduced by what he gave up (அரசுதுறந்து), so the work's narrator stands from the first line in the posture of renunciation, though the patikam makes no doctrinal claim about it.
event: The hill kuravar report to Ilango that they saw a one-breasted woman carried to heaven with her husband, and Saathan offers to explain it.

reading: Saathan tells how Kovalan, a merchant of the Chola's Puhar, lost his great wealth living with a dancing courtesan, came to Madurai to sell an anklet of his wife Kannaki, and showed it to the royal goldsmith, who told him to wait, went off, and said to the king that he had found, in a stranger's hand, the thief of the anklet he himself had once taken.
nuance: The summary already lets the listener know the goldsmith is the thief: பண்டுதான் கொண்ட சிலம்பு, the anklet he himself took earlier, so the accusation is shown as a cover for his own theft before any karma is mentioned. The courtesan is not named here; the loss of wealth is put down to Kovalan's own way of life (ஆடிய கொள்கையின்).
event: Kovalan, ruined, brings Kannaki's anklet to Madurai to sell, and the royal goldsmith who had stolen the queen's anklet denounces him as the thief.

reading: Saathan says that because it was the time for the deed to ripen, the Pandya did not inquire, called his guards and ordered them to kill the thief and bring the anklet; Kovalan's wife, finding no ground to stand on, wept, and being a pathini, twisted off her breast and set fire to Madurai so that the Pandya fell, and this is the woman the kuravar saw, the pathini praised by many.
nuance: Two causes stand side by side: the ripening of the deed (வினைவிளை காலம் ஆதலின்) explains why the king failed to inquire (தேரானாகி), and Kannaki's being a pathini (பத்தினி யாகலின்) explains the city's ruin. Karma here does not excuse the king's fault; it is given as the reason the fault happened, and the burning falls on the king all the same.
event: The Pandya, without inquiring, has Kovalan killed; Kannaki weeps, tears off her breast and burns Madurai.

reading: Ilango asks what deed it was that ripened, and Saathan answers that, lying at night in the silver hall of Madurai, he saw the great goddess of Madurai appear before the grieving pathini and tell her that their ripe deed had run its course because of a curse laid in a former birth by the wife of Sangaman, a merchant of Singapuram, and that she would see her husband after fourteen days only in the form of the gods, not in human form; this unbiased word, he says, he heard.
