nuance: The patikam names only the curse and its author, the widow of Sangaman, and not what was done to Sangaman; the reader learns only in the Katturai Kaathai that Kovalan in that birth had him killed as a spy. Saathan vouches for the account as a witness, not as a sage: he overheard it (கேட்டனன் யான்). Lines 50 to 53 are repeated almost word for word at Silappathikaram 23.173-176.
event: Asked about the deed that ripened, Saathan reports overhearing the goddess of Madurai tell Kannaki that a curse from a former birth has come to fruit and that she will see her husband in divine form after fourteen days.

reading: Ilango declares that, to show that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship, that the great praise a renowned pathini, and that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat its fruit, he will set down a song-poem named Silappathikaram with the anklet as its cause; told that it belongs to all three crowned kings and that he himself should compose it, he composes, and the list of its kaathais begins: the benediction, the wedding household, Madhavi's debut, the evening, the Indra festival, the sea bathing.
nuance: The three morals are stated as theses the poem will show (ஆவதூஉம், ஏத்தலும், என்பதூஉம்), and the title is derived from the anklet as the cause (சிலம்பு காரணமாக) of all three. The first is narrowed to kings (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு), where the venba of the Vazhakkurai Kaathai gives it as a general saying about all wrongdoers. The third sits beside the first without being reconciled with it: the poem holds both that the king's error is punished and that the past deed had to come. Who speaks lines 55 to 60 is not marked; the யாம் of நாட்டுதும் can be read as Ilango's resolve, with lines 61 and 62 as Saathan's reply, or as Saathan's proposal; this marking follows the first.
event: Ilango resolves to compose the Silappathikaram on the three morals, and is urged to do so as a poem for all three kings.

reading: The list of the thirty kaathais continues from the Kaanal Vari through Madhavi's lament, the dream, the journey, the killing and the plea, to the burning, the goddess's word, the hill kuravai and the five Vanchi kaathais ending with the Varantharu Kaathai, and the patikam closes by saying that this song-poem with prose set among it was composed by Adigal and heard by Saathan the grain merchant of Madurai.
nuance: Line 86 (இவ்வா றைந்தும், six fives) gives the count of thirty, which the list bears out. The closing lines describe the form, verse with prose between (உரையிடை இட்ட பாட்டுடைச் செய்யுள்), and name Saathan as the first hearer, so the frame that began with him telling the story ends with him receiving the poem.
event: Adigal composes the poem and Saathan, the grain merchant of Madurai, hears it.

title: மங்கல வாழ்த்துப் பாடல்
theme: The benediction that opens the epic: three-line venbas hail the moon, the sun, the rain and Puhar, each for being like the Chola's umbrella, wheel, grace and line; the narrative then calls Puhar a city the learned never speak of as declining, introduces Kannaki at twelve and Kovalan at sixteen as children of its two great merchant houses, and tells their wedding, with the Vedic circling of the fire, the women's blessing that she never be parted from her lover, and a closing praise of the Chola's wheel.
source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 68 lines as shown against the edition's printed last line 65; the short connecting words set on lines of their own (ஆங்கு, அதனால், அவளுந்தான், அவனுந்தான், அவரை, அவ்வழி) may be counted differently in the edition.
Lines 48 and 62 carry repaired TSCII characters (ு + ட read as ூ); the repaired forms (மாலைதாழ், தீதுஅறுக) read correctly.
Line 46 lacks a space after the comma in பணிலம்,வெண்குடை.

Lines 64 to 68: the syntax joining the women's seating of the bride (ஏற்றினார், தங்கிய) to the closing praise of the Chola (எனவே) is unclear, so whether the praise is the women's or the poet's cannot be fixed.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
Kannaki's father, a great merchant of Puhar
Kovalan's father, a great merchant of Puhar
the two fathers (the elders of the two houses) who arrange the wedding
the aged Brahmin priest who conducts the wedding rite
the adorned women who bless the bride and lead her to the marriage couch
the unnamed Chola king of Puhar, praised as சென்னி, காவிரி நாடன், செம்பியன்

reading: Four short venbas each hail a power twice, the moon, the sun, the great rain and the city Puhar, and give as the reason for praising each that it resembles the Chola: the moon his cool white umbrella sheltering the world, the sun his wheel of rule circling Meru, the rain his bounty pouring on the sea-girt earth, and Puhar his lineage rising and spreading.
nuance: The comparison runs backwards from the usual royal praise: the king is not likened to the sun and moon, the heavenly bodies are praised because they are like the king (the ablative ஆன் of அளித்தலான், திரிதலான், சுரத்தலான், ஒழுகலான் gives the reason). The opening worship names no god; nature and the city stand where an invocation would be, and the king is in every stanza without being named except by the titles சென்னி and காவிரி நாடன்.

reading: The narrator says that the learned, whatever they say of Pothiyil, the Himalaya or Puhar of the ancient families who never leave it, speak of these only as standing unshaken and never of their decline, and in that city he introduces the twelve-year-old daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan, Kannaki, whom women worship as Lakshmi's beauty and the faultless northern star's virtue.
nuance: Puhar is set beside two mountains as a thing that does not move, and the claim is given to the wise of complete learning (முடித்த கேள்வி முழுதுணர்ந்தோர்), so the epic opens on a confidence in the city's permanence that its sequel will undo. Kannaki is first named by her father's house and by others' praise: she does nothing in the unit, and the star of the faultless wife (வடமீன், the Arundhati star) is what women see in her before her story begins. Her name ends the unit with மன்னோ, the particle of something past and lasting.
event: The narrator introduces Kannaki, twelve-year-old daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan of Puhar.

reading: The narrator introduces Kovalan, sixteen, son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, master of great wealth who pours out his coming riches for others and whose house stands with the families that the king of the whole earth honours, a youth whom women hail as Murugan come again; then the two fathers, delighting to see them married, set the bride on an elephant's neck and announce the wedding to the city.
nuance: Both introductions are built alike (அவளுந்தான் / அவனுந்தான், ending பாள்மன்னோ / பான்மன்னோ), so bride and groom are presented as a matched pair of houses before they are persons; Kovalan's praise, though, is all of women's admiration (மதிமுக மடவார், ஆயத்துப் பாராட்டி), a hint of the charm that will draw him to Madhavi. The father's wealth is praised for being given away (வருநிதி பிறர்க்குஆர்த்தும்).
event: The two fathers arrange Kovalan and Kannaki's marriage and announce it to the city from an elephant's back.

reading: Drums, conches and the royal umbrella go out as if a king rode forth; under a pearl canopy on diamond pillars, at the hour the moon joins Rohini, Kovalan circles the fire with Kannaki as the aged Brahmin shows the Vedic way, and the adorned women, scattering flowers and blessing her never to part from her lover nor loosen her embrace, seat the Arundhati-like bride on the marriage couch; the unit closes hailing the Chola who set his tiger on the Himalaya and rolls his single wheel everywhere.
nuance: The women's blessing (காதலற் பிரியாமல் கவவுக்கை ஞெகிழாமல் தீதுஅறுக) names exactly the harm the story will bring: separation and loosened arms. Line 53 exclaims what vow (நோன்பு) the onlookers must have kept to see the circling of the fire, treating the sight as the fruit of past observance. The rite is Vedic in form (மறைவழி, தீவலம்), led by a Brahmin, though the families are merchants. How lines 64 to 68 attach is not plain: தங்கிய and எனவே may make the praise of the Chola part of the women's words, or the poet's own close.
event: Kovalan and Kannaki are married with the circling of the fire, and the women bless her and lead her to the marriage couch.

title: மனையறம்படுத்த காதை
theme: The kaathai of setting up the household: in Puhar's inexhaustible wealth the newly married Kannaki and Kovalan, likened to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity, climb to the terrace of their mansion on a spring evening; Kovalan pours out an unmeasured praise that has the gods surrender their weapons to her body and asks why her maids adorned a beauty that needs nothing; then an elder lady sets Kannaki up in a household of her own for charity and the hosting of guests, some years pass, and a closing venba says the two enjoyed every pleasure inseparably, as if they had seen that nothing on earth lasts.
source_issues: The edition prints 90 as the last line: the count covers the akaval (lines 1-90) and leaves out the closing venba (91-94).
Line 72 has என்உற் றனர்க்கொல் with a doubled க், against என்உற் றனர்கொல் on line 66; probably a misprint.
Lines 62 and 73-75 carry full stops after vocatives (கோதை.நின், பொன்னே., முத்தே.), editorial punctuation for exclamation; line 62 lacks a space after the stop.
Lines 49-50 (பெறுமுறை இன்றியும் இறுமுறை காணும் இயல்பினின்) are hard to construe, so the reason given for the six-faced god's gift is uncertain.
Line 91: the sense of தூமப் பணிகள் (smoky or dark serpents) is not certain.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the great lady of the house who sets Kannaki up in a household of her own; the unit does not name her, and the story suggests an elder of the family, likely Kovalan's mother

reading: The narrator describes Puhar, city of famed merchants, so rich that its stores would not run short if the whole sea-girt world came to it, filled with rare goods brought by ship and cart, home of wealthy houses that never fall from their lineage, and there sets the flower-eyed bride and her loving husband, who appear like those who completed hard austerity and are born to enjoy in Uttarakuru.
nuance: The couple's happiness is introduced through a simile of reward: Uttarakuru is the land where the fruit of austerity is enjoyed (அருந்தவம் முடித்தோர்), so the marriage is pictured as a store of merit being spent, and what is spent can run out. The unit is the subject of a sentence that runs on to line 37 without a main verb; the couple are named only by epithets (கயமலர்க் கண்ணியும் காதல் கொழுநனும்).

reading: Seated on a jewelled couch like Maya's work in the middle storey of their tall mansion, the couple see the fragrant southern breeze enter through the latticed window with bees that have fed on the field flowers and on the thaazhai, the maadhavi creeper and the champak grove, and delighted and deepened in love they climb to the open terrace where spring sits enthroned with its arrows of flowers.
nuance: Spring with its flower-arrows (விரைமலர் வாளியொடு வேனில்) is the love god's season, so the breeze is a messenger of desire. Among the scents it carries is the மாதவி creeper (line 18), the same name the dancer bears who will take Kovalan from this house in the next kaathai; the text does not point to it, and the echo may be no more than a reader's.
event: Kovalan and Kannaki, delighted by the spring breeze in their chamber, climb to the terrace of their mansion.

reading: On the flower bed Kovalan paints sugarcane and creeper on her shoulders, the two shine together like sun and moon lighting the world, their garlands tangle, and gazing at her face in love he speaks: the great god should give her the crescent moon he wears as her brow, since it is her sibling; the bodiless god gave his cane bow as her two brows; the king of gods gave the middle of his thunderbolt as her waist, since she appeared before the nectar; and the six-faced god gave his one spear as her two eyes.
nuance: Lines 28 to 37 are the narrator's and the speech begins at 38. The praise makes the gods hand over their weapons, as one gives arms to a champion at the front (lines 42-43), so her body is imagined as an armoury that conquers; the moon being her sibling and her appearing before the nectar both suggest she is likened to Lakshmi, born of the churned sea, though the text does not name her. Line 37 calls the speech குறியாக் கட்டுரை, an unmeasured or unconsidered speech, which may judge Kovalan's excess as well as describe it.
event: Kovalan paints his bride's shoulders and begins a long praise of her beauty.
unit_note: End moved from line 50 to line 52: the question about the six-faced god's spear, begun at line 49, closes with ஈத்தது? on line 52.

reading: Kovalan goes on: the peacock beaten by her grace has fled to the forest, the swan beaten by her gait hides among the lotus pools, and the parrot, pained by her prattle that is sweeter than flute, lute and nectar, still will not leave her hand; then he asks why those who praise her beauty decked her with ornaments beyond the auspicious one, with garlands beyond the flowers of her hair, musk beyond incense, and a strand of pearls beyond the painting on her breasts, making her small waist suffer.
nuance: The parrot is pitied (அளிய தாமே) because it loses to her and still stays, unlike the peacock and swan that withdraw; the catalogue of adornments turns into a reproach of her attendants, the convention that beauty is burdened by what is added to it. The faultless auspicious ornament (மறுஇல் மங்கல அணி, line 63) is the one ornament he allows, the wife's mark, set against the rest.
unit_note: Start moved from line 51 to 53 (see the previous unit) and end from line 66 to 72: the run of questions about her ornaments, begun at line 62, ends with என்உற் றனர்க்கொல்? on line 72.

reading: Kovalan calls her flawless gold, pearl of the right-whorled conch, pure fragrance, sugarcane, honey, rare doll, medicine of his life, innocent daughter of the great merchant house, and asks whether to call her a gem not born of mountains, nectar not born of the sea, music not born of the lute; so he delights with her, and as the days go the great lady of the house, wishing to see Kannaki's charity and her household that welcomes guests flourish, sets her up apart with her own retinue, and some years pass for Kannaki in the dignity of the house.
nuance: Lines 73 to 80 are Kovalan's words, closed by என்று at line 80; from line 81 the narrator speaks. The title's மனையறம் is given its content here: the household is set up so that its charity (அறப் பரிசாரம்) and hospitality (விருந்து புறந்தருஉம்) may be seen, which is the life Kannaki will later say she has lost. 'Some years passed' (யாண்டுசில கழிந்தன) closes the happy time in four words. Who the great lady is the unit does not say.
event: After Kovalan's praise, an elder lady of the family sets Kannaki up in a household of her own, and some years pass.
unit_note: Start moved from line 67 to 73: the questions about her ornaments end at line 72, and the run of endearments that the narrator closes with என்று at line 80 begins at line 73.

reading: A closing venba says that the two, joined like intertwined serpents and never parting, hand in hand as husband and wife, enjoyed every pleasure whose name does not fade, standing on the earth like people who had seen its impermanence.
nuance: The last line turns the knowledge of impermanence into a reason for haste in pleasure rather than for renunciation, as the ethics books use it; the simile 'as if they had seen' (கண்டவர்ப்போல்) leaves open whether they did see it. ஒருவார், 'they did not part', is undone in the next kaathai. The image of தூமப் பணிகள் (smoky or dark serpents coiled together) is not certain in its first word.

title: அரங்கேற்று காதை
theme: Madhavi's debut: after seven years of training she is presented to the Chola king with a troupe each of whose masters is described by his art, on a stage built to the treatise's measures; the talaikkol, a war trophy worshipped as Indra's son, is carried round the town, she dances, wins the title and 1008 kazhanju, and her garland, priced at that sum and offered in the street, is bought by Kovalan, who goes to live with her and forgets his home.
source_issues: The kaathai has 179 lines as shown: 175 lines of nilaimandila akaval, matching the edition's printed last line 175, and a closing venba of 4 lines (176-179).
Lines 40, 44 and 158 carry repaired TSCII characters (ு + ட read as ூ); the repaired forms (நன்னூல், நன்குகடைப்) read correctly.
Lines 30 and 31 both read தேசிகத் திருவின் ஓசை; the repetition may be the poem's linking device or a doubled half-line, which I cannot settle.

Words are split across a space in several lines (புலமை யோனுடன் 94, ஆமந் திரிகை 142-143, ஐந்துமண் டிலத்தால் 152, வந்தவா ரம்வழி 153, நன்குகடைப் பிடித்து 158), apparently metrical division carried into the text.

cast.role: the dancer of Puhar, of a line traced to the heavenly women freed from a curse
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the unnamed Chola king of Puhar, here சூழ்கடல் மன்னன், காவல் வேந்தன்
Madhavi's dance master
the singer of the troupe
the poet of the troupe, master of Tamil and the drama treatise
the master of the thannumai drum
the flute player
the yaazh player who tunes the modes
the king's five great assemblies
the instrumentalists
the senior dancing women who sing the opening vaaram
the doe-eyed woman, unnamed here, who calls Madhavi 'our creeper' and sends her garland out for sale
the hunchbacked maid who carries the garland into the street

reading: Madhavi, of a birth not falling short of the heavenly women freed at the place of the talaikkol from the curse a holy sage of the divine mountain laid on them with Indra's son, trains seven years in dance, song and beauty, lacking in none of the three, to show her art to the sea-girt king in her twelfth year.
nuance: The sage gives the curse 'as grace' (அருள எய்திய சாபத்து), so the curse is framed as a gift. Whether Madhavi descends from the freed heavenly women or only matches them (பிறப்பிற் குன்றா, a birth not less than theirs) cannot be fixed from these lines; the sage and the heavenly woman are not named. The three arts are counted as a set that must be whole (ஒன்றுகுறை படாமல்), so beauty stands among the trained skills, not as a gift of nature.
event: Madhavi trains seven years in dance, song and beauty to be shown to the Chola king in her twelfth year.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the first unit ends at line 11 (காட்டல் வேண்டி), where the account of Madhavi's training gives way to the dance master; the old unit 1-16 ran five lines into his description.

reading: The dance master is described: he knows the marks of the two kinds of koothu, joins the many kinds to the interludes, knows the eleven dances with their song and drumming, the four kinds of hand gesture and how a gesture of one style is dropped into another, and directs the kuravai and vari without mixing them.
nuance: The four lines 20 to 23 are built as a chiasmus (கூடை into வாரம், வாரம் into கூடை, பிண்டி into ஆடல், ஆடல் into பிண்டி): the verse performs the exchange of gestures it describes. The master is praised for knowing where each gesture must stop, not for invention.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 12 (இருவகைக் கூத்தின்) to line 25, which closes the dance master's description with ஆசான் தன்னொடும்.

reading: The singer is described: he fits the song to yaazh, flute, beat, voice and drum, keeps to the sound of the regional styles and knows them all without fault, and when the poem's intent, the dance and the parts of the song are set together, lays out his flawless learning.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 26 (யாழும் குழலும்) to line 36, which names the singer (இசையோன் தானும்) and closes his description.

reading: The poet is described: knowing all of Tamil so that the Tamil land within the sea knows it, holding to the drama treatise in its two kinds, the king's style and the common style, he understands where the singer bends the melody and sets it in the fixed tradition, and knows the faults that rivals charge.
nuance: The poet's office is partly defensive: he must know the blame (வசைமொழி) that others will speak, so the performance is judged against a rule that critics also hold. The pair வேத்தியல் பொதுவியல் recurs in the Manimekalai's list of Madhavi's arts.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 37 (இமிழ்கடல் வரைப்பில்) to line 44, which names the poet (நன்னூல் புலவனும்).

reading: The drum master is described: knowing dance, song, melody, Tamil, mode, beat, rhythm, the lame measure and the regional styles, he lets the yaazh, flute and voice be heard in the measures of the dance, strikes the stroke at its sign, and swells or restrains it so that it never overpowers.
nuance: The drummer's excellence is restraint: ஆக்கலும் அடக்கலும் மீத்திறம் படாமை, raising and holding back without excess. The loudest instrument is praised for not drowning the others.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 45 (ஆடல் பாடல் இசையே) to line 55, which names the drum master (தண்ணுமை அருந்தொழில் முதல்வனும்).

reading: The flute player is described: knowing the fixed figures and the four ornaments, hearing the two strings kural and ili as one, keeping in step with the drum master and the tuned yaazh, he follows the singer's melody, carries on what has come and anticipates what comes, and plays each syllable on the wet stops without fault.
nuance: The terms of art (சித்திர வஞ்சனை, வர்த்தனை, ஈர நிலம்) are not explained in the verse, and their exact sense is a reading I cannot fix without commentary.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 56 (சொல்லிய இயல்பினிற்) to line 69, which names the flute player (குழலோன் தானும்).

reading: The yaazh player is described: to fix the seven palai modes from the fourteen strings, he moves notes by their kin, the high and low parts of the scale passing to one another until the red palai, then the other palais, are set, and he matches the yaazh and flute so that strong, soft and level are all in tune.
nuance: The notes are treated as women who leave or join their kin (கிளைவழிப் பட்டனள், ஏனை மகளிரும் கிளைவழிச் சேர): the modal shift is told as a family moving house. The technical sequence (படுமலை, செவ்வழி, கோடி விளரி) is the verse's own, but which note becomes the tonic at each step is beyond what I can fix.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 70 (ஈர்ஏழ் தொடுத்த) to line 94, which names the yaazh player (புலமை யோனுடன்) and ends the list of accompanists.

reading: The stage is built as the treatise's authors prescribe: on chosen ground, with a bamboo from the holy mountain whose internodes are a span apart, a measuring rod of twenty-four finger-breadths fixes it seven rods wide, eight long and one high, four rods between the planks, two doors, the guardian beings painted above and worshipped, lamps set so no pillar casts a shadow, and three kinds of curtain.
nuance: Every measure is given as a number from the book (நூல்நெறி மரபின்), and the rod itself is taken from a holy mountain: the stage is a ritual space before it is a theatre. The lamps are placed so the pillars' shadows fall outside, so nothing on the stage is hidden.
event: The stage is measured and built by rule, with painted guardians, lamps and three curtains.

reading: Pearl garlands are hung from the painted canopy; the talaikkol, cut from the shaft of a white umbrella taken from great kings who fled, its joints set with nine gems and bound in gold, is worshipped in the king's palace as Jayanta son of Indra, bathed from a golden pot, garlanded, set in the state elephant's hand on an auspicious day, and carried round the town by the king and the five great assemblies to be set before the stage.
nuance: The dancer's staff of honour is a war trophy: the shaft of a defeated king's umbrella. The emblem of an art is made from the emblem of a lost kingdom, and worshipped as a god, so the dance's highest title carries the Chola's victory and the Indra myth at once. What கவிகைக் கொடுப்ப (line 127) gives, and to whom, is unclear to me.
event: The talaikkol, worshipped as Jayanta, is bathed, garlanded and carried on the state elephant round the town by the king and the five great assemblies, then set before the stage.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 111 (ஓவிய விதானத்து) to line 128, where the procession ends with புகுந்துமுன் வைத்துஆங்கு; the old unit stopped at 126 in mid-procession.

reading: The musicians take their places by order; the dancer steps onto the stage right foot first and goes to the right pillar as custom requires, while the senior dancing women at the left pillar sing the two vaaram for good fortune and to keep off harm; the instruments follow one another, yaazh after flute, drum after yaazh, muzhavu after drum, the aamanthirikai with them, through eleven rounds, and then the dance begins on the palai mode in its counted measures.
nuance: Madhavi is not named here; she is known from the right-foot entry, a rule of conduct (வழக்குஎனப் பொருந்தி). The order of the instruments is itself a hierarchy, each standing 'behind' (வழி) the one before. The counted measures of lines 148 to 153 are technical and I read only their outline.
event: Madhavi enters the stage right foot first, the senior dancers sing the two vaaram, the orchestra plays in its order, and the dance begins.
unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 129 (இயல்பினின் வழாஅ) to line 153, where the opening rounds end with மயங்கிய பின்றை; the old units 127-137 and 138-153 split the entry from the music it opens.

reading: Having shown the dance as the treatise prescribes, Madhavi receives from the king the leaf garland and the talaikkol title and, by rule, a thousand and eight kazhanju of gold; the doe-eyed woman sets that sum as the price of the garland and sends it by a hunchbacked maid into the street of the town's young men as if for sale; Kovalan buys it, enters the bridal house with Madhavi, and in his union with her, infatuated and knowing no letting go, forgets his own house of flawless distinction.
nuance: The garland's price is exactly the king's reward, so the courtesan house turns a royal honour into a sale price. The sale is staged (பகர்வனர் போல்வதோர் பான்மையின், 'in the manner of those who sell'): the street offer is a custom, not a bargain. The narrator passes no verdict on Madhavi; his one judgment is the praise of what Kovalan forgot (வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின்தன் மனையகம்), and the forgetting is told as infatuation (மயங்கி, விடுதல் அறியா விருப்பினன்), not as fate. Who the doe-eyed woman is, Madhavi's mother or another of the house, the chapter does not say.
event: The king gives Madhavi the talaikkol and 1008 kazhanju; her garland, priced at that sum, is offered in the street, and Kovalan buys it, goes to live with Madhavi and forgets his home.

reading: A closing venba says that Madhavi of Puhar, with her golden bangles, came onto the dancing stage and by her art displayed on earth the counts and letters, the five modes of composition, the four panns and the eleven dances set to music.
nuance: The venba sums up the chapter as Madhavi's achievement and says nothing of the sale or of Kovalan: the closing praise and the narrative's last line (Kovalan forgetting his home) are set side by side without comment.

title: அந்திமாலைச் சிறப்புசெய் காதை
theme: The kaathai of the evening: in one long sentence the poet brings dusk on Puhar like a usurping king, lets the Pandya crescent take the sky, and goes through the city's nights, Madhavi giving Kovalan love and its quarrels, the wives asleep on their husbands' chests, Kannaki stripped of every ornament but the marriage one, the parted women sleepless and weeping, until at dawn the god of desire, who patrolled all night, is declared the city's best watchman; a venba sets the moon as a king's umbrella, shade to Madhavi and heat to Kannaki.
source_issues: The kaathai has 88 lines in the core text but the edition's printed numbering ends at 80, so line numbers here (the kaathai's own, 1-88 as `show` prints them) differ from the printed ones.
Line 66 (துணைபுணர் அன்னத் தூவியிற் செறித்த) carries a repaired encoding flag (a TSCII leftover read as ூ); the repaired reading makes sense and I marked it as written.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, left alone in his house
Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer with whom Kovalan now lives
the wives of Puhar who sleep on their husbands' chests through the night
the women of Puhar parted from their lovers
Kama, the god of desire, with the makara banner, flower arrows and sugarcane bow

reading: The poet brings evening on Puhar as a political disaster: the sun, sole wheel-ruler of the world, is gone, the earth like a woman in grief weeps with pale face and wet eyes as if her king were lost, and evening camps in the city like a foreign king who seizes a land whose victorious king is absent, sides with the traitors and leaves the loyal wringing their hands; lovers apart are grieved and lovers together delighted, a bee hums in the jasmine beside the herdsmen, the little breeze scatters scent through the streets and women light the gem lamps.
nuance: The whole kaathai is one sentence, and this opening sets its frame: evening as a usurper in a kingless land (lines 8 to 12), a figure drawn from the state rather than from love. Lines 13 and 14 announce the chapter's plan, the same hour bringing grief to the parted and joy to the joined, which the following units fill in house by house. The herdsmen of line 15 are கோவலர், the hero's name in the plural; the chapter does not stress the pun, and I note it only as a sound a listener would hear.
event: Evening falls on Puhar and the women of the houses light the gem lamps.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 21|22 to 20|21: line 20 (மாலைவந்து இருத்தென) closes the clause of evening's arrival, and lines 21 to 22 (இளையர் ஆயினும் ... குலமுதல் ஆகலின்) give the reason for the crescent's power in the next clause.

reading: Because it is the founder of the line of the Pandyas, who drive off hostile kings even when young, the white crescent rises in the evening sky, routs the raiding gloom, spreads milk-white rays without swerving from its nature and rules the stars; under its light Madhavi, adorned, on the high moonlit terrace among beds of jasmine and mallikai, gives Kovalan both love-making and the feigned quarrel, meeting him with an eager heart.
nuance: The moon that took over the sky from the beaten evening is a Pandya; in a book whose second half turns on a Pandya's justice, its first praise of that line is of a ruler that does not swerve (பான்மையில் திரியாது). Madhavi is given both கலவி and புலவி, union and the lovers' sulk, as a skill she offers Kovalan (அளித்து), an art and not only a feeling. The unit ends on அன்றியும் ('and besides'): she is the first item in a list of the city's nights.
event: Madhavi, adorned on her moonlit terrace, receives Kovalan with love-making and lovers' quarrels.
unit_note: Start moved from 22 to 21 to take in the whole reason clause (lines 21 to 22) that belongs to the crescent of line 23; the unit still ends at 34 (மாதவி அன்றியும்).

reading: Besides Madhavi, the other wives of the city lie on rich flower beds strewn with western white incense, eastern dark agil, northern stone-ground and southern sandal, lotus, lily and garlands mixed with fine powder, and, drowsy in the gentle south wind, sleep in delight folded on their husbands' chests.
nuance: The four directions of the perfumes (குடதிசை, குணதிசை, வடமலை, தென்மலை) make the bed a map of the merchant city's trade, so the joy of these couples is also a picture of Puhar's wealth. Their wedded sleep (கொழுநர் அகலத்து ஒடுங்கி) is the one thing Kannaki, also a wife, lacks in the next unit.
event: The wives of Puhar sleep in delight on their husbands' chests.
unit_note: End moved from 44 to 46: the sentence of the scented beds runs on through lines 45 and 46 and closes at களித்துயில் எய்த; Kannaki's description begins at line 47.

reading: Kannaki, with a helpless heart, has left off the anklets from her feet and the girdle from her waist, draws no saffron on her breast, takes pleasure in no ornament but the auspicious one, has put away her earrings, forgets the collyrium of her eyes, loses the tilaka from her brow and the oil from her hair, and her bright smile is lost to Kovalan.
nuance: Each line strips one ornament, and the verbs are of absence and forgetting (ஒழிய, நீங்க, மறப்ப, இழப்ப), not of protest: she makes no speech in the chapter. Only one loss is charged to another, the smile Kovalan forfeits (தவள வாள்நகை கோவலன் இழப்ப, line 55). Line 50 (மங்கல அணியின் பிறிதுஅணி மகிழாள்) answers Kovalan's own praise at the wedding night (silappathikaram:2:51-66), and the first anklet of the epic appears here, laid aside.
event: Kannaki, alone at evening, puts off her anklets and every ornament but the auspicious marriage ornament.
unit_note: Both boundaries moved: the unit now starts at 47 (அணிசிலம்பு ஒழிய, the first item of Kannaki's description) and ends at 57, where கண்ணகி அன்றியும் closes it; the original 45-62 split her description from its subject's name and ran into the parted women.

reading: The women parted from their lovers sigh like the bellows of a smith's furnace and shrink into themselves; they leave the summer bedroom, close the small windows of the cool-season room, keep sandal and pearl strings off their breasts, shun beds strewn with lily and red waterlily and find no sleep on pillows stuffed with the down of mated swans; and in their sulking with their husbands their long eyes, red at the corners, rain pearls of lonely tears.
nuance: Lines 58 and 59 repeat almost word for word the Akananuru's evening of a woman left behind (akananuru:71: காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த புலம்பின் நோதக, and the breath blown in a furnace), so a single heroine's lament becomes one class of the city's women. The swan-down pillow is of 'mated swans' (துணைபுணர் அன்னம்), a comfort made from the union they lack. Lines 68 to 71 shift to the time of ஊடல் with husbands, and I cannot fix whether these are the same parted women remembering past quarrels or another group of wives in a quarrel now.
event: The women parted from their lovers lie sleepless, refusing the comforts of their rooms.
unit_note: The original unit 63-84 is split, and its start moved to 58: the parted women's sentence begins at காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த மாதர் (line 58) and its tears close at உறைப்ப (line 71); the dawn scene opens at line 72.

reading: Until dawn comes and night departs, when the pond, a woman with a swan's gait, lily breath, lotus mouth and hair of sand, wakes to bees singing a mournful mode and opens her blue-lily eyes, and drums and conches sound in turn and rouse the sea-girt town, Kama of the makara banner, carrying his flower arrows and sugarcane bow, roamed sleepless at midnight and by day, and so the city's watch was kept supremely well.
nuance: The closing word is a joke on the chapter's political opening: the city that evening invaded like a usurper is guarded all night, and its guard is the god of desire, whose 'patrol' is what kept the parted women awake. நோதிறம், the mode the bees sing at dawn, is a pann of grief, so even the waking of the pond carries the night's sorrow.
event: Kama roams Puhar through the night until drums and conches wake the town at dawn.
unit_note: Split from the original 63-84: the dawn clause starts at அன்னம் மெல்நடை (line 72) after the parted women's tears close at உறைப்ப (line 71); the unit ends where the kaathai does (line 84).

reading: The closing venba says that the night, when the moon riding the sky spread its light and opened the buds, showed itself to Madhavi who was with her lover and to Kannaki like the guardian king's white umbrella, which is shade to those joined to him and heat to those who are not.
nuance: கூடினார், 'those joined', serves both halves of the simile: allies of the king and lovers together. Madhavi is called கூடிய and Kannaki is given no epithet, so the poem's sorting of the two women is done by one word and by its absence.

title: இந்திர விழவு ஊர் எடுத்த காதை
theme: Indra's festival at Puhar: a survey of the city's two quarters and the market between them, the warrior women's possessed blessing and the warriors' head-offerings at the guardian spirit's altar, the halls brought from the north by Thirumavalavan, the five marvellous courts that guard against theft, disease, hidden wrong and a bent sceptre, the bathing of Indra and the rites of all the gods; then Kovalan roaming with Madhavi, the festival's women seen as moon, lotus and Death in disguise, and the omen of Kannaki's and Madhavi's throbbing eyes.
source_issues: Lines 83 and 125: the text tool repaired a stray space before a dead consonant.
Line 164 (ஆயிரத்து ஓர்எட்டு அரசுதலைக் கொண்ட) is obscure as it stands: it is unclear whether the thousand and eight are kings, pots or fords.
Lines 227-234: the construction of the chaste wives' fear is hard to parse and may be corrupt or elliptical.

cast.role: the unnamed reigning Chola king of Puhar, for whose victory and welfare the rites are made
the guardian spirit sent by Indra to remove the Chola king's distress, worshipped at its altar in the market
the women of the old warrior houses who dance possessed and bless the king
the fighting men of Maruvur and Pattinappakkam who offer themselves at the altar
a Chola king of the past remembered for his northern campaign to the Himalaya
the king of the Vajra country who gave Valavan a pavilion as tribute
the king of Magadha who, defeated, gave Valavan a hall of debate
the king of Avanti who gave Valavan an arched gateway in friendship
the spirit of the crossroads (பூத சதுக்கம்) that seizes and devours wrongdoers
the five great councils of the king, acting together at the festival
the eight groups of royal attendants, acting together at the festival
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
Kovalan's wife, daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan
Kama, the bodiless god of love, whose army of festival beauty assails the town

reading: The sun, rising over the mountain and lifting the dark cloak from the earth pictured as a woman with the sea for dress and hills for breasts, lights up Puhar's terraced mansions, its storerooms, the rich men's houses, the quarter by the harbour where Yavanas live, the shore settlements of foreign traders who came with the ships, and the streets where scents, powders, sandal, flowers and incense are hawked.
nuance: The catalogue of Maruvurppakkam begins with the outsiders: the Yavanas whose quarter dazzles onlookers are called people who do not know how things are used (பயன்அறிவு அறியா), and the foreigners are those who came with the ships' wealth and stay mingled with the town. Puhar is first a port.
unit_note: Moved the end from line 16 to line 15: line 15 closes the item 'the town streets where they hawk scents' (நகர வீதியும்), while line 16 begins the weavers' item that ends on line 17.

reading: The catalogue goes on through the weavers of silk, hair and cotton, the broad streets heaped with cloth, coral, sandal, agil, pearls, gems and gold beyond measuring, the grain street, the sellers of cakes, toddy, fish, salt and meat, the brass-smiths, coppersmiths, carpenters, blacksmiths, painters, potters, goldsmiths, jewellers, tailors and leather-workers, the great bards who play the seven notes faultlessly, and the makers of small crafts, all of which together are the shore quarter, Maruvurppakkam.
nuance: Line 21 (வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும்) is word for word the closing line of the Pattinappaalai's list of goods pouring into Puhar (its line 193), so the epic's survey of the same city is built on the older poem's praise. The list names crafts and trades by the worker, not the guild or caste, and puts the bards (பெரும்பாண்) among the skilled trades.
unit_note: Starts at line 16 (the weavers' item of lines 16-17) and ends at line 39, where மருவூர்ப் பாக்கமும் names and closes the whole first quarter; the core units broke at 32 and 47, inside the catalogue.

reading: The second quarter, Pattinappakkam, is listed: the royal street and chariot street, the market square, the mansions of the great merchant families, the Brahmins' quarter, the farmers, the physicians and astrologers, the gem-setters and conch-cutters, the bards, heralds and panegyrists, the time-keepers, actors, courtesans and dancing women, flower-sellers and maids, drummers and players, jesters, and the horsemen, elephant-drivers, charioteers and fierce warriors camped round the palace.
nuance: The inner town is ordered around the king: it opens on the royal and chariot streets and closes with the soldiers who ring the palace (இருந்துபுறம் சுற்றிய), with the courtesans (காவல் கணிகையர்) placed among the king's own servants, the world Madhavi belongs to.
unit_note: Starts at line 40, the first item after மருவூர்ப் பாக்கமும் (line 39), and ends at line 58 (பட்டினப் பாக்கமும்), which names and closes the second quarter; the core units broke at 47 and 62.

reading: Between the two quarters, like the no-man's-land between two kings' battle lines, lies the day market in a grove of close-set trees loud with buyers and sellers; there, when the month of Chittirai brings the full moon of Chitra, the women of the old warrior houses heap rice, cakes, flowers and incense on the altar of the guardian spirit that Indra sent to remove the king's trouble, dance possessed, and bless the king that hunger, disease and enmity may leave his land and plenty and abundance flow.
nuance: The festival begins not with Indra but with the spirit he sent (தேவர் கோமான் ஏவலின் போந்த காவல் பூதம்), and with women who speak as possessed (வலவையின் உரைக்கும்): the blessing for the whole land is uttered in trance. The comparison of the market to the ground between two armies makes peace look like a truce.
event: At the Chitra full moon the women of the warrior houses make offerings at the guardian spirit's altar, dance possessed and bless the king.
unit_note: Starts at line 59, where the market between the two quarters is introduced (இருபெரு வேந்தர் முனையிடம் போல), and ends at line 75, where the old women's blessing closes (ஓதையின் பெயர); the core units broke at 62 and 80.

reading: The fighting men of both quarters hurry first to the altar of the great sacrifice and, praying that the king's trouble be removed and that the offering be a bulwark of his strength, the slingers and spearmen who have won hard battles cut off their own dark heads with fierce reddened eyes, set them on the altar crying 'may the victorious king win', and with the thunder of the drum feed the spirit that eats life-offerings.
nuance: The life-offering (உயிர்ப்பலி) here is the warriors' own heads offered for the king's victory; the narrator gives it no judgment, setting it among the festival's opening rites. The sense of 'cut off their heads' is taken from the head placed on the altar (கருந்தலை ... நற்பலி பீடிகை ... வைத்து); the verb itself is not stated.
event: Warriors of both quarters offer their own heads at the altar for the king's victory.
unit_note: Starts at line 76 with the warriors (மருவூர் மருங்கின் மறம்கொள் வீரரும்) and ends at line 88 (வான்பலி ஊட்டி), the end of their offering; the core units broke at 80 and 98.

reading: The narrator recalls how Thirumavalavan, finding no match for his war-lust on earth, set out to the holy north with sword, umbrella and drum, asking that his arms find foes, and, stopped by the Himalaya, carved his tiger on its peak; on his way back the king of the Vajra land gave him a pavilion, the defeated king of Magadha a hall of debate, and the king of Avanti, gladly, an arched gate, gifts of gold and gems that no craftsman could make, made by Mayan, which now stand together in Puhar as a hall the great praise.
nuance: The episode is told as the past (அந்நாள்), to explain monuments of the festival city; the king's name, திருமா வளவன், is the name of the Pattinappaalai's patron, and the Tamil supports no more than that shared name. The mountain halts him rather than any rival (பகைவிலக்கியது இப் பயம்கெழு மலை). Who received Mayan's help in lines 107-108 (அவர் தொல்லோர் உதவிக்கு) is not clear.
event: Thirumavalavan goes north to the Himalaya, sets his tiger emblem there, and receives a pavilion, a debating hall and a gateway from three northern kings.
unit_note: Starts at line 89 with Valavan's campaign (இருநில மருங்கின் பொருநரைப் பெறாஅ) and ends at line 110, where the three gifts are summed up as the hall the great praise (மண்டபம் அன்றியும்); the core units broke at 98 and 113.

reading: Besides the hall, Puhar has the open court where traders' bundles marked with their names lie unguarded without lock or keeper, because any thief is made to carry his load on his head and whirl round; the court of the pool where the hunchbacked, dwarfs, dumb, deaf and lepers bathe, gain a flawless form and leave after circling it; and the court of the tall stone where those deceived and maddened, poisoned, snake-bitten or struck by demons come round, worship and are freed of their pain.
nuance: The courts (மன்றம்) do the work of watchmen and physicians: theft is prevented by the place itself, and healing comes by circling and worship rather than by medicine. The city's safety is presented as a marvel, not as the king's police.
unit_note: Starts at line 111 with the open court (வம்ப மாக்கள் தம்பெயர் பொறித்த) and ends at line 127 (நிழல்கால் நெடுங்கல் நின்ற மன்றமும்), closing the third court; the core units broke at 113 and 127.

reading: At the crossroads of the spirit, a spirit roars across four kathams that hypocrites who hide behind penance, unchaste women who hide their wrong, ministers who betray, men who desire others' wives, false witnesses and backbiters will fall into the noose in its hand, and it beats and devours them.
nuance: The spirit's list is a list of hidden wrongs: each kind of offender is one whose fault is concealed (மறைந்து ஒழுகும் twice), betrays a trust or speaks falsely behind others' backs, so the punishment exposes what ordinary justice cannot see.
unit_note: Split the core unit 128-142 at line 134, where the crossroads of the spirit (பூத சதுக்கமும்) closes its item; the image court begins on line 135.

reading: There is also the court of the image, where if the king's sceptre bends or a judge in the hall of justice bends the law-book and takes one side, the image weeps without a word; and in all five of these courts, praised by those who know the truth, rare offerings are made.
nuance: The image weeps for two failures, not one: the king's bent sceptre and the judge who twists the treatise (உரைநூல் கோடி), so the court is a check on the king's justice and on his court's learning. It cannot speak or act (நாவொடு நவிலாது); it can only grieve.
unit_note: Split the core unit 128-142: starts at line 135 with the image court (அரைசுகோல் கோடினும்) and ends at line 140, where offerings in all five courts (ஐவகை மன்றத்தும் அரும்பலி உறீஇ) close the survey of the courts.

reading: The festival drum is taken from the Vajra temple and set on the neck of an elephant, the start of the festival is proclaimed at the temple of the white elephant, the auspicious flag is raised to the sky at the temple of the wish-granting tree, and in every street the gates of the mansions are hung with pearl-mouthed arches, golden pots, lamps held by figures, banners, whisks and fragrant powder.
event: The festival drum goes out on an elephant, the festival is proclaimed and its flag raised, and the streets are decorated.
unit_note: Starts at line 141, the drum taken from the Vajra temple (வச்சிரக் கோட்டத்து மணம்கெழு முரசம்), and ends at line 156, where the street decoration closes (வீதியில் செறிந்துஆங்கு); the core units broke at 142 and 158.

reading: The five great councils and the eight groups of attendants, princes, sons of merchants, horsemen, elephant-men and charioteers gather, wishing victory to the famed king, carry in golden pots the holy water of the Kaveri's great ford, and bathe the lord of the gods in it, to the wonder of earth and sky.
nuance: Line 164 (ஆயிரத்து ஓர்எட்டு அரசுதலைக் கொண்ட) is unclear: it may describe the ford where a thousand and eight kings bathed, or the pots or kings who bear the water; the reading here leaves it open. The festival's central rite, the bathing of Indra, is performed by the king's councils on the king's behalf.
event: The king's councils and attendants bathe Indra's image in Kaveri water carried in golden pots.
unit_note: Starts at line 157 with the councils (ஐம்பெருங் குழுவும்) and ends at line 168 (விண்ணவர் தலைவனை விழுநீர் ஆட்டி), the bathing of Indra; the core units broke at 158 and 173.

reading: In the temples of the Unborn One, of six-faced Murugan, of the white-bodied elder brother, of the dark tall god and of the king of the white umbrella, on one side Vedic fire rites follow the ancient way; on another the many classes of gods each have their festival; on another the monasteries of the virtuous and the alms-halls give charity as the wise prescribe; on another kings who would not join the Chola are freed from their fetters; and on another musicians, lute-players and bards make music.
nuance: The repeated ஒருபால் ('on one side') sets Vedic sacrifice, the gods' festivals, the charity of the அறவோர் பள்ளி and the release of captive kings side by side without ranking them; the release of the fettered kings is called grace (அருள்). The temple of the 'king of the white umbrella' may be Indra's or a royal shrine; the Tamil does not say.
event: Rites of every kind go on at once in Puhar's temples, and captive kings are released.
unit_note: Starts at line 169 with the temples (பிறவா யாக்கைப் பெரியோன் கோயிலும்) and ends at line 186, the last ஒருபால் clause; line 187 begins the sentence of the festival streets that leads to Kovalan, so it goes with the next unit. The core units broke at 173 and 187.

reading: In the festive streets where the drums never sleep, the southern breeze wanders with the bees and the young spring like Kovalan, who roams with Madhavi, garlanded in jasmine and lily, a woman never parted from her lover to become the talk of the town, delighting in love, bathing in groves, entering new flower gardens, with bards and town gallants; and the onlookers begin to wonder whether the moon itself, carrying a dark cloud and painting two dark carp with a kumizh flower between them, has come down to wander here for fear of the serpent in the sky.
nuance: Kovalan enters the chapter only inside a simile, as the measure of the spring wind's wandering (திரிதரு மரபின் கோவலன் போல), and Madhavi is praised as one who has never been parted from her beloved (காதல் கொழுநனைப் பிரிந்துஅலர் எய்தா), the word கொழுநன், a husband, given to the man who is Kannaki's. The question at lines 204-207 opens a run of wonderings closed by என at line 223; who wonders is not named, and whether the face like the moon is Madhavi's or any festival beauty's is not fixed.
event: Kovalan roams the festival streets and gardens with Madhavi.
unit_note: Starts at line 187 (முழவுக்கண் துயிலாது முடுக்கரும் வீதியும்), which with line 188 sets the scene for Kovalan's wandering, and ends at line 207, the first question closed by உண்டுகொல்; the core unit began at 188.

reading: The wondering goes on: does the heavenly creeper that Kama grew, nourished on the moon's nectar, come here too, and, as if Lakshmi had entered the city to show the king its wealth, does a false lotus wander here with ilavam, mullai, kuvalai and kumizh blooming on it, seeking a partner in its painted disguise?
nuance: Each question turns a woman's face into a thing out of place: a creeper from heaven, a lotus walking the streets, its flowers being lips, teeth, eyes and nose. The 'disguise' (உள்வரி கோலம்) suggests the festival's masked or costumed women; the speakers are still the unnamed onlookers.

reading: Or, they ask, has Death, which drinks many lives, afraid that the king's sceptre will forbid its work, changed its manly form but not its deadly task, and come wandering as a woman with a modest look, a smiling face and a voice like the lute; and against those it meets, Kama's great bodiless army fights, painting their bodies with love's lines, while the wives of Arundhati-like chastity, living with husbands who came home with guests, tremble helpless, wondering whether the earth holds any cure if the red-cornered glance of their eyes does not end with the guest.
nuance: The conceit makes the king's just rule the reason women are deadly: under the Chola's sceptre Death cannot kill openly, so it kills as a woman. The last lines (227-234) are hard: whose eye wounds whom, and whether the wives fear their husbands' new loves or suffer their own longing, is not clear from the Tamil.
unit_note: Split the core unit 218-240 at line 234, which ends the wondering and the wives' fear with the festival's midday (நல்வினை நடுநாள்); the omen of the two women's eyes begins on line 235.

reading: Like a red lily whose heart is so full of pollen that it trembles and spills its honey, Kannaki's dark eyes and Madhavi's red eyes, hiding what filled them within, shed tears, and throbbed, in that order, the left and the right, on the day of the festival of the king of the gods.
nuance: The eyes throb 'in the order counted' (எண்ணுமுறை), so the left goes with Kannaki, named first, and the right with Madhavi; read as omens for women, the wife's is the good sign of a husband's return and the courtesan's the bad sign of parting. The chapter's festival thus closes on the two women together, each weeping, at the moment of their fortunes' turn.
event: On the festival day Kannaki's left eye and Madhavi's right eye throb and both weep.
unit_note: Split the core unit 218-240: starts at line 235, a new sentence with its own simile (உள்அகம் நறுந்தாது), and ends at line 240, the chapter's close.

title: கடலாடு காதை
theme: The sea-bathing chapter: a vidyadhara and his beloved fly from the silver mountain to Puhar's Indra festival, where he explains its guardian bhuta and halls as Indra's gifts to a Chola, traces Madhavi's line to a celestial dancer cursed to earth and names the eleven dances of the gods she performs; after the festival Madhavi adorns herself, gives the sulking Kovalan union and sulk, and at the full moon they ride at dawn through Puhar's streets and lamp-lit market to the crowded shore, where she sits with him in a bower and takes up the lute.
source_issues: The kaathai header says the text has 178 lines but its printed last line number is 170; the akaval runs to line 174 here and the closing venba is 175-178, so the edition's own numbering and this count differ.
Lines 73 and 111 carry a repaired TSCII leftover (a ு plus a following letter read as ூ), flagged by show; the repaired lines read sensibly.
Lines 145-147 (இடிக்கலப்பு அன்ன ஈர்அயில் மருங்கில் கடிப்பகை காணும் காட்சியது ஆகிய) are obscure and their reading is uncertain.
Lines 20-24: the syntax leaves unclear whether the cursed மங்கை மாதவி is Urvasi or another celestial dancer.

cast.role: a vidyadhara (sky-dwelling being) of the silver mountain who visits Puhar's festival
the vidyadhara's beloved, to whom he speaks
the dancer of Puhar of the celestial dancer's line, Kovalan's lover
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, living with Madhavi
Madhavi's attendant
the auspicious women who scatter flowers, grass and paddy before the couple

reading: A vidyadhara warrior, holding a love-feast with his long-eyed beloved in a grove on the slopes of the silver mountain, tells her that this is the day a rich city in the south begins its festival for Indra, and proposes that they go to see the place where the great bhuta sits and eats offerings, the bhuta the king of the gods sent to the lance-bearing king who guarded the royal city against the asuras and turned back their deceit, and the order of the five assembly-halls that king won from the immortal for guarding Amaravati and set upon earth.
nuance: Puhar is not named: it enters the epic's second festival chapter as 'a rich city in the south' seen from a heavenly being's distance, and what he wants to see first are its sacred fixtures, which the unit explains as heaven's rewards to a Chola who once guarded Indra's own city. The festival is thus framed as a debt between the gods and the Chola line. The king is named only by epithets (தொடுகழல் மன்னன், திருந்துவேல் அண்ணல்).
event: A vidyadhara feasting with his beloved on the silver mountain proposes that they fly south to see the Indra festival of Puhar.

reading: He goes on: they will hear the song that knows the beauty of Narada's lute and the refrain sung by the leading singer, and see the dance of the snake-hipped girl born in the line of the maiden Madhavi, who, when Urvasi failed in her dance before the thousand-eyed Indra and the music lost its auspiciousness, was cursed to stay on earth with the lute; and he ends by hailing his coral-lipped, drum-waisted beloved.
nuance: The syntax of lines 20 to 24 is hard to fix: the one cursed is called மங்கை மாதவி, and whether that is Urvasi herself under another name or a second celestial dancer is not settled by the lines. What is clear is that the earthly Madhavi's art is presented as an inheritance from a heavenly dancer's fall: her dancing on earth is the continuation of a curse. Line 26 closes the vidyadhara's speech with a vocative.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the source unit 18-29 ran on into the next sentence; the vidyadhara's first speech closes at line 26 with the vocative துடிஇடை யோயே, and line 27 begins the narration of his journey, so the unit now ends at 26 and the next begins at 27.

reading: Saying they will worship the lord of the immortals, he shows his beloved the Himalaya, the Ganga, Ujjain, the Vindhya forest, the Venkatam hill and the Kaveri country, reaches Puhar, worships there in due order, sings the songs to Mayon, to the bhutas of the four varnas and to the moon, and then begins to point out the dances: the kodukotti that Siva, with Uma as one half of him, danced when the three cities burned at the gods' request and the fiery arrow obeyed, and the pandarangam he danced with the four-faced Brahma watching from before the chariot.
nuance: The flight runs north to south across the whole subcontinent and ends at the Kaveri, so Puhar's festival is set at the end of a sacred geography. The dances are told as myths of origin: each stage form is what a god once danced at a victory, and the Tripura burning is given as a literal event (the gods asked, the arrow obeyed). பாரதி ஆடிய பாரதி அரங்கத்து (line 39) names Siva and his stage by a title whose sense the lines do not fix.
event: The vidyadhara flies with his beloved over the northern mountains and rivers to Puhar, worships Indra, sings, and begins to name the dances.
unit_note: Boundary moved: begins at line 27 (formerly inside unit 18-29), where the narration of the journey starts after the speech that ends at line 26; it ends at 45 as before.

reading: The vidyadhara names the rest of the eleven dances, each a god's dance at a victory: Krishna's alliyam against Kamsa's deceit and his wrestling dance, Murugan's drum dance on the sea's wave-stage after overcoming Sur and his umbrella dance before the disarmed asuras, the pot dance of the one who measured the earth in Bana's city, Kama's dance in a woman's guise, Durga's stilt dance, Lakshmi's doll dance and Indrani's kadaiyam at the northern gate, and bids his beloved see them performed with each one's costume, stances and songs in strict rule.
nuance: Almost every dance is the celebration of a god overcoming an asura or a deceit (வஞ்சம்), and the gods are drawn from every cult (Siva, Krishna, Murugan, Kama, Durga, Lakshmi, Indrani) under one festival for Indra. Lines 66 and 67 repeat almost word for word the formula of Madhavi's training in the third kaathai (பதினோர் ஆடலும் ... விதிமாண் கொள்கையின் விளங்க), so the dances learned there are here performed.
event: The vidyadhara points out to his beloved the eleven dances of the gods as they are performed at the festival.

reading: Having told his beloved that this is Madhavi of the line of the Madhavi he spoke of in the grove, the vidyadhara rejoices; and when the festival that the sky-dwellers come to watch unseen, and its dances, costumes and ornaments have ended, Madhavi, to please the man who sat sulking, washes her fragrant hair in water steeped with ten astringents, five scents and thirty-two herbs, dries it in smoke, works musk paste into it, and colours her small feet with lac.
nuance: The unit turns from heaven to the bedroom in one sentence: the heavenly watcher's recognition (மாதவி மரபின் மாதவி இவள்) is the last of the celestial frame, and the next person seen is a man sulking after the festival. Why Kovalan sulks the text does not say; that it follows her public dancing is a reader's inference. The man in ஊடல் கோலம் is unnamed here and is Kovalan by line 109.
event: The vidyadhara identifies Madhavi to his beloved; after the festival Madhavi bathes and perfumes her hair and paints her feet to please the sulking Kovalan.

reading: Madhavi puts five kinds of anklet on her feet, a ring on her thigh, a girdle of thirty-two strands of pearl over fine cloth, armlets of pure gems, bangles of gold, conch and coral on her forearms, and rings shaped like a fish's mouth, of red gems and of diamond and emerald on her soft fingers.
nuance: The catalogue is the poem's own display of wealth worn on a body, moving from foot to finger; among its first items are anklets of five names (பரியகம் நூபுரம் பாடகம் சதங்கை அரியகம்), in a story whose turn will rest on one anklet.
event: Madhavi adorns her feet, thighs, waist, arms and fingers with anklets, girdle, armlets, bangles and rings.

reading: She puts fine chains and a necklace on her throat, a string of gems to hide the small of her back, ear-ornaments of sapphire and moonstone and the god's crest, the conch and other jewels on her dark hair; and she who had given Kovalan both union and sulking and sat on the couch fit for song, when the full moon came to the old city and crowds streamed toward the sea, longed to see the sea-play on the flowering shore and asked for it.
nuance: Line 109 makes union and sulking things Madhavi gives (அளித்து) to Kovalan: the woman dispenses both sides of love's play, and the one who sulked was he (line 75). The wish to see the sea-play is hers, so the outing that will part them starts from her desire.
event: Adorned, Madhavi, having given Kovalan union and sulking, asks to go to see the full-moon sea bathing on the shore.

reading: At dawn, when the birds of the lotus pond cry, the cock announces the watch and the morning star clears the dark, Kovalan of the rain-like giving hand mounts a mule and deer-eyed Madhavi a carriage, and they pass the street of piled wealth and the altar street where auspicious women carrying lamps scatter flowers, grass and paddy with jingling ornaments, go straight past the seat of the goddess of fortune and down the city's middle street, toward the quarter where foreign merchants raise flags on the sea sand.
nuance: Kovalan is named here by his liberality (வான வண்கையன், the man whose hand gives like the sky), and the couple's road runs through the heaped wealth and 'the seat of Tirumagal' (line 127); a reader who knows that his wealth will be gone by the ninth kaathai may hear the passage as a farewell to fortune, but that is interpretation, not the text's statement.
event: At dawn Kovalan rides a mule and Madhavi a carriage through Puhar's rich streets, greeted by auspicious women with lamps, flowers, grass and paddy.

reading: They reach the evening quarter by the market, where the lamps of every trade shine together beyond counting, those of sellers of colours, sandal, flowers, powders and goods, of skilled craftsmen, of sweet-makers and pancake-sellers, of women hawkers and fish-sellers, the lighthouse on the shore, the lamps of the net-fishers' boats, of foreign-tongued strangers and of the watchmen of cargo, and beside them the lotus waters and the bounds of the farmland appear.
nuance: The lamps are counted by trade, so the catalogue is a census of the port: each light belongs to a livelihood, from the hawker woman to the lighthouse and the foreigners whose speech is strange (பொழிபெயர் தேஎத்தர்). Lines 145 to 147 (the sand like pounded flour, கடிப்பகை காணும் காட்சியது) are obscure and the reading of them is a guess.
event: Kovalan and Madhavi pass through the market and shore of Puhar lit by the lamps of every trade.

reading: On the neythal shore hedged with thazhai, where ships unload the goods of hill and sea and princes, merchants' sons, dancing and singing women and many companies gather behind screens, with different costumes and noises, like the first day of Karikal Valavan's festival of the cool water, and the clamour of the four varnas fills the Kaveri's mouth, Madhavi of long flower-eyes sits with Kovalan on a canopied couch under a punnai inside a thazhai fence, taking the tuned lute from Vasanthamaalai.
nuance: The crowd is compared to Karikal Valavan's festival with the phrase தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் தலைநாள், the same words (தண்பதம் கொண்டு) that Akananuru 376 uses for Karikal's water festival at Kazhar: the epic recalls the Sangam king as a past glory, not as the ruling Chola. The unit closes with the lute passing into Madhavi's hand, the instrument of the songs in the next kaathai that will part the lovers.
event: On the crowded Puhar shore Madhavi sits with Kovalan in a screened bower under a punnai and takes the lute from Vasanthamaalai.

reading: A closing venba says that the jewel-like bee that slept at evening inside the white petal of the seaside thazhai went at morning to suck the pollen of the honeyed flower, and the beautiful bright sun's chariot appeared.
nuance: On its face a dawn scene; read against the story it may picture Kovalan, the bee who spent the night in one flower and leaves it at morning for another, which the next kaathai makes real. That second sense is an interpretation; நறவம் may be honey or the name of a flower.

title: கானல் வரி (1/3)
theme: On the shore after the sea festival, Madhavi tunes the yazh and hands it to Kovalan, who sings the Kaveri as the Chola's wife whose chastity is not to sulk at his other loves, then a run of neithal songs in the voices of the shore girls and of the smitten man, calling the fisher girl moon, goddess and Death in disguise; the songs, chosen by him for pleasure, carry the hint of another love that Madhavi will answer and that ends their union.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
the river Kaveri, addressed in the songs as the Chola's wife

reading: On the seashore Madhavi takes up the yazh, adorned like a bride and free of faults in body, neck, pegs and strings, worships it, runs through the eight ways of handling the strings and tests by ear the eight ways of fingering, then holds it out to Kovalan asking what song he commands, and he begins to play songs of the Kaveri and of the shore groves to delight her.
nuance: The unit is a catalogue of the lute-player's craft (two named lists of eight techniques, lines 5-8 and 12-15), and the instrument is dressed like a bride before the songs begin. The act that matters for the story is small: Madhavi hands the yazh to Kovalan (line 18), so the songs that follow are his choice, and the kaathai's close (line 289) will lay the parting on what the two sang over this yazh.
event: Madhavi tunes the yazh and hands it to Kovalan, who begins to play songs of the Kaveri and the seashore for her.

reading: Kovalan hails the Kaveri: though the Chola of the moon-white umbrella, wielding his just sceptre, unites with the Ganga, she does not sulk, and he says he knows that this not sulking, carp-eyed one, is the great chastity of a noble woman.
nuance: The river is the Chola's wife and the Ganga the other woman his northern conquest has taken; the praise of the king is turned into a picture of marriage in which the wife's virtue is to bear his other union without sulking. Sung by a married man to the courtesan he lives with, while his own wife waits at home, the stanza touches all three; the kaathai shows Madhavi reading a hidden meaning in these songs (lines 144-148).

reading: The second stanza repeats the praise with the Kanni, the southern maiden river, in place of the Ganga: though the Chola of the unbending sceptre unites with her, the Kaveri does not sulk, and that is a woman's lasting great chastity.
nuance: With the Ganga in the north and the Kanni in the south, the two stanzas give the king a rival bride at each end of the land, so the Kaveri's patience covers the whole reach of his conquest. வளையாச் செங்கோல் (line 30) makes the uniting with another a mark of his just rule, not a fault.

reading: The third stanza hears the Kaveri walking amid the shouts of ploughmen, the roar of sluices and breaking water and the cries of the festival crowds, and calls all that she has walked through, loud with the Mazhavar warriors, the very wealth of the Chola Valavan.
nuance: After two stanzas of the river as wife, this one makes her the source of the king's prosperity, so the couple of river and king is both a marriage and an economy. The sense of வாய்காவா (line 42), said of the Mazhavar, is not settled.

reading: In the voice of the shore girls, the singer asks the lover how they, simple as they are, could have known that the man who showed the sea god again and again before the dark-eyed girl and swore a hard oath would break it and prove without virtue, and names their town as Puhar, where the water lily opens its buds taking white conches and pearls for the moon and stars.
nuance: This is the akam friend's charge against a man who has broken his oath, sung as a set piece; the closing refrain (புகாரே எம்மூர்) turns each stanza into a boast of the city. The lily that mistakes conches and pearls for the moon and stars is the same mistake the girl made in trusting appearances.

reading: The girls ask how they could have known that the man who became their lover, following them in the backwater grove with gifts, would stand like a stranger while they plead, and name Puhar as their town, where the bee swings unable to tell women's eyes from the blue lilies that bloom paired with the moon's reflection in the water.
nuance: The lover's change is set as a turn from காதலர் to ஏதிலர் (lines 53, 55): the same man, first the one who followed with gifts, now the one they must beg. The bee that cannot choose between eye and flower mirrors the lover's wavering.

reading: The third stanza pictures a conch, battered by old waves, ploughing through and spoiling a girl's sand-play on the striped beach, and the girl, distressed, flinging her kuvalai garland at it with soft fingers so that the flowers seem to glance sidelong, and in this Puhar those who pass cannot leave.
nuance: Only here, of the three stanzas, there is no accusation; the girl's small anger is enough to hold the passers-by, and the garland's flowers, like eyes, do the looking. The spoiled sand-play is a stock neithal sign of the lover's first coming.

reading: The singer sets the scene of the shore grove, where the trace the conch ploughed in the sand is hidden under the fine pollen of punnai flowers, and wonders whether the incurable sickness that her moon-bright face and carp eyes have given will be cured only by her soft breasts with their golden spots.
nuance: The trace in the sand covered by falling pollen may stand for a union that leaves no sign, but the song does not say so. The syntax of தீர்க்கும் போலும் (line 75) leaves open whether the singer hopes or only supposes that the one who caused the sickness can cure it.

reading: In the man's voice, the singer says that he did not know that in the fragrant shore grove there dwelt a goddess who, with driving birds from drying fish as her pretext, walks holding fresh njaazhal flowers swarmed by bees, and that had he known he would not have come.
nuance: The refrain அறியேன் அறிவேனேல் அடையேன் (lines 81-82) makes first sight a danger the man would have avoided if warned; the girl's work, guarding the drying fish, is called a mere pretext for a goddess's presence.

reading: The second stanza says that in the fishers' quarter, where nets dry before the houses, another being, a cruel Death with long eyes like killing spears, has taken a form of its choosing and lives in the cool shore grove, holding flowers, on the pretext of drying fish for sale; he did not know, and had he known he would not have come.
nuance: வேண்டுஉருவம் கொண்டு (lines 85-86) makes the girl a disguise: Death has chosen to take a woman's shape, which is stronger than calling her eyes deadly.

reading: The singer bids his hearers look: the face on which carp, bow, cloud and Kama's work have been drawn is the moon, which, fearing the serpent in the beautiful sky, has come to live in the boatmen's little village.
nuance: The features are listed as things painted (எழுதி) on the face, eyes as carp, brows as bow, hair as cloud, and the moon is given a motive for coming down to earth: fear of the eclipse serpent.

reading: He bids them look again: the stained spear-like eyes that run to either side as her bangles ring are fierce Death, which in the sea-dwellers' little village has become a girl of soft and innocent grace.
nuance: The stanza joins the deadliest name to the gentlest: கடுங்கூற்றம் becomes மடம்கெழுமென் சாயல் மகள் (lines 96-97), so innocence is the form the killing takes.

reading: He bids them look a third time: the goddess who brings anguish to those who see her driving birds from the white drying fish has taken the form of a woman with five-braided hair in the cool shore grove where the adumbu creeper grows.
nuance: The three nilaivari stanzas name her moon, Death and goddess in turn, each come down to the fishing village in human form. The force of அலவநோய் (line 99) is not certain.

reading: The singer lists the grove's fragrant flowers, the fresh-scented sand, her flawless words, her young breasts, her moon-like face, her curved brows and her waist too fine to paint, and says these are what brought him distress.
nuance: Each line runs two vocatives, and the place and the woman are mixed in one list, so the grove itself is among the causes of the sickness.

reading: The second stanza lists the ford where waves spread, the broad sand, the fragrant flowers, the thick grove, her braided hair, her moon-like face and her paired carp eyes as what brought him distress.

The third stanza lists the ford where conches grow, the fragrant grove, the opening flowers, the place where she walks alone, her budding smile, her moon-like face and the young girl's breasts as what brought him distress.
nuance: தனிஅவள் திரிஇடமே (line 111) adds the one hint of a meeting: the place where she wanders alone.

reading: The singer tells the fisher girl that her elders live by going into the sea and taking lives, and she too lives by going into bodies and taking lives, and warns her that under the weight of breasts no strength can contain, her waist, sinking in distress, will be lost.
nuance: The fishers' trade of killing is taken as the plain fact of the coast and turned into a compliment: the daughter inherits the family work, killing lives, with her body as the net. The warning about the waist is the usual hyperbole of praise.

reading: The second stanza says her father kills lives with a crooked-meshed net and she kills lives with the net of her long eyes, and warns her that with breasts bearing strands of pearls her waist, swaying like lightning in rain, will snap.
nuance: The pun is in வலை: கொடுங்கண் வலை, the net of crooked mesh, against நெடுங்கண் வலை, the net of long eyes (lines 118-119).

title: கானல் வரி (2/3)
theme: Kovalan ends his songs of the fisher girl whose eyes and brows kill, and Madhavi, reading a hidden meaning in them, takes the yazh in a sulk and answers: she sings the Kaveri as a wife whose grace proves her husband's straight sceptre, mocks a lover who comes to the shore on a trader's pretext, and voices a deserted shore woman who will not forget the one who forgot her and whose last trace of him the tide erases.
source_issues: Lines 183 and 189 carry TSCII repairs (ு + ட read as ூ); 189's sense in any case turns on how புண்தோய்வேல் and பரதர் attach, so 186-189 is marked uncertain.
Lines 206 and 210 are the same line: the stanza at 206-209 and the one at 210-213 open alike and the song runs across the chapter boundary; this is the song form, not a doubled unit.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
the river Kaveri, addressed in the songs as the Chola's wife

reading: The third stanza tells the fisher girl that her brothers take lives with their running boats, and she takes lives with her bending brows, and warns her that, carrying her breasts with no thought for the pain she gives others or for her own state, her small soft waist will waste away and be lost.
nuance: The refrain of the three stanzas (114-125) moves the killing from the father's net and the brothers' boats to the girl's eyes and brows: the fisher family's trade in lives becomes her inheritance. கோடும் புருவத்து makes the brow's curve itself the weapon, where the earlier stanzas used the net and the eye.

reading: The singer says the girl who holds a coral pestle in her hand and pounds white pearls has red-lined eyes that are no blue lilies but cruel, cruel things.
nuance: Pounding pearls with a coral pestle is a fisher household's work made precious: the girl's ordinary labour is given in the shore's own riches. The line that names her eyes is sung twice, as the song form requires.

reading: The singer says the girl who walks as the swan walks on the flesh-smelling shore in the punnai shade has red eyes fierce to no purpose, and calls them Death, Death.
nuance: கொன்னே, 'to no end', makes the eyes' cruelty gratuitous: they kill without aiming at anyone, which is the singer's complaint.

reading: The singer says the girl who holds a honey-mouthed blue lily in her hand and drives the birds from the drying fish has red eyes that are not white spears and yet are fierce, fierce.
nuance: She carries a flower as the thing she scares birds with, and the singer denies her eyes are spears only to say they are worse: the stanza's work is the reversal of a gentle gesture into a weapon, as in 126-129.

reading: The singer tells the young swan not to follow the girl who wanders churning the wave-washed shore, since it cannot match her gait.
nuance: This is the last of Kovalan's songs before Madhavi takes the lute. The compliment that the swan is beaten by a woman's walk is one he once paid Kannaki in their bridal chamber; here it goes to an imagined fisher girl, sung before Madhavi.

reading: Having heard the kaanal vari, Madhavi decides that Kovalan's songs carry some hidden intent and that he has lost himself in another, and, seeming glad of their union but in a sulk, takes the yazh and, as if she too had a hidden meaning, begins to sing her own kaanal vari in a voice joined to the instrument, so that the land's deity marvels and the people rejoice.
