nuance: The whole break turns on குறிப்பு: she reads one into his songs (144) and sings as one who has her own (148). Neither intent is confirmed; the poet says only that she seemed (போல்) glad and seemed to have a meaning. The quarrel that ends the union at 286-300 begins here as two readings of songs, not as any act.
event: Madhavi, reading a hidden meaning into Kovalan's songs, takes the yazh in a sulk and begins to sing kaanal vari of her own.

reading: Madhavi hails the Kaveri, who walks with bees humming at her sides, wearing a garment of jewel flowers and opening her dark kayal eyes, and says she knows that all this graceful going comes from her husband's well-set sceptre not bending.
nuance: Madhavi keeps Kovalan's figure of the Kaveri as the Chola's wife but changes what the wife's grace proves: in his stanzas (21-36) it proved her patience with his other unions; in hers it proves his justice. The epic's later turn, Kannaki's case against a king whose sceptre did bend, makes this praise of the Chola sceptre a standard the Pandya will fail.

reading: Madhavi hails the Kaveri, who walks as the peacock dances in the flower groves, cuckoos sing and lovely garlands sway at her sides, and says she knows all this going from seeing the strength of her husband's dread spear.
nuance: Set beside 154-161, the second stanza grounds the same graceful flow in the king's spear rather than his sceptre: justice and force are given as two causes of one ease, stanza by stanza.

reading: Madhavi blesses the Chola's rich land and the Kaveri who, becoming a mother who rears it like a child, never stops her great help that carries the world through the ages, and says that this unceasing flow that sustains life is the grace of the day-bringer who rules the wheel.
nuance: ஆழி ஆள்வான் பகல்வெய்யோன் can be the sun, or the Chola as the sun who rules the wheel of command; the evening passage of kaathai 4 calls the sun the world's sole wheel-ruler, so the river's bounty is credited to a ruling power either way. ஊழி here is the age of the world, not fate.

tamil: தீங்கதிர் வாள்முகத்தாள் செவ்வாய் மணிமுறுவல் ஒவ்வா வேனும்
வாங்கும்நீர் முத்துஎன்று வைகலும் மால்மகன்போல் வருதிர் ஐய
வீங்குஓதம் தந்து விளங்குஒளிய வெண்முத்தம் விரைசூழ் கானல்
பூங்கோதை கொண்டு விலைஞர்போல் மீளும் புகாரே எம்மூர்.
reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi tells the man that, though the pearls cannot match the girl's smile, he comes every day like Kama's son saying he wants the pearls the waters bring, and names their town Puhar, where the swelling tide brings shining white pearls to the fragrant shore and goes back, like traders, carrying off flower garlands.
nuance: The man's excuse is a buyer's excuse, and the refrain makes the tide itself a merchant bartering pearls for garlands. Sung to Kovalan, a great merchant's son, the stanza mocks a lover who disguises desire as trade.

tamil: மறையின் மணந்தாரை வன்பரதர் பாக்கத்து மடவார் செங்கை
இறைவளைகள் தூற்றுவதை ஏழையம் எங்ஙனம்யாங்கு அறிகோம் ஐய
நிறைமதியும் மீனும் எனஅன்னம் நீள்புன்னை அரும்பிப் பூத்த
பொறைமலிபூங் கொம்புஏற வண்டுஆம்பல் ஊதும் புகாரே எம்மூர்.
reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi asks how simple folk like them could know that in the fishing hamlet the bangles slipping from girls' red hands proclaim those who married them in secret, and names Puhar, where swans climbing the budding punnai look like the full moon among stars and bees hum at the water lilies.
nuance: The secret is betrayed by the girl's own wasting body: the bangles loosening on a thinning arm do the gossiping (தூற்றுவதை), so the scandal is the man's doing but written on her.

tamil: உண்டாரை வெல்நறா ஊண்ஓழியாப் பாக்கத்துள் உறைஒன்று இன்றித்
தண்டாநோய் மாதர் தலைத்தருதி என்பதுயாங்கு அறிகோம் ஐய
வண்டல் திரைஅழிப்பக் கையால் மணல்முகந்து மதிமேல் நீண்ட
புண்தோய்வேல் நீர்மல்க பரதர் கடல்தூர்க்கும் புகாரே எம்மூர்.
reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi asks how they could know that in the hamlet where strong toddy and food never run out he would bring a girl an unending sickness without any cure, and names Puhar, where girls whose sand-houses the waves have wrecked scoop sand with their hands and, their long spear-like eyes brimming, try to fill up the sea.
nuance: The reading turns on உறை (a cure, or a single drop?) and on how புண்தோய்வேல் and பரதர் attach in 188-189; line 189 also carries a repaired character. The image of girls weeping as they try to fill the sea that wrecked their play-houses is clear and makes a child's futile revenge the picture of the girl's grievance.

reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells her friend of the curled five-plaited hair that the lord of the loud-waved shore, who looked at the spotted crab playing with its mate, at the flowering grove and at her, went away so that her senses left her, and she does not know his mind.
nuance: The crab with its mate is the scene of union he watched before leaving, so the stanza sets what he saw against what he did. வண்ணம் உணரேன் is ambiguous between not knowing his nature and not knowing her own state.

reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, asks whether he has left them, forgetting with his cool grace and his horse-drawn chariot, says let him go, and tells the soft-clustered adumbu creepers and the swans that she will not forget those who forgot her.
nuance: The stanza turns on the shift from 'they' to 'we': he forgot, we will not forget. Sung to Kovalan, the vow of remembering is at once a lament and a reproach, which is how Kovalan hears it in 286-300.

reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells the honey-mouthed neythal that, unlike her own eyes which weep in the sorrowful evening, it suffers no pain and gets to sleep, and asks whether in its dreams it sees the cruel man coming to the shore grove.
nuance: The neythal closes at dusk, so the flower is said to sleep; she cannot, and so she is shut out even from the dream in which she might see him, and must ask a flower for news of it.

reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells the clear tide that it has broken up every trace of the path where the wheel of his bird-swift horse-chariot went, and asks what she can do, since the tide, which stays with her and with those here, does not understand.
nuance: The wheel-track is the last thing left of him, and the tide erases it while staying beside her: the grievance is that the sea is near her and still unfeeling.

reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, asks the flower grove, the swans that play in pairs and the cool ford whether they will not tell the tide, which rolls in erasing the path of their pledged lover's tall strong chariot, that this is not right.
nuance: நேர்ந்த, 'who pledged', makes the lover one who gave his word; the stanza appeals to the shore's creatures as witnesses to a wrong done to that pledge. The same opening line begins the next stanza (210), which carries the song on.

title: கானல் வரி (3/3)
theme: Madhavi's answering shore songs end and the union breaks: she sings, in the voice of the akam heroine, of the tide that wiped out the lover's chariot tracks, the mother who may find out, three evenings asked whether they reach the absent man's land, a man who spoiled their sand-play, and, after changing mode, evening as killer and besieger, closing with a plea to the sea god to pardon a false oath; Kovalan hears the songs as her love for another, and the narrator, giving it to his ripening former deed, has him leave her on the shore.
source_issues: Line 284 reads பூக்கமழ் கனலில் (in the flower-fragrant fire); the setting and the song cycle suggest கானலில் (in the shore grove), and the line may be faulty.
Lines 262 and 263 are the same line; it is the refrain of the form, as show flags, not a doubling.

cast.role: the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived, who sings the second set of shore songs
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, who hears Madhavi's songs and leaves her
Kovalan's servants, who go with him from the shore
the god of the sea, addressed in the last song

reading: The third stanza of the song to the tide: the singer hails the sea tide that ran over and broke the track her lover's tall wheeled chariot made, and says that it seemed to have done with her but has not.
nuance: The three stanzas (202 to 213) turn on one image: the wheel ruts are the only trace the man left, and the tide that wipes them takes even that. The last line (எம்மொடு தீர்ந்தாய்போல் தீர்ந்திலையால்) can be read as the tide seeming to leave with him yet staying to torment her, or as its harm seeming finished and not being so; the unit does not fix which.

reading: In a stanza of mixed landscapes the singer hails the lord of the shore, where the waves, wearing pearls and coral, roam even the red-paddy fields, and asks what she will do if her mother sees the fresh wounds that the god of the fish banner shot into her in the punnai grove, wounds she hid by her own guile.
nuance: The sea decked in pearl and coral reaches into the paddy fields, which is why the rubric calls these stanzas மயங்கு திணை, mixed landscapes. The heroine fears not the wound but its discovery by the mother, the akam fear of secret love becoming known.

reading: The second stanza hails the shore where the sea smiles with pearls and opens coral lips before the fishers' net-yards, and asks what she will do if her mother, seeing the girl take the colour of the rain-season peerku flower, decides a god has done this cruelty.
nuance: The pallor likened to peerku blossom is the sign of love-sickness, and the feared misreading (கடவுள் வரைந்து, settling it on a god) is the akam mother's mistake that leads to the frenzy rite; the stanza names the mistake without the rite. The phrase is compressed, and its sense as 'the mother fixing on a god as cause' is a reading.

reading: The third stanza hails the shore whose waves, grieving at their own fish smell, enter the cool grove and come away fragrant with fallen flowers, and asks what she will do if her mother learns of the unknown sickness the girl suffers alone, a longing that no single cause makes firm.
nuance: The waves cure their own smell in the grove while the girl's sickness has no cure; பலஉற்று ஒருநோய் திணியாத suggests a sickness built of many pains that no one name fits, which is why the mother could not read it.

reading: The singer tells her companion, woman of loosened flower-hair, that young darkness has spread, the sun has hidden and her eyes pour unstoppable tears, and asks whether this bewildering evening, which came scattering fire and loosening her bangles, exists in the land of the man who left.
nuance: The question is barbed: if evening came to his land too, he would feel what she feels and come back. The song is sung to a lover who sits beside her, and the absent man is a persona, which is the ambiguity Kovalan will hear as a confession.

reading: The second stanza repeats the complaint, the sun gone and dark cloud spreading, the eyes like opposed flowers shedding tears of pain, and asks the moon-faced companion whether this evening, which spat out the moon and swallowed the sun, is found in the land of the one who went.

The third stanza adds that the birds' songs have stopped and the full moon sharpens her sickness, and asks whether this evening, which came like an enemy upon her life, exists in the land of the one who abandoned her.
nuance: The verb for the man hardens across the three stanzas, from தணந்தார் (who went apart) to போனார் (who went) to துறந்தார் (who abandoned).

reading: In the first stanza of the saayal vari the singer tells her companion that a man came by the backwater fenced with screw-pine, spoiled their sand-play and went, and that he will not leave their infatuated heart.
nuance: The repetition of the second line in the third is the form's refrain, and it turns the closing claim into a double meaning: he will not leave the heart, though he has left the place.

reading: The second stanza says that a man came by the backwater fenced with the shore grove and stood saying 'grant me grace', and that he will not forget their deer-like glance.
The third stanza says that a man stood yesterday gazing as a swan played with its mate, and that he will not leave the golden freckles on her breast.
nuance: The man who watched mated swans has learned the lesson of pairing, which is the stanza's hint that he will return.

reading: The singer bids the heron not to settle in their shore grove, repeating the bidding, because it did not tell the lord of the breaking waves the sickness she suffers.
nuance: The heron is refused for failing as a messenger; the doubled line 263 is the refrain of the form.

reading: The narrator says that the woman of fine jewels, having sung thus, then raised on the yazh, with her soft kaanthal-like fingers, the sweet sevvazhi palai set on kaikkilai and kural, and sang by its rules, changing to another mode.
nuance: The change of mode marks a change of mood: the songs that follow are evening laments in a mode of grief, and the narrator records it as a musician's choice before the reader learns what Kovalan makes of it.
event: Madhavi finishes the shore songs and shifts the yazh to another mode for the evening songs.

reading: The singer tells evening that it has struck the sweet palai the fisherfolk sing in vilari so that it settles in ili and kilai, and says that if it is so skilled in melody it may take her life.
nuance: Evening is addressed as a fellow musician, and the musical terms (விளரி, இளி, கிளை) describe how the shore's own songs sound at dusk; how exactly the modes are meant to change is beyond what the lines settle.

reading: The singer tells evening that it stands outside the lives of those who live pining in the shade of the great grace the departed lover tenderly promised, and asks what it will be, so placed, if not a king outside the fort against a king within who cannot hold out.
nuance: The image is a siege: the woman's life is a fort whose inner king, weakened, cannot resist the king camped outside its wall, and the promise of grace is her only shelter. The construction of the last line is compressed and the reading of it as a siege is offered as a reading.

reading: The singer says that as her grief grows and the sun goes down, bewildering evening comes and the world shuts its eyes, and that if this is what evening is and this is what the man who wed her is, the world itself has become poor.

The singer, in the last song, says that with these words of grief spoken without weighing them in this bewildering evening that came like fire, she bows at the flower feet of the god of the great sea and asks it to bear the false oath sworn in the fragrant grove.
nuance: The plea presumes that the sea god punishes a false oath sworn before it, and the heroine asks it to hold its hand: she shields the man who lied. Line 284 reads கனலில் (in the fire); the sense of the grove (கானல்) suits the song cycle, and the text may be faulty here. Whose false oath is meant is not said, which is the opening for Kovalan's reading of the song as Madhavi's own.

reading: The narrator says that Kovalan, hearing this, thought that while he had sung the shore songs she, her mind on another, had sung as a woman of lying tricks, and because his former deed had come in wrath through the yazh music he loosened his embrace and, saying the time had passed, left with his servants while she stayed seated, and Madhavi, her heart helpless, quieted her company in the flower grove and went home in her carriage without her lover, while the Chola's garlanded white umbrella shaded the earth.
nuance: Two causes are given in one sentence: Kovalan's own judgement of the song (lines 287 to 288, in his voice) and the narrator's ஊழ்வினை வந்து உருத்தது (line 289), the patikam's own phrase for karma. The narrator does not say Madhavi had another in mind; the hidden intent exists only in Kovalan's reading. The closing four lines, opened by ஆங்கு, end the kaathai with a blessing on the Chola king and are not part of the scene.
event: Kovalan, deciding Madhavi's songs betray love for another, leaves her on the shore, and she goes home alone.

title: வேனில் காதை
theme: The kaathai of spring: spring arrives over the Tamil land as the herald and army of Kama, Madhavi, left by the sulking Kovalan, plays the yaazh and writes him a letter on a flower leaf, and Kovalan refuses it, recalling every sign of her love as a dancing woman's role, so that the quarrel at the shore becomes the break that sends him back to Kannaki.
source_issues: The kaathai has 126 lines in the core text but the edition's printed numbering ends at 115, so line numbers here (the kaathai's own, 1-126 as `show` prints them) differ from the printed ones.
Line 9 (இளங்கால் தூதன் இசைத்தனன் ஆதலின்) carries a repaired encoding flag (a TSCII leftover read as ூ); the repaired reading makes sense and I marked it as written.
Lines 109 (ஆயிழை.) and 115 (மாண்இழை.) end in a full stop in mid-sentence; the sense runs on into the next line in both, so I read through the stops.
The closing unit 119-126 holds two separate venbas (119-122 and 123-126) in one core unit; I marked it as one unit because boundaries may not move inside the venba block.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, who has left Madhavi after the quarrel at the shore
the dancer of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived
Madhavi's companion, who carries her letters to Kovalan
Kama, the god of desire, here also மாரன் and உருஇலான், the formless one
the young southern breeze from Pothiyil, herald of spring
the cuckoo, a soldier of Kama's army who proclaims his command

reading: The young southern breeze, messenger born of the great sage of fertile Pothiyil, announces that sweet young spring, the delighting companion of king Maran, has come to the cool land whose Tamil bounds are cut by the hill of the tall god and the sea of the bangled goddess, where kings sit in Madurai, Uraiyur, Vanji and Puhar; and as if the army of the makara-bannered youth were putting on its flawless array, the cuckoo, a soldier in that army, calls the command through the crowded groves.
nuance: Spring arrives as a king's affair: a herald (தூதன்), an army (சேனை, படை), an order spoken by a soldier (பணிமொழி). The setting is the whole Tamil land, named by its two bounds and the capitals of all three crowns, not Puhar alone, so the season that will break Kovalan and Madhavi is announced as a law over every Tamil city. The breeze is 'born of the sage' of Pothiyil because the south wind blows from that hill.
event: The southern breeze announces the coming of spring and the cuckoo calls in the groves.

reading: Madhavi, whom Kovalan left without joining her after he sulked at the sea-sport on the flowering shore, goes in her longing up to the spring chamber on the high terrace, takes the court of saffron on her breasts, where the southern sea's pearls and the southern hill's sandal pay their dues, as her offering, takes up the yaazh of steady tradition and, lost in feeling, sings a sweet song.
nuance: Line 15 gives Kovalan's leaving at the end of the Kaanal Vari as a sulk (ஊட) that would not end in union (கூடாது), a lover's quarrel; the narrator there (7:289) gave it as Kovalan's ஊழ்வினை rising to bear fruit. The epic so names two causes for one departure, fate and pique, and neither cancels the other. The pearls and sandal paying tribute (கடன் இறுக்கும்) to her breasts carry on the opening unit's language of kings and dues.
event: Left by the sulking Kovalan, Madhavi climbs to her spring chamber and sings to the yaazh.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 29|30 to 24|25: line 24 (மதுர கீதம் பாடினள் மயங்கி) closes the account of her going up and singing, and lines 25 to 44 are one run describing how she sits, tunes and plays.

reading: Seated in the first of the nine postures, her right hand set to the yaazh's neck and four fingers of her left on the pegs, Madhavi, knowing the skill that removes the string faults named by the treatise, ties the fourteen strings from ulai to kaikkilai, tests the four relations of notes, listens to kural and ili, plays the scales of five and seven beginning and ending on ulai and on kural, the four kinds of marutham and the three movements, until in one outer measure the flowering creeper herself is lost in it.
nuance: The catalogue is a performer's checklist, the same craft the yaazh player of 3:70-94 is praised for, now done alone by Madhavi for no audience. The modes she plays are the marutham ones; marutham is in Tamil poetics the landscape of the lovers' quarrel, so the music fits her situation without the poem saying so. All this control ends in மயங்கி: mastery tips into self-loss. Many terms (இணை கிளை பகை நட்பு, மூவகை இயக்கம், புறத்துஒரு பாணி) are technical and I read them only in outline.
event: Madhavi tunes the yaazh, tests its notes and plays the marutham modes until she loses herself in the music.
unit_note: Start moved from 30 to 25 with the change at 24|25 (see silappathikaram:8:14-24); the end at 44 (பூங்கொடி மயங்கி) is unchanged.

reading: Bound up with champak, madhavi, tamaalam, karumugai, white jasmine with vetiver, red kazhuneer and kattigai flowers, Madhavi takes the curved white leaf of a ripe thaazhai, and, ready to send the royal letter that the whole world bows to by order of the one man whose single sceptre rules the earth with fragrant flower-arrows, she dips into the thick red lac and takes a pithigai bud as her stylus.
nuance: The letter is called திருமுகம், the word for a king's writ, and Madhavi writes it 'by the order' (ஆணையின்) of Kama's 'single sceptre' (ஒருதனிச் செங்கோல்). The figure is love as sovereign, not a claim about kingship; but the epic that will turn on a bent sceptre in Madurai here gives a sceptre to desire, whose order Kovalan is about to refuse. Her own name, மாதவி, stands in the flower list at line 45.
event: Madhavi takes a thaazhai leaf, red lac and a jasmine bud to write a letter to Kovalan.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 60|61 to 55|56: line 55 (ஆணி கைக்கொண்டு) ends the preparation, and line 56 begins the words of the letter, which run to line 63 (அறிந்தீ மின்என).

reading: Madhavi writes that young spring, the prince who joins every living being to its mate, and the moon born in the bud of evening are not kind: if joined lovers let time come between them, or parted lovers forget their partners, it is no wonder that love takes their lives with flower-arrows, so let them know it; she writes this with all sixty-four arts at her command yet in the unformed lisp of a lonely desire, then, pale with longing, calls Vasantamalai and bids her give Kovalan the flower garland with all its meaning and bring him back, and Vasantamalai gives it to him in the grain-market street.
nuance: The letter is a warning in the plural and impersonal, not a plea: it never names Kovalan or herself, and puts the blame for delay on the lovers who let time divide them. Line 68 plays three ways on மாலை: the evening of her pain, Vasanta-maalai her messenger, and the flower maalai that carries the writing. Kovalan is found not at home but in the grain-market street.
event: Madhavi writes her letter on the garland and sends Vasantamalai, who gives it to Kovalan in the grain-market street.
unit_note: Start moved from 61 to 56 (see silappathikaram:8:45-55); end moved from 77|78 to 73|74: line 73 (கோவலற்கு அளிப்ப) closes the delivery, and line 74 begins Kovalan's answer, the catalogue of Madhavi's love-plays.

reading: Kovalan answers by naming, one by one, the love-plays Madhavi has shown him: the glance of eyes meeting in love from a face like a sword; the play of coming when called and going when sent, showing her pearl smile; the inner play when, seeing his distress at evening, she hid her parrot speech, swan gait and peacock grace and came alone dressed as a serving maid; and the outer play when she danced outside with anklets wailing and girdle ringing, looking lovingly at his changed and wretched state.
nuance: Each memory is given a technical name ending in வரி (கண்கூடு வரி, காண்வரிக் கோலம், உள்வரி, புன்புற வரி), the names of acted love in the dance treatise. Kovalan is recalling real tenderness, her coming to him disguised as a maid when he was low, but by filing each act under a genre of performance he turns their life together into a repertoire.
event: Kovalan answers Vasantamalai by listing Madhavi's past shows of love as dance roles.
unit_note: Start moved from 78 to 74 (see silappathikaram:8:56-73); the end at 93 (புன்புற வரியும்) is unchanged.

reading: Kovalan goes on: the stirring play when, hearing her maids carry back his replies full of quarrel-making double meanings hidden within union, her grace drooped and her soft hair stirred; the play of careful telling when, parted from him, she told her own grief to his kin; the play of the dazed lover who told her state to whoever saw her; and the play of the lifted swoon when she fainted again and again before them and they raised her: since she is a dancing woman, he says, all of these were fitting achievements for her.
nuance: Lines 109 and 110 are the verdict, and the verdict is a refusal (the next unit calls it மறுத்தது): ஆடல் மகள் names her by her calling and makes the calling the proof that her grief was art. The narrator had blamed the first break on Kovalan's ஊழ்வினை (7:289); this second break is in Kovalan's own words and names no fate, so the story lays the choice on him too. The judgment is answered later by Kovalan himself, who reads her second letter and says she is without fault and the fault is his (13:93-95).
event: Kovalan refuses the letter, saying every sign of Madhavi's love was a role that suits a dancing woman.
unit_note: Unit 94-118 split at 110|111: line 110 (பாடுபெற் றனஅப் பைந்தொடி தனக்குஎன) closes Kovalan's speech, and line 111 turns to Vasantamalai's return.

reading: Grieving that the jewelled letter written on an ornamented leaf by the jewelled woman was refused, Vasantamalai, her heart wilted, hurries back and tells Madhavi, who says that though he will not come this evening they will see him in the morning, and lies on her flowered bed with a helpless heart, unable to rest.
nuance: Her last words set evening against morning (மாலை ... காலை), and the morning she waits for does not bring him: the next kaathai has Kovalan at Kannaki's door. The 'helpless heart' (கையறு நெஞ்சம்) is a phrase her second letter will ask him to take away.
event: Vasantamalai reports the refusal, and Madhavi lies sleepless, hoping to see Kovalan in the morning.
unit_note: New unit from the split of 94-118 at 110|111 (see silappathikaram:8:94-110); it ends at the kaathai's akaval close, line 118 (மாதவி தான்என்).

reading: Two closing venbas: the first says that with the red lotus opening, mango shoots trickling and the strong ashoka unfolding its buds, clustered young spring has come, and asks what will become today of the heart of the woman with spear-bright eyes; the second says that the cuckoo has proclaimed the formless one's command, 'all you who have sulked, unite', and bids the one who, troubled by the shore song, spurned the soft flower letter of her who joined in the long spring song, to see it.
nuance: The second venba sets two songs against each other: the கானல் பாணி, the shore songs of 7 that started the quarrel, and the வேனல் பாணி, the spring song in which Madhavi wrote. I read அலந்தாய் as addressed to Kovalan, who refused the letter, but the line is compressed and the addressee is not named.

title: கனாத்திறம் உரைத்த காதை
theme: The kaathai of the dream: as Puhar's women light the evening lamps, the poet tells how the god Pasanda Saathan once took a dead child from a desperate mother, gave her a child that was himself, grew up as a Brahmin youth, married Devanthi and left her for his temple; Devanthi, worshipping there, comes to bless Kannaki, hears her ominous dream of a great city, a false charge, a plea before the king and harm to the city, blames a vow broken in a former birth and urges bathing in the shore tanks, which Kannaki declines as unworthy; then Kovalan comes home ashamed of his lost wealth, takes her anklets as capital and leaves with her for Madurai before dawn, driven, the narrator says, by the deed at its term.
source_issues: The kaathai has 83 lines but the edition's printed last line number is 75 (`show`: 'printed last line 75'); line numbers here are `show`'s 1 to 83.
Line 28 carries a repaired encoding flag (TSCII leftover read as ூ in தூய); the repaired reading fits the sense.

Lines 82-83 of the closing venba repeat lines 78-79 word for word (வினைகடைக் கூட்ட வியம்கொண்டான் கங்குல் / கனைசுடர் கால்சீயா முன்); this looks like the venba's deliberate echo of the kaathai's last lines, not a doubling, but it is recorded.
Line 55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) and lines 51-54 (தீக்குற்றம் போலும் ... நகைஆகும்) are obscure in wording; the readings of those units are marked uncertain.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, alone in his house
Kannaki's husband, returning from Madhavi
the dancer Kovalan has left; named only in the closing venba
Kannaki's friend, a Brahmin woman whose husband was the god Saathan
a Brahmin's wife whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it
the god Saathan of the sects, who takes the form of a young woman, then of the dead child, and becomes Devanthi's husband
the corpse-eating demoness of the burning-ground shrine
a young serving woman of Kannaki's house

reading: While the women of the inner city scatter jasmine buds and paddy and show the lamps at dusk, the poet goes back to an earlier day: Maalathi, whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it, fearing that the Brahmin and his wife would blame her unjustly, carried the child round every shrine of the city begging the gods to cure her grief and lay prostrate before Pasanda Saathan, who came as a young woman, told her that gods grant no boon to those without tapas, took the body to the burning-ground shrine where the corpse-eating demoness swallowed it, then, as she wept, bade her see her child alive and, becoming that child in a koel-haunted grove, put the magic child in its mother's hands.
nuance: The catalogue of lines 9 to 13 takes Maalathi through the shrines of Indra's tree, the white elephant, the white Naga, the sun, the city, Vel, the thunderbolt, the god outside the town, the Nigantha (Jain) shrine and the moon: the city's gods stand side by side with no school set above another, and the one who answers is the god of the sects (பாசண்டம்). Saathan's rule (line 17) is stated and then exceeded by his own act: Maalathi has no tapas, he says, yet he gives her back a child, by becoming it. Her fear is of a false charge (படாதன, line 7), the same shape as the false word in Kannaki's dream later in this kaathai. Lines 1 to 4 belong to the frame of the whole kaathai: the tale of Saathan is told as a digression hung on மேல்ஓர்நாள்.
event: Maalathi carries her co-wife's dead baby to every shrine; Saathan, as a young woman, gives the body to the burning-ground demoness and then returns to her as the child himself.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 15|16 to 28|29, merging the old units 1-15 and 16-31's first part: line 15 (பாடு கிடந்தாளுக்கு,) is a dative that needs the speech of lines 16 to 19, and the miracle sentence closes in line 28 (தாய்கைக் கொடுத்தாள் அத் தையலாள்); line 29 (தூய மறையோன்பின் மாணியாய்) begins the child's life as a Brahmin youth.

reading: The child grew up a Brahmin student, mastered the learning of the scriptures, and after the death of his foster-parents settled the inheritance with the kin and paid the rites owed to father and mothers; he married Devanthi, showed her his own ageless youth, told her to come to his shrine, and left; Devanthi, telling people her husband had gone to bathe at every holy ford and making that her pretext, keeps worship at the shrine to win him back, and now, sensing that Kannaki has a lack, comes scattering arugu, poolai flowers and paddy and blesses her to have her husband.
nuance: Devanthi is a wife whose husband is a god, and she worships that god to have the husband back: the rival of Kannaki's way, where the husband is the only god (see the link to Kural 55). Her public story, that he has gone on pilgrimage to the fords (line 38), is a cover she lays on something (ஒன்றன் மேல் இட்டு, line 39), and the blessing she brings is the household rite of arugu and paddy, which Kannaki answers with a dream rather than thanks. That the god does the funeral and inheritance duties of a son (lines 30 to 32) makes his human life complete before he leaves it.
event: Saathan, grown as a Brahmin, marries Devanthi, reveals himself and leaves; Devanthi worships at his shrine and comes to bless Kannaki.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 31|32 and 47|48 to 28|29 and 44|45: line 29 begins the child's grown life, and line 44 closes Devanthi's blessing (பெறுக கணவனோடு என்றாள்) before Kannaki's reply begins; the one word பெறுகேன் at the end of line 44 opens her answer and is read with the next unit.

reading: Kannaki answers that she will have him, but that her heart is shaking from a dream: he took her hand, they went into a great city, the people there laid on him a word that did not belong to him, as one drops a scorpion, a harm befell Kovalan, she made a plea before the king, and with the king there was a harm to the city too, of which she will not speak; it is like an evil omen, she says, and if her friend heard the good that came to her with the one she had joined, she would laugh.
nuance: The dream is the poem's plot in small, told before the journey begins: city, false charge, harm to Kovalan, her plea before the king, the city's harm, and a last good that sounds absurd. She refuses to tell the city's harm (உரையாடேன், line 51), and the final good is told only as something that would be laughed at; the poem's later units show both. The scorpion image (இடுதேள், line 48) makes the charge something thrown on, not earned. Lines 51 to 54 are dense, and which of the repeated உற்ற forms refers to Kovalan and which to the 'harm' is not certain.
event: Kannaki tells Devanthi a dream of a false charge on Kovalan in a great city, her plea before the king and harm to the city.
unit_note: Unit runs 45-54, from the start of Kannaki's dream (கடுக்கும்என் நெஞ்சம் கனவினால்) to the end of her speech in line 54 (நகைஆகும்); the old boundary 47|48 split the dream mid-sentence.

reading: Devanthi answers that Kannaki is not one who has failed her husband in this life, but in a former birth she broke a vow to him, and bids that fault be gone; on the shore grove where the sea and the Kaveri meet there are two tanks, the Moon's and the Sun's, and women who bathe there and worship at the shrine of Kama enjoy their husbands in this world and are born again in the land of enjoyment, so let them bathe one day; Kannaki says it is not worthy and sits on, and then a young serving woman announces that Kovalan has come to the gate.
nuance: Devanthi gives a cause for Kannaki's lack, a vow broken in a former birth, and the remedy of a rite; the poem later gives another cause, a curse on Kovalan's own former birth told by the goddess of Madurai (Silappathikaram 23), and does not take up Devanthi's. Kannaki's பீடு அன்று (line 64) refuses the rite for herself without disputing its power: she does not say the tanks fail, only that seeking a husband through Kama's shrine is beneath her, which the poem's later venba turns into a wife whom the gods worship. போகம்செய் பூமி is a land of enjoyment where the next birth is spent; the term is at home in Jain cosmology, but the unit does not tie it to a school. Line 55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) is obscure; I read it as 'you have not wronged him (in this life)', and other readings are possible.
event: Devanthi urges Kannaki to bathe in the shore tanks and worship at Kama's shrine; Kannaki refuses, and a maid announces Kovalan's return.
unit_note: Unit runs 55-66 (the old unit 48-66 less its first seven lines, which go with Kannaki's dream): it opens with Devanthi's reply (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) and ends, as before, with the maid's announcement in line 66.

reading: Kovalan enters the bedchamber, sees her wasted body and her pain, and says that having sported with a deceiver of deceitful ways, the poverty of losing the mountain of wealth his family gave him shames him; with a bright smile she offers the anklets, and he answers that with the anklets as his beginning he will earn back the wealth that is gone, and bids her rise and go with him to Madurai; driven by the deed at its term, he sets out before the night's dark is cleared.
nuance: Kovalan blames Madhavi (சலதி, line 69) and names his own feeling as shame at poverty, not remorse toward Kannaki; she answers with no word of reproach, only the anklets. His plan is an ordinary remedy, to trade and recover; the narrator's last line gives the plan another author, the deed that drives him to its term (வினைகடைக் கூட்ட, line 78). The anklet enters the story here as capital (சிலம்பு முதலாக, line 74), the thing that will become the charge in the dream.
event: Kovalan returns ashamed of his lost wealth, takes Kannaki's offered anklets as capital and leaves with her for Madurai before dawn.

reading: The closing venba says that, as the dream his beloved saw and Madhavi's word came to nothing, the deed of old driving him to its end, he set out before the night's dark was cleared.
nuance: The venba puts the old deed (மூதை வினை) where the kaathai's last line had only வினை. What 'made Madhavi's word empty' means is not certain: it may be Madhavi's word sent to Kovalan in the preceding kaathai, now come to nothing because he has left with Kannaki; the syntax of காதலி கண்ட கனவு beside it is also open.
event: Kovalan sets out from Puhar before dawn.

title: நாடுகாண் காதை
theme: The kaathai of seeing the country: driven by their past deed, Kovalan and Kannaki slip out of Puhar before dawn past its temples and viharas, take the Jain nun Kavunthi as guide, and walk slowly through the Chola country of the Kaveri; a Charana tells Kavunthi that a strong deed returns like a sown seed and cannot be put off, she vows every sense to the Arhat, and at Uraiyur's edge she curses two mockers into jackals and, at the wronged couple's plea, sets them a term of release.
source_issues: The edition prints 245 as the last line number, but the kaathai has 248 lines as cut; line numbers here are the core file's.
Lines 41, 51, 200 and 224 carry repaired encoding (a TSCII leftover and stray spaces), flagged by show; the repaired readings are used.

cast.role: Kannaki's husband, a merchant's son of Puhar, setting out for Madurai to recover his wealth
Kovalan's wife
a Jain nun living by the Kaveri outside Puhar, who goes with the couple to Madurai
a Jain Charana, a sky-walking sage, who appears on the stone seat and preaches (named in the honorific plural)
a wanton courtesan who mocks the travellers and is cursed into a jackal
the idle-tongued man with the courtesan, cursed into a jackal with her

reading: Before dawn on the last dark night of the month, with the deed of the past driving them and their own minds pressing, the couple leave by the long gate of their mansion, pass the temple of the sapphire-hued god asleep on the serpent, and go past the seven Indra viharas where sky-walkers proclaim the word of the dharma-teacher under the five-branched bodhi.
nuance: Line 4 gives two drivers side by side: ஊழ்வினை pushes and the heart urges (உள்ளம் துரப்ப), so the narrator names the past deed as cause at the very moment the couple act of their own will; Kovalan's own spoken reason, the wish for wealth in Madurai, comes at line 51. The road out of Puhar is a tour of the city's faiths, a Vishnu temple and Buddhist viharas, before the Jain shrine of the next lines. Whether வலம்செயா (line 10) means they circled the temple or passed it without circling turns on the form; I read it as the poetic absolutive, having circled.
event: Kovalan and Kannaki leave their Puhar mansion secretly before dawn and pass the Vishnu temple and the Buddhist viharas.

reading: They come to the Arhat shrine of those who gave up flesh and keep an unfailing vow, where lay votaries have set a shining stone seat for the Charanas who come at the festivals, worship it and circle it, and then flow out of the city's passages like a great river leaving the hills, past the outer wall of the king's pleasure garden where the southern breeze pays its tribute with spring.
nuance: The seat is worshipped empty: it is set up against the chance (தகுதி) that the sky-walking Charanas will come, which prepares the Charana who appears on such a seat at line 161. உலக நோன்பிகள் are those who keep the vow while living in the world, the lay counterpart of the ascetics described in lines 15 to 17.
event: The couple worship and circle the Charanas' stone seat at the Jain shrine and leave the city by the garden wall.
unit_note: The boundary between the original units 15-29 and 30-51 is moved from after line 29 to after line 31: lines 28-31 are one clause ending at போகி (line 31), the departure past the garden wall.

reading: Going west along the Kaveri's north bank they reach after one kaatham the flower grove of the Jain nun Kavunthi's retreat; Kannaki, aching in feet and waist, asks in her child's speech which of these is Madurai, and Kovalan laughs that it is thirty kaathams beyond their land; they worship the nun, who asks why people of their form, family, conduct and vow have left home like the afflicted, and Kovalan answers that he seeks wealth in old Madurai.
nuance: Kannaki's question after one kaatham, and Kovalan's laughing answer that thirty is near, measure the distance between her sheltered life and the journey. Kavunthi credits the couple with a vow that never strays from the Great One's word (line 47), which counts them among the lay faithful. Kovalan's stated motive, wealth (வரைபொருள் வேட்கை), stands against the narrator's ஊழ்வினை at line 4.
event: Kannaki asks how far Madurai is, the couple meet the Jain nun Kavunthi at her retreat, and Kovalan tells her he goes to Madurai for wealth.
unit_note: Starts at line 32 because lines 30-31 were moved to the preceding unit; the unit still ends at line 51, where Kovalan's answer closes the exchange.

reading: Kavunthi says the forest-broken country is hard going for the girl's small anklet feet and that they will not turn back though told to, so she too, wishing to hear dharma from the learned and praise the Knower, will go to Madurai with them; Kovalan worships her and says her grace would end his wife's distress, and she begins to list the dangers of the road if they take the delicate girl into the shady groves.
nuance: The nun's motive for the journey is her own: to hear the teaching at Madurai (lines 56-59). Her joining makes her the couple's guardian on the road, the role she hands on in Madurai.
event: Kavunthi decides to go with the couple to Madurai, and Kovalan accepts her as their guide.

reading: Kavunthi warns that in the groves a pit dug for tubers and hidden under fallen champak pollen can trap the unwary, ripe jackfruit and thorny jack-seeds in the turmeric and ginger thickets can hurt, and if they take the fields instead a vaalai fish leaping from an otter's jaws may frighten the girl, and honey dripping from the cane may cloud the pond.

She goes on: the girl, thirsty past bearing, might scoop that honeyed water in her palm or step unknowing on lilies thick with bees, and on the shore a careless step may harm the crab and the snail, a grief that cannot be borne; since there is no path but fields and groves, Kovalan must read the signs with his beloved and avoid each one.
nuance: The danger in lines 90-93 runs both ways: the step may hurt the girl and it may hurt the crab and the snail she does not see, and the nun counts the second as a sorrow beyond bearing. ஊழ் here (line 92) is the order of the steps, not fate. The warning against drinking honeyed water may reflect a Jain avoidance of honey, but the lines give thirst and confusion of mind (அறிவு அஞர்) as the danger, not a rule.
unit_note: The original unit 84-98 ends one line early, at line 97 (குறுகாது ஓம்புஎன), where Kavunthi's warning ends; line 98 begins the list of what she takes up for the road.

reading: Kavunthi takes up her flawless begging bowl, the cloth for her shoulder and the peacock-feather brush, and praying that the god who is the meaning of the word be their companion they set out into the Chola country, where even when Saturn smokes, a comet shows and Venus moves south, the new flood of the Kaveri comes down with the hills' goods to meet the sea's wealth, so that only its roar is heard at the sluices and no water-lift creaks, among paddy, cane, lotus pools and waterbirds.
nuance: The omens of lines 102-103 are the Sangam formula for drought, kept here to praise the Kaveri, which fails no one when the sky fails. மொழிப்பொருள் தெய்வம் (line 100) I take as the god whose word is the truth, but the phrase is compressed.
event: Kavunthi takes her bowl, cloth and peacock-feather brush, and the three set out through the Kaveri's fields.
unit_note: Starts at line 98 instead of 99: line 98 (தோம்அறு கடிஞையும் சுவல்மேல் அறுவையும்) is the first of the things Kavunthi takes up at line 99, so it is moved out of the preceding unit.

reading: The fields ring with the many cries of geese, herons, waterhens and crows like the camp of a victorious king, with the shouting of the dark-handed labourers when a mud-caked buffalo rubbing against the granary spills its paddy, and with the new song of the field-women who, having drunk hot toddy, transplant seedlings with mud on their bangled arms.

With the plough festival of the ploughmen who wear arugu and lily, the reaping songs at the threshing floors and the drums of the kinai bards in their ears, the travellers go on without grief past the Brahmins' auspicious settlements, whose sacrificial smoke wraps the mansions like mist on hills under the tiger-flag king's might, and past the old towns of the Kaveri's sons, moving only a kaatham a day and halting many days.
nuance: The Vedic sacrifice is praised as part of the land's good order (மங்கல மறையோர் இருக்கை) in the same journey that the Jain nun leads; the text sets the faiths side by side and does not weigh them here.
event: The three travel slowly through the Chola country, a kaatham a day, halting many days.

reading: One day, at a grove on a river island near a place where the gods dwell, a Charana appears on the stone seat set by the great ascetics, proclaiming the true dharma of the Great One's wonder; the travellers fall at his feet with Kavunthi praying that their old deed may perish, and though he knows by the lamp of his mind why they have come, he does not grieve, being a hero who has put away desire and hatred.
nuance: The Charana foresees what is coming to the couple and says nothing of it; the narrator explains his silence by his freedom from desire and hatred (ஆர்வமும் செற்றமும்), not by indifference. Their prayer, பண்டைத் தொல்வினை பாறுக, asks for the very thing his sermon will say cannot be had.
event: A Jain Charana appears on the stone seat, and the travellers and Kavunthi fall at his feet praying that their old deeds perish.
unit_note: The original unit 156-170 ends one line early, at line 169 (விழுமம் கொள்ளான்): line 170 opens the Charana's speech to Kavunthi and is moved to the next unit.

reading: The Charana tells Kavunthi that the strong deed, which will not go when bidden, comes back like a sown seed to face its doer and cannot be put off once it clings, that lives do not stay long in bodies, like a lamp set in a windy open place, and that, unless the light of the Veda spoken by the Lord reaches them, souls will not open the bundle of births; he names that Lord by a long run of titles, Knower, Jina, Siddha, Arhat, the one of eight qualities, Sankara, Isa, the self-born and four-faced.
nuance: The verb ஊட்டும் is the patikam's (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும், line 57 of the patikam), so the epic's third moral is here given to a Jain sage as doctrine, with one addition the patikam lacks: a way out of birth through the Jina's word. The titles take names other schools use for their own gods (சங்கரன், ஈசன், சதுமுகன், வேத முதல்வன்) and claim them for the Arhat. The syntax of lines 174-175 is compressed; I read the lamp in the wind as the image of life in the body.
unit_note: Runs from line 170 (moved from the preceding unit) to line 191, where the Charana's speech ends (பொதிஅறை யோர்என); lines 192-195 were moved to the next unit because they begin Kavunthi's reply.

reading: Hearing the Charana, Kavunthi lays her hands on her head and vows that her ears open only to the word of the one who quenched the three, her tongue speaks only the thousand and eight names of the conqueror of desire, her eyes see only the feet of the conqueror of the five, her body touches earth only before his holy form, her hands join only for the Arhat, her head bears only his flower feet and her mind moves only for his word; the sage rises a cubit from the ground, blesses her that the bond which brings birth may perish, and goes through the sky, and the travellers worship and go on.
nuance: The vow goes organ by organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head, mind, and each line has the same 'only for him' (அல்லது) shape, so devotion is described as the closing of every sense to all else. The Charana's blessing names பாசம் and பவம்: the bond is what brings birth.
event: Kavunthi vows every sense to the Arhat, and the Charana blesses her and departs through the sky.
unit_note: Starts at line 192 (சாரணர் வாய்மொழி கேட்டு), where Kavunthi's reply begins after the Charana's speech closes at line 191; ends as before at line 213.

reading: Crossing the Kaveri by a ghat to its south bank, the three rest in a grove, where a wanton courtesan and an idle-tongued man come up, ask the fasting nun who these two, like Kama and his consort, are; when she answers that they are her children, human beings, and bids them stand off from the weary pair, the two jeer whether people born of one womb live together as man and wife, and call her learned.
nuance: Kavunthi's 'my children' is the nun's shield for a married couple, and the mockers turn it into an insinuation of incest. நோற்றுஉணல் யாக்கை (line 223), the body that eats only after fasting, is how they address her, and her austerity is what gives force to what follows.
event: A courtesan and a loose-tongued man mock Kavunthi and the couple, insinuating that the pair are siblings living as lovers.

reading: Kannaki stops her ears and trembles before her husband; Kavunthi, calling the two scorners of her flower-garlanded girl, curses them to become old jackals of the thorn forest, and the curse that her penance gives takes hold; when the couple, trembling at the jackals' howls, plead that the improper words of those who have left the path are ignorance and ask her to name a time of release, she rules that, having fallen into low birth by ignorance, they shall suffer twelve months by the Uraiyur hedge and then regain their former form, and the three enter Uraiyur.
nuance: Lines 233-234 use the same formula as the patikam's curse of the former birth (இட்ட சாபம் கட்டியது ஆகலின், patikam line 49), but this curse is given a term and a return to former form, at the plea of the very couple who were wronged. The pardon comes from the victims: it is Kovalan and Kannaki who name the insult ignorance, and Kavunthi takes their word (அறியாமையின், line 241) into her release.
event: Kavunthi curses the two mockers into jackals and, at the couple's plea, sets a twelve-month term of release, and the three enter Uraiyur.

title: புகார்க் காண்டம் கட்டுரை
theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Puhar book: a single long sentence lists what the first ten kaathais set out about the Chola line and its land (righteousness, valour, the old city, its festivals, the divine Kaveri, the unfailing sky) and about its arts of stage, dance, vari songs and the lute, all seen as one; a venba then wishes Puhar, built by fame for the sea-moated earth, to live like the morning sun and the evening moon.
source_issues: Line 4 was repaired from a TSCII leftover (ு + ட read as ூ), as show flags.
The chapter header counts 24 lines but the edition's last printed number is 20: the closing venba is numbered 21 to 24 by the tool, not by the edition.

Line 19 (ஒரு பரிசா நோக்கிக் கிடந்த) has no named king with ஓடு before it, unlike the Madurai summary (பாண்டியன் நெடுஞ்செழியனோடு) and the Vanchi summary (செங்குட்டுவனோடு) built on the same frame; the text does not show whether the Puhar summary names no king by design or a line is lost.
Line 20 (புகார்க் காண்டம் முற்றிற்று) is a colophon that also completes the sentence of lines 1 to 19 (கிடந்த governs காண்டம்), so it is marked as part of the unit.

reading: The narrator sums up the Puhar book as one that keeps in single view the righteousness, valour and strength of those born in the Chola line among the three crowned kings, the excellence of their ancient city, its festivals and the visits of the gods, the people and abundant food of their land, the evil-removing divine Kaveri, the unfailing sky pouring new floods, and the arts of stage, dance, rhythm, vari songs, the lute and its modes, and declares the book complete.
nuance: The same formula, nearly word for word, closes the Madurai and Vanchi books with the Pandya and Chera lines put in place of the Chola, so the praise of aram, maram and an unfailing sky belongs to the frame given every crowned line, not to a judgment on this one. What differs is the close: the Madurai summary looks at its book as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan who died on his throne with his queen, the Vanchi summary with Senguttuvan, while this one names no king and gives most of its lines to music and dance (lines 10 to 16, the arts of Madhavi's kaathais). The music terms of lines 13 to 16 (சகோடம், இடநிலைப் பாலை, தாரத்து ஆக்கம், ஊரகத் தேர்) are technical and are left unglossed here; the reading does not turn on them.

reading: A closing venba wishes that Puhar, which fame has made for the earth whose moat is the sea, may live on like the sun that buds and blooms in the morning and the moon of the evening.
nuance: The wish for the city's lasting life is a blessing, not a claim that it will last; the poem calls the sea the earth's moat (வேலை அகழால் அமைந்த அவனி), the sea that the Manimekalai later makes the city's end. The kandam opened (silappathikaram:1:1-12) by praising the moon and the sun for being like the Chola; here they are the measure for the city, and no king is named.

title: காடுகாண் காதை
theme: On the road from Uraiyur to Madurai the travellers meet a Vaishnava brahmin who praises the Pandya line and maps three roads, with a cave of wish-granting pools on one; the Jain ascetic Kavunthi answers that truth and care for life reach the same ends, and in the forest a goddess in the form of Madhavi's maid tries to delude Kovalan until a mantra unmasks her, before the three reach the hunters' shrine of Aiyai.
source_issues: The kaathai has 216 lines in the core text but the edition's printed last line is 215, so line numbers here (the kaathai's own, as `show` prints them) differ by one from the printed ones somewhere in the kaathai.
Lines 102 to 103 repeat இட்ட சித்தி (இட்ட சித்தி எய்துவி ராயின் / இட்ட சித்தி எய்துவிர் நீரே); this looks like the text's own wordplay rather than a doubled line, and I marked it as written.

cast.role: the merchant's son of Puhar, travelling to Madurai
Kovalan's wife
the Jain ascetic woman who guides them to Madurai (named here காவுந்தி ஐயை, கவுந்தி அடிகள், மாதவத்தாட்டி)
the Jain Charanas, wandering sages, who speak at the shrine grove
the old Vaishnava brahmin of Maankadu in the western hills who tells the roads to Madurai
the forest goddess who takes Vasantamalai's form to delude Kovalan
the courtesan dancer, Kovalan's former companion (only reported here)

reading: After worshipping the Arhat seated under the triple umbrella beneath the flowering pindi tree, and after the Charanas and then the great ascetic woman had spoken their good words at the shrine grove, the three stay the night at their lodging and, eager to go south, set off at the last watch before dawn and enter a grove of young trees beside watered fields and ponds.
nuance: The chapter opens in an explicitly Jain setting (the triple umbrella, the pindi or asoka tree, the Charanas, அறிவன் for the omniscient one), so the Vaishnava pilgrim who appears next is met by travellers who have just come from another shrine.
event: Kovalan, Kannaki and Kavunthi worship at a Jain shrine, rest the night, and set out south at dawn into a grove.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 1-16 to 1-14: line 14 (இளமரக் கானத் திருக்கை புக்குழி) ends the journey clause, and line 15 begins the brahmin's blessing of the Pandya (வாழ்க எங்கோ).

reading: A voice in the grove hails the Pandya: may he guard the world age after age, he whose lance the sea would not bear and who, when the sea took the Pahruli river and the Kumari peak with its hills, took the Ganga and the Himalaya in the north and ruled the south; he of the lunar line who wears Indra's necklace on his chest, who broke a crown, and who, when the thundering clouds withheld their rain, bound them and made the harvest unfailing.
nuance: Lines 17 to 22 tie the loss of southern land to the sea to a king's quarrel with it and set a northern conquest against it; the epic gives this as praise, not as history. Line 26 (முடிவளை உடைத்தோன்) is compressed and whose crown was broken is not stated. The praise of a faultless line (தீதுதீர் சிறப்பின் தென்னனை, line 30) is spoken on the road to the city where the reigning Pandya will condemn himself.
event: An old brahmin sitting in the grove sings a blessing on the Pandya kings.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 17-32 to 15-30: line 30 (தீதுதீர் சிறப்பின் தென்னனை வாழ்த்தி) closes the blessing, and line 31 turns to the brahmin and Kovalan's question.

reading: Kovalan asks the old brahmin where he comes from and why he is here, and the brahmin of Maankadu in the western hills answers that his heart pressed him to see with his own eyes the form in which Vishnu lies on the thousand-hooded serpent at the river island of the Kaveri and the form in which he stands, conch and discus in hand like a dark cloud girt with lightning, on the peak of Venkatam between sun and moon, and that having seen the Pandya land's excellence he stayed to praise it.
nuance: The pilgrim's wish is to see (என்கண் காட்டு, line 52): his devotion is to the god's visible postures, reclining and standing, which the chapter will set beside the Jain nun's inward discipline.
event: Kovalan questions the brahmin, who says he is on pilgrimage to see Vishnu at Srirangam and Venkatam and stopped to praise the Pandya land.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 33-47 (with 31-32 from 17-32 and 48-56 from 48-61) to 31-56: line 31 opens the exchange with the brahmin and line 56 (இதுவென் வரவென) ends his answer; the core cuts fell inside his speech.

reading: Kovalan asks the brahmin for the straight road to Madurai, and the brahmin tells him he has come with his lady at the season when summer and the burning sun, like a wide land that has lost its royal order because its king bent with his officers, twist the mullai and kurinji out of their nature into the form called paalai, and that he must cross this long waste of rock, hill and maze-like paths to the bank of the great tank of Kodumbai, where the road forks like the trident of the crescent-crowned god.
nuance: The simile at lines 60 to 66 makes paalai a state of land rather than a region: forest and hill turned by heat into waste, as a kingdom is turned by a bent sceptre (கொற்றவன் கோடி). It is spoken on the road to the kingdom whose sceptre will bend.
event: Kovalan asks the way to Madurai and the brahmin describes the summer waste up to the three-way fork at Kodumbai.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 62-77 (with 57-61 from 48-61) to 57-71: line 57 starts Kovalan's question, and line 71 (கொடும்பை நெடுங்குளக் கோட்டகம் புக்கால்) ends the stretch of road before the fork.

reading: If they take the right-hand branch, the brahmin says, past dead kadambu and omai, scorched ulinjil and dry bamboo, where deer cry for water, and through the hunters' pass, they will see the Pandya's Sirumalai rising among rice, cane, millet, turmeric, plantain, areca, coconut, mango and jack; keeping that hill on the right, they should go on to the wide city.
event: The brahmin describes the right-hand road through the waste past Sirumalai to Madurai.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 62-77 and 78-88 to 72-86: line 72 begins the fork, and line 86 (அம்மலை வலங்கொண் டகன்பதிச் செல்லுமின்) closes the right-hand road with a strong break.

reading: If they take the left-hand branch, past fields, groves and many forests to Thirumal's hill, there is a cave that dispels great confusion and three pools praised by the gods, Punniya Saravanam, Bhavakaarini and Ishtasiddhi: bathing in the first gives the treatise of the king of the gods, in the second the knowledge of one's former birth, and in the third whatever one wishes.
nuance: The brahmin offers three goods from water: learning, memory of past lives, and wishes granted. Kavunthi answers the second directly at lines 156 to 157 without denying the pools' power; see 150-165.
event: The brahmin describes the left-hand road to Thirumal's hill, its cave and its three pools.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 78-88 and 89-103 to 87-103: line 87 (அவ்வழிப் படரீ ராயின்) opens the left-hand road, and line 103 closes the pools' account with a strong break.

reading: To enter the cave, the brahmin says, they must worship the high one of the hill, set his feet in their minds and walk round the hill three times; then by the Silambaaru a bangled woman will appear among karnikara blossoms and ask them to tell her the joy of this life, the joy of the next, and the state that stands in perfection beyond both, saying she is Varottamai who lives at the hill's foot, belongs to those who answer, and will open the door to the worthy.
nuance: Varottamai's riddle lays out a scale of three ends, joy here, joy hereafter, and a third beyond both, which looks like release; the chapter never gives the answer.
event: The brahmin explains the rite for entering the cave and the guardian woman's riddle at its door.

reading: Inside, the brahmin goes on, are many gates; above a joined gate a slender maiden will ask them to tell her the joy that has no end and promise them what they seek, or else send them unharmed back to the road, and to those who answer she shows the three pools; there, reciting together the two mantras of five and of eight letters, they may bathe in the one they want, but better, thinking of none of these, to fix the heart on the golden lotus feet of the god on the hill, whose bird banner will then appear, and having reached the joy of his feet that ends sorrow, to go on to Madurai.
nuance: The brahmin himself ranks the pools below devotion (மற்றவை நினையாது, line 133), so the pilgrim's account already moves from outer water to the god's feet. Lines 128 to 132, on the two mantras and what is not to be seen, are compressed and my reading of them is tentative; the text says only five and eight letters, not which formulas.
event: The brahmin describes the inner gates, a second riddle, the mantras for the pools, and the higher way of devotion to the hill god.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 118-136 (with 137-140 from 137-149) to 118-140: line 136 (புணர்நிலை தோன்றும்) runs on into 137 (தோன்றிய பின்), and line 140 (காண்டகு பிலத்தின் காட்சி யீதாங்கு) closes the account of the cave.

reading: If they take neither branch, the middle way is the straight road: past forests set between towns there is on the hard way a goddess of great affliction who appears gently and, doing no harm, holds back those who pass, and then the Madurai highway; as for himself, the brahmin says, he goes to worship the feet of the tall-crowned lord who strode across the wide earth.
nuance: The warning is brief and its last verb (தாங்கும், line 146) can mean to hold back or to bear up travellers; Kovalan recalls it at lines 192 to 193 as a warning of a deluding goddess, which supports the first sense.
event: The brahmin describes the middle road, warns of a goddess on it, and takes his leave to worship Vishnu.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 137-149 to 141-149: line 141 (அந்நெறிப் படரீ ராயின்) begins the third road after the cave account ends at line 140; line 149 ends the brahmin's speech.

reading: Kavunthi answers the brahmin that there is no need to enter the cave: does he not see clearly, by the book that the Indra of the heavens taught, that what was gained in past births is seen in this one, and is there any rare thing beyond the reach of those who never swerve from truth and who protect living beings; let him go and worship the god he loves, and they will take their long road; so the travellers part from him, rest that day in a town and go on.
nuance: She does not deny the pools: she says their ends are reached by truth and care for life, and answers Bhavakaarini's promise of one's former birth (line 101) with the claim that past births show in this one. She then sends the brahmin courteously to his own god. கப்பத்து இந்திரன் (line 154) seems to be the Indra of a heaven (கற்பம்) and the book a scripture; which book is not said. The narrator calls her reply a கட்டுரை, a weighty word, which I take as endorsement.
event: Kavunthi tells the brahmin the cave is unnecessary and sends him to his god; the travellers rest a day in a town and go on.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 150-172 to 150-165: line 165 ends the day's march, and line 166 begins the scene at the roadside where Kannaki and Kavunthi rest.

reading: While Kannaki and Kavunthi rest by the road, Kovalan goes by a side path to a pool, thirsty, and the forest goddess, thinking he will yield to love, appears in the form of Vasantamalai, falls at his feet weeping and tells him that over the message written in the garland Madhavi, distraught and saying Kovalan had been cruel, declared the courtesan's life the lowest, one that the noble, the learned and the discerning cast off as a disease, tore off her string of pearls and in anger dismissed her too, so that she came with a caravan to Madurai and now asks his command.
nuance: The goddess's story takes up the thread left loose in the Venil kaathai, where Kovalan refused Madhavi's garland letter (8:94-118), and puts in Madhavi's mouth a verdict on her own calling which the later story has her live out in renouncing it. Lines 176 to 177 (தீதிலேன் பிழைமொழி செப்பினை) are hard to divide between Madhavi's words and the maid's; I read them as Madhavi blaming the maid for her message.
event: The forest goddess, in the form of Madhavi's maid Vasantamalai, meets Kovalan at a pool and tells him Madhavi has cast her off.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 150-172 and 173-192 to 166-191: line 172 (நல்குவன் இவனென) runs on into 173 (வயந்த மாலை வடிவில் தோன்றி), and line 191 (நின் பணிமொழி யாதென) ends the false maid's speech.

reading: Because the brahmin had said a deluding goddess haunts this forest, Kovalan resolves to know the woman by the mantra that undoes deceit, and since the mantra he speaks is that of the goddess Paaykalaippaavai, the spirit confesses that she is Vanasaarini who deluded him, begs him not to tell his wife or the holy lady, and goes; Kovalan then brings cool water in a lotus leaf and relieves Kannaki's thirst.
event: Kovalan unmasks the goddess with a mantra; she confesses and leaves, and he brings water to Kannaki.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 173-192 and 193-216 to 192-202: line 192 begins Kovalan's recall of the warning, and line 202 (அருந்துயர் தீர்த்து) ends the episode before the march resumes.

reading: As the sun climbs hot and the forest grows hard to cross, Kovalan, Kannaki and the ascetic come through the bewildering waste to the shrine of Aiyai in a grove of kuravam, maravam, kongu and vengai, the virgin goddess with the eye in her brow, to whom the bow-ploughing hunters, who get no wealth from rain but only from those who cross the waste, bring the spoils of raids on other lands as they wait on the duty of great valour.
nuance: Lines 209 to 210 say the hunters' only harvest is the traveller: they plough with the bow. The travellers reach the shrine of the people who live by the road's danger, which sets up the next kaathai, the hunters' song.
event: The three travellers reach the shrine of the hunters' goddess Aiyai as the midday heat begins.
unit_note: Adjusted from the core cut 193-216 to 203-216: line 203 begins the resumed march after the goddess episode ends at 202; line 216 ends the kaathai.

title: வேட்டுவ வரி (1/2)
theme: The first half of the hunters' song: at Aiyai's shrine in the dry country, where Kovalan and Kannaki rest, the possessed Saalini demands the goddess's due because the hunters' raids have failed; they dress a maiden of their clan as Kotravai and worship her; Saalini, still possessed, hails Kannaki as the jewel of the world, which Kannaki takes for confusion; and the hunters sing the goddess as Shiva's half, Mal's sister, the slayer of the buffalo-demon and the light above the Vedas, and their own clan as the first of clans through the girl who wears her form.
source_issues: The show header gives the kaathai 168 lines but says the edition's printed last line number is 70, so the edition's printed line numbers do not match the core's count; line numbers here are the core's.
The four akaval units were cut at weak breaks (break score 0 at line 35, and 16 and 51 fall inside speeches); they were moved to 1-19, 20-44, 45-53 and 54-74.
Lines 75-86 carry the rubric உரைப்பாட்டுமடை together with வேறு, though they are three regular sung stanzas; the rubric may belong to a prose passage not in the core.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, walking with him to Madurai
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the ascetic woman travelling with Kovalan and Kannaki to Madurai
a woman of the hunters' fighting clan, bound to its old duty to the goddess, who is possessed in the rite
the bow-bearing hunters of the dry country, who sing the vari
the hunter women who carry the offerings
the maiden of the hunters' clan dressed as the goddess
the war goddess of the dry country, also called Aiyai, the goddess of the stag

reading: Footsore from the road under the scorching sun, Kannaki rests with her husband in a corner of Aiyai's shrine, while Saalini, a woman of the hunters' fighting clan bound to its old duty to the goddess, is seized by the deity, dances in the village common and says that the goddess of the stag gives victory to the bow only when her due is paid, since the hunters' cattle-raids have failed and they have fallen quiet.
nuance: Lines 12-15 set the cause of the rite: the herds in the big villages thrive, the hunters' common lies waste, and the fighting clan, its raiding yielding nothing, has subsided 'like a clan of dharma' (அறக்குடி போல, line 15), so the poet makes peace the hunters' misfortune. Lines 16-19 are Saalini's words, closed by எனவாங்கு; the sense of 18-19 (மட்டுண் வாழ்க்கை, கட்டுண் மாக்கள் கடந்தரும்) is not secure, but the demand is plain: the goddess's debt (கடன்) must be paid before she gives victory.
event: Kovalan and Kannaki rest at Aiyai's shrine, and Saalini, possessed by the goddess, dances in the hunters' common and says the goddess will give victory only when her due is paid.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 19: line 15 closes the narrator's sentence, but Saalini's speech runs 16-19 and is closed by எனவாங்கு (line 19); the new dressing sentence begins at line 20.

reading: The hunters take a maiden of their old unyielding clan, bind her hair with a young white snake, set a boar's curved tusk on it like the crescent moon, hang a row of tiger's teeth on her as a tali, gird her with a striped and spotted skin, put a bow in her hand and seat her on a stag with twisted horns, and, with dolls, parrots, jungle fowl, peacocks, balls and play-stones laid before her and the women of the clan carrying colours, powders, sandal, boiled grain, sesame cakes, rich rice, flowers and incense behind, they sound drums, horns, flutes and bells and worship the goddess of the stag at her altar of bought offerings.
nuance: The unit turns a hunter girl into the goddess by costume: each item (snake, boar tusk as crescent, tiger teeth, skin girdle, bow, stag mount) is one of the goddess's emblems that the later songs give back to the goddess herself (lines 58-62, 99-104). The opening phrase (இட்டுத் தலையெண்ணும் எயினரல்லது சுட்டுத் தலைபோகா, lines 20-21) praises the girl's clan as one that never bows its head to any but its own, but the exact sense of the two head-phrases is not secure. விலைப்பலி (line 43) is an offering given in return, as a price, which fits Saalini's talk of the goddess's due.
event: The hunters dress a maiden of their clan as the goddess, seat her on a stag, and with offerings, drums and horns worship the goddess at her altar.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 44 (and 16 to 20): the old break at 34 fell in the middle of the list of gifts (break score 0 at 35), while line 44 closes the worship of the goddess (கைதொழு தேத்தி) before the scene turns to Kannaki at line 45.

reading: As Kannaki, her small feet aching, sits with her husband, the possessed Saalini points to her and says that this woman is the goddess of Kongu and of the western hills, the shoot of the penance done by the Tamil maiden, a single great jewel risen to light the world; Kannaki, thinking the old wise woman has spoken in confusion, shrinks behind her husband's broad back with the shy smile of a stranger.
nuance: This is the first time in the story anyone calls Kannaki divine, and it comes from a possessed hunter woman in a desert shrine, not from the great. Kannaki's own judgement is that the words are பேதுறவு, bewilderment (line 51); the story will prove the priestess right. The three regions she names (கொங்கு, குடமலை, தென்றமிழ், lines 47-48) are where Kannaki will later be worshipped, so the speech reads as prophecy, though the unit itself does not say so.
event: Possessed, Saalini hails Kannaki as a great jewel born for the world, and Kannaki, taking the words for confusion, hides behind her husband and smiles.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 53 (and 45 begins the unit): Saalini's speech runs 47-50 and is closed by the narrator at 51 (என்று); lines 52-53 give Kannaki's response, ending with the clause அரும்பினள் நிற்ப, after which the list of the goddess's epithets begins at 54.

reading: The goddess is hailed in a long chain of names: she wears the crescent, has the unwinking eye in her split forehead, coral lips and white teeth, a throat dark from the poison, bends the great mountain with a snake for string, wears a cobra as breast band, holds the trident, wears the elephant's hide and the lion's skin, is Kotravai of the true sword, the maiden standing on the head of the two-formed asura, Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli, the younger kin of Mal, Aiyai, the red one, the doll of the leaping stag; and it is declared that she, in the maiden's guise come for her people to worship, has given her grace and the vari rite has borne fruit.
nuance: The epithets fuse the hunters' war goddess with Shiva (crescent, forehead eye, dark throat, bending Meru with a snake, elephant hide), with the slayer of the buffalo-demon (line 65-66) and with Vishnu, whose younger kin she is called (மாலவற் கிளங்கிளை, line 68). The unit ends with எனவே, so these are someone's words, most likely the hunters' or Saalini's; the text does not name the speaker.
event: The goddess in the guise of a maiden is declared to have given her grace, and the vari rite is said to have succeeded.
unit_note: Unit begins at 54 instead of 51: lines 51-53 close Saalini's speech and give Kannaki's response (now in 45-53); the chain of the goddess's names starts at line 54 and runs to the closing எனவே at 74.

reading: The first song of the court: before the shrine of the goddess who rules half the body of the forehead-eyed god, nagam and narantham spread their scent, aa and sandal trees grow tall everywhere, and red deer and other beasts crowd together.

The second song: before the shrine of the goddess whose matted hair holds the moon, the vengai sheds its golden flowers, the red-petalled silk-cotton heaps its blossoms and the punku scatters white puffed-rice flowers.
The third song: before the shrine of the goddess who is the kin of Tirumal, maravam, paathiri, punnai, kuravam and kongam bloom on their branches and swarms of bees hum together like a yazh.
nuance: The three refrains give the goddess's court to three figures in turn: Shiva's half (line 78), the one with the moon in her matted hair (line 82), and the kin of Mal (line 86), so the court of the forest goddess is placed between the two great gods.

reading: The singers ask what penance this golden-bangled girl did, that she stands wearing Kotravai's own adornment, and answer that the clan of bowmen hunters in which she was born is the clan among clans.
nuance: The question (தவமென்னை கொல்லோ) treats the girl's present glory as the fruit of some penance, and the answer moves the credit from her to her birth-clan: the girl's merit makes the hunters' clan the first of clans. The same pattern is sung twice more with different names for goddess and clan (91-94, 95-98).

reading: The second stanza asks what penance this girl did, that she stands wearing the adornment of Aiyai, and answers that the clan of the Eyinar of the shooting bow, in which she was born, is the clan among clans.

The third stanza asks what penance this well-bangled girl did, that she stands wearing the adornment of the doll of the leaping stag, and answers that the clan of the Eyinar with bamboo bows, in which she was born, is the clan among clans.

The singers tell the goddess that she stands on the black head of the forest buffalo, wrapped in an elephant's hide and girt with a tiger's skin, and that, worshipped by the gods, she stands unshaken as the secret beyond the Vedas and the shoot of wisdom.
nuance: The same stanza joins the cult image (the buffalo's head under her feet, the hides) to the highest doctrinal title: மறைமேல் மறை, the mystery above the Veda. Elephant hide and tiger skin are Shiva's emblems elsewhere, here worn by the goddess.

reading: The singers tell the goddess that, sword in her bangled hand, she killed the great buffalo-demon and stands on the black stag with twisted horns, and that she abides as the light of spreading rays in the heart-lotus of Hari, Hara and the one on the flower.
nuance: The claim places the goddess as the light within all three gods, Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma alike, so she is not ranked under Shiva here; the saiva tag on the claim follows the cycle's other stanzas (99, 109), which make her Shiva's, and should be read with that caution.

reading: The singers tell the goddess that, holding conch, discus and lotus in her hands, she stands on the angry bull of the red-eyed one, and that she stands as the woman's form in the share of the forehead-eyed god who wears the Ganga in his hair, praised by the Veda.
nuance: The goddess carries Vishnu's conch and discus while standing as the left half of Shiva, so one stanza gives her both great gods. The phrase செங்கண் அரிமால் சினவிடை (line 108) can be read as the angry bull or as a lion with Mal's name; the mount is not certain.
