reading: Thus, with a thick garland of kondrai and tulasi flowers woven together laid on her shoulders, the maiden enters the dance that the goddess in maiden form danced for the gods when the asuras withered.
nuance: The garland joins Shiva's kondrai and Vishnu's tulasi, as the songs before it joined the two gods' emblems. Whether the subject of கூத்துள் படுமே is the dressed hunter girl entering the dance, or the song itself counting as part of the goddess's dance, is not clear from the lines.
event: Garlanded with kondrai and tulasi, the dressed maiden enters the goddess's victory dance.

title: வேட்டுவ வரி (2/2)
theme: The second half of the hunters' vari: songs that see the goddess dance her victory and walk before the cattle raider, three songs that show the seized herds filling the yards of smith, bards, toddy seller, augur and elders, and stanzas offering her blood and bali as the hunters' due while praising her as Siva's consort and Mal's kin; it closes by wishing the vetchi on the Pandya of Pothiyil.
source_issues: silappathikaram:12:136-140: line 140, துறைப்பாட்டுமடை, is a rubric introducing the following stanzas but is counted as a verse line of the last herd song.
The kaathai header reports a printed last line of 70 against 168 counted lines; the numbering here follows show.

silappathikaram:12:153-156 to 161-164: the three stanzas are counted as three 4-line units though each pairs a refrain line (உண்குவாய்) with a praise line (செய்குவாய்/சேர்த்துவாய்); the boundaries look right.

cast.role: the hunters (Maravar) of the forest beside the Aiyai shrine, who sing the vari
the goddess of victory (Aiyai, Kumari, Neeli) worshipped by the hunters
a young hunter woman addressed in the songs of the seized herds
the woman who sells toddy to the hunters

tamil: ஆய்பொன் னரிச்சிலம்பும் சூடகமும் மேகலையும் ஆர்ப்ப வார்ப்ப
மாயஞ்செய் வாளவுணர் வீழநங்கை மரக்கான்மேல் வாளமலை யாடும் போலும்
மாயஞ்செய் வாளவுணர் வீழநங்கை மரக்கான்மேல் வாளமலை யாடுமாயின்
காயாமலர்மேனி யேத்திவானோர் கைபெய் மலர்மாரி காட்டும் போலும்;
reading: The hunters sing that the goddess, her fine anklets, wristlets and girdle ringing, seems to dance the victory sword-dance on stilts as the deceiving asuras fall, and that the gods, praising her body dark as the kaya flower, seem to shower flowers from their hands.
nuance: Every line ends in போலும் (it seems): the singers describe the costumed girl of the rite as if she were the goddess dancing her battle, so the song is a seeing-as rather than a report. The dance on stilts (மரக்கால்) over the falling asuras is the myth's dance of victory; the dark body (காயா மலர்மேனி) ties her to Mal, whose younger kin the first half of the kaathai calls her.
event: The goddess dances on stilts as the asuras fall and the gods shower flowers on her.

tamil: உட்குடைச் சீறூ ரொருமகன்ஆ னிரைகொள்ள உற்ற காலை
வெட்சி மலர்புனைய வெள்வா ளுழத்தியும் வேண்டும் போலும்
வெட்சி மலர்புனைய வெள்வா ளுழத்தியும் வேண்டின் வேற்றூர்க்
கட்சியுட் காரி கடிய குரலிசைத்துக் காட்டும் போலும்;
reading: When a man of the small village inside the forest sets out to seize cattle, the goddess who plies the white sword seems to want to wear the vetchi flower too, and if she does, the kaari bird in the enemy village's forest seems to cry its harsh omen.
nuance: The goddess takes the raider's own badge, the vetchi flower of cattle seizure, so the raid becomes her act; the omen bird crying in the enemy's grove (கட்சி) is the sign of their loss. The song turns on condition (வேண்டின்): her wish is what makes the omen fall.
event: A hunter sets out to seize cattle and the goddess takes the vetchi with him while an omen bird cries in the enemy's grove.

tamil: கள்விலை யாட்டி மறுப்பப் பொறாமறவன் கைவில் ஏந்திப்
புள்ளும் வழிப்படரப் புல்லார் நிரைகருதிப் போகும் போலும்
புள்ளும் வழிப்படரப் புல்லார் நிரை கருதிப் போகுங் காலைக்
கொள்ளும் கொடியெடுத்துக் கொற்றவையும் கொடுமரமுன் செல்லும் போலும்
reading: When the woman who sells toddy refuses him, the warrior who cannot bear it takes his bow and goes, with birds leading the way, to seize the cattle of his foes, and as he goes the goddess of victory seems to raise her banner and walk before his bow.
nuance: The raid starts from a small want: the toddy seller will not pour (மறுப்ப), so the hunter goes for cattle to pay her. The song sets this trade motive and the goddess's banner side by side without embarrassment; the birds on the road (புள்ளும் வழிப்படர) are the omens of the way.
event: Refused toddy by the toddy seller, a hunter takes his bow and goes to raid cattle, and the goddess goes before him with her banner.

reading: The singers bid the young hunter woman look: the fine herds her brothers brought back from yesterday's raid now fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the skilled yazh-playing bards.
nuance: The spoil is not kept: it goes at once to the craftsmen and musicians of the raid (the smith who makes the weapons, the துடி drummer, the bards). The address to the girl (இளமா எயிற்றி) makes her the witness of her brothers' valour shown as giving.
event: The herds seized in the raid are given out and fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the bards.

reading: Again the young woman is bidden to look: the herds her brothers seized while the karanthai men cried out fill the yards of the toddy seller, the forest man who picks good bamboo, and the augur who read the bird omen.
nuance: The list pays the debts of the raid one by one: the toddy seller who refused credit in lines 124-127 is now paid in cattle, and the augur (கணி) is paid for the omen that sent them out. கரந்தை here names the defenders of the herd by their flower.
event: The seized herds fill the yards of the toddy seller, the bamboo-cutter and the augur.

reading: A third time the young woman is bidden to look: the herds her brothers drove off while the neighbouring village wailed fill the yards of the grey-bearded old Eyinar and Eyinar women, and a rubric marks the songs to the goddess that follow.
nuance: The third song ends with the elders of the hunters' own kin; the neighbouring village's wail (அயலூர் அலற) is the price, stated plainly. Line 138 (நயனில் மொழியின்) is hard: it may describe the old men's rough speech; the sense is not secure. Line 140, துறைப்பாட்டுமடை, is a rubric, not a verse line.
event: The herds seized from a neighbouring village fill the yards of the old Eyinar men and women.

reading: The hunters say they worship the goddess's paired feet, which grant grace to the sages and gods who wander with the sun so their distress ends, and that this is the due the mighty Eyinar owe as they touch her feet: blood flowing from the throat, the price of the victory she gives.
nuance: The hymn joins the goddess's grace (அருளும்) and the price of blood (விலையே) in one stanza: victory is a purchase and blood the payment. Whose throat bleeds is not said: an animal's, a captive's, or the hunters' own offered blood; I leave it open.
event: The hunters touch the goddess's feet and offer throat-blood as their due for victory.

reading: The hunters worship her flower feet, jewel-formed, to which the crowned gods and their king bow, and say this is the due offered by the victorious Eyinar who come in a full band: blood with fat dripping from it, the price that crushes their rivals.
nuance: The second stanza repeats the first's frame (தொழுதேம் ... கடனிது ... விலையே) with the gods' king in place of the sages, and fat (நிணன்) added to the blood: the offering is flesh as well as blood.
event: The hunters offer blood and fat at the goddess's feet as the price of victory over rivals.

reading: The Eyinar who come bursting out at midnight like killing tigers, with drum, small drum and horn sounding, touch the maiden goddess's feet, and this, they say, is the due they owe: the offering of food at the head of the bali.
nuance: The night raid and the night offering are the same band in the same noise: the drums that sound for the attack (வெடிபட வருபவர்) sound for the rite. படுகடன், the debt that has fallen due, makes the bali an obligation rather than a gift.
event: The hunters come at midnight with drums and lay the bali at the goddess's feet.

reading: The hunters pray that travellers may multiply and the road grow rich, and ask the goddess, Sankari, Antari, Neeli, who sets the red-eyed snake and the crescent on her matted crown, to eat the due of the Eyinar of strong bows and arrows.
nuance: To a highway robber a road rich with travellers (வம்பலர் பல்கி) is a rich harvest: the prayer for safe, busy roads is, from these singers, a prayer for prey. The goddess carries Siva's snake and crescent, so the hymn makes her his consort.

reading: They ask her to eat the due of the pitiless Eyinar who fall on sleeping villages with the startling drum, and praise her who, while the gods who ate nectar still die, ate the poison none would eat and sits granting grace.
nuance: Two contrasts are packed together: the gods who drank amrita still die, while she who drank poison lives and gives grace; and the hunters who have no eyes for pity (கண்ணில்) are fed by her grace. The poison-swallowing is Siva's act; the hymn gives it to the goddess as his other half.

reading: They ask her to eat the due of the graceless Eyinar, who show no mercy to anyone but take his goods and wound him, and praise her who walked between the marutham trees and kicked to pieces the rolling cart of deceit her uncle sent.
nuance: The singers call themselves அருளில் (without grace) in the same stanza that praises the goddess's grace (அருள் செய்குவாய்); the hymn does not ask her to change them, only to eat their due. The feats of the marutham trees and the cart sent by the uncle are Krishna's, given to her as Mal's kin.

reading: The vari closes with a blessing: may the hill-lord of high Pothiyil, mighty and eager for victory, wear the vetchi so that the groves and karanthai of other lands go to ruin.
nuance: The hunters' raid becomes the king's war: the vetchi they wore for cattle is wished on the Pandya, the lord of Pothiyil, unnamed here. Line 165 (மறைமுது முதல்வன் பின்னர் மேய) is obscure: it may set the king after an ancient first lord, but the reference cannot be fixed. The kaathai that hailed Kannaki as the goddess ends by praying for the victory of the king who will die before her word.

title: புறஞ்சேரியிறுத்த காதை
theme: Guided by the ascetic, Kovalan and Kannaki travel the Pandya land by night trusting its fame for safety; in a Brahmin village Kovalan meets Kausikan with Madhavi's letter, clears her and owns the fault as his own, sends the letter on to his parents, and with bards on the road comes by breeze, dawn sounds and the Vaigai to Madurai, where river, flowers and flags grieve and warn as if they knew what is coming, and the couple enter the outer settlement of the virtuous.
source_issues: Lines 89-90: the word குலப்பிறப்பாட்டியொடு is split across the line end (பாட்டியோ / டிரவிடை), and the cut between units 76-89 and 90-114 fell inside it; the boundary was moved to line 92.
Lineation: the kaathai has 196 lines as shown but the edition's printed last line is 195, so the printed numbering is one short somewhere.
Lines 106-112: the technical terms of tuning the yazh (திவவு, உழை முதல் கைக்கிளை இறுவாய், மூவகைத் தானத்து) are taken as written; their sense was not checked against any source.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, travelling to Madurai
Kovalan's wife, travelling with him
the woman ascetic who guides the couple to Madurai; in this kaathai named only by epithets (புண்ணிய முதல்வி, மாதவத்தாட்டி, அறவி)
a Brahmin youth of Puhar, Madhavi's messenger, who finds Kovalan on the road
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar whom Kovalan left
Madhavi's maid and companion
Kovalan's father, the wealthy merchant of Puhar
Kovalan's mother, the mistress of the great house
wandering bards met on the road to Madurai
the Earth, personified as a woman
the moon, named as the founder of the Pandya line
the river Vaigai of Madurai, personified as a woman

reading: After the forest guise has been put off, someone at the holy lady's feet reasons that this young woman cannot bear the fierce summer sun and her small feet have never trodden the hot pebbled forest, and that the fame has spread everywhere of the land guarded by the Pandyas of the straight sceptre, where the bear does not dig the anthill, the tiger does not attack the deer, and serpent, demon, crocodile and thunder do no harm to those who depend on it.
nuance: The safety of the road is given as reputation (இசை, line 10), heard of rather than seen, and it reaches past men to beasts, demons and thunder. The text does not name the speaker: the deliberation runs into the next unit and ends with குரவரும் நேர்ந்த (line 14), the elder's consent, so it is most likely Kovalan proposing night travel to the ascetic. The praise of the Pandya's straight sceptre is set on the threshold of the realm where the Pandya will kill Kovalan without inquiry.
event: On the road to Madurai the travellers weigh the summer heat against the safety of the Pandya's land before going on.

reading: Since the moonlight protects living beings better than daylight and there is no danger in passing the long road by night, the elder agrees, and the travellers, who wait for the hour of sunset like the subjects of a cruel king, see the moon, the founder of the Pandya line, rise with its host of stars spreading milk-white rays, while the Earth asks the summer moon, with the southern breeze born on Malaya and grown in Madurai, to pour its white light on the young woman whom no star-garland, sandal paste, flower garland or leaf-chaplet now touches.
nuance: The sun is likened to a cruel king whose subjects wait for him to set (line 15), and the moon that brings relief is the Pandya's own ancestor (line 18): the image of a bad reign and a protecting lineage are set side by side in the passage that admits the travellers to the Pandya land. The Earth's request (lines 19-28) is spoken before she is named in the next unit (பார்மகள், line 29); that the 'doll' (பாவை) is Kannaki, unadorned in her exile, is my reading.
event: With the elder's consent the travellers wait for sunset and set out by night as the moon rises.

reading: When the Earth has sighed and grown still, Kovalan, seeing his wife toil on the hard road, gives her his shoulder for her bangled hand and bids her not fear the roaming tiger, the calling owl and the growling bear; having heard the ascetic's teaching of dharma, free of harsh words, they pass the road, and at cock-crow reach a village of thread-wearing Brahmins versed in the Vedas, where he leaves his wife with the ascetic in a safe enclosure and goes beyond the thorn fence for water, sighing like a smith's bellows that he has brought her into the forest, so changed by grief that Kausikan does not know him.
nuance: The bellows simile (ஊதுலைக் குருகின், line 45) gives Kovalan's grief a cause he owns: he is pained that his wife has come with him into the forest (line 44). The ascetic's teaching is described only as அறவுரை free of the speech of violence (மறவுரை நீத்த, line 34); its content is not given. The last three lines begin Kausikan's address to a creeper, which the next unit completes.
event: Kovalan leads Kannaki through the night forest to a Brahmin village, leaves her with the ascetic and goes for water, unrecognised by Kausikan.

reading: Resting in the shade of a green-leaved kurukkatthi arbour, Kausikan addresses the creeper as Madhavi, saying it suffers in the harsh summer with its flowers shed like Madhavi of the long eyes when Kovalan left her; Kovalan asks what he means, and Kausikan, saying he has found him unharmed, tells how Kovalan's father and mother became like serpents that had lost their gem, the kin fell into a sea of grief like a body without life, servants went everywhere to seek him, the great city was bewildered like Ayodhya when the hero left for the forest, and Madhavi, hearing from Vasanthamaalai, grew pale and fell on her couch, and when he went to her in her grief she wrote with her own hand, worshipping Kovalan's feet and asking him to end her sorrow, bidding Kausikan show it to him.
nuance: Kausikan's speech to the creeper is a ruse of purpose (கொள்கையின் உரைப்போன், line 56): the creeper's name is the courtesan's, and the word Madhavi draws out the man he cannot recognise. The Ayodhya simile (lines 63-66) sets Puhar's loss of one merchant's son beside the city that lost Rama; the sense of அரசே தஞ்சம் (line 64) in the simile is not clear to me. Kovalan's family and Madhavi grieve in one report, the household and the courtesan side by side.
event: Kausikan, sent from Puhar, recognises Kovalan and tells him of his parents' grief, the city's search and Madhavi's collapse and letter.

reading: Kausikan says Madhavi gave him the clay-sealed letter and that he has wandered the roads and lands with it, and when he holds it out, Kovalan, knowing by the scent of the oil from her curled hair pressed into the clay seal the fragrance she spoke of when they lived together, cannot let it go, opens it and reads: she falls at his feet and asks him to take her guileless words to heart, she does not know her fault that made him leave by night with his high-born wife, against the service owed to his elders, and she asks him to remove the confusion of her helpless heart, hailing him as one of flawless sight.
nuance: The letter names his elders' claim (குரவர்பணி, line 89) and his wife's birth (குலப்பிறப் பாட்டியொடு, lines 89-90), and asks for no return: it only asks what her fault was. The letter is the courtesan's speech in her own hand; the narrator voices the frame. தீத்திறம் புரிந்தோன் (line 78) I read as Kausikan naming himself as a Brahmin who keeps the sacred fire; it could refer to someone else.
event: Kausikan hands Kovalan Madhavi's letter, which he knows by the scent of her hair on the seal, and he reads her plea.
unit_note: Adjusted: the boundary at line 89/90 split the word குலப்பிறப்பாட்டியொடு (பாட்டியோ / டிரவிடை) and the letter's sentence; the end was moved from line 89 to line 92, where the letter closes with போற்றி.

reading: Understanding the words she wrote, Kovalan decides she is without fault, his weariness leaves him, and seeing that the fault was his own, he says the letter's sense fits as well for his parents, bids Kausikan show it to them with his worship of their feet and sends him off to relieve their distress; then he returns to the ascetic, who sits with his wife of spotless chastity, joins a group of bards who sing the dance of the goddess, tunes the yazh with them and hears the paalai melody of the goddess of the leaping deer, and, singing along, asks them how far it is to Koodal.
nuance: This is the one place in the journey where Kovalan names the cause of his ruin as his own fault (என்தீது, line 95), and he does it in answer to the courtesan, whom he clears (தன்றீ திலள், line 94). Later Kannaki tells the king that ஊழ்வினை drove him to Madurai (kaathai 20, line 69). The same letter, sent on to his parents, serves as his own plea to them. The musical lines (106-112) are technical and I have not tried to fix their terms.
event: Kovalan, reading Madhavi's letter, holds her blameless and himself at fault, sends it on to his parents by Kausikan, and joins wandering bards on the road, asking them the distance to Madurai.
unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 90 to line 93 so that the letter (lines 87-92) stays whole; line 92 ends it and line 93 (என்றவள் எழுதிய) begins Kovalan's response.

reading: The bards answer that the Madurai breeze has come here, unlike the Pothiyil breeze of the poets' tongues: it carries the smells of eaglewood and sandal paste, saffron, civet and musk, the flowers of the houses, the smoke of kitchens and of the cake-sellers' sweets, the incense men and women burn in the mansions and the smoke of the fire offerings, mingled with the fragrance of the Pandya's palace, so his prosperous old city is not far off, and even if they go alone none will stop them.
nuance: Madurai is first reached by smell, and the city's breath mixes the kitchens, the merchants, the lovers' incense and the sacrificial fire with the king's own palace. The breeze itself is the Pandya land's (lines 25-26 of this kaathai already sent it from Malaya through Madurai). The closing assurance of safety for the lone traveller (line 134) repeats the opening fame of the Pandya's road.

reading: With the ascetic as before they travel on in the dark, and the uproar of Koodal, loud as the dark sea, comes out to meet them and ends their sorrow: the morning drums of the great temple of the fierce god and of the king's palace, the chant of the Brahmins of the four Vedas, the recitation of the ascetics, the day drum of the warriors in the king's honour, the trumpeting of elephants taken in war and in pits, the neighing of horses in their stalls and the dawn songs of the kinai bards.
nuance: The city's dawn is heard, not seen, from outside the walls, and it heals the travellers' grief (ஆரஞர் நீங்கி, line 150). The catalogue sets the temple and the palace side by side and the Brahmins' chant beside the ascetics' (மாதவர், line 142), and several items, the stalled horse (பணைநிலைப் புரவி, line 147) and the captured elephants, are those of the Sangam Madurai dawn in Maduraikkanchi.
event: Travelling on by night, the three hear Madurai's dawn sounds and their grief lifts.
unit_note: Adjusted: the end was moved from line 151 to line 150; line 150 (ஆரஞர் நீங்கி) closes the dawn catalogue, and line 151 begins the list of flowers that dress the Vaigai.

reading: The Vaigai is drawn as a woman whose banks of kuravam, vakulam, kongu, vengai and many other flowering trees are her girdle, whose sand heaps are her hips, whose flowered islet is her breasts, whose fallen kavir petals her red mouth, mullai her smile, carp her long eyes and dark water her flowered hair, the never-failing creeper of the Pandya clan, of high conduct that feeds the world, who, as if she knew what was to befall the young wife, wraps herself in a garment of holy fragrant flowers and hides her eye-filling flood, so that the woman of the swan's gait and her lord worship her, saying this is not a river of water but a river of flowers.
nuance: The river's flowers, which the travellers read as beauty and worship, are given by the narrator as a veil over her tears (கண்ணிறை நெடுநீர் கரந்தனள், line 173): she knows the wife's fate and hides it. 'Never-failing' (பொய்யா, line 170) and 'feeds the world' are the Pandya river's old praise, and the poet names it as the poets' Vaigai (புலவர் நாவிற் பொருந்திய, line 169). Only the reader is told the river's grief; the couple see a river of flowers.
event: The travellers reach the Vaigai, covered in flowers, and worship it as a river of flowers.
unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 152 to line 151, where the flower list begins, and the end from line 174 to line 175, since the river's sentence (என, line 174) closes with the couple's worship (தொழுது, line 175).

reading: Passing by the great ford where boats with horse, elephant and lion faces ply, they cross with the ascetic on a log raft to the flowering southern bank, and, judging it fitting to go round Madurai where the gods dwell, they skirt the moat girded with guard forest, where the blue lily, white lily and lotus, as if they knew for certain the lone sorrow that would come to the wife and her husband, weep and tremble with humming bees, and the long war-flags on the fort wave back as if saying 'do not come', and through fields, groves, tanks, lakes and gardens of coconut, plantain, areca and bamboo they enter the outer settlement of the old city where only those devoted to dharma dwell.
nuance: Two omens are given as the narrator's 'as if' (போல, lines 186 and 190): the moat's flowers weep and the fort's flags wave the couple away. Both say plainly what the Vaigai's flowers hid. The couple avoid the royal ferry for a humble raft, and their first lodging in Madurai is the outer quarter of those devoted to dharma (lines 195-196), outside the walls where the king's justice will fail them.
event: The three cross the Vaigai on a raft, skirt Madurai's moat past weeping flowers and waving flags, and enter the city's outer settlement.
unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 175 to line 176, because the couple's worship on line 175 (தொழுது) closes the river's sentence and line 176 begins the crossing.

title: ஊர்காண் காதை
theme: Kovalan, at dawn, leaves Kannaki in Kavunthi's keeping, and the nun answers his self-reproach with a teaching that the deed ripens on its doer and that suffering comes to those bound to women, citing two exiled kings who lost their wives, and assures him that he, unlike them, keeps his wife; he then walks through Madurai's courtesans' quarter through all its seasons, its dancers' streets, bazaar, gem, gold, cloth and grain streets, and goes back outside the walls pleased with the city that will kill him.
source_issues: The kaathai header gives 218 lines but the printed last line number is 215; the edition's line numbering and the file's sequence differ by three lines somewhere in the kaathai, and line numbers here follow the file.
Line 6 reads ஒங்குயர் where ஓங்குயர் is expected, likely a lost long vowel mark.
Lines 188 and 190 carry the tool's repair of ௌ before a vowel sign to ெள (தெளித்தனைய); the repaired forms read correctly.

cast.role: the merchant's son of Puhar, Kannaki's husband
the woman ascetic who guides Kovalan and Kannaki to Madurai
Kovalan's wife

reading: At dawn, as birds rise crying from the groves, pools and fields and the sun opens the lotus, Madurai of the sword-bearing Seliyan wakes, and in the temples of the three-eyed god, of the one who raised the eagle banner, of the white one with the plough banner and of the one with the cock banner, in the monasteries of the righteous and in the king's palace the morning drums sound with the conch.
nuance: The list sets the shrines of four gods and the பள்ளி of the அறவோர் (the renouncers' monasteries) beside the palace, the seat of மறம், as one waking city: line 11's அறத்துறை and line 12's மறத்துறை are paired, and Kavunthi will use the same two words a few lines on (27-28) for the paths of harm and of virtue. The sun is called the orb the world worships that makes kings tremble (line 5), a mild foretaste in a kaathai that ends at this king's city.
event: Dawn breaks over Madurai and the morning drums sound in its temples, monasteries and palace.
unit_note: Moved the end of the first unit from line 12 to line 14: the list of temples in lines 7-12 is the subject of இயம்ப in line 14, which closes the sentence of the dawn.

reading: Kovalan goes to Kavunthi, who keeps to her vows, worships her and says that, having become like those who strayed from the right path, he has brought distress on his tender wife and suffered among strangers in an unknown land, and asks whether, until he has made his state known to the merchants of the old city and returned, any harm could come to her here in the lady's keeping.
nuance: Kovalan names his own fault (நெறியின் நீங்கியோர் நீர்மையேன், line 17) before Kavunthi names karma (line 27): the two causes, his choice and the ripening deed, are set side by side within a few lines, and the nun's answer moves the weight from the first to the second. மன்னர் பின்னோர் (line 21), 'those after the kings', is read here as the merchant order, to whom Kovalan as a merchant's son would go.
event: Kovalan asks Kavunthi to keep Kannaki safe while he goes into Madurai to make himself known to its merchants.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 13 to line 15 and the end from line 29 to line 24: Kovalan's speech runs from line 15 to என்றலும் in line 24, and Kavunthi's answer begins at line 25.

reading: Kavunthi tells Kovalan that the unlearned do not take the drum-like cry of the righteous to leave the ways of harm because the hard deed will feed its fruit, and are bewildered when that deed ripens, while the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds; that the pains of parting, of union and of the bodiless god's punishment belong to those who join with women and not to the strong who live alone; that those who took women and food for pleasure have met grief ever since; and that he surely knows the old story of the one who went with his wife at his father's word and suffered when she was taken from him.
nuance: Kavunthi's word for the deed's coming, உருத்த (line 31), is the verb of the patikam's third moral (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்): the epic's thesis is first spoken inside the story here, by a nun consoling the man it will kill. She names neither hero of her exempla: the one 'who begot the first of the Veda' (line 48) is the god who fathered Brahma, here in his birth as the prince exiled with his wife, and the reader must supply the name. Her account of desire as the root of suffering is a renouncer's, yet she does not urge Kovalan to leave his wife; the speech consoles a householder with an ascetic's diagnosis. தவந்தீர் மருங்கின் (line 26) may mean that his lone suffering comes from a lack of past penance; the reading does not turn on it. The unit does not name a school; the speaker is the Jain nun of the earlier kaathais.
event: Kavunthi answers Kovalan with a teaching on karma and on the suffering that comes through desire, citing the prince who lost his wife in exile.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 30 to line 25: Kavunthi's speech begins at கவுந்தி கூறும் (line 25), and lines 25-29 begin the sentence that ends at கொள்ளார் (line 30). The end stays at line 49 (நெடுமொழி யன்றோ).

reading: Kavunthi adds the example of the king who lost his land at the dice and went into the cruel forest with his wife, not parted from her for want of love nor she guilty of any fault, and asks whether his leaving her in the forest at midnight was not strong karma, and whether Kovalan would not say so if anyone blamed the woman; Kovalan, she says, is not even like him, for he has a life never parted from his wife, so let him go without grief, learn a fitting place in the king's Koodal and come back.
nuance: The nun's comfort is that Kovalan, unlike the dice-ruined king, keeps his wife at his side (பிரியா வாழ்க்கை, line 59); the story will part them within days, and Kannaki will name the same driving deed (ஊழ்வினை) in the Pandya's court. The exemplum clears the abandoned wife of blame and lays the abandonment on karma rather than on the husband's will. Line 57 (சொல்லலும் உண்டேற் சொல்லா யோநீ) is compressed; it is read here as an appeal to Kovalan to answer anyone who blames the wife.
event: Kavunthi cites the dice-ruined king who abandoned his wife in the forest and sends Kovalan into Madurai to find a lodging.
unit_note: Moved the end from line 59 to line 61: Kavunthi's speech closes with போதீங் கென்றலும் (line 61), so lines 60-61 belong to it rather than to the entry into the city.

reading: Kovalan goes along the tunnel road beside the moat where elephant herds pass, enters the guarded gate unsuspected by its Yavana swordsmen, and comes into the walled city that opens like Indra's jewel casket, with banners waving in the west wind, where courtesans with their lovers play in the Vaigai's flood at the marutham-shaded ford and wear mullai, kuvalai and other flowers.
nuance: The Yavana guards at the gate are a detail of the city's wealth and order; that they do not question the stranger is the first of the many ways the city lets Kovalan in without knowing him.
event: Kovalan enters Madurai through its guarded gate and begins his walk through its streets.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 60 to line 62: lines 60-61 close Kavunthi's speech (என்றலும், line 61), and Kovalan's walk into the city begins at line 62.

reading: The courtesans, garlanded with lilies, jasmine and red waterlily and wearing Korkai pearls, smear Malaya sandal and play in the groves, sit at evening on moonlit terraces in red silk with hill flowers, saffron and coral to show Indra the red adornment of Koodal, and, besides the season when the cloud-king comes with the north wind, warm themselves by agil fires with their men and close the small windows in the cold.
nuance: The description runs through the seasons in a single sentence (lines 70-145): each season is a new setting for the same pleasures of the courtesans' quarter, and their dress follows the seasons' colours. Which season each sub-scene names is not always clear from the Tamil, and the reading keeps to what the lines show.

reading: In the early dew season, when the sun has gone south and white clouds rarely show, the men and women of rich houses enjoy the young sun on moonlit terraces, and besides that the east wind comes in bearing the agil, silk, sandal, scents and camphor that the people of Thondi have loaded on their ships.

Wondering where the king of dew has gone at the union of Panguni and where the young spring is, which comes with the south wind from Pothiyil when the madhavi creeper lifts its banner, the women count the seasons with their husbands; and when the summer king who ruled Koodal with forest fires departs on the last day of fierce heat, carriages, palanquins and jewelled couches are given them.
nuance: Line 113's கோதை மாதவி is the madhavi creeper whose flowering marks spring, but in an epic whose Madhavi is the courtesan Kovalan left, the creeper raising its banner over a courtesans' quarter is hard to read without her.

reading: Given chowries, gold betel-pouches and sharp swords by the prince, the women of unfailing wealth take new lovers, drink the toddy their maids bear in gold bowls, and in their sulks show the unspoken laugh, the fight of the eye's corner, the curled brow and the sweat on the small forehead, in the street where rich men who wait on their moods and the kings of the earth take delight.
unit_note: Moved the end from line 143 to line 145: the list of the women's sulking signs closes with வீதியும் (line 145), which ends the description of this street.

reading: There are also the two great streets of those of the sixty-four arts, whose sweet words outdo song: the houses of flawless fame before which crowned kings bow, where women who know the two styles of dance, its measures, the vari, songs and beats and the instruments, the four kinds of gesture and the stage of seven levels, the talaikkol dancer, the singer of the vaaram and the dancers of the lead and middle songs, receive the thousand and eight kalanju by fixed rule each day, and in the net of whose glances even ascetics lose their hard-won wisdom, while young men and the fools of love's feast sleep secure.
nuance: The fee, ஆயிரத் தெண்கழஞ்சு with எட்டுக் கடைநிறுத்த, and the praise வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின் are the words used when Madhavi received her title and price in Puhar; here they describe a daily rate across a whole profession. சுடுமண் ஏறா (line 146) is obscure and the reading leaves it aside; தாக்கணங்கு (line 160) is the goddess who strikes those who look on her.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 144 to line 146 and the end from line 156 to line 167: the dancers' quarter begins at line 146 and its sentence ends at இருபெரு வீதியும் (line 167).

reading: There is the bazaar street, desired by kings for its wealth, where carriages, chariot parts, armour, goads, leather shields, chowries and shields of boar-hide and of wood lie heaped with work in copper and bronze, things of silk and garlands, polished wares, worked horn and ivory, incense, sandal and flowers, so mixed in plenty that their kinds cannot be told apart.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 157 to line 168 and the end from line 172 to line 179: the list of the bazaar's goods begins at line 168 and ends with அங்காடி வீதியும் (line 179).

reading: There is the gem street, safe from any enemy, where men who can tell gems apart gather: diamonds free of the four flaws the treatises name, in the colours of the four orders, emeralds free of dark spots, rubies of every lawful kind, topaz, crystal and stones dark or of two colours, gems whose flaws from wind, earth, stone or water have been cut away, pearls round as the moon, Jupiter and Mars, and coral without twist.
nuance: Each gem is named with the flaws it lacks, so the street is a street of judgment as much as of wealth: its people know by rule what is true and what is false in a stone. The epic will bring a gem-filled anklet before this king, and his verdict will be made without any such testing.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 173 to line 180 and the end from line 195 to line 200: the gems begin at line 180 and the sentence closes at வீதியும் (line 200).

reading: Past the gold street, where assayers of the four kinds of gold raise their flags free of doubt, the cloth street of cotton, hair and silk in bundles past counting, and the grain street where weighers, measurers and those with the measuring pot go everywhere among heaped grain and sacks of pepper, Kovalan wanders the four-caste streets, junctions, squares, halls and lanes, and, glad at having seen the king's great city under the shade of banners the sun cannot pierce, goes back outside the walls.
nuance: பொலந்தெரி மாக்கள் (line 203), the men who test gold, are the trade of the goldsmith who will accuse Kovalan; the tour ends in pleasure (மகிழ்வெய்தி) at the city whose verdict will kill him.
event: Kovalan walks through the gold, cloth and grain streets and, pleased with the city, returns outside its walls.
unit_note: Moved the start from line 196 to line 201: line 200 closes the gem street, and line 201 opens the gold street.

title: அடைக்கலக் காதை
theme: On the eve of entering Madurai, the Brahmin Maadalan recounts Kovalan's good deeds (naming his daughter Manimekalai after the goddess who saved an ancestor for his gifts, saving a Brahmin from an elephant, paying for a Brahmin wife's expiation, offering his life to the spirit for a false witness) and asks whether his suffering is the fruit of a former birth; Kovalan tells a dream of ruin and release, and Kavunthi entrusts Kannaki to the herdswoman Maadari, praising her as a deity and binding Maadari to the charge with a Jain tale of a monkey raised to the gods by a housewife's gift.
source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed last line is 215 against 219 lines as shown, so its printed numbers run four behind by the end; line numbers here are the kaathai's own as `show` prints them.
Chapter 20 of this marking is the fifteenth kaathai (அடைக்கலக் காதை, unit ids silappathikaram:15:...); the brief's 'Silappathikaram 20' (the plea before the Pandya) is kaathai 20, chapter 26.
Line 94 விருத்தகோபால: the word division and sense of விருத்த are unclear.
Line 80 பட்டோன் றவ்வை: தவ்வை may be the man's mother or elder sister.

Brahmin of Thalaichengaanam, returning from pilgrimage to Kumari, who knows Kovalan's past deeds
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom Kannaki is entrusted
the dancer of Puhar, mother of Kovalan's daughter Manimekalai
the elder courtesans who propose to name Madhavi's daughter
the sea goddess, Kovalan's family deity, who at Indra's command saved a shipwrecked ancestor
the aged Brahmin, coming to receive gifts, whom Kovalan saved from an elephant
the rogue elephant that seized the Brahmin
the Brahmin who left his wife and went north after the mongoose's death
the Brahmin's wife who sought someone to take the fruit of her wrong deed
the poor man who bore false witness against a chaste wife
the spirit of Puhar's crossroads that seizes false witnesses with its noose and devours them
the mother (or elder sister) of the false witness seized by the spirit
the herdsmen of Madurai carrying axes and pot-slings who walk with Maadari
the herdswomen who walk with Maadari
the Jain charanas (wandering sages) who preach dharma under the asoka at Puhar; their chief (இறையோன்) tells the monkey's story
the Jain lay hearers at Puhar
the god, once Saayalan's monkey, who appears with a monkey's hand on one side
the wife of the merchant Etti Saayalan of Puhar, who raised the monkey and gave gifts in its name
the town monkey that ate the sage's leftovers
the great ascetic fed at Saayalan's house, who bids the wife cherish the monkey

reading: Having seen Madurai, whose kings' straight sceptre, cool umbrella and victorious spear keep a city that has never had to flee, Kovalan returns to the grove of the ascetics' outer quarter and tells Kavunthi of the evil-free city and the Pandya's might; meanwhile the Brahmin Maadalan of Thalaichengaanam, returning from circling the sage's hill and bathing at Kumari, enters the grove to rest, Kovalan bows at his feet, and the Brahmin begins to speak.
nuance: Kovalan's report of a Madurai 'free of evil' (தீதுதீர் மதுரை) and of the straightness of its kings' sceptre (கோலின் செம்மை) is the last praise of the Pandya before the killing; the next kaathai will show that sceptre bend on him. Line 7 calls the outer quarter the place of those with dharma-bearing hearts, which line 107 turns into the reason Kovalan must leave it.
event: Kovalan returns from seeing Madurai to the ascetics' grove and tells Kavunthi of it; the Brahmin Maadalan arrives from Kumari and Kovalan bows to him.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the old first unit ended at line 16 in mid-sentence (தாழ்பொழி லாங்கண், 'in that grove'); the unit now runs to line 20, where the narration closes with உரைப்போன் and Maadalan's speech begins.

reading: Maadalan recalls the day the elder courtesans proposed to name the infant daughter of Madhavi, and Kovalan said that an ancestor of his, shipwrecked at midnight on the sea, had been kept afloat because of his meritorious gifts until the goddess Manimekalai came at Indra's bidding, told him not to fear because the merit of his great giving does not fail, and saved him; so the child must bear the name of that family deity, and a thousand courtesans hailed her Manimekalai while Kovalan, with Madhavi, poured gold from his hands.
nuance: This is the first naming of Manimekalai in the epic, and it ties her name to a sea goddess who rescues for merit, the role the goddess plays for Manimekalai herself in the sequel. The rescue is credited to giving (புண்ணிய தானம், பெருந் தானம்), not to devotion, and the goddess acts on Indra's command (இந்திரன் ஏவலின்).
event: At the naming of Madhavi's daughter Kovalan has her called Manimekalai after the goddess who saved his shipwrecked ancestor, and pours out gold gifts.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 21 with Maadalan's speech (the old unit began at 17, mid-narration) and ends at line 41, where the naming scene closes with the gold poured out (பொழிய); the next clause opens a new episode, the Brahmin who came for gifts.

reading: Maadalan goes on: on that day an aged Brahmin, bent and leaning on a staff, coming to receive gifts, was seized by a rogue elephant that had thrown off its driver, and Kovalan, shouting, freed the man from its trunk, entered between its tusks, sat on its neck like a vidyadhara on a black hill and tamed it, and Maadalan hails him as the compassionate warrior who subdued the elephant.
nuance: The vocative கருணை மறவ joins compassion and martial courage in a merchant; the feat is told as one more of Kovalan's good deeds in a list that will end in the question why such a man suffers (lines 91 to 94).
event: A rogue elephant seizes an old Brahmin who came for gifts, and Kovalan frees him and tames the elephant.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the old units 33-48 and 49-64 split the elephant episode in mid-sentence at line 48; this unit runs from line 42 (the Brahmin's arrival) to line 53, which closes the episode with the vocative கருணை மறவ.

reading: Maadalan tells how a Brahmin, after the mongoose they kept as a child came to its death, left for the north with his grieving wife following, telling her that living on food from her hand was no longer his duty and giving her a leaf written in Sanskrit to be placed in the hands of men who know duty; she went from house to house through the merchants' streets crying for someone to take the fruit of her deed, and Kovalan called her, heard her trouble, took the leaf, gave her wealth, had her wrong removed by gifts as the Brahmins' books lay down, brought back her husband and set them on a good path, and Maadalan hails him as one whose wealth never fails.
nuance: The text says only that the mongoose came to its death (பெரும்பிறிது ஆக) and that the wife was scorned (எள்ளிய); that she herself caused the death is implied by line 71, which calls her the one who did a harmful deed (தீத்திறம் புரிந்தோள்), not told. Kovalan does not take the sin on himself: he pays for the expiation the Brahmins' law books prescribe, and the merchant's wealth is what makes the rite possible.
event: A Brahmin leaves his wife after their pet mongoose dies; Kovalan pays for her expiation by gifts and brings her husband back.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 54 (the mongoose) to line 75, where the episode closes with the vocative செல்லாச் செல்வ; the old boundary at 64/65 fell between her cry and her answer.

reading: Maadalan tells how a poor man who bore false witness to a chaste wife's husband about what he did not know was caught in the noose of the spirit that beats and devours, how Kovalan, seeing the man's mother grieve, ran to the spirit and offered his own life for the man's, and how the spirit refused, saying it had no way of taking a good life for a hell-bound one and losing the higher state, and struck the man dead before him; Kovalan went away with the grieving woman and for many years fed the dead man's kin, and Maadalan, having listed these good deeds of this birth, asks whether it is the fruit of a former birth that Kovalan now suffers alone with his jewel of a wife.
nuance: Maadalan's question (உம்மைப் பயன்கொல்) is the first time in the Madurai book that a character reasons from undeserved suffering to a deed of a former birth: the good deeds of this life (இம்மைச் செய்தன யானறி நல்வினை) are known and cannot explain it, so the cause must lie further back. It is put as a question, not a verdict. The spirit's refusal shows its justice cannot be bought even with a good man's life. விருத்தகோபால (line 94) is an address to Kovalan; whether விருத்த means 'old', 'vowed' or something else here is not clear. Whether தவ்வை (line 80) is the man's mother or his elder sister is not settled by the line.
event: The spirit seizes a false witness; Kovalan offers his life for the man's, the spirit refuses and kills him, and Kovalan supports the dead man's family for years.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the old boundary at 82/83 cut Kovalan's offer from the spirit's answer; the unit runs from line 76 (the chaste wife) to line 94, where Maadalan's question ends with வினவ.

reading: Kovalan answers with a dream he had at midnight as vivid as waking: in the guarded city of the king, because of a petty man, his wife fell into trembling distress, his garment was seized and he rode a horned beast; then, with his wife, he reached the state of those who have cut their bonds, Kama flung his flower arrows on the bare ground and stood helpless, and Madhavi gave Manimekalai before the virtuous one of the shining Bodhi tree; and he fears that something bad will soon come.
nuance: The dream compresses the rest of the story in order: the petty man (குறுமகன்) is the goldsmith to come, the seized garment and the ride on a horned beast are signs of death, the couple's reaching the state of the unbound (பிணிப்பறுத்தோர் தம் பெற்றி) is their afterlife, and Madhavi's giving her daughter before the Buddha (போதி அறவோன்) is the Manimekalai's opening. Kovalan reads only the first part, as a coming harm; he does not answer Maadalan's question about a former birth.
event: Kovalan tells Maadalan a dream of his wife's distress, his own seizure and death-ride, and Madhavi's giving their daughter to the Buddha.
unit_note: Unit split: the old unit 83-98 and 99-113 cut the dream at line 98; this unit runs from line 95 (கோவலன் கூறும்) to line 106, where the dream closes with கடிதீங் குறுமென.

reading: Kavunthi and Maadalan tell Kovalan that this outer quarter is fit only for those on the path of dharma, that the merchants of the inner city will receive him at the mention of his name, and that he should enter great Madurai with his wife before the sun sets.
nuance: Lines 107 and 108 make the ascetics' quarter unfit for a householder, so the couple must leave the place the narration called 'dharma-bearing' (line 7) for the city where the killing will happen. அரைசர் பின்னோர் ('those after the kings') names the merchant class by rank.
event: Kavunthi and Maadalan urge Kovalan to leave the ascetics' quarter and enter Madurai with his wife before sunset.
unit_note: Unit split: the unit runs from line 107 to line 114, where the sentence closes with கூறுங் காலை; the old unit 99-113 ended one line before the verb.

reading: As they speak, the old herdswoman Maadari, coming back from offering milk rice to the yakshi of the outer quarter, worships Kavunthi; Kavunthi, judging that the life of herders who tend cows and give their yield has no crookedness and that this old woman is blameless and kind, tells her that when Kovalan's people hear whose son he is they will receive him like a guest of great worth, and that until he enters a rich man's house she gives Kannaki to Maadari as a charge in her keeping.
nuance: This is the act that names the kaathai: அடைக்கலம் here is a ward placed in another's protection, the sense the rest of the chapter builds on, not the Saiva self-surrender to the Lord that the concept usually tags elsewhere. Kavunthi's trust rests on a judgment of the herders' way of life as a whole (கோவலர் வாழ்க்கை), not on knowledge of Maadari herself. பூங்கண் இயக்கி is a yakshi goddess, and Maadari, a herdswoman, worships her and a Jain ascetic alike.
event: Maadari worships Kavunthi, who judges her trustworthy and entrusts Kannaki to her keeping.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 115 (அறம்புரி நெஞ்சின்), with Maadari's arrival, since line 114 closes the sentence of Kavunthi's and Maadalan's advice; it ends at line 130, where Kavunthi's entrusting closes with அடைக்கலந் தந்தேன்.

reading: Kavunthi tells Maadari to bathe Kannaki, line her eyes, put flowers in her hair, dress her in clean cloth and be her companions, guard and mother; she says the earth never knew this girl's small feet, that in the scorching sun she grieved for her husband's pain and never for her own, that she has seen no goddess fairer than this one who bears the vow of the chastity a wife cannot be without, and asks whether Maadari does not know the good saying that where chaste wives live the sky does not fail, plenty does not falter and the victory of kings does not decay.
nuance: Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity (இத்தெய்வம்), the strongest claim yet about her, and grounds it in her bearing pain for her husband and not for herself. The saying of lines 145 to 147 is quoted as common wisdom (அத்தகு நல்லுரை), not as Jain teaching, and it pledges the king's victory to the presence of pathini women: the Pandya of this very city will fall because of one.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 131 (the bathing) to line 148, where the saying closes with அறியா யோநீ; the old boundary at 147/148 cut the saying from its question.

reading: Kavunthi adds that a charge held for the ascetics, however small, yields very great joy, and tells a story: at Puhar, under the flowering asoka on the shining stone seat the world's ascetics had set up, where the charanas preached dharma, there appeared a god with a body bright as a rainbow, garlands and gold ornaments, a form the world cannot see, with a black-fingered monkey's hand on one part of him, and when the lay hearers worshipped the charanas and asked why he came, the chief of them spoke.
nuance: தவத்தோர் அடைக்கலம் can be read as a charge entrusted by ascetics, as Kavunthi has just entrusted Kannaki, or as refuge given to ascetics; the story that follows (a monkey that a sage bids a housewife cherish) fits the first. The setting is Jain throughout: the asoka (பிண்டி), the charanas (சாரணர்), the lay hearers (சாவகர்).
event: At Puhar a god with a monkey's hand appears before the Jain charanas, and the lay hearers ask why.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 149 with Kavunthi's maxim (the old unit began at 148, the last line of the saying); its end at 162 is unchanged.

reading: The chief charana tells that in the house of Etti Saayalan, where many fasting ascetics came, as the lady of the house was receiving a great ascetic, a small town monkey crept in, touched his feet, drank a little of the leftover food and the water he had spilled, and looked up into his face, and the sage, pleased, told the lady to cherish it as her own children.
nuance: The monkey's merit begins with eating an ascetic's leftovers (மிச்சில்) and looking into his face, and with the sage's word that turns an animal into a ward: the story is built to fit Kavunthi's maxim of a charge held for ascetics.
event: A monkey eats a visiting ascetic's leftovers in Saayalan's house, and the ascetic bids the housewife raise it as her child.

reading: The charana goes on: keeping the sage's true word, the woman cared for the monkey, and when it died she set aside a share of her gifts in its name so its evil might end; so it was born the son of Uttara Kauttan in Varanasi of the middle country, excellent in form, fortune and understanding, made many gifts, and after thirty-two years died and took the form of a god; and, saying that all the fruit of this was the virtue of the gift of the woman who had raised him, and that the monkey's small hand on part of the god's body shows he became this form through Saayalan's wife's gift, the chief showed him to the hearers, and the god's son appeared.
nuance: Merit here passes from one being to another: the woman's gift, made for the monkey's share (அதற்கொரு கூறு), raises it to a human birth, and that birth's own gifts raise it to the gods. The god's body keeps the monkey's hand, so the reward of merit is itself a birth that still bears the mark of the one before. That the woman made the gift so that the monkey's evil should end (தீதறுக) treats an animal birth as the fruit of evil to be cleared.
event: The charana tells how the monkey, through the housewife's gift in its name, was reborn a prince and then a god, and shows the god to the hearers.

reading: Kavunthi ends that those who took the charanas' good words as precious and turned to dharma, the ascetics of that city, the lay hearers who lived restrained lives and the merchant and his wife of the gift, reached the final world of unbroken joy; and she tells Maadari that, having heard this, she should go with the girl without delay.
nuance: The giving couple reach not another heaven but the final world (முடிவுலகு), and the line ties this to hearing the charanas and turning to dharma (அறந்தலைப் பட்டோர்), not to the gift alone. Kavunthi tells the story to bind Maadari to her charge; the story promises great joy to the keeper, which the later kaathais do not give Maadari.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit runs from line 192 to line 199, where Kavunthi's speech closes with நீபோ கென்றே; the old unit 192-207 ran on into the narration of Maadari's walk home.

reading: When Kavunthi has spoken, Maadari praises her gladly and, as the sun goes down and cows call for their calves, sets out with the wise young Kannaki, herdsmen with axes on their shoulders and pot-slings and herdswomen around them, passes through the gate of Madurai, bristling beyond its moat with the fort's engines, bows, slings, boiling oil and molten metal, hooks, stakes and iron bars, spears and every other device, where the day's banners wave, and enters her house, holding to what she had taken on.
nuance: The long list of war engines on Madurai's wall (lines 207 to 216) is the city's defence against siege at the very moment it admits the woman whose wrong will burn it. Among the engines is a black-fingered monkey (கருவிர லூகம்), set against the black-fingered monkey (கருவிரற் குரங்கு, line 159) of Kavunthi's tale. The closing word கொள்கையிற் புணர்ந்து says Maadari took on the charge as her resolve.
event: Maadari takes Kannaki through Madurai's fortified gate at sunset and brings her home.
unit_note: Boundary moved: the unit begins at line 200 (கவுந்தி கூற), where the narration resumes, and runs to the end; the old boundary at 207/208 fell in the middle of the list of engines.

title: கொலைக்களக் காதை
theme: The killing: lodged with the herdswoman Maadari, Kannaki cooks Kovalan's last meal, he confesses his heedlessness and she her silent endurance, and he goes to sell one anklet; the goldsmith who stole the queen's anklet accuses him, the king orders the thief killed without inquiry, the goldsmith talks down the guards' doubts with a lore of thieves' arts, and a drunken guard cuts Kovalan down; the narrator and the closing venba give the king's bent sceptre and Kovalan's former deed as causes of the one death.
source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 221 lines as shown (217 of akaval and a four-line venba) against the edition's printed last line 215.
Lines 41, 128 and 174 carry the repair of ௌ read as ெள from old fonts (தெளித்து, வெளிப்படா, தெளிகுவர்); the repaired readings make sense.

Unit boundaries fall inside speeches: 33-47 ends in the middle of the herdswomen's question, 48-61 holds both their wonder and the start of Kovalan's speech, 62-73 and 74-90 each hold the end of one speech and the start of the reply, and 178-193 ends in the middle of the goldsmith's tale; the units are kept as cut because other chapters already link to 62-73 and 74-90.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, lodged with the herdswoman Maadari in Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom the ascetic Kavunthi entrusted Kannaki (named here as இடைக்குல மடந்தை and தவ்வை)
Maadari's daughter, who serves Kannaki
the herdswomen of Maadari's settlement, acting together
the royal goldsmith of Madurai who accused Kovalan of theft
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as தென்னவன், வேம்பன், காவலன், மன்னவன்)
the Pandya's chief queen
the Pandya's guards who carry out the killing
a young spearman among the guards who tells of a thief who took his sword
the drunken, unlettered guard whose sword kills Kovalan

reading: Glad to have received Kannaki as a ward, the herdswoman Maadari lodges her in a guarded little house apart from the herders' dwellings, has the herdswomen bathe her, tells her that her daughter Aiyai will be her servant and that she will keep her as if wrapped in gold, and so settles her in a place she thinks free of harm.
nuance: Maadari's praise turns Kannaki's lack of ornament into a beauty that spoils the worth of the Madurai women's gold (செய்யாக் கோலம்), and she bows to her ward. The last line's ஏதம் இல்லா இடம் repeats the word with which Kavunthi judged it safe to leave Kannaki with Maadari (15:124, ஏதம் இன்று), so the 'harmless place' is named on the day of the killing.
event: Maadari lodges Kannaki in a guarded house, has her bathed and gives her Aiyai as a servant.

reading: Maadari bids the herdswomen bring at once good vessels for cooking the day's meal, since Kovalan is a lord who keeps the lay disciple's vow, and they bring the vessels with gourds, vegetables, pomegranate, mango and plantain, rice and milk, which Kannaki takes and begins to cut and cook until her face sweats and her eyes redden in the smoky kitchen.
nuance: சாவக நோன்பிகள் names Kovalan as one under the vow of a lay disciple; in the preceding kaathai the word சாவகர் is used for the lay hearers of the Jain charanas (15:190, 195), and the meal of the day (நாள்வழிப் படூஉம் அடிசில்) may point to the lay rule of eating before dark, though the Tamil does not say so. The merchant's daughter cooking with her own hands, her soft fingers reddening, is the first housekeeping she has done since Puhar. நும்மகனார் and நாத்தூண் நங்கை (the husband's sister) give the herders kin-terms for their guests, but whom each names is not clear.
event: The herdswomen bring vessels and provisions at Maadari's word, and Kannaki starts cooking.

reading: With Aiyai lighting the fire, Kannaki cooks with her untrained hands, seats Kovalan on a mat of palm leaf, washes his feet from an earthen bowl, sprinkles water on the ground as if to clear the earth goddess's distress, spreads a young plantain leaf and bids him eat, and he eats after completing the rites proper to the merchant order, while the herders' women begin to wonder whether he is the dark god Yasoda bore.
nuance: Kovalan, just called a lay disciple under vow, first performs what the sacred text (அருமறை) prescribes for those after kings (அரசர் பின்னோர், the merchant order), so the meal joins a vow-keeper's diet to caste rite without comment. The water sprinkled 'as if to clear the bewilderment of the earth-woman' (மண்ணக மடந்தையை மயக்கொழிப் பனள்போல், line 40) returns at line 215, when the same earth-woman's grief grows under his blood. The unit ends in the middle of the women's question, which runs on into the next.
event: Kannaki cooks with Aiyai's help, washes Kovalan's feet and serves him, and he eats after his rites.

reading: Aiyai and her mother marvel that the man eating is the god of the flower-dark hue and the woman the lamp of their own clan who once relieved his distress in the Yamuna, a sight their eyes cannot hold; Kannaki gives Kovalan betel, and he draws her close, asks how her soft feet bore the stony desert path, and wonders aloud what has befallen his old parents and whether this is illusion or a strong former deed.
nuance: The herders see their guests as Krishna and his herd-clan consort (the Tamil does not name Pinnai here), the pair whose kuravai Maadari will dance in the next kaathai to ward off coming harm. Kovalan's மாயங் கொல்லோ வல்வினை கொல்லோ is a question, not a claim: he does not yet know whether to blame illusion or karma, and in the next lines he blames himself.
event: Aiyai and Maadari liken the couple to Krishna and his consort; Kovalan, given betel, asks Kannaki how she bore the road.

reading: Kovalan says his mind is confused and he knows nothing, that keeping company with men of empty talk and idle rakes he grew heedless, that he failed the bidding of his parents and wronged his wise young wife, and asks what she has done in rising to come with him to this city; Kannaki begins her answer, that she had lost the giving to the virtuous, the tending of Brahmins, the receiving of ascetics and the welcoming of guests.
nuance: Karma and his own fault stand side by side: the line before asked whether this was வல்வினை, and now he names பொச்சாப்பு, bad company and disobedience as his own failures. Lines 65-66 (பொருளுரை யாளர் நச்சுக்கொன் றேற்கும் நன்னெறி யுண்டோ) are hard; they seem to ask whether there is any good way left for one who has spurned the counsel of the wise, but the sense of நச்சு is doubtful. Kannaki's four lost duties are the householder's duties, which she could not keep without her husband.
event: Kovalan confesses his heedlessness and wrongs, and Kannaki begins to answer.

reading: Kannaki goes on: when his mother and his wealthy father set aside their old anger and praised her lovingly, her smile that seemed to deny the grief she hid only pained them more; though he followed unworthy ways, she, whose life does not gainsay him, rose and came; Kovalan answers by praising her, who left kin, servants and companions with modesty, innocence and chastity as her only companions and has removed his sorrow, as gold, creeper, doll of modesty and lamp of the wide earth.
nuance: Kannaki's reply blames his conduct plainly (போற்றா வொழுக்கம் புரிந்தீர்) while setting her own rule as not opposing him (மாற்றா உள்ள வாழ்க்கை); the epic lets her name the fault and still follow. The grief she hid behind a smile before his parents is told only here. Kovalan's praise counts karpu as a companion (பெருந்துணை) in place of the kin and servants she left.
event: Kannaki tells why she followed Kovalan, and he praises her chastity and companionship.

reading: Calling her the shoot of chastity, Kovalan says he will take one anklet from her small foot, go and exchange it and return, embraces her alone with burning heart and hidden tears, and leaves; walking unsteadily through the streets he does not know as an ill omen the humped bull that comes against him, since reading such signs is not his class's knowledge, and in the bazaar street he meets a goldsmith with a hundred craftsmen behind him and asks whether he can price an anklet fit for the queen.
nuance: The narrator excuses Kovalan's blindness to the omen by his birth (தன்குலம் அறியுந் தகுதியன்று), not by his fault; the herders, whose knowledge it is, will read their own bull's tears as coming harm in the next kaathai. The goldsmith is drawn before he speaks, walking aslant (விலங்குநடை) in a tunic with tongs in hand, and Kovalan takes him for the craftsman honoured with the Pandya's name.
event: Kovalan takes one anklet, leaves Kannaki, passes an ill omen unheeded and asks a goldsmith to price the anklet.

reading: The goldsmith, a messenger of Death, bows and says he makes the crowns and jewels of kings, examines the anklet's workmanship, declares that it fits none but the queen, tells Kovalan to wait in his hut near the temple while he informs the king, and resolves to pass off on this stranger the queen's anklet that he himself had stolen before his theft comes to light.
nuance: The narrator reveals the goldsmith as the real thief here, before the accusation, so the reader watches the whole frame-up knowingly. His verdict that the anklet fits only the queen is the claim the breaking of the anklet will disprove (20:74-91), since Kannaki's holds gems and the queen's pearls.
event: The goldsmith inspects the anklet, lodges Kovalan in his hut and plans to blame him for his own theft.

reading: The goldsmith goes on with calm hidden heart; the king, whose queen, sulking because the dances and songs of Madurai's women had captured his heart, had pleaded a headache and gone away, leaves his council for her palace with her maids, and at its gate the goldsmith falls at his feet and tells him that the thief who took the palace anklet without breaching wall or using a forked pole, putting the gatekeepers to sleep by a spell, is hiding in his hut.
nuance: The accusation reaches the king when he has left his ministers (மந்திரச் சுற்றம் நீங்கி) to make peace with a sulking queen; the epic gives this setting without naming it a cause, and in the next lines the narrator gives the cause as the ripening of a deed. The goldsmith's tale of a thief working by mantra prepares his later lecture on thieves' arts.
event: At the queen's gate the goldsmith tells the king that the thief of the palace anklet is in his hut.

reading: Since it was the time for the deed to ripen, the neem-garlanded king, inquiring into nothing, calls the city guards and orders them to kill the thief if he holds the queen's anklet and bring it; the goldsmith, his purpose achieved, brings them to Kovalan, caught in the net of his ripened evil deed, and shows them the anklet, but the guards say that a man who bears himself by the marks of good birth is not one to be put to death.
nuance: One ripening is given two subjects: the time of the deed (வினைவிளை காலம்) makes the king fail to inquire, and the net of the matured evil deed (தீவினை முதிர்வலை) holds Kovalan, so whose deed ripens is left open between them. The order கொன்றச் சிலம்பு கொணர்க condemns before any hearing. The guards' doubt is the one hesitation in the chain.
event: The king, without inquiry, orders the thief killed; the goldsmith leads the guards to Kovalan, who they say does not look like a thief.

reading: Laughing inwardly at the guards, the goldsmith lectures them that thieves roam with eight aids, mantra, deity, drug, omen, technique, place, time and tool, and that if they use a drug the guards will suffer worse than from the king, if mantra they will be as invisible as Indra's sons, if a divine form they will show the stolen thing in hand and still go, and if they cloud the guards' eyes with drugs, the guards will not even keep their names and place.
nuance: The real thief makes himself the expert on theft and turns the guards' good judgement of Kovalan's bearing into a sign of the thief's skill: the better the man looks, the more dangerous. The eightfold list is set out as a lore with its own order (இழுக்குடை மரபு), named a faulty tradition even in his mouth.
event: The goldsmith lectures the guards on the eight aids of thieves.

reading: The goldsmith goes on through the other aids, that with a true omen a priceless thing falls into their hands, with technique they would take even the garland from Indra's chest, with the right place and time no one sees or stops them, with tools no one on earth can catch them, and night and day are one to them, and begins a tale of a thief who in a messenger's guise and then a woman's slipped through the dark and the lamp's shadow toward a prince's shining necklace.
nuance: The lecture goes item by item in the order of the list (omen, technique, place, time, tool), and its claim that the thief has no refuge if one asks for his hiding place (கரவிடங் கேட்பினோர் புகலிட மில்லை) presses the guards to act at once. The unit breaks in the middle of the tale, whose verb comes in line 194.

reading: The goldsmith ends his tale, how the thief took the prince's necklace, dodged his sword and slipped away, and asks who in the world can match such men; a young spearman tells of a thief with a digging chisel and blue cloth who took his own sword from his hand one rainy midnight and vanished, and bids the guards do what is fit, since such men's deeds are hard to know and the king will punish them; then a drunken, unlettered guard throws his sword and cuts Kovalan across, his blood floods the ground and the earth goddess grieves, and Kovalan falls as the king's sceptre bends, his former deed come in wrath.
nuance: The killer is not the king or the guards who doubted but a கல்லாக் களிமகன், a drunken man without learning, so the bent sceptre works through its least fit instrument. The last two lines give two causes in one sentence, the king's sceptre bent (செங்கோல் வளைஇய) and Kovalan's former deed come in wrath (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து), the patikam's first and third morals at once. Line 210 (அலைக்கும் வேந்தனும்) is read as the king who will punish them, but the sense is not certain.
event: After the goldsmith's and a young guard's tales of uncatchable thieves, a drunken guard cuts Kovalan down with his sword.

reading: The closing venba bids all, since both kinds of deed will surely reach them, to turn to good dharma, for the never-bending sceptre bent on earth because of Kannaki's husband, the fruit of an old deed come to ripeness.
nuance: The moral drawn is not only that kings should judge carefully but that every hearer should do good, since good and evil deeds alike come back; the bent sceptre is made the fruit of Kovalan's old deed, which lifts the blame from the king in the same breath as it names the bending.

title: ஆய்ச்சியர் குரவை (1/2)
theme: The first half of the herdswomen's kuravai: on the morning after Kovalan's killing, Madari finds the milk, butter and cattle showing signs of a coming sorrow, and to avert it sets seven herd girls, each pledged by the bull-catch formula to a bull's tamer and named for one of the seven notes, to dance before Kannaki the kuravai of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai; the first song asks that the herders' god come among the cows today.
source_issues: Line 13 reads உருகா உருகும் where the prose restatement (lines 18 to 19) has உருகாமையும்; the couplet's sense is unsure.
Line 18 was repaired by the build (a doubled vowel sign reduced to one).

Lines 31 to 32 and 37 to 38 pledge girls to the rider of a young bull in nearly the same words, as do lines 33 to 34 and 35 to 36 for the spotted white bull; the text may carry a doubling, though seven bulls are needed for seven girls.
Line 58 (முத்தைக்கு நல்விளரி தான்) is obscure, and vilari is placed twice (lines 56 and 58).

cast.role: the old herdswoman of Madurai in whose house Kannaki was lodged (named here இடைமுதுமகள்)
Madari's daughter
the seven herd girls of Madari's kuravai, named for the seven notes and cast as Mayavan, his elder brother, Pinnai and the rest

reading: Because the morning drum will sound in the palace of the Pandya, whose fish is inscribed on the brow of the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow and whose orders the kings of Navalam obey, the old herdswoman, saying that today is their turn to bring ghee, calls her daughter Aiyai and comes out with churning rope and churn.
nuance: The kaathai opens on the Pandya's glory and the ordinary round of service his house draws from the herders (நெய்ம்முறை, their turn to supply ghee) on the morning after his men have killed Kovalan; the king is praised by his emblem and not named. Unlike the Kalittokai's boast that the fish replaced the tiger and the bow, the fish here stands beside them (அயலெழுதிய).
event: Madari, saying it is their turn to supply ghee to the palace, calls her daughter Aiyai and comes with churning rope and churn.

reading: The first sign: the milk in the pots will not set, and tears run from the eyes of the bull with the heaped hump; something is coming.
nuance: Each of the three couplets ends on the same refrain (வருவதொன் றுண்டு), and the prose that follows (lines 17 to 20) gathers them as the old woman's own reading, so the voice is hers though no line names her.
event: The milk in the pots fails to curdle and the bull sheds tears.

reading: The second sign: the fragrant butter in the hanging pot does not melt, and the lambs do not leap and play; something is coming.
nuance: Line 13 reads உருகா உருகும், which taken literally sets 'does not melt' against 'melts'; the prose restatement at lines 18 and 19 has only உருகாமையும் (its not melting), and this reading follows it.
event: The butter will not melt and the lambs lie still.

reading: The third sign: the cows stand trembling and lowing in pity, and the bells of the cattle fall; something is coming.
event: The cows tremble and low, and the cattle's bells drop to the ground.

reading: Summing up the signs as a sorrow to come, the old woman tells her daughter not to be troubled: with Kannaki, the ornament of the women of the earth, looking on, they will dance the kuravai that Mayavan danced with his elder brother and with long-eyed Pinnai among the boyhood plays of the cattle-yard of Ayarpadi, so that the distress of the cows and calves may pass.
nuance: The remedy is a rite: a re-enactment of Krishna's childhood dance among the herds, set against an evil the signs do not name. The reader knows what the herders do not, that Kovalan was killed the day before (16:194-217), so the distress of cows and calves the dance is meant to lift stands for a loss already done. Kannaki is placed as the dance's onlooker, not a dancer.
event: Madari reads the omens as a coming sorrow and resolves to dance the kuravai of Mayavan before Kannaki to avert it.

reading: This girl, garlanded with honeyed flowers, will love the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, leapt upon it.
nuance: The pledge is the bull-catch formula of the herders (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான், as in Kalittokai 104), but here no bull is penned and no man leaps: the old woman names each girl by the bull her tamer would take, as the first of the dance's roles. The speaker is inferred from lines 41 to 44, where she sets the seven girls in order.

reading: The shoulders of this girl with golden bangles belong to the man who subdues the red bull with the mark on its brow.
This girl with mullai flowers in her hair belongs to the man who rides the strong young bull.
nuance: This couplet and lines 37 to 38 both pledge a girl to the rider of a young bull (மழவிடை யூர்ந்தாற்கு), told apart only by the epithets மல்லல் and வென்றி.

reading: The shoulders of this creeper-like girl go only to the man who subdues the white bull with fine spots.
This good, creeper-like girl with soft breasts goes only to the men who subdue the white bull with golden spots.
nuance: Nearly the same couplet as lines 33 to 34, with பொற்பொறி for நுண்பொறி and the plural அடர்த்தார்க்கே for the singular.

reading: This girl with konrai flowers in her hair belongs to the man who rides the victorious young bull.
This girl like a fresh poovai flower belongs to the man who subdues the pure white bull.
nuance: With the black bull of line 27, this makes seven bulls for seven girls.

reading: So, saying to her daughter that these are the seven young girls for whom bulls were raised in the pen, the old herdswoman sets them in the ancient order and names them, going round from the west, after the seven notes: kural, tuttam, kaikkilai, uzhai, ili, vilari and taram, the names the flower-haired one wanted.
nuance: The ring of dancers is laid out as the circle of the seven notes, so the dance is also a scale. Whose wish the closing words name (விரிதரு பூங்குழல்) is not clear: the old woman, her daughter, or each girl.
event: Madari sets the seven herd girls in a ring and names them after the seven notes.

reading: She called kural Mayavan, ili the victorious Vellai (his elder brother), and tuttam the herd girl Pinnai, and said the rest keep their former names in order.
event: Madari gives three of the notes the roles of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai.

reading: She sets the places: Pinnai and taram stand in Mayavan's measure, uzhai and vilari in white Vellai's, kaikkilai stands at Pinnai's left, and vilari to the right.
nuance: The places seem to follow the concords between the notes, so who stands beside whom is a matter of the scale. Line 58 (முத்தைக்கு நல்விளரி தான்) is obscure, and vilari is named in both lines 56 and 58.
event: Madari assigns each dancer her place in the ring.

reading: Of them, the one who lays the cool tulasi garland on Mayavan enters the ceaseless kuravai, and the herd girl cries out in wonder that this bangled one is their own Pinnai, set beside the Tiru on the chest of him who measured the world.
nuance: The sense of திருநோக்கா (line 62) is unsure: whether Pinnai is one Tiru looks upon, or one who does not look to Tiru, the herd girl ranks the herders' own Pinnai with the goddess on Vishnu's chest. Which herd girl cries out (ஆயர் மகள், line 64) is not clear.
event: The girl playing Pinnai garlands the girl playing Mayavan with tulasi and joins the dance.

reading: Standing in a true circle with their hands joined in the crab clasp, they work out the dance measures; the first, kural, looks to her kin and says they will sing the sweet mullai tune of the one who broke the kurundu tree in the field, and as she takes kural low, ili level, tuttam strong and vilari low in their due order, her companion takes up the song after her.
nuance: The kurundu tree recalls a feat of Krishna's boyhood, so the tune chosen is itself a story of the god among the herds.
event: The seven girls join hands in the ring and begin the mullai song.

reading: The first song: if Mayavan, who knocked down the fruit using a calf as his throwing stick, comes among our cows today, shall we not hear from his lips the sweet konrai flute, friend?
nuance: The wish that the herders' god come among the cows today (இன்று) is the rite's answer to the omens, but the herdsmen's guest, whom the household likened to the gem-coloured god (16:48-61), is already dead. The konrai flute is the herders' flute of konrai pods.

title: ஆய்ச்சியர் குரவை (2/2)
