theme: The second half of the Aaychiyar Kuravai: the herdswomen sing Maayavan's herd-village play with Pinnai, set their ring by the gods they enact, praise the three crowned kings in the ulvari as bearers of Vishnu's deeds, address Maal with the paradox of the cosmic god bound and thieving, define ear, eye and tongue by his praise, and close by asking the god to end the cattle's distress and the Pandya's drum to win daily, on the very day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan.
source_issues: Lines 146-147 spell the refrain கண்ணென்ண கண்ணே with ண where the parallel refrains have என்ன (செவி என்ன செவியே, நாவென்ன நாவே); likely a typing slip for கண்ணென்ன.
The god's consort is spelt both பின்னை (lines 85, 105, 107) and பிஞ்ஞை (line 101) within the kaathai.

cast.role: the herdswomen of the Madurai outskirts, led by the old herdswoman, who dance and sing the kuravai
Maal (Thirumaal, Narayana), the god praised in the kuravai, addressed in the second-person stanzas

reading: The herd girls open the kuravai song: if the wonder-working one who churned the sea with a snake for rope came among their cattle, would they not hear the sweet aambal-mode flute at his lips?
nuance: The cosmic deed (the churning) and the herd-village wish (his flute among 'our cattle', நம் ஆனுள்) are set in one line pair; each stanza of this song names one deed of Maayavan and one flute mode (கொன்றை, ஆம்பல், முல்லை), so the song is also a demonstration of modes.

reading: The third stanza wishes for the mullai flute of the one who broke the kurundu tree on the hill slope, and the girls turn to sing the beauty of Pinnai who danced with the lord of the Yamuna ford.
nuance: Lines 85-86 are the turn of the song from Maayavan to Pinnai (பின்னை அணிநிறம் பாடுகேம் யாம்), which the next three stanzas carry out.

reading: The girls ask what words could tell the form of him who hid the garment as Pinnai's soft grace swayed, and the face of her who wilts as he plays on.
nuance: The stanza is built as a chiasmus: each half-line answers the other, his form and her face, so the lovers' play is shown as mutual. The garment hidden (அறுவை யொளித்தான்) is the god's prank at the river.

reading: The girls ask what to call the self-possession of her who stole the heart of the trickster in the Yamuna, and the form of the trickster who took her self-possession and her bangles.
nuance: நிறை, a woman's self-containment, is here lost and won in a game: she takes his heart and he takes her நிறை and bangles. Who seized whose heart turns on how கவர்ந்தாள் is construed; the reading taken is that she captured his.

reading: The girls sing that the maiden, robbed of garment and bangles, hid her face in her hands, and that he, seeing the hidden face, suffered infatuation.
nuance: The trickster ends caught himself: மைய லுழந்தான், he laboured in infatuation. The modesty of the hidden face (கையி லொளித்தாள் முகம்) is what defeats him.

reading: The dance's arrangement is told through the myth: Pinnai stands at the left of the sea-coloured one who hid the sun with his discus and at the right of his moon-fair elder, others keep her measure, and Narada, versed in the old Veda, plucks the strings in their first order.
nuance: Part 1 of the kaathai gave each girl the name of a god and a note of the scale; this block names their places in the ring by the gods they play. 'Hid the sun with the discus' (கதிர்திகிரி யான்மறைத்த) alludes to a Krishna story the line does not tell.

reading: The second stanza turns the ring: Pinnai is now at the right of the peacock-necked Maayavan and the left of his elder, and Narada among the musicians plucks the strings in the tuned measure.
nuance: Left and right are exchanged from the stanza before, so the pair of stanzas records the dancers moving round. கயிலெருத்தம் கோட்டிய (line 105) is a rare phrase for Pinnai's bent neck.

reading: The dancers praise the kuravai danced on the dusty common by Maayavan with his elder and bangled Pinnai, the herd girls' hair garlands slipping and Asodhai praising with joined hands, as fitting.
nuance: The mythic kuravai of Ayarpadi is the model the Madurai herdswomen are copying, so praising it praises their own dance; the herd mother Asodhai worships the child-god she raises.

reading: One of the women calls all of them to praise the god whose mount is the bird, taking up the ulvari tune.
event: The herdswomen call one another to praise the bird-riding god in the ulvari mode.

reading: The first ulvari stanza says the hill's pearl string, the sea's pearl string and the necklace of the king of the gods are on the chest of the Pandya, and that the one who wears the gods' king's necklace, they say, grazed the herds at Dvaraka and broke the kurundu tree.
nuance: The 'inner vari' (உள்வரி) has the singers take on another person: the Pandya is hailed with Krishna's herd-deeds, so king and god are fused. The fusion is ironic in the story, since this king has that day ordered Kovalan's death.

reading: The second stanza hails the Chola Valavan of walled Puhar, who carved his tiger on the Himalaya and ruled the earth, as the one, they say, who bears the golden discus as weapon.
nuance: Each of the three crowns is given a mark of Vishnu: the Chola the discus (திகிரி), as the Pandya the herd-deeds and the Chera the churning. The refrain doubles line 120.

reading: The third stanza hails the Chera of prosperous Vanchi, who went into the sea and threw down the ageless kadambu, as the one who, they say, churned the sea with his stone-strong arms.
nuance: The Chera's sea-raid is renamed with the churning of the ocean (கடல்கடைந்தான்), the deed this song gave Maayavan at line 79. The stanza names only 'the Chera, king of kings', not a particular Cheralathan.

reading: Addressing the lotus-naveled god, the women say that he who once churned the sea with the north mountain for staff and Vasuki for rope had the same hand bound by Asodhai's churning cord, and ask whether this is his maayam, for it bewilders them.
nuance: Cosmic churning and the herd mother's churning rope (கடைகயிறு, the tool the old herdswoman carried in at line 9) meet in one hand. The refrain மாயமோ மருட்கைத்தே asks rather than explains.

reading: The women tell the god that, while the hosts of gods praised him as the final truth, he swallowed the whole world without hunger, and the same mouth ate stolen butter from the hanging pot.
nuance: Again the god's greatest act and his smallest theft share one organ, here the mouth; 'without hunger' (உறுபசியொன் றின்றியே) marks the swallowing of the world as play, not need.

reading: The women tell Thirumaal that with his two red-lotus feet he strode the three worlds so their darkness lifted, that the same feet walked as envoy for the Pandavas, and that he became a lion and killed the foe.
nuance: The stanza joins the cosmic stride to a humble errand, the envoy's walk, on the same feet (நடந்தஅடி repeated).

reading: Turning to the third person, the women ask what ear it is that has not heard the glory of the hero who, after his feet had spanned the three worlds in two strides, went to the forest with his brother and destroyed old Lanka, and of Thirumaal.
nuance: The 'praise in the third person' (படர்க்கைப் பரவல்) defines each sense organ by its devotion: an ear that has not heard his praise is no ear. The stanza ties the Vamana stride to the Rama story as one person's deeds.

reading: The women ask what eye it is that has not seen the great dark one, the god of the lotus navel who holds all the worlds, whose eyes, feet, hands and mouth are red, and what eyes are those that blink while looking at him.
nuance: Line 147 sharpens line 146: even an eye that sees him is faulted if it blinks, since the gods do not blink; the devotee should look unblinking.

reading: The women ask what tongue it is that does not praise or name Narayana, who overcame Kamsa's deceit and walked as envoy to the hundred for the Pandavas, then close the kuravai: may the god it praised take away the distress fallen on their cattle, and may the drum of the Pandya, who broke the crown of the thunder-armed god, bring victory day after day.
nuance: The close returns to the omens that opened the kaathai (the curd that would not set, the bulls' tears): the dance was a rite to avert them. Its last wish, victory for the Pandya's drum, is set on the day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan, so the blessing turns to irony; the next kaathai brings the news. The god is asked to protect the herd, and the king's fate is asked of his drum.
event: The herdswomen end the kuravai praying that the god remove the cattle's distress and that the Pandya's drum bring victory.

title: துன்ப மாலை
theme: Madari returns from her river worship with news heard in the town; Kannaki, not finding her husband, presses for what people say, learns that he is called the thief of the palace anklet and that the guards have killed him, laments that the king's straying sceptre has made her a widow, and calls on the sun as witness, which answers that he is no thief and that fire will eat the city.
source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai shows 53 lines against the edition's printed last line 50; short rubric-like lines (ஆங்கு, அவள்தான், எல்லாவோ, சொன்னது:-, எனக் கேட்டு, காணிகா) are counted as lines here.
Line 27 repeats line 26 (கரையாமல் வாங்கிய கள்வனாம் என்றே): flagged and kept as the song form's refrain.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, waiting in the herders' quarter for his return
Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai as a thief
the aged herdswoman (ஆயர் முதுமகள்) who leads the kuravai and in whose house Kannaki lodges
the young herdswomen who danced the kuravai with Madari
the sun, whom Kannaki calls on as witness and whose voice answers her (the next kaathai opens என்றனன் வெய்யோன்)
the Pandya's guards who carry out the killing
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as மன்னவன், தென்னவன்)

reading: Madari, who had gone to the long-flowing Vaigai with flowers, incense and garlands to worship Mal at the end of the kuravai, hurries back on hearing a stir in the town and stands without a word, while Kannaki, unable to find her husband, says her heart heaves like a forge's bellows and asks her friend what the strangers have been saying.
nuance: The refrain form (a line, then its second half repeated as the next line with அன்றே turned to ஆயின், closing on 'what did they say, friend?') makes the dread grow through the repetition before any news is told. Madari's silence is itself the message: the poem has her come back with news and not speak it. Lines 8 to 10 play on சொல்லாடாள் and சொல்லாடும், and it is not certain whether they mean Madari's silence speaks to Kannaki or that Kannaki speaks while Madari is silent; the reading here takes the second.
event: Madari returns from worship at the Vaigai having heard a rumour, and Kannaki, not finding Kovalan, asks her friend what people are saying.

reading: Kannaki's refrain continues that she trembles at noon and suspects some treachery, and the answer comes that men say he was a thief who silently took an anklet from the king's palace and that the guards with ringing anklets set out to kill him; hearing it, she rises, falls like the moon dropping with the clouds to earth, and weeps, calling for her husband.
nuance: The charge comes as hearsay: கள்வனாம் ('a thief, they say') is reported speech, and the line is repeated as the song form's refrain, so the town's word is heard twice before Kannaki falls. Her suspicion of வஞ்சம் (line 21) comes before the news and frames it as a deception. The answer does not name who tells it; the reading takes it as what the townsfolk said, carried by the friend.
event: Kannaki hears that Kovalan was called the thief of the palace anklet and marked for death by the guards, and falls weeping.

reading: Kannaki asks whether, now that the king has erred and his sceptre has strayed from right, she must waste away in grief like the women who lose their husbands to the pyre and keep the hard observances of widowhood, losing even her good name in this life; then she bids the kuravai girls listen and asks the sun, who knows all in the sea-girt world, whether her husband is a thief, and a voice answers that he is not, and that fire will eat this city.
nuance: In each of the three stanzas the cause is the king's fault alone (மன்னவன் தவறிழைப்ப, with the sceptre that wanders with cruelty and has gone beyond straightness), though the narrator had closed the killing with the king's bent sceptre and Kovalan's former deed together (16:216-217), and Kannaki herself will later name ஊழ்வினை before the king (20:69). Her question sets her apart from the widows who bathe at the ghats and keep the observances: the form 'shall I perish like them?' prepares her refusal of that path. அறனென்னும் மடவோய் (line 41) can be read as an address to Dharma itself as a simpleton that has failed her, or as an address to a naive woman; the sense is uncertain. The voice is unnamed here (ஒருகுரல்); the next kaathai opens என்றனன் வெய்யோன், making it the sun's.
event: Kannaki laments the king's wrong, calls the sun to witness whether her husband is a thief, and a voice answers that he is innocent and that fire will consume Madurai.

title: ஊர்சூழ் வரி
theme: After the Sun's answer, Kannaki walks the streets of Madurai holding her one anklet and calls the city's chaste women to witness that her husband was no thief; the townspeople read her grief as the bending of the Pandya's sceptre and the coming of a new goddess, show her Kovalan's body at dusk, and hear her lament couple the king's fault with a deed that must be eaten; Kovalan rises in a vision among the immortals, wipes her tears and leaves, and she, refusing to rejoin him until her anger is spent, goes to the king's gate.
source_issues: Core unit silappathikaram:19:1-21 ends inside the townspeople's speech (line 21 runs on into 22); boundaries moved to 1-14 and 15-34.
Line 34 is printed ஒலிபடைத்த தூர்; the word division is probably ஒலிபடைத்தது ஊர்.

Lines 73 and 74 nearly repeat each other (நின்றாள் நினைந்தாள் / நின்றால் நினைந்தாள்), and lines 74 and 75 read நின்றால் and சென்றால் where the sense wants நின்றாள் and சென்றாள்; probably a doubling or misprint.

The kaathai is one block in the core, though the metre changes at line 39 (the three lament stanzas), at line 51 (the refrain questions) and at line 72 (the closing lines); no rubric marks the changes.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, who goes through Madurai with her anklet
Kannaki's husband, killed as a thief, seen here dead and then in a vision among the immortals
the Sun, whose answer to Kannaki closes the preceding kaathai
the chaste wives of Madurai whom Kannaki calls to witness
the people of Madurai, who grieve with Kannaki and show her Kovalan's body
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as அரசன், தென்னவன், பாண்டியன், மன்னவன், தீவேந்தன்)

reading: With the Sun's word just spoken, Kannaki does not stand still but, holding her one anklet, calls on the chaste wives living in the city of a king without justice to hear her: she has suffered what none has suffered, her husband was no thief but was killed for the price of her anklet, and she will see him before the women and hear a faultless word from his mouth, or let them scorn her as one who did a wrong.
nuance: Each of her six statements closes with ஈதொன்று, 'this is one thing', so the speech is built as a count of grievances and vows. She calls her witnesses நிறையுடைப் பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர், giving the women of the city the same standing she claims, and puts herself under their judgment: if she does not hear her husband's word, they may scorn her (எள்ளல்). The charge against the king is already in her address, முறையில் அரசன், before anyone in the city has spoken.
event: Kannaki, holding her one anklet, calls on the chaste women of Madurai to hear that her husband was killed as a thief for the price of her anklet.
unit_note: End moved from line 21 to line 14: Kannaki's speech closes on line 14 with இதுவொன்றென்று, and line 15 begins the narration of the townspeople; the core boundary at 21 fell inside their speech, whose sentence runs on into line 22.

reading: The people of Madurai, seeing her weep beyond bearing, ask in bewilderment whether this is the unbending sceptre bent, the Pandya's victory broken, the cool umbrella breeding heat, a new great goddess come among them for their sake, a woman possessed; the crowd shows her her husband, she sees him who cannot see her, and as the sun hides behind the mountain her cry fills the dusk and the city resounds.
nuance: The townspeople, not Kannaki, are the first to name the king's fault: their refrain இதுவென்கொல் moves from the bent sceptre and the umbrella that cools the earth now giving heat to a stranger goddess (வம்பப் பெருந்தெய்வம்) come 'for our sake', so the city reads one woman's grief at once as the failure of rule and as the arrival of a deity. Madurai is called a city whose people spread the king's blame (மன்பழி தூற்றுங் குடியதே). Line 15 (அல்லலுற் றாற்றா தழுவாளை) is close to Kural 555's opening, but the verb differs and the run is shorter than four words, so it is not marked as an echo. Line 34 is printed ஒலிபடைத்த தூர், probably ஒலிபடைத்தது ஊர.
event: The people of Madurai grieve with Kannaki, ask whether the king's sceptre has bent, and show her Kovalan's body as the sun sets, and her cry fills the city.
unit_note: Start moved from line 22 to line 15 (Kannaki's speech ends at 14); end kept at line 34, where the sentence closes with ஊர் and the next line begins the scene at the body.

reading: She who that morning took the garland from her husband's hair for her own tresses sees him at evening with blood flowing from his wounds, and laments that his fragrant golden body lies in the dust before her, alone in the dusk, while she does not know the cruel deed behind the king's harm, and asks whether no one will tell her: this is the deed that tears, the deed that must be eaten, now that the Pandya has erred and the world spreads his blame.
nuance: The three stanzas of the lament hold both causes in each closing pair of lines: the king commits the fault (பாண்டியன் தவறிழைப்ப, மன்னவன் தவறிழைப்ப) and yet what has come is a வினை to be eaten (உண்பதோர் வினை), and she calls herself one who has a harsh deed (கடுவினை யுடையேன்). She does not know which deed (மறவினை யறியாதேற்கு); the patikam's goddess will name it. The morning garland and the evening wound frame one day of the marriage.
event: Kannaki sees Kovalan's wounded body at dusk and laments over it.

reading: Kannaki asks whether there are wives who bear their husbands' affliction, worthy men who raise the children they beget, or any god in the Koodal of a king who erred with the sword; as she embraces her husband's chest he rises, wipes her tears saying her moon face has faded, and when she falls and grasps his feet he rises whole among a host of immortals, bids her stay, and goes; she asks whether it was illusion or a deluding god, vows not to join him until her anger cools and to face the cruel king, and, remembering her evil dream, goes weeping to the palace gate.
nuance: Her vow in the opening speech, to hear a faultless word from his mouth, is answered only by a tender word about her faded face and the command to stay (இருந்தைக்க, a rare form), and she herself judges it no word of substance (பொருளுரையோ இதுவன்று). She rejects the vision as a reason to grieve and turns to judgment: காய்சினந் தணிந்தன்றிக் கணவனைக் கைகூடேன். The three questions (பெண்டிரும், சான்றோரும், தெய்வமும் உண்டுகொல்) test the city's wives, its men and its god in turn. Lines 73 and 74 nearly repeat each other.
event: Kovalan rises from death in a vision, wipes Kannaki's tears and departs among the immortals, and Kannaki goes to the king's palace gate to confront him.

title: வழக்குரை காதை
theme: Kannaki pleads her husband's case before the Pandya: the queen's dream of the falling sceptre is told, Kannaki indicts the king as one who did not inquire and sets the Chola precedents of justice against him, the broken anklet proves her right, and the king, naming himself the thief, dies by his own sentence; three closing venbas restate the moral that dharma is death to the wrongdoer and credit the king's death to the sight and words of the wronged wife.
source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed line numbers run 14 behind from line 20 (printed 15) and end at 80 against 103 lines as shown.
Line 54 repeats line 53 (கணவனை இழந்தாள் கடையகத் தாளே): probably the gatekeeper's refrain, but possibly a doubled line.

Block labels: lines 1-7 carry no metre label ('-') and lines 8-91 are labelled கருப்பம், a label the other kaathais do not use; lines 1-7 are in a different refrain metre from the akaval of 32 onward, and lines 8-29 are in short lines, so the single கருப்பம் block spans more than one metre.
Line 73: Kannaki's speech ends and the king's reply (பெண்ணணங்கே) begins mid-line, so no unit boundary can fall on the speech change.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, who pleads his case before the Pandya
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as தென்னவன், செழியன், கொற்கை வேந்தன்)
the Pandya's chief queen
the gatekeeper of the Pandya's palace
the queen's retinue of women and attendants

reading: The Pandya queen tells a companion, line by line, the omens she saw in her sleep: the umbrella and sceptre falling, the gate bell trembling, the eight directions shaking, darkness swallowing the sun, a rainbow by night and stars dropping by day.
nuance: Every omen is a disorder of the king's world or of the sky, and the first is the fall of the umbrella and sceptre, the signs of just rule; the refrain காண்பென்காண் எல்லா marks it as spoken to a companion. The lines stand in a block of their own, apart from the akaval that follows, and open with ஆங்குக், tying the scene to the moment Kannaki reaches the palace gate.
event: The Pandya queen tells a companion her ill-omened dream of the king's umbrella and sceptre falling.

reading: The queen, reading the dream as a coming harm to the king, goes to tell him, attended by women bearing mirror, jewels, cloth, colours, musk, garlands, fly-whisk and incense and by a crowd of hunchbacks and dwarfs, and tells her dream to the king seated on his lion throne.
nuance: Lines 8 to 15 restate the omens in the queen's own words and end in her resolve (வருவதோர் துன்பமுண்டு, மன்னவற்கு யாம் உரைத்தும்), so the king is warned before the accuser arrives. The long list of what the attendants carry sets the full ceremony of the court against the lone woman with one anklet who comes next.
event: The queen, with her retinue, goes to the king on his lion throne and tells him her evil dream.
unit_note: End moved from line 28 to line 33: line 28 (ஈண்டுநீர் வையங்காக்கும்) runs on into line 29 (பாண்டியன்பெருந் தேவிவாழ்கென), and the queen's scene closes at line 33 with the king on his throne; இப்பால் there turns to Kannaki.

reading: Kannaki bids the gatekeeper announce to the king who has strayed from right rule that a woman holding one anklet, who has lost her husband, is at the gate, and the gatekeeper, hailing the Pandya, tells him that a woman who is neither Kotravai nor Kali but seems as angry stands there.
nuance: Kannaki's message already pronounces the verdict: the king is one whose mind has lost its wisdom and who has erred in the rule of kingship (இறைமுறை பிழைத்தோன்), which recalls the patikam's அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர். The gatekeeper denies she is the war goddess or Kali while piling up their images, preparing her later standing as a goddess, and hails the king as the Panchava who never walks with blame (பழியொடு படராப் பஞ்சவ) just before the blame falls.
event: Kannaki asks the gatekeeper to announce her, and he tells the king that a widow holding one anklet, fierce as a goddess, waits at the gate.
unit_note: Start moved from line 29 to 34 (the queen's scene closes at 33 with இப்பால்); end moved from line 53 to 54, since line 54 repeats the gatekeeper's refrain and closes his speech with என, while the core boundary fell between the refrain and its repetition.

reading: Admitted at the king's word, Kannaki answers his question by calling him a king who did not inquire, recalls the Chola kings of her city who relieved a bird's distress and crushed their own son under the chariot wheel for a cow's grief, and names herself as the wife of Kovalan, who came to Madurai driven by former deeds and was killed at the king's order while selling her anklet.
nuance: The plea gives two causes in one breath: she indicts the king as தேரா மன்னா, the one who failed to inquire, and yet says Kovalan entered Madurai because ஊழ்வினை drove him (line 69). The two Chola precedents (the kings are not named in the Tamil) set the standard of a justice that spares not even the king's own son, and they are her own city's kings, offered to a Pandya. The king's reply begins on the last line (பெண்ணணங்கே).
event: Brought before the king, Kannaki names the Chola precedents of justice, her city, her husband's lineage and herself as the wife of the Kovalan he had killed.
unit_note: Start moved from line 54 to 55: the gatekeeper's speech ends with என on line 54, and the king's summons (வருக மற்றவள்) begins the new scene.

tamil: மன்னவன் வாய்முதல் தெறித்தது மணியே, மணி கண்டு
reading: The king answers that killing a thief is no cruel rule but royal justice; Kannaki says her anklet holds gems and the king that the queen's holds pearls; she breaks her anklet, a gem leaps to the king's mouth, and he, his umbrella lowered and sceptre slack, declares that he who heeded the goldsmith is no king but the thief, that the guarding of the southern land has failed first with him, prays his life to end and falls, while the queen, trembling, falls worshipping his feet.
nuance: Where the patikam and the narrator of the killing scene give former deeds as the reason the king did not inquire, the king here names only his own fault, heeding the goldsmith's word (பொன்செய் கொல்லன் தன்சொற் கேட்ட), and sentences himself; karma and the king's fault both stand as causes in the story, and he takes the second. தாழ்ந்த குடையன் தளர்ந்தசெங் கோலன் fulfils the queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre. The queen's words before she falls (கணவனை இழந்தோர்க்குக் காட்டுவது இல்) can be read as 'there is nothing left to offer those who lose their husbands'; the line does not say outright that she dies.
event: Kannaki breaks her anklet and a gem flies to the king's mouth; the king declares himself the thief, wishes his life ended and falls, and the queen falls at his feet.

reading: A closing venba says the saying of many assemblies, that dharma becomes death to those who do wrong, is not false, and bids the queen of the king who did the scarring wrong see what the speaker, a woman of harsh deeds, will do.
nuance: வயவேந்தன் றேவி may be addressed (the queen is told to watch) or may be the subject (see what the queen does, and what I will do); the first-person கடுவினையேன் points to Kannaki, who opens the next kaathai calling the queen கோவேந்தன் தேவி and herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன், but the speaker is not named. The first line restates the patikam's first moral (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று) as a common saying now proved.

reading: A second venba says that seeing the tears from her blue-lily eyes, the lone anklet in her hand, her form like one whose life had left, and her dark hair spread like a forest, the lord of Koodal took fright and became a lifeless husk.
nuance: The pun கூடலான் கூடு ஆயினான் (the lord of Koodal became a mere frame) makes the city's name the measure of the king's ruin. Here sight alone kills, not the king's own verdict of line 87. The first-person பாவியேன் is unexplained: it may be the poet's cry, or a speaker's who is not named.
event: The Pandya, seeing Kannaki's tears, lone anklet and spread hair, dies of fear.

reading: A third venba says that the lord of the Vaigai, at the sight of her dust-covered body, loosened hair, lone anklet and tears, lost, and when her words entered his ears, lost his life.
nuance: தோற்றான் is said twice: he lost first as a party loses a case, at the sight of her (the kaathai is the telling of the case, வழக்குரை), and then lost his life at her words. The three venbas give three accounts of how the king died, by her power, against the akaval's self-sentence.
event: The Pandya, beaten at the sight of Kannaki, dies on hearing her words.

title: வஞ்சின மாலை
theme: Kannaki, standing over the fallen king and queen, names herself the heir of the chaste women of Pukar, swears that if she is a true pathini she will not let the kingdom or Madurai survive, tears off her left breast and flings it at the city, and the fire god, who says he long held an order to burn it on the day she was wronged, burns Madurai sparing only those she names; the closing venba says chastity ate the city and its gods withdrew.
source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 55 against 61 lines held; the closing venba (58-61) and perhaps a difference of count in the akaval account for the gap.
Line 61 மாத்துவத் தான்மறைந்தார் has an unclear word (மாத்துவம்) and may be corrupt.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, who vows the destruction of Madurai and sets it burning
the Pandya's chief queen, fallen at his feet at the end of the last kaathai, addressed here as கோவேந்தன் தேவி
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as வழுதி, நற்றேரான்)
the fire god, who appears in a Brahmin's form (எரியங்கி வானவன்)
the women and men of Madurai, whom Kannaki calls to witness
the guardian gods of Madurai, who withdraw as the city burns

reading: Kannaki tells the king's queen that she, a woman of cruel fate who knows nothing, still knows that he who harms another in the forenoon sees his own harm in the afternoon, and begins to list the chaste women of Pukar: one who made a vanni tree and a kitchen stand as witnesses, one who, told in play that a sand doll on the Ponni bank was her husband, would not leave it and was spared by the tide, and Karikal Valavan's daughter, who followed her Vanchi husband into the flood that took him until the sea brought him back to her.
nuance: Kannaki calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன், a woman of harsh deeds or harsh fate, the same self-naming as the last kaathai's closing venba; she places herself under karma while, in the same breath, she threatens the king's house with the forenoon-afternoon law, so the deed's return is both a law and something she is about to carry out. The queen she addresses has just fallen at the king's feet, so the speech is made over the dead or dying. The exempla are told in clipped allusion and depend on stories the poem does not tell; who the sand-doll woman was and what the vanni tree witnessed are not given in these lines.
event: Kannaki, addressing the Pandya queen, recalls the chaste women of Pukar one after another.

reading: Kannaki goes on with the women of Pukar, one who stood turned to stone until her husband came home, one who threw her own child into the well after her co-wife's child and brought both up, one who made her face a monkey's while her husband was away because another man stared, and the girl who, learning that her mother had promised her in play to a friend's son, put on new cloth and went with bowed head to him, then says that she was born in their city and, if she too is truly a pathini, will not let the kingdom live, will destroy Madurai, and the queen will see her vow kept.
nuance: Lines 23 to 31 are nested speech: the girl's mother, telling the father, reproaches herself for not heeding the wise who say that a woman's wit is folly (பெண்ணறிவு என்பது பேதைமைத்தே) and for the careless word she spoke at the sand-house game; the saying is reported as a mother's self-blame, not asserted by the poem, and where the mother's speech begins is not certain. The vow is conditional on Kannaki's own virtue (பத்தினியே யாமாகில்), so the burning that follows is presented as the test that proves her a pathini, not only as revenge. The kaathai's name, வஞ்சின மாலை, takes the warrior's vow and gives it to a widow.
event: Kannaki finishes her list of the chaste women of Pukar, vows to destroy the Pandya's kingdom and Madurai if she is a true pathini, and leaves the palace.

reading: Kannaki calls the women and men of Madurai, the gods and the ascetics to hear that she, without fault, has raged against the royal city that wronged her beloved husband, twists off her left breast, circles Madurai three times and flings the breast into the street; the fire god appears as a Brahmin with red matted hair and white teeth and says he long held an order to feed this city to the fire on the day she was wronged and asks whom he should spare, and at her bidding to leave Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children and go only to the side of the wicked, smoke and flame fill Koodal.
nuance: Two causes stand side by side: Kannaki's own act and charge (சீறினேன் குற்றமிலேன் யான்) and the fire god's word that he had an order from long before (பண்டேயோர் ஏவ லுடையேன்), which makes the burning already decreed; who gave the order is not said. The fire takes a command from her (ஏவ, line 56), so a god serves the pathini's word. The exemptions limit her rage by a code of protected persons, and the city is burned as the king's, not as the guilty one's.
event: Kannaki proclaims her grievance to Madurai, tears off her left breast and flings it at the city; the fire god appears, she names those to be spared, and Madurai burns.

reading: The closing venba says that the Pandya, his women, his palace, his army bright with bows and his horses and elephants were consumed as chastity ate fierce Koodal, and that the city's divine guardians vanished too.
nuance: The venba names the agent of the burning as கற்பு itself, not Kannaki or the fire god. The sense of மாத்துவத் தான் (line 61) is not secure, so how the gods are said to vanish is uncertain.
event: The fire consumes the Pandya's household, palace and army, and the guardian gods of Madurai withdraw.

title: அழற்படு காதை
theme: With the Pandya dead on his throne, the fire Kannaki commanded breaks out: the four guardian bhutas of Madurai, each in the form of one order of society, leave the city because its king erred, the fire spares the virtuous, the cows, the children and the elders and burns the rest, the city's housewives judge her revenge no cruelty, all rites cease, and the city goddess, unable to bear the heat, comes before the grieving pathini.
source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 161 lines as shown but the edition's printed last line is 160, so the printed numbering is one short somewhere; the edition's doubted spans (17-33, 37-50, 67-84, 89-96, 111) were applied as given to the lines as shown, and on sense they fit them (each doubted span is a fuller portrait of a bhuta whose kept lines remain).
Line 47 (முகிழ்த்தகைச்) is a single word on a line of its own, probably a broken or split line.
Lines 81-82 (சூழொளித் தாலு மியாழும், விலைந்துபத மிகுந்து) are obscure as written and may be corrupt.
Line 113: விடாது can be read as sparing or as clinging to the virtuous; the sparing reading is taken from the exemptions in 21:53.

cast.role: the fire god, here called the god under command (ஏவல் தெய்வம்), who burns Madurai at Kannaki's bidding
the guardian gods of Madurai, who close the city's gates
the Pandya king of Madurai, now dead on his throne (named here as செழியன்)
the palace household: the preceptor, astrologer, judges, ministers, accountants, servants and women of the court
the Pandya's elephant-men, horse-masters, charioteers and swordsmen at the palace gate
the first of Madurai's four guardian bhutas, in the form of a Brahmin of the three fires
the royal guardian bhuta of Madurai, in the form of a conquering king
the guardian bhuta of Madurai in a merchant's form, bearing plough and balance
the fourth guardian bhuta of Madurai, bearing the artisans' tools and versed in dance and song
the four guardian bhutas of Madurai together
Kovalan's wife, the pathini whose command has set Madurai burning
the women and men of Madurai
the mistresses of Madurai's great households, keepers of hospitality
the dancing and singing women of Madurai, versed in the sixty-four arts
the guardian goddess of Madurai, who comes before Kannaki

reading: The fire god under command opens its blazing face and the guardian gods shut the city's gates; not knowing that the Pandya, who gave up his life for the fault of his bent sceptre and so showed the earth a straight one, lies dead on his throne with his queen, the court officials sit still as painted figures, and the elephant-men, horsemen, charioteers and swordsmen crowd in confusion at the palace gate and halt at the sight of the fire.
nuance: The narrator recasts the king's death as a gift (உயிர் ஆணி கொடுத்து) by which he showed the straight sceptre to the earth (இருநில மடந்தைக்குச் செங்கோல் காட்ட): the death that ends the bent sceptre is itself counted as an act of just rule. The fire is called ஏவல் தெய்வம், the god who takes orders, so the burning is presented as obedience, not as the fire's own wrath. The queen is praised for flawless chastity (புரைதீர் கற்பின்) even as she dies beside the king whose fault brought the fire.
event: The fire breaks out and the gates are shut while the court, unaware the king is dead, freezes and the guards halt before the flames.
unit_note: End moved from line 10 to line 15: the sentence that begins with the court (lines 7-10) runs on through the painted stillness (11) and the guards at the gate to தாமிடை கொள்ள (15); the description of the first bhuta begins at line 16.

reading: The first guardian bhuta of Madurai is described in a Brahmin's form: moon-bright with pearl ornaments, crowned with white lotus and arugu, in unbleached cloth and sandal, receiving offerings of honey, milk and sweet smoke at bathing ghats, temples and Veda schools, carrying umbrella, staff, water-pot, kindling and darbha, the thread on his chest, never failing the rule of the three-fire life, with the sacrificial implements of the Veda.
nuance: The edition marks lines 17-33, almost the whole portrait, as doubted by many commentators; the lines it keeps (16, 34-36) give only the pearl ornament, the unfailing three-fire life and the Vedic sacrificial tools, so no claim is built on the fuller description. The four bhutas that follow are each drawn from one order of society, and this one, the 'first bhuta', is the Brahmin's.
unit_note: Start moved from line 11 to 16 (the court-and-gate sentence closes at 15); end moved from line 42 to 36, where ஆதிப் பூதத்து அதிபதிக் கடவுளும் closes the first bhuta's portrait; the second begins at 37.

reading: The royal guardian bhuta is described: bright as the conquering sun, crowned and jewelled, wearing champak and red flowers, saffron on the chest and red silk, receiving hot rice offered in gold, coral-red in body, holding drum, white umbrella, fly-whisk, banner, goad, spear and rope like the ruler of the sea-girt earth, a god like Nediyon who drives off kings, takes their land, wields the straight sceptre, puts down cruel deeds and guards the four lands.
nuance: Lines 37-50 are doubted in the edition; the kept lines 51-61 carry the whole charter of the royal spirit, ending in செங்கோல் ஓச்சிக் கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து: wielding the straight sceptre and putting down cruel deeds. That is the very office the Pandya claimed when he had Kovalan killed as a thief, so the portrait of the king's own guardian spirit stands as the measure he failed, just before the spirit leaves him.
unit_note: Start moved from line 43 to 37 (the first bhuta closes at 36); end moved from line 59 to 61, since நானிலம் புரக்கும் (59) runs on through நெடியோன் அன்ன (60) to அரைச பூதத்து அருந்திறற் கடவுளும் (61), which closes the royal bhuta.

reading: The third guardian bhuta is described in a merchant's form: golden in body, wearing kings' ornaments but no crown, guarding the land by the trading way, holding plough and balance, garlanded with flowers of every landscape, receiving offerings of pulses at threshing floors, fields and market platforms, bringing goods of hill and sea to those who need them, called the master of the faultless life that sustains farming, a great god in the form of the crescent-wearing lord.
nuance: Lines 67-84 are doubted in the edition, so the kept portrait is short: golden body, kings' ornaments without the crown (64), the trading tradition, plough and balance, and the crescent-crowned form (85-88). The doubted lines garland him with vetchi, thazhai, ambal, neythal, poolai and marutham together, flowers of different landscapes, as if trade gathered every region. Lines 81-82 (தாலு, விலைந்துபத) are obscure and were not resolved.
unit_note: The core units 60-79 and 80-93 are recut at the bhutas' own closes: this unit starts at line 62, after அரைச பூதத்து அருந்திறற் கடவுளும் (61), and ends at line 88 with விளங்கொளிப் பூத வியன்பெருங் கடவுளும்; line 79 (அவனே) only resumes the subject.

reading: The fourth bhuta, dark as the karuvilai flower, in dark cloth with flowers of tree, creeper, water and land in his hair, bearing the artisans' tools and versed in dance and song, the chief of the bhutas that receive offerings in Koodal, appears too; and the bhutas say that there is a rule that on the day the king errs in the order of rule this city is to be eaten by fire, and since they know it as their charge, it is not fitting for them to stay.
nuance: Lines 89-96 are doubted in the edition; the kept portrait (97-102) gives the gem-like body, the dark cloth, dance and song, and the title of chief of Koodal's offering-receiving bhutas. The bhutas' words (103-106) give the burning a law of its own: it is the city's lot (திறன்) when the king errs, and the guardians leave because they know it as their duty (முறை), not because they are driven off. Which order of society the fourth bhuta stands for is not named in the kept lines.
event: The fourth guardian bhuta appears, and the bhutas declare that the city must burn because its king has erred and that they will leave.
unit_note: Start moved from line 94 to 89, where the fourth bhuta's portrait begins (கருவிளை புரையு மேனியன்) after the third closes at 88; the end stays at 106, where the bhutas' words close with எனக்.

reading: Before the victorious lady who aimed her breast, the four bhutas leave each to its own quarter; the grain street, the chariot streets and the four streets of the separate orders are thrown into turmoil as on the day the monkey-bannered bowman fed the forest to the fire; the flame spares the side of the virtuous and crowds into the quarter of the fighting men, the cows and calves, untouched by fire, reach the broad street of the righteous herdsmen, and the war elephants, cow-elephants and swift horses flee beyond the walls.
nuance: The fire sorts the city as Kannaki ordered in the previous kaathai: the virtuous (அறவோர்) and the cows are kept from it while the warriors' quarter (மறவோர் சேரி) burns, and the pun அறவோர் / மறவோர் may also mean the righteous against the wicked. விடாது in line 113 is taken as 'not letting the flame loose' on the virtuous, which is how the exemption of 21:53 is fulfilled; read as 'not leaving', it would say the opposite, so the reading is marked uncertain. Line 111, the bowman who burned the forest (the Mahabharata's Arjuna), is doubted in the edition.
event: The guardian bhutas leave and the fire sweeps the streets of Madurai, sparing the virtuous and the cows while the warriors' quarter burns and the elephants and horses flee.
unit_note: Start stays at 107; end moved from line 117 to 118, since the sentence on the elephants (117) closes only with புறமதிற் பெயர்ந்தன (118).

reading: Young women with sandal-smeared breasts and kohl-dark eyes, roused from love-play with their men, stagger in confusion; mothers wake their lisping little sons from cotton beds and go out with the white-haired women; and the mistresses of the great houses, who never failed the household duty of feeding guests, saying with great gladness that the breast-battle of the jewelled lady who lost her husband and won with her anklet is not a cruel thing, worship and praise the god of the blazing fire.
nuance: The verdict on the burning is given to the wives who keep household dharma (வருவிருந் தோம்பி மனையற முட்டா), and they meet it with great gladness (பெருமகிழ்வு) and worship of the fire: the women of the city it destroys judge Kannaki's act just. The children and elders who leave together are the ones she exempted (மூத்தோர் குழவி, 21:54).
event: The townspeople flee the fire with their children and elders, and the housewives of Madurai worship the fire god, calling Kannaki's revenge no cruelty.
unit_note: Start moved from line 118 to 119 (see the previous unit); end moved from line 133 to 137, since the housewives' sentence (132-133) closes only with தொழுதனர் ஏத்தினர் (137).

reading: The dancing women of the sixty-four arts, as if robbed of their stage, ask what land and whose daughter is the lone woman who, having lost her husband in this land and city, defeated the king who did not inquire with her anklet and set this city on fire; the evening festival, Vedic chant, fire offering, worship of gods, lighting of house lamps and the beat of drums all cease; and before the heroic pathini, burning with grief for her lost husband, sighing like a smith's bellows and wandering street to street in anguish, Madurapathi, unable to bear the heat of the fire, comes and appears.
nuance: The ceasing of rites (ஆரண ஓதை, செந்தீ வேட்டல், தெய்வம் பரவல்) shows a burning that stops the city's worship altogether, including the Brahmins' fire offerings that her command spared from harm. The city's own goddess comes because she cannot bear the fire (கொந்தழல் வெம்மைக் கூரெரி பொறாஅள்): a deity is put under the pathini's fire. The dancers' question names Kannaki only as 'one woman' (ஒருமகள்) who won with the anklet, so the city knows the deed before it knows her.
event: The city's dancers ask who the woman is, all rites in Madurai stop, and the goddess of Madurai appears before the grieving Kannaki.
unit_note: Start moved from line 134 to 138 (the housewives' sentence closes at 137); the end stays at 157, the close of the akaval.

reading: The closing venba says that Madurapathi, a lady of victory who holds what Lakshmi, Saraswati and the queen who killed the buffalo demon possess, came before the woman who cut off her young breast.
nuance: The venba gives the city goddess the powers of three goddesses at once (மாமகள், நாமகள், the slayer of Mahisha), and still has her come to the mortal woman, not the woman to her. கொற்றத்தாள் with தாம்படைத்த is read as the goddess holding the victory the three possess; the syntax allows other readings.
event: The goddess of Madurai comes before Kannaki.

title: கட்டுரை காதை
theme: In the Katturai Kaathai the goddess of Madurai, the Pandya's family deity, pleads the justice of his line with legends of Pandya self-punishment and repair, then gives Kannaki the cause from a former birth, Kovalan's killing of Sangaman and the widow Neeli's curse, and the pathini goes up from Murugan's hill to heaven with her husband.
source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed line numbers end at 200 against 204 lines as shown (the closing venba is unnumbered or counted apart).

Lines 25 to 30 are three short couplet-like pairs (each a long line and a short one) set inside the akaval block with no metre rubric; line 30 ends one pair and resumes the akaval mid-line (வினை; காதின்).
Line 121 (இருநில மடந்தைக்குத் திருமார்பு நல்கியவள்) has an unclear word division (நல்கி அவள் or நல்கிய அவள்), and lines 121 to 122 are hard to construe.
Line 160 to 161: Neeli's cry (அரசர் முறையோ ... சேரியீர் முறையோவென) runs across the unit boundary at 160/161; the boundary was left as cut because other chapters already link to these unit ids.

cast.role: the guardian goddess of Madurai, family deity of the Pandyas, who tells Kannaki the cause from a former birth (calls herself மதுரா பதி)
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai

a learned brahmin of the Chola land who won gifts from the Chera
Vaarthikan's small son, named after the god under the banyan, who recites the Veda before Parasaran
a brahmin of Thangal, imprisoned on the charge of taking treasure
Vaarthikan's wife
the Pandya's officers who seize Vaarthikan
the Pandya of old who freed Vaarthikan and made amends (not named in the Tamil)
the goddess Kotravai, whose temple door stays shut (also கலையமர் செல்வி, கொற்றவை)
a merchant of Singapuram in Kalinga, killed as a spy in a former age
Kovalan in his former birth, a king's officer who had Sangaman killed
king of Singapuram in Kalinga, at enmity with his kinsman Kumaran
Sangaman's wife, who laid the curse
the retinue of the king of the gods who take Kannaki to heaven

reading: The narrator describes the goddess of Madurai, half dark and half golden, a lotus in her left hand and a sword in her right, a warrior's anklet on one foot and a woman's anklet on the other, who, as the family goddess of the Pandya, does not come before the grieving pathini but appears behind her and asks her to hear her plea.
nuance: The goddess's two halves, the woman's anklet (சிலம்பு) on one foot and the hero's anklet (கழல்) on the other, set the book's emblem on a divided body. She stands behind Kannaki (பின்னிலைத் தோன்றி) because she is the Pandya's own family goddess (குலமுதற் கிழத்தி ஆதலின்), and the word she uses is குறை, a petition: the city's deity comes as a pleader for the king.
event: The goddess of Madurai appears behind Kannaki and asks her to hear her plea.

reading: Kannaki turns and asks who follows her and whether she knows her grief; the goddess answers that she knows it, names herself the deity of Madurai, grieved for what befell Kannaki's husband, asks her to hear what came to her king when his former deed arrived and what came to her husband, and says the Pandya kings' ears heard only the sound of the Veda, never the sound of the justice bell.
nuance: The goddess gives the one cause to both men: ஊழ்வினை came to her king (line 28) and the deed came to harm Kannaki's husband (line 30), so the king is not the only one whose fault is being judged. Lines 25 to 30 are three short couplet-like pairs set inside the akaval. Her boast that the bell was never rung answers Kannaki's plea before the Pandya, where the Chola's gate bell trembled for the cow.
event: Kannaki asks who follows her, and the goddess names herself and asks to be heard.

reading: The goddess says the Pandya's sceptre brings blame on his people only when they are kings who will not bow to him, that in this noble line joined to good conduct even untamed youth, an elephant in must not yet held by the goad of learning, brings no fault, and begins the tale of the wife of the poor brahmin Keeranthai, at whose door someone knocked one night.
nuance: The claim that the line's youth stays blameless without learning is made by the line's own goddess, in the chapter that tells how its present king failed. The masculine புடைத்தனன் (line 43) leaves who knocked to the next lines, where the king's response shows it was he.
event: One night a man knocks at the door of Keeranthai's wife, whose husband is away.

reading: Keeranthai's wife cries that her husband left her saying there is no fence but the king's, and asks whether that fence does not guard her today; the king, his heart burned as if a hot nail were driven into his ear, cuts off his own hand, the hand that broke Indra's crown, and the goddess turns to a second tale, of the brahmin Parasaran of the Chola land, who set out to see the Chera famed for his gifts and came among the brahmins of the three fires and four Vedas.
nuance: The king punishes his own hand for a wrong of approach that the wife only feared, so the goddess sets a Pandya against the Chola exemplars Kannaki had thrown at him; she even names the Chola of the dove and the calf (line 58) here, as the ruler of Parasaran's land, and the burning heart (நெஞ்சஞ் சுடுதலின்) is the phrase Kannaki used of the Chola who killed his son.
event: Hearing the woman's reproach, the Pandya cuts off his own hand; Parasaran sets out for the Chera court.

reading: Parasaran wins the brahmins' victory garland in debate, receives fine jewels and, going home, rests at Thangal, a brahmins' town of the Pandya, under the pipal of its common hall, setting down his staff, water pot, umbrella and bundle, and hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea and carved his bow on the hill, the Poraiyan of the Porunai, Mantharam Cheral.
nuance: A Chola-land brahmin, standing in a Pandya village, sings the Chera's praise; the four வாழி lines join epithets the Sangam books give to different Cheras, and the Tamil does not say whether they name one king or several.
event: Parasaran, enriched by the Chera, rests at Thangal and blesses the Chera king.

reading: Parasaran calls the playing children to recite with him for his bundle, and Vaarthikan's small son, named after the god under the banyan, recites the Veda without fault though his tongue still lisps; Parasaran, delighted, gives Thakkinan a pearl thread, bangles and earrings and goes home, and the king's officers, unable to bear the boy wearing them, seize Vaarthikan as a brahmin who took treasure without the king's leave.
nuance: The charge (கோமுறை அன்றிப் படுபொருள் வௌவிய) is the officers' own; the text gives envy as their motive (பொறாஅராகி), not any order of the king.
event: Parasaran rewards the boy who recites the Veda, and the king's officers seize the boy's father as a thief.

reading: Vaarthikan is put in prison; his wife Kaarthigai weeps and rolls on the ground, the door of Aiyai's temple will not open, and the king, asking whether his sceptre has bent, learns the truth, declares that his rule has strayed through ignorant men and asks the people to bear his fault, gives Thangal and Vayalur to Vaarthikan, and lies prostrate on the earth to soothe Kaarthigai's grief.
nuance: The king reads a shut temple door as the sign of a bent sceptre (கொடுங்கோ லுண்டுகொல், line 111) and owns the wrong of his servants as his own (என் இறைமுறை பிழைத்தது). Lines 121 to 122 (திருமார்பு நல்கியவள் ... தணித்தனனே) may mean that he lay with his chest to the earth before her, or something else; the word division is unclear.
event: When Aiyai's temple door stays shut, the king learns of the wrongful arrest, frees Vaarthikan and grants him villages.

reading: The goddess's door opens, the king has it proclaimed by drum on an elephant's neck that the prisons be broken and the guilty set free and that treasure found or laid by belong to those who hold it, and the goddess tells Kannaki to hear how a king of this line that proclaimed justice came to err, for there is also a saying that on the eighth day of the dark half of Aadi, under Krittika, on a Friday, fire will eat Madurai and its king will perish.
nuance: Line 131 to 132 may set the proclaiming king against the present one, or say that the same line which proclaimed justice now erred; either way the goddess adds a fixed omen-day (lines 133 to 136) to the deed of a former birth, so the burning is foretold as well as earned.
event: The temple door opens and the king proclaims the release of prisoners; the goddess cites a prophecy of Madurai's burning.

reading: The goddess tells how in Kalinga two kings of one line, Vasu of Singapuram and Kumaran of Kapilapuram, were at war so that none could cross the land between, how the merchant Sangaman came secretly with his wife to sell jewels in the market, and how Kannaki's husband in his former birth, Bharatan, an officer of the king who had left his vow, seized him as a spy and had him killed, so that his widow Neeli cried whether this was the justice of kings or of the Bharatas.
nuance: This is the former deed the patikam only names: Kovalan once played the part the goldsmith plays now, bringing a stranger with goods before a king as a criminal and having him killed. The text gives Bharatan's motive as a dislike that came from having left his vow (விரத நீங்கிய வெறுப்பினன்), so his own fault, not only fate, is named.
event: In a former birth Bharatan seizes the merchant Sangaman as a spy and has him killed.

reading: Neeli cried through the halls and streets, and after fourteen days climbed a hill to join her slain husband in the sky and, falling, laid the curse that those who caused her sorrow should suffer the same; the goddess tells Kannaki that she and her husband are under that curse, that when the deed of a former birth rises penance does not help those not upright, and that she will see her husband within fourteen days, but only in a god's form.
nuance: Neeli's curse is for exact repetition (எம்முறு துயரம் ... தம்முறு துயரம்), and the story repays it in kind: a wife again cries through a city's streets after her husband's killing. செம்மையிலோர் (line 172) is not named; it may be Bharatan's past, or a general rule.
event: Neeli curses the killers as she falls from a hill; the goddess tells Kannaki she will see Kovalan in fourteen days in divine form.

reading: After the goddess has told the pathini the course of fate and the fire has withdrawn, Kannaki vows neither to sit nor stand until she sees her husband, breaks her bangles at Kotravai's gate, says she came in by the east gate with her husband and goes out by the west alone, follows the Vaigai's bank night and day, climbs Murugan's hill and under a flowering vengai mourns that she is a woman of fiery deeds, and after fourteen days the retinue of the king of the gods praises her, rains flowers and takes her up in the sky car with Kovalan.
nuance: Kannaki now calls herself தீத்தொழிலாட்டி, a doer of the deed of fire, where at the burning she declared herself faultless; Kovalan is still கோநகர் பிழைத்த, he who erred against (or perished in) the royal city, even as he is taken to heaven.
event: Kannaki leaves Madurai by the west gate, climbs the hill and after fourteen days is taken to heaven with Kovalan.

reading: A closing venba says it is certain that the gods worship the woman who worships her husband rather than a god, for Kannaki, ornament of the women of earth, has become the guest of the women of heaven.
nuance: The first line takes up three words of Kural 55's first line (தெய்வந் தொழாஅள் கொழுநற்), short of the four-word echo rule, and changes the reward: not rain at the wife's command but the gods' own worship of her.

title: மதுரைக் காண்டம் கட்டுரை
theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Madurai book: one long sentence lists what the book set out about the Pandya line and its land (righteousness, valour, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the Vaigai's plenty, the unfailing sky, the two dramatic modes and the vari and kuravai songs) and says the book lies viewed as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan, victor over the northern Aryan armies, who slept on his royal couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
source_issues: Lines 14, 15, 18 and 19 are short lines inside the akaval frame (வடஆரியர் படைகடந்து, தென்றமிழ்நா டொருங்குகாணப், நெடுஞ்செழியனோ டொருபரிசா, நோக்கிக் கிடந்த); the Puhar and Vanchi summaries built on the same frame have full lines here, so the edition's line division may differ from the metre.

Line 6 reads அவருடை நாட்டுக் where the Vanchi summary has அவருறை நாட்டுக்; line 18 reads ஒருபரிசா where the Vanchi summary has ஒருபரிசு நோக்கி. Either may be a variant or a misprint; the sense is unaffected.
Line 20 (மதுரைக் காண்டம் முற்றிற்று) is a colophon that also completes the sentence (கிடந்த governs காண்டம்), so it is marked as part of the unit.

reading: The narrator closes the Madurai book by gathering into one view the righteousness, valour and strength of the Pandya line among the three crowned kings, their old city, its festivals and divine visitors, the people and harvests of their land, the Vaigai that feeds it, the sky that never fails its rain, the two modes of drama and the vari and kuravai songs, all seen together with Nedunjeliyan, who defeated the northern Aryan armies and, before all the Tamil south, came to lie still on his throne-couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
nuance: The opening lines repeat, nearly word for word, the frame that closes the Puhar book, with the Vaigai for the Kaveri; so the praise of aram and of a sky that never fails (பொய்யா வானம், line 9) is given to the very line whose king the book has shown condemning an innocent man, and the summary does not take it back. The book's judgment shows only at the close, where the whole book is set beside a death: துஞ்சிய (line 17), 'slept', is the courtly word for a king's dying, and the queen's death at his feet (20:88-91) becomes a shared lying on the royal couch. The summary gives the epithet of flawless chastity (புரைதீர் கற்பின்) to the Pandya's queen, and does not name Kannaki, Kovalan or the burning of the city at all. The epithet வடஆரியர் படைகடந்து (line 14) matches the name under which tradition files Purananuru 183 (ஆரியப் படை கடந்த நெடுஞ்செழியன்); the Tamil here gives the epithet, not a proof that the two are one king, so no link is built on it. Lines 10 to 13 name two dramatic modes (ஆரபடி, சாத்துவதி) and the songs and say they appear together 'with other matter set in' (பிறபொருள் வைப்போடு); the reading does not turn on the technical terms.

title: குன்றக் குரவை
theme: The hill women of the Chera country meet Kannaki under a vengai, hear her name her fate, see the gods take her to heaven with her husband and make her their clan's goddess; their kuravai then weaves the cult into an akam love story, mocking the velan's rite, praying to Murugan for the lover's wedding, and crediting the new pathini of their millet field when the lover comes, before blessing the Chera king.
source_issues: Line 7: இறைஞ்சியஞ் looks corrupt (perhaps இறைஞ்சி யஞ்சி, 'bowing in fear'); the sense of bowing is clear.
Lines 31-42: the closing line of each stanza (மற்றையார் ...னோம்தோழி நெஞ்சன்றே) is obscure in our text and the stanzas are marked uncertain.
Line 20: பரவுலும் is probably பரவலும.
The kaathai's printed last line number is missing (show prints None); the text has 134 lines.

cast.role: the young women of the hill kuravar hamlet who meet Kannaki and sing and dance the kuravai
the hill girl in a secret love, the heroine of the kuravai's love songs
the hill girl's friend, who speaks to her and to her lover
the hill girl's mother, who calls the velan
the hill girl's lover, the man of the hill (also சிலம்பன், வெற்பன்)
the hill god addressed in the kuravai by epithets (இறைவன், கடம்பன், அறுமுக வொருவ, மலைமகள் மகன்); the unit does not use the name முருகன்
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the hill-dwelling kuravar who saw the one-breasted woman taken to heaven
the gods who rain flowers and take Kannaki to heaven with her husband
the Chera king, blessed here only as king of the Kudavar who ruled Kolli and the Himalaya; the next kaathai names him Senguttuvan

reading: The hill women tell how, coming back from scaring birds off the millet and bathing in the falls, they met under a mountain vengai a woman who had lost a breast and asked who she was, and she answered that she was the one of cruel deeds who had lost her husband there when strong karma pressed on her and Madurai and its kingship came to ruin; as they bowed, the gods rained flowers and took her away with her husband while the hill folk watched, and the women call the hamlet to take her as its god, with drums, horn, bells, kurinji song, incense and flowers, so that the great hill may never sleep but yield its wealth.
nuance: Kannaki gives two causes in one breath: the strong deed of the past that came and pressed (வல்வினைவந் துருத்தகாலை, the patikam's ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும் and the Madurai goddess's உம்மை வினைவந் துருத்த காலை), and herself as the doer, கடுவினையேன், the woman of cruel deeds. The women compare her to Valli (வள்ளிபோல்வீர்) before they know her, and the reason they give for the cult is plain: no deity of their clan is as great as she (line 10). The prayer asks for the hill's fertility, the boon the Kural gives to the chaste wife's word.
event: The hill women meet the one-breasted Kannaki under a vengai, she tells them who she is, the gods take her to heaven with her husband, and the women call the hamlet to worship her.

reading: A hill girl bids her friend look at the falls that come down coloured like the rainbow with the earth's collyrium, orpiment and vermilion, and says they will bathe in the falls of the cloud-wrapped grove, the falls of the man who said 'do not fear', enjoyed her beauty and gave no grace.
nuance: The lover's 'do not fear' (அஞ்சலோம் பென்று) is the promise of the secret union; the bathing song turns at once from the beauty of the falls to his failure to keep it, which is the complaint the whole kuravai will try to cure by asking for his wedding.
event: The hill girls go to bathe in the waterfall, and one complains of the lover who promised and did not return.

reading: The girl says she finds no cause to sulk, for the fresh flood that came washing the stones of his hill is the water they bathed in, and closes with an obscure line on others and the heart.
nuance: The three stanzas differ only in what the water touched on his hill (stone, gold, flowers) and in the verb of bathing with others (உற்று, முன், மீது). The water from his hill stands for the man himself, so bathing in it undoes the quarrel. The last line, மற்றையார் ... ஆடினோம் தோழி நெஞ்சன்றே, may mean that others bathed in it too, or that it was not the heart that sulked; I cannot fix it.

reading: The girl says she finds no cause to sulk, for the fresh flood that came washing the gold of his hill is the water they bathed in, and closes with an obscure line on others and the heart.
nuance: The three stanzas differ only in what the water touched on his hill (stone, gold, flowers) and in the verb of bathing with others (உற்று, முன், மீது). The water from his hill stands for the man himself, so bathing in it undoes the quarrel. The last line, மற்றையார் ... ஆடினோம் தோழி நெஞ்சன்றே, may mean that others bathed in it too, or that it was not the heart that sulked; I cannot fix it.

reading: The girl says she finds no cause to sulk, for the fresh flood that came washing the flowers of his hill is the water they bathed in, and closes with an obscure line on others and the heart.
nuance: The three stanzas differ only in what the water touched on his hill (stone, gold, flowers) and in the verb of bathing with others (உற்று, முன், மீது). The water from his hill stands for the man himself, so bathing in it undoes the quarrel. The last line, மற்றையார் ... ஆடினோம் தோழி நெஞ்சன்றே, may mean that others bathed in it too, or that it was not the heart that sulked; I cannot fix it.

reading: Having bathed until their eyes reddened, the girl bids her friend come and, raising praise to the spear that killed the mango of the strong sea, link hands in a kuravai and sing.
event: The girls leave the water and begin the kuravai dance in praise of Murugan's spear.

reading: The first spear song says the spear in the hand of the god who never leaves Senthil, Sengodu, Venkunru and Erakam is the bright-leaved white spear that once went into the dark sea and cut down Sur's mango.
nuance: The four hills named are the kuravar's list of Murugan's seats; it is not the six of the guide poem.

reading: The second spear song says it is the spear held by the one who alone has six fair faces and twelve hands, the white spear that, riding Pinimukam, killed so that the asuras lost their pride and the lord of the sky praised him.

The third spear song says it is the spear of the one who drank at the breasts of six mothers in the Saravana lotus bed, the long spear that split the chest of the asura and killed the mountain named for the crane.

The friend laughs to the girl that mother, not knowing how to cure the sickness the lord of the pepper hills caused, says it is the Kadamba god's and, wanting the veri rite, has told the velan to come.
nuance: The mother's belief that the god has seized the girl is answered in the next three stanzas (lines 63 to 74), which call the velan and the god himself foolish if they come to cure a sickness a man gave; hence 'refuted'.
event: The girl's mother calls the velan to hold the veri rite for a sickness she thinks Murugan sent.

reading: The friend says it is laughable: if the velan comes to cure the sickness the man of the great hill caused, the velan is a fool, and more foolish than he is the one who killed the crane mountain, if he comes.
The velan who comes to cure the sickness the man of the fragrant hill caused is a fool, the friend repeats, and more foolish still is the son of the one under the banyan, if he comes.
The friend says, not in jest, that if the god of the dark kadamba garland comes to cure the hot sickness the chest of the man of the hill gave, he is more foolish than the velan who comes to cure it.
nuance: நகையா (line 71) may be read 'not laughing' against the refrain's இதுநகையாகின்றே, turning the last stanza from jest to earnest; the same girls have just praised this god's spear, and the mockery is of his coming to the wrong rite, not of his power.

reading: If the son of the one under the banyan comes on his blue bird with his bride to the veri ground where the velan dances, the girls say, they will ask him for the wedding of the man of the great hill.
nuance: The rite the friend mocked is put to another use: if the god does come, they will ask him not to cure the sickness but to bring the marriage that alone cures it.

reading: The girls tell the son of the lord of Kailasa that they have worshipped his feet, which are like asoka flowers, asking that the girl of the hill folk, peacock-like with a moon brow, be spared another's marriage and given the marriage of her lover.
nuance: அயல்மணம் is the fear behind the prayer: a match the family might make with someone else, which would break the secret bond.
event: The hill girls pray to Murugan that the girl be married to her lover and not to another.

reading: The girls tell the son of the mountain's daughter, the god of high station, that they have worshipped his feet asking that the girl of the kuravar of the high hills be wed in the marriage that many know.
nuance: பலரறி மணம், the marriage many know, is the public wedding that ends the secret union.

reading: Calling the six-faced one's kurava wife their own clan's daughter, the girls say they have worshipped his feet with her, asking that those who touch his feet at the bathing place be granted a good marriage and spared a wrong one.
nuance: குறமகள் அவள் எம குலமகள்: the hill women claim the god's wife, Valli, as a girl of their own clan, so their prayer goes to a god who is their kinsman by marriage.

reading: The friend tells the girl that the man of the hill, who had heard their song from hiding, was going away when she went before him, worshipped his feet and told him that he comes to this village for a girl's sake wearing kadamba and carrying a spear, yet has no six faces, no peacock and no kurava bride, so the hamlet's people, who will not take him for the kadamba god, are simple folk.
nuance: She treats the lover in the god's own forms, bowing at his feet as the girls bowed at Murugan's, and then lists what he lacks of the god. Lines 99 and 100 (கடம்பூண் தெய்வ மாக நேரார் மடவர்) can be read either way: the folk are simple for not seeing that the girl's god is this man, or for taking him for the god; the reading turns on நேரார்.
event: The hidden lover overhears the girls' song, and the friend stops him as he leaves and speaks to him.

reading: When she told him that gossip had arisen, the friend says, the man of the hill who had turned away with a withering heart seems now about to marry; so they will sing of the pathini who with her breast destroyed great Madurai, to whom the gods with their kin brought her husband and showed him, singing in praise of her who burned Koodal when the royal order failed, and as they sing they ask for the lover's wedding, for a woman whom chaste wives praise and worship is in their own millet field.
nuance: Here the cause of the burning is the king's failure, கோமுறை நீங்க (line 111), where Kannaki in the first unit named the strong deed of the past and her own cruel act: the chapter gives both causes, in her voice and in the hill women's. The love story and the cult are joined: the friend's report of gossip moves the lover to marry, and the girls credit the new goddess of their field with the boon.
event: The lover, told that gossip has spread, turns to marry, and the girls begin to sing the praise of the pathini in their field.

reading: The girls sing that even after the gods brought her husband to her they do not cease their praise, that the gods of heaven worship the woman under the fragrant forest vengai, that she has gone with her husband to the life of heaven and will not come back, and that the village which sings her has gained a distinction, to see the gold-bangled girl's lover wed; seeing the kuravai, their lovers have come, and they bless themselves to live and feast every day, and the king of the Kudavar who ruled Kolli and the Himalaya where the bow was carved.
nuance: மறுதரவில்லாள் (she has no return) closes the story of Kannaki on earth: the hill folk keep her as a deity under the vengai, not as one who will come back. The closing blessing turns from the hill to the Chera king, who in the next kaathai hears of her; the bow carved on the Himalaya is a Chera emblem the Sangam poems give to Cheralathan, and the kuravai does not name which king it means.
event: The girls finish the kuravai in praise of the pathini, their lovers come to marry them, and they bless the Chera king.

title: காட்சிக் காதை
theme: On a journey to the hills, Senguttuvan hears from the hill people of the one-breasted woman taken to heaven and from Saathan of the burning of Madurai; he reads the Pandya's death as a bent sceptre straightened, his queen chooses Kannaki for worship, and he resolves to bring the goddess's stone from the Himalaya, which his ministers turn into a summons to the northern kings.
source_issues: The edition prints the last line as 190 but the kaathai has 194 lines; line numbers here are show's.
Line 126: a leftover HTML quote mark was removed in the build (show flags the repair).
Lines 59 and 60 both begin வானவர் போற்ற; possibly a doubled phrase, kept as written.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi (here வாய்வாட் கோதை, வானவன், மன்னர் கோமான்), who hears the pathini's story and resolves to fetch her stone from the Himalaya
Senguttuvan's queen (மாபெருந் தேவி), not the poet Ilango
the hill women who sing the kunra kuravai
the hill-dwelling kuravar who saw the one-breasted woman taken to heaven (here மலைமிசை மாக்கள்)
the grain merchant of Madurai and Tamil poet (தண்டமிழ் ஆசான்), who tells the king the story
the Pandya king of Madurai (here தென்னர் கோமான்), whose death Saathan reports
the Pandya's chief queen (here பெருங்கோப் பெண்டு), who died with him
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai
the learned men of the Chera court, consulted on the stone
Senguttuvan's minister, who recounts his victories
a chief of Senguttuvan's court who advises proclaiming the campaign by drum
the proclaiming drum, beaten from an elephant's neck, whose message the last unit gives

reading: The Chera king, scion of the line that threw down the kadambu in the sea and set its bow on the Himalaya, sitting in the silver mansion with his queen Ilango Venmal, resolves to see the hills, and leaves Vanchi with his retinue for the groves and river banks.
nuance: The queen named here (இளங்கோ வேண்மாள், line 5) is Senguttuvan's wife, not the poet Ilango. Whether the kadambu and Himalaya feats of lines 1 to 2 are the king's own or his line's turns on whether the participles qualify வானவர் or தோன்றல் (line 3); the Patitruppattu preface gives the carved bow to his father Imayavaramban. The kaathai opens as a pleasure trip, so the news of the pathini reaches the king by chance, not by petition.
event: Senguttuvan sets out from Vanchi with his queen and retinue to see the mountain country.

reading: The royal camp spreads its halls on the sandbanks of the great river like the god riding his vast elephant, where fallen flowers hide the stream, and from every side rise the kuravai of the hill women, the velan's song to Murugan, the millet-pounders' vallai and the calls of the field-watchers and toddy-drinking kuravar.
nuance: The catalogue of hill sounds (ஓதை, repeated line after line into the next unit) sets the Chera court inside the kurinji world whose people witnessed Kannaki's ascent; the kuravai named at line 24 points back to the previous kaathai's kunra kuravai.
event: The king's camp is pitched on the river bank amid the songs and noises of the hill people.

reading: Amid the din of the moving army, the hill people come carrying goods beyond counting, like enemy kings who stand bearing tribute at Vanchi's court without finding the king's hour, and the list begins: tusks, aloe wood, yak-tail whisks, pots of honey, sandal, vermilion, collyrium, orpiment, cardamom, pepper, arrowroot, coconuts, mangoes, jack fruit, cane and flowering creepers.
nuance: The simile turns a free gift of hill produce into tribute: the hill folk stand at the king's camp as defeated enemies stand at his court, which prepares the kaathai's turn from wonder to conquest.
event: The hill people arrive at the camp laden with the produce of the mountains.

reading: Carrying on their heads plantain and areca clusters and the young of lion, tiger, elephant, bear, mountain goat, deer, musk-deer, mongoose, peacock, civet, jungle fowl and parrot, the hill people hail the king as his servants for seven births and tell him that under a forest vengai a woman who had lost her breast, alone in her grief, joined her husband and went to heaven while the gods praised her; they do not know her country or whose daughter she is, and they wish him long life.
nuance: The witnesses repeat the patikam's report to Ilango almost image for image (the vengai, the lost breast, the ascent), but now to the reigning king, and they confess they do not know her (நின்னாட்டு யாங்கள் நினைப்பினும் அறியேம்): the pathini enters the Chera land as a nameless stranger before Saathan names her. Lines 59 and 60 both begin வானவர் போற்ற.
event: The hill people offer their gifts and tell the king of the one-breasted woman they saw taken up to heaven under the vengai.
unit_note: End moved from line 61 to 63: the hill people's speech runs on to its closing blessing ending வாழியரென on line 63, and line 64 turns to Saathan.

reading: Saathan, the teacher of cool Tamil, who sat beside the king rapt with joy, offers to tell all that befell the woman: how, the anklet of an evil deed being the cause, her husband met his end, how she went with her anklet to plead before the king, and how the great pathini threw down the anklet before the queen, made her vow and burned the old city of Madurai with the fire that rose from her breast.
nuance: Saathan's account to the king calls the anklet தீவினைச் சிலம்பு (line 69), placing the evil deed in the object, and leaves out the former-birth curse he explained to Ilango in the patikam; told publicly to a king, the story is the case, the vow and the burning.
event: Saathan begins to tell Senguttuvan the story of Kannaki's loss, her case before the Pandya and the burning of Madurai.
