unit_note: Start moved from line 62 to 64: the hill people's speech ends at line 63 (வாழியரென), and the narration of Saathan begins at line 64.

reading: Saathan goes on: the Pandya on his lion throne, unable to bear her grief, fell senseless; his queen, stroking his feet and finding no answer, unshaken yet unable to bear the pain, said she would go where the king went and died with him as if seeking the life that had taken hers; and the maiden, as if to show the king the nature of the Pandya's bent sceptre, did not go to her own land alone but came to the Chera's, and Saathan blesses the king's victory for age upon age.
nuance: In the Vazhakkurai the queen only trembles and falls at the king's feet; here she dies by her own resolve (மன்னவன் செல்வுழிச் செல்க யான், line 84). Saathan gives the pathini's coming to Chera land a purpose, to show another king what a bent sceptre comes to (lines 87 to 88), which turns a refugee goddess into a lesson for kings. Line 82 (தலைத்தாள் நெடுமொழி தன்செவி கேளாள்) is obscure.
event: Saathan tells how the Pandya king died, how his queen died with him, and how Kannaki came into the Chera country.
unit_note: End moved from line 93 to 92: Saathan's speech closes with his blessing ending கொற்றமென on line 92, and line 93 begins the sentence about the king who heard it.

reading: Senguttuvan, grieving at the Pandya's fiery end, says it is well that the king's life left before word of his straying from justice reached kings like himself, that his departing life straightened into a just sceptre what strong former deeds had bent, and that to be born in a good line that guards the people, in great fear when rain fails and greater fear when any life is wronged, is only suffering and nothing to be revered; then he asks which of the two women the fair-browed queen admires more, the one who went with her husband's life or the one who came here in wrath.
nuance: Both causes are given in one line: the sceptre was bent by வல்வினை (line 98), yet the king's own death is what straightens it, so karma bends and the king's choice repairs. This is the patikam's first moral (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று ஆவது) read by a fellow king as a mercy: death came before the shame. The question at lines 107 to 109 sets the two kinds of wifely virtue side by side for the queen to judge.
event: Senguttuvan laments the Pandya's death, reflects on the burden of kingship and asks his queen which of the two women is greater.
unit_note: Start moved from line 94 to 93: the sentence that introduces the king's speech begins at line 93 (தென்னர் கோமான் தீத்திறங் கேட்ட) and runs into line 94.

reading: The great queen answers that the woman who died without seeing her husband's grief may gain great fortune in heaven, but that they must worship this pathini goddess who has come to their wide land; the king, pleased, looks to the learned men, who say that a stone taken from Pothiyil or from the Himalaya will become the goddess, and that bathing it in the Ganges or the Kaveri is fitting.
nuance: The queen settles the king's question by dividing the two women: the Pandya queen's reward is in heaven (வானகத்து), Kannaki's is a cult on earth (பத்தினிக் கடவுளைப் பரசல்). The learned men offer two sources, south and north, as equal.
event: The queen proposes that they worship the pathini as a goddess, and the learned men advise on the stone and its bathing.
unit_note: End moved from line 120 to 121: the learned men's advice ends with தகவோ உடைத்தென on line 121, and the king's reply begins at line 122.

reading: Senguttuvan answers that taking a stone from Pothiyil and bathing it at the Kaveri's ford is no deed of honour for those born to his line of the sword, and that if the king of the great northern mountain, with his matted, thread-wearing, three-fire-tending twice-born, will not give a stone to carve the goddess of the great pathini, then the kaanchi themes of lives gone fruitless, of the daughter given to the moon-crowned god, and of the long kaanchi set against the north will follow.
nuance: The cult becomes a matter of the king's honour: the near southern stone is rejected because it brings no glory, and the Himalaya's king, whose daughter married Siva (lines 133 to 134), is threatened with the kaanchi of war. The run of kaanchi turai names (lines 131 to 136) is compressed and its exact sense is not sure.
event: Senguttuvan rejects the southern stone and resolves to take one from the Himalaya, threatening war if its king refuses.
unit_note: Start moved from line 121 to 122: the learned men's speech ends at line 121, and the king's reply begins at line 122.

reading: The king goes on that they shall see his moon-touching head crowned with a garland of mandaram and vengai, and that his army shall wear the vanchi of the true sword outside the golden city in all its kinds, the umbrella, victory, assembly, conquest and great feast; and Villavan Kothai, wishing the king long years, speaks to him.
nuance: The speech is built from the names of the vanchi turai of the grammar of war, so the campaign is announced as a sequence of literary themes. Where the king's words end and Villavan Kothai's begin (line 140, 149 or 150) is not certain.
event: Senguttuvan declares that he will wear the vanchi garland and march north.

reading: Villavan Kothai recalls that kings who rose against him brought the fish banner from the Kongu field and their fame reached the elephants of the quarters, that his hunt among Aryans and Tamils is still before the minister's eyes, and that on the day his mother was bathed in the Ganges, Death saw him stand alone against a thousand Aryan kings; there is none in the world who would oppose him, so let letters bearing the bow, fish and tiger go to the northern kings; and Azhumbil Vel adds that the spies of enemy kings, who never leave Vanchi's gate, will carry the news, so let the drum be beaten.
nuance: The minister argues that fame will do the work of war: the Himalaya journey is only for a stone (line 169), and the northern kings need only wear the three Tamil emblems. Line 165 (இமிழ்கடல் வேலியைத் தமிழ்நா டாக்கிய) uses the Patitruppattu preface's phrase for his father. Azhumbil Vel turns the enemy's spies into the king's heralds.
event: The minister recounts the king's victories and urges a summons to the northern kings, and Azhumbil Vel advises proclaiming it by drum.
unit_note: End moved from line 175 to 177: Azhumbil Vel's counsel runs from line 173 to அறைபறை யென்றே ... உரைப்ப on line 177, and line 178 begins the king's assent.

reading: The king consents and enters great Vanchi, and the drum, raised on an elephant's neck, proclaims through the city: long live our lord; since he goes to take a stone from the Himalaya, let the northern kings come with tribute and live hearing of the kadambu thrown down in the sea and the bow carved on the cleft, or else live in a renunciation that leaves their wives; long live the king and his army's front.
nuance: Renunciation appears here as a threat: the alternative to tribute is a துறவு that gives up one's wives (line 190), the defeated king's forced exile, in a poem whose author by tradition renounced the Chera throne. The proclaimed feats (lines 187 to 188) are those the kaathai's opening gave to the Chera line.
event: Senguttuvan returns to Vanchi and the drum proclaims his northern campaign, calling the northern kings to tribute.
unit_note: Start moved from line 176 to 178: Azhumbil Vel's counsel ends on line 177 (உரைப்ப), and line 178 begins the king's consent and the proclamation.

title: கால்கோட் காதை
theme: The Chera king vows to bring a stone for a god from the Himalaya on the heads of the northern kings who scorned Tamil strength, marches north with Siva's feet on his crown, is charged by sky-faring sages to protect the northern Brahmins, refuses his allies' offer of a stone, crosses the Ganga, defeats the Aryan kings and captures Kanakan and Vijayan, while the demons hail his battlefield as a field of dharma; he then takes the stone for the pathini.
source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 250 against 254 lines held.
Line 8 உயந்த்தோங்கு is probably a misprint for உயர்ந்தோங்கு.
Line 57 இறைஞ்சாக் சென்னி has a wrong sandhi consonant; the sense requires இறைஞ்சாச் சென்னி.
Line 179 ஒங்குநீர் has a short ஒ where ஓங்குநீர் is expected.
Every unit boundary was moved to a sense break; the cut units split speeches and lists at lines 22, 69, 94, 106, 128, 139, 149, 168, 184, 201, 213 and 244.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanji who leads the northern expedition for the pathini's stone (also குட்டுவன், வானவன், காவலன் here)
the king's preceptor, who counsels him to calm his anger
the royal astrologer, master of the five branches of reckoning, who fixes the hour of departure
the assembled warriors and chiefs whom the king addresses
the king's councils and officers, who take the sword and umbrella to the outer shrine
those who bring the prasada of the god reclining on the serpent
the dancing women of Vanji, who bless the departing king
the court praisers who hail the king as he sets out
sages who travel through the sky and stop at the camp on their way to Malaya
performers from Konkan and Karnataka who sing at the camp
performers of the western hills (Kudagu) who sing the rainy-season kuravai
praise-singers who hail the king
the gatekeepers who announce the envoys
chief of the envoys sent by the Nootruvar Kannar
northern rulers allied with the Chera, who supply the boats to cross the Ganga
the thousand robed officers who bring gifts and tribute
the scribes who hand sealed letters to the kings
son of Balakumaran, a northern king who scorned Tamil strength
son of Balakumaran, Kanakan's brother and ally
the northern (Aryan) kings Uttaran, Vichitran, Rudran, Bhairavan, Chitran, Singan, Dhanuttaran, Svetan and others who fight the Chera
the demon women of the battlefield, who dance, sing and cook the battle feast
the Chera's commander, with whom he completes the campaign

reading: After the drum proclaims the campaign, the king takes the lion throne before his preceptor, astrologer, ministers and generals and vows that, since the boast of the northern kings reported to him by the Himalayan ascetics would shame kings like him if it went unanswered, his sword will not come back empty without a stone, laid on the crowned heads of the northern kings, from which to carve a god, or else let him be a king whose sceptre makes his own people tremble instead of his foes.
nuance: The vow is in the old conditional form: the penalty he accepts is not death or loss in battle but becoming a cruel king to his own subjects, so the fear his sceptre must cause is either the enemy's or his people's. The insult is only reported, carried by ascetics from the Himalaya (இமையத் தாபதர்), and அமையா வாழ்க்கை அரைசர் may mean kings of restless or unworthy life; the words of the boast are not given here. The god to be carved is not yet named as Kannaki in these lines.
event: The Chera king, enthroned before his council, vows to bring back a stone for a god on the heads of the northern kings or be a tyrant to his own people.
unit_note: End moved from line 22 to line 18: the king's vow closes with ஆகென on line 18, and lines 19-24 are the preceptor's reply, which ends with ஆசான் கூற on line 24.

reading: The preceptor asks whether any king, besides the Chola and Pandya who wear the aar and the neem, would stand against his vow, tells him that those two have not scorned him and bids his anger settle; then the astrologer, master of the five branches of reckoning, rises to hail his victory and declares that this very moment is the auspicious hour for marching in the chosen direction.
nuance: The preceptor's counsel is double: it flatters (no northern king can face you) and restrains (the only equals, the other two Tamil crowns, are not the offenders), so the anger is turned wholly north. The astrologer's முழுத்தம் makes the departure an act of timing as much as of will.
event: The preceptor calms the king's anger and the astrologer declares the hour for setting out north.
unit_note: Start moved from line 23 to line 19 (see the previous unit) and end from line 38 to line 31: the astrologer's speech closes with என்று ஏத்த on line 31, and line 32 begins the king's response.

reading: Hearing the astrologer, the king orders his sword and umbrella moved northward; with drums roaring, the councils and officers hail him, carry the sword and white umbrella on an elephant's neck into the outer shrine, the king who strings the vanji with the palmyra feasts his eager generals with the great rice, wears on his crown the vanji that blossoms in flowerless Vanji, and the morning drum sounds at the gate.
nuance: பூவா வஞ்சியிற் பூத்த வஞ்சி plays on the city's name and the vanji flower worn for an invading march: the garland of conquest is said to bloom in a city that bears the flower's name but not the flower. The great rice (பெருஞ்சோறு) shared with the generals binds them to the campaign before it starts.
event: The sword and umbrella are moved north to the outer shrine, the generals are feasted with the great rice, and the king puts on the vanji garland.
unit_note: Start moved from line 39 to line 32 (see the previous unit): the king hears and gives the order at lines 32-33, and the long sentence of preparations closes with எழுதலும் on line 53.

reading: The king sets the feet of the moon-crowned god who fills the world upon his head with the vanji garland, bows the head that bows to no one, circles the shrine and mounts his war elephant amid the Brahmins' oblation smoke; when some bring the prasada of the god who sleeps on the serpent in the golden hall, he takes it on his shoulder, since Siva's feet are on his crown, and the dancing women everywhere bless him to go with the victor's flowers on his elephant's brow.
nuance: The king worships both gods but ranks them on his body: the matted god's feet on the crown, Vishnu's prasada on the shoulder, and the narrator gives the reason (வைத்தலின்) without comment. இறைஞ்சாச் சென்னி இறைஞ்சி: the head that bows to no king bows to the god. ஆடக மாடம் may name a particular Vishnu shrine; the lines do not say which.
event: The king worships Siva before setting out, takes Vishnu's prasada on his shoulder, and is blessed by the dancing women.
unit_note: Start unchanged at line 54; end moved from line 69 to line 73: the dancing women's blessing, begun at line 68, closes with ஆகென on line 73.

reading: Bards, panegyrists and heralds, elephant riders, horse captains and sword warriors hail him; like Indra leaving his city against the asuras he leaves Vanji, his army spreading like a white-crested sea, bending mountain backs and cutting paths through the land, camps on the slopes of the Nilagiri, and, praised by his men, lies down on the great couch amid the din of the moving army.
nuance: The comparison with Indra marching on the asuras makes the northern kings the demons of the simile before any battle is fought.
event: Praised by bards and soldiers, the king marches out of Vanji and camps at the Nilagiri.
unit_note: Start moved from line 70 to line 74 (see the previous unit) and end from line 94 to line 92: the march and the camp close at line 92, and the sky-faring sages' descent, begun at line 93, runs to line 97.

reading: Sages who travel the sky, wishing to see the Indra-like ruler, descend into the hall where the king rises and bows to them, and tell the Vanavan born in Vanji by the grace of the red-haired god that they are going to Malaya, and since his purpose is the great Himalaya, where Brahmins of the hard Vedas live, guarding them is his duty; they bless him and leave.
nuance: The sages turn the campaign's road into a duty: on the way to punish northern kings, the Chera is charged to protect the northern Brahmins. He keeps the charge at the close of the kaathai (lines 248-250), when he orders the Veda-keepers of the north guarded before he takes the stone.
event: Sky-faring sages visit the camp and charge the king to protect the Brahmins of the Himalaya.
unit_note: Start moved from line 95 to line 93 and end from line 106 to line 104: the sages' descent begins with விசும்பியங்கு முனிவர் on line 93, and their speech and departure close with போந்ததற் பின்னர் on line 104.

reading: Performers from Konkan and Karnataka in the dress of their peoples come with dark-eyed women singing that spring has come and the lover has not, the Kudagar come singing the rainy-season kuravai, asking a bangled girl whether it is the rain cloud that has come or her lover's chariot with his work done, and the Ovar hail the king who will finish his sword-work to live an aeon; he rewards them all with jewels beyond their hopes.
nuance: The camp's songs are songs of separation sung to a man setting out: the spring song says the lover has not come, the rain song imagines his chariot returning with his work done (செய்வினை முடித்து), so the performers set the king's campaign in the frame of a woman waiting for the return. கூத்துள் படுவோன் காட்டிய முறைமையின் may mean the rewards followed the rule the dance-master showed; the phrase is not clear.
event: Performers from Konkan, Karnataka and Kudagu sing at the camp and the king rewards them.
unit_note: Start moved from line 107 to line 105 and end from line 128 to line 127: the new scene begins after போந்ததற் பின்னர் on line 104, and the king's gifts close the scene at line 127; line 128 begins the gatekeepers' list.

reading: The gatekeepers announce to the king of the bow banner that there have arrived one hundred and two dancing women, two hundred and eight musicians, a hundred jesters versed in the ninety-six kinds of sect, a hundred chariots, five hundred elephants, ten thousand horses, twenty thousand carts of northern goods marked in writing, and a thousand robed officers led by Sanjayan.
nuance: தொண்ணூற் றறுவகைப் பாசண்டத் துறை நண்ணிய நூற்றுவர் நகைவேழம்பர்: the jesters are said to know the ninety-six sects, perhaps because their comedy imitates the sects' teachers; the number ninety-six is the conventional count of the heterodox schools, but the line does not say how the jesters use it.
event: The gatekeepers announce the arrival of the allied envoys and their gifts.
unit_note: Start moved from line 129 to line 128 (see the previous unit) and end from line 139 to line 140: the gatekeepers' announcement closes with வாயிலோர் என on line 140.

reading: The king bids the dancers, performers and musicians come in with Sanjayan; Sanjayan enters, bows, presents the hundred and two and the craftsmen, and reports the Nootruvar Kannar's message that if the Chera's march north is only for a stone to carve a god, they themselves will take one from the Himalaya, bathe it in the Ganga and bring it to him.
nuance: The allies' offer would give the king his stone without a war; the next unit declines it, so the stone must be taken by battle for the vow to be kept, not merely obtained.
event: Sanjayan presents the gifts and reports the Nootruvar Kannar's offer to fetch and bathe the stone for the king.
unit_note: Start moved from line 140 to line 141 (see the previous unit) and end from line 149 to line 155: Sanjayan's report of the Kannar's offer closes with என்றனர் என்று ... வாழ்கென on lines 154-155.

reading: The king answers that Kanakan and Vijayan, the sons of Balakumaran, of unguarded tongue, joined with visiting kings, have not known the strength of Tamil; let Sanjayan tell the Kannar that an army like Death is coming and have them build rows of boats to cross the Ganga; Sanjayan leaves, and the thousand robed officers bring sandal, pearls and the Pandya's tribute, while the scribes hand the kings sealed letters.
nuance: The insult is now named: two kings, Kanakan and Vijayan, whose fault is a careless tongue (காவா நாவின்) and ignorance of அருந்தமிழ் ஆற்றல். The quarrel is cast as the honour of Tamil, not of the Chera alone, which is why the Pandya's tribute arrives in the same breath.
event: The king refuses the allies' stone, names Kanakan and Vijayan as the offenders, and asks the Kannar for boats to cross the Ganga.
unit_note: Start moved from line 150 to line 156 (see the previous unit) and end from line 168 to line 171: the delivery of gifts and letters closes with அளித்தாங்கு on line 171.

reading: When the envoys have gone, the ruler of the sea-girt earth, hailed by the lords of the land, leaves his camp, crosses to the northern bank of the Ganga on the Kannar's boats, is received by them, passes through their country and enters the northern land, making camp in enemy territory.
event: The Chera crosses the Ganga on the Kannar's boats and camps in the enemy's northern country.
unit_note: Start unchanged at line 172; end moved from line 184 to line 181: the crossing and the camp in enemy land close at line 181, and the list of enemy kings begins at line 182.

reading: Before him Uttaran, Vichitran, Rudran, Bhairavan, Chitran, Singan, Dhanuttaran, Svetan and all the kings of the north, saying they will see the strength of southern Tamil, come on in league with Kanaka and Vijaya, and the king falls on them like a lion that, hunting, sees a herd of elephants, while drums, conches and horns shake every quarter and archers, spearmen, charioteers, elephant riders and horsemen close in.
nuance: The northern kings take up the very phrase of the quarrel, தென்றமிழ் ஆற்றல் காண்குதும், so the battle is staged as a test of Tamil power. The drum that eats the offering of lives (உயிர்ப்பலி யுண்ணும்) makes the war itself a rite.
event: The northern kings, allied with Kanaka and Vijaya, march to test Tamil strength and the Chera attacks.
unit_note: Start moved from line 185 to line 182 and end from line 201 to line 199: the list of enemy kings begins at line 182, and the lines 200-203 on the dust that silences bells and conches form one sentence with the next unit.

reading: The great dust of battle blinds the earth and stills the tongues of the elephants' bells and the conches, garlands tangle with garlands, archers' shoulders and heads lie severed in heaps, headless trunks stumble over corpses, and demon women dance to the drum and loosen their hair in the fat-laden blood that carries the bodies.
unit_note: Start moved from line 202 to line 200 (see the previous unit) and end from line 213 to line 210: the description of the carnage closes at line 210, and line 211 begins the sentence on the Aryan kings' armies.

reading: The king slays the fighting men of the Aryan kings and heaps them on the field, lays waste their chariots, elephants and horses so that the Aryan kings learn on the battlefield that the buffalo-rider eats a whole host of lives in a single day, wears the thumbai with the palmyra after the war dance, and Kanakan and Vijayan, who scorned rich Tamil trusting their swords, fall with fifty-two chariot warriors into Senguttuvan's net of anger.
nuance: Death (the buffalo-rider) is made the Chera's teacher: the Aryan kings learn in one day what they did not know of Tamil strength. The capture, not the killing, of Kanakan and Vijayan keeps them for the humiliation that follows (they will carry the stone).
event: Senguttuvan destroys the Aryan kings' armies and captures Kanakan and Vijayan with fifty-two chariot warriors.
unit_note: Start moved from line 214 to line 211 and end from line 228 to line 224: the sentence on the Aryan kings' armies begins at line 211, and the capture of Kanakan and Vijayan closes with படுதலும் on line 224.

reading: The other northern kings throw away their swords and slip off wherever they wish in disguise, as matted ascetics, robed monks, ash-smeared devotees, peacock-feather vow-keepers, singers, players and dancers, while the elephant-riding guardians tremble; and the demons praise the battlefield of the sword-ploughman who threshed it with tuskers yoked and the sword for goad, sing of the churning of the sea, the war in Lanka and the dark god's chariot war, dance the kuravai before and behind the chariot, and cook a meat-rice in pots on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms, which the demon cook serves, hailing the one who made a field of dharma by the victory of the just sceptre.
nuance: The disguises cover the whole range of ascetics (matted hair, robes, ash, the peacock-feather fan of the great vow) and performers, so the defeated kings survive by wearing the marks of renunciation and art; the text says only that they went where they wished, not that the victor spared them knowingly. The demons' blessing calls the slaughter an அறக்களம் made by the செங்கோல்: the battle feast is given the name of dharma by those who eat it. விச்சைக் கோலத்து (the guise of the arts they had mastered) is not certain in sense.
event: The surviving northern kings flee in the guise of ascetics and performers, and the demons sing and cook their battle feast for the victor.
unit_note: Start unchanged at line 225; end moved from line 244 to line 246: the demons' feast and blessing, begun at line 240, close with ஊழி வாழ்கென on line 246.

reading: Kuttuvan, having finished the battle, orders that the northern guardians of the Vedas, whose cool life keeps the great fire unquenched, be protected, sends out his many armies under Villavan Kothai to complete the conquest, and takes from the golden-peaked Himalaya the stone for the peerless pathini.
nuance: Only now is the god of the vow (line 14) named: the stone is for the பத்தினி, Kannaki. The order to protect the Veda-keepers keeps the charge of the sky-faring sages (lines 102-103). காற்றூதாளர், those who blow the fire, is a rare word for the fire-tending Brahmins.
event: Senguttuvan orders the northern Brahmins protected, sends his armies on with Villavan Kothai, and takes the stone for the pathini from the Himalaya.
unit_note: Start moved from line 245 to line 247 (see the previous unit); end unchanged at line 254.

title: நீர்ப்படைக் காதை
theme: At the Ganga the Chera Senguttuvan has the pathini's stone bathed, rewards his warriors, and hears from the Brahmin Maadalan the aftermath of Madurai: Madari's fire, Kavunthi's fast, the renunciations and deaths of the parents, Madhavi's taking of robes, the new Pandya's offering of a thousand goldsmiths and the soundness of the Chola sceptre; then he rewards the Brahmin, sends the captives away and returns to Vanchi as the songs of hill, field, pasture and shore announce him.
source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 255 against 256 lines held; the count differs by one somewhere in the kaathai.
Line 135 reads நிரைமணிப் புரவி ஓரழ் பூண்ட; ஓரழ் is not a word and is probably a corruption of ஓரேழ் (the sun's seven horses).
Line 188 spells ஈரைஞ் ஞூற்றூவர் where line 128 has ஈரைஞ் ஞூற்றுவர்; one of the two is a misprint.
Lines 7 to 12 (the reckoning of the slaughter by years, months, days and hours, and the number ஒன்பதிற்று இரட்டி) are compressed and may be damaged; the count cannot be fixed from the text.
The given boundary after line 33 broke a phrase; units 18-33 and 34-56 were re-cut as 18-42 and 43-56.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the pathini's stone from the Himalaya and bathed it in the Ganga (named here also குடவர் கோ, பொறையன், வில்லவன், வானவன்)
the Brahmin of Puhar (மாடல மறையோன்) who brings the Chera king news of what followed Kovalan's death
Kanaka and Vijaya, the northern (Arya) princes who defied the Tamil king and were made to carry the stone on their crowns
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini whose stone the Chera has brought
the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived
the old herdswoman of Madurai in whose house Kannaki was lodged
the Jain nun who went with the couple to Madurai
Kovalan's father, a great merchant of Puhar (named here கோவலன் தாதை)
Kovalan's mother (named here துறந்தோன் மனைவி)
Kannaki's father, a great merchant of Puhar (named here கண்ணகி தாதை)
Kannaki's mother, the wife of the merchant who gave gifts
Madhavi's mother
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan
the young Chola king, the Chera's cousin (மைத்துனன்), whose rule nine kings would not bear
the nine kings of one mind who rose against the young Chola
the Pandya of Korkai who took the throne of Madurai after the king's death
the Chera king's astrologer, who reckons the time since the army left Vanchi
the northern kings taken captive in the campaign
the thousand chamberlains (cloaked officers) sent to show the captives to the other two kings
the Chera king's chief queen, waiting in Vanchi
the queen's nurses of her retinue
the hunchbacked and dwarf attendants of the women's quarters
the hill women who sing on the millet-watch platform
the ploughmen of the Chera land, who sing to their oxen
the cowherds of the Porunai ford, who play the flute
the girls of the shore who play kazhangu with pearls and sing the vanji

reading: The narrator recounts that, after the stone for the goddess-pathini had been taken from the Himalaya and set on the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya, the Chera, whose army had reckoned its slaughter of the northern kings who fought him not knowing Tamil strength, came with his host to the bank of the Ganga and had the pathini deity bathed by men learned in the rite.
nuance: The kaathai is named for this bathing (நீர்ப்படை), told in a single subordinate clause (lines 15 to 16) before the poem turns to the camp; the rite is done by நூற்றிறன் மாக்கள, men who know the treatise, not by the king. The pathini is called கடவுட் பத்தினி and பத்தினிக் கடவுள், a goddess, before any temple is built. Lines 7 to 12, where the work of the old death-dealer swells and the army reckons years, months, days and hours, and the eighteen (ஒன்பதிற்று இரட்டி) and the one day's span are given, are compressed and the count is not clear.
event: Senguttuvan, the northern kings beaten in a day's battle, reaches the Ganga and has the pathini's stone bathed there.

reading: The king enters the camp on the open ground of the Ganga's south bank, in halls, pavilions, groves and pools that the Arya kings had built for him, and the narrator lists the warriors he will honour: those who broke enemy kings' hearts and were wed like brides of the gods, those who lay with head and shoulders paid for in battle, those who died with their swords as the hollow-eyed demoness sang their praise in her kuravai, those who wore the victor's garland and stood red with their wounds.
nuance: The list puts the dead and the living in one catalogue: the dead are given the heavenly marriage (வானவர் மகளிரின் வதுவை) and a demoness's praise, the living are marked by wounds, and all are the same grammatical subject of the honours given in the next lines. The Arya kings' building of the camp for the conqueror (line 22) is tribute, not hospitality.
event: Senguttuvan enters the camp the Arya kings built for him on the Ganga's south bank.
unit_note: The boundary between the second and third units was moved from after line 33 to after line 42. Line 33 broke a phrase (கிளர்பூண் ஆகத்து / வளையோர் மடிய); line 42 ends with மறவர், the head noun of the whole list of warriors, and line 43 begins the king's giving.

reading: Calling his wounded warriors forward, the king gives them golden vaagai leaves through the long festival hour, and as he sits in state, crowned with palmyra and thumbai, the Brahmin Maadalan appears and hails him, saying that Madhavi's seaside song crushed the crowned heads of Kanaka and Vijaya, and the king asks what this jest, unknown to the kings of the enemy lands, means.
nuance: Maadalan's riddle makes a courtesan's song the first cause of a northern war: the kaanal vari split Kovalan from Madhavi, which led to Madurai, to Kannaki, and to the stone the northern kings now carry. The king calls it நகைத்திறம், a jest, and asks for its sense; the next units are the answer.
event: Senguttuvan rewards his warriors, and Maadalan arrives and tells him Madhavi's song crushed the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya.
unit_note: The unit begins at line 43, where the boundary was moved from after line 33 (see the previous unit); it ends where the given unit ended, at line 56.

reading: Maadalan explains that at the sea-play on the cool shore, in a time of sulking, with Madhavi's vari song, the deed of the past rose in wrath, Kovalan left her and went with his wife to Madurai, was killed, and his wife came into the Chera's land and rose onto the crowns of the northern kings; then he tells why he came: returning from circling Pothiyil and bathing at Kumari, by karma's fruit perhaps he went to Madurai, heard that the woman had beaten the king with her anklet, and saw Madari rise in the common and cry that Kovalan was blameless, the king had erred, and she had lost the one put in her keeping.
nuance: Line 59 gives two causes in one breath: the lovers' sulk (ஊடற் காலத்து) and the deed of the past rising (ஊழ்வினை உருத்தெழ). Maadalan then puts even his own arrival at Madurai under karma, as a question (ஊழ்வினைப் பயன்கொல்), while Madari blames the king outright (கோமகன் பிழைத்தான், line 75) and her own failure to guard her charge. So the unit sets karma, the king's fault and a guardian's failure side by side without choosing among them. Madari's அடைக்கலம் is a ward entrusted to her, not a devotee's refuge at a god's feet.
event: Maadalan tells Senguttuvan how Kovalan left Madhavi, died in Madurai, and how Madari cried out that the king had erred.

reading: Maadalan goes on: Madari entered the fire in the middle of the night; Kavunthi, the ascetic, in her anger at the king, asking whether the couple's deed had risen against her too, gave up her life by the vow of not eating; having learned all that befell Madurai he went home to Puhar and told it, and Kovalan's father, hearing what came to his son, his son's wife and the king, gave away great wealth, entered the seven Indra viharas and renounced before the three hundred sky-walkers who strive to end the birth of the body.
nuance: Kavunthi's question (line 82) is the striking thing: a Jain nun, who has taught that deeds come back to their doers, asks whether the couple's deed has come back on her, the one who led them, and answers with the fasting death. Lines 80 to 81, with the king's departing life and the patient woman, are hard to construe: whether the king's death is the time of her fast, or what she could not bear, is not clear. Kovalan's father renounces at the Indra viharas, which the poem placed in Puhar under the five-branched bodhi (Silappathikaram 10), so his renunciation is in the Buddhist order; the unit does not state the doctrine, only the aim of ending birth.
event: Madari enters the fire, Kavunthi fasts to death, and Kovalan's father, told by Maadalan, gives away his wealth and becomes a renouncer.

reading: Maadalan says that Kovalan's mother, unable to bear her son's grief, died; Kannaki's father gave gifts before the Ajivika ascetics in their godlike guise and took their dharma, and his wife died too; and Madhavi, hearing it, told her mother that Manimekalai must never see the courtesan's guise that brings great sorrow, cut off her hair with its garland and took dharma with a gift at the bodhi; since those who heard the news from his mouth died, he has come to bathe in the Ganga; and the king asks what the Pandya land has done since its king died.
nuance: The same news ends in renunciation for the two fathers and Madhavi and in death for the two mothers. The two merchants turn to different orders, Kovalan's father to the Indra viharas, Kannaki's father to the Ajivikas (ஆசீவகர், line 99), and Madhavi to the bodhi (போதித் தானம், line 108); the poem names the orders without ranking them. Madhavi's reason is her daughter: she renounces so that Manimekalai will not take up the courtesan's life, the thread the Manimekalai follows. Maadalan bathes in the Ganga because his telling caused deaths (line 109), a messenger's guilt for the news he carried.
event: Kovalan's mother and Kannaki's mother die of grief, Kannaki's father joins the Ajivikas, and Madhavi cuts her hair and renounces; Senguttuvan asks about the Pandya land.

reading: Maadalan answers by first praising the king, who, when nine kings of one mind would not bear the young rule of his cousin the Chola Killi, destroyed their nine umbrellas in a single day, and who felled the neem guarded by Pazhaiyan, and then tells that Vetrivel Cheliyan of Korkai, in one day, fed the lives of a thousand goldsmiths as an offering to the pathini who cut off one breast, and, when Madurai had lost its king in its time of distress, mounted the throne of justice as the morning sun mounts the god's chariot.
nuance: The new Pandya's first act is an offering of lives (உயிர்ப்பலி) to the pathini: the craft of the one goldsmith who lied is punished a thousandfold, and the poem gives it as worship, not as a sentence. The unit does not say the goldsmiths were guilty. Maadalan's praise of the Chera for the Chola succession shows the three crowned houses bound by kinship: the Chera intervenes for a cousin of his mother's line.
event: Maadalan tells how Vetrivel Cheliyan offered a thousand goldsmiths to the pathini and took the Pandya throne.

reading: Maadalan ends that the heir of the moon's line has ascended to guard the world age after age, and as the king sits listening, evening falls, the sky reddens and the white crescent shows; the astrologer rises and tells him thirty-two months have passed since he left Vanchi; the king goes back through the streets of the camp to his hall, has Maadalan called by the gatekeepers and asks whether, since the young princes died, the Chola's rule and its sceptre are still sound.
nuance: The sun-and-moon image of lines 137 to 138 turns the Pandya succession into a change of lights: the line descended from the moon goes on as the sun goes down. The astrologer's count of thirty-two months reminds the king, and the reader, how long the vow for the stone has kept him from home. Who the young princes (இளங்கோ வேந்தர், line 159) were is not said in the unit.
event: At evening the astrologer tells Senguttuvan he has been away thirty-two months, and the king asks Maadalan about the Chola's rule.

reading: Maadalan answers that the victory of the Chola line, who destroyed the three forts the gods marvelled at, and the dharma-giving sceptre of the one who cut his own body to end the little dove's distress and the hawk's hunger, can never turn; there is no fault, even in a time of trouble, with the lord of the land the Kaveri guards.
nuance: The assurance rests on lineage: the sceptre cannot bend because of what an ancestor did. The dove story, which Kannaki threw at the Pandya as a reproach, is here a guarantee offered to a Chera about a Chola. The answer is given as a rhetorical question (திரிந்துவேறு ஆகுங் காலமும் உண்டோ), not as a report of how the Chola has ruled.

reading: The king honours the Brahmin and gives him gold to fifty times his own weight, sends the hundred Arya kings back toward their lands, and with them the princes of great armies who saved their lives in ascetics' guise, the Arya pedis with curled beards, flower-hair, long eyes, bangles and anklets, and the chamberlains who refuse the commands of the defiant kings.
nuance: The gold is measured against the king's own weight (தன்னிறை), the giver's body as the unit of the gift. The princes who escaped in ascetic guise (தாபத வேடம்) are a jibe: the renouncer's garb worn as a disguise to live. The pedis are described with a mix of male and female marks (a beard with a woman's eyes, bangles and breasts); what their role was is not said. Whether all these groups go home with the hundred kings or are sent elsewhere, and how ஐயிரு பதின்மர் and ஆடகப் பெருநிறை ஐயைந்து இரட்டி are to be counted, is not certain; the sentence runs on into the next unit.
event: Senguttuvan gives Maadalan gold of fifty times his weight and sends the captive Arya kings away.

reading: The king sends a thousand chamberlains to show Kanaka and Vijaya, who fought not knowing Tamil strength, to the two other great kings, and before he has slept, as the young sun rises over the eastern hills and bees hum in the Ganga's lotus fields, the western king, wearing the northern thumbai and vaagai, turns south with his army toward his treasure-filled city.
nuance: Showing the captives to the Chola and the Pandya makes the northern victory a message to the other two Tamil crowns; the Tamil strength the northerners did not know (அருந்தமிழ் ஆற்றல், line 189) is the same phrase as the kaathai's opening (line 5), so the campaign is framed as Tamil against Arya. From line 200 the unit has already moved to the queen's palace in Vanchi.
event: Senguttuvan sends Kanaka and Vijaya to be shown to the Chola and Pandya kings and sets out south for Vanchi.

reading: In Vanchi, the queen lies sleepless on a golden bed of swan-down in her gem-set hall; the nurses who know the king's chariot victories sing that her grief at parting will end and wish her long life; the hunchbacks and dwarfs come to tell her that her lord has come and her hair should take its festival adornment; and the hill women on the watch platform sing their kurinji song, telling the wild elephant that came to eat the millet while the toddy-drunk watchman dropped his sling to leave the path of the king's war elephant.
nuance: The return is told through the queen's waiting and the voices that reach her: first those of the palace, then the hill women. The kurinji song turns its own landscape's scene (the elephant raiding the millet) into news of the king, so that each region's song, here and in the next units, bends to the same refrain that he has come. The queen's sleep is ambiguous: துயிலாற்றுப் படுத்து suggests she was laid to sleep, while the nurses sing to end her grief.
event: The queen's nurses and attendants announce the king's coming, and the hill women sing of it in their kurinji song.

reading: The ploughmen sing their own song, that the lord of the west, the ploughman who yoked donkeys and sowed kavadi on the ruined forts of the northern kings, has come, that tomorrow the oxen will not wear the yoke, and that this is the white festival that frees kings from their fetters; and at the Porunai ford, bright with the colours, powders and flowers the bathers left, the cowherd boys perched on a thazhai branch call that Villavan has come back from the Himalaya and the herds should be taken to the water.
nuance: The ploughmen's title for the king, the donkey-plough ploughman of the enemy's forts, is a war rite (ploughing a ruined fort and sowing it with worthless seed) that the field-workers sing as their own; the same song gives their oxen a holiday. The white festival that frees kings' fetters (line 229) seems to be a release of captives at the king's return, but the line is brief and its sense not sure.
event: The ploughmen and the cowherds of the Porunai sing that the king has come.

reading: The cowherds play their flute as the king's herds bathe at the ford, the girls of the shore lift pearls born of the right-whorled conch in their bangled hands for the kazhangu game and sing that Vanavan has come and they will sing the vanji with thumbai and palmyra; the queen listens to all these songs, and the king, under the white umbrella, crowned with vaagai and high on his swift elephant, is met by the city with a train of elephants and enters Vanchi.
nuance: The four songs, of hill, field, pasture and shore, make the four landscapes of the Chera land greet one king, and the queen hears them all (line 251) before she sees him. The kaathai ends with the king's name (செங்குட்டுவன்), as the stone, the bathing and the news of Madurai give way to the triumph.
event: Senguttuvan, met by the city with elephants, enters Vanchi while the shore girls sing and the queen listens.

title: நடுகற் காதை
theme: Back in Vanchi after the northern campaign, the Chera hears through Neelan the Chola's and Pandya's taunts that captives who fled in ascetics' guise are no victory; the brahmin Maadalan calms his anger and preaches that body, wealth and youth pass and the soul goes by its deeds, and urges a Vedic sacrifice in place of the sacrifice of war; the king performs it, frees the prisoners, and installs the Himalayan stone as the pathini's jewelled image with daily worship, while the narrator sums up the three lessons the pathini gave the three kings.
source_issues: The kaathai has 234 lines in the core file but the edition's printed last line number is 230; the four-line difference is in the edition's numbering, and this file uses the core file's line numbers.
Line 115 reads வியுலூ ரெறிந்தபின்; the place is வியலூர் in the Patitruppattu's fifth preface, so வியுலூர் is probably a misprint.
Line 40 (காட்டி நீங்க) and line 41 (வழிமொழி கேட்ப) are hard to construe; unit 39-54 is marked uncertain.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi, returned from the northern campaign with the Himalayan stone (named here குட்டுவன், கோமகன், வேந்தன், வடதிசை வணக்கிய மன்னவர் ஏறு)
the Chera's queen (வதுவை வேண்மாள்)
the Chera queen's women and attendants
the women of Vanchi who greet the evening and the returned warriors
the Chakkaiyan dancer of Paraiyur who performs Siva's koṭṭicētam
the chief of the chamberlains (கஞ்சுக மாக்கள்) sent to escort the Aryan kings to the Chola and Pandya
the brahmin of Thalaichengaanam, of unfailing learning, who counsels the Chera
the Chola king in his old city, the Chera's cousin (named கிள்ளி in the previous kaathai)
the Pandya now reigning at Madurai after the fire (வெற்றிவேற் செழியன் in the previous kaathai), not the Nedunjeliyan who died
the northern kings beaten by the Chera and paraded before the other two kings
the Chera's commander
the Chera's officer sent with the revenue accountants
the brahmins of the field of dharma who go with the king to the temple
the king's great astrologer
the skilled artisans who made the image

reading: At evening in the Chera's old city of Vanchi, women holding white-wicked lamps scatter flower offerings and hail the king of the world, and the warriors with palmyra garlands who finished his war come home with chests pressed by elephant tusks and torn by spear, arrow and sword.
nuance: The opening sentence does not close in this unit: the list of the warriors' wounds is the object of what the women do with them in the next lines. The wounds are counted by weapon, so the homecoming is told through the body of the fighter, not through the king's victory.
event: Evening falls on Vanchi; lamp-bearing women hail the king as the wounded warriors return.

reading: The dark-eyed young women soothe those wounds with the warmth of their breasts, their perfumed hair loosened, their glances shot like Kama's flower arrows, and they praise this evening as both the go-between and the medicine, smiling with fresh smiles.
nuance: The evening, elsewhere in the tradition the hour when longing hurts, is here called தூதும் மருந்தும் (lines 20-21): it brings the lovers together and heals what war did. The scene sets up, before the brahmin's sermon, the pleasures of a victorious city that the sermon will call passing.
event: The women of Vanchi tend the returned warriors' wounds with their embrace and praise the evening.

reading: The mango-leaf-skinned women give their delights to the young men, set mirrors before them to see their hair, garlands and adornment, take up the curved small yaazh and play in the old order of the paalai and kurinji modes like the singing women, and so feast the men as guests, while the narrator begins to liken the coming moon to the face of Kuttuvan.
nuance: Lines 33-35 use technical terms of tuning (குரல், துத்தம், பாலை, குறிஞ்சி) whose exact sense belongs to the musical lore of the time. The simile at 37-38, the king's face when he protects his people, runs on into the next unit.
event: The women adorn themselves before mirrors, play the small yaazh and feast the young men.

reading: The moon rises, worshipped by the world, showing the famed city a face like Kuttuvan's, and takes possession of the moonlit terraces, flower beds, stages, bowers and couches where Kama reigns; and in the jewelled hall of the golden palace that stands in the middle of the walled city like Meru in the middle of the earth, the queen Venmal comes to see the moon's beauty while bangled women carrying lamps spread on one side singing her many years.
nuance: காட்டி நீங்க (line 40) and வழிமொழி கேட்ப (41) are hard to fix: whether something departs as the moon shows itself, and whose words the men and women hear, is not clear to me. The queen is named only as வதுவை வேண்மாள் மங்கல மடந்தை.
event: Queen Venmal comes to the jewelled hall of the palace to see the moon, with lamp-bearing women singing blessings.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 55/56 to 54/55: line 54 closes the first ஒருசார் clause (பரந்தன வொருசார்); line 55's drums and yaazh begin the second, which ends at 56.

reading: On every side the queen's attendants press round: drums and yaazh and ripe songs on one side, hunchbacks and dwarfs carrying musk and white sandal on another, eunuchs dressed as women carrying colours, powders and garlands on another, flowers, incense and perfume round the couch, and maids carrying mirrors, clothes and jewels.
nuance: The retinue repeats almost item by item the Pandya queen's train in the twentieth kaathai (mirror, cloth, colours, musk, hunchbacks); here the same splendour surrounds a queen whose city is at peace.
event: The queen's attendants gather round her with music, scents, garlands, mirrors, clothes and jewels.
unit_note: Unit cut from the original 56-70: it now starts at 55 (see the previous unit) and ends at 64, the last ஒருசார் clause; line 65 (ஆங்கு) begins the king's ascent with the queen.

reading: The king who rules the earth ascends the jewelled stage with the queen and watches the koṭṭicētam of the god whose one side is Uma, danced by the Chakkaiyan of Paraiyur of the four-Veda brahmins, with the anklet sounding, the drum beating, the thousand eyes giving their signs and the red matted hair sweeping the quarters on one half while on the other half nothing stirs; pleased, he praises the dancer, goes to the royal hall, and Neelan and the chamberlains come with the brahmin Maadalan, announce themselves through the gatekeepers and bow.
nuance: The dance shows the god as half woman: the lines on what moves (anklet, drum, matted hair) and what does not (bangle, girdle, breast, earring, hair knot) divide the one body between Siva's fury and Uma's stillness. The Chakkaiyan acts the god's dance; the god himself is not on the stage. A Saiva performance sits in a Chera court that also hears a Vedic sermon and will found a pathini's temple.
event: The king and queen watch the Chakkaiyan dance Siva's koṭṭicētam; then Neelan and the chamberlains come with Maadalan to the royal hall.
unit_note: Unit made from 67-70 of the original 56-70 and 71-83 of the original 71-84: it starts at 65 (ஆங்கு, the king ascending) and ends at 83, where the chamberlains bow; line 84 is the vocative that opens Neelan's report.

reading: Neelan reports that when they reached the Chola's old city and went with the Aryan kings beaten in battle to bow before the Chola, seated in the painted hall gathered from Vajra, Avanti and Magadha, the Chola told his army chief that to take in a winning war those who had flung away sword and umbrella on the field and saved their lives in the guise of men who do not kill is no victory.
nuance: கொல்லாக் கோலம், the guise of those who do not kill, points back to the end of the Kaal Kol kaathai, where the beaten kings escaped dressed as matted, ash-smeared ascetics, singers and dancers. The Chola's words are a judgment on the Chera's triumph made in the Chera's own envoy's hearing.
event: Neelan reports that the Chola, shown the captive Aryan kings, said it was no victory to take men who had saved their lives in ascetics' guise.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 84/85 to 83/84 and from 96/97 to 95/96: the unit begins with Neelan's vocative (line 84) and ends at 95, where the Chola's words close with their subject after the verb (உரைத்தனன் ... செம்பியர் பெருந்தகை).

reading: Neelan goes on: when, after the Chola left, they showed the Aryan kings on elephants under the umbrellas taken from them to the Madurai king, the Pandya Cheliyan said that the conquest of a man who turned his burning anger on those who, having bowed to the god whose half is Uma on the Himalaya's peak, gave up the field to the king and took the great guise of penance, was a new kind of victory; and Neelan tells all these long words of the two kings.
nuance: புதுவது, 'new', is ironic: a victory over men who had already renounced is no victory. The Pandya calls the Chera கொதியழற் சீற்றம் கொண்டோன் (106), the burning-fire anger the patikam and this kaathai's line 219 give to Kannaki's breast. The Pandya here is the new king at Madurai after the fire, not the Nedunjeliyan who died.
event: Neelan reports the Pandya's taunt that defeating kings who had put on ascetics' guise was a strange victory.
unit_note: Boundaries moved from 96/97 to 95/96 and from 112/113 to 109/110: the unit runs from the turn to the Pandya (ஆங்குநின் றகன்றபின், 96) to the close of Neelan's report at 109 (நீலன் கூற).

reading: Hearing it, the king's lotus eyes turn the colour of fire and he laughs; Maadalan of unfailing learning rises, hails him as king of kings, and recounts his victories: Viyalur of the small-stemmed neythal destroyed, nine kings beaten in the standing battle at the Neri gate, the camp outside Idumbil, the sea driven back, and the Aryan kings who came against him beaten at the Ganges.
nuance: The laugh is anger, not amusement, as the next unit's 'let your anger subside' shows. Maadalan begins with praise before he counsels; the list of victories is close in wording to the preface of the fifth decad of the Patitruppattu.
event: The king's eyes redden and he laughs in anger; Maadalan rises and recounts his victories.
unit_note: Boundary moved from 112/113 to 109/110: the unit now opens with the king's anger and laugh (110-111) and Maadalan's rising (112), which lead into his speech; it ends at 122 as before.

reading: Maadalan asks the king, a bull among kings who understands with the wise, to let his anger rest, wishes him days more than the sands of the Porunai, and asks him to hear without scorn: after fifty years of guarding the world he has nowhere performed the sacrifice of the field of dharma, only the sacrifice of the field of war; and he begins to list the king's ancestors, the one who cut the kadamba in the sea, the one who carved the bow on the mountain, the one who took a four-Veda brahmin's poem and sent him to the upper world.
nuance: அறக்கள வேள்வி against மறக்கள வேள்வி (131-132) turns the bards' old figure of battle as a sacrifice against the king: his wars were a sacrifice of the wrong kind. The fifty years, ஐயைந்து இரட்டி, use the same count as the gold Maadalan received in the last kaathai. The blessing by the sands of a river is an old formula (Purananuru 9 ends with the sands of the Pahruli).
event: Maadalan bids the king calm his anger and tells him he has performed only the sacrifice of war, never the sacrifice of dharma.

reading: Maadalan finishes the list, the one who held back Death bidding it take lives only in order, the one who ruled the land of the harsh-tongued Yavanas and entered the golden mountain, the one who destroyed Agappa, the one who bathed in Ayirai and the two seas, the one who brought the crossroads spirits into Vanchi and offered the honey sacrifice, and says that since none of these exalted ones remains the king knows the body does not last, and that he has seen from the Aryan kings who scorned Tamil that wealth does not last.
nuance: The ancestors are named by feats, not names; several of the feats (Agappa, Ayirai, the two seas, the bow on the Himalaya, the kadamba) are those of the Patitruppattu's prefaces. The proof that wealth passes is the king's own victory over the Aryans: his triumph is turned into a lesson against triumph.

reading: Maadalan adds that the wise need not tell the king youth does not last, since he sees his own greying body, and that, as those of unfailing sight teach, a good soul that came in a god's form may turn into a human one, a soul wearing a human body may enter a beast's, and a soul in a beast's body may come among the hell-dwellers, for like dancers the soul does not stay in one costume but goes by the way of the deeds it did; and he blesses the king's wheel of rule.
nuance: The four states, gods, humans, beasts and hell-beings, are the scheme of the Jain gatis, but the text names no school: a brahmin cites them as the word of பொய்யில் காட்சியோர். The introducing phrase பொய்யில் ... பொருளுரை is the formula the brief cites from Manimekalai 22 for a Kural quotation, but what follows here is not a Kural couplet. கோலம், costume, is the word the kaathai used of the Aryan kings' disguise (92, 105).

reading: Maadalan says he is not one who seeks rich gifts, but cannot bear that the king, beyond the poets' measure, should go the common way by which lives leave this world; the brahmin of sacrifice learned in the four Vedas will open to him the way the gods praise, and he must perform the great sacrifice that the Veda sets for kings, for if he says he will do dharma tomorrow, a life rich in learning may leave today.
nuance: Maadalan disclaims the gift-seeker's motive just after (in the last kaathai) the king gave him gold by weight. The 'dharma' that must not be deferred is here a Vedic royal sacrifice performed by priests, not the giving or conduct the ethical books usually mean.
event: Maadalan urges the king to perform the great Vedic sacrifice without delay.

reading: Maadalan ends: no one in the old world has known the fixed span of his days, so may the king, with this lady of the sacrifice, guard the world aeon upon aeon while crowned kings praise his feet, and live long.
nuance: The sermon on impermanence closes, as court speech must, with a wish for a reign of aeons; the queen is called வேள்விக் கிழத்தி because a king performs the sacrifice with his wife.
event: Maadalan closes his counsel with a blessing on the king and queen.
unit_note: Unit cut from the original 181-201: it ends at 186, where Maadalan's speech closes (நெடுந்தகை யென்று).

reading: The brahmin having ploughed with his Veda tongue and sown its meaning in the field of the king's ear, the harvest ripens: the king, wishing to enjoy it, orders the Veda-learned priests to hold the sacrifice and its festival as Maadalan prescribed, frees the Aryan kings from prison, lodges them in the Velavikko mansion in the park outside Vanchi, and tells Villavan Kothai to send them home after the sacrifice and do for them what befits kings, orders the prisons opened everywhere and the towns' taxes remitted, and sends Azhumbil Vel with the revenue accountants through the city.
nuance: The narrator's ploughing figure (187-189) endorses the sermon: it bears fruit at once in acts of clemency. The release of prisoners and remission of dues are the usual festival acts of a king, here prompted by a lesson on impermanence.
event: The king orders the sacrifice, frees the Aryan kings and all prisoners, and remits the towns' taxes.
unit_note: Unit made from 187-201 of the original 181-201 and 202-206 of the original 202-214: no sentence ends between 187 and 234, so it closes at 206 (ஏவி), the last of the orders of release, before the pathini clause begins at 207.

reading: The narrator recalls the pathini whom the world worships: she gave the garlanded Chola the proof of the ancients' Tamil saying that unless kings rule justly the chastity of famous women does not shine, gave the southern king the lesson that a king does not live once his sceptre bends, gave the western king the lesson, made known to the northern kings, that kings' fierce anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled, and, having ruined old Madurai with the burning anger she brought forth from her breast, came to the good land and stood in the shade of the flowering vengai.
nuance: The three lessons go one to each crowned king and do not match the patikam's three morals: karma is absent, and the third is about the Chera's own vow. What 'gave to the Chola' means (that her chastity's glory waited on the Pandya's justice being tested, or that the Chola learned it from her story) is not plain to me, and I mark the reading uncertain. The phrase கொதியழற் சீற்றம் கொங்கையின் விளைத்து repeats the patikam (line 44).
unit_note: Unit made from 207-214 of the original 202-214 and 215-221 of the original 215-234: it holds the whole relative clause on the pathini, closing at 221 on its object நங்கையை; line 222 turns to the king's going to her temple.

reading: The king who bent the north goes with the brahmins of the field of dharma, the teacher, the great astrologer and the skilled artisans, worships the god of the Himalaya's peak, and in the pathini's temple laid out by men of the texts has the divine image carved by masters adorned with every jewel, offers flowers, sets guards at the door, ordains sacrifice and festival every day, and commands that the goddess's auspicious rite be done.
nuance: The kaathai is named நடுகல், the hero-stone; the stone fetched from the Himalaya becomes a jewelled image in a temple with Brahmin priests and daily sacrifice, so the old warrior's stone is turned into a goddess's shrine. This fulfils the patikam's உரைசால் பத்தினிக்கு உயர்ந்தோர் ஏத்தல்.
event: The king installs the jewelled image of the pathini in her temple and ordains daily sacrifice, festival and worship.
unit_note: Unit cut from the original 215-234: it starts at 222, where the king's own acts begin, and ends at the kaathai's close.

title: வாழ்த்துக் காதை (1/2)
theme: The first half of the Vaazhthu Kaathai: a prose summary recalls Senguttuvan's northern campaign for the Himalaya stone and its consecration, then Kannaki's friends from Puhar arrive at her shrine and lament before the image, telling of the deaths of the mothers, the renunciations of both fathers, of Madhavi and Manimekalai, and of Maadhari's death for a broken charge; Kannaki appears in the sky, declares the Pandya faultless and herself his daughter, and the women of Vanchi sing her and bless both the Pandya and the Chera lines.
source_issues: Block labels misplace three rubrics: the block காவற்பெண்டு சொல் (42-52) contains the rubric அடித் தோழி சொல் at line 47, so lines 48-52 are the maid's speech; the block தேவந்தி யரற்று (53-63) contains the rubric காவற்பெண் டரற்று at line 58, so 59-63 are the foster mother's; the block செங்குட்டுவன் கூற்று (74-83) contains the rubric at lines 78-79 (செங்குட்டுவற்குக் கண்ணகியார் கடவு ணல்லணி காட்டியது), so 80-83 are Kannaki's words. The rubric lines are counted as verse lines.

Lines 1-36 are prose (உரைப் பாட்டு மடை) broken into lines of the edition's own making, with words split across line ends (16-17 கங்கைப்பேர் / யாற்று, 18-19 நீண் / முடி, 19-20 பூச / லாட்டி, 25-26 மன் / னரசர், 27-28 துறப் / பவும்).
The kaathai header reports the printed last line as None.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi, son of Cheralathan by a Chola princess, who brought the Himalaya stone for the pathini and consecrated it
Senguttuvan's father, the Chera who ruled the world from Kumari to the northern Himalaya
the northern Aryan kings whose taunt provoked the expedition and who were made to carry the stone on their heads
the great ascetics living in the north who brought word of the Aryan kings' taunt
Kovalan's wife, the pathini, now worshipped as a goddess at Vanchi and appearing in the sky
Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed and died of his own verdict (named here காவலன், தென்னவன், கோவேந்தன்)
the royal goldsmith of Madurai, called here the petty man
Kovalan's father, who renounced on hearing of the deaths
Kannaki's father, who also renounced
Kovalan's mother, Maasaathuvan's wife, who died of grief
Kannaki's mother, who died of grief
the dancer of Puhar, Kovalan's companion, who renounced before the Buddhist monks
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, who renounced with her
Kannaki's friend, the Brahmin woman who lived with the god Saathan
Kannaki's foster mother, who calls herself her தாயர்
Kannaki's personal maid-companion, daughter of the foster mother
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom Kannaki was given in charge, dead of grief at failing that charge
Maadhari's unmarried daughter, who comes with the Puhar women to Vanchi
the Jain nun who placed Kannaki in Maadhari's charge, named here only by an epithet if that is the reading
the women of Vanchi who call one another to sing Kannaki
the company of women whose venba sets the two kings' claims to Kannaki side by side
Indra, king of the gods, whose palace receives the Pandya as guest

tamil: மைந்தன் கொங்கர் செங்களம் வேட்டுக் கங்கைப் பேர்
வஞ்சியுள் வந்திருந்த காலை, வட ஆரிய மன்னர் ஆங்
இமய நெற்றியில் விளங்கு வில் புலி கயல் பொறித்த
நாள் எம்போலும் முடிமன்னர் ஈங்கில்லை போலும் என்ற
வெம்மை நீங்கி வஞ்சிமா நகர்புகுந்து நிலவரசர் நீண்
முடியாற் பலர்தொழு படிமங் காட்டித் தடமுலைப் பூச
reading: The prose opening tells how Senguttuvan, son of the world-ruling Cheralathan by the Chola's daughter, after the Kongu war and the Ganga campaign, heard from the northern ascetics that the Aryan kings had laughed that no crowned kings like themselves were left in the Tamil south, as on the day bow, tiger and fish were cut on the Himalaya's brow; stung, he routed them, made them carry the Himalaya stone on their crowned heads, bathed the lady in the Ganga, came back to Vanchi with his rage spent, and consecrated the image, worshipped by many kings' crowns, of the pathini as a goddess.
nuance: The cause given is not devotion but a slight to Tamil kingship: the taunt touches the Chera's pride, and the stone for the goddess is quarried by humbling the kings who made it, so worship and conquest are one act. The ascetics are the ones who carry the word that starts a war. The stone is first called a stone that is to be a god (கற்கடவுள், line 13) and only after the Ganga bathing and consecration a படிமம் and a goddess; the poem marks the stages by which a stone becomes a deity. The three emblems carved on the Himalaya belong to the three Tamil crowns, not the Chera alone.
event: Senguttuvan, told by northern ascetics of the Aryan kings' taunt, defeats them, makes them carry the Himalaya stone, bathes it in the Ganga and consecrates it at Vanchi as the pathini's image.
unit_note: Moved the boundary from after line 16 to after line 20. Line 16 ends in the middle of the word கங்கைப்பேர் / யாற்று, which runs into line 17; the stone's journey and consecration close at கடவுண் மங்கலஞ்செய்த பின்னாள் on line 20, the next clause, Kannaki's shrine and the kings' tribute, begins with that line's last word கண்ணகி, which stays in this unit because no line end in the prose (lines 1 to 36) falls on a phrase break.

tamil: மதிமுகத்திற் சில செங்கயல் நீர் உமிழப் பொடியாடிய
reading: On a later day, as Senguttuvan was receiving the tribute of earthly kings at Kannaki's shrine, the women of Puhar came: the prose recalls how Kannaki, her moon face streaming with tears and her dark hair loose with dust, reviled dharma when Kovalan's deed rose up and the petty goldsmith had him killed, went to the king, and how the king lost his life at her tears; how Maasaathuvan, told by a Brahmin, renounced and his wife died; and how the foster mother, the maid and Devanthi went to Madurai to see Kannaki, met Maadhari's daughter Aiyai, and with her followed the Vaigai up the great hill to the queen's shrine, where they tell the king what happened.
nuance: In one breath the prose names three causes of Kovalan's death: his own former deed rising up (வினையுருத்து), the goldsmith who brought it about (குறுமகனால்), and the king who caused the killing. Kannaki's response is to blame dharma itself (அறம்பழித்து), a protest the poem records without answering here. Maadhari is not named; she is the herding woman who died having lost the charge entrusted to her (அடைக்கலமிழந்து உயிரிழந்த, line 32). The shrine on the hill is reached by following the Vaigai, which ties the Vanchi cult back to Madurai.
event: As Senguttuvan takes tribute at Kannaki's shrine, Kannaki's foster mother, maid and Devanthi, who went to Madurai and came on with Aiyai, arrive and tell him what befell.
unit_note: Moved the boundary from after line 16 to after line 20 (see the unit 1-20); this unit begins with the clause about Kannaki's shrine and the kings' tribute (its first word கண்ணகி stands at the end of line 20), and ends at line 36, where the long prose sentence closes with திறமுரைப்பர் மன்.

reading: Devanthi tells the king to see in her the friend of the bangled one who was born on the divine northern Himalaya, guarded by the three crowned kings, and came after bathing in the swift Ganga: the friend of the doll of the Chola country.
nuance: The words describe the stone as much as the woman: born in the Himalaya and bathed in the Ganga is the history of the image told in lines 1 to 20, and Devanthi speaks of it as Kannaki herself, so the image and the woman are one in her grief. The refrain names Kannaki by her home country, the Chola land.
event: Devanthi, before the image, declares herself the friend of Kannaki.

reading: The foster mother says she is the mother of the wide-eyed girl who, taking her loving husband's hand away from soft-mannered Madhavi without reproach, came through the cruel forest of wells no pot can reach: the mother of the doll of cool Puhar.
nuance: கடம்படாள் is hard: it may mean that Kannaki did not hold Madhavi to account, or that she owed no duty to her; either way the line sets her taking back her husband apart from any quarrel with the dancer. தாயர் is the foster mother's own title, not birth.
event: The foster mother declares herself Kannaki's mother.

reading: Under the rubric 'the maid's word', the maid says that the gold-bangled lady who took chastity as her duty and followed her lover left without a word to the mother who bore her, to the foster mother who guarded her, or to the maid herself: she is that lady's friend, the friend of the doll of flowering Puhar.
nuance: The grievance is that Kannaki left in secret; the same deed that the poem praises as chastity (கற்புக் கடம்பூண்டு) cost those at home a farewell. The phrase கற்புக் கடம்பூண்ட is the one Kavunthi used of Kannaki when she gave her into Maadhari's care (15:131-148, line 143).
event: Kannaki's maid declares herself her friend and complains she left without a word.

reading: Devanthi laments that she, who had done no penance, heard the ill dream and did not grasp what it would bring, and asks her friend whether she has heard that on the day of the outcry of her breast her mother died, and her mother-in-law too.
nuance: Devanthi blames her own lack of penance (செய்தவம் இல்லாதேன்) for failing to read the dream; in the dream kaathai she had read it as the fruit of a vow broken in a former birth and prescribed a bath in the tanks, and now she owns that she did not see what it portended. முலைப்பூசல் names the burning of Madurai by the breast. The friend she addresses is Kannaki, now the image.
event: Devanthi tells Kannaki that her mother and her mother-in-law died on hearing of the burning.

reading: Under the rubric 'the foster mother's lament', she asks whether Kannaki has heard that Maasaathuvan, grieving that the king gave up his life when the petty man brought about Kovalan's death, held that death itself was now his life, made many gifts and renounced, and that Maanaaygan renounced too.
nuance: The renunciation is grief's, not doctrine's: the father turns away because life after the news is no life (சாவதுதான் வாழ்வு), and the gifts come as part of leaving the world. The cause of Kovalan's death is put on the petty man, and the king's death is what the father heard of.
event: The foster mother tells Kannaki that both fathers, Maasaathuvan and Maanaaygan, gave gifts and renounced.

reading: The maid asks whether Kannaki has heard that Madhavi, grieving at her lover's death and at Kannaki's fate and hearing the blame of strangers, made gifts of merit before the great ascetics under the Bodhi tree and renounced, and that Manimekalai renounced too.
nuance: Madhavi's renunciation is placed under the Bodhi tree before the monks, a Buddhist setting, and is moved partly by what strangers say of her (ஏதிலார் ஏச்சுரை); the story the Manimekalai tells begins here. The text states the act, not a doctrine.
event: The maid tells Kannaki that Madhavi and Manimekalai renounced before the monks under the Bodhi tree.

reading: Devanthi, showing Aiyai, asks Kannaki whether she sees the unmarried girl with fine teeth, daughter of the mother who gave up her life saying she had fallen into madness because she could not guard the charge given her by the one of clear vision: the young daughter of her mother-in-law.
nuance: ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி, 'of vision freed from doubt', seems to name Kavunthi, the Jain nun who gave Kannaki into Maadhari's care, though it could qualify the charge itself. Maadhari dies of the failure to keep a trust, not of any wrong she did. Calling Maadhari மாமி, mother-in-law, makes Aiyai a kinswoman by the bond of the charge; the kinship term is affectionate and its exact sense is not sure.
event: Devanthi shows Aiyai to Kannaki and tells of Maadhari's death.

reading: Senguttuvan cries out three times what this can be: a lightning creeper with a golden anklet, a girdle, bangled arms, fine diamond earrings and ornaments of Jambu gold appears high in the sky.
nuance: The king sees first only a flash of jewels and lightning, not a person; the anklet is the first ornament named, the thing the story turned on.
event: Kannaki appears in the sky as a lightning-like figure in jewels, and Senguttuvan cries out in wonder.

reading: Under the rubric 'Kannaki shows Senguttuvan her goddess's form', Kannaki says that the Pandya is without fault and has become a welcome guest in the palace of the king of the gods; she is his daughter; she will not leave the playground on the hill of the one of the victorious spear; and she calls her friends to come with her.
nuance: This is the sharpest turn in the epic's judgment of the king: the woman who called him a king who strayed from right rule and burned his city now declares him faultless and claims him as father. His self-sentence and death have cleared him. The hill of the spear-bearer is Murugan's, near where the kuravar saw her taken up.
event: Kannaki, appearing as a goddess, tells Senguttuvan the Pandya is faultless and in Indra's palace, and calls her friends.

reading: The women of Vanchi call one another, women with waists like the vanchi creeper and companions of the fierce-speared king, to come and sing her who with her breast ruined the city of Koodal and with her red anklet overcame the king, the Pandya's daughter, the bangled doll who came to this land when our king's just tongue declared that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends.
nuance: The songs praise Kannaki for destroying a city and defeating a king, and in the same stanza they call her that king's daughter, taking up her own claim. The saying about the Pandyas is put in the mouth of the Chera king (எங்கோ முறைநா), so a rival line honours the Pandyas for dying of their own injustice.

reading: A venba says that while we called her the daughter of our king the Chera, she called herself the creeper born of the king of the Vaigai's people; so let us praise the Chera, and the divine woman will praise the lord of the Vaigai.
nuance: Two kings claim one goddess, and the dispute is settled by dividing the praise: the people of Vanchi keep their own king, and the goddess keeps the Pandya, the king who wronged her.

reading: Long live the great king who gave his life when the tears of her who suffered by an old deed killed him, long live the ancient line of the lord of Madurai, circled by the Vaigai's flowing water.
nuance: Both causes stand in one line: her suffering came by an old deed (தொல்லை வினையால்), and the king died of her tears. The blessing falls on the king who caused the wrong, praised for paying with his life, and on his whole line. Who sings these stanzas is not named; they follow the women's songs.

reading: Long live the king who set the young doll born of the mountain king on the long crowns of the kings of the earth, long live the ancient line of the lord of Vanchi, circled by the cool Porunai.
nuance: மலையரையன் பெற்ற மடப்பாவை fits both the Himalaya stone and the mountain king's daughter, the goddess Uma, so the image is praised in a goddess's terms; the doll set on kings' crowns recalls the defeated kings made to carry the stone. The stanza answers the Pandya's blessing line for line.

title: வாழ்த்துக் காதை (2/2)
theme: The second half of the Vaazhthu Kaathai is a cycle of women's play songs that divides the praise among the three crowns: the ammanai songs sing the Chola's ancestral deeds and Puhar, the ball songs hail the Pandya whom Kannaki has just declared blameless, the swing songs sing the Chera line's deeds, the pounding songs give each city its women and its king, and the close has Kannaki herself praise Senguttuvan; no karma is named in this half.
source_issues: Lines 105-107, the Chola stanza of the benediction, have three lines where the Pandya and Chera stanzas (97-100, 101-104) have four, no deed and no வாழியரோ refrain, and line 105 (எல்லா நாம்) is a half line; the stanza may be a different form or a damaged one.
The edition prints song number 21 after song 28 at line 174; read as 29 (show flags it).
Line 172 reads வாழ்த்தல் where the sense ('find it hard to live') wants வாழ்தல்; possibly a misprint.
Line 137 ends நீணிலம் and line 138 begins தன்னினின்று, so the line division runs across the phrase; the sense of 137-138 is not secure.

cast.role: the women of Vanchi who play the ammanai, ball, swing and pounding songs of the Vaazhthu Kaathai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai, now a goddess
Madari's daughter
the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the stone from the Himalaya for Kannaki's image

reading: The last stanza of the benediction calls the company to sing, and sing again, the lord of the Kaveri country and Puhar of the flower-strewn tresses.
nuance: The Pandya and Chera stanzas before it (97-100, 101-104) each praise a deed of the king and close with வாழியரோ and the king's old line; this Chola stanza has no deed and no வாழியரோ, only the call to sing, so it is either a shorter form or a broken one. The Chola is named only by his country, and the line gives Puhar the woman's epithet பூவிரி கூந்தல், as if the city were a woman.

reading: The first ammanai song asks, as the women toss their play-stones, who ruled the sea-fenced world and guarded the high fortress of the king of the gods, answers that it was the Chola who destroyed the three hanging forts in the sky, and bids them sing his city Puhar.
nuance: The ammanai form is a riddle and its answer: one line asks யார் அம்மானை, the next repeats the clue and answers with காண் அம்மானை, and the refrain turns from the king to his city. So the two deeds, guarding Indra's fort and cutting down the hanging forts, are set as one king's, and the song names no Chola king by his own name.

reading: The second ammanai song asks who was the king who, while heaven praised him, entered the scale for a dove and cut his own flawless body, answers that he was the guardian who gave justice to the milch cow that came before him, and bids them sing his flowering Puhar.
