nuance: The riddle's form makes the body-cutting king and the king who judged for the cow one answer, where Kannaki's plea at the Pandya's court (20:55-73) gave them as two Chola precedents; whether the song means one man or one line is not settled by the Tamil. The deeds Kannaki used to accuse a Pandya are sung here, in the Chera capital, as the plain glory of Puhar.

reading: The third ammanai song asks who stamped his sword-bright tiger on the northern mountain while the eight mountains of the quarters looked on without blinking, answers that it was the victor who took the eight directions under the shade of his umbrella and protected them, and bids them sing his Puhar.
nuance: The song does not name the king; the tiger on the Himalaya is the deed the Puhar book gives to Thirumavalavan (5:89-110), where the mountain halts him. Here the eight guardian mountains only watch, and the halt has become a rule over all eight quarters.

reading: The fourth ammanai song, of the women themselves, asks what is the worth of the singing the jewelled women do in their homes with the ammanai in their hands, answers that it is that the garlanded king should come to their round, painted breasts, and says that if the king of the line comes there, they will sing his lovely Puhar.
nuance: The game turns from the king's deeds to the singers' desire for him: the play-song is offered as a lure for his embrace. The king is again only தார்வேந்தன், குலவேந்தன், not named, and the refrain still ends on Puhar.

reading: The first ball song shows a girl like a golden creeper, her gold garland flashing and her girdle-bells ringing, running everywhere and striking the ball while she cries long live the Southerner, long live the one whose chest bears the gods' necklace.
nuance: The ball songs praise the Pandya alone (தென்னன், and தேவர் ஆர மார்பன், the king who wore the necklace of the king of the gods): sung in the Chera city after the Pandya's death, they follow Kannaki's word just before (78-83) that the Pandya is blameless and is now Indra's guest.
event: The girls play at ball, crying blessings on the Pandya with each stroke.

reading: The second ball song likens the player, darting back and forth on every side, rising and turning, to a young creeper of lightning come down to the wide earth, as she strikes the ball with the same cries for the Pandya.
event: A girl runs and leaps after the ball, crying blessings on the Pandya.

reading: The third ball song says the ball, coming close, never rested in the hand and, rising from the long earth, never reached the heights, and closes with the same cries for the Pandya as it is struck.
nuance: Lines 137-138 seem to describe the ball kept always between hand and sky, never caught and never lost upward; மந்தரம் may be the sky or Mount Mandara, and the sense is not sure.
event: The girls keep the ball in the air, crying blessings on the Pandya.

reading: The first swing song bids the girls seat Aiyai on the jewelled swing hung on ropes, push it together with lifted hands, and swing with long eyes darting, singing the guardian who cut the kadamba down at its root and the emblem of the curved bow.
nuance: The swing songs belong to the Chera. கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த is the Patitruppattu's own phrase for Neduncheralathan's deed (patitruppattu:20), but the song names no king, so the deed is sung as the Chera line's glory before Senguttuvan. ஐயை may be Madari's daughter, whom Devanthi has just pointed out among the heavenly company (72), or a word for a lady; the singers' own swing would make the second reading possible.
event: The girls set a companion on the swing and push it as they sing.

reading: The second swing song sings the might of the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, who without stint fed the great feast to the war in which the Five and the twice fifty rose against each other, and bids them swing with dark hair flying, singing his cutting of the kadamba.
nuance: The feast at the war of the five and the hundred is the deed Purananuru 2 gives by name to Uthiyan Cheralathan; the song gives it to the Chera by his house names (சேரன், பொறையன், மலையன்) and sets it beside the kadamba deed of another king, so it praises the line, not one man.

reading: The third swing song sings the might of the king who guards all living people, the lord of the bow who, it seems, holds the fish and the tiger, and who ruled from the rich land of the harsh-tongued Yavanas and the great mountain to Kumari in the south, and bids them swing with slender waists swaying, singing the emblem of the victorious bow.
nuance: செருவிற் கயற்புலியான் can be read as the king of the battle-bow who also bears (or has taken) the Pandya's fish and the Chola's tiger; if so, the Chera song folds all three crowns' emblems into its own king, where the Madurai kuravai (17:1-10) set the three side by side on the Himalaya. The reading of the compound is not certain.

reading: The first pounding song says the women of Puhar, in the shade of flowering kaanchi, pound rich pearls with sweet sugarcane for pestles, and that the song to sing is the one of the Chembiyan of the strong chariot with the wheel banner and the shoulders like great hills, the one the girls cry out.
nuance: Each of the three pounding songs gives one city its women, its pestle and its king: the luxury is formal (pearls in place of grain, cane or coral or ivory in place of a pestle), and the work song is turned to praise. The order here is Chola, Pandya, Chera, ending on the host.

reading: The second pounding song says the women of towered Madurai pound pearls worthy of song with coral pestles, and that the song to sing is of the fish banner of the Panchavan, whose shoulders shine with the necklace of the king of the gods, the song that sinks into the heart of the neem-garlanded king.
nuance: The last line, the song that 'melts' or 'enters' the heart of the neem-garlanded one (வேப்பந்தார் நெஞ்சுணக்கும்), lets the song reach the Pandya himself, now in Indra's world by Kannaki's word.

reading: The third pounding song says the women of Vanchi pound fine pearls in a sandalwood mortar with ivory pestles, and that the song to sing is the one that spread over the land and covered it, the report of the Chera of the conquering garland who cut down the kadamba, the song that wins the palmyra-wearer's heart.

The close says that the kings of the long earth who do not bow at the good feet of Poraiyan of the long bow find it hard to live, and that, her vow fulfilled, our king's lady too praised him: long live Senguttuvan for ages.
nuance: எங்கோ மடந்தை takes up the Vanchi women's claim earlier in the kaathai (93) that Kannaki is the Chera's daughter, against the Madurai women's claim that she is the Pandya's; so the close ends with the goddess on the Chera's side. சூளொழிய may mean that her vow (to destroy Madurai) is now spent, or 'without an oath'; and வாழ்த்தல் in line 172 may be a slip for வாழ்தல், which the reading follows. This is the only unit in the song cycle that names a living king.
event: Kannaki, now a goddess, joins in praising Senguttuvan.

title: வரந்தரு காதை
theme: The last kaathai (வரந்தரு காதை) closes the story by showing deeds and loves of the past bearing fruit in the present: Devanthi tells the Chera of Manimekalai's renunciation, is possessed by the god Saathan, and through water from a spring that restores former births three girls in Vanchi are shown to be Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari reborn near the pathini; Maadalan explains it as the old law of births and deeds, the king endows the pathini's temple, foreign kings beg her presence and a voice grants the boon, the goddess tells the poet's own renunciation, and the poet ends with a string of commands to his hearers.
source_issues: The kaathai has 202 lines in the core file, but the edition prints its last line as 200; the numbering here follows the core file.
Line 179: a stray space before a vowel sign was repaired in the core file (வாயிற்).
Line 164 reads றேழுந்த with a long ஏ, where the sense (a voice rose) needs எழுந்தது; probably a typing error for றெழுந்த.
Line 190 has a stray space before its semicolon (தாங்குமின் ;); the closing lines carry modern punctuation not found elsewhere in the kaathai.
Lines 97 to 111 run the cries of the three reborn girls together without naming who speaks which line; the division among them is inferred.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the stone from the north and set up the pathini's temple; called here வானவர் பெருந்தகை, குறிஞ்சிக் கோமான், மன்னர் கோ
Kannaki's friend, the Brahmin woman whose husband was the god Saathan; here possessed by him
the god Saathan of the sects, who once took the form of Maalathi's dead child and became Devanthi's husband; here he speaks through her
Brahmin of Thalaichengaanam who knows Kovalan's past deeds and explains the rebirths to the king
a Brahmin's wife whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it
the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived, mother of Manimekalai
Madhavi's mother, who asks Madhavi what is to be done with the grown Manimekalai
the daughter of Madhavi and Kovalan, given to the Buddhist dharma as a girl (not the sea goddess of the same name)
Kama, the bodiless god of love
the unnamed Chola king of Puhar
the ascetics of true speech of Puhar to whom Manimekalai announces her renunciation

the three little girls of Vanchi, the twin daughters of Arattan Chetti and the young daughter of Sedakkudumbi, who on being sprinkled recall former births as Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari
the aged herdswoman (ஆயர் முதுமகள்) of Madurai in whose house Kannaki lodged, reborn as Sedakkudumbi's daughter
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini, now a goddess (இமையோர் இளங்கொடி)
the visiting kings before the Chera: the Aryan kings freed from prison, the kings released from the great prison, the Kongar of Kudagam and the Malava kings
Gajabahu, king of sea-girt Lanka, among the kings who beg the goddess's presence
the Chera prince who gave up kingship; the poet, who here speaks in the first person
the hearers of the poem, whom the poet addresses at its close

reading: After the goddess's form has passed from his sight, the Chera king turns to Devanthi and asks who the Manimekalai is for whom she cried out and why she renounced; Devanthi, wishing his rule and land prosperity, begins: the girl had come to full youth, her eyes knew love's craft though she herself did not, her body had ripened in every part, the dance master stood ready behind her, and Madhavi's mother asked Madhavi what she intended and what she should do.
nuance: The catalogue of the girl's ripened body (lines 10 to 19) is the courtesan house's reckoning of a daughter ready for the stage, with the dance master already waiting (line 20); the renunciation that follows is set against exactly this readiness. Line 21, that the chief men of the clan would not take her by their custom, can be read as the courtesan house's worry or as the families' refusal of a courtesan's daughter in marriage; the reading leaves it open. Line 13 makes a small irony: the eyes knew the craft of love, she did not.
event: Senguttuvan asks Devanthi why Manimekalai renounced, and Devanthi begins by telling how Madhavi's mother, seeing the girl grown, asked Madhavi what to do with her.
unit_note: End moved from line 22 to line 23: the mother's question at lines 22 and 23 is one clause, and line 23 names who asks it.

reading: Madhavi called her young daughter Manimekalai and, while Kama flung his great bow and fragrant arrows on the bare ground, removed the garland together with the girl's hair and gave her at the Bodhi seat into the dharma; the king and the city, hearing it, grieved like men who have dropped a fine gem into the sea, and the ascetics of true speech said with love and grace that the girl had declared her renunciation to them.
nuance: Who removes the hair is not named: the sentence runs on from Madhavi's call, and the next unit says the girl herself left off her adornment. போதித் தானம் (line 28) can be the gift made at the Bodhi or the Bodhi as a place; either way the giving is the scene of Kovalan's dream (15:101-104), where Madhavi gives Manimekalai before the dharma-one of the Bodhi and Kama casts his arrows on the bare ground, here told as done. The grief of king and city (lines 29 to 31) treats a girl's renunciation as a public loss, the loss of the gem of the town's arts.
event: Madhavi gives Manimekalai to the Buddhist dharma, her hair and garland removed, and Puhar's king and people grieve while the ascetics receive her.
unit_note: Start moved from line 23 to line 24 and end from line 33 to line 34: line 33 ends in என்றே, and the sentence closes with கூறினர் at line 34.

reading: Devanthi tells the king she wailed because the girl left off her adornment before her time; then her hair falls loose, her brows quiver, she bites her lip, her words blur, her face sweats, her eyes redden, she flings her arms and rises, and possessed by a god she speaks before the hill-country king: among the women come to see the goddess's consecration are the twin daughters of Arattan Chetti's wife and the young daughter of Sedakkudumbi, servant of the god who lies on the serpent.
nuance: The signs of possession are listed one per half-line (lines 38 to 44) in the same piled style as the girl's body in the first unit, so the kaathai sets a body made ready for desire beside a body taken by a god. The voice is not Devanthi's own: the god names himself only at line 69. The three girls are introduced by their present parents before anything is said of who they were.
event: Devanthi explains her cry, falls into possession and, before Senguttuvan, points out three girls among the women at the consecration.
unit_note: Start moved from line 34 to line 35 and end from line 50 to line 52: the sentence naming the three girls closes with ஈங்குளள் at line 52.

reading: The possessing voice says that on the high hill by the shrine of the Lady of Good Fortune, among the pools filling the ridge, there is a spring of grinding stones and splashing water in which those who bathe become again the persons of their former birth, and that it brought that water and gave it, in a pot hanging in a sling, into the hand of the one sitting in the assembly at the lady's shrine as a token.
nuance: The spring does not purify or grant a wish, the usual work of a holy tank; it makes a past birth come back into the present body. The one addressed (இருந்தோய், line 62) is Maadalan, as line 70 shows.
event: Speaking through Devanthi, the god tells of a spring on the hill that restores former births and says he once gave its water to Maadalan in a pot.
unit_note: Start moved from line 51 to line 53: the sentence about the three girls ends at line 52.

reading: The voice says the water keeps its divine power till sunset and bids Maadalan sprinkle the three girls so that their hidden births appear, naming itself Paasandan come upon the Brahmin woman; the king is amazed, and Maadalan tells him the story: Maalathi's co-wife's baby, fed at her breast, died when an old deed flared up, she lay in vigil at Paasandan's shrine, the god came in the child's form, grew up in the old Brahmin family, married Devanthi, and after eight years showed his ageless youth, told her to come to his shrine and left; later, appearing as a Brahmin at the shrine of the Lady of Good Fortune, he gave Maadalan the pot and a token and went away for good.
nuance: Maadalan's telling repeats the Maalathi story of the dream kaathai (9:1-44) with a change: there Maalathi carried the child round the city's shrines, here she lies in vigil at Paasandan's own shrine, and the child's death is put down to பழவினை (line 75), an old deed flaring up, which the earlier telling does not say. The god's parting words to Devanthi, எம் கோட்டத்து நீ வா, are given here as என் கோட்டத்து நீவா (lines 86 to 87), and the chapter shows how they are kept: he comes back to her not as a husband but as the god who possesses her.
event: The god tells Maadalan to sprinkle the water on the three girls, and Maadalan tells the amazed king how Saathan came as Maalathi's dead child, married Devanthi and later gave him the pot.
unit_note: End moved from line 80 to line 91, absorbing the former unit 81-96 up to line 91: line 80 ends in a quotation still running into line 81, and the account of Saathan closes with போயினன் வாரான் at line 91.

reading: Maadalan says that because he brought the water, the knowing god has now appeared on this Brahmin woman and told him to sprinkle it, and he sprinkles the girls; their hidden births return and they cry out: one as a mother to the daughter she bore, who suffered alone with her husband in a strange land, one as a mother whose heart cannot bear that her son went off into the dark with the girl who lived with her, and one who came back from the Vaigai's ford, heard the news, found the house empty and asks the young one where she has hidden.
nuance: The girls do not say who they were: the three griefs (for a daughter, for a son and for a girl who had lodged in the house) identify Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari, and Maadalan names them only in the next units. Lines 102 and 103 run several forms of address together (daughter, companion, lady who ends grief), and how the lines divide among the three voices is not certain. The scene is offered as proof of former birth seen by a whole court.
event: Maadalan sprinkles the water on the three girls, and they cry out in the voices of the mothers of Kannaki and Kovalan and of Maadari.
unit_note: Start moved from line 97 to line 92 and the former units 81-96 and 97-111 regrouped: the sprinkling (line 96) and its result (line 97) are one sentence, so the account of the pot from line 92 joins the laments.

reading: When the lisping little girls have wept in the courtyard with the words of old women before the king, he looks at Maadalan, who blesses him and explains: because the mothers loved the wife of the man who entered the elephant's trunk to end a Brahmin's distress and so won the form of the gods, and had not done the unfailing dharma that goes with those of the upper world, they came as twins to Arattan Chetti's wife in old Vanchi, near the woman of the golden creeper whom they loved.
nuance: Two fruits of deeds are set side by side: Kovalan's rescue of the Brahmin from the elephant (15:42-53) has earned him a god's form, while the mothers' love, without the dharma that leads upward, has earned them a new birth near the beloved. Love here is not condemned; it decides where they are born. The phrase கையகம் புக்கு (line 121) repeats the wording of the rescue scene (15:49).
event: Maadalan tells the king that Kannaki's and Kovalan's mothers, bound by love for Kannaki, were reborn as Arattan Chetti's twins in Vanchi.
unit_note: End moved from line 126 to line 131: line 126 is mid-sentence, and the account of the twins closes with தோன்றினர் at line 131.

reading: Maadalan goes on that the old herdswoman, out of love for the girl from her former birth, has become Sedakkudumbi's young daughter; that the good reach the golden world, those of loving heart go where their attachment leads, the fruits of virtue and of wrong ripen, the born die and the dead are born, and none of this is new but the ancient way of life; and that the king, born by the grace of the one who rides the bull, has seen the fruit of austerity and the forms of the great as if in his hand, and should live and guard the world age after age.
nuance: Lines 136 to 140 are the kaathai's general law, and they finish what the patikam set out (0:55-57): there the deed of the past comes in wrath to be eaten; here good deeds ripen as surely as wrong ones, and love is a force like deed that carries a person to a new birth. The Brahmin calls the Chera born of Siva's grace (line 141); this is his praise of the king, not a claim the poem makes about the pathini cult.
event: Maadalan says Maadari was reborn as Sedakkudumbi's daughter, states the law of births and deeds, and blesses the king.
unit_note: Start moved from line 127 to line 132 and end from line 144 to line 146: Maadalan's speech closes with the blessing ending என்ற at line 146.

reading: Glad with Maadalan, the king endows the temple of the pathini of unaging body who twisted off her breast so that fierce fire spread through Koodal of the Pandya land, orders a festival there every day, gives Devanthi charge of its flowers, incense and scents, and goes round it three times and bows; before him the Aryan kings freed from prison, the kings released from the great prison, the Kongar of Kudagam, the Malava kings and Gajabahu of sea-girt Lanka pray her to come to the festival they will hold in their lands as on this day of the Chera's sacrifice, and a voice rises: I have granted the boon.
nuance: The kaathai's name comes from line 164, and the boon is asked by foreign and conquered kings, some just let out of the Chera's prison: the cult of the Madurai pathini spreads through the very kings defeated in the campaign for her stone. The temple is identified by the burning of Madurai, not by Kannaki's name. The epithet இமய வரம்பன் (line 161) is given here to the Chera holding the sacrifice; in the Patitruppattu's second decade the name belongs to Senguttuvan's father, so the two uses should not be merged. Line 162's construction (whose festival, held where) is compressed and the reading follows the plainest sense.
event: Senguttuvan endows the pathini's temple with daily worship under Devanthi, the visiting kings beg the goddess to come to their lands, and a voice grants the boon.
unit_note: Start moved from line 145 to line 147 and end from line 160 to line 164: the kings' prayer runs from line 157 to line 163 and is answered at line 164.

reading: When the king, the kings and the army have praised in turn and the king has left the sacrificial hall with Maadalan, who longs for the true path like those who have seen release, the poet says that he too went, and the young creeper of the gods, shining on Devanthi, rose before him and told his own story: that when he sat in his father's shade in the jewelled hall of Vanchi and a man said he bore the mark of one who will sit as king, he looked at the man in anger and, to end Senguttuvan's distress, put away the burden of the wide earth and became, far beyond where thought can reach, a king ruling endless bliss; and he calls the hearers good people who have heard clearly these words that told her story.
nuance: Only here does the narrator say 'I' (யானுஞ் சென்றேன், line 171), and the poem's frame closes in a circle: the goddess whose story the poet told tells the poet's own story, and the poem is named in line 184 as the words that told hers. The patikam (0:1-2) only says that Ilango gave up the throne; this unit gives the cause, a prophecy of kingship that would have set brother against brother, and makes the renunciation an act of care for Senguttuvan. பகல்செல் வாயில் (line 179), the gate of the day's going, places where he lives; the patikam names the eastern-gate shrine, and the unit's phrase is left as written.
event: The poet follows the king out of the sacrificial hall, and the goddess, appearing on Devanthi, tells how he renounced the throne on hearing a prophecy that he would be king.
unit_note: Start moved from line 161 to line 165: the kings' prayer and the boon close at line 164.

reading: The poet bids his hearers put away grief and trouble, trust the god and honour those who trust, fear lying and guard against backbiting, give up eating flesh and killing, give gifts and keep many austerities, not kill a kindness done or keep bad friends, never bear false witness or leave words of substance, keep near the assembly of the virtuous and avoid others, fear another's wife and protect suffering lives, guard the house of dharma and drive off what is not, and shun liquor, theft, lust, lies and idle company; since youth, wealth and body do not last, they should, without waiting on the days they have, seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
nuance: After thirty kaathais of story the poem ends in plain commands, almost one to a half-line, and several of them name what the story has shown: false witness (the poor man seized by the spirit, 15:76-94), another's wife, flesh and killing. The list of things to shun (liquor, theft, lust, lies) resembles lay vows of the Jain and Buddhist traditions, but the unit names no school, so the claims are tagged general. The last three lines turn from conduct to impermanence: the reason for all the commands is the journey after death.

title: வஞ்சிக் காண்டம் கட்டுரை
theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Vanchi book: one sentence lists what the book set out about the Chera line, rulers of the west (its righteousness, valour and strength, its old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the wealth and grain of its land, its vari and kuravai songs), and says the book lies viewed as one with Senguttuvan, whose army of true swords fought in keeping with aram, drove back the sea and reached the bank of the Ganga.
source_issues: Line 7 reads அவருறை நாட்டுக் where the Madurai summary has அவருடை நாட்டுக்; line 14 reads ஒருபரிசு நோக்கிக் where the Madurai summary has ஒருபரிசா நோக்கிக். Either may be a variant or a misprint; the sense is unaffected.
Line 15 (கிடந்த வஞ்சிக் காண்ட முற்றிற்று) joins the closing participle of the sentence to the colophon, so the colophon is marked as part of the unit, as in the Madurai summary.

reading: The narrator closes the Vanchi book by gathering into one view the righteousness, valour and strength of those born in the garlanded Chera line who rule the west among the three crowned kings, the excellence of their old city of ancient victories, its festivals and divine visitors, the wealth of the families and the plenty of grain in their land of unbroken joy, and the vari and kuravai songs, all seen together with Senguttuvan, whose army of unfailing swords completed the deeds of war joined to righteousness, who drove back the sea and went to the bank of the great Ganga, and declares the book complete.
nuance: Lines 4 to 8 repeat the frame that closes the Puhar and Madurai books, but the frame is cut short: there is no river and no unfailing sky here, and the arts shrink to the vari and kuravai (line 9), the hill-folk's and herders' songs of this book. Where the Madurai summary ends on a king's death, this one adds a phrase of its own, அறத்தொடு பொருந்திய மறத்துறை (lines 10 to 11), valour 'fitted to aram', and makes war the book's centre. The summary names neither Kannaki nor the Pattini stone for which the march to the north was made (25:113-130); it keeps only the king, his sea and the Ganga. கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி (line 12) is the epithet under which the Patitruppattu's fifth decad names Senguttuvan (கடல் பிறக்கோட்டிய செங்குட்டுவன்); the shared epithet is the Tamil's ground for taking the epic's king as the decad's patron, not proof that the two portraits are one man's history.

title: நூற் கட்டுரை
theme: The closing summary of the whole work (நூற் கட்டுரை): one sentence says that within the Tamil land bounded by Kumari, Venkatam and the two seas, the Silappathikaram gathers the matter of akam and puram, the three aims of virtue, wealth and pleasure for humans and gods alike, song, the lute, melody, rhythm, the stage and dance, the vari, the kuravai and the other forms, and makes its meaning plain as a good mirror shows a tall hill, its story's matter being completed in Manimekalai.
source_issues: The edition's printed numbering ends at line 15 while the summary has 18 lines as cut; the printed numbers may count the short lines or the closing colophon differently.
Line 18 (சிலப்பதி காரம் முற்றும்) is a colophon that also completes the sentence (முற்றிய in line 17 governs it), so it is marked as part of the unit.

reading: The narrator closes the epic by saying that, in the cool Tamil country bounded by Kumari, Venkatam and the eastern and western seas, with its two kinds of Tamil, the work joins the virtue, wealth and pleasure of the five landscapes, fitting for humans and gods alike, to conduct that keeps the tradition, sets the meaning that rises from words in faultless metre as akam and puram, gathers song, the lute, melody, rhythm, the stage, its rules and dance, and the vari, kuravai and other forms, and lays out its intent as a good mirror shows a vast hill, being the Silappathikaram whose story's matter is completed in Manimekalai.
nuance: The close describes the work by its land, its language and its arts, and not by the three morals the patikam announced at 0:55-57: karma, the pathini and the death of the king who erred are not named here, and aram appears only as the first of the three aims of poetry's matter (line 4). Lines 5 and 6 claim the epic's matter is valid for gods as well as humans, which fits a story that ends with Kannaki's ascent and her worship. The simile of lines 15 and 16 claims that a large matter is shown whole in a small compass, as a mirror holds a hill. மணிமேகலைமேல் உரைப்பொருள் முற்றிய (line 17) can be read as the story's matter being completed in the work Manimekalai or upon the person Manimekalai, Kovalan and Madhavi's daughter; either way the line declares the epic's story unfinished within its own covers, and the reading here does not choose between the two.

title: valayapathi 0-23 (1/3)
theme: The first run of Valayapathi fragments, quoted mostly in the Purattirattu: an invocation to the knower that asks release from old deeds, verses on the rarity of human birth, a cluster of harsh sayings on women's inconstancy set against praise of the chaste wife, and a sermon in plural commands against lying, theft, killing, flesh-eating and other men's wives, closing on penance, release without return, and the blindness of desire.
source_issues: 0: line 2 is badly divided ('ஏத்துமாண்' runs into 'டிலக மாய திலறறி வனடி'); 'திலறறி' is doubtful and the epithet of the knower cannot be fixed.
6: line 3 'அத்துனை' is a misspelling of அத்துணை.
13: line 3 'என்றெண்னி' has ன் for ண் (என்றெண்ணி).
14: line 2 repaired by the tool ('·' for ஃ in அஃது).
17: line 4 'மாண்டருகல்' is obscure and may be corrupt.
18: line 2 'குற்றம்' may be a slip for சுற்றம் (kin), which line 4 uses; the sense of the line turns on it.
20: line 1 'பொருளடு' is probably பொருளொடு with the vowel sign lost (flagged by the tool).
21: line 2 'மனமொழி யடுமெயிற்' is probably மனமொழியொடு மெயிற் with the vowel sign lost, and line 3 'கய்தலொ(டு)' probably காய்தலொடு with ா lost; neither is flagged by the tool.

cast.role: the voice of a fragment whose speaker the surviving text does not name
the group a speaker addresses as his own people (verse 16)

reading: The poet says he bows, with a faultless heart and in purity, at the feet of the knower whom the three worlds praise together, so that his ancient deeds may leave him.
nuance: The god is named only as அறிவன், the knower, praised by three worlds; no creating role is given, and the hoped-for fruit of worship is the removal of old deeds (தொல்வினை), not a gift of grace. Line 2 is badly divided in the text, so the exact epithet is not secure.

tamil: வினைபல வலியி னாலே வேறுவே(று) யாக்கை யாகி
நனிபல பிறவி தன்னுள் துன்புறூஉம் நல்லு யிர்க்கு
மனிதரின் அரிய(து) ஆகும் தோன்றுதல், தோன்றி னாலும்
இனியவை நுகர எய்தும் செல்வமும் அன்ன தேயாம்.
reading: For the soul that suffers through very many births, taking one different body after another by the force of its many deeds, birth as a human is rare, and even when it comes, wealth enough to enjoy sweet things is just as rare.
nuance: The verse stacks two rarities: the human body and, inside it, the means of enjoyment. It does not yet say what the rare birth is for.

tamil: உயர்குடி நனியுள் தோன்றல் ஊனமில் யாக்கை யாதல்
மயர்(வு)அறு கல்வி கேள்வித் தன்மையால் வல்ல ராதல்
பெரி(து)உணர் அறிவே யாதல் பேரறம் கோடல் என்றாங்(கு)
அரி(து)இவை பெறுதல் ஏடா பெற்றவர் மக்கள் என்பார்.
reading: Birth in a high family, a body without defect, learning and listening that clear away confusion, an understanding that grasps much, and taking up the great dharma are hard to get, the speaker tells a man, and only those who get them are called human.
nuance: The address ஏடா shows a speaker talking to one man, but the fragment does not say who either is. 'Human' (மக்கள்) is made a title earned by a list that runs from birth to dharma, so high birth sits beside virtue as a condition.

reading: Praise from country and town, and rain that falls when bidden to fall, belong, when the able men of Koodal speak of the good, to the illustrious chaste wife.
nuance: The rain at the wife's word is one honour in a list, beside the praise of country and town, and it is credited to what the learned of Koodal say. Whether கூடல் ஆற்றவர் means an assembly at Madurai or simply learned men is not clear from the line.

reading: Fish used to the old water of a pond still long for a new flood when they see one, and so, the speaker tells someone to know, the heart of a garlanded woman turns and melts for another even if she is with the love god himself.
nuance: Addressed to one listener (கொள்நீ, 'take it'), so the view belongs to an unknown speaker in a lost scene, not plainly to the poet. 'Even with Kaman' makes the claim independent of the husband's merit.

reading: There is a guard for food, a guard for wealth and a guard for precious learning, but those who have learned and seen the world said that there is no way to guard women.
nuance: The speaker cites the learned (கற்றறிந்தோர்) as the authority. The verse puts women in the list of possessions a man keeps, and then denies that this one can be kept by any outward means.

reading: As many as the grains of sand in rivers, the drops of water, the dew on grass, the leaves fallen from trees and the fine hairs, so many men thought they had entered the hearts of sweet-speaking women and found themselves shut in a closed room.
nuance: பொதியறைப் பட்டார் is read here as being trapped in a sealed chamber, that is, deceived; the image could also be of being suffocated. The counting similes make the deceived men beyond number rather than describing a single case.

reading: Like a single cool raindrop on a lotus that stays only as long as the wind allows, women are steady only for the short while the man who cherishes them is watching; otherwise they waver and do not stay.
nuance: The last phrase துணைவனைக் கையார் is hard: it may mean they do not openly spurn their partner, which would make the inconstancy hidden. The raindrop image ties women's steadiness to outward conditions rather than to an inner guard.

tamil: பொறையிலா அறிவு போகப் புணர்விலா இளமை மேவத்
துறையிலா வசன வாவி துகிலிலாக் கோலத் தூய்மை
நறையிலா மாலை கல்வி நலமிலாப் புலமை நன்னீர்ச்
சிறையிலா நகரம் போலும் சேயிலாச் செல்வ மன்றே.
reading: Wealth without a child is like knowledge without patience, youth without pleasure, a tank without steps, finery without cloth, a garland without fragrance, scholarship without learning's goodness, and a town without a moat of good water.
nuance: Each item in the list is a thing that exists but lacks what makes it usable or whole; the child is placed as the completion of wealth, not as a good in itself.

reading: It can raise a man, cast him into hard fetters, ruin him and send him to the vile hell: of the five senses that must be guarded, none needs guarding so much as the tongue.
nuance: The tongue is counted among the five senses (இந்திரியம் ஐந்து), so it is both the organ of taste and of speech; the verse does not choose, and புலைநகரம், a hell called 'vile', can carry a hint of flesh.

reading: Hold to your wife and her good and stand firm: town and country will surely rejoice, and the victorious gods will praise you and come to receive you with honour.
nuance: The plural command (தலைநின்மின்) addresses a group. தாரம் நல்லிதந் தாங்கி is read as cherishing one's wife; if so, the same praise from town and country that verse 3 gives the chaste wife is here promised to the faithful husband.

reading: The great sorrow that comes from women cannot be counted even by the most thoughtful; the heavy, entangling deed rises against one, so whatever happens, keep away from another man's woman.
nuance: The verse opens with a charge against women in general and closes on a narrower command about the other man's wife (ஏதில்பெண்); the karma of line 3 is what joins them.

reading: Do not lie, do not backbite, revile no one, do not try to escape by saying what is unfitting, do not spend your days killing living beings and eating them, and do no evil in company with base people.
Steal nothing that is theft; do not accept a dharma that comes joined with killing; scorn no one as poor; and do not befriend or approach another man's woman.
nuance: கொலை கூடி வரும் அறம் rejects any dharma that involves killing; the line names no rite or school, though sacrifice is the obvious case.

reading: If one asks why someone gathered food into a single mouthful and set a finger on it, the reason is the conviction that however many flawless gifts there are, none equals a mouthful of rice.
nuance: The verse explains a gesture whose scene is lost; who makes it and for whom cannot be told. The point is a ranking of gifts, with the smallest gift of food placed above the rest.
event: Someone gathers food into one mouthful and lays a finger on it, and the gesture is explained.

reading: Show grace to all precious lives, spread dharma, do not draw near to wrong, cast off excess deceit and pride, and keep these as your wealth.

One should not hoard wealth as if it were wealth but do dharma with grace as one's wealth; when one does dharma so, the speaker asks his own people, how could one come to the dark state in the world above?
nuance: The last line is read as இருள் இயல்பு எய்தாதது, not reaching the dark state; the address நமரங்காள் shows a speaker talking to a group he counts as his own.

reading: No sin exceeds killing a life wrongly; the one who eats at a price his craving sets wants flesh to multiply, and the one who kills other creatures with nets, as a trapper, and sells the flesh at that price also wants more of them to die.
nuance: The verse joins buyer and seller through one price set by craving (அவா விலை): the eater's demand and the trapper's trade feed each other. Line 4's மாண்டருகல் is obscure and read loosely.

reading: Looked at within the ocean of births, no one is free of fault in killing, and those who eat flesh without weighing dharma have eaten their own kin without remainder.
nuance: The argument rests on rebirth: every creature has at some birth been one's kin, so flesh is always a relative's. Line 2 is hard; its குற்றம் may stand for சுற்றம் (kin), which would say that no being is not one's kin.

reading: Protect living beings, do not eat flesh from craving, shed your faults and give up anger, and you will be born in good states, spotless like the moons that those who see them worship.
nuance: கதி, the state of the next birth, is the term Jain and Buddhist works use for the destinations of rebirth; the verse promises a good one rather than release.

reading: Even if you are joined to wealth and pleasure, practise the hard penance that is fit for grace; going to the state free of darkness, you will not come back here again; if you would gain clarity, gain it in that.
nuance: Release here is reached by one's own penance, with no god granting it, and it is marked by no return (இனி இவண் வாரீர்). The verse speaks to people still in wealth and pleasure, not to monks.

reading: Except for the lord of penance who dwells above penance, it is hard to end delusion, to hold mind and speech with the body, to be without liking and loathing, to have grace for every kind of life, and to give up wealth with longing; know that as well.
nuance: The three restraints of mind, speech and body are named together; only the perfected ascetic (தவத்து இறை) is said to achieve them all. Addressed to one listener (அறிநீ).

reading: Desire decides without thinking, runs any way it likes, melts one from within, takes no counsel from the wise, comes without closeness, longs for those who do not love, and, standing in the eye, fells those who desire too much.

When the arrow Kama lets fly strikes the body, men do not see the blame they invite standing alone while the wise recoil, will not take the word of their elders, and stain a fame that held up the sky.
nuance: The verse judges the lover from outside, by what he loses in others' eyes; the next verse (24) goes on to the madal.

title: valayapathi 24-47 (2/3)
theme: Fragments preserved in the Purattirattu on the madness of love, the dangers and fleetingness of wealth, killing and truth, the late turn to renunciation and the futility of trying to escape karma while still attached; their order is the editor's and no story can be rebuilt from them.
source_issues: 24 line 2: யஎன்(று) ... சுடுப is probably corrupt; the verse reworks Kuruntokai 17 (பூவென ... எருக்கங் கண்ணியும் சூடுப), so பூஎன்று and சூடுப ('wear') are likely the true readings for யஎன்று and சுடுப ('burn').
29 line 3 and 42 line 3: the checker flags பொய்யடு and பொருளடு as possibly -யொடு/-ளொடு with the vowel sign lost; the sense ('with') supports -ொடு in both, as in verse 20's பொருளடு.
42 line 3 begins யுய்த்தவம், with an initial யு that cannot begin a Tamil word; it looks like a broken sandhi from the line before (உய்த்தவம்).
32 lines 1 and 4 (ஒழிந்த பிறவறன் உண்டென்பார் உட்க; கல்லாப் பிலரே) do not yield a sure sense and may be corrupt.
41 lines 1-2 are obscure; the verse may be the second half of a comparison of the என்னொக்கும் ... ஆறே type (as 39, 42, 46) whose first half is lost or garbled.
47 line 2 (மாண்வினைப் பாவை மறைநின்று கேட்குறிற்) does not fit a clear syntax.

cast.role: an unnamed first-person or arguing voice in a fragment; the verse does not say who speaks

reading: When the sickness of love takes deep root, men ride the palm-stem calling it a horse in every public square, put on erukku clusters, and stand like the possessed while others jeer.
nuance: The verse reworks Kuruntokai 17 almost phrase for phrase (மா என... மடல் ஏறுப, எருக்கு, ஆர்ப்ப, காழ்க்கொள்), but recasts the lover's own boast as a symptom: it adds புன்மை (baseness), பேய் (possession) and நோய் (disease). Line 2 is damaged (see source_issues).

reading: Lovesick men laugh till their sides split, feel shame and then want none, lie where they have crept in, live on dreams and fancies, forget food, weep and cannot sleep; desire for a woman's fine shoulders makes a suffering the whole country knows.
nuance: A catalogue of symptoms in the manner of the akam books, but told from outside and without sympathy; the last line's நாடறி துன்பம் turns private longing into public talk (alar).

reading: Those who befriend kings live off their realm and those who befriend snakes make them dance for a living, but of women with bangled forearms the ancients said no art avails, and let them go.
nuance: The sense of விரகிலர் (no art, no means) and the subject of விடுத்தனர் are not certain; the verse may instead mean the women themselves are without guile. This is the fragment's view of women, one of several in the chapter (46, 47).

reading: Those who carry off by stealth many goods from others' houses reap this fruit: they are gathered, held fast by hand and foot, and cut so they cannot run.
nuance: The punishment is presented as the theft's own பயன் (fruit), in this life; the verse does not name the king, only the seizing and cutting.

reading: Give up lying, take on truthfulness and walk the path of dharma without doubt: those who do are seen to reach a world without daily pain or reproach.
nuance: Truth here is a companion of dharma, worn like an ornament (பூண்டு), not the whole of it; கண்டதே ('this is what has been seen') rests the promise on observation.

reading: Lack of learning, loss of wealth in hand, affliction and being drawn into lie after lie surely follow from something the verse calls only 'that'; forbid it and guard yourselves.
nuance: அது in line 4 has no antecedent in the verse: the vice was named in a lost context (drink or gambling would fit the list, but the verse does not say). Line 2's நல்லில் செல்லல் is unclear.

reading: If you want lasting fame that lights the world, and fear the boundless pain of reeling among the four states of birth, give up deceitful killing that terrifies living beings: so the knowing have said.
nuance: கதி நான்கு, the four states (gods, humans, beasts, hell), is the Jain reckoning of births; the verse rests its rule on the authority of அறிந்தார் rather than stating it in its own voice.

reading: Wealth slips from the hand and departs by flood, by negligence, by mighty kings, by fire, by kinsmen's claims and by thieves; those who give up the wealth in their house without clinging to it pass beyond the scorned grief of great suffering.
nuance: The six thieves of wealth (flood, forgetfulness, kings, fire, heirs, robbers) are a list; the last line could also be read as saying those who cling suffer more, so the verse's direction is not fixed.

reading: Those who let go of the borrowed wealth that perishes and passes to others, and who did not seek even a little of it, the verse appears to say, are free of great suffering.
nuance: வம்பப் பொருள் ('wealth that is a stranger's', borrowed) is the key image; line 1 and the close of line 4 do not yield a sure sense.

reading: Poverty is disgrace and possession is fear for one's life; wealth lasts little, deludes much and brings baseness, so the renunciation of those who never went near it is excellent.
Wealth is hard to gather and easy to lose, gives little joy and much trembling, and is ignoble by nature; the strength of those who never wanted it is excellent.
nuance: A companion to 33 with the same closing frame (ஒழிந்தார் ... விழுமிதே), turning from renunciation (துறவு) to the strength (விறல்) it takes.

reading: Without wealth there is no living, with it base men kill you and the taken die; whether one has it or not, it shows itself worthless for this life and the next and is nothing to hold.
nuance: Line 2's கொளப்பட்டும் வீடுவர் is compressed; it may mean the robbed die, or the rich are seized and killed.

reading: A speaker says that now the spear-eyed young women no longer desire him, the staff shows his road and killing Death is near; past forty, with grey hair come as messenger, he resolves to renounce, for youth does not last.
nuance: The motive is mixed: renunciation is chosen when desire has already left him (மடவார் விழைவு ஒழிய). யாம் may be a plural of dignity or a group; the fragment does not say who speaks.
event: An unnamed speaker, past forty and greying, resolves to renounce.

reading: Youth does not last, pleasures do not stay, wealth is the same and floods of sorrow come daily; so for the state you will go to, always, like farmers who plough, sow and water, make your provision.
For those set on cutting off birth, even the body is excess, so what further ties; while these remain, karma clings and the soul wanders among many wombs, hard to escape.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are Kural 345 almost word for word; lines 3-4 add the reason the couplet leaves unstated, a chain from attachment to karma to யோனிகள் (wombs).

reading: Trying to drive off sin born of attachment while still standing in attachment is like washing a blood-stained cloth by dipping it in the same blood.

A speaker laments: we gave no gifts and did no penance, but spent ourselves in moonlit groves; is there escape for us and the musk-haired one? The word of those whose creed has cast off pride is not false.
nuance: நானம் தோய்குழல் may be a vocative to a woman or the woman whose love distracted the speaker; the 'pride-free' ones (மானம்தீர் கொள்கையார்) are probably ascetics, whose warning the speaker now accepts.

reading: The verse bids the hearers stop some heartfelt rejoicing (lines 1-2 are obscure) and closes on the saying that there is one mighty being in the world who removes fearful suffering.
nuance: Whether the closing saying is affirmed (a deliverer such as a Jina) or held up as a false comfort cannot be fixed from the fragment; என்னும் ஆறே suggests it is the second half of a comparison whose first half is unclear.

reading: Yoking oxen and ploughing hard yet expecting the green crop without seed is like the man without austerity toiling and suffering for wealth and pleasures.
nuance: Austerity is the seed, not the labour: effort without past merit grows nothing.

reading: In the rich land the sweet sugarcane, rivalling the red paddy, rises in anger at the areca, and the areca, refusing to look, hides its face in the clouds.
nuance: A description of fertile country by rivalry of crops, the kind of country-praise that opens the long epics; nothing in the verse ties it to a place.

reading: Learning got from the family brings things to completion, wealth relieves the wasting hunger of struggling kin; is there any shame in crossing the long, ground-splitting wasteland to bring it back?
nuance: The voice is an arguer for going after wealth, as in the akam books' parting for wealth; the fragment does not say who argues, and its editor's order sets it among verses that condemn wealth (33-35).

reading: When a ruined man says 'this is my state' and seeks refuge, the many kin who were no true friends say what they please, scorn him and go stand where he cannot reach them.
Hoping to unite a woman's divided mind is like longing to gather back oil that has spread on clear water and gone in every direction.
nuance: The fragment's view of women; the simile is of something past recall, not merely difficult.

reading: Forcing love is like tearing open a long bud by hand; when care and affection are born, a woman, bewildered, embraces the man of herself.
nuance: Line 2 (a finely wrought doll standing hidden and listening) does not fit a sure syntax, and the verse may say instead that love comes by stealth, as one overhears from behind a screen.

title: valayapathi 48-71 (3/3)
theme: The last run of the Valayapathi fragments: a verse against a blind guide to release, then the sequence (49-60) in which an old courtesan gives her daughter ten models, from the river to the chaste wife, and each is glossed as a way of following wealth; gnomic verses on poverty, household virtue and the conditions without which goods are void; and fragments from commentaries, Jain sages and a proud lute master, and two refrains to the heart on the burning of the adorned body and the striving that leads to attainment.
source_issues: 49 line 1: யாறொடி, where the list of similes needs யாறொடு (river, with ...); the gloss in 51 confirms the river. Likely a misprint or a wrong division.
53 lines 2-4: the division of கரண மெனுமிலர், திரணி உபாயத்திற் றிரண்பொருள் and கரணி is doubtful, and the line-level sense cannot be fixed.
60 line 2: பருக்கரடு is obscure.
61 line 1: மக்க்ள் has a stray pulli; the word is மக்கள்.
63 line 2: repaired character (the old encoding '·' for ஃ in அஃகுப).
69 line 1: அன்றைப் பகற்கழிந் தாளின் றிராப்பகற் is hard to divide; the verse is an incomplete sentence (ஆர்ப்பவும்).

Order is the editor's. 48-66 are from புறத்திரட்டு, 67-69 from Adiyarkku Nallar's commentary on the Silappathikaram, 70-71 from the Yapparungala virutti, so the run mixes three sources and verses 67-69 need not belong together.

cast.role: the aged dancer-courtesan who instructs her daughter (49-50)
an unnamed player who bows to the Jain sages and sets the story to the lute (67)
an unnamed master of the ninety-six kinds of musical sequence (68)
the speaker's own heart, addressed in the refrains of 70 and 71

reading: Someone without sound knowledge who offers to destroy wholly the faults done before and tells the way to blissful release to one who does not know it is like a blind man telling a blind man the road.
nuance: The verse names no school and no teacher; whose rival guide is meant belonged to the lost story. முந்துசெய் குற்றம் (faults done before) makes the false teacher's offer a promise to clear past deeds, so the charge is that he lacks the knowledge such clearing needs.

reading: The aged dancer-courtesan tells her daughter to behave like the river, the lute, the fire-drill, the moon, the climbing creeper, the ship, the chaste wife and the beast, and the verse says these are best shown in another place.
nuance: Line 4 promises that the comparisons will be opened out elsewhere, and verses 51-60 do so in the order of this list (river 51, lute 52, fire-drill 53, moon 54, creeper 55, ship 56, chaste wife 57, beast 58), with 50's monkey and bee in 59 and 60. The chaste wife stands in a list of things and animals: that placement is the satire.
event: An aged dancer-courtesan instructs her daughter to conduct herself like a list of things, among them the chaste wife.

reading: Without preface she adds the monkey and the bright-winged bee as models, and the verse seems to say that these too fit those who come trusting the daughter's shoulders and bringing great wealth.
nuance: பாயிரம் இன்றி, without preface, may mean she taught bluntly, with no introduction. நின் in line 3 addresses the daughter, so lines 3-4 may still be the mother's words; the syntax of line 4 is hard to fix.
event: The old courtesan adds the monkey and the bee to her list of models for her daughter.

reading: Courtesans are like a river: their love swells as the inflow of wealth swells and shrinks as it shrinks, as the stream rises with the rain and dries away completely.
nuance: வாரி serves twice: the flood of a river and the inflow of income. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like the lute: whoever holds the wealth, their love is suited to him, as a lute plays for whatever bard takes it up.
nuance: The repeated எங்ஙனம் ... அங்ஙனம் (however ... so) makes the love a function of the wealth, whatever its source. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like the fire-drill: by many arts and devices, once men are in their hands, they draw wealth out of them as the drill-stick turned in the hands draws fire.
nuance: The image is friction: the stick yields fire only while it is worked. Line 2 (கரணம் எனும் இலர்) and line 3's word division are hard, so the exact sense of who lacks means is not certain. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like the bright moon: the love that grows day by day they let waste day by day, as the moon waxes day by day and wanes day by day.
nuance: Each line opens with நாடொறும் நாடொறும், so the verse's own form waxes and wanes in a steady rhythm. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like a flowering creeper in the field, humming with bees: even men without beauty, if they are not without means, they cling to and stand by as the creeper takes whatever support it finds.
nuance: The reading of வன்மையிலோரை and of line 2 is not certain; the sense that looks or worth do not matter, only means, is the likeliest. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like a ship that sinks in the open sea with the merchants who loaded it with fine goods: they harshly cast off those whose love for them has grown excessive.
nuance: The merchants have staked everything on the ship, so the image puts the ruin on the side of the most devoted. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans resemble chaste wives in conduct: toward men who give them wealth enough, they serve and follow in every way.
nuance: The verse grants the courtesan the outward form of the பத்தினி's devotion (வழிபட்டு ஒழுகல்) and puts the whole difference in ஒத்த பொருளான், the condition of matching wealth. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Flower-eyed courtesans are like a grazing beast: leaving the man whose wealth has perished, they fix their desire on another man of great wealth, as a beast whose pasture is bare moves into another's field.
nuance: One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like the monkey that lives in the branches: having used up the man of little wealth, they take the man of great wealth, as a monkey leaps from branch to branch.
nuance: The gloss on the monkey added in 50. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Courtesans are like the striped-winged bee: however bright and handsome a man may be, like the red flame-of-the-forest flower, they give no thought to one without substance.
nuance: The bee passes over the bright முருக்கு blossom because it holds little honey, so beauty without wealth draws no courtesan. பருக்கரடு in line 2 is obscure, and the reading of 'substance' as wealth rests on the series. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

reading: Those who know call begetting children and keeping the household's dharma the chief virtue; spending one's life in pleasure with deceitful-tongued women yields nothing.
nuance: The verse is attributed to 'those who know' (என்ப), not to the poet. தோற்றம் ஒன்று இன்று may mean no issue at all, against the children of line 1, or simply no good result. A Jain epic by tradition here praises the householder's life, not renunciation; the fragment does not say whether a higher path was set above it.

reading: The verse calls mockery very bad and enmity very bad, even, it seems, toward those who do not bow and give, and says those who never transgress, holding these as the weightiest matters, reach the many-tiered heaven and live there.
nuance: Line 1's division (துனி நன்றி யார்க்கும், or துனி நன்று இயார்க்கும்) is unclear, so whether sulking is praised, blamed or left out cannot be fixed.

reading: If a man stands in an empty house without wealth, his women will not respect him, his great kin will shrink back at the hints of cunning men, they will all crowd off and leave, and even his own children will not cling to him.
nuance: வெண்டறை (bare floor) and the sense of line 2 are uncertain; line 2 also carries a repaired character.

reading: The poor do not speak in the assembly, the good who weigh things finely do not esteem them, and the learning the poor teach fades away dull: take this as truth.
nuance: The addressee, நீ in line 4, is unnamed. The failure is laid on the hearers too: even the நல்லவை, the assembly of the good, discounts the poor man.

reading: Even a servant, if he has food to give, is surrounded as birds surround a fruiting tree; even the noble, once their wealth is spent, are left as birds leave a fruit tree that has fallen.
nuance: The two halves turn on one image, the fruit tree standing and fallen, and they reverse rank: the servant (தொழுமகன்) is courted, the noble (விழுமியர்) abandoned.

reading: A lineage without wealth, a vow without forbearance, dharma without grace and a kingdom without ministers: the undeluded poets declare these darkness put inside darkness.
nuance: Each good is paired with the condition without which it fails. The verse speaks through மருள் இல் புலவர், the undeluded poets, so it presents itself as received wisdom.

reading: Having fallen at the feet of the hosts of sages in the Nirgrantha garb, whose faultless vision wipes away sorrow, and having done the customary courtesies, he set that story to the lute.
nuance: நிக்கந்த வேடம் names the Jain monks' garb outright, the clearest Jain mark in these fragments. Who the player is and what அக்கதை (that story) was belonged to the lost context; the verse survives in a commentary on the Silappathikaram.
event: A lute player bows at the feet of the Jain sages, pays his courtesies, and sets the story to the lute.

reading: He was a master of all ninety-six kinds of musical sequence, faultless and pre-eminent in melody and mode, and even if those who travel the sky-path were his hearers he would look at them askance and laugh harshly.
nuance: The editor places this after 67, but nothing shows it is the same player. The harsh laugh at even the sky-travelling beings marks a pride the verse states without judging it here.

reading: When the day had passed, the calves' cries and the milch cows' bells sounded, and the herdsmen's flutes of konrai pod and ambal, with the bees humming like strings, filled the air.
nuance: Pastoral sound is drawn as an orchestra: flutes and bees' hum as strings. The sentence is incomplete (ஆர்ப்பவும், 'and as they sounded'), and line 1's இன்று இராப்பகல் is hard to construe.

reading: The speaker tells his heart that the dark, oiled, flower-decked, carefully dressed hair and the rich tuft will burn in the fire of time, and asks why, even seeing them burn, it is still so bewildered.
nuance: Each line hands its phrase on to the next (கோலம் குயின்ற குழல், காலக் கனலெரியின்), so the verse moves step by step from adornment to the pyre. The heart has already seen the burning: its fault is not ignorance but bewilderment that survives the sight.

reading: The speaker bids his heart see the glory of heads crowned with craftsmen's bright crowns come to ruin, not to be bewildered at it, to stand in the highest good path, and to be sure that if it strives there, attainment will follow.
nuance: சித்தி is the Jain word for the released state, and the companion of 70 moves from diagnosis to remedy; but the verse names no school and no god, so the claim is tagged general. The remedy is the heart's own effort (ஊக்கம்), with no refuge in another named.
